constraints_guess.notes: Reads an integer n then n integers, computes sum and squared deviations. Typical competitive-programming constraints are up to 2e5 or 1e5; exact limit not specified, this is a guess.

dominant_ops: O(n) to parse n integers from stdin into a list
O(n) to compute sum(var_2)
O(n) loop to accumulate squared differences from the rounded mean

complexity.why: The code stores all n integers in a list and scans them twice: once for sum and once to accumulate squared differences. Input reading is also linear in n. No extra data structures beyond the array of size n.

bottlenecks.detail: Introduces multiple small wrapper functions (func_1, func_3, etc.) around sys.stdin.readline(). Each call adds a Python function-call overhead compared with using input() directly for these small-sized inputs.

Defines several lambdas and helper functions (func_2, func_4, func_5, func_6, func_7, func_8, var_4, var_6, var_7) that are never used in this solution. They add minor module initialization cost and noise without benefiting performance.

The computation requires two passes over the data (one for sum, one for variance accumulation). While this is optimal in asymptotic terms, it prevents streaming the data without storing it, which could matter for very large n or tight memory limits.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the same O(n) algorithm but with minimal indirection: read n, read the list of integers directly with input().split(), compute the rounded mean, and accumulate squared differences in a straightforward loop without extra helper layers.

complexity.why: Still reads and stores n integers in a list and performs two linear passes over them (sum and squared-difference accumulation). The improvement is in constant factors due to fewer function calls and simpler I/O handling, not in asymptotic complexity.

complexity_delta.from: O(n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: Both versions have identical asymptotic complexity; the change only reduces constant overhead in Python-level function calls and unused helpers.

transformation_steps: Remove unused helper functions and lambdas (func_2, func_4–func_8, var_4, var_6, var_7) that are not needed for this problem.
Inline the main logic instead of routing through func_9(), reducing one level of Python function-call overhead.
Use direct input() and simple list construction to read the numbers instead of multiple custom wrappers around sys.stdin.readline().
Keep the core algorithm (compute mean, then sum squared deviations) unchanged to preserve correctness and linear-time behavior.
trigger_signals: The so-called optimized version is cluttered with generic I/O utilities that are unused or called only once, suggesting unnecessary abstraction for a simple, single-testcase problem.

Profiling or reasoning shows runtime dominated by straightforward O(n) arithmetic on a single array, leaving little room for algorithmic speedups; thus constant-factor reductions (fewer wrappers, less indirection) are the natural target.
Problem constraints are likely modest (typical /CP style for such a simple task), making heavy custom I/O scaffolding unnecessary and possibly counterproductive.
pitfalls: Using eval(input()) (in the fast_code) is generally unsafe and slower than int(input()); it works in a controlled judge environment but is a bad practice in production or untrusted contexts.

Python's round() uses banker's rounding (ties to even). If the problem expects a different tie-breaking rule for the mean, both versions could produce off-by-one results; integer-based formulas may be safer.

If the first integer n and the actual count of numbers on the next line diverge, the two versions behave slightly differently (one uses len(var_2), the other uses n in the denominator); relying on malformed input can cause subtle discrepancies.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer N; solution relies on iterating up to sqrt(N), so N is likely as large as 1e12–1e13 in Python. Time limit suggests O(sqrt(N)) or slightly above is acceptable.

dominant_ops: Two separate loops up to int(sqrt(N)) with modulo checks: (N-1) % i and N % i.
Inner while-loop repeatedly dividing N by a divisor candidate until not divisible.
Appending many divisor candidates to a list then converting to a set to deduplicate.

complexity.why: The first for-loop scans all i from 1 to floor(sqrt(N)) to collect divisors of N-1, costing O(sqrt(N)). The second for-loop also scans 2..sqrt(N), doing an O(1) modulo each iteration and an inner division loop only when i | N. The inner loop divides by that i until the factor is removed, so overall divisions across all i are bounded by O(log N) per distinct prime factor. The list of candidates var_2 contains at most O(d(N)) elements (number of divisors), and set(var_2) also uses O(d(N)) memory and time.

bottlenecks.detail: Divisors of N and N-1 are extracted via separate sqrt-based scans without reuse or factoring; the second scan runs over all i up to sqrt(N), even though only divisor candidates are useful.
For N-1 being a perfect square, the code appends both i and (N-1)//i even when they are equal, relying on set() later to deduplicate, which adds minor overhead.
The second loop checks N % var_3 for all var_3 in [2, sqrt(N)], even though only the relatively few actual divisors of N will lead to further work.
Building a potentially large list var_2 and then converting it into a set at the end adds extra allocations and hash operations for each candidate.

FastAudit.core_idea: Factor N and N-1 into their divisors explicitly once via a helper func_1 (iterating up to sqrt), then perform the main condition check only over the actual divisors of N and N-1 rather than over all integers up to sqrt(N). This concentrates the work on relevant candidates and centralizes divisor generation.

complexity.why: func_1 computes all divisors of a number M in O(sqrt(M)) by scanning 1..sqrt(M) and adding complementary divisors, so computing divisors of N and N-1 is O(sqrt(N)). Then the outer loop runs only over actual divisors of N, whose count is d(N), and for each divisor performs a while-loop similar to the original (bounded by the exponent of that factor, hence total O(log N) factoring-style operations). Collecting candidates into var_1 and then deduplicating with set(var_1) remains O(d(N)) in time and space. Thus the asymptotic complexity matches the original but reduces unnecessary checks and clarifies divisor handling.

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(N) + d(N) * log N) time, O(d(N)) space
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(N) + d(N) * log N) time, O(d(N)) space with reduced constant factors on divisor processing
complexity_delta.note: The big-O bounds are essentially unchanged, but the work is focused on actual divisors rather than all integers up to sqrt(N). Some redundant operations and duplicate insertions are removed; correctness is also improved by including divisors > sqrt(N).

transformation_steps: Introduce a helper function func_1 to compute all divisors of a given integer M in one pass over 1..sqrt(M), appending both i and M//i and avoiding duplicates for perfect squares.
Use func_1(var_5) to obtain the full divisor list of N once, instead of scanning 2..sqrt(N) and testing N % i != 0 for each i.
Iterate only over those divisors (excluding 1) when applying the division-while-possible and remainder condition, rather than over every integer up to sqrt(N).
Similarly, use func_1(var_5 - 1) to get all divisors of N-1 instead of manual two-value appends per divisor and relying on set to clean duplicates.
Aggregate all valid candidates into a single list var_1, merge with divisors of N-1, then deduplicate via set(var_1) and adjust the final count (subtracting 1 to account for excluding k = 1).
trigger_signals: Multiple explicit loops of the form for i in range(1, int(n**0.5)+1) performing similar divisor checks suggest consolidating divisor logic.
Use of (n-1) % i followed by unconditional appends of both i and (n-1)//i hints at potential duplicate handling inefficiencies and an opportunity to centralize divisor generation.
A second full sqrt-range scan over N with a cheap guard (if N % i != 0: continue) indicates most iterations do almost no work, suggesting iterating over known divisors instead.
Reliance on len(set(list_of_divisors)) to fix duplication is a signal that divisor enumeration could be structured more cleanly and efficiently.
pitfalls: When generating divisors, it is crucial to avoid double-counting the sqrt(N) divisor for perfect squares; this is handled in func_1 via a conditional check var_3 != var_5 // var_3.

Switching to a divisor-based loop changes which candidates are considered; care must be taken to include all divisors, including those greater than sqrt(N), to preserve (and in this case, correct) the intended logic.

Subtle off-by-one or exclusion choices around the divisor 1 (e.g., skipping var_3 == 1 and subtracting 1 at the final count) must be consistent with the mathematical definition of valid k to avoid logical errors.

Precomputing divisors increases peak memory usage from O(1) in the scan loops to O(d(N)), which is safe for typical constraints here but could matter for problems with many test cases or larger ranges.
The continued use of eval(input()) is a security and performance smell; for competitive programming it is usually acceptable but should generally be replaced with int(input()) in production code.

constraints_guess.notes: n is length of the array; solution in Code A is O(n). Typical AtCoder constraints suggest n up to around 1e5. Answer size can reach 2^n but Python big integers handle it.

dominant_ops: Repeated computation of combinations via factorial (math.factorial) inside loops over k
Summation over all non-empty subsets of evens and many subsets of odds using binomial coefficients

complexity.time: O(n^2 * F(n)) where n is number of elements; practically dominated by O(n^2) calls to big-integer factorial/combination routines
complexity.space: O(n * log n) bits transiently for large factorials and combination results
complexity.why: For each k in [1..var_2] and many k in [1..var_6], func_1 computes C(n,k) using three factorials: factorial(var_8), factorial(k), factorial(var_8-k). Each factorial on large n is at least linear in n in terms of arithmetic operations on big integers. Looping over O(n) k values leads to roughly O(n^2) big-int work, which is far too slow when n is up to ~1e5.

bottlenecks.detail: The slow code explicitly sums binomial coefficients to count valid subsets, while the problem only depends on the presence of at least one odd number. A simple parity argument collapses the count to a closed-form expression.
math.factorial is called repeatedly on large arguments (up to n). Each call allocates and multiplies big integers; doing this inside loops over k causes severe overhead.
func_1 recomputes factorial(var_8) for every k even though var_8 is constant; similarly, factorial(k) and factorial(var_8-k) are recomputed without any reuse or DP.

The algorithm sums C(neven, k) over k and C(nodd, k) over k (restricted by parity), effectively iterating over counts of subsets instead of using identities like sum_k C(n,k) = 2^n and the simple parity structure.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use parity only: the number of subsets with sum having a given parity depends solely on whether at least one odd element exists. If there is any odd, exactly half of all 2^n subsets have even sum and half have odd sum, giving 2^(n-1). If all elements are even, every subset sum is even, so there are 2^n even-sum subsets and 0 odd-sum subsets. This eliminates all combinatorial summation and factorial use.

complexity.space: O(1) extra (ignoring input storage and the output integer size)
complexity.why: The fast code scans the array once to check for an odd element, then performs at most a constant number of exponentiations (2^n or 2^(n-1)), which are implemented efficiently in Python. No nested loops or factorials are involved.

complexity_delta.from: ≈O(n^2 * F(n)) with large-argument factorials and many binomial computations
complexity_delta.to: O(n) with a single linear scan and a constant number of power operations
complexity_delta.note: The key improvement is not micro-optimization of factorials but a change in viewpoint: from explicit combinatorial summation to a closed-form parity argument.

transformation_steps: Recognize that only the parity (odd/even) of each element matters for the subset sum parity, not their actual magnitudes.
Count whether there exists at least one odd number in the array instead of counting combinations of evens/odds.
Use the identity that if there is at least one odd, exactly half of all subsets (2^(n-1)) have sum parity 0 and half 1; if all are even, all subset sums are even.
Replace the explicit combinatorial summations and factorial-based C(n,k) calculations with a simple conditional on presence_of_odd and the requested parity var_5/var_9.
Remove calls to math.factorial and loops over k, leaving only a single loop through the input array and a constant-time power computation.
trigger_signals: Presence of math.factorial inside loops whose bounds depend on n, indicating potential factorial recomputation on large inputs.
Double loops over k to sum binomial coefficients up to var_2 and var_6 (both O(n)), which is suspicious under typical -like constraints.
Known combinatorial identity for subset parity counts suggesting that the extensive combination summation is unnecessary.
Mismatch between expected competitive-programming constraints (n up to 1e5) and the heavy big-integer factorial computations.
pitfalls: Assuming you must sum explicit binomial coefficients rather than leveraging parity identities leads to factorial-heavy, quadratic or worse solutions.
Using math.factorial repeatedly for combinations severely degrades performance for large n due to big-integer arithmetic, especially inside Python loops.

While 2^n can be very large, computing it once with integer exponentiation is much cheaper than summing many C(n,k) terms; however, memory/time can still explode if constraints allow extremely large n (which they typically do not here).

When refactoring to the fast solution, ensure that the interpretation of the parity parameter (var_5/var_9) matches the problem statement (0 for even, 1 for odd); an off-by-one in parity handling can silently give wrong answers.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic AtCoder-style problem: N nodes in a line (1..N) plus one shortcut edge between nodes X and Y. Need counts of shortest-path lengths for all unordered pairs (i,j). Time limit implies O(N^2) is intended; O(N^3) would be too slow.

dominant_ops: Breadth-first search (BFS) from every starting node (outer loop over all N nodes, inner BFS over N nodes and edges).
Repeated initialization of distance array of size N for each BFS.
Queue operations (deque append/popleft) and float('inf') comparisons in the BFS loop.

complexity.why: There are N starting nodes (outer loop over var_4 in range(var_7)). For each start node, BFS over a graph with N vertices and O(N) edges (a line plus one extra edge) takes O(N + E) = O(N). Thus total time is O(N * N) = O(N^2). Memory holds a distance array of size N plus the result counts array, so O(N) space.

bottlenecks.detail: Performs BFS from every node, recomputing all single-source shortest paths N times even though the graph has a simple, highly structured form (a line with one extra edge) that admits a direct formula for distances.
Uses float('inf') and min() on every pop from the queue, adding extra comparisons. A standard BFS would mark 'visited' once and avoid repeated min() operations.
Does not prevent enqueuing already-seen nodes; it only checks on pop (var_3[var_5] != inf), so nodes may be enqueued multiple times before being finalized, increasing queue operations.
Allocates a fresh distance list of length N for each of the N BFS runs, causing repeated O(N) allocations and writes.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the specific structure of the graph (a simple path 1..N plus one shortcut edge between X and Y) to derive a closed-form expression for the shortest distance between any pair (i,j). Then iterate over all unordered pairs once and update counts based on this O(1) distance computation, avoiding BFS entirely.

complexity.why: There are C(N,2) ≈ N^2/2 unordered pairs generated by itertools.combinations(range(1, N+1), 2). For each pair, the code does a constant amount of arithmetic and a min() over three values to get the shortest distance. Thus time is O(N^2). The only significant extra memory is the counts array of size N, so space is O(N).

complexity_delta.from: O(N^2) time, O(N) space (BFS per node on a sparse graph with N BFS runs).
complexity_delta.to: O(N^2) time, O(N) space (direct pair iteration with O(1) distance formula).
complexity_delta.note: Big-O time and space complexities remain O(N^2) and O(N) respectively, but the new method removes BFS overhead, repeated allocations, and queue operations, resulting in significantly fewer constant-factor costs and simpler control flow.

transformation_steps: Recognize the graph structure: nodes 1..N arranged in a path (i connected to i±1) plus a single extra undirected edge between nodes X and Y.

Derive formulas for path lengths between any two nodes (i,j): direct line distance is abs(i-j). Using the shortcut: one path is |X-i| + 1 + |Y-j|, and the other is |Y-i| + 1 + |X-j|. The shortest distance is the minimum of these three values.
Replace the nested pattern of 'for each start node, run BFS over the entire graph' with 'for each unordered pair of nodes, compute distance using the formula'.
Implement pair enumeration via itertools.combinations(range(1, N+1), 2) to iterate over all unordered pairs (i,j) efficiently.
For each pair, compute the three candidate distances using abs() and integer addition, take the min, and increment the counter for that distance.
Remove all BFS-related data structures (distance arrays per start node, deque, visited/inf checks), leaving a simpler and more cache-friendly computation.
Retain a single result array to count how many pairs have each distance from 1 to N-1, and print these counts at the end.
trigger_signals: Presence of an outer loop over all nodes combined with an inner BFS traversal over all nodes and edges, effectively repeating similar work N times.
Graph is extremely structured (a linear chain plus one extra edge), suggesting that general-purpose BFS may be overkill and that a direct arithmetic formulation could be possible.
Constraints hint that N around 2000 makes O(N^2) feasible but O(N^3) or overly heavy O(N^2) with big constants risky in Python.
Distance calculations in BFS are simple increments; there is no dynamic edge change, reinforcing that a closed-form distance expression might exist.
Use of float('inf') and min() in a tight loop, which is a red flag for unnecessary per-node overhead.
pitfalls: While removing BFS, it is easy to mis-derive the distance formula and get off-by-one errors, especially around including the teleport edge ('+1' step for using the shortcut). Careful reasoning about the path lengths is required.

Must ensure to count each unordered pair exactly once. Using nested loops incorrectly (e.g., both i<j and i>j) can double-count pairs; itertools.combinations helps avoid this but indices must be chosen correctly.
Distances start from 1 up to N-1. Indexing the counts array must align with these distances; allocating an array of size N and ignoring index 0 (as in the provided fast_code) is intentional.

Casting to 1-based vs 0-based node indices can be a source of bugs. In the fast code, nodes are treated as 1..N; in the slow BFS code, indices are 0-based. Mixing these conventions during refactor can break correctness.

Although both approaches are O(N^2) asymptotically, careless implementation of the combinational approach (e.g., adding extra nested loops or redundant computations) could accidentally worsen the runtime beyond acceptable limits.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style constraint for single-array prefix-sum task; needs O(n) with low constant factors.

dominant_ops: Allocation and fill of suffix-sum array of size n+1
Two full passes over the array (suffix sums, then counting)
Counter (hash map) lookups and updates per element
Extra arithmetic and conditional checks inside main loop

complexity.why: One O(n) loop to build the suffix-sum array and one O(n) loop to count, each iteration doing O(1) average hash-map work; suffix-sum array and Counter both store up to O(n) entries.

bottlenecks.detail: Building a separate suffix-sum list var_6 of length n+1 doubles the memory traffic and adds an extra O(n) pass.
Using collections.Counter adds method/indirection overhead compared to a plain dict; every access/assignment is slightly slower.

Inside the main counting loop, each iteration performs multiple array index operations (var_6[var_8], var_1[var_8]), a branch on var_1[var_8] == 0, and two Counter accesses, increasing per-element cost.
Storing both the original array and a full suffix-sum array increases peak memory and cache footprint, which hurts runtime for large n.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a single forward prefix-sum scan and a hash map from prefix_sum -> frequency to count zero-sum subarrays in one pass without auxiliary arrays.

complexity.why: Single loop over n elements; for each element, compute running prefix sum and do O(1) average-time dict get/update. The dict can store up to O(n) distinct prefix sums.

complexity_delta.from: O(n) time, O(n) space with two array-sized structures (input + suffix sums) and higher per-iteration overhead via Counter
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space with a single pass and a plain dict, minimizing memory traffic and per-iteration operations
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged (still linear), but constant factors are significantly reduced: one fewer full-array pass, no suffix array, and a lighter-weight mapping structure.

transformation_steps: Replace the suffix-sum formulation with a direct prefix-sum formulation: maintain a cumulative sum var_6 while scanning the array once.
Eliminate the explicit suffix-sum array var_6[...] and its backward-construction loop; compute the running sum on the fly inside the main loop.
Replace collections.Counter with a plain dict (var_4), using dict.get(sum, 0) for frequency retrieval and manual increment for updates.
Remove special-case counting of single zero elements via separate if checks; the prefix-sum frequency method automatically counts length-1 zero subarrays.
Simplify input handling and remove unused utilities (lambda readers, debug printer, recursionlimit adjustment) to reduce overhead and noise.
trigger_signals: Presence of two O(n) loops where logically only one pass over the data is required for prefix-sum counting.
Use of a full-sized auxiliary array (suffix sums) when the operation can be streamed with a single running sum variable.
Use of collections.Counter in a tight loop where a plain dict with integer counts suffices.
Problem pattern matches a standard 'count subarrays with sum zero' template well-solved by a minimal prefix-sum + hashmap solution.
pitfalls: Ensuring correctness when switching between suffix-sum and prefix-sum formulations; off-by-one mistakes in indices can silently change which subarrays are counted.
When using a dict of prefix sums, it is crucial to initialize the frequency dict with {0: 1} to count subarrays that start at index 0; forgetting this undercounts results.
Hash-map based methods assume average O(1) operations; adversarial data is unlikely in contest settings but, in theory, can degrade performance.
For very large n, using unnecessary auxiliary arrays (like suffix sums) can lead to higher memory usage and potential cache misses, even if asymptotic space is still O(n).

constraints_guess.notes: Typical of AtCoder-style problem: first input N up to ~1e4, second input M up to ~1e9. Need prime factorization of M and count ways to distribute prime exponents over N slots using combinations.

dominant_ops: Precomputation of factorials, modular inverses, and inverse factorials up to O(N) in func_3
Trial-division prime factorization of M up to sqrt(M) in func_4

complexity.why: func_3 runs a single loop from 2 to (N+100), filling factorial/inverse arrays: O(N) time and O(N) memory. func_4 runs trial division up to sqrt(M): O(sqrt(M)). Combination queries are O(1) each using precomputed factorial and inverse factorial.

bottlenecks.detail: func_3(var_3 + 100, var_2) always precomputes factorials and inverses up to N+100 even though the number of combinations actually evaluated is very small (only one per distinct prime factor). For small number of queries this O(N) precompute dominates.

Each iteration in func_3 performs multiple modular multiplications; for N up to ~1e4 this is not asymptotically bad, but it is a large constant overhead compared to the tiny number of binomial evaluations needed.
func_4 performs naive trial division up to sqrt(M). This is acceptable for M up to ~1e9 but remains an O(sqrt(M)) hotspot and is shared with the fast version.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial/inverse precomputation and instead compute each needed binomial coefficient with a small O(k) multiplicative loop on Python integers, then reduce modulo at the end. This trades O(N) precomputation for a handful of very small loops because the combination parameters have small k (the prime exponents).

complexity.why: Prime factorization func_2 is O(sqrt(M)) like in the slow version. For each distinct prime (P is small, typically <10 for M<=1e9) with exponent e (E is small, <=30), func_1 computes C(n, e) via k=min(e, n-e) multiplications/divisions, so O(e) iterations. The intermediate integers can grow, but for n≈1e4 and e≈30 the bit-length is only a few hundred bits, so cost_bigint is modest. No O(N) precomputation arrays are kept, so memory is constant apart from the factor map.

complexity_delta.from: O(N + sqrt(M)) time, O(N) space due to factorial/inverse tables
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + P * E * cost_bigint) time, O(1) space (apart from small factor map)
complexity_delta.note: Given that the number of binomial evaluations is small and each exponent e is small, direct computation avoids the linear-in-N precompute and reduces both time and memory for typical constraints.

transformation_steps: Eliminate global factorial and inverse factorial arrays (var_8, var_7, var_10) and their initializer func_3.
Replace O(1) formula for nCk using precomputed factorials with a direct multiplicative implementation of nCk using a loop of length k=min(r, n-r) on Python integers (func_1 in fast_code).
Keep the prime factorization logic conceptually the same: factor M, obtain exponents, and for each exponent e compute C(N-1+e, e).

Defer modular reduction: accumulate the product of combinations in Python integers and apply modulo only at the end (or per factor), leveraging Python's big-int support instead of modular factorial tables.
trigger_signals: Number of combination queries is very small (one per distinct prime factor of M).
k (the second parameter of nCk, here the exponent e) is small for all queries (for M<=1e9, e<=30).
N is moderately sized, making the O(N) factorial/inverse precompute a visible overhead compared to a handful of tiny loops.
Memory usage of storing arrays up to N+100 is unnecessary when each nCk can be computed independently in k steps.
pitfalls: If N were much larger (e.g., up to 1e6) or if many nCk queries were needed, the factorial precomputation approach could become superior; direct multiplicative binomial would then be slower overall.

Without modular reduction inside the binomial loop, intermediate integers can grow; Python handles big integers, but if parameters ever become significantly larger, performance might degrade. The current constraints keep them small.
Prime factorization remains O(sqrt(M)) in both versions; for significantly larger M a more advanced factorization (e.g., Pollard’s rho) or pre-sieved primes might be required.
Care must be taken to use integer division (//) in the direct binomial loop to avoid floating-point precision issues; the fast_code correctly uses integer arithmetic.

constraints_guess.notes: Matches AtCoder ABC160 D (Line++): N up to about 2*10^3, compute counts of shortest-path lengths between all pairs of vertices in a path graph 1..N with one extra edge between nodes X and Y.

dominant_ops: Repeated Dijkstra (or similar SSSP) over an N-vertex graph, likely once per source vertex
Heap operations for priority queue in each Dijkstra run (heapq.heappush/heappop)
Iteration over adjacency lists for every vertex and every relaxation
Object overhead from Python class-based graph and edge representations

complexity.why: The graph for this problem has O(N) vertices and O(N) edges (line 1..N plus a single extra edge). The slow code defines a Dijkstra-style routine func_9 that uses a heap and adjacency lists. For all-pairs shortest paths, the natural way with this structure is to run Dijkstra once from each vertex: N runs * O((N + E) log N) per run ≈ O(N * N log N) = O(N^2 log N). Space is O(N + E) = O(N) for adjacency lists and distance arrays; per-run extra memory is also O(N).

bottlenecks.detail: Using a general Dijkstra-based all-pairs approach for a very special, unweighted graph (a path with one extra edge) is overkill. This introduces an extra log N factor and large constant overheads versus a direct O(N^2) combinatorial computation.
Running a full SSSP (Dijkstra) from every vertex leads to N invocations of a relatively heavy algorithm, instead of exploiting symmetry or structure of the line graph to avoid repeated work.

The graph is represented via a class with nested edge class and method calls (self.V(), self.G, self.Edge), all defined inside func_8. This adds Python-level overhead to every edge relaxation compared to direct integer arithmetic on indices.
Dijkstra and heap operations in Python are comparatively slow for N^2-scale workloads when cheaper closed-form distance computations exist.
Use of eval in func_2 (int(eval(...))) is unnecessary and slow, though likely not the dominant cost compared to O(N^2 log N) Dijkstra.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the special structure of the graph: vertices 1..N form a path, and there is a single extra edge between two vertices X and Y. For any pair (i, j) with i < j, the shortest path distance is the minimum of three explicit expressions: direct path along the line, or paths that go via the extra edge in either direction. This allows computing distances in O(1) per pair using pure integer arithmetic, and counting frequencies with a Counter over all pairs.

complexity.why: The fast code iterates over all unordered vertex pairs using itertools.combinations(range(1, N+1), 2), which generates Θ(N^2) pairs. For each pair, it does O(1) work: three absolute differences, a few additions, and a min. Distances are accumulated in a Counter with at most N-1 keys, so additional memory is O(N). There is no log N factor, and no per-vertex graph search.

complexity_delta.from: O(N^2 log N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N^2) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: By eliminating repeated Dijkstra runs and using a direct formula for distances in the specific line-plus-one-edge graph, the log N factor and heavy graph overhead are removed, yielding purely quadratic integer-arithmetic work.

transformation_steps: Recognize the exact input graph structure: vertices 1..N in a line (edges i–i+1), plus a single extra edge between nodes X and Y.
Derive closed-form expressions for shortest path distance between any pair (i, j): direct distance |i-j| along the line, and two candidate routes that go via the extra edge (i→X→Y→j and i→Y→X→j).
For each pair (i, j) with i < j, compute the three candidate distances in O(1) time and take their minimum instead of running a graph search.
Count distances with a frequency map (Counter) indexed by the distance value, rather than storing or recomputing all paths.
Iterate over all pairs using combinations (or nested loops) once, removing all graph class overhead, heap operations, and per-source SSSP invocations.
trigger_signals: The graph is unweighted and extremely structured (a path plus one extra edge), which suggests there may be closed-form formulas for distances instead of generic shortest-path algorithms.
The task only requires counts of distances, not the actual paths or per-source distance arrays, hinting that heavy graph machinery may be unnecessary.
Constraints (N ≈ 2000) allow O(N^2) solutions comfortably, but repeated Dijkstra (N times) with heaps in Python risks high constant factors and timeouts.
The distance between two vertices on a path is simply |i-j|, and adding a single extra edge between X and Y yields only a small set of alternative paths, making case-by-case analysis feasible.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors: indices in the formula-based solution must be consistent with the problem’s 1-based or 0-based indexing; the fast code uses 1..N directly, so mixing 0-based conversions can easily miscount distances.
Double counting pairs: when iterating over all pairs, ensure each unordered pair {i, j} is processed once (i < j). Using combinations helps avoid this mistake.
Incorrect distance formulas: it is easy to forget one of the two directions via the extra edge (i→X→Y→j vs i→Y→X→j) or to omit the +1 edge length between X and Y.
Using a general shortest-path algorithm even after deriving formulas: some implementations still build the full graph and run BFS/Dijkstra per node, which reintroduces unnecessary overhead.

Memory/performance issues if combinations are materialized: one must rely on combinations as an iterator; converting the list of all pairs explicitly (e.g., list(combinations(...))) would create an O(N^2) list in memory, which is borderline and unnecessary.
Retaining eval-based input parsing or heavy class structures from the slow version in the optimized solution can waste time even if the core algorithm is improved.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: N up to about 1e5, M up to about 1e9. Need to factor M (O(sqrt(M))) and compute products of binomial coefficients modulo 1e9+7. Single test case.

dominant_ops: 1) Precomputing factorials up to N+100 in func_3 (single O(N) loop with modular multiplications). 2) Trial division factorization of M in func_4 up to sqrt(M). 3) For each prime factor exponent e, computing nCk via factorial table and two modular exponentiations (pow with exponent ~1e9+5).

complexity.why: func_3 runs a loop from 2 to var_12 = N+100, giving O(N) time and O(N) space for the factorial list. func_4 uses trial division up to sqrt(M). For each prime factor (at most P ≈ O(log M)), func_1 performs two modular exponentiations using pow(..., MOD-2, MOD), each O(log MOD). The factorial list dominates memory at O(N).

bottlenecks.detail: Unconditionally precomputing factorials up to N+100 (func_3) costs O(N) time and memory even though each binomial coefficient needs only O(e) work where e is a small exponent (≤ ~30 for M ≤ 1e9). For large N this dominates runtime.

Each call to func_1 uses pow(..., MOD-2, MOD) twice to compute modular inverses. Although asymptotically O(log MOD), the large constant factors from repeated exponentiation are noticeable when P (number of prime factors) is not tiny.
Global lists var_7 and var_10 are never used; they consume a small amount of memory and add noise, though they do not materially affect performance.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial precomputation and modular inverse exponentiations. Instead, compute each required binomial coefficient C(n, k) directly via the multiplicative formula: repeatedly multiply the numerator terms (n, n-1, ..., n-k+1) and denominator terms (k, k-1, ..., 1), then take an exact integer division at the end. Since k is just the exponent of a prime in M's factorization and is very small (≤ ~30), this yields O(k) work per binomial, independent of N.

complexity.why: Factorization func_2 is still O(sqrt(M)). For each prime factor with exponent e, func_1 runs a simple loop of length e, performing integer multiplications and divisions, for total O(sum_e). There is no O(N) preprocessing and no extra arrays, so auxiliary space is constant aside from a small list of factors.

complexity_delta.from: O(N + sqrt(M) + P * log MOD) time, O(N) space (precompute factorials up to N+100 and use modular exponentiation for inverses).
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + sum_e) time, O(1) space (compute each binomial coefficient directly in O(e) without any factorial table).
complexity_delta.note: For realistic constraints where N can be up to ~1e5 while each prime exponent e is small (≤ ~30), the O(N) factorial precomputation dominates. Switching to the direct multiplicative nCk removes that dependence on N and reduces both time and memory usage.

transformation_steps: 1) Remove the global factorial list and precomputation function (var_8 and func_3).

2) Replace the binomial computation func_1 that used factorials and modular inverses with a direct multiplicative implementation that builds the binomial coefficient as an exact integer product n*(n-1)*.../(k!); apply the modulus only after the integer result is obtained.
3) Keep the prime factorization logic intact (trial division) to obtain the exponents e for each prime factor of M.
4) In the main loop, for each exponent e, call the new O(e) binomial function to compute C(e+N-1, e) and multiply it into the answer modulo 1e9+7.
5) Eliminate unused globals (var_7, var_10) and unnecessary stdin wrappers to keep the implementation lean.
trigger_signals: Runtime dominated by func_3 (factorial precomputation) in profiles for large N and small prime exponents.
High memory footprint due to storing factorials up to N+100 when only a handful of small-k binomial coefficients are needed.
Observation that exponents from factorization of M ≤ 1e9 are very small (≤ ~30), so binomial computation can be done in O(e) time without precomputed factorials.
No need for repeated modular inverses when the binomial coefficients themselves remain relatively small and can be formed via exact integer arithmetic.
pitfalls: If future constraints increase exponents e or require much larger n for the binomial, the direct multiplicative method can produce very large intermediate integers; although Python big integers are exact, extremely large values may cause performance degradation. In that case, reverting to factorial + inverse factorial tables in modular arithmetic might become preferable.

The direct nCk implementation must keep the denominator multiplication and final integer division exact; any attempt to interleave modular reduction before division would break correctness because modular division requires modular inverses, not plain integer division.

The naive trial-division factorization remains O(sqrt(M)); if M were allowed to be much larger (e.g., ≥ 1e12), this part would become the actual bottleneck and might require optimization (e.g., better bounds or a sieve-based approach).

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case with coordinates up to around 1e7; solution must be roughly O(n) or better. Problem is the classic counting of paths with knight-like moves (1,2) and (2,1) to reach (x,y).

dominant_ops: Linear search over all possible counts of one move type, plus per-iteration modular exponentiation to update a binomial coefficient.

complexity.time: O(X + K * log MOD), where X is the first input (var_6) and K is the number of steps of one move type (var_2).
complexity.why: The outer loop iterates var_6 + 1 times to find a solution of the linear system. If a solution exists, the second loop iterates var_2 times, and each iteration performs pow(var_4, MOD-2, MOD), which is O(log MOD). Only a few integer variables are stored, so space is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: Brute-force search over var_4 in range(var_6 + 1) to solve a simple system of linear equations relating the numbers of (1,2) and (2,1) moves. This is unnecessary because the system can be solved in O(1) with algebra.

Inside the combinatorial loop, a modular inverse is computed in every iteration using pow(var_4, MOD-2, MOD). This causes an extra O(log MOD) factor per loop iteration and dominates runtime when var_2 is large.

The binomial coefficient C(var_2 + var_3, var_2) is built via incremental multiplication and repeated inverses instead of factoring numerator and denominator once and inverting a single product. This leads to many redundant exponentiations.

FastAudit.core_idea: Solve the linear equations for the counts of each move type directly, check feasibility with divisibility and non-negativity conditions, then compute the resulting binomial coefficient using a single pass over k terms and a single modular inverse of k!.

complexity.time: O(k + log MOD), where k = var_10 is the smaller of the two move counts derived from the inputs.
complexity.why: Algebraic manipulation yields the total number of steps n = (x + y) / 3 and one of the move counts k in O(1). The helper func_1 computes C(n, k) by forming the product of k terms for numerator and denominator and then performing one modular exponentiation to invert the denominator, costing O(k + log MOD) overall with constant extra memory.

complexity_delta.from: O(X + K * log MOD) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(k + log MOD) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: The linear scan over possible move counts and repeated modular exponentiations per iteration are replaced by a closed-form solution for the counts and a single-pass binomial computation with one modular inverse.

transformation_steps: Recognize the combinatorial structure: reaching (x, y) using moves (1,2) and (2,1) corresponds to choosing an order of two move types, giving a binomial coefficient once the counts of each move type are fixed.

Replace the brute-force loop over var_4 with algebra: solve the linear system for the two move counts in terms of x and y, using conditions like (x + y) % 3 == 0 and non-negativity to check feasibility in O(1).
Reparameterize the problem using n = (x + y) / 3 and k derived from the difference between x and y (var_6 and var_10 in the optimized code) to directly obtain the two move counts.

Redesign the binomial computation: instead of multiplying by (n - i + 1) and by inv(i) in each iteration, compute the numerator as a falling product and the denominator as k!, then perform a single modular inverse pow(denominator, MOD-2, MOD).
Minimize modular exponentiation: restrict pow calls to just one for the denominator inverse, eliminating the per-iteration exponentiation present in the slow implementation.
trigger_signals: Presence of a loop over all possible counts of one move type to satisfy a simple linear condition relating x and y, hinting that algebraic elimination is possible.
Nested use of pow(base, MOD-2, MOD) for modular inverse inside a loop whose iteration count can be large (up to input scale).
Overall time complexity combining a large linear loop with repeated logarithmic-cost operations, which is suspicious for typical competitive programming constraints.
Problem structure clearly resembling a standard lattice path / knight-move combinatorics task where closed-form binomial formulas are well known.
pitfalls: Getting the feasibility conditions wrong: both the divisibility check (sum must be multiple of 3) and non-negativity constraints on derived move counts must be handled carefully, including equality edge-cases.
Off-by-one errors in mapping n and k into the combinatorial function (e.g., how var_10 is used in the loop and how many terms are taken in the numerator product).
Integer division ordering: when forming expressions like (var_5 - var_6) // 2 and (var_2 + var_3) // 3, the arithmetic must be structured to avoid truncation mistakes before divisibility checks.
Modular arithmetic consistency: all intermediate products must be reduced modulo MOD to prevent overflow and ensure correctness of the final modular inverse.

Assuming symmetry without checks: while the problem is symmetric in the two coordinates, the derivation of move counts uses max/min; mishandling this can lead to negative counts or swapped parameters that break the combinatorial formula.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder 'Coprime' constraints: 1 <= N <= 1e5, 1 <= A[i] <= 1e6. Need to determine if the array is pairwise, setwise, or not coprime.

dominant_ops: Building full factor table var_14 for all integers up to 1e6 with nested loops
Factoring each input number via repeated division by precomputed largest prime factors
Recursive gcd calls over the entire array

complexity.time: O(A_max log log A_max + n log A_max)
complexity.why: func_2 first builds var_14 up to var_1 = 1e6. The outer loop runs for all k from 2..A_max and the inner loop runs over multiples of k, visiting each integer up to A_max once per distinct prime factor; this is effectively O(A_max log log A_max) like a sieve. Then each of the n values is factorized by repeatedly dividing by its current largest prime factor, costing O(log A_max) per value in the worst case. A defaultdict of size up to number of distinct primes encountered is kept, so space is O(A_max) for var_14 plus O(n) for the input.

bottlenecks.detail: func_2 always precomputes var_14 for all numbers up to 1e6, even if the actual input uses few primes. This unconditional O(A_max log log A_max) sieve dominates runtime for large constraints.

The sieve assigns var_14[var_10] = var_6 for every multiple without checking whether it was already set to a smaller factor, so each composite may be updated multiple times (once per prime factor). This increases constant factors compared to a canonical SPF sieve.

The nested for-loops over range(2, 1_000_001) and range(var_6, 1_000_001, var_6) are executed entirely in Python, which is relatively slow for ~1e6-scale loops even if the asymptotic complexity is acceptable.
func_1 implements gcd recursively instead of using math.gcd; although the depth is small (O(log A_max)), recursive calls in Python add overhead compared to the optimized C implementation.
Reading n using int(eval(var_7())) adds overhead and is unsafe; a simple int(var_7()) would suffice. This is a minor overhead but avoidable.

FastAudit.core_idea: Instead of precomputing prime factors for the whole [1..1e6] range, factorize only the actual input numbers by trial division and, for each prime factor encountered, mark all its multiples in a global used-array exactly once. If a later number shares any marked prime factor, we can immediately conclude the array is not pairwise coprime. In parallel, maintain the global gcd of all numbers to distinguish setwise/not coprime. This input-driven sieving plus early stopping removes the cost of a full unconditional sieve and reduces work when primes repeat.

complexity.time: O(A_max log log A_max + n log A_max) in the worst case, typically much less due to input-driven sieving and early exit
complexity.why: For each distinct prime p that appears in the factorization of at least one A[i], func_1 runs a marking loop over multiples of p: O(A_max / p). Summed over all such primes, this is bounded by O(A_max log log A_max) in the worst case and is often smaller if only few primes appear. Factorization per number via trial division is O(sqrt(A[i])) but in practice closer to O(log A[i]) because numbers shrink quickly when divided by found factors. The gcd computation is O(n log A_max). The global mark array var_3 of size A_max and the input array dominate memory.

complexity_delta.from: O(A_max log log A_max + n log A_max) with a full, unconditional sieve over [1..A_max]
complexity_delta.to: O(A_max log log A_max + n log A_max) worst-case but only sieving primes that actually occur in the input, with early termination once a shared prime is found
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic big-O remains the same, but the fast version avoids a full sieve and redundant prime-factor processing, substantially reducing constant factors and typical runtime.

transformation_steps: Replace the global precomputation of prime factors for all numbers up to 1e6 with an input-driven factorization: for each A[i], factor it on the fly by trial division.
Introduce a global boolean/int array (var_3) indexed by prime, used to record whether a prime has already appeared in any previous A[i].

For each new prime factor p of the current number, mark all multiples of p (p, 2p, 3p, ...) in var_3, so that any later A[j] with a factor whose remaining value hits a marked index is detected immediately as sharing a prime factor.
Short-circuit the pairwise-coprime check: if func_1 detects that any prime factor is already used (via var_3[var_11] == 1), return False early without further factorization or marking.
Compute the overall gcd using math.gcd in a simple loop, instead of a custom recursive gcd, to decide between setwise coprime and not coprime after the pairwise check.
Maintain the existing output logic, but rely on the more efficient factoring/marking scheme to ensure scalability.
trigger_signals: Presence of a full sieve up to a constant upper bound (1e6) regardless of actual input distribution.
Nested Python loops over ~1e6 with an inner loop also potentially visiting a large fraction of that range.
A factor table (var_14) built for the entire domain, even though only a relatively small subset of values is ever queried.
Use of a custom recursive gcd instead of the optimized math.gcd, indicating missed opportunities to leverage built-in primitives.
No early exit from the sieve when pairwise coprimality has already been invalidated; work continues even after the answer is determined.
pitfalls: When switching to input-driven sieving, it is crucial to avoid double-counting the same prime factor within a single number; otherwise, you may incorrectly conclude non-pairwise coprime. The slow_code correctly uses a set(var_13) per number; the fast approach must ensure it logically mirrors this behavior.
The marking scheme in the fast_code operates over all multiples of a prime up to A_max; incorrect bounds or off-by-one errors can lead to either missed conflicts or out-of-bounds access.
Early termination in pairwise checks should not prevent the gcd computation from being completed; otherwise, the setwise vs. not coprime classification can be wrong.
Replacing gcd with trial-division factorization only is dangerous; gcd is needed to distinguish setwise coprime from not coprime when pairwise coprime fails.
Using eval on raw input is both slower and unsafe; any refactor should remove eval and rely on direct integer parsing to avoid security and performance issues.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style array problem. N is small-to-medium (<= 2e3 or 1e5), but array values can span a large range (e.g., up to |a_i| <= 1e9). The slow solution is bottlenecked by value range (max(a)-min(a)), not N.

dominant_ops: Loop over all candidate target values from min(a) to max(a)
For each candidate, compute vectorized squared differences (np.sum((var_2 - var_5) ** 2))
Repeated np.min (min(var_2)) inside the loop

complexity.why: Let N = number of elements, R = max(a) - min(a) + 1. The code iterates over every integer target value in [min(a), max(a)], i.e., R iterations. In each iteration, it computes (var_2 - var_5) ** 2 and np.sum(...), both O(N) operations on the N-length array. Thus total time is O(N * R). The array var_2 of size N dominates memory usage, giving O(N) space.

bottlenecks.detail: Brute-force search over all integer targets between min(a) and max(a), yielding O(N * (max(a) - min(a))) time. If the value range is large (e.g., up to 1e9), this is infeasible despite vectorization.

min(var_2) is recomputed inside the loop each iteration when defining var_5. Although np.min is in C and relatively fast, doing it R times adds unnecessary overhead on top of the already large O(N * R) work.
Using NumPy inside a Python loop negates much of the benefit of vectorization. Each iteration still incurs Python-level loop overhead and repeated allocation/operations on the entire array.
The loop length depends on the numeric range of input values, not N. With large a_i (e.g., up to 1e9), R becomes enormous even if N is small, leading to guaranteed TLE.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical fact that the sum of squared deviations is minimized at the mean. For integer targets, it suffices to check floor(average) and ceil(average) and take the minimal sum of squared differences, eliminating the brute-force scan over all values between min(a) and max(a).

complexity.why: The code computes the sum of the array O(N), derives two candidate target values var_6 and var_7 (floor and floor+1 of the mean), and then performs one pass over the N elements to accumulate the squared differences to each candidate. That totals a constant number of O(N) passes, yielding O(N) time. The list of N integers dominates memory usage, so space is O(N).

complexity_delta.from: O(N * R) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: R = max(a) - min(a) + 1. The fast solution removes dependence on the value range by exploiting the mean-minimizes-squared-error property, cutting out the scan over all possible target values.

transformation_steps: Recognize the objective: minimize sum_i (a_i - x)^2 over integer x.
Use calculus / algebra: for real x, the minimizer of sum_i (a_i - x)^2 is x = (sum_i a_i) / N (the arithmetic mean).
Account for integer constraint: the optimal integer x must be either floor(mean) or ceil(mean); these are equivalent here to sum(var_1)//N and sum(var_1)//N + 1.
Replace the brute-force iteration over x from min(a) to max(a) with evaluating the sum of squared differences at just these two candidate values.
Implement a single pass over the array accumulating sums for both candidates simultaneously, avoiding NumPy and Python-level loops over the candidate-space.
Take the minimum of the two accumulated sums and output it.
trigger_signals: Loop bounds depend on value range: range(max(a) - min(a) + 1) with potentially large span.
Inside the loop, an O(N) operation (np.sum on a length-N array) is performed for each candidate.
Vectorized NumPy operations are nested inside a Python loop, indicating partial or ineffective vectorization.
Problem structure: minimizing sum of squared differences around a central value, which is a classical mean/variance optimization pattern.
Potential constraints suggesting large coordinates (e.g., typical problems allowing |a_i| up to 1e9).
pitfalls: Using only floor(mean) without also checking ceil(mean) could miss the optimal integer when the mean is fractional.
Computing the mean with floating-point and then rounding can introduce precision issues; using integer sum // N and +1 is safer.
For languages with fixed-width integers, accumulating squared differences can overflow; while Python's ints are arbitrary precision, other languages would need 64-bit or larger types.
Assuming the optimal x must lie between min(a) and max(a) is correct, but using that to do a full scan over the range is unnecessary and leads to O(N * R) behavior.
Relying on NumPy for performance in an online judge environment may not help if the algorithmic complexity is too high; algorithmic improvements usually dominate micro-optimizations.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style constraints where O(n log n) with small constants is required; O(n^2) will TLE.

dominant_ops: Per-element Fenwick/BIT-style prefix operations (log n each) combined with very heavy input handling via eval and multiple wrapper functions.

complexity.time: O(n log n) (intended; worse if BIT used in nested loops)
complexity.why: The presence of a Fenwick-like Class_1 suggests per-prefix update/query operations costing O(log n). For n prefix sums, this is O(n log n). Memory is linear in n for prefix sums and BIT tree. However, constant factors are very large due to slow IO (eval on each integer), extra function call layers, and generic helper constructs.

bottlenecks.detail: func_1 reads integers via int(eval(func_12())), which invokes Python’s expression parser for every number. This is an order of magnitude slower than int(sys.stdin.readline()) or int.split-based parsing, and dominates runtime for large inputs.
Layers of tiny helpers (func_1, func_2, func_3, func_12) around basic input operations add Python function-call overhead in tight loops without algorithmic benefit.

Helpers like func_13/func_14/func_15 build large 2D/3D lists. Even if not called, such patterns indicate a template-heavy style; if any are used accidentally or for debugging, they blow up memory and time.

Class_1 implements a Fenwick tree, allocating its size as the next power of two and using while-loops for every update/query. For Python, the per-operation overhead (index arithmetic, bounds checks, Python integers) is large; if used on every prefix, runtime can be close to the time limit even though it’s O(n log n) asymptotically.

If the Fenwick tree is used in nested loops (e.g., an O(n) outer loop plus multiple BIT operations per inner iteration), effective complexity can drift toward O(n log^2 n) in practice, which is risky for n≈2e5 in Python.

Generic helpers (YES/NO printers, ceil functions, multi-dimensional array generators) increase cognitive load and risk of accidental extra work. While not asymptotically bad, they contribute to constant-factor slowdown if used in hot paths.

FastAudit.core_idea: Transform the array via a[i] := a[i] - T, build prefix sums, then count pairs (i < j) such that prefix[j] >= prefix[i] using a divide-and-conquer merge-sort-style algorithm on the prefix array. This counts subarrays whose sum is >= T (or a similar threshold) in O(n log n) with low overhead.

complexity.why: func_3 builds prefix sums in O(n). func_1 recursively performs a merge sort on the prefix array; each level merges in O(n) time, with O(log n) levels, giving O(n log n). Space is linear for prefix sums and temporary merge buffers. The implementation uses only list operations and tight loops, minimizing Python overhead.

complexity_delta.from: O(n log n) (Fenwick tree plus heavy IO and template overhead; potentially worse if misused)
complexity_delta.to: O(n log n) (clean divide-and-conquer counting on prefix sums, minimal overhead)
complexity_delta.note: Both approaches aim for O(n log n), but the fast version uses a lean merge-sort-based counting method with simple IO, which is significantly faster in Python than a template-heavy BIT solution with eval-based inputs.

transformation_steps: Replace eval-based input parsing with direct int and split on sys.stdin.readline, removing func_1/func_2/func_3 IO indirection.
Eliminate the generic competitive-programming template helpers (multi-dimensional list constructors, YES/NO wrappers) from the hot path.
Discard the Fenwick-tree-based counting approach and instead compute prefix sums once and count valid pairs via a merge-sort-style divide-and-conquer (func_1 + func_2).
Ensure the merge step maintains descending order on prefix sums and uses a sentinel (e.g., -1<<60) to avoid bounds checks inside the merge loop.
Accumulate the answer during merge when left_value <= right_value (or the appropriate inequality), leveraging the sorted order to count many pairs at once.
trigger_signals: Runtime near or exceeding the time limit for n around 10^5–2×10^5 despite an ostensibly O(n log n) algorithm.
Profiling or logging showing a large percentage of time spent in eval, input wrapper functions, or BIT update/query loops.
High CPU usage with low memory growth, indicative of Python-level loop overhead dominating.
Difficulty reasoning about performance due to a large, generic template obscuring the true hot path.
pitfalls: Using eval for numeric input is extremely slow and dangerous; always prefer int() on raw strings.

When re-implementing the merge-sort-based counting, it’s easy to invert the inequality or misplace the count update, changing the condition from prefix[j] >= prefix[i] to the opposite and silently breaking correctness.
The merge implementation relies on appending a very small sentinel value (-var_7) to each half; using the wrong sign or magnitude for the sentinel can corrupt sort order and counts.
Deep recursion in func_1 may hit recursion limits if n is very large or if Python’s recursion limit isn’t high enough, though for ~2e5 elements the given recursion depth is typically safe.

If one keeps both the BIT code and the merge-sort code in the same file, it is easy to accidentally mix them (e.g., double-counting or leaving unused heavy structures), reintroducing performance issues.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder setting (ABC126C Dice and Coin): N up to 1e5, K up to about 1e9. Single test case, simple loop-based solution required.

dominant_ops: Outer loop over i=1..N; for each i, a while-loop repeatedly doubling a value until it reaches K, and calling np.power in each iteration to compute (1/2)^var_5.

complexity.why: For each of N values (var_4 from 1 to var_2), var_6 is doubled until var_6 >= var_1. The number of doublings is ceil(log2(var_1 / var_4)) when var_4 < var_1, giving O(log K) iterations per outer step in the worst case. Each inner iteration performs only O(1) work (a few arithmetic ops and np.power). No extra data structures scale with N, so space is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: The inner while loop `while var_6 < var_1: var_6 *= 2; var_5 += 1` performs up to ~log2(K/var_4) iterations for each outer iteration, adding a logarithmic factor in K.
Both the outer for-loop and the inner while-loop are executed in pure Python, making per-iteration overhead significant for N up to around 1e5.

np.power is called once per outer iteration (or more if moved), which is expensive because each call crosses the Python–NumPy boundary. Here, NumPy is used in scalar mode, forfeiting its vectorization benefits and adding overhead.
Using NumPy for a simple scalar power of 1/2 is slower than using Python's built-in exponentiation or math functions; np.power does extra type checks and dispatch logic.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace the inner doubling loop with a direct mathematical formula using logarithms: the number of doublings needed to reach at least K from i is ceil(log2(K/i)), truncated at zero; then compute (1/2) to that power directly with normal exponentiation, eliminating the inner loop and any NumPy overhead.

complexity.why: The code runs a single loop over var_2 from 1 to var_4. For each iteration, it performs a constant amount of work: a division, a log2 call, a max and ceil, and a single exponentiation. There is no nested loop, so the time scales linearly with N. No auxiliary data structures proportional to N are allocated, so space remains constant.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log K) in terms of operations per test (log K inner steps per i) with significant constant factors from NumPy calls
complexity_delta.to: O(N) with a small constant factor using direct math.log2 and Python exponentiation
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically, for fixed K, both behave like O(N), but the fast version removes the explicit logarithmic inner loop and heavy NumPy scalar overhead, giving a substantial constant-factor speedup. The key change is reducing each iteration to O(1) work with simple math operations.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the while loop doubling var_6 until it reaches var_1 computes the minimal number of doublings t such that var_4 * 2^t >= var_1, i.e., t = ceil(log2(var_1 / var_4)) when var_4 < var_1, and 0 otherwise.
Replace the inner while loop with a direct computation of t using math.log2 and math.ceil, wrapped with max(..., 0) to handle cases where var_4 >= var_1.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic AtCoder-style problem: line graph of size N with one extra edge (X,Y), count number of pairs by shortest-path distance. Typical constraints N ≤ 2000 so O(N^2) is acceptable but O(N^3) is not.

dominant_ops: For each start node i (1..N), perform a BFS over the entire graph (O(N) edges) to compute distances to all nodes.
After each BFS, loop over all target nodes j ≥ i to update distance frequency counts.
Allocate a fresh distance array of size N+1 for every BFS run.

complexity.why: The graph is a path of N nodes plus one additional edge, so |E| = O(N). For each of the N start nodes, BFS traverses O(N) edges, costing O(N) time per start, totaling O(N^2). After each BFS, an additional loop over j from i..N contributes another O(N^2) across all i. Overall time is O(N^2). Space is dominated by the adjacency list O(N) and the distance array O(N).

bottlenecks.detail: BFS is executed N times in pure Python (N BFS runs, each doing O(N) queue operations and neighbor traversals). Even though asymptotically O(N^2), the overhead of repeated deque operations and per-element processing is large.
A new distance list var_11 = [-1] * (N+1) is allocated for every start node, causing O(N^2) total element constructions and garbage, increasing runtime and memory churn.

A general BFS on an explicit adjacency list is used despite the graph having a very regular structure (a line plus one extra edge) that allows distances to be computed via direct arithmetic without graph traversal.
Distances between many node pairs are recomputed multiple times through different BFS runs, rather than using a direct formula that computes them once in a simple nested loop.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the special structure of the graph (a path 1..N with an extra edge between X and Y) to compute the shortest path distance between any pair (i, j) directly by simple arithmetic, avoiding BFS entirely. For each pair i < j, the shortest distance is the minimum of: (1) the direct path length j - i along the line, (2) the length going via X then Y, and (3) the length going via Y then X. Count how many pairs realize each distance using a double loop and increment a frequency array.

complexity.why: The algorithm consists of a double loop over all ordered pairs (i, j) with 1 ≤ i < j ≤ N. This is Θ(N^2/2) iterations, each performing O(1) arithmetic and a single array increment. No BFS or queue operations are used. The frequency array var_1 has size N, so space is O(N). Compared to the slow version, the asymptotic time is the same O(N^2), but the constant factors are much smaller due to the absence of graph traversal, distance arrays, and deques.

complexity_delta.from: O(N^2) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N^2) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: Both versions are O(N^2), but the slow code uses N BFS traversals and repeated allocations, while the fast code uses only arithmetic in nested loops, drastically reducing constant factors and Python overhead.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the underlying graph is a simple path 1..N with one extra edge (X, Y), so distances need not be computed with a general-purpose BFS.
Derive the closed-form shortest-path length for any pair (i, j) as the minimum of: direct distance |j - i|, distance via X then Y, and distance via Y then X.
Replace the repeated BFS-from-each-node pattern with a single nested loop over all i < j pairs computing distance via arithmetic.
Eliminate per-source distance arrays and queues, using a single frequency array indexed by distance to count pair occurrences.
Simplify memory usage to only the counts array, removing adjacency lists and BFS state.
trigger_signals: The graph is almost a path (line) with one additional edge, a structure that is highly amenable to direct formulas instead of general graph traversal.
The slow code performs BFS from every node, a pattern that is often a red flag for potential simplification when the graph has special structure.
Fresh distance arrays and deques are allocated in the innermost performance-critical loops, which is expensive in Python for N up to around 2000.
Editorial and known solutions for similar problems use direct distance formulas rather than BFS when possible.
pitfalls: When switching from BFS-based distances to an arithmetic formula, it is easy to make off-by-one errors in the computed path lengths, especially around the extra edge and 1-based indexing.
Care must be taken to consider both directions via the extra edge (i -> X -> Y -> j and i -> Y -> X -> j). Omitting one direction can underestimate some distances.
The counting must only consider pairs with i < j to avoid double counting; using loops with correct bounds (for var_5 in range(1, N) and var_6 in range(var_5+1, N+1)) is crucial.
The output array indices must align with distance values (distance k is stored at index k in var_1); index 0 is unused and should be skipped when printing.
For larger constraints than assumed (e.g., N >> 2000), even O(N^2) may become too slow, so while this transformation significantly reduces constants, it does not change the asymptotic complexity.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical union-find / connected components problem: N nodes, M edges; N,M up to ~2e5 in Python on AtCoder-like judge.

dominant_ops: Repeated DSU find operations (without path compression) plus redundant work: extra finds per union, building and storing the entire edge list, and a final O(N) floating-point aggregation.

complexity.why: Union is by size (tree height O(log N)), but find has no path compression, so each find is O(log N). Each edge can trigger multiple finds (in the if condition, in union, and via size queries). The final loop over all N nodes does extra work with floating-point divisions. Edge list var_9 stores all M edges, giving O(N + M) memory.

bottlenecks.detail: find() is implemented recursively without path compression; although union-by-size bounds height to O(log N), every operation costs more than strictly necessary and recursion adds call overhead.
For each edge, code calls func_2/func_3 multiple times (up to ~6 finds per union), inflating the constant factor in the DSU hot path.
All edges are appended to var_9 but never used later; this adds O(M) memory and push overhead.

The number of connected components is reconstructed by summing 1/size for each node and rounding, which requires an O(N) pass and floating-point operations instead of maintaining an integer component count incrementally.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a standard DSU (union-find) with path compression and union by rank, while maintaining an explicit group counter. Avoid storing unused edges and skip the final floating-point aggregation by directly outputting the maintained component count.

complexity.why: Path compression plus union by rank makes each find/union amortized inverse-Ackermann time α(N), effectively constant. Each edge is processed with a constant number of DSU operations, and components are tracked via grp without an extra pass. Only parent and rank arrays of size N are stored.

complexity_delta.from: O((N + M) log N) time, O(N + M) space
complexity_delta.to: O((N + M) α(N)) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic improvement comes from adding path compression and removing the O(M) edge list plus O(N) post-processing; the dominant practical improvement is reduced constant factors in the DSU operations and elimination of extra passes.

transformation_steps: Replace the global-array DSU without path compression by a class-based union-find with parent and rank arrays and path-compressed find.
Introduce a grp counter initialized to N and decremented exactly once per successful union to track the number of connected components in O(1) per union.
Remove storage of all edges (drop var_9) and process each edge online as it is read from input.
Eliminate size-based floating-point reconstruction of the component count (sum of 1/size over all nodes and rounding); instead, directly print grp.
Reduce redundant find calls by structuring union so that roots are computed once per argument and reused inside the operation.
trigger_signals: Time-limit exceed (TLE) or near-TLE behavior on the largest inputs when using the original DSU with many repeated finds and extra passes.
Profiling or reasoning showing that DSU operations and the final O(N) floating-point loop dominate runtime.
High memory usage from storing the entire edge list despite it not being needed after unions are applied.
pitfalls: Incorrect method naming or calls in the refactored DSU class (e.g., defining func_1 but calling find, defining func_4 but calling unite) will cause runtime errors despite the algorithm being faster in theory.

Path compression implemented recursively can still risk recursion limits if not carefully written (e.g., accidental loss of union-by-rank/size leading to tall trees); an iterative find is safer for extremely large N.
Maintaining grp requires updating it only on successful unions; decrementing it when joining already-connected nodes would undercount components.

Switching from the floating-point reconstruction to an integer counter changes how the answer is derived; one must ensure grp exactly matches the intended problem definition (number of connected components) before removing the old computation.
If the original edge information (var_9) is later needed for other queries, removing it would break functionality; ensure that the problem only needs the final component count.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder ABC-style constraints; N (=var_2) and K (=var_1) on the order of 1e5–1e6, K possibly up to about 1e9. Single test case, no explicit queries.

dominant_ops: Per-iteration floating-point division var_1 / (var_4 + 1)
Per-iteration math.log2 call
Per-iteration math.ceil on log2 result
Per-iteration list creation for max([0, ...])
Per-iteration power operation 2 ** (−k)

complexity.why: The loop runs var_2 times. Inside each iteration, a constant number of O(1) operations are performed: a division, a log2, a ceil, a small list allocation plus max, and a power. No data structures grow with N.

bottlenecks.detail: math.log2 and 2 ** exponent are relatively expensive transcendental operations executed N times. These dominate runtime for large N.
max([0, x]) allocates a new list object on every iteration just to compare with 0; this adds overhead in both time (allocation) and GC pressure.
Repeated floating-point operations (division, log2, pow) can be slower than simple integer arithmetic and may introduce small precision quirks, though accuracy is likely acceptable here.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace the closed-form logarithm-based computation of the required number of doublings with an explicit simulation: for each starting value i in [1, N], keep doubling i until it reaches at least K, halving the probability weight each time. This removes expensive transcendental math and list allocations, relying only on integer multiplies and simple float multiplies/divides.

complexity.time: O(N log K) in the worst case; effectively O(N) for typical constraints where log K is small (e.g., K ≤ 1e9 ⇒ log2 K ≤ ~30).
complexity.why: The outer loop runs N = var_2 times. For each i, the inner while loop doubles i until i ≥ K. The number of doublings for a given i is t_i = max(0, ceil(log2(K / i))). Summed over all i, this is at most N * log2 K. Each iteration uses only a few integer and float multiplications and comparisons, and no extra data structures are allocated.

complexity_delta.from: O(N) with very high per-iteration constant due to math.log2, 2**x, and list allocation
complexity_delta.to: O(N log K) worst-case but with very small constant, and for typical constraints log K is bounded (~30), making it effectively linear and faster in practice
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically, the modified code may appear to add a log K factor, but in competitive programming constraints K is small enough in log scale that the cheaper operations dominate. The empirical speedup comes from eliminating heavy transcendental functions and allocations.

transformation_steps: Reformulate the probability term from an analytic expression using log2 and powers to an iterative doubling process that directly simulates the number of coin tosses/doublings as in the original model.
Replace math.log2(var_1 / (var_4 + 1)) and ceil + max + pow with a simple loop that multiplies the current value by 2 and halves the probability weight until the threshold is reached.
Remove per-iteration list allocation 'max([0, x])' and instead rely purely on control flow (while condition) to enforce non-negativity of the number of doublings.
Use only primitive arithmetic operations (integer multiply, compare; float multiply/divide) inside the tight loop, reducing CPU cost per iteration and avoiding function call overhead.
Preserve the overall probability sum logic but in a more numerically transparent and computationally efficient way.
trigger_signals: Presence of math.log2 inside the main loop, which is an expensive transcendental function.
Use of 2 ** exponent in the inner loop, another typically heavy operation compared to simple multiplications.
Allocation of a Python list '[0, x]' for every loop iteration just to call max, indicating avoidable overhead.
All heavy operations occur O(N) times with no caching or precomputation, suggesting a constant-factor bottleneck rather than a purely asymptotic one.
pitfalls: The fast code modifies the loop variable var_3 inside the while loop; although safe in Python (the for-range is precomputed), it can be confusing and error-prone to readers or if ported to other languages.
Both implementations rely on floating-point arithmetic for probabilities; extreme parameter values could accumulate rounding error, though for typical contest constraints this is acceptable.
If constraints were such that K could be astronomically large (making log2 K nontrivial), the added log K factor could become a real asymptotic concern; this must be checked against problem limits.

Care must be taken to maintain equivalence between the analytic log2 formulation and the iterative doubling method; off-by-one errors in the loop condition (e.g., '< K' vs '<= K') would change the computed probability.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style setting: N up to ~1e5, M up to ~1e9 so that prime factorization by trial division to sqrt(M) is feasible. Only one test instance per run. Needed nCr arguments go up to about N + max_prime_exponent, with max exponent < ~40 for M <= 1e9; code uses a safe margin +100.

Trial-division prime factorization of M up to sqrt(M)
O(#prime_factors) combinations using precomputed factorial tables

complexity.space: O(B), storing three length-B arrays for factorials, modular inverses, and inverse factorials
complexity.why: The main loop `for var_8 in range(2, 2 * 10**5 + 1)` builds factorials (var_6), modular inverses (var_9), and inverse factorials (var_7) in O(B) time and space. Factorization `func_2` runs in O(sqrt(M)) which is smaller than B under inferred constraints. The final multiplicative loop over prime factors is O(#factors) with #factors << B.

Each iteration of the precompute loop performs several modular multiplications and one indexed access into var_9 using `var_10 % var_8`, making the constant factor non-trivial over 2*10^5 iterations.
The `math` module is imported but not used; this does not materially affect performance, but is a small sign of unneeded code.

FastAudit.core_idea: Tighten the upper bound for factorial and inverse precomputation to depend on N (var_2) plus a small constant for the maximum needed exponent from the prime factorization of M, instead of using a large fixed global bound.

complexity.time: O(N + sqrt(M)), where the precomputation loop runs to limit = N + 100
