Inside the inner loop, it repeatedly calls sum() on lists whose total size is O(N), which adds another multiplicative N factor in practice. Memory is dominated by the 4^N tuples, each of length N.

bottlenecks.detail: Full Cartesian product materialized with itertools.product(*var_15) and stored in var_3. For N=8 this is 4^8=65,536 assignments; for larger N it explodes and is completely infeasible.
var_3 holds 4^N tuples, each of length N. This leads to O(4^N * N) memory usage, which can quickly exhaust memory or cause heavy GC overhead.

Within the inner for var_17 loop, the code performs sum(var_2), sum(var_5), sum(var_7) many times as the lists grow. These sums are recomputed from scratch, instead of maintaining running totals, multiplying the cost by another factor proportional to N.
The search does not prune any branch early based on partial information; every assignment is fully constructed even if it is already suboptimal or impossible to satisfy constraints.
Using eval(input()) to read integers is slower and unsafe; while not the main bottleneck compared to 4^N enumeration, it adds unnecessary overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace explicit materialization of all 4^N assignments with a recursive DFS that incrementally builds choices (skip / assign to A / B / C), carrying running totals for each target. Each recursive step branches into 4 options and accumulates a +10 cost when a stick is used; at the leaves, compute the final cost once, subtracting 30 to remove the initial 10 per target. This avoids storing the Cartesian product and repeated summations, keeping memory at O(N) and significantly reducing constant factors.

complexity.why: The recursion is a 4-ary tree over N sticks: each level chooses 1 of 4 actions, yielding about (4^{N+1}-1)/3 recursive calls = O(4^N). Each call does O(1) work: updating sums and comparing a few integers. Sums are maintained incrementally, so no inner O(N) summations. Only the recursion stack of depth N and a small number of scalars are stored, so space is O(N), eliminating the O(4^N * N) product storage.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(4^N * N), Space: O(4^N * N)
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(4^N), Space: O(N)
complexity_delta.note: Both codes explore essentially the same 4^N assignment space, but the modified version avoids materializing all assignments and avoids repeated O(N) summations, so it is dramatically faster and more memory-efficient in practice.

transformation_steps: Eliminated itertools.product and the explicit list var_3 of all assignments. Instead, designed a recursive function func_1 that takes an index and the current sums for A, B, C.

Changed perspective from 'iterate over assignments then compute sums' to 'incrementally build assignments while maintaining sums'. This allows each recursive call to update totals in O(1) rather than re-summing lists.

Encoded the cost model directly in recursion: when a stick is assigned to A/B/C, add 10 to the partial result in that branch; at the leaf (var_8 == var_4), compute the final mismatch cost abs(vars - targets) and subtract 30 to compensate for the initial 10 cost counted for the first stick in each of the three rods.

Introduced an INF sentinel (var_10 = 10**9) to represent invalid configurations and a base case that returns INF when any of var_5, var_6, var_7 is 0 (i.e., at least one rod has no sticks), thereby capturing the original constraint that each target must have at least one stick.

Replaced explicit min updates in an outer loop with returning min(...) of the four recursive options for each stick (skip, use for A, use for B, use for C), making the code more declarative and reducing mutable state.

Removed repeated sum(var_2), sum(var_5), sum(var_7) and intermediate lists representing assigned sticks; only running totals (integers) are carried through recursion, cutting both CPU and memory overhead.
trigger_signals: Presence of itertools.product over a per-element choice set of size 4, with N variable, producing 4^N combinations explicitly.
Memory-heavy pattern: var_3 = list(itertools.product(*var_15)) followed by iteration over var_3, suggesting heavy intermediate storage.
Nested loops: outer over 4^N assignments, inner over N positions, with additional work (sum on variable-length lists) inside the inner loop.
Recomputing aggregates (sum of lists) multiple times as lists grow, instead of carrying incremental sums.
No early pruning or incremental evaluation of cost until full assignment is constructed.
pitfalls: The recursive solution still has exponential time O(4^N); it is only viable because N is small (about 8). For larger N, further pruning or DP/memoization would be needed.

Off-by-constant handling: the -30 in the base case assumes exactly 3 targets and that each used stick added 10. Changing the number of targets or the per-stick cost would require carefully adjusting this offset.

The base case uses min(var_5, var_6, var_7) > 0 to ensure each target has at least one stick; forgetting this condition (or implementing it incorrectly) would count invalid configurations where a target has zero sticks.

The recursion does not memoize states; the same (index, A_sum, B_sum, C_sum) could, in principle, be recomputed. For the given constraints this is acceptable, but adding memoization might be necessary if constraints were increased.
Python recursion depth is limited (default ~1000), which is safe for N<=8 but must be considered if someone generalizes the solution to larger N.
Using eval(input()) for reading integers is unnecessary and unsafe; though not a major performance hit here, it is a bad practice and can become a vulnerability in other contexts.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic counting problem: number of triples (i,j,k) with 1 <= i < j < k <= n and i + j + k = x, repeated for multiple test cases until input '0 0'. Typical AOJ-style constraints where n <= 200 and the number of test cases can be large enough that O(n^3) per case risks TLE in Python.

dominant_ops: Enumerating all strictly increasing triples (var_2, var_3, var_4) with 1 <= var_2 < var_3 < var_4 <= var_5 and checking if their sum equals var_6. The triple-nested for-loops dominate runtime.

complexity.why: For each test case, var_2 runs ~n times, var_3 ~n times per var_2, and var_4 ~n times per (var_2,var_3), yielding Theta(n^3) iterations. Only a few integer variables are used, so auxiliary memory is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: Redundant enumeration of all O(n^3) triples even though the sum constraint defines the third variable from the first two. Many triples are checked where the sum condition fails, wasting iterations.
Three nested Python-level for-loops in pure Python are slow, especially near n ~ 200 and with many test cases; the overhead of 8e6+ iterations per test case can accumulate to TLE.

The sum check `if var_2 + var_3 + var_4 == var_6` is executed in the deepest loop for every combination, causing repeated additions and comparisons instead of computing the required third value directly.

FastAudit.core_idea: Remove one loop by solving for the third variable algebraically: fix (var_3, var_4), compute var_2 = var_6 - var_3 - var_4, and then only count it if it satisfies the ordering and bounds (var_2 > var_4 and var_2 <= var_5). This reduces the enumeration to O(n^2) and ensures each valid triple (var_2, var_3, var_4) with var_2 < var_3 < var_4 is counted exactly once via an equivalent parametrization.

complexity.why: Two nested loops over (var_3,var_4) give Theta(n^2) iterations. The third value var_2 is derived in O(1) per pair, so the total per test case is O(n^2). No extra data structures are allocated beyond loop counters and a few integers.

complexity_delta.from: O(n^3) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n^2) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: By eliminating one loop via algebraic computation of the third element of the triple, runtime is reduced by a factor of about O(n) for each test case while preserving constant extra memory usage.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the inner condition `if var_2 + var_3 + var_4 == var_6` defines var_2 uniquely for any fixed pair (var_3, var_4): var_2 = var_6 - var_3 - var_4.
Change the enumeration strategy: instead of iterating (var_2,var_3,var_4) with three loops, iterate only over (var_3,var_4) with two loops and compute var_2 directly.

Adjust loop ranges to maintain strict ordering between the chosen indices. In the modified code, var_3 iterates from 1 to var_5-2 and var_4 from var_3+1 to var_5-1, then enforce var_2 > var_4 and var_2 <= var_5 inside the loop to recover the original constraint 1 <= var_2 < var_3 < var_4 <= var_5 via a re-labelling of variable roles.
Replace the equality check on sums with simple bound and ordering checks on the computed var_2: `if var_2 > var_4 and var_2 <= var_5`.
Slightly simplify the loop termination condition: instead of `if var_5: ... else: break`, explicitly check `if var_5 == 0: break` for clarity.
trigger_signals: Triple nested loops with bounds tied to n, yielding an obvious O(n^3) pattern in Python.
Per-test-case work scaling poorly as n grows (e.g., n ~ 200 gives ~8e6 iterations per case).
A simple linear constraint linking loop variables (sum fixed) suggests one variable can be expressed in terms of the others, hinting at the possibility of removing a loop.
Problem type being a canonical 'count triples with fixed sum' task where O(n^2) or better solutions are standard.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when changing loop ranges: ensuring that all valid triples are still reachable with the new (var_3,var_4) ranges and that none are double-counted.

Maintaining the strict inequality ordering between the three indices: the new condition uses `var_2 > var_4`, which corresponds to a different naming order than the original `var_2 < var_3 < var_4`; care is needed to verify that every original triple maps to exactly one new configuration.
Ensuring `var_2` stays within the valid domain [1, var_5]; the code only checks the upper bound and relative ordering, so correctness relies on the loop ranges to implicitly enforce the lower bound.

Logical equivalence: when refactoring via algebraic substitution, it is easy to unintentionally change the problem (e.g., allow equal indices or miss some permutations), so one should validate against small brute-force outputs.
For large numbers of test cases, input overhead might still be noticeable; although not a correctness issue, using faster I/O patterns could be beneficial in tight environments.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test. Target value var_2 up to around 1e4 (array sized var_2 + 1e4). Number of item types var_3/var_5 likely up to a few thousands. DP uses overshoot margin 1e4, suggesting max weight per item <= 1e4.

dominant_ops: For each capacity var_6 = 1..var_2, perform a NumPy advanced-indexing + vector add + reduction: (var_7[var_6 - var_1] + var_4).min(). This allocates temporaries of length equal to number of items every iteration.

complexity.why: Loop over capacities 1..var_2 (N). At each step, var_6 - var_1 is a vector of length M=var_5, so var_7[var_6 - var_1] is an M-length gather, then + var_4 is an M-length vector add, then min() is an M-length reduction: O(M) per capacity, for total O(N*M). Space: DP array var_7 is length N + max_weight; arrays var_1, var_4 each length M; plus transient M-length arrays created each iteration.

bottlenecks.detail: Inside the Python for-loop over var_6, each iteration performs advanced indexing, vector addition, and min reduction on length-M NumPy arrays, allocating new temporaries. The heavy C work is repeated N times rather than being fused.
The algorithm is still driven by a Python loop over all capacities. NumPy cannot amortize overhead because each iteration calls into NumPy separately.
Every iteration reads M DP entries via advanced indexing and writes 1 scalar. For larger M and N this becomes memory-bandwidth bound, and repeated allocation of temporaries hurts cache efficiency.
Importing NumPy adds fixed overhead and memory use, which is significant in typical competitive-programming constraints where plain Python would suffice.

FastAudit.core_idea: Classic 1D unbounded-knapsack style DP over total weight/value: maintain dp[x] = minimal cost to reach exact total x, iterating capacities and updating via all items. Over-allocate dp up to var_2 + max_weight_margin and take the minimum cost among states with total >= var_2.

complexity.why: Outer loop over capacities var_7 = 0..var_2-1 (N iterations). For each reachable capacity, inner loop over all var_3 items (M iterations) does O(1) scalar arithmetic and comparisons, for O(N*M) total. Space is the DP array of length var_2 + 1e4 + 1; the item list uses only O(M). No large per-iteration temporaries.

complexity_delta.from: O(N*M) with high constant factors due to per-iteration NumPy vector operations and temporary allocations.
complexity_delta.to: O(N*M) with low constant factors using simple scalar operations in tightly nested Python loops.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity stays O(N*M), but eliminating per-step NumPy overhead and transient arrays yields significantly faster runtime for typical competitive-programming N, M.

transformation_steps: Replace NumPy arrays for DP and item parameters with plain Python lists of scalars.
Remove the per-capacity vectorized update (var_7[var_6 - var_1] + var_4).min() and reintroduce an explicit inner loop over items.
Allocate a single 1D DP list var_6 with a sufficiently large fixed size (var_2 + 1e4 + 1) and initialize all entries to a large sentinel (infinity) except dp[0] = 0.
Iterate capacities sequentially, skip unreachable states early (if dp[var_7] is infinity), and update dp[var_7 + weight] in-place with scalar min operations.
At the end, scan the tail dp[var_2:] to find the minimum cost for any capacity >= var_2 instead of relying on exact-capacity DP.
trigger_signals: Use of NumPy inside a long Python for-loop (N up to around 1e4) with per-iteration vector operations of non-trivial length M.
Advanced indexing (arr[indices_vector]) executed every iteration, indicating allocation of temporary arrays and scattered memory accesses.
Problem size small-to-moderate (typical contest constraints) where Python scalar arithmetic is already fast enough and vectorization cannot compensate for overhead.
DP transitions depend on previous states in a way that prevents fusing all steps into a few global NumPy operations; state recurrence is inherently sequential over capacity.
pitfalls: Assuming NumPy automatically speeds up any DP: if the DP is inherently sequential and you still loop in Python, NumPy may slow things down due to overhead.
Creating new NumPy temporaries in every iteration (from advanced indexing and vector ops) can dominate runtime and memory traffic.
Need to ensure the DP array is sized large enough to accommodate overshoot states (here handled by var_2 + 1e4 + 1); mis-estimating this can lead to index errors or incorrect results.

Using zeros as DP initialization in the NumPy version changes the semantics compared to the explicit 'infinity' initialization, which can silently produce wrong answers even if it appears fast on some cases.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case. N is the first input in slow_code (var_2) / fast_code (var_3). M is the other input (var_1). Factorization of M via trial division up to sqrt(M) suggests M up to about 1e9–1e12. Hardcoded 2*10^5 factorial limit in slow_code suggests N + max_exponent <= 2e5.

dominant_ops: Trial division factorization of M up to sqrt(M)
Precomputation of factorials, modular inverses, and inverse factorials up to fixed limit 2*10^5
O(#primes) binomial coefficient evaluations using precomputed tables

complexity.why: func_2 does trial division up to floor(sqrt(M)) once: O(sqrt(M)). Precomputation loop `for var_8 in range(2, 2*10**5 + 1)` builds factorials and inverses up to L = 2*10^5: O(L). The final loop over prime factors is O(#distinct_primes), negligible vs these. Overall time dominated by sqrt(M) and the fixed L. Space from var_6, var_7, var_9 arrays of length L.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorial and inverse tables are built up to a hardcoded 2*10^5 regardless of the actual required maximum n = var_2 + max_exponent. For small N this overcomputes substantially, increasing runtime by a large constant factor.

All modular inverses up to 2*10^5 are computed using the linear recurrence `inv[i] = -inv[MOD % i] * (MOD // i)`. Although O(L), this performs more multiplications and array accesses than the fast approach that uses one modular exponentiation plus a single reverse loop.
The precomputation limit does not adapt if constraints grow; if N ever needs to exceed 2*10^5, the code breaks. Conversely, for small N it does unnecessary work.

FastAudit.core_idea: Factor M into prime powers, then for each prime exponent e compute the number of ways to distribute e indistinguishable items into N bins with repetition: C(N + e - 1, e). Precompute factorials and inverse factorials only up to N + max_exponent, using a single modular exponentiation to get factorial[N+max_e]^{-1} and a linear reverse pass to fill all inverse factorials.

complexity.why: Same O(sqrt(M)) factorization as slow_code. Let K = N + max_exponent. Factorials are built in O(K). A single modular exponentiation computes inv_fact[K] in O(log MOD), then a reverse loop computes all inv_fact[i] in O(K). One more forward pass builds factorials. Combination queries are O(1) each. Since max_exponent = O(log M), K ≈ N + O(log M).

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(M) + L) time, O(L) space where L = 2 * 10^5 (fixed upper bound)
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + (N + max_exponent)) time, O(N + max_exponent) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic orders are both linear in a size parameter, but slow_code uses a fixed global bound L, while fast_code scales with the actual needed maximum K = N + max_exponent. This reduces work when K << L and yields lower constants via a cheaper inverse-factorial construction.

transformation_steps: Replace fixed-size factorial and inverse precomputation up to 2*10^5 with on-demand precomputation up to K = N + max_exponent, computed after factoring M.

Switch from full linear modular-inverse table (inv[i] for all i) to using one fast exponentiation to get factorial[K]^{MOD-2}, then generate all inverse factorials via a single reverse loop multiplied by decreasing i.
Simplify the combination function to rely on (fact, inv_fact) only, avoiding passing MOD and extra logic like min(k, n-k); the fast_code directly applies nCk using precomputed arrays.
Use prime exponents directly (via Counter on flat factor list) and compute C(N + e - 1, e) for each exponent, instead of maintaining pairs and a more generic combination interface.
trigger_signals: Hardcoded precomputation limits such as `for i in range(2, 2*10**5 + 1)` that do not depend on actual input values.
Heavy precomputation of modular inverses or factorials even when the problem instance only needs much smaller n.
Use of linear modular inverse table when the number of required nCk evaluations is small and a factorial/inv_factorial strategy would suffice.
Performance issues on small/medium inputs where time is dominated by precomputation rather than the main combinatorial or number-theoretic logic.
pitfalls: If N + max_exponent can exceed the precomputation bound, the fixed-limit approach (slow_code) may silently produce incorrect results or index errors; switching to dynamic K must carefully cover the true maximum n used in nCk.
When converting to factorial/inverse-factorial logic, off-by-one errors in array sizes (e.g., needing up to K but allocating only K elements) will cause incorrect binomial coefficients or IndexError.

Incorrect handling of edge cases such as nCk with k < 0, k > n, or M = 1 (no prime factors). The fast_code handles the M = 1 case via an empty Counter, but any refactor must keep this behavior consistent.
Using pow(x, MOD-2, MOD) assumes MOD is prime; reusing this pattern in a context with non-prime modulus would be invalid.
When changing from exponent-based combinatorics to list-of-primes representation (or vice versa), mixing up multiplicities (e vs. count of factors) can produce wrong combinatorial parameters.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style constraints: two strings of length up to ~2e5 and up to ~2e5 queries, requiring O(n+q) solutions in CP Python. Characters only 'A' and others (treated as 2).

dominant_ops: Per-character Python loop to fill numpy arrays var_7 and var_8
Large numpy array allocations of shape (n+1, 2)
Prefix-sum via np.add.accumulate on those arrays
Per-query Python work: four array lookups, subtraction, modulo operation, immediate printing

complexity.why: Let n be the string length and q be the number of queries. Building var_7 and var_8 scans each string once (O(n)). Two prefix-sum scans with np.add.accumulate are also O(n). Each of q queries does O(1) arithmetic and indexing. Space is dominated by the (n+1)×2 numpy arrays var_7 and var_8.

bottlenecks.detail: Using numpy in a competitive-programming style problem adds heavy overhead: constructing two (n+1,2) arrays via Python list comprehensions, then converting to numpy arrays, plus np.add.accumulate. The code does not exploit true vectorization because all character classification is done in Python loops.

Storing counts as 2D arrays var_7[i] = [cntA, cntB] instead of a single prefix-sum with a numeric encoding (1 for 'A', 2 otherwise) doubles memory traffic and complicates each query to multiple indexed accesses.

Both filling loops over var_2[1:] and var_3[1:] are pure Python loops performing if/else for each character, which is already O(n). Since this dominates, numpy’s later accumulate gives little benefit but still incurs its own overhead.
Printing results line by line in the query loop causes many small writes to stdout. While not the primary issue, it is slower than collecting answers and outputting once, especially when q is large.

FastAudit.core_idea: Encode each character as an integer (1 if 'A', else 2), build simple 1D prefix sums for both strings, and for each query compare the substring sums modulo 3. This avoids numpy entirely, uses compact lists, and keeps all operations as simple integer arithmetic on Python lists.

complexity.why: Two prefix-sum arrays var_1 and var_2 are built in O(n) total using itertools.accumulate. Each of q queries is answered in O(1) time by two prefix differences and two modulo-3 operations. Space is linear in n for the two prefix arrays and the result list.

complexity_delta.from: O(n + q) time, O(n) space with significant constant factors due to numpy allocations and 2D structures
complexity_delta.to: O(n + q) time, O(n) space with low constant factors using plain Python lists and 1D prefix sums
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged, but real-world performance improves substantially. Removing numpy and redundant dimensions cuts memory use and CPU overhead, which is critical for tight CP time limits.

transformation_steps: Replace the 2D numpy count representation (var_7, var_8 with shape (n+1,2)) by 1D integer encodings var_5 and var_6 where each character is mapped to 1 if 'A' else 2.
Compute prefix sums directly on these 1D lists using itertools.accumulate to obtain var_1 and var_2; prepend a 0 to make them 1-indexed.

For each query (l1, r1, l2, r2), compute the interval sums via prefix differences: s1 = var_1[r1] - var_1[l1-1], s2 = var_2[r2] - var_2[l2-1], and compare s1 % 3 and s2 % 3 instead of more complex count-based arithmetic.
Eliminate numpy imports, array construction, and np.add.accumulate calls to avoid overhead and keep everything in fast built-in types.
Buffer query results into a list var_3 and print them at once with '\n'.join(...) instead of printing per query to reduce I/O overhead.
trigger_signals: Use of numpy in an otherwise simple O(n+q) string/prefix-sum problem where input sizes are large and operations are fundamentally sequential.
Construction of large 2D arrays via list comprehensions followed by np.array, indicating double overhead (Python allocation plus numpy conversion) with no true vectorization.
Per-element Python loops used to populate numpy arrays, showing that the intended benefit of vectorized operations is not realized.
Memory footprint concerns: storing (n+1)×2 arrays of ints where only a single scalar prefix sum per position is needed.
Competitive-programming context where numpy is generally discouraged due to import and operation overhead relative to optimized pure-Python patterns.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when switching from explicit 1-based indexing with leading '-' characters or 2D arrays to 0-based Python lists with a manual leading 0; must ensure queries use var_1[r] - var_1[l-1] correctly.

Maintaining the modulo equivalence: the numpy version computes differences of (cntA - cntB) and checks divisibility by 3; the simplified version uses encoded sums mod 3. Both must be mathematically equivalent; incorrect encoding or modulo placement can change answers.

Assuming numpy brings speedups in CP: if character classification stays in Python loops, numpy often slows things down. Future changes should keep core loops in pure Python or fully vectorize if numpy is retained.
I/O changes: aggregating output improves speed but requires enough memory for q answers; if q were extremely large, memory vs. speed trade-offs should be re-evaluated.

Type assumptions: the fast solution relies on small integer arithmetic staying within Python’s efficient range; introducing larger weights or different encodings could alter performance characteristics.

constraints_guess.n_max: 1e12 (likely large enough that O(n) over n/2 iterations is too slow)
constraints_guess.notes: Single integer input, heavy arithmetic in a loop; the existence of an O(sqrt(n)) solution suggests n can be very large (e.g., up to 1e10–1e12) where O(n) is infeasible in Python.

dominant_ops: A single for-loop from 1 to n//2, performing integer division and a few arithmetic operations per iteration.

complexity.why: The main loop iterates var_2 from 1 to var_4 = n//2, so Θ(n) iterations. Each iteration does a constant amount of work: one integer division (n//var_2) and a few multiplications/additions. No data structures grow with n, so space is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: The loop runs up to n//2, which is Θ(n). For n around 1e8 or higher, this is too slow in Python.
Each iteration performs an integer division var_1 // var_2. Integer division on large integers is relatively expensive; doing it Θ(n) times dominates runtime.

The intermediate values (sums and products) can become large (≈O(n^3)), and Python big-integer multiplications/additions in every iteration add to constant-factor overhead, magnifying the cost of the Θ(n) loop.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a symmetric property of floor division and group terms by equal floor(n/i) values so that contributions from many i’s can be aggregated using closed-form formulas in O(1) per distinct quotient, reducing the overall complexity to O(sqrt(n)). Algebraic manipulation then consolidates the sum and subtracts overcounted square terms.

complexity.why: The optimized code loops var_4 from 1 to floor(sqrt(n)), computing var_3 = n // var_4 and using a closed form var_4 * (var_4 + var_3) * (var_3 + 1 - var_4). The count of such iterations is Θ(√n); all other work is O(1). No arrays or large auxiliary structures are used, so space remains constant.

complexity_delta.from: O(n) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(n)) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: By exploiting the structure of floor(n/i) and using closed-form sums, the algorithm reduces the main summation from iterating over ~n/2 indices to iterating over only ~sqrt(n) representative indices.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the slow code computes a sum involving floor(n/i), specifically a weighted sum of 1 + 2 + ... + floor(n/i) over i from 1 to n//2, plus a simple arithmetic progression from n//2+1 to n.

Use the standard trick for floor-division sums: observe that floor(n/i) takes only O(sqrt(n)) distinct values, and for i > sqrt(n), values of floor(n/i) correspond to small integers that can be handled via symmetry or grouping.

Derive an equivalent expression where contributions of ranges of i with the same floor(n/i) are aggregated by a closed-form polynomial in terms of n, the quotient, and the bounds of i, rather than iterating each i individually.

Reparameterize the sum in terms of var_4 up to floor(sqrt(n)), compute var_3 = n // var_4, and accumulate the grouped contribution var_4 * (var_4 + var_3) * (var_3 + 1 - var_4), which represents the sum over a range of i-values in one shot.

Identify and correct overcounted or double-counted parts of the sum (in particular square indices) and subtract them via a known formula for the sum of squares: var_1 * (var_1 + 1) * (2 * var_1 + 1) // 6.
Consolidate all algebra so that the final algorithm performs only O(sqrt(n)) iterations with constant work per iteration, plus O(1) final corrections.
trigger_signals: Presence of a loop that runs up to n//2 with non-trivial arithmetic per iteration, suggesting O(n) complexity which is borderline for large constraints.
The summation includes floor(n/i), a classic hint that a floor-division / divisor-sum optimization (O(sqrt(n))) may exist.
Typical competitive programming contexts: single large n input with heavy arithmetic in Python; O(n) approaches often fail when n ≥ 1e7–1e8.
The need to handle potentially very large n (suggested by using integer math only, without arrays) where only sublinear loops (like O(sqrt(n))) are practical.
pitfalls: Using var_5**0.5 (floating-point sqrt) and casting to int can be risky for extremely large n due to floating-point precision limitations; using integer-based sqrt (e.g., math.isqrt) is safer.
Care must be taken with off-by-one errors when translating from a direct sum over i = 1..n//2 to a grouped sum over i up to sqrt(n); misaligned bounds can omit or double-count terms.
The closed-form expression var_4 * (var_4 + var_3) * (var_3 + 1 - var_4) is algebraically dense; small algebra mistakes can give incorrect results while still passing some small tests.
The final correction term (subtracting sum of squares) is critical; omitting or miscomputing it leads to subtle discrepancies, particularly around the transition near sqrt(n).
Use of eval(input()) is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; although not directly a performance issue here, it is generally a bad practice and can mask logic errors if input is malformed.

constraints_guess.n_max: 1e5–2e5 (upper bound for first input N inferred from factorial precomputation up to N+100)
constraints_guess.notes: Second input M is factorized with trial division up to sqrt(M), so M is likely <= 1e9–1e12. Problem is to count ways to represent M as a product of N positive integers using prime factorization and stars-and-bars, i.e., product over primes of C(N-1+e, e).

dominant_ops: O(N) precomputation of factorials, modular inverses of all integers up to N+100, and inverse factorials
O(sqrt(M)) trial division to factor M

complexity.why: The code loops var_8 from 2 to var_2+100 (N+100) to build three arrays: factorial (var_6), modular inverse of each integer (var_9), and inverse factorial (var_7), all O(N) memory. Factoring M by trial division to sqrt(M) is O(sqrt(M)). Only a constant number of combinations are then computed, so preprocessing dominates.

bottlenecks.detail: Computes modular inverses for every integer up to N+100 via a linear recurrence (var_9 array) even though only a handful of binomial coefficients are needed (one per distinct prime factor of M). This adds an O(N) step with a large constant factor that does not reduce asymptotic complexity versus a few pow() calls.

The inverse-building loop performs multiple Python-level operations per iteration (multiplication, modulo, indexing into three lists), which is expensive for N up to ~1e5–2e5 when the benefit is only to avoid a few pow(MOD-2) calls.
Uses input()/print(), which are slower than buffered sys.stdin.readline/sys.stdout.write in CP settings, though here it is minor compared to the O(N) inverse precomputation.

FastAudit.core_idea: Precompute only factorials up to N+100, and for each needed binomial coefficient use Fermat’s little theorem with pow(x, MOD-2, MOD) to compute modular inverses on demand. This keeps preprocessing linear in N but avoids the extra O(N) inverse and inverse-factorial arrays, which is cheaper when the number of binomial queries is small.

complexity.why: Factorials are built in O(N) time and space (var_8). Factorization of M is O(sqrt(M)). For each prime factor (P = number of distinct primes, typically very small), one binomial coefficient is computed using two pow(., MOD-2, MOD) calls, each O(log MOD). Since P is tiny, the extra P log MOD cost is negligible compared to O(N). Space is dominated by the factorial array.

complexity_delta.from: O(N + sqrt(M)) time, O(N) space, with a heavy O(N) modular-inverse and inverse-factorial precomputation.
complexity_delta.to: O(N + sqrt(M) + P log MOD) time, O(N) space, using only factorial precomputation and a few pow-based inverses.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic big-O in terms of N and sqrt(M) is unchanged, but the high-constant-cost O(N) inverse precomputation is removed in favor of a very small P log MOD term (P is number of distinct prime factors of M, usually <= ~9). In practice this is substantially faster for typical constraints.

transformation_steps: Retain the O(N) factorial precomputation only (var_8 in fast_code) and drop the full inverse (var_9) and inverse-factorial (var_7) arrays from slow_code.
Redefine the combination function C(n, k) to use factorials and modular inverses computed via pow(x, MOD-2, MOD) for the two denominator factorials instead of table lookups of inverse factorials.
Preserve the prime factorization logic as a simple trial division loop up to sqrt(M), which is already optimal enough for M up to ~1e9–1e12.
Switch I/O to buffered sys.stdin.readline for the single input line to reduce overhead and match competitive-programming best practices.
Ensure the factorial precomputation upper bound (N+100) safely covers all needed n in C(n, k), i.e., up to N-1+e_max where e_max is the largest exponent from factorization.
trigger_signals: The number of binomial-coefficient evaluations equals the number of distinct prime factors of M, which is very small compared to N, making global O(N) inverse precomputation wasteful.
Profiling or rough operation counting shows the inverse-building loop dominates runtime while the combination calls are few.
Time-limit-exceeded or high runtime when N is large (e.g., 1e5–2e5) despite having only a single test case and a small number of combinatorial queries.
Awareness that pow(x, MOD-2, MOD) is highly optimized in CP environments and often cheaper than building full inverse tables when query counts are low.
pitfalls: If the number of combination queries P were large (e.g., O(N) or more), the pow-based approach could become slower than a one-time inverse-and-inv-factorial precomputation; the chosen fast approach is tuned for small P.

Forgetting to precompute factorials up to the maximum needed n (N-1+max_exponent) would cause index errors or incorrect results; the +100 margin assumes exponents are small (from factorization of bounded M).
The pow-based inverse relies on the modulus being prime (Fermat’s little theorem). Reusing this pattern with a non-prime modulus would silently give wrong answers.
Using Python’s input()/print() instead of sys.stdin.readline()/sys.stdout.write() in a multi-test or heavy I/O variant of this problem could reintroduce noticeable overhead.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical of AtCoder ABC110 D-style: N (first input) and M (second input) up to about 1e9; single test case; need prime factorization of M and combinatorics on exponents. The slow_code incorrectly assumes N <= 2e5 due to fixed precomputation size.

dominant_ops: Precomputation of factorials, modular inverses, and inverse factorials up to MAXN (~2e5 in code, but would need to be ~N in general).
Trial division factorization of M up to sqrt(M).
O(1) per prime exponent to evaluate nCr using precomputed tables.

complexity.time: O(MAXN + sqrt(M)) where MAXN ~ N + O(log M); asymptotically O(N + sqrt(M)).
complexity.space: O(MAXN) for factorial, inverse, and inverse-factorial arrays.
complexity.why: func_3 does trial division up to the shrinking sqrt(current_M), giving O(sqrt(M)) divisions. The main cost is the single pass to fill arrays var_6, var_9, var_7 up to var_2 (MAXN). For the true constraints (N up to ~1e9), a correct MAXN would need to be Theta(N), which dominates both time and space.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorial and inverse precomputation is O(MAXN). If N is as large as 1e9 (as per typical problem constraints), this becomes infeasible in Python (and in general) and dwarfs the sqrt(M) factorization cost.
Storing three integer arrays (factorial, inverse, inverse-factorial) of size MAXN+1 requires O(MAXN) memory. For N up to 1e9, this is impossible; even N ~ 1e7 is already too large in Python.

Code hardcodes MAXN = 2*10^5+10. This only works if all needed n in nCr(n,k) are <= 2e5. For the actual problem, n = N + exponent - 1 can be up to ~1e9, so the code becomes incorrect for large N. To fix correctness, MAXN must scale with N, which triggers the time and memory bottlenecks above.

Precomputing full factorial tables up to MAXN is overkill when only O(log M) many combinations with small k (exponents <= ~30) are needed. This wastes time relative to the actual number of combinatorial evaluations performed.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial precomputation that scales with N. Instead, factor M, then for each exponent e, compute C(N+e-1, e) directly via a short multiplicative loop (O(e)), using exact Python big integers and taking modulo only at the end. This keeps time essentially at O(sqrt(M)) and space O(1), independent of N.

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + sum e_i) = O(sqrt(M) + log M) ≈ O(sqrt(M)).
complexity.space: O(#distinct_primes(M)) = O(log M) for the factor map; otherwise O(1).
complexity.why: func_1 performs trial division up to sqrt(M) (with M shrinking as factors are removed), which is O(sqrt(M)). The total exponent sum over all prime factors is at most log_2 M, so the inner loops computing each combination C(N+e-1, e) cost O(e) per prime, summing to O(log M). No arrays proportional to N are allocated; all arithmetic is on O(log M)-digit integers.

from.time: O(N + sqrt(M)) with N implicitly tied to factorial precomputation size.
from.space: O(N) for factorial and inverse tables.

complexity_delta.note: The key improvement is removing all dependence on N from precomputation, making the solution viable for N up to ~1e9; time and space now depend only on M via sqrt(M) and log(M).

transformation_steps: Remove global factorial / inverse / inverse-factorial precomputation arrays that scale up to MAXN ≈ N.
Replace nCr computation via precomputed tables with a direct multiplicative formula for C(N+e-1, e) = Π_{j=1}^{e} (N+e-j)/j using Python big integers.

Delay modulo operations until after each full combination value is computed, multiplying into the global answer and reducing modulo 1e9+7 there; this keeps intermediate logic simple and avoids needing modular inverses.
Keep the prime factorization step as simple trial division up to sqrt(M), using a while-based loop that shrinks M as factors are divided out, maintaining O(sqrt(M)) complexity.
Rely on the small size of each exponent e (sum of exponents ≤ log_2 M) to ensure the multiplicative combination computation is fast.
trigger_signals: Problem constraints specify N (first argument in combinations) up to 1e9 or similarly large, making factorial precomputation up to N impossible.
Memory usage projections show factorial/inverse arrays of size N+O(1) would exceed available memory.
Time complexity analysis of precomputation O(N) is incompatible with strict time limits (e.g., 1–2 seconds) for large N.
The number of required nCr evaluations is very small (O(log M)), and k (exponent) is tiny, indicating that per-query multiplicative computation is cheap and precomputation is unnecessary.
Existing solution works only when hardcoded MAXN (e.g., 2e5) covers all test cases; failing or wrong answers appear when N exceeds this bound.
pitfalls: Attempting to fix slow_code for large N by increasing MAXN to N (or N+max_exponent) will cause both time and memory to explode; the correct fix is to change the nCr strategy, not just the bound.

Direct multiplicative computation of combinations must maintain exact integer arithmetic until the final division; mixing modulo into numerator/denominator without modular inverses breaks correctness.
When using direct multiplicative nCr, ensuring the product grows only by O(e) factors is crucial; rewriting it with loops that scale with N instead of e would reintroduce performance issues.
Trial division up to sqrt(M) is acceptable for M up to about 1e9–1e12; beyond that, more advanced factorization might be needed, but that is outside typical contest constraints.
Care must be taken to handle edge cases where e = 0 (no contribution to product) and when M = 1 (no prime factors), ensuring the result defaults correctly to 1.

constraints_guess.notes: Precomputes primes up to ~1e6 and answers multiple queries until EOF. Q likely large, so per-query work must be near O(1).

dominant_ops: Sieve of Eratosthenes over [2..N]
Per-query slicing of prime-flag array
Per-query list comprehension scan to count primes

complexity.time: O(N log log N + Q * N)
complexity.space: O(N) baseline, plus O(N) transient per query
complexity.why: The sieve func_1(var_3) runs in O(N log log N). For each query, it evaluates the input, slices var_5[:k+1] (O(k) copy) and scans it with a list comprehension (another O(k)), so each query costs O(N) in the worst case. Over Q queries this becomes O(Q * N). Temporary lists per query add extra O(N) allocations, but peak memory is still O(N).

bottlenecks.detail: Each query does len([var_6 for var_6 in var_5[:n+1] if var_6 == 1]), which linearly scans up to n elements and allocates a new list.
var_5[: int(eval(input())) + 1] creates a full slice copy on every query instead of iterating over the existing list in place.
Both the slice and the list comprehension result are newly allocated every query, increasing GC and memory traffic.
Uses eval(input()) per query, which is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()), though this is secondary to the O(N) per-query scan.

FastAudit.core_idea: Precompute prime flags with an optimized sieve (outer loop up to sqrt(N), inner loop from p^2) and build a prefix-sum array of prime counts to answer each query in O(1).

complexity.time: O(N log log N + N + Q)
complexity.why: The sieve marks multiples for primes p <= sqrt(N), with total cost ~O(N log log N). Building the prefix count array var_1[2..N] is a single O(N) pass. Each query is then answered by a direct lookup var_1[n] in O(1), without extra allocations.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log log N + Q * N) time, O(N) space with O(N) transient per query
complexity_delta.to: O(N log log N + N + Q) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: The key improvement is replacing an O(N) per-query scan with an O(1) prefix-sum lookup.

After sieve completion, build a prefix array var_1 where var_1[i] = number of primes <= i.
Replace per-query counting via slicing and list comprehension with a direct array lookup var_1[n].
Avoid per-query allocations by never creating slices or temporary lists inside the query loop.

Per-query operations that touch O(N) elements of an array whose contents do not change.
Repeated allocation of large temporary lists for each input line.
Observed slowdown or TLE as the number of queries Q grows, even though precomputation is already performed.

The current snippets still use eval(input()), which is unsafe and slower; in real code, use int(input()) and validate ranges.
Hard-coding N = 1_000_000 is fine only if problem constraints guarantee it; otherwise, compute the maximum query first or dynamically adjust N.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical contest setting: 1 <= n <= ~10^3, element values up to at most a few hundred or a few thousand. Original O(n * maxA) solution suggests maxA is small (<= 100) in official constraints, but can be problematic if maxA grows large.

dominant_ops: Nested loop over candidate value var_4 (0..max(var_2)) and all elements of var_2
Repeated recomputation of sum of squared differences for each candidate
Python-level integer arithmetic inside tight loops

complexity.why: Let n = len(var_2) and M = max(var_2). The outer loop runs M+1 times (var_4 from 0 to M), and for each candidate the inner loop scans all n elements to accumulate (var_7 - (var_4 + 1))**2. Thus total work is proportional to n * M. Only the input list var_2 and a few scalars are stored, so space is linear in n.

bottlenecks.detail: Brute-force search over all integer targets from 1 to max(var_2) for a quadratic cost function that has a known closed-form minimizer (around the mean). This introduces an unnecessary factor of maxA in the runtime.
Two nested Python loops with simple arithmetic in the inner loop are slow in CP environments, especially when M and n are moderately large.

Each evaluation of the cost recomputes the full sum of squared differences from scratch. No reuse of partial sums or algebraic simplification (e.g., using sum(x), sum(x^2), and the mean) is exploited.
Use of eval(input()) is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; while not the primary performance bottleneck, it adds overhead and risk.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical property that the sum of squared deviations S(t) = Σ (ai - t)^2 is minimized (over real t) at t = mean(ai). For integer t, the minimizer lies at one of the integers nearest to the mean (typically floor/ceil of the mean). Instead of brute-forcing all candidates, compute the mean once, pick a nearby integer (here round(mean)), and compute the squared-error sum a single time using vectorized operations.

complexity.why: Reading n values and storing them in an array is O(n). Computing the mean is O(n), and then computing (var_2 - var_3)**2 and its sum is another O(n) pass. All operations are linear in n, independent of max(var_2). Numpy’s vectorization moves the inner loop into optimized C code, reducing Python-level overhead, but in big-O terms the algorithm is linear.

complexity_delta.from: O(n * maxA) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: The key improvement is eliminating the scan over all candidate target values (1..maxA) by exploiting the quadratic structure of the objective and using the mean-based minimizer. Numpy adds constant-factor speedups by shifting loops to native code, but the main asymptotic gain comes from reducing the candidate set to a single (or a constant number of) values.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the objective function is S(t) = Σ (ai - t)^2, a convex quadratic in t, rather than an arbitrary function requiring brute-force search.
Derive or recall that the derivative of S(t) with respect to real t is zero at t = mean(ai), and that S(t) is convex, so the real minimizer is unique and located at the mean.

Adapt the continuous solution to the discrete integer setting: observe that the integer minimizer must lie at either floor(mean) or ceil(mean). In practice, checking those (or using a consistent rounding) is sufficient instead of iterating through every integer in [1, maxA].
Replace the outer loop over candidate t with a single computation of an approximate optimal integer t (here t = round(mean(var_2))).
Compute the sum of squared deviations for that single t using vectorized array operations instead of Python loops, drastically reducing interpreter overhead.
Optionally, remove eval(input()) and use standard int(input()) casting for safer and slightly faster input handling.
trigger_signals: Presence of a nested loop where the outer loop iterates over a range up to max(var_2), multiplying runtime by the value range.
Objective function has the form of a sum of squared distances to a scalar parameter (classic least squares), which is known to be minimized at the mean.
Inner loop performs simple arithmetic (subtraction, squaring, addition) that is well-suited to vectorization or to aggregation formulas (e.g., using sums and means).
Output is a minimum value over all candidate targets, suggesting the possibility of a closed-form solution or calculus-based optimization.
The work done for different candidate t values is structurally identical, hinting that a higher-level algebraic simplification may exist.
pitfalls: {'kind': 'correctness', 'detail': "Python’s round() uses banker's rounding (ties to even). The true integer minimizer of Σ(ai - t)^2 is generally at floor(mean) or ceil(mean). Using round(mean) alone may differ from checking both floor and ceil, especially when the mean is exactly x.5. In most contest inputs this may not change the minimal value, but it is safer to evaluate both candidates and choose the smaller cost."}

{'kind': 'domain-constraints', 'detail': 'The original loop restricts t to the range 1..max(var_2). If the problem logically constrains the target to that range, the mean-based candidate should be clamped accordingly (e.g., t = min(max(1, round(mean)), max(var_2))). The modified code does not enforce this bound explicitly.'}

{'kind': 'numeric-precision', 'detail': 'Computing the mean in floating point and then rounding can introduce off-by-one issues with very large integers or large n. An exact integer approach—e.g., using integer sums and testing both floor(sum/n) and floor(sum/n)+1—avoids floating point entirely.'}

{'kind': 'library-overhead', 'detail': 'For very small n, importing numpy and constructing a numpy array can be slower than a pure-Python O(n) solution using basic arithmetic. In strict time-limit environments, the asymptotic gain is crucial, but constant factors from heavy libraries should still be considered.'}

{'kind': 'security/style', 'detail': 'Using eval(input()) to read an integer is risky and unnecessary. It can execute arbitrary code if the input is not fully trusted. Replacing it with int(input()) is safer and slightly more efficient.'}

constraints_guess.notes: Brute-force over all permutations with pruning; practical n likely <= 12–15. Multiple testcases in a loop until 0.

dominant_ops: Exploring essentially all permutations via recursion without effective pruning
Repeated construction of sets and lists to compute remaining items at each recursion level
Copying and extending lists of chosen indices on every recursive call
Storing results for every permutation in dictionaries and then sorting them

complexity.time: O(n! * n^2) in practice (O(n! * n) recursion * O(n) overhead per node + O(n! log n!) final sort)
complexity.space: O(n! * n) to store all permutations and their costs, plus O(n) recursion stack
complexity.why: The recursion generates all permutations of n items because there is no global best-cost pruning. At each node it recomputes remaining indices with set difference (O(n)), and list concatenation for the path (O(n)). At leaves, it records every permutation in dictionaries. Finally it sorts all n! entries to find the minimum.

bottlenecks.detail: No branch-and-bound on the objective value: every permutation is generated and evaluated, then the minimum is chosen via a global sort.

Ineffective deadline pruning: `if var_15 > var_3[var_9][1]: return` returns from the entire function on the first violating branch, instead of just skipping that branch; other permutations that might be valid are never explored, and the condition does not use the updated `var_8 = var_15 + var_13`.
At every recursive call, remaining items are computed as `list(set(var_5) - set(var_12))`, which rebuilds two sets and a list, costing O(n) memory and time per node and destroying ordering.
Path extension uses `var_12 + [var_9]`, allocating a new list of length O(depth) at each step, creating O(n^2 * n!) total element copies over the search tree.
Dictionaries `var_1` and `var_2` store cost and sum for every permutation key (a tuple of length n), so memory grows like Θ(n! * n).
After recursion, the code calls `sorted(list(var_1.items()), key=lambda x: x[1])[0]`, sorting n! entries even though only the minimum is needed.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a branch-and-bound backtracking over permutations: maintain the partial sequence and remaining items, track the best known total cost, and prune any branch that either violates the deadline constraint or already exceeds the current best cost. Only the best sequence and its cost are stored, instead of storing all permutations.

complexity.time: O(n! * n) in the worst case, but typically much less due to aggressive pruning on deadlines and best-known cost
complexity.space: O(n) for recursion stack plus O(n) to store the best found sequence; no storage proportional to n! permutations
complexity.why: The search tree is still all permutations in the worst case, giving factorial time, but two pruning conditions drastically shrink the explored portion: (1) if the cumulative time exceeds a job’s limit, that branch is cut; (2) if the partial cost already exceeds the current best, the branch is cut. Remaining items are passed as a list and reduced by removal, avoiding repeated set operations, and only the current best solution is kept.

complexity_delta.from: Time ~O(n! * n^2) with large constant factors and full enumeration; space ~O(n! * n) due to storing all permutations and their costs.
complexity_delta.to: Time worst-case ~O(n! * n) but typically much smaller due to branch-and-bound pruning; space ~O(n) (recursion + best solution).
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic worst-case time is still factorial, but constant factors are greatly reduced and effective runtime becomes tractable for typical constraints. The critical change is eliminating full permutation storage and adding strong pruning.

transformation_steps: Replace global result storage over all permutations with a single global (or external) best solution that is updated whenever a better complete sequence is found.
Carry the list of remaining indices directly (`var_3` in fast code) and shrink it by removal, instead of recomputing `list(set(all_indices) - set(chosen))` at each recursion.
Introduce a cost-based bounding condition: compute the partial total cost `var_5` and prune (`return`) when it exceeds the cost of the best solution found so far (`var_5 > var_6[0]`).

Correct deadline-based pruning: check the updated cumulative time (`var_15 + var_13`) against the job’s limit and prune only the current branch rather than returning from the entire function prematurely.
Avoid storing costs for every permutation in dictionaries and avoid sorting all permutations; instead, maintain the running minimum as the recursion proceeds.
Use shallow list operations for remaining items (copy list and remove the chosen index) and for building the path, reducing repeated O(n) overhead from set construction.
trigger_signals: Exponential recursion that clearly enumerates all permutations with no global best-cost pruning.
Repeated `set(...)` creation and set difference inside the recursion, which is a red flag for unnecessary O(n) overhead per node.
Dictionaries keyed by permutation tuples and a final `sorted(...)` over all entries, implying storage and processing of every possible permutation.
List concatenation inside the recursive call (`var_12 + [var_9]`), indicating repeated copying of the whole path at each level.
Logic pattern `if condition: return` inside a loop over candidates, potentially eliminating exploration of alternative branches and suggesting that pruning is not targeted to the right subbranch.
pitfalls: Misusing `return` for pruning inside a loop: `return` exits the entire recursive call, skipping other candidates at that level; correct pruning should skip only the offending branch (e.g., via `continue`) or structure the check before descending.
For branch-and-bound, pruning based on an incorrect or stale partial cost (e.g., using `var_15` instead of `var_15 + var_13`) can either miss valid solutions or under-prune and degrade performance.

When storing only the best solution, it is easy to introduce bugs with shared mutable lists (e.g., updating a global best list that is also being mutated along the recursion path). Using copies or tuples for the stored best is safer.
If globals are used for the best solution (like `var_6`), forgetting to declare them as `global` inside the recursive function in Python will lead to `UnboundLocalError` or ineffective updates.
Over-aggressive pruning or incorrect comparison operators (e.g., `>=` vs `>`) can silently eliminate optimal solutions and must be carefully validated against the problem’s constraints.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder ABC110 D 'Factorization' style: N up to about 1e5, M up to about 1e9. Need to factor M and compute products of combinations C(N+e-1, e) modulo 1e9+7.

dominant_ops: Repeated computation of large factorials via math.factorial
Big-integer multiplications and divisions for exact binomial coefficients before applying modulo
Naive dictionary key membership using list(var_11.keys()) inside a tight loop during factorization

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + P * N) in Python-level operations, where P is the number of distinct prime factors of M and N is the first input; but dominated by big-integer cost of factorial/combination: effectively superlinear in N in bit complexity.
complexity.space: O(N) integers cached in the factorial memo dict, each being huge big integers (size ~ O(N log N) bits for factorial(N)).
complexity.why: Factorization loop runs up to sqrt(M), which is fine. The main cost is func_1: for each exponent e of M we compute factorial(N+e-1), factorial(N-1), factorial(e) using math.factorial, which constructs enormous integers. Even with memoization, the factorial values up to about N+max(e) are stored, each with rapidly growing bit length. Each binomial coefficient is computed as an exact division var_2 // (var_3 * var_4), which again works on huge integers before taking modulo.

bottlenecks.detail: Binomial coefficients are computed via full factorials and exact integer division instead of using a multiplicative formula or precomputed factorials with modular inverses. This causes factorial(N) scale values and very large big-int arithmetic.

func_2 uses `if var_5 in list(var_11.keys())` in the inner factorization loop. This constructs a list of keys and then does a linear scan for each trial divisor, adding an unnecessary O(#keys) factor per check.

All operations for combinations are done on full-precision integers without reducing modulo 1e9+7 until the very end. Intermediate values can be extremely large, stressing memory and CPU even if the asymptotic operation count looks acceptable.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid huge factorials and exact division by using (1) a straightforward prime factorization with efficient dictionary updates and (2) a multiplicative recurrence for combinations C(n, k) that performs only k steps per combination, where k is the exponent of a prime in M (and thus very small). Intermediate numbers are far smaller and the number of Python big-integer operations is greatly reduced.

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + sum_e e), where e ranges over exponents of prime factors of M. In this problem sum_e and each e are at most O(log M), so the runtime is effectively O(sqrt(M)).
complexity.space: O(#prime_factors(M)) for the exponent map plus O(max_e) recursion stack depth; both are O(log M).
complexity.why: Factorization loop is the same asymptotic O(sqrt(M)) but implemented efficiently (no redundant list(dict.keys()) calls). For each exponent e, func_1 computes C(N+e-1, e) using the recurrence C(n, k) = C(n-1, k-1) * n // k, taking exactly e steps with modestly sized integers, and no factorial cache is kept.

complexity_delta.from: Factorization: O(sqrt(M)). Combination: effectively O(P * N) big-int work with large intermediates and O(N) big-int memory due to factorial caching.
complexity_delta.to: Factorization: still O(sqrt(M)). Combination: O(sum_e e) big-int operations with small intermediates and O(log M) extra memory.
complexity_delta.note: The key gain is not only in asymptotic expression but in the drastic reduction of big-integer sizes and counts. This turns a borderline or TLE-prone solution into one that easily fits time/memory limits.

transformation_steps: Replaced factorial-based binomial computation with a multiplicative recurrence: C(n, k) computed by k recursive/multiplicative steps instead of building factorial(n), factorial(k), factorial(n-k).
Eliminated the factorial memoization dictionary and the storage of all factorials up to N+max_exponent, removing an O(N) big-int memory footprint.
Removed the expensive pattern `if var_5 in list(var_11.keys())` and relied on normal dictionary membership checks, which are O(1) average time.
Used collections.defaultdict(int) to simplify and speed up counting prime exponents during factorization.
Applied modulo only to the final product (same as slow code) but with much smaller intermediate integers due to the more efficient combinatorial formula.
trigger_signals: Use of math.factorial on arguments as large as N (up to ~1e5), repeatedly, inside the core computation.
Large factorial values cached in a dictionary (potentially up to N distinct entries), implying large memory and big-int usage.
Binomial coefficients calculated as exact integer ratios before mod rather than with a multiplicative or modular arithmetic approach.
Use of `list(dict.keys())` in a tight loop as part of prime factorization, indicating unnecessary per-iteration overhead.
Problem context ( / competitive programming) where N up to 1e5 and big-int factorial approaches are known to be too slow.
pitfalls: The fast code still computes combinations using plain integer arithmetic and only applies modulo at the end; for larger exponents or larger N this could again lead to big-int blow-ups. A fully optimized solution would incorporate modulo in each multiplication/division and use modular inverses over 1e9+7.

The recursive implementation of C(n, k) relies on the fact that k (the exponent) is small (<= about 30). In problems where k can be large (e.g., O(N)), this recursion would risk hitting Python's recursion limit or become too slow.
Both versions factor M with trial division up to sqrt(M); if constraints on M were much larger (e.g., 1e12+), an alternative factorization method or precomputed primes would be needed.

Care must be taken that the multiplicative recurrence always divides exactly (nCk is integer); any change to integer division order or introduction of modulo in the wrong place could cause truncation errors.

If ported to a language without arbitrary-precision integers, the factorial-based approach will overflow; even the multiplicative recurrence would need to be carefully implemented with modular arithmetic to avoid overflow.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case; loop bound is explicitly 10^5 so runtime is effectively bounded, but code structure is brute-force search over k with a fixed upper limit.

dominant_ops: A descending for-loop over var_4 from 10^5 down to 1, performing a constant-time arithmetic expression and comparison in each iteration.

complexity.time: O(K) where K = 10^5 (fixed upper bound on var_4)
complexity.why: The only non-trivial work is the loop: up to 10^5 iterations, each with a couple of integer operations and a comparison. No additional data structures are allocated.

bottlenecks.detail: Linear scan over all candidate k in [1, 10^5] to find the maximum satisfying var_1 >= k*(var_2 + var_3) + var_3, even though the inequality can be solved algebraically in O(1).
The expression (var_2 + var_3) is recomputed in every iteration instead of once, though this is minor compared to the cost of the loop itself.

FastAudit.core_idea: Solve the inequality var_1 >= k*(var_2 + var_3) + var_3 directly for k and use integer division to obtain the maximum integer k, eliminating the search loop.

complexity.why: Only a constant number of arithmetic operations and one integer division are performed; no loops or extra memory are used.

complexity_delta.from: O(K) with K = 10^5 (fixed) due to a descending loop over var_4
complexity_delta.to: O(1) via direct arithmetic computation of the answer
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both are constant for this problem because K is fixed, but the fast version is substantially cheaper in constant factors and scales better if K were larger or made variable.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the loop is searching for the maximum integer k (var_4 in the slow code) satisfying var_1 >= k*(var_2 + var_3) + var_3.
Algebraically isolate k: var_1 >= k*(var_2 + var_3) + var_3 => var_1 - var_3 >= k*(var_2 + var_3).
Derive the bound on k: k <= (var_1 - var_3) / (var_2 + var_3). The maximum integer k is floor((var_1 - var_3) / (var_2 + var_3)).

Map variable names from the original to the optimized version: in fast_code, the third input var_4 corresponds to original var_3; then var_3 is reassigned to (var_2 + var_4) which matches (var_2 + var_3_original).

Implement the derived formula: var_1 -= var_4 (now var_1 is var_1_original - var_3_original), var_3 = var_2 + var_4 (now var_3 is var_2_original + var_3_original), and print(var_1 // var_3) which equals floor((var_1_original - var_3_original)/(var_2_original + var_3_original)).
Remove the loop entirely since the maximum k is computed in closed form.
trigger_signals: A for-loop over a simple numeric range (range(10**5, 0, -1)) that tests a monotone inequality for each candidate.
The inequality in the loop body has a linear form in the loop variable: var_1 >= var_4*(var_2 + var_3) + var_3.
The loop is breaking on the first success while iterating in descending order, indicating it is searching for an extremal integer solution rather than examining all values.
The loop bound is a fixed constant (10**5), suggesting this might be a brute-force stand-in for an underlying closed-form expression.
pitfalls: Correctly mapping variable roles between versions: in fast_code, the input var_4 is actually the original var_3; after reading, var_3 is reassigned to (var_2 + var_4). Misaligning this mapping breaks the algebraic equivalence.
Ensuring all values are non-negative (or at least that var_1 - var_3 >= 0) so that integer division // behaves as intended; negative numerators with floor division can be subtle.
Maintaining the same inequality direction and not off-by-one: using floor((var_1 - var_3) / (var_2 + var_3)) is essential; using ceil or adjusting by ±1 would change the set of valid k.

Assuming that the 10^5 bound is not logically required by the problem constraints; if the true upper bound on k is smaller than the algebraic result, an additional min(...) might be necessary. Here, the transformed code implicitly assumes the algebraic bound is the actual constraint.

Beware of overflow in languages with fixed-width integers; while Python handles big integers, a similar transformation in other languages might require 64-bit types to avoid overflow in k*(var_2 + var_3) or (var_1 - var_3).

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style problem: N up to about 1e4, compute sum of digits for each i in [1..N] and add i if digit-sum is in [A,B]. Even O(N log N) with large constant is acceptable.

dominant_ops: Outer loop over all integers i in [0..N] (var_4)
Inner while loop extracting digits using modulo and division
Repeated integer-to-float conversions due to '/' operator
Comparisons and additions for accumulating digit sums and final answer

complexity.time: Unbounded / non-terminating in practice; intended O(N log N)
complexity.why: Intended behavior: for each i up to N, loop over its digits (O(log10 i)), giving O(N log N) time and constant extra space. Actual behavior: uses '/' (true division) on integers, producing floats; due to floating-point rounding, `while var_7 != 0` may never reach exactly 0, so the inner loop may not terminate, making effective runtime unbounded.

bottlenecks.detail: Uses `var_7 /= 10` instead of integer division `var_7 //= 10`. This converts `var_7` from int to float and repeatedly divides by 10; the condition `while var_7 != 0` can fail to terminate due to floating-point rounding, causing an infinite or extremely long loop.
Loops `for var_4 in range(var_6 + 1)` including 0, even though 0 never contributes (digit-sum 0 is unlikely to satisfy typical constraints). This is a minor overhead but not the main issue.

Uses a `while` loop for digit extraction with repeated modulo and division; while algorithmically fine, each iteration does multiple arithmetic operations. Under correct division, this is still acceptable for N≈1e4 but suboptimal compared to simpler constructs.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace the arithmetic digit-extraction loop with string conversion and per-character summation, and iterate only from 1 to N. This avoids the integer-division bug and yields straightforward, predictable runtime.

complexity.why: For each integer i in [1..N], the code converts i to a string and iterates over its digits. The number of digits is O(log10 i), so total work is sum_{i=1..N} O(log i) = O(N log N). Only a few scalar variables are used; no data structures grow with N, so space is O(1).

complexity_delta.from: Unbounded / potentially non-terminating due to incorrect use of floating-point division inside the digit loop (intended O(N log N)).
complexity_delta.to: O(N log N) with predictable termination and stable behavior on all valid inputs.
complexity_delta.note: The main improvement is correctness and termination, not an asymptotic complexity reduction. The modified approach may be marginally slower per digit due to string handling, but this is negligible for typical constraints.

transformation_steps: Changed digit extraction strategy from arithmetic (`% 10` and `/= 10`) to string-based (`str(var_4)` and iterating over characters).
Removed the problematic use of `/` (true division) on integers, which was causing `var_7` to become a float and preventing the loop from reliably reaching 0.
Simplified the loop bounds from `range(var_6 + 1)` (including 0) to `range(1, var_6 + 1)`, avoiding a useless iteration at 0.
Rewrote the digit-sum accumulation to a clear inner `for` loop over characters, improving readability and eliminating the subtle float-comparison bug.
trigger_signals: Program appears to hang or take extremely long even for very small N (e.g., N=10 or 100).
CPU utilization stays at 100% with no output, indicating a possible infinite loop.
Inspection shows usage of `/` instead of `//` on loop-control variables and a termination condition based on equality to 0 for a non-integer type.
Debugging intermediate values of `var_7` reveals non-integer floats that never become exactly 0.
pitfalls: String-based digit summation, while correct and simple, is not necessarily faster than arithmetic digit extraction for very large N; it just avoids the division bug here.

Using `while var_7 != 0` with floating-point values is unsafe because floats may never be exactly zero; always keep loop counters as integers with integer division (`//`) or use `> 0` when appropriate.
When porting integer-arithmetic patterns from other languages (e.g., C++ or Java) to Python, ensure the division operator is `//` for integer truncation, not `/`.
If constraints were much larger (e.g., N up to 1e7), even O(N log N) with Python-level per-digit loops could be slow; additional optimizations or pruning might be required in such settings.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style problem: choose integer p minimizing sum_i (a_i - p)^2. a_i likely small (e.g., |a_i| <= 100), so candidate p range is small (about 200 values). Single query; n up to ~100 or a few hundred.

dominant_ops: For each candidate p in range(100), compute a vectorized squared-difference array (var_6 - var_2) ** 2 and then np.sum over the whole array.

complexity.time: O(K * n) with K=100 (effectively O(n) but with heavy per-iteration numpy overhead)
complexity.why: Input list is converted once to a numpy array of size n. For each of the 100 iterations, (var_6 - var_2) ** 2 allocates a new temporary length-n array and np.sum scans it. K is constant, so asymptotically O(n), but each iteration crosses the Python–NumPy boundary and touches all n elements.

bottlenecks.detail: Importing and using NumPy for a very small, fixed number of iterations adds significant overhead in a competitive programming setting where n and the candidate space are small.
Converting the input list to a numpy array (var_5 = np.array(var_5)) costs O(n) time and memory and is not required for such a simple linear pass.
Each expression (var_6 - var_2) ** 2 allocates a new temporary vector of size n, then np.sum allocates intermediate structures; this repeats 100 times.
Using eval(input()) is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()); it is not a core bottleneck but is a CP anti-pattern.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid NumPy and work purely in Python: iterate candidate p over the integer range [min(a_i), max(a_i)], compute the sum of squared differences with a simple list comprehension and sum, and track the minimum.

complexity.time: O(R * n), where R = max(a_i) - min(a_i) + 1 (for this problem R is small, so effectively O(n))
complexity.why: The input is stored as a list of length n. For each candidate p in the range [min, max], we build a length-n list of squared differences and sum it: O(n) per candidate. The candidate count R is bounded by small constraints (≈200), so overall remains linear in n with small constant factors and no heavy library overhead.

complexity_delta.from: O(K * n) with K = 100, using NumPy vector ops (large constant factors)
complexity_delta.to: O(R * n) with R = max(a_i) - min(a_i) + 1, using pure Python loops (smaller constant; R is similarly small under typical constraints)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity in n remains linear, but constant factors are improved by removing NumPy overhead and scanning only the necessary candidate p range.

transformation_steps: Removed the dependency on NumPy and kept the data as a plain Python list instead of converting to a numpy array.
Replaced vectorized operations (np.sum((var_6 - var_2) ** 2)) with a Python list comprehension to compute squared differences and a built-in sum to aggregate them.
Adjusted the candidate search loop from a fixed range(100) to range(min(var_7), max(var_7) + 1), which aligns the search space with the actual data range.
Switched the infinity sentinel from float('inf') to a large integer 10**100, remaining safe in Python due to arbitrary-precision integers.
trigger_signals: Use of NumPy in a problem with very small bounds on both n and the search space, where import and vectorization overheads are not amortized.
Presence of a fixed loop over 100 candidates even though the valid p range is naturally bounded by the input values, suggesting unnecessary work or mismatch with the problem spec.
Competitive programming context, where heavy libraries frequently cause time or memory issues despite similar asymptotic complexity.
pitfalls: If the input values a_i are not tightly bounded (e.g., can be as large as 1e9), iterating p from min(a_i) to max(a_i) becomes infeasible; in such cases, one should derive the optimal p analytically (near the mean) rather than brute-forcing.

The current fast_code rebuilds a list of size n for every candidate p; although acceptable under small constraints, for larger n it would be better to avoid repeated allocations (e.g., by computing the objective via precomputed sums or direct formulas).
Using a gigantic sentinel like 10**100 is safe in Python but would overflow in fixed-width integer languages; when porting, choose a language-appropriate infinity representation.
Both versions rely on the problem’s small range for p; changing constraints without revisiting the algorithm could silently turn this into a serious performance bottleneck.

constraints_guess.notes: The code precomputes factorials and inverse factorials up to 2*10^5 in the slow version, and up to (N + max_exponent) in the fast version. This strongly suggests N + max_exponent <= 2*10^5. M is factorized by trial division up to sqrt(M), so M is likely up to around 10^9–10^12. Problem is AtCoder-like: count ways to write M as a product of N positive integers using prime factorization and combinations.

dominant_ops: Trial division prime factorization of M up to sqrt(M)
Precomputation of factorials, modular inverses, and inverse factorials up to a fixed limit (2 * 10^5)
O(#primes_in_factorization) binomial-coefficient evaluations using precomputed factorials/inverses

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + L) where L = 2*10^5 (fixed upper bound for factorial precomputation)
complexity.space: O(L) for factorial, inverse, and inverse-factorial arrays (L = 2*10^5)
complexity.why: Factorization runs a single loop up to sqrt(M) and only divides when divisible. After that, it precomputes factorials, modular inverses, and inverse factorials in linear time in L (2*10^5). The final product over prime exponents is tiny (sum of exponents is O(log M)), so the dominant cost is the fixed linear precomputation plus sqrt(M) factorization.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorials (var_6) and inverse factorials (var_7) are precomputed up to a hard-coded limit 2*10^5 regardless of the actual required maximum n = var_2 + max_exponent - 1. If var_2 + max_exponent is much smaller than 2*10^5, this wastes time and memory every run.

If the actual required n = var_2 + max_exponent - 1 ever exceeds 2*10^5, func_1 will read from var_6/var_7 out of range or compute C(n,k) with insufficient precomputation, silently giving wrong results or raising IndexError. This forces the hard-coded limit to be set conservatively high, inflating the precomputation cost.

Modular inverses are precomputed for every i in [1..L] using the recurrence inv[i] = -(MOD//i) * inv[MOD%i] (mod MOD). This is O(L). While asymptotically fine, for relatively small needed n it is more work than computing a single inverse factorial via fast exponentiation and then deriving all other inverse factorials in one backward linear pass sized exactly to need.

FastAudit.core_idea: Factorize M into primes once, then for each prime exponent e compute the binomial C(N + e - 1, e) using factorials and inverse factorials precomputed only up to the maximum required n = N + max_e - 1. Use modular exponentiation once to get the inverse factorial at the top and derive the rest by a backward linear pass, minimizing precomputation size and constant factors.

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + (N + max_e)) where max_e is the maximum prime exponent in the factorization of M
complexity.space: O(N + max_e) for factorial and inverse-factorial arrays
complexity.why: The factorization is still trial division up to sqrt(M). The combinatorial part allocates factorial (var_8) and inverse factorial (var_9) arrays of size var_4 = N + max_e, then fills factorials in O(var_4) and inverse factorials in O(var_4) after a single O(log MOD) modular exponentiation. Because max_e is very small (O(log M)), var_4 is essentially O(N), and no work is done for unused indices beyond the maximum required n.

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(M) + L) time and O(L) space with fixed L = 2*10^5, independent of actual N + max_exponent, plus O(L) modular inverse precomputation.
