complexity.why: Prime factorization via trial division runs while p*p <= current_M and divides out factors as they are found, so the upper bound shrinks as M is reduced, yielding O(sqrt(M)) in the worst case. Only primes that actually divide M are stored in a dict, so P, the number of distinct primes, is O(log M). Each exponent e contributes a binomial computation done in two simple loops of length e (one for numerator, one for denominator), so total combination work is O(E) with simple integer multiplications and divisions. The dictionary for factors uses O(P) space; other state is O(1).

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(M) + E * log MOD) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + E) time, O(P) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically, both are dominated by the sqrt(M) factorization, but the slow version pays an extra log MOD inside the small E-term and more constant overhead during factorization. The fast version removes expensive modular exponentiation and avoids generating many useless exponent=0 values.

transformation_steps: Replace the generator-based factorization that yields an exponent for every odd candidate (including non-divisors) with a dictionary-based factorization that only records primes that actually divide M.

Tighten the trial-division loop by using the shrinking current value (var_5 in fast_code) in the loop condition (var_1 ** 2 <= var_5), reducing the number of candidate checks when M has small factors.

Change binomial coefficient computation from multiplicative formula with modular inverses inside the loop to a pure integer multiplicative/divisive computation (compute C(n, k) by multiplying n*(n-1)*... and dividing by 1*2*...*k) relying on Python big integers.
Move modular reduction out of the hot combinatorial loops and apply % MOD only once to the final result, reducing the number of modulo operations.
Eliminate repeated pow(.., MOD-2, MOD) calls from the innermost loop, removing the O(log MOD) cost per step and replacing it with simple integer division.
trigger_signals: Observation that func_1 yields many exponent values equal to 0, indicating redundant work in factorization.
Presence of pow(x, MOD-2, MOD) inside a nested loop that already runs per exponent, a typical performance red flag in Python for CP tasks.
Use of the original number in the factorization loop condition instead of the progressively reduced value, preventing early termination.
Frequent modulo operations in inner loops where exact arithmetic would suffice and modulo could be applied once at the end.
pitfalls: When switching to direct integer binomial computation, using integer division (//) is required; any mismatch in numerator/denominator balancing can silently truncate if not carefully implemented.
Relying on big-integer arithmetic for combinations is safe in Python but would overflow in fixed-width integer languages; the same strategy is not portable without arbitrary-precision support.
Changing factorization logic must preserve the multiset of exponents exactly; off-by-one errors in exponents or missing factors change the result even if complexity is improved.

Delaying modulo to the end assumes intermediate products fit within reasonable memory and time bounds; with much larger constraints, a fully modular combinatorial approach might be required again, but then care must be taken to precompute factorials/inverses rather than calling pow repeatedly in inner loops.

constraints_guess.notes: Likely AtCoder ABC 110 D "Factorization": input N, M with 1 <= N <= 1e5, 1 <= M <= 1e9. Single test case. Need product over prime factors p^e of C(N-1+e, e) mod 1e9+7.

dominant_ops: Precomputing factorials up to 2*10^5 under modulo (loop of length 2e5)
Precomputing modular inverses and inverse factorials up to 2*10^5
Trial-division prime factorization of M up to sqrt(M)
O(1) binomial-coefficient queries using precomputed factorials

complexity.why: Factorial/inverse arrays var_6, var_7, var_9 are all grown to size 2e5+1 regardless of actual N or required combination sizes. Factorization is standard trial division up to sqrt(M). Each combination query is O(1) using precomputed factorials.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorials, modular inverses, and inverse factorials are computed up to a hard-coded limit 2*10^5 even though only a handful of combinations with small extra exponent e are needed.
The upper limit 2*10^5 is independent of the input and may be much larger than N + max_exponent(M), causing needless O(2e5) modular multiplications.
Prime factorization uses int(-(-(var_11**0.5) // 1)) to get ceil(sqrt(n)), introducing floating-point sqrt and ceiling logic instead of a simple integer while-loop bound.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial and inverse precomputation entirely by exploiting that each exponent e of M's prime factorization is small; compute C(N-1+e, e) directly via a short multiplicative loop in integers, and only then reduce modulo 1e9+7.

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + sum_e e) ≈ O(sqrt(M) + log M)
complexity.why: Prime factorization is still via trial division up to sqrt(M). For each prime factor with exponent e, the code computes C(N-1+e, e) in O(e) time by multiplying a product of e terms in numerator and denominator, with e small because M ≤ 1e9. No O(MAXF) factorial precomputation is performed, and only a Counter over prime factors is stored.

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both are dominated by sqrt(M) for the given constraints, but removing the O(2e5) factorial/inverse precomputation significantly reduces constant factors and memory usage. The new combination routine is O(e) where exponents e are at most ~30 for M ≤ 1e9, so the overhead is negligible.

transformation_steps: Removed global precomputation of factorials, modular inverses, and inverse factorials up to a fixed bound (2*10^5).

Replaced the O(1)-per-query modular binomial using precomputed factorials with a direct integer binomial computation func_1(a, b) based on multiplicative products of length b (where b is the exponent e of a prime factor).
Simplified the prime factorization routine to a standard while-loop with condition var_6 * var_6 <= var_8, eliminating floating-point sqrt and ceiling operations.
Changed the representation of factorization output: instead of (prime, exponent) pairs, func_2 now returns a flat list of prime factors and uses collections.Counter to obtain exponents.
Applied the modulo 1e9+7 only to the final product accumulation, relying on Python big integers for intermediate binomial computations.
trigger_signals: The binomial coefficient is only ever called with parameters of the form (N-1+e, e) where e is derived from the exponent of a prime factor of M, and M is relatively small (≈1e9), implying e is always small.
The code performs a large fixed-size factorial precomputation (2e5) even though it only needs a handful of combinations for a single test case.
Memory footprint (arrays of size 2e5) is disproportionate to the real combinatorial work required (a few small-e combinations).
Problem constraints indicate many operations on modest-sized integers but not a high volume of binomial queries; optimizing per-query speed via precomputation is unnecessary.

constraints_guess.notes: Input: N then N integers (values likely in [1,100]). Need min over integer P in [0..100] or [1..100] of sum_i (a_i - P)^2. Algorithm is O(100*N), fine up to ~1e5 or more with proper vectorization.

dominant_ops: Repeated NumPy array arithmetic ((var_6 - var_3) ** 2) inside a Python for-loop over 101 candidate P values
Python built-in sum() applied to NumPy arrays, causing Python-level iteration over array elements
Re-allocation of temporary NumPy arrays for each candidate P

complexity.why: For each of ~101 candidate P values, the code computes (var_6 - P) ** 2 (O(N) NumPy op) and then sum(...) (O(N) traversal). No extra asymptotic factor beyond the constant 101; only one main array of size N is stored.

bottlenecks.detail: Outer loop over P in range(0, 101) stays in Python, invoking multiple heavy NumPy operations per iteration instead of fusing them.
Using built-in sum((var_6 - var_3) ** 2) iterates in Python over NumPy scalars instead of leveraging NumPy’s internal reduction (np.sum). This is extremely slow for large N.
Each iteration allocates a new temporary NumPy array for (var_6 - var_3) ** 2, incurring repeated allocation and deallocation overhead.
open(0).read().split() is actually reasonably fast but reads whole input into memory and parses all tokens at once; not a major bottleneck here but less explicit than line-based reading.

FastAudit.core_idea: Eliminate Python-level loops and Python reductions over NumPy arrays by fully vectorizing over candidate P values: construct all candidate P (1..100) as a NumPy array, broadcast against the data array to form a 2D (100 x N) difference matrix, square and sum along axis=1 in pure NumPy C loops, then take the minimum. Also use NumPy’s own reduction (np.sum, np.min) instead of Python’s sum.

complexity.why: Broadcasting var_2 (shape (N,)) against np.arange(1,101).reshape(100,1) (shape (100,1)) forms a conceptual 100xN array of differences; squaring and summing along axis=1 also touch each element once. This yields the same asymptotic time as the original (factor 100 from the candidate P range), but all heavy work is done in optimized C loops. Space increases to hold the 100xN intermediate differences/squares, but that is still linear in N with a small constant factor (100).

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(100*N) with heavy Python overhead per element (Python sum on NumPy arrays inside a Python loop). Space: O(N).
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(100*N) with nearly all work in NumPy C loops (np.sum + broadcasting + np.min). Space: O(100*N) due to 2D broadcasted intermediates.

The forward-transition DP relies on the invariant that all dp[i] with i < current index are finalized when processing i; changing iteration order (e.g., iterating i backwards) would break correctness for unbounded knapsack.

If N were much smaller than W_max and solutions relied heavily on very large overshoots, trimming the outer loop to N is still correct but makes reasoning about the required DP range (N + buffer) more subtle; the buffer must still cover the maximal single-step overshoot.
When adapting this pattern to different constraints, one must recompute or explicitly read the max item size to size the DP array safely, instead of hard-coding 10**4.

constraints_guess.notes: Inputs are likely up to ~1e9 (typical for AtCoder-style integer problems). Naive looping proportional to the numeric range can TLE if the step size is small.

dominant_ops: A while-loop that repeatedly adds a constant (var_3 + var_4) to var_1 until exceeding an upper bound var_2, counting iterations.

complexity.why: Each loop iteration performs only O(1) integer operations, but the number of iterations grows linearly with the range between var_4 and var_2 divided by the step size var_3 + var_4.

bottlenecks.detail: The while True loop increments var_1 by a fixed amount until passing var_2. If var_2 is large and var_3 + var_4 is small, the loop may execute up to about 1e9 times, which is too slow in Python.
The logic effectively counts how many times a constant step fits into an interval, which can be computed directly via integer division instead of step-by-step simulation.

FastAudit.core_idea: Identify that the loop is counting how many full steps of size (var_3 + var_4) fit into the usable range (var_2 - var_4), then replace the simulation with a direct arithmetic formula using integer division: floor((var_2 - var_4) / (var_3 + var_4)).

complexity.why: The optimized code performs a constant number of integer additions/subtractions and a single integer division, independent of the numeric size of the inputs.

complexity_delta.from: O(K) loop where K ≈ (var_2 - var_4) / (var_3 + var_4)
complexity_delta.to: O(1) direct computation
complexity_delta.note: Replaced repeated addition and boundary checks with a single integer-division-based formula, removing dependence on the size of the numeric range.

transformation_steps: Observe the loop invariant: var_1 starts at var_4, and each iteration adds a constant step S = var_3 + var_4 while var_1 + S <= var_2.
Express var_1 after k iterations as var_1(k) = var_4 + k * S.
Translate the loop condition to an inequality in k: var_4 + (k + 1) * S <= var_2.
Solve for k to count valid iterations: k_max + 1 = floor((var_2 - var_4) / S), so the answer is floor((var_2 - var_4) / (var_3 + var_4)).
Rewrite the code to compute this count directly: precompute S = var_3 + var_4, compute the effective range (var_2 - var_4), then perform integer division range // S.

Relabel input variables in the fast version so that var_1 holds the original upper bound (var_2 in the slow code), var_2 holds the original step component (var_3), and var_4 is unchanged, then apply the derived formula.
trigger_signals: A while-loop or for-loop that increments a variable by a constant amount until it exceeds a bound, with no other state-dependent branching.
Loop body that only performs simple arithmetic and a counter increment, essentially simulating a linear progression.
Constraints or typical competitive-programming context suggesting inputs may be as large as 1e9, making linear iteration infeasible.
Pattern of repeated addition that resembles counting fits of a segment into an interval, which often can be replaced by integer division.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when converting the loop condition var_1 + S <= var_2 into a division formula; miscounting by 1 is easy if the starting offset (var_4) is not handled correctly.

Negative or very small ranges: if var_2 <= var_4, the effective range (var_2 - var_4) is non-positive and the count should be zero; relying on Python's floor division behavior for negatives requires care, though typical problem constraints may ensure var_2 > var_4.
Division by zero if the step size S = var_3 + var_4 could be zero; usually ruled out by constraints (e.g., positive integers), but must be conceptually considered.
Variable remapping between slow and fast code (inputs renamed as var_1, var_2, var_4 in the fast version) can be confusing and may lead to incorrect formula application if not tracked carefully.
Assuming floating-point math: using integer division is crucial to avoid precision issues and to match the discrete count of iterations exactly.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical Lunlun-number problem (e.g., AtCoder ABC161 D). Input N up to about 1e5; need to generate the N-th number whose adjacent digits differ by at most 1.

dominant_ops: Repeated heap operations: heappush / heappop on a growing heap
Frequent string conversions for every generated number: int -> str, slicing, concatenation, then back to int
Maintaining a visited set of all numbers generated
Final conversion of set to list and full sort of all generated numbers

complexity.why: The algorithm generates O(N) unique Lunlun numbers plus a constant extra (N+100). Each accepted number incurs multiple heappush calls and at least one heappop, each O(log H) where H ~ O(N). Final sorting of all collected numbers is another O(N log N). L is the digit length (<= ~10), coming from repeated string conversions. Overall this yields roughly O(N log N) behavior with a relatively large constant factor from string work and heap overhead.

bottlenecks.detail: Using a min-heap plus a visited set and then sorting all results emulates ordered generation but introduces an extra O(log N) per operation compared to a simple queue-based BFS that inherently preserves order.

Loop runs until var_3 reaches -100 (condition var_3 + 100 >= 0). Starting at N and decrementing once per newly accepted number, this enforces generation of N+100 numbers, a constant-factor overhead but unnecessary.

Every new number is converted to string (var_9 = str(var_9)), then first and last digits are extracted via indexing and reconverted to int, and new numbers are created via string concatenation plus int(). These conversions are relatively expensive in tight loops.

Duplicates are pushed to the heap even if already present in the visited set; they are only filtered when popped. This inflates the heap size and the number of heap operations, increasing the log factor cost.

After generation, the set is converted to a list and fully sorted: var_5 = [int(var_6) for var_6 in var_5]; var_5.sort(). This complete sort is O(N log N) and unnecessary if numbers are generated in order.
Using eval(input()) is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()), though its performance impact is negligible relative to the generation loop.

FastAudit.core_idea: Perform a BFS over Lunlun numbers in strictly increasing order using a simple queue (deque). Start from 1–9, repeatedly pop the front, and append valid successors formed by appending a digit differing by at most 1 from the last digit. Because BFS expands in numeric order under this construction, the N-th popped element is the N-th Lunlun number, eliminating the need for a heap, visited set, or final sort.

complexity.why: Each number up to the N-th Lunlun number is enqueued once and dequeued once. For each dequeued number, we perform O(1) arithmetic to compute up to three successors and append them. Queue operations (popleft/append on deque) are O(1) amortized. There is no sorting and no log-factor heap overhead, leading to linear time in N. The queue holds O(N) numbers in the worst case, yielding O(N) space.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log N * L) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: The key shift is from a priority-queue-based generation with sorting (heap + visited + final sort) to a queue-based BFS that directly produces Lunlun numbers in increasing order. This removes the log N factor and avoids expensive string manipulation inside the hot loop.

transformation_steps: Replace the min-heap (heapq) with a FIFO queue (collections.deque). Initialize the queue with [1, 2, ..., 9] instead of a heapified list.
Remove the visited set and final sorting. The BFS construction ensures numbers are generated in increasing order without duplicates, so we can directly take the N-th dequeued number.

Change the generation loop from a while-based condition (using var_3 and an extra +100 margin) to a for-loop that runs exactly N-1 iterations, popping from the queue each time. After N-1 pops, the next pop is the N-th Lunlun number.

Generate successors using integer arithmetic instead of string slicing and concatenation. In the fast code, only the last digit is used (var_3 % 10), and successors are formed via multiplication and addition, avoiding repeated int/str conversions.
Drop the expensive postprocessing: no need for converting a set to a list and sorting; simply print the final popped value from the queue.
trigger_signals: Use of heapq for what conceptually is a level-order or monotonic sequence generation that can be done via a simple queue.
Presence of a visited set plus a final sort of all generated numbers, which is a red flag for avoidable O(N log N) work.
Repeated int<->str conversions and string concatenations in an inner loop for digit operations.
A loop condition that overshoots the needed count (N+100) instead of targeting exactly N elements, indicating potential constant-factor overhead.
Known pattern: Lunlun/stepping number generation problems are often solvable via straightforward BFS/queue in O(N).
pitfalls: Order correctness: When migrating from a heap to a queue, it is essential that the BFS expansion rule preserves numeric ordering of generated Lunlun numbers. An incorrect successor-enqueue scheme could produce numbers out of order, making the N-th popped element incorrect.

Queue growth control: Unconditionally appending successors without a condition like len(queue) < N (or an equivalent stopping criterion) may cause the queue to grow much larger than necessary for given constraints, potentially leading to memory issues.
Digit-boundary handling: When generating successors, carefully handle edge digits 0 and 9 (e.g., do not generate digits -1 or 10). The fast code explicitly checks var_4 != 0 and var_4 != 9.

Off-by-one errors: The fast approach uses for var_1 in range(1, var_2): then outputs var_5.popleft() as the answer. Misaligning these bounds (e.g., looping var_2 times or starting from 0) yields the wrong index for the N-th Lunlun number.

Avoiding string-based logic: Reintroducing string conversions inside the BFS loop (e.g., to inspect digits) can significantly increase constant factors; arithmetic on digits (% 10, // 10) is faster and should be preferred.
Input parsing and safety: Although not the main performance issue, continuing to use eval(input()) is both slower and unsafe; int(input()) is preferable in a production-quality solution.

constraints_guess.notes: Input is two integers N,M. M is up to about 1e9 (since trial division to sqrt(M) is used). N can be as large as 1e9 in the original AtCoder problem (ABC110 D - Factorization). Number of distinct prime factors of M is small (O(log M)).

dominant_ops: Trial division factorization up to sqrt(M) with incremental divisor
Computing factorial(N-1) as a Python big integer
Building very large intermediate integers for combinations before taking modulo
Python big-integer multiplication and factorial computations

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + N log N) in big-integer arithmetic; practically dominated by factorial(N-1) and huge intermediate products when N is large
complexity.space: O(log M) for factorization map plus O(N log N) bits for storing factorial(N-1) and intermediate combination products
complexity.why: Factorization via trial division is O(sqrt(M)) and cheap for M<=1e9. The critical issue is math.factorial(N-1): when N can be up to 1e9, factorial(N-1) produces an astronomically large integer; computing and storing it dominates both time and memory. Additionally, combination products are formed as plain integers without modular reduction until the very end, causing intermediate values with lengths proportional to N log N bits.

bottlenecks.detail: Use of factorial(N-1) with N derived directly from input; for N as large as 1e9 this is completely infeasible. The result is never actually used in the final formula, so it is pure overhead.

Combination computation multiplies large integers var_3 and var_11 without applying modulo in the loop, so integers grow exponentially before the final `% (10**9+7)`, leading to extremely slow big-integer arithmetic and huge memory usage.
The code computes `var_5 = factorial(var_2 - 1)` and then never uses var_5. This wasted O(N log N) big-int work is the main practical reason for TLE or MLE.

Using integer division `var_3 // factorial(var_12)` outside modular arithmetic is safe mathematically but forces exact big-int division on huge operands instead of efficient modular inverses on small residues.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the prime factorization approach for M, but compute each combinatorial term C(e + N - 1, e) purely in modular arithmetic using the multiplicative formula with small e (the exponent of each prime). Avoid computing factorial(N-1) entirely and apply modulo 1e9+7 at every multiplication and division (via modular inverses). This uses O(e) operations per prime factor, with e small (sum of exponents = O(log M)), and keeps all numbers bounded by MOD.

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + (sum e_i) * log MOD) ≈ O(sqrt(M) + log M * log MOD)
complexity.why: Factorization remains O(sqrt(M)). For each prime factor with exponent e, the multiplicative formula C(N-1+e, e) can be computed in O(e) modular multiplications and modular inverses: `res = res * (N-1 + k) * inv(k) mod MOD` for k=1..e. Since e is small for M≤1e9 (sum of e_i ≤ ~30), this is effectively O(log M). All operations are on residues modulo MOD, so there are no enormous big integers and both time and memory remain small.

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(M) + N log N) time with huge big-integer constants; O(N log N) bits memory due to factorial(N-1) and large intermediate products.
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + log M * log MOD) time and O(log M) space, using only fixed-size modular integers.
complexity_delta.note: The asymptotic change in terms of M is modest, but the removal of factorial(N-1) and of giant intermediate integers transforms the solution from practically impossible for N up to ~1e9 into easily fast enough.

transformation_steps: Remove the computation of factorial(N-1) entirely since it is not needed for the combinatorial formula in this problem.
Maintain the prime factorization logic, but return a simple mapping from prime -> exponent.

For each prime exponent e, compute C(N-1+e, e) in modular arithmetic using the multiplicative formula: initialize comb = 1; for k from 1 to e: comb = comb * ((N-1 + k) % MOD) % MOD; comb = comb * pow(k, MOD-2, MOD) % MOD.
Accumulate the total answer as the product of these comb values modulo MOD, applying `% MOD` after each multiplication to keep numbers bounded.
Use Python's pow(x, MOD-2, MOD) for modular inverses, which is valid because MOD=1_000_000_007 is prime.
Avoid any use of math.factorial on values depending on N; limit factorial or precomputation (if used at all) to small values bounded by max exponent e only.
trigger_signals: Presence of math.factorial called with an argument derived directly from input (N-1) where N is unconstrained in code and known from the problem to be as large as 1e9.
Combination formula with extremely large n and tiny r implemented via exact factorials or products without early modulo, suggesting big-int explosion.
Only taking modulo at the very end of a long chain of multiplications and divisions.
Unexpected memory/time blowup in tests with larger N despite simple mathematical logic, indicating heavy big-integer operations.
Prime factorization of M via trial division is already optimal for M≤1e9, so any additional slowness must stem from the combinatorics layer.
pitfalls: Using factorial(N-1) or precomputing factorials up to N when N can be ~1e9 is infeasible; combinations must be computed via a multiplicative formula that iterates over small exponents only.
When converting to modular arithmetic, every multiplication and division must be reduced modulo MOD; forgetting `% MOD` leads to the same big-int growth as the original.
Division in modular arithmetic must be implemented as multiplication by a modular inverse (pow(k, MOD-2, MOD)); using plain integer division will break correctness.

The optimization relies on exponents e being small; if a future variant allows very large exponents, the O(e) loop per prime could become a bottleneck and may require a different combinatorial approach.

Ensure that factorization loop bounds are correct: iterating up to int(sqrt(M)) and handling the remaining M>1 as a prime factor; off-by-one errors in factorization can silently corrupt the prime exponent counts and thus the final answer.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical 'number of divisors of n!' style problem (e.g., AtCoder ABC 052 C) where n is around 1000. Larger n would make computing n! as a big integer and factoring it by trial division too slow or memory-heavy.

dominant_ops: For each k in [1..n], factorize k by trial division against all candidate primes up to k, and after each k rebuild an O(n) array of accumulated exponents.

complexity.time: O(n^2) integer operations (plus an O(n^(3/2)) naive primality sieve), dominated by nested loops over k and candidate divisors.
complexity.space: O(n) for prime flags and exponent arrays; additional O(n) temporary lists rebuilt n times.
complexity.why: func_2 does a naive primality test for every number up to n, costing about sum_{x<=n} sqrt(x) = O(n^(3/2)). The main loop calls func_1 for each k in [1..n]; func_1 iterates up to k indices and may do several divisions, leading to ~sum_{k<=n} k = O(n^2) work. Inside the outer loop, var_9 is rebuilt via a full O(n) list comprehension each time, adding another O(n^2) term.

bottlenecks.detail: func_2 tests each number up to n by trial dividing up to its square root, instead of using a proper sieve of Eratosthenes.
func_1 factorizes every k in [1..n] separately, scanning through all candidate bases up to k and dividing while possible, even though the goal is only to aggregate prime exponents for n!.
In the outer loop, var_9 = [var_9[i] + var_3[i] for i in range(n)] rebuilds an O(n) list on every iteration, adding an extra O(n^2) overhead in Python list operations.
Inside func_1, var_5 = var_5 / (var_2 + 1) uses floating-point division instead of integer division (//), which is slower and potentially unsafe for exact arithmetic on large integers.
Exponent arrays have length n and are maintained for all indices, even though only prime indices are meaningful, wasting memory traffic and cache.

FastAudit.core_idea: Compute n! once, factorize this single big integer by trial division from 2 upward, count multiplicities of each prime factor with a Counter, then use the multiplicities to compute the divisor count product Π (e_i + 1) modulo 1e9+7.

complexity.time: O(n) big-integer multiplications to form n! plus O(n) big-integer divisions/comparisons during trial division up to n, which is acceptable for n up to about 10^3.
complexity.space: O(size(n!)) bits for the factorial value plus O(n) for storing prime factors and their counts.
complexity.why: The loop that search-divides factors starts from 2 and increases var_5 by 1, never needing to exceed the largest prime ≤ n because all prime factors of n! are ≤ n. Thus the number of trial divisions is O(n). math.factorial computes n! in roughly linear time in n (with big-int cost), and Counter aggregation plus the final product is linear in the number of distinct primes ≤ n, which is about n/log n.

complexity_delta.from: O(n^2) scalar operations (plus O(n^(3/2)) naive primality tests) with heavy Python-level overhead on lists and repeated factorization of each k in [1..n].
complexity_delta.to: O(n) big-integer multiplications and divisions by trial division up to n, with a single factorization of n! and linear-time aggregation of exponents.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically in n, the new approach reduces the combinatorial work from quadratic to roughly linear in the bound n, but introduces big-integer arithmetic cost and a large intermediate n!. For n≈10^3 this is still significantly faster in Python than repeatedly factorizing all k=1..n.

transformation_steps: Changed the perspective from 'sum prime exponents over all numbers 1..n' to 'factorize the single number n! and read exponents directly'.
Removed the custom naive prime-detection func_2 and per-k factorization func_1, which both used nested loops and repeated trial division.
Introduced math.factorial to compute n! directly, avoiding the need to track exponents across many intermediate products.
Replaced manual exponent-tracking arrays of length n with a flat list of prime factors and used collections.Counter to aggregate multiplicities compactly.
Computed the number of divisors as a simple product over (exponent + 1) while maintaining the result modulo 1e9+7, eliminating repeated list rebuilding and large intermediate products.
trigger_signals: Nested loops over both the range 1..n and all candidate divisors for each k, indicating O(n^2) or worse complexity.
A primality check executed for every integer up to n using trial division, instead of a single sieve or direct use of known primes.
Reallocation of a full O(n) list (var_9) on each iteration of an outer loop that runs O(n) times.
Using a factorization routine (func_1) repeatedly on many small numbers when the mathematical goal is to understand the factorization of n! as a whole.
Float division (/) on integer-like values in tight loops, which suggests both correctness and performance concerns.
pitfalls: The optimized version depends on building the full factorial n!, which grows extremely quickly; for n much larger than the intended constraints (e.g., n>>10^3), big-int size and multiplication/division costs could dominate or exhaust memory.
Trial division on n! is only efficient here because all prime factors are ≤ n, and n is small; for large n, a direct method for exponents (e.g., sum floor(n/p^k) for primes p) would be superior.
Relying on math.factorial may hide big-int costs; if the environment has tighter memory or time limits, a streaming prime-exponent accumulation approach might be necessary instead.
The trial division step still increments var_5 by 1 (checking composite bases as well as primes); this is acceptable for n≈10^3 but would become a bottleneck if constraints were raised significantly.
Using eval(input()) is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; while not the dominant performance cost here, it is a pattern to avoid in production or contest code.

constraints_guess.notes: Single array of N integers; typical AtCoder-style constraints N <= 100, values in [1,100]. Task: choose an integer P (likely 1..100) minimizing sum_i (a_i - P)^2.

dominant_ops: Single pass to sum elements (for mean) plus another pass to accumulate squared differences over N elements.

complexity.why: Input is stored as a list of N integers. Computing sum(var_2) is O(N), and the for-loop accumulating (var_9 - var_5)**2 is another O(N). All other work is O(1).

bottlenecks.detail: For N <= 100, the linear pass with simple integer arithmetic is already optimal. The overhead from helper functions and lambdas is negligible at these scales.
Using sys.stdin.readline is slightly faster than input(), so I/O is already efficient. The only extra cost is a floating-point division and round() to compute the mean.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the small fixed search space for P (1..100) by brute-forcing all candidate integer centers, computing the total squared distance for each, and keeping the minimum. Early break relies on unimodality of the quadratic objective.

complexity.why: Outer loop runs at most 100 iterations for P in [1,100]. Inner loop recomputes the cost over all N elements each time, giving 100*N operations in the worst case. The array of N integers is stored once, so space is O(N). The early-break optimization can reduce the constant factor but not the worst-case asymptotics.

delta_type: algorithm_change_non_asymptotic (from direct mean-based formula to fixed-range brute-force search with early break)

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(N), Space: O(N)
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(100 * N) ≈ O(N), Space: O(N)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity stays linear; the modified code performs up to ~100x more per-element work but still trivial for N <= 100. The main change is constant-factor and correctness-oriented (searching all integer P) rather than asymptotic speedup.

transformation_steps: Remove helper I/O functions and switch from sys.stdin.readline to input(), reading N and the list directly.
Replace the mean-based closed-form choice of P (round of average) with an explicit search over candidate integer centers P = 1..100.
Introduce a nested loop: outer over candidate P (var_1 + 1), inner over all elements to recompute sum (a_i - P)^2 from scratch each time.
Track the best (minimum) cost seen so far (var_4) and update it when a lower cost is found.
Add an early break condition when the cost stops decreasing, leveraging the convex/unimodal shape of the squared-error function in P.
Use only integer arithmetic in the objective evaluation, avoiding float division and round().
trigger_signals: The candidate center P is restricted to a small fixed integer range (typically 1..100), making brute-force feasible.
The objective sum (a_i - P)^2 is a convex/unimodal function of P, enabling an early break once costs start increasing.
Problem constraints are tiny (N around 100), so even a 100x constant-factor increase is acceptable, allowing simpler brute-force logic.
Using mean directly involves floating-point arithmetic and assumes the unconstrained integer optimum matches the problem's discrete domain, which may not always be aligned with the statement.
pitfalls: Using eval(input()) to read an integer is slower and potentially unsafe in general; int(input()) is preferable and clearer.
The brute-force loop hardcodes the range(100) and assumes the optimal P lies in [1,100]. If actual constraints change, this must be updated or parameterized.
Early break relies on the unimodality of the cost function in P; if the search range or objective changed to a non-convex shape, this heuristic could skip the true optimum.
The modified solution performs more total arithmetic than the original O(N) mean-based approach; for larger N, it would be strictly slower despite identical asymptotics.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical scheduling-with-deadlines greedy problem (sort by deadline, accumulate durations). Likely n up to ~2e5, times/deadlines up to about 1e9. Time limit around 1–2s in Python, so input and constant factors matter.

dominant_ops: Reading n lines of input and parsing integer pairs
Sorting the list of n jobs by deadline: O(n log n)
Single linear scan over sorted jobs to accumulate durations and compare with deadlines

complexity.why: The algorithm builds a list of n pairs, then sorts it (O(n log n)), followed by a single O(n) pass. Extra helper functions and imports do not change asymptotic complexity, only constant factors. Memory is dominated by storing the n job records.

bottlenecks.detail: Imports of sys, math, itertools, bisect, copy, deque, Counter, Decimal and setting a huge recursion limit are unused in this solution. They add minor startup/initialization overhead and clutter.
Both func_4 and func_7 use eval(input()). Using eval is slower and unsafe versus int(input()). Here it is also redundant because the input is already a plain integer.

Each line is read via func_1() (and the first via func_4()), introducing an extra Python function call per iteration compared to inlining input().split() and map(). This slightly increases constant time per job.
Multiple helper functions (func_2, func_3, func_5, func_6, func_7) are defined but never used, increasing code size and bytecode parsing time without benefit.
Jobs are stored as lists [deadline, duration] instead of tuples. This has marginally higher memory and construction overhead per element compared to tuples, which are smaller and immutable.
The function name func_2 is later reused as a list variable, which is confusing and risks mistakes. While not a performance issue directly, it complicates reasoning and refactoring.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the classic greedy scheduling strategy: read all tasks as (deadline, processing_time), sort by deadline, then accumulate processing times in that order. If at any point the cumulative time exceeds the current task's deadline, the schedule is infeasible; otherwise it is feasible.

complexity.why: As in the slow version, the main cost is sorting n tasks by deadline, which is O(n log n). Storing the tasks requires O(n) memory, and the feasibility check is a single O(n) scan. The optimized code reduces constant factors mainly by simplifying I/O and data handling, not by changing asymptotic complexity.

complexity_delta.from: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: Both implementations share the same greedy-by-deadline algorithm and thus identical asymptotic complexity. Improvements are in constant factors (fewer function calls, no unused helpers/imports, lighter data structures).

transformation_steps: Removed unused imports and helper functions (func_2, func_3, func_5, func_6, func_7) that were never called in the core logic.
Inlined input reading and parsing instead of using wrapper functions (replaced func_4 and func_1 calls with direct int(eval(input())) and map(int, input().split())).
Simplified data structure from mutable lists [deadline, duration] to tuples (deadline, -duration), allowing a straightforward cumulative-sum logic with a sign flip and slightly cheaper objects.
Removed variable/function name shadowing (e.g., func_2 used both as function and list), improving code clarity and avoiding potential overhead or bugs.
Replaced explicit index-based loops over range(var_4) with direct iteration over the sorted list, reducing index operations and attribute lookups.
Avoided calling exit() inside the loop; instead used a boolean flag and a break to control flow, which is cheaper and more idiomatic inside competitive-programming style solutions.
trigger_signals: Presence of a heavy, generic template (many unused imports and helper functions) around a simple core algorithm.
Use of eval(input()) or int(eval(input())) for plain integer reading, which is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()).
Frequent tiny wrapper functions around I/O and parsing in tight loops with n up to about 10^5–10^6.
Profiling or timing indicates most runtime is spent in input/parsing and interpreter overhead rather than the core O(n log n) logic.
TLE or borderline runtime on large inputs despite an optimal O(n log n) algorithm, suggesting constant-factor overhead is the remaining bottleneck.
pitfalls: Continuing to use eval for input conversion: replacing int(eval(input())) with int(input()) is both safer and faster; forgetting this may leave unnecessary overhead.
Over-focusing on micro-optimizations while accidentally altering the algorithm (e.g., changing the sort key incorrectly) can break correctness; the sort-by-deadline order is essential.
Using exit() in the middle of logic can complicate testing or reuse of the code; although fast, it may be undesirable in modularized contexts.
Tuples vs lists: while tuples are slightly more efficient, care must be taken when porting logic that mutates list elements; here the algorithm is read-only so tuples are safe.

Assuming the template helpers (like gcd-based LCM) are free: defining many unused functions does have a small cost in load time and memory, which matters when multiple test files are run or when time limits are tight.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical task: count integers in [1, N] with an odd number of digits (similar to AtCoder 'Uneven Numbers'). N is likely up to around 1e9; a per-number loop is too slow, motivating a formula-based solution. Provided fast_code only handles N < 1e6 but the pattern is easily extendable.

dominant_ops: Linear loop from 1 to N
Per-number digit counting via repeated integer division
Function-call overhead for each number
Modulo operation per number

complexity.why: The main loop runs for every integer var_3 in [1, var_4]. For each var_3, func_1 repeatedly divides by 10 until the number becomes 0, performing O(d) operations where d is the number of digits (~log10(var_3)). Thus total time is sum_{i=1..N} O(log10 i) = O(N log N). No extra data structures are used, so space is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: The algorithm iterates over every integer from 1 to N and recomputes the digit count from scratch for each number, yielding O(N log N) runtime which is infeasible when N is up to ~1e9.
func_1(var_4) is called N times and performs a while-loop of integer divisions per call, making it the tight inner loop and dominating runtime.
A Python function call for every integer in [1, N] adds overhead on top of the already expensive per-number digit processing.
Using int(eval(input())) is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()). While not the primary asymptotic bottleneck, it is an avoidable cost and a security risk.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid iterating over all numbers. Instead, use a closed-form count of integers with an odd number of digits by splitting [1, N] into digit-length ranges and summing contributions from ranges with odd digit lengths.

complexity.time: O(1) for given code (finite branch chain; conceptually O(log10(N)) if extended to larger N)
complexity.why: The solution directly computes the answer from N using a small fixed number of comparisons and arithmetic expressions. Each branch corresponds to a digit-length interval (1-digit, 2-digit, etc.), so the number of operations does not grow with N under the provided constraints, yielding constant time and constant space.

complexity_delta.from: O(N * log10(N)) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(1) time (for given covered range), O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: The transformation replaces a per-number digit-counting loop with a small constant number of arithmetic cases based on digit ranges. In a generalized form covering larger N, the time would still be only O(log10 N) because the number of digit ranges grows logarithmically with N.

transformation_steps: Recognize that func_1(x) computes the number of digits of x by integer division, and that func_1(x) % 2 is 1 exactly when x has an odd number of digits.
Identify that the slow solution is counting how many integers in [1, N] have an odd number of digits.
Reframe the problem mathematically: for each digit length d, count how many numbers with d digits lie within [1, N], and include only odd d.

Derive a closed-form expression by digit ranges: e.g., for N < 10, the count is N; for 10 <= N < 100, it is 9 (all 1-digit numbers); for 100 <= N < 1000, it is 9 + (N - 99) = N - 90; and similarly for higher ranges.
Implement the derived piecewise formula with a small set of if/elif comparisons, eliminating the explicit loop over all integers.
Retain constant memory usage while drastically reducing the number of operations from O(N log N) to a fixed constant per query.
trigger_signals: Presence of a for-loop iterating from 1 up to N where N can be large (e.g., up to 1e9).
An inner while-loop per iteration performing repeated integer division to compute digit counts.
Use of a simple numeric property (number of digits) whose distribution is regular and amenable to closed-form counting.
Typical competitive-programming constraints where N is large enough that O(N) or O(N log N) iterations in Python will time out.
Function calls in the innermost loop, exacerbating the cost of each iteration.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when computing range boundaries such as 9, 99, 999, etc.; careful attention is needed to write expressions like (N - 90) or (N - 9090) correctly.
Failing to cover all possible values of N: in the provided fast_code, N >= 1e6 produces no output because there is no final else or further range branches.
Miscounting numbers at digit-length transitions (e.g., including 10 or 100 incorrectly), which can shift counts by ±1 and break edge cases.
Assuming the constant-branch solution is universally valid without extending it to handle larger N when constraints grow beyond 1e6.
Continuing to use eval(input()), which is unnecessary and unsafe, even though the main inefficiency is algorithmic rather than from input parsing.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder 'Coprime' task: N up to 1e5, each A_i in [1, 1e6]. Need to classify as pairwise/setwise/not coprime.

dominant_ops: Building an array of largest prime factors up to 1e6 with a double loop sieve.
For each input number, repeatedly dividing by its largest prime factor to factorize it, maintaining a per-number set of prime factors.
Recursive gcd computation over all N numbers.

complexity.time: O(M log log M + N log A_max) where M=1e6 and A_max<=1e6
complexity.space: O(M + K) where M=1e6 for the factor table and K is the number of distinct prime factors appearing in inputs
complexity.why: The sieve-style construction of the largest-prime-factor table runs in harmonic-like sum_{i<=M} M/i = O(M log log M) steps. Each number is then factorized via repeated division by its largest prime factor, which is O(log A_i) per number in the worst case, summed to O(N log A_max). The gcd over N numbers adds O(N log A_max) but with relatively small constant. Memory is dominated by the factor table of size M+1 and the defaultdict for counting primes.

bottlenecks.detail: Always sieves up to a fixed upper bound of 1e6 regardless of the actual maximum input value. If max(A_i) is much smaller, this is unnecessary work.
The sieve uses Python-level nested loops over ranges up to 1e6 with repeated assignments into a list, which is heavy in pure Python at this scale.
For each of up to N=1e5 numbers, a new set of prime factors is created and updated, leading to many small allocations and hash operations.
gcd is implemented recursively; for many calls this adds Python call overhead compared to an iterative loop using math.gcd.

FastAudit.core_idea: Instead of factorizing each number individually, precompute a sieve up to max(A_i), count the frequency of every value, and for each prime p accumulate how many input numbers are multiples of p. If no prime divides more than one number, the set is pairwise coprime; if some prime divides all N numbers, they are not coprime; otherwise they are setwise coprime. This avoids per-number factorization and per-number set allocations.

complexity.time: O(M log log M + N) where M = max(A_i)
complexity.why: The sieve to mark primes up to M runs in O(M log log M) using the standard Eratosthenes pattern over multiples. Counting frequencies over the N inputs is O(N). For each prime p, iterating over its multiples contributes sum_{p prime<=M} M/p = O(M log log M). The overall complexity is therefore O(M log log M + N). Memory is dominated by the structures of size ~M (boolean primality map, counts per value, counts per prime).

complexity_delta.from: Effectively O(M log log M + N log A_max) with large constant factors from per-number factorization and set allocations (M fixed at 1e6).
complexity_delta.to: O(M log log M + N) with reduced per-number overhead; sieve is bounded by max(A_i) instead of always 1e6.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both are dominated by the sieve term, but the modified approach removes the per-number factorization and set operations, and can reduce M in practice, yielding a substantial runtime improvement in Python.

transformation_steps: Replace the largest-prime-factor table and per-number factorization with a sieve that only tracks primality up to max(A_i).
Count occurrences of each input value once in a frequency map, avoiding repeated division loops per number.
For each prime p, scan multiples p, 2p, 3p, ... to aggregate how many input numbers share factor p; use the maximum such count to determine pairwise versus setwise versus not coprime.

Eliminate recursive gcd computation over the array by inferring the global gcd from the maximum multiplicity of any prime factor (if some prime appears in all numbers, gcd>1; else gcd==1 when not pairwise).
Stop relying on per-number sets of prime factors; instead, use aggregated counts, which significantly reduces allocation and hashing overhead.
trigger_signals: Runtime close to or exceeding limits for worst-case input where N is large (≈1e5) and many A_i are near the upper bound (≈1e6).
Profiling or informal timing showing the sieve + factorization and set-handling dominating total execution time.
Observation that the same prime factors are recomputed and re-handled for many numbers, suggesting an opportunity to aggregate work by primes instead of by numbers.
pitfalls: Using Python dicts for arrays up to size 1e6 (as in fast_code) is still memory- and overhead-heavy; a further optimization would be to use plain lists for frequency and prime-multiplicity arrays.

Care must be taken that the logic `max_count < 2`, `max_count < N`, `else` correctly matches the definitions of pairwise and setwise coprime; the correctness relies on the fact that if gcd>1 then some prime must divide all N numbers.

If the actual constraints on A_i exceeded 1e6 significantly, both approaches would become too slow or memory-hungry in Python; then either a tighter bound based on max(A_i) or a different strategy (e.g., factoring only necessary primes) would be required.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style GCD-of-array problem: single test, N up to ~1e5, A[i] up to ~1e9.

dominant_ops: Initial sort of the array: sorted(var_4)
First loop reducing all elements modulo the smallest: for i in range(1, n): var_4[i] %= var_4[0]
Repeated while-loop: while len(var_4) > 2 with inner for-loop performing modulus by var_4[1]
Inside while-loop: repeated conversion to set and sort: var_4 = sorted(list(set(var_4)))

complexity.time: O(n^2 log n) in the worst case (heuristically), dominated by repeated full passes over the array and repeated sorted(list(set(...))) calls inside a loop whose iteration count depends on value distribution.
complexity.space: O(n) for storing the list and its set-converted variants; extra temporary containers in each iteration.
complexity.why: The algorithm repeatedly rebuilds the container using set() and sorted(), which is O(m log m) per iteration (m = current length). The outer while-loop can run many times when values decrease slowly under the modulo operations, leading to quadratic-like behavior in n. Modulo operations themselves are O(1) per element, but their repetition across passes amplifies cost.

bottlenecks.detail: Uses a list-transforming loop with repeated modulus by the smallest elements and deduplication via set() instead of a linear-time fold using the Euclidean GCD, leading to many passes over the data.
Calls sorted(list(set(var_4))) inside the while-loop on each iteration, repeatedly sorting almost the same data.
Each sorted(list(set(...))) rebuilds the entire list and set, causing O(n) allocations and deallocations per while-loop iteration.
Reads integers using int(eval(var_3())), which is slower and unsafe compared to int(var_3()). The performance impact is small compared to algorithmic issues but still unnecessary.

FastAudit.core_idea: Compute the GCD of all numbers by iteratively applying the Euclidean algorithm in a single pass over the sorted array, maintaining the running GCD.

complexity.time: O(n log C) where C is the maximum absolute value of the integers; practically dominated by a single sort O(n log n) plus O(n log C) for GCD computations.
complexity.space: O(n) to store the input array; O(1) additional working space for the running GCD.
complexity.why: Each GCD(a, b) computes in O(log min(a, b)) via the Euclidean algorithm. Folding GCD over n elements costs O(n log C). The algorithm touches each element once (after sorting) and does not rebuild large containers in loops.

complexity_delta.from: Approximately O(n^2 log n) worst-case due to repeated sorted(list(set(...))) and multiple full passes over the list with modulus operations.
complexity_delta.to: O(n log n + n log C) ≈ O(n log n) using a single pass of Euclidean GCD over the array (after one sort).
complexity_delta.note: The key gain is eliminating repeated deduplication and resorting loops in favor of a mathematically direct GCD fold.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the intended computation is the GCD of all elements, not iterative modulus-based reduction with deduplication.
Replace the while-loop with repeated sorted(list(set(...))) by a single running GCD variable updated as gcd(current_gcd, next_value).
Remove the repeated modulus-by-second-smallest-element pass; the Euclidean algorithm already performs optimal modular reduction internally.
Eliminate set()-based deduplication and repeated sorting; keep at most one initial sort if the problem truly requires it.
Simplify input handling: avoid int(eval(...)) and unnecessary helper functions/imports when not used.
Use a tail-recursive or, in CP contexts, preferably iterative GCD implementation to keep both time and memory overhead low.
trigger_signals: Presence of while len(var_4) > 2 with a full for-loop and heavy operations (mod, set, sort) inside.
Pattern sorted(list(set(var_4))) appearing inside an iterative loop over the same container.
Algorithm seems to be converging values to a common divisor using modulus steps, suggesting a GCD problem that can be solved directly.
Multiple imports and helper functions that are unused in the core logic, indicating copy-pasted template code rather than a minimal solution.
Use of eval for reading integers, which is unsafe and typically unnecessary in competitive programming input patterns.
pitfalls: If the recursive GCD function were used on extremely large integers with pathological inputs, recursion depth could matter, but for typical 32/64-bit integers the depth is O(log C) and safe in CP constraints.
Removing the initial sort is possible for pure GCD computation; if the original problem had additional constraints relying on ordering, blindly removing sort could break logic.
Using eval on input is not only slower but also a security risk; in more general settings it must be avoided even if performance seems acceptable.
In languages without guaranteed tail-call optimization, deeply recursive GCD should be converted to an iterative loop, though in Python the depth here is small enough for standard constraints.

constraints_guess.notes: Precomputation up to 2*10^5+10 for factorials suggests n + max_exponent <= 2e5. Single (n, m) input pair; m up to around 1e9–1e12 based on trial-division factorization.

dominant_ops: Precomputing factorials and modular inverses up to N = 2e5 (single pass loops with modular multiplications)
Trial-division prime factorization of m up to sqrt(m)
O(1) modular combination queries per prime exponent

complexity.why: The global loops that fill var_6 (factorials), var_9 (modular inverses), and var_7 (inverse factorials) each run once up to N, giving O(N) time and space. Prime factorization tries divisors up to sqrt(m) and shrinks m by dividing out prime factors, yielding O(sqrt(m)) in the worst case. Each combination C(n+e-1, n-1) is computed in O(1) using precomputed factorials and inverse factorials.

bottlenecks.detail: Three arrays of size ~2e5 (factorials, modular inverses, inverse factorials) are fully precomputed on every run, even though only a small number of combinations are ultimately queried (one per distinct prime factor of m). This O(N) setup dominates when m and n are small.

Prime factorization by trial division is O(sqrt(m)); for worst-case m close to the upper limit, this loop is the main non-trivial per-test cost, though for typical competitive constraints it is acceptable.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global precomputation of factorials and modular inverses by computing exact factorials with math.factorial on demand and caching them in a dictionary; use integer binomial coefficient nCr = n! / ((n-r)! r!) with normal integer division, then apply modulo at the very end.

complexity.time: O(sqrt(m) + K * F) where K is the number of distinct factorial arguments requested and F is the cost of math.factorial at the largest argument (super-linear in that argument due to big-integer arithmetic); effectively much worse than O(N) modular precomputation for N ≈ 2e5.
complexity.why: Factorization remains O(sqrt(m)). Each factorial is computed via math.factorial, which constructs a huge Python integer with magnitude n! (bit-length Θ(n log n)), leading to super-linear cost in the argument. Although results are cached, the stored factorials themselves are enormous, so both time per operation and memory footprint scale poorly compared with storing factorials modulo 1e9+7.

complexity_delta.from: O(N + sqrt(m)) time and O(N) space with small integers bounded by the modulus; O(1) per combination query.
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(m) + K * F) time with F being the cost of big-integer factorial and significantly higher constant factors; space grows with the size of cached exact factorials, which are huge integers.
complexity_delta.note: The new approach removes linear modular precomputation but replaces it with repeated big-integer factorial computations and storage, which are asymptotically and practically more expensive for N around 2e5.

transformation_steps: Replaced defaultdict-based prime factorization (func_3) with a plain-dict implementation (func_2) that uses a while loop over trial divisors; complexity remains O(sqrt(m)).
Removed global precomputation of factorials, modular inverses, and inverse factorials modulo 1e9+7.
Introduced math.factorial to compute exact (unmodded) factorials on demand, caching results in a dictionary keyed by the factorial argument.
Changed combination computation from modular nCr using precomputed factorials and inverse factorials to exact integer nCr = n! // ((n-r)! * r!), followed by a single modulo operation at the end.
Introduced repeated dictionary-key checks via `if var_5 in list(var_11.keys())`, creating temporary lists of keys inside loops, adding extra overhead.
trigger_signals: Switch from modular factorial arrays to math.factorial suggests potential increase in big-integer sizes and arithmetic costs.
Use of integer division on very large factorial values (n! // ((n-r)! * r!)) indicates heavy big-integer division operations.
Removal of precomputed modular inverses and inverse factorials removes the O(1) combination evaluation path that was optimized for many queries.
Repeated creation of list(dict.keys()) within tight loops indicates additional avoidable overhead.
pitfalls: Big-integer factorials grow extremely fast; computing and storing n! as a Python int for n up to ~2e5 is far more expensive than maintaining values modulo 1e9+7. This can cause both timeouts and high memory usage.
Integer division of huge factorials (n! // ((n-r)! * r!)) is much slower than modular multiplication with precomputed inverses; it also obscures the originally clear O(1) per-combination cost.

The new combination logic is not modular in its internal steps; all arithmetic is performed on full integers and only reduced modulo 1e9+7 at the end, which forfeits the performance benefits of modular arithmetic.
Using `if key in list(d.keys())` creates a new list every time and is O(len(d)) instead of O(1) for `if key in d`, adding unnecessary overhead inside the factorization loop.

For large inputs aligned with the original constraints (N ≈ 2e5), the modified code is very likely slower and at higher risk of exceeding typical competitive-programming time/memory limits compared with the original precomputation-based modular solution.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic AtCoder-style task: choose integer P minimizing sum_i (a_i - P)^2. Typical constraints: 1 <= N <= ~100, a_i in small integer range (e.g., 0..100). Original solution brute-forces over the value span [min(a), max(a)], which implies that span is also modest.

dominant_ops: For each candidate integer P across the full value range from min(a) to max(a), the code computes the sum of squared differences over all N elements. This is a nested loop: outer over candidate P, inner over all elements.

complexity.why: Sorting var_3 costs O(N log N). Then var_8 = max(a) - min(a) defines R = var_8 + 1 candidate P values. For each candidate, a full pass over N elements computes the quadratic cost, giving O(N * R). Memory is dominated by storing the list of N integers.

bottlenecks.detail: Brute-force search over every integer P in the range [min(a), max(a)]. When the value range R is large, the double loop O(N * R) becomes the dominant cost.
Inner loop over all N elements for each candidate P recomputes the sum of squared differences from scratch instead of exploiting algebraic structure.
Sorting the array to obtain min/max is O(N log N); min and max could be obtained in O(N) without sorting.
Using eval(input()) to read an integer introduces unnecessary overhead and potential security issues, though it is not the primary performance bottleneck for competitive programming constraints.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical fact that the sum of squared deviations f(P) = sum_i (a_i - P)^2 is a convex quadratic in P, minimized at the mean of the data. For integer P, the optimum lies at floor(mean) or ceil(mean). Thus it suffices to evaluate the cost at those two candidates and take the minimum, eliminating the search over the full value range.

complexity.why: Compute the sum of elements once (O(N)), derive two candidate P values (floor and ceil of the average) in O(1), then compute the sum of squared differences for each candidate in O(N). Overall linear time in N with no dependence on the value range R other than constant factors. Space is for storing the N-element list.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log N + N * R), where R = max(a) - min(a)
complexity_delta.to: O(N)
complexity_delta.note: The improvement removes the dependence on the value range R by replacing exhaustive search over P with a constant-number-of-candidates evaluation based on the mean.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the objective function sum_i (a_i - P)^2 is a convex quadratic in P, analytically minimized at P = mean(a).
Observe that P must be an integer, so only floor(mean) and ceil(mean) need to be checked instead of the full [min(a), max(a)] range.
Eliminate the outer loop over candidate P by replacing it with a fixed small set of candidate values (two in this case).
Remove the sorting step, since the algorithm no longer needs the data ordered or explicit min/max; it only needs N and sum(a).
Compute the total sum once, derive the two candidate P values via integer division, and compute the sum of squared deviations for each candidate in a single pass over the data.
Drop the explicit N == 1 special case, as the mean-based formula naturally returns 0 when all elements are equal or when there is only one element.
trigger_signals: The original code performs a search over all integer points between the minimum and maximum data values, a characteristic pattern suggesting possible analytical minimization.
The objective has the form sum of squared differences from a scalar P, a classic textbook case where the mean minimizes squared error.
The inner computation repeats the same algebraic pattern (P - a_i)^2 for each P, indicating that an algebraic simplification is likely available.
Constraints (small N but potentially non-trivial value range) and competitive programming context suggest that O(N * R) is riskier than necessary and that more direct formulas are expected.
The function in P is univariate and convex, which is a strong signal that the minimum can be characterized analytically rather than via exhaustive search.
pitfalls: Integer mean handling: For integer P, using only floor(mean) or only ceil(mean) can be incorrect if the true minimum is at the other side; both candidates must be evaluated.

Off-by-one in average computation: Carefully compute floor and ceil of sum(a) / N as (S // N) and (S + N - 1) // N; naive rounding can behave differently for negative values in other languages (though here values are likely non-negative).
Precision and overflow: In languages with fixed-width integers, (a_i - P)^2 can overflow for large values; Python's unbounded ints avoid this, but other environments need attention.
Edge cases: N = 1 or all a_i equal are naturally handled by the mean-based method, but if special-casing is reintroduced, it must match the general formula to avoid inconsistencies.
Input handling: Retaining eval(input()) is unnecessary and risky; safer to use int(input()). While not a performance pitfall under typical constraints, it is a maintainability and security concern.

Order-independence: The optimized solution assumes that the order of elements is irrelevant (only sums and squared differences matter). Any additional logic depending on ordering must not be lost during refactoring.

constraints_guess.notes: Single sequence processing problem. Dominant operation is sorting; typical AtCoder constraints imply n up to ~2e5 for Python-feasible O(n log n) solutions.

dominant_ops: Sorting the array of n integers: sorted(var_1)
Full scans to check signs: all([var_6 > 0 for var_6 in var_1]) and all([var_6 < 0 for var_6 in var_1])
Summation of absolute values: sum(map(abs, var_1))
Construction of helper arrays var_2 and var_3 with O(n) appends
Multiple linear passes over the array to print operation pairs

complexity.why: Sorting var_1 dominates with O(n log n). All other work (sign checks, building var_2/var_3, summations, and output construction loops) is O(n). Additional lists var_2 and var_3, plus transient lists from comprehensions, take O(n) extra space.

bottlenecks.detail: Two full passes with all([...]) to test all-positive and all-negative cases allocate temporary lists and traverse the entire array even though subsequent logic also reprocesses the data.
Helper arrays var_2 and var_3 each grow to O(n) size, duplicating information derivable from a single running accumulator. This increases memory footprint and Python-level loop overhead.
Three separate control-flow branches (all positive, all negative, mixed) each contain independent loops and constructions, increasing overhead and making it harder to optimize access patterns.
Several explicit for-loops append to lists and compute differences one element at a time, keeping the interpreter in tight Python-level loops instead of minimizing passes.
Use of eval(input()) is slower and unnecessary compared to int(input()), although this is a small constant-factor overhead relative to O(n log n) work.

FastAudit.core_idea: Normalize all cases via sorting, compute the optimal final value with a single formula using endpoints and middle absolute values, then construct the required sequence of subtraction operations in a single linear pass using one accumulator variable instead of multiple auxiliary arrays and sign-specific branches.

complexity.why: Sorting var_1 still dominates with O(n log n). The sum over middle elements and the single construction loop are O(n). Aside from the sorted array, only O(1) additional state (accumulator var_6 and a few scalars) is kept; the list comprehension for absolute values adds transient O(n) space.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(n log n), Space: O(n) with multiple O(n)-sized helper arrays and repeated passes.
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(n log n), Space: O(n) with a single main array and O(1) extra state plus one transient comprehension.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged, but the modified code reduces the number of full passes, list allocations, and Python-level loops, improving constant factors and practical performance.

transformation_steps: Unify handling of all sign patterns (all-positive, all-negative, mixed) by sorting the array once and using a single greedy scheme instead of three separate large branches.
Replace multiple global absolute-sum computations and sign checks with one formula: max - min + sum(abs(middle_elements)).
Eliminate large helper arrays (var_2, var_3) and replace them with a single accumulator (var_6) updated in-place during construction.
Reduce the number of full-pass scans: avoid all([...]) sign checks and var_2/var_3 building loops; use one main loop over indices to emit operation pairs.
Simplify each iteration to constant-time work with local variables (var_3, var_4) using max/min, improving cache locality and branch predictability compared to more complex branch logic.
Streamline printing by emitting pairs directly in the main loop instead of staging them via intermediate arrays.
trigger_signals: Presence of multiple independent O(n) scans over the same data (all([...]) checks, repeated list-building loops).
Allocation of additional O(n)-sized lists (var_2, var_3) that mirror information that could be tracked with a single running value.
Complex branch structure with separate implementations for all-positive, all-negative, and mixed cases, suggesting consolidation via sorting and a unified greedy approach.
Heavy reliance on Python for-loops with list appends, which are significantly slower than minimized-pass, accumulator-based constructions.
Use of eval(input()) for integer input, hinting at non-optimized I/O and parsing practices.
pitfalls: Ensuring the unified greedy construction reproduces correct behavior for edge cases: all-positive inputs, all-negative inputs, and arrays containing zeros.
Careful index management in the sorted list: using var_1[1:-1] for middle elements assumes n >= 2; if n is small, this slice and the main loop bounds must still behave correctly.

The direction of each subtraction (which value is minuend vs subtrahend) is crucial; errors in the max/min selection or the conditional that flips the order (based on the next element’s sign or being the last step) can silently change the final result.

Relying on the sorted order and sign of upcoming elements (var_1[var_5 + 1] < 0) requires that the logic fully matches the mathematical proof of optimality; any deviation can break correctness even if performance is improved.

Constructing the final value with max - min + sum(abs(middle)) must match the problem’s definition exactly; omitting or mis-indexing endpoints would yield an incorrect total despite efficient implementation.

constraints_guess.n_max: 1e5–2e5 (needs better than O(n^2))
constraints_guess.notes: Computes sum over all unordered pairs a[i]*a[j]; presence of O(n^2) vs O(n) solutions suggests large n. Single test case, single array.

dominant_ops: Nested Python loops over all index pairs (i, j) with i < j, performing a[i]*a[j] and accumulating.

complexity.why: Two nested for-loops: outer over i in [0, n-1], inner over j in [i+1, n-1]; number of iterations is n*(n-1)/2, each doing a Python-level multiply and add.

bottlenecks.detail: Quadratic pairwise iteration (double loop) is inherently too slow for large n (e.g., n ~ 1e5 leads to ~5e9 operations).
Each iteration does Python integer multiplication and addition in pure Python, which is relatively slow compared to vectorized or formula-based approaches.
Multiple small helper functions for input add minimal overhead but are negligible compared to the O(n^2) loop.
Using eval(input()) for reading an integer is unsafe and slower than int(input()), though performance impact is minor compared to the double loop.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the algebraic identity ∑_{i<j} a[i]*a[j] = ((∑ a[i])^2 - ∑ (a[i]^2)) / 2 and compute the needed sums in a single pass using vectorized operations (NumPy).

complexity.space: O(n) for the array (same asymptotic as slow code)
complexity.why: Only a constant number of passes over the array: one to read, then np.sum(var_2) and np.sum(var_2**2) both run in linear time in C. No nested loops over pairs.

complexity_delta.from: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space (beyond input array)
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space (same asymptotic space as reading input array)
complexity_delta.note: The critical improvement is removing the quadratic pairwise iteration in favor of an O(n) formula-based computation; NumPy further reduces constant factors via C-level loops.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the target quantity is the sum of a[i]*a[j] over all unordered pairs (i<j).
Apply the algebraic identity: (∑ a[i])^2 = ∑ a[i]^2 + 2*∑_{i<j} a[i]*a[j], rearranging to ∑_{i<j} a[i]*a[j] = ( (∑ a[i])^2 - ∑ a[i]^2 ) / 2.
Replace the double nested loop that accumulates pairwise products with computation of two scalar sums: total_sum = ∑ a[i], squares_sum = ∑ a[i]^2.
Implement these as linear-time operations using NumPy: var_2 = np.array(var_2); total = np.sum(var_2); squares_sum = np.sum(var_2**2).
Compute the final answer as ((total**2 - squares_sum) // 2) and print it.
Optionally (for environments without NumPy), implement the same identity with pure Python sums to retain O(n) complexity.
trigger_signals: Presence of a double nested loop over indices with inner loop bounds depending on the outer index (range(var_3+1, var_5)).
Computing something over all pairs of elements (a classic pattern for combinatorial sums).
Constraints implying n can be around 1e5 or higher, making n^2 iterations infeasible.
Use of Python integer arithmetic inside deeply nested loops, which is expensive.
Similarity to known algebraic identities (e.g., pairwise sum/product formulas) suggesting there may be a closed-form or O(n) alternative.
pitfalls: Integer division: In languages with different division semantics, using regular division instead of integer division can cause precision issues; here, // 2 is correct because the numerator is always even for integer inputs.
Overflow in other languages: While Python integers are unbounded, in C++/Java the intermediate (sum)^2 may exceed 32- or 64-bit integer limits unless 64-bit or big integers are used.
NumPy import overhead: For very small n, importing NumPy may dominate runtime; in strict competitive programming environments, a pure Python O(n) solution using the same identity is preferable.
Input consistency: The first integer (n) must match the length of the array read; the slow version relies on this for indexing safety (var_1[var_3], var_1[var_4]).
Use of eval: Both versions use eval(input()) to read an integer, which is unsafe and unnecessary; it should be replaced by int(input()) in production code.
Type consistency: When porting away from NumPy, ensure all computations remain in integer arithmetic to avoid floating-point rounding errors in the final division by 2.

constraints_guess.n_max: 10^4–10^5 (needs to be at least a few thousand for original to TLE but still typical for n! divisor-count problems)
constraints_guess.notes: Task is to compute the number of divisors of n! modulo 1e9+7. Typical competitive-programming constraints put n up to 10^4 or 10^5; original code would time out well before that.

dominant_ops: For each i from 1 to n, func_1(i, n) recomputes primality of all numbers up to i via func_2 using naive trial division, then (conditionally) factors i. This nests an O(i^{3/2}) primality routine inside an outer loop over i, leading to roughly sum_{i=1..n} i^{3/2} operations.

complexity.time: Θ(n^{5/2}) in terms of elementary integer ops (ignoring growth of values); more precisely, sum_{i=1..n} Θ(i^{3/2}) from func_2 dominates, plus smaller factorization overhead.
complexity.why: Outer loop runs i = 1..n. For each i, func_2(i) makes a list of length i and for each k ≤ i performs trial division up to sqrt(k), costing Θ(i^{3/2}) total work. func_1(i, n) allocates arrays of length n and i, but the maximum over all i is O(n). The accumulation array var_9 is also size n.

bottlenecks.detail: func_2 performs naive primality checks for every k ≤ i via trial division up to sqrt(k), and func_2 is called separately for every i = 1..n. This is roughly Θ(n^{5/2}) total, far too slow for n in the thousands or higher.
The primality / sieve information is recomputed from scratch for each i. Primes up to i are recomputed for every i instead of computing primes once up to n and reusing them.
Each i is factored independently, instead of using a formula for exponents of primes in n! (e_p(n!) = sum floor(n/p^k)) or reusing factorization results incrementally.
func_1 allocates an array of length n for every i, even though meaningful exponents exist only up to i. This increases per-iteration memory traffic.

FastAudit.core_idea: Compute n! once as a big integer, then factor that integer by trial division starting from 2. Track the exponent of the current divisor; when the divisor changes, multiply a running product by (exponent) (effectively building the product of (e_p + 1) factors) and reset the exponent counter. Finally, multiply in the last exponent and take the result modulo 1e9+7. This avoids per-i sieving and aggregates factorization to a single pass over the factors of n!.

complexity.time: If treating big-int operations as unit cost: Θ(n) divisions/multiplications after computing n! in Θ(n) multiplications, so overall Θ(n). In realistic bit-complexity terms: factorial construction and repeated big-int trial divisions on n! cost roughly polynomial time in n with large constants (bit-length ≈ Θ(n log n)); still asymptotically much better than Θ(n^{5/2}) elementary ops from the original.
