Ensuring that the modular inverse precomputation is done once and reused; repeatedly constructing the Class_1 object per query or in a loop over many test cases would reintroduce unnecessary O(K) overhead each time.

constraints_guess.notes: Array size and number of operations are on the order of 3e5. Operations are range updates and range max queries; naive per-element handling will TLE.

dominant_ops: Building a segment tree over the initial array
Point updates on the segment tree (func_3) called repeatedly for each element in an update range
Range max queries (func_1) on the segment tree
Extra list allocation in build: reversed(list(range(...)))

complexity.time: O(n log n + sum_over_updates(len_range) * log n + q_query * log n)
complexity.why: The class implements a standard max segment tree with point updates (func_3) and range max queries (func_1). A single point update or query is O(log n). If the problem’s logical operation is a range update [l, r) and it is implemented as a loop of point updates, each such operation costs O((r-l) log n), leading to O(n * q * log n) in the worst case. Tree build is O(n log n) in this implementation due to the inefficient reversed(list(range())) pattern, and the segment tree itself stores O(n) elements.

bottlenecks.detail: Range updates are likely realized as many point updates via func_3 inside a loop over all indices in the interval, giving per-update time O(range_length * log n) instead of O(log n). With up to ~3e5 operations and large ranges, this becomes prohibitive.

Tree build uses reversed(list(range(var_9 - 2))) which constructs an intermediate list of size O(n) and then iterates it in reverse, instead of a direct reversed range (e.g., range(var_9 - 2, -1, -1)). This adds unnecessary allocation and time.

Heavy use of method calls (Class_1.func_3 / func_1), attribute lookups (self.node), and a separate func_2 wrapper around max() adds call overhead on every internal node visit, amplifying the cost of each O(log n) operation when executed hundreds of thousands of times.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace repeated point updates with a segment tree supporting true range assignment updates via lazy propagation, implemented iteratively with flat arrays and bit operations. This reduces per-update complexity from O(range_length * log n) to O(log n) and aggressively minimizes Python-level overhead by avoiding classes, recursion, and intermediate allocations.

complexity.why: The fast code preallocates segment tree arrays sized to the next power of two >= 300001 (var_5). It supports range assignment updates and range maximum maintenance with lazy propagation: func_4 performs a range update [l, r) in O(log n) by updating O(log n) segment tree nodes and lazily marking them in var_15. func_1 computes the nodes on the paths that need their lazy values pushed down, and func_2 pushes those values to children before updates. Each operation touches only O(log n) nodes, giving overall O((n + q) log n) time. The tree arrays var_9 (values) and var_15 (lazy tags) are O(n) in size.

complexity_delta.from: Per range update implemented as O(range_length * log n) via repeated point updates; total worst case O(n * q * log n) when ranges are large. Build phase also has extra O(n) allocation overhead.
complexity_delta.to: Per range update and per range query in O(log n) using an iterative lazy segment tree; overall O((n + q) log n).
complexity_delta.note: The key asymptotic change is in how range updates are handled (true lazy propagation vs. many point updates). Additional gains come from removing per-operation Python overhead (classes, extra lists, redundant function wrappers).

transformation_steps: Identify that problem operations are range-based (assign or update over [l, r)) combined with range maximum queries, making repeated point updates asymptotically suboptimal.
Redesign the data structure from a point-update segment tree to a lazy segment tree that directly supports range assignment updates in O(log n) per operation.
Switch from an object-oriented, method-based segment tree to a flat-array, function-based implementation to reduce Python attribute lookup and call overhead.
Avoid intermediate list allocations in tree processing by using bit-level index arithmetic and compact loops instead of reversed(list(range(...))).

Introduce lazy tag array (var_15) to defer propagation of range assignments, and a targeted push-down mechanism (func_1 + func_2) that only touches necessary nodes on paths relevant to each operation.
Use fast I/O (sys.stdin.readline) and precomputed tree size (next power of two) to reduce input parsing and allocation overhead.
trigger_signals: Constraints suggest n and q up to ~3e5 with many range operations; a solution with per-element loops inside each operation is likely to exceed time limits.
Original design provides only point updates (func_3) but the problem semantics require range updates, implying a loop over the range in user code.
Profiling or reasoning shows that the majority of time is spent in repeated calls to update over contiguous ranges, each performing log n work.
Presence of reversed(list(range(...))) and small wrapper functions around built-ins (func_2 wrapping max) indicates avoidable Python overhead in inner loops.
pitfalls: Implementing lazy propagation incorrectly (e.g., failing to push tags before reading children, or mishandling overlapping ranges) can lead to subtle wrong answers that only appear on specific corner cases.

Off-by-one errors in translating between array indices and segment tree positions (0-based vs 1-based, [l, r) vs [l, r]) are easy to introduce when converting from a simple point-update tree to an iterative lazy one.

Mixing assignment semantics (overwrite) with max semantics in the tree requires clear invariants: lazy values must represent the operation correctly, and internal node values must always be recomputable from children.

Using Python recursion for segment tree operations with large n risks hitting recursion limits or incurring extra overhead; an iterative design like in the fast code avoids this but is more index-arithmetic heavy and error-prone.
Relying on bit operations for path decomposition (e.g., (x & -x).bit_length()) is efficient but can be fragile if indices or inclusivity rules change without carefully updating the logic.

constraints_guess.notes: Two integers input. First (call it N) is up to about 1e5 (since factorial tables are sized to 2e5). Second (call it M) can be up to around 1e9–1e12 (trial division up to sqrt(M) is used). Single test case. Number of primes/exponents from factorization is O(log M).

dominant_ops: Trial-division factorization of var_1 up to sqrt(var_1) in func_2
Precomputation of factorials, modular inverses, and inverse factorials up to 2*10^5 (three arrays: var_6, var_7, var_9)
A small number of nCk evaluations via O(1) table lookups in func_1

complexity.time: O(P + sqrt(V)) where P = 2*10^5 (precomputation bound for factorial tables) and V = var_1 (value to factor)
complexity.space: O(P) extra memory for factorial, inverse, and inverse-factorial arrays of length ~2*10^5
complexity.why: Factorization via trial division to sqrt(V) is O(sqrt(V)). On top of that, the code always precomputes factorials and inverses up to 2*10^5 regardless of actual N or number of combinations needed. That precomputation loop is linear in P. The number of combination queries is equal to the number of distinct prime factors, which is O(log V), and each query is O(1) using precomputed tables, so those are negligible compared to the precompute and factorization costs.

bottlenecks.detail: The factorial and modular-inverse tables (var_6, var_7, var_9) are built up to 2*10^5 even though only O(log var_1) combinations are computed and each combination’s n = var_2 + exponent - 1 might be far below that bound. This adds a fixed ~2*10^5-iteration cost on every run.
Three arrays of size ~2*10^5 are allocated and filled, which is non-trivial memory traffic compared to the actual problem size (only a handful of primes and small exponents).
Each step in the precomputation involves modular multiplication and accessing arrays; the constant factor is relatively high and dominates runtime when var_1 is not extremely large.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid heavy global precomputation for combinations and instead compute each required binomial coefficient directly with a short multiplicative/divisive loop that runs in O(k), where k is the exponent of a prime factor (which is small). The only significant work is factoring var_1 by trial division and then doing a few small integer-arithmetic loops, followed by a final modulo.

complexity.time: O(sqrt(V) + sum k_i) where V = var_1 and k_i are prime exponents in its factorization; sum k_i = O(log V), so effectively O(sqrt(V))
complexity.space: O(log V) for storing the multiset of prime factors and their counts (via Counter); no large global tables are allocated.
complexity.why: Factorization cost remains O(sqrt(V)) as in the slow code. However, each nCk is computed via two simple loops of length k (the exponent), independent of N = var_3. Since k is at most O(log V), the total extra work is negligible compared to sqrt(V). There is no O(P) precomputation, which eliminates a large fixed runtime and memory cost.

complexity_delta.from: O(P + sqrt(V)) time, O(P) space with P = 2*10^5 for factorial and inverse tables in the slow version.
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(V)) time, O(log V) space in the fast version, since combinations are computed on-the-fly with only small O(k) loops per prime exponent.
complexity_delta.note: As P is a fixed large constant chosen as a safety upper bound rather than a tight requirement, removing the O(P) precomputation significantly reduces runtime and memory traffic for the actual input sizes used.

transformation_steps: Remove global factorial / inverse / inverse-factorial precomputation loops (arrays var_6, var_7, var_9) which were sized up to 2*10^5.

Replace table-based combination computation func_1(n, k, mod) that uses precomputed factorials and inverse factorials with a direct multiplicative implementation func_1(n, k) that computes C(n, k) by multiplying n*(n-1)*... and dividing by k! in small loops of length k.

Keep trial-division prime factorization but simplify its output representation: the fast version returns the multiset of prime factors and then compresses it via Counter to obtain exponents, instead of constructing a list of [prime, exponent] pairs during factorization.

Defer modular reduction until after the aggregate product of combinations is computed, exploiting Python's big integers; this avoids per-operation modular overhead but relies on the fact that the total bit-length remains manageable for these constraints.
trigger_signals: The number of combination evaluations equals the number of distinct prime factors of var_1, which is very small (O(log var_1)), so heavy precomputation for many possible nCk queries is unnecessary.
The precomputation bound for factorials (2*10^5) is far larger than any actual n involved in combinations for typical inputs, indicating wasted work.
Running-time profiling or intuition shows a large fixed startup cost regardless of var_1’s size, pointing to precomputation as the dominant cost.
Memory use includes multiple large arrays despite the logical problem needing only a few integer values per prime factor, suggesting over-allocation.
pitfalls: If the first input (N or var_3/var_2) were significantly larger and many different combinations were needed, the direct multiplicative nCk implementation could become slower than a table-based factorial/inverse approach; the optimization assumes few queries and small k.

In languages without arbitrary-precision integers, computing combinations via raw multiplication before taking modulo can overflow; in such contexts, modular multiplication at each step or precomputed factorial tables with modular inverses are safer.

The direct division-based nCk relies on exact integer division (the intermediate numerator is always divisible by the denominator). Algorithmic mistakes (e.g., wrong loop bounds) could cause non-integer intermediate results and errors.

If constraints change so that var_1 is extremely large (making sqrt(var_1) too big), the trial-division factorization itself becomes the bottleneck; a more advanced factorization algorithm might then be required.

constraints_guess.notes: Two integers N, K. Single pass over i=1..N computing probabilities; typical AtCoder constraints suggest N up to about 1e5 and K up to about 1e9.

dominant_ops: math.log called once per loop iteration
math.ceil called once per loop iteration
power operation 0.5 ** var_3 once per loop iteration
division var_1 / (var_4 + 1) per iteration
list creation for max([...]) per iteration

complexity.why: Single for-loop over range(var_2) with a constant number of scalar operations per iteration; no data structures growing with N. However, the constant factor is large due to transcendental math operations and unnecessary temporary objects.

bottlenecks.detail: math.log is relatively slow and is called N times. For large N this dominates runtime even though asymptotic complexity is O(N).
max is called with a list literal [math.log(...), 0], allocating a new list each iteration. Using max(x, 0) would avoid the list.
0.5 ** var_3 uses the generic pow operator on floats. Although O(1), it has a nontrivial constant cost and is repeated N times.
var_1 / (var_4 + 1) performs a float division each iteration; for large N this cost accumulates.
Combination of log, division, and power inside a tight Python loop leads to heavy per-iteration overhead compared with simple integer operations.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace per-iteration logarithm and exponentiation with a small integer-multiplication loop that simulates doubling until reaching K, accumulating probability via repeated halving. This trades expensive math.log and pow calls for cheap integer compares and multiplies, which are faster in CP Python even with a few extra loop iterations.

complexity.why: Outer loop runs N times. For each i (var_3), the while-loop doubles var_3 until it is at least K; the number of iterations is about ceil(log2(K / i)) when i < K and 0 otherwise. Summed over i, the total iterations are bounded by O(N log K). All operations are scalar integer/float ops; no additional storage proportional to N is used.

complexity_delta.from: O(N) time, O(1) space with heavy per-iteration math (log, ceil, pow, division, list creation).
complexity_delta.to: O(N log K) time, O(1) space using only integer comparisons and multiplications plus simple float multiplies.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time complexity formally increases, but in practice log2(K) is small (≈30 for K≤1e9) and the removal of expensive math functions and object allocations makes the modified version faster for typical contest constraints.

transformation_steps: Eliminate use of math.log and math.ceil to compute the number of doublings needed; instead, simulate the doubling process directly with a while-loop on an integer.
Replace 0.5 ** var_3 with iterative halving of a probability variable var_4 (multiplying by 0.5 each step).
Avoid repeated division var_1 / (var_4 + 1) by working directly with the current score (loop index) and comparing against K (var_1).
Remove list allocation in max([x, 0]) and the associated overhead altogether by replacing the expression with control flow in the while-loop.
Fold the final division by N into the running probability (start each iteration with var_4 = 1 / var_2 and accumulate directly into the answer).
trigger_signals: math.log or other transcendental functions called in a tight loop over a potentially large N.
Use of pow or ** on floats inside per-element loops in performance-sensitive code.
Creation of small temporary containers (like lists) purely to pass arguments to functions like max or min in hot loops.
Profiling or timeouts indicating that, despite O(N) complexity, the code is too slow in CP Python for upper-bound inputs.
Problem structure suggests a simple iterative or combinatorial interpretation (number of doublings) that can replace explicit logs.
pitfalls: The while-loop must guarantee progress (var_3 must strictly increase) to avoid infinite loops; incorrect condition or update could hang.
Floating-point rounding: repeated multiplications by 0.5 can accumulate small errors, but for this problem the precision of double-precision floats is sufficient.

Although faster in this context, the O(N log K) approach could become slower than the O(N) log-based approach if K were extremely large or if using an implementation where math.log is highly optimized.
Starting probability var_4 must be initialized correctly as 1 / N for each i; moving or misplacing this initialization would change the computed expectation.
Care must be taken that var_3 in the fast code is a local loop variable; reusing or mutating it incorrectly outside the intended scope can change semantics.

constraints_guess.notes: Single query; larger input value (call it M) is likely up to about 1e12, which makes O(M) scans too slow but O(sqrt(M)) divisor enumeration feasible.

dominant_ops: A linear downward scan over candidate divisors, testing each with a modulo operation until a valid divisor of var_2 is found.

complexity.why: Let V be the larger numeric input (var_2 in slow_code). var_3 = var_2 // var_1, and the loop runs from var_3 + 1 down to 1. In the worst case var_1 = 1, so var_3 ≈ var_2, and the loop performs Θ(var_2) iterations, each doing a modulo and branch. No extra asymptotic memory is used beyond a few scalars.

bottlenecks.detail: Naively tests every integer from floor(var_2 / var_1) + 1 down to 1 as a potential divisor of var_2. This is a linear scan in the magnitude of var_2 instead of exploiting divisor structure.
When var_1 is small (especially var_1 = 1) and var_2 is large (up to about 1e12), the loop may require ~var_2 iterations, which is far beyond typical time limits (~1e7–1e8 basic operations).
Early break only helps if a large divisor is encountered quickly; adversarial cases where var_2 is prime or has only small factors force traversal of nearly the entire range.

FastAudit.core_idea: Enumerate all divisors of the relevant number via sqrt decomposition: loop up to sqrt(M), and for each factor i of M, add both i and M // i. Then select the maximum divisor that satisfies the bound (<= M // K) instead of linearly scanning all candidates.

complexity.why: The modified code treats the second input (var_1) as the main number M, iterating var_4 from 1 to floor(sqrt(M)). Each time var_1 % var_4 == 0, it pushes at most two divisors into var_3. This yields all divisors in O(sqrt(M)) time. The final list comprehension and max run in O(d(M)), where d(M) (number of divisors) is at most about 10^4 for M <= 1e12, negligible compared to sqrt(M). Space usage is proportional to the number of divisors stored.

complexity_delta.from: O(V) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M)) time, O(d(M)) space
complexity_delta.note: Replaced a linear scan over candidate divisors (up to the magnitude of the number) with a sqrt-based divisor enumeration that exploits the pairing property of divisors.

transformation_steps: Reinterpreted the task as: find the maximum divisor d of a given number M (var_1 in fast_code) such that d <= M // K (K = first input, var_2 in fast_code).
Swapped input roles to work directly on the number whose divisors are needed, simplifying the logic.
Introduced a loop from 1 to floor(sqrt(M)) to identify divisors efficiently, using the fact that if i divides M, then both i and M // i are divisors.
Collected all divisors into a list and then filtered it to keep only those not exceeding the required upper bound (M // K).
Used max() on the filtered divisor list instead of a manual descending scan with early break.
trigger_signals: Presence of a for-loop whose bound scales with the numeric value of an input (range(var_3 + 1, 0, -1) where var_3 ~ var_2 / var_1).
Potential worst case when var_1 can be 1, forcing Θ(var_2) iterations.
Typical competitive programming constraints (M up to 1e12) incompatible with O(M) factor search.
Number-theoretic structure (searching for divisors) suggests standard sqrt-based divisor enumeration as an optimization.
pitfalls: Building the entire divisor list uses extra memory; for extremely large numbers with many divisors, one could instead track the best candidate on the fly while iterating up to sqrt(M).
Care is needed with integer operations: use integer division (//) and avoid floating-point errors when computing sqrt or bounds.
The fast approach assumes all calculations fit within Python integer arithmetic; although Python's big integers handle this, excessive intermediate growth should still be avoided in other languages.

The final max() call will fail if the filtered list is empty; the logic assumes at least one valid divisor exists under the constraint (which should be guaranteed by the problem: at minimum, 1 must satisfy the bound).

constraints_guess.notes: Minimize sum of squared differences between array elements and an integer x in [1,100]. Typical competitive programming task; actual constraints likely small (n<=100), but slow solution would not scale if range or n grew.

dominant_ops: Outer loop over candidate x values in range(1, 101)
Inner loop over all elements var_2 to accumulate (var_9 - var_4) ** 2
Integer arithmetic for squared differences and accumulation

complexity.why: Reads n numbers into a list (O(n) space). Then for each candidate integer x in [1,100] (R=100), it scans the entire list and computes a squared difference and add per element, giving O(R*n) operations. R is constant here but the 100x factor is significant in Python.

bottlenecks.detail: Brute-force search over all integer x in [1,100], recomputing the entire sum of squared differences for each candidate.
For every candidate x, the code re-traverses the full array and recomputes (var_9 - x)**2 from scratch, even though the optimal x can be derived directly from the mean.
Nested Python-level loops (over candidate x and over elements) incur substantial interpreter overhead compared to a single pass.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the statistical property that the sum of squared differences is minimized at the mean of the data (for integer x, at round/floor/ceil of the mean), so compute the mean once and then a single pass to accumulate squared differences.

complexity.why: Reads n values into a list (O(n) space). Computes sum(var_2) once (O(n)), derives var_5 as the rounded mean, then makes a single O(n) pass to compute the squared differences. No extra loop over candidate x values.

complexity_delta.from: O(R * n) with R=100 (about 100n operations) and nested Python loops
complexity_delta.to: O(n) with a single pass over the data after computing the mean
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both are O(n) because R is constant, but removing the 100x factor and one full Python-level loop yields a substantial speedup in practice, especially if the candidate range or constraints grow.

transformation_steps: Recognize the objective: minimize sum_i (a_i - x)^2 over integer x, which is a standard least-squares problem.
Use the fact that the unconstrained minimizer is the mean of the a_i; for integer x, the optimum lies at round/floor/ceil of the mean (and within [1,100] this coincides for typical constraints).
Replace the brute-force outer loop over candidate x in 1..100 with a direct computation of x = round(sum(a)/n).
Keep a single loop over the array to accumulate (a_i - x)^2, eliminating recomputation of the sum of squares for different x.
Simplify control flow: no need to track a running minimum over candidate x; directly compute the sum for the chosen x.
trigger_signals: Fixed small search range (1..100) being scanned with a full pass over the array for each candidate.
Repeated identical pattern: inner loop recomputing sum of squared deviations for each candidate x.
Objective function is sum of squared errors, strongly suggesting a closed-form solution based on the mean.
Presence of nested loops where the outer loop is over possible parameter values rather than input data itself.
pitfalls: Rounding behavior: for integer minimization of squared error, both floor(mean) and ceil(mean) may need checking in general; using round() assumes typical constraints where this is safe or symmetric behavior.
Constraint bounds on x: if x must lie in [L,R], the optimal x should be clipped to that interval; the fast code assumes the mean lies within [1,100] given the data constraints.
Use of eval(input()) in the fast code is unnecessary and can be unsafe; int(input()) is preferable, though it does not affect performance materially.
Potential float precision issues if values or n are large when computing the mean; here, small integers keep this safe.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder 'Coprime' constraints: N up to ~1e5, each A_i up to ~1e6. Single test, no queries; need near O(N log A_max) or O(N * sqrt(A_max)) with good constants.

dominant_ops: For each array element (until the first shared prime factor is detected), trial-divide up to sqrt(a_i) to get prime factors, and for each new prime factor p mark all multiples of p up to 10^6 in a global array. Also compute running GCD across the array.

complexity.time: O(N * sqrt(A_max) + A_max log log A_max)
complexity.why: Each number a_i is factorized by trial division: worst-case O(sqrt(A_max)) per element, so O(N * sqrt(A_max)). For every distinct prime factor p that appears in the input, func_1 marks all multiples of p up to var_4 = 10^6, costing O(A_max/p) per prime; over possible primes this behaves like O(A_max log log A_max). The global mark array var_3 is of size A_max+1, giving O(A_max) space.

bottlenecks.detail: func_1 marks every multiple of each newly discovered prime factor p up to 10^6 (a sieve-like loop) even though the algorithm only needs to know whether prime p has been seen before, not whether its multiples exist in the input. This adds an unnecessary O(A_max/p) loop per distinct prime factor.

Pairwise-coprime check is embedded into a factorization routine that relies on trial division up to sqrt(a_i); with N up to ~1e5 and A_max up to ~1e6, a worst-case O(N * sqrt(A_max)) ≈ 10^8 trial divisions is borderline in Python.
Input is read using input() and n is parsed via eval(input()), which is slower and unnecessarily powerful compared to int(sys.stdin.readline()).
The array is sorted even though the algorithm’s logic does not require sorted order for correctness; this costs O(N log N) extra work, though this is secondary compared to the factorization cost.

FastAudit.core_idea: Directly factor each number to obtain its distinct prime factors, and maintain a boolean array indexed by prime values that records whether each prime has already appeared. If any prime repeats, the set is not pairwise coprime. In parallel, compute the GCD of all numbers to distinguish between setwise coprime and not coprime. Avoid global sieving over all multiples and use faster I/O.

complexity.why: func_1 factorizes each a_i by trial division up to sqrt(a_i), giving O(sqrt(A_max)) per element and O(N * sqrt(A_max)) overall. For each distinct prime factor p of a_i, it performs only O(1) work to check and set var_4[p]; there is no O(A_max/p) sweeping over multiples. The GCD is updated once per element in O(log A_max) time, which is dominated by trial division. var_4 is a boolean array of length max(a_i)+1, hence O(A_max) space.

complexity_delta.from: O(N * sqrt(A_max) + A_max log log A_max) time, O(A_max) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N * sqrt(A_max)) time, O(A_max) space
complexity_delta.note: Removed the per-prime O(A_max/p) 'mark all multiples' sweep, transforming a hybrid factorization + partial sieve approach into a pure on-demand factorization with O(1) marking per prime factor. Input and control-flow optimizations reduce constant factors.

transformation_steps: Replace the global multiples-marking scheme: instead of, for each discovered prime p, looping var_10 from p to 10^6 and marking var_3[var_10], the fast version simply stores a boolean flag var_4[p] to remember whether prime p has appeared before.

Simplify pairwise coprimality detection: for each number, factor it into distinct primes, then check var_4[p]; if already True, the set is not pairwise coprime and factorization for subsequent elements can be skipped.
Retain but decouple the GCD logic: compute the GCD of all elements in a simple loop (func_2), used at the end to distinguish 'setwise coprime' (gcd == 1) from 'not coprime'.
Avoid unnecessary sorting: the fast code processes the numbers in input order, eliminating the O(N log N) sort.
Optimize I/O: use sys.stdin.readline() instead of input() and remove eval() for integer parsing, reducing overhead.
Use a tight factorization loop: iterate var_6 from 2 up to int(var_10**0.5) and divide var_10 completely by var_6 once it is detected as a factor, minimizing repeated work for the same prime.
trigger_signals: Profiling or inspection shows func_1 dominating runtime due to the inner loop that marks all multiples of each prime factor up to 10^6.

Time limit exceeded (TLE) or near-timeout behavior on test cases with many elements and numbers dense in small prime factors, where many distinct primes appear and the O(A_max log log A_max) marking term becomes costly.
Code review reveals eval(input()) and unnecessary sorting in a performance-critical section.
Awareness that only per-prime presence is needed (not per-multiple status) for pairwise coprime detection, indicating that the global multiples marking is overkill.
pitfalls: The fast version still relies on trial division up to sqrt(a_i), giving O(N * sqrt(A_max)) complexity; for larger A_max (e.g., >10^7) this would be too slow. A more scalable approach would precompute smallest prime factors (SPF) via a sieve in O(A_max log log A_max) and then factor each a_i in roughly O(log A_max).
Recursive GCD (func_2) is fine for these constraints because the recursion depth is O(log A_max), but for stylistic and robustness reasons an iterative gcd or math.gcd is usually preferable.
Using max(var_2) to size var_4 assumes all a_i are non-negative and reasonably bounded; if constraints changed to allow much larger values, the boolean array would become a memory hotspot.

If inputs are adversarially chosen to be large primes close to A_max and N is large, the O(N * sqrt(A_max)) trial division becomes the dominant cost; any further optimization should then focus on faster factorization (SPF sieve or probabilistic methods for larger ranges).

constraints_guess.notes: Single query (one pair of integers). Precomputation in slow_code up to 1e6+10 suggests n (the larger combinatorial parameter) is <= ~1e6. Modulus is 1e9+7.

dominant_ops: Linear precomputation of factorials and modular inverses up to N = 1e6+10, followed by O(1) binomial coefficient evaluation.

complexity.time: O(N_max) for precomputation + O(1) for the single combination query
complexity.why: The loop `for var_5 in range(2, var_1 + 1)` builds factorial (var_3), inverse (var_6), and inverse factorial (var_4) arrays of length ~N_max. The combination `func_1` then just does three array accesses and multiplications.

bottlenecks.detail: The initialization loop up to 1e6+10 dominates runtime for a single query; all values are computed regardless of the specific n,k needed.
Three arrays of size O(N_max) (var_3, var_4, var_6) keep O(N_max) integers in memory even though only one combination value is used.
The code is hard‑wired to var_1 = 1e6+10; supporting larger n would require increasing this and doing even more precomputation.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial/inverse arrays; compute C(n,k) on demand via a multiplicative formula for numerator and denominator, then use fast modular exponentiation to invert the denominator.

complexity.why: For k = var_13, the code performs two loops of length k: one to build the numerator product (n−k+1..n) and one to build k! (denominator). Then it calls `func_1`, which does a single modular exponentiation `pow(denominator, MOD-2)` via divide‑and‑conquer recursion, taking O(log MOD) steps.

complexity_delta.from: O(N_max) time + O(N_max) space (factorial/inverse precomputation, O(1) per query)
complexity_delta.to: O(k + log MOD) time + O(1) space (per query, no precomputation)
complexity_delta.note: For a single query and N_max around 1e6, both are feasible. The modified version trades the one‑time O(N_max) cost and memory usage for a per‑instance cost proportional to k, which is favorable when N_max is large or unknown and queries are few.

transformation_steps: Remove global precomputation of factorials and modular inverses (`var_3`, `var_4`, `var_6` and the loop up to 1e6+10).
Introduce a modular exponentiation routine (`func_2`) implementing binary exponentiation to compute a^(MOD-2) mod MOD for modular inverses.
Define `func_1` as a thin wrapper around `func_2` to compute the modular inverse (a^(MOD-2) mod MOD) of the denominator.

Replace the O(1) table‑based nCk computation with a multiplicative computation of numerator (product of n−k+1..n) and denominator (k!), followed by multiplying by the modular inverse of the denominator.
Retain the same combinatorial conditions on inputs ((x+y)%3==0 and non‑negative transformed coordinates) but compute the binomial coefficient without relying on large global tables.
trigger_signals: Only a single query is processed, so heavy factorial precomputation is not amortized over many operations.
Concern about memory usage or about supporting larger n than the fixed precomputation bound (1e6+10).
Desire to make the solution less dependent on a fixed N_max and more adaptable to input sizes determined at runtime.
Profiling or intuition showing that startup/precomputation time is a significant share of total runtime.
pitfalls: For large k (e.g., k close to 1e6), the per‑query O(k) loops in the fast_code can still be substantial; if there were many queries, the original precomputed approach might be faster overall.

The recursive modular exponentiation (`func_2`) introduces function‑call overhead; while recursion depth is only O(log MOD) (~30), an iterative implementation would be slightly faster and safer for larger exponents or different environments.

Care must be taken that intermediate products are taken modulo MOD at each multiplication to prevent large integer growth; the fast_code does this, but omitting `% var_1` inside the loops would degrade performance.

The modified approach computes numerator and denominator in two separate loops; small code changes (e.g., off‑by‑one in bounds) could silently break the combinatorial identity, so correctness relies on precise loop limits.

If inputs were such that n became larger than what the slow_code precomputes for, slow_code would fail, whereas the fast_code scales without that particular bound but at the cost of linear dependence on k.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: N up to around 100, each value between 1 and 100. Need to choose an integer p in [1,100] (or [min(a), max(a)]) minimizing sum_i (a_i - p)^2.

dominant_ops: For each candidate p, compute (var_2 - p) ** 2 as a NumPy vector operation and then np.sum(...) over all elements
Within the loop, repeatedly compute min(var_2), which scans the entire NumPy array each time

complexity.why: Let n = number of elements, R = max(var_2) - min(var_2) + 1. The loop runs R times. Each iteration does: (1) a min(var_2) call, which is O(n) because Python’s min iterates over the NumPy array, and (2) a vectorized difference, square, and np.sum over n elements, which is also O(n). So overall time is O(R * n). The NumPy array var_2 plus per-iteration temporaries of size n give O(n) space.

bottlenecks.detail: Importing and using NumPy in a competitive programming environment has large constant overhead, especially for small n and small R; crossing the Python-NumPy boundary R times is expensive.
min(var_2) is recomputed in every iteration of the outer loop, scanning the entire array each time, even though min(var_2) is invariant; this adds an unnecessary O(R * n) component.
Each iteration allocates temporary NumPy arrays for (var_2 - var_5) and (that result) ** 2 before summing, creating repeated allocation/GC overhead.
Using eval(input()) is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()); NumPy also slows startup vs. plain Python for small inputs.
The code searches over [min(a), max(a)] computed from data; in this problem, constraints allow fixing the search range to [1, 100], which simplifies logic and avoids extra calls to min/max.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid NumPy and heavy per-iteration allocations; use fast buffered input, exploit that the optimal p lies in the small fixed range [1,100], and compute the squared error sum with a simple nested loop in pure Python.

complexity.why: Read all integers once into a Python list (size n+1 including N). Then loop p from 1 to 100 and, for each p, linearly scan the list of values to accumulate sum (a_i - p)^2. The outer loop cost is 100 (constant), inner loop is O(n), so total is O(100 * n). Memory is O(n) for the list; only O(1) extra working variables are used.

complexity_delta.from: O(R * n) time, O(n) space with sizable NumPy and eval overhead; R <= 100 but each step uses heavy vector ops and repeated min() scans
complexity_delta.to: O(100 * n) time, O(n) space with lightweight pure-Python arithmetic and minimal overhead
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity in n is effectively the same for this problem’s bounded R, but the constant factors and overhead are drastically reduced by removing NumPy, avoiding repeated min() inside the loop, and using fast I/O.

transformation_steps: Replace eval(input()) with direct integer parsing via sys.stdin.read and map(int, ...), improving safety and I/O performance.
Remove dependency on NumPy; store the sequence in a plain Python list instead of a NumPy array.
Exploit problem constraints: iterate candidate p over the fixed range [1,100] instead of dynamically using min(var_2) and max(var_2).
Replace vectorized (var_2 - p) ** 2 and np.sum(...) with a simple inner for-loop accumulating (value - p) ** 2 in a scalar variable.
Avoid recomputing min(var_2) inside the loop; the modified version does not need min/max at all.
Use a single pass over pre-read input via sys.stdin.read, minimizing input overhead and avoiding multiple input() calls.
trigger_signals: Use of NumPy in a small, tight loop for a problem with very small constraints suggests unnecessary overhead.
Presence of eval(input()) for reading a single integer, indicating avoidable overhead and unsafe usage.
Recomputing min(var_2) inside the main search loop, even though the array does not change.
Creating new temporary arrays (var_2 - var_5) and squaring them in each iteration, hinting at repeated allocation and GC work.
Competitive programming context where import time and heavy libraries are penalized for otherwise trivial numeric loops.
pitfalls: The optimized code assumes the valid p-range is exactly 1 to 100; if the true constraints allow values outside this interval, the result could be wrong.
Using sys.stdin.read and unpacking var_2, *var_6 assumes the first integer is N followed by at least N more integers; malformed input will raise errors.
For extremely large n (far beyond the intended constraints), a naive double loop might need further optimization (e.g., using precomputed sums) even without NumPy.
Relying on constant bounds like 100 ties the solution to problem-specific constraints; reusing the pattern elsewhere requires revisiting these magic numbers.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic 3-choice per day DP (Vacation-like). Typical constraints ~1e5–2e5 days; constant 3 activities per day.

dominant_ops: Reading and storing all n triplets into a list of length n
Allocating an n x 3 DP table (list of lists)
O(n) DP transition with nested loops and repeated list indexing/branching
Use of eval(input()) for reading a single integer

complexity.why: For each of n days we store its 3 values and compute transitions using only the previous day, but we still allocate and maintain an n x 3 DP table plus the n x 3 input array.

bottlenecks.detail: Stores both the entire input var_2 (n x 3) and the full DP table var_4 (n x 3), leading to O(n) memory usage and worse cache behavior.
Creates the DP table with a nested list comprehension [[0 for ...] for ...], incurring O(n) list allocations before any transitions.
Inner loop over var_6 in range(3) uses three if branches to update the same row; this performs multiple conditional checks and repeated assignments to the same DP cells, inflating constant factors.
Heavy use of 2D indexing var_4[i][j] and var_2[i][j] inside the hot DP loop adds Python-level overhead compared to working with a few scalar variables.
Uses eval(input()) instead of int(input()) for reading var_1, which is slower and unnecessary, though this is a minor constant-factor effect compared to DP and allocations.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit that each day's DP state depends only on the previous day and there are exactly 3 activities, so keep just three running values (var_6, var_7, var_8) representing the best scores if you pick activity 0, 1, or 2 today. Update them in one tuple assignment using the previous state, eliminating the O(n) DP table and the stored input array.

complexity.why: Still processes each of the n days exactly once with a constant amount of work per day (a few max operations), but only keeps 3 DP values in memory instead of an entire n x 3 table.

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time complexity remains linear, but memory is reduced from linear to constant and constant factors in the inner loop are significantly improved (fewer allocations, indices, and branches).

transformation_steps: Recognize the DP relation: DP[i][a] = max over b != a of (DP[i-1][b] + value[i][a]) for a in {0,1,2}. Each state depends only on the previous day.
Observe that the number of activities (3) is constant and small, so we can keep only three running values for DP[i-1][0], DP[i-1][1], DP[i-1][2].
Remove storage of the entire input array var_2; instead, read each day's triplet (var_2, var_3, var_4) and immediately apply the DP transition.
Replace the n x 3 DP table var_4 with three scalar variables (var_6, var_7, var_8) holding the current day’s best scores for choosing each activity.
Express the DP update as a single parallel tuple assignment: (new0, new1, new2) computed from the old (var_6, var_7, var_8) and the new input triplet, then assign back to (var_6, var_7, var_8).
Eliminate the nested loops and branching on var_6; transitions are encoded directly in the tuple assignment using max calls, reducing Python-level overhead.
Output the final answer as max(var_6, var_7, var_8) after processing all days instead of max over the last row of a DP table.
trigger_signals: DP recurrence depends only on the previous time step (i-1), suggesting a rolling-state optimization.
The state dimension (3 activities) is a small compile-time constant, making scalar variables more efficient than lists.
Memory footprint is O(n) with a simple per-step dependency, a classic pattern where you can usually reduce to O(1) space.
The original code keeps full history (n x 3 DP table) even though only the last row is needed at the end.
The inner loop includes conditional branches that just encode the same recurrence that can be written algebraically without branching.
pitfalls: Incorrect in-place updates: When compressing the DP table to three scalars, you must compute all new values based on the previous state. If you update var_6 first and then use var_6 again for var_7’s update, you’ll mix old and new states and break the recurrence. Using a single tuple assignment ensures atomicity.

Mis-mapping activities: The compact form assumes a fixed mapping (e.g., var_6->activity0, var_7->activity1, var_8->activity2). Any mismatch between this mapping and the original DP transitions will yield wrong results.

Edge case for the first day: The original code initializes var_4[0] explicitly from var_2[0]. The optimized code must implicitly handle the base case correctly (starting from zeros and processing the first day or setting initial DP equal to the first day’s values).

Over-aggressive micro-optimization: While reducing DP to scalars helps, avoid obfuscating the transition logic; errors in rewriting the max expressions (using the wrong pair of previous states) are easy to introduce and hard to debug.

Reliance on eval(input()): Although unchanged, using eval instead of int for reading var_1 is a security and minor performance issue; if the environment ever changes, this could break or slow the solution unnecessarily.

constraints_guess.notes: Single array of length N, one pass feasible; solutions that iterate over value range (max(A)-min(A)) would TLE if values are large (e.g., up to 1e9). Values appear to be integers; objective is to find integer x minimizing sum (a_i - x)^2.

dominant_ops: Python-level for-loop over all candidate centers x in [min(A), max(A)]
Per-iteration numpy vector operations: (var_2 - var_5) ** 2 and np.sum(...)
Repeated Python built-in min(var_2) inside the loop, scanning the array each time

complexity.why: Let N = len(var_2), R = max(var_2) - min(var_2) + 1. The loop runs R times. Each iteration computes (var_2 - var_5) ** 2 and np.sum(...), both O(N) over the array, and also calls min(var_2) once per iteration which is O(N) on a numpy array when using Python's built-in min. Total per-iteration cost is Theta(N), so total time is Theta(R * N). The array var_2 dominates memory, giving O(N) space.

bottlenecks.detail: Brute-force search over every integer between min(var_2) and max(var_2) for the minimizer of sum (a_i - x)^2, leading to O(R * N) time where R can be large.

Use of Python built-in min(var_2) on a numpy array inside the loop adds an extra O(N) scan each iteration instead of using a precomputed scalar min or numpy.min; this multiplies the already expensive loop cost.
The code repeatedly performs full-array numpy computations ((var_2 - var_5) ** 2 and np.sum) for each candidate x, even though the optimal x has a closed-form expression (the mean).
For constraints where an O(N) pure-Python solution is enough, importing and using numpy adds overhead, though this is minor compared to the algorithmic issue.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical fact that the sum of squared deviations S(x) = sum_i (a_i - x)^2 is minimized over real x by x = mean(a_i); for an integer solution, choose an integer nearest to the mean (here via round). Compute the objective once at that x instead of brute-forcing over the entire value range.

complexity.why: Computing np.mean(var_2) is a single pass over N elements in C (O(N)). The final expression sum((var_2 - var_3) ** 2) is one vectorized difference and one sum over N elements (O(N)). There is no loop over candidate x values, so total time is Theta(N). The array var_2 still dominates memory usage, giving O(N) space.

complexity_delta.from: O(R * N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: R = max(var_2) - min(var_2) + 1 can be large when the value range is wide; replacing the brute-force scan over all integer centers with a single evaluation at the (rounded) mean removes the multiplicative factor R.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the objective function sum (a_i - x)^2 is quadratic in x and is minimized at the arithmetic mean of the data.
Replace the outer for-loop over x in [min(A), max(A)] with a single computation of x* = round(mean(A)).
Remove the repeated evaluation of min(var_2) inside the loop by no longer scanning over the range at all.
Compute the sum of squared deviations only once at x* using a single vectorized expression sum((var_2 - x*) ** 2).
Keep input parsing and storage similar, but avoid repeated full-array operations that depend on candidate x.
trigger_signals: Loop bounds depending on max(array) - min(array), indicating algorithmic complexity grows with value spread rather than just element count.
Full-array operations (numpy vector math and reductions) executed in every loop iteration.
Recomputing min(var_2) inside a loop, signaling unnecessary repeated scans of the data.
Objective function is clearly a sum of squared differences, which is a classic case with a known analytic minimizer (mean).
pitfalls: Using round(np.mean(var_2)) for integer x can behave subtly for .5 ties due to banker's rounding (e.g., 0.5 -> 0, 1.5 -> 2). For strict contest guarantees it may be safer to check both floor(mean) and ceil(mean) and take the minimum.
Floating-point precision in np.mean may cause off-by-one in the chosen integer x when values are large or N is big; again, evaluating both neighbors around the mean mitigates this.
The improvement is algorithmic, but using numpy still incurs import and runtime overhead; for very small N, pure-Python arithmetic can be faster despite similar complexity.
The original code uses eval(input()) for reading N, which is unsafe and unnecessary; while not a performance bottleneck, it is a potential security risk and should be avoided in general.

constraints_guess.notes: Computes Lucas numbers L_n (L_0=2, L_1=1, L_n=L_{n-1}+L_{n-2}); typical constraints allow at least up to 10^7 with linear-time solutions. Only a single integer N is read.

dominant_ops: Allocation and initialization of an array of size n+1
Single for-loop performing O(n) additions and array reads/writes
Use of eval(input()) for parsing the integer

complexity.why: The code builds the entire DP table var_2[0..n] and fills it in a single pass. Each of the n-1 iterations performs constant-time work, so time is linear in n. The array var_2 of length n+1 dominates memory, giving linear space usage.

bottlenecks.detail: Keeps an array of size n+1 (var_2) even though only the final value var_2[n] is printed, wasting O(n) memory.
Array-based DP requires indexed loads and stores on every iteration; this is more expensive than keeping just a few scalar variables in registers.
Uses eval(input()) to read an integer, which is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()).
Multiple early exits and repeated prints add minor overhead and complexity, though not asymptotically significant.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit that the recurrence L_n = L_{n-1} + L_{n-2} only depends on the previous two (or three tracked) values; compute iteratively while maintaining a constant number of variables, avoiding the DP array entirely and using safe int(input()) parsing.

complexity.why: The while-loop runs exactly n iterations, performing a fixed number of arithmetic and assignment operations each time, so time remains linear. It tracks only three scalars (current and next Lucas numbers), so memory usage is constant, independent of n.

complexity_delta.from: Time O(n), Space O(n)
complexity_delta.to: Time O(n), Space O(1)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time complexity is unchanged (still one linear pass), but memory usage drops from linear to constant and per-iteration overhead is reduced by avoiding list indexing and allocation.

transformation_steps: Replace eval(input()) with int(input()) for safer and lighter input parsing.
Recognize that the recurrence L_n = L_{n-1} + L_{n-2} only needs a constant number of previous terms, not the full DP table.
Remove the DP array var_2 and the range-based for-loop; instead, maintain scalar variables (var_1, var_2, var_3) representing consecutive terms of the Lucas sequence.
Initialize these scalars to match the base cases (L_0=2, L_1=1, L_2=3) and iterate exactly n times, updating them in a tuple assignment.
Print the scalar corresponding to L_n after the loop, instead of reading it from an array.
trigger_signals: The original code only prints var_2[var_1] (the last DP state), never accessing intermediate DP values.
Array var_2 is sized to n+1 even though intermediate results are not reused after their immediate successors are computed.
The recurrence is a simple second-order linear recurrence, a textbook pattern for O(1)-space iterative computation.
Use of eval(input()) indicates avoidable overhead and potential security risks when only an integer is expected.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when converting from array indices to iterative updates: the scalar initialization must correctly reflect L_0, L_1, and the update order must ensure that after k iterations the printed variable indeed holds L_k.
Incorrect handling of n=0 and n=1 edge cases; the scalar-based loop must be structured so that these values are returned without extra special-case branches.

Potential integer overflow in languages with fixed-width integer types; although Python handles big integers, translating this approach to other languages requires checking that the maximum n stays within numeric limits.
Ensuring that the variable roles (current, next, and next+1 term) remain consistent across iterations; a wrong assignment order can silently corrupt the sequence.

constraints_guess.notes: Single-array optimization problem. Original code initializes best value with 10**6, suggesting n*max_a^2 ≈ 1e6 → likely n ≤ 100, |a_i| ≤ 100. Exact constraints unknown but time optimization not strictly necessary at that scale; transformation is more about using the mathematical property of the mean.

dominant_ops: For each integer p between min(a) and max(a), compute sum((a_i - p)^2) over all elements.

complexity.why: Sorting the n numbers takes O(n log n). Then the outer loop iterates over p in [min(a), max(a)], where R = max(a) - min(a) + 1, and for each p the inner loop scans all n elements to accumulate squared differences, giving O(n * R). Storing the input list dominates space at O(n).

bottlenecks.detail: The double loop over every candidate integer p in the full range [min(a), max(a)] and every element in the list leads to O(n * R) operations. If R is large relative to n, this becomes slow.

The sum of squared deviations from p is a convex quadratic in p with a unique minimum at the mean. Scanning all integer p in the range is unnecessary; the optimum must lie near the mean, so the full range search is overkill.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical fact that the sum of squared deviations Σ(a_i - p)^2 is minimized at p equal to the mean of a_i. Since p must be an integer, it suffices to check floor(mean) and ceil(mean) and take the better of the two.

complexity.why: The algorithm reads the n elements, computes their sum (O(n)), derives two candidate integers (floor and ceil of the mean), and in one pass computes Σ(a_i - p)^2 for both candidates simultaneously (O(n)). No sorting or range-based candidate enumeration is used. Space remains O(n) to store the input list.

complexity_delta.from: O(n log n + n * R) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: The key improvement is replacing a brute-force scan over all integer p in [min(a), max(a)] with a constant-size candidate set derived from the mean of the data, exploiting convexity of the squared loss.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the objective function F(p) = Σ(a_i - p)^2 is a convex quadratic in p with derivative zero at p = mean(a).
Use the fact that the real-valued minimizer is p* = (Σ a_i) / n; for integer-constrained p, the optimum must be at floor(p*) or ceil(p*).
Replace the outer loop over all p in [min(a), max(a)] with computation of two candidate integers p_floor and p_ceil from the average.
Retain a single pass over the array to compute Σ(a_i - p_floor)^2 and Σ(a_i - p_ceil)^2 simultaneously, and return the smaller value.
Drop the initial sort, since the order and global min/max of the array are no longer required.
trigger_signals: Presence of a nested loop where the outer loop iterates over a continuous integer range derived from min and max of the data, and the inner loop sums a smooth function over all elements.
Objective function is a sum of per-element terms depending on a scalar parameter p in a polynomial (quadratic) form.
Use of squared differences (a_i - p)^2, a standard scenario where the mean minimizes total squared error.
Sorting is only used to obtain min and max while not otherwise affecting logic, suggesting the algorithm is brute-forcing over an interval rather than exploiting order.
pitfalls: When using integer division for the mean, you must consider both floor and ceil; checking only floor(sum / n) can be wrong if the exact mean is not an integer and the function is not symmetric around that integer.
Repeatedly computing sum(a) (as in the modified code) is slightly wasteful; store it once to avoid redundant O(n) work, especially if constraints are larger than expected.

If negative numbers are allowed, be careful with integer division semantics: in Python, // is floor division, so floor and ceil handling must be explicit; still, the floor/ceil-of-mean principle remains valid.
Avoid using eval(input()) for reading integers; besides safety issues, it can introduce subtle overhead or bugs if the input is not exactly an integer literal.

constraints_guess.n_max: 1e9 (n in combinations), prime exponents sum ≲ 60 (m up to about 1e9–1e12)
constraints_guess.notes: Typical of AtCoder-style problem: input (n, m) with 1 ≤ n ≤ 1e9, 1 ≤ m ≤ 1e9; need number of ways to write m as product of n positive integers. Requires prime factorization of m and combinatorial counts modulo 1e9+7.

dominant_ops: Computing factorial(var_2 - 1) where var_2 (n) can be very large (up to about 1e9).
Big-integer multiplications in factorial and combination loops without early modulo reduction.
Trial division factorization up to sqrt(m) (acceptable but secondary to factorial cost).

complexity.time: O(sqrt(m) + n) big-integer multiplications, where n = var_2
complexity.space: Θ(log m + log(result)) bits for necessary values, but factorial(var_2-1) inflates to Θ(n log n) bits if it were to complete.
complexity.why: func_1 does straightforward trial division up to sqrt(m), which is O(sqrt(m)). The main loop then computes factorial(var_2 - 1) once, costing O(n) multiplications and generating an integer with Θ(n log n) bits. This factorial is never used subsequently, so all that work is wasted. For n as large as 1e9 this is completely infeasible, and even for much smaller n, factorial growth makes each multiplication extremely expensive. The later combination-like products per prime exponent e are small (sum of exponents is O(log m)), so they are not the bottleneck compared to factorial(var_2-1).

bottlenecks.detail: Unnecessary computation of factorial(var_2 - 1) for potentially huge n dominates time and memory; its result is never used in the final answer.
All combination-related multiplications are done on full big integers without reducing modulo 1e9+7 until the very end, increasing intermediate integer size and cost of arithmetic.
For large n, factorial(var_2 - 1) is so large that it may not finish within time/memory limits, effectively making the solution unusable even though the result does not require this factorial.

FastAudit.core_idea: Remove the massive and unnecessary factorial(var_2 - 1) computation and instead compute each required binomial coefficient C(n + e - 1, e) using a multiplicative formula that only iterates over the smaller parameter e, then apply the modulus as part of the per-prime loop. Factorization remains trial division but is already efficient enough for m up to about 1e9.

complexity.time: O(sqrt(m) + Σ_e e) ≈ O(sqrt(m) + log m)
complexity.space: O(#distinct_primes(m)) extra space, typically O(log m); all intermediate values kept to reasonable size by frequent modulus application.
complexity.why: func_1 still does trial division up to sqrt(m), which is acceptable for m up to around 1e9. After factorization, each prime exponent e contributes one call to func_2 computing C(N, K) with K = e and N = e + n - 1. func_2 runs in O(K) by multiplying N·(N-1)·...·(N-K+1) and dividing by 2···K. The sum of exponents over all primes dividing m is O(log m), so Σ_e e is small. MOD is applied to the running product var_1 in the main loop, preventing values from blowing up. This eliminates the O(n) factorial work and enormous big integers from the original version.

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(m) + n) big-integer operations with factorial(var_2 - 1) dominating, and huge intermediate integer sizes due to full factorial computation and late modulo.
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(m) + Σ_e e) with Σ_e e ≈ O(log m), and controlled integer sizes via localized combination computation and per-step modulo in the accumulation.
complexity_delta.note: The refactor removes an O(n) factorial that depends on potentially huge n and replaces it with O(log m) combination computations, making the solution feasible even for very large n as long as m is moderately sized (≈1e9).

transformation_steps: Identify that the mathematical core of the answer is product over primes of C(n + e - 1, e), where e is the exponent of each prime in the factorization of m.
Remove the computation of factorial(var_2 - 1), which was mathematically unnecessary and never used in the final formula.
Encapsulate the binomial coefficient computation into func_2 that uses a multiplicative formula in O(min(k, n-k)) time, avoiding precomputing large factorial tables or a huge single factorial.
Apply the modulus 1e9+7 to the running product var_1 after each multiplication of a binomial term to keep intermediate values small and arithmetic fast.

Retain trial-division factorization but streamline it using repeated divmod inside the loop and computing the sqrt bound once at the start; this keeps factorization cost acceptable for the given m range.
trigger_signals: Presence of factorial(var_2 - 1) where var_2 can be large, while its result is not used in any subsequent computation.
Observed pattern that the inner loops are implementing falling factorials divided by factorial(e), which is exactly a binomial coefficient C(n + e - 1, e).
Lack of modular reduction around large multiplications, implying unnecessarily large intermediate big integers.
Known constraints from similar contest problems (n up to around 1e9) that make computing factorial(n) directly impossible.
pitfalls: func_2 performs integer division in the binomial computation before applying modulo. This is safe only because the binomial coefficient is an integer and divisions are exact; one must not apply modulo to numerator or denominator before the division unless modular inverses are used.

Although mod is applied in the outer loop, func_2 itself can still create relatively large integers if parameters grow; if constraints on n or e increased significantly, it would be safer to interleave modulo reductions inside func_2 as well.
Trial division factorization is only viable while m is up to about 1e9–1e12; for significantly larger m, a faster factorization method or precomputed primes would be required.

Using int(sqrt(var_9)) + 1 as an upper bound is correct, but care must be taken that var_9 mutates during factorization; recomputing the bound dynamically could shave some iterations but is not necessary at these scales.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical scheduling/greedy problem from contest platforms; O(n log n) with n up to ~1e5–2e5 is standard. Input is n tasks with (duration, deadline), check feasibility by sorting by deadline and accumulating durations.

dominant_ops: Reading n lines of pairs via input() and int conversion: O(n)
Sorting the list of tasks: O(n log n)
Single pass to accumulate durations and compare to deadlines: O(n)

complexity.why: All helper functions and extra imports are negligible compared to building an array of n tasks and sorting it. The sort on func_2 dominates with O(n log n) time, and storing all tasks uses O(n) additional space.

bottlenecks.detail: Sorting func_2 (the list of [deadline, duration] pairs) is O(n log n) and is the main cost. This is expected and necessary for the greedy scheduling approach.

Per-line input is taken via input() inside a helper (func_1) called in a loop. The extra Python function call for each line adds overhead compared to inlining the parsing, though it does not change Big-O.

Large import list (math, itertools, bisect, copy, deque, Counter, Decimal) and several unused helper functions (func_2, func_3, func_5, func_6, func_7) slightly increase load/parse time and clutter the namespace, though they have no asymptotic impact.

int(eval(input())) is used for reading n. eval introduces unnecessary parsing overhead and potential safety issues; using int(input()) would be faster and safer. This is only done once, so its impact on performance is minor here.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the same greedy algorithm (sort tasks by deadline, accumulate durations, fail if any prefix exceeds its deadline) but remove unused helpers/imports and inline input parsing and sorting criteria to reduce constant-factor overhead and improve clarity.

complexity.why: The fast version still reads n tasks, sorts them (now by specifying a key on deadline), and performs one linear pass to validate feasibility. Sorting remains the dominant O(n log n) step, and storing all tasks requires O(n) space.

complexity_delta.from: O(n log n)
complexity_delta.to: O(n log n)
complexity_delta.note: Both implementations use the same greedy scheduling strategy with the same asymptotic complexity. Improvements are in constant factors, readability, and removal of unused code rather than algorithmic changes.

transformation_steps: Remove unused imports (sys, math, itertools, bisect, copy, deque, Counter, Decimal) and helper functions (func_2, func_3, func_5, func_6, func_7) that were never called.
Inline input parsing for tasks: replace calling func_1() inside the loop with direct list(map(int, input().split())), removing a function-call layer per task.

Simplify data representation: in the fast code each task is stored as [duration, deadline] and sorted with key=lambda v: v[1]; in the original code tasks were stored as [deadline, duration] and sorted by default. Both result in tasks ordered by deadline, but the key-based sort makes the intention explicit.
Remove extraneous global variables and settings (sys.setrecursionlimit, var_3, var_8) that are unused in this solution.
Retain the core greedy check loop but rename variables for more straightforward accumulation (var_2) and immediate exit on failure.
trigger_signals: Presence of many unused imports and helper functions relative to the actual logic used.
Per-iteration helper calls for trivial operations (like reading and splitting input) in tight loops.
Use of generic list.sort() on two-element lists without an explicit key, obscuring the intent of sorting by deadline.
Global configuration such as recursion limit and gcd helper that are not relevant to a non-recursive, non-number-theoretic solution.
pitfalls: Both versions still use int(eval(input())) for the first integer; replacing this with int(input()) would remove unnecessary overhead and potential security issues, even if those are not critical in contest environments.

Changing the internal representation of tasks (from [deadline, duration] to [duration, deadline]) requires carefully updating indices in the sort key and in the accumulation loop; mixing indices can lead to subtle logic bugs.
Optimizing away helper functions should not change behavior; ensure that the inlined code preserves the same parsing semantics (number of integers per line, their order, and types).
Any attempt to micro-optimize beyond this (e.g., custom sort or avoiding list allocation) is unlikely to yield meaningful gains relative to the O(n log n) sorting cost and may hurt code clarity.

constraints_guess.notes: Input is an index K (up to about 1e5) of 'Lunlun' numbers (integers whose adjacent digits differ by at most 1). Output is the K-th such number. All answers < 3.3e9 (fits in 10 digits).

dominant_ops: Per-call construction of a 3D DP table var_5 of size O(D * 2 * 11), where D = number of digits of var_12
Triple nested loops over var_8 in {0,1}, var_9 in [0..9], var_11 in [var_9-1..var_9+1] for each digit position (transition step of digit DP)
Outer loop over digit positions var_7 from 1 to D-1
Binary search loop calling func_2 O(log MAX_VAL) times
Final summation over last DP layer to count valid numbers

complexity.why: For a given mid value var_12 (≤ 3.234566667e9), its digit length D ≤ 10. Inside func_2, DP transitions run in O(D * constant) because loops are over small fixed ranges (10 digits, 2 tight/loose states, ±1 neighbors). Binary search over [0, 3234566667] takes O(log MAX_VAL) ≈ 32 iterations, so total is O(D * log MAX_VAL) operations, effectively constant for the given bounds. The DP table var_5 has size (D+1) * 2 * 11 = O(D) states, so memory is linear in the number of digits, i.e., constant for this problem.

bottlenecks.detail: Each call to func_2 allocates a fresh 3D list var_5 of size (D+1)×2×11, incurring Python list and object allocation overhead O(D) per binary search step.

Inner DP transitions are implemented with three nested Python loops (over var_8, var_9, var_11) and multiple Python-level integer operations and condition checks, which have relatively high constant factors even though the iteration counts are small.
The DP recomputes counts from scratch for each mid in the binary search, rather than reusing any structure across calls, leading to repeated O(D) work about 30+ times.

The digit-DP + binary-search approach solves a counting problem for all N up to MAX_VAL, whereas the task only needs the K-th Lunlun number for a relatively small K (≤1e5), so the algorithm does more general work than necessary.

FastAudit.core_idea: Generate Lunlun numbers directly in increasing digit-length layers starting from 1–9, by extending each current number with allowable next digits (last_digit-1, last_digit, last_digit+1 where valid). Maintain a global set of generated numbers until at least K distinct numbers exist, then sort them and return the (K-1)-indexed element.

complexity.why: Each Lunlun number is generated at most once in the iterative process; from each current frontier value var_4 we generate at most 3 children (or 2 at the boundaries 0/9), so the total number of generated values is Θ(K). Insertions into Python sets are average O(1), making the generation loop O(K). At the end, sorted(list(var_2)) sorts K elements, which costs O(K log K). The space used is dominated by storing all generated numbers in var_2 and var_5, both O(K).

complexity_delta.from: O(D * log MAX_VAL) time, O(D) space (digit DP + binary search, effectively constant for these constraints)
complexity_delta.to: O(K log K) time, O(K) space (direct generation plus final sort)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically in terms of K, the new method has higher theoretical complexity but avoids per-call DP table creation and multiple passes; it leverages simple arithmetic and set operations, which can be performant and is conceptually simpler for the problem's actual constraint range (K up to about 1e5).

transformation_steps: Eliminate binary search over the answer range [0, 3234566667] and the associated digit DP counting routine func_2.
Reformulate the problem as constructive generation of Lunlun numbers, starting from base digits 1–9.
Maintain two sets: var_5 for the current frontier (numbers of the current length) and var_2 for all accumulated Lunlun numbers.

For each number in the current frontier, obtain its last digit and append allowed neighbors (last_digit-1, last_digit, last_digit+1) as next digits to form new candidates, adding them into the next frontier set var_6.
Iterate frontier expansion until the size of var_2 reaches or exceeds K, ensuring that there are at least K generated Lunlun numbers.
Replace the counting-and-compare strategy with a direct selection: sort the accumulated set var_2 and return the (K-1)-th element of the sorted list.
trigger_signals: The recognition that the underlying task is the well-known 'K-th Lunlun number' problem, which has a standard constructive solution via BFS-like generation.
Single-query input (only one K) with K relatively small (around 1e5), making direct enumeration feasible within time and memory limits.
Original approach uses non-trivial digit DP and repeated binary search calls, suggesting over-engineering compared to simpler state enumeration.
DP table indices and transitions are somewhat opaque, which can hinder maintainability; a generation-based approach closely matches the definition of Lunlun numbers and is easier to reason about.
pitfalls: Using a set for var_2 loses numeric order; explicit sorting is required at the end, which introduces the O(K log K) factor and must not be forgotten.

The approach stores all generated Lunlun numbers up to the K-th; if K were much larger (e.g., ≥1e6–1e7), memory and sort time might become an issue compared to a streaming/BFS solution using a queue without a global set.
Relying on sets assumes that duplicates are either not generated or are acceptable to deduplicate; the transition logic must be correct to avoid unintended duplication or omission of valid numbers.
The use of eval(input()) is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; for competitive programming environments this usually works but int(input()) is safer and has slightly less overhead.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style pair counting: n up to ~2e5, values up to ~2e5. Original code allocates an array of size 10**7, suggesting an upper bound around that scale for i + a[i].

dominant_ops: Allocation of a large zero-initialized list of length 10**7
Single pass over n elements with constant-time list indexing and updates

complexity.why: Time is dominated by initializing var_4 = [0] * 10**7 (O(M), M = 10**7) plus an O(n) loop over the input; space is dominated by the 10**7-element list regardless of actual n or value ranges.

bottlenecks.detail: var_4 = [0] * 10**7 is ~80MB of integers in CP Python, which risks MLE and increases GC/cache pressure, especially if n is much smaller than 10**7.
Zero-filling 10**7 elements has non-trivial startup cost even for small n, making the approach inefficient when the actual key space (i ± a[i]) is sparse.
The constant bound 10**7 is chosen to be "big enough"; if the true maximum of i + 1 + a[i] exceeds this, the code breaks, but if it is much smaller, the extra space/time is wasted.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace the large dense array used as a frequency table with two sparse hash maps (defaultdict) that count occurrences of i + a[i] and i - a[i], then sum over matching keys using frequency products. This keeps both time and space proportional to n instead of a fixed large upper bound.

complexity.why: Building var_1 and var_2 requires one pass over n elements with O(1) average-time hash operations. The second loop iterates over at most O(n) distinct keys. No large fixed-size array is allocated; memory tracks actual distinct values of i ± a[i], which is bounded by n.

complexity_delta.note: Eliminates dependence on a large constant bound for indices (10**7) by switching from a dense array to sparse hash maps keyed by i ± a[i]. This reduces both memory footprint and initialization time, especially when n << 10**7.

transformation_steps: Reinterpret the original condition (j + 1 + a[j] == i + 1 - a[i]) as j + a[j] == i - a[i], removing the constant offset and making the expressions symmetric.
Accumulate frequencies of i + a[i] into var_1 and frequencies of i - a[i] into var_2 using defaultdict(int), instead of indexing into a preallocated array.
Compute the number of valid pairs by iterating over keys in var_1, and for each key also present in var_2, add var_1[key] * var_2[key] to the answer.
Remove the fixed-size array var_4 and all index-bound checks tied to 10**7, letting the key space be implicitly bounded by input size via the dictionaries.
trigger_signals: Presence of a very large fixed array var_4 = [0] * 10**7 despite an input-dependent effective key range.
Key expressions (i + 1 ± a[i]) are linear in the index and value, suggesting they may be sparsely populated over the 0..10**7 range.
Risk of MLE/TLE in competitive programming contexts due to the 10**7-scale allocation for Python ints.
Overall logic is pure frequency matching on transformed indices, which is naturally expressible with hash maps.
pitfalls: Using list(var_1.items()) creates an extra list; while still O(n), it adds overhead and memory usage. Iterating directly over var_1.items() would be slightly more efficient.
Hash map operations are O(1) on average but can degrade in adversarial cases; for competitive programming inputs this is typically acceptable.
Care must be taken to maintain the correct 0/1-based index offsets when transforming from (i + 1 ± a[i]) to (i ± a[i]); an off-by-one error would silently change the set of counted pairs.

eval(input()) is unnecessary and can be unsafe in general; int(input()) is adequate and avoids parsing arbitrary expressions, though this does not materially affect performance in this specific context.

constraints_guess.notes: Single list of jobs (time, deadline); typical scheduling/greedy problem, likely up to 1e5–2e5 jobs based on use of sorting and fast I/O patterns.

dominant_ops: Reading N lines of two integers each
Sorting the list of N pairs by deadline
Single linear scan to accumulate processing time and compare to deadlines

complexity.why: All jobs are stored in memory and sorted by the second element (deadline). Sorting dominates with O(N log N); reading and the final loop are O(N).

bottlenecks.detail: Overall algorithm is already optimal for this classic scheduling feasibility check; no asymptotically faster exact method than sorting by deadline is known in this model.
Uses sys.stdin.readline, which is already fast; no real I/O bottleneck for typical contest constraints, but repeated helper functions add tiny overhead (negligible vs sort).
Stores all N pairs before processing; for extremely large N this requires O(N) memory, but this is standard and required by the sort-based approach.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the same greedy algorithm: read all (time, deadline) pairs, sort by deadline, then accumulate processing times in order and ensure accumulated time never exceeds the current deadline.

complexity.why: Still reads and stores all N jobs, sorts them by deadline using sorted(), then performs a single O(N) pass. As in the original, sorting dominates.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N log N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: The algorithm and asymptotic complexity are unchanged. The main differences are in I/O style and minor control-flow refactoring; these do not improve complexity and may slightly hurt constant factors due to eval() and slower input().

transformation_steps: Replaced sys.stdin.readline-based helpers with direct input() calls.
Replaced func_7() + list comprehension of tuples with direct list(map(int, input().split())) building a list of lists.
Replaced in-place list.sort(...) with sorted(...), which produces a new list but has the same O(N log N) complexity.
Removed the explicit boolean flag var_6 and final conditional print in favor of a for-else pattern that prints "No" on early failure and "Yes" if the loop completes.
Introduced eval(input()) instead of plain int(input()).
trigger_signals: Desire for shorter or more idiomatic-looking code (for-else instead of a flag, fewer helper functions).
Misconception that using sorted() or list literals instead of tuples materially impacts performance.
