constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: choose integer p minimizing sum_i (a_i - p)^2. Usual constraints: 1 <= n <= 100, a_i in a small bounded range (e.g., 1..100). No separate queries; single computation on one array.

dominant_ops: Triple-nested looping over candidate p values and array elements: an outer loop over a value-range [min(a), max(a)], inside which a full search over the same value-range is repeated, and each candidate p evaluates sum of squared differences over all n elements.

complexity.why: Let n = len(var_7), R = max(a) - min(a) + 1. Sorting costs O(n log n). The outer loop over var_4 runs R times but does not use var_4; inside, it computes one O(n) sum (for p = min) and then a loop over var_2 with ~R iterations, each doing an O(n) sum. Per outer iteration: O(n + Rn) = O(Rn). Multiplied by R outer iterations gives O(R^2 n). Space is dominated by storing the n-element array.

bottlenecks.detail: The outer loop over var_4 in range(var_7[0], var_7[-1] + 1) does not use var_4 and repeats the entire inner search for the best p R times, multiplying work by a factor of R.
Loop variable var_4 is never referenced in the body. Its sole effect is to cause recomputation of identical sums, a classic signal of redundant looping.

The effective search over candidate p is done in the inner loop over var_2 from min+1 to max-1. Combined with the redundant outer range loop, this yields a quadratic dependence on the value range, R^2, instead of linear.
var_7.sort() is used only to access min and max; sorting incurs O(n log n) though min and max can be obtained in O(n) without sorting.
Using eval(input()) to read an integer is both slower and unsafe compared to int(input()), though this is a minor performance issue compared to the algorithmic redundancy.

FastAudit.core_idea: Eliminate the redundant outer loop and restrict the candidate p search to a fixed small range (1..100). For each candidate p, compute the sum of squared differences in a single pass over the n elements and track the minimum.

complexity.why: The modified code loops var_1 from 0 to 99 (C = 100 candidate p values). For each p, it performs one inner loop over the n elements to accumulate the squared differences. That yields O(C * n) operations; with C treated as a constant (100), this is linear in n. No sort or extra nested range loop remains; space is still just the array of n integers.

complexity_delta.from: O(R^2 * n + n log n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(100 * n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: By removing the unused outer loop and replacing a data-dependent candidate range [min, max] × [min, max] with a fixed 1..100 range, the modified version avoids the R^2 factor. Under the assumption that the optimal p lies in this fixed range, the runtime becomes effectively linear in n with a small constant.

transformation_steps: Remove the outer for-loop over var_4, which did not influence the computation and only caused repeating the same search multiple times.
Drop the inner loop over var_2 spanning [min(a) + 1, max(a) - 1]; instead, use a single loop over a fixed set of candidate integer p values (here 1..100).
For each candidate p, compute the cost sum_i (a_i - p)^2 in one pass over the array and maintain the minimum cost seen so far.
Avoid sorting the input array; simply read the values into a list and operate directly on them.
Initialize the current best cost to a large sentinel (var_4 = 10000000) and update it if a lower cost is found.
trigger_signals: Presence of a loop whose index (var_4) is never used inside the loop body, indicating redundant repeated computation.
Triple-nested loops with two loops effectively spanning the same numeric range of candidate p values, implying a potential R^2 blow-up in operations.
Sorting used only to obtain min and max values, suggesting unnecessary O(n log n) overhead on top of heavy nested loops.
Recomputing the same structure of sums from scratch many times without any change that would affect the result, a common pattern behind time limit exceed errors.
pitfalls: Hard-coding the candidate p range to 1..100 assumes all relevant a_i and the optimal p lie in that interval; if inputs can be outside that range, results become incorrect even though faster.
The modified solution still reads n via eval(input()), which is unsafe and slower than int(input()); while not the main performance issue, it is a bad practice.

If actual constraints allow a much larger value range for a_i, the correct approach is to either search p in [min(a), max(a)] (O(R * n)) or exploit the fact that the minimizing p is near the mean of a_i, rather than hard-coding 100.

If n or the value range grow in future problem variants, assuming C = 100 as a constant may silently break correctness; such optimizations must be validated against the specification, not just typical tests.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style combinatorics with MOD=998244353. Expect n (here var_8) and m (var_5) up to ~2e5, k (var_6) up to MOD. Single test, no queries.

dominant_ops: Python built-in pow(base, exp, MOD) with varying exponent inside the main loop
Repeated modular inverses via Fermat: pow(i+1, MOD-2, MOD) per iteration
Big-integer modular multiplications and additions in a tight Python loop

complexity.time: O(m * (log MOD + log n)) where m = var_5
complexity.why: Loop runs m+1 times. Each iteration calls pow(var_6-1, var_7-var_4-1, MOD) whose cost is O(log(var_7-var_4-1)) ⊆ O(log n), and pow(var_4+1, MOD-2, MOD) which is O(log MOD). Other arithmetic is O(1) per step. No arrays depending on n or m are allocated, so extra space is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: pow(var_6 - 1, var_7 - var_4 - 1, var_1) recomputes (k-1)^(n-i-1) from scratch each iteration, costing O(log n) per loop.
pow(var_4 + 1, var_1 - 2, var_1) computes modular inverse of (i+1) using exponent MOD-2 in every iteration, an O(log MOD) cost per step.
The combination of multiple pow calls and big-int multiplications in a Python for-loop stresses the time limit for large m (≈2e5).

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid per-iteration exponentiation by (1) maintaining the power term k*(k-1)^{...} multiplicatively using a precomputed inverse of (k-1), and (2) precomputing modular inverses 1..m in O(m) via the linear recurrence inv[i] = -(MOD//i)*inv[MOD%i] % MOD. This lets us update binomial coefficients C(n-1, i) iteratively with O(1) work per step.

complexity.why: The main loop still runs m times, but all heavy pow calls are removed from the loop. We precompute inv[i] for i = 1..m in O(m) using a simple recurrence. Each iteration then does only O(1) modular multiplications and additions. An array of size m+1 is used to store inverses, yielding O(m) extra space.

complexity_delta.from: O(m * (log MOD + log n)) time, O(1) extra space
complexity_delta.to: O(m) time, O(m) extra space
complexity_delta.note: Time is improved by eliminating per-iteration exponentiation and Fermat inverses at the cost of storing an inverse table of size m+1.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the expression being summed is k * C(n-1, i) * (k-1)^{n-1-i} for i from 0 to m, i.e., a combinatorial sum over binomial coefficients and powers.
Replace repeated pow(var_6-1, var_7-var_4-1, MOD) with a single initial power var_10 = k*(k-1)^{n-1} and then iteratively multiply by the modular inverse of (k-1) each loop: var_10 *= inv(k-1).
Precompute inv[k] = (k-1)^{MOD-2} once outside the loop via pow(var_6-1, MOD-2, MOD), and reuse it in each iteration instead of calling pow(..., ..., MOD) repeatedly.
Replace per-iteration modular inverses pow(i+1, MOD-2, MOD) with a linear-time inverse table inv[1..m] built using the recurrence inv[i] = -(MOD//i)*inv[MOD%i] % MOD with inv[1] = 1.

Update binomial coefficients C(n-1, i) multiplicatively using inv[i]: maintain var_9 = C(n-1, i) with var_9 = var_9 * (n - i) * inv[i] % MOD instead of recomputing via factorials or expensive operations.
Special-case the k=1 scenario (var_6 == 1 and n-1 == m) where the formula collapses to 1, avoiding invalid inverse computations and potential corner-case errors.
Accumulate the answer incrementally in var_11, ensuring all intermediate values are reduced modulo MOD to keep integers small and operations fast.
trigger_signals: Presence of pow(base, exponent, MOD) inside a loop where the base and MOD are constant but the exponent changes linearly with the loop index.
Pattern pow(x, MOD-2, MOD) appearing in a loop, signaling repeated computation of modular inverses via Fermat's little theorem.
A combinatorial-looking update of a running coefficient var_3 (or var_9) that resembles a binomial coefficient recurrence.
Use of 998244353, a standard NTT-friendly prime, strongly suggesting intended O(n) or O(n log n) combinatorial solutions with precomputed inverses.
Large possible bounds on m (var_5) inferred from typical contest settings (≈2e5), making O(m log MOD) Python solutions risky.
pitfalls: Incorrect handling of the k=1 edge case: (k-1) has no modular inverse, so trying to precompute inv(k-1) would fail; this is why the fast code explicitly returns 1 when k=1 and n-1=m.
Off-by-one errors in the binomial update: var_9 = var_9 * (n - i) * inv[i] % MOD must align exactly with C(n-1, i); mis-indexing i or using wrong upper bounds will change the combinatorial factor.
Building the inverse table requires careful indexing: inv[0] is unused and must not be referenced by the recurrence, and the recurrence must be computed up to at least m.
Forgetting to apply modulo after multiplications can cause extremely large Python integers, hurting performance and possibly memory.
Using max(1, ...) incorrectly: it is used here only to avoid touching index 0; replacing it or altering its logic without understanding the inverse recurrence can silently break correctness.
Assuming constraints too small and keeping pow in the loop; this might pass small tests but will likely TLE on worst cases.

constraints_guess.notes: Likely AtCoder-style problem (similar to ABC110 D - Factorization): N (var_3/var_2) up to around 1e5, M (var_1) up to around 1e9. M has few prime factors, total exponent sum <= ~30.

dominant_ops: Prime factorization of M by trial division up to sqrt(M), then for each prime factor exponent computing a binomial coefficient via an O(N) loop with modular exponentiation per iteration.

complexity.why: The factorization loop `for var_5 in range(2, var_1 + 1)` breaks at sqrt(var_1), so O(sqrt(M)). The main cost is `func_1(var_7, var_6)` where var_6 = var_3 - 1 ≈ N-1. It loops from 1 to N-1 and on each iteration computes a modular inverse via `pow(var_5, var_2 - 2, var_2)` which is O(log MOD). This is done once per distinct prime factor (P is small but N can be large). The dictionary `var_8` stores at most P entries, so space is O(P).

bottlenecks.detail: Combination computation `func_1(var_7, var_6)` loops var_6 = N-1 times, even though the exponents of the prime factors are small (sum of exponents is O(log M)). This makes the cost scale linearly with N instead of with the much smaller exponents.

Each iteration in `func_1` calls `pow(var_5, var_2 - 2, var_2)` to compute a modular inverse, which is an O(log MOD) exponentiation. Doing this inside an O(N) loop leads to O(N log MOD) work per prime factor.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep trial-division factorization but rewrite the combinatorial part so that, for each prime exponent e, the binomial C(e+N-1, e) is computed by iterating only e times and using factorial(e) for division, instead of iterating N-1 times with modular inverses. This exploits that e is small while N may be large.

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + N log N + sum_e log e)
complexity.why: Factorization in `func_1(var_8)` still runs in O(sqrt(M)). For each prime with exponent e, the code builds a product of e terms (loop of length e) and divides by factorial(e); sum_e over all primes is O(log M), so these loops are tiny. However, the call `factorial(var_2 - 1)` is computed once and its result is never used; this is an O(N log N) big-integer operation and can dominate runtime for large N. Apart from this unnecessary factorial, the algorithmic core of the combination computation is O(sum_e) with small constants. Space remains O(P) for the factor-exponent map.

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(M) + P * N * log MOD)
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + N log N + sum_e log e)
complexity_delta.note: If the unused factorial(var_2 - 1) call is removed, the effective complexity becomes O(sqrt(M) + sum_e log e), which is typically much smaller than O(P * N * log MOD) because sum_e << N. As written, the extra factorial introduces an O(N log N) overhead that can offset or even outweigh the algorithmic gain.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the number of ways can be expressed as a product over prime factors of combinations C(e_i + N - 1, e_i), where e_i are the exponents of M's prime factors.
Change the combination computation to iterate over e_i multiplicative terms instead of over N-1 terms, reducing the inner-loop length from O(N) to O(e_i) per prime.

Replace repeated modular inverses inside the loop with integer arithmetic: build the numerator product as a standard Python integer, divide once by factorial(e_i) to form C(e_i + N - 1, e_i), then multiply into the global product and apply the modulus at the end.
Factorization logic is kept essentially the same (trial division up to sqrt(M)), but factored out into a helper function for clarity.
trigger_signals: A nested structure where an inner loop in `func_1` runs up to var_6 = N-1 for each prime factor, indicating potentially ~1e5 iterations times number of primes.
Use of `pow(x, MOD-2, MOD)` within a large loop, signaling many modular exponentiations and a likely hotspot.
Problem structure where the total exponent of prime factors of M is very small (O(log M)), suggesting that a formulation whose cost depends on exponents e_i instead of N would be far more efficient.

Presence of factorial-based or precomputation patterns in typical reference solutions for similar problems (binomial coefficients under modulo), hinting that direct O(N) loops for each combination are suboptimal.
pitfalls: In the modified code, `var_5 = factorial(var_2 - 1)` is computed but never used; for N up to ~1e5, this is an expensive O(N log N) big-integer operation and can negate the intended speedup. It should be removed.

Using plain Python factorial and big integers for large arguments without modular reduction can cause high memory usage and runtime; for larger constraints, it is safer to precompute factorials and inverse factorials modulo 1e9+7.

Performing integer division `var_3 // factorial(var_12)` before applying the modulus relies on exact divisibility (which holds mathematically for combinations) but can be numerically expensive because both numerator and denominator are large big integers.
If constraints were tighter on M (e.g., much larger than 1e9), trial division up to sqrt(M) could become the real bottleneck; a more advanced factorization method would then be needed.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case with two integers (n, m). m is up to about 1e9 (due to trial division to sqrt(m)); original solution precomputes factorials up to n+50, which suggests n could be as large as 1e5–1e9, motivating the optimization to avoid O(n) memory.

dominant_ops: Trial division prime factorization up to sqrt(m) with repeated division for each factor
Precomputation of factorials up to (n + 50) under modulo
Precomputation of inverse factorials up to (n + 50) under modulo
Final product of a small number of binomial coefficients using precomputed factorials

complexity.why: Factorization loop iterates up to about sqrt(m) with repeated divisions: O(√m). Then two linear passes to build factorial and inverse factorial arrays of size ~n+50 dominate when n is large: O(n) time and O(n) memory. The final loop over distinct prime exponents is tiny (sum of exponents is O(log m)), so its cost is negligible compared to factorial precomputation.

bottlenecks.detail: Two full linear passes over arrays of size ~n+50 to compute factorials and inverse factorials under modulo. For large n this becomes the main cost even though only O(log m) binomial coefficients are actually needed.
Stores two arrays of length ~n+50 (factorials and inverse factorials). If n is large (e.g., up to 1e7 or more), this is memory-heavy and can cause TLE/MLE or cache inefficiency.

To compute a product over a handful of combinations C(n + e_i - 1, e_i), the code precomputes factorials for all values up to n+50, even though only binomials with small e_i (sum e_i = O(log m)) are required.

Prime factorization via trial division up to int(sqrt(m)) is O(√m). While usually acceptable for m up to 1e9, this component becomes noticeable if m is near the upper bound; it is, however, not the primary bottleneck compared to O(n) factorial precomputation when n is large.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial and inverse-factorial precomputation by computing each binomial coefficient C(n + e - 1, e) multiplicatively as a short product using modular inverses on the fly, so total work depends on the sum of prime exponents of m (O(log m)) instead of n.

complexity.why: Factorization still uses trial division up to about sqrt(m): O(√m). For each prime exponent e, the code builds C(n + e - 1, e) via a loop of length e, performing a constant number of modular multiplications and one pow-based modular inverse per step: O(e · log MOD). The sum of exponents Σe is O(log m), so the overall binomial part costs O(log m · log MOD). No arrays of size n are allocated; only O(1) extra space is used.

to.time: O(√m + (Σe) · log MOD) ≈ O(√m + log m · log MOD)

complexity_delta.note: The dominant cost shifts from linear in n (factorial precomputation and storage) to depending only on the logarithmic sum of prime exponents of m. This is especially beneficial when n is large while m remains reasonably small (e.g., ≤ 1e9).

transformation_steps: Reformulate the combinatorial expression: recognize that the answer can be written as a product over prime exponents e of combinations C(n + e - 1, e) (stars and bars formulation).
Replace global factorial and inverse-factorial precomputation with an incremental formula for C(n + e - 1, e): C(n + e - 1, e) = product_{k=0..e-1} (n + e - 1 - k) / (k + 1).
Implement the division in modular arithmetic via Fermat's little theorem: for each term divide by (k + 1) using pow(k + 1, MOD-2, MOD) to get the modular inverse.
Turn the prime factorization into a generator function (func_1) that yields the exponent for each candidate factor, and iterate over these exponents directly, skipping work when the exponent is zero.
Eliminate the O(n) arrays (factorial and inverse-factorial tables) and their construction loops, reducing memory from O(n) to O(1) and avoiding linear-time precomputation.
trigger_signals: The presence of large arrays sized as n+50 and loops that touch each element even though the number of required binomial coefficients is small.
Constraints or problem context suggesting n can be significantly larger than log m, making O(n) precomputation disproportionate to the actual combinatorial work needed.
Use of factorial-based binomial computation in a context where only combinations with small second argument e are needed, indicating a mismatch between implementation cost and mathematical structure.
Potential memory pressure or timeouts when scaling n upward, detectable via profiling or from problem constraints.
pitfalls: Each modular inverse pow(var_6 + 1, MOD - 2, MOD) is O(log MOD); if Σe were large (e.g., m huge with many factors), this could become costly. For current constraints (m around 1e9), Σe is small and this is safe.

The fast factorization loop in func_1 uses the condition while var_6 * var_6 <= var_7 (original m) instead of the shrinking var_8; this does not worsen asymptotic complexity but may waste iterations compared to using the reduced value.
The generator func_1 yields exponent counts, including zeros for non-dividing candidates; callers must ensure they skip any O(e)-size work when e=0 (as the provided code does via range(var_5)).
Modular inverses via pow(x, MOD-2, MOD) assume MOD is prime and x is not divisible by MOD. Changing the modulus or allowing x to be a multiple of MOD would break correctness.

Directly translating this pattern to languages or environments with slower big-integer exponentiation or without built-in pow with modular exponentiation may change the performance balance; in such cases, batch precomputation of inverses might be more efficient.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style constraints: N up to ~1e5, M up to ~1e9 or slightly larger (fits in 64-bit). Only one query (single test case).

dominant_ops: Trial division prime factorization up to sqrt(M)
Precomputation of factorials up to N+50 under modulo
Precomputation of inverse factorials up to N+50 under modulo
O(1) binomial coefficient evaluation per prime exponent using precomputed tables

complexity.why: Prime factorization loop runs up to O(sqrt(M)). Factorial and inverse-factorial arrays are size O(N), built with linear loops. The number of distinct prime factors and exponents is tiny, so the final product over exponents is negligible in comparison.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorials and inverse factorials are precomputed up to N+50 even though the number of binomial coefficients required is equal only to the number of distinct prime factors of M (typically <= 9 for M <= 1e9). This introduces an O(N) cost regardless of how small the exponents are.
Two arrays of size N+50 are maintained (factorial and inverse factorial), each storing Python ints modulo 1e9+7, which is unnecessary when only a handful of combinations are needed.
Every step of factorial / inverse factorial precomputation uses modular multiplication, which is relatively costly compared to a small number of big-int multiplications when exponents are small.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial / inverse factorial precomputation by computing each required binomial coefficient directly using integer arithmetic based on the small exponents obtained from prime factorization, then taking modulo at the end.

complexity.why: Prime factorization remains O(sqrt(M)). The exponents e_i of the prime factors of M are small; the total sum of exponents is O(log M). For each exponent e_i, func_1 computes C(N+e_i-1, e_i) via products of length e_i for numerator and denominator. No O(N) precomputation is performed, so time and space depend only on the factorization, not on N.

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(M) + N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + sum(e_i)) time, O(sum(e_i)) space
complexity_delta.note: Since sum(e_i) is typically O(log M) and independent of N, the modified approach removes the linear dependence on N, which dominates for large N.

transformation_steps: Replace exponent-counting factorization with a factor-list factorization (func_2) and use collections.Counter to derive exponents; complexity remains O(sqrt(M)) but logic is modularized.
Remove global factorial and inverse factorial precomputation arrays sized O(N).
Introduce func_1(n, k) that computes binomial coefficients directly using products over k terms in numerator and denominator with Python big integers, and returns the exact integer C(n, k).
In func_3, for each prime exponent e, call func_1(N + e - 1, e), then multiply the result into the running answer modulo 1e9+7, avoiding modular inverse/table lookups entirely.
Short-circuit the special case M == 1 (no prime factors) to immediately output 1, saving unnecessary work.
trigger_signals: Observation that the number of required binomial coefficients is equal to the number of distinct prime factors of M, which is very small (typically <= 9 for M up to 1e9).
Recognition that factorial precomputation up to N+50 is O(N) and dominates running time when N is large but sum of exponents is small.
Realization that direct combinatorial computation using big integers is feasible because k (each exponent) is small, making the product loops short and the big-int sizes moderate.
pitfalls: The direct binomial computation in func_1 uses exact integer arithmetic and can become extremely slow or memory-hungry if exponents e_i grow large; the optimization relies on exponents being small (which holds for this problem but might not generalize).

Building lists via list(range(...)) in func_1 adds overhead; while safe here due to tiny lengths, it would be inefficient for larger k. An iterator-based or incremental product would be preferable in more general settings.
The factorial-based original method scales better when many binomial coefficients are required or when k can be large; replacing it with direct products in such contexts would be a regression.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case. Indices and a[i] small enough that i + a[i] stays below ~4e5 (as seen from fixed array size 400005). Typical AtCoder-style constraints (n up to 2e5).

dominant_ops: Reading input using eval(input()) and input() (slow text parsing and unnecessary expression parsing)
Initializing var_4 with 400005 append operations
Single pass over n elements updating and querying the frequency array var_4

complexity.time: O(K + n) where K = 400005; effectively O(n) for asymptotics but with a large fixed constant and slow I/O
complexity.space: O(K) for the frequency array var_4
complexity.why: The code first performs a loop of length 400005 to build var_4 (O(K)), then a loop over n elements to do constant-time array lookups and updates (O(n)). K is fixed but large; combined with slow eval(input()) and input(), this hurts performance.

bottlenecks.detail: Use of eval(input()) is significantly slower than plain integer parsing and is unsafe; plain input() is slower than buffered sys.stdin.readline for large inputs.
var_4 is initialized via a Python loop with append 400005 times instead of using list multiplication ([0] * 400005), incurring extra Python-level overhead.
The array size 400005 is scanned in full even if n is much smaller, wasting time on unnecessary operations when n << 4e5.

FastAudit.core_idea: Transform the condition into two derived sequences: L[i] = i - a[i] and R[i] = i + a[i]. Count how many times each R value occurs using a hash map (defaultdict), then for each L[i], sum the frequency of the same value in R. This counts all valid pairs in a single pass using hashing.

complexity.why: Building lists var_3 and var_4 takes O(n), populating the defaultdict with counts of var_4 is O(n), and summing var_11[var_9] over var_3 is another O(n). Hash operations are amortized O(1), so the overall complexity is linear in n. Space is O(n) for the two lists plus the dictionary.

complexity_delta.from: O(K + n) time, O(K) space with slow I/O (K = 400005 fixed initialization cost)
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space with faster buffered I/O and hash-based counting
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time is effectively linear in both versions, but the optimized code removes the large fixed initialization loop and uses faster I/O and more direct list/dictionary operations, improving constant factors and practicality under tight time limits.

transformation_steps: Replace eval(input()) with strict integer parsing using sys.stdin.readline() and int().
Switch from input() to a buffered reader (sys.stdin.readline) to reduce per-line overhead.
Avoid manual loop-based array initialization; either switch to [0] * needed_size or, as in the optimized version, use a dictionary keyed by i + a[i] instead of a large fixed array.
Reformulate the counting logic using two derived arrays (i - a[i] and i + a[i]) and a hash map to count frequencies, enabling a clean linear pass.
Use list comprehensions for building derived sequences and for the final summation to leverage optimized C-level loops.
trigger_signals: Use of eval(input()) for reading integers (red flag for performance and safety).
Fixed-size loop of 400005 iterations regardless of n, suggesting unnecessary work.
Manual Python-level list building via append in a large loop instead of using vectorized-like constructions.
Problem pattern matching a classic frequency-counting / hashing solution where O(n) hash map logic is natural.
pitfalls: If the bounds on i + a[i] or i - a[i] were larger than expected, the fixed-size array approach (slow_code) would break or silently ignore valid pairs; the dictionary-based approach (fast_code) avoids this but uses more memory for very large n.
Misusing eval for input parsing is both a security risk and a performance trap; it should be entirely avoided in competitive programming.
While both solutions are O(n) in time, relying solely on Big-O can hide constant-factor issues like large fixed loops and slow I/O that cause TLE in practice.
Care must be taken to keep all hash-map accesses within amortized O(1) expectations; extremely adversarial patterns could cause degradation, though this is usually not an issue in contest settings.

constraints_guess.notes: Sequence DP over indices; inner window-based search suggests n up to around 1e5–2e5. Values can be up to about max(a[i]) ~ 1e5–1e9 but are later used in a segment tree of size max(a)+1 after possible coordinate compression.

dominant_ops: For each index i, iterate j over a fixed backward window (i-99 .. i) and check abs(a[i] - a[j]) <= D
Compute max(dp[j]) over the window in pure Python using a generator expression
Random-access reads/writes on large Python lists for dp and the value array

complexity.why: The outer loop runs for each of n positions (var_3 in range(var_6)). For each position, a generator iterates at most W ≈ 100 previous indices (range(var_3 - 99, var_3 + 1)) to compute a max subject to a value difference predicate. Thus the overall complexity is O(n * W). The dp array var_2 and value array var_1 are both O(n).

bottlenecks.detail: Transition dp[i] = 1 + max_{j in window and |a[i]-a[j]|<=D} dp[j] is implemented by a linear scan over the window for each i, which becomes O(n * W). If W grows with n or constraints are tight (e.g., W ~ 1e5), this becomes effectively quadratic and will time out.

Even with W ≈ 100, the inner Python loop does heavy work: loop control + abs + comparison + max evaluation for each j, giving roughly 100 operations per index over n up to ~2e5, which can be borderline in Python under strict time limits.

A huge preallocated dp array var_2 = [0] * 6**8 (≈1.7M entries) is used as a safety cushion. This increases memory usage and cache footprint unnecessarily if the actual n is much smaller, slightly harming locality and performance.
Use of a Python generator expression inside max for every position i adds overhead: generator creation, iteration protocol, and Python-level function calls for abs and comparisons.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace the per-position linear scan over the backward window with logarithmic-time range queries on a segment tree keyed by value (or by dp length). Maintain for each value (or value bucket) the best index/DP achievable, allowing queries over all values within [a[i]-D, a[i]+D] and updates when processing each new position. This turns the DP transition from O(W) per index to O(log M), where M is the size of the value domain or compressed coordinate range.

complexity.why: The segment tree Class_1 is built over an array of length roughly max(a)+1 (or the number of compressed coordinates), giving M leaves and O(M) build time. Each DP step performs an O(log M) range query (func_1) and an O(log M) point update (func_2). Doing this for n indices gives O(n log M). Additional per-value sets or buckets (var_9) cost O(n) total. Memory is dominated by the tree O(M) plus DP/index bookkeeping O(n).

complexity_delta.from: O(n * W) time, O(n) space (with W the backward window size, implemented by a linear scan per i)
complexity_delta.to: O(n log M) time, O(n + M) space (M is the size of the value domain or its compressed coordinate range)
complexity_delta.note: In practice, when W can be large (comparable to n), this moves from near-quadratic behavior to near-linearithmic. For small fixed W (≈100) complexity is theoretically similar but segment tree reduces worst-case risk and generalizes to larger windows/constraints.

transformation_steps: Recognize the DP recurrence structure: dp[i] depends only on a limited set of previous states filtered by both index window and value difference |a[i]-a[j]| <= D.
Observe that the limiting factor is finding max(dp[j]) under constraints efficiently, which is a range-maximum (or range-minimum over positions) query problem in the value space, not index space.
Introduce a segment tree (Class_1) supporting associative operations (here min or max) with identity element, enabling O(log M) range queries and updates.
Map value constraints |a[i]-a[j]| <= D into an index range on the segment tree by using value as the tree index (possibly after coordinate compression to ensure a compact [0..M) domain).

For each i: query the segment tree over the interval [a[i]-D, a[i]+D] to obtain the best previous DP candidate, compute dp[i], and update the tree at position a[i] (or appropriate bucket) with the new information.

Optionally maintain auxiliary per-DP-length sets or per-value sets (var_9) to tie together indices and DP lengths, allowing the segment tree to store minimal index achieving each DP length and support updates/removals efficiently.

Replace slow generator-based max over a Python loop with iterative or iterative-recursive segment tree logic implemented in tight loops inside Class_1.func_1 and func_2, minimizing Python overhead and exploiting array-based tree representation.
trigger_signals: Nested loop where the inner loop scans a sliding window or prefix for each index, producing O(n * W) or O(n^2) operations under problem constraints.
Use of max(...) over a comprehension/generator that depends on the current index and ranges over many previous indices.
Constraints in the original problem statement indicating n up to ~1e5 or higher with unrestricted or large windows, making naive O(n^2) or heavy O(n * W) infeasible.
Value-based constraint |a[i]-a[j]| <= D suggesting that the data could be indexed by value in a balanced tree or segment tree for faster range queries.
Presence of explicit DP recurrence description in the editorial that mentions segment trees, Fenwick trees, or coordinate compression.
pitfalls: Segment tree indexing: off-by-one errors when converting between 0-based array indices, 1-based tree internals, and inclusive/exclusive range semantics in func_1 can produce subtle incorrect DP results.
Handling value bounds: the range [a[i]-D, a[i]+D] must be clamped to the valid value domain [0, max_value]; missing this can lead to index errors or missed candidates.

Coordinate compression: if values are large (e.g., up to 1e9), failing to compress them before building the tree leads to excessive memory usage. Conversely, incorrect compression mapping can break the range queries.

Identity element and operation choice: the segment tree is instantiated with min and an identity of var_3 (treated as INF). Choosing the wrong identity or operation (min vs max) leads to incorrect DP transitions.

Initial conditions: the tree must be initialized correctly so that positions with no valid previous state do not falsely influence DP (e.g., INF for min-based structures or 0/-INF for max-based ones).

Performance in Python: although asymptotically faster, a poorly implemented segment tree (e.g., recursive recursion for each query) can negate gains. Iterative implementations and tight loops over preallocated lists, as in Class_1, are important.

Negative index tricks: the slow code uses negative indexing semantics with an oversized array as a hack to avoid bounds checks. Reusing such tricks in the optimized solution would be dangerous and harder to reason about; explicit bounds handling is safer.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AOJ-style problem: given N and S, count triples (a,b,c) with 1 <= a < b < c <= N and a + b + c = S, repeated for multiple test cases until '0 0'. N and S likely up to around 1000.

dominant_ops: Triple nested for-loops over ranges up to N (var_6, var_4, var_2).
Per-iteration creation of a temporary list [var_6, var_4, var_2] and calling sum() on it.

complexity.why: Outer loop var_6 runs ~N times, middle loop var_4 runs O(N) times per var_6, inner loop var_2 runs O(N) times per (var_6, var_4). Total iterations ~sum_{i=1..N} sum_{j=i+1..N} (N-j) = O(N^3). Only a few scalar integers are stored, so auxiliary space is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: The triple nested loops produce O(N^3) iterations, which becomes too slow when N is up to ~1000 (10^9 iterations scale in Python).
The innermost loop body is extremely light but executed O(N^3) times, making Python loop overhead dominant.
Using sum([var_6, var_4, var_2]) allocates a new list and computes its sum in every inner iteration; this is significantly slower than a direct arithmetic comparison var_6 + var_4 + var_2 == var_7.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the structure a < b < c and a + b + c = S to remove one loop: fix the largest element c, derive b and a via arithmetic so that a + b is determined by S and c, then move (a, b) towards each other (a increases, b decreases) while maintaining a < b and counting valid positive solutions. This effectively turns the O(N^3) enumeration into an O(N^2) process.

complexity.why: The outer while loop iterates over possible values of c (var_1) from N down to roughly (S+1)/3, i.e., O(N) values. For each c, the inner while loop iterates over pairs (a, b) with a + b fixed, adjusting a and b until a >= b; this is O(N) steps in the worst case for each c. Combined, this yields O(N^2) iterations overall. Only a constant number of integers are stored.

complexity_delta.from: O(N^3) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N^2) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: The key improvement is eliminating the innermost loop by deriving and iteratively adjusting the remaining two variables for each fixed largest element.

transformation_steps: Recognize the mathematical structure: we are counting 1 <= a < b < c <= N such that a + b + c = S.
Fix the largest element c and observe that a + b = S - c. Because a < b and both are positive integers, we can start with an extreme pair (a, b) and walk inward.
For each fixed c, initialize b = c - 1 and a = S - c - b so that a + b remains constant and equal to S - c.
Iteratively adjust (a, b) via a++ and b-- while maintaining a + b = S - c; for each step where a > 0 and a < b, count a valid triple.
Stop the inner process when a >= b, because there are no further valid pairs (a, b) with a < b for this c.
Stop the outer loop when c <= a (equivalently, when c is no longer strictly larger than the smallest candidate a); the condition `if not var_1 > var_3: ... break` encodes this.
Avoid constructing temporary collections and calling sum() inside tight loops; use direct arithmetic with scalar variables instead.
trigger_signals: Presence of three nested loops over a similar range (1..N) where inner loop body is simple arithmetic and comparisons.
Constraints indicating N can be up to the low thousands, making N^3 ~ 10^9 iterations infeasible in Python.
The logical condition in the innermost loop is a simple equality on the sum of loop indices (i + j + k == S), which suggests algebraic relationships can eliminate a loop.
Repeated list allocation and sum() calls in the innermost loop, which are red flags for micro-inefficiencies on hot paths.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors in ranges when converting from inclusive mathematical bounds (1 <= a < b < c <= N) to Python range() semantics.
Forgetting to enforce the strict ordering a < b < c, which may cause overcounting if permutations of the same triple are counted separately.
Failing to ensure a > 0 when adjusting a and b; negative or zero values should not be counted as valid elements of the triple.
Incorrect termination conditions for the outer while loop (e.g., breaking too early or too late if the relationship between c and a is miscomputed).
Translating the optimized logic without preserving the invariant a + b + c = S on each inner iteration, which can silently change the counted set of triples.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style problem (ABC139 C: Lower). N up to about 2e5, values up to around 1e9.

dominant_ops: Reading N integers and doing a single pass of adjacent comparisons over the array.

complexity.why: The solution stores all N integers in a list and iterates once over N-1 adjacent pairs; no nested loops or extra data structures.

bottlenecks.detail: Uses input() and eval(input()) instead of buffered stdin.readline and int(), which is slower for large N.
Loads many unused modules (math, collections, decimal, etc.) and defines unused helper functions, increasing startup time and memory footprint.
Uses eval(input()) to read an integer, which is both slower and less safe than int(input()).

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep only the current and previous value while streaming the sequence from stdin, maintaining the length of the current non-increasing streak and its maximum, with minimal imports and faster I/O.

complexity.why: Still reads N integers into a list and scans them once, but with reduced constant factors due to faster I/O and fewer overheads.

delta_type: constant-factor optimization / I/O optimization (asymptotic complexity unchanged)

complexity_delta.from: Time O(N), Space O(N) with heavier constants (input(), many unused imports).
complexity_delta.to: Time O(N), Space O(N) with smaller constants (stdin.readline, trimmed imports, simpler loop).
complexity_delta.note: Algorithmic structure remains a single linear pass; improvements are mainly in I/O speed and reduced overhead.

transformation_steps: Replace input()-based reading with stdin.readline for the integer list to speed up input.
Remove unused imports and helper functions (factorial-based comb, divisor generator, etc.) to cut startup and memory overhead.
Switch from index-based adjacent comparisons to a streaming comparison using the last seen value and a current streak counter.
trigger_signals: Problem is a simple linear scan with N up to around 1e5–2e5, making Python I/O a frequent bottleneck.
Presence of many heavy but unused imports in a small logic problem.
Use of eval(input()) where a simple int(input()) would suffice, indicating unnecessary overhead and risk.
pitfalls: Initializing the previous value to 1e9+7 assumes all inputs are <= 1e9+7; if an element is larger, the first comparison logic changes and can undercount the initial streak.
The modified code ignores the provided N and trusts the second line length; malformed input could lead to inconsistent behavior.
Mixing input() and stdin.readline() works here but can be confusing; using a single input method consistently is safer.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style constraint: n up to about 1e5, each ai up to around 1e9, product must not exceed 1e18 or output -1. Single test case, one array read.

dominant_ops: Reading n integers into a list via sys.stdin
Single pass over the list to multiply elements and check product > 1e18
Second pass-style operation via `0 in var_3` to test for zero

complexity.why: The code reads n integers into a list (O(n)). It then loops once over all elements to multiply and compare against 1e18 (O(n) multiplications and comparisons). After that, `0 in var_3` performs a linear scan over the list (O(n)), so the total is O(n) with a constant factor of about two passes. The list storage is O(n).

bottlenecks.detail: Two traversals of the array in the worst case: one for the product computation and another for checking if 0 is in the list. This doubles the linear scan cost, though still O(n).
Large set of unused imports (bisect, math, itertools, collections, array) and helper lambdas add module import overhead at startup, which can be noticeable but still small relative to O(n) loop cost.
Zero handling is deferred until after the product loop; when zeros are present, the multiplications are unnecessary, though they do not affect asymptotic complexity.

FastAudit.core_idea: Strip template overhead and simplify logic: read and ignore n, read the array once, first check for any zero to short-circuit to 0, otherwise compute the product with an early break when exceeding 1e18. This keeps the algorithm linear while reducing overhead and unnecessary work in zero-containing cases.

complexity.why: Reading n integers is O(n) and storing them in a list is O(n). The call to `var_2.count(0)` is a linear scan (O(n)). If no zero is found, a second linear scan computes the product with early exit when the product exceeds 1e18 (O(n) in the worst case). So the complexity remains O(n) time, O(n) space. When zeros exist, only the count scan is performed before returning, which can reduce work in practice but not the worst-case big-O.

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time and space complexities are unchanged (linear in n), but constant factors differ slightly due to fewer imports and adjusted control flow for zero handling. The modified code may do less work when zeros exist, but retains two O(n) scans in the zero-free case.

transformation_steps: Removed unused imports and global helper variables that were part of a generic competitive-programming template, reducing module import overhead.

Changed input handling from sys.stdin.readline to the default input(); used eval(input()) only to consume and ignore the first integer (n), simplifying the signature but not affecting algorithmic complexity.
Reordered the logic to first check for the presence of zero using var_2.count(0); if any zero exists, the result is immediately set to 0 and the multiplication loop is skipped.
Kept an early-break condition during product accumulation to set the result to -1 and stop once the product exceeds 10**18, maintaining the overflow guard behavior.
Simplified branching and variable usage, reducing structural overhead while preserving the same computational pattern (linear scans over the array).
trigger_signals: Presence of a full competitive-programming template with many unused imports and helpers for a very small, single-array problem.
Linear pass over the array followed by an additional membership test (`0 in list`), suggesting potential duplicate scans or redundant work.
Overflow guarding in Python by manual threshold checks, indicating that the primary cost is in repeated multiplications and comparisons over n elements.
Problem type is a straightforward product with an upper bound, with no indication that anything beyond an O(n) single or double pass is required.
pitfalls: Using eval(input()) to read and discard n is unnecessary and can be dangerous in non-judge environments; direct int(input()) would be safer and clearer without performance penalty.

var_2.count(0) always scans the entire list even if the first element is zero; a pattern like `if 0 in var_2` or checking during the product loop could short-circuit earlier, though this does not change the worst-case complexity.
Switching from sys.stdin.readline to input() may slightly increase I/O overhead in Python for very large inputs, although it typically remains negligible compared to O(n) computation for n ≈ 1e5.

Both versions rely on Python’s big integers; while the explicit 10**18 bound addresses the problem’s requirement, developers should remember that Python will not overflow but will slow down if numbers grow extremely large; here, the early break prevents pathological growth.
Removing template code is good for performance clarity, but care must be taken not to lose useful patterns (e.g., robust input reading) in more complex problems where they are beneficial.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic AOJ-style problem: count triples (1 <= i < j < k <= n) with i+j+k = x, repeated for many (n,x) pairs until '0 0'. Typical limits around n <= 1000, x <= 3000, and up to a few thousand test cases.

dominant_ops: Triple nested loops over indices i, j, k up to n
Integer additions and comparisons for each (i,j,k) triple
Early-break on sum > target, but still cubic in worst-case

complexity.why: There are three nested loops: i from 1..n, j from i+1..n, k from j+1..n. This yields Θ(n^3) triples in the worst case. The early break on (i+j+k) > target reduces iterations somewhat when the target is small, but for moderate/large target values it still approaches the full cubic behavior. Only a few scalar counters are stored, so space is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: The triple nested loops enumerate all O(n^3) strictly increasing triples (i,j,k). For n up to ~1000 this yields up to ~1e9 iterations, which is infeasible in Python.
The innermost loop recomputes (var_1 + var_2 + var_3) twice per iteration (for == and > checks), adding constant-factor overhead on top of the cubic iteration count.
The process repeats for many (n,x) pairs until '0 0'. Even if a single test might barely pass in isolation, multiple tests compounded make the cubic algorithm far too slow.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid enumerating all triples explicitly. For each possible middle value j, derive analytically how many i (and thus k) satisfy 1 <= i < j < k <= n and i + j + k = x. This collapses three loops into one by turning the inner two loops into a range-counting formula based on bounds derived from positivity, ordering, and sum constraints.

complexity.why: The code chooses a single loop variable (effectively the middle index of the triple) and iterates it over a constrained range between about x/3 and min(n, x-3). For each value it performs O(1) arithmetic to compute the valid count contribution. Thus runtime is linear in the smaller of n and x. Only a few integer variables are used, so memory usage remains constant.

complexity_delta.from: O(n^3) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(min(n, x)) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: The key improvement is replacing explicit enumeration of all triples with a direct combinatorial count per chosen middle element, reducing three nested loops to a single loop.

transformation_steps: Reformulate the problem: count the number of triples (i,j,k) with 1 <= i < j < k <= n and i + j + k = x instead of explicitly enumerating them.
Fix one index as the primary loop variable (the middle index j). For each j, deduce constraints on i and k: i < j < k, 1 <= i, k <= n, and i + k = x - j.

Use inequalities from ordering and bounds to derive the valid interval for i: derive lower and upper bounds from (i < j), (j < k), (1 <= i), (k <= n), and i + k = x - j. Translate these into simple formulas of the form i_min(j) and i_max(j).
Express the number of valid triples for a given j as max(0, i_max(j) - i_min(j) + 1). Implement this as O(1) arithmetic per j instead of nested loops over i and k.
Determine the valid range of j itself (roughly from floor(x/3)+1 up to min(n, x-3)) so that the derived intervals for i and k are non-empty and indices remain within [1,n].
Replace the triple nested loops with a single for-loop over j, accumulating the count using the derived bounds, and keep the outer read-loop structure unchanged.
trigger_signals: Presence of three nested loops whose bounds are up to n (var_6), leading to an estimated O(n^3) runtime.
Typical competitive-programming constraints (n around 1000) where 1e9 operations are known to be too slow in Python.
Problem structure is pure counting of integer triples with linear constraints (sums and inequalities), which strongly suggests a closed-form or near-linear-time combinatorial counting solution.
Repeated test cases until a sentinel line ('0 0'), amplifying the impact of a high per-case complexity.
pitfalls: Deriving the bounds for the transformed single-loop algorithm is error-prone: off-by-one mistakes in i_min, i_max, or the loop limits for the middle index can undercount or overcount solutions.
Integer division and floor behavior (e.g., x // 3, (x - j) // 2) must be chosen carefully; incorrect rounding can exclude valid triples or include invalid ones.
Edge cases for small n or x (e.g., n < 3, x very small or very large relative to n) must be handled so that computed ranges do not become negative or reversed (i_max < i_min).

Maintaining the strict ordering i < j < k is subtle when converted into algebraic bounds; it is easy to accidentally allow equality or incorrect ordering if the inequalities are not carefully propagated.

The sentinel condition '0 0' must still be correctly recognized after refactoring the algorithm; swapping input variables (n and x) or misinterpreting them in the formulas can break termination or counting.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical for this pattern (ways to write M as product of N integers): N and M up to about 1e9, single test case. Prime factorization runs up to sqrt(M); combinatorial part uses exponents of prime factors, whose sum is O(log M).

dominant_ops: Trial division prime factorization up to sqrt(M) (both versions do this).
Precomputation of factorial and inverse-factorial tables inside Class_1 up to MAX ≈ N + (small slack).
nCk evaluation using the precomputed tables (O(1) per query, but only a handful of queries).
Extra generic helpers (eval-based input reader, unused multi-dimensional array constructors) add overhead in code size and constant factors, though not asymptotic.

complexity.why: Factorization via trial division takes O(sqrt(M)). From the visible Class_1 pattern, MAX is set from var_3 (N) plus 1; the standard combinatorics helper then precomputes factorial and inverse factorial arrays up to MAX, costing O(MAX) time and memory. Since the number of combinations actually needed is only the number of distinct prime factors (≲ log M), the precomputation dominates for large N.

bottlenecks.detail: Class_1 sets self.MAX = var_3 + 1 and (based on common templates) precomputes factorial and inverse factorial lists up to that size. If var_3 (N) is large (e.g., 1e7–1e9), this results in huge time and memory usage that is unnecessary for just a few nCk evaluations with very small k (prime exponents).

Only O(#primes) combinatorial queries of the form C(N + e_i - 1, e_i) are required, with each exponent e_i ≪ N (e_i = O(log M)). Precomputing factorial tables up to N instead of computing each combination on the fly wastes work, especially under tight limits.

The use of eval in func_1 (return int(eval(func_10()))) to parse integers is slower and unsafe compared to int(). While this is not asymptotically dominant, it introduces unnecessary overhead and potential security issues.

Generic helpers func_11/func_12/func_13 allocate multi-dimensional arrays but are unused in the main solution. Their presence indicates a generic template; if accidentally used with large dimensions, they can easily cause O(N^2) or worse memory/time blowups.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial precomputation and instead compute each required combination C(n, k) directly via a multiplicative formula with O(k) operations, where k is the small exponent of a prime in the factorization of M. Combine this with standard trial division factorization of M and multiply the per-prime combination contributions modulo 1e9+7.

complexity.space: O(1) additional (beyond input and small counters)
complexity.why: Prime factorization by trial division runs in O(sqrt(M)). Let e_i be the exponent of each prime factor of M; we need to compute products of C(N + e_i - 1, e_i). Each nCk is computed with k = min(e_i, N + e_i - 1 - e_i) = e_i multiplications/divisions, so O(e_i) per prime. Since sum e_i = O(log M) for M ≤ 1e9, this part is negligible. No factorial arrays are stored; only a few integers and the Counter of prime factors are used, so extra space is constant.

from.time: O(sqrt(M) + MAX) with MAX ≈ N (precomputing factorials/inverses)
from.space: O(MAX) for factorial and inverse factorial arrays

to.time: O(sqrt(M) + sum e_i) with sum e_i = O(log M)

complexity_delta.note: The main improvement removes the linear-in-N factorial precomputation and replaces it with on-the-fly combinatorial calculation whose cost depends only on the (small) exponents of M's prime factors, not on N itself.

transformation_steps: Drop the combinatorics helper class (Class_1) that precomputes factorial and inverse factorial tables up to MAX = N + 1 or similar, removing O(MAX) precomputation time and memory.

Implement a direct nCk function (func_1 in the fast code) that computes C(n, k) via multiplicative loops: multiply n, n-1, ..., n-k+1 and then divide by 1, 2, ..., k, using k = min(k, n-k) to minimize loop length.

Keep the prime factorization logic but simplify it: factor M (var_1) into a list of primes (func_2), then count exponents with collections.Counter instead of maintaining a dict manually during factorization.
For each prime exponent e, compute C(N + e - 1, e) with the new O(e) nCk function and multiply all such values together under modulo 1e9+7.

Use straightforward, safe input parsing (input().split(), int()) and remove eval-based input helpers and unused multi-dimensional array constructors, reducing constant-factor overhead and potential errors.
trigger_signals: Presence of a factorial/inverse-factorial precomputation up to a size derived directly from a potentially large input parameter (e.g., N up to 1e7–1e9) in a problem that only needs a handful of combinations.
Memory footprint or time cost dominated by building large combinatorics tables when the combinatorial parameters (k = prime exponents) are very small (O(log M)).
Use of generic competitive-programming template code (many helper functions, combinatorics class) where most helpers are unused but one heavy precomputation (factorials) remains.
Use of eval for reading integers, which is a smell both for performance and safety, especially in code that otherwise only needs simple int parsing.
pitfalls: When switching from factorial-based nCk to multiplicative nCk, failing to minimize k to min(k, n-k) can multiply the number of operations by up to a factor of two, which might matter when k is not tiny.

In languages without arbitrary-precision integers, computing the full product before division can overflow; one must carefully interleave multiplication and division (or work modulo a prime with modular inverses). Python avoids overflow but other languages do not.

If one later introduces a true modulus into the multiplicative nCk (e.g., reducing modulo 1e9+7 at each step), using integer division // will no longer be valid; instead, modular inverses must be used. The current fast code relies on exact integer arithmetic and only applies the modulus at the end.

For larger M than initially expected, trial division up to sqrt(M) can become the bottleneck; in that case, more advanced factorization (e.g., Pollard's Rho) might be required. For M ≤ 1e9, trial division is adequate.

constraints_guess.notes: Fixed 10x10 cost/adjacency matrix (digits 0–9). Grid size given by (var_3, var_4) ≈ (H, W), likely up to about 200x200 cells in typical AtCoder-style tasks, so H*W ~ 4e4.

dominant_ops: Importing and initializing SciPy (scipy.sparse.csgraph.floyd_warshall), which has heavy startup and binary loading costs
Converting the 10x10 Python list-of-lists into SciPy’s internal matrix representation
Running floyd_warshall on a 10x10 graph (C-level, but negligible compared to import/initialization here)
Iterating over all H rows and their W entries to sum distances to node 1, skipping -1

complexity.time: O(10^3 + H*W) ≈ O(H*W) in asymptotics, but with a very large constant factor from SciPy import and conversion
complexity.space: O(10^2) for the distance matrix plus additional opaque SciPy internal structures; effectively O(1) w.r.t. H and W
complexity.why: The graph portion is fixed-size (10 nodes), so Floyd–Warshall is constant work asymptotically. However, importing SciPy and constructing its sparse/dense structures introduces substantial constant-time overhead that dominates when the APSP problem is this small. The grid processing is linear in the number of cells and is unchanged between versions.

bottlenecks.detail: Using scipy.sparse.csgraph.floyd_warshall forces importing SciPy, which is heavyweight (binary modules, compiled extensions). In typical competitive programming environments this either fails or costs a significant fraction of the time limit just to import.
The 10x10 Python list-of-lists is converted to SciPy’s internal representation and then back to something indexable. For such a tiny matrix, this overhead dominates the O(10^3) arithmetic operations.
SciPy’s floyd_warshall is a general solver (sparse/dense handling, possibly float handling), which is overkill compared to a hand-rolled triple loop tailored to a fixed 10x10 integer matrix.

FastAudit.core_idea: Remove the heavy SciPy dependency and implement Floyd–Warshall directly in pure Python over the fixed 10x10 matrix, then iterate through the H×W grid using the precomputed all-pairs distances to node 1.

complexity.time: O(10^3 + H*W) with very small constants; effectively O(H*W) and dramatically faster in practice because it avoids SciPy import and conversion costs.
complexity.space: O(10^2) for the 10x10 distance matrix plus O(1) extra; still O(1) w.r.t. H and W.
complexity.why: The triple nested loops for Floyd–Warshall do at most 10^3 updates, which is trivial in Python. The grid traversal remains linear in the number of cells. By eliminating SciPy, the program runs almost entirely in straightforward Python loops and integer arithmetic, avoiding the heavy constant-time costs of importing and using a large numerical library for a tiny fixed-size problem.

complexity_delta.from: Theoretical O(10^3 + H*W) but dominated in practice by SciPy import, matrix conversion, and generic floyd_warshall machinery.
complexity_delta.to: O(10^3 + H*W) with minimal constant factors, implemented as a simple triple loop over a 10x10 matrix plus straightforward grid iteration.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged, but the constant factor drops massively because the problem size for APSP is tiny and SciPy is an extreme overkill. In competitive programming contexts, this change often is the difference between TLE/RE and AC.

transformation_steps: Remove the import of scipy.sparse.csgraph.floyd_warshall and the call to floyd_warshall(var_2).
Implement a dedicated Floyd–Warshall function (func_1) that runs three nested loops over range(10) and updates var_2[i][j] = min(var_2[i][j], var_2[i][k] + var_2[k][j]).
Call func_1(var_2) to compute all-pairs shortest paths directly on the in-place 10x10 matrix.

Slightly restructure the grid summation to iterate explicitly with indices (for var_6 in range(var_3), for var_7 in range(var_4)) and index var_1[var_6][var_7], still skipping -1 and accumulating var_2[value][1].
Preserve the core logic of summing shortest-path costs to node 1 for all grid cells that are not -1, ensuring output remains identical to the original algorithm.
trigger_signals: Presence of SciPy (or other heavy scientific libraries) in a competitive programming solution is a red flag due to import overhead and environment incompatibility.
The graph dimension is clearly tiny and fixed (10x10), which makes a hand-coded O(10^3) Floyd–Warshall both trivial and more than fast enough.
The library call handles much more general cases (sparse structures, floats, larger graphs), which is unnecessary here and increases constant factors.
Time limits and environment hints for typical online judges indicate that third-party heavy numerical libraries are either disallowed or too slow to import.
pitfalls: If the matrix size were not fixed at 10 or could grow large, a pure-Python Floyd–Warshall (O(N^3)) might become too slow; this optimization assumes N=10.

Care must be taken to handle unreachable edges correctly (often represented by a large INF value rather than -1) when re-implementing Floyd–Warshall. Misinterpreting -1 as an actual weight rather than impossibility can change the semantics if the original library handled it differently.
In-place updates in Floyd–Warshall require the standard loop order (k, i, j or equivalently var_8, var_6, var_7 here). Changing loop nesting incorrectly can break the algorithm.

Type consistency matters: using Python ints throughout avoids precision issues seen in some floating-point APSP implementations; a careless reimplementation with floats could introduce rounding errors compared with an integer-based reference.
Relying on third-party libraries in online judges can cause import errors or missing-module runtime errors; the fast version avoids this but any future refactor must maintain this independence.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical array-GCD problem (e.g., AtCoder). N up to ~1e5–2e5, each Ai up to ~1e9. Single test case; requires near O(N log V) or better.

dominant_ops: Single pass over the N integers, maintaining running GCD using the Euclidean algorithm (mod operations in func_7).

complexity.why: For each of the N-1 remaining elements, func_7 computes gcd(current_g, a[i]) using the Euclidean algorithm, which takes O(log V) modulus steps where V is the maximum magnitude of the numbers. No extra data structures beyond a few scalars.

bottlenecks.detail: Asymptotically this approach is already optimal for computing the GCD of all elements: O(N log V). There is no better fundamental algorithmic improvement for this task in Python.
Using eval(var_5()) in func_1 to parse an integer is slower and unsafe compared to int(var_5()). This is a micro-bottleneck for large input but does not change complexity.

Many heavy standard-library modules (collections, itertools, bisect, heapq, math, operator) are imported but never used. This increases startup time slightly, though still minor compared to O(N log V) computation on big inputs.

FastAudit.core_idea: Repeatedly sort the list, use the smallest element as a divisor, replace each other element by its remainder modulo the smallest, and remove zeros until only one element (the GCD) remains. This simulates the multi-number Euclidean algorithm but uses full-list sorts and repeated passes.

complexity.time: O(T * (N log N + N)) ≈ O(N log N log V) in the worst case
complexity.why: Each while-iteration sorts the entire list (O(N log N)) and then performs a linear pass applying modulo and filtering out zeros (O(N)). The number of iterations T is bounded by how many times the minimum can be used to reduce the other elements before they become 0 or equal to the GCD; in adversarial or large-value cases T can be on the order of log V. This yields roughly O(N log N log V), worse than a single linear GCD pass. The entire list is stored and repeatedly rebuilt, so space is O(N).

complexity_delta.from: O(N log V) time, O(1) extra space (pairwise Euclidean GCD accumulation)
complexity_delta.to: O(N log N log V) time, O(N) space (repeated sort + modulo reduction over full list)
complexity_delta.note: Replacing a single linear pass of Euclid’s algorithm with repeated global sorts and full-array modulo passes significantly worsens performance, especially for large N.

transformation_steps: Replaced the running GCD computation func_7(g, a[i]) inside a single for-loop with a while-loop that operates on the full list until its length becomes 1.
On every while-iteration, introduced a full sort of the array (var_1.sort()), making each pass O(N log N).
Performed modulo operations for all elements with respect to the smallest element in each iteration, instead of just processing the next element against the running GCD.
Rebuilt the list on every iteration via a list comprehension to filter out zeros, increasing constant factors and memory churn.
Switched from a scalar state (current GCD) to maintaining and repeatedly mutating the entire list, increasing both time and space usage.
trigger_signals: The algorithm starts to sort the full list inside a loop whose iteration count depends on the data, a common red flag for superlinear time.
The amount of work per element is no longer bounded by a constant or log V; elements can be processed multiple times across iterations.
Memory usage grows to O(N) with repeated list allocations and copies, versus the O(1) scalar GCD accumulator.
Theoretical comparison: computing gcd of all numbers has a well-known optimal O(N log V) algorithm; any approach with repeated sorting of N items is asymptotically worse.
pitfalls: Believing that mimicking the pairwise Euclidean reduction by repeatedly using the smallest element over a list will be as efficient as the direct GCD accumulation, while ignoring the cost of sorting each round.
Underestimating the cost of list operations and Python-level loops for large N, especially when they are nested (while * sort * for).
Assuming that repeatedly shrinking numbers via modulo inherently leads to fast convergence without quantifying the number of iterations T.
Using eval on raw input, which is slower and unsafe; while not the main complexity issue, it is a bad practice that can mask where the real bottlenecks are.

constraints_guess.n_max: 1e5–2e5 (var_3, because factorials are precomputed up to var_3 + max exponent)
constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style constraints: var_1 up to about 1e9–1e12 (trial division to sqrt(var_1) is used), modulus is 1e9+7, multiple binomial coefficients C(var_3 + e - 1, var_3 - 1) / C(var_3 + e - 1, e) must be computed for prime exponents e of var_1.

dominant_ops: 1) Prime factorization of var_1 by trial division up to sqrt(var_1). 2) For each distinct prime factor exponent e of var_1, computing a binomial coefficient via func_1(n, k) using a length-k loop with modular multiplications and a pow(var_5, var_2 - 2, var_2) call on every iteration (per-step modular inverse via binary exponentiation).

complexity.time: O( sqrt(var_1) + ω(var_1) * var_3 * log MOD ), where ω(var_1) is the number of distinct prime factors
complexity.why: Factorization loop runs var_5 from 2 while var_5^2 <= var_1, so O(sqrt(var_1)) divisions in the worst case. The dict var_8 stores one entry per distinct prime factor. For each exponent e in var_8.values(), func_1(var_3 + e - 1, var_3 - 1) is called with var_6 = var_3 - 1, and the internal loop runs from 1 to var_6, i.e. O(var_3) iterations. Each iteration does constant-time modular multiplications but also pow(var_5, var_2 - 2, var_2), which is modular exponentiation in O(log MOD). Hence about ω(var_1) * var_3 pow calls, giving O(ω(var_1) * var_3 * log MOD). Memory holds only the factor counts, so O(ω(var_1)).

bottlenecks.detail: Binomial coefficient computation via func_1 is O(var_3 * log MOD) per call because it loops up to var_3 and recomputes a modular inverse pow(var_5, MOD-2, MOD) on every iteration. This dominates runtime for large var_3.
Each call to func_1 recomputes a full binomial value from scratch, even though multiple calls share overlapping ranges of factorial terms; there is no reuse via factorial / inverse-factorial tables.
The inner for-loop in Python with a pow call per iteration is slow in CPython, especially when var_3 can be large (e.g., up to 1e5 or more).

Factorization loop uses range(2, var_1 + 1) with an early break on var_5 * var_5 > var_1; this maintains the correct complexity but is slightly less direct than using a fixed sqrt bound and keeps var_1 mutated inside the loop, which may confuse optimizations.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the same number-theoretic structure (factorize var_1 into primes, then use stars-and-bars style binomials), but replace per-binomial O(var_3 * log MOD) loops with a single O(L) factorial and inverse-factorial precomputation up to L = var_3 + max_exponent, so each binomial C(n, k) is O(1). The modular inverses are obtained by one modular inverse of var_9[L] and a backward pass, rather than calling pow in every step.

complexity.time: O( sqrt(var_1) + L + ω(var_1) ), where L = var_3 + max_exponent_of_var_1 and ω(var_1) is the number of distinct prime factors
complexity.why: Prime factorization via func_2 still does trial division up to floor(sqrt(var_14)), so O(sqrt(var_1)) as before. Let e_max = max(var_7.values()), then var_4 = var_3 + e_max. Arrays var_9 (factorials) and var_10 (inverse factorials) are built in O(var_4), plus one modular inverse via func_3, which is O(log MOD). Each binomial func_1(var_3 + e - 1, e) is then computed in O(1) using three table lookups and modular multiplications. The total for all exponents is O(ω(var_1)). Memory is O(var_4) for the factorial and inverse factorial arrays.

complexity_delta.from: O( sqrt(var_1) + ω(var_1) * var_3 * log MOD ) time, O( ω(var_1) ) space
complexity_delta.to: O( sqrt(var_1) + (var_3 + e_max) + ω(var_1) ) time, O( var_3 + e_max ) space, where e_max is the maximum exponent in the prime factorization of var_1
complexity_delta.note: The factorization complexity is roughly unchanged; the major improvement is replacing per-call O(var_3 * log MOD) binomial computation with O(1) using precomputed factorial and inverse factorial arrays.

transformation_steps: Identify that func_1 is computing binomial coefficients C(var_7, var_6) via a multiplicative formula that iterates over k and uses pow(k, MOD-2, MOD) to get modular inverses, causing O(var_3 * log MOD) per call.

Observe that the required binomials are of the form C(var_3 + e - 1, var_3 - 1) or equivalently C(var_3 + e - 1, e) for exponents e of the prime factors of var_1, and that all relevant n, k are bounded by var_3 + e_max for e_max = max exponent.
Introduce factorial precomputation: build an array var_9 where var_9[i] = i! mod MOD for i up to var_4 = var_3 + e_max using a single forward pass.

Compute inverse factorials via a single modular inverse of var_9[var_4] using fast exponentiation (func_3), and then fill var_10[i] = (var_10[i+1] * (i+1)) % MOD in a backward loop, giving inv_fact[i] for all i.
Redefine func_1 to compute binomial coefficients in O(1) as var_9[n] * var_10[k] % MOD * var_10[n-k] % MOD instead of looping and calling pow in each iteration.
Slightly refactor factorization using func_2 and Counter to get exponents, but keep the same O(sqrt(var_1)) behavior while clarifying the logic.
Change the second argument of func_1 in the product to use exponent e directly (func_1(var_3 + e - 1, e)) instead of var_3 - 1; these are mathematically equal (C(n, e) = C(n, n - e)).
trigger_signals: Presence of a loop from 1 to var_3 (or var_3 - 1) inside a function called once per prime factor exponent, leading to O(ω(var_1) * var_3) iterations.
Use of pow(var_5, var_2 - 2, var_2) inside the inner loop, signaling repeated modular exponentiations that are expensive, especially when var_3 is up to 1e5 or more.
Overall structure computing binomial coefficients repeatedly with no factorial precomputation, a common TLE pattern in combinatorial problems with large parameters.
Constraints (in the original problem) likely allow var_3 around 1e5 and var_1 large enough to have several prime factors, making ω(var_1) * var_3 * log MOD too slow for Python.
Code style typical of an initial straightforward implementation that passes small tests but fails on maximal inputs due to nested loops with heavy operations.
pitfalls: Must ensure factorial arrays are sized to at least var_3 + max_exponent; if mis-sized, binomial calls will index out of range or silently produce wrong results.

When switching from C(n, var_3 - 1) to C(n, e) in func_1, need to rely on combinatorial identity C(n, k) = C(n, n - k); mixing up which parameter is which can introduce off-by-one or swapped-argument errors.

Precomputing factorials and inverse factorials increases memory usage from O(ω(var_1)) to O(var_3 + e_max); for extremely large var_3 this can become an issue, though it is acceptable under typical contest constraints.
The modular inverse precomputation step using func_3 must use exponent MOD - 2 and a correct fast exponentiation implementation; any mistake there corrupts all inverse factorials.

Factorization via trial division to sqrt(var_1) assumes var_1 fits in integer range and that sqrt(var_1) is not too large; if constraints were much larger than expected, a different factorization method would be required.

Care must be taken not to reuse the original mutable var_1 inside the factorization loop in a way that affects subsequent logic; the fast version isolates factorization in func_2 and returns a factor list, which is safer.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical of AtCoder ABC110 D "Factorization": N and M up to about 1e9, single test case. Need to factor M (<=1e9) and for each prime exponent e compute C(N+e-1, e) mod 1e9+7. Exponents e are very small (<= ~30).

dominant_ops: Precomputing factorials and inverse factorials up to a limit var_11 that comes from the input N (potentially ~1e9) and then using O(1) nCk queries.

complexity.why: Class_1.__init__ builds two arrays of length var_11+1 (fact and invs) with a linear loop forward to fill factorials and a linear loop backward to fill inverse factorials. When var_11 is chosen based on N+max_exponent-1 and N can be up to 1e9, both time and space become linear in N and completely dominate the relatively cheap O(sqrt(M)) prime factorization.

bottlenecks.detail: Arrays fact and invs of size var_11+1 when var_11 is on the order of N (≈1e9) require several gigabytes of memory (two arrays of 1e9 Python ints). This will not fit in typical contest limits and will lead to MemoryError or severe swapping.

The loops in Class_1.__init__ iterate from 2 to var_11 and then from var_11-1 down to 1, each doing a modular multiplication. For var_11 ≈ 1e9 this is ~2e9 operations, far beyond what can be completed within time limits.

The algorithm assumes it is feasible to precompute factorials up to the maximum n used in combinations. In this problem n = N+e-1 where N can be ≈1e9, but k=e is tiny (≈<=30). This is exactly the regime where factorial precomputation is inappropriate and a multiplicative O(k) formula is required.
Even if var_11 were capped smaller than N, choosing it based on the input without verifying against constraints can silently pass small tests but fail on large hidden tests due to TLE/MLE.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid any precomputation that scales with N. Factor M by trial division up to sqrt(M). For each prime factor with exponent e, compute the combination C(N+e-1, e) using a multiplicative formula in O(e) time, where e is very small. Multiply all these contributions and take the final result modulo 1e9+7.

complexity.why: Prime factorization of M by trial division up to floor(sqrt(M)) takes O(sqrt(M)) operations with small constant factors since M <= 1e9. The exponents e_i are small (at most about log_2(M) ≈ 30), and the combination function func_1(n, k) uses a multiplicative recurrence that effectively costs O(k) per call with k=e_i. The total sum of exponents over all primes is O(log M), so combination computation is negligible. Only a handful of prime factors and their exponents are stored, yielding constant or logarithmic space usage.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(N + sqrt(M)) dominated by factorial precomputation with N up to ~1e9. Space: O(N) for arrays of size N.
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(sqrt(M) + sum(e_i)) ~ O(sqrt(M) + log M). Space: O(#primes in factorization of M) ~ O(1–log M).
complexity_delta.note: The key improvement is eliminating linear dependence on N (which can be as large as 1e9) and replacing it with dependence only on the small exponents e_i of M's prime factorization.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the combination arguments are (N+e-1, e), where N can be huge (~1e9) but e is tiny (≈<=30). This invalidates the usual factorial precomputation strategy.
