transformation_steps: Inline and localize input operations: Replace helper functions like func_7 and func_3 with a direct binding var_5 = sys.stdin.readline and inline map(int, ...) inside the comprehension. This removes extra Python function calls per line.

Simplify sorting: Instead of sort(key=lambda x: x[1]) on [a, b], reverse each pair to [b, a] and use default sorted(...). This avoids an extra Python lambda call per element and leverages native list comparison.

Add early exit on infeasibility: In the fast version, break immediately once cumulative time exceeds the current deadline, using a for-else construct to decide the final answer. This can save up to O(n) work in failing cases.
Tighten loop variables and logic: Use a direct running sum and immediate print inside the loop, avoiding an extra boolean flag that is checked only after the loop.
trigger_signals: n can be large (around 1e5–2e5), making Python-level overhead in tight loops and input wrappers non-negligible.
The original code performs the full pass over all jobs even when the schedule is already known to be infeasible.
Presence of multiple small helper functions wrapping stdin.readline in a competitive-programming context, where minimal per-iteration overhead is important.
pitfalls: The fast version uses eval to parse the first line (var_6 = int(eval(var_5()))). While it executes only once and is fast enough here, eval is generally unsafe if input is not fully trusted and should be avoided in non-CP contexts.

Changing the sort logic must preserve the intended order. Reversing pairs to rely on default sorting assumes a fixed and known field order (deadline first, duration second). A mistake here can silently break correctness.

Relying on early break requires that any needed side effects after failure are either done before break or handled via the for-else structure; otherwise code might skip necessary cleanup or reporting.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic digit-parity counting problem (e.g., AtCoder ABC136 B - Uneven Numbers). N is up to about 1e5 so numbers have at most 5 digits; we count how many integers in [1, N] have an odd number of digits.

dominant_ops: Outer loop over all integers from 1 to N
Per-integer digit counting via repeated integer division by 10
Function call overhead inside the tight loop

complexity.why: For each i in [1, N], func_1 performs O(log10(i)) integer divisions to count digits. Summed over i, this is Θ(∑_{i=1..N} log i) = Θ(N log N). Only a few scalar variables are used, so space is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: Counts digits for every number from 1 to N individually instead of using the fact that digit length is constant on contiguous ranges [1,9], [10,99], [100,999], etc.
Inside the main loop, each call to func_1 performs several integer divisions and updates; this log-scale work is paid N times.
func_1 is called N times in a tight loop; even if digit counting were O(1), the call overhead adds unnecessary cost compared with inlining or using a formula.
Using eval(input()) is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()); however, this is a minor performance issue relative to the O(N log N) algorithm.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit that all numbers within a digit-length range share the same digit count. Count contributions in bulk for ranges with odd digit lengths (1-digit: [1,9], 3-digit: [100,999], 5-digit: [10000,99999]) by clamping each range to N, instead of iterating through every number.

complexity.why: The optimized code iterates over at most 9 + 900 + 90000 fixed values corresponding to the 1-, 3-, and 5-digit ranges. Since N ≤ 99999 in the intended problem, the number of iterations is bounded by a constant independent of N, giving O(1) time and O(1) space in terms of N.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log N) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(1) time (for N up to 1e5), O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: Replaces per-number digit counting with constant-number loops over digit-length ranges; asymptotically constant-time in terms of N for the given constraints. For larger possible N (more digits), this general approach still gives O(#digit_ranges) instead of O(N log N).

transformation_steps: Recognize that the property of interest (odd digit count) depends only on the number of digits, not on the specific value, and that digit length is constant on ranges [1,9], [10,99], [100,999], [1000,9999], [10000,99999], etc.
Observe that only ranges with an odd digit length (1, 3, 5, ...) contribute to the answer, so even-digit ranges can be completely skipped.

Replace the full loop from 1 to N with loops over fixed digit-length ranges: [1,9], [100,999], [10000,99999], each clamped by N. For each range, increment the count for each integer ≤ N within that range.
Eliminate the digit-counting function and its repeated integer divisions. Instead, use the fact that the digit length is implicit in which range is being processed.
Keep range lengths hardcoded to match the problem's maximum N (up to 99999), making the runtime independent of N within these constraints.
trigger_signals: A loop from 1 to N where N can be as large as 1e5 or more, with per-iteration work that depends on the digits of the loop index.
Use of repeated integer division by 10 to compute digit counts inside a tight loop.
The presence of clearly structured ranges (powers of 10) where a property (digit length parity) is constant, suggesting aggregation per range instead of per element.
Performance requirements or timeouts when scaling N higher, indicating that an O(N log N) approach may be unnecessary for a highly regular property like digit length.
pitfalls: Hardcoding digit ranges makes the solution tightly bound to the input constraints; if N can exceed 99999 (introducing 7-digit or 9-digit ranges), the code must be updated or generalized.
Off-by-one risks at boundaries (e.g., ensuring ranges like [1,9], [100,999], [10000,99999] are inclusive and correctly clamped at N).

The optimized code still manually iterates inside each range; while constant under the given limits, it could be further improved by using pure arithmetic formulas such as max(0, min(N, upper) - lower + 1) for each odd-digit range.
Using eval(input()) instead of int(input()) is unnecessary and can be unsafe, though it is not the primary performance bottleneck in this problem.
If the constraints change to allow N = 0, the logic must explicitly handle the empty range [1, 0] (no numbers) to avoid incorrect counting assumptions.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical of AtCoder-style problem: given N (up to ~1e5) and M (up to ~1e9), compute product over prime factors e of C(e+N-1, e) mod 1e9+7. Single test case; M small enough for trial-division factorization in O(sqrt(M)).

dominant_ops: Precomputation of factorial array up to MAXN = 2*10^5
Precomputation of inverse factorial array up to MAXN = 2*10^5
Trial-division prime factorization of M up to sqrt(M)

complexity.why: Two global arrays of size MAXN are filled: factorial (forward loop) and inverse factorial (backward loop), each O(MAXN). Factorization of M via trial division from 2 to sqrt(M) is O(sqrt(M)). Binomial queries themselves are O(1) using precomputed factorials/inverses and are called only for each distinct prime factor (small count).

bottlenecks.detail: Always builds factorial and inverse factorial arrays up to 2*10^5 regardless of actual N and maximum needed n in nCk. This fixed MAXN can be substantially larger than N+max_exponent, wasting time and memory.

Inverse factorials for all indices are precomputed even though the number of distinct binomial coefficient evaluations is very small (only per prime factor of M). This turns a handful of modular inverses into O(MAXN) work.
Uses built-in input() instead of buffered sys.stdin.readline; negligible for one line but suboptimal style when aiming for maximal performance.

FastAudit.core_idea: Reduce combinatorial precomputation to only what is required: build a factorial table up to N+constant lazily, and compute modular inverses on demand with pow(..., MOD-2, MOD) instead of a full inverse-factorial array. Keep the same O(sqrt(M)) trial-division factorization, and switch to fast I/O via sys.stdin for small additional gains.

complexity.why: Factorials are computed once up to N+100 in a single forward loop O(N). For each binomial coefficient, modular inverses are computed with pow in O(log MOD) time, but the number of such calls equals twice the number of distinct prime factors of M, which is tiny in practice, so this cost is negligible. Factorization remains O(sqrt(M)). Only one factorial array of size ~N is stored, yielding O(N) space.

delta_type: constant-factor optimization with reduced precomputation and slightly faster I/O

complexity_delta.from: O(MAXN + sqrt(M)) time, O(MAXN) space with MAXN fixed at 2*10^5 and two full arrays (factorial and inverse factorial) always built.
complexity_delta.to: O(N + sqrt(M)) time, O(N) space with factorials built only up to N+margin and modular inverses computed lazily via pow for a small number of binomial evaluations.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity class is unchanged, but constants are reduced: roughly half the precomputation and half the memory, plus avoiding a backward loop for inverse factorials. For typical constraints (N <= 1e5), this can be the difference between borderline TLE and acceptance in Python.

transformation_steps: Replace fixed-size precomputation (MAXN = 2*10^5) with factorial precomputation up to the exact required bound (N + safety margin) using a single forward loop.
Remove global inverse factorial array and its O(MAXN) backward construction; instead, compute modular inverses using pow(x, MOD-2, MOD) inside the combination function.
Compute nCk using factorials and on-the-fly modular inverses, avoiding storage of O(MAXN) inverse factorials.

Retain trial-division prime factorization but express it with a simple while loop (var_9*var_9 <= var_12) rather than a for loop over precomputed sqrt; this keeps the same complexity but can be slightly leaner.
Switch input handling from input() to sys.stdin.readline for marginally faster I/O on competitive-programming judges.
trigger_signals: Large fixed MAXN (2*10^5) used for precomputation irrespective of actual N.
Presence of both factorial and inverse factorial arrays when the number of combination queries is very small.
Backward loop over the entire range to build inverse factorials despite only a handful of nCk evaluations.
Use of input() in performance-sensitive code, a common sign that more optimal I/O may be beneficial.
pitfalls: When computing nCk via factorials plus pow for modular inverses, correctness relies on the modulus being prime (so that x^(MOD-2) is the modular inverse). This approach breaks for non-prime moduli.
The factorial table must be built to at least the maximum n used in nCk (here, max(e_i + N - 1)); underestimating this bound causes index errors or incorrect results.
If the problem were extended to many queries (large Q), using pow for every inverse might become a bottleneck compared with a one-time inverse-factorial precomputation.
Using a global list that is extended by func_3 assumes single test case or monotonic growth; multiple independent test cases may require careful reinitialization or bounds checks.
Trial-division factorization O(sqrt(M)) is adequate for M up to about 10^9; for much larger M the approach would need to change (e.g., faster factorization algorithms) to avoid TLE.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: given N and M, count ways to write M as a product of N positive integers, order matters, modulo 1e9+7. M is small enough for trial division (likely M <= 1e9..1e12). N can be as large as about 1e5, but the sum of prime exponents of M is small (O(log M)).

dominant_ops: Trial division factorization of M up to floor(sqrt(M)) in func_2.
Precomputation of factorials up to var_4 = N + max_prime_exponent in var_9.
Precomputation of inverse factorials up to var_4 via one modular inverse (binary exponentiation) and a backward loop in var_10.
O(1) number of binomial coefficient queries using precomputed factorials/inverse factorials.

complexity.why: Factorization loops up to sqrt(M). Then var_4 = N + max_exp; building factorial and inverse-factorial arrays is linear in var_4. func_3 uses binary exponentiation (O(log MOD)) once for modular inverse of var_9[var_4]. Only a few combinations are evaluated using O(1) array accesses each.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorials and inverse factorials are precomputed for all values up to N + max_exp even though only as many C(n, k) calls are made as there are distinct prime factors of M (very small, <= O(log M)). This introduces O(N) work and memory where the effective combinatorial workload is O(sum exponents).
Two arrays of length var_4 (factorials and inverse factorials) are stored, which is unnecessary when the number of combinations is very small and k (each exponent) is tiny.
Using reversed(list(range(var_4))) materializes a list of size var_4 before reversing, instead of iterating reversed(range(var_4)) lazily. This is a small but avoidable overhead for large N.

Binary exponentiation for computing the modular inverse of var_9[var_4] is asymptotically efficient, but here it becomes redundant given that we could avoid modular inverses entirely by computing binomial coefficients via exact integer arithmetic for small k.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit that the exponents of prime factors of M are small: instead of precomputing full factorial and inverse-factorial tables, compute each required binomial coefficient C(n, k) directly via the multiplicative formula in O(k) time using exact integer arithmetic, then apply the modulo at the end. Keep the simple trial-division factorization, and add a fast early exit for the M == 1 case.

complexity.why: Factorization remains trial division up to sqrt(M). For each prime with exponent e_i, computing C(N + e_i - 1, e_i) via product of e_i terms in numerator and denominator is O(e_i). The number of distinct primes and the exponents are bounded by O(log M), so Σe_i is very small. No arrays of size N are maintained; memory is dominated by a few short lists created for the multiplicative binomial computation and the factor list itself.

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(M) + (N + max_exp) + log MOD) time, O(N + max_exp) space
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + Σe_i) time, O(1) additional space (up to small factor lists)
complexity_delta.note: The dependence on N (the first input) drops from linear precomputation O(N) to only appearing inside binomial parameters with cost O(e_i) per prime exponent. For typical constraints where N can be large and Σe_i is tiny, this is a substantial constant-factor and practical complexity improvement.

transformation_steps: Removed global factorial (var_9) and inverse-factorial (var_10) precomputation up to var_4 = N + max_exp.

Replaced the combinatorial routine using precomputed factorials and modular inverses with func_1 that computes C(n, k) via the multiplicative formula: product(n * (n-1) * ... * (n-k+1)) // product(1 * 2 * ... * k).
Deferred modulus application in fast_code to after the exact integer binomial calculation, avoiding modular inverses entirely.
Simplified prime factorization: switched from for var_8 in range(2, floor(sqrt(n)) + 1) to a while var_3 * var_3 <= var_6 loop with a single evolving sqrt-bound, avoiding repeated sqrt/floor calls.
Added a fast early-exit branch when the second input (M) equals 1, immediately printing 1 and skipping factorization and combinatorics.
Removed dependency on binary modular exponentiation (func_3 in the original) for inverse computation, relying on exact arithmetic and integer division instead.
trigger_signals: You see factorial and inverse-factorial precomputation up to a large N even though the number of C(n, k) queries is small and each k is tiny.
Problem constraints indicate that one parameter (here, exponents of prime factors) is small, while another (N) can be large, and combinations are always of the form C(N + small, small).
A modular inverse implementation (e.g., pow(x, MOD-2, MOD) or a custom binary exponentiation) is used heavily but could be avoided by doing work in plain integers and taking modulo only at the end.
Memory usage is dominated by large precomputed tables that are used only a handful of times.
pitfalls: The fast approach uses exact integer arithmetic for binomial coefficients; for significantly larger exponents or many more combination calls, intermediate integers could become huge, harming performance or memory. It is safe for this problem only because each exponent e_i is very small.

Changing func_2 to return [1] when input is 1 alters its semantics compared to the original (which returned an empty factor list). In this code, correctness is preserved because M == 1 is handled by an early exit and func_2 is not called in that case, but reusing func_2 elsewhere could be incorrect.

Relying on exact integer division var_9 // var_2 in func_1 requires that the binomial formula is implemented correctly; any mismatch in numerator/denominator ranges would cause a subtle bug (non-integer division).

While eliminating large factorial arrays is good here, for problems with many binomial queries or larger k values, precomputing factorials modulo MOD and using modular inverses can be asymptotically superior to repeated multiplicative binomial computations.

The algorithm still uses trial division for factorization; if M’s constraints were raised significantly (e.g., up to 1e15 or higher), this step would become the new bottleneck and might require a faster factorization method.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: count integers in [1, N] with an odd number of digits. The optimized solution hardcodes ranges up to 10^6, suggesting N is at most around 10^5–10^6. No multiple queries.

dominant_ops: Iterate over all integers from 1 to N and, for each, repeatedly divide by 10 to count its digits, then test if the digit count is odd.

complexity.why: For each integer up to N, the code performs a loop that divides by 10 until the value is 0; the number of divisions is proportional to the number of digits, i.e., O(log_10 i). Summed over i from 1 to N, this is O(N log N). Only a constant number of integer variables are used, so space is O(1).

bottlenecks.detail: Linear scan over all numbers from 1 to N, even though we only need aggregated counts per digit-length range.
For each number, a while-loop repeatedly performs integer division by 10 to count digits, adding a log10 factor to runtime.
Integer division inside the innermost loop is relatively expensive compared to simple arithmetic or a constant-time formula.
Use of eval(input()) is unnecessary (int(input()) suffices) and potentially unsafe, though it is not the main performance bottleneck.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the structure of decimal lengths: count how many numbers up to N have 1, 3, 5, ... digits using closed-form expressions per digit-length interval instead of iterating through each integer. For each range [10^(k-1), min(N, 10^k - 1)] where k is odd, add its size to the answer.

complexity.why: The solution uses a fixed sequence of conditional checks and a small number of arithmetic operations to compute the count directly from N. This work does not scale with N, so time is constant. No additional data structures are used, so space remains constant as well.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log N)
complexity_delta.note: Replaced per-number digit counting with a constant-time formula based on digit-length intervals (1–9, 100–999, 10000–99999, ...).

transformation_steps: Identify the computed quantity: the original loop increments the counter whenever the number of digits of the current integer is odd, so it counts integers in [1, N] with an odd number of digits.
Recognize that all numbers with the same digit length form contiguous ranges: 1–9 (1 digit), 10–99 (2 digits), 100–999 (3 digits), etc.
Observe that for each odd digit length k, the contribution is simply the size of the intersection between [1, N] and [10^(k-1), 10^k - 1].
Derive closed-form counts for each relevant range: e.g., if N < 10, answer is N; if 10 ≤ N < 100, answer is 9; if 100 ≤ N < 1000, answer is 9 + (N - 99); and similarly for higher odd lengths.
Encode these formulas as a small set of if/elif branches on N, using constant expressions (like 9, 909, 90909) or simple linear expressions (like N - 90, N - 9090).
Remove the explicit loop and digit-counting while-loop, leaving only O(1) arithmetic and branch operations.
trigger_signals: Presence of an outer loop from 1 to N with inner digit-counting logic, indicating at least O(N log N) operations.
Problem structure depending only on digit length, not on specific digit patterns, which often allows range-based counting.
Expected constraints where N can be large (e.g., up to 10^5 or more), making per-integer processing potentially slow in Python.
Use of repeated integer division inside a tight loop, which is relatively expensive in Python.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors at interval boundaries (e.g., correctly handling transitions at N = 9, 10, 99, 100, 999, etc.).
Forgetting to include all odd-digit ranges that might be needed if N can exceed the hardcoded maximum (e.g., N ≥ 10^6 in this implementation is not handled).
Miscomputing constants like 90, 909, or 9090 when converting mathematical ranges to code, which can subtly skew results.
Assuming N is always positive; negative or zero inputs are not logically handled by the counting formula or the original code.
Continuing to use eval(input()) instead of int(input()), which is unnecessary and unsafe, even if performance is improved elsewhere.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style scheduling/feasibility task; main cost is sorting tasks by deadline. Likely n up to 2e5–3e5, no extra queries.

dominant_ops: Sorting list of n tasks by deadline
Reading and constructing list of tasks

complexity.why: n tasks are stored in a list; sorting that list dominates with O(n log n). The subsequent single pass over the list is O(n). Input helpers and overhead are linear at most.

bottlenecks.detail: Uses eval(input()) and an indirection via func_4() for the initial integer, plus wrapper input functions; eval is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()) and direct map(int, ...).
Redefines func_2 from a function to a list, reuses func_4 as both function and loop index, and calls helper functions for each line read, adding Python-level overhead in tight loops.

Imports math, itertools, bisect, copy, deque, Counter, Decimal, and defines helper functions (func_3, func_5, func_6, func_7) that are never used, slightly increasing startup and namespace management cost.
Constructs each task as [var_2, var_1] to sort by deadline, which is fine but entails explicit reordering instead of directly sorting original pairs by key. This is a minor constant-factor cost.

FastAudit.core_idea: Preserve the same greedy scheduling-by-deadline algorithm but streamline the implementation: read tasks directly into a list, sort them by their deadline field using a key function, and perform a single cumulative-duration check. Remove unnecessary helpers and imports to reduce Python overhead.

complexity.why: As in the original, the sort over n tasks dominates with O(n log n); reading input and the cumulative check each scan the list once in O(n). The memory footprint is storing the list of n tasks plus a few scalar variables, so O(n) space.

complexity_delta.from: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged; improvements are from reducing Python-level overhead (fewer function calls, less eval use, simpler data layout) and minor simplifications around sorting.

transformation_steps: Inline the initial input parsing: replace func_4() wrapper + eval(input()) with a direct int(eval(input())) for the task count (still using eval but with less indirection).
Remove unused helper functions (func_1, func_2, func_3, func_5, func_6, func_7) and global constants that are never referenced in the core logic.
Eliminate unnecessary imports (sys, math, itertools, bisect, copy, deque, Counter, Decimal) that were not used in the solution.
Read each task directly into a list as [duration, deadline] instead of reordering to [deadline, duration] for sorting.
Sort the tasks using sorted(var_5, key=lambda var_6: var_6[1]) to order them by deadline (second element) rather than constructing swapped pairs and using default sort.
Retain a single linear pass to accumulate durations and check against deadlines, using straightforward variables and indexing without function indirection.
Avoid reassigning function names to data (e.g., func_2 being reused as a list), making the runtime environment simpler and reducing potential name resolution overhead.
trigger_signals: Presence of eval(input()) for parsing integers, which is slower and unsafe compared to direct int(input()).
Multiple small wrapper functions around simple I/O operations used in tight loops, indicating unnecessary function-call overhead.
Large set of unused imports and helper utilities, typical of template code that was not pruned for performance-critical submissions.
Algorithm already optimal (greedy with sorting), implying that any remaining performance improvements must come from constant-factor optimization rather than algorithmic changes.
pitfalls: Continuing to use eval for numeric input can remain a performance and security concern; replacing eval(input()) with input() and then explicit parsing (int, map(int, ...)) is safer and slightly faster.
Relying on sort key positions requires consistent understanding of the data layout; mixing up indices (duration vs deadline) would break correctness even though the performance is fine.
If constraints were significantly smaller, these micro-optimizations would be unnecessary and could reduce readability; balance clarity and performance based on problem limits.
In more complex variants (e.g., additional constraints or weights), similar greedy logic might not stay correct even though the pattern of sorting by deadlines and accumulating time looks similar.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical Lunlun-number task: input is a single integer K (1-indexed). K is up to around 1e5 in common contest problems; maximum digit length is effectively bounded (<= ~10–11) by construction.

dominant_ops: Recursive DFS over the digit tree of Lunlun numbers (branching factor up to 3, depth up to ~10–11).
Per-node integer-to-string conversion and length check: len(str(var_2)) and str(var_2)[-1].
Appending every generated number into a global Python list.
Full sort of the list of all generated Lunlun numbers before indexing the (k-1)-th element.

complexity.why: Let D be the maximum number of digits (here effectively ~10) and M be the number of Lunlun numbers generated up to that digit length. The DFS explores roughly 9 * 3^(D-1) states (constant for fixed D), each doing O(D) string work. After generation, it sorts all M numbers, which costs O(M log M). All numbers are stored simultaneously, so memory is O(M). For the intended constraints (D small, K up to ~1e5), this is practically fine but asymptotically it scales with the total search space instead of the requested rank K.

bottlenecks.detail: Always generates the entire set of Lunlun numbers up to length ~10–11, even if the requested index K is small. Complexity is tied to total possible states (M) rather than the required rank K.
Sorts the entire list var_4 of Lunlun numbers, although the DFS could in principle be structured to generate in sorted order or to stop once the K-th value is reached, avoiding O(M log M) sorting.
Deep recursion in Python for digit-DFS; while depth here is bounded (~11), recursion still incurs Python call overhead per node and can be fragile if digit bound is ever increased.

For every DFS node, it converts the current number to a string multiple times (len(str(var_2)), int(str(var_2)[-1])). This adds an O(D) factor to each node expansion instead of maintaining digits as integers.
It never stops generation early when var_4 contains at least K elements; it continues to enumerate all possible Lunlun numbers up to the depth bound, regardless of K.
Uses eval(input()) instead of int(input()), which is slower and insecure. Not a big asymptotic cost, but a notable code-smell.

FastAudit.core_idea: Re-architect around direct construction and validation of Lunlun numbers via digit-wise operations (func_2) and iterative arithmetic, instead of recursive tree traversal with string conversions. The helper func_2 checks the Lunlun property by scanning adjacent digits, making it possible to iterate over candidates numerically and test them. The surrounding structure (func_11, while True, base-10 arithmetic) appears intended to compute successive valid numbers using integer arithmetic and digit boundaries rather than exploring the whole DFS tree explicitly.

complexity.why: From the visible part, func_2 runs in O(d) where d is the digit count of a candidate number. func_11 iterates var_9-1 times (suggesting it tries to get the var_9-th Lunlun number), and in each iteration it performs some inner while True arithmetic and likely a small number of func_2 checks. If designed as a sequential 'next valid number' generator without exploring a full DFS tree, the effective time is proportional to K times a small digit-wise cost C_digit, and it does not need to store all previously generated values, yielding O(1) auxiliary space (besides call stack and constants). Exact asymptotics depend on the missing tail of func_11, but the structural goal is to tie cost to K rather than to the whole search space M.

complexity_delta.from: O(3^D * D + M log M) time, O(M) space (DFS over entire search space with final sort).
complexity_delta.to: O(K * C_digit) time, O(1)–O(K) space depending on implementation details of the iterator (ideally no global list or sort).
complexity_delta.note: The key conceptual improvement is shifting work from 'generate and sort all possible Lunlun numbers up to max length' to 'generate or search directly for the K-th valid number', thus making runtime depend on K rather than on the total number of candidates M. For typical constraints (K up to 1e5, D ~ 10), both are fast enough, but the latter scales more gracefully if K or allowed digits grow.

transformation_steps: Replace recursive DFS that builds numbers by appending digits and converting to strings with an iterative, digit-based numeric approach (e.g., using integer arithmetic and digit differences).
Introduce a dedicated Lunlun-check function (func_2) that verifies abs(diff between adjacent digits) <= 1 in O(d) time without constructing new strings repeatedly.

Shift from 'generate all then sort and index' to 'iteratively compute the next Lunlun number until the K-th' (or a mathematically guided construction), eliminating the need for a global list and final sort.
Avoid accumulating all results in memory; instead, maintain only the current candidate (and possibly a small amount of auxiliary state), returning the answer when the rank is reached.
Remove or minimize string conversions in the hot loop by operating directly on digits via integer division/modulo or by pre-extracted digit arrays.
Use iterative loops instead of deep recursion to limit Python call overhead and avoid recursion-depth issues if the digit limit increases.
trigger_signals: Presence of a DFS that enumerates the full combinatorial space of digit sequences up to a fixed depth, irrespective of the requested K.
Use of a global list that stores every generated candidate and is then fully sorted even though only the K-th element is needed.
Repeated conversions between integers and strings within the inner loop (len(str(x)), str(x)[-1]) for every node.
No early-termination condition tied to reaching the K-th valid number; execution continues to explore all branches.
Introduction in the modified code of a specialized predicate (func_2) and arithmetic manipulations around powers of 10, indicating a move toward digit-based reasoning rather than tree traversal.
pitfalls: If the 'fast' iteration still linearly scans many invalid candidates (e.g., simply incrementing the integer and checking with func_2), it can become slower than the original DFS for large K, as it may effectively be O(answer_value * d) instead of O(M).
A while True loop without careful break conditions (as seen partially in func_11) risks devolving into very long or infinite loops for certain edge cases, which is worse than the predictable DFS.
Trying to be too clever with digit-arithmetic skipping can easily introduce off-by-one errors, especially around boundaries like transitions between digit lengths (e.g., 9→10, 19→20, 99→100).
Removing recursion in favor of iteration must preserve the generation order; if order is not monotone, simply stopping at the K-th generated value may not return the K-th smallest number.

Micro-optimizations (large import list, debugging timers, stderr logging) can clutter the solution and add overhead without changing asymptotic behavior; they should be kept out of the hot path in performance-sensitive contexts.

The original code’s length cutoff (len(str(var_2)) > 10) is slightly subtle: the append occurs before the check, inadvertently including 11-digit numbers; when reworking the algorithm, it’s easy either to change the effective search space or to misalign with the original behavior if problem constraints rely on a specific bound.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder 'Coprime' problem: N up to 1e5, each A_i up to about 1e6. Need to classify: pairwise coprime, setwise coprime, or not coprime.

dominant_ops: Building a smallest-prime-factor sieve up to 10^6, then for each number repeatedly dividing by its smallest prime factor while doing Python set insert/lookup operations.

complexity.time: O(A_max log log A_max + n log A_max)
complexity.why: func_2 runs an Eratosthenes-like sieve up to 10^6: sum_{p prime<=A_max} A_max/p = O(A_max log log A_max). func_3 then factors each of the n numbers via repeated division by smallest prime factors, needing O(log A_i) divisions per number, so O(n log A_max) overall, plus O(total distinct prime factors) set operations. func_1 adds an O(n log A_max) gcd fold, but this is dominated by the sieve and factorization.

bottlenecks.detail: Sieve size is hard-coded to 10**6 in func_3 regardless of the actual maximum value in the input, forcing a full 10^6-scale sieve even when unnecessary.
func_2 implements the sieve entirely in Python with nested for-loops over up to 10^6 indices; this has substantial interpreter overhead compared to more linear scans.

For each prime factor of each number, func_3 performs membership checks and insertions into two Python sets (var_8 and var_9). These operations are O(1) average but relatively slow, and are in the inner factorization loop.

Every number is factored individually via repeated division by smallest prime factors. Even though asymptotically acceptable, it incurs many Python-level divisions and loop iterations when there are many inputs or larger values.
The global gcd is computed separately in func_1 by folding gcd over all elements, even though the factorization phase already contains enough information to infer setwise vs not coprime in principle.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid explicit per-number factorization and sets; instead, count frequency of each value, then for every integer d from 2 to max(A_i) aggregate counts of multiples of d. The maximum such aggregate tells whether any common divisor occurs in at least 2 elements (pairwise test) and whether some divisor occurs in all elements (setwise vs not).

complexity.why: Building the frequency array var_2 is O(n). The main loop over d = 2..A_max does sum(var_2[d::d]), which iterates over roughly A_max/d elements for each d. The total work is sum_{d=2..A_max} A_max/d = A_max * H_{A_max} = O(A_max log A_max). No per-element factorization or sets are used, so the constant factors are smaller and the code is cache-friendly.

complexity_delta.from: O(A_max log log A_max + n log A_max) time, O(A_max) space, with high Python overhead from sieve and set-based factorization.
complexity_delta.to: O(A_max log A_max + n) time, O(A_max) space, using a frequency array and divisor-multiples aggregation with fewer Python-level operations.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both depend linearly (up to log factors) on A_max, but the fast version removes per-number factorization and set overhead, and converts the logic into a single structured multiples scan, which is much faster in CP Python.

transformation_steps: Replace smallest-prime-factor sieve (func_2) and per-number factorization (func_3) with a single frequency array var_2 of size max(A_i)+1 that counts occurrences of each value.
For each integer d from 2 to max(A_i), compute how many input numbers are divisible by d by summing var_2 at indices d, 2d, 3d, ... (i.e., sum(var_2[d::d])). Track the maximum such count var_6.

Use var_6 to classify: if var_6 < 2 then no divisor > 1 appears in two different numbers (pairwise coprime); else if var_6 < n then some divisor > 1 appears multiple times but none appear in all numbers (setwise coprime); else var_6 == n implies some divisor > 1 divides all numbers (not coprime).
Remove explicit gcd folding (func_1) and the prime-factor-set logic (func_3/func_4); the classification is now derived solely from the divisor-multiples counts.
Tighten memory layout to a single integer list var_2; avoid sets and auxiliary arrays from the sieve.
trigger_signals: Presence of a full sieve up to a fixed large bound (10**6) even when the maximum input value can be smaller.
Nested Python for-loops over ranges proportional to 10^6 in func_2, indicating potentially millions of interpreted iterations regardless of input.
Inner loops that perform repeated division and Python set operations for each prime factor of every number in func_3.
Separate gcd folding pass over all elements in addition to the factorization-based analysis, suggesting redundant computation.
The problem structure (checking common divisors over a bounded integer domain) naturally suggests a frequency-and-multiples approach instead of explicit factorization.
pitfalls: Using sum(var_2[d::d]) creates a new list slice for each d, which is extra overhead and memory churn; a more optimal variant would manually loop k in range(d, maxA+1, d) and accumulate var_2[k] without slicing.
The multiples-based logic assumes A_i >= 1; if zeros or negatives were allowed, the divisor counting and gcd interpretation would need adjustments.

If max(A_i) were much larger (e.g., up to 10^7 or more), the O(A_max log A_max) scan over all d could become too slow or memory-heavy; then a different strategy (e.g., factoring each number with a faster sieve or using a hashmap of prime counts) might be preferable.

The correctness of classifying setwise vs not coprime using only the maximum multiples count depends on the fact that gcd > 1 iff there exists at least one prime dividing all numbers; this must be remembered if adapting the pattern to more general domains.
Care must be taken that the length of var_2 is max(A_i)+1, and that indices are not off-by-one; any shift would corrupt the divisor counts and misclassify the coprimality.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical 'K-th Lunlun number' style task. K (input) up to about 1e5, numbers fit in 64-bit integer. Need to generate numbers whose adjacent digits differ by at most 1, then output the K-th smallest.

dominant_ops: Exhaustive DFS generation of all valid numbers up to fixed depth (10 digits)
Appending every generated number into a Python list
Global sort of the full list of generated numbers
Recursive call overhead for each node in the DFS tree

complexity.time: O(T log T) where T is the total count of generated numbers (≈ 9 * 3^9 < 2e5 for depth 10). Independent of requested index K.
complexity.space: O(T) to store all generated numbers before sorting.
complexity.why: DFS visits every valid number up to depth 10 and appends it to var_1. After generation, sort() is applied once to the full list, costing O(T log T). Memory must hold all T numbers concurrently; recursion stack is O(L) where L=10 (constant).

bottlenecks.detail: Generates all Lunlun-like numbers up to 10 digits regardless of the requested index var_4 (K). For small K, almost all generated work is unused.
Performs a global sort of the entire collection of numbers even though only the K-th element is required.
Python recursion for every node in the search tree adds function call overhead. Safe here due to depth 10, but costly relative to an iterative queue-based solution.
All generated numbers are kept in var_1 simultaneously; peak memory is proportional to the total count of valid numbers, not to K.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use BFS (queue) over valid numbers in increasing order so that the sequence is generated in sorted order by construction. Start from 1..9, repeatedly pop the smallest current number, extend it by appending digits in {last_digit-1, last_digit, last_digit+1} (within [0,9]) and push back to the queue. After K pops, the last popped value is exactly the K-th smallest number; no global sort or full enumeration is needed.

complexity.time: O(K): Each loop iteration pops one number and pushes up to 3 new ones; constant work per generated element, repeated K times.
complexity.space: O(K) in the worst case for the queue, typically on the same order as the number of generated-but-not-yet-popped numbers.
complexity.why: BFS ensures numbers are produced in non-decreasing order by magnitude and lexicographic structure. Since we terminate after K pops, the algorithm’s cost scales directly with K, avoiding processing of unnecessary higher-index elements.

complexity_delta.from: O(T log T) time, O(T) space with T ≈ total count of valid numbers up to fixed depth (independent of K).
complexity_delta.to: O(K) time, O(K) space where K is the requested index.
complexity_delta.note: For the typical constraint K ≤ 1e5 and T ≈ 2e5, both are feasible, but the BFS solution scales directly in K and avoids the overhead of generating and sorting all numbers, making it more robust if limits increase.

transformation_steps: Replace recursive DFS generation of all numbers with an iterative BFS using a queue (collections.deque).
Initialize the queue with base numbers 1..9 instead of recursively starting from each digit.
At each iteration, pop the front of the queue as the next smallest number, append valid next states by using last_digit-1, last_digit, last_digit+1 (with boundary checks on 0 and 9).
Count how many numbers have been popped; once the count reaches K, output the last popped number and terminate.
Remove the global list and final sort, since BFS order guarantees sorted output by construction.
trigger_signals: The original code computes the full set of candidates and sorts them despite needing only the K-th element.
Presence of a global list accumulating all results and a final sort() often indicates a potential streaming/BFS alternative.
Recursive implementation with small fixed depth suggests it’s modeling a tree/graph traversal that can be made iterative.
The pattern 'generate all -> sort -> index[K]' is a classic candidate for online generation in sorted order.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors: ensuring that after K iterations of popping, the last popped number corresponds exactly to the K-th element (careful with 0-based vs 1-based counting).
Using a plain list instead of deque for the queue would make popleft() O(n), degrading performance to roughly O(K^2).
Boundary handling for last_digit==0 and last_digit==9 must be correct to avoid generating invalid digits or missing valid ones.
Changing recursion depth or problem constraints in the original DFS solution could hit Python’s recursion limits, whereas the BFS solution avoids this but still must consider integer size limits.
Using eval(input()) is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; while not the main performance bottleneck, it is a practice to avoid.

constraints_guess.n_max: ≈ 1e5 for N (first input); M (second input) up to about 1e9–1e12 so that trial division to sqrt(M) is feasible
constraints_guess.notes: Typical of AtCoder ABC-style problem (e.g., factorize M and use combinations with repetition: ∏ C(e_i + N - 1, e_i) mod 1e9+7). Need to support large N but relatively small max exponent sum.

dominant_ops: Naive trial division factorization up to sqrt(M) using while var_5**2 <= var_9
Repeated calls to math.factorial for arguments up to N + max_exponent
Large integer multiplications and divisions when computing nCk = fact(n) // (fact(k) * fact(n-k)) in full precision before applying modulo
Repeated construction of list(var_11.keys()) inside the factorization loop

complexity.time: O(√M + K * F(N)) where K is number of distinct prime factors of M (small) and F(N) is the cost of computing factorials of size up to N+max_e with big integers (superlinear, roughly Θ(N^2) bit-ops in practice). Effectively much slower than O(N).
complexity.space: O(K + U * N_bits) where K is number of primes and U is number of distinct factorial arguments cached in var_1; each factorial value is a huge big integer whose size grows as Θ(N log N) bits.
complexity.why: Trial division is standard O(√M), but the real cost is math.factorial on large n: computing and storing huge exact factorials and then doing big-int arithmetic (multiplication, division) for each binomial coefficient. The cache var_1 avoids recomputing some factorials but still stores large values. Converting dict.keys() to a list inside the factorization loop adds an unnecessary O(K) factor on each iteration, though this is minor compared to factorial costs.

bottlenecks.detail: Combinations are computed via exact factorials and integer division (var_2 // (var_3 * var_4)) instead of using modular factorials and modular inverses. This forces all operations to use large arbitrary-precision integers, dramatically increasing time and memory usage.

Even with caching, math.factorial is called on several large arguments (≈ N, N+e_i, e_i). Factorial is Θ(n) multiplications on increasing big integers, and each call recomputes from scratch rather than building incrementally.

Using `if var_5 in list(var_11.keys())` inside the factorization loop rebuilds the keys list on every iteration. Proper use of `if var_5 in var_11` would be O(1); the current code is O(K) per check, adding overhead if M has many small factors.
Modulo 1e9+7 is applied only at the very end (`var_12 % var_7`), so all intermediate combinatorial values grow to the exact size of factorials, instead of staying bounded by MOD.

FastAudit.core_idea: Factorize M as ∏ p_i^{e_i} using trial division, then compute the answer as ∏ C(e_i + N - 1, e_i) modulo 1e9+7. Precompute factorials and inverse factorials up to max_n = N + max(e_i) under the modulus, using O(max_n) time and O(max_n) memory, and use them to evaluate each binomial coefficient in O(1) with only modular arithmetic.

complexity.time: O(√M + max_n + log MOD) where max_n = N + max_exponent ≤ N + O(log M). Trial division factorization is O(√M). Factorial and inverse-factorial arrays are built in O(max_n). One modular exponentiation via fast binary exponentiation runs in O(log MOD). Each binomial coefficient is then O(1), so total is effectively linear in N plus √M.
complexity.space: O(max_n) for two integer arrays (factorials and inverse factorials) plus O(K) for the prime factorization map, all under 64-bit modular arithmetic.
complexity.why: All heavy combinatorial work is moved into a single linear precomputation of factorials and inverse factorials modulo MOD, which uses only primitive integer operations. Binomial coefficients are computed as C(n,k) = fact[n] * invfact[k] * invfact[n-k] mod MOD, avoiding big-int factorials and divisions. Factorization cost stays the same order as in the slow version, but the dominant combinatorial portion drops from big-int factorials to simple modular multiplications.

complexity_delta.from: Factorization O(√M) plus expensive big-int factorial and division for each binomial: effectively superlinear in N with large constant factors, dominated by math.factorial and big-int arithmetic.
complexity_delta.to: Factorization O(√M) plus O(N + max_exponent) modular precomputation and O(K) O(1)-time binomial evaluations: overall O(√M + N) with small constants using fixed-width modular arithmetic.
complexity_delta.note: The key improvement is replacing repeated exact factorial computations and integer division with a single linear modular precomputation and O(1) modular binomial evaluations.

transformation_steps: Replaced Python's math.factorial-based nCk with a modular combinatorics framework: precompute factorials fact[i] and inverse factorials invfact[i] for i up to N + max_exponent under MOD = 1e9+7.

Introduced fast modular exponentiation (binary exponentiation) to compute fact[max_n]^(MOD-2) mod MOD (Fermat's little theorem) and then filled invfact[] in a single backward pass, turning inversion of all factorials into an O(max_n) process.
Computed binomial coefficients as C(n,k) = fact[n] * invfact[k] * invfact[n-k] mod MOD in O(1) per query, eliminating repeated big-int factorial calls and integer divisions.
Kept all arithmetic under the modulus throughout, which avoids growth of intermediate values to enormous factorial sizes and keeps operations in the range of native integers.
Improved factorization bookkeeping by storing exponents in a defaultdict(int) keyed by primes, avoiding repeated list(var_11.keys()) construction and using O(1) dictionary updates.
Precomputed factorials once globally (arrays var_8 and var_9) instead of caching factorial results in a dictionary per argument, greatly reducing both overhead and memory footprint.
trigger_signals: Use of math.factorial with arguments tied to N (potentially up to 1e5 or higher) and then dividing large factorial values before applying modulo suggested heavy big-int arithmetic and avoidable cost.
Presence of a fixed prime modulus 1e9+7, which is a strong hint that modular combinatorics (factorials + inverse factorials or Pascal-style DP) should be used instead of raw factorials.
Repeated computation (and caching) of factorials for related arguments (N-1, e_i, N-1+e_i), suggesting that a single linear precomputation over a contiguous range would be more efficient.
Creation of list(var_11.keys()) inside a while loop during factorization signaled unnecessary per-iteration overhead in a core numeric loop.
General pattern: computing combinatorial numbers with exact integers first and only taking modulo at the end is a classic anti-pattern for performance in modular arithmetic problems.
pitfalls: When switching to modular combinatorics, max_n (the upper bound for factorial arrays) must be chosen correctly as N + max_exponent; underestimating it leads to index errors or incorrect binomial values.
The modular inverse technique using Fermat's little theorem requires MOD to be prime. For other moduli, a different inversion strategy (e.g., extended GCD per value) would be needed.
Care must be taken to keep all intermediary products reduced modulo MOD; missing a `% MOD` can reintroduce large integers and degrade performance.
The binary exponentiation function must use the correct exponent (MOD-2) and correct modulus parameter; miswiring the parameters (e.g., wrong named argument) can silently break inverse computation.
For extremely large N beyond typical contest constraints, even O(N) precomputation may be too slow or memory-heavy; then alternative combinatorial or number-theoretic approaches would be required.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style combinatorics problem with modulo 998244353. Single query (n, m, k). k can be up to n-1. Needs O(n) or O(k log MOD) solution; O(n^2) would TLE.

dominant_ops: Precomputation of factorials, modular inverses, and inverse factorials up to n+10 in func_3 via a linear loop
Main accumulation loop over k+1 terms, each term computing a binomial coefficient C(n-1, i) using precomputed tables
Repeated modular exponentiation pow(m-1, MOD-2, MOD) inside the main loop to update a geometric factor

complexity.why: func_3 builds factorial, inverse, and inverse factorial arrays up to size Θ(n) in O(n) time and space. The main loop in func_2 runs for (k+1) iterations; each iteration does O(1) arithmetic plus one modular exponentiation pow(m-1, MOD-2, MOD), which costs O(log MOD). Therefore total time is O(n + k log MOD). Arrays var_7, var_6, var_9 store O(n) values, giving O(n) memory.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorials and inverse factorials are precomputed up to n+10 regardless of the actual k. When k << n, this O(n) preprocessing dominates the runtime even though only C(n-1, i) for i <= k are needed.
Inside the main loop, pow(m-1, MOD-2, MOD) is recomputed on every iteration to divide by (m-1). This modular inverse of a constant could be computed once and reused, avoiding O(k log MOD) work.
Although asymptotically linear, the factorial precomputation involves multiple modular multiplications and reciprocal computations, adding noticeable constant-factor overhead for large n (e.g., 2e5).

FastAudit.core_idea: Eliminate global factorial/inverse tables and instead iterate directly over the k+1 terms using a multiplicative recurrence for binomial coefficients combined with per-term modular powers for the geometric factor. This reduces preprocessing from O(n) to O(1) and makes runtime depend mainly on k.

complexity.why: The optimized code iterates over var_4 from 0 to var_5 (k) and in each iteration: (1) computes pow(var_6 - 1, var_7 - var_4 - 1, MOD), and (2) updates the combinatorial factor var_3 using a multiplicative formula with pow(var_4 + 1, MOD-2, MOD). Each pow call is O(log MOD), so each iteration is O(log MOD). With k+1 iterations, total time is O(k log MOD). Only a constant number of integers are stored, so memory usage is O(1).

complexity_delta.from: O(n + k * log MOD) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(k * log MOD) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: Removed the O(n) factorial and inverse-table precomputation and switched to an on-the-fly multiplicative binomial update, making the algorithm depend primarily on k rather than n.

transformation_steps: Removed global factorial, inverse, and inverse factorial arrays (var_7, var_6, var_9) and their O(n) precomputation in func_3.
Replaced table-based binomial evaluation C(n-1, i) with an iterative multiplicative recurrence maintained in var_3: C(n-1, i+1) = C(n-1, i) * (n-1-i) * inv(i+1) mod MOD.

Folded the separate loops (one for building the initial geometric factor m*(m-1)^{n-1} and another for summation) into a single loop that directly uses pow(var_6-1, var_7-var_4-1, MOD) to compute the needed power term for each i.
Reduced memory usage by working with scalar variables only (var_1..var_7), eliminating the O(n) arrays.
Avoided reliance on sys.stdin and custom read helpers for this single-query scenario, simplifying IO overhead (though this is a minor performance aspect compared to the algorithmic changes).
trigger_signals: Presence of factorial and inverse arrays sized up to n even though the summation only depends on C(n-1, i) for i in [0, k], suggesting potential over-precomputation when k << n.
Repeated modular exponentiation of the same base (m-1) for its inverse inside the main loop, which is a known performance smell.
Typical constraints (n up to around 2e5) where an O(n) precomputation plus k log MOD can be borderline if constants are large, motivating a more k-focused approach.
Observation that the combinatorial term C(n-1, i) naturally supports a simple multiplicative recurrence, enabling elimination of factorial tables.
pitfalls: Incorrectly implementing the multiplicative recurrence for binomial coefficients can lead to off-by-one errors: the recurrence must use (n-1-i) in the numerator and (i+1) in the denominator when iterating from i to i+1.

Computing modular inverses per iteration via pow(x, MOD-2, MOD) is still O(log MOD); if k is close to n and n is large, a hybrid strategy (precomputing inverse prefix) could be faster, but would reintroduce higher memory usage.
Care must be taken to avoid computing an inverse of zero: ensure that the loop bounds and parameters guarantee var_4+1 != 0 mod MOD when calling pow(var_4+1, MOD-2, MOD).

Replacing factorial-based combinatorics with recurrence-based updates can reduce robustness against future changes: if the problem later requires arbitrary C(n, r) queries, the lack of precomputed tables may become a bottleneck.

Floating between different formulations (original sum as m*(m-1)^{n-1-i} * C(n-1, i) vs the new one) risks algebraic mistakes; the transformation must be checked carefully against sample tests or derived identities.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic AtCoder-style brute-force problem (ABC119C Synthetic Kadomatsu). N is small (≈8), targets and lengths up to around 10^3, enabling 4^N enumeration.

dominant_ops: Enumerating all 3^N assignments of rods to the three targets and, for each group, running a heavy recursive search (func_1) over all subsets/combinations using list slicing.

complexity.time: Θ(3^N * T_rec(N)), where T_rec(k) ≈ k * T_rec(k-1) + O(k) (factorial-like), effectively super-exponential in N for non-trivial inputs.
complexity.space: Θ(3^N * N) to store all assignments materialized as a list + O(N) recursion stack and repeated list copies.
complexity.why: The outer loop pre-materializes all itertools.product([0,1,2], repeat=N) results (3^N tuples of length N). For each assignment, func_1 is called up to three times on groups of size ≤N. func_1 recursively explores combinations by removing one element at each level using slicing (var_12[:var_9] + var_12[var_9+1:]), causing an explosion in the number of states because there is no memoization and each recursive call allocates a new list.

bottlenecks.detail: func_1 performs a naive recursive search over all combinations of rods to approximate the target length, without memoization. The branching factor is up to the current group size, leading to roughly k! subcalls for a group of size k in the worst case.
Each recursive call of func_1 constructs a new list via var_12[:var_9] + var_12[var_9+1:], which is O(k) per call and multiplies the cost of the already explosive recursion.
var_8 = list(itertools.product([0, 1, 2], repeat=var_5)) stores all 3^N assignments in memory before processing, inflating memory usage and cache pressure instead of streaming them.

The solution decomposes the problem into: (1) assigning rods to three groups, and then (2) solving a separate exponential subproblem per group to approximate the target length. The intended problem can be solved by directly evaluating the cost of each assignment in linear time, so this decomposition is unnecessarily expensive.

FastAudit.core_idea: Enumerate all assignments of each rod to one of {A, B, C, unused} using product([0,1,2,3], repeat=N). For each assignment, accumulate the total length per target and the join cost (10 for every additional rod beyond the first in a target). After building three non-empty targets, add the adjustment cost |A-sumA| + |B-sumB| + |C-sumC| and take the minimum over all assignments.

complexity.space: Θ(N) extra (for small arrays and loop variables, product is streamed).
complexity.why: There are exactly 4 choices (A,B,C,unused) for each of N rods, giving 4^N assignments. For each assignment, the code does a single pass over N rods to accumulate lengths and join costs, then O(1) work to compute the final cost. product(...) is consumed directly in the loop, so intermediate assignments are not stored.

complexity_delta.from: Super-exponential-ish: Θ(3^N * T_rec(N)) with T_rec(k) ~ k! in the worst case due to recursive, non-memoized combination search per group.
complexity_delta.to: Controlled brute-force: Θ(4^N * N), which is feasible for N≈8.
complexity_delta.note: The key gain is eliminating the recursive subset search and computing the combination and adjustment costs in one linear pass per assignment. Even though the outer enumeration grows from 3^N to 4^N, the overall runtime plummets because each assignment is handled in O(N) instead of an exponential subroutine.

transformation_steps: Removed func_1 and the entire recursive subset/combination search over each group of rods.
Redesigned the state representation from 'group of rods then recursively decide subsets' to a single global assignment per rod: each rod is assigned to A, B, C, or unused.
Extended the assignment space from [0,1,2] (only the three targets) to [0,1,2,3] by introducing an explicit 'unused' option, allowing the correct modeling of rods that are not used for any target.

Inlined cost computation: during the scan over one assignment, track the current total length per target and add 10 to the cost whenever a rod is added to a non-empty target (implementing 10 * (number_of_pieces - 1) per target).

After the scan, skipped assignments where any of the three targets has zero total length (invalid because each must use at least one rod) and then added the adjustment cost as a sum of absolute differences between target and actual lengths.
Switched from materializing list(itertools.product(...)) to iterating directly over product(...), avoiding Θ(3^N) intermediate storage. (In the fast code, product is directly used in the for loop.)
trigger_signals: Presence of deeply recursive function (func_1) called repeatedly with overlapping subproblems and no memoization.
Use of list slicing in recursion (var_12[:var_9] + var_12[var_9+1:]), a classic TLE pattern for exponential recursion.
3^N outer enumeration combined with another exponential inner procedure, which is clearly excessive for even moderate N if constraints are small enough to allow a simpler brute-force.
Problem structure (three targets, small N) strongly suggests a global assignment-based brute-force (4^N) is intended and sufficient.
Memory-heavy pattern: list(itertools.product(...)) storing all combinatorial states at once instead of streaming them.
pitfalls: When switching to the assignment-based brute-force, it is easy to miscompute the join cost. The correct cost is 10 * (number_of_rods_assigned_to_target - 1) per target, implemented by adding 10 each time a non-empty target receives an additional rod.
Assignments where any of the three targets gets no rods must be excluded; failing to enforce this leads to undercounting the true minimal cost.
While 4^N * N is fine for N≈8, blindly applying the same brute-force for larger N would quickly become infeasible; the redesign assumes small N as given by the problem constraints.
Care must be taken not to reintroduce hidden exponential behavior (e.g., a secondary recursive check inside each assignment). All per-assignment processing must remain O(N).
Using eval on numeric input is unnecessary and slightly slower as well as unsafe in general contexts; though not a big performance bottleneck here, it is best replaced by int(input()).

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder ABC161 D (Lunlun Number) style: N up to about 1e5, single query; answer fits in 64-bit integer.

dominant_ops: Main BFS loop repeatedly popping from a deque and pushing up to 3 children per number
Per-iteration digit extraction via modulo (`var_13 % 10`) and integer arithmetic to form new numbers
Branching over neighbor offsets `(-1, 0, 1)` with bounds check `if 0 <= var_4 + var_7 <= 9`
Python loop and function-call overhead from the more generalized scaffolding (extra helpers, decorators, imports) around the core logic

complexity.why: The algorithm performs a breadth-first generation of Lunlun numbers: each iteration pops one number, computes its last digit, and conditionally enqueues up to 3 successors whose last-digit difference is at most 1. To obtain the N-th valid number it generates O(N) such numbers; each requires O(1) arithmetic and queue operations, giving O(N) time. The deque may hold Θ(N) numbers in the worst case, giving O(N) space.

bottlenecks.detail: The BFS uses a more generic pattern `for var_7 in (-1, 0, 1)` with `if 0 <= var_4 + var_7 <= 9` inside a tight loop, which adds an extra branch and loop control overhead for each generated neighbor compared with directly handling the 0 and 9 edge cases.

The file imports many unused modules (bisect, heapq, math, random, decimal, itertools, etc.) and defines generic I/O and timing helpers. While asymptotically irrelevant, this adds minor startup and function-call overhead relative to a minimal solution.

The BFS is written in a less constrained, more open-ended style (`while True` and manual termination logic in the missing tail), which typically implies additional checks per iteration compared with a known-bounds `for` loop over N-1 iterations.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a straightforward BFS over integers whose adjacent digits differ by at most 1: initialize a queue with [1..9]; then for exactly N-1 steps, pop the front number, generate successors by appending digits (last_digit-1, last_digit, last_digit+1) within [0,9], push them back, and after the loop the front of the queue is the N-th Lunlun number.

complexity.why: Each iteration pops one number and enqueues up to 3 new numbers, all via O(1) operations. The loop runs exactly N-1 times, so total work is Θ(N). The queue contains at most a constant multiple of N numbers, hence Θ(N) memory usage. The implementation is tight: minimal branching and no superfluous helper calls inside the critical loop.

complexity_delta.from: O(N) time, O(N) space (generic BFS with extra branching and scaffolding)
complexity_delta.to: O(N) time, O(N) space (specialized BFS with tighter loop and minimal overhead)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged (both are linear in N), but the fast version reduces per-iteration overhead in the hot loop and removes non-essential scaffolding, improving runtime by a constant factor.

transformation_steps: Specialized the BFS to this specific problem: use a fixed-count loop `for var_1 in range(1, var_2)` so exactly N-1 numbers are expanded, instead of a more open-ended or conditionally terminated `while True` pattern.

Replaced the generic neighbor-generation pattern `for offset in (-1, 0, 1) if 0 <= last_digit + offset <= 9` with explicit checks for `last_digit != 0` and `last_digit != 9`, avoiding one loop and one bounds check per neighbor.

Removed unused imports and general-purpose helpers (timing decorator, multiple I/O wrappers, math/itertools/decimal utilities) from the main execution path, slightly reducing startup and interpretive overhead.
Kept the core data structure (a deque) and BFS generation order but simplified control flow so that the queue operations and arithmetic dominate execution with minimal extra Python-level logic.
trigger_signals: The task requires enumerating the N-th element of a recursively defined sequence, which is naturally suited to a BFS-style generation with one expansion per sequence element.
Presence of many unused imports and helpers in the original file, indicating potential non-essential overhead unrelated to the algorithmic core.
A tight Python loop (`while True` or similar) with extra branching and generic neighbor enumeration in the hot path, suggesting that simplifying the loop structure could improve constant factors.
Knowledge that constraints for this problem (N up to around 1e5) make Python viable only if the per-iteration overhead is kept small.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when deciding how many times to expand the BFS: the correct pattern is to start with [1..9] and run N-1 expansion steps, then take the next value from the queue.
Forgetting to handle the edge digits 0 and 9 correctly when generating neighbors, which can lead to invalid digits or missed valid Lunlun numbers.
Using an unbounded generation loop without careful termination conditions, which could over-generate numbers and waste time.

Relying on `eval(input())` for reading integers (as in the fast code) is slightly slower and generally unsafe in other contexts; for competitive settings it is acceptable but should be avoided in reusable libraries or untrusted environments.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style problem: count shortest path lengths between all pairs (i, j) on a line graph 1..N with one extra edge (X, Y). Double nested loops over all pairs suggest N is at most around 2000 in Python; otherwise O(N^2) would be too slow.

dominant_ops: Nested loops over all pairs (i, j) with 0 <= i < j < N: O(N^2) iterations
Appending each pairwise distance into a Python list var_2: O(N^2) list growth and allocations
Building a Counter over var_2, iterating over all stored distances again: O(N^2) extra work

complexity.why: There are N(N-1)/2 distinct pairs (i, j). For each pair, the code computes a constant-time expression and appends the resulting distance to var_2, giving Θ(N^2) operations. Counter(var_2) then scans all these Θ(N^2) entries again to build frequency counts, adding another Θ(N^2) time but not changing the asymptotic complexity. The list var_2 itself stores Θ(N^2) integers, so memory usage is quadratic in N.

bottlenecks.detail: The list var_2 stores every pairwise distance, requiring O(N^2) integers. For N≈2000, this means ~2 million items; for larger N it becomes prohibitively large and can cause MLE or heavy GC overhead.

Distances are first materialized into var_2 and then counted by Counter. In fact, only frequency counts per distance are needed; storing all raw distances is unnecessary and doubles both passes over O(N^2) data.

Each appended distance is a separate Python int object in a list. Combined with Counter's internal dictionary objects, this leads to a large number of Python objects, increasing overhead, cache misses, and GC pressure.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid storing all pairwise distances. Instead, count frequencies on the fly during the nested loops by incrementing a preallocated array var_4 indexed by distance. This preserves the O(N^2) pairwise enumeration but reduces memory from O(N^2) to O(N) and removes the extra Counter pass.

complexity.why: The optimized code still has a double loop over all ordered pairs (var_6, var_7) with var_6 < var_7, resulting in Θ(N^2) iterations and constant-time work per iteration. However, instead of pushing distances into a list and then recounting them, it directly increments var_4[var_5], making only a single pass over all pairs. Memory use is dominated by the result array var_4 of length N, hence Θ(N) space, since no O(N^2) intermediate storage is kept.

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time complexity remains quadratic because all pairs must still be examined, but space complexity improves from quadratic to linear. The reduction in allocations and passes over data significantly improves real runtime and memory behavior.

transformation_steps: Replace the accumulation of all pairwise distances in a list var_2 with direct counting into a frequency array var_4.
Preallocate var_4 = [0] * N to hold counts of each possible distance (1..N-1).
In the nested loops, compute var_5 as the shortest distance between the current pair and immediately do var_4[var_5] += 1 instead of appending to a list.
Remove the Counter construction and subsequent dictionary lookups; output counts directly from var_4[1:].
Slightly optimize the distance expression by using var_7 - var_6 instead of abs(var_6 - var_7) given the enforced ordering var_6 < var_7.
trigger_signals: Presence of a list that stores one value per pair (i, j), i.e., size ≈ N(N-1)/2, indicates O(N^2) memory usage.
Using collections.Counter on a very large list whose values are used only as frequencies reveals an unnecessary materialization step.
Observed or potential Memory Limit Exceeded (MLE) or significant slowdown due to handling millions of Python objects.
The logical requirement is only counts of distances, not the distances themselves, suggesting an opportunity for streaming aggregation.
pitfalls: Indexing off-by-one: when switching from Counter to a frequency array, ensure that distance d is stored at index d and that index 0 is unused or handled properly; the fast code addresses this by printing var_4[1:].

Maintaining correct pair orientation: the fast code uses nested loops (var_7 in range(N), var_6 in range(var_7)) so that var_7 > var_6, allowing var_7 - var_6 instead of abs(var_6 - var_7). Any change to loop bounds must preserve this ordering; otherwise the distance formula breaks.

Consistency of 0-based vs 1-based endpoints: both versions convert X and Y to 0-based indices (decrement by 1). When modifying or reusing this approach, mixing index bases will silently produce incorrect distances.
Potential overflow in other languages: while Python ints are unbounded, porting similar logic to languages with fixed-size integers must ensure indices and counts fit within chosen types.

constraints_guess.notes: Two strings of length n over alphabet {'A','B'} (or similar); about q range queries. Typical AtCoder-scale constraints (n,q up to 2e5) where O((n+q) log n) is fine and O((n+q)^2) is not.

dominant_ops: Building and manipulating large 2D NumPy arrays for prefix counts, plus Python loops to fill them and query ranges.

complexity.why: Two passes over each string to fill var_8 and var_9 (O(n)), two cumulative-sum passes with np.add.accumulate (O(n)), and a single loop over q queries performing O(1) arithmetic each (O(q)). Arrays store per-position info so memory is linear in string length.

bottlenecks.detail: Importing NumPy and creating large NumPy arrays introduces heavy constant-factor overhead. For competitive programming inputs (n ~ 1e5–2e5), pure Python arithmetic on lists/tuples with prefix sums is typically faster than NumPy due to import and bridge costs.

var_8 and var_9 are 2D arrays of shape (n+1, 2). Creating the initial Python list [[0,0] for _ in range(len(var_2))] is O(n) in Python objects, followed by conversion to a NumPy array, then another full pass to fill counts. This adds extra passes and object allocations.

Storing two separate counts per position (A and non-A) in a 2-column structure and then always using the difference (A-B) wastes memory and vectorization potential. A single scalar prefix sum with encoded values (1 or 2) suffices.

Large contiguous numeric buffers in NumPy are fast for vectorized bulk operations, but here most work is done in Python loops (per-character and per-query). The big arrays increase memory footprint with limited payoff.

FastAudit.core_idea: Encode each character as an integer (1 for 'A', 2 for others), build 1D prefix sums with itertools.accumulate, and answer each range query by comparing differences of these prefix sums modulo 3, all in pure Python with O(1) per query.

complexity.why: Single pass over each input string to map chars and accumulate prefix sums (O(n)), plus a loop over q queries where each query uses a constant number of arithmetic operations and array accesses (O(q)). Prefix arrays are length n+1, giving linear memory.

complexity_delta.from: O(n + q) time, O(n) space (NumPy + Python overhead)
complexity_delta.to: O(n + q) time, O(n) space (pure Python prefix sums)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged, but constants are greatly reduced by eliminating NumPy, 2D structures, and redundant passes.

transformation_steps: Replace per-character 2D count arrays with scalar encoding: map 'A' -> 1, others -> 2 to represent contributions directly in Z_3.
Build 1D prefix sums using itertools.accumulate and store them in tuples with a leading 0 for convenient 1-based indexing.
Derive the segment value as prefix[r] - prefix[l-1] for both strings, and compare their difference modulo 3 to answer queries.
Eliminate NumPy import and array creation; rely entirely on Python integers and built-in iteration for better performance in CP environments.
Optimize query loop to use direct input().split() parsing and minimal temporary variables, doing only O(1) arithmetic operations per query.
trigger_signals: Use of heavy numerical libraries (NumPy) in environments where import and Python<->C boundary overhead dominate for n ~ 1e5–2e5.
Multiple passes and conversions: list-of-lists creation, then conversion to NumPy arrays, then another pass to fill them.
2D data structures when a 1D prefix sum or difference array is mathematically sufficient.
Time limit exceeded or borderline performance despite nominally optimal O(n + q) complexity due to large constant factors.
pitfalls: Indexing off-by-one: switching from arrays sized len(var_2) with a manual leading '-' to tuples with a leading 0 requires careful adjustment of l-1 / r indices.
Encoding correctness: the mapping 'A' -> 1, other -> 2 and the modulo 3 logic must match the original A/B difference test; an incorrect encoding breaks equivalence.
Using input() instead of sys.stdin.readline in some environments can be slightly slower; ensure constraints are still safe or revert to buffered input if needed.
Tuple immutability: building prefix sums as tuples is fine for read-only access, but attempts to mutate them later would fail; code must treat them as immutable.
Modulo with negatives: in Python, x % 3 is always in {0,1,2}, but in other languages negative modulo behaves differently; the approach is Python-specific in that regard.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style heap problem: first integer N=var_3, then 3N array values. N likely up to ~1e5 so total elements ~3e5.

dominant_ops: Maintains two custom heap-wrapped classes and, in each of O(N) iterations, performs multiple heap pops/pushes plus Python-level max/min and method calls; then an additional O(N) scan over prefix arrays.

complexity.why: Initialization heapifies two heaps on O(N) data. The main loop (range(N)) does several heap operations per iteration (pop + push for left heap, pop + push for right heap). Each heap op costs O(log N), so overall O(N log N). Two auxiliary arrays of length N+1 plus stored heaps contribute O(N) memory.

bottlenecks.detail: In each of N iterations: var_6.pop() + var_6.push(...) and var_7.pop() + var_7.push(...). That is ~4 heap operations per index versus 2 heappushpop calls in the optimized version. Each extra heap op is O(log N), doubling the dominant cost.
Implements the update as an explicit pop followed by a conditional push with max/min logic instead of using heappushpop, causing extra sift-up/sift-down operations inside heapq.
Heap operations are wrapped in Class_1 methods (func_1/func_2 or pop/push). Every loop iteration incurs multiple Python method lookups and calls, which are expensive in a tight O(N log N) loop.
Per-iteration use of max(0, ...) and min(0, ...) plus repeated max/min when deciding what to push adds Python-level arithmetic and branching on top of heap operations.

Maintains two full prefix-sum arrays var_9 and var_10 of length N+1, then scans them, instead of combining prefix contributions on the fly. This is still O(N) but increases memory traffic and cache misses.
Uses eval(input()) and line-by-line input(), which are slower and riskier than bulk reading via open(0).read() used in the fast code. For large inputs this adds noticeable overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a dedicated helper func_1 that (1) builds a heap from the first N elements, (2) maintains the running sum, and (3) for each of the next N elements performs a single heappushpop to update the heap and sum, yielding the sum after each step.
