Huge integer factorial computation factorial(N-1) using math.factorial (result not even used later)
For each prime exponent e: building a large integer via e multiplications of numbers up to N+e-1
For each prime exponent e: computing factorial(e) via math.factorial on Python big integers
Late modular reduction (mod 1e9+7) only at the final print, so all intermediate combinatorial values are full-precision big integers

complexity.time: O( sqrt(M) + F(N) + sum_e ( e + F(e) ) ) where F(k) is the cost of math.factorial(k) on big integers
complexity.space: O( log M + B(N) ) where B(N) is the bit-length of factorial(N-1) and intermediate combinatorial products
complexity.why: Prime factorization by while var_7*var_7 <= var_8 is O(sqrt(M)). The call factorial(var_2 - 1) creates a massive big integer even though it is never used, dominating both time and space for large N. Each binomial factor is formed by multiplying e terms of magnitude ≈ N, building integers whose size grows with N and e, and factorial(e) also relies on big-int arithmetic. Because no modulo is applied until the very end, all arithmetic is performed with arbitrarily large integers, making constant factors huge and effectively rendering the solution non-viable for large N.

bottlenecks.detail: math.factorial(var_2 - 1) is computed and stored but never used. For N up to around 1e5 or larger, factorial(N-1) is enormous and its computation dominates runtime and memory.

Combinations C(N+e-1, e) are computed using plain integer arithmetic (products and factorial(e)) with no modular reduction until the very end. Intermediate values grow super-exponentially with e and N and are extremely slow to manipulate in Python.
factorial(e) is recomputed from scratch for each prime exponent e instead of using a shared precomputed table of factorials/inverses.
Modulo 1e9+7 is applied only at output, preventing the program from leveraging small modular integers and forcing all arithmetic to use gigantic Python big ints.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep all combinatorial computations strictly under modulo 1e9+7 using precomputed factorials and inverse factorials, so each binomial coefficient C(N+e-1, e) is obtained in O(1) modular time and space. Factor M as before, collect the exponents e_i, then compute the product ∏ C(N+e_i-1, e_i) modulo 1e9+7 using nCr via factorial and inverse factorial arrays whose size is only O(N + max_e).

complexity.why: Prime factorization remains O(sqrt(M)), unchanged. The key improvement is that factorial and inverse factorial arrays of size about N+50 are built once, in O(N) modular operations. Each binomial coefficient C(N+e-1, e) is then computed as fact[N+e-1] * invfact[N-1] * invfact[e] mod MOD in O(1) time per exponent. All arithmetic is modular, so costs are small and independent of the actual magnitude of combinations. Memory usage is linear in N due to the factorial and inverse factorial arrays.

delta_type: Algorithmic and numerical optimization (big-int elimination via modular precomputation)

complexity_delta.from: Effective runtime dominated by large big-integer factorial and combination computations; factorial(N-1) and full-precision combinations cause extremely high constant factors and may be practically superlinear in N in terms of bit operations.
complexity_delta.to: Runtime dominated by O(sqrt(M)) factorization plus O(N) modular precomputation, with each combinatorial term computed in O(1). Space reduced from holding enormous big integers (factorial(N-1)) to storing O(N) modular factorial arrays.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic big-O in terms of operation counts on integers may look similar, but the cost per operation drops drastically by avoiding enormous big integers. This transforms the solution from non-viable/TLE to easily passing under typical CP constraints.

transformation_steps: Remove the unused computation of factorial(var_2 - 1) on big integers, eliminating a dominant and unnecessary cost.
Change the representation of the prime exponent multiset from a defaultdict to a simple list of exponents var_5, reducing overhead and simplifying later loops.
Introduce a constant modulus MOD = 1_000_000_007 and ensure that all combinatorial arithmetic is performed modulo MOD from the beginning.
Precompute factorials fact[i] = i! mod MOD for i in [0, var_2 + 50) in a single forward pass, O(N) time.

Precompute inverse factorials invfact[i] = (i!)^{-1} mod MOD using Fermat's little theorem: first compute invfact[last] = fact[last]^(MOD-2) mod MOD, then fill the rest in a single backward pass via invfact[i-1] = invfact[i] * i mod MOD.
Replace the manual product/quotient combination construction with a direct modular binomial formula: for each exponent e, compute C(N+e-1, e) as fact[N+e-1] * invfact[N-1] * invfact[e] % MOD.
Accumulate the final answer as a product of these modular binomials, applying % MOD at each multiplication to keep values bounded.
Retain the basic sqrt(M) trial division factorization logic, but operate on the exponents only (which are small) when computing combinatorial factors.
trigger_signals: Use of math.factorial on N-1 where N can be large, especially when the result is not reused or is unused.
Combinatorial calculations (nCr, products of consecutive integers) without any modular reduction until the very end, causing massive intermediate integers.
Repeated calls to math.factorial inside loops over prime exponents.
Performance issues or TLE when N or M are moderately large (e.g., N ≈ 1e5) despite conceptually simple combinatorial formulas.
Memory spikes due to construction of gigantic integers (e.g., factorial of large N) in Python.
pitfalls: Incorrect bounds for factorial arrays: the code must ensure arrays cover all indices up to N + max_exponent; here var_2 + 50 assumes max exponent < 50, which is valid only if M constraint guarantees that (e.g., for M ≤ 1e12 or 1e18). For different constraints, the buffer must be adjusted.
Off-by-one errors in factorial and inverse factorial indexing can silently yield wrong binomial coefficients. Careful alignment of indices for fact[n], invfact[k], invfact[n-k] is crucial.
The modular inverse technique via pow(x, MOD-2, MOD) relies on MOD being prime. Using a non-prime modulus would make this invalid.
Using floating-point sqrt (M ** 0.5) for factorization bounds can be slightly tricky; the loop upper bound must be chosen conservatively (e.g., +2) to avoid missing a factor due to rounding.

If N were significantly larger (e.g., > 2e6), precomputing factorial up to N+50 might be too slow or memory-heavy in Python; in that case, a different combinatorial technique (e.g., multiplicative formula per combination using precomputed inverses up to max_e) would be necessary.
Sorting the exponent list is not required for correctness and has a negligible but nonzero cost; although minor, unnecessary work should be avoided in tighter environments.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic AOJ-style problem: count triples (i,j,k) with 1 <= i < j < k <= n and i+j+k = x, repeated until '0 0'. Typical intended solution is O(n^3) brute force, implying n is small (≈100). Exact constraints not provided; this is an educated guess.

sum([var_6, var_4, var_2]) in the innermost loop creating a list and summing each iteration
Integer comparisons and increments in the innermost loop

complexity.why: The outer loops iterate over all strictly increasing triples (var_6, var_4, var_2) with 1 <= var_6 < var_4 < var_2 <= n. The number of such triples is C(n,3) = O(n^3). Each iteration performs constant-time arithmetic and comparison, plus creation of a 3-element list and a sum, which are O(1) but with a large constant factor. No data structure grows with n; only a few scalar variables and a small temporary list are used.

All three nested loops are executed at Python level (not vectorized or in C), so every operation inside the innermost loop is performance-critical. Extra function calls (sum) and allocations (list) are costly here.
Reading input with a list comprehension [int(var_3) for var_3 in input().split()] is slightly more overhead than tuple(map(int, ...)), but this is negligible compared to the O(n^3) computation.

The ranges implicitly enforce var_1 > var_2 > var_3, so the condition var_1 > var_2 > var_3 is redundant but cheap. Overall, this removes unnecessary overhead inside the O(n^3) innermost loop.

complexity.why: The three nested loops still enumerate all strictly ordered triples with values in [1, n], giving C(n,3) = O(n^3) iterations. Each iteration performs only direct integer additions and comparisons without extra list allocations or function calls, so the constant factor is lower but the asymptotic complexity remains O(n^3). Memory usage is constant, with only scalar variables and no per-n data structures.

The loop condition in func_1 uses float division (var_4 / 10 >= 1), which repeatedly creates intermediate float values, while the update uses integer division (var_4 // 10). The float division in a tight loop is substantially slower than integer operations.
func_1 is called once for each var_2 in 1..N. The Python function call overhead inside the hot loop adds nontrivial constant-factor cost.
The core logic is pure Python looping; no use of built-in bulk operations beyond the range iteration, so performance is bound by Python’s per-iteration overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid a manual digit-counting loop and instead leverage Python’s optimized string conversion and len(str(x)) to obtain digit counts, all within a list comprehension driven by C-level iteration over range.

complexity.why: Each number from 1 to N is converted to a string once and its length is computed. String conversion and length are O(d) where d is the number of digits, so the total work is still O(N log N). However, these operations are implemented in C and avoid explicit per-digit Python loops, reducing constant factors. The comprehension builds a list of all qualifying numbers, so it stores up to O(N) integers, giving O(N) auxiliary space.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(N log N), Space: O(1)
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(N log N), Space: O(N)
complexity_delta.note: Both approaches have the same asymptotic time complexity but differ substantially in constant factors. The modified (fast) version trades extra memory (building a list) for lower per-iteration overhead by relying on C-level operations.

transformation_steps: Replace the custom digit-counting routine (func_1 with a while-loop and repeated divisions) with len(str(x)) to obtain the number of digits using optimized built-ins.
Inline the digit-counting logic directly in the comprehension condition instead of calling a separate function for each number, avoiding Python function-call overhead.
Use a list comprehension driven by range(1, N+1) to perform filtering in a compact, C-accelerated pattern rather than a manual for-loop body with multiple Python-level steps.
Rely solely on integer-to-string conversion and len to determine digit counts, eliminating the float division inside the hot loop.
trigger_signals: Presence of a nested loop pattern: an outer loop over all numbers 1..N and an inner while-loop per number to count digits.
Use of float division (/) inside a loop that runs for every digit of every number, a classic sign of unnecessary overhead for simple integer digit counting.
A separate function (func_1) that is invoked in the core counting loop, indicating repeated Python call overhead.
The task is simple (count numbers with odd digit length), suggesting that built-in operations (str, len) or arithmetic digit-length formulas could replace manual loops.
pitfalls: Both versions still use eval(input()), which is unsafe and unnecessary; int(input()) is preferable. This is a correctness/security issue rather than a performance one, but it’s easy to overlook.

The fast version allocates a full list of all qualifying numbers just to measure its length, using O(N) extra memory. For very large N, this can increase memory usage and potentially slow down due to allocations; using a generator with sum(...) would avoid this.

Despite being faster in practice, len(str(x)) does not change the asymptotic complexity; for very large N (e.g., N up to 10^12), both codes can still be too slow, and an O(1) arithmetic formula over digit ranges would be preferable.

If ported to other languages or constrained environments, assuming that string conversion is always faster than arithmetic digit counting may not hold; performance characteristics can differ between runtimes.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style coprime classification problem (ABC 177 E-like). Likely 1 <= N <= 1e5, each A_i <= 1e6. Single test, no extra queries.

dominant_ops: Building smallest-prime-factor table with a Python-level sieve up to fixed 10**6
Per-element prime factorization via repeated division using the SPF table
Per-element allocation and updating of Python sets while checking pairwise coprimality

complexity.time: O(M log log M + N * log A_max)
complexity.why: func_2 builds an SPF array up to var_7 = 10**6: the outer loop over odd var_5 and inner loop over multiples var_6 gives about sum_{p prime<=M} M/p ≈ M log log M operations in Python. Then func_3 factorizes each of the N numbers by repeatedly dividing by SPF; each number has O(log A_max) prime factors in the worst case. Sets var_8 and var_9 introduce extra hash-work per factor. Overall asymptotically near-linear in M with a log factor, but dominated by Python-level nested loops and set operations.

bottlenecks.detail: func_2 implements the sieve entirely in Python with nested for-loops over up to 10**6 values and their multiples. This leads to ~10^7+ Python-level iterations, which is expensive in CP time limits.
func_2(10**6) always sieves up to 1e6 regardless of the actual maximum value in var_1. For inputs where max(A_i) << 1e6, a large fraction of the sieve work is wasted.

In func_3, for each input number a fresh set var_8 is created and populated with its prime factors, while var_9 tracks global factors. Frequent set allocations and membership checks add significant constant-factor overhead.
Repeated divisions var_3 //= var_2[var_3] cause non-sequential accesses to the SPF array and repeated Python integer operations, which are slower than contiguous scanning/aggregation with built-ins.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid explicit prime factorization and sieving by instead counting occurrences of each value up to max(A_i), then for each possible divisor d accumulate counts of numbers divisible by d using strided slices var_2[d::d] and built-in sum. This shifts the heavy work into highly optimized C-level loops (slicing and summation) and only loops over d in Python.

complexity.why: var_2 is a frequency array of size M = max(A_i). For each input number, we increment var_2[a] (O(N)). Then for each d from 2 to M, sum(var_2[d::d]) touches about M/d elements. Total elements processed is sum_{d=2..M} M/d ≈ M log M, but this iteration is executed inside C (slice construction and sum), so Python-level overhead is only O(M) for the outer loop. Space is O(M) for var_2 plus O(N) for the input.

complexity_delta.from: O(M log log M + N log A_max) time with heavy Python-level nested loops and set operations; O(M + N) space.
complexity_delta.to: O(M log M + N) time where the log-factor work is mostly done in C via slicing and sum; O(M + N) space.
complexity_delta.note: Big-O is comparable, but the key improvement is moving the dominant inner work from Python loops and dynamic sets into contiguous array operations implemented in C, dramatically reducing interpreter overhead.

transformation_steps: Replace global SPF sieve func_2 up to fixed bound 10**6 with a frequency array sized only up to max(var_1).
Eliminate per-number prime factorization and per-number temporary sets; instead, count frequency of each integer value directly in var_2.

For each candidate divisor d from 2 to max(var_1), compute how many inputs are divisible by d as sum(var_2[d::d]) using slicing and built-in sum, which are implemented in C and avoid Python-level inner loops.
Track the maximum such count (var_6) and classify as pairwise/setwise/not coprime based on comparisons with N, replacing explicit factor overlap tracking via sets var_8 and var_9.
Remove the separate gcd-based pass (func_1) since the divisibility-count method already distinguishes all three coprimality cases.
trigger_signals: Presence of a hand-written sieve with nested Python loops up to a large fixed limit (10**6) regardless of input maximum.
Use of per-element prime factorization and repeated divisions in Python for every input number.
Allocation and update of Python sets inside an inner loop over prime factors, indicating heavy overhead for membership checks and hashing.
Observed or anticipated runtime dominated by millions of Python-level iterations rather than vectorized or built-in operations.
Awareness that frequency-based divisor counting can be implemented via strided slices and sum, pushing heavy work into C.
pitfalls: The fast approach builds a frequency array up to max(A_i); if constraints allowed A_i to be much larger (e.g., >1e7), memory and O(M log M) time could become problematic. It assumes A_i are reasonably bounded (≈1e6).

The use of var_2[d::d] creates a new list for each d; while this is efficient under the given constraints, for much larger M it would incur heavy allocation costs. An alternative is to accumulate using a simple loop over multiples, trading C-level speed for memory savings.

Both versions use eval(input()) for reading integers, which is unnecessary and potentially unsafe in non-CP contexts; replacing with int(input()) is recommended, though not a performance bottleneck here.

If input distribution is pathological (e.g., many large identical numbers), the frequency method still performs well, but an implementation mistake (like iterating up to a fixed large bound instead of max(A_i)) could reintroduce avoidable overhead similar to the slow version.

Relying on Python built-ins for speed requires awareness of their complexity: sum over a slice is linear in the slice length; misusing it in nested patterns can reintroduce hidden O(M^2) behavior if not carefully structured as here (single outer loop over d).

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: one array of small integers (likely within [-100, 100] or [0, 100]); single-shot computation, no queries. Both given solutions are linear in n, which is sufficient even if n up to 1e5.

dominant_ops: Repeated NumPy vectorized subtraction and squaring inside a Python for-loop (100 iterations)
np.sum on the same array 100 times
Python↔NumPy boundary overhead on each loop iteration

complexity.time: O(K * n) where K = 100 (loop range), effectively O(n) but with a large constant factor from NumPy calls in a loop
complexity.why: The algorithm loops var_2 from 0 to 99, and for each candidate value computes np.sum((var_6 - var_2) ** 2) on an n-length array. The array itself is reused, so memory is linear in n, but we pay for 100 full passes over the data plus NumPy call overhead.

bottlenecks.detail: Brute-force search over 100 candidate centers instead of using the mathematical minimizer (mean/rounded mean) for sum of squared deviations.
Using NumPy inside a tight Python loop causes repeated Python↔C transitions and repeated full-array operations; for competitive programming input sizes, pure Python arithmetic is often faster.
The same array var_5 is processed 100 times; the optimal center can be computed directly from the mean of the array in O(n) total time with a single pass.
Using eval(input()) for reading an integer is unnecessary and potentially unsafe, though not the main performance bottleneck.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the property that the sum of squared deviations \(\sum (a_i - p)^2\) is minimized when p is the mean of the data (rounded to the nearest integer if p must be integer). Compute the rounded mean once in O(n), then compute the squared deviations in a single pass.

complexity.why: Two linear passes over the input: one to compute the sum and thus the mean, and one to compute the sum of squared deviations. The list of n integers is stored, so memory is linear in n. No extra multiplicative factors or heavy library calls per candidate.

complexity_delta.from: O(K * n) with K = 100 and heavy per-iteration NumPy overhead
complexity_delta.to: O(n) with simple Python arithmetic and list comprehension
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both are linear in n, but the optimized version eliminates the factor 100 brute-force search and the substantial NumPy call overhead, making it significantly faster in practice.

transformation_steps: Recognize the mathematical structure: minimizing sum of squared deviations from a constant p over integers.
Use the known fact that the minimizer of \(\sum (a_i - p)^2\) is the mean of a_i; when p must be an integer, test the nearest integers, here effectively handled by round().
Replace the explicit for var_2 in range(100) loop and repeated np.sum calls with a single computation of the rounded mean var_3.
Remove NumPy and operate directly on Python lists and integers to avoid Python↔C overhead and repeated vector operations.
Compute the final answer in one list comprehension that accumulates (var_4 - var_3) ** 2 for each element.
trigger_signals: Presence of a small fixed-range brute-force search (for var_2 in range(100)) around what looks like a mean/center optimization problem.
Repeated full passes over the same data (np.sum((var_6 - var_2) ** 2)) for different candidate centers.
Use of a heavy numerical library (NumPy) in a competitive-programming context for simple scalar operations.
Observation that the task output math matches the form of variance / sum of squared deviations, which has a known closed-form minimizer.
pitfalls: Using round() can be subtly different across languages or when dealing with .5; ensure the problem’s rounding specification matches Python’s round-to-even behavior, or explicitly handle floor/ceil if required.
If the allowed range of p were constrained (e.g., must be within [0, 100]), the direct mean-based solution must still clamp or adjust to that range; blindly using the mean might violate constraints.
Avoid introducing floats for large sums if constraints allow very large n or values; here, integers are small, but in general, prefer integer arithmetic or use exact rational computations if needed.
Retaining eval(input()) is unnecessary and dangerous in general; for production or contest code, plain int(input()) should be used instead.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AOJ BFS problem (ALDS1_11_C): up to about 100 vertices, adjacency given as 'u k v1 ... vk', BFS from vertex 1. Edges ~O(n^2) worst-case but small n, so even O(n^2) Python solutions pass.

dominant_ops: Single-source BFS over an adjacency list using a deque as the queue; linear scan over neighbors of each vertex; one-time parsing of all input lines.

complexity.why: Each vertex is enqueued and dequeued at most once (deque operations are O(1)); each edge is examined at most once. Arrays var_12 (color/visited) and var_9 (distance) are size O(V). Adjacency list var_7 stores each edge once, O(E).

bottlenecks.detail: Algorithm is already optimal BFS in O(V+E); no asymptotically faster graph-traversal algorithm exists for this task. For very large graphs, the main cost would simply be the Python-level overhead of the BFS loops.
Uses sys.stdin.readlines(), which loads all input into memory at once. For the small constraints of this problem this is fine, but for huge inputs this could be memory-heavy.

func_1 is defined as func_1(var_16) but called as func_1(v_init=1), which will raise a TypeError (unexpected keyword argument) and prevent the BFS from running. This is not a performance issue but makes the code unusable as-is.

Uses 'is' for integer comparison (if var_12[var_4] is var_2). This happens to work for small interned integers like 0 in CPython but is semantically wrong; use '==' instead. It does not materially affect performance here.

FastAudit.core_idea: Also performs a BFS from the start vertex over an adjacency list, but uses a plain Python list as the queue with pop(0) to dequeue, and uses the distance array both as a distance record and as a visited marker (−1 means unvisited). Input is read line-by-line with input().

complexity.why: Each pop(0) on a Python list is O(V) because it shifts all remaining elements. In the worst case the BFS performs O(V) queue operations, making the queue-management cost O(V^2). Edge traversals still cost O(E). Memory is dominated by the distance array and adjacency list, O(V+E).

complexity_delta.from: O(V + E) time, O(V + E) space (deque-based BFS queue)
complexity_delta.to: O(V^2 + E) time, O(V + E) space (list.pop(0)-based BFS queue)
complexity_delta.note: Switching from deque.popleft() (O(1)) to list.pop(0) (O(V)) degrades the asymptotic performance of the BFS. For this problem's small constraints (V≈100) it may still pass, but it is strictly worse in scalability.

transformation_steps: Replaced a deque-based BFS queue (append / popleft) with a Python list used as a queue (append / pop(0)), changing queue operations from O(1) to O(V).
Changed indexing scheme: slow_code uses 1-based indexing with arrays of length n+1; fast_code uses 0-based indexing with arrays of length n and adjusts vertex IDs when reading/using them.
Replaced explicit visited-state array (var_12 with color states) with using the distance array (var_3) as both distance and visited marker (−1 for unvisited).
Switched input method from sys.stdin.readlines() followed by manual splitting and mapping to repeated calls to input().split() per line.
Simplified adjacency representation from a tuple of lists (fixed-size container) to a simple list of lists built directly from input lines.
trigger_signals: Profiler or manual inspection shows a very large number of list.pop(0) calls dominating runtime.
Runtime grows roughly quadratically when V is increased (e.g., doubling the number of vertices leads to ~4x runtime) even though BFS should be linear.
For larger test cases or if constraints are increased, the list-based BFS starts timing out while deque-based BFS still passes.
Memory usage is not a limiting factor but CPU time is, suggesting algorithmic or data-structure inefficiency rather than excessive memory.
pitfalls: Using list.pop(0) as a BFS queue in Python: this is O(V) per pop and will cause O(V^2) behavior; always prefer collections.deque for FIFO queues.
Relying on 'is' for integer comparison (slow_code) is semantically wrong and can lead to subtle bugs in other contexts; always use '==' for value comparison.
Changing indexing (1-based to 0-based or vice versa) can easily introduce off-by-one errors in array sizes and neighbor indexing.

Overloading the distance array as a visited marker (using −1 as sentinel) is common and efficient, but forgetting to initialize it correctly or accidentally reusing it across test cases can break correctness.
Using eval(input()) (fast_code) is slower than int(input()) and is unsafe in general; it should be avoided in competitive programming and production code.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer N; goal is to output the N-th number whose adjacent digits differ by at most 1 (often called Lunlun numbers). N is relatively small (≈1e5), while the value of the numbers themselves can be up to around 1e10.

dominant_ops: Recursive DFS expansion of all reachable numbers up to a large numeric cutoff
Appending every generated number into a global list
Final sort of the entire generated list of numbers

complexity.why: Let M be the total count of generated numbers <= 3234566667 that satisfy the adjacency rule. func_1 performs a DFS tree traversal with branching factor up to ~3 per digit, and it does not stop after collecting the first N results; it generates every possible valid number up to a fixed numeric limit. Each number is appended to var_2, and then sorted at the end in O(M log M) time. Memory also scales with M because all numbers are stored.

bottlenecks.detail: func_1 explores the full search space up to 3234566667 regardless of N. Even if N is small (e.g., 1e5), the algorithm still generates and stores all valid numbers up to the bound, making M much larger than N.
sorted(var_2) sorts the entire list of M generated numbers in O(M log M). For N ≪ M, this dominates the runtime unnecessarily.
All generated numbers are kept in var_2 simultaneously, leading to O(M) memory usage which can become very large for a high numeric cutoff.

The DFS implementation is recursive and repeatedly calls func_1 for each child. Python function call overhead and recursion depth (managed via sys.setrecursionlimit) both add non-trivial cost compared to an iterative approach.
The work done is almost independent of the input N; increasing N from 1 to 1e5 does not significantly change the amount of generated numbers, because the upper bound 3234566667 is fixed.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a min-heap to perform a best-first (by value) generation of valid numbers, always expanding the smallest unseen number next. This inherently produces numbers in ascending order, and by stopping after enough numbers are extracted, it avoids exploring the entire search space. A visited set prevents duplicate processing.

complexity.why: Each iteration pops the smallest candidate from the heap and pushes a constant number of successors (based on altering first and last digits). The loop runs for roughly O(N) successful extractions plus some overhead from extra pushes due to the +100 margin and duplicates. Each heap push/pop is O(log K) where K = O(N) is the heap size. Thus, overall time is about O(N log N). A set tracks visited numbers and the heap/list of results only grows proportional to the number of distinct numbers near the first N, giving O(N) space.

complexity_delta.from: O(M log M) time, O(M) space (M = total valid numbers up to a fixed large bound)
complexity_delta.to: O(N log N) time, O(N) space (N = index of the requested number)
complexity_delta.note: The key change is switching from generating the whole domain up to a numeric bound (M-anchored) to generating only as many numbers as needed in ascending order (N-anchored).

transformation_steps: Replace the full recursive DFS generation (func_1) with an incremental generation strategy driven by a min-heap that always yields the smallest next value.

Avoid a fixed hard-coded numeric cutoff (3234566667) and instead control exploration by how many numbers have been extracted; the while var_3 + 100 >= 0 condition ensures generating slightly more than N numbers as a safety margin.
Introduce a visited set (var_5) to prevent reprocessing the same number multiple times, reducing both unnecessary heap operations and duplicate storage.
Generate successors locally from the current minimum element by modifying its first and last digits, rather than recursing blindly deeper for every node in the tree.
Post-process only the collected set of visited numbers (var_5) by sorting once and selecting the (N-1)-th element, instead of sorting an entire space defined by an external numeric bound.
Remove recursive calls and replace them with iterative heap operations, eliminating recursion overhead and call-stack related costs.
trigger_signals: Runtime dominated by func_1 recursion and final sorting, observable in profiling for even moderate N.
Memory usage grows large and does not depend strongly on N, indicating that the algorithm is exploring far beyond what is needed.
Presence of a large hard-coded cutoff (3234566667) suggests that the algorithm is bounded by value range instead of by the requested count N.
Recursion depth approaching or exceeding the default limit, requiring sys.setrecursionlimit adjustments, signaling an overly deep search tree.
Performance does not scale smoothly with N, because most of the work is fixed by the upper bound rather than the query size.
pitfalls: The heap-based approach still performs string-int conversions for generating successors; these are acceptable for N around 1e5 but could be a hotspot for tighter limits. A fully integer-based digit manipulation would be faster if needed.

The while var_3 + 100 >= 0 condition relies on an empirical margin (100). If N were substantially larger than intended by the original problem, this margin might be insufficient, requiring adjustment to guarantee enough numbers are generated.

Maintaining a visited set for all generated numbers means memory scales with the number of distinct numbers near the first N; if constraints were mis-estimated and N were very large, this could become a memory bottleneck.

Both implementations finally sort the collected numbers; if one only needs the N-th smallest and the set is large, using selection algorithms or generating strictly in order without extra margin can further optimize and avoid full sorting.

Switching from recursion to iterative heap-based logic changes the traversal order; correctness depends on ensuring that the generation rules in the heap version produce exactly the same valid number set as the DFS version.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical of AtCoder ABC 110 D: second input (here var_4 / var_3) up to ~1e5; number to factor (var_1 / var_15) up to ~1e9. Exponents of prime factors are at most ~30, and the number of distinct primes is small (<10).

dominant_ops: Precomputation of factorials and inverse factorials up to var_2 = 2 * 10^5
Trial division prime factorization up to sqrt(N)
O(1) binomial evaluations using precomputed factorial tables

complexity.why: func_1 runs a trial division loop up to sqrt(N) => O(sqrt(N)). Before using combinations, code precomputes factorials and inverse factorials up to var_2 with two linear passes and one modular exponent => O(F) time and O(F) memory. Each combination func_2 is then O(1) and called only a handful of times (once per distinct prime factor). The precomputation dominates for single-query usage.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorials and inverse factorials are built up to 2 * 10^5 regardless of the actual exponents, which are very small (≤ ~30). For a single query, the cost of this precomputation outweighs the savings from O(1) nCk.
The factorial and inverse factorial arrays are filled in pure Python loops, incurring significant interpreter overhead for ~2e5 iterations each, plus one reverse loop of similar size.
Two arrays of length ~2e5 for factorials and inverse factorials consume more memory than necessary when only a few small binomial coefficients are required.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial/inverse-factorial precomputation and instead compute each required binomial coefficient C(m + e - 1, e) directly using a small multiplicative loop, exploiting that exponents e are tiny. Keep the prime factorization as simple trial division.

complexity.why: Prime factorization via while var_7 * var_7 <= var_8 runs in O(sqrt(N)) time and uses O(1) extra space. For each exponent e (very small), the combination is computed with a loop of length e in pure integer arithmetic; total work over all primes is O(sum e) = O(log N) and negligible relative to sqrt(N). No O(F) precomputation or large tables are used.

complexity_delta.from: O(F + sqrt(N)) time, O(F) space where F ≈ 2 * 10^5 due to factorial tables
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(N)) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: By eliminating factorial and inverse factorial tables and computing binomial coefficients with short multiplicative loops, the algorithm removes the linear-in-F cost and memory overhead, which dominated for single-query use.

transformation_steps: Remove global factorial (var_10) and inverse factorial (var_12) arrays and their O(F) initialization loops.
Replace general-purpose func_2(n, k) based on factorial tables with an in-place multiplicative computation of C(m + e - 1, e) using a loop over j = 1..e.
Perform binomial computation directly inside the prime-exponent loop, keeping only scalar variables and applying modulo at the end of each combination multiplication.
Retain the simple trial-division prime factorization (func_1) since its complexity is already optimal for these constraints and dominates runtime.
trigger_signals: The size of precomputed arrays (var_2 = 2 * 10^5) is fixed and large relative to the number of actual combination queries (only as many as prime factors of N).
Exponents of prime factors (k in C(m + k - 1, k)) are known to be very small, making O(k) per combination effectively constant-time.
Single test case; there is no amortization benefit from expensive precomputation across multiple queries.
Memory and startup time dominated by factorial table setup rather than core number-theoretic logic.
pitfalls: When removing factorial tables, it is important to ensure the multiplicative combination formula uses exact integer arithmetic before applying the modulus; do not mix modular division without using modular inverses when necessary.

The direct multiplicative computation must carefully handle the product (m + k - j) / j to avoid integer truncation errors; using integer division is only safe because the product is mathematically divisible at each step or in total.

If problem constraints change to allow much larger exponents or many queries, the factorial precomputation approach could become preferable again; the chosen optimization assumes small k and few calls.
Care must be taken to keep intermediate values under control if exponents grow; although Python supports big integers, excessive growth could impact performance if k ceases to be small.

constraints_guess.notes: Single scalar input, no loops or collections; runtime dominated by Python startup and I/O, not algorithmics.

dominant_ops: One eval(input()) call plus a couple of constant-time arithmetic operations and a print.

complexity.why: The program performs a fixed sequence of operations regardless of input magnitude or content; no loops or data structures that scale with input size.

bottlenecks.detail: Computes 24 - var_1 + 24 instead of directly 48 - var_1, adding extra arithmetic steps (though still O(1)).
Wraps logic in func_1 and uses an if __name__ == '__main__' guard for a single expression, adding a function call overhead and extra syntax without functional gain in this tiny script.
Casts eval(input()) to int() when the numeric type from eval may already be suitable; this adds a small constant-time overhead and changes semantics for non-integer numeric input.

FastAudit.core_idea: Inline the computation and simplify the arithmetic expression (24 - x + 24) to (48 - x), eliminating the helper function and redundant int() conversion.

complexity.why: The optimized version still performs a single eval(input()), one subtraction, and one print, all independent of input size.

complexity_delta.from: O(1) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(1) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged; only constant factors (fewer operations and no function call) are improved.

transformation_steps: Algebraically simplify 24 - var_1 + 24 to 48 - var_1.
Inline the logic into the module-level scope and remove the func_1 definition and the if __name__ == '__main__' guard.
Drop the int() cast around eval(input()) to use the value from eval directly.
Collapse to a single statement: print(48 - eval(input())).
trigger_signals: Very small script where extra function and redundant arithmetic provide no structural benefit.
Obvious constant folding opportunity (24 - x + 24).
Desire to minimize constant overhead in tight or code-golf-style solutions.
pitfalls: Removing int() changes behavior: the original coerced the result of eval(input()) to an integer (e.g., '3.9' would become 3), while the new version uses the raw evaluated type (e.g., float), potentially altering outputs for non-integer numeric input.
Both versions rely on eval(input()), which is unsafe for untrusted input; this is a security rather than performance issue but is a significant practical concern.
The micro-optimizations provide negligible real-world speedup because execution time is dominated by I/O and interpreter startup, not arithmetic or function call overhead.

constraints_guess.notes: Input var_1 is the 1-based index of a 'Lunlun' number (digits differ by at most 1 between neighbors). Known from AtCoder-style tasks where N <= 1e5. Original solution generates all Lunlun numbers up to a hardcoded upper bound 3234566667 (10-digit cap) regardless of N.

dominant_ops: Recursive DFS calls in func_1 over the implicit digit graph
List appends to var_2 for every generated number
Integer arithmetic: multiplication by 10, additions, modulo
Full sort of all generated numbers before indexing

complexity.time: O(G log G), where G is the total count of Lunlun numbers <= 3234566667 (a fixed but relatively large constant, independent of input N). In terms of the digit cap D, G is O(3^D) and the sort is O(G log G).
complexity.space: O(G), to store all generated numbers in var_2 before sorting.
complexity.why: The DFS explores the entire search tree of valid Lunlun numbers starting from digits 1..9 until exceeding the fixed upper bound. Every generated number is stored in a list. Only after generating all of them does the code sort the list and pick the N-th element, so work does not scale with N but with the global enumeration size G.

bottlenecks.detail: func_1 recursively generates all Lunlun numbers up to 3234566667 even when var_1 (N) is small, performing work independent of the actual query size.
After generating all G numbers, the code performs sorted(var_2), which is O(G log G). This is costly given that only the N-th smallest is needed.
Deep recursive DFS (though depth-bounded) introduces function call overhead and requires raising the recursion limit, which is less efficient and less robust than an iterative approach.
