Repeated int->str conversions per node to check length and last digit
Appending every generated number to a global list
Sorting the entire generated list of numbers

complexity.why: Let M be the total number of Lunlun numbers up to 10 digits (about 1e6). The recursive DFS visits each such number once and performs O(1) work (constant-length string operations) per node, so generation is O(M). All M numbers are stored in a list and sorted, costing O(M log M), which dominates. Memory stores all M integers plus small recursion stack depth (<= 10), giving O(M) space.

bottlenecks.detail: Always generates the full search space of Lunlun numbers up to length 10 regardless of the requested K. When K is much smaller than M (~1e6), most of this work is wasted.
Sorts the entire array of M generated numbers even though only the K-th value is needed. Sorting dominates time for large M.
For each number var_2, the code performs len(str(var_2)) and int(str(var_2)[-1]), i.e., multiple int->str conversions per node. With ~1e6 nodes, this becomes a noticeable constant-factor cost.
Recursive DFS with Python function calls for each node adds overhead. The depth is small (<= 10), but the number of calls is large (~M), so cumulative call overhead is significant.
Uses eval(input()) instead of int(input()), which is slower and unsafe. This is a minor constant-factor issue compared to the algorithmic ones.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace full-depth recursive DFS with iterative, breadthwise generation using sets, and stop expanding once the total count of generated Lunlun numbers reaches or exceeds K. Only the numbers actually generated up to that stopping depth are collected, then flattened and sorted to pick the K-th.

complexity.why: Let L be the number of Lunlun numbers generated until the cumulative count first reaches K. The while-loop processes each generated number once, performing constant-time digit checks and neighbor generation, giving O(L) generation time. All generated numbers are stored in a list var_11 of size L and then sorted in O(L log L) time, which dominates. Memory usage is proportional to the total number of generated numbers across all levels, i.e., O(L). For typical constraints (K <= 1e5), L is on the order of K, so complexity behaves like O(K log K) time and O(K) space.

complexity_delta.from: O(M log M) time, O(M) space where M is the total number of Lunlun numbers up to fixed maximum length (about 1e6).
complexity_delta.to: O(L log L) time, O(L) space where L is the number of Lunlun numbers actually needed to reach K (typically L = Θ(K)).
complexity_delta.note: The modified code avoids generating the entire search space and only expands levels until it accumulates at least K numbers, turning the work from being tied to a fixed global maximum depth M to being essentially proportional to K.

transformation_steps: Replaced recursive depth-first search with an iterative breadthwise process using a list of sets (var_1) to represent each frontier (numbers of a given digit length).
Introduced an early stopping condition in the while-loop based on the cumulative count of generated numbers (var_3 >= var_7), so the search halts once at least K numbers are available.
Stored numbers per level in sets instead of a single global list, allowing controlled expansion by levels and counting new numbers each iteration (len(var_10)).
After generation, flattened all per-level sets into a single list (var_11) and sorted it once, then indexed the (K-1)-th element to output the answer.
Swapped the input variable name but preserved semantics, reading K as var_7 instead of var_1 to avoid conflicting with previous naming.
trigger_signals: The original solution generates all Lunlun numbers up to length 10 unconditionally, independent of K, indicating unnecessary work when K is small or moderate.
Presence of a deep recursion over a combinatorial tree and then a global sort of all generated values suggests potential performance issues for large search spaces.
Known constraints for similar problems (K up to around 1e5) imply that generating ~1e6 numbers and sorting them may be near time limits in Python, especially with heavy string conversions.
Use of DFS with a fixed maximum depth instead of a demand-driven approach (stopping when K numbers are found) hints that a more efficient BFS or incremental strategy is possible.
pitfalls: Using sets for per-level storage loses generation order; correctness is preserved only because a final sort is done. If the sort were removed or changed, relying on set iteration order would be incorrect and non-deterministic.

The modified code still performs repeated int->str conversions and back, and still sorts all generated numbers. A more optimized BFS could avoid sorting entirely by generating numbers in increasing order and taking the K-th directly.

There is no explicit limit on the maximum number of digits in the new implementation. If K exceeded the total number of possible Lunlun numbers under given constraints, the loop could become very large or non-terminating in other contexts (not an issue for the presumed contest constraints).
Memory usage can still grow to O(M) in the worst case when K is close to the total number of Lunlun numbers; the improvement mainly benefits cases where K is significantly smaller than M.
Use of eval(input()) remains; while not the main performance issue, it is both unsafe and slightly slower than int(input()).

constraints_guess.notes: Classic 3D variant of AtCoder 'Patisserie' style problem: N points (x,y,z), choose M (var_1) to maximize |sum_x|+|sum_y|+|sum_z|. Typical constraints N up to 1e5, M<=N.

dominant_ops: Outer loop over selected count: for _ in range(var_1)
Inner full scan over all points each iteration to choose next point (var_7 loop)
Multiple abs() calls and additions for each candidate point
Additional full scans over all points to find max-absolute coordinate per axis

complexity.time: O(N * M + N^2) ≈ O(N^2) in worst case (M up to N)
complexity.why: The selection phase has a nested loop: for each of the M selections, it iterates over all N points, computing a score with several abs operations. With M<=N, this is Θ(N^2). The later adjustment part (max abs coordinate search) also scans all N points a few times, which is O(N) and dominated by the Θ(N^2) selection loop. Storage is just the list of N triples plus a few O(N) boolean/index arrays.

bottlenecks.detail: Greedy selection loop: for _ in range(var_1) contains an inner loop over all N points. With N up to ~1e5 and M≈N, this becomes ~1e10 per-point evaluations, which is far beyond feasible limits for Python.

For each candidate point inside the inner loop, the code performs 6 abs() calls and several additions/subtractions to compute var_15. Even if asymptotically dominated by N^2, this heavy constant factor exacerbates runtime.

After the greedy building of var_16, the code performs additional full scans over all points (to compute var_11/var_10 arrays) and then appears to start another selection process (incomplete in snippet). These extra O(N) or worse passes add overhead without reducing overall complexity.

The greedy heuristic chooses the next point based on immediate gain in |sum_x|+|sum_y|+|sum_z|, but the correct optimal structure is to fix one of 8 (sign_x, sign_y, sign_z) patterns and then globally sort by projected value. The greedy per-step choice prevents benefiting from this global ordering and forces repeated rescans.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the identity max over sign choices: |X|+|Y|+|Z| = max over s_x,s_y,s_z∈{+1,-1} of s_x*X + s_y*Y + s_z*Z. For each of the 2^3 sign combinations, project every point (x,y,z) to v = s_x*x + s_y*y + s_z*z, sort these values in descending order, and sum the top M. The answer is the maximum over all 8 sign patterns.

complexity.time: O(8 * (N log N + N)) = O(N log N)
complexity.why: For each of the 8 bitmasks (var_4 in range(2**3)), the code: (1) builds a 3-element sign mask (O(1)); (2) scans all N points to compute transformed sums v (O(N)); (3) sorts the resulting N values (O(N log N)); (4) sums the first M entries (O(M)⊆O(N)). Summed over 8 masks, the dominant term is 8 * N log N. Only the list of N triplets (var_9) and a temporary list of N projected values (var_7) are stored, giving O(N) memory usage.

complexity_delta.from: O(N^2) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N log N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: Replacing a per-step greedy selection (rescan all N for each of M selections) with an 8-pattern global projection + sort eliminates the quadratic factor.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the objective |sum_x|+|sum_y|+|sum_z| can be rewritten as a maximum over 8 fixed sign combinations: for any chosen subset, its contribution for a fixed sign pattern is simply the sum of per-point signed projections.
Instead of iteratively picking the next best point via a greedy scan, precompute for each of the 8 sign combinations the projected value v_i = s_x*x_i + s_y*y_i + s_z*z_i for all points.

For each sign pattern, sort the list of v_i in descending order once and compute the prefix sum of the top M entries. This exploits a global ordering rather than recomputing local marginal gains each step.
Take the maximum result over the 8 patterns as the final answer, since one of these patterns attains |sum_x|+|sum_y|+|sum_z| for the optimal subset.
Remove repeated O(N) scans driven by greedy updates and abs() recalculations; replace them with a fixed number (8) of scans and sorts over the entire data.
trigger_signals: Presence of nested loops where the outer loop runs up to M (number of items to select) and the inner loop scans all N elements, especially when problem constraints allow N≈1e5.
Use of a greedy incremental choice criterion for a problem with an L1-norm objective (sum of absolute values), which often has known global sign-pattern tricks.
Total operations estimate approaching or exceeding ~1e8–1e9 in Python (e.g., N*M with N≈M≈1e5 → 1e10), which is an immediate red flag.
Multiple full-array scans with substantial per-element work (several abs calls) occurring inside another loop over selection count.
Contest/problem discussions or editorials hinting at a bitmask + sort solution, suggesting that a greedy O(N^2) approach is not intended.
pitfalls: Assuming that a locally optimal greedy choice (maximizing immediate increase in |sum_x|+|sum_y|+|sum_z|) is globally optimal; this is not guaranteed and also leads to much worse complexity.
Underestimating the cost of nested loops when both loop bounds can approach N, especially in Python where ~1e8 operations is already near the upper practical limit.
Overcomplicating the solution with additional heuristics (e.g., re-choosing points based on max absolute coordinate per axis) instead of using the clean sign-pattern projection.
Failing to exploit algebraic transformations of absolute values to linear forms with fixed signs, which can turn a combinatorial selection problem into a sorting problem.
Micro-optimizations (e.g., reducing abs calls) cannot compensate for an O(N^2) algorithm when the intended solution is O(N log N).

constraints_guess.notes: This is effectively counting numbers i in [1, N] whose digit count is odd. The style matches AtCoder ABC136 B 'Uneven Numbers' where N ≤ 1e5. Both codes iterate up to N, so N is not huge.

dominant_ops: Repeated string conversions: len(str(var_4)) inside loops
Unnecessary precomputation of all odd-digit numbers up to 99999
Membership checks in a dictionary that encodes the same property already checked via len(str(...))

complexity.why: Let N = var_5 (input upper bound), D = number of digits (~log10 N). First loop: range(1, 100000) does ~1e5 iterations, each with len(str(var_4)) → O(D_const) string creation and length. This is a fixed precomputation cost P ≈ 1e5 * D. Second loop: range(1, N+1) and for each var_4, len(str(var_4)) again for even/odd digit check, plus O(1) dict membership. Overall time ~O(N * D + 1e5 * D). Space: list of all odd-digit integers up to 99999 and a dict mapping each to itself → O(1e5) auxiliary space.

bottlenecks.detail: Using len(str(var_4)) inside per-element loops repeatedly allocates strings and counts their lengths, which is significantly slower than pure integer arithmetic for digit counts.
The first loop builds var_3 for var_4 in range(1, 100000) regardless of the actual input N. If N is smaller than 100000, this is pure overhead.

var_2 is a dict {var_4: var_4 for var_4 in var_3}, but the later logic recomputes the odd-digit property via len(str(var_4)) and then only checks membership. The dictionary encodes no additional information beyond the same predicate; the membership test is redundant.

In the second loop, the code first checks len(str(var_4)) % 2 == 0 to continue, then checks var_4 in var_2, where var_2 only contains numbers with odd digit counts. This performs two logically equivalent checks for the same condition.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace string-based digit counting and redundant precomputation with a direct arithmetic digit-count function applied on the fly. Eliminate the list and dictionary and just count how many integers in [1, N] have an odd number of digits by using repeated division by 10.

complexity.why: The loop still runs over all integers from 1 to N. For each var_2, func_1(var_2) counts digits via repeated division by 10: at most D iterations per number, where D ≈ floor(log10 N)+1. So time is O(N * D). No precomputation or auxiliary collections are kept; space usage is constant aside from small scalars.

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both are linear in N times digit count, but the modified code removes a fixed ~1e5 * D precomputation and avoids costly string operations and dictionary structures. This mainly improves constants and memory footprint.

transformation_steps: Remove precomputation loop that builds var_3 (list of odd-digit numbers up to 99999).
Remove construction of var_2 dictionary that maps each number to itself.
Eliminate the membership test var_4 in var_2, as it duplicates the odd-digit property check.
Introduce func_1(var_4) to compute the number of digits using integer division by 10 instead of converting to string.
Replace len(str(var_4)) % 2 checks with func_1(var_2) % 2 checks inside the main loop.
Avoid any auxiliary lists or dicts; maintain only a running count var_1.
trigger_signals: Presence of len(str(x)) inside a loop up to N, indicating per-iteration string allocations.
Precomputation to a fixed bound (range(1, 100000)) independent of input N, suggesting unnecessary work for small N.
Data structures (list, dict) that encode a simple property (odd digit count) which can be recomputed cheaply.
Double-checking the same logical condition (odd digit count) twice for each element.
pitfalls: In func_1, the condition uses var_4 / 10 >= 1, which performs floating-point division in Python 3. While correct, it is slightly slower and less idiomatic than using integer comparison (e.g., while var_4 >= 10:). Using // in both places would be cleaner and avoids float operations.

The algorithm still runs in O(N * D), which is fine for N up to around 1e5–1e6. For much larger N (e.g., 1e9), a purely arithmetic counting by digit ranges (e.g., summing contributions of ranges [1,9], [100,999], etc.) would be preferable to avoid iterating over all integers.
If ported to other languages, be careful about integer division semantics; some languages differ between / and //, which can affect loop termination conditions.

constraints_guess.notes: Two integers N, K (mapped to var_4/var_10 and var_1/var_9). Sum is over k in [0, min(K, N-1)]. Fast code explicitly caps k by N-1 and loops up to K; slow code precomputes factorials up to fixed 5e5, suggesting K or required max nCr arguments are <= 5e5 while N itself may be large (up to ~1e9).

dominant_ops: Precomputation of factorials up to 5*10^5 with modular multiplication
Precomputation of inverse factorials up to 5*10^5 using one modular exponentiation and a backward linear pass
Single loop over k in [0, min(N, K+1)] performing O(1) combination calculations per iteration

complexity.time: O(F + L) where F = 5*10^5 (fixed factorial & inverse factorial precompute) and L = min(N, K+1)
complexity.space: O(F) for two arrays of size ~5*10^5 each (factorials and inverse factorials)
complexity.why: The code always builds factorial and inverse-factorial arrays of length 5*10^5, independent of actual N and K. That is two linear passes over 5*10^5 elements plus a pow with exponent ~1e9 (log MOD factor). The main combinatorial sum is a single loop whose bound is min(N, K+1), with O(1) work per k via array lookups and a few multiplications; this is asymptotically cheaper than or comparable to the fixed precompute.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorials and inverse factorials are computed up to a hard-coded limit 5*10^5 (var_2), regardless of the actual maximum k used in the sum. For small K this dominates runtime and memory.
The inverse factorials loop uses reversed(list(range(1, var_2 + 1))) which constructs a full list of ~5*10^5 elements before iterating, instead of using range(var_2, 0, -1) directly.

The design assumes all combinations can be handled via precomputed factorials up to 5*10^5. If N (var_4) exceeds this bound, the method becomes invalid; even when valid, it's more work than necessary when K is much smaller.

func_1 and func_2 are called inside the main accumulation loop. While O(1) each, Python function call overhead adds a noticeable constant factor compared with inlining the multiplicative recurrence that the fast solution uses.
The call pow(var_6[var_2], var_3 - 2, var_3) is O(log MOD). It is not asymptotically critical but adds overhead compared to the fast solution’s purely linear inverse precomputation.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial precomputation and instead (1) precompute modular inverses of integers 1..K in O(K) using the standard recurrence inv[i] = -(MOD//i) * inv[MOD%i] mod MOD, and (2) maintain the needed binomial coefficients C(N, k) and C(N-1, k) iteratively using multiplicative recurrences. The sum \sum_k C(N, k) * C(N-1, k) can then be evaluated in a single O(K) pass, with both time and space depending only on the actual K used (capped at N-1) rather than on a large fixed limit.

complexity.space: O(K_eff) for the inverse array; O(1) additional for a few running combination values
complexity.why: The fast code only performs work proportional to the maximum k used in the sum. First, modular inverses for 1..K_eff are computed via a simple linear recurrence. Then, in a single loop over k=1..K_eff, it updates C(N, k) and C(N-1, k) from their previous values using inverse[k] and multiplies them to accumulate the answer. There is no dependence on a global fixed factorial bound, and no logarithmic modular exponentiation inside the main computation.

complexity_delta.from: O(F + L) time, O(F) space with F = 5*10^5 fixed and L = min(N, K+1)
complexity_delta.to: O(K_eff) time, O(K_eff) space with K_eff = min(K, N-1)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both are linear in the relevant k-bound, but the slow version pays an additional fixed precomputation cost F independent of K and N, and carries larger arrays than necessary. The fast version scales purely with the actual K used and avoids expensive operations like pow inside the precompute.

transformation_steps: Replace global factorial and inverse-factorial precomputation with a linear precomputation of modular inverses inv[1..K_eff] using inv[i] = -(MOD // i) * inv[MOD % i] mod MOD.

Exploit multiplicative recurrences for binomial coefficients: maintain running values cur_C_n_k = C(N, k) and cur_C_n1_k = C(N-1, k), updating via cur_C_n_k *= (N - k + 1) * inv[k] and cur_C_n1_k *= (N - k) * inv[k] modulo MOD.
Inline the combination logic into the main summation loop, eliminating repeated nCr calls and Python function-call overhead.
Cap the summation index as k <= N-1 (var_9 = min(var_9, var_10 - 1)), aligning the algorithm with the combinatorial constraints and preventing any attempt to form invalid terms.
Remove unused or redundant structures (e.g., factorial arrays, reversed(list(range(...))) construction) to reduce memory footprint and constant factors.
trigger_signals: Presence of large fixed-size precomputation (factorials up to 5*10^5) regardless of actual input K.
Use of pow(..., MOD-2, MOD) to compute a single inverse factorial for the full range, indicating an opportunity to switch to linear inverse precomputation if only 1..K are needed.
Allocation of multiple O(F) arrays when the core sum only needs combinations up to K, suggesting that a streaming or iterative combination computation could suffice.
High constant-factor operations in setup compared to a relatively simple main summation loop, signaling that setup cost dominates runtime.
pitfalls: Correctness for large N: factorial-based precomputation with a fixed upper bound fails if N or N-1 exceed that bound. The iterative method used in the fast code avoids this but must compute inverse[i] for all i up to K_eff without off-by-one errors.
Modular inverse recurrence: inv[i] = -(MOD // i) * inv[MOD % i] % MOD requires MOD to be prime and > i, and careful implementation to avoid sign or indexing mistakes.
Loop bounds: the cap K_eff = min(K, N-1) is essential; omitting this can introduce invalid combinatorial terms and may cause logic errors or unnecessary work.

Overflow and data types: while Python’s big integers handle large intermediate values, forgetting to take modulo frequently enough would degrade performance. The fast code carefully reduces modulo MOD at each multiplicative step.

Indexing alignment: when switching from factorial-based C(n, k) to multiplicative updates, matching the initial values (k=0 term) and update formulas is crucial; an off-by-one in k or in N - k terms will silently produce wrong sums.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case. Inputs: (var_2=n, var_1=m). Likely n up to ~2e5 and m up to ~1e12 or smaller (e.g., 1e9), since factorization is done by trial division to sqrt(m). Number of distinct prime factors and each exponent are small (sum of exponents O(log m)).

dominant_ops: Precomputation of factorials and modular inverses up to O(n+100) under modulo 1e9+7
Trial division factorization of m up to O(sqrt(m))

complexity.why: Let n = var_2, m = var_1, k = number of distinct prime factors of m. func_2 does trial division from 2 to ceil(sqrt(m)), giving O(sqrt(m)). The loop building var_6 (factorials), var_9 (modular inverses), and var_7 (inverse factorials) runs from 2 to n+100, so O(n) time and O(n) memory. Each binomial coefficient via func_1 is O(1) using precomputed factorials/inverse factorials, and it is called once per prime factor, so O(k) extra.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorials and modular inverses are precomputed up to n+100 even though the required binomial coefficients only depend on small exponents (sum of exponents is O(log m)); this yields an O(n) cost that can dominate when n is large relative to sqrt(m) and log m.
Three arrays (factorials, modular inverses, inverse factorials) of length O(n) are stored, which is unnecessary given that the problem only needs a handful of binomial coefficients with small k.

The factorization function uses a somewhat awkward sqrt ceiling expression int(-(-(var_11**0.5) // 1)), involving floating-point sqrt and ceiling. Although asymptotically still O(sqrt(m)), it incurs minor constant-factor overhead compared to using integer sqrt/floor directly.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial/inverse precomputation and compute each needed binomial coefficient combinatorially using a multiplicative formula with small k (the prime exponent). Factor m by trial division with integer sqrt, accumulate prime exponents in a dictionary, and for each exponent e compute C(n+e-1, e) via a simple recursive multiplicative relation, then take the product modulo 1e9+7.

complexity.why: Factorization: the loop from 2 to floor(sqrt(m)) with inner division reduces m in O(sqrt(m)) operations. Let e_i be the exponent of each prime factor; sum_e = Σ e_i ≤ log_2(m). The recursive func_1 computes C(N, k) in O(k) arithmetic ops and stack frames with k = e_i, so total cost across all primes is O(sum_e) = O(log m). There is no O(n) precomputation, and memory is dominated by the recursion stack and the small dictionary of primes, both O(log m) in the worst case.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(n + sqrt(m) + k), Space: O(n) due to factorials and inverse factorials up to n+100.
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(sqrt(m) + log m), Space: O(log m) for recursion stack and a small prime-exponent dictionary; no dependence on n in the asymptotic cost.
complexity_delta.note: The main improvement is removing the O(n) factorial/inverse precomputation and replacing O(1) binomial queries with O(e) combinatorial computations where e (prime exponent) is very small (sum of e is O(log m)). Thus, when n is large and m is modest, the modified code is significantly faster and lighter in memory.

transformation_steps: Replace the nested func_3 structure with a flat script that reads (n, m) once at the top level.
Change prime factorization to use floor(sqrt(m)) with integer sqrt from math, and accumulate exponents in a defaultdict(int) via repeated division in a while loop.
Remove global factorial and modular inverse precomputation arrays (var_6, var_7, var_9) and the associated O(n) initialization loop.
Redefine the binomial computation as func_1(n, k) using a recursive multiplicative formula C(n, k) = C(n-1, k-1) * n / k, which runs in O(k) time with k being the exponent (typically very small).
Iterate over the exponent values from the factorization map, compute C(n + e - 1, e) for each exponent, multiply them into an accumulator, and only then reduce the final result modulo 1e9+7.
trigger_signals: The sum of exponents of the prime factors of m is bounded by O(log m), but the original solution pays O(n) to precompute factorials and inverses regardless of how many combinations are needed.
Memory usage grows linearly with n due to factorial-related arrays, even though only a few combinations with small k are ever computed.
The precomputation loop dominates runtime for large n while combination queries themselves are very cheap, indicating a mismatch between precomputation cost and query volume.
The problem structure involves computing a small number of combinations with small k but potentially large n, making multiplicative formulas more appropriate than full factorial tables.
pitfalls: {'kind': 'recursion_depth', 'detail': "func_1 is implemented recursively. Although k (the exponent) is small in typical constraints (O(log m)), if constraints change or input is adversarial (large k), this could hit Python's recursion limit or incur overhead. An iterative implementation would be safer for general use."}

{'kind': 'big_integer_growth_before_mod', 'detail': 'The fast version computes binomial coefficients using integer arithmetic and division, only applying modulo 1e9+7 at the very end. For larger or different constraints, intermediate values C(n, k) can grow very large, increasing CPU and memory cost; in extreme cases this may be slower than modular factorial-based methods that keep numbers bounded.'}

{'kind': 'integer_division_exactness', 'detail': 'The combination formula uses integer division (//) and assumes divisibility at every step (which is mathematically correct for binomial coefficients). Any mistake in the recurrence or argument order would silently produce wrong results via truncated division.'}

{'kind': 'loss_of_general_scalability', 'detail': 'While the modified solution is efficient under small exponents (typical for factoring a single m), it does not scale as well as the precomputed factorial approach in scenarios where many binomial coefficients with large k need to be computed. The original O(1) per-query binomial using factorials would then be preferable.'}

constraints_guess.notes: Classic task: choose integer p minimizing sum_i (a_i - p)^2. Likely AtCoder beginner-level with small N (≤100) and small coordinate range (e.g., |a_i| ≤ 100). Range-based brute force over integer p is acceptable.

dominant_ops: Triple-nested looping over value range and array elements: an outer loop over candidate range that redundantly wraps an inner double-loop over the same candidate values, recomputing the same sums of squared differences many times.

complexity.why: Let N = len(var_7) and R = var_7[-1] - var_7[0]. The outer loop: for var_4 in range(var_7[0], var_7[-1] + 1) runs ~R+1 times. Inside, we do: (1) a loop over all N elements to compute var_6 at p = var_7[0], then (2) an inner loop for var_2 in range(var_7[0] + 1, var_7[-1]) with about R-1 iterations, each iteration looping over all N elements again. Per outer iteration: Θ(N + R*N) = Θ(R*N). Multiplied by the outer R+1 iterations gives Θ(R^2 * N). The list var_7 itself is the main data structure, so space is Θ(N).

bottlenecks.detail: The outer loop for var_4 in range(var_7[0], var_7[len(var_7) - 1] + 1): does not use var_4 at all. All computations inside depend only on var_7 and var_2, not on var_4, so the same work is repeated R+1 times.

For each candidate p (var_2), the code recomputes var_6 from scratch via a loop over all array elements: for var_1 in range(len(var_7)): var_6 += (p - var_7[var_1]) ** 2. This is unavoidable in a naive brute-force, but here it is nested inside an unnecessary outer loop, effectively multiplying cost by another factor of R.

The first inner loop always evaluates the cost at p = var_7[0], and the second inner loop evaluates p from var_7[0] + 1 to var_7[-1] - 1. Because all of this is wrapped in an outer loop that does not change any of these values, the algorithm repeats the identical search for the minimal var_6 in each outer iteration.

All sums of squared differences are performed via explicit Python loops over the list, incurring Python-level overhead per element. With N up to ~100 this is not catastrophic, but combined with the redundant R factor it becomes unnecessarily slow compared to a vectorized approach.

FastAudit.core_idea: Eliminate the redundant outer search and compute the cost for each candidate integer p exactly once, using numpy vectorized operations to perform (a_i - p)^2 and the summation in optimized C code.

complexity.why: The loop for var_4 in range(max(var_2) - min(var_2) + 1): iterates over each candidate p from min to max once, so there are R+1 ≈ R candidate values. For each p, the expression np.sum((var_2 - var_5) ** 2) computes N squared differences and sums them; under the hood, this is Θ(N) work, albeit in fast C. Total work is thus Θ(R * N). The numpy array var_2 of length N dominates memory usage, giving Θ(N) space.

complexity_delta.from: O(R^2 * N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(R * N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: The key improvement is removing an unnecessary outer loop over R and relying on a single pass over the candidate range, coupled with vectorized arithmetic to reduce constant factors.

transformation_steps: Remove the outermost loop over var_4 that redundantly wraps the inner search; instead, iterate once over the candidate integer p in the range from min(a_i) to max(a_i).
For each candidate p, compute the sum of squared deviations sum_i (a_i - p)^2 exactly once rather than recomputing the same costs in multiple outer iterations.

Replace explicit Python loops over indices with numpy vector operations: construct a numpy array of the inputs, then use (array - p) ** 2 followed by np.sum(...) to evaluate the cost in optimized C rather than Python.
Track the running minimum of the cost across candidates using a scalar variable (var_3) rather than recomputing or resetting intermediate minima inside nested loops.
Simplify the search bounds by using min(var_2) and max(var_2) directly; rely on range(max - min + 1) and offsetting by min to generate all candidate p values.
trigger_signals: Presence of a loop variable (var_4) that is never used in the loop body, suggesting redundant repeated computation.
Nested loops over both the value range and the array indices, whose total number of iterations multiplies to R^2 * N, while the problem conceptually only requires R * N work at worst.
Recomputing the same sum of squared differences for identical candidate p values multiple times within different loops.
Use of pure Python loops for numeric aggregation over arrays where vectorization (numpy) is available and natural.
pitfalls: Assuming numpy always guarantees asymptotic improvements: while vectorization reduces constant factors dramatically, the algorithmic improvement here is primarily due to removing a redundant R factor; numpy alone does not change the Θ(R * N) nature of the brute force.

For very small N and very small R, the overhead of importing numpy may outweigh the gains from vectorization in some environments, though in typical competitive programming constraints this is not an issue.
Relying on eval(input()) for reading input is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; int(input()) or map(int, ...) is preferable. It does not affect performance here but is a robustness concern.

If N or the value range R were much larger than guessed (e.g., N up to 2e5, range up to 1e9), even the optimized O(R * N) brute force would be infeasible; a different approach using the mean and precomputed sums would be required.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer input n (var_8). Original code precomputes factorials and inverse factorials up to 1e6 unconditionally, suggesting n <= 1e6 and single test case.

dominant_ops: O(1e6) modular multiplications/additions in global precomputation loop for factorials and inverse factorials
O(n) modular multiplications in the first main loop building var_3
O(n) modular subtractions/additions in the second main loop computing weighted sum
Array indexing on large lists (size up to ~1e6)

complexity.why: Before reading input, the code always runs a loop up to var_1=1_000_006, computing three arrays: factorials (var_4), inverse factorials (var_6), and an auxiliary inverse-related array (var_7). This is O(1e6) time and space regardless of the actual input n. After that, two loops each up to n do O(n) work on var_3 and accumulate var_9. Total is dominated by the fixed 1e6 precomputation when n is smaller, and the arrays stored are sized by var_1 plus an additional array of size n.

bottlenecks.detail: The precomputation loop `for var_5 in range(2, var_1)` always runs up to 1_000_006, even if the input n (var_8) is much smaller. This adds a fixed O(1e6) cost per run.
Three large arrays var_4, var_6, var_7 of size ~1e6 are always allocated, regardless of input size. This can be heavy in memory and cache, especially in Python.

The result is computed via building var_3 in one pass and then transforming it with a second pass (difference and accumulation). This requires two O(n) passes and an extra array that are not strictly necessary.
Using `eval(input())` instead of `int(input())` is slower and unsafe. While minor compared to O(1e6) loops, it is still an avoidable cost.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace the fixed-size (1e6) global precomputation of factorials and inverse factorials with on-demand computation up to n-1 using a factorial generator and a single modular inverse via pow, then compute inverse factorials in a single backward pass. Use these to compute the required combinatorial-weighted sum in one loop without materializing the intermediate var_3 array or performing a second differencing pass.

complexity.why: The factorials up to n-1 are generated in O(n) time (func_1). A single modular exponentiation pow(var_4[n-1], MOD-2, MOD) costs O(log MOD), then inverse factorials are built in O(n) time in func_2. The main summation loop runs from roughly n/2 to n-1, which is O(n). Two arrays of length ~n (var_4 and var_13) are stored, so space is O(n). There is no unconditional O(1e6) work if n is smaller.

complexity_delta.from: O(10^6 + n) time, O(10^6 + n) space with a large constant from unconditional precomputation
complexity_delta.to: O(n + log MOD) time, O(n) space with cost directly proportional to input n

constraints_guess.notes: Problem counts the number of distinct triples (i<j<k) with values in [1..n] whose sum equals x, repeated for multiple input pairs until '0 0'. Exact limits not given; typical AOJ-style constraints suggest n up to ~50–200 and many test lines.

complexity.why: The core loop structure is for i in [0..n-3], j in [i+1..n-2], k in [j+1..n-1], which enumerates all C(n,3) = n(n-1)(n-2)/6 triplets ⇒ Θ(n^3) operations. FastAudit.core_idea: Reduce the triple enumeration to a double loop by solving for the third element algebraically: for each ordered pair (a,b) with 1 ≤ a < b ≤ n, compute c = x − a − b and check if b < c ≤ n. This counts each valid triple exactly once with only O(n^2) iterations.

complexity.why: Two nested loops: a in [1..n-2], b in [a+1..n-1] ⇒ about n(n-1)/2 iterations = Θ(n^2). Inside, only constant-time arithmetic and comparisons, with a single integer counter var_1; no auxiliary arrays are needed, so space usage is constant.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial precomputation entirely. Factorize M by trial division, then for each prime exponent e compute C(N+e-1, e) using a direct multiplicative formula with small ranges; multiply these contributions together modulo 1e9+7.

complexity.why: Prime factorization of M via trial division runs up to sqrt(M). The total sum of prime exponents is O(log M). For each exponent e, the combination C(N+e-1, e) is computed with O(e) multiplications where e is small (since M is at most about 1e9). No O(N) or O(L) precomputation is done, and only lists of prime factors and small ranges are stored.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic AtCoder-style problem: given N (up to about 100) and N integers a_i in [1,100], choose integer p in [1,100] to minimize sum_i (a_i - p)^2.

Allocating a NumPy array from a Python list (np.array(var_2))
Vectorized arithmetic (var_2 - var_4) ** 2 and np.sum(...)

bottlenecks.detail: Importing NumPy (import numpy as np) is expensive in the -style single-test, short-runtime environment; the import/initialization cost can dominate the total runtime for very small n.
Creating np.array(var_2) copies all n elements from a Python list into a NumPy buffer; for n ≤ 100 this conversion plus Python→C boundary crossings is slower than staying in pure Python.

NumPy’s vectorized operations are optimized for large arrays; for tiny arrays (n around 10–100), the fixed overhead of dispatch and temporary array allocation outweighs any speed-up compared to simple Python arithmetic.

Computing var_4 = round(np.sum(var_2) / var_1) uses floating-point division and rounding where a purely integer-based search or integer formula would suffice; this adds minor overhead and potential subtlety without a clear win at this scale.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the tiny search domain (candidate p from 1 to 100) and compute the objective sum_i (a_i - p)^2 directly with nested loops, staying entirely in pure Python and avoiding heavy libraries.

complexity.why: For each of the 100 candidate p values we iterate over all n numbers and accumulate the squared differences, yielding 100 * n operations. Since 100 is a small constant, this is effectively linear in n. Space is linear due to storing the n input integers.

complexity_delta.from: O(n) with heavy constant factors due to NumPy import and array machinery
complexity_delta.to: O(100 * n) ≈ O(n) with very small constant factors using pure Python loops
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is effectively the same, but in the real contest environment with n ≤ ~100, avoiding NumPy’s import and conversion overhead makes the simple double loop faster.

transformation_steps: Removed the NumPy dependency entirely (no import numpy as np).
Eliminated conversion of the input list into a NumPy array (np.array(var_2)), keeping the data as a plain Python list.
Replaced the vectorized computation of the optimal p via mean and broadcasting with an explicit enumeration of p from 1 to 100.
For each candidate p, computed sum (a_i - p)^2 using straightforward nested Python loops and tracked the minimum value.
Used an early-stopping break when the objective value starts increasing, leveraging the convex/unimodal nature of the squared error function over integer p.
trigger_signals: Very small problem size: n and the domain of p are both at most around 100, making heavy numerical libraries unnecessary.
Single-shot competitive-programming environment where NumPy imports are known to be slow and often discouraged.
Profile or intuition indicating that startup and conversion overhead dominate for tiny arrays.
Objective function is simple (quadratic) and easy to brute-force over a small integer range.
pitfalls: The mathematical optimization shortcut (p is the rounded mean) relies on p being unconstrained or at least within the domain of the ai; if constraints change or p’s domain is larger/different, the formula may need adjustment.

Using floating-point mean and round (as in the NumPy version) can introduce off-by-one issues if the mean is exactly halfway between integers due to tie-breaking rules; brute-force enumeration avoids such subtleties.

The early-break heuristic in the fast code assumes the objective is unimodal in p; while this holds for sum of squared differences, extending this pattern to non-convex objectives could miss the true minimum.
The fast code uses eval(input()) to parse N, which is unnecessary and potentially unsafe in general; it should be replaced with int(input()) in production-quality code.

Hash table operations (insert, lookup) are amortized O(1), so overall time is linear in n. The dictionaries can hold up to O(n) distinct keys, and var_2 stores n tuples, so space is O(n).

constraints_guess.notes: Sequence DP over N elements; segment tree sized ~3.3e5 and value range capped at 300001 suggest N and value domain up to ~3e5. Window size over indices is fixed at 100 in slow_code.

dominant_ops: For each position i, scanning up to 100 previous positions j in [i-99, i] and taking a max over dp[j] subject to |a[i] - a[j]| <= K, combined with an enormous padded input/dp array (size 6**8) and converting all of it through map(int, ...).

complexity.time: Θ(N * W) for the DP transitions with W=100 (so ~100N) plus Θ(N + 6**8) for input processing and padding; asymptotically Θ(N) but with very large constants.
complexity.space: Θ(N + 6**8) integers; in practice dominated by the preallocated array of size 6**8 ≈ 1.68e6.
complexity.why: The main loop computes dp[i] via a max over at most 100 candidates (j from i-99 to i), so about 100 operations per element. Additionally, the code builds a huge list from open(0).read().split() + var_2, where var_2 has length 6**8; map(int, ...) then traverses every element, and var_2 is reused as the dp array. This padding dominates memory and adds ~1.6M extra int conversions regardless of N.

bottlenecks.detail: For each index i, the expression max(var_2[var_4] for var_4 in range(var_3 - 99, var_3 + 1) if abs(var_1[var_3] - var_1[var_4]) <= var_5) performs up to 100 Python-level iterations, branches, and array lookups. With N up to ~3e5, that’s roughly 30M loop iterations, which is heavy in pure Python even though asymptotically linear.

var_6, var_5, *var_1 = list(map(int, open(0).read().split() + var_2)) forces map(int, ...) over all real inputs plus 6**8 zero padding integers. This adds ~1.6M unnecessary int() calls and creates a massive temporary list combining the true tokens with padding.
var_2 = [0] * 6**8 allocates an array of ~1.68M integers regardless of N. This dominates memory usage and cache footprint; it is used both as padding for input unpacking and as the dp array.

range(var_3 - 99, var_3 + 1) for small var_3 yields negative indices; in Python lists, negative indices wrap around from the end, so the DP may read unrelated padded elements instead of treating j < 0 as invalid. Even if the padding is intended, this couples correctness to Python’s negative indexing behavior and the padding size.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace the per-position scan over up to 100 prior indices with a segment tree that maintains, over the value domain, the maximum dp value among currently active positions. For each a[i], query the segment tree over values in [a[i] - K, a[i] + K] to obtain the best dp candidate in O(log V), then update the tree at position a[i] with dp[i]. Use a sliding window over indices (size 100) to expire dp values for positions older than 99 steps by resetting their contribution in the tree. Also, streamline input to incremental reading via sys.stdin.readline and avoid constructing huge padded arrays.

complexity.time: Θ((N + V) log V), where V ≈ 3.3e5 is the value-domain size of the segment tree. Each element does one range-max query and one point update in O(log V); initializing the tree is also O(V).
complexity.space: Θ(V + N), where V is the size of the segment tree array (≈ 2 * 330000) and N for storing the sequence values; no large artificial padding like 6**8 is used.
complexity.why: The DP transition is transformed into a range-maximum query over the value axis instead of scanning explicit candidate indices. A segment tree supports both range-max and point-update in O(log V). The index-window constraint (|i - j| ≤ 99) is enforced separately by invalidating dp contributions that fall out of the window, so at any time the tree only reflects active indices. This trades an O(W) scan per element (W=100) for O(log V) hierarchical operations with significantly lower constant factors in CP Python.

complexity_delta.from: Θ(N * W) DP with W=100 via explicit Python loops plus Θ(N + 6**8) input/padding overhead; effectively linear with large constants and huge padding cost.
complexity_delta.to: Θ((N + V) log V) with V≈3.3e5 using a segment tree over values, plus linear input reading; still near-linear in N but with better constants and no 6**8 padding.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically, both are O(N) if W is treated as constant and V is bounded, but in practice the naive implementation’s constants (100-way scans in Python, 1.68M-element padding, and large intermediate lists) are much worse. The segment tree shifts work into tight array operations (log V ≈ 19 per query/update) and removes the massive padding overhead, which is a substantial practical speedup.

transformation_steps: Recognize the DP recurrence: dp[i] = 1 + max{ dp[j] | j in [i-99, i], |a[i] - a[j]| <= K }, with base case handled by treating missing candidates as 0.
Abstract the constraint |a[i] - a[j]| <= K into a value-range query: all valid predecessors j must have a[j] in [a[i] - K, a[i] + K].
Introduce a segment tree (or similar range-max structure) over the value domain [0, 300000], storing for each value x the maximum dp seen so far for active indices with that value.
For each index i: compute L = max(0, a[i] - K) and R = min(MAXV, a[i] + K); query the segment tree for max dp over [L, R], then set dp[i] = 1 + that maximum.
Update the segment tree at position a[i] with dp[i] via a point update, combining via max.

Maintain the index-window constraint (j >= i-99) by tracking past indices and, when an index leaves the window, clearing its contribution from the segment tree (e.g., updating at a[old] to the max dp among remaining active indices with that value, or to 0 if none).

Refactor IO: use sys.stdin.readline to read N, K and each a[i] incrementally instead of open(0).read().split() + padding. Allocate arrays only up to the needed sizes (e.g., dp length N, tree length ~2 * 330000).
Implement the segment tree with an explicit identity element X_unit = 0 and a binary operation X_f = max, and ensure all queries respect half-open [l, r) semantics for correctness and performance.
trigger_signals: Presence of a DP step that scans a window of up to 100 previous indices for every position i using Python loops and max over a generator.
Use of an enormous constant-sized array var_2 = [0] * 6**8 combined with open(0).read().split() + var_2, indicating artificial padding and excessive memory use.
Constraints inferred from the fast solution: segment tree sized to ~330000 and values clamped to [0, 300001], which suggest large N and value range where naive per-element scans are too slow.
The condition |a[i] - a[j]| <= K naturally forming a value-interval filter, which is a classic signal for range-query data structures like segment trees or Fenwick trees.
Need to enforce a sliding window over indices (|i - j| <= 99), which is more efficient with a data structure that supports fast insertions and deletions/expirations than explicit rescan.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors in segment tree range queries: the implementation uses a half-open interval [l, r); care must be taken to query [var_11, var_14 + 1) when the desired range is inclusive [var_11, var_14].
Incorrect identity value: for a range-maximum segment tree, X_unit must be 0 (or -inf if negative values are allowed). Using an incorrect identity leads to inflated dp values or missed optimums.

Forgetting to enforce the index-window constraint (|i - j| <= 99) in the fast solution. If expired positions are not removed or neutralized in the tree, dp values from outdated indices will leak into later states and overestimate the answer.

Value-domain bounds: a[i] - K and a[i] + K must be clamped to [0, MAXV], where MAXV matches the tree’s size (here 300001 / 330000). Off-by-one in MAXV or clamping can cause index errors or missed candidates at the boundaries.

I/O quirks: in the fast code, using eval(var_9()) for reading numbers can be significantly slower and potentially unsafe compared to int(var_9()). This may reintroduce performance issues if N is large.

Method naming/usage mismatch: the snippet references var_16.fold(...) while the class defines func_2; in a complete implementation these must be consistent, and the fold function must indeed perform the segment tree query as intended.
Memory layout: choosing a segment tree size that is too small for the possible value range will cause out-of-bounds writes; oversizing it excessively wastes memory and might impact cache performance.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace manual streaming selection of the two smallest times per group with batched sorting of each group using Python's built-in sorted (implemented in C), accumulate the relevant entries into a list for the final round, and iterate over those groups in a single compact loop built from list comprehensions.

complexity.why: For 3 heats of size 8 and a final of size 6, the code sorts four lists: three of length 8 and one of length 6. In general, for H heats of size K each and a final of size O(H), the cost is roughly H * K log K for sorting each heat plus a small sort for the final. With N = H * K, this is O(N log K). The original algorithm performs only linear streaming selection. The fast version also stores all input lines and intermediate selections in Python lists, using O(N) extra space instead of constant space.

complexity_delta.from: O(N) time, O(1) extra space
complexity_delta.to: O(N log K) time, O(N) extra space (here N is total records, K group size; in the given code N and K are constants)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically, replacing streaming selection with full sorting is a regression (linear to N log K). For the fixed small sizes in this problem (3 groups of 8 and a final of 6), the practical performance difference is negligible and may even favor the sorted version due to highly optimized C-level sort and reduced Python branching.

transformation_steps: Batch input per heat: use a nested list comprehension [[input() for _ in [0] * 8] for _ in [0] * 3] to read each heat into a list instead of streaming line-by-line processing.

Replace manual top-2 maintenance (comparisons and func_1 calls in the inner loop) with a single sorted(var_2, key=lambda var_3: var_3.split()[1]) call per group, then slice var_1[:2] for the two smallest entries.
