constraints_guess.n_max: ≈1e5 total entries (e.g. N,M up to ~10^2–10^3)
constraints_guess.notes: Typical contest setting where total number of (person, item) pairs is up to around 1e5. Requires O(N*M) or O(total_items) behavior; extra linear factors on M inside deep loops are risky.

dominant_ops: Double loop over people and item indices, with each iteration performing list membership checks (`x in list`) and `list.remove`, both O(L) in the list length. This turns a nominal O(N*M) scan into roughly O(N*M^2) in the worst case.

complexity.time: O(N * M^2) in the worst case
complexity.why: Let N = var_2 (number of groups/people), M = var_1 (number of item types). The outer loop runs N times, the inner loop runs M times, giving N*M iterations. Inside each iteration: (1) `var_3[var_6] in var_4` is O(|var_4|), up to O(M); (2) `var_3[var_6] in var_7[var_5]` is O(size_of_group), up to O(M); (3) `var_4.remove(...)` is O(|var_4|) = O(M). So each inner iteration can cost O(M), leading to O(N*M^2) overall. Space is O(N*M) because all groups are stored in `var_7`, plus O(M) for `var_3` and `var_4`.

bottlenecks.detail: Using Python lists (`var_4`, `var_7[...]`) for membership tests (`x in list`) and removals (`list.remove`) leads to O(L) per operation. This is inappropriate when these operations are executed inside nested loops over N and M.

The algorithm simulates a set intersection by scanning all M possible items for every group and conditionally removing from `var_4`. Each item can trigger multiple linear scans and removals, which inflates the complexity from O(N*M) to O(N*M^2) in dense cases.

All input rows are stored in `var_7` before processing. While not the primary bottleneck, this adds O(N*M) memory and prevents streaming-style processing that could be simpler and slightly more cache-friendly.

FastAudit.core_idea: Represent the current candidate items as a set and iteratively intersect it with the set of items from each group. Set intersection (`&=`) and membership are O(1) amortized per element, giving an overall O(N*M) solution that matches the natural mathematical formulation of the problem.

complexity.time: O(N * M) in the worst case (or O(total_items))
complexity.why: Initialize `var_3` as a set of size M. For each of N groups, read K_i items, convert them to a set in O(K_i), and compute `var_3 &= set(var_1)`. Each intersection touches at most the smaller of the two sets, and the size of `var_3` is non-increasing, so the total cost across all groups is O(sum K_i) ≤ O(N*M). Only `var_3` (size ≤ M) and one temporary set per line are needed, so space is O(M).

complexity_delta.from: O(N * M^2) time, O(N * M) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N * M) time, O(M) space
complexity_delta.note: The key improvement is switching from list-based membership/removal inside nested loops to native set intersection on shrinking sets.

transformation_steps: Replace the list `var_4` (current candidates) with a set `var_3` initialized as `set(range(1, M+1))` to represent the items common so far.
Avoid storing all groups in memory (`var_7`); instead, process each input line as it is read to allow streaming intersection and reduce space usage.
For each group, ignore the count `var_2` and read the remaining values directly into a list, then convert that list to a set once: `set(var_1)`.

Use set intersection assignment `var_3 &= set(var_1)` to update the running set of common items in one O(K_i) operation, instead of iterating over all M items and conditionally removing them with `list.remove`.
Remove redundant arrays (`var_3` and `var_4` in the slow code) and duplicated representations of the candidate universe, keeping only a single set for candidates.
trigger_signals: Nested loops over both N and M (`for var_5 in range(var_2):` and `for var_6 in range(var_1):`) combined with non-constant-time operations inside.
Use of `x in list` within the inner loop, which is O(L) and therefore dangerous when L can be as large as M.
Use of `list.remove` inside deeply nested loops, which is also O(L) and can be called many times.
Manual simulation of set behavior (membership + removal) using Python lists, rather than using the built-in `set` type.
Storing all input groups in an array (`var_7`) even though groups can be processed independently, a sign that a streaming or incremental approach might be simpler and more efficient.
pitfalls: If one keeps lists instead of sets for the candidate items, even a conceptually correct algorithm can degrade to O(N*M^2) due to linear-time membership and removal operations.

Repeatedly calling `list.remove` while iterating over indices or values can lead to subtle logic bugs in other contexts (index shifting) and always incurs O(L) time; sets do not suffer from this when calling `set.remove` or `set.discard`.
Converting each group’s items to a set is important; intersecting a set with a list directly is not supported, and repeatedly checking `x in list` would negate the performance benefits.

For very large M, constructing `set(range(1, M+1))` still costs O(M); if M could be extremely large compared to total listed items, a different representation (like counts per item) might be considered, but under typical constraints this is acceptable.

Care must be taken to read and ignore the per-line count correctly (`var_2`), ensuring that all and only the listed items are included in each group’s set for intersection; off-by-one or parsing errors would silently change the result.

constraints_guess.n_max: ≈ 1e5 (first input, number of factors / N in combinations)
constraints_guess.notes: Second input (the number to factor, M) is ≲ 1e9. Classic AtCoder-style task: count ways to distribute prime exponents of M among N items using ∏ C(N + e_p - 1, e_p) mod 1e9+7.

dominant_ops: Precomputing factorials and modular inverse factorials up to O(N) where N is input-dependent (loop up to var_2 + 100)
Trial division factorization of M up to O(sqrt(M)) using floating-point sqrt and repeated division
Computing several binomial coefficients C(N + e - 1, N - 1) via table lookups

complexity.why: Factorization by trial division up to sqrt(M) is O(sqrt(M)). The loop building var_6, var_7, var_9 runs from 2 to var_2 + 100, i.e., O(N) multiplications and modular operations, and the arrays themselves grow to size O(N). The final product over primes is small (sum of exponents ≲ log M) so its cost is negligible compared with the O(N) precomputation.

bottlenecks.detail: Building factorial (var_6) and inverse factorial (var_7) tables up to var_2 + 100 dominates runtime and memory when var_2 (N) is large. For N as big as 1e5 this is noticeable but OK; for larger N (e.g., 1e7–1e9) it becomes infeasible (TLE/MLE).
Arrays var_6, var_7, var_9 store O(N) integers. This is unnecessary given that only O(log M) binomial computations are needed; the fast solution achieves O(1) extra space instead.

Factorization uses a for-loop up to ceil(sqrt(M)) with float exponentiation (var_11**0.5) and a ceiling trick. While asymptotically similar to the fast version, using integers and updating the bound based on the remaining factor can be slightly cheaper and clearer.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial/inverse-factorial precomputation and instead compute each required binomial coefficient C(N + e - 1, e) on the fly using the multiplicative formula res *= (N - 1 + e - k) / (k + 1) modulo 1e9+7 with modular inverses via pow(). Combine this with a lightweight prime factorization that yields only the exponents, using a generator so no large tables are built.

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + log M * log MOD) ≈ O(sqrt(M))
complexity.why: Factorization still uses trial division up to about sqrt(M), same as the slow version. However, for each exponent e_p the code performs only e_p iterations of an O(log MOD)-time modular inverse via pow, and the total sum of exponents is O(log M). Thus the additional cost over factorization is O(log M * log MOD), which is tiny relative to sqrt(M). No arrays proportional to N are allocated, so extra space is constant.

complexity_delta.from: O(N + sqrt(M)) time, O(N) space (slow_code with factorial tables up to N)
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M)) time, O(1) space (fast_code with on-the-fly binomial computation)
complexity_delta.note: The key gain is eliminating O(N) factorial/inverse factorial precomputation and storage, leveraging the small total exponent sum (≈ log M) to compute each combination directly.

transformation_steps: Removed the global factorial (var_6) and inverse factorial (var_7) arrays and the accompanying O(N) initialization loop.

Replaced the nCk helper that used precomputed factorial/inverse factorial tables with an in-place multiplicative computation of C(N + e - 1, e) using a short loop over k = 0..e-1 and modular inverses pow(k + 1, MOD - 2, MOD).

Simplified the prime-factor data structure from a list of [prime, exponent] pairs to a generator that yields only exponents in a fixed order (2, 3, 5, ... plus possibly a final prime > sqrt(M)); this avoids materialization overhead and intermediate storage.

Kept factorization cost roughly the same (trial division up to sqrt(M)), but structured the loop using integer arithmetic and a single running remainder var_8, which can be marginally more efficient than the float-based ceiling sqrt used in the slow version.

Structured the main accumulation loop so that exponents equal to zero incur no work: the inner loop over range(var_5) simply does not run when var_5 == 0, avoiding conditional checks per potential prime.
trigger_signals: Precomputation loops whose upper bound depends directly on a potentially large input parameter (e.g., for i in range(2, N + 100)): suggests O(N) work that might dominate.
Large auxiliary arrays sized by input N (factorials and inverse factorials) when the problem structure implies only O(log M) combinatorial evaluations are needed.
Constraints indicating N can be large (e.g., up to 1e5 or more) combined with a single query and small secondary parameters (like exponents of prime factors).
Observed or anticipated TLE/MLE when N is increased, with profiling showing most time spent in the precomputation phase rather than in the core mathematical logic.
Editorial or mathematical insight that the number of required combinations is very small (at most one per prime factor), which makes heavy table precomputation unnecessary.
pitfalls: Incorrect modular inverse usage: when replacing factorial-table-based nCk with the multiplicative formula, each division must be converted to a multiplication by the modular inverse using pow(denominator, MOD - 2, MOD). Forgetting MOD - 2 or mixing integer division and modular arithmetic will break correctness.

Overflow or missing modulo: intermediate products must always be reduced modulo 1e9+7; skipping a % operation in the multiplicative combination loop can overflow Python's implicit assumptions in other languages (or just hurt performance elsewhere).

Off-by-one in combination indices: the fast version uses numerators (N - 1 + e - k). Misaligning this (e.g., (N + k) instead) changes the binomial from C(N + e - 1, e) to a different coefficient, yielding wrong answers that might still pass small cases.

Factorization loop bounds: using var_6 * var_6 <= var_7 (original M) instead of the shrinking remainder could do extra iterations; using var_8 (the remaining unfactored part) is a micro-optimization but must be done carefully to avoid missing a prime factor.

Handling the final prime factor correctly: after the trial division loop, if the remaining value > 1, it corresponds to a leftover prime with exponent 1. Missing this case or adding it incorrectly changes the number of combination factors.

Corner cases M = 1 or N = 1: when M = 1 there are no prime factors and thus the product over combinations should be 1; when N = 1, each exponent must be assigned to a single number, so the answer should also be 1. Both formulas handle this, but ad-hoc rewrites can accidentally special-case them incorrectly.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: first integer N, then N integers a_i with 0 <= a_i <= 100. Objective: minimize sum_i (a_i - p)^2 over integer p in some small range (often [0,100] or [min(a),max(a)]).

dominant_ops: Import and initialization of NumPy (large fixed startup cost)
Loop over candidate p in range(0, 101) with vectorized operations: (var_6 - p) ** 2 and sum(...) for each p

complexity.time: O(N) with a large constant factor: 101 full passes over the data via NumPy plus NumPy import overhead
complexity.why: N elements are stored once in a NumPy array. The loop tests 101 candidate p values; each evaluation is a vectorized O(N) operation in C. The candidate range is fixed-size (101), so asymptotically it is O(N), but with 101 passes over the data and non-trivial NumPy startup cost.

bottlenecks.detail: Importing NumPy and creating a NumPy array is expensive relative to the small input size typical of this problem.
Brute-force scan over all integer p in [0,100] does 101 separate evaluations of sum_i (a_i - p)^2, although for a quadratic objective the minimizer can be found analytically from the mean of the a_i.
Even though the per-p computation is vectorized, the Python-level loop over 101 values of p adds overhead that can dominate when N is small.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical property that the sum of squared deviations sum_i (a_i - p)^2 is minimized at the (real) mean of the a_i. For integer p, it suffices to check the floor and ceiling of the mean, so only 2 candidate p values are evaluated instead of scanning an entire fixed range. This avoids NumPy and reduces the number of full passes over the data from ~100 to 2.

complexity.why: Read N values once, compute their sum in O(N), compute the mean and two integer candidates, then evaluate sum_i (a_i - p)^2 for p in {floor(mean), ceil(mean)} (two more O(N) passes). The candidate set size is constant (2), so total time is linear in N with a very small constant factor. The list of values is stored once, so space is linear in N.

complexity_delta.from: O(N) with a large constant: 101 evaluations of the cost function plus NumPy import and array allocation
complexity_delta.to: O(N) with a very small constant: 1 pass to sum and 2 passes to evaluate the cost at floor/ceil of the mean
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time remains O(N), but the number of full passes over the data drops from ~101 to 2 and heavy library overhead (NumPy) is removed. For competitive programming constraints, this difference is substantial.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the objective function sum_i (a_i - p)^2 is a convex quadratic in p, whose minimizer over the reals is the mean of the a_i.
Observe that when p must be an integer, it suffices to check the integer(s) nearest to the mean: floor(mean) and ceil(mean).
Replace the brute-force search over p in range(0, 101) with computation of the total sum of a_i and derivation of the two candidate p values via integer division.
Evaluate the cost sum_i (a_i - p)^2 only for these two candidates and take their minimum.
Remove NumPy dependency and use pure Python lists and arithmetic for better startup and execution performance in a contest environment.
trigger_signals: Objective is a sum of squared differences: sum_i (a_i - p)^2, a classic quadratic form with a well-known analytic minimizer.
The code brute-forces p over a fixed small range (0..100), hinting that the solution might not be using the structure of the objective.
Use of NumPy in a problem with small constraints, where import and array conversion cost likely outweighs any benefit.
Repeated full-data scans inside a Python loop when the mathematical form allows an O(N) single-pass formula.
pitfalls: Ensuring that the floor/ceil of the mean are valid candidates if the problem restricts p to a specific range (e.g., must be in [0,100] or [min(a), max(a)]). If there is a range constraint, candidates should be clamped accordingly.
Handling integer division correctly: using // and (sum + N - 1) // N to get floor and ceil mean reliably for non-negative integers.
Avoiding the use of eval(input()) for reading integers; it is unnecessary and unsafe in general, though in an online judge it typically passes. Prefer int(input()).
Ensuring that the cost computation uses integers with enough range (Python ints are arbitrary precision, so overflow is not an issue, but in other languages it would be).
Not overfitting to the 0..100 bound: if constraints or value ranges change, the brute-force 0..100 loop may become invalid or inefficient, whereas the mean-based approach generalizes cleanly.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style single array problem: read N, then N integers; linear solution strongly suggests N up to about 2e5–1e6. No explicit queries; single pass computation.

dominant_ops: In func_7: building an array of N integers from stdin, then a single for-loop over N-1 positions doing integer division, modulo, comparisons, and a few array reads/writes.

complexity.why: func_7 reads N, then creates a list var_1 of length N and iterates over it once (plus a constant-time final element handling). All other defined functions are unused in the hot path. The work per element is O(1) (a few arithmetic operations and branches), so overall time is linear in N; space is linear because the full list of N integers is stored.

bottlenecks.detail: Reading N separate integers with sys.stdin.readline inside a list comprehension is standard but still dominates runtime for large N; however, it is already using fast buffered I/O, so this is close to optimal in pure Python.

The loop must special-case the last index: range(var_2 - 1) plus an extra final computation var_1[var_2 - 1] // 2. This adds an extra conditional path and slightly more code complexity, though it does not change asymptotic cost.

Multiple unused functions (func_6, func_8–func_11, input helpers) and heavy imports (bisect, itertools, heapq, math, random, deepcopy, Counter, defaultdict, deque) are present. They do not affect asymptotic complexity but add minor import-time overhead and noise, making it harder to identify the actual hot path.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the same greedy linear algorithm on the array of counts, but simplify the loop by appending a sentinel 0 to the list so that every index i can safely look at i+1. This removes the need for separate handling of the last element and keeps all logic in one uniform loop.

complexity.why: The fast_code reads N, builds a list of N integers plus a single sentinel element, then iterates from 0 to N-1 once. Each iteration performs O(1) arithmetic and branch operations. The sentinel adds only constant extra work and memory, so time remains O(N) and space O(N).

complexity_delta.from: Time O(N), Space O(N) for a single-pass greedy over the array with explicit last-element handling.
complexity_delta.to: Time O(N), Space O(N) for the same greedy logic but with a sentinel element to unify the loop.
complexity_delta.note: Algorithmic complexity is unchanged (linear in N). The changes mainly simplify the core loop and remove unused scaffolding, slightly improving constant factors and readability. Note that fast_code’s use of eval(input()) is actually slower and unsafe compared to int(sys.stdin.readline()).

transformation_steps: Restrict the implementation to the relevant greedy routine, dropping unused functions like func_6, func_8–func_11 and extra helpers/imports that are not involved in the computation.
Inline the logic of func_7 into a single entry-point function (func_1 in fast_code) to clarify the data flow: read N, read the N integers into a list, process them, and print the result.
Append a sentinel 0 to the list of counts so that for each index i (0 <= i < N) the code can safely inspect and modify var_1[i+1] without special casing the last index.
Unify the greedy pairing logic in one loop: accumulate var_1[i] // 2; if var_1[i] is odd and the next element is positive, consume one from the next and add an extra pair.
Reduce minor branching and separate final-element logic by eliminating the explicit post-loop handling of var_1[N-1] and incorporating its contribution into the unified loop with the sentinel.
trigger_signals: The presence of a single loop over the array with simple arithmetic indicates that O(N) is already optimal; opportunities are in constant-factor and code-structure improvements, not asymptotic ones.
Manual special casing of the last element (loop to N-1, then a separate computation for index N-1) suggests the possibility of using a sentinel value to simplify the loop body.

Multiple unused helper functions and imports in the slow_code hint at template or boilerplate code, meaning cleaning up to the minimal hot path can clarify performance analysis and reduce minor overhead.
The greedy structure (looking at current and next elements only) is naturally compatible with a sentinel-based approach, making the transformation straightforward.
pitfalls: The fast_code uses eval(input()) instead of int(input()), which is both slower and insecure if the input is not trusted. For performance and safety, int(sys.stdin.readline()) or int(input()) should be preferred.

Appending a sentinel element relies on the assumption that accessing var_1[i+1] for i in range(N) is always valid and that the extra 0 does not alter the logical outcome. Misplacing the sentinel or looping to the wrong bound can introduce off-by-one errors.
Removing special-case handling for the last element requires careful verification that the old logic (explicit final var_1[N-1] // 2) is fully incorporated into the unified loop with the sentinel.

If constraints are very large (N >> 10^6), pure-Python I/O and per-element arithmetic will dominate; neither version changes the asymptotic limit, so a language change or further I/O optimization might be required instead of micro-optimizations.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder/AOJ style: N up to ~1e5–2e5, coordinates/lengths up to about 1e9. Needs O(N log N) or better; exponential/backtracking infeasible.

dominant_ops: Recursive backtracking over interval choices (func_1): effectively exploring many combinations of intervals.
Sorting intervals by right endpoint: O(N log N).
Per-node recursion overhead and Python function call cost.

complexity.time: O(2^N) in the intended recursive algorithm; O(N log N) in the actually executed greedy part
complexity.space: O(N) for storing intervals + O(N) recursion stack (if recursion used)
complexity.why: func_1 performs a depth-first search over interval indices, with a branch at almost every level (either extend from the same 'last index' or reset). In the worst case, pruning via var_10 (global best) does not cut much, so the search explores an exponential number of states in N. Additionally, recursion stack depth scales with N. The bottom part of slow_code already has an O(N log N) greedy, but the conceptually intended solution via func_1 is exponential and thus non-viable for large N.

bottlenecks.detail: func_1 is a brute-force/backtracking search that branches at almost every interval, leading to O(2^N) behavior in the worst case. This cannot handle N in the thousands or more.
Deep recursion with Python function calls at every node adds significant constant factor overhead and risks hitting recursion limits or stack overflow for large N.

Pruning via var_10[0] (current best) only compares counts of selected intervals and does not leverage any structural property (like sorted endpoints) to strongly reduce the search tree in worst cases.
Although func_1 is not actually invoked in the shown slow_code, keeping such an exponential helper often leads to accidental use or confusion and obscures that a simple greedy suffices.

FastAudit.core_idea: Transform each (x, l) into a closed interval [x - l, x + l], sort by the right endpoint, then greedily select intervals in order of increasing right endpoint, always picking the next interval whose left endpoint is not less than the right endpoint of the last chosen interval. This is the classic optimal algorithm for maximizing the number of non-overlapping intervals.

complexity.why: Creating the list of intervals and their transformed endpoints is O(N). Sorting by the right endpoint costs O(N log N). The subsequent single pass to greedily count compatible intervals is O(N). No recursion or exponential branching is used; memory usage is linear in the number of intervals.

complexity_delta.from: Conceptual O(2^N) backtracking (func_1) + O(N log N) preprocessing
complexity_delta.to: Pure O(N log N) greedy interval scheduling
complexity_delta.note: The key improvement is recognizing that this is a standard unweighted interval scheduling problem, allowing a provably optimal greedy solution based on sorting by right endpoints instead of exploring combinations.

transformation_steps: Model the input pair (x, l) as an interval on the line: left = x - l, right = x + l.
Observe that the objective is to maximize the number of non-overlapping intervals, which matches the classic interval scheduling problem.
Use the known optimal strategy: sort all intervals by increasing right endpoint.

Replace recursive/backtracking search with a single linear scan: maintain the right endpoint of the last chosen interval; for each interval in sorted order, pick it if its left endpoint is >= the current right endpoint.
Simplify state representation: store intervals directly as (right, left) tuples so the default sort order by the first element gives the correct ordering and allows a fast, tight inner loop.
Optimize I/O and data handling for Python: use open(0).read().split() and map to integers in one shot, and use zip with an iterator trick to pair coordinates, minimizing Python-level overhead.
trigger_signals: Naive or recursive solution shows explosive runtime growth as N increases slightly (e.g., fine for N <= 20 but times out for N ~ 30–40).
Presence of a recursive function exploring different choices per interval, with weak pruning based only on a global best counter.
Problem structure matches well-known patterns (interval scheduling / non-overlapping segments) where a greedy algorithm is known to be optimal.
Constraints on N (likely up to 1e5 or more) are incompatible with any exponential or high-polynomial solution.
Need to set sys.setrecursionlimit(10**7) is a red flag that recursion depth or search tree is too large for Python.
pitfalls: Off-by-one or comparison mistakes when deciding overlap: using the wrong inequality (e.g., > vs >=) can change whether touching intervals are allowed.
Sorting by the wrong key (e.g., by left endpoint or by length) instead of by right endpoint breaks the optimality of the greedy algorithm.
Incorrect endpoint transformation (mixing up x + l and x - l, or using radius/length inconsistently) leads to wrong interval boundaries.
Assuming the exponential recursive helper is necessary or beneficial when a simple greedy scan suffices.
For large inputs, using slow input patterns (repeated input() calls and per-line processing) can cause additional overhead; the fast solution mitigates this with a single bulk read.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer input n. Arrays are precomputed up to ~1e6 in the slow version, suggesting n ≤ 1e6. Heavy use of factorials and modular inverses under MOD = 1e9+7.

dominant_ops: O(N_max) precomputation loop up to var_1 = 1_000_006 for factorials and modular inverses
O(n) forward loop to build var_3 with combinatorial terms and factorial products
O(n) backward loop to convert var_3 into differences and accumulate the weighted sum

complexity.time: O(N_max + n) ≈ O(10^6 + n), effectively O(10^6) per test
complexity.space: O(N_max) for arrays var_4 (fact), var_6 (invfact), var_7 (inv), and O(n) for var_3
complexity.why: Precomputation always iterates up to a fixed upper bound (1_000_006) regardless of the actual input n. Then two linear passes over size ~n arrays are used to build and process a difference array.

bottlenecks.detail: The initial loop runs up to var_1 = 1_000_006 even if the input n is much smaller, wasting time for small/medium n.

func_1 returns var_4[var_10] * var_6[var_11] * var_6[var_10 - var_11] without taking modulo. Later, this result is multiplied by two more factorial terms before a final % MOD, causing intermediate values to grow to ~MOD^5 and forcing Python to perform expensive big-integer multiplications.
Lack of `% var_2` inside func_1 keeps values large throughout the combinatorial computation, increasing CPU time and cache pressure compared to keeping all intermediates in the modular range.

The algorithm uses a difference array var_3 and then a second O(n) backward loop to convert differences and accumulate the final sum. This doubles the number of passes over the array compared to a telescoping single-pass formulation.
The slow code performs multiple list lookups and appends (var_3, var_4, var_6, var_7) and touches more elements per iteration than the fast version’s tight loops.

FastAudit.core_idea: Compute factorials up to n−1 and inverse factorials via a single modular exponentiation and a linear backward pass, then use a telescoping recurrence to accumulate the weighted sum in a single forward loop over the necessary index range, with all operations reduced modulo MOD to avoid big integers.

complexity.why: func_1 generates factorials for 0..n−1 in O(n). func_2 computes invfact[n−1] with a single pow (O(log MOD)) and then uses a backward linear pass to derive all inverse factorials in O(n). The final loop runs only from ceil(n/2) to n−1, each step doing O(1) modular operations. All intermediates are kept modulo 1e9+7, so arithmetic is on small integers with low constant factors.

complexity_delta.from: Time ~ O(1e6 + n) with heavy big-integer multiplications and two O(n) passes; space O(1e6).
complexity_delta.to: Time ~ O(n) with only modular-size integers and a single O(n) pass after factorial precomputation; space O(n).
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both are linear in n, but the slow version has a fixed linear precompute to 1e6 and big-int arithmetic, while the fast version scales exactly with n and keeps all operations within modular bounds, drastically reducing constants.

transformation_steps: Size precomputation to the actual input n instead of a hard-coded upper bound (1_000_006), computing factorials only up to n−1.

Replace the inv[i] + prefix-product scheme with a factorial + inverse factorial scheme built via one modular exponentiation (pow(fact[n−1], MOD−2, MOD)) and a backward linear recurrence, avoiding extra arrays and work.
Introduce modular reduction at every multiplication so that all intermediates remain within [0, MOD), preventing Python from promoting values to large big integers.

Remove the explicit difference-array var_3 and the backward loop; instead, maintain the previous term (var_9) and exploit the telescoping structure so the weighted sum is accumulated in a single forward pass.
Restrict the main loop to the mathematically active range [(n+1)//2, n−1], skipping indices where the contribution is known to be zero, reducing the number of iterations by roughly half.
Streamline array usage: store factorials and inverse factorials in compact lists and index them directly, avoiding multiple nested list multiplications before modulo.
trigger_signals: Hard-coded precomputation bound (var_1 = 1000006) significantly larger than typical input n.
Combinatorial expressions formed as products of several factorial-like terms without intermediate modulo reductions, leading to very large integers.
Two separate O(n) passes over the same array (building a difference array and then processing it) when the final expression looks telescopable.
Use of Python big integers in tight loops (multiplying several MOD-sized numbers) visible in profiling or from code inspection.
Competitive-programming context with n up to ~1e6 and Python time limits around 1–2 seconds, where O(n) is acceptable only with small constants.
pitfalls: Forgetting a `% MOD` in the combinatorial helper (like func_1) reintroduces big-int overhead and can silently hurt performance without changing correctness for small tests.
Misaligning factorial and inverse-factorial indices (off-by-one between n, n−1) will produce incorrect binomial coefficients; the fast code carefully builds them for 0..n−1.
If multiple test cases are present, recomputing factorials for each test instead of reusing a global precompute up to max(n) can negate the performance gains.
Using eval(input()) is unnecessary and slightly slower than int(input()); in strict environments it may also be disallowed.
Memory usage of O(n) arrays is fine up to ~1e7 elements in CP, but pushing n or the precompute bound higher without care can lead to MemoryError or cache thrashing.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: two integers N,M with N up to about 1e5 and M up to about 1e9. M is factorized by trial division up to sqrt(M), so M is not extremely large; number of distinct prime factors is small (O(log M)).

dominant_ops: Trial division factorization of M up to sqrt(M)
For each prime exponent e: computing C(N+e-1, N-1) via an O(N) multiplicative loop with modular multiplications and modular inverses using pow(..., MOD-2, MOD)

complexity.why: Factorization uses trial division up to sqrt(M): O(sqrt(M)) divisions. Let N = var_3 and M = original var_1. The binomial coefficient is computed by a loop of length N-1, and each iteration uses pow(i, MOD-2, MOD) which internally is O(log MOD) modular multiplications, giving O(N log MOD). Only a small number of distinct prime factors exists, so the outer product over prime exponents is O(#primes) = O(log M) and negligible. Memory is dominated by storing the few prime factors and constant-size integers.

bottlenecks.detail: The binomial coefficient C(n, k) is computed via a loop of length k (here k ≈ N) with a modular exponentiation pow(i, MOD-2, MOD) in each iteration. For large N (≈1e5), this is notably heavier than necessary; one could precompute factorials and inverse factorials in O(N) time and use a single pow for inv_fact, reducing the log MOD factor.

The factorization loop uses trial division from 2 upward. While complexity is acceptable for M up to about 1e9, it is still the main cost when N is small. A minor micro-optimization is possible (e.g., skip even numbers after 2, or stop as soon as candidate^2 exceeds the current residual), but overall this is not a severe bottleneck for typical constraints.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the same basic mathematics (factor M, then for each exponent e compute C(N+e-1, e) and take the product), but switch from an in-loop modular multiplicative formula to direct use of math.factorial and exact integer binomial coefficients, caching factorials in a dictionary and reducing modulo 1e9+7 only at the very end.

complexity.why: Factorization is still trial division up to sqrt(M): O(sqrt(M)). The heavy change is in combinatorics: instead of modular arithmetic on fixed-size ints, it calls math.factorial on arguments up to about N + e_max - 1 and stores these huge integers in a cache. The cost of computing factorial(k) is superlinear in k due to big-integer multiplications; overall this is roughly O(max_k^2 log max_k) bit-operations for the largest k involved. Binomial coefficients are then computed using big-int multiplications and divisions, also superlinear in k. Space usage grows with the number and size of cached factorials: storing factorial(k) requires O(k log k) bits. Therefore, the new version is asymptotically and practically much slower and more memory hungry than the original modular approach.

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(M) + N * log MOD) time, O(log M) space with only fixed-width modular integers.
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + max_k^2 * log max_k) bit-operations time and O(max_k^2 * log max_k) bits space due to repeated big-integer factorials and binomial computations, where max_k ≈ N + max_exponent.
complexity_delta.note: The change from streaming modular arithmetic to exact big-integer factorial and binomial computations dramatically increases arithmetic cost and memory consumption, so the so-called fast_code is actually slower and less scalable than the original.

transformation_steps: Replaced defaultdict(int)-based factor exponent counting with a plain dict and explicit key checks (func_2). This introduces repeated list(var_11.keys()) calls, adding unnecessary O(#keys) overhead in the inner loop.

Changed the combinatorial computation from an incremental modular product with modular inverses to a direct binomial coefficient formula nCk = factorial(n) // (factorial(k) * factorial(n-k)), implemented using math.factorial on unbounded Python integers.
Introduced a cache (dictionary) for factorial values to avoid recomputing the same factorial multiple times, but still storing full big integers rather than values reduced modulo MOD.
Deferred taking modulo 1e9+7 until after all binomial coefficients have been computed and multiplied together as big integers, instead of applying modulo at each arithmetic step.
trigger_signals: Use of math.factorial on potentially large arguments (up to around N + max_exponent) in a performance-critical combinatorics routine.
Integer division (//) with huge operands to compute binomial coefficients, rather than modular inverse-based division.
Modulus applied only once at the end (var_12 % var_7), not throughout the computation, causing intermediate values to grow to enormous big integers.
Repeated list(dict.keys()) in the inner factorization loop, adding avoidable overhead proportional to the current number of distinct prime factors.
Replacement of a purely modular arithmetic approach (fixed-width ints) with exact big-integer arithmetic inside tight loops.
pitfalls: math.factorial grows extremely fast: factorial(1e5) is an astronomically large integer whose computation and storage are very expensive. Computing and caching several such factorials can easily exceed time and memory limits.

Deferring modulo until the end allows intermediate products and factorials to become huge; even though the final answer fits modulo 1e9+7, intermediate big-int operations dominate runtime and memory usage.
Using integer division (//) on huge integers is far slower than modular inverse-based division on fixed-size ints; bitlength growth makes each operation progressively slower.
The list(var_11.keys()) pattern in the factorization function creates a new list of keys on every membership test, turning what should be O(1) dict lookups into O(#keys) operations in a nested loop.

Caching factorials as raw big integers consumes space proportional to their bitlength (O(k log k)), and the cache holds multiple such values; on large inputs this can lead to memory blow-ups or garbage collector pressure.

Mathematically the combinatorics are correct (C(e+N-1, e) = C(e+N-1, N-1)), but the implementation disregards typical competitive-programming constraints that require working modulo a prime throughout to keep both time and space manageable.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder 'Coprime' style: n up to ~1e5, each a_i up to ~1e6. Need to classify as not/pairwise/setwise coprime using gcd and prime factorization.

problem_type_tags: prime factorization with SPF (smallest prime factor)

dominant_ops: Building smallest-prime-factor table up to fixed limit 10^6+5 with sieve-like nested loops
Prime factorization of each a_i using precomputed SPF
GCD fold over all elements

complexity.time: O(M log log M + n log A)
complexity.why: M = 10^6+5 fixed sieve upper bound; sieve with while var_6 * var_7 <= M over primes gives ~O(M log log M). For each of n numbers, SPF-based factorization does O(log A) divisions in worst case. Space stores arrays var_3, var_10, var_2 of size Theta(M).

bottlenecks.detail: The sieve and SPF table var_3 are built up to a hard-coded 10^6+5 regardless of the actual max(a_i). If max(a_i) << 10^6, a large fraction of the sieve work is wasted.
Allocates arrays of size 10^6+10 and 10^6+5 even if input values are much smaller, increasing memory footprint and cache pressure.

FastAudit.core_idea: Make the sieve/SPF precomputation adaptive: build the smallest-prime-factor table only up to max(a_i) instead of a fixed global upper bound, so work and memory scale with actual data rather than worst-case bound.

complexity.time: O(A_max log log A_max + n log A_max)
complexity.why: A_max = max(a_i). Class_1.__init__ builds SPF only up to A_max, so sieve cost is proportional to that value. Factorization of each a_i via func_2 still costs O(log a_i) divisions, giving total ~O(n log A_max). Arrays MINFact and var_2 have length A_max+1, reducing memory compared to a fixed 10^6 bound when A_max is smaller.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(M log log M + n log A) with M fixed at 10^6+5. Space: O(M) with M fixed at 10^6+5.
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(A_max log log A_max + n log A_max). Space: O(A_max).
complexity_delta.note: When A_max << 10^6, both time and memory usage drop proportionally. In worst-case A_max ~= 10^6, asymptotic bounds remain similar but constant factors may improve due to tighter allocation.

transformation_steps: Compute the maximum value in the input array: var_6 = max(var_1).
Replace the global, fixed-size SPF array (var_3 size 10^6+10) with a per-instance MINFact array sized to var_6+1 inside Class_1.
Run the sieve/SPF construction loop only up to var_12 = var_6 instead of a hard-coded 10^6+5.
Allocate the prime-count array var_2 with length var_6+1 instead of 10^6+5.
Wrap SPF logic in a class (Class_1) and perform factorization via a method (func_2 / prime_factor) using the adaptive-sized tables.
trigger_signals: Precomputation loops over a large fixed upper bound (10^6) while actual input maxima may be much smaller.
Large auxiliary arrays whose size is independent of actual data range.
Time limit tight for worst-case but many test cases likely use smaller values, suggesting room for data-dependent optimization.
Memory usage close to contest limits due to globally sized tables.
pitfalls: If A_max is allowed to be very large (e.g., > 2e8 as guarded in Class_1), the adaptive SPF table can become too big in time and memory; the guard raises, but a real solution would need a different factorization strategy for such ranges.
Off-by-one errors when sizing arrays to max(a_i); need length A_max+1 to index by prime value directly.
Multiple test cases would benefit from reusing one sieve up to the global max instead of rebuilding per test; rebuilding every time could negate performance gains.

The posted fast_code appears to call var_9.prime_factor instead of the defined func_2 method and ends with an incomplete else-branch; in a real implementation this must be corrected, or it will fail at runtime irrespective of complexity benefits.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style combinatorics with modulus 998244353. Single test case, parameters like n (<= 2e5), m (<= 2e5), k (<= n-1). Needs near O(n) or O(k) solution in Python.

dominant_ops: O(n) factorial and inverse-factorial precomputation
O(k log n) modular exponentiation via custom Python loop for each term in the sum
Heavy and unnecessary imports (numpy, decimal, queue, etc.) increasing startup overhead

complexity.why: func_3 precomputes factorials and inverse factorials up to n -> O(n). The main loop runs for i in [0..k], and each iteration calls func_1 which is a hand-written binary exponentiation in Python, costing O(log(n)) operations per call, giving O(k log n). Arrays for factorials and inverse factorials each of size n+1 give O(n) space.

bottlenecks.detail: Using custom modular exponentiation func_1 inside the main loop causes O(k log n) Python-level operations. Built-in pow with modulus would be significantly faster, but even that would still be O(k log n) overall.
Full factorial and inverse factorial arrays up to n are computed although only combinations C(n-1, i) for i <= k are needed; this forces O(n) work regardless of k.
Hand-written binary exponentiation in Python (while loop, bit operations) is slower than using Python’s built-in pow(base, exp, mod) implemented in C.
Large set of unused imports (math, collections, bisect, itertools, fractions, copy, heapq, decimal, queue, numpy) increase import and startup time, which matters in tight time limits.
Storing two arrays (factorial and inverse factorial) of length n+1 uses O(n) memory; if n is large (e.g., 2e5 or higher), this is acceptable but not minimal given only k (<= n-1) is needed.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit incremental formulas to avoid heavy precomputation and repeated exponentiation: (1) maintain C(n-1, i) iteratively using C(n-1, i) = C(n-1, i-1) * (n-i)/i with precomputed modular inverses of 1..k; (2) maintain the geometric factor m * (m-1)^{n-1-i} by multiplying once per step by inv(m-1) instead of recomputing pow each time; (3) compute modular inverses 1..k in linear time using the standard recurrence inv[i] = MOD - (MOD//i) * inv[MOD % i] % MOD.

complexity.why: Precomputing modular inverses of 1..k is O(k). Each loop iteration does O(1) arithmetic: update combination factor C(n-1, i), update the power term by multiplying by inv(m-1), and add to the answer. A single pow call is used for (m-1)^(n-1), costing O(log MOD) (log of exponent’s magnitude). Arrays of size k+1 for inverses give O(k) memory usage.

complexity_delta.from: O(n + k log n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(k + log MOD) time, O(k) space
complexity_delta.note: For typical constraints with k up to n (e.g., <= 2e5), this reduces both asymptotic work in the inner loop and constant factors by replacing repeated custom exponentiation and full factorial tables with incremental binomial coefficients and linear-time inverse precomputation.

transformation_steps: Remove unused heavy imports and unnecessary global configuration (e.g., numpy, decimal, queue, sys.setrecursionlimit) to reduce startup overhead.
Replace the custom modular exponentiation function with a single built-in pow for computing (m-1)^(n-1) and another pow for inv(m-1), eliminating the O(k log n) inner-loop exponentiation.
Avoid full factorial and inverse-factorial precomputation up to n; instead, compute C(n-1, i) incrementally: C_{i} = C_{i-1} * (n-i) * inv[i] mod MOD, using that only i up to k is required.
Precompute modular inverses of 1..k in O(k) using the recurrence inv[i] = MOD - (MOD//i) * inv[MOD % i] % MOD (implemented via the var_3 array), so each combination update is O(1).
Maintain the power term m * (m-1)^{n-1-i} iteratively by multiplying by inv(m-1) each iteration instead of calling pow with a decreasing exponent.
Handle edge cases explicitly (e.g., m == 1 and n-1 == k) where the general formula could be degenerate, returning the correct constant answer immediately.
Restructure input handling into a single function that consumes all lines at once, minimizing I/O overhead and allowing easy unit testing.
trigger_signals: Observation of repeated modular exponentiation inside a loop over k (k+1 times) for exponents on the order of n-1-i.
Use of a hand-written binary exponentiation in Python rather than built-in pow(base, exp, mod).
Full factorial / inverse factorial precomputation up to n, while the main sum only needs combinations C(n-1, i) for i <= k.
Presence of many unused imports and global definitions, typical of template code, which suggests non-essential overhead can be removed.
Constraints indicating n, k can be up to ~2e5, making O(k log n) with Python-level loops borderline or too slow in a 1–2 second time limit.
pitfalls: When switching to incremental C(n-1, i), it is easy to get the recurrence wrong; the correct update is C_i = C_{i-1} * (n-i) * inv[i] mod MOD (with C_0 = 1). Off-by-one mistakes in n-i or loop bounds will give wrong answers.
The modular inverse precomputation via inv[i] = MOD - (MOD//i) * inv[MOD % i] % MOD relies on MOD being prime and i < MOD; using it under other conditions is invalid.

Care must be taken with negative intermediate values; always apply % MOD after multiplications. The fast code’s use of max(1, ...) is non-standard and would be incorrect if the expression could ever produce 0, though this should not occur under the stated assumptions.
Edge cases like m = 1 need special handling: powers of (m-1) become 0^something, and the combinatorial interpretation may reduce to a single valid configuration.
If k >= n, the upper bound of the summation should effectively be n-1; ensuring the loop range and combination updates respect this constraint is important to avoid index errors or incorrect counts.
Misinterpreting the formula and omitting the leading factor m (i.e., using only (m-1)^{...} * C(…) ) would undercount configurations by a factor of m.

constraints_guess.notes: Single array of integers, computing a rounded mean and sum of squared deviations. Typical AtCoder/contest-style constraints suggest n up to ~1e5–2e5; both solutions are O(n) and easily fit in time for these ranges.

dominant_ops: Reading n integers into a list, computing their sum once to get the mean, then a single pass over the list to accumulate (a_i - mean)^2.

complexity.why: func_3 reads all n integers into a Python list (O(n) time and space). sum(var_2) is O(n). The for-loop over var_2 computing var_3 += (var_9 - var_5)**2 is another O(n). Constants are low; there is no nested loop or extra asymptotic factor.

bottlenecks.detail: I/O cost is already optimized with sys.stdin.readline; no real bottleneck for typical contest constraints.

Multiple small wrapper functions (func_1, func_3, etc.) and lambdas add a tiny amount of call overhead, but this does not change asymptotic behavior and is negligible relative to O(n) array processing.
Storing the entire list var_2 requires O(n) memory. This is standard for this kind of problem but may be a consideration if n is very large (e.g., >10^7).

FastAudit.core_idea: Inline the logic: read n and the list directly with input(), compute the rounded mean once, and compute the sum of squared deviations using a list comprehension wrapped in sum().

complexity.why: list(map(int, input().split())) is O(n) time and space. sum(var_2) is O(n). The list comprehension [(var_4 - var_3) ** 2 for var_4 in var_2] builds another list of size n in O(n) time and O(n) extra space before summing it. Overall still linear but with a slightly larger constant factor and higher peak memory than the original loop-based accumulation.

complexity_delta.note: Both implementations are linear in n and store the full input list. The modified code introduces an extra O(n) temporary list for squared differences and uses eval(input()), which may be marginally slower and riskier despite identical big-O complexity.

transformation_steps: Replaced sys.stdin.readline()-based helpers with direct input() calls.
Replaced func_1() with int(eval(input())) for reading n.
Replaced func_3()-style input parsing with inline list(map(int, input().split())).
Replaced explicit for-loop accumulation of squared deviations with a list comprehension inside sum().
Removed all unused helper functions and module-level boilerplate, inlining logic at the top level.
trigger_signals: Desire to shorten and inline logic for brevity instead of using multiple helper functions.
Perception that comprehensions and one-liners are more 'Pythonic' or faster than explicit loops.
No actual algorithmic performance issue: the original was already optimal in big-O terms.
pitfalls: Using eval(input()) is unsafe for untrusted input and is slower than int(input()); it should be avoided in competitive programming and production code.
The list comprehension for squared deviations allocates an additional list of size n, increasing peak memory and constant factors versus the original in-place accumulation loop.
Switching from sys.stdin.readline() to input() can slightly degrade I/O performance for very large n, though for typical constraints the difference is minor.

Relying on round(sum(var_2) / var_1) has language- and version-specific rounding behavior (banker’s rounding in Python 3); if the problem expects a specific rounding rule, this must be confirmed against the statement.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic AtCoder-style combinatorics: compute a single binomial coefficient C(n,k) mod 1e9+7 where n ≈ (x+y)/3. Typical constraints have x,y up to ~1e6, so n up to ~2e6.

dominant_ops: factorial_precomputation up to N = (x + y) / 3
modular inverse precomputation for all 1..N via linear recurrence
list growth/appends for three arrays of length N+1

complexity.why: Let N = (x + y) / 3. The loop `for var_10 in range(2, var_3 + 1)` performs O(N) iterations, each doing O(1) modular arithmetic and appending to three lists (factorials, inverse factorials, and modular inverses). The actual binomial evaluation `func_1` is O(1). Memory is dominated by storing three arrays of size Θ(N).

bottlenecks.detail: Three lists var_8 (factorials), var_9 (inverse factorials), var_11 (modular inverses) each of length N+1. For large N (≈10^7) this can consume hundreds of MB and risk MemoryError or cache thrashing.
Python-level loop up to N in the precomputation. If N approaches ~10^7, the O(N) loop with Python arithmetic and list appends becomes a significant runtime cost.
Multiple helper input functions (func_2, func_5, func_6, func_3) are unused in this particular solution; they do not affect asymptotics but add noise and minor import/definition overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial/inverse tables and compute a single binomial coefficient C(n, k) using a multiplicative formula with one modular inverse obtained via fast exponentiation. This trades O(N) memory for O(1) memory and retains linear time in k while keeping exponentiation O(log MOD).

complexity.time: O(N) with much lower constant memory and an O(log MOD) factor
complexity.why: The new code computes coordinates (a,b) such that n = a + b = (x + y) / 3 and k = b. The main cost is `func_1`, which loops `for var_6 in range(var_11)` where var_11 = k, performing O(k) modular multiplications: O(N) in the worst case. It then calls `func_2` to compute var_5^(MOD-2) using binary exponentiation (`func_3`), which takes O(log MOD) steps; log2(1e9+7) ≈ 30, so this is negligible. No arrays of size N are stored, so memory is Θ(1).

complexity_delta.note: Both solutions are linear in N ≈ (x + y) / 3. The main practical gain is removing O(N) memory and the corresponding overhead of large lists; time asymptotics are similar, though constants differ.

transformation_steps: Replace global factorial and inverse factorial precomputation with an on-the-fly multiplicative computation of C(n, k) using the identity C(n,k) = n*(n-1)*...*(n-k+1) / (k*(k-1)*...*1) mod MOD.
Introduce a fast modular exponentiation function (binary exponentiation) to compute modular inverses via Fermat's little theorem: inv(x) = x^(MOD-2) mod MOD.
Derive the transformed coordinates a and b directly: a = (2x - y)/3, b = (-x + 2y)/3, then compute C(a+b, b) when a,b ≥ 0 and (x+y) % 3 == 0.
Remove large auxiliary arrays (factorials, inverse factorials, modular inverses) and the O(N) precomputation loop.
Keep only simple integer variables for running products and a single modular inverse, achieving O(1) extra memory.
trigger_signals: Presence of factorial precomputation up to a problem-dependent N where N can be as large as ~10^6–10^7.
Use of arrays proportional to N for a problem that requires only a single binomial coefficient, not many queries.
Memory-heavy patterns: multiple lists of length N storing factorials, inverse factorials, and intermediate inverses.
Single-query nature of the problem (no need to amortize factorial precomputation across many queries).
pitfalls: The new approach still has O(N) time via the loop in func_1; for extremely large N it may still be too slow in Python. In such cases, using factorial precomputation with PyPy/CPython optimizations or moving critical loops to C (e.g., via C++ or numba) might be necessary.

Recursive implementation of fast exponentiation (func_3) is slightly slower than using Python's built-in pow(base, exp, mod) and, in other contexts, deep recursion could hit recursion limits (not an issue here with depth ~30). Replacing with pow(var_4, var_1 - 2, var_1) is preferable.

Care is needed to ensure that derived coordinates a and b are integers and non-negative; incorrect integer division or sign errors will produce wrong results even if the combinatorial core is correct.
Both methods assume MOD is prime to use Fermat's little theorem or the modular inverse recurrence; changing MOD to a non-prime would invalidate inv computations.

For multiple queries or varying N, the trade-off can flip: the original factorial-table method becomes more efficient when many C(n,k) evaluations are required with shared N, whereas the fast version recomputes products per query.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical for this AtCoder-style problem: two integers N and M, each up to about 1e9. M is factorized by trial division up to sqrt(M). Number of distinct prime factors and total exponent sum are O(log M).

dominant_ops: Trial division factorization of M up to sqrt(M).
For each prime factor, computing a binomial coefficient C(N+e-1, N-1) via a loop of length O(N) with modular inverses using pow in every iteration.

complexity.why: Factorization uses a simple i from 2 upward until i*i > M, giving O(√M). The main cost is func_1: it loops var_6 = N-1 times and calls pow(var_5, MOD-2, MOD) in each iteration. Exponentiation with mod is O(log MOD), so each binomial is O(N log MOD). There are as many binomial evaluations as distinct prime factors of M, which is O(log M) but small in practice. Space holds just the factor counts in a dict.

bottlenecks.detail: func_1(var_7, var_6) uses var_6 = N-1. With N up to ~1e9, this is an impossible loop count; even with N=1e5 it is very slow.
Computes C(N+e-1, N-1) using k = N-1 instead of the symmetric smaller parameter e in C(N+e-1, e). This ignores the key optimization of using min(k, n-k).
Inside the large loop, pow(var_5, MOD-2, MOD) is called for every 1 <= var_5 <= N-1, adding a log MOD factor to an already too-large loop.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the symmetry C(n, k) = C(n, n-k) to express C(N+e-1, N-1) as C(N+e-1, e), where e is the (small) prime exponent from factoring M. Then compute C(n, k) with a multiplicative formula over k = min(k, n-k), avoiding any O(N) loops or per-iteration modular exponentiation. Factorization remains O(√M).

complexity.time: O(√M + sum_over_primes e_i * polylog(C(N+e_i-1, e_i))) ≈ O(√M + sum e_i) in CP terms
complexity.why: Factorization is still trial division up to sqrt(M). For each prime with exponent e, func_1 now uses k = min(e, N-1), which for this problem is just e since N is large and e is small (O(log M)). constraints_guess.notes: Typical for this AtCoder-style problem: input is (N, M) with N up to about 1e5 and M up to about 1e9. Prime factorization cost is O(sqrt(M)) ~ 3e4. Sum of prime exponents of M is small (<= ~30 for M <= 1e9).

Precomputation of factorials up to N+50 with a linear loop
Precomputation of inverse factorials up to N+50 with a linear backward loop after one modular exponentiation

Compute each nCk directly by a short multiplicative loop on integers, keeping the per-prime cost O(e) and eliminating the O(N) factorial precomputation. Factorization is done with an integer-based while-loop up to sqrt(M), which is efficient for M up to about 1e9.

complexity.why: Factorization via while var_7 * var_7 <= var_9 performs trial division up to sqrt(M). The sum of exponents sum_e is bounded by O(log M) and is very small in practice (<= ~30), so the overall complexity is effectively O(sqrt(M)). For each k in [1..n], recomputing var_9 via a full length-n list comprehension (vector addition of exponent arrays)

In the main loop, for each k from 1..n: func_1 has a for-loop of length k (∑k=1..n k = O(n^2)), and each iteration does at most a small constant number of divisions, plus the aggregation var_9 = [...] is O(n) per k. Therefore total is dominated by O(n^2) list operations and function-call overhead, which is too slow in Python for moderate n.

func_1 refactorizes each k from scratch and iterates over all indices < k, causing ∑k O(k) = O(n^2) work just to rebuild exponent vectors.

In func_1, var_5 is updated with division var_5 = var_5 / (var_2 + 1), which in Python 3 is floating-point division; this is both slow and numerically unsafe for large integers (even if logically it divides evenly).

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the definition of the divisor-count function: if n! has prime factorization ∏ p_i^{e_i}, then the number of divisors is ∏ (e_i + 1). Compute n! once via math.factorial, then factor n! by trial division from 2 upward, counting the multiplicity (exponent) of each divisor. Maintain a running product of (e+1) values modulo 1e9+7 without storing full exponent arrays.

complexity.time: ≈O(n) Python-level iterations, with big-integer arithmetic cost roughly O(n^2 log n) bit operations under the hood
complexity.space: O(1) additional Python-space beyond the big integer representing n!
complexity.why: At the Python loop level, the code performs: (1) a single call to math.factorial(n) implemented in optimized C, and (2) one while-loop that increments the trial divisor var_4 from 2 upward while dividing out factors from var_1. The number of iterations is O(max divisor tested) ≈ O(n). Each iteration is a handful of big-int operations. No per-k refactorization or length-n arrays are built, so Python overhead is linear in n rather than quadratic.

complexity_delta.from: O(n^2) Python-level operations + O(n^{3/2}) naive primality test, with repeated allocation of length-n arrays
complexity_delta.to: O(n) Python-level iterations over trial divisors, with heavy work moved into optimized C big-integer routines (overall ≈O(n^2 log n) bit operations, but very fast in practice for the intended n)
complexity_delta.note: The key win is cutting a nested O(n^2) Python loop and repeated factorizations down to a single global factorial computation and one pass of factorization. Even though big-integer arithmetic is non-trivial, the reduction in Python interpreter overhead dominates for realistic constraints.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the required quantity is the number of divisors of n!, which equals the product over its prime exponents plus one: ∏ (e_p(n!) + 1).
Avoid factorizing every integer k ≤ n separately; instead, work with n! directly so that each prime factor is processed only once in aggregate.
Use math.factorial(n) to compute n! efficiently in C rather than building it in Python loops.

Factor n! using a single increasing trial divisor var_4, counting how many times each divisor divides var_1 (the current remaining factor). For each completed exponent e, multiply an accumulator by (e + 1) modulo 1e9+7 instead of storing full exponent arrays.
Eliminate all length-n exponent vectors and per-iteration vector additions, thereby removing the O(n^2) list operations and freeing memory.

A main loop from 1 to n where each iteration calls a function (func_1) that itself loops up to the current index and may perform repeated division.
List comprehensions that build length-n arrays on every iteration of an outer loop over n, indicating O(n^2) list processing.
Re-factorization of each k independently instead of aggregating prime exponents globally.
Use of Python-level loops and lists for operations that could be pushed into math / big-integer primitives implemented in C.

Trial division of n! by all integers starting at 2 is still not optimal asymptotically; using primes only or using exponent formulas e_p(n!) = ∑ floor(n / p^k) would be more scalable. For larger n, this factoring strategy may still time out.
Use of eval(input()) is unsafe and unnecessary; it should be replaced with int(input()) in production code to avoid security vulnerabilities and parsing overhead.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style product-with-overflow problem. n up to about 1e5, values up to ~1e9, threshold 1e18; single test case, no queries.

dominant_ops: Reading n integers from stdin
Single pass multiplying all elements with overflow threshold check

Obfuscated variable names and generic helper lambdas make reasoning and potential further optimization harder, though they do not change runtime complexity.

complexity.why: Still reads n numbers into a list and performs a single linear pass multiplying them. Early exit can reduce runtime on instances where the product exceeds 1e18 early, but worst-case remains O(n). The list of all inputs still requires O(n) memory.

constraints_guess.notes: Tree on up to ~50 nodes. Number of path-queries small (<=~17), enabling 2^Q subset enumeration. Uses bitmasks to represent nodes/edges and precomputes popcount up to 1<<17.

Per-query path computation by walking ancestors up the tree in func_1
2^Q-scale subset enumeration (in the truncated tail) combining per-query path bitmasks
Use of eval(input()) for every integer read

complexity.time: O(N + Q * H + 2^Q * poly(Q, N)) where H is tree height (<= N). With typical constraints N<=50, Q<=17 this is dominated by 2^Q * something but bounded in practice.
complexity.why: Building the tree and DFS are linear in N. func_1 walks up from both endpoints to their LCA; worst-case O(H) per call, done Q times. The later (truncated) part builds arrays of size 1<<Q and 1<<17 and loops from 1 to (1<<17)-1 to precompute popcounts: O(2^17). The main counting logic (not shown) will iterate over all subsets of queries (1..(1<<Q)-1), combining precomputed path bitmasks and using popcount, so O(2^Q * cost_per_subset). Cost_per_subset depends on how they combine bitmasks (likely O(Q) or O(1) per query bitmask).

bottlenecks.detail: Use of eval(input()) for reading integers. eval is much slower than int() and dangerous; repeated usage significantly increases constant factors when inputs are large.

During DFS: `for var_12 in var_9[var_17][::-1]: ... var_9[var_12].remove(var_17)`. Removing from Python lists is O(deg(var_12)) due to linear search; although each edge is removed once, the overhead and cache-unfriendliness increase constant factors versus using a static adjacency structure and parent array.

func_1 climbs ancestors for both endpoints until they meet. Each call can be O(H) where H is tree height; in a skewed tree, H≈N. For small Q this is fine, but it is still Python-level looping on every query.

Precomputation `var_1` (popcount table) over range(1, 1<<17) is O(2^17) regardless of actual Q used. If Q is substantially smaller, this is wasted work. The main DP later (over 1<<var_5) also uses Python-level loops rather than bit operations as much as possible.
Using eval() on arbitrary input is not just slow but unsafe. While not a typical contest concern, it is a red flag in performance-sensitive code.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use faster I/O (sys.stdin.readline), represent edges with indices, compute per-query paths once via BFS that records (parent, edge_id), and then work with sets of edge indices for later subset-combination logic. The main optimization is reducing overhead of tree processing and I/O while keeping the same exponential subset-enumeration structure in Q.

complexity.time: Still O(N + Q * N + 2^Q * poly(Q, N)), but with significantly better constants: each query path is found with a non-modifying BFS, and subsequent subset processing operates on precomputed sets.
complexity.space: O(N + Q * N_edge_repr + 2^Q) ; asymptotically similar to the original, dominated by structures of size 2^Q and storage of per-query paths.
complexity.why: func_3 reads input via buffered sys.stdin.readline, which reduces per-line overhead. func_2 performs BFS on the tree from a source to a target, storing for each node its parent and the edge index used; this is linear in N per query but implemented with simple lists and integer tuples. Paths are then stored as sets of edge indices, which can be unioned in subset-iteration. The subset enumeration (partially shown) loops over masks 1..(1<<Q)-1 and combines the relevant precomputed sets; the overall asymptotic exponent in Q is unchanged but the operations are more primitive and cache-friendly than mutating adjacency lists or walking ancestors repeatedly.

complexity_delta.from: Roughly O(N + Q * H + 2^Q * poly(Q, N)) with slow I/O (eval(input())) and some unnecessary overhead (list.remove in DFS, fixed 2^17 precomputation).
complexity_delta.to: O(N + Q * N + 2^Q * poly(Q, N)) with fast I/O, simpler BFS-based path discovery, and a cleaner representation of paths (sets of edge IDs). Asymptotic order in N and Q remains similar, but constant factors are improved and unnecessary work is reduced.
complexity_delta.note: The key practical gain is from lowering constant factors (fast input, no eval, no list.remove in inner loops) and from cleaner path representation, not from a change in big-O exponent. Given N≈50 and Q≤17, constants are crucial.

transformation_steps: Replace eval(input()) with buffered sys.stdin.readline() and int() conversion for all integer inputs.
Avoid mutating adjacency lists during DFS. Instead, store parent and depth arrays (or use BFS per query as in func_2) on an immutable adjacency structure.
Switch from node-based bitmask construction in func_1 (climbing ancestors each time) to per-query BFS that records parent and edge indices, then reconstruct a path once per query.
Represent paths as collections of edge IDs (sets or bitmasks), so later subset DP combines precomputed structures rather than recomputing paths.
Precompute only as much popcount / helper data as needed for actual Q instead of hardcoding up to 1<<17.
Use iterative loops and primitive operations (bit ops, list access) inside the 2^Q subset enumeration to reduce Python-level overhead.

Mutation of adjacency lists (list.remove) inside a traversal loop, a known performance smell.
Multiple Python-level loops over ranges up to 1<<17 irrespective of actual Q used.
Per-query ancestor-walking in func_1 rather than reusing more structured preprocessing (LCA or BFS parent arrays).
Incomplete and slightly inconsistent tail (e.g., var_1[var_18] = v in the original snippet), hinting at ad-hoc development and opportunities to simplify the DP.
pitfalls: Misusing eval instead of int can both slow programs and introduce security issues; in contests it mainly hurts performance.
Mutating lists while iterating related structures (like removing neighbors during DFS) can be both fragile and slower than using read-only adjacency plus parent arrays.
When Q changes, hardcoded precomputation up to 1<<17 can either do too much work or, if Q>17, break correctness; always tie precomputation bounds to actual parameters.

Relying on operator precedence in expressions like `1 << var_20 - 1` is error-prone and can lead to subtle bugs; clearer forms like `1 << (var_20 - 1)` are safer and often easier for humans to optimize.

In subset DP over 2^Q masks, any non-O(1) per-subset operation (like repeated BFS or costly set operations) can make an otherwise feasible algorithm too slow; ensure per-subset work is minimal and uses precomputed data.

Switching representations (nodes vs edges, sets vs bitmasks) must preserve the combinatorial meaning (e.g., counting edges on paths vs nodes), or you risk silent logical errors even if performance improves.

constraints_guess.notes: Grid size is (N+1) x (N+1); solution uses an explicit N^2 table, so N is likely <= O(500–2000). Number of points/queries (var_2, var_4) can be large (up to ~2e5) where O(1) per query after preprocessing is valuable.

dominant_ops: Building and updating a segment tree array (var_22) via Python loops (func_3 for build, func_9 for point updates).
Performing range queries on the segment tree via func_7 with a while-loop and multiple Python-level operations per queried interval.
Repeated function calls (func_7, func_8) inside hot loops, adding Python call overhead on top of O(log N) tree traversals.
General Python list and index manipulation for the tree rather than contiguous numeric operations.

complexity.time: O((B + U + Q) * log N) in terms of the segment-tree size N (or worse if tree is sized to ~N^2). B: number of initial elements used to build the tree (var_16), U: number of updates (func_9), Q: number of range queries (func_7).
complexity.space: O(N_tree) where N_tree is the segment-tree capacity (typically ~2 * 2^{ceil(log2 base_size)}). If misapplied to a 2D problem via flattening, this could approach O(N^2).
complexity.why: Segment tree operations (build, point update, range query) are logarithmic in the base array length: each query or update touches O(log N) nodes. In pure Python, each node visit involves multiple interpreted operations (indexing, arithmetic, function calls), creating large constant factors. If the underlying logical structure is 2D, and the author tried to encode 2D relationships with a 1D segment tree (or a segment tree per row/column), the effective N_tree can be large relative to the actual constraints, amplifying both time and memory usage.

bottlenecks.detail: A full segment tree is used for what is essentially counting points in axis-aligned ranges that admit a simple prefix-sum solution. As a result, each query becomes O(log N) instead of O(1), with heavy constant factors.

The hot path (func_7 for range queries and func_9 for updates) is dominated by Python-level loops, branching, and function calls (func_8 for combining values). This overhead accumulates when Q and U are large.

Use of global-like variables (var_17, var_22, var_9, var_16) and generic segment tree helpers makes it hard for CPython to optimize or for a human to simplify; each operation requires several pointer dereferences and index calculations.

The original problem is 2D in nature (counting pairs (a, b) within ranges). A 1D segment tree abstraction is not a natural match; if encoded naively (e.g., separate trees or flattened indexing), it leads to unnecessary complexity and overhead compared to a direct 2D prefix-sum array.

Helpers like sys.setrecursionlimit and generic IO wrappers are present but not addressing the main bottleneck. The code carries segment-tree machinery even though a non-recursive, array-based prefix-sum approach is enough.

FastAudit.core_idea: Model the problem as counting points (a, b) on an N x N grid, build a 2D prefix-sum array over the grid, and answer each rectangular query in O(1) time using inclusion–exclusion. Use NumPy to perform the 2D prefix accumulation via vectorized column-wise and row-wise additions implemented in C, eliminating Python-level loops over the inner dimension.

complexity.time: O(N^2 + M + Q), where N = var_3 (grid size), M = var_2 (number of points), and Q = var_4 (number of queries). Building the grid is O(M), computing 2D prefix sums is O(N^2), and each query is O(1).
complexity.space: O(N^2) for the 2D array var_8 of size (N+1) x (N+1).
complexity.why: The grid is explicitly created as a (N+1)x(N+1) integer array. Each of the two prefix-sum passes (first over columns, then over rows) touches every cell once, yielding O(N^2) work. NumPy executes var_8[:, k] += var_8[:, k-1] and var_8[r, :] += var_8[r-1, :] in compiled C loops, so the per-element cost is low. Range queries [l, r] are converted to rectangle sums via a constant number of array accesses and integer operations using the 2D prefix-sum identity: sum(l..r, l..r) = S[r,r] - S[l-1,r] - S[r,l-1] + S[l-1,l-1].

complexity_delta.from: O((B + U + Q) * log N_tree) time with significant Python overhead, plus possible O(N_tree) or worse memory if mis-sized segment trees are used for a 2D structure.
complexity_delta.to: O(N^2 + M + Q) time and O(N^2) memory via a direct 2D prefix-sum over an (N+1)x(N+1) grid, with each query answered in O(1).
complexity_delta.note: Given that N is relatively small (grid-based solution is feasible), the N^2 preprocessing cost is modest and dominated by the benefit of very cheap O(1) queries implemented in vectorized NumPy operations.

transformation_steps: Reinterpret the problem purely as counting occurrences of pairs (a, b) on an N x N grid, eliminating the need for tree-like dynamic structures.
Allocate a 2D list var_8 of size (N+1) x (N+1) initialized to zero; for each input pair (a, b) increment var_8[b][a].
Convert the Python list of lists into a NumPy array to enable fast vectorized arithmetic on contiguous memory.

Compute the 2D prefix sums: first sweep columns (for k from 1 to N, var_8[:, k] += var_8[:, k-1]) to accumulate horizontally, then sweep rows (for r from 1 to N, var_8[r, :] += var_8[r-1, :]) to accumulate vertically.
Replace segment-tree range queries with O(1) prefix-sum rectangle queries using the inclusion–exclusion formula on var_8 for each [l, r] query.
Remove the segment tree machinery (func_3, func_7, func_8, func_9, and associated global-size management) as it is no longer needed.
trigger_signals: The core question is counting points in many axis-aligned ranges, a classic use-case for prefix sums rather than segment trees in low-dimensional settings.
N is small enough that an N^2 array is clearly feasible within memory limits, while the numbers of points and queries can be large, making O(1) query time attractive.
The segment-tree code is structurally complex and heavy with Python-level loops and function calls around each query and update, which is problematic for large Q under CP constraints.
The presence of a simple, static data set (points are inserted once, not dynamically updated over queries) suggests that preprocessing (prefix sums) can replace dynamic data structures.
Micro-benchmark intuition: NumPy vectorized operations tend to outperform Python loops by orders of magnitude for bulk numeric array processing.
pitfalls: Memory growth: The 2D prefix-sum approach is O(N^2) in memory. If N were much larger than expected, this could cause memory issues; the approach relies on N being moderate.

Indexing off-by-one: The grid and prefix sums use 1-based logical indices via a (N+1)x(N+1) array. Care is required to align (a, b) and (l, r) properly and to use [l-1] indices correctly in the inclusion–exclusion formula.

NumPy import and startup cost: On some competitive programming environments, importing NumPy adds overhead; for very small inputs this overhead may dominate, though for large M, N^2, and Q it is usually amortized.

Integer type and overflow: Depending on defaults, NumPy might choose a platform-dependent integer dtype. If counts can exceed 2^31-1, explicitly using a 64-bit dtype (e.g., np.int64) may be necessary to avoid overflow.

Assumed constraints: This optimization assumes no online updates after preprocessing. If future requirements demanded dynamic insertions/deletions of points, the static 2D prefix-sum approach would not apply directly.

Axis order confusion: The code stores counts at var_8[b][a] and queries rectangles [l..r] x [l..r]. Misinterpreting which axis corresponds to which original parameter could lead to incorrect results when modifying or extending the solution.

constraints_guess.notes: Counts nonnegative integer solutions to a1*x + a2*y + a3*z = S with small S (likely S <= 3000, as seen from the hard-coded 3000 in the fast code). Triple-loop-like search over sums; single test case.

dominant_ops: Nested Python for-loops over candidate (x, y) pairs
Integer multiplications/additions to build partial sums
Modulo operation in the innermost loop to test divisibility

complexity.time: O((S / a1) * (S / a2)) ≈ O(S^2) in the worst case (e.g., a1 = a2 = 1, S = var_3)
