Constructed each job as list(map(int, var_5().split()))[::-1], effectively storing (deadline, duration) so that Python's default tuple/list comparison sorts by deadline without an explicit key.
Used sorted(...) directly on the jobs list instead of list.sort with a key lambda, eliminating the overhead of calling a Python function for key extraction on each element.
Simplified the feasibility check loop to early-print 'No' and break on violation, and used a for-else construct to print 'Yes' only if the loop completes without breaking.
trigger_signals: Presence of sort with a simple key function (lambda on a small index) on potentially large lists: var_1.sort(key=lambda var_8: var_8[1]).
Multiple thin wrapper functions around sys.stdin.readline for basic parsing (integers, floats, strings) suggest avoidable per-line overhead for a performance-sensitive problem.
Typical contest context where N can be up to 1e5–2e5 and sorting dominates runtime; reducing per-element overhead in sorting and I/O can be significant.
Dead code and unused helpers (func_1, func_2, func_4, func_5, func_6, func_8) hint that the template isn't tailored to the specific problem, leaving room for cleanup and optimization.
pitfalls: Using eval on raw input (var_6 = int(eval(var_5()))) is unsafe in general and slower than necessary; it should be replaced by int(var_5()) for safety and performance.

Relying on reversing the list ([...][::-1]) to align with default sorting semantics can reduce readability; future maintainers must remember that elements are stored as (deadline, duration) rather than (duration, deadline).
The optimization assumes each line has exactly two integers; if the input format changes, the index order and reverse operation could introduce subtle bugs.

Although removing the sort key lambda is faster in CP settings, it couples data layout to sort criteria; adding a new sort criterion later may require changing the data shape rather than a simple key adjustment.

constraints_guess.notes: Input is a single integer k; output is the k-th positive integer whose adjacent digits differ by at most 1 ("Lunlun" number). Original code pre-generates all such numbers up to length 10, implying k is at most on the order of 2e5.

dominant_ops: Depth-first recursive generation of all valid numbers for every length from 1 to 10 and starting digit 1..9
List append for every generated number to a global vector
Final full sort of all generated numbers
Recursive call overhead for each partial number

complexity.why: Let M be the total count of generated Lunlun numbers up to length 10. DFS explores all valid digit strings of length up to 10 regardless of requested k, doing O(M) work and then sorts the entire list, adding an O(M log M) term. Memory stores all M numbers simultaneously.

bottlenecks.detail: Generates the full set of Lunlun numbers up to length 10 for every run, even when k is much smaller than the total count, leading to unnecessary exploration.
Performs a full sort of all generated numbers just to access the k-th element, instead of generating them directly in sorted order.
Heavy use of recursion for what is essentially a breadth-wise enumeration; recursion depth is moderate (<=10) but incurs overhead on each call.
Uses eval(input()) instead of int(input()), which is slower and unsafe, though not the main performance issue here.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a BFS/queue-based enumeration of Lunlun numbers in increasing order, starting from digits 1..9. Each time, pop the smallest current number, generate its at-most-3 valid extensions by appending last_digit-1, last_digit, last_digit+1, and push them to the queue. Repeat until the k-th number is popped. This produces numbers directly in sorted order and stops as soon as the k-th one is found, avoiding full pre-generation and sorting.

complexity.why: Each Lunlun number up to the k-th is generated once, with O(1) work to pop it and enqueue up to three successors. No global sort is needed because BFS from smaller numbers naturally yields numbers in ascending order. Memory usage is linear in the number of numbers held in the queue/prefix, which is on the order of k for these constraints.

complexity_delta.from: O(M log M) time, O(M) space, where M is the total number of Lunlun numbers up to length 10 (independent of k).
complexity_delta.to: O(k) time, O(k) space, where k is the requested index of the Lunlun number.
complexity_delta.note: The optimized approach generates only the prefix of size k in correct order and avoids sorting, so running time scales with the actual query instead of the maximum search space.

transformation_steps: Replace DFS-based generation over fixed lengths 1..10 with BFS/queue enumeration starting from digits 1..9.
Ensure BFS progresses in increasing numerical order (e.g., by using a queue initialized with 1..9 and always appending larger successors).
Stop the enumeration as soon as the k-th Lunlun number is dequeued instead of generating the entire set.
Remove the global list accumulation and final sort; the queue order itself represents sorted order.
Replace eval(input()) with faster and safer int(input()) (or equivalent fast input helper).
trigger_signals: The original code constructs all valid numbers up to a fixed max length regardless of the requested index k.
Presence of a final sort even though only the k-th smallest value is needed.
Recursive DFS over a bounded depth where a BFS naturally matches the problem’s ordering requirement.
Constraints on k are much smaller than the total generatable space, making full pre-generation wasteful.
pitfalls: Ensuring BFS actually yields numbers in strictly increasing order; using a plain queue seeded with 1..9 and expanding them in FIFO order with monotone growth is crucial.
Handling edge cases for last_digit-1 and last_digit+1 properly (must stay within 0..9).
Avoiding off-by-one errors in counting the k-th dequeued number (1-indexed vs 0-indexed).
Not accidentally exploding memory by pushing successors beyond what is needed; enumeration must stop when the k-th number is obtained.

constraints_guess.notes: Single query. Presence of sqrt(N) optimization in fast code suggests N may be as large as 1e12; an O(N) scan would TLE while O(sqrt(N)) is acceptable.

dominant_ops: Single descending loop over up to ~var_2/var_1 values, performing a modulo (var_2 % var_4) each iteration.

complexity.time: O(var_2 / var_1) in general; in the worst case (var_1 = 1) this is O(var_2).
complexity.why: var_3 = int(var_2 / var_1); func_1 iterates for var_4 in range(var_3 + 1, 0, -1), so loop length is ~var_3+1 ≈ var_2/var_1. Each iteration does a constant amount of work (one modulo and a comparison), and no extra data structures are allocated.

bottlenecks.detail: When var_1 is small (especially var_1 = 1), var_3 ≈ var_2 and the descending loop may run up to O(var_2) iterations. For large var_2 (e.g., up to 1e12), this linear scan is far too slow.
The algorithm treats divisor search as a brute-force scan on a large interval, instead of leveraging the fact that divisors come in complementary pairs around sqrt(var_2) or sqrt(var_1).

FastAudit.core_idea: Use divisor pair enumeration up to sqrt(N) (here N = var_1) to find a suitable divisor instead of linearly scanning up to N or N/M. For each factor var_3 of var_1 found in [2, sqrt(var_1)], check both var_3 and its complementary factor var_1 // var_3 against the constraint involving var_2, keeping the maximum valid divisor. This reduces the search space from O(N) to O(sqrt(N)).

complexity.why: The loop runs var_3 from 2 to int(var_1**0.5) + 1. For each var_3, only a constant number of operations are performed: a few modulo, comparison, and max assignments. Divisor checks exploit that every divisor d of var_1 has a partner var_1 / d, so all candidates can be examined using only O(sqrt(var_1)) iterations.

complexity_delta.from: O(var_2 / var_1) time, which in worst case is O(var_2) when var_1 is small (e.g., 1); O(1) space.
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(var_1)) time; O(1) space.
complexity_delta.note: Under typical constraints with var_1 (the factored number) up to around 1e12, the worst-case number of iterations decreases from about 1e12 to about 1e6, which is easily feasible within time limits.

transformation_steps: Reinterpret the goal as a divisor search problem on a single integer (var_1) with a constraint involving the other parameter (var_2).
Replace the linear scan up to ~var_2/var_1 with an enumeration of candidate divisors var_3 in the range [2, sqrt(var_1)].
For each var_3 that divides var_1, consider both var_3 and its complementary divisor var_1 // var_3 as candidates and apply the constraint checks (>= var_2).
Initialize the best answer appropriately (1, or var_1 if var_2 == 1) and update it via max() as better candidates are found.
Remove function call overhead and redundant modulus operations associated with scanning a large range.
trigger_signals: The slow code uses a for-loop whose bound var_3 is derived as var_2 / var_1, meaning in the worst case (var_1 small) the loop length is proportional to var_2.
No usage of sqrt or divisor-pair logic in a problem that clearly revolves around divisibility, indicating a naive divisor search.

The potential problem domain (-style, integer constraints) and the presence of a simple modulo test in a wide loop suggest a standard pattern where divisor enumeration via sqrt optimization is expected.
Early exit (break) does not meaningfully help in the worst case because the required divisor might be small relative to the range.
pitfalls: Off-by-one and direction issues when converting from a descending range on candidate values to a sqrt-based ascending range on potential divisors; it is easy to skip the boundary cases or mishandle 1.
Forgetting to check both the divisor and its complementary pair can lead to missing the true maximum or minimum satisfying divisor.
Handling edge cases such as var_2 == 1 (where the answer is trivially var_1) must be explicit; relying on the general loop can be incorrect or more complex.
Overflows or precision issues if using floating-point sqrt for very large integers; must ensure the loop upper bound is correctly computed as int(var_1**0.5) + 1.
Misinterpreting which variable represents the number to factor (var_1 or var_2) versus the threshold/constraint can lead to O(sqrt(wrong_variable)) behavior and incorrect results.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic 3-choice per day DP (AtCoder-style 'Vacation'). N is large (1e5–2e5 range) so O(N) or O(N log N) is fine, but O(N^2) is not. Only transitions from day i-1 to i are needed.

dominant_ops: For each of N-1 transitions, iterate over 3 states and update 2 target states via max and list indexing; plus reading and storing all N lines of input and maintaining an N x 3 DP table.

complexity.why: The DP loop runs (N-1) * 3 iterations with O(1) work per iteration, giving O(N) time. However, it stores all activity values in var_2 (size N x 3) and all DP states in var_4 (also N x 3), so memory grows linearly with N.

bottlenecks.detail: Stores both the entire input matrix var_2 (N x 3) and the full DP table var_4 (N x 3) even though only the previous day’s DP row is needed at any step.
Uses a 2D list var_4 with Python list-of-lists overhead and repeated var_4[var_5 + 1][*] indexing inside loops, increasing constant factors.
Reads and keeps all N days in var_2 before performing the DP; this prevents streaming and increases peak memory.
Inner loop over var_6 in range(3) with if var_6 == 0/1/2 branches encodes a fixed 3x3 minus diagonal transition pattern in a verbose way, adding Python-level branching overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Stream the input day by day and keep only two 1D DP arrays of length 3 (previous and current day), performing all transitions in-place and discarding older data. This converts the DP from an N x 3 table to a rolling 3-element state.

complexity.why: For each of N days, the code runs a 3x3 nested loop (9 iterations) with constant work per iteration, so time is linear in N. It maintains only two lists of length 3 (var_5 and var_9) and the current input triple, so extra memory usage is constant with respect to N.

complexity_delta.from: time O(N), space O(N) with full N x 3 DP table and stored input
complexity_delta.to: time O(N), space O(1) with rolling 3-element DP and streaming input
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time remains linear, but constant factors improve slightly, and space is reduced from Θ(N) to Θ(1), eliminating memory pressure and improving cache behavior.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the DP transition for day i depends only on DP values from day i-1, not on earlier days.
Replace the N x 3 DP table var_4 with two 1D arrays of size 3: one for the previous day (var_5) and one for the current day (var_9).
Change input handling from pre-reading and storing all days in var_2 to reading each day's 3 integers on the fly inside the main loop.

Encode transitions generically with a double loop over previous state var_8 and current state var_7, skipping the same-state transition (var_7 != var_8), instead of hard-coded if var_6 == 0/1/2 branches.
After computing var_9 for the current day, assign var_5 = var_9 and reinitialize var_9 to [0] * 3 to prepare for the next iteration.
Compute the final answer as max over the last DP array (var_5) instead of accessing var_4[N-1].
trigger_signals: DP table indexed as var_4[day][state] with day going up to N and only transitions from day-1 to day are used.
Input values stored for all N steps (var_2 list of length N) even though they are consumed sequentially and never revisited.
A fixed small state dimension (3 activities) suggesting that only O(1) state per step is fundamentally required.
Memory footprint proportional to N (two N x 3 structures) in Python, which can be significant for N around 1e5–2e5.
Hard-coded transitions between a small number of states, which are natural candidates for rolling-array DP.
pitfalls: When using rolling arrays, mistakenly aliasing lists can corrupt DP: e.g., var_5 = var_9; var_9[:] = [0,0,0] would also zero var_5; the code avoids this by reassigning var_9 = [0] * 3, not mutating in place.
Forgetting to reset the current DP array (var_9) each day would cause transitions to accumulate from earlier days incorrectly.
Mis-implementing the transition condition var_7 != var_8 could allow same-activity repetitions on consecutive days, changing the problem’s constraints.
Off-by-one errors when converting from a full DP table (indexing day i and i+1) to a rolling scheme, particularly in initializing the first day and computing the final answer.

Continuing to use eval(input()) instead of int(input()) introduces unnecessary overhead and potential security risks in more general settings; though not the main performance issue, it is a code-quality concern.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AOJ-style problem: multiple test cases (terminated by 0 0), N relatively small (<=200) but potentially many test cases. Brute-force O(N^3) may be borderline in Python, O(N^2) is very safe.

dominant_ops: Triple-nested for-loops over indices (var_6, var_7, var_8)
Array indexing into var_2 inside the innermost loop
Integer additions and comparisons in innermost loop
Appending to list var_1 for each valid triplet

complexity.why: var_6 ranges from n-1 down to 2, var_7 from var_6-1 down to 1, and var_8 from var_7-1 down to 0, giving Θ(n^3) triplets in the worst case. Each iteration does constant work: 3 array accesses, 1 addition of 3 numbers, and up to 2 comparisons plus an append. var_2 is a list of size n, so space is O(n). The result list var_1 can be at most O(n^3) in theory but in this problem it effectively stores at most O(number_of_triplets_with_given_sum), and because it only stores the sum value repeatedly, it is upper-bounded by the number of valid triplets; still, the dominating auxiliary structure is var_2 of size n and temporary loop variables.

bottlenecks.detail: Triple nested loops over n (O(n^3) combinations) dominate runtime. Even with an early break when var_5 < var_3, the asymptotic order is cubic in n.
The innermost loop over var_8 is doing a linear scan to find c such that a[i] + a[j] + a[k] == target, instead of solving directly for the third value.
Repeated indexing into var_2 for var_2[var_6], var_2[var_7], var_2[var_8] inside the tightest loop adds overhead on top of the cubic iteration count.

The list var_1 collects the sum value var_5 for each valid triplet, only to take len(var_1) at the end. Storing all hits is unnecessary; a simple counter would reduce memory usage and slight overhead from list appends.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the structure of the problem (choosing 3 distinct integers in [1..n] that sum to X) by iterating over the first two values a and b (with a < b) and solving directly for the third value c = X - a - b. Instead of a third loop, check with constant-time inequalities that c is within bounds and greater than b (to ensure distinctness and ordering). This eliminates the innermost loop and reduces time complexity from O(n^3) to O(n^2).

complexity.why: The fast version uses two nested loops: var_1 (a) from 1 to n-2 and var_2 (b) from a+1 to n-1, giving Θ(n^2) pairs (a, b). For each pair, it computes (implicitly) c = var_4 - var_1 - var_2 and checks the condition `var_2 < var_4 - var_1 - var_2 <= var_3`, which is O(1) per pair. No extra arrays proportional to n are used; the comprehension materializes a list of 1s whose length equals the number of valid triplets, but this could be replaced with a simple counter, and the algorithm itself does not require more than constant additional space.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(n^3), Space: O(n)
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(n^2), Space: O(1) (or O(k) where k is number of solutions in the list-comprehension version)
complexity_delta.note: The main gain is removing the innermost loop by algebraically determining the third element of the triplet. This reduces the iteration space from Θ(n^3) triplets to Θ(n^2) (a, b) pairs, with constant-time checks for c.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the original code is enumerating triplets (i, j, k) that correspond to distinct integers 1..n whose sum equals a target value.
Replace the array var_2 = [1, 2, ..., n] and index-based sums var_2[var_6] + var_2[var_7] + var_2[var_8] with direct number variables a, b, c in the ranges 1..n, respecting ordering a < b < c.

Change the structure from three nested loops over indices (i, j, k) to two nested loops over a and b (the first two numbers in the triplet), enforcing a < b via loop bounds: for a in range(1, n-1), for b in range(a+1, n).
Derive the third element c via the equation c = target - a - b instead of scanning a third loop. This removes the innermost O(n) loop and replaces it with O(1) arithmetic.

Impose constraints on c using inequalities instead of enumeration: check that b < c <= n (to ensure distinctness and ordered triplets) and implicitly c >= 1 (already satisfied if target and ranges are valid). This is encoded as `if var_2 < var_4 - var_1 - var_2 <= var_3`.

Remove the list var_1 of all matching sums and replace it with a direct count of valid triplets. The provided fast_code uses a list comprehension of constant elements and then takes its length; in a further micro-optimization, this could be changed to increment an integer counter instead of building a list.

Simplify input handling: directly read (n, x) as integers via map. Swap the naming so that var_3 represents n and var_4 represents the target sum in the optimized version, and keep the termination condition based on both being zero.
trigger_signals: Empirical runtime grows very quickly with increasing n, characteristic of O(n^3) behavior (e.g., runtime roughly multiplies by ~8 when n doubles).
Profiling or code inspection shows that the vast majority of execution time is spent inside the innermost loop over var_8, with repeated additions and comparisons.
The existence of an early break in the innermost loop that still does not prevent timeouts for larger inputs suggests that the underlying complexity is still cubic.

Conceptual recognition that the problem is counting triplets (a, b, c) with a linear constraint a + b + c = X and simple bounds, which usually admits an O(n^2) solution by fixing two variables and solving for the third.
Multiple test cases with repeated N up to the upper limit exacerbate the cubic behavior, making an O(n^3) algorithm unsuitable in a competitive programming or online judge context.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors in loop boundaries when moving from index-based loops (0..n-1) to direct value loops (1..n). For example, the fast_code uses `range(1, var_3 - 1)` for a and `range(var_1 + 1, var_3)` for b; incorrect boundaries would miss valid triplets or count invalid ones.

Incorrect inequality for the third value c. It must satisfy b < c <= n and implicitly c >= 1; encoding this as a chained inequality must be done carefully. Using `<=` instead of `<` between b and c would allow duplicated or unordered triplets.

Maintaining the one-to-one correspondence between (a, b, c) triplets in the original version (enforced by three nested loops with strictly decreasing indices) and the (a, b, c) generated via two loops plus inequality conditions. Failing to enforce strict ordering can result in overcounting permutations of the same combination.

Misinterpreting input variable roles when refactoring. In the original code, (var_4, var_3) correspond to (n, target); in the optimized code, the order in the input line is reversed (var_3, var_4) but logically they represent (n, target). Mixing them up will lead to incorrect ranges and conditions.

List comprehension in the fast_code builds a list of length equal to the number of solutions, which is generally small but in worst-case could still be non-trivial. Using a counter instead of materializing a list avoids unnecessary memory use and overhead, which could matter on tighter constraints.

Assuming that the early break optimization in the triple loop is sufficient. While it prunes part of the search space, the worst-case pattern (e.g., when the target sum is near the upper bound) still leads to Θ(n^3) iterations, so it's not a reliable optimization for larger n.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer N converted to a 1-indexed base-26 (a-z) string, similar to Excel columns but lowercase. Typical AtCoder constraints put N up to about 1e12–1e16.

dominant_ops: Repeated pow(26, k) computations
While-loop subtracting blocks of size 26^k from N to determine string length
Per-character pow(26, k) and division/mod operations
String concatenation in a loop

complexity.why: Let L be the length of the resulting string (~log_26 N). The length-determining while-loop runs O(L) iterations. The for-loop also runs O(L) iterations, but each iteration performs string concatenation on an increasingly long string, leading to O(1 + 2 + ... + L) = O(L^2) character copies. Arithmetic (pow/div/mod) is O(L) but dominated by string concatenation.

bottlenecks.detail: The code manually finds the number of digits by repeatedly subtracting powers of 26: while var_1 > 26^k: var_1 -= 26^k; k++. This is an O(L) process that can be avoided by direct base conversion via division/mod operations.

pow(26, var_4) and pow(26, var_3 - 1) are recomputed on each iteration. Although pow is optimized, repeated exponentiation adds non-trivial constant factors compared to repeated multiplication or simple division/mod by 26.
Building var_2 via var_2 += ... in the loop causes O(L^2) behavior due to repeated reallocation and copying of strings as they grow.

Separate handling of the last character (if var_3 > 1 else ...) and repeated state updates var_1 %= pow(26, var_3 - 1) increase code complexity and risk of off-by-one/logic bugs without providing asymptotic benefits.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use direct 1-indexed base-26 conversion by repeatedly decrementing N, taking N % 26 as the next character, and dividing N //= 26, then reversing the accumulated string. This eliminates the need to precompute the string length or subtract powers of 26.

complexity.why: The loop runs once per character (L ≈ log_26 N), with O(1) arithmetic per iteration (decrement, mod 26, div 26). String concatenation var_1 += char in Python is still O(L^2) in the worst case due to repeated reallocation, and final reversal var_1[::-1] is O(L). Arithmetic cost is negligible compared to string building. Space is O(L) for the result string.

complexity_delta.from: O(L^2) time, O(L) space (with extra overhead from redundant exponentiation and length-detection loop)
complexity_delta.to: O(L^2) time, O(L) space (same asymptotics but with fewer operations and simpler arithmetic)
complexity_delta.note: Both versions are asymptotically O(L^2) in Python due to string concatenation, but the fast version removes an O(L) pre-processing loop and many pow(26, k) calls, substantially improving constant factors and clarity.

transformation_steps: Replace the initial while-loop that subtracts powers of 26 to determine the number of characters with a direct base-conversion loop that runs until N becomes zero.
Eliminate repeated pow(26, k) calls and replace them with simple modulo and integer division by 26 in each iteration.
Shift from a most-significant-digit-first construction (and complex index handling) to a least-significant-digit-first construction followed by a final string reversal.
Remove the conditional handling of the final character (if var_3 > 1 else ...) by using a uniform per-iteration formula: decrement N, take N % 26 to select a letter, divide N //= 26.
Retain overall string-building pattern but with cleaner state updates, reducing arithmetic and control-flow overhead.
trigger_signals: Manual length detection using a loop that subtracts powers of 26 from N rather than directly converting via division/mod.
Multiple pow(26, k) calls inside loops, indicating repeated exponentiation that can be replaced by simpler base operations.
Complex index-based logic to pick digits (separate branches for last digit) instead of a uniform conversion rule.
Presence of both a pre-processing loop and a main loop where the pre-processing loop only serves to compute the digit length.
pitfalls: 1-indexed base-26 conversion is subtle: you must decrement N before taking N % 26, otherwise mappings for boundaries like 26, 27, 52, etc. will be off by one.
For very large N, Python string concatenation in a loop can be a performance concern; in more extreme constraints it would be better to accumulate characters in a list and ''.join(list) at the end.
The final result must be reversed when constructing from least-significant digit to most-significant digit; forgetting the reversal produces the string in reverse order.
Using eval(input()) is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; int(input()) is sufficient and safer, though this is more of a security/robustness issue than a performance one under contest conditions.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical scheduling/deadline feasibility problem; O(n log n) with Python and fast I/O implies n is likely up to around 1e5–2e5.

dominant_ops: Reading n lines of input with input() and eval()
Sorting the list of tasks: O(n log n)
Single pass over the sorted tasks to accumulate time and compare with deadlines

complexity.why: All implementations build an array of n tasks and sort it; the subsequent feasibility check is a linear O(n) pass. The asymptotic cost is therefore dominated by sorting.

bottlenecks.detail: Uses input() in a loop (func_4 and func_1), which is significantly slower than sys.stdin.readline for large n.
Wraps input reading in several layers of function calls (func_4 -> eval(input()) -> int(...), func_1 -> list(map(int, input().split()))), adding call overhead on every line.
Uses eval(input()) just to parse integers. eval is slower than direct int() parsing and is unsafe; it also prevents certain optimizations by the interpreter.
Imports math, itertools, bisect, copy, deque, Counter, Decimal and defines multiple unused helper functions. This increases startup time and code size without benefit for this problem.
Reassigns names like func_2 from function to list, reducing clarity and making it harder to see the tight loop’s true operations when profiling.

FastAudit.core_idea: Same greedy algorithm: read all (duration, deadline) pairs, sort tasks by deadline (then duration as tiebreaker), and accumulate total duration; if at any step cumulative_time > current_deadline, answer is "No", otherwise "Yes". The optimization is in using sys.stdin.readline and minimizing per-line overhead.

complexity.why: Still builds and sorts an n-element list of tasks; sorting dominates at O(n log n). The cumulative check over the sorted list is O(n). Memory holds the task list plus a few scalars, so O(n) space.

complexity_delta.from: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged; the improvement is in constant factors, especially I/O and per-iteration overhead.

transformation_steps: Replaced high-overhead input() calls with sys.stdin.readline, reducing latency per line of input.
Eliminated multiple wrapper functions (func_1, func_4) around input/parsing, cutting function-call overhead in the tight input loop.
Built the list of tasks using a list comprehension over sys.stdin.readline rather than append in a Python for loop, which is generally faster in CP scenarios.
Removed unused libraries and helper utilities (math, itertools, bisect, copy, deque, Counter, Decimal, lcm helper, etc.), reducing import/startup overhead and code noise.
Simplified the scheduling loop to iterate directly over the list of tasks (for var_2, var_3 in var_1) instead of indexing through an intermediate array, slightly reducing Python-level overhead.
trigger_signals: Uses input() inside a loop that runs up to n times, which is a known bottleneck for large n in Python.
Multiple layers of small helper functions wrapping input() and parsing, which add function-call overhead with no algorithmic benefit.
Large number of unused imports and utilities suggesting template code carried over from other problems, often a source of unnecessary overhead.
Same high-level algorithm and complexity as typical editorial solutions, implying that any TLE is due to constant factors (I/O, call overhead) rather than asymptotic inefficiency.
pitfalls: Both versions still use eval for parsing the first integer; eval is slower than int() and unsafe if input is not trusted. For performance and security, prefer int(sys.stdin.readline()) or int(input()).
Changing the sort order incorrectly would break correctness; tasks must be ordered by deadline (and optionally by duration as tiebreaker) for the greedy check to be valid.
Be careful not to introduce extra data structures (e.g., priority queues) unnecessarily; they can increase constant factors without improving complexity for this simple feasibility check.
If further micro-optimizing, ensure early exits (printing "No" and exiting) are preserved, as they can significantly reduce runtime on negative instances with early violations.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style brute-force over integer x minimizing sum (a_i - x)^2; input N small (~<=100), each a_i small (e.g., |a_i|<=100), so enumerating x from min(a) to max(a) is acceptable.

dominant_ops: Outer loop over candidate centers x: range(max(var_2) - min(var_2) + 1) ~ O(R) where R = max(a) - min(a).
Inside loop, repeated Python built-in min(var_2) each iteration: O(N) per iteration on a numpy array via Python iteration.
Vectorized numpy expression (var_2 - var_5) ** 2 creating temporary arrays and np.sum for each candidate x: O(N) numeric work plus allocation per iteration.

complexity.why: Let N = number of elements, R = max(a) - min(a) + 1. The for-loop iterates R times. In each iteration: (1) min(var_2) scans N elements in Python; (2) (var_2 - var_5)**2 and np.sum perform O(N) numeric operations and allocate temporaries. So each iteration is O(N), giving O(N * R) total time. Storing the input as a numpy array costs O(N) space; each iteration also uses O(N) temporary space for the broadcasted difference and squared array, but these are short-lived. Asymptotically O(N) extra space.

bottlenecks.detail: min(var_2) is recomputed inside the loop for every candidate x, costing O(N) Python-level work per iteration. min and max could be computed once before the loop.

Using Python's min() on a numpy array iterates element-by-element in Python rather than using np.min, leading to high overhead compared to precomputing min and max via np.min/np.max or converting to a Python list.
Each iteration allocates new numpy temporaries for (var_2 - var_5) and the squared array before np.sum, which is expensive when repeated many times even if N is modest.

On many competitive programming judges, numpy has significant import and per-call overhead and may not be optimized, making repeated vectorized calls slower than simple Python integer loops for small N.

Both the slow_code and fast_code use the same O(N * R) brute-force over all candidate x. No mathematical simplification (e.g., using the mean of a_i) is applied, so if R is large the approach would still be slow regardless of micro-optimizations.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid numpy and Python-level min() inside the main loop by operating on a sorted Python list: enumerate candidate x from the first to the last element, and compute the sum of squared differences using plain integer arithmetic in a nested loop. This keeps the same brute-force algorithm but with lower constant factors and no heavy numpy overhead.

complexity.why: Sorting var_2 costs O(N log N). The outer loop runs over x in [var_2[0], var_2[N-1]], which has length R = max(a) - min(a) + 1. For each candidate x, the inner loop sums (var_6 - var_4)^2 over N elements: O(N) work. Thus the main computation is O(N * R). For typical constraints (small N and small value range), N * R dominates sorting and is acceptable. The list of values takes O(N) space and the algorithm uses O(1) additional space inside the loops (no large temporaries per iteration).

from.note: Original uses numpy with repeated Python min(var_2) and per-iteration temporary arrays; theoretical complexity O(N * R) time and O(N) space, but with high constant factors and overhead.

to.note: Modified uses a sorted Python list and plain integer loops; same O(N * R) brute-force structure but substantially cheaper per iteration, plus a one-time O(N log N) sort that is negligible for small N.

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time and space complexities remain effectively the same; improvements come from removing per-iteration redundant min() calls and numpy overhead. Sorting is not strictly necessary for correctness but bounds the x-range using constant-time index lookups instead of recomputing min/max.

transformation_steps: Replace numpy array with plain Python list: var_2 = np.array(...) -> var_2 = list(map(int, input().split())). This removes numpy overhead and Python-numpy conversion costs.
Avoid repeated min(var_2) and max(var_2) calls: instead of computing min(var_2) inside the loop, sort var_2 once and use var_2[0] and var_2[var_1-1] as fixed bounds for the candidate x range.
Replace vectorized numpy operations with explicit integer loops: np.sum((var_2 - var_5) ** 2) -> inner loop accumulating (var_6 - var_4) ** 2 in a scalar variable var_5.
Add a special-case early exit for N == 1: if var_1 == 1: print(0); exit(). This avoids unnecessary loop overhead when there is only one element, where the optimal sum of squares is trivially 0.
Minor structural changes: use min(var_5, var_3) in pure Python instead of numpy types, reducing type conversion and interop overhead.
trigger_signals: Use of numpy in a tight Python for-loop where N and the range R are small indicates vectorization benefits are limited but overhead is high.
Repeated min(var_2) inside the loop over candidate x reveals avoidable O(N * R) Python-level work on a numpy container.
Competitive programming context (single test, tight time limits, no need for full numpy power) favors simple integer loops over heavy libraries.

Small integer domains and brute-force search over a short range suggest that algorithmic complexity is already acceptable and that micro-optimizations and removing library overhead will likely suffice.
pitfalls: Sorting var_2 is not necessary to compute the minimum and maximum; a single pass or built-in min/max on the list would give O(N) instead of O(N log N). For typical small N this is irrelevant, but for larger N the extra log N factor could matter.

Both versions still run in O(N * R) time; if the value range R becomes large (e.g., up to 1e9), this approach will time out regardless of numpy usage. A mathematically optimal solution would use the mean of a_i (testing floor/ceil) in O(N) time.
Using eval(input()) is unnecessary and unsafe for general code, though it does not dominate performance here. int(input()) should be preferred for robustness.

Integer overflow is not an issue in Python due to arbitrary-precision ints, but in languages with fixed-width integers, summing (a_i - x)^2 may require 64-bit types; porting this logic must consider that.

The fast_code assumes that the input list var_2 is non-empty when accessing var_2[0] and var_2[var_1 - 1]. If constraints allowed N = 0, this would raise an error; the problem likely guarantees N >= 1.

constraints_guess.notes: Matches typical constraints of AtCoder ABC 153 E: H (HP) up to ~1e4, N (number of spells/attacks) up to ~1e2; damage per attack up to ~1e4. Objective: minimum total cost to reduce HP to 0 or below using unbounded number of attacks.

dominant_ops: Nested DP loops over spells (var_6 in range(var_9)) and HP (var_7 in range(var_5)), performing multiple 2D list accesses and a 3-way min() per cell update.

complexity.why: The DP table var_4 has dimensions (var_9 + 1) x (var_5 + 1). Each of the (N * H) cells is visited once and updated via constant-time operations, giving O(NH) time and O(NH) memory.

bottlenecks.detail: Using a 2D DP table var_4[(N+1) x (H+1)] for an unbounded knapsack–style problem where a 1D DP over damage/HP is sufficient. This increases memory footprint and constant factors for each transition.

Each transition computes min() of up to three expressions: var_4[var_6][var_7 + 1], var_4[var_6][var_7 + 1 - wt] + cost, var_4[var_6 + 1][var_7 + 1 - wt] + cost. This implies multiple Python-level list index operations and additions per state.
2D Python lists incur extra indirection and can reduce cache friendliness compared to a flat 1D array. Every DP read/write has to traverse two indices, adding overhead.
Building var_4 via a nested list comprehension allocates (N+1)*(H+1) large-INF values up front, which is relatively costly in Python for N≈100 and H≈1e4.

The 2D DP is initialized with all entries = INF (10**8) and never explicitly sets a base case like var_4[0][0] = 0. While this is mainly a correctness issue, attempts to fix it often further complicate the transitions and add overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a 1D DP over total damage dealt, modeling an unbounded knapsack where dp[x] is the minimum cost to deal exactly x damage. Iterate damage from 0 to H-1 and relax transitions for each attack, then take the minimum cost among dp[H..H+max_damage]. This removes the redundant DP dimension and reduces per-state operations.

complexity.why: The DP array var_8 has size var_3 + var_2 + 1 ≈ H + 1e4. The outer loop runs over var_9 in range(var_3) (≈H) and the inner loop over all N attacks. Each state update is O(1), yielding O(NH) time. Space is linear in the DP length, which is O(H + max_damage), significantly smaller than O(NH) when N is up to ~1e2.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(N * H), Space: O(N * H)
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(N * H), Space: O(H + max_damage)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time complexity remains O(NH), but the constant factors are much lower: fewer memory accesses, a smaller DP array, simpler transitions, and early skipping of unreachable states. Space improves from roughly N*H states to about H + max_damage states.

transformation_steps: Recognize the problem as an unbounded knapsack over cumulative damage/HP where the order of attacks does not matter and each attack may be used unlimited times.
Replace the 2D DP dp[item_index][hp] with a 1D DP dp[damage] that stores the minimum cost to achieve a given damage total.
Choose a safe DP size: H + max_damage, so that overshooting the target HP is allowed and the result is the minimum cost among all dp[damage] with damage >= H.
Iterate damage from low to high so that each attack can be used multiple times (unbounded knapsack property) without requiring a second DP dimension.

Simplify each transition to a single comparison: if dp[cur_damage] + cost < dp[cur_damage + damage], then update dp[cur_damage + damage]. This removes the 3-way min() and multiple DP table accesses from the slow version.
Add a reachability check (skip states where dp[cur_damage] is INF) to avoid propagating from impossible states, reducing unnecessary work in the outer loop.
Use a flat Python list for the DP array instead of a list-of-lists matrix to reduce memory usage, avoid an extra level of indirection, and improve cache locality.
trigger_signals: A DP solution uses a (items+1) x (capacity+1) table for a problem where items can be used unlimited times and only the total capacity (HP/damage) matters, indicating an unbounded knapsack pattern.

Nested loops over number_of_items and capacity with transitions that reference both dp[i][w] and dp[i][w - weight_i], or both dp[i][w] and dp[i+1][w - weight_i], suggesting that a 1D rolling or flat DP can encode the same information.
High memory usage from DP tables approaching ~1e6 cells or more in Python, which is workable but expensive, especially when each cell update performs several operations.
Use of min() over multiple DP expressions in every inner-loop iteration, which often can be simplified to a single comparison in an optimized DP formulation.
Problem statement or editorial hints that the solution is an unbounded knapsack or simple cost-minimization over a one-dimensional state (HP, capacity, sum, etc.).
pitfalls: When switching from 2D to 1D DP in an unbounded knapsack, the iteration order matters: iterating the capacity/damage dimension in the wrong direction can change the meaning from unbounded to 0/1 knapsack or lead to under-counting. Here, iterating damage increasing is correct for unbounded use of attacks.
The DP array must be sized to allow overshooting the target HP (H + max_damage). If sized only to H, optimal solutions that exceed H slightly may be missed.

INF values and reachability checks must be handled carefully: only propagate transitions from states dp[x] that are not INF; otherwise, arithmetic on INF can mask logical errors or add unnecessary work.
Be careful with indices when converting from HP-based to damage-based DP; off-by-one errors around dp[0] and the inclusive range of min(dp[H:]) are common and can silently produce wrong answers.

If constraints are tighter than assumed (e.g., H or N significantly larger), even O(NH) may become borderline in Python, and further optimizations (pruning, faster I/O, or a different algorithmic approach) might be necessary.

constraints_guess.notes: Inputs: (var_4 or var_2) ~ up to 1e5, (var_1) up to about 1e9 so that trial division up to sqrt(var_1) is feasible. Binomial arguments reach up to var_4 + max_exponent - 1; max_exponent is small (<= ~30 if var_1 <= 1e9), hence factorial size ~1e5+O(1) is sufficient.

dominant_ops: Trial division prime factorization up to sqrt(var_1)
Precomputation of factorials and inverse factorials up to a fixed limit (2 * 10^5)
Modular multiplications for binomial coefficients for each prime factor

complexity.why: Let X = var_1 (the number to factor) and F = 2 * 10^5 (fixed factorial precompute size). func_1 does trial division up to sqrt(X), giving O(sqrt(X)) divisions in worst case. Factorial and inverse factorial arrays are filled with two linear passes over size F, costing O(F) time and O(F) memory regardless of the actual input sizes. The final loop over prime factors is O(k) where k is the number of distinct primes (<= log X), negligible compared to sqrt(X) and F.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorial and inverse factorial arrays var_10 and var_12 are always allocated and filled up to 2 * 10^5 elements, even when var_4 (M) and exponents are much smaller, leading to unnecessary O(F) work.
Two arrays of size 2 * 10^5 (var_10 and var_12) are stored, using more memory than necessary for many inputs.
Each factorial entry requires a modular multiplication; at size 2 * 10^5 this is a large fixed constant cost for a single test case.
Using collections.defaultdict(int) for prime exponents introduces some overhead versus a simple list or direct accumulation into a list, though this is minor compared to the factorial precompute.

FastAudit.core_idea: Resize the factorial and inverse factorial precomputation to depend on the input parameter var_2 (M) plus a small margin for exponents, instead of a fixed global upper bound; keep the same mathematical approach (prime factorization of var_1 and stars-and-bars binomial coefficients) but avoid over-allocating and over-computing factorial tables.

complexity.why: Prime factorization remains O(sqrt(X)) using trial division. Let M = var_2 and E = max exponent of primes in var_1 (~<= 30 for typical constraints). Fast code allocates factorial/inverse factorial arrays of length L = M + 50, which is O(M + E). Filling factorials and inverse factorials is O(L). Computing the final product over prime exponents is O(k), negligible compared to O(L). Thus total time is O(sqrt(X) + M + E) and memory is O(M + E). Asymptotically similar to the slow version but with the linear term tied to input size rather than a fixed ceiling.

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(X) + F) time, O(F) space with F = 2 * 10^5 fixed
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(X) + (M + E)) time, O(M + E) space with M = first input (var_2) and E = max prime exponent
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic form remains linear in the precomputation size, but the previous fixed F is replaced by a value derived from inputs (M + small constant), reducing constant factors and memory usage for smaller M. For worst-case M near 1e5, time is comparable; gains are substantial when M is much smaller than F.

transformation_steps: Replace the global fixed factorial size var_2 = 2 * 10^5 with a size that scales with the input M (var_2 in the fast code), specifically arrays of length var_2 + 50 to cover all needed n in C(n, k).
Inline the prime factorization logic instead of using func_1 with defaultdict, collecting only the exponents into a list (var_5) rather than a dict keyed by prime values.

Use a single factorial array var_7 and a single inverse factorial array var_6 sized to var_2 + 50, computing factorials in a forward pass and inverse factorials via one modular inverse at the end and a backward pass.

Compute binomial coefficients using precomputed factorials/inverse factorials in the loop over exponents, directly using the formula C(M + e - 1, e) with M = var_2 and e = exponent, matching the original combinatorial logic but with smaller tables.
Remove minor overheads such as defaultdict and .items() iteration in favor of simple list operations, and avoid recomputing sqrt bounds repeatedly.
trigger_signals: Presence of a large fixed-size factorial precomputation (2 * 10^5) in a single-testcase problem where actual needed maximum n depends on input M.
Memory footprint and initialization time dominated by factorial tables rather than the problem's intrinsic operations.
Tight time limits combined with a noticeable constant cost from always initializing 2 * 10^5 factorials even for small M.
Observation that the binomial argument upper bounds are directly expressible as M + max_exponent - 1, suggesting that a dynamic sizing strategy is safe.
pitfalls: Ensuring factorial table size: The fast code uses length var_2 + 50. This relies on the assumption that max exponent E of any prime in var_1 is < 50. If constraints allowed var_1 to be very large (e.g., > 10^15), E could exceed this margin, causing out-of-bounds accesses when computing C(M + E - 1, E). The margin must be chosen based on guaranteed constraints.

Float-based sqrt: Using var_1 ** (1 / 2) instead of math.sqrt may introduce off-by-one issues due to floating-point rounding for very large var_1. The extra +2 in the loop bound mitigates this, but for significantly larger constraints, it is safer to use integer math or math.isqrt.

Correctness of binomial indexing: When resizing factorial arrays, it is crucial that they cover all n used in C(n, k) = C(M + e - 1, e). Any miscalculation of the necessary maximum n leads to incorrect results or index errors.

Inverse factorial generation: The fast method computes only one modular inverse (for the last factorial) and fills others backward. Any off-by-one or index misalignment in this loop silently corrupts all binomial coefficients.

Sorting exponents: The fast code sorts the exponent list var_5. This is not needed for correctness and costs O(k log k). Though k is small, this is an unnecessary step and should not be generalized to larger k without noting the overhead.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder B-level: n up to ~100, |a_i| up to a few hundred. Objective: choose integer P minimizing sum_i (a_i - P)^2; optimal P is floor/ceil of mean.

dominant_ops: For each candidate integer P in range(100), compute a full vectorized squared-distance sum over all elements using NumPy.

complexity.time: O(C * n) with C=100 (effectively O(n) but with a large constant from NumPy ops in a loop)
complexity.why: Input is stored as a NumPy array (O(n)). Each of the 100 iterations performs (var_5 - scalar)**2 and np.sum(...), both scanning the entire array (O(n) per iteration).

bottlenecks.detail: Brute-force scanning all P in range(100) ignores the known property that the minimizer of sum (x_i - P)^2 lies at floor/ceil of the mean; this adds a factor 100 more passes over the data.
Using NumPy inside a Python loop incurs repeated array operations and function call overhead; for small n, plain Python arithmetic in a single pass is typically faster.
var_6 = var_5 inside the loop does nothing but is executed 100 times; minor, but unnecessary.
Using eval(input()) instead of int(input()) is slower and unsafe, though not the main performance issue.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical fact that the sum of squared deviations is minimized at the mean; for integer P, the optimum lies between floor(mean) and ceil(mean). Compute both candidates directly and take the minimum in a single pass over the array.

complexity.why: Two passes to compute sum(var_1) (can be reduced to one) and one pass to accumulate squared differences for two fixed P values. No extra per-candidate scanning beyond this single pass.

complexity_delta.from: O(100 * n) time, O(n) space (NumPy-based brute force over candidate P)
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space (direct computation for at most two optimal P values)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both are O(n), but removing the factor-100 loop and NumPy overhead yields a significant constant-factor speedup, especially for small to medium n.

transformation_steps: Recognize the objective function as sum_i (a_i - P)^2, which is a convex quadratic in P with minimum at the mean of the data.
Use the fact that for integer P, it suffices to test P = floor(mean) and P = ceil(mean).
Replace the brute-force loop over range(100) with direct computation of these two candidate P values via integer division of the total sum by n.
Iterate over the list once, accumulating squared differences to both candidate P values in simple Python integers.
Remove NumPy entirely, avoiding repeated vectorized operations and associated overhead.
Replace eval(input()) with int(input()) for safer and slightly faster input parsing.
trigger_signals: Loop over a fixed, arbitrary range (range(100)) with full-array computation each iteration.
Use of heavy numerical library (NumPy) for very small vectors and simple arithmetic.
Objective is a quadratic function in P, suggesting a closed-form or near-closed-form minimizer.
Constraints and typical problem patterns (sum of squared deviations) hint at mean-based solutions instead of scanning many candidates.
pitfalls: Forgetting that the minimizer must be checked at both floor(mean) and ceil(mean); using only floor or only round can be wrong when mean is fractional.
Recomputing sum(var_1) multiple times instead of storing it; minor but unnecessary overhead.
Using NumPy with default dtypes could cause overflow in other languages or environments with fixed-width integers; Python ints avoid this but keeping pure Python helps maintain correctness.
Retaining eval(input()) in performance-sensitive or security-sensitive contexts; should be replaced with int(input()).

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder single-testcase array problem: N up to ~1e5–2e5 integers; all processing must be O(N) with small constants.

dominant_ops: One pass to compute sum(var_2) over N elements
One pass to accumulate squared deviations (var_3 += (var_9 - var_5) ** 2) over N elements
Input parsing: reading N and a list of N ints into memory

complexity.why: The code stores all N integers in a list (func_3) and iterates over that list a constant number of times (two passes: one in sum(var_2), one in the for-loop), so time is linear in N and extra space is linear for the array.

bottlenecks.detail: The mean is computed as var_5 = round(sum(var_2) / var_1), which uses float division (/) and round(). Floating-point operations are slower than pure integer arithmetic and can introduce subtle rounding issues for large values, even though asymptotic complexity remains O(N).

Input is wrapped through multiple tiny helper functions (func_1, func_3, etc.) and lambdas. This adds some function-call overhead compared to direct use of built-ins. The cost is constant-factor only and small, but present.

Only one candidate center var_5 (rounded mean) is evaluated. For integer minimization of sum (x_i - a)^2, both floor(mean) and ceil(mean) should be considered. This is primarily a correctness/robustness issue rather than a performance one, but it also prevents pruning to the true optimum if round() chooses the farther neighbor in .5 cases.

FastAudit.core_idea: Compute the integer mean via floor division and also the next integer (floor+1), evaluate the objective sum (x_i - a)^2 for both candidates using pure integer arithmetic, and output the smaller value. This exploits the fact that the optimal integer a lies at floor(mean) or ceil(mean).

complexity.why: The code reads N integers into a list and computes sum(var_1) twice (two O(N) passes) plus one O(N) loop for squared deviations, resulting in O(N) time overall. The list of N integers dominates memory, so extra space is O(N).

complexity_delta.from: O(N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: Both implementations perform a constant number of passes over the N-element array and store it entirely. The primary changes are in arithmetic style (float+round vs integer floor/ceil) and the number of passes, which only affect constant factors and correctness, not asymptotic complexity.

transformation_steps: Changed input style: from sys.stdin.readline() wrappers to direct input()/eval(input()). This simplifies the code but does not improve asymptotic performance; direct input() can be slightly slower than buffered sys.stdin in very tight constraints.
Replaced floating-point mean computation var_5 = round(sum(var_2) / var_1) with integer candidates var_6 = sum(var_1) // var_2 and var_7 = var_6 + 1, avoiding floating-point arithmetic.

Extended the candidate search: instead of evaluating sum of squares at a single rounded mean, the fast_code evaluates the objective at two neighboring integers (floor and floor+1) and takes the minimum, which matches the known minimizer set for sum (x_i - a)^2 over integer a.

Switched arithmetic inside the loop from (var_9 - var_5) ** 2 to abs(var_3 - var_6) ** 2 and abs(var_3 - var_7) ** 2. The abs() call is not strictly necessary before squaring and adds a tiny constant-factor overhead, but keeps data strictly non-negative before exponentiation.

Increased the number of passes over the data: slow_code performs two passes (one for sum, one for squared deviations), whereas fast_code performs three (two sums plus one squared-deviation loop). This is still O(N) but with a slightly larger constant factor.
trigger_signals: Recognition that minimizing sum (x_i - a)^2 over integer a is linked to the mean, and that for integer a the optimum lies in {floor(mean), ceil(mean)}, indicating that evaluating only round(mean) can miss the optimum.
Concern about using floating-point division and round() for a problem that can be solved entirely with integer arithmetic for better precision and usually better performance.

Desire to express the mathematical insight explicitly by checking both neighboring integer centers rather than relying on round()’s behavior, which depends on ties-to-even semantics and floating-point representation.
Refactoring away from over-abstracted IO helpers in favor of more straightforward code, even at the potential cost of minor IO performance differences.
pitfalls: In the slow_code, using sum(var_2) / var_1 with round() can lead to incorrect centers for .5 cases due to round-ties-to-even semantics and possible floating-point error; this is a semantic pitfall more than a performance one.
In the fast_code, sum(var_1) is computed twice; for very large N this slightly increases runtime. A micro-optimization would be to store the sum once and reuse it.
The fast_code uses eval(input()) to read an integer, which is unnecessary and potentially unsafe in other contexts; int(input()) is sufficient and typically preferred.
Adding abs() before squaring, as in the fast_code, is redundant because squaring removes the sign; this adds a minor constant overhead per element.

Switching IO models (sys.stdin vs input()) under very tight time limits can matter: sys.stdin.readline() is often faster than input(), so the so-called fast_code may actually be marginally slower on extremely large inputs despite better arithmetic choices.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical greedy scheduling/deadline problem: N jobs, each with (duration, deadline). Likely N up to 1e5–2e5, durations/deadlines up to about 1e9. Needs O(N log N) solution in Python.

dominant_ops: Reading N job pairs from stdin into a list
Sorting the list of N jobs by deadline (second element)
Single linear pass over the sorted jobs to accumulate durations and compare against deadlines

complexity.why: The sort of N pairs dominates with O(N log N). Input storage and the subsequent single pass are O(N).

bottlenecks.detail: No early termination in the main loop: even after detecting var_5 > var_4 (schedule impossible), the loop continues over all remaining jobs, only flipping a flag. This wastes work when the schedule becomes impossible early.
Uses a boolean flag (var_3) plus a final conditional print instead of breaking immediately or exiting. Each iteration after failure does an unnecessary comparison and addition.

Uses sys.stdin.readline with a thin wrapper (func_3). Per-line function call adds small overhead, but raw readline is slightly faster than built-in input(). Overall IO cost is not dominant compared to sorting, but the extra wrapper is unnecessary.

Defines multiple helper functions (func_1, func_2, func_4, func_5, func_6, func_8) that are never used. This does not significantly affect runtime in competitive settings but introduces noise and potential confusion without benefit.

FastAudit.core_idea: Greedy scheduling: sort all jobs by deadline, maintain cumulative processing time, and verify at each step that the cumulative time does not exceed the current job’s deadline. Immediately terminate the program on the first violation.

complexity.time: O(N log N) worst-case, with better best/average-case when a violation occurs early due to immediate exit
complexity.why: The sorting step remains O(N log N). The linear scan is O(N) in the worst case (all jobs feasible or violation only near the end), but may terminate early as soon as a deadline is missed. Space usage is for storing N pairs.

delta_type: micro-optimization / control-flow improvement with unchanged asymptotic complexity

complexity_delta.from: O(N log N) time, O(N) space; always scans all N jobs in the final pass even after failure.
complexity_delta.to: O(N log N) time, O(N) space; linear pass short-circuits on first failure, improving best/average-case constants while keeping worst-case the same.
complexity_delta.note: The core algorithm (sort by deadline + cumulative sum check) is identical. The key practical improvement is early termination on infeasibility.

transformation_steps: Preserve the main algorithm: read all (duration, deadline) pairs, sort by deadline, accumulate durations and compare with deadlines.
Replace the boolean-flag pattern with an immediate exit on first failure. In the fast code, upon detecting var_2 > var_5[var_4][1], it prints 'No' and calls exit(), stopping further iterations.
Avoid a final conditional check on a flag; instead, rely on early program termination for the negative case and a single 'Yes' print after successfully processing all jobs.
Use direct tuple unpacking in the loop (for var_2, var_4 in var_1) rather than indexing inside the loop, reducing per-iteration overhead slightly.
Simplify the surrounding code by not carrying unused utility functions for various input types, focusing only on what is required for this problem.
trigger_signals: Observed TLE or tight runtime margins in Python when N is large (e.g., 1e5–2e5) and many test cases are infeasible early but the implementation still iterates over all jobs.
Profiling indicates that a significant portion of time is spent in the main feasibility-check loop even after infeasibility has already been established.
Code reviews showing unnecessary use of flags and lack of early termination in critical loops.
Online judge or benchmarking environment with strict time limits where constant-factor improvements in hot loops materially affect pass/fail outcomes.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical for this AtCoder-style problem (ABC110 D: Factorization): N up to 1e5, M up to ~1e9. Single test case. M factorization cost O(sqrt(M)) is acceptable; main challenge is handling combinations C(N+e-1, e) for multiple primes efficiently under modulo 1e9+7.

dominant_ops: Trial division factorization up to sqrt(M) in a for-loop with early break
For each prime exponent, computing C(N+e-1, N-1) via a multiplicative loop from 1 to N-1
Inside that loop, repeated modular exponentiation pow(i, MOD-2, MOD) to get modular inverses

complexity.why: Factorization uses a loop var_5 from 2 upward and breaks once var_5*var_5 > var_1, giving O(sqrt(M)). After factorization there are P distinct primes. For each exponent, func_1(var_7, var_6) loops var_6 = N-1 times; each iteration performs one pow(var_5, MOD-2, MOD), which is O(log MOD). Thus combination computation is O(N * log MOD) per prime, overall O(P * N * log MOD). Space holds only the exponents map of size P.

bottlenecks.detail: Combination C(n, k) is recomputed from scratch with a loop up to k = N-1 for every prime exponent. This scales linearly with N per prime factor.
Inside the inner loop, pow(i, MOD-2, MOD) is called for every i from 1 to N-1 and for every prime. Modular exponentiation is relatively heavy; this leads to O(P * N * log MOD) work just for inverses.

Factorials and inverse factorials of 0..(N+maxExponent) are not precomputed; instead, the binomial coefficient is built via multiplicative formula repeatedly, missing an O(1) per-query combination using factorials.

FastAudit.core_idea: Precompute factorials and inverse factorials up to N + max_possible_exponent once, then evaluate each combination C(N+e-1, e) in O(1) time using nCr = fact[n] * inv_fact[r] * inv_fact[n-r] mod. This avoids per-iteration modular exponentiation and large per-combination loops.

complexity.why: Factorization remains O(sqrt(M)), now with explicit sqrt bound. Factorials and inverse factorials are precomputed in O(N + K) where K≈50 is a safety margin for the maximum exponent; this includes one pow for inv_fact[last] and a linear pass to fill the rest. Each prime exponent then costs O(1) to compute C(N+e-1, e). Thus overall time is dominated by O(sqrt(M) + N). Arrays of length N+50 dominate the space usage, giving O(N) memory.

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(M) + P * N * log MOD)
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + N + P)
complexity_delta.note: The key improvement is replacing O(N * log MOD) per prime for combinations with O(1) via factorial / inverse-factorial precomputation, and doing only one modular exponentiation (for inverse factorial of the largest index) instead of O(P * N) such calls.

transformation_steps: Keep the same mathematical formulation: the answer is the product over primes p dividing M of C(N + exponent(p) - 1, exponent(p)) (or equivalently C(N + exponent(p) - 1, N - 1)).

Preserve trial division factorization but change the loop upper bound from 'for i in range(2, M+1) with break when i*i > M' to 'for i in range(2, int(sqrt(M)) + 2)', making the sqrt bound explicit and slightly reducing iteration overhead.
Collect the prime exponents into a list (var_5) rather than a dict, since only the exponents are needed for the combinatorial product.
Introduce global factorial array var_7 of size (N + constant_margin) initialized with var_7[0] = 1 and filled by var_7[i+1] = var_7[i] * (i+1) % MOD, precomputing n! values.

Introduce inverse factorial array var_6 of the same size. Compute var_6[-1] as pow(var_7[-1], MOD-2, MOD) once (modular inverse of the largest factorial), then fill the rest backwards via var_6[i-1] = var_6[i] * i % MOD, which uses only modular multiplications.
Use the identity C(a, b) = fact[a] * inv_fact[b] * inv_fact[a-b] % MOD to compute each C(N+e-1, e) in constant time during the final product loop, avoiding inner loops and repeated pow calls.
Sort the exponent list (var_5.sort()). This does not affect correctness or complexity significantly but is harmless and may help in some variants; it is not performance-critical here.

Use of pow(x, MOD-2, MOD) inside a frequently executed inner loop. pow with modular exponentiation is O(log MOD) and relatively heavy.
Computations of binomial coefficients via iterative multiplicative formula instead of factorial-based precomputation, especially when the same N is used repeatedly.
Single-test-case competitive programming problem with tight time limits and large N, which usually calls for O(N) precomputations rather than O(N log MOD) per query.

constraints_guess.notes: Two integers N,M; N is the count of factors, M is the value to factor. Likely M <= 1e9–1e12 (trial division factorization still used), N up to around 2e5 (since factorials are precomputed up to N+100). Single test case.

dominant_ops: Prime factorization of M by trial division up to sqrt(M)
Heavy use of Python big integers via math.factorial and large intermediate products
Repeated binomial-like computation using plain integer arithmetic and division

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + N * cost_bigint_mult) where factorial(N-1) and large intermediate products dominate; factorization itself is O(sqrt(M)).
complexity.space: O(number_of_prime_factors(M)) for the factor map; but effective space is dominated by the size of huge big integers created by factorial and intermediate products.
complexity.why: func_1 factors M in O(sqrt(M)). The main loop computes combinations using plain integer arithmetic: factorial(N-1) (unused) and products of size roughly on the order of binomial(N+e-1, e). Because it does not reduce modulo until the very end, Python integers grow to thousands of bits, so each multiplication/division becomes increasingly expensive. This big-integer growth, plus an entirely redundant factorial(N-1), dominates runtime.

bottlenecks.detail: Intermediate products var_3 and var_11 are computed without modulo reduction, so their magnitude grows roughly like the product of multiple large binomial coefficients. Each subsequent multiplication/division operates on very large integers, causing superlinear overhead.
factorial(var_2 - 1) is computed and stored in var_5 but never used. For large N this is a very expensive, completely unnecessary computation.

Each C(N+e-1, e) is built via a loop of length e multiplying descending integers and then dividing by factorial(e). Even though e is small, doing this with full-precision integers (not modulo) and repeated factorial calls is much slower than using precomputed factorials and modular inverses.
Modulo 1e9+7 is only applied once at the very end: print((var_11 % (10**9 + 7))). This maximizes the size of intermediate integers and slows all arithmetic.
Uses input().split for reading; not a major issue here, but slower than buffered sys.stdin in tight settings.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use number-theoretic precomputation: factor M as before, but compute each binomial coefficient C(N+e-1, e) modulo MOD using precomputed factorials and modular inverse factorials. Precompute factorials, modular inverses, and inverse factorials up to N+max_exponent once via linear DP (func_3). Then evaluate all combinations with O(1) modular multiplications and keep all intermediates reduced modulo 1e9+7.

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + N) where sqrt(M) is for prime factorization and N (actually N + small margin) is for precomputing factorials and inverses; each binomial is O(1) after precomputation.
complexity.space: O(N) for the factorial, inverse, and inverse-factorial tables (var_8, var_10, var_7). Additional space for factorization is O(number_of_prime_factors(M)).
complexity.why: func_3 builds factorials and modular inverses up to N+100 in a single linear pass, using the recurrence inv[i] = -inv[MOD % i] * (MOD // i) mod MOD. Once these tables are available, each binomial C(n,k) is computed as fact[n] * invfact[k] * invfact[n-k] mod MOD with constant-time operations. All arithmetic stays within 32–64-bit words due to modulo, eliminating big-int blowup. Factorization cost remains O(sqrt(M)), which is acceptable for typical M constraints.

complexity_delta.from: Effectively O(sqrt(M) + N * cost_bigint_mult + cost_of_redundant_factorial) with very large constant factors due to big-integer arithmetic and unused factorial computation.
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + N) with only modular integer operations and O(N) extra space for precomputed tables.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic loop counts may look similar at first glance, but the shift from arbitrary-precision factorial computations and large intermediates to fixed-width modular arithmetic produces a massive constant-factor improvement and removes the redundant factorial(N-1) completely.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the required quantity is the product over prime exponents e of the combinations C(N + e - 1, e) modulo a prime MOD (1e9+7).
Eliminate the unused computation factorial(N-1), which was a major redundant cost in the slow version.

Replace per-query factorial and combinational arithmetic using Python big integers with a one-time precomputation of factorials fact[i] and modular inverses inv[i], invfact[i] up to N + margin via func_3.
Implement modular inverses using the linear-time recurrence inv[i] = -inv[MOD % i] * (MOD // i) mod MOD to avoid repeated exponentiation.
Compute each C(n,k) as fact[n] * invfact[k] * invfact[n-k] % MOD using only O(1) modular multiplications, avoiding divisions and extra factorial calls.
Apply modulo reduction after each multiplication when aggregating the product of combinations to keep all intermediate values within machine word size.
Switch to faster buffered I/O (sys.stdin.readline) for robustness under tighter time limits.
trigger_signals: Use of math.factorial on large arguments when the final answer is required modulo a prime (e.g., 1e9+7).
Combinatorial formulas implemented using plain integer division (// factorial(k)) rather than modular inverses.
Intermediate integer values (products, factorials) that grow extremely large, followed by a modulo at the very end.
Redundant heavy computations, such as factorial(N-1) being computed but never used in downstream logic.
Patterns involving distributing prime exponents among N factors (stars-and-bars), which naturally map to binomial coefficients modulo a prime.
pitfalls: The precomputation bound in func_3 must be at least max(N + max_exponent) for all combinations C(N+e-1, e); underestimating this bound leads to index errors or incorrect results.
The modular inverse recurrence used assumes MOD is prime; changing MOD to a non-prime would break the inverse computation and all combinations.
Off-by-one errors in factorial arrays (e.g., starting from 0 vs 1) can silently corrupt binomial coefficients; keeping consistent definitions (fact[0] = 1) is essential.
For extremely large N (e.g., > 2e6), O(N) precomputation may become too slow or memory-heavy; additional optimizations or alternative combinatorial methods might be needed.

Mixing up arguments in func_1 (n,k,MOD) or computing C(k,n) instead of C(n,k) can pass small tests but fail on larger cases; carefully maintain the combinatorial meaning (here, distributing each prime exponent e across N factors).

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style constraints for this pattern: N up to ~2e5, M up to ~1e9. Need combinations C(n, k) mod 1e9+7 for n up to about N + (sum of prime exponents of M) (~N+60). Single query.

dominant_ops: Global precomputation of factorial, modular inverse, and inverse-factorial arrays up to a fixed MAX_N = 2e5+10
Trial-division prime factorization of M up to sqrt(M)
Evaluation of O(#prime_factors) binomial coefficients and modular multiplications

complexity.why: Factorials/inverses are filled with a single forward pass up to MAX_N (2e5), which is linear. Prime factorization via trial division from 2 up to sqrt(M) is O(sqrt(M)). The loop over exponents is bounded by the number of distinct prime factors of M, which is very small (<= ~9 for M <= 1e9), so its cost is negligible compared to the linear precomputation.

bottlenecks.detail: var_6, var_7, and var_9 are sized to 2e5+10 regardless of the input N, so for small N most of this O(2e5) work and memory is unnecessary.
Prime factorization stores exponents in a defaultdict(int). While asymptotically fine, it has higher constant-factor overhead than a simple list of (prime, exponent) pairs.
Uses the built-in input() which is slower than buffered sys.stdin methods in tight time limits, though this is a minor factor compared to the O(MAX_N) precomputation.

FastAudit.core_idea: Precompute factorials and inverse factorials only up to the strictly necessary bound (N + small margin) using dynamic append on global arrays, use a lightweight list-based representation for prime factors, and rely on buffered I/O. This keeps the same asymptotic complexity but reduces constant factors and wasted work when N is smaller than the global MAX_N in the slow version.

complexity.why: func_3 precomputes factorial and inverse factorial values up to N+100 via a single pass, which is O(N). func_4 performs trial-division factorization up to sqrt(M), same as in the slow version. The products over factors are again over a tiny set. Overall, the work scales linearly with the actual N instead of a fixed upper bound (2e5), reducing time when N << 2e5 while keeping the same big-O form.

complexity_delta.from: Theta(MAX_N + sqrt(M)) with MAX_N fixed at ~2e5 regardless of N
complexity_delta.to: Theta(N + sqrt(M)) using N+100 as the precomputation bound
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic class remains linear in the relevant precomputation bound plus sqrt(M), but the bound is tightened from a global constant 2e5 to the actual N (plus a small margin). For inputs with N much smaller than 2e5, this is a significant speedup; for N near 2e5, runtimes are comparable.

transformation_steps: Replace fixed-size precomputation (arrays of length 2e5+10) with a precomputation sized to N+100 (func_3 in the fast code builds var_8, var_10, var_7 only up to that bound).
Switch from defaultdict-based factor-count storage to a simple list of (prime, exponent) pairs in func_4, reducing hash-table overhead.
Use buffered I/O via sys.stdin.readline instead of input(), shaving overhead on reading the single line of input.

Compute nCr directly via precomputed factorials and inverse factorials with minimal range checks, avoiding extra wrapper indirection (slow code’s func_2 calls func_1; fast code calls func_1 directly with appropriate parameters).

Observed runtime scales roughly with 2e5 regardless of N, suggesting over-provisioned precomputation.
Tight time limits where constant factors in Python loops and dictionary operations matter.
Memory pressure or concern about global arrays sized to a high upper bound without necessity.
