When capping k to n-1, failure to do so or incorrect capping can include invalid terms (e.g., C(n-1, i) with i > n-1), which are mathematically zero but may not be treated as such by the recurrence if not properly constrained.

Transitioning from factorial-based to multiplicative binomial computation changes numerical stability and overflow patterns; all intermediate multiplications must be taken modulo MOD to avoid large integer growth and performance degradation.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder coprimality problem: N up to ~1e5, each A[i] up to ~1e6. Single test case, offline.

dominant_ops: Building smallest-prime-factor array up to a fixed bound 10**6 using a sieve-like process.
For each input value, repeatedly dividing by its smallest prime factor (factorization using SPF).
Maintaining and querying Python sets to track prime factors seen per-number and globally.

complexity.time: O(M log log M + n log A)
complexity.why: Let n be the number of inputs, A = max(a_i), and M = 10^6 (hard-coded). func_2 creates an SPF-like array up to M using a sieve: this is O(M log log M) time and O(M) space. func_3 then factors each a_i via repeated division by SPF, O(log a_i) per value in the worst case, totalling O(n log A). Set operations (membership/insert) add O(k log P) where k is number of distinct prime factors and P is size of global set, but k is small and dominated by the sieve+factorization cost.

bottlenecks.detail: func_2 always builds SPF up to 10**6 regardless of the actual maximum value in the input. If max(a_i) << 10**6, most of this work is wasted.
Each number is factorized via a while-loop with repeated division and Python-level control flow and set lookups. This adds noticeable constant-factor overhead for large n.

Tracking prime factors with Python sets (per-number set var_8 and global set var_9) involves hashing and dynamic resizing; this is heavier than simple integer counting arrays when only frequency of multiples is needed.

SPF array accesses are cache-friendly, but the logic repeatedly interleaves random-access into var_2 with set operations in var_8/var_9, hurting locality compared to a single structured sieve+count pass.

FastAudit.core_idea: Instead of factorizing each number individually, build a sieve up to max(a_i), identify primes, and for each prime count how many input numbers are multiples of that prime. If any prime divides at least two numbers, the array is not pairwise coprime. Then use a single global gcd check (from the problem editorial, though not included verbatim here) to decide setwise vs not coprime. This transforms per-number factorization and per-prime-set bookkeeping into a structured sieve plus counting multiples.

complexity.why: Let V = max(a_i). A sieve-like pass marks composites in var_3 for all integers up to V. As in the Eratosthenes sieve, the total number of composite-marking operations is sum_{k=2..V} V/k = O(V log log V). Counting occurrences of each value uses O(n). For each prime p, counting elements divisible by p via stepping in multiples adds sum_{p} V/p ≈ O(V log log V) operations. Overall, O(V log log V + n) time and O(V) memory for the maps used as frequency arrays.

complexity_delta.from: O(M log log M + n log A) time, O(M) space with fixed M = 10^6 and per-value factorization + set tracking.
complexity_delta.to: O(V log log V + n) time, O(V) space with V = max(a_i), using a sieve and multiple-counting over primes.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both precomputations are similar when V ≈ M, but the fast version adapts to the actual max value and removes per-number factorization and set overhead, giving a large constant-factor improvement, especially when max(a_i) << 10^6 or n is large.

transformation_steps: Replace hard-coded sieve bound 10**6 with a dynamic bound V = max(2, max(a_i)) to avoid unnecessary work.
Switch from computing smallest prime factor for every number to a boolean is_prime-like sieve (var_3) to identify primes only.
Abandon per-number factorization and per-number prime-factor sets; instead, build a global frequency map var_2 of input values.
For each prime p (keys in var_4), accumulate count of how many input numbers are multiples of p by iterating j = p, 2p, 3p, ... up to V and summing var_2[j].
Determine pairwise coprimality by checking if the maximum multiple-count over all primes is at most 1 (var_11 < 2).
Determine setwise vs not coprime via comparing var_11 to n (or equivalently via gcd over all values), mapping to 'pairwise', 'setwise', or 'not coprime' outputs.
Use contiguous integer-keyed containers (dicts here, though lists would be faster) as frequency tables instead of many Python set operations on prime factors.
trigger_signals: Presence of a large fixed bound (10**6) for sieve precomputation regardless of input maximum.
Per-element while-loop factorization inside the main input-processing loop, indicating potentially high overhead for large n.
Use of Python sets for every number plus a global set, with membership checks in a tight loop.
context with tight time limits and typical constraints n up to 1e5 and A up to 1e6, suggesting need for linear or near-linear passes without heavy Python-level loops.
pitfalls: Using Python dicts instead of lists for the sieve and frequency tables (var_3, var_4, var_2) introduces unnecessary hash overhead; lists indexed by integers would be faster and more memory-efficient.
The sieve must be carefully implemented to avoid off-by-one errors on bounds (inclusive handling of V).

The logic that classifies 'setwise' vs 'not' coprime must ensure that the gcd over all numbers is computed correctly; relying only on prime multiple counts without gcd can be subtle if implemented differently.
If V is much larger than necessary (e.g., due to input errors or extreme constraints), both approaches can still be heavy; memory usage grows linearly with V.
Early return logic in the original code (when a repeated prime factor is detected) is replaced by a global pass; while usually faster, it loses the ability to short-circuit on very early conflicts.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case with two integers; typical AtCoder-style constraints suggest |A|,|B| up to about 1e9 or similar 32/64-bit range.

dominant_ops: Process import-time initialization of many heavy standard-library modules (math, itertools, heapq, collections, re, random, etc.)
Define several helper functions (func_1..func_5) that are mostly unused
Single read from stdin via sys.stdin.readline and list comprehension to parse two ints
A few integer operations: max(), min(), subtraction, modulo, division

complexity.why: The program performs a constant number of arithmetic operations and no data structures that grow with input size; there are no loops dependent on input size. All overhead is constant-time initialization and a few function calls.

bottlenecks.detail: Imports many large standard-library modules that are never used. Module loading and initialization adds avoidable startup time and memory overhead for a trivial constant-time task.
Defines func_1, func_3, func_4, func_5 but only func_2 and func_6 are actually used. Function definitions incur constant initialization cost and add indirection without benefit.
Core logic is wrapped in func_6, which is called once just to print its return value. This extra function call adds minor overhead compared with inlining the few arithmetic operations.

Uses max(var_1, var_2) and min(var_1, var_2) to compute the difference, then calls max(var_1, var_2) again in the return expression. This repeats comparisons that could be avoided with a single normalization/swap step.

func_2 constructs a list via a comprehension and then immediately unpacks it into two variables. While also present conceptually in the fast code, the layered helper call plus list creation adds a bit more overhead than a single direct map+unpack at top level.

FastAudit.core_idea: Strip the solution down to the minimal arithmetic on two integers: normalize order with one conditional swap, check parity of the difference using a bitwise AND, and compute the midpoint directly without extra modules or helper functions.

complexity.why: Like the slow version, it performs a fixed number of arithmetic and comparison operations and a single input read, but with fewer function calls and no heavy imports. Asymptotic complexity is unchanged, but constant factors are improved.

complexity_delta.from: O(1) time, O(1) space, with significant constant overhead from imports and indirection
complexity_delta.to: O(1) time, O(1) space, with minimal constant overhead
complexity_delta.note: Both implementations are asymptotically identical; the improvement is in startup cost and per-run constant factors (less importing, fewer function calls and redundant operations).

transformation_steps: Remove all unused heavy imports (math, itertools, heapq, collections, etc.) to reduce startup and memory overhead.
Eliminate unused helper functions (func_1, func_3, func_4, func_5) and inline the core logic instead of wrapping it in func_6.
Avoid repeated max/min calls by normalizing the order of the two values once via a simple conditional swap (if var_1 > var_2: swap).
Replace the modulus-based parity check (var_7 % 2 == 1) with a bitwise check ((var_2 - var_1) & 1), which is slightly cheaper and more idiomatic for parity.
Compute the midpoint directly from the normalized values (var_1 + (var_2 - var_1) // 2) instead of recomputing max and difference.
Print the result directly and exit early on the impossible case, avoiding extra layers of return and print.
trigger_signals: A very simple mathematical problem was solved with a template containing many imports and helpers, suggesting unnecessary overhead.
Presence of large import list at the top of the file for a solution that only needs basic I/O and integer arithmetic.
Helper functions that are defined but never used, hinting at auto-generated or copy-pasted template code.
Repeated calls to max/min for just two integers instead of a single normalization step.
pitfalls: Over-optimizing such a trivial constant-time problem is rarely necessary; the main value is code clarity, not performance.
When simplifying, ensure that behavior for negative or large integers (if allowed) remains correct; the midpoint and parity logic must be robust for the full constraint range.

Using input() instead of sys.stdin.readline is fine for single test cases, but in high-frequency IO scenarios the choice of IO method can matter; align with the broader contest style if multiple test cases are later introduced.

Removing template elements (like recursion limit settings) is safe here but in larger problems the same template might rely on them; keep separate minimal vs. full templates to avoid accidental regressions elsewhere.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder ABC110 D: inputs N, M up to about 1e9. Need product over prime exponents e of C(e+N-1, e) mod 1e9+7. Number of distinct primes and sum of exponents are small (O(log M)).

dominant_ops: Trial division prime factorization of M up to sqrt(M).
Precomputing factorial array fact[0..N+max_e] modulo MOD.
Precomputing inverse factorial array invfact[0..N+max_e] modulo MOD via reverse loop.
Answering each binomial coefficient with O(1) arithmetic using precomputed factorials.

complexity.why: After factorization, var_8 = N + max_exponent, then two lists var_2 and var_5 of length var_8+1 are filled by linear loops. With N up to 1e9 this is a billion-scale array and billion-iteration loops, completely dominating the small √M factorization cost.

bottlenecks.detail: Allocates lists var_2 and var_5 of size var_8+1 where var_8 = N + max_e. For N up to ~1e9, this requires several GB of RAM and will not fit in typical contest limits.
Loops `for var_4 in range(1, var_8 + 1)` and `for var_4 in range(var_8 - 1, -1, -1)` each do Θ(N) modular multiplications, which is far beyond feasible when N is large (up to 1e9).

The solution treats N as a precomputation bound for factorials, but the problem only needs combinations C(N+e-1, e) where e is small (sum of exponents ≤ ~30 for M ≤ 1e9). Using O(N) precomputation for O(log M) queries is asymptotically unnecessary.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit that each exponent e of M's prime factorization is small, so C(N+e-1, e) can be computed directly via multiplicative formula on big integers with only O(e) multiplications, then reduced modulo MOD at the end. This avoids any dependence on N in time/space complexity beyond using it as a value in the products.

complexity.time: O(√M + Σ e_i * cost_bigint) ≈ O(√M + log M)
complexity.space: O(1) additional (aside from small lists of factors and counters)
complexity.why: Factorization by trial division is O(√M). The number of distinct primes and the magnitudes of their exponents e_i are both O(log M). func_1 for each exponent e_i runs a loop of length e_i, performing big-int multiplies/divides, but e_i ≤ ~30 for M ≤ 1e9, keeping this cheap. No arrays sized by N are allocated.

complexity_delta.note: The slow version scales linearly in N due to factorial/inv-factorial construction, while the fast version scales only with √M and the small prime exponents of M, eliminating any O(N) term.

transformation_steps: Stop precomputing factorials up to N+max_e; remove arrays var_2 and var_5 and the associated linear loops.

Implement a direct binomial combination function func_1 that computes C(a, b) using multiplicative formula: multiply numerator terms (a, a-1, ..., a-b+1) and denominator terms (b, b-1, ..., 1), then divide at the end.
Use Python big integers (default int) to hold exact intermediate values in func_1 and only apply modulo 1e9+7 to the final product across primes.
Retain the same prime factorization logic (func_2) since its O(√M) cost is already optimal enough for the given constraints.
Iterate over prime exponents e and for each compute C(N+e-1, e) with func_1, multiplying them into the running answer and taking modulo at each step.
trigger_signals: Constraint inspection: N can be as large as 1e9, so any O(N) array or loop is infeasible.
Memory limit issues: attempts to allocate arrays of size ~1e9 cause MemoryError or exceed contest memory limits.
Runtime concerns: per-test runtime dominated by loops over range(N) even though the combinatorial queries only depend on small exponents of M.
Asymptotic mismatch: recognition that exponent counts e_i are tiny (sum ≤ ~30), so precomputing factorials up to N is unnecessary overhead.
pitfalls: In other languages without automatic big integers, switching from modular factorials to direct multiplication can cause overflow; here Python int makes it safe but slower than pure modular arithmetic for large e. The key is that e is very small in this problem.

func_1 must perform the division only after constructing the full numerator and denominator to preserve integer correctness; interleaving modulo operations into numerator/denominator separately would break exact divisibility.

Returning [1] for func_2(1) in the slow version is mathematically odd but performance-neutral; when simplifying or porting the code, ensure that the M=1 edge case is still handled correctly (answer = 1).
If problem constraints were instead N up to 2e5 or similar, the factorial precomputation approach would be superior; the optimization here is specific to very large N and small exponents of M.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer n and an array of length n. Typical competitive-programming constraints, likely n up to 1e5–2e5, single test case, 1s time limit.

dominant_ops: A single linear pass over the array comparing adjacent elements to count lengths of contiguous non-increasing runs; plus unnecessary module imports and unused helper definitions executed at startup.

complexity.why: The main logic loops once from 0 to n-2 and performs O(1) work per iteration (one comparison, simple integer updates, and an occasional max). No data structures scale with n beyond the input array itself.

bottlenecks.detail: Imports many heavy modules (math, collections, decimal, fractions, itertools, copy, etc.) that are never used in the main logic. This adds parsing and initialization overhead before the actual O(n) loop runs.
Defines func_1 (divisors), func_2 (duplicate check), func_3 (combinations) which are never called. Defining these functions costs extra bytecode parsing and function object creation for no benefit.
Uses int(eval(input())) to read n. eval is slower and less safe than int(input()) and adds unnecessary overhead, especially if input size is small but repeated in many test runs.
Global lists var_3 and var_4 (direction vectors) are created but never used, adding small but unnecessary allocation and memory footprint.

FastAudit.core_idea: Still performs a single pass over the array but keeps track of the start index of the current strictly increasing segment and records the length of the preceding non-increasing run into a list, then takes the maximum. The code removes all unused imports and helper functions.

complexity.why: The loop from 0 to n-2 does O(1) work per element (one comparison, one append, and a possible index update). However, it stores a length value for each position in var_4, which grows linearly with n, so auxiliary space is O(n).

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(n), Space: O(1) (plus heavy import/startup overhead)
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(n), Space: O(n) for the auxiliary length list
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time remains linear in both versions. The modified (fast) code is faster in practice mainly because it eliminates many unused imports and helper definitions, reducing startup and constant factors, at the cost of an extra O(n) list.

transformation_steps: Removed all unused standard-library imports and global variables that were not contributing to the core computation.
Removed unused helper functions (factorial-based combination, divisor listing, duplicate detection) that added definition overhead without being called.

Kept the core algorithm as a single linear pass over the array but changed the implementation style: instead of maintaining the current streak length directly, it tracks the start index of the last strictly increasing segment and records non-increasing run lengths into a list.
Handled the n == 1 edge case explicitly in the fast_code to short-circuit and avoid unnecessary loop logic.
Retained eval for integer input (could be further optimized by using int(input()) if needed).
trigger_signals: Code contained many heavyweight imports and helper functions that were never referenced in the main logic, indicating unnecessary overhead.
Profiling or inspection would show that almost all real work is done in a simple O(n) loop, so any performance issues are likely due to constant factors and startup time, not algorithmic complexity.
Memory and readability concerns: extraneous definitions clutter the namespace and make it harder to see the actual algorithm.
pitfalls: Both versions still use eval on input. Replacing int(eval(input())) with int(input()) is advisable to avoid unnecessary overhead and security risks.

The fast_code allocates an O(n) list (var_4) of intermediate lengths; for very large n or tight memory limits, it would be better to track only the current best length in a single scalar to keep O(1) extra space.
Edge cases like n == 1 must be handled explicitly; missing such a guard can lead to index errors when accessing a[i+1].

When refactoring for performance, it's easy to inadvertently change the condition (>= vs > or < vs <=); such changes would alter the definition of 'non-increasing' streaks and give wrong answers even if the complexity is sound.

constraints_guess.n_max: var_2 up to about 1e12 (so that sqrt(var_2) ~ 1e6 is feasible, but linear in var_2 is not)
constraints_guess.notes: Single test case; time limit likely around 1s-2s. Code pattern (sqrt search over divisors) suggests var_2 can be large (1e9–1e12).

dominant_ops: A descending loop from floor(var_2 / var_1) + 1 down to 1, performing var_2 % candidate on each iteration until a divisor is found.

complexity.time: O(var_2 / var_1) in the general case; worst-case O(var_2) when var_1 is small (e.g., var_1 = 1).
complexity.why: The function func_1 iterates over every integer candidate in [1, floor(var_2 / var_1) + 1], checking divisibility. In the worst case (e.g., when the first valid divisor near floor(var_2/var_1) is small or when var_2 is prime and var_1 does not divide var_2), the loop can approach floor(var_2 / var_1) iterations. Each iteration does a constant-time modulo, so total time is proportional to the upper bound on the loop.

bottlenecks.detail: The descending for-loop over all candidate divisors from floor(var_2/var_1)+1 to 1 can require up to O(var_2 / var_1) iterations, which becomes O(var_2) when var_1 is small. For large var_2 (e.g., 1e9 or higher), this is too slow.
If var_2 has no large divisors below var_2/var_1 (e.g., var_2 is prime or almost prime and var_1 does not divide var_2), the loop scans almost the entire range, hitting the worst-case time.

FastAudit.core_idea: Enumerate divisors of var_2 up to sqrt(var_2), use divisor pairing (d and var_2/d) to collect all divisors, then select the maximum divisor not exceeding floor(var_2 / var_1). This reduces the search space from all integers up to var_2/var_1 to only actual divisors of var_2, found in O(sqrt(var_2)) time.

complexity.space: O(number_of_divisors(var_2)) ≈ O(sqrt(var_2)) in the worst case.
complexity.why: The loop iterates var_3 from 1 to floor(sqrt(var_2)), performing a constant amount of work per iteration. For each divisor var_3, it records both var_3 and var_2 // var_3. The number of iterations is bounded by sqrt(var_2), and collecting divisors is also bounded by O(sqrt(var_2)) in the worst case. The subsequent scan over the divisors list is also at most O(sqrt(var_2)), so overall time is O(sqrt(var_2)).

complexity_delta.from: O(var_2 / var_1) worst-case O(var_2), O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(var_2)) time, O(sqrt(var_2)) space (in worst case for divisor storage)
complexity_delta.note: For small var_1, the slow code is linear in var_2, which is prohibitive for large var_2. The fast code bounds runtime by sqrt(var_2), a substantial asymptotic improvement when var_2 is large.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the task is to find the largest divisor of var_2 that does not exceed floor(var_2 / var_1).
Replace brute-force scanning of all integers in [1, floor(var_2 / var_1) + 1] with enumeration of only actual divisors of var_2.
Use the standard divisor-enumeration pattern: iterate i from 1 to floor(sqrt(var_2)); when i divides var_2, add both i and var_2 // i to a divisors list.
After collecting all divisors, iterate through them and track the maximum divisor that satisfies divisor <= floor(var_2 / var_1).
Retain the fast-path shortcut: when var_2 % var_1 == 0, answer is exactly var_2 / var_1, so skip divisor enumeration entirely.
trigger_signals: Loop bounds depend directly on var_2 / var_1, making the algorithm effectively O(var_2) for small var_1.
Typical competitive programming constraints and patterns: problems involving divisors of large integers rarely intend naive O(n) divisor search.
Presence of math.sqrt in alternative solutions suggests that a sqrt-based divisor enumeration is the intended approach.
Timeouts or performance warnings when testing with large values of var_2 (e.g., 1e9 or more) using the naive descending search.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors in the sqrt loop: ensuring the range includes floor(sqrt(var_2)) and not stopping one too early.
Missing paired divisors: whenever var_3 divides var_2, both var_3 and var_2 // var_3 must be considered; forgetting the second would miss larger divisors.
Not filtering divisors by the constraint divisor <= floor(var_2 / var_1), which would produce incorrect answers when the largest divisor is larger than the allowed bound.

Using floating-point division instead of integer division for thresholds (e.g., var_2 / var_1 vs var_2 // var_1) can cause subtle off-by-one or precision issues; integer division should be used for bounds.

constraints_guess.notes: Single scalar input, trivial arithmetic; runtime not dependent on input size.

dominant_ops: eval(input()) to parse the input expression
simple integer arithmetic (24 - x + 24)
printing the result

complexity.why: Only a single input is read and a constant number of arithmetic operations and a print call are executed, independent of the input value.

bottlenecks.detail: Redundant arithmetic (24 - var_1 + 24) instead of directly computing 48 - var_1.
Wrapping the logic inside func_1 and calling it from the main guard adds a small but unnecessary function call overhead for such a trivial operation.
int(eval(input())) performs an extra int() conversion; eval already produces a numeric type if a numeric literal or expression is given.
Using eval(input()) is potentially unsafe and slower than int(input()) if only integers are expected, because eval parses and executes arbitrary Python expressions.

FastAudit.core_idea: Inline the computation and simplify the arithmetic expression to a single constant-minus-input operation, removing the extra function, redundant arithmetic, and explicit int() conversion.

complexity.why: As with the original, the optimized version performs a single eval(input()), one arithmetic expression, and a print call, all independent of input size; only constant factors are reduced.

complexity_delta.note: No change in asymptotic complexity; improvements are in constant factors via fewer operations and no function wrapper.

transformation_steps: Algebraically simplified (24 - var_1 + 24) to (48 - var_1), then written as -var_1 + 48.
Inlined the computation into a single top-level print(...) call, removing the func_1 definition and its invocation.
Removed the explicit int() conversion, relying on eval to produce a numeric result directly.
Eliminated intermediate variable storage (var_1), using the expression result directly in the print call.
trigger_signals: Very small function with a single use and trivial logic, suggesting it can be inlined.
Redundant arithmetic pattern of constant - x + constant that can be collapsed.
Use of an intermediate variable that is only used once.
Presence of int(eval(input())) indicating possible redundant conversion and overpowered parsing.
pitfalls: Using eval(input()) is unsafe if the input is not fully trusted; it can execute arbitrary code. For competitive programming or simple numeric input, int(input()) or float(input()) is safer and typically faster.

Removing int() changes behavior slightly: the original coerced the result of eval to int; the new version will preserve non-int numeric types (e.g., floats) and might produce a float output where the original truncated/rounded via int().
Relying on algebraic simplification assumes standard integer/float arithmetic; if input expressions relied on side effects (unusual with eval, but possible), reordering might theoretically matter.
Micro-optimizations like removing a single function call or arithmetic operations have negligible impact in real-world scenarios compared to algorithmic changes or I/O bottlenecks.

constraints_guess.notes: Directed graph, vertices labeled 1..n. Input gives adjacency for each vertex. Task: BFS from vertex 1 (index 0) and print minimum distance (or -1 if unreachable). Typical AOJ / competitive-programming constraints with n <= ~100.

dominant_ops: Building an n×n adjacency matrix: nested list comprehension O(n^2)
For each dequeued vertex, list comprehension scanning the full adjacency row to find neighbors: O(n) per vertex
Queue implemented as a Python list with pop(0): O(n) per dequeue due to element shifting

complexity.why: Graph is stored as an n×n matrix => O(n^2) build cost and memory. BFS loop processes up to n vertices; each iteration does pop(0) (O(n)) and scans the entire row via list comprehension (O(n)), so per vertex O(n) work, giving O(n^2) overall. Edges do not influence asymptotics because the matrix scan cost dominates.

bottlenecks.detail: Adjacency matrix representation var_2 of size n×n consumes O(n^2) memory and forces scanning all n potential neighbors for every vertex, even if the vertex has very few outgoing edges.

In each BFS iteration, var_12 = [ ... for var_5, var_13 in enumerate(var_2[var_11]) if (var_13 == 1) and (var_4[var_5] == 0)] enumerates the entire row var_2[var_11], incurring O(n) work just to identify neighbors.
Queue is a plain list var_1; using var_1.pop(0) is O(n) per pop because all elements are shifted. For up to n pops, this adds another O(n^2) component.
Distance update uses var_3[var_5] = min(var_3[var_11] + 1, var_3[var_5]) even though BFS discovers vertices in nondecreasing distance order, so the min() call is unnecessary overhead.

Visited state var_4 is only marked for the current node (var_4[var_11] = 1) inside the neighbor loop instead of immediately upon discovery of neighbors; logic works here but is more convoluted than using a simple visited or distance-check pattern.
Using eval(input()) instead of int(input()) is slower and potentially unsafe; while not a major bottleneck for these constraints, it is unnecessary overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid the O(n^2) adjacency matrix and row scans by storing adjacency lists directly from the input and iterating only over actual neighbors during BFS. The BFS state is tracked with a single distance array where -1 denotes unvisited.

complexity.why: Graph is represented as adjacency lists var_1, where the total number of stored neighbor entries is O(m). BFS visits each edge at most once, contributing O(m). However, the queue is still a list with pop(0), costing O(n) per pop in the worst case, giving an O(n^2) upper bound when all n vertices are processed. Space uses O(n + m) for distances and adjacency lists, which is much smaller than O(n^2) for sparse graphs.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(n^2), Space: O(n^2) (adjacency matrix + list.pop(0) queue)
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(n^2 + m) (dominated by list.pop(0) but only iterating over actual neighbors), Space: O(n + m) (adjacency lists)
complexity_delta.note: Switching from an adjacency matrix to adjacency lists removes unnecessary O(n^2) neighbor scans and reduces space to O(n + m). Both versions still use a list as a queue, so worst-case time remains O(n^2), but the fast version has significantly smaller constants and better behavior on sparse graphs.

transformation_steps: Replace the n×n adjacency matrix with adjacency lists built directly from the input (store only the listed neighbors per vertex).
In BFS, iterate directly over each vertex's stored neighbors instead of scanning an entire row and filtering entries with value 1.
Simplify visit tracking by using a single distance array initialized to -1; use distance >= 0 as the visited condition instead of a separate visited array plus min() updates.
Inline the BFS logic into the main flow and print distances directly, avoiding an extra function layer and post-processing of unreachable nodes.
trigger_signals: Initialization of a 2D array var_2 = [[0 for ...] for ...] of size n×n suggests O(n^2) memory and build time regardless of the number of edges.
Neighbor discovery via enumeration of all entries in var_2[var_11] (list comprehension over the full row), which reveals an O(n) per-vertex scanning pattern.
Use of list.pop(0) in a BFS-like loop, which is a classic sign of an O(n) per-pop queue implementation in Python.
Problem semantics (unweighted BFS on a graph where m can be much smaller than n^2) naturally favor adjacency lists and O(n + m) neighbor traversal.
pitfalls: When switching to adjacency lists, maintain correct index conversions between 1-based labels in input and 0-based Python indices to avoid off-by-one errors.
Ensure that BFS still initializes the starting vertex’s distance correctly (0 for the source, -1 for others) and that the visited condition is consistent with how distances are stored.

Both versions currently use a Python list as a queue (pop(0)); for larger n, this becomes a serious bottleneck. A further optimization would be to use collections.deque, which changes the time complexity to O(n + m). Forgetting this can result in unexpected quadratic slowdowns on larger inputs.
In the fast code, neighbors are stored as strings and converted to int inside the BFS loop; if performance is critical and inputs are large, converting to int once at read time is preferable.
Avoid using eval(input()) for numeric input parsing; while not the main performance issue here, it is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()).

constraints_guess.notes: Two integers N (var_3) and M (var_1). M is factorized by trial division so M is likely up to about 1e9. N can be as large as 1e5 in typical AtCoder combinatorics problems. No explicit queries; single computation.

dominant_ops: trial_division_factorization up to roughly sqrt(M) with repeated division
for each distinct prime factor, a binomial computation loop of length N-1 using modular multiplication and modular inverse via pow

complexity.why: Factorization: loop var_5 from 2 up while var_5^2 <= current var_1, so in worst case O(√M) trial divisions and repeated divisions when a factor divides M. P is the number of distinct prime factors of M, which is small (<= log2 M). For each exponent e of a prime, func_1 is called as func_1(var_3 + e - 1, var_3 - 1) so var_6 = N-1. The loop in func_1 runs from 1 to var_6 (≈ N) and each iteration performs a modular inverse with pow(var_5, MOD-2, MOD) taking O(log MOD) time, plus a few modular multiplications. Hence binomial part is O(P * N * log MOD). Only a defaultdict of size P is stored, so space is O(P).

bottlenecks.detail: func_1 computes C(var_7, var_6) with var_6 = N-1, so the loop length scales linearly with N, which can be up to ~1e5. This yields up to ~1e5 * P iterations with an expensive pow() call each time.

Within func_1, modular inverses are recomputed from scratch via pow(i, MOD-2, MOD) for every i in 1..(N-1). This is significantly more expensive than using precomputed factorials / inverse factorials or at least computing binomial with the smaller of k and n-k.
pow(base, MOD-2, MOD) inside the inner loop introduces a high constant factor due to repeated modular exponentiation, even though the asymptotic is still acceptable for the constraints.

The factorization loop starts from 2 up to var_1+1 with a break on var_5 * var_5 > var_1. Although var_1 shrinks as factors are removed, this pattern is slightly less direct than looping to sqrt(initial M); however, this cost is dominated by the combination loop and is not the main bottleneck.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the same number-theoretic structure (prime factorization of M and a product of binomial coefficients) but drastically reduce the cost of each binomial coefficient by computing C(n, k) with k equal to the prime exponent (which is small, <= O(log M)) and using the symmetry k = min(k, n-k). Compute C(n, k) as an exact integer via a short multiplicative/divisive loop and only apply modulo at the very end. Factorization is also written against a fixed sqrt(M) bound for clarity.

complexity.why: Factorization: func_2 runs var_7 from 2 to floor(sqrt(M)) with repeated divisions, so O(√M) time, with M reduced as factors are removed. P is the number of distinct primes. For each exponent e, func_1 is called as func_1(N + e - 1, e); it sets k = min(e, N+e-1-e) = e because e << N, so the loop length is O(e). Each binomial coefficient is computed using at most 2e ≈ O(e) big-integer multiplications/divisions. Since e <= log2 M and P <= log2 M, this is O(P * log M * B) where B is the cost of big-int arithmetic on numbers of size ≈ log C(N+e-1, e) bits. With N up to ~1e5 and e <= ~30, B is modest and the total is far smaller in practice than the original O(P * N * log MOD). Space holds only the list of factors and a Counter, both O(total number of prime factors), thus O(P).

complexity_delta.from: O(√M + P * N * log MOD) time, O(P) space
complexity_delta.to: O(√M + P * log M * B) time, O(P) space
complexity_delta.note: The key win is replacing a binomial loop that scales with N (potentially 1e5) and uses modular exponentiation at each step with a loop that scales with the small prime exponent e (<= ~log M, about 30) and uses only big-integer multiplication/division. As a result, the practical running time drops by roughly a factor of N / log M for large N.

transformation_steps: Reformulate the binomial argument: instead of computing C(N + e - 1, N - 1), compute the equivalent C(N + e - 1, e) and then further reduce to C(n, k) with k = min(k, n-k). Since e is small compared to N, this guarantees a very short loop.

Replace the modular multiplicative formulation with modular inverses inside the loop by an exact integer binomial computation: multiply the numerator n * (n-1) * ... * (n-k+1) and divide by the denominator k! using integer division. This leverages Python's arbitrary-precision integers and avoids repeated pow() calls.
Move modulo operations out of the inner binomial loops: compute each C(n, k) as a pure integer and take mod 1e9+7 only once at the end of the full product, minimizing modular arithmetic overhead.

Simplify and clarify factorization: implement a factorization helper func_2 that iterates var_7 from 2 to floor(sqrt(M)) and collects prime factors into a list, then convert that list into a Counter to get exponents. This keeps factorization complexity at O(√M) and separates concerns cleanly.
Use Counter instead of defaultdict for counting prime exponents, which is more semantically direct for counting occurrences and avoids manual increment-and-store patterns.
trigger_signals: Presence of a loop from 1 to N-1 inside func_1, where N comes directly from input and can be large (e.g., up to 1e5). This suggests the running time scales with the larger input rather than with the small combinatorial parameter (the prime exponent).
Use of pow(i, MOD-2, MOD) inside the innermost loop, indicating repeated modular exponentiation per iteration, a classic performance red flag in competitive programming code.

Theoretical observation that the binomial C(N + e - 1, N - 1) has a symmetric form C(N + e - 1, e) where e is the exponent of a prime in M and hence bounded by O(log M). Not exploiting this symmetry wastes potential complexity reductions.

Empirical understanding that Python's big integers handle modestly-sized exact binomial computations well, making an exact arithmetic approach viable and often faster than modular inverses in tight loops.
pitfalls: The optimized combinatorial routine relies on Python's arbitrary-precision integers. Porting this approach directly to languages without built-in big integers (like C++ without libraries) would cause overflow; in such languages, one must keep arithmetic modulo MOD throughout.

Integer division in the binomial computation must be exact at every step. The numerator and denominator loops must be correctly aligned to compute C(n, k) to avoid truncation or rounding errors; reordering or modifying these loops incorrectly would break correctness.

Computing the modulus only once at the very end means intermediate integers can grow very large if N were significantly bigger. For the guessed constraints (N up to ~1e5 and exponents small), this is fine, but for substantially larger N a more careful modular combinatorics approach with precomputed factorials would be safer.

The factorization in func_2 iterates up to floor(sqrt(initial M)) even as M is reduced by repeated division. Although asymptotically fine, this can be slightly slower than dynamically shrinking the bound (as in the original code). If M were much larger, a more advanced factorization method or early-termination logic might be necessary.

The optimization assumes that using k = exponent is always the smaller side of the binomial (i.e., exponent << N). If constraints changed and exponents could be large relative to N, then k = min(k, n-k) must be carefully maintained to keep loops short.

constraints_guess.n_max: 1e5–1e7 (typical CP: often 1e5)
constraints_guess.notes: Input is a single integer N; task is to count integers in [1, N] whose decimal representation has an odd number of digits.

dominant_ops: Outer loop over all integers from 1 to N
For each integer, repeated integer division by 10 to count digits

complexity.why: For each number var_3 in [1, N], the while-loop divides by 10 until 0, performing O(log_10 var_3) ≈ O(log N) iterations; summing over all var_3 gives O(N log N). Only a constant number of integer variables are used.

bottlenecks.detail: Digit count computed via repeated division for every number individually: while var_4 > 0: var_4 //= 10; this induces a log-factor per element.
The inner while-loop introduces Python-level branching and integer arithmetic for each digit of each number, which dominates runtime as N grows.
Using eval(input()) is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()); minor in complexity but undesirable in competitive settings.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace manual digit-counting via repeated division with computing the decimal representation as a string and using its length to determine the number of digits.

complexity.why: For each integer var_3, converting to string (str(var_3)) and building a list of its characters both take time proportional to the number of digits, O(log var_3) ≈ O(log N). Across all N numbers, this is still O(N log N). The transient list/str objects per iteration require O(d) = O(log N) space, but peak additional space is bounded by one number’s digit-length.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log N) time, O(1) space (ignoring tiny temporaries)
complexity_delta.to: O(N log N) time, O(log N) transient space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically unchanged; in practice, the string-based version can even be slower due to object allocations and list creation.

transformation_steps: Replaced manual digit-count loop (while var_4 > 0: var_4 //= 10; var_5 += 1) with conversion to string: str(var_3).
Replaced integer digit-count variable (var_5) with len(var_4), where var_4 is a list of characters derived from the string form of var_3.
Preserved the overall counting logic: increment var_2 when the digit count is odd.
trigger_signals: Desire to simplify digit-counting logic into a more readable form using built-in string operations.
Observation that digit count equals string-length in base-10 representation.
No evident need to change the overall O(N log N) approach due to moderate expected constraints.
pitfalls: No asymptotic speedup: both versions run in O(N log N); relying on this change for big performance gains is incorrect.
String conversion plus list() allocation adds overhead; for tight time limits, the original arithmetic-based digit counting may actually be faster.
The list conversion var_4 = list(str(var_3)) is unnecessary; using len(str(var_3)) would avoid an extra list allocation.

Both versions still iterate over all numbers up to N; for very large N (e.g., >1e7), a formula-based approach by digit ranges (1–9, 100–999, 10000–99999, etc.) would be required for O(1) or O(#digit-blocks) time.
eval(input()) remains a security and performance concern in both versions; it should be replaced with int(input()).

constraints_guess.notes: Graph has vertices for indices 1..n plus source/sink and edges for each divisor relation j = k*i, so E ≈ n log n. Dense (n+2)×(n+2) matrix is already too heavy once n ≳ 5000, indicating the intended solution must be sparse and roughly O(n log n)–O(n^(3/2)) time.

dominant_ops: Allocation and use of a dense (n+2)×(n+2) int64 NumPy matrix for capacities
Repeated calls to scipy.sparse.csgraph.dijkstra on a dense graph inside the max-flow augmentation loop
Python-level reconstruction of each augmenting path and per-edge residual capacity updates

complexity.time: ≈ O(K * V^2) with V = n+2 and K = number of augmenting paths; with V ≈ n this is ≈ O(K * n^2) and can approach O(n^3) in bad cases.
complexity.space: Θ(V^2) = Θ(n^2) due to the dense capacity matrix.
complexity.why: The capacities are stored in a dense matrix var_10 of shape (n+2, n+2). Each augmentation runs dijkstra(...) over this matrix, which, for dense graphs, is effectively O(V^2). Because max-flow is implemented as repeated shortest-path augmentations, the total time multiplies this by the number of augmenting paths. Memory is dominated by the O(n^2) matrix, not by the O(n log n) logical number of edges.

bottlenecks.detail: var_10 is an (n+2)×(n+2) int64 NumPy array. Memory usage is about 8·(n+2)^2 bytes. At n = 2e5 this would be ~64 TB, completely infeasible; even at n = 2e4 it's already several GB.

Max-flow is implemented using repeated single-source shortest paths (Dijkstra) on the residual graph. With an effectively dense representation this behaves like O(K * n^2), where K is the number of augmenting iterations, which is too slow for large n.

Using scipy.sparse.csgraph.dijkstra per augmentation is expensive and SciPy is typically unavailable in competitive programming environments. Even if available, calling a heavy-weight generic routine repeatedly is inefficient.
Most entries in var_10 are zero (no edge), but they are still stored and processed as part of the dense matrix. This wastes both time (Dijkstra scans non-edges) and memory.
Path reconstruction and residual updates are done in Python loops over each edge in the augmenting path; with many iterations this overhead becomes non-trivial.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace the dense capacity matrix + SciPy Dijkstra-based max-flow with a sparse adjacency-list max-flow (e.g., Dinic) implemented in pure Python. Build only the actual edges implied by the divisibility relations and run a BFS/DFS-based blocking-flow algorithm from source (0) to sink (n+1). This reduces both time and memory from quadratic to nearly linear in the number of edges (Θ(n log n)).

complexity.time: For V = n+2 and E ≈ n log n (from all j = k*i edges), Dinic on this sparse network runs in roughly O(E * sqrt(V)) or better in practice; more conservatively O(E * V^(2/3)) in unit-capacity style cases, both acceptable for n up to about 1e5–2e5.
complexity.space: Θ(E) = Θ(n log n) for adjacency lists and residual edges, plus Θ(V) for node arrays.
complexity.why: Adjacency lists store only real edges instead of all V^2 pairs. Dinic’s algorithm uses alternating BFS (to build level graphs) and DFS (to find blocking flows), touching each edge only a limited number of times per phase. For a network defined by divisibility constraints, where E is about n log n, this yields near-linear behavior in the input size, as opposed to n^2 for the dense-matrix Dijkstra runs.

complexity_delta.from: Time: ≈ O(K * n^2) with K augmentations; Space: Θ(n^2) via a dense capacity matrix and dense Dijkstra processing.
complexity_delta.to: Time: ≈ O(E * polylog(V)) or O(E * sqrt(V)) with E ≈ n log n; Space: Θ(E + V) ≈ Θ(n log n).
complexity_delta.note: The asymptotic improvement is from quadratic (or worse) in n to near-linear in the actual number of edges. Practically, this changes the problem from impossible for large n to easily solvable within typical contest limits.

transformation_steps: Switch graph representation from a dense (n+2)×(n+2) NumPy matrix to a sparse adjacency list (vector of edge lists), storing only existing edges and their residual capacities.

Replace the SciPy-based Dijkstra loop with a dedicated max-flow algorithm (e.g., Dinic or Edmonds–Karp on adjacency lists). For performance at large n, Dinic with BFS level graph + DFS blocking flow is preferred.

When constructing the graph, iterate i = 1..n and for each i, add edges (j -> i) with large capacity only for multiples j = 2*i, 3*i, ..., ensuring overall edge count ≈ n log n. Keep the original source->node and node->sink capacities based on the sign of a[i].

Maintain residual capacities explicitly in the edge structs (cap, rev index) instead of storing and mutating them in a dense matrix. For each original edge, also create a reverse edge with 0 capacity for the residual graph.
Compute the maximum flow once with the chosen algorithm on this sparse graph, then output sum(positive a[i]) - max_flow as in the original reduction to maximum closure.

Remove all SciPy and NumPy dependencies, reducing startup overhead and ensuring compatibility with standard judges; rely purely on Python built-ins and possibly minimal standard library structures like lists and deque.
trigger_signals: Use of a dense NumPy array for graph capacities despite the graph arising from a structured divisibility relation (which is inherently sparse).
Presence of scipy.sparse.csgraph.dijkstra in a while-loop, indicating repeated all-edges shortest path computation for a flow-like algorithm.
Residual capacity updates (var_10[u][v] -= f; var_10[v][u] += f) suggest a home-grown max-flow on top of Dijkstra, a known performance anti-pattern for large graphs.
Theoretical memory blow-up from Θ(n^2) storage for a graph where counting logical edges shows only Θ(n log n) real edges.
Typical contest environments do not provide SciPy, hinting that a pure-Python graph algorithm is the intended solution.
pitfalls: INF capacity choice: The large capacity (10**12) must exceed any possible sum of positive a[i] (upper bound of total flow) but still fit safely in 64-bit integers; when porting, keep INF within 1e18 if using int64-like constraints.

Indexing and node mapping: Carefully preserve the mapping of nodes (0 as source, 1..n as original indices, n+1 as sink). Off-by-one errors will silently produce incorrect flows or disconnect required dependencies.

Edge construction cost: When adding edges for multiples j = 2*i, 3*i, ..., use integer stepping loops. Avoid nested O(n^2) loops; the correct pattern is `for i in range(1, n+1): for j in range(2*i, n+1, i): ...` which yields O(n log n) edges.
Recursion depth: If the max-flow DFS is implemented recursively, either keep recursion shallow or use sys.setrecursionlimit / iterative DFS to avoid hitting recursion limits on deep graphs.

Performance tuning: In Python, avoid per-edge overhead from heavy objects or attributes inside the inner BFS/DFS loops. Represent edges as small tuples/objects, preallocate arrays where possible, and avoid unnecessary Python-level checks inside tight loops.

Correctness of maximum-closure reduction: Ensure that edges are directed as in the original reduction (from dependent node to prerequisite node) and that only pairs with a[i] < 0 and a[j] > 0 get the infinite edges; flipping these conditions breaks the closure semantics even if the max-flow implementation is fast.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: given N integers (likely N <= 100, values around 1..100), choose integer t to minimize sum_i (a_i - t)^2. Original solution brute-forces t in [1,100].

dominant_ops: Python-level for-loop over candidate centers t in range(max(a) - min(a) + 1)
Within each iteration, computing min(var_2) (O(N) each time)
Vectorized numpy arithmetic (var_2 - var_5) ** 2 creating temporary arrays
np.sum over length-N array for each candidate t

complexity.why: Let N = number of elements, R = max(a) - min(a) + 1 candidate centers. For each of R candidate t: we recompute min(var_2) in O(N) time, then allocate a temporary vector (var_2 - t)**2 and sum it in O(N). Overall O(R * N) time and O(N) extra space for the temporary vector.

bottlenecks.detail: min(var_2) is recomputed inside the loop for every candidate t, costing O(N) per iteration instead of O(1) if precomputed.

Numpy is used inside a Python loop over t. Each iteration allocates new temporary arrays (var_2 - var_5) and (..) ** 2 and then calls np.sum, causing significant overhead for small N typical of this problem.
Vectorization is only across N, but the outer loop over R is still in Python. Given small N and small R, the constant-factor overhead of numpy outweighs the gains versus simple Python arithmetic.
Using numpy in a competitive-programming environment often slows execution because of import cost and Python–C boundary crossing for small arrays.
Using eval() for integer input is unnecessary and can be unsafe, though it does not dominate performance here.

FastAudit.core_idea: Pure-Python double loop over a fixed small range of candidate t (1..100), accumulating squared differences directly in integers and using early break once the sum stops decreasing due to convexity of the quadratic.

complexity.why: The outer loop runs at most 100 iterations (constant bound from constraints), and the inner loop scans all N elements computing integer arithmetic. Hence O(100 * N) time, which is effectively linear in N. Only the input array of size N is stored, so O(N) space.

complexity_delta.from: O(N) time, O(N) space (fixed small outer loop with early break)
complexity_delta.to: O(R * N) time, O(N) space (R = max(a) - min(a) + 1) with additional per-iteration overhead from numpy and repeated min())
complexity_delta.note: As implemented, the numpy version adds heavy constant factors and an extra O(N) inside the loop; with small N and small R typical of the problem, this is slower than the minimalistic pure-Python approach.

transformation_steps: Replaced pure-Python list of ints with a numpy array var_2.
Changed candidate t-range from fixed range(100) to range(max(var_2) - min(var_2) + 1), increasing dependence on data spread R.
Inside the loop, used numpy broadcasting (var_2 - var_5) ** 2 and np.sum, which allocates temporary arrays and crosses the Python–C boundary for every t.
Recomputed min(var_2) on every iteration of the loop instead of precomputing it once.
Removed the early-break optimization based on monotonicity/convexity of the objective.
trigger_signals: Use of numpy operations ((var_2 - var_5) ** 2, np.sum) inside a Python for-loop over candidate values.
Repeated computation of min(var_2) inside the loop body.
Small problem constraints (N and value range small), making vectorization overhead comparatively expensive.
Competitive programming context where numpy import and per-iteration allocations are known to be slow.
pitfalls: Assuming that introducing numpy always speeds up numeric code; for small N and many Python-level iterations, it can be slower than simple loops.
Forgetting to hoist invariant computations (like min(var_2)) out of loops, leading to hidden O(N^2) patterns for larger spreads.
Dropping early-termination logic (break when objective stops decreasing) that exploits the convex shape of the cost function.
Using eval() on input instead of int(), which is unnecessary and potentially dangerous, even if not the main performance issue.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style problem: first line n (up to ~2e5), second line n integers with magnitude up to around 1e9. Need to compute minimal sum of squared differences to an integer mean.

dominant_ops: Parsing n integers from input: list(map(int, sys.stdin.readline().split())) -> O(n)
Creating NumPy array from Python list: np.array(var_2) -> O(n) time and O(n) extra memory
Summing elements with np.sum(var_2) -> O(n)
Element-wise operations to form (var_2 - var_4) ** 2 -> O(n) time and O(n) extra memory
Summing squared differences with np.sum(...) -> O(n)

complexity.why: The algorithm performs a constant number of full passes over n elements: one to read input, one to build the NumPy array, and at least one more to compute and sum squared differences. It also stores the data in both a Python list and a NumPy array plus a temporary squared-differences array, all of size n.

bottlenecks.detail: Holds the input as a Python list, then copies it into a NumPy array, and then creates another size-n array for (var_2 - var_4) ** 2. This roughly triples the memory footprint for large n.

Element-wise NumPy operations ((var_2 - var_4) ** 2) and multiple np.sum calls introduce overhead. While each is O(n), they add constant-factor cost compared to computing aggregated statistics in a single pass.
Using NumPy in a competitive-programming-style environment for a single linear pass adds import and array-management overhead, which can be significant relative to the total time budget.

The mean is computed as var_4 = round(np.sum(var_2) / var_1), which uses floating-point and Python's bankers rounding semantics, potentially differing from the exact integer minimizer strategy and introducing unnecessary float work.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid building and traversing full difference/squared arrays by using the algebraic identity sum_i (x_i - m)^2 = n*m^2 - 2*m*sum(x_i) + sum(x_i^2), and search only the two relevant integer means (floor and ceil of the true mean) using integer arithmetic.

complexity.why: The optimized code still needs to read n elements and compute sum(x_i) and sum(x_i^2), which is inherently O(n). It stores the input list and one NumPy array of squares (size n), so space remains O(n), but it removes the extra temporary array of squared differences and the repeated element-wise operations.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(n) with several full-array NumPy operations and extra passes; Space: O(n) with multiple size-n arrays (original list, NumPy copy, squared-differences array).
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(n) with fewer passes, focusing on aggregate sums and a single squaring pass; Space: O(n) with only the input list and one squared array.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity remains linear in n, but constant factors in both time and memory are significantly improved by eliminating superfluous arrays and element-wise operations.

transformation_steps: Replace direct computation of sum((a_i - m)^2) via full vector operations with the algebraic identity sum_i (x_i - m)^2 = n*m^2 - 2*m*sum(x_i) + sum(x_i^2), so the cost is dominated by computing sum(x_i) and sum(x_i^2).
Stop constructing an explicit (var_2 - var_4) ** 2 array; instead, compute sum of squares (via np.power or pure Python) once and reuse it in the formula.

Switch from floating-point mean with round(...) to integer-only computation of floor and ceil means (var_2 = sum // n, var_3 = -(-sum // n)) and evaluate the objective at these two candidates, which guarantees the minimum sum of squared differences without floating-point rounding.
Reduce the use of NumPy vector operations to a single squaring pass (np.power(var_6, 2)) instead of multiple chained operations; the remaining operations are scalar arithmetic on aggregated values.
Inline I/O handling (input()) rather than helper wrappers, simplifying control flow and avoiding some indirection overhead (though this is a minor contribution compared to array-creation costs).
trigger_signals: Use of NumPy arrays for simple one-dimensional statistics (mean/variance) in a tight time-limited environment; importing and managing NumPy arrays is often heavier than a single linear pass with basic arithmetic.
Creation of multiple temporary arrays of length n ((var_2 - var_4) ** 2) purely to sum them once, indicating redundant memory traffic.
Float-based rounding (round(sum / n)) where an integer optimization problem is intended, hinting that an algebraic or integer-arithmetic reformulation could be more efficient and precise.
Observed or anticipated time/memory limits being hit when scaling n up (e.g., around 10^5–10^6 elements) due to extra passes and allocations.
pitfalls: The modified code still calls sum(var_6) three times; while asymptotically harmless, it introduces extra linear passes. In very tight constraints, sum(var_6) should be computed once and stored.
Using eval(input()) for reading an integer is both slower and potentially unsafe in a general context; a plain int(input()) is preferable and sufficient.

Retaining NumPy only for squaring (np.power(var_6, 2)) may still be overkill; a pure-Python pass (e.g., a comprehension computing both sum and sum of squares) could be faster and avoid NumPy entirely.

Care must be taken to ensure that the floor/ceil mean approach exactly matches the original specification: for minimizing sum of squared deviations over integer m, evaluating both floor and ceil is correct, but if the problem required a specific tie-breaking rule tied to round(), the behavior might differ.

When porting this algebraic approach to languages with fixed-size integer types, sum(x_i^2) and n*m^2 can overflow; Python's big integers avoid this, but in other environments explicit 64-bit checks or modular arithmetic might be needed.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder array/pair-count problem; input is n and an array of length n. Indices used are i±a[i], suggesting |a[i]| and n are around 2e5–1e6 at most.

dominant_ops: Initialization of a length-10**7 list and a single pass over n elements with array accesses and bounds checks.

complexity.why: The code creates var_4 = [0] * 10**7 upfront, which costs Θ(10^7) time and memory regardless of n. The loop itself is Θ(n), doing constant work per element. Combined, this is Θ(n + 10^7) time and Θ(10^7) space.

bottlenecks.detail: The fixed array var_4 of size 10**7 stores int counters. In CP Python this can exceed typical memory limits (tens to hundreds of MB) and causes MLE or heavy GC and cache pressure.
Creating [0] * 10**7 is a large upfront Θ(10^7) operation even if n is much smaller (e.g., 2e5). This dominates runtime when n << 10^7.

Indices used are var_6 = (i+1) - a[i] and var_7 = (i+1) + a[i]. In typical constraints, the number of distinct indices touched is O(n), but the code reserves space for 10^7 positions regardless, wasting memory and time.

Negative indices and indices >= 10**7 are silently ignored due to bounds checks. While not a performance bottleneck itself, this indicates the array is not truly modeling the needed (potentially unbounded) index space and could force even larger arrays if constraints grew.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a defaultdict as a sparse frequency map keyed by transformed indices (i ± a[i]) instead of a huge preallocated array. Only actually used indices are stored, so both time and space scale with the number of relevant keys rather than an arbitrary upper bound.

complexity.space: O(k) where k is the number of distinct (i + a[i]) values, typically O(n)
complexity.why: The loop runs once over the array (i from 1 to n), and each iteration does O(1) expected-time dict operations: a read var_3[i - a[i]] and an increment var_3[i + a[i]]. No large preallocation. The map holds at most O(n) keys, so memory and runtime are linear in n.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(n + 10^7), Space: O(10^7) due to preallocated list.
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(n), Space: O(k) with k = O(n) using a sparse defaultdict.
complexity_delta.note: The main win is removing the fixed-size 10^7 array and instead using a hash map keyed by only the actually used indices. This removes the Θ(10^7) time/space overhead and improves cache behavior.

transformation_steps: Replace the fixed-size array var_4 = [0] * 10**7 with collections.defaultdict(int) to store counts sparsely.
Change index usage to mirror the dictionary approach: directly access var_3[key] for both reading and incrementing without bounds checks, letting the dict grow only where needed.
Iterate with 1-based logical indices (range(1, n+1)) and use a[i-1] to match the original mathematical formulation, simplifying index arithmetic and aligning with the fast solution.
Remove arbitrary index caps (like 10**7) and rely on the dictionary's unbounded key space to correctly handle all possible i ± a[i] within constraints.
trigger_signals: Presence of a very large fixed-size list ([0] * 10**7) whose size is not clearly tied to input n.
Constraints (inferred or explicit) indicating n is around 2e5 while the code reserves 10**7 slots.
Memory limit in the environment being close to or below the footprint of a 10**7-element Python list of ints.
Profiling or observed behavior showing large startup time or MLE/TLE before the main loop does much work.
pitfalls: Choosing an array size based on a guessed upper bound (10**7) can either waste memory (if too large) or silently break correctness (if too small for worst-case i ± a[i]).
Assuming array-based indexing is always faster than dict lookups; for sparse key spaces or large unused ranges, dicts can be faster and far more memory efficient.
Ignoring constant factors: Θ(10^7) operations for initialization can dominate runtime when n is only ~10^5–10^6.
Forgetting that Python lists of ints have high per-element overhead, making large preallocations much more expensive than in low-level languages.
Switching to dict without considering key formulation: mixing 0-based and 1-based indices incorrectly can alter keys (i ± a[i]) and silently give wrong pair counts.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer input; typical AtCoder-style task computing ceil(n/2). Complexity constraints irrelevant; constant-time solution is expected.

dominant_ops: Module imports (itertools, sys, math, numpy, collections, functools) at startup
eval(input()) for reading a single integer
math.ceil(var_1 / 2) using floating-point arithmetic

complexity.why: Both reading a single integer and computing ceil(n/2) are constant-time; no loops or data structures growing with input size. However, constant factors are inflated by heavy imports and floating-point operations.

bottlenecks.detail: Imports of itertools, math, numpy, collections, functools, and setting a very large recursion limit are unnecessary for this trivial computation and add startup time.
numpy, deque, combinations, reduce, lru_cache are never used but incur import cost and can be significant in short-running programs.
math.ceil(var_1 / 2) performs a float division and a library function call instead of pure integer arithmetic.
Wrapping the logic in func_1 and calling it once adds a small but unnecessary call overhead in a program dominated by constant-time work.
eval(input()) is slower and less safe than plain int(input()); it parses Python expressions instead of plain integers.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use minimal code with integer-only arithmetic and no unnecessary imports: compute ceil(n/2) via (n + 1) >> 1 directly on the integer.

complexity.why: The program does a single integer parse and a constant number of integer operations (addition and bit shift). No imported modules, no extra call stack, and no floating-point or library function calls, so constant factors are minimized.

complexity_delta.from: O(1) time, O(1) space with heavy constant factors due to imports and floating-point math.
complexity_delta.to: O(1) time, O(1) space with minimal constant factors using pure integer arithmetic and no imports.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged, but runtime in a short-lived script can be noticeably improved by removing import overhead and using bit-level integer math.

transformation_steps: Remove all unused imports (itertools, sys, math, numpy, collections, functools) and recursion limit configuration.
Inline the main logic instead of wrapping it in a separate function for this trivial one-shot script.
Replace math.ceil(var_1 / 2) with integer-only arithmetic (var_1 + 1) >> 1 to avoid float conversion and library calls.
Retain the same effective behavior for non-negative integers while reducing overhead.
Preserve the single input and single output structure to match the original problem specification.
trigger_signals: Very small input size (single integer) where startup and import costs dominate total runtime.
Presence of multiple heavy imports (especially numpy) that are never used in the core logic.
Use of math.ceil on a simple integer expression that can be expressed via integer arithmetic.
Function indirection for a one-line computation in a script that runs only once.
pitfalls: Bit-shift-based formula (n + 1) >> 1 assumes var_1 is non-negative; for negative inputs its behavior differs from math.ceil(n/2). If negatives must be handled exactly like ceil, use integer formula (n + 1) // 2 or a more general expression.
Using eval(input()) is unnecessary and unsafe for arbitrary input; int(input()) is safer and faster, but both versions currently use eval for compatibility with the original code.
Over-optimizing via bit tricks can reduce readability; in some codebases, (n + 1) // 2 might be preferred for clarity while still avoiding floating-point math.

constraints_guess.notes: Single array input; typical competitive-programming constraints where O(n) with low constant factor is required.

dominant_ops: Multiple full traversals over the n-element list: statistics.mean (sum+len), optional counting comprehension, and squared-difference comprehension.

complexity.why: Reading n integers and storing them takes O(n) space. statistics.mean iterates over the list (O(n)). In the var_7 == 0.5 branch, a list comprehension creates another list of size up to n for counting. The final squared-differences list is also size n. Overall linear time with multiple passes and linear auxiliary lists.

bottlenecks.detail: statistics.mean(var_5) performs its own pass over the list separate from the later squared-difference pass.
len([var_2 for var_2 in var_5 if var_2 > var_7]) materializes a temporary list solely for counting; this is an additional O(n) memory and time in the rare var_7 == 0.5 case.
Using statistics.mean introduces extra Python-level overhead compared with a direct sum / n computation for a simple numeric mean.

Imports of statistics.mean, math.floor, and math.ceil are performed inside the function. While cached after the first call, the name lookups are still less direct than built-in arithmetic and round().

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace statistics.mean with an explicit sum/size mean and round it directly, eliminating extra passes and library overhead while computing squared differences in a single additional pass.

complexity.why: One pass to sum the list (O(n)) and one pass to compute squared differences (O(n)); list of inputs and squared-difference list are both size n. Asymptotic complexity remains linear, but constant factors are reduced by simpler operations and fewer traversals.

complexity_delta.from: O(n) time, O(n) space with multiple traversals and extra temporary list in a branch.
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space with fewer traversals and no branch-specific extra list.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged, but practical performance improves from reduced Python-level overhead and fewer passes over the data.

transformation_steps: Replace statistics.mean(var_5) with sum(var_2) / var_1 using simple arithmetic.
Remove the special-case logic around mean == 0.5 and manual floor/ceil selection in favor of a single round(sum / n) call.
Eliminate the list-building count len([x for x in arr if x > mean]) that was only used when mean == 0.5.
Inline the core logic at module level and use only built-in operations (sum, round) to reduce overhead.
Keep a single list comprehension for squared differences without extra conditionals.
trigger_signals: Use of statistics.mean in a tight, performance-sensitive loop in Python.
Multiple full traversals over the same list for simple aggregate computations (mean, counts, squared differences).
Creation of temporary lists solely for counting elements (len([...])) instead of using streaming or direct arithmetic.
Presence of heavy conditional logic around a simple rounding decision.
Need to meet strict time limits for large n (e.g., up to 10^5–10^6 elements).
pitfalls: Behavioral change in rounding semantics: Python's round() uses bankers rounding (ties to even), whereas the original code used custom logic (floor for <=0.5 except a special mean==0.5 tie-breaking rule using majority). This can produce different results for .5 cases.
Reliance on eval(input()) remains; while not a performance issue here, it is unsafe and unnecessary for pure integer inputs (int(input()) is preferable).

Both versions allocate a full list for squared differences; for extremely large n and tight memory constraints, using a generator in sum (sum((x - m) ** 2 for x in arr)) would reduce peak memory usage.
If the problem specification required the original bespoke rounding rule, the simplified round() approach may be logically incorrect despite being faster.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical of AtCoder-style problem (sum over i=1..N with inner loop ~log K). N up to about 1e5, K up to about 1e9; single test case.

dominant_ops: For each i from 1..N, repeatedly double a value until it reaches at least K, adjusting a probability factor each time; this inner while loop runs O(log K) times for small i.

complexity.why: Outer for-loop over var_3 runs N times (1..var_5). For each iteration, the while loop doubles var_2 until var_2 >= var_4. Starting from var_3, the number of doublings is about ceil(log2(var_4 / var_3)) when var_3 < var_4, which is at most O(log K) where K ≈ var_4. Summed over all i, worst case is Θ(N log K). Only a few scalar variables are used, so space is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: The inner while loop `while var_2 < var_4: var_2 *= 2; var_6 /= 2` executes up to O(log K) times per outer iteration, making the total runtime O(N log K).
Repeated floating-point division `var_6 /= 2` and the initial `var_6 = 1 / var_5` occur every iteration; the division inside the while loop is particularly frequent.
Using the built-in `input()` for reading can be slower than `sys.stdin.readline()` in tight time limits, though this is a constant-factor issue.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the same probabilistic simulation structure but reduce constant factors: faster input via sys.stdin, avoid some divisions by using a multiplicative accumulator (var_7 *= 0.5) and moving the division by N outside the inner while loop.

complexity.why: The modified code still has an outer loop over i=1..N and, for i < K, an inner loop doubling the value until it reaches K. The number of doublings per such i is still O(log K), so the asymptotic time complexity remains O(N log K). Memory usage is still constant, with only a fixed number of scalar variables.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log K) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N log K) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexities are unchanged; improvements are only in constant factors (I/O and arithmetic organization).

transformation_steps: Replaced `input()` with `sys.stdin.readline` to reduce input overhead.
Reordered variable roles but preserved the structure: var_2 (N), var_1 (K) instead of var_5, var_4.
Introduced an accumulator `var_7` initialized to 1, multiplied by 0.5 in each inner-loop step instead of doing division on `var_6`.
Moved the division by N (`/ var_2`) outside the inner while loop so it is done once per outer iteration (`var_5 += var_7 / var_2`) instead of repeatedly adjusting a fraction inside the loop.
Added a guard `if var_3 < var_1:` to skip the inner while loop entirely when the index is already >= K, clarifying control flow; in the original code, the while condition covered this implicitly.
trigger_signals: Presence of a nested loop where the inner loop’s iterations depend on logarithmic growth (`var_2 *= 2` in a while condition).
Use of `input()` in a problem likely to have up to 1e5 iterations, where faster I/O is often preferred.
Repeated floating-point divisions inside a tight loop (`var_6 /= 2`).
Same algorithmic structure in both versions, indicating that performance changes are targeted at constants rather than big-O improvements.
pitfalls: Both versions rely on floating-point arithmetic for probabilities; large N or deep inner loops can accumulate rounding error, though typical constraints make this acceptable.

Using 0.5 multiplication instead of division by 2 is numerically similar but still subject to floating-point precision limits; an exact rational or logarithm-based approach would be more precise but is not used here.
Assuming that replacing `input()` with `sys.stdin.readline()` meaningfully changes big-O is incorrect; it only affects constant factors.

Further optimization (e.g., replacing the inner loop with `t = ceil(log2(K/i))` and computing `0.5**t`) would change constants but might not be necessary and can introduce overhead from math operations if not carefully implemented.

constraints_guess.notes: Single query with two integers (N, M). Pattern matches combinatorics-on-prime-factorization problems (e.g., N up to around 1e7, M up to around 1e12). The slow solution’s O(N) factorial precomputation strongly suggests N can be large enough that linear precompute is a bottleneck, while the number of binomial evaluations is small (number of distinct prime factors of M).

dominant_ops: Global precomputation of factorials and modular inverses up to N+100 in func_3, followed by O(1) binomial evaluations for each prime exponent.

complexity.why: func_3(var_3 + 100, MOD) runs a loop from 2 to N+100, performing several modular multiplications per iteration to fill factorial, inverse, and inverse-factorial arrays (var_8, var_10, var_7). Prime factorization of M via trial division is O(sqrt(M)), but is typically dominated by the O(N) precompute when N is large. The binomial calls themselves are O(1) each, using precomputed factorials.

bottlenecks.detail: func_3 builds factorial and inverse arrays up to N+100 regardless of how large the exponents e of primes in M actually are. The number and size of required combinations depends on the sum of exponents of M (typically small), not on N itself.

Arrays var_8 (factorials), var_7 (inverse factorials), and var_10 (modular inverses) all grow to size O(N). For large N this increases memory footprint and cache misses, and can trigger Python-level overhead in list growth and indexing.

The O(N) precomputation loop in pure Python performs multiple big-integer modular arithmetic operations each iteration. For N on the order of millions, this loop dominates runtime more than the relatively cheap sqrt(M) factorization and few binomial evaluations.

The code prepares to handle combinations up to N+100 even though the largest n in C(n, k) is only (N - 1 + max_exponent(M)), and max_exponent(M) is at most log2(M), which is usually tiny relative to N.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial/inverse precomputation and instead compute each binomial coefficient C(n, k) on demand via an O(k) multiplicative formula. Since the exponents of primes in M are small, this drastically reduces total work compared to an O(N) precompute.

complexity.why: Prime factorization of M by trial division up to sqrt(M) is O(sqrt(M)). For each prime exponent e in the factorization of M, func_2 computes C(N-1+e, e) via two loops of length min(e, n-e), so O(e) per exponent. The sum of exponents e over all primes dividing M is at most log2(M) (and typically much less), so total cost of binomial computations is small. No arrays of size O(N) are allocated; only a few scalar integers are used, so space is O(1) beyond the factors dictionary.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(N + sqrt(M)), Space: O(N) due to factorial/inverse precompute up to N+100.
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(sqrt(M) + sum_e e), Space: O(1) using per-query multiplicative binomial computation.
complexity_delta.note: When N is large and M’s prime exponents are small (sum_e e ≪ N), eliminating the O(N) factorial precomputation yields a substantial speedup and memory reduction. The cost shifts from N-dependent to exponent-dependent, which better matches the actual scale of required combinatorial computations.

transformation_steps: Remove the global factorial, inverse, and inverse-factorial arrays (var_8, var_10, var_7) and their O(N) initialization in func_3.
