Replace factorial-based binomial evaluation func_1(N, K, MOD) = fact[N] * invfact[K] * invfact[N-K] % MOD with a multiplicative implementation that computes C(n, k) using: result = prod_{i=0..k-1} (n - i) / (i + 1) mod MOD, implemented as integer multiplications followed by integer divisions before taking modulo.
Keep the prime factorization strategy (func_4 / func_1 in fast_code) but factor M into primes once and compute exponents e for each prime.
For each (prime, exponent) pair, compute C(N-1+e, e) via the new multiplicative combinator and multiply it into the running answer modulo 1e9+7.
Ensure that at each multiplication step you take modulo 1e9+7 to keep numbers within reasonable size, as in the fast_code’s loop updating var_1.
trigger_signals: Observation that factorial/inverse arrays are sized in proportion to N, while the number of binomial evaluations is bounded by the number of distinct prime factors of M and the exponent sizes, which are much smaller.
Runtime dominated by a single large Python for-loop over range(2, N+100), with line-level profiling or timing indicating func_3 consumes most of the execution time.
Memory profiling or inspection shows large global lists (var_8, var_7, var_10) whose size scales with N, even though the rest of the algorithm only needs a handful of binomial values.
Knowledge that multiplicative binomial formulas are competitive or superior when the number of queries is small and k (or exponents) stay modest, avoiding the overhead of full factorial tables.
pitfalls: {'kind': 'performance-regression-if-exponents-large', 'detail': 'The multiplicative nCk implementation runs in O(k). If the exponents e can be large (e.g., comparable to N), this approach could become slower than a factorial-based method. The refactor assumes that sum_e e is small relative to N.'}

{'kind': 'integer-division-ordering', 'detail': 'The fast_code computes products and integer divisions in Python before applying modulo. This relies on the exact arithmetic of Python integers. Reordering operations or taking modulo too early could break correctness because modular division is not the same as integer division. The pattern used—compute the exact binomial as an integer then apply % MOD—is safe as long as intermediate integers fit in memory.'}

{'kind': 'maintaining-modulo-correctness', 'detail': 'If one tries to mix modular inverses into the multiplicative formula to keep numbers smaller, it is easy to introduce mistakes (e.g., forgetting to precompute inverses or using non-coprime denominators). If the problem were changed to require many binomial queries over varying n and k, the lack of factorial precomputation would become a bottleneck; in such cases, reverting to an O(N) precompute might be beneficial.'}

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style problem: count numbers in [1, N] whose decimal representation has odd length. N is likely up to 1e5–1e7; solution is linear in N with small per-element work.

dominant_ops: Per-number digit counting via explicit Python while-loop with division and floor-division
Function calls (func_1) inside the main for-loop over the entire range [1, N]

complexity.why: For each integer k in [1, N], func_1 performs a loop that divides k by 10 until it becomes < 1. This takes O(d) operations where d ≈ floor(log10(k)) + 1, so total cost is sum_{k=1..N} O(log k) = O(N log N). Only a constant number of integer variables are maintained, so space is O(1).

bottlenecks.detail: Digit length is computed via a Python-level while-loop using repeated division (var_4 / 10 and var_4 // 10), resulting in ~O(log10(k)) interpreted operations per number.
The loop condition uses float division (var_4 / 10 >= 1) instead of integer comparison (var_4 >= 10). This introduces unnecessary float operations and conversions on every iteration of func_1.
func_1 is called once per number in [1, N]. This adds Python function call overhead N times, exacerbating the cost of the inner digit-counting loop.

Effective nested loops: outer for-loop over N numbers, inner while-loop over O(log10(k)) digit divisions. This leads to large interpreter overhead even though the asymptotic complexity is acceptable for moderate N.
Use of eval(input()) instead of int(input()) is unsafe and slower, although its performance impact is negligible compared to the digit-counting loop.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace the explicit Python-level digit-counting loop with Python's built-in string conversion and len() to obtain the number of digits in C-optimized code, keeping the outer loop but dramatically reducing per-iteration overhead.

complexity.why: For each integer k in [1, N], str(k) creates a string whose length is the number of digits d ≈ floor(log10(k)) + 1; len(str(k)) is O(d). Summed over k in [1, N], this is O(N log N) total work. No extra data structures proportional to N are stored, only a few scalar variables, so space remains O(1). The key improvement is a much smaller constant factor due to C-level loops inside str() and len().

complexity_delta.from: O(N log N) time, O(1) space, with heavy Python-level per-digit operations and function call overhead
complexity_delta.to: O(N log N) time, O(1) space, using C-implemented string conversion and length computation to reduce constant factors
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged, but the constant factor is significantly reduced by moving digit-processing work from Python loops to optimized C code.

transformation_steps: Inline digit-count computation: remove func_1 and compute the digit count directly inside the main loop.
Replace repeated division-based digit counting with len(str(var_3)), leveraging CPython's efficient integer-to-string conversion and C-level length computation.
Change the parity check from 'func_1(var_2) % 2 == 1' to 'len(str(var_3)) % 2 != 0', which is logically equivalent but operates on the new digit-length method.
Eliminate per-iteration function call overhead by removing func_1; digit length is now computed inline without Python call overhead.
Slightly simplify variable handling by reading input directly into var_1 and using var_2 as the counter, though this is stylistic rather than performance-critical.
Keep the loop bounds and overall counting logic identical so that the observable behavior (count of numbers with odd digit length) remains the same.
trigger_signals: Presence of an outer loop over all integers up to N combined with an inner while-loop that processes each digit of the number.
Use of repeated division and floor-division inside Python-level loops for a task (digit counting) that has well-known, efficient builtin alternatives.
Use of a helper function in the hot path (called N times) whose body is very small and consists only of simple arithmetic, suggesting that overhead dominates.
Potential timeouts or slow execution when N is near the upper bound, due to the effective nested loop structure.
Opportunity recognized to replace Python loops with builtins (str, len) that are implemented in optimized C and reduce interpreter overhead.
pitfalls: Although faster in practice, the string-based approach still has O(N log N) time complexity; if N is extremely large (e.g., 1e9), a true O(1) mathematical counting formula over digit ranges would be necessary to avoid TLE.
Repeated creation of strings for each integer allocates many temporary objects; while acceptable for typical competitive-programming constraints, it can create GC pressure for very large N.
Use of eval(input()) in the original code is unsafe and unnecessary; the modified code correctly uses int(input()) but retaining eval would pose both security and minor performance concerns.
If the problem used a different base or allowed leading zeros, len(str(k)) would no longer correspond directly to the intended digit count; assumptions about representation must be consistent.

Relying solely on big-O notation may hide that both versions are O(N log N); the benefit here is entirely from constant-factor reduction via C-implemented operations, which should not be mistaken for an asymptotic improvement.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical Lunlun-number problem: input is one integer N (up to about 1e5). Need to output the N-th number in a specially defined digit sequence.

dominant_ops: Repeated heap operations (heappop/heappush) on potentially many duplicate values
Frequent membership checks and insertions into a Python set
Per-element int<->str conversions and string concatenations to build next numbers
Final conversion of set to list and full sort of all generated numbers

complexity.time: O(P log P + N log N)
complexity.why: Let N be the requested index and P be the total number of heap pops (including duplicates). The loop continues until about N+O(1) distinct numbers are found, but it may perform many extra heap pops for duplicates. Each pop/push is O(log H) where H is heap size (Θ(P)), yielding O(P log P). Each unique number also incurs string processing cost. After the loop, all distinct numbers (~Θ(N)) are copied into a list and sorted, adding O(N log N). Memory is dominated by storing all visited numbers in the set plus heap elements, giving O(P) space.

bottlenecks.detail: Generates numbers in a complex way from both first and last digits, creating many duplicates and unnecessary candidates; relies on a set to deduplicate and a final global sort, instead of directly generating the sequence in the needed order.
Using a min-heap with a large number of duplicate entries leads to many wasted pop operations that do not advance progress (they are immediately skipped due to set membership).
Each processed number is converted to a string, indexed, and then turned back into integers via string concatenation, adding heavy overhead in Python for every node expansion.
After generation, it converts the whole set to a list and sorts it, which is an O(N log N) step that is avoidable if the sequence is produced in order.
The loop condition `while var_3 + 100 >= 0` is indirect and allows many redundant heap pops over duplicates; effective work is not tightly coupled to N.

FastAudit.core_idea: Model the Lunlun numbers as a breadth-first traversal over a digit graph: start from 1..9, repeatedly pop the smallest-depth number, and push extensions formed by appending digits that differ by at most 1 from the last digit. The BFS order directly corresponds to the required sequence order, so the N-th popped value is the answer without any sorting or deduplication.

complexity.why: Each iteration dequeues exactly one sequence element and enqueues at most 3 new candidates based on the last digit. There are Θ(N) iterations to reach the N-th number, and each operation (modulo, multiplication, queue put/get) is O(1). No sorting or deduplication is needed because BFS inherently generates values in the correct order. The queue size is proportional to the frontier of the BFS, which is O(N) in the worst case.

complexity_delta.from: Roughly O(P log P + N log N) time and O(P) space with many redundant heap operations and a final sort over ~N elements.
complexity_delta.to: O(N) time and O(N) space, with strictly one primary operation per sequence element via BFS over a queue.
complexity_delta.note: The main win is eliminating duplicates, string-heavy generation, and global sorting by switching from a heap+set+sort pipeline to a linear BFS that emits the sequence in-order.

transformation_steps: Interpret the problem as generating a sequence where each number’s valid successors are defined solely by its last digit (difference at most 1), not by both first and last digits.
Replace the priority queue (heap) with a FIFO queue implementing pure BFS from the initial digits 1..9.

Remove the visited set and deduplication logic, because BFS from these roots with the given transition guarantees each number is produced exactly once in growing 'length then lexicographic' order appropriate for the target sequence.
Eliminate all int<->str conversions; compute the next numbers using arithmetic on the last digit: last = x % 10, then push x*10 + (last-1/last/last+1) when in range.
Drop the final set-to-list conversion and sort; instead, maintain a running count of popped values from the queue and stop when reaching the N-th pop, printing it directly.
trigger_signals: Use of a heap combined with a visited set and a final sort for what is conceptually a simple incremental sequence generation problem.
Frequent int-to-string and string-to-int conversions inside the innermost loop, which are known hotspots in Python.
Presence of many duplicates in the heap (condition `if var_9 in var_5: continue` being hit often), indicating wasted work.
Loop condition that is not tightly N-bounded (`while var_3 + 100 >= 0`), suggesting the number of iterations may significantly exceed the desired sequence length.
Postprocessing step that sorts all generated candidates just to select the k-th element, instead of generating elements directly in sorted/sequence order.
pitfalls: Assuming a priority queue is needed just because numbers should be in increasing order; for this sequence, BFS over a simple queue already yields the correct order.
Overusing deduplication with sets when the underlying graph/traversal can be structured to avoid generating duplicates in the first place.
Relying on string manipulation for digit operations instead of arithmetic, which is substantially slower in Python at scale.
Adding an extra global sort step at the end of generation, which both increases time complexity and memory usage unnecessarily.
Using indirect or slack loop conditions that break the tight coupling between N and the total work performed, making performance harder to reason about and more likely to exceed limits.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: given N and M, count the number of ways to write M as a product of N positive integers. M is likely <= 1e9~1e12 so that trial division up to sqrt(M) is feasible; N is up to around 1e4. Single test case.

dominant_ops: Trial division prime factorization of M up to floor(sqrt(M)) with repeated division and Counter updates
Initialization of a general combinatorics class (Class_1) that likely precomputes factorials and inverse factorials up to some MAX = O(N + total_exponent)
Use of layered input helpers and eval-based integer parsing in func_1/func_2 introducing extra overhead

complexity.why: func_9 factors M by testing all integers up to sqrt(M): this is O(sqrt(M)) divisions. The partially shown Class_1 pattern matches a standard combinatorics helper that precomputes factorials/inverses up to self.MAX, which costs O(MAX) time and space. MAX is typically chosen as N plus the sum of prime exponents or another upper bound on n in nCk, so factorial precomputation adds O(MAX) time and memory even though only a handful of combinations are actually needed.

bottlenecks.detail: Precomputing full factorial and inverse factorial tables in Class_1 up to MAX for modular combinations, even though the problem only needs combinations C(e+N-1, e) for very small e (sum of exponents is O(log M)). This injects an O(MAX) cost independent of the actual number of combinations evaluated.

Large template with many generic helpers (multi-dimensional list builders, multiple YES/NO printers, eval-based input conversion) that are unused or heavier than necessary for a single small computation; this inflates constant factors and obscures the core logic.
Use of eval in func_1 to parse integers is slower and riskier than direct int() conversion; though likely not asymptotically dominant, it adds avoidable overhead in tight timing environments.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the structure of the problem directly: factorize M into primes, count exponents e_p, and use stars-and-bars. The number of ways to distribute exponent e over N factors is C(e + N - 1, e). Compute prime exponents with straightforward trial division and evaluate each needed combination with a simple multiplicative nCk routine whose cost is proportional to the small exponent e, avoiding any large factorial precomputation.

complexity.why: func_2 performs trial division: for each integer d from 2 to floor(sqrt(M)), it divides out d as many times as possible. This is O(sqrt(M)) operations in the worst case. The exponents e_p obtained satisfy sum_e = O(log M). For each exponent e, func_1 computes C(e + N - 1, e) via a multiplicative loop of length e-1, so total combination cost is O(sum_e). The factorization result is stored as a list and then counted by Counter, which uses O(number_of_distinct_primes) additional space.

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(M) + MAX) time, O(MAX) space (factorization plus global factorial/inverse precomputation for combinations)
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + log M) time, O(number_of_distinct_primes) space (factorization plus direct multiplicative nCk on small exponents)
complexity_delta.note: The asymptotic term sqrt(M) from trial division is unchanged, but the combinatorial part shrinks from an O(MAX) precomputation to O(sum_e) ~ O(log M). For the given constraints, this materially improves constants and eliminates unnecessary memory use.

transformation_steps: Remove the general-purpose combinatorics class and any global factorial/inverse factorial precomputation; instead, compute only the specific combinations needed on the fly.

Replace generic nCk infrastructure with a direct multiplicative combination function that runs in O(k) where k is the small exponent e in C(e+N-1, e), applying the modulus at each multiplication to control intermediate sizes.
Keep the straightforward trial-division factorization of M, but streamline the data path: return a flat list of prime factors, then use Counter to obtain exponents.
Simplify input handling by reading the two integers directly with input().split() and int(), avoiding layers of wrapper functions and eval.

Eliminate unused helpers (multi-dimensional list constructors, multiple YES/NO printing functions, recursion-limit tweaks) from the hot path so the code is lean and easier for the interpreter to optimize.
trigger_signals: Profiler or manual timing shows a disproportionate amount of time spent in combinatorics helper initialization (__init__) and factorial precomputation relative to the small number of combinations actually evaluated.
Constraints indicate that the exponents of the prime factors of M are small (sum_e = O(log M)), so a heavy general-purpose nCk implementation is unnecessary.
Memory usage or startup time appears high despite a single simple test case, suggesting large global arrays (factorials, inverse factorials) are being allocated.
Code complexity is high relative to the mathematical structure of the solution (stars and bars with small k), indicating that a simpler direct implementation is possible.
pitfalls: When replacing factorial-based nCk with a multiplicative formula, it is easy to introduce off-by-one errors in the loop bounds or to swap n and k; thorough small-test checking is needed.
Each multiplication in the direct nCk computation must be reduced modulo 1e9+7, otherwise intermediate integers can grow large and slow down execution even in Python.

Trial division factorization works comfortably only if M’s upper bound keeps sqrt(M) within time limits; if constraints were tighter (e.g., M up to 1e12 with many test cases), a more advanced factoring method or precomputed primes might be required.

If the problem were extended to multiple test cases, naive recomputation of combinations per test could become expensive; in that scenario, some level of shared precomputation (e.g., factorials up to a true global maximum) might be beneficial again.

Care must be taken that the integer division in the multiplicative nCk (var_3 // var_4) is exact at each step; the implementation assumes the classic product formula where intermediate division is safe.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic AtCoder-style problem: given N and M, factorize M and compute product over prime exponents e of C(e+N-1, e) mod 1e9+7. M is likely up to around 1e9–1e12 so trial division up to sqrt(M) is acceptable. N up to about 1e5 is implied by precomputing factorial tables of size N+O(1).

dominant_ops: Trial division prime factorization of M (while var_5**2 <= var_9)
Repeated calls to math.factorial on large arguments (up to ~N + max_exponent)
Big-integer multiplications/divisions when computing factorials and binomial coefficients in full integer arithmetic

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + P * F(K)), where P is number of distinct prime factors of M (<= ~log M), K ≈ N + max_exponent, and F(K) is the cost of computing factorials on K-sized big integers (superlinear in K; practically near O(K^2) operations with growing integer sizes). Overall effectively much worse than O(N * sqrt(M)) for N ~ 1e5.
complexity.space: O(P + U * log K), where U is the number of distinct factorial arguments cached in var_1 (up to O(N)), and each factorial value is a huge integer with O(K log K) bits. This leads to very large memory usage for N around 1e5.
complexity.why: Factorization itself is fine (O(sqrt(M))) and similar in both codes. The bottleneck is computing factorials as exact Python integers for arguments up to ~N+e (N as large as 1e5) multiple times, and then dividing these huge integers for binomials before taking modulo. math.factorial grows extremely fast in both value size and computation cost; storing all those full-precision factorial values in a dict causes large time and memory overhead. No modular reduction is applied during factorial computation, so intermediate integers can have tens or hundreds of thousands of bits.

bottlenecks.detail: Binomial coefficients are computed via full integer factorials: C(a, b) = factorial(a) // (factorial(a-b) * factorial(b)), with all factorials computed as big integers and only then reduced modulo 1e9+7. This is asymptotically and practically far slower than doing all operations modulo a prime and using precomputed factorials and inverse factorials.

In func_2, membership checks use `if var_5 in list(var_11.keys()):` which constructs a list of keys on every iteration and then performs a linear search. This converts an intended O(1) dict membership into O(K) per check, where K is the current number of distinct factors. While K is small here, this is still an unnecessary inefficiency.

Using math.factorial without modular reduction produces extremely large integers (size ~K log K bits). Repeated multiplications and integer divisions on such large values dominate CPU time and increase memory pressure.

Even with caching in var_1, factorial arguments span many values (e.g., all integers up to N+max_exponent). Computing and storing factorial(k) individually for many k duplicates work compared to a single incremental precomputation of factorials up to max K.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the same mathematical formula but compute binomial coefficients efficiently under modulo arithmetic. Factor M by trial division to get exponents e_i. Precompute factorials and inverse factorials modulo 1e9+7 up to about N + max(e_i). Then compute each C(N + e_i - 1, e_i) as fac[N+e_i-1] * inv_fac[N-1] * inv_fac[e_i] mod MOD in O(1) per exponent using Fermat's little theorem for modular inverses. This avoids huge integers and replaces many expensive factorial calls with a single linear precomputation.

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + N + log MOD). Factorization of M by trial division is O(sqrt(M)). Precomputing factorial and inverse factorial arrays of size O(N) is O(N). Modular exponentiation to obtain the inverse of fac[-1] is O(log MOD). Each combination evaluation is O(1), and there are at most O(log M) such evaluations.
complexity.space: O(N). Two arrays of size about N+50 are stored: one for factorials (var_7) and one for inverse factorials (var_6). The list of exponents var_5 has size O(log M). All arithmetic is modulo 1e9+7, so integer sizes remain bounded.
complexity.why: Modular factorial precomputation leverages the recurrence fac[i+1] = fac[i]*(i+1) mod MOD, allowing us to compute all factorials up to N+max_exponent in a single linear pass. Inverse factorials are computed from fac[max]^{-1} via a backward linear pass using inv_fac[i-1] = inv_fac[i]*i mod MOD. This converts repeated heavy factorial calls on large integers into cheap table lookups and a few modular multiplications, which are constant-time on typical hardware.

complexity_delta.from: Time dominated by repeated big-integer factorial computations and divisions: effectively superlinear in N with very large constants, on top of O(sqrt(M)) factorization; memory dominated by storing huge factorial values as big integers (up to O(N * K log K) bits).
complexity_delta.to: Time reduced to O(sqrt(M) + N + log MOD) with small constants, using only modular arithmetic and O(N) memory for factorial tables.
complexity_delta.note: The critical change is computing all combinatorial values via precomputed factorials and inverse factorials modulo 1e9+7 instead of raw integer factorials and exact integer division.

transformation_steps: Preserve the mathematical structure: the result is the product over prime exponents e of C(N + e - 1, e) modulo 1e9+7. Only the method of computing C is changed.

Replace the on-demand big-integer factorial calls with a single precomputation of factorials modulo MOD up to at least N + max_exponent. In code B, a safe bound N+50 is used, exploiting that for the given constraints the sum of exponents of M is small (e.g., <= ~30).
Introduce an array var_7 where var_7[i] = i! mod MOD, built iteratively: var_7[i+1] = var_7[i] * (i+1) % MOD. This costs O(N) time and O(N) space.

Compute inverse factorials via Fermat's little theorem: first compute inv_fac[max] = fac[max]^(MOD-2) mod MOD using fast exponentiation, then fill inv_fac[i-1] = inv_fac[i] * i % MOD in a backward pass. This yields all factorial inverses in O(N + log MOD) time.
Implement binomial coefficients using the identity C(a, b) = fac[a] * inv_fac[b] * inv_fac[a-b] mod MOD. This gives O(1) time per binomial evaluation with no large integers.
Simplify dictionary usage in factorization: instead of storing a map from prime to exponent, store just the exponents list (var_5). This avoids the `list(keys)` overhead and simplifies iteration.
Avoid any full-precision integer division in the main combinatorial computation; all operations are modular multiplications and exponentiations with bounded integer sizes.
trigger_signals: Use of math.factorial on arguments as large as N+e without any intermediate modular reduction.
Very large intermediate integers (factorials of size up to (N+e)! for N around 10^5).
Repeated computation of factorials for many closely spaced arguments instead of a single incremental precomputation.
Integer division of huge factorial products to form binomial coefficients before taking modulo.
Unnecessary `list(dict.keys())` calls in tight loops, indicating non-O(1) membership checks.
pitfalls: Ensuring the factorial and inverse factorial arrays are large enough: they must cover indices up to max(N + e_i - 1). Using N+50 assumes constraints that guarantee sum of exponents is small; for more general problems, one should compute or bound max_e explicitly.
Off-by-one errors in factorial and inverse factorial index computations when translating C(a, b) into fac/ifac accesses (e.g., ensuring fac[a], inv_fac[b], inv_fac[a-b] are all in range).
Relying on Fermat's little theorem requires MOD to be prime; here 1_000_000_007 is prime, but this approach would fail for composite moduli.
Handling edge cases such as M = 1 (no prime factors, result should be 1) or very small N correctly in the combinatorial formula.
Maintaining mod reduction at every multiplication to avoid integer growth and prevent overflow in languages without big-int support (Python is safe but slower with large ints if mod is not applied).

constraints_guess.notes: Two integers N, M. N can be as large as 1e9 (cannot precompute factorials up to N). M up to about 1e9–1e12 (prime factorization with sqrt(M) loop is acceptable). Single test case.

dominant_ops: Precomputation of factorials and modular inverses up to N+100 under modulo 1e9+7
Trial division prime factorization of M up to sqrt(M)

complexity.why: The loop `for var_8 in range(2, var_2 + 100 + 1)` builds factorial (`var_6`) and inverse factorial (`var_7`) arrays up to size ~N, which dominates when N is large. Factorization via trial division is O(sqrt(M)), but for the intended constraints this is much smaller than N.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorials and inverse factorials are precomputed up to N+100 even though only combinations C(N+e-1, N-1) for small exponents e (sum of exponents is O(log M)) are needed. For N up to 1e9 this is impossible in time and memory.
Arrays `var_6`, `var_7`, and `var_9` grow linearly with N, requiring O(N) memory. This does not fit typical limits when N can be ~1e9.
The pattern of linear factorial and modular inverse precomputation scales only to N around 1e6–1e7 in Python. Any larger N leads to TLE or MLE, making the solution invalid for high constraints.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit that the exponents in the prime factorization of M are small (sum O(log M)) and compute each binomial C(N+e-1, e) with a direct multiplicative formula in O(e) time, avoiding any O(N) factorial or inverse-factorial precomputation. Still factor M by trial division, accumulate exponents with Counter, use exact integer arithmetic for binomials, and apply the modulo only at the end.

complexity.why: Prime factorization by trial division up to sqrt(M) is O(sqrt(M)). Each binomial coefficient C(N+e-1, e) is computed in O(e) using multiplication and division loops; the total of all exponents sum_e is O(log M) in the worst case. No work depends linearly on N, so N can be as large as ~1e9 without performance issues. Only a Counter of prime factors and a few integers are stored, giving O(#prime_factors(M)) space.

complexity_delta.from: O(N + sqrt(M)) time, O(N) space (due to factorial and inverse-factorial precomputation up to N+100)
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + log M) time, O(#prime_factors(M)) space (no dependency on N in precomputation)
complexity_delta.note: The new code removes the linear dependence on N by avoiding global factorial tables and using a multiplicative binomial computation whose cost depends only on the (small) exponents from M’s factorization.

transformation_steps: Keep the same mathematical formulation: factor M, and for each prime factor with exponent e, multiply by C(N+e-1, e) (equivalently C(N+e-1, N-1)) under modulo 1e9+7.

Replace the prime factorization helper with a simpler function `func_2` that returns the multiset of prime factors directly (list of primes, one per occurrence), then use `collections.Counter` to aggregate exponents.
Remove global precomputation of factorials and modular inverses (`var_6`, `var_7`, `var_9`) that iterated up to N+100.

Introduce a direct combinatorial helper `func_1(n, k)` computing C(n, k) by multiplicative formula: multiply n * (n-1) * ... * (n-k+1) and then divide by 1 * 2 * ... * k, using exact integer arithmetic; apply symmetry k = min(k, n-k) to reduce loop length.
Apply modulo 1e9+7 only to the final product (and implicitly via Python’s big integers during intermediate steps), eliminating modular inverses and modular factorial arithmetic.
Retain the overall result aggregation loop: for each exponent e in the factorization, update the answer with C(N+e-1, e), then output the result modulo 1e9+7.
trigger_signals: N appears only as a parameter of binomial coefficients, but the original implementation builds factorial tables up to N+100, which is infeasible for N as large as 1e9.
Typical problem pattern (-style factorization/combinations) indicates that the sum of exponents of M is small (O(log M)), suggesting that per-exponent work, not per-N work, is sufficient.
Memory growth O(N) in arrays `var_6`, `var_7`, and `var_9` is incompatible with large N constraints and is clearly unnecessary given only a handful of binomial evaluations.
The combination values C(N+e-1, e) are exactly integers; therefore, a multiplicative formula without modular inverses is safe and can avoid expensive modular precomputation.
pitfalls: When using the multiplicative binomial computation, it is crucial to operate in exact integer arithmetic (no floating point) and ensure that the divisions are exact at each step; Python’s big integers guarantee this as long as the combinatorial identity is correct.

The new approach applies the modulo only at the end. While safe for Python due to arbitrary-precision integers and small total exponents, in other languages or with larger exponents this might cause overflow and would require modular multiplication with modular inverses instead.

The factorization routine must handle the case M == 1: the factor list is empty, Counter is empty, and the neutral element 1 should be returned as the final product. The provided fast code does this correctly because it initializes the result as 1 and multiplies over an empty collection.

For problems where M can be extremely large (e.g., > 1e12), trial division up to sqrt(M) may become the bottleneck; a more advanced factorization algorithm might then be required, but this is consistent with the original solution’s complexity assumptions.

Care must be taken not to reintroduce an implicit O(N) dependency—for example, by attempting to precompute factorials for modular binomials again. The key is to keep all combinatorial work dependent only on the small exponents from M’s factorization.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder DP with two sequence lengths n=var_3, m=var_1. Overall algorithm is O(n*m) with a full (n+1)*(m+1) DP table. Practical n,m likely up to ~2000 so that n*m≈4e6 cells is just acceptable in Python if inner loops are in C (NumPy), but borderline with pure Python nested loops.

dominant_ops: Double nested Python loops over i in [0..var_3-1] and j in [0..var_1-1]
Per-iteration list indexing and assignment on 2D Python lists var_5 and var_6
Per-iteration integer arithmetic (+, -, %) in Python (big-int semantics)
Per-iteration branch on value comparison var_9[var_7] != var_10[var_8]

complexity.why: The algorithm fills two (n+1) x (m+1) tables (var_5 and var_6). Each of the n*m cells is computed exactly once via constant-time operations, for total O(n*m) time. Space is proportional to the number of DP cells stored, i.e., (n+1)*(m+1) = O(n*m).

bottlenecks.detail: The core DP is implemented with explicit Python for-loops: for var_7 in range(var_3): and inner for var_8 in range(var_1):. Each of the n*m iterations incurs Python interpreter overhead, which dominates when n*m is on the order of millions.

Within the inner loop, multiple integer operations (+, -, %) are performed per cell update: var_6[...] = var_6[...] + var_6[...] - var_6[...] + var_5[...]; and then modulo. Python integers are arbitrary-precision, so these operations are relatively expensive compared to fixed-width arithmetic in C.

Accesses like var_6[var_7][var_8 + 1], var_6[var_7 + 1][var_8], var_6[var_7][var_8] are nested list lookups (outer list -> inner list) for each cell. This repeated indirect addressing adds overhead on top of the loop cost.
The if var_9[var_7] != var_10[var_8]: branch executes in the innermost loop, introducing mispredicted branches and additional Python-level work for every of the n*m iterations.
The modulo operation var_6[var_7 + 1][var_8 + 1] %= var_2 is done inside the inner loop per cell. Modulo with a large integer modulus is comparatively expensive.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the same O(n*m) DP recurrence but push the inner loop into optimized C code using NumPy. For each row i, compute matches against all columns j at once via a boolean vector (var_7 = var_6[var_5] == var_8). Use array slicing and masked assignment to update the matching positions in the new row from the previous row (shifting by one). Then compute the required prefix-sum DP transition along the row using NumPy's cumsum, which runs in C over contiguous memory. This removes Python from the n*m critical path and replaces it with a small Python loop over rows (O(n)), with each row handled in vectorized O(m) fashion by NumPy.

complexity.why: The fast version still processes an (n+1) x (m+1) DP table (var_4). Each row is updated once using vectorized operations: one equality comparison over length m, one masked assignment, and one cumulative sum over m entries. These are all O(m) in C per row, so total time is O(n*m). Memory remains proportional to the DP table size, O(n*m), stored as a NumPy array of int64.

complexity_delta.from: O(n*m) time in pure Python loops with large constant factors; O(n*m) memory in nested lists of Python ints.
complexity_delta.to: O(n*m) time with inner work performed in optimized C (NumPy), drastically reducing constant factors; O(n*m) memory in a contiguous NumPy int64 array.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged (still O(n*m)), but the constant factor improvement from eliminating Python-level work in the inner loop is large enough to cross typical AtCoder time limits for n,m up to ~2000.

transformation_steps: Replace Python lists var_9 and var_10 with NumPy arrays (var_6 and var_8 in the fast code) to enable vectorized comparisons across an entire row.
Collapse the two DP tables (value DP and its 2D prefix-sum DP) into a single NumPy 2D array var_4 and express the recurrence in terms of row-wise prefix sums.
For each i (row index), precompute a boolean mask var_7 = (current_element_of_first_sequence == entire_second_sequence_array) to identify matching positions j in one vectorized equality operation.
Use masked assignment var_4[i+1, 1:][var_7] = var_4[i, :-1][var_7] to update all DP transition contributions for matching pairs (i,j) in a single vectorized step, rather than branching per cell.

Leverage NumPy's cumsum along the row to implement the prefix-sum-based DP transition: var_4[i+1] = (var_4[i+1].cumsum() + var_4[i]) % MOD; this encodes the same recurrence as the slow code's 2D prefix handling but in O(m) C-level operations per row.
Apply the modulus operation once per row after cumsum instead of once per cell, significantly reducing the number of expensive modulo operations.
Use fixed-width integer dtype (int64) in NumPy to ensure efficient arithmetic while keeping results safe under repeated additions before modulo.
trigger_signals: Presence of a double nested Python loop over both dimensions of the DP table (for var_7 in range(var_3): for var_8 in range(var_1):), indicating O(n*m) Python-level work.
Per-iteration arithmetic and branching (if comparison + three additions/subtractions + modulo) in the innermost loop, signaling heavy interpreter overhead.
Constraints suggesting n*m up to a few million cells, where pure Python DP is known to be borderline with typical 1–2 second limits.
DP recurrence that can be expressed using prefix sums and element-wise operations, which map naturally to NumPy's vectorized primitives (equality, masked assignment, cumulative sum).
Availability of NumPy in the environment (as evidenced by the original fast solution using import numpy as np).
pitfalls: Correctness of the vectorized DP: the transformation from the explicit 2D prefix DP (var_6) + match DP (var_5) to the single-array row-wise prefix DP must be algebraically equivalent. Any off-by-one in slicing (e.g., 1: vs :-1) or row indexing can silently produce wrong counts.

Integer overflow: although NumPy int64 can hold values well beyond 1e9+7, repeated additions without timely modulo could overflow if the DP values grow combinatorially. Ensuring dtype=int64 and applying modulo every row keeps values safe in typical constraints, but using smaller dtypes (e.g., int32) could break correctness.

Boolean masking semantics: expressions like var_4[i+1, 1:][var_7] = var_4[i, :-1][var_7] rely on NumPy's advanced indexing rules. Misunderstanding when views vs. copies are created can lead to unintentional extra allocations or no effect if a temporary copy is modified instead of the original array.

Memory footprint: storing an (n+1) x (m+1) int64 array uses about 8*(n+1)*(m+1) bytes. For larger-than-expected constraints this can become a memory issue; the pure Python version also uses O(n*m) space but with different overhead characteristics.

Modulus placement: moving from per-cell modulo to per-row modulo changes when reductions happen. For very large intermediate sums, delays in modulus application could cause overflow or performance issues; here, applying modulo once per row is safe, but extending this pattern carelessly to other problems might not be.

Environment assumptions: the fast solution depends on NumPy being available and performant. In restricted judges without NumPy, this optimization path is not applicable, and alternative micro-optimizations in pure Python would be needed.

Cache behavior and layout: NumPy uses row-major contiguous memory, so operations along the row (axis=1) are cache-friendly. Rewriting the DP to operate row-by-row is appropriate; attempting to vectorize in a column-major manner without regard to memory layout could degrade performance.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style small constraints: N items, M groups, sum of group sizes likely <= 10^4. The modified code's use of a buffer of length 10001 suggests an official upper bound around that value.

dominant_ops: Writing all group elements into a preallocated list of length 10001
Building a set from the entire 10001-element list to count distinct values

complexity.why: Let S be the total number of input integers across all groups (sum k_i). The inner for-loop writes exactly S elements into var_4. Regardless of S, set(var_4) traverses the entire list of length L=10001, hashing each element. Thus the runtime is O(S) for filling plus O(L) for constructing the set. Memory usage is dominated by the fixed-length list of size 10001.

bottlenecks.detail: var_4 is allocated with a hard-coded length of 10001: var_4 = list(int() for _ in range(10001)). When N and M are small (e.g., up to ~100), this overshoots the actual required capacity by up to two orders of magnitude, but the whole list is still processed later.

set(var_4) scans and hashes all 10001 elements, including many trailing zeros that were never overwritten by input values. For small problem sizes where N * M << 10001, this constant overhead dominates total runtime.

Using set(var_4) introduces per-element hashing and dynamic hash-table management. In this problem, the value universe is small and bounded (1..N); simple integer counting or boolean presence flags are cheaper than a set of size up to N+1.
The pattern var_4[var_9 + var_8] in a flat buffer, then a separate pass via set(var_4), results in more scattered memory access and an extra full pass compared to directly updating per-item counters.
Using eval(input()) to read an integer is slower and unnecessarily powerful compared to int(input()). While not the dominant factor here, it adds avoidable overhead inside a loop.

FastAudit.core_idea: Represent group membership as an M×N 0/1 matrix, then sum each column to count how many times each item appears, and finally count items whose column sum is zero (never selected). This avoids hashing and large overallocated buffers, and all loops are tightly bounded by the actual N and M.

complexity.why: Building the matrix var_3 requires O(MN) writes (initializing zeros) plus O(S) writes for setting ones at positions corresponding to group memberships. Summing columns is another O(MN). Counting zeros in var_4 costs O(N). For small constraints where MN <= 10^4, these nested loops are fast and involve only simple integer operations with good cache locality. Memory is O(MN) for the matrix plus O(N) for the column sums.

complexity_delta.from: O(MN + S) time, O(MN + N) space (matrix-based per-item counting)
complexity_delta.to: O(S + L) time, O(L) space with L=10001 (flat buffer + set for distinct counting)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically, both are linear in the input size, but the modified version introduces a large fixed constant L=10001 and hashing overhead. When MN is at most a few thousand, replacing MN with a fixed 10001-element scan and set construction increases the actual amount of work, making the 'optimized' version slower in practice.

transformation_steps: Replaced an explicit M×N incidence matrix (var_3) with a 1D buffer (var_4) intended to store all group elements sequentially.
Eliminated the explicit column-summing loops and the zero-counting loop, and instead used set(var_4) to obtain the number of distinct values that appeared (plus zero).
Introduced a hard-coded buffer length of 10001 for var_4 instead of sizing the data structure from N, M, or sum k_i.
Relied on the identity (N + 1) - len(set(var_4)) to compute how many values in 1..N never appeared, leveraging the fact that the buffer is initialized with zeros and zero is not in 1..N.
Kept use of eval(input()) for reading group sizes, preserving an unnecessary overhead inside the input loop.
trigger_signals: Problem constraints indicate N and M are small (M×N comfortably below 10001), so a fixed-size buffer of length 10001 is much larger than needed.
Profiling or timing shows most time is spent in set(var_4) even when the number of actual input values S is small.
The modified solution uses a hash-based set operation across a large, mostly redundant buffer, while the original uses only integer increments in nested loops.
The new approach introduces a magic constant (10001) unrelated to the input sizes, a common smell for hidden performance or correctness issues.
pitfalls: Assuming that a set-based distinct-count computation is always faster than simple counting. For small bounded universes (1..N with small N), direct counters or boolean flags per element are typically faster than constructing and hashing a large set.

Using a large fixed-size buffer (10001) instead of sizing based on actual constraints can dominate runtime via unnecessary memory scans, especially when later operations (like set()) always traverse the entire buffer.

Relying on implementation tricks like including the default zero value in the set and then adjusting with (N + 1) - len(set(...)) makes the code brittle: changing initialization, length, or domain of values can silently break correctness or performance.
Keeping eval(input()) in performance-critical code; while not the main bottleneck here, it is slower than int(input()) and unsafe in general.

Optimizing for perceived asymptotics without considering the actual constant factors and real constraint ranges; with MN small and fixed L large, the micro-optimized-looking code is empirically slower.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer input; intended to work for general positive n (likely up to around 1e9). Original slow version hard-codes powers up to 2^6, so it is probably from a small-constraint problem, but the fast version scales to large n.

dominant_ops: List comprehension to precompute small table of powers of two
Membership test `var_1 in var_2` (linear scan)
Appending to list and sorting `sorted(var_2)`
Linear search via `var_2.index(var_1)`

complexity.time: O(1) for given code (fixed list size 7); conceptually O(k log k) with k = number of precomputed powers
complexity.space: O(1) extra space (fixed-size list of powers)
complexity.why: The code constructs a constant-sized list of seven powers, does linear scans and a sort on that list. With the list size fixed, the complexity is constant, but the constant factor includes multiple passes over the list and a sort.

bottlenecks.detail: Precomputes a list of powers of two instead of computing the answer directly from n.
Sorts `var_2` on every execution even though the list is nearly sorted and of fixed structure.
Uses `in` and `index` on the list, incurring multiple O(k) scans even though a direct mathematical formula exists.
Hard-codes powers up to 2^6; for n > 64 the result is no longer guaranteed to be the largest power of two ≤ n.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical identity: largest power of two ≤ n is 2^floor(log2(n)), computed directly with `math.log2` and exponentiation.

complexity.why: The computation consists of a single logarithm call, a cast to int (floor), and one exponentiation; no auxiliary data structures or loops are used, so both time and space are constant with very small constant factors.

complexity_delta.from: O(1) with relatively high constant factor due to list creation, sorting, and repeated scans; limited correctness range.
complexity_delta.to: O(1) with a minimal constant factor using a single logarithm and exponentiation; correct for all valid n in range of data type.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is constant in both versions, but the optimized version dramatically reduces constant overhead and generalizes correctly beyond the small fixed table.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the goal is to output the greatest power of two not exceeding the input n.
Express this goal as 2^floor(log2(n)).
Replace the precomputed powers list and conditional/sorting logic with a direct computation using `math.log2(n)` and `2 ** int(math.log2(n))`.
Remove all list-related operations (comprehension, append, sort, in, index) as they are no longer needed.
trigger_signals: Presence of a hard-coded list of powers of two constructed via a loop.
Use of sorting and index search on a nearly static, tiny list.
Pattern of choosing the previous element in a sorted powers-of-two list, which matches the definition of 2^floor(log2(n)).
Problem semantics clearly mapping to a known mathematical function (log base 2).
pitfalls: Floating-point precision: `math.log2` on extremely large integers may be subject to rounding errors, potentially impacting `int(math.log2(n))` for boundary values, though typical contest ranges (≤ 1e12 or 1e18) are usually safe in Python.
Domain of log2: `math.log2` is undefined for n ≤ 0; inputs must be positive integers.
Use of `eval(input())` is unsafe and unnecessary; `int(input())` should be preferred for real-world code.
If exact integer behavior is required for very large n, an alternative is to use bit operations (e.g., bit_length) instead of floating-point logarithms.

constraints_guess.notes: Digit DP over the decimal representation of N. Let D = len(str(N)), K = given second integer. DP table size is O(D * K). Typical constraints: D, K <= ~100 so O(D*K) is fine but O(D*K*10) with heavy Python overhead can be borderline in tight limits.

dominant_ops: Four nested loops: pos (0..D-1), used_nonzero (0..K), tight_state (0..1), digit (0..9)
Per-iteration 3D list reads/writes on var_4[pos][used][tight]
Repeated conversion int(var_12[pos]) inside inner loops

complexity.why: DP state dp[pos][used_nonzero][tight] with transitions trying all 10 possible next digits for each state. D positions, K+1 counts, 2 tight states, 10 digits; 2 and 10 are constants but large enough to matter in Python due to interpreter and indexing overhead.

bottlenecks.detail: The innermost digit loop `for var_8 in range(10)` multiplies total iterations by 10 for every DP state, leading to ~10 * D * K * 2 iterations with several Python operations each.
`var_3 = int(var_12[var_5])` is recomputed for every (used_nonzero, tight_state) even though it depends only on pos; it could be hoisted out of inner loops.
Heavy use of 3D-list indexing `var_4[var_9][var_10][var_11]` in the deepest loop adds substantial interpreter overhead when executed millions of times.

FastAudit.core_idea: Recognize that the digit loop can be aggregated: instead of iterating over all 10 digits per state, group digits into classes (0, non-zero digits below the current limit digit, non-zero digits above, etc.) and update DP counts in bulk using multiplication. This removes the explicit digit loop and keeps only loops over position and used_nonzero.

complexity.why: The optimized DP still has states indexed by (pos, used_nonzero, tight), but transitions are computed with constant-time arithmetic expressions per state, without an inner loop over all 10 digits. Thus each (pos, used_nonzero, tight) combination is processed O(1) times.

delta_type: constant-factor optimization via algebraic digit-DP transition aggregation

complexity_delta.from: O(D * K * 10) time, O(D * K) space (digit-by-digit transitions)
complexity_delta.to: O(D * K) time, O(D * K) space (grouped transitions without explicit digit loop)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic Big-O remains O(D*K), but the constant factor drops by about 10x and removes much of the Python-loop overhead, which is critical under tight time limits.

transformation_steps: Identify DP state meaning: both versions use dp over (position, count_of_nonzero_digits, tight_flag). The slow version materializes all 10 next digits; the fast version infers counts combinatorially.

Classify outgoing digits from each state: for tight=0 (on the limit prefix), allowed digits are 0..current_digit, with 0 preserving nonzero count, digits 1..current_digit-1 increasing count and moving to loose state, and digit=current_digit increasing count but staying tight. For tight=1 (already below limit), digits 0..9 are always allowed and always stay loose.

Replace the explicit `for var_8 in range(10)` loop with aggregated contributions: use formulas like `*9` for the 9 non-zero digits in loose state and `*(var_7 - 1)` for digits between 1 and current_digit-1 in tight state. This directly updates dp[pos+1][new_tight][new_count] from dp[pos][tight][count].
Adjust DP array layout: fast_code uses `var_3[pos][tight][used_nonzero]` and allocates `used_nonzero` dimension of size K+2 to safely handle `+1` updates without extra bounds checks.
Remove repeated computations and simplify inner logic: compute current digit once per position, avoid per-digit comparisons, and collapse multiple similar transitions into a few arithmetic updates.
trigger_signals: Presence of a 4-deep loop with a fixed small loop bound (10) for digit iteration in Python.
Digit DP pattern where transitions can be naturally grouped into classes of digits (zero vs non-zero, below/at/above limit digit).
Performance issues or potential TLE when D and K are large enough that D*K*10 is borderline for Python.
Repetitive, structurally similar update logic inside the innermost loop, suggesting it can be algebraically summarized.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors in DP dimensions: when aggregating transitions that increase the non-zero count, ensure the DP array is sized to at least K+2 and that states exceeding K are either not updated or safely ignored.

Mis-handling tight vs loose states: when grouping transitions, it is easy to incorrectly move states from tight to loose or to omit the exact-equality digit case (digit == current_digit) that keeps tight=0.
Incorrect digit group sizes: constants like 9 (non-zero digits) or (current_digit - 1) must be applied only when current_digit > 0; otherwise they should contribute 0.
Boundary conditions at the last position: ensure that only dp[D][K][*] is summed and that intermediate over-counting does not occur when K is small relative to D.
Maintaining correctness while changing loop order: reordering indices or changing DP layout can introduce subtle bugs if initial conditions and final aggregation indices are not updated consistently.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical 'sum of digits in [A,B] for 1..N' problem (e.g., AtCoder ABC083B). N up to around 10^4–10^5, A,B small.

dominant_ops: Outer loop over all integers 0..N (range(var_6 + 1))
Inner while loop doing repeated `% 10` and `/= 10` on a float
Integer-to-float promotion and repeated floating-point division
Branch and accumulation for each i that satisfies the digit-sum condition

complexity.time: O(N * K) with K ≈ 300+ float divisions per number (effectively O(N) but with a very large constant factor)
complexity.why: For each integer var_4 in [0, var_6], the code computes a digit sum via a while loop on var_7. Because it uses `var_7 /= 10`, var_7 becomes a float. The loop condition `while var_7 != 0` keeps dividing the float by 10 until it underflows to 0.0. That takes on the order of a few hundred iterations per number, regardless of the actual digit count. Thus, the total time is linear in N with a large constant, dominated by repeated float divisions and comparisons.

bottlenecks.detail: Digit-stripping uses `var_7 /= 10` (true division) instead of `var_7 //= 10` (integer division). This converts var_7 to float and causes the while loop to continue until floating-point underflow, producing ~300+ iterations per number instead of ~digits(var_4).
The inner `while var_7 != 0` loop performs many more iterations than the number of decimal digits, multiplying work per outer iteration by a large constant factor.
Using `while var_7 != 0` on a float is fragile: floating-point values decay toward zero but only hit exactly 0.0 after many divisions and eventual underflow, not after stripping decimal digits.
Looping from 0 to N with `range(var_6 + 1)` includes 0, which contributes nothing to the sum; a smaller loop from 1 to N is slightly cheaper.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace the buggy float-based digit-stripping loop with a straightforward digit-sum computation on the string representation of each number. For each i in 1..N, convert i to string, sum its character digits, and check if the sum lies between A and B. This avoids float underflow and keeps the number of operations per i proportional to the actual digit count.

complexity.time: O(N * log10(N)) ~ O(N) for typical constraints (each number processed in time proportional to its digit length)
complexity.space: O(1) auxiliary (plus transient O(log N) per-iteration string storage)
complexity.why: The outer loop runs N times. For each i, `str(i)` creates a string of length equal to the number of digits, and the helper `func_1` loops over those characters, doing O(d) work where d = digits(i) = O(log10 N). No extra nested unbounded loops or float underflow effects are present; the digit-sum work matches the actual number of digits.

complexity_delta.from: Asymptotically O(N), but with K≈300+ floating-point iterations per number due to `while var_7 != 0` on a float, making it effectively too slow for typical N.
complexity_delta.to: O(N log N) in theory because digit count grows as log10(N), but with a small constant factor and operations tightly tied to true digit length.
complexity_delta.note: Big-O notation does not fully capture the change: the original bug introduces a huge hidden constant factor via float underflow iterations. The new approach trades this for predictable O(digits) work per number, which is far smaller for realistic N.

transformation_steps: Correct the digit-stripping logic by avoiding floating-point division. Instead of mutating a float with `/= 10` and looping until it happens to underflow to zero, compute the digit sum explicitly in a bounded loop.
Refactor digit-sum computation into a helper (func_1) that takes the string representation of the number and sums its digits, ensuring a fixed number of iterations equal to the digit length.
Change the outer loop bounds from `range(var_6 + 1)` to `range(1, var_7 + 1)` so that 0 is excluded and the input variable naming matches its semantic meaning (N).
Remove unintended reliance on floating-point behavior and underflow; operate solely on integers (or their string representations) for predictable performance.
Retain the original condition `if var_1 <= digit_sum <= var_3` and accumulation logic while making the per-number digit-sum computation efficient and well-bounded.
trigger_signals: Use of `/` instead of `//` in a loop intended to strip digits from an integer (`var_7 /= 10` instead of `var_7 //= 10`).
Loop condition `while var_7 != 0` on a variable that has become a float, potentially causing many more iterations than intended.
Unexpectedly high runtime or TLE despite apparently simple O(N) logic.
Inner loop whose iteration count does not clearly depend on the problem's natural parameter (digit count) but instead on floating-point underflow behavior.
pitfalls: Assuming `/` on integers is safe for digit stripping: in Python 3 it produces floats, not truncated integers; always use `//` for integer division.
Using equality checks `!= 0` on floats for loop termination; floating-point values may not reach exactly zero until underflow after many steps.
Believing the original code is O(N log N) with small constants when, due to float underflow, the constant factor is actually very large.

In the optimized version, repeatedly calling `str(i)` and iterating characters is fine for small to moderate N, but for very large N (e.g., 10^7 or higher) further micro-optimizations (e.g., precomputing or using integer arithmetic with `// 10`) might be preferable.
Changing range bounds (0..N to 1..N) alters which elements are considered; in this problem 0 contributes nothing so it is safe, but this kind of change must be reasoned about carefully in general.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic Lunlun-number style task (e.g., AtCoder ABC 161 D). Input is a single integer k (1-indexed), asking for the k-th positive integer whose adjacent digits differ by at most 1. k is up to about 1e5, requiring generation of ~1e5 such numbers in increasing order.

dominant_ops: Recursive DFS (func_2) exploring all valid digit-extensions up to length 10 for each starting digit 1..9
Frequent Python function calls and recursion overhead at every digit extension
Digit operations in tight loops: modulo, abs, multiplication, range(10) iteration
Appending all generated numbers to a Python list var_2
Final global sort(sorted(var_2)) over all generated numbers

complexity.time: O(T + M log M), where T is the total number of explored states in the recursive tree and M is the number of generated Lunlun numbers (up to length 10). With branching factor <= 3 and max length L=10, T and M are on the order of a few *10^5, but conceptually T = Θ(9 * B^L) with B≈3. Note that this cost is paid regardless of the input k; it does not stop early when the k-th element is reached.
complexity.space: O(M), to store all generated numbers in var_2 plus recursion call stack O(L). M is the number of Lunlun numbers of length 1..10; L=10 is small but fixed.
complexity.why: The algorithm precomputes all Lunlun numbers up to 10 digits for all starting digits 1..9, then sorts them to extract the k-th element. This means it explores the entire search space (DFS) and performs a sort, even when k is small. The recursion and Python call overhead occur at every node in the tree, and the final sort dominates once the number of generated numbers grows.

bottlenecks.detail: Generates all Lunlun numbers of length 1..10 for every run, independent of the requested index k. For small k, the majority of work is wasted; for large k, it still performs more work than needed since numbers beyond the k-th are also generated and sorted.

Calls sorted(var_2) on the full list of generated numbers. The DFS generation does not guarantee order, so a full O(M log M) sort is required, even though only the k-th smallest number is needed and generation could be done directly in sorted order.

Deep recursive calls (up to depth 10) for every path, with Python function-call overhead in the innermost loops. The use of sys.setrecursionlimit hints at concern over recursion depth and contributes additional overhead.

Inner loop over var_7 in range(10) checks all digits 0..9 then filters by abs((var_8 % 10) - var_7) < 2. This does up to 10 checks per step where only at most 3 digits are valid, increasing constant factors in the tightest loop.
Uses eval(input()) instead of int(input()), which is slower and unnecessarily powerful for reading a single integer, though this is a minor cost compared to the DFS and sort.

FastAudit.core_idea: Generate Lunlun numbers in increasing numeric order using an iterative BFS-like traversal over the current list of numbers, appending only valid next-digit extensions, and stop as soon as the list size exceeds k so that the k-th number is available without a global sort.

complexity.time: O(k * D), where D is the number of digits of the k-th Lunlun number (max about 10–11 in this problem). For each current number processed before reaching length k, the code performs O(1) work plus a small constant number of string conversions and appends. It stops early via `if len(var_4) > var_3: break` once enough numbers are generated, so work is proportional to k, not to the full precomputable universe of Lunlun numbers.
complexity.space: O(k), since var_4 stores all Lunlun numbers generated up to slightly beyond index k. No additional large structures or recursion stack are required.
complexity.why: The for-loop `for var_1 in var_4:` combined with appending to var_4 implements a natural BFS over the implicit graph of Lunlun numbers (nodes are numbers, edges are valid digit extensions). BFS from small to large numbers ensures that numbers are encountered in non-decreasing numeric order. Because this order coincides with the desired sorted order, there is no need for a final sort. The early break condition ensures that only as many nodes as necessary (k+something) are generated.

complexity_delta.from: O(T + M log M) with T, M ≈ size of full Lunlun search space up to 10 digits; cost is largely independent of k and always generates and sorts all such numbers.
complexity_delta.to: O(k * D) time and O(k) space, where work scales directly with the requested index k and avoids global sorting and full search-space enumeration.
complexity_delta.note: Conceptually, the change moves from a full DFS + sort of the entire fixed-depth search tree (with exponential dependence on max digit length L) to a BFS that directly enumerates the sequence in sorted order and stops after reaching the k-th element. For typical constraints (k up to ~1e5), this reduces constant factors significantly and eliminates the O(M log M) sort.

transformation_steps: Switched from recursive DFS (func_2) that explores all possible valid digit extensions up to fixed max length to an iterative BFS-like generation by iterating `for var_1 in var_4` while appending children.

Removed the accumulation of all candidates in a global list followed by `sorted(var_2)`, instead generating numbers in inherently sorted order via BFS over increasing-length numbers starting from 1..9.
Introduced early stopping: the BFS stops once len(var_4) exceeds the requested index var_3 (k), so no unnecessary numbers beyond the k-th are generated.

Replaced the generic `for var_7 in range(10)` + abs-check branching with direct digit-transition rules based on the last digit (0 -> {0,1}, 9 -> {8,9}, else -> {d-1,d,d+1}), lowering constant factors in the innermost loop.
Eliminated recursion and the associated call stack, relying solely on iterative list traversal which is more cache-friendly and faster in Python.
Avoided the separate length dimension (var_5) entirely: instead of parameterizing recursion by current length and target length, BFS inherently grows numbers by one digit at each step as needed.
trigger_signals: Presence of sys.setrecursionlimit(10**6) and deep recursive DFS, which is a common hint that recursion depth and overhead might be a bottleneck in Python.
Final use of sorted(var_2)[var_1 - 1], indicating that the algorithm generates an unsorted collection of all candidates, then performs a full sort just to retrieve the k-th smallest element.
Inner DFS loop iterating over all digits 0..9 with a filtering condition, despite the problem structure allowing direct transitions to only a few valid next digits.
The algorithm ignores the actual input value k when deciding when to stop generating numbers: it always generates the entire pre-defined search space (length up to 10) regardless of k.
Use of a separate max-length loop (for var_4 in range(1, 11)) which shows that generation is bounded by a static parameter instead of demand-driven by k.

Any change to loop or break conditions must preserve this indexing convention; otherwise, it’s easy to return the (k+1)-th or (k-1)-th number accidentally.'}

If the child-generation rules or starting set are changed, this property might break and would require either a re-derivation or an explicit sort.'}

{'kind': 'string_conversion_overhead', 'detail': 'The fast implementation uses repeated str(var_1) and slicing to get the last digit. While still fast enough here, for larger-scale problems, it would be better to keep digits as integers (e.g., last_digit = var_1 % 10) to minimize per-node overhead.'}

{'kind': 'hardcoded_depth_limits', 'detail': 'The slow code hardcodes lengths 1..10; this works only because constraints guarantee the answer lies within these lengths. If the required k increases (e.g., > 1e6), this approach may fail or require changing magic constants, whereas the BFS approach naturally extends by continuing the loop as needed.'}
