constraints_guess.notes: Likely AtCoder-style problem: choose integer p in [1,100] (or 0..99) minimizing sum (a_i - p)^2; n appears small (≈100) from typical tasks and the fixed 100-candidate search.

dominant_ops: For each candidate integer (100 iterations), compute (array - candidate)**2 and sum via NumPy; the repeated Python-level loop around NumPy operations dominates runtime.

complexity.why: Each loop iteration does O(n) work on the length-n array (subtract, square, sum). There are 100 such iterations. Only O(n) storage for the main array plus per-iteration O(n) temporaries that are freed, so asymptotically O(n) extra space.

bottlenecks.detail: The for-loop runs 100 times in Python, each time invoking multiple NumPy operations ((var_6 - var_2)**2, np.sum). This incurs repeated Python<->C dispatch overhead and prevents fusing work.
Each iteration allocates new temporary arrays for (var_6 - var_2) and its square, causing repeated O(n) allocations instead of a single batched computation.
Using eval(input()) to read an integer is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()); while not the main bottleneck for typical constraints, it is unnecessary overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Eliminate the Python loop by vectorizing across all 100 candidate integers at once using NumPy broadcasting, then reduce with sum (axis=1) and min entirely in C.

complexity.why: Computes (var_2 - np.arange(1, 101).reshape(100, 1))**2, which forms a 100×n array and processes all candidates in one batched operation. This still performs Θ(100n) arithmetic but in a single, highly optimized C-level kernel, removing Python-loop overhead. Space increases to store the 100×n broadcasted difference/squared array.

complexity_delta.from: O(100 * n) with heavy Python-loop overhead and per-iteration temporaries
complexity_delta.to: O(100 * n) in a single batched NumPy computation with higher spatial but much lower constant-time factors
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time complexity remains linear in n, but the new version shifts nearly all work into optimized NumPy kernels and removes Python-control overhead at the cost of O(100*n) memory.

transformation_steps: Replaced the explicit Python for-loop over 100 candidate integers with a vectorized set of candidates using np.arange(1, 101).reshape(100, 1).
Used NumPy broadcasting to compute (var_2 - candidates)**2 for all candidates at once, forming a 100×n array of squared differences.
Aggregated over the element dimension with np.sum(..., axis=1) to get the total squared error per candidate, then took the minimum via np.min.
Switched from eval(input()) and generic input() parsing to sys.stdin.readline-based input, removing eval overhead and making I/O slightly leaner and safer.
trigger_signals: Presence of a small fixed-range loop (range(100)) that repeatedly calls NumPy operations inside the loop body.
Pattern of recomputing the same type of reduction (sum of squared differences) for many similar scalar shifts of the same array.
Use of NumPy arrays without leveraging multi-dimensional broadcasting or axis-wise reductions.
Use of eval(input()) for reading integers, suggesting an easy I/O micro-optimization and safety improvement.
pitfalls: The vectorized version allocates a 100×n intermediate array; if n is much larger than expected, this can increase peak memory and potentially hurt cache behavior, so for very large n a different approach (e.g., analytical minimizer or streaming) may be preferable.

The candidate range changed from range(100) (0..99) in the slow code to np.arange(1, 101) (1..100) in the fast code; this may alter the mathematical result if 0 is a valid candidate in the original problem.
Heavy reliance on broadcasting semantics: the shape of var_2 must be 1D; unexpected shapes can lead to shape-mismatch errors or unintended broadcasts.
If input values are large and kept as integer dtype, squaring may overflow fixed-width integer types; using a wider dtype or float may be needed in other contexts.
I/O refactoring relies on sys.stdin.readline; missing trailing newlines or different input layout would require careful handling to avoid ValueError on int conversion or .split() on empty strings.

notes: Single test case combinatorics problem under modulo 998244353
Typical AtCoder-style constraints: n, k up to ~2e5
Python needs roughly O(n log MOD) or better with low constants

dominant_ops: Precomputation of factorials and modular inverses up to n via linear loop
Linear construction of (m-1)^(n-1) via repeated multiplication in a loop
Repeated computation of the same modular inverse pow(m-1, MOD-2, MOD) inside a loop
Big-int modular multiplications and additions in a loop of length k+1

why: func_3(var_4 + 10, MOD) runs one loop up to n+10, doing O(1) work per i (factorial and inverse factorial building) → O(n) time and O(n) memory for the global arrays
var_11 power build: for _ in range(n-1): var_11 *= (m-1) → an extra O(n) loop to compute m * (m-1)^(n-1)
Main sum: for t in range(k+1):
- Combination func_1(n-1, t, MOD) is O(1) using precomputed factorials
- var_11 *= pow(m-1, MOD-2, MOD) calls pow with a fixed base and exponent inside the loop
pow(base, exp, mod) with big ints is O(log exp) multiplications (~log MOD ≈ 30 steps), so the sum loop costs O(k * log MOD)
Global arrays var_7, var_6, var_9 store factorials and inverse factorials up to n → O(n) space

bottlenecks.detail: Computes (m-1)^(n-1) by n-1 repeated multiplications instead of a single pow(m-1, n-1, MOD), adding an O(n) overhead.
Inside the main loop, recomputes pow(m-1, MOD-2, MOD) on every iteration even though m is constant, causing O(k * log MOD) extra work with a large constant factor.
Precomputes factorials and inverse factorials up to n+10 regardless of actual k, increasing memory and time when k is smaller or comparable to n.
Stores three lists (factorials, inverse factorials, and inverse array) each of size O(n), which is unnecessary for the optimized iterative-combination approach.

core_idea: Avoid global factorial and inverse factorial precomputation; instead, build binomial coefficients C(n-1, i) iteratively in the loop using the recurrence:
C(n-1, i) = C(n-1, i-1) * (n - i) / i  (using modular inverses for division).
Compute the initial power m * (m-1)^(n-1) with a single pow call instead of a linear loop.
Precompute the modular inverse of (m-1) once as inv_m1 = pow(m-1, MOD-2, MOD) and update powers by repeated multiplication: cur_power *= inv_m1.
Replace heavy global I/O and global state with a single pure function that reads input once and returns the result as a string.

why: Initial power: var_9 = m * pow(m-1, n-1, MOD) uses pow once with exponent n-1 → O(log n) or O(log exponent), negligible versus loop.
Precomputes inv_m1 = pow(m-1, MOD-2, MOD) once → O(log MOD).
Loop for i in 1..k:
- Updates combination var_8 using var_8 *= (n - i) * pow(i, MOD-2, MOD) % MOD:
each iteration calls pow(i, MOD-2, MOD) → O(log MOD) time with a small constant; all other operations are O(1).
- Updates current power var_9 via var_9 *= inv_m1 and accumulates contribution into var_10 in O(1).
Thus the loop is O(k * log MOD) time overall, matching the dominant term in the slow code but with reduced constants and without extra O(n) passes.
No factorial arrays or large lists are stored; only O(1) integers are maintained throughout → O(1) additional space.

note: Asymptotically, both variants are dominated by O(k * log MOD) due to modular inverses, but the original includes additional O(n) passes and O(n) memory.
The optimized code removes the linear power-building loop and the factorial precomputation, reducing both time (for large n) and space.

transformation_steps: 1. Replace linear power construction with pow: - Original: var_11 = m; for _ in range(n-1): var_11 *= (m-1) % MOD. - Optimized: var_9 = m * pow(m-1, n-1, MOD) % MOD.

2. Hoist invariant modular inverse out of the loop: - Original: var_11 *= pow(m-1, MOD-2, MOD) recomputed each iteration. - Optimized: var_3 = pow(m-1, MOD-2, MOD) once; then var_9 *= var_3 inside the loop.

3. Remove global factorial/inverse factorial arrays and binomial helper that depend on them: - Original: func_3 builds var_7, var_6, var_9 arrays; func_1 reads from these arrays for combinations. - Optimized: uses iterative combination update var_8 = C(n-1, i) via multiplicative recurrence with pow(i, MOD-2, MOD); no large arrays.

4. Convert from procedural main to a pure function interface: - Original: uses sys.stdin, global state, and top-level main driver. - Optimized: func_1(*lines) parses input string and returns the answer, improving clarity and reducing I/O overhead.
5. Simplify control flow and special cases: - Retain the early-return case when m == 1 and k == n-1 but implement it directly in the functional style; avoid exit(), globals, and side effects.
trigger_signals: Repeated pow(base, MOD-2, MOD) inside a loop with base constant (m-1), a red flag for redundant work.
Linear loop computing base^(n-1) via repeated multiplication rather than pow(base, exponent, mod).
Global factorial and inverse factorial arrays allocated up to n even though iterative combinatorics can avoid them.
High memory usage patterns (O(n) arrays) in a problem that only needs sequential binomial values.
Use of multiple global lists and globals for simple combinatorial expressions, indicating refactoring potential.
pitfalls: Modular inverse strategy: - The optimized code still calls pow(i, MOD-2, MOD) per iteration to divide by i in binomial recurrence; while asymptotically fine, this can be heavy if k is extremely large. One must ensure constraints are small enough or consider precomputing inverses if needed.

Requirement of prime modulus: - Using pow(x, MOD-2, MOD) to compute modular inverses assumes MOD is prime (Fermat's little theorem). This is valid here (998244353 is prime) but would fail for non-prime moduli.

Off-by-one and index correctness in recurrence: - The recurrence var_8 = var_8 * (n - i) * inv(i) corresponds to C(n-1, i) from C(n-1, i-1). Incorrect ordering or bounds on i can easily shift to C(n, i) or similar; tests around small n, k are important.

Overflow vs. modulo placement: - All multiplicative updates should be modulo-reduced to keep intermediate big-int sizes manageable; mixing modulo order incorrectly can still be correct logically but much slower.

Input handling differences: - Moving from sys.stdin.readline to open(0).read().splitlines() changes how trailing newlines and extra whitespace are treated; care is needed if the original problem allows multiple lines or extra spaces.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical competitive-programming I/O task: read many pairs of integers until sentinel '0 0', sort each pair, print. Performance dominated by input/output rather than computation; number of lines may be up to ~1e5–1e6.

dominant_ops: High-level input() calls with parsing on every iteration
String splitting and int() conversion per line
Function call overhead for func_1 on each pair
Multiple assignments for manual swap

complexity.why: For T input pairs until the sentinel, each iteration performs a constant amount of work: read a line, split, convert two integers, possibly swap, and print. No additional data structures grow with T.

bottlenecks.detail: Uses built-in input(), which is significantly slower than sys.stdin.readline() for large numbers of lines due to additional safety and decoding overhead.
Each pair is passed through func_1, adding Python function call overhead in the tight loop for a trivial conditional swap.
Manual swap with a temporary variable var_4 instead of a direct comparison-and-print, plus repeated re-parsing logic inside the loop (int conversion duplicated around the loop condition).

Loop condition uses while (0 != var_1) or (0 != var_2), which is slightly less direct than a sentinel check inside the loop; also does an extra read before entering the loop, leading to more scattered logic.

FastAudit.core_idea: Eliminate function-call overhead and optimize input by using sys.stdin.readline() directly in the loop, performing the comparison and ordered printing inline without extra swaps or helper functions.

complexity.why: Still one pass over T input pairs with constant work per pair (read, compare, print). Asymptotic complexity is unchanged, but constant factors are reduced by faster IO and fewer indirections.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(T), Space: O(1) with high constant factors due to input() and helper calls.
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(T), Space: O(1) with reduced constant factors via sys.stdin.readline() and inline logic.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity remains linear in the number of lines, but performance improves substantially in CP judges because IO dominates runtime.

transformation_steps: Replace input() with sys.stdin.readline() to speed up line reading for many iterations.
Inline the swap logic by directly comparing var_1 and var_2 and printing them in the correct order, removing func_1 and its call overhead.
Use map(int, ...) to convert both integers in one expression, simplifying parsing code.
Adopt an explicit infinite loop with a sentinel check (break when '0 0') for clearer control flow and slightly less overhead.
Avoid extra temporary variables for swapping and avoid re-reading/parsing before and inside the loop separately.
trigger_signals: Problem is dominated by simple per-line processing with potentially large input size.
Use of input() inside a tight loop in Python, a known performance bottleneck for up to 1e5+ lines.
Unnecessary helper function calls in a very small, frequently executed code path.
Online judge context where Python solutions using input() often TLE or run close to time limits on IO-heavy tasks.
pitfalls: Using sys.stdin.readline().split() without guarding against empty lines or trailing whitespace can raise ValueError if input format deviates from expectations.
If there is an extra blank line at EOF, list(map(int, ...)) may fail; robust versions often check the result of readline() and break on empty string.

Printing tuples, e.g., print((var_1, var_2)), outputs '(a, b)' instead of 'a b'; some judges may expect space-separated numbers. While both codes do this, a fully correct optimized version would typically use print(var_1, var_2).
Assumes that every non-sentinel line contains exactly two integers; any deviation in input format could crash the fast version more abruptly because it does less defensive work.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic AOJ-style problem: count triples 1 <= i < j < k <= n with i + j + k == x. Typical constraints n <= 100, x <= 300, multiple test cases until '0 0'.

dominant_ops: Triple nested loops over i, j, k with an equality check (i + j + k == x) per iteration.

complexity.why: Outer loop i runs ~n times, middle loop j runs up to ~n times for each i, inner loop k runs up to ~n times for each (i, j). Constant work (sum + comparison) per iteration, so overall ~n^3 operations; only a few integer counters stored, so constant extra space.

bottlenecks.detail: Inefficient enumeration of all i < j < k by explicitly looping k instead of deriving it from i, j, and target sum x. This introduces an unnecessary O(n) factor for the innermost loop.
Three nested Python for-loops in interpreted code cause substantial overhead in per-iteration bytecode execution compared to a two-loop solution.
Many k candidates are tested even when i + j is already close to or exceeds x, but the loop still iterates up to n without early pruning.

FastAudit.core_idea: Eliminate the innermost loop by solving for the third value k = x - i - j and only checking whether this k is in the valid range and maintains the ordering i < j < k <= n.

complexity.why: Two nested loops over i and j give O(n^2) (about n(n-1)/2) candidate pairs. For each pair, computing k and checking bounds is O(1). No additional data structures are kept beyond counters.

complexity_delta.from: O(n^3) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n^2) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: Removed the explicit enumeration of k by deriving it algebraically from i and j, reducing one loop level.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the problem is to count triples (i, j, k) with 1 <= i < j < k <= n and i + j + k == x.
Observe that for fixed i and j, the third value is uniquely determined as k = x - i - j; no need to loop over all possible k.
Replace the innermost k-loop with a constant-time calculation of k.
Enforce ordering and range constraints via inequalities: j < k <= n (and implicitly k >= 1 given ranges of i, j and typical x).
Count how many (i, j) pairs yield a valid k instead of iterating over all (i, j, k) triples.
trigger_signals: Presence of three nested loops over ranges up to n with a simple arithmetic condition in the innermost body.
A constraint of the form i + j + k == constant, where one variable can be solved from the others.
Strict ordering constraints i < j < k that allow the range of variables to be tightly bounded.
Competitive programming / online judge context where cubic algorithms for n up to ~100 may borderline pass but are suboptimal.
pitfalls: Failing to correctly enforce i < j < k after eliminating the k loop; the optimized code must ensure j < k, not just k in [1, n].
Off-by-one errors in loop ranges: using range(1, n) vs range(1, n + 1) when interpreting constraints 1 <= value <= n.
Neglecting the upper bound on k (k <= n) or the fact that k must be positive, which could count invalid triples.
Relying on list construction for counting (e.g., len([...])) can add overhead; for very tight constraints, a simple integer counter increment in the loops is marginally faster.

constraints_guess.notes: n = number of skills/attributes (bit positions); q = number of books/items. Fast solution uses DP over all subsets: O(q * 2^n), so n is likely <= 12–15 and q <= ~100. Costs are small enough that 2e7 is a safe INF sentinel.

dominant_ops: Full enumeration of all 2^n bitmasks multiple times
Nested enumeration over all masks and many candidate submasks using precomputed buckets by popcount
For each mask, scan all items to find a covering item
String-based popcount: bin(mask).count('1') in a loop

complexity.why: Precomputation: for each of 2^n masks, convert to binary string and count bits (O(n) per mask) → O(n * 2^n). Then for each mask, scan all q items → O(q * 2^n). The DP combination step tries to partition each mask into two parts: for each of the 2^n masks, it iterates over var_19[size] which, across sizes, covers essentially all 2^n masks again. This double over-all-masks effect yields ~O((2^n)^2) = O(4^n) checks, each with constant-time bit operations and comparisons.

bottlenecks.detail: DP formulation is based on recursively splitting each subset into two smaller subsets, checking all possible splits via global buckets of masks grouped by popcount. This explores a combinatorial number of decompositions and results in approximately O(4^n) operations.

The innermost DP loop over var_18 iterates over var_19[var_14], which contains all masks of a given popcount, irrespective of whether they are submasks of the current mask. The submask check (var_18 & var_6 == var_18) is applied after enumeration, so most candidates are useless but still visited.
For each mask, var_13[mask] is computed by scanning all items to find those whose mask is a superset. This is O(q * 2^n) and is later only a lower bound that is refined by the expensive split DP.

Using bin(mask).count('1') for popcount introduces an O(n) string conversion and scan for each of the 2^n masks. A built-in bit operation (like Python 3.8+ int.bit_count()) or iterative DP on popcount would avoid this overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a classical bitmask DP over items/books: state dp[i][S] = minimum cost to achieve subset S of skills using only the first i books. Transition: either skip the i-th book (dp[i+1][S] <= dp[i][S]) or take it (dp[i+1][S | mask[i]] <= dp[i][S] + cost[i]). The answer is dp[m][(1<<n) - 1], where m is the number of books. This directly models selecting a subset of books to cover all skills with minimal sum cost.

complexity.why: There are q stages (one per book) and at each stage we iterate over all 2^n masks. For each (i, S) we do O(1) work: a couple of comparisons and a bitwise OR for the transition. Thus time is Θ(q * 2^n). The DP table var_11 has dimensions (q+1) × 2^n, giving Θ(q * 2^n) space; this could be reduced to O(2^n) by rolling arrays over i if needed.

complexity_delta.from: ≈ O(4^n + q * 2^n) time, O(2^n + n * 2^n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(q * 2^n) time, O(q * 2^n) space (reducible to O(2^n) space)
complexity_delta.note: The slow version effectively tries all ways to partition each subset into smaller subsets using a global enumeration of masks, causing a near O(4^n) blow-up. The fast version instead progresses over items once, using a simple 0/1-choice DP on a 2^n state space, which is optimal for typical constraints (n <= 12–15).

transformation_steps: Reinterpret the problem as selecting a subset of books/items to cover all skills, where each book is a bitmask and has a cost. The goal is to reach the full mask (all skills) with minimal total cost.

Redefine the DP state: instead of dp[mask] = best combination cost and then recursively splitting masks into submasks, introduce a 2D DP dp[i][mask] that represents the minimal cost to obtain 'mask' using the first i books.
Replace the combinatorial partition DP with a linear-in-items iterative DP: for each book i and each mask S, update dp[i+1][S] (skip book) and dp[i+1][S | book_mask[i]] (take book).
Eliminate global buckets of masks by popcount and the associated bin().count('1') precomputation, which removed an O(n * 2^n) and a hidden O(4^n) factor.
Keep state transitions local and monotone in i (only move from i to i+1), which guarantees a single pass over the state space rather than repeatedly revisiting states via arbitrary subset splits.
trigger_signals: Presence of multiple nested loops over the full 2^n state space, notably a loop over all masks combined with another loop that scans global lists of masks grouped by popcount.
Use of bin(mask).count('1') inside a loop over all masks, indicating per-state string processing on top of bitmask DP.
A DP recurrence that tries all possible ways to decompose a mask into two submasks for every mask (subset convolution-like pattern) without constraints on decomposition size or structure.

The existence of a much simpler and well-known DP formulation for 'minimum cost to cover all skills given items with bitmasks', suggesting the original approach is overcomplicating the state transitions.
pitfalls: Memory usage of the fast DP: var_11 is of size (q+1) × 2^n. For larger constraints (e.g., n=20, q=200), this may still be large. A one-dimensional rolling DP array over masks is safer in general.

Correct initialization of the INF sentinel: using a value too small could cause overflow or incorrect minima; fast_code uses var_4 = 2 * 10**7, which is safely above any possible total cost under typical constraints but must be adjusted if costs or q are larger.
Bitmask construction: off-by-one errors when doing shifts (1 << (skill - 1)) can silently corrupt states. Both codes assume skills are 1-indexed, so this convention must be preserved.

Input parsing consistency: the fast solution ignores one of the read integers per book (var_2/var_9). If that parameter actually encodes the number of skills on the line or another constraint, the implementation must ensure it still matches the input format and doesn't rely on undefined behavior.

Time behavior in Python: although O(q * 2^n) is fine for n up to about 20 and q up to around 200, using Python-specific costlier operations (like repeated list copying or expensive I/O per transition) could still cause timeouts; care must be taken to keep inner loops tight and rely on simple integer and list operations only.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical of AtCoder ABC110 D 'Factorization': input is two integers N, M. Need to factor M (M up to about 1e9) and for each prime factor p^e of M, multiply C(N+e-1, e) modulo 1e9+7. Total sum of exponents e is small (O(log M)).

dominant_ops: Trial division factorization of M up to sqrt(M)
Precomputation of factorial array fact[0..N+O(1)] modulo MOD
Precomputation of inverse factorial array invfact[0..N+O(1)] via one modular inverse and a backward linear pass
Constant-time binomial coefficient evaluations using fact/infact for each exponent e

complexity.why: Factorization loop runs up to floor(sqrt(M)) iterations in worst case. After that, the code allocates two arrays of size N+50 and fills them with O(N) modular multiplications. The number of prime factors and their exponents is very small (sum e = O(log M)), so the per-prime work after precomputation is negligible compared to the O(N) preprocessing.

bottlenecks.detail: Unconditionally precomputes factorials and inverse factorials up to N+50, costing O(N) time and O(N) memory even though only binomial coefficients with small k (the exponents e) are needed.
Inverse factorials are derived via a full backward pass over the array: one pow(fact[-1], MOD-2, MOD) (O(log MOD)) plus an O(N) loop. With only a single query, this cost is not amortized.
The list of exponents var_5 is sorted, but the order of processing exponents does not affect the product; the sort is logically redundant (though its cost is tiny compared to O(N)).
Two arrays of size N+50 are stored, which is overkill when the number of binomial evaluations is only the number of distinct prime factors of M (often < 10).

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial and inverse-factorial precomputation. Instead, compute each required binomial coefficient C(n, k) directly with a short multiplicative loop in O(k) arithmetic operations on Python integers, then take the result modulo 1e9+7. Because all k are small exponents of prime factors of M, this removes the O(N) preprocessing and uses only O(1) extra memory.

complexity.why: Factorization remains O(sqrt(M)). After factorization, for each exponent e (where e is the exponent of a prime factor of M), func_1 computes C(N+e-1, e) by looping from 1 to e-1, i.e., O(e) operations. The total sum of exponents sum_e is upper-bounded by O(log M), so the post-factorization cost is O(log M), asymptotically smaller than the O(N) factorial precomputation. No large auxiliary arrays are kept; only a few scalar variables are used.

delta_type: algorithmic (binomial computation strategy and memory usage)

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(M) + N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + sum_e e) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: Under typical constraints (N up to ~1e5, M up to ~1e9), N can be much larger than sum_e (which is O(log M), often < 30–60). Eliminating the O(N) factorial and inverse-factorial precomputation removes the dominant cost for large N.

transformation_steps: Removed global factorial and inverse-factorial arrays (var_7 and var_6) sized to N+50 and the associated O(N) initialization loops.

Replaced constant-time factorial-based binomial computation with a direct multiplicative combination function func_1 that computes C(n, k) via products of consecutive integers in numerator and denominator, followed by an exact integer division.
Switched from modular arithmetic throughout the combination computation to exact integer arithmetic with a modulus applied only once per combination (var_11 = var_11 * func_1(...) % MOD).

Reduced auxiliary data saved from full exponent list (and its sort) to only the exponents used in per-prime combination calls, thereby keeping post-factorization work proportional to the number and size of prime exponents instead of N.
trigger_signals: N appears in array sizes (N+50) and loop bounds, indicating an O(N) preprocessing step even though only a handful of binomial values are needed.
Single-query problem: factorial precomputation cannot be amortized across multiple test cases.
Constraints where N is large (up to ~1e5) while M is relatively small (~1e9), implying the total exponent sum of M is much smaller than N.
Observed or anticipated TLE/MLE/slowdowns when N is near its upper bound despite the mathematical structure suggesting only O(log M) work should be necessary after factorization.
pitfalls: Big-integer overhead: The direct combinatorial computation in func_1 temporarily creates very large integers (C(N+e-1, e)), and Python’s big-int multiplications have super-constant cost. For extremely large N and even modest e, big-int arithmetic can become the new bottleneck despite better asymptotic operation counts.

Correctness relies on exact integer division: func_1 returns var_3 // var_4 with no modular arithmetic inside. This is valid only if the product formulation exactly equals the binomial coefficient; introducing intermediate mod operations would break the divisibility and corrupt results.

If the problem were extended to many test cases, the original factorial-based approach (done once and reused) could become preferable, as its O(N) cost would then be amortized; moving to per-call multiplicative combinations is optimal mainly in a single-query or very few-query setting.

The factorization step remains O(sqrt(M)) in both versions. For larger M (e.g., up to 1e12 or beyond), trial division itself may become the dominant cost and would need further optimization (e.g., precomputed primes, Pollard’s rho, or better bounds).

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style: N up to 1e5, each a_i up to about 1e9; output -1 if product exceeds 1e18 or 0 if any element is 0.

dominant_ops: Single pass over N integers computing their product with early termination if product exceeds 1e18.

complexity.why: All N integers are stored in a list and iterated once; each step performs a constant-time multiplication and comparison.

bottlenecks.detail: Large competitive-programming template: many heavy imports (bisect, math, itertools, collections, etc.) and global lambdas/constants are loaded even though almost all are unused in this problem. This increases startup and parsing time.
Custom input lambdas (var_2, var_1) add extra indirection and branching compared to direct input()/map() usage, slightly increasing constant factors, though still O(N).
The template keeps references to many unused functions and constants, increasing memory footprint for no benefit, though asymptotic complexity is unchanged.

FastAudit.core_idea: Read N and the list directly with built-in input/map, check for zero early, otherwise accumulate the product and stop as soon as it exceeds 1e18, then print the product or -1.

complexity.why: Stores N integers in a list and performs a single traversal with constant-time operations per element; no additional data structures are used.

complexity_delta.from: O(N) time, O(N) space with heavy constant overhead from imports and lambdas.
complexity_delta.to: O(N) time, O(N) space with minimal constant overhead and simpler control flow.
complexity_delta.note: Both versions are linear; the improvement is purely in startup time, code size, and micro-level overhead, not in Big-O complexity.

transformation_steps: Remove unused imports (bisect, math, itertools, collections, etc.) and global constants/lambdas that are not needed for this problem.
Replace custom input helper lambdas with direct calls to input(), int(), and list(map(int, ...)) for clarity and reduced indirection.
Inline the main logic instead of wrapping it in a function with extra flags, simplifying the control flow.
Directly assign -1 to the product when exceeding 1e18 rather than using a separate boolean flag, slightly reducing branching.
trigger_signals: Presence of a large competitive-programming template with many unused utilities for a very simple problem.
Imports of multiple standard-library modules where only basic input and arithmetic are required.
Extra layers of indirection in I/O (lambda wrappers) without functional benefit.
Code size and startup time being disproportionate to the simplicity and constraints of the task.
pitfalls: Using eval(input()) in the fast version is unnecessary and can be unsafe in general; int(input()) is sufficient and safer.
Ensure that early termination for overflow (>1e18) happens before printing; off-by-one mistakes in the condition could yield wrong -1 behavior.
When refactoring away from templates, avoid accidentally changing the overflow threshold or comparison direction (e.g., using >= instead of > if the problem requires strict >1e18).
If constraints were larger or memory tighter, one might avoid storing the entire list and instead stream-process the inputs; both current versions still store all N numbers.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder coprime problem: n up to ~1e5, each a_i up to ~1e6. Need to classify as pairwise / setwise / not coprime using divisor counting + gcd.

dominant_ops: Allocation of frequency array of fixed size 1e6+1 regardless of max(a_i).
For each d in [2..1e6], iterating over the slice var_7[d::d] to sum counts of multiples of d (creates a new list per d).
Final linear pass computing gcd over all input numbers.

complexity.time: O(M log M + n log A), where M = 1e6 (fixed upper bound), A ≈ 1e6
complexity.why: The pairwise-coprime test is essentially a divisor sieve: for each d up to 1e6, it inspects all multiples of d; the total number of inspected cells is ∑_{d=1}^{M} M/d = O(M log M). Each slice var_7[d::d] is materialized as a new list, so work and memory traffic scale with the same harmonic sum. The gcd pass is O(n log A).

bottlenecks.detail: Loop upper bound fixed at 1e6 (var_1), even if max(a_i) is much smaller, causing wasted O((1e6 - max(a)) log 1e6) work.
Using var_7[d::d] allocates a new list for every d; this adds heavy constant factors in time and memory, especially for small d where the slices are long.
Always allocates an array of size 1e6+1 even when input values are small, increasing memory usage and cache pressure.

FastAudit.core_idea: Tighten the sieve domain to the actual maximum value in the input array instead of a fixed global bound, so the divisor-iteration loops only up to max(a_i), reducing unnecessary work when max(a_i) ≪ 1e6.

complexity.time: O(V log V + n), where V = max(a_i)
complexity.why: The frequency array is sized to V+1. For each d in [2..V], it sums var_2[d::d]; total elements visited across all d is ∑_{d=1}^{V} V/d = O(V log V). Building the frequency array is O(n). In terms of the problem’s official constraints (A_max ≈ 1e6), both versions are O(1e6 log 1e6), but the modified version’s cost scales with the realized maximum V rather than the fixed A_max.

complexity_delta.from: O(1e6 log 1e6 + n log A) time, O(1e6 + n) space (fixed bound 1e6 regardless of input).
complexity_delta.to: O(V log V + n) time, O(V + n) space, where V = max(a_i). For V ≪ 1e6 this is significantly cheaper; for V ≈ 1e6, asymptotics match but constants differ.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically (in terms of theoretical A_max) both are O(A_max log A_max). The improvement is practical: the work now depends on the actual maximum input value, potentially much smaller than the global bound.

transformation_steps: Replaced the fixed-size frequency array of length 1e6+1 with an array sized to max(a_i)+1 (var_4 + 1).
Adjusted the divisor loop upper bound from the constant 1e6 to max(a_i) (var_4), avoiding scanning unused larger values.

Removed the separate gcd-based setwise-coprime check; instead, reused the divisor-count-based maximum (var_6) combined with n (var_5) to classify pairwise/setwise/not coprime (note: this is a correctness change, not just a performance change).
Simplified input handling to store n explicitly and reuse it for the classification thresholds.
trigger_signals: Use of a hard-coded large upper bound (1e6) instead of the actual range of input values.
Long-running nested sieve-style loop with a fixed upper limit, regardless of smaller input magnitude.
High overhead from repeated list slicing over a large array in inner loops.
pitfalls: Correctness risk: Replacing the gcd-based setwise coprime check with conditions based only on maximum divisor multiplicities can misclassify some cases; performance changes must not silently alter problem semantics.
Remaining slicing overhead: var_2[d::d] still creates a new list for every d; for further optimization, one should iterate multiples via indices (j += d) without slicing.

If max(a_i) is close to the known global bound (≈1e6), asymptotic performance is similar to the original; perceived speedup primarily arises when input values are much smaller than the maximum allowed.
Continued use of eval(input()) for reading integers is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; it also adds minor overhead compared to int(input()).

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case. Second input (M) is factorized by trial division, so M is likely up to around 1e9. First input (N) only appears as a parameter in binomial coefficients C(exp + N - 1, exp); algorithms must be essentially independent of N in runtime.

dominant_ops: math.factorial(var_2 - 1) with potentially huge argument (N-1)
trial division prime factorization up to sqrt(M)
big-integer multiplications/divisions for binomial coefficients without intermediate modulo

complexity.time: O(√M + F(N)) where F(N) is the cost of factorial(N-1), effectively superlinear and enormous for large N
complexity.space: O(log answer + log factorial(N)) bits due to huge intermediate integers, dominated by factorial(N-1)
complexity.why: The prime factorization loop is O(√M). For each prime exponent e, building the numerator via a loop of length e is cheap (e ≤ O(log M)). However, computing factorial(var_2 - 1) once has cost roughly proportional to N times big-int arithmetic cost, and creates a gigantic integer that is never used. This dominates both time and memory when N is large. Additionally, delaying modulo until the very end allows intermediate products to grow to the full size of the final answer (product of combinations), increasing big-int cost.

bottlenecks.detail: Computes factorial(var_2 - 1) where var_2 is the first input N. For realistic constraints N can be up to ~1e9, making this factorial computation astronomically expensive and completely unnecessary because var_5 is never used afterwards.
Use of math.factorial on a very large argument allocates and manipulates an enormous big integer, causing severe time and memory usage even though the result is discarded.

Modulo 10**9+7 is applied only once at the very end (print(var_11 % MOD)). All intermediate binomial products are kept as full Python integers, which can grow very large and make every multiply/divide slower.
Conversion list(var_9.values()) is unnecessary; direct iteration over var_9.values() would avoid a small extra allocation. This is negligible compared to the factorial issue.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid any factorial on large N and compute each binomial coefficient C(exp + N - 1, exp) via a short multiplicative loop whose length is only the exponent (≤ O(log M)), then take modulo at each step to keep integers small. Factorization remains trial division, which is acceptable for M up to about 1e9.

complexity.space: O(1) extra space beyond input/output and a small list of prime factors
complexity.why: Prime factorization by trial division up to sqrt(M) is O(√M). The sum of exponents in the factorization of M is at most O(log M) (e.g., for powers of 2). For each exponent e, func_1 runs a loop of length e − 1, independent of N, so the total binomial cost is O(Σ e_i). Intermediate values are reduced modulo 1e9+7 at each multiplication, so integer sizes remain bounded, giving effectively constant extra space and cheap arithmetic.

complexity_delta.from: O(√M + cost_of_factorial(N-1)) time with huge memory due to an unnecessary factorial on N-1 plus large intermediate products without modulo
complexity_delta.to: O(√M + log M) ≈ O(√M) time and O(1) extra space by removing the large factorial and keeping numbers reduced modulo 1e9+7
complexity_delta.note: The key change is eliminating factorial(N-1), whose cost dominates when N is large, and ensuring computations depend only on the small exponents of M.

transformation_steps: Remove the computation of factorial(var_2 - 1), which produced an unused but enormously expensive value.
Use a multiplicative formulation for binomial coefficients C(n, k) that loops only k times (k = exponent), independent of N, instead of relying on large factorials in the denominator.
Apply modulo 1_000_000_007 during accumulation of the result (after each multiplicative update) instead of only at the very end, bounding integer sizes and speeding up arithmetic.
Represent the prime factorization as a simple list of (prime, exponent) pairs and iterate directly over it, avoiding unnecessary conversions.
Keep the algorithm’s runtime dependent on the size and factorization of M rather than on N, matching intended constraints.
trigger_signals: Use of math.factorial or combinatorial functions on arguments that can be as large as the original input N without any constraint reduction.
Large-integer multiplications and divisions without intermediate modulo in a modular arithmetic problem.
Variables computed once with heavy cost (e.g., factorial(var_2 - 1)) and then never used (dead computation).
Combination formulas implemented directly via factorials of large numbers instead of multiplicative or modular-friendly forms.
Trial division factorization combined with additional superlinear work in N, suggesting a mismatch between algorithm and typical -style constraints.
pitfalls: Calling math.factorial on a large input (like N up to 1e7 or more) is practically infeasible in contest settings and must be avoided unless N is provably small.
Relying on exact factorials or binomial coefficients without reducing modulo can cause integer blowup and slow down every subsequent arithmetic operation.
Introducing heavy computations whose results are never used (dead code) can dominate runtime even if the main algorithm is otherwise efficient.
Assuming that Python’s bigint performance will hide superlinear computations: for combinatorics with large parameters, algorithmic complexity must be controlled explicitly.

In modular combinatorics, use multiplicative formulas or precomputed factorials with modular inverses tailored to the constraint ranges; avoid naive factorials when the domain size is unclear or very large.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical of AtCoder ABC110 D-like: N up to ~1e4, M up to ~1e9. Single test, need prime factorization of M and combinatorics over exponents.

dominant_ops: Prime factorization of M by trial division up to sqrt(M), plus (likely) factorial / inverse-factorial precomputation for nCr and heavyweight I/O helpers (eval, Counter, repeated imports).

complexity.why: func_9 factors var_20 with a for-loop up to int(sqrt(var_20)) and repeated division in the inner while, giving O(√M) in the worst case. The (truncated) Class_1 strongly suggests precomputing factorial and inverse factorial arrays up to about N+max_exponent, costing O(N_precompute) time and space. Additional constant-factor overhead comes from using collections.Counter, importing inside the factorization function, and eval-based input parsing.

bottlenecks.detail: Precomputing factorial / inverse factorial tables up to MAX ≈ N+max_exponent for just a handful of binomial coefficients causes O(N) time and memory overhead where only O(log M) work is logically necessary (since each exponent of M is small).
Using collections.Counter for the prime exponent map and importing sqrt and Counter inside func_9 on every call adds non-trivial constant factors compared to a simple dict.

Input helpers use eval(func_10()) to parse integers, which is significantly slower and more complex than int(). Also, a large template of unused helpers (func_11, func_12, func_13, etc.) is included, increasing code size and startup overhead without contributing to the solution.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use straightforward trial-division factorization of M into primes and exponents, then for each exponent e compute C(e + N - 1, e) via direct multiplicative formula with k = min(e, (e+N-1)-e) = e (since e ≪ N). No factorial precomputation, just small O(e) loops per prime factor, and multiply all results modulo 1e9+7.

complexity.why: func_2 performs trial division while var_1**2 <= var_5, so in the worst case it runs up to √M with a small constant for repeated division; ω(M), the number of distinct prime factors, is at most about log M. For each exponent e, func_1 evaluates C(e + N - 1, e) with two loops of length e (because e ≪ N and var_8 is min(k, n-k)), so the combinatorial part is O(Σ e) = O(log M). Only a dict of prime→exponent is stored, giving O(ω(M)) space.

complexity_delta.from: O(√M + N_precompute) time, O(N_precompute + ω(M)) space (factorization + factorial table for nCr, plus Counter and heavy helpers).
complexity_delta.to: O(√M + log M) time, O(ω(M)) space (factorization + direct multiplicative nCr over small exponents).
complexity_delta.note: For large N and single-query combinatorics, avoiding factorial-table precomputation converts an unnecessary O(N) term into a much smaller O(log M) term, and dropping Counter/eval further trims constants.

transformation_steps: Replace factorial-table-based combination logic (implied by Class_1) with a direct multiplicative nCr implementation (func_1) that loops only over the small exponent e of each prime factor.
Simplify prime factorization: use a plain dict keyed by primes instead of collections.Counter, and keep imports at top-level instead of inside the function.
Remove eval-based integer input; use direct int(input().split()) to parse N and M, avoiding the overhead and risk of eval.
Eliminate unused generic helper functions and multidimensional-initialization utilities that do not participate in the computation, reducing code size and startup overhead.
Operate entirely with primitive loops and arithmetic, avoiding unnecessary abstraction layers and object allocations in the hot path.
trigger_signals: Single test case with large-ish N but very small number of required combinations (only one combination per distinct prime factor).
Profiling or inspection reveals a dominant cost in factorial/inverse-factorial precomputation and library-heavy constructions (Counter, repeated imports) despite the combinatorial results being few.
Use of eval to read integers, which is a red flag for performance and security, especially when only simple numeric parsing is needed.
Presence of a large competitive-programming template where most helpers are unused in this solution, suggesting that trimming could improve performance and clarity.
pitfalls: Direct multiplicative computation of nCr must use the identity nCk = nC(n-k) to keep k small; otherwise, if k were large (e.g., O(N)), the loops would become O(N) and reintroduce a large linear factor.

While Python integers are arbitrary-precision, performing multiplication before modular reduction can temporarily create very large intermediates; in tight constraints, it is safer to reduce modulo at each step if necessary, though here the number of steps is small.
The trial-division prime factorization is only acceptable because M ≤ about 1e9; for significantly larger M, a faster factorization method (or stronger constraints) would be required.

Removing factorial-based combinatorics is only safe because the number of combinations needed is extremely small; in multi-query settings, precomputing factorial and inverse factorial tables may become advantageous again.

Be careful not to repeatedly create lists of dict keys in hot loops (e.g., list(var_7.keys())); although cheap here due to few primes, in other contexts this pattern can silently add an O(number_of_keys) factor per iteration.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical 'K-th Lunlun number' style: input is K up to about 1e5, generate all lunlun numbers (adjacent digits differ by at most 1) below ~1e10, then output the K-th smallest.

dominant_ops: Recursive DFS calls for each lunlun number candidate
Repeated conversion int->str: len(str(var_2)) and str(var_2)[-1]
Repeated conversion str->int: int(str(var_2)[-1])
List appends to var_4 for every generated number
Final sort of the generated list var_4

complexity.why: Let M be the number of generated lunlun numbers (up to all lunlun numbers with <= 10 digits) and L the maximum digit length (~10). The DFS generates O(M) nodes. Each node performs string conversions len(str(var_2)), str(var_2)[-1], and int(...), each costing O(L). So generation is O(M * L). After generation, var_4.sort() costs O(M log M). Space is dominated by storing all generated numbers: O(M).

bottlenecks.detail: In every recursive call, len(str(var_2)) and int(str(var_2)[-1]) are executed. These are O(L) operations repeated for each of O(M) nodes, inflating runtime by a large constant factor.
str(var_2) is constructed twice per call (for len and for indexing). This allocates and traverses strings repeatedly instead of using arithmetic on integers.

Recursion depth can reach the maximum number of digits (~10), which itself is fine, but the large number of recursive calls combined with Python function-call overhead contributes significantly to runtime. No iterative optimization or memoization is used.

All generated numbers are stored in var_4 before sorting and indexing, which is necessary for this approach but increases memory usage to O(M). Not a big asymptotic issue vs fast_code, but still a resource hotspot.
Using eval(input()) is slower and less safe than int(input()). The cost is minor compared to DFS and string operations but still unnecessary overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Generate lunlun numbers via DFS using pure integer arithmetic and an explicit numeric upper bound; obtain the last digit via modulo, branch on it to append next digits, and avoid all string conversions. Collect all values in a list and sort once at the end, then index the (K-1)-th element.

complexity.why: DFS still explores O(M) lunlun numbers, but each node does O(1) work using arithmetic: var_5 % 10 and simple integer comparisons, plus up to 3 recursive calls. There is no per-node O(L) string cost. Sorting the resulting list is O(M log M). Space is the same O(M) for storing all generated numbers.

complexity_delta.from: O(M * L + M log M) time, O(M) space
complexity_delta.to: O(M + M log M) time, O(M) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity in terms of the number of generated lunlun numbers M is similar, but removing per-node string operations (O(L)) significantly reduces the constant factor; effectively time goes from O(10 * M + M log M) to O(M + M log M), which is a large practical improvement.

transformation_steps: Replace string-based digit handling with integer arithmetic: use var_3 = var_5 % 10 to obtain the last digit instead of int(str(var_2)[-1]).
Remove length-based termination len(str(var_2)) > 10 and instead terminate recursion using a numeric upper bound (var_5 > 3234566667), which corresponds to the maximum required lunlun value.

Simplify child-generation logic: instead of branching separately for last digit 0, 9, and middle digits via ranges, use three direct checks (var_3-1 >= 0, always var_3, and var_3+1 < 10) to generate valid next digits.
Avoid repeated string creation: eliminate len(str(...)) and str(...)[-1] calls entirely; every operation is on integers.
Preserve the overall enumeration structure: still DFS from starting digits 1..9, still append to a global list, and still sort the list once at the end before indexing.
Increase recursion limit via sys.setrecursionlimit(10**5) to safely support the necessary recursion depth and call count in CP environments.
trigger_signals: Recursive function performing str() conversion on every call (len(str(var_2)), str(var_2)[-1]).
Repeated construction of the same string representation of an integer in a tight recursion loop.
Digit-oriented logic expressed via strings instead of integer modulo and division.
Performance issues or timeouts when input size K grows even though the mathematical search space is moderate.
Use of eval(input()) instead of simpler and faster int(input()) in a competitive-programming-like context.
pitfalls: Recursion depth: although the depth in digits is small, the total number of recursive calls is large; forgetting to adjust sys.setrecursionlimit may lead to RecursionError in some environments.

Upper bound correctness: the numeric cutoff (3234566667) must be chosen to ensure all required lunlun numbers for the maximum K are generated; a too-small bound yields wrong answers, too-large bound increases runtime.
Memory usage: both approaches store all generated lunlun numbers, so memory remains O(M); this can still be large if constraints are tighter than assumed.
Ordering and duplicates: changing generation rules incorrectly can introduce duplicates or skip numbers, affecting the sorted order and hence the K-th element.
Use of eval: retaining eval(input()) (as in both versions) is unsafe and slightly slower; replacing with int(input()) is recommended to avoid accidental code execution and minor overhead.

constraints_guess.notes: Likely AtCoder ABC 083B (Some Sums): N up to 10^4, single pass over 1..N, no additional queries.

dominant_ops: Outer for-loop over all integers from 1 to N
Inner while-loop doing digit extraction using modulo and floating-point division
Repeated calls to math.floor on small integers

complexity.time: O(N * D) in theory, but effectively unbounded / extremely large due to float-based division in the digit loop
complexity.why: Nominally, each number requires O(D) digit operations (D ~ log10 N). However, using `var_4 /= 10` turns `var_4` into a float and divides by 10 indefinitely towards 0 without reaching it quickly in integer steps, so the while-loop may run an enormous number of iterations before `var_4` underflows to 0.0. This dominates runtime.

bottlenecks.detail: Uses `var_4 /= 10` instead of integer division `var_4 //= 10`. This changes `var_4` from int to float and causes it to decrease by a factor of 10 as a float, so `while var_4 > 0` can take a huge number of iterations before reaching 0.0, effectively behaving like a near-infinite loop for each number.
Unnecessary `math.floor(var_4 % 10)` on a value that is already an integer digit; this adds function-call overhead and imports the math module without algorithmic benefit.

Digit extraction is implemented as a Python-level while-loop with repeated modulo and division operations, which is slower than leveraging optimized C-level operations such as `str()` and list comprehensions for these constraints.

FastAudit.core_idea: Iterate over 1..N, convert each integer to a string, map each character back to an int, sum the digits, and accumulate the integer if its digit sum lies within [A, B]. This avoids problematic float operations and uses efficient C-implemented string and list operations.

complexity.why: For each of the N numbers, converting to string and summing digits is proportional to the number of digits D (~log10 N). The temporary string and list for a single number at a time require O(D) space and are reused per iteration, so peak space is O(D). No hidden superlinear factors.

complexity_delta.from: Effectively worse than O(N * D) due to a near-non-terminating inner while-loop caused by float division; practical runtime can blow up.
complexity_delta.to: O(N * D) with small, predictable constants.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity in terms of integer digit operations is similar, but the modified fast version removes the float-division bug and drastically reduces constant factors by avoiding unnecessary math functions and pathological loops.

transformation_steps: Replace arithmetic digit extraction loop using `while var_4 > 0: var_7 += math.floor(var_4 % 10); var_4 /= 10` with string-based digit extraction: `str(var_5)` -> list of chars -> `int` conversion -> `sum`.
Eliminate the use of `math.floor` and the math module entirely, since `% 10` on an integer already yields an integer digit.
Remove the erroneous use of `/=` (true division) and rely on string conversion, thereby avoiding float arithmetic and type changes inside the loop.
Simplify condition checks to idiomatic chained comparisons (`if var_1 <= var_7 <= var_2:`) and range usage (`range(1, var_7 + 1)`), ensuring clean, linear iteration.
trigger_signals: Program appears to hang or run extremely slowly even for relatively small N (e.g., N ≈ 10^4).
High CPU usage with no output progress, suggesting an inner loop not terminating as expected.
Use of `/=` on what should be an integer loop variable in a digit extraction loop, changing the type to float.
Presence of `math.floor` around an expression that is already an integer, indicating unnecessary overhead.
pitfalls: If one insists on arithmetic digit extraction, forgetting to use integer division (`//`) instead of `/` will reintroduce both correctness and performance issues.
Relying on float comparisons (`while var_4 > 0` with var_4 as a float) can lead to non-obvious non-termination or extremely long loops due to gradual underflow.
For much larger constraints (e.g., N up to 10^9), even the optimized O(N * D) approach in Python would be too slow; a more advanced mathematical or combinatorial approach would be required.
Over-optimizing by manually unrolling digit extraction in Python often loses to simple, idiomatic string-based solutions that use compiled C-level operations.

constraints_guess.notes: N is read once and then a fixed 100 candidate target values (1..100) are tested. Typical AtCoder-style constraints for this pattern are N ≤ 100 and |Ai| reasonably small (e.g., |Ai| ≤ 100), so an O(100·N) solution is intended.

dominant_ops: Double nested Python loops: outer over 100 candidate targets, inner over N elements
Per-iteration arithmetic: subtraction, squaring, and addition for each (candidate, element) pair

complexity.why: For each of 100 candidate target values, the code scans the entire list of N elements and accumulates (Ai - t)^2. No extra data structures of size > N are allocated; only scalars and the input list exist.

bottlenecks.detail: The inner loop `for var_2 in range(var_3)` performs Python-level iteration and arithmetic N times for each of the 100 candidates, resulting in ~100·N Python ops. For larger N this overhead dominates.
Each `(var_6[var_2] - (var_1 + 1)) ** 2` involves Python integer objects and exponentiation. Even though exponent is 2, `**` is more expensive than a simple multiplication.
`var_3 = int(eval(input()))` incurs unnecessary `eval` parsing overhead and is unsafe. While not the biggest bottleneck for large N, it is slower and unnecessary.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace nested Python loops with NumPy vectorized operations that compute all squared differences for all 100 candidate targets in one go using broadcasting, and then reduce with a single sum and min over axes. Use faster stdin methods to minimize I/O overhead.

complexity.why: The vectorized version materializes a 100×N array of differences `(var_2 - arange(1, 101).reshape(100, 1))`. Computing squares and sums is still linear in the number of elements (100·N), but the operations are executed in optimized C loops, dramatically reducing constant factors. Memory use increases to hold the 100×N intermediate array.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(100 * N) Python-level loops, Space: O(N)
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(100 * N) with NumPy C-level loops, Space: O(100 * N)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time complexity remains linear in N, but actual runtime drops significantly due to vectorization. Space increases because of the 100×N broadcasted array.

transformation_steps: Parse input once using sys.stdin.readline instead of eval(input()) and input(), removing eval and reducing I/O overhead.
Store the N integers into a Python list, then convert to a NumPy array for efficient vectorized arithmetic.
Create a 100×1 NumPy array of candidate targets using np.arange(1, 101).reshape(100, 1).
Use broadcasting to form a 100×N matrix of differences between each candidate and each element: (var_2 - targets).
Square the matrix elementwise and sum along axis=1 to get a length-100 array of costs for each candidate.
Take the minimum of this array using np.min and print the result.
trigger_signals: Presence of a fixed small outer loop (100 iterations) with an inner loop over all N elements performing arithmetic, suggesting high Python loop overhead.
Use of exponentiation `** 2` inside tight loops, which is more expensive than multiplication and a natural candidate for vectorization.
Reliance on input()/eval in code that may be run with large N, hinting potential I/O overhead issues.
Pattern of computing the same expression over all pairs of (candidate, element), which maps cleanly to NumPy broadcasting semantics.
pitfalls: NumPy dependency: The fast solution requires NumPy; in some competitive programming environments, NumPy may not be available or may have higher startup overhead than pure Python for very small N.

Memory usage: Creating a 100×N array of intermediate results increases memory usage from O(N) to O(100·N). For extremely large N, this could be problematic, although typical constraints here are small.

Integer overflow: NumPy typically uses fixed-width integers (e.g., int64). If Ai and the target range were much larger, squaring could overflow; Python’s built-in ints in the slow version do not overflow.
Over-optimization for tiny inputs: When N is very small, NumPy import and array creation overhead can dominate, making the pure-Python loop competitive or even faster in microbenchmarks.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer N; iterate over 1..N and count numbers whose decimal representation has an odd number of digits.

dominant_ops: Loop from 1 to N
Per-iteration int-to-str conversion: str(var_3)
Per-iteration list creation from string: list(str(var_3))
Length check and conditional increment

complexity.why: Each of the N iterations converts the current number to a string and then to a list, both proportional to the number of digits (≈log10 N). The temporary list var_4 is thrown away each time, so no growing memory usage.

bottlenecks.detail: Converting str(var_3) to a list just to get its length (len(list(str(var_3)))) is unnecessary; len(str(var_3)) is enough.
Python-level for-loop with manual counter updates is relatively slow for large N compared to vectorized or comprehension-based constructs.
Using eval(input()) is slower and unsafe; int(input()) should be used instead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace the explicit Python for-loop and manual counter with a list comprehension and take its length, letting CPython execute the loop in C-level where possible.

complexity_delta.to: Time: O(N log N), Space: O(N)

Redundant construction: converting a string to a list solely to measure its length.
Per-iteration Python overhead in a simple counting loop over a contiguous integer range.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style constraints: N up to about 1e4, M up to about 1e9. Need to factor M and use exponents in combinatorics. Prime exponents are at most O(log M) ≈ 30.

dominant_ops: Trial-division prime factorization up to sqrt(M) in func_9.
Construction of Counter/dict for prime exponents.
Generic I/O helpers using eval and multiple layers of wrappers.
Extraneous helper functions and class definitions increasing load-time and namespace overhead.

The map of prime->exponent is size O(log M). Additional helpers and imports add constant-factor overhead but do not change the asymptotic bound.

func_9 performs imports (sqrt, Counter) inside the function and uses a Counter when only exponents are needed. This adds avoidable overhead if called multiple times.
Input helpers use eval(int(eval(func_10()))) and multiple wrapper functions, which are slower than a direct int(input()) or map(int, input().split()).

Large number of unused helpers (multi-dimensional array initializers, YES/NO printers, Class_1 skeleton) incur parse and load-time cost and noise, making optimization and reasoning harder even if not asymptotically expensive.

FastAudit.core_idea: Factor M via trial division once to obtain prime exponents, then for each exponent e compute the number of ways to distribute that many identical prime factors among N slots using combinations C(N+e-1, e). Multiply these contributions modulo 1e9+7. Implementation is streamlined: minimal imports, direct input, simple factorization that returns a prime list and uses Counter, and a direct multiplicative formula for combinations without global precomputation.

complexity.why: func_2 performs trial division up to sqrt(M), which dominates with O(sqrt(M)). The total number of prime factors (with multiplicity) is O(log M), so Counter(func_2(M)) uses O(log M) time and space. For each exponent e, func_1 computes C(n, e) using O(e) multiplications, and sum(e) over all primes is O(log M). Therefore, combination work is O(log M) total. Memory usage is dominated by storing the prime factors list and Counter, both O(log M).

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(M) + overhead) time, O(log M) space with heavy generic helpers and inner-function imports.
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + log M) time, O(log M) space with reduced constant factors and simpler data flow.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time remains dominated by sqrt(M) trial division, but the fast version cuts constant factors (no eval I/O, no inner imports, focused helpers) and keeps the combination step linear in the small exponents. This is crucial under tight time limits and Python’s relatively slow per-operation cost.

Remove unused utilities (multi-dimensional array constructors, YES/NO printers, incomplete Class_1) from the hot path to reduce load-time work and cognitive noise.

Implement combinations via a direct multiplicative formula localized in func_1 instead of relying on a heavier combinatorics framework or precomputed global arrays; keep operations minimal and only as large as needed for the small exponents.

trigger_signals: The problem involves factoring a single integer M up to about 1e9 and using prime exponents in a combinatorial formula (e.g., distributing factors among N slots).
A solution template includes many generic helpers (array builders, multiple I/O wrappers, unused classes) that are not specific to the current problem.
Factorization or combinatorics utilities import modules or set up data structures inside functions that may be called multiple times.
Combinations are computed via heavy machinery (e.g., global factorial arrays or generalized libraries) even though the required n and k are small or few.

Forgetting to reduce k to min(k, n-k) in the multiplicative combination formula, which can double the work and slow down computation.

Applying the modulus inside every multiplication in the combination function for very small k, incurring unnecessary overhead; better to keep integer arithmetic there and mod only at aggregation sites.

Using eval on input lines, which is both slower and unsafe, and unnecessary when only integers are read.

constraints_guess.notes: Single-input combinatorial/modular-arithmetic problem. Original code precomputes up to a fixed cap 1_000_006 regardless of the actual input n, suggesting n <= 1e6. Modulus is 1e9+7 (prime).

dominant_ops: Linear-time precomputation of modular inverses up to 1_000_006 using recurrence inv[i] = inv[MOD % i] * (MOD - MOD // i) % MOD
Linear-time precomputation of factorials and inverse-factorial-like prefix products up to 1_000_006
Two additional passes up to O(n) for building var_3 and then converting it into a difference array and accumulating the answer

complexity.why: The first for-loop always runs from 2 to 1_000_006, independent of input, and fills three arrays (var_4, var_6, var_7). Subsequent loops are O(n). Arrays var_4, var_6, var_7 each store ~1e6 integers, plus var_3 up to size n.

bottlenecks.detail: Precomputes modular inverses, factorials, and prefix products up to a fixed upper bound 1_000_006 for every run, even if the input n is much smaller.
Maintains three large arrays (var_4, var_6, var_7) of length ~1e6 plus var_3, totaling around 4e6 Python integers, which is heavy in memory and cache-unfriendly.
Builds var_3 in one pass and then performs a backward pass to transform it into a difference array while accumulating the result; this second pass can be algebraically folded into the main summation.
The cap var_1 = 1_000_006 is hard-coded and dominates runtime even when n is small, making the algorithm effectively O(1e6) per test regardless of input size.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace the explicit precomputation of all modular inverses and the separate difference-array pass with a factorial/inverse-factorial scheme driven by the actual input n. Compute factorials up to n-1, then compute the entire inverse-factorial array in linear time from a single modular exponentiation (pow(fact[n-1], MOD-2, MOD)). Use these to evaluate the same combinatorial expression directly in one pass while maintaining a running previous-term value to implicitly handle the difference-array behavior.

complexity.why: func_1 builds factorials up to n-1 in O(n). func_2 builds inverse factorials up to n-1 from a single modular exponentiation in O(n). The final loop over var_4 in range((n+1)//2, n) is O(n). Arrays var_2 and var_11 store only n values each, both proportional to the input rather than a global cap.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(N_max + n) with N_max = 1_000_006; Space: O(N_max)
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(n); Space: O(n)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both versions are linear in n, but the original is tied to a fixed upper bound 1e6 and maintains three large precomputed arrays. The optimized version scales work and memory with the actual input n and reduces constant factors by using factorial/inverse-factorial arrays and removing an extra pass.

transformation_steps: Identify that var_4 is factorials, var_7 holds modular inverses of integers, and var_6 is effectively the inverse factorial prefix product (1 / i! mod MOD). Recognize var_3 construction and the backward pass as a finite-difference transformation over a sequence of combinatorial terms.

Eliminate the fixed upper bound var_1 = 1_000_006 and drive all precomputation sizes directly from the input value n (var_6). This avoids unnecessary work when n << 1e6.

Combine the separate difference-array pass with the accumulation of the final answer: use var_9 to store the previous combinatorial term (analogous to a_k), compute the current term var_10 (a_k), and add (var_10 - var_9) * k to the running result var_1 in a single loop.
Remove the array var_3 entirely by performing the difference and weighted sum on the fly, reducing both time (one less O(n) pass) and memory (no need to store the full sequence of differences).

Tighten index ranges: iterate k (var_4) from ceil((n+1)/2) to n-1 so that the term index 2*k-n used in invfact (var_11) is always valid and non-negative, matching the original conditional (k*2 - n >= 0) but without needing to explicitly store zeros.
trigger_signals: Presence of a large hard-coded upper bound (1_000_006) used for precomputation regardless of input size.

Use of a classic O(N) modular inverse recurrence to build inv[i] for all i up to a cap, followed by a separate prefix product to build another array, suggesting they could be collapsed into a more compact factorial/inverse-factorial representation.
A pattern where an array is filled and then immediately converted with a linear difference pass before summation, indicating potential to algebraically combine those passes.
High memory footprint from multiple parallel arrays of the same size storing related combinatorial quantities (factorial, inverse, inverse factorial).
Final computation depending only on a subsequence of precomputed values (indices constrained by 2*k - n >= 0), yet the code precomputes everything up to the global maximum.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when constructing factorial and inverse-factorial arrays: ensuring that var_2[i] truly corresponds to i! for i in [0, n-1] and that var_11 indices match the required invfact values.

Correctness of the inverse-factorial generation: the recurrence invfact[i-1] = invfact[i] * i mod MOD is valid only if invfact[n-1] is correctly initialized as (n-1)!^(MOD-2) mod MOD and MOD is prime (which holds for 1e9+7).

Index range safety for 2*var_4 - var_6 when accessing var_11: the refactor must ensure the loop bounds on var_4 match the original condition (2*k - n >= 0) so that all indices into var_11 are within [0, n-1].

Losing the telescoping structure when merging the difference-array pass into the main loop: one must maintain a running previous-term variable (var_9) and update it correctly each iteration to emulate var_3[k] = a_k - a_{k-1}.

Memory trade-offs: while the optimized version uses fewer large arrays, it still stores factorial and inverse-factorial arrays; for even tighter memory constraints, one might need a streaming or more algebraically reduced formulation.
Use of eval(input()) is unnecessary and potentially unsafe in general; although not a performance bottleneck here, it is a source of risk and should usually be replaced with int(input()).

constraints_guess.notes: Typical GCD-of-array / AtCoder-style problem: N up to ~1e5, values up to ~1e9. Single query: compute gcd of all numbers.

dominant_ops: Repeated full-array modulo operations inside a while loop
Rebuilding a list via set() to deduplicate in every iteration
Sorting the entire array (sorted()) in every loop iteration

complexity.time: O(T * M log M) where M is current length of the number list and T is number of while-loop rounds (typically O(log V) but can be large in practice)
complexity.why: Initial sort costs O(N log N). The key cost comes from the while len(var_4) > 2 loop: each iteration does O(M) modulo operations plus a set() and sorted() on up to M elements, which is O(M log M). The number of iterations T until the list collapses to two numbers depends on how quickly new remainders disappear; in worst-case patterns this can be high, making the approach substantially slower than a linear fold with Euclid's algorithm.

bottlenecks.detail: Instead of using Euclid’s pairwise gcd, the code repeatedly reduces all elements by modulo with the smallest elements, maintaining a set of remainders. This multi-pass reduction of the entire array is inherently more expensive than necessary.
The while len(var_4) > 2 loop repeatedly scans almost the entire list (for i in range(2, len(var_4))) performing modulo operations on each element.
Each iteration does var_4 = sorted(list(set(var_4))). Converting to a set and then sorting is O(M log M) every time; this dominates runtime when the while loop runs many times.

Using set() + sorted() to maintain uniqueness plus order is overkill for this task and leads to repeated full rebuilds of the array instead of incrementally updating a small state such as a scalar gcd.
Various unused imports and constants (Counter, deque, combinations, etc.) don’t change complexity but indicate template code; they slightly increase startup overhead and obfuscate the core logic.
Using eval() to parse integers (func_1 and func_3) is slower and unsafe, although this is not the primary performance bottleneck compared to the algorithm itself.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use Euclid’s algorithm to compute the gcd of the array by folding from left to right: gcd_all = gcd(a1, a2, ..., an) computed via repeated pairwise gcd(a, b). Each gcd step runs in O(log V) time, and only a single scalar is carried forward.

complexity.why: Each gcd(var_2, var_3) call performs a logarithmic number of modulus operations in the magnitude of the numbers (O(log V)), and we call it once per element after the first, so total time is O(N log V). The algorithm only stores the current gcd and the next element, so additional space usage is constant.

complexity_delta.from: Approximately O(T * M log M) with repeated full-array processing and sorts inside a while loop (T iterations, M up to N).
complexity_delta.to: O(N log V) using a simple linear fold with Euclid’s gcd.
complexity_delta.note: The optimized version replaces multiple passes over the evolving array and expensive deduplication/sorting with a single pass that maintains only the scalar gcd.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the required result is simply the gcd of all input numbers, which is associative: gcd(a1, ..., an) = gcd(...gcd(gcd(a1, a2), a3)..., an).
Replace the multi-step remainder-set algorithm (modding all elements by the smallest ones, appending 0, deduplicating with set, and sorting) with a standard pairwise Euclidean gcd computation.
Collapse the state from an evolving list var_4 to a single scalar accumulator var_6 that stores the gcd so far.
Remove the while len(var_4) > 2 loop and inner for-loops; instead, iterate once over the input list and update var_6 = gcd(var_6, current_element).
Keep recursion depth safe: Euclid’s algorithm depth is O(log V), so recursion is acceptable here; alternatively, it can be trivially converted to an iterative loop if needed.
Avoid repeated set() and sorted() operations entirely, since they are unnecessary once we maintain only the scalar gcd.
trigger_signals: A while loop whose termination condition depends on the size of a container (len(var_4) > 2) combined with heavy operations (modulo, set, sorted) inside signals potential superlinear or unpredictable runtime.
Patterns like var_4 = sorted(list(set(var_4))) executed repeatedly indicate repeated full reconstruction of a data structure, which is often a red flag when N can be large.
The presence of known mathematical structure (gcd) suggests there is a canonical O(N log V) solution; any solution doing repeated full-array transformations is suspect.
Multiple nested loops where the outer loop has no clear small bound in terms of N (here, bounded only by eventual convergence of a number-theoretic process) suggest possible T * N * log N behavior.

A solution that maintains a growing or fluctuating list of remainders instead of a small fixed-size state (gcd accumulator) indicates missed opportunities to exploit associativity and idempotence of gcd.
pitfalls: Assuming that the repeated remainder-and-dedup process will converge quickly for all inputs; adversarial or worst-case inputs can keep the list size large for many iterations.
Underestimating the cost of set() + sorted() in every iteration; these operations are O(M log M) and dominate the runtime when done repeatedly.
Relying on eval() for integer input can introduce both performance overhead and security issues; although minor compared to algorithmic cost, it is still a bad practice.

If converting the gcd function to recursive form, one must ensure that recursion depth stays within bounds; however, Euclid’s algorithm guarantees O(log V) depth, which is safe for typical constraints.

Overcomplicating the solution with generic templates (multiple unused helper functions and imports) can obscure the simple gcd-fold approach and make it harder to recognize the straightforward O(N log V) method.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical Lunlun-number problem (e.g., AtCoder) where input is K (1-indexed) up to around 1e5; need the K-th number in increasing order.

dominant_ops: Level-by-level BFS over all generated numbers using Python sets
Repeated string conversions per number to inspect/append last digit
Flattening list-of-sets into a single list
Global sort of all generated numbers before indexing
