complexity.why: The BFS-style expansion generates O(K) numbers in total, but after generation it flattens all levels into a list and sorts it. Sorting the K numbers dominates with O(K log K) time. Space holds all generated numbers plus intermediate structures, which is O(K).

bottlenecks.detail: After generating enough numbers, the code flattens all sets into var_11 and calls sort(), which costs O(K log K) and dominates runtime.

Each level of numbers is stored as a set inside a list (var_1). This incurs hashing and set-management overhead, even though duplicates are largely controlled by the generation rules and only one visit per parent is needed.
All levels are kept in memory simultaneously and then copied again into var_11, effectively duplicating storage and doing extra passes over O(K) elements.

For every number in every level, the code converts the number to string several times (for var_9 and for concatenation) inside nested loops, adding significant constant-factor overhead on top of an already more expensive O(K log K) algorithm.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a single list as a BFS queue over Lunlun numbers ordered by value, appending children in such a way that the sequence is generated directly in increasing order. This removes the need for sets and for a final sort: we just extend the list until it has at least K elements and then index the (K-1)-th element.

complexity.why: Each iteration processes exactly one existing number, generates 2–3 children with a constant amount of work (including a few string operations), and appends them. To reach K numbers we execute O(K) iterations and do O(1) work per iteration on average, so total time is O(K). Only the list of generated numbers is stored, giving O(K) space use.

complexity_delta.from: O(K log K) time, O(K) space
complexity_delta.to: O(K) time, O(K) space
complexity_delta.note: The main asymptotic improvement comes from eliminating the final global sort and avoiding per-level set structures, instead generating Lunlun numbers in sorted order via a simple list-based BFS.

transformation_steps: Replace the list-of-set levels (var_1) with a single list (var_2) that simultaneously acts as storage and a BFS queue.
Remove the global flatten-and-sort phase. Instead of generating unordered layers and sorting at the end, design the BFS so that appended children preserve increasing order of the global sequence.
Switch from set insertion and membership semantics to plain list append operations, relying on the construction rules to avoid problematic duplicates in the context of this problem.
Track a simple index (var_3) into the list to indicate the current BFS frontier element, incrementing it each iteration while appending new children to the end of the list.
Stop generation as soon as the list length reaches K and directly access the (K-1)-th element, rather than counting via a separate counter and then rebuilding/sorting the entire collection.
trigger_signals: Presence of a full sort (var_11.sort()) after an already-complete BFS-like enumeration of all candidate numbers.
Use of sets for each BFS level when only a single visit per parent is required and duplicates are not conceptually central.
Flattening multiple containers of numbers (var_1 -> var_11) before the final selection, indicating unnecessary copying and materialization.
Overall pattern: generate many values, then sort and index one element, which often signals an opportunity to generate directly in order.
pitfalls: When removing the final sort, it is crucial that the BFS generation order actually matches numeric ascending order; otherwise, directly indexing into the list will produce the wrong K-th number.
Changing from sets to lists can introduce duplicates if the generation logic is not carefully controlled; duplicates would break both correctness (wrong rank) and performance (effective K grows).

Relying heavily on string operations in the hot path can still be costly for very large K; while asymptotically linear, the constant factor matters, so unnecessary recomputations (multiple str() calls on the same number) should be minimized if further optimization is needed.

Using list concatenation (var_2 += [...]) repeatedly can be slightly less efficient than append/extend patterns if K becomes large; care should be taken if porting to constraints much larger than the original problem.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical 'Lunlun numbers' task (e.g., AtCoder ABC161 D): given N (up to about 1e5), output the N-th positive integer where adjacent digits differ by at most 1.

dominant_ops: Recursive DFS over all valid numbers up to fixed digit length (depth ~10, branching <=3)
Frequent int->str conversions and slicing inside recursion
Global list append for every generated number
Sorting the entire generated list at the end

complexity.why: L is the maximum digit length (here effectively 11 due to the len(str(var_2)) > 10 cutoff); each node in the recursion tree does O(L) work due to str() and indexing, and branching is up to 3 per digit, giving roughly O(3^L) nodes. K is the total count of generated numbers (~9 * (3^L - 1) / 2). After generation, a full sort of size K costs O(K log K). Memory holds all K numbers in var_4.

bottlenecks.detail: Generates all Lunlun numbers up to digit length >10 regardless of the requested index var_1; work is independent of N and tied only to the fixed depth limit.
Each recursion level converts the current integer to a string twice (len(str(var_2)), int(str(var_2)[-1])), incurring O(d) cost per node where d is the number of digits.
Deep recursive calls (depth up to 11) with Python function-call overhead at every node in the 3-ary tree.
Sorting the full list of all generated values O(K log K) even if only the first var_1 elements are needed.
Stores all generated numbers in a single list var_4 instead of only maintaining the frontier or the first N numbers.

FastAudit.core_idea: Iteratively generate Lunlun numbers level by level (by digit-length) using a BFS-like expansion on the last digit with arithmetic instead of strings, and stop as soon as we have generated at least N distinct numbers. Maintain a global set of discovered numbers and a frontier set for the current digit-length, then sort once at the end to pick the N-th element.

complexity.why: Each iteration of the while loop expands every number in the current frontier var_4 to up to 3 children, and var_2 accumulates all seen numbers. The process stops when |var_2| >= N, so total expansions are O(N). Operations per expansion are O(1) (arithmetic, set add). Final sorting of |var_2| elements costs O(N log N). Memory usage is dominated by storing all generated numbers in var_2 and the current frontier var_4, both O(N).

complexity_delta.from:
Time: O(3^L * L + K log K) and independent of N; Space: O(K), where K is the total number of Lunlun numbers up to fixed length L>10.
L is fixed but the algorithm always pays for all depths up to L regardless of requested N.
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(N log N); Space: O(N), where N is the requested index var_1 (number of required Lunlun numbers). Work now scales with N rather than with a fixed maximal depth.
complexity_delta.note: In the typical constraint regime (N up to ~1e5), the new method avoids generating and sorting many unneeded large numbers, especially when N is much smaller than the total count for L-digit numbers, and avoids per-node string overhead and recursion.

transformation_steps: Replace recursive DFS with an iterative BFS-style expansion using a loop and an explicit frontier (var_4) representing all Lunlun numbers of the current digit length.

Eliminate repeated int->str conversions and digit extraction via strings; instead, compute the last digit using arithmetic (var_3 % 10) and build new numbers with integer arithmetic (var_3 * 10 + offset).

Change the stopping condition from a fixed digit-length limit (len(str(var_2)) > 10) to a demand-driven condition (while len(var_2) < var_1), ensuring we generate numbers only until we have at least N.

Use a set (var_2) to accumulate all generated numbers to avoid duplicates and support efficient membership and merging; maintain var_4 as the current layer, and var_5 as the next layer in each iteration.
Generate children based directly on the last digit case (0, 9, or middle digits) to ensure adjacency difference <= 1 while avoiding string slicing.
After generation completes, convert the accumulated set var_2 to a list, sort it once, and index the (var_1 - 1)-th element, rather than sorting a huge list built via recursion.

Remove global shared mutable state for recursion (the list var_4 in the slow version) and instead use local sets for current and next layers to better reflect the BFS structure and to constrain memory growth to what is needed.
trigger_signals: Presence of a deeply recursive function (func_1) called from a loop over starting digits, with no dependence on N in the termination condition besides a fixed maximal length.
Use of len(str(var_2)) and str(var_2)[-1] inside the recursive core, indicating O(d) string operations per node on top of the graph expansion.
Global collection var_4 that is appended to for every recursion node, implying all generated numbers are kept irrespective of N.
Post-generation full sort var_4.sort() over all collected values, indicating that sorting cost grows with total generated states rather than with N.
Fixed digit-length cutoff (>10) in the slow code, suggesting potential mismatch between work and requested N and motivating a more output-sensitive approach.
Opportunity to interpret the generation as a graph/BFS on last digits (edges between digits differing by at most 1), which naturally suggests an iterative frontier-based solution.
pitfalls: Using sets for var_2 and var_4 means iteration order is arbitrary; correctness depends on the final sorted(list(var_2)) call to impose numeric order before indexing. Forgetting the final sort or relying on set order would be incorrect.

While the new method is demand-driven in N, it still stores all numbers up to the N-th one; for very large N this can be memory-intensive. Streaming approaches or priority queues (e.g., a min-heap) could reduce memory by not storing all intermediates.

If constraints required indexing far beyond the range for which Lunlun numbers are reasonably small, BFS by digit-length may still result in large integers and increased arithmetic cost; in the given context this is acceptable but should be noted.

The original fixed-length cutoff (len(str(var_2)) > 10) implicitly restricts the search space; removing it for a general N must be done carefully to ensure termination and performance under the actual problem constraints.
Using eval(input()) is fragile and slower than int(input()); it is unchanged between versions but should be avoided for robustness, even though it is not the primary performance bottleneck.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case; var_1 likely up to around 1e12 given need to replace O(N) linear scan with O(sqrt(N)) divisor enumeration.

dominant_ops: Single for-loop from 1 to floor(var_1 / var_2), performing subtraction and modulo each iteration.

complexity.time: O(var_1 / var_2) (worst-case O(N) when var_2 is small, especially var_2 = 1)
complexity.why: The loop `for var_4 in range(1, var_1 // var_2 + 1)` dominates, doing O(1) arithmetic and a modulo per iteration. No auxiliary data structures grow with input size.

bottlenecks.detail: Iterates up to var_1 // var_2 times; with var_2 = 1 this is O(var_1), which is too slow if var_1 can be as large as ~1e12.
Each iteration computes `var_5 = var_1 - var_4 * var_2` and `var_5 % var_4`, so the modulo is executed O(var_1 / var_2) times.

Condition `(var_1 - var_4 * var_2) % var_4 == 0` simplifies to `var_1 % var_4 == 0`, i.e., checking divisors of var_1. The code searches linearly over all candidates instead of using a divisor-enumeration strategy.

FastAudit.core_idea: Recognize that the loop is effectively searching for the largest divisor d of var_1 such that d <= var_1 / var_2 (equivalently d * var_2 <= var_1). Instead of scanning all d from 1 to var_1 / var_2, enumerate all divisors of var_1 in O(sqrt(var_1)), sort them in descending order, and pick the first one satisfying d * var_2 <= var_1.

complexity.time: O(sqrt(var_1) + D log D), where D is the number of divisors of var_1 (typically D << sqrt(var_1))
complexity.why: Divisors are generated by iterating var_5 from 1 to floor(sqrt(var_6)) and adding both var_5 and var_6 // var_5 when they divide evenly, giving O(sqrt(var_1)) divisor checks. The divisor list `var_4` contains D elements which are then sorted in O(D log D). Memory is dominated by storing these D divisors.

complexity_delta.from: O(var_1 / var_2) time, O(1) space (worst-case O(N) when var_2 is small)
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(var_1) + D log D) time, O(D) space, where D is the number of divisors of var_1
complexity_delta.note: For large var_1 and small var_2 (especially var_2 = 1), this transitions from linear in N to roughly O(sqrt(N)), which is typically required for N up to about 1e12 in Python.

transformation_steps: Algebraic simplification: Start from `var_5 = var_1 - var_4 * var_2` and condition `var_5 % var_4 == 0`. Observe `(var_1 - var_4 * var_2) % var_4 == 0` is equivalent to `var_1 % var_4 == 0`, since `var_4 * var_2` is always divisible by `var_4`.

Problem reformulation: The original loop maintains `var_3` as the largest var_4 up to floor(var_1 / var_2) such that `var_1 % var_4 == 0`. Thus the task is to find the maximum divisor d of var_1 such that `d <= var_1 / var_2` (or equivalently `d * var_2 <= var_1`).

Switch from linear scan to divisor enumeration: Instead of testing all candidates up to var_1 / var_2, enumerate all divisors of var_1 by iterating up to sqrt(var_1) and adding both the small divisor and its complementary large divisor.
Ordering for early exit: Sort the divisor list in descending order so the first divisor satisfying `d * var_2 <= var_1` is the maximum valid d, allowing an early exit without checking all divisors.

Replace explicit case handling: The original code had a fast path for `var_1 % var_2 == 0`. The new method handles this uniformly by enumeration, where the divisor `var_1 // var_2` naturally appears and is selected by the `d * var_2 <= var_1` condition.
trigger_signals: Loop bound proportional to the magnitude of the input value (`range(1, var_1 // var_2 + 1)`), suggesting potential O(N) time.
Heavy-use arithmetic inside the loop, especially modulo, repeated O(N) times.
Single numeric input with no arrays or complex structures, indicating a number-theory style optimization (e.g., divisor enumeration) is likely.
Simplifiable modulo expression `(var_1 - var_4 * var_2) % var_4` where the loop variable also appears as the modulo base.
Known competitive-programming pattern: searching over divisors or factors often admits an O(sqrt(N)) solution.
pitfalls: Floating-point sqrt: Using `var_6**0.5` introduces floating-point arithmetic; for very large var_6 there is a theoretical risk of rounding errors when converting to int. For typical constraints (<= 1e12) this is safe, but `math.isqrt(var_6)` would be more robust.

Sorting cost: Sorting divisors O(D log D) is acceptable because D is small, but if D were large or if the logic was extended, a more direct way to iterate divisors in descending order without sorting might be preferable.

Behavioral equivalence: It is crucial that the new condition `var_3 * var_2 <= var_1` exactly matches the original bound `var_4 <= var_1 // var_2`. Any off-by-one error would change answers for edge cases.

Early return and I/O: The fast version returns from inside the loop after printing, which is fine for a single test case. For multiple test cases or reused functions, this early exit pattern would need reconsideration.

Implicit removal of the explicit `var_1 % var_2 == 0` branch: While the new logic covers that case, care must be taken to ensure that previously special-cased scenarios are fully subsumed by the generalized algorithm.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer N; output the N-th positive integer whose adjacent digits differ by at most 1 (a.k.a. Lunlun / stepping number). Based on common tasks like AtCoder ABC161 D.

dominant_ops: Recursive DFS that generates all Lunlun numbers up to 10 digits, repeated string conversions per node, and a global sort of all generated numbers.

complexity.time: O(M log M) where M ≈ 9 * 3^L with L = 10 (max length), effectively a fixed upper bound but independent of input N.
complexity.why: The code explores the full branching tree of Lunlun numbers up to length 10 via recursion, stores every generated number in a list, then sorts the entire list before indexing the N-th element.

bottlenecks.detail: Generates all Lunlun numbers up to 10 digits regardless of N; work is not proportional to the requested rank and can be wasteful when N is relatively small.
Uses deep recursion (depth up to 10) with a function call per generated number, combined with multiple str() and int() conversions in each call.
For every node, converts the current number to string twice (for length and last digit), which is costly in tight loops compared to pure integer arithmetic.
Performs a global sort of all M generated numbers (O(M log M)), even though only the N-th smallest is needed.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a min-heap (priority queue) to perform a best-first traversal of Lunlun numbers in increasing order, expanding from current numbers by adding digits adjacent to the first and last digit, and stop after generating roughly N unique numbers tracked in a visited set.

complexity.time: O(K log K) with K ≈ N (number of unique Lunlun numbers popped from the heap)
complexity.why: Each newly discovered number is inserted into the heap and set once; each heap push/pop is O(log K). The loop runs until about N+100 unique numbers are processed, then the visited set is converted to a list and sorted (O(K log K)), on the same order as the heap work.

complexity_delta.from: O(M log M) time and O(M) space to precompute and sort all Lunlun numbers up to 10 digits, where M ≈ constant (≈ 5e5) and independent of N.
complexity_delta.to: O(N log N) time and O(N) space, generating only about N unique numbers plus a small margin and avoiding full enumeration of the search space.
complexity_delta.note: As constraints grow (e.g., larger maximum digit length or generalized variants), the original approach scales with the full combinatorial space, while the heap-based approach scales with N (requested rank), making it more robust.

transformation_steps: Replaced global recursive DFS enumeration with a priority-queue-based best-first search that naturally yields numbers in increasing order.
Introduced a visited set to skip duplicates introduced by expanding on both ends of the number, ensuring each Lunlun number is processed once.
Stopped relying on generating the entire search space up to a fixed depth; instead, the loop runs until enough (≈ N+100) unique candidates have been produced.
Deferred global sorting to a much smaller set (the visited numbers) and only after limiting its size via the heap-driven traversal.
Shifted the dependence of the runtime from the full space size (all sequences up to length 10) toward the requested index N.
trigger_signals: Full combinatorial generation (DFS over all valid numbers up to a fixed length) even though only the N-th smallest number is required.
Use of recursion with per-node string conversions in a performance-sensitive enumeration.
Global sort of a large list of candidates as a separate step before selecting the N-th element.
Problem context suggests N can be as large as around 10^5, making naive enumeration plus sort close to time limits in Python.
pitfalls: The heap-based solution still performs multiple string-int conversions per iteration; using pure integer arithmetic on digits would further improve performance.
The stopping condition uses a heuristic margin (N+100); if the margin were too small in a variant of the problem, it could fail to cover the true N-th number.
Maintaining both a heap and a visited set increases memory usage; for very large N, careful consideration of memory growth is required.
Relying on eval(input()) is both stylistically unsafe and slightly slower than int(input()); replacing eval with int is recommended for robustness.

constraints_guess.notes: Computing the number of divisors of n! modulo 1e9+7. Typical contest constraints push for at least ~1e4, often up to ~1e5, requiring something close to sieve-based prime exponent accumulation.

dominant_ops: Nested trial-division loops for every k in [2..n]
Integer modulo and division operations inside the inner loops
Appending all prime factors to a Python list, then counting with collections.Counter

complexity.why: For each integer k from 2 to n, the code runs a for-loop var_4 from 2 up to k and tests divisibility. For prime k this does ~k modulo operations; summing over k gives ~sum_{k=2}^n k = O(n^2) Python-level iterations. The factor list var_5 stores every prime factor of every k ≤ n. The total number of prime factors up to n is Θ(n log log n), which is upper-bounded by O(n log n), so the list and Counter both scale accordingly.

bottlenecks.detail: Each number k in [2..n] is factored from scratch using naive trial division up to k, yielding an O(n^2) algorithm for collecting exponents for n!.
Two nested Python loops (over var_6 and var_4) with inner while loops perform many small interpreted operations (mod, division, loop control), which are expensive in CPython.
All factors of all k are appended to var_5, then materialized into a Counter. This uses O(number of factors) extra memory and adds overhead for hashing and counting.

The outer while var_6 != 1 combined with for var_4 in range(2, var_6 + 1) restarts scanning divisors for each k, instead of reusing prime information (e.g., via sieve or cumulative exponent formulas for n!).

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid factoring every k in [2..n] individually in Python. Instead, compute n! once using math.factorial (implemented in optimized C with big integers) and then factor that single large number by repeated division in a single while loop, tracking multiplicity runs and accumulating the product of (exponent-like counters) on the fly without materializing all factors or using Counter.

complexity.time: O(n) Python-level loop iterations plus super-linear big-integer arithmetic cost
complexity.space: O(size(n!)) in big integers, but only O(1) additional Python containers
complexity.why: At the Python level, var_4 increases from 2 up to at most n while var_1 is repeatedly divided; the while-loop body performs O(n) divisor steps (each with one or more big-int divisions). The number of successful divisions is O(log n!) because each division reduces var_1 by at least a factor of 2. However each big-int operation costs Θ(log n!) bit-time, so the true bit-complexity is super-linear (roughly quadratic in log n!). Despite this, the design minimizes Python interpreter overhead by relying on math.factorial and big-int operations written in C, and avoids storing all factors or using Counter.

delta_type: constant-factor and implementation-level shift (Python loops -> C-level big-int operations)
with similar or worse asymptotic bit-complexity but far fewer Python interpreter steps.

complexity_delta.from: O(n^2) Python-level trial divisions and list operations, with O(n log n) extra space for storing all prime factors of all k ≤ n.
complexity_delta.to: O(n) Python-level loop iterations plus heavy big-integer arithmetic in C, with only O(1) extra Python container space but O(size(n!)) for the big integer itself.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically in terms of arithmetic bit operations, factoring n! via big integers is not fundamentally better and can even be worse. The practical speedup mainly comes from eliminating a quadratic number of Python-level interpreted operations and leveraging optimized C routines.

transformation_steps: Replace per-integer factorization of each k in [2..n] with a single computation of n! using math.factorial, shifting multiplication work into optimized C big-int code.
Remove the list var_5 and Counter; instead, accumulate multiplicities on the fly during factorization via simple scalar variables (var_2, var_3).
Collapse the nested for loops over k and potential divisors into a single while loop over divisors var_4, reducing Python-level loop nesting from two levels to one.
Eliminate repeated construction of ranges and redundant scans from 2..k for every k, relying instead on repeated division of a single composite (n!).
trigger_signals: Presence of nested loops where the inner loop bound depends linearly on the outer loop variable (here: for var_6 in [2..n], inner for var_4 in [2..var_6]), which suggests O(n^2) behavior.
Per-element naive trial division up to the value itself (for var_4 in range(2, var_6 + 1)) with no reuse of previous factorization or precomputed primes.
Construction of a large list of all prime factors and then passing it through collections.Counter, indicating unnecessary memory traffic and hashing overhead.
The mathematical structure of the problem (divisors of n!) hints at closed-form exponent formulas or sieve-based accumulation; brute factoring every integer is a red flag.
pitfalls: Computing factorial(n) directly leads to enormous integers for large n; even if Python can represent them, time and memory usage for big-int operations can explode and become worse than a more nuanced prime-sieve-based approach.
Factoring n! via trial division over all integers (including composites) is mathematically redundant and inefficient; it over-divides by composite factors and complicates correct exponent tracking.

Although Python-level operations are reduced, the algorithm still has super-linear cost in terms of bit operations; for large n, both versions can be impractical and a genuine number-theoretic optimization (e.g., accumulating prime exponents via floor(n/p^k)) would be preferable.
Use of eval(input()) is unsafe and unnecessary; while not primarily a performance issue, it is a security and robustness hazard that should be replaced with int(input()).

The modified logic (tracking var_3 per divisor rather than per prime) is easy to get wrong relative to the intended formula product (e_i + 1) over prime exponents, so correctness must be reverified, not just performance.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic AtCoder-style problem: choose M of N 3D points to maximize |sum x|+|sum y|+|sum z|. Typical constraints N up to around 1e5, coordinates up to ~1e9.

dominant_ops: For each of the 8 sign combinations: build a list of N quadruples [score, sx*xi, sy*yi, sz*zi], sort this length-N list in descending order, then run three separate passes over the top M elements to compute coordinate sums with abs.

complexity.time: O(8 * N log N + 8 * (N + M)) = O(N log N)
complexity.why: For each of the 8 iterations over var_2 in range(2**3), the code fills _xyz with N elements (O(N)), sorts it (O(N log N)), then slices and sums over the first M elements three times (O(M)). N log N dominates for large N; everything is repeated 8 times.

bottlenecks.detail: Instead of storing a single scalar key per point, each element of _xyz is a list of 4 integers: [sum(_abc), sx*xi, sy*yi, sz*zi]. Sorting and slicing this larger structure increases memory footprint and constant factors for comparisons and moves.

After sorting, the code computes _r by running three separate sum() calls over generators on _xyz[:var_4] (indices 1, 2, and 3). This means 3*M accesses and Python-level additions for every sign combination, even though a single scalar objective per point would suffice.

The inner loop over var_3 (0..N-1) creates _abc via a Python list comprehension and then wraps it again in a new list when appending to _xyz. That is a lot of small list allocations and Python arithmetic in tight loops.

For every sign pattern var_2, the sign vector var_1 is rebuilt bit-by-bit in a loop. While small (only 3 elements), it’s still repeated 8 times and can be simplified or inlined logically as nested loops as in the fast version.

FastAudit.core_idea: For each of the 8 sign combinations (sx, sy, sz), project each 3D point to a single scalar score = sx*xi + sy*yi + sz*zi, sort these scores, and sum the top M. The maximum over all sign patterns equals the desired maximum of |sum x|+|sum y|+|sum z|, so we only need scalar scores instead of keeping per-coordinate sums explicitly.

complexity.time: O(8 * N log N + 8 * (N + M)) = O(N log N)
complexity.why: For each of the 8 (sx,sy,sz) combinations, we build a list var_4 of N integers (O(N)), sort it (O(N log N)), then sum the first M elements (O(M)). The operations are the same order as the slow version but use only scalars and a single sum per combination, which significantly reduces constant factors.

complexity_delta.from: O(8 * (N log N + N + M)) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(8 * (N log N + N + M)) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged (still 8 sorts of N elements), but the fast code eliminates per-point coordinate storage and repeated summations, reducing constant factors and memory traffic.

transformation_steps: Recognize that for a fixed sign pattern (sx, sy, sz), maximizing |sum x|+|sum y|+|sum z| over a chosen subset is equivalent to maximizing sum(sx*xi + sy*yi + sz*zi) for that subset.
Instead of storing [score, sx*xi, sy*yi, sz*zi] for each point, store only the scalar score = sx*xi + sy*yi + sz*zi in a list var_4.
Sort var_4 in descending order and compute the objective for that sign pattern as sum(var_4[:M]), removing the need for three separate abs(sum(...)) calculations over coordinates.
Replace the bit-manipulation loop that constructs var_1 in the slow code with explicit nested loops over (1, -1) for each coordinate, which is clearer and removes a small overhead.
Avoid re-creating and handling larger temporary lists in inner loops; work with simple integers wherever possible to minimize Python-level overhead.
trigger_signals: Use of large composite list elements (e.g., length-4 lists) when a single scalar key would suffice for sorting and selection.
Multiple passes with sum(...) and abs(...) over the same top-M slice for each iteration of an outer loop.
Inner loops that construct temporary lists (_abc, _xyz elements) for every point and every configuration.
Same O(N log N) structure as known accepted solutions but with significantly heavier operations per element, leading to timeouts near upper constraints.
pitfalls: When switching from explicit coordinate sums to scalar projections, it’s easy to get the sign logic wrong; the equivalence relies on choosing (sx, sy, sz) among all 8 combinations so that the projected sum matches |sum x|+|sum y|+|sum z| for the chosen subset.
If the number of dimensions or the number of sign combinations changes, hard-coding nested loops over (1, -1) or the exponent 2**3 must be updated accordingly.

Using slicing and sum on very large lists can still be expensive; if constraints grow further, one might need to avoid full sorting and instead use partial selection (like nlargest) or counting-like optimizations.

Changing the data representation (from full coordinate storage to scalars) must preserve numerical correctness; in languages with fixed-width integers, overflow could become an issue when summing large coordinates, though Python’s big integers avoid this.

constraints_guess.notes: Computes a linear recurrence similar to Fibonacci with base cases a[0]=2, a[1]=1. The original code preallocates an array of size 1e6, suggesting n is intended to be <= 1e6.

dominant_ops: Single loop from 2 to n performing constant-time integer additions and list writes
Initialization of a large fixed-size list of length 1_000_000

complexity.why: The recurrence requires one pass over indices 2..n, so time grows linearly with n. However, the list is always of size 1_000_000 regardless of n, so space is proportional to that fixed maximum N_max instead of the actual n.

bottlenecks.detail: Allocates a list of 1_000_000 elements even when n is much smaller, wasting memory and increasing initialization time.
Creating and zero-initializing a 1_000_000-length list incurs unnecessary work when n is small.
If the intended constraints grow beyond 1_000_000, the fixed-size list can either be too small (logic error) or need to be increased further, raising the risk of hitting memory limits.

FastAudit.core_idea: Allocate the DP array exactly to size n+1 instead of a fixed large upper bound, so memory usage scales with the actual input and list initialization work is minimized.

complexity.why: The loop structure and per-iteration work remain unchanged, so time complexity stays linear in n. The list length is now n+1, so memory usage is proportional to the actual input size, improving from a fixed upper bound to input-sensitive space usage.

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time remains linear, but list initialization work and memory footprint now grow with n instead of a fixed upper bound, reducing overhead for small n and improving cache locality.

transformation_steps: Replace fixed-size list allocation `var_1 = [0] * 1000000` with size based on input: `var_1 = [0] * (var_2 + 1)`.
Keep the recurrence and loop bounds unchanged so that computation remains identical for all valid n.
Retain base case assignments `var_1[0] = 2` and `var_1[1] = 1` and the final output `print(var_1[var_2])`.
trigger_signals: Presence of a large magic constant (1_000_000) used for array sizing instead of depending on input.
Memory usage disproportionately large compared to given n values in tests.
Potential Memory Limit Exceeded (MLE) or slow start-up due to frequent full re-initialization of a large list.
Code comments or problem statements indicating upper bounds different from the hardcoded capacity.
pitfalls: If n can be 0 or 1, the code must ensure the allocated list length is at least 2 before assigning `var_1[1]`; here it assumes n >= 1. For n=0, `var_1[1]` would be out of range.
If actual constraints permit n > 1_000_000, the original code would index out of bounds; the new version scales correctly but may use a lot of memory for extremely large n.
Using `eval(input())` is unsafe and unnecessary; it should be replaced with `int(input())` to avoid security and performance issues when untrusted input is possible.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical CP setting: N people, M food types. Fast solution uses a single frequency array over foods; slow solution would TLE if N,M or total favorites are large (e.g., up to 2e5).

dominant_ops: Triple nested loops: for each food id (1..M), for each person (1..N), scan that person's list of liked foods linearly to check membership.

complexity.time: O(M * sum_K) (worst-case O(N * M^2) when each person lists O(M) foods)
complexity.why: Input is stored as a list of lists: var_1[person] holds [Ki, foods...]. Outer loop runs over all M foods. For each food, we iterate over all N people, and for each person we scan up to Ki entries. Total inner work per food is O(sum_K) in the worst case, giving O(M * sum_K). Storing all lists costs O(sum_K) integers.

bottlenecks.detail: The loops over food (var_6), over people (var_7), and over each person’s food list (var_8) create O(M * sum_K) membership checks.
For each food id, the code linearly searches every person’s list again instead of reusing previous work or using an index structure.
Iterating food ids from 1..M and then scanning lists to see if the id appears is more expensive than iterating the given pairs (person, food) once and counting.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a single frequency array over foods and count, in one pass over all (person, food) pairs, how many people like each food; then count foods whose frequency equals N.

complexity.why: Each input pair (person, food) is processed exactly once: we increment var_3[food-1]. Counting how many foods have frequency N is an additional O(M). The frequency array over M foods uses O(M) space; no need to store all person lists.

complexity_delta.from: O(M * sum_K) time, O(sum_K) space
complexity_delta.to: O(sum_K) time, O(M) space
complexity_delta.note: Eliminated repeated scans of each person’s list for every food id by aggregating counts in a frequency array during a single pass.

transformation_steps: Stop iterating over every food id and then searching all lists for that id.
Instead, as each person’s line is read, immediately update a frequency array var_3 indexed by food id (after converting to int and shifting by -1).
After processing all people, scan the frequency array once and count how many positions equal N (the number of people).
Remove storage of the full person->foods matrix where not needed; only cumulative counts per food are kept.
trigger_signals: Presence of a triple nested loop over (food id) x (person) x (person’s foods).
Membership checking implemented as repeated linear scans through lists.
Outer loop ranges over the domain of food ids rather than iterating actual (person, food) pairs once.
Total operations grow as M times the total size of all lists, which is unnecessary for simple counting.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when mapping 1-based food ids to 0-based array indices (need food_id-1).
Forgetting to convert input tokens to integers before indexing or incrementing the frequency array.
Misinterpreting the first value on each line (Ki) as a food id instead of the count of subsequent foods.
Incorrectly counting foods that appear at least once instead of exactly N times (must compare frequency to N, not >= 1).

constraints_guess.notes: Classic ‘number of divisors of N!’ type task (e.g., AtCoder ABC 052 C). N is typically up to around 10^4 so that sieve-based O(N log N) solutions pass but naive O(N^2+) do not.

dominant_ops: For each k from 1 to N, recompute primality up to k using trial division (func_2).
For each k from 1 to N, scan all numbers up to k to extract prime exponents and fill a length-N vector (func_1).
For each k from 1 to N, elementwise add two length-N arrays (var_9 accumulation).

complexity.why: For a given k, func_2 runs a naive prime sieve: sum_{i=2..k} O(sqrt(i)) = O(k^{1.5}). Then func_1 scans up to k and does O(1) work for most positions plus a few divisions, i.e. O(k). This is called for every k from 1 to N, giving sum_{k=1..N}(k^{1.5} + k) = O(N^{2.5}). Arrays var_6, var_9, var_10 are at most length N, so memory is linear.

bottlenecks.detail: func_2 recomputes prime information from scratch for each k, using nested loops over all integers up to k and all possible divisors up to sqrt(i). This alone is ~O(N^{2.5}) across all calls.
Prime list for all numbers ≤k is recomputed for every k, although primes ≤N are the same regardless of k.

func_1 builds a length-N exponent vector for each k (even though only primes ≤k are relevant) and then the main loop repeatedly adds these length-N vectors elementwise, leading to O(N^2) array operations on top of the already heavy prime generation.
Instead of counting prime exponents of N! directly, the code factors each i from 1..N into a full exponent vector, which is overkill when only aggregate prime exponents are needed.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid recomputing prime tables and large exponent vectors. Directly factor each integer 2..N by trial division (with a small optimization to skip even non-2 divisors), collect all prime factors into one list, then count exponents with Counter and compute the product of (exponent+1) modulo 1e9+7.

complexity.space: O(N log N) in prime-factor multiset size (practically much smaller for N≈10^4)
complexity.why: func_1(k) loops var_3 from 2 to k, doing O(1) work most of the time and some divisions when var_3 divides k. The upper bound per call is O(k). Doing this for all k from 2 to N yields sum_{k=2..N} O(k) = O(N^2). Collecting all prime factors into var_8 stores each prime factor of each k; across 2..N, this is at most O(N log N) elements. Counter and the final product over distinct primes are O(number_of_distinct_primes) = O(N / log N), negligible compared to the factorization loop.

complexity_delta.from: ≈O(N^{2.5}) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N^2) time, O(N log N) space for factor multiset (still dominated by time)
complexity_delta.note: The modified code removes the heaviest nested recomputation (per-k prime sieve and per-k length-N vector operations). While still not optimal compared to a sieve-based O(N log N) factorial factorization, it reduces the exponent in the time complexity and greatly cuts constant factors.

transformation_steps: Remove the separate prime sieve (func_2) and the large per-number exponent vector construction in func_1. Instead, let func_1(k) return just the prime factors of k as a list.
Replace the outer accumulation of length-N exponent arrays with a single global multiset of prime factors (var_8) collected over all k from 2..N.
Use collections.Counter to compress the global factor multiset into exponent counts per prime, removing the need for fixed-size arrays indexed by position.
Compute the final answer as the product over primes of (exponent+1) modulo 1e9+7, avoiding any high-dimensional vector arithmetic.
trigger_signals: Nested loops where both bounds depend on N (e.g., prime checking inside a loop over k) leading to super-quadratic behavior.
Recomputing primality / prime lists for each k instead of reusing results or using a single sieve up to N.
Creating and processing O(N) sized arrays inside an O(N) loop (e.g., per-k exponent vectors of length N) causing O(N^2) memory traffic.
Use of naive trial division for each i up to itself or up to i (rather than sqrt(i) or precomputed primes), indicating potential for large constant factors and unnecessary iterations.
pitfalls: The fast version still uses trial division up to k for each k; for larger constraints this O(N^2) approach can still TLE. A more scalable approach is to generate primes up to N once (e.g., sieve) and then count prime exponents in N! via floor(N/p) + floor(N/p^2) + ... or by factoring each i using those primes up to sqrt(i).
func_1 does not early-break when var_7 becomes 1; it continues the loop up to k, doing useless mod operations. While correct, this is an avoidable overhead.
Building the big list var_8 of all prime factors and then passing it to Counter costs extra memory; exponents could be updated directly in a Counter during factorization to reduce peak memory usage.
Using eval(input()) is unnecessary and can be unsafe in general; int(input()) suffices and avoids code execution risks.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder Lunlun-number task (e.g., ABC161D). Input is a single integer K up to about 1e5; need to output the K-th "Lunlun" number (adjacent digits differ by at most 1). Original code caps length at 10 digits, which is enough to cover the first 1e5 Lunlun numbers.

dominant_ops: Recursive DFS over the implicit digit tree of Lunlun numbers starting from 1..9 up to length 10
Repeated string conversions per node: len(str(var_2)) and int(str(var_2)[-1]) in every recursive call
Appends to a global list for every generated number
Final full sort of all generated numbers before indexing the (k-1)-th element

complexity.time: O(M log M), where M is the total number of Lunlun numbers with up to 10 digits (effectively O(3^L) with L=10)
complexity.why: The DFS explores the full search space of valid numbers up to length 10 regardless of input K. Each new number causes constant work plus string conversions. After generation of M numbers, a sort over all M elements is performed, leading to M log M time. The list storing all numbers is O(M) space.

bottlenecks.detail: Generates all Lunlun numbers up to 10 digits even if K is small; work is essentially independent of input size and bounded by the maximum search depth instead.
After generating the entire set, it sorts the full list var_4, costing O(M log M). This dominates runtime given that M is fixed but large.
Deep recursive DFS with a branching factor up to 3 adds significant Python function call overhead for each node in the digit tree.
Every recursive call executes len(str(var_2)) and int(str(var_2)[-1]), repeatedly converting integers to strings and back, which is expensive and avoidable.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use BFS with a queue (deque) to generate Lunlun numbers in strictly increasing order and stop as soon as the K-th number is reached, avoiding full search-space generation and sorting.

complexity.why: Initialize a queue with digits 1..9, then perform K-1 iterations: each iteration pops one number (constant time) and, if the queue size is still below K, pushes up to three successors derived from its last digit. The total number of push operations is O(K), and each iteration does O(1) arithmetic and queue operations. The queue size is kept below K, giving O(K) space usage.

complexity_delta.from: O(M log M) time and O(M) space with M = number of Lunlun numbers up to fixed max length (about 3^10); generation and sorting of the full set regardless of K.
complexity_delta.to: O(K) time and O(K) space, where K is the input value (desired rank of the Lunlun number); only first K numbers are generated and no sorting is needed.
complexity_delta.note: As K grows, the new approach scales with K instead of with the full search-space size M and avoids the expensive sort; for K up to ~1e5 this is crucial in Python.

transformation_steps: Replace recursive DFS generation with iterative BFS using collections.deque, which naturally yields Lunlun numbers in increasing order.
Initialize the queue with base numbers 1 through 9 instead of recursively seeding from them.
On each step, pop the smallest current Lunlun number from the left of the deque and treat it as the next number in sequence.
Compute the last digit via modulo (var_3 % 10) instead of converting the whole number to a string, avoiding repeated str/int conversion.
Generate up to three valid successors (last_digit-1, last_digit, last_digit+1 when in [0,9]) and append them to the deque.
Limit queue growth using a size check (len(var_5) < var_2) so that at most O(K) numbers are stored and extended, ensuring memory and time scale with K.
Eliminate the global accumulation list and final sort; instead, after K-1 pops, the next popped value is directly the K-th Lunlun number.
trigger_signals: Presence of a full search with fixed depth cut-off (len(str(var_2)) > 10) that does not depend on input K, indicating potential overgeneration.
Use of recursion with heavy branching (DFS over a combinatorial tree) implemented in Python, which is often slow and limited by recursion depth.
Repeated string conversions inside performance-critical loops or recursion (str(var_2) and int(str(var_2)[-1]) every call).
A large container (var_4) being populated for all generated elements followed by a full sort, which is a red flag for k-th element selection tasks.
The problem only requires the K-th smallest value, yet the algorithm computes and sorts the entire candidate set.
pitfalls: Ensuring BFS maintains numeric ascending order: the queue must always pop the smallest current candidate; starting from 1..9 and pushing successors in correct order guarantees this for Lunlun numbers.

The queue-size condition (len(var_5) < var_2) is subtle: implemented incorrectly, it could under-generate or over-generate numbers. It must ensure that enough future candidates exist to reach the K-th pop without unnecessarily growing memory.
Care must be taken with boundary digits 0 and 9 so as not to generate invalid successors (digits outside [0,9]); the conditions var_4 != 0 and var_4 != 9 handle this.
Beware of off-by-one errors in the BFS loop: running the loop for range(1, K) and then outputting the next popped element ensures the printed number is the K-th.
Relying on eval(input()) is unsafe in general; while common in competitive programming constraints, using int(input()) is preferable for robustness.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical job scheduling / deadline feasibility problem (e.g., AtCoder-style). Needs O(n log n) or better; n likely up to 1e5–2e5.

dominant_ops: Read n lines, each with two integers (processing time, deadline)
Sort list of n pairs by second element (deadline)
Single linear pass accumulating processing times and comparing to deadlines

complexity.why: Building an array of n pairs is O(n). Sorting by the second element with list.sort(key=lambda ...) dominates at O(n log n). The final feasibility loop is O(n). Space is O(n) for storing all jobs.

bottlenecks.detail: var_1.sort(key=lambda var_8: var_8[1]) is the asymptotic hotspot at O(n log n); unavoidable for this greedy-by-deadline approach.
Using a Python lambda as a key adds some per-element overhead compared to sorting pre-reordered structures, though it is minor relative to the sort itself.
Per-line parsing with split+map(int) is standard; however, relative to pure computation, I/O still contributes significantly when n is large, though using sys.stdin.readline mitigates this.

FastAudit.core_idea: Same greedy scheduling algorithm: sort jobs by deadline, then check that the cumulative processing time never exceeds the current job's deadline. Implementation changes representation of each job to [deadline, duration] so that a plain sort() works without a key.

complexity.why: Still reads n jobs (O(n)), sorts them (now as [deadline, duration]) with list.sort() which is O(n log n), then scans once (O(n)). Memory holds all jobs simultaneously, so O(n) space. No asymptotic change from the slow_code.

complexity_delta.from: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: Big-O complexity is unchanged; micro-level choices (eval(input()), deque-to-list conversion) are actually likely slower in practice than the original sys.stdin-based version.

transformation_steps: Switched input handling from sys.stdin.readline and helper functions to direct input() calls with eval for the first integer.
Changed data representation from list of (duration, deadline) tuples to a deque of [deadline, duration] lists, then converted back to a list before sorting.
Avoided an explicit sort key by storing [deadline, duration] so that default list.sort() orders by deadline.
Replaced the end-flag pattern (boolean var_6 and final conditional print) with immediate print-and-exit on detecting an infeasible schedule.
trigger_signals: Desire to express the greedy idea more directly by storing (deadline, duration) so a natural sort suffices.
Refactoring toward shorter, more linear-looking code without helper I/O functions.
Attempt to micro-optimize by avoiding a lambda key in sort, though offset by slower I/O and extra data structure conversions.
pitfalls: Using eval(input()) is significantly slower than int(input()) and introduces serious security risks if input is not trusted.
Creating a deque and then converting it to a list (var_1 = deque(); var_1 = list(var_1)) adds unnecessary overhead; a plain list would be simpler and faster.
Built-in input() is slower than sys.stdin.readline() for large n, which can matter under tight time limits.
The algorithm itself is unchanged; any performance gain from avoiding a key function in sort is likely outweighed by the slower I/O and extra conversions.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style pair-counting problem (i + a[i] == j - a[j]). Indices up to ~2e5, a[i] can be large (up to ~1e9), so key space for i±a[i] is too large for dense arrays.

dominant_ops: Initialization of a length-10^7 Python list: var_4 = [0] * 10**7
Single pass over n elements with random access into var_4

complexity.why: The core loop is O(n), but creating and storing a list of size M=10^7 dominates both time and memory. Each entry is a Python int, so memory is very large; initialization of 10^7 elements also takes significant time.

bottlenecks.detail: var_4 is a Python list of size 10^7 containing ints. This can require hundreds of MB in CPython, easily causing MLE or heavy paging.
Zero-initializing 10^7 counters is done regardless of actual n or the number of distinct keys i±a[i] that will be used. If n≈2e5, this is ~50× larger than needed.

The magic bound 10**7 does not reflect the true range of i±a[i] (which can be much larger if a[i] is large). The guards var_6>=0 and var_7<10**7 silently drop valid pairs, harming correctness and making the optimization unsafe.
All counts are stored as boxed Python integers in a list; every access and update involves Python-level operations with significant overhead compared to using a sparse dict sized to O(n).

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid a huge fixed-size frequency array and instead count frequencies of (i + a[i]) and (i - a[i]) in hash maps (dicts), then compute the total number of matching pairs by summing cnt_plus[x] * cnt_minus[x] over all keys x.

complexity.why: Each index contributes O(1) average-time updates to two dictionaries. Then we iterate over the keys (at most O(n)) to accumulate the answer. No dependence on an artificial upper bound like 10^7, and memory usage scales with the actual number of distinct expressions rather than a fixed large domain.

complexity_delta.note: Replaced a large dense array keyed by (i±a[i]) with sparse hash maps keyed directly by these values, removing the dependence on a fixed 10^7 bound.

transformation_steps: Reformulate the counting: recognize that we need to count pairs (i, j) such that i + a[i] == j - a[j].
Introduce two frequency maps: one for values (i + a[i]) and one for (i - a[i]) across all indices.
Perform a single pass over the array to populate the two dictionaries instead of updating a fixed-size list.
Combine the two frequency maps by summing cnt_plus[x] * cnt_minus[x] over keys x; avoid online counting that depends on an arbitrary fixed bound.
Remove the massive [0] * 10**7 allocation and all bounds checks tied to that artificial array size.
trigger_signals: Use of a magic constant 10**7 for array size without reference to constraints, suggesting a potential mismatch between key domain and allocated space.
Very large memory footprint for a simple counting task; likely to cause MLE on typical competitive programming limits.
Guard conditions that discard values outside [0, 10**7), hinting at correctness issues for larger a[i].
Asymmetry between actual key range (i±a[i]) and a fixed array bound, while n is only up to ~2e5.
pitfalls: Double-counting: combining plus/minus maps by iterating over both and then dividing by 2 (as in the fast_code) requires care. An alternative is to iterate over the intersection of keys once to avoid the need for //2.
Potential integer overflow or range issues in other languages if indices or a[i] are large; dict-based approach avoids the need to size arrays to cover extreme key ranges.
Dict operations have higher constant factors than list indexing; for very small bounded domains an array could be faster, but here the domain is too large and sparse.
Using eval for reading integers is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; although not the main performance issue, it should be replaced with int(input()) in production code.

constraints_guess.n_max: 10–15 (number of bits/skills; 2^n DP in Python)
constraints_guess.q_max: ≈50–200 (number of items/books; linear factor in DP)
constraints_guess.notes: Both versions allocate arrays of size 2^n, so n is small. Time limit likely around 1–2s, making O(q * 2^n * n) feasible but anything ~3^n or worse too slow.

dominant_ops: Enumeration of all masks 0..(2^n-1)
For each mask, iterating over many candidate submasks from pre-grouped lists
Nested mask-submask loops with expensive membership checks and DP transitions
Repeated popcount via bin(x).count('1') over all masks

complexity.time: Θ(m * 2^n + n * 2^n + 2^n * Σ_{k≤n/2} C(n, k)) ≈ Θ(3^n) or worse for practical n
complexity.why: First, popcount and grouping over all masks is O(n * 2^n). Then computing var_13 costs O(m * 2^n). The critical part is computing var_12: for each mask, it iterates over all subsets grouped by size up to half the mask popcount, but those groups are global for all masks (var_19[k] contains all subsets of size k, independent of mask). This effectively enumerates many subset pairs multiple times, leading to a combinatorial explosion roughly on the order of 3^n (each element can be in subset A, subset B, or neither), multiplied again over all masks.

bottlenecks.detail: DP over subsets with pairwise partitioning. For each mask var_6, it tries all subsets var_18 taken from global groups var_19[popcount], not restricted to being submasks of var_6 except via a conditional check. This leads to ~3^n explorations, far too many compared to 2^n-based methods.

Triple nesting: for each mask var_6 (2^n states), for each subset size var_14 up to half its popcount, for each subset var_18 in var_19[var_14]. The size of var_19[var_14] is C(n, var_14) regardless of var_6, so many irrelevant subsets are scanned and discarded by `if var_18 & var_6 == var_18`.

The partition-based DP recombines smaller masks to form larger ones even though the optimal cost can be computed by directly transitioning from current coverage to `coverage | item_mask` as in Code A. The decomposition step duplicates work and revisits states many times.
Using `bin(var_6).count('1')` for popcount inside a 2^n loop incurs an O(n) per-state overhead. While not the primary asymptotic bottleneck, it adds noticeable constant factors.

FastAudit.core_idea: Standard bitmask DP over coverage states: maintain dp[mask] = minimum cost to achieve skill set 'mask'. Initialize dp[0] = 0. For each item/book with cost c and skill bitmask S, relax all states: dp[mask | S] = min(dp[mask | S], dp[mask] + c). Answer is dp[(1<<n)-1]. This uses one pass over all items, each performing transitions over all 2^n states but with O(1) work per transition.

complexity.why: The DP table has 2^n entries and is updated for each of m items. Each update involves a constant-time bitwise OR and comparison. Mask construction from input for each item costs O(k) where k is the number of skills listed for that item; summed over all items, this is at most O(m * n). No combinatorial subset-partition enumeration is done.

complexity_delta.from: ≈Θ(3^n) (subset-partition DP with global subset groups and repeated recombinations)
complexity_delta.to: Θ(m * 2^n) (direct transitions on DP over coverage states)
complexity_delta.note: The optimized solution removes the expensive subset-partitioning phase and instead applies each item once across all DP states, the classic 2^n bitmask DP pattern.

transformation_steps: Recognize that we need the minimum cost for each coverage state (bitmask of skills) and that items independently contribute skill subsets with associated costs.

Discard the attempt to build optimal costs for masks by recursively partitioning them into smaller masks via global subset groups (var_19, var_22, and partition loops). This is unnecessary for this set-cover style objective.
Adopt a single-layer DP: dp[mask] = min cost to achieve 'mask'. Initialize dp with large INF and set dp[0] = 0.
Precompute each item's bitmask S directly while reading input (as in Code A, using bit shifts or sum of powers of two). Store only cost and mask per item.
For each item, iterate mask from 0 to 2^n - 1 and relax dp[mask | S] using dp[mask] + cost. This ensures each state is improved using each item exactly once.
After processing all items, read dp[(1<<n)-1]; if it is still INF, output -1, otherwise output the minimum cost. This matches Code A.

Optionally, micro-optimize by avoiding allocations inside loops (e.g., avoid list comprehensions for mask building in inner loops, reuse variables, etc.), though the main speedup comes from the algorithmic change.
trigger_signals: Presence of dp arrays indexed by masks of size 2^n combined with more than double-nested loops over masks and subsets, suggesting exponential blow-up beyond 2^n.
Use of global subset collections (var_19) and popcount arrays (var_22) followed by nested loops over all subsets of given popcount values for every mask.
Conditional checks of the form `if sub & mask == sub` inside deep loops, indicating that many candidate subsets are generated and then filtered rather than iterating only over actual submasks.
bin(x).count('1') usage inside large loops over all masks, hinting at inefficiencies in per-state computations.
Comparing against a known simpler solution pattern (bitmask DP over coverage) that achieves the same goal with a clear O(m * 2^n) complexity.
pitfalls: Accidentally reintroducing subset-partition enumeration when trying to 'optimize' DP transitions, which can push complexity back toward 3^n.
Forgetting to initialize dp[0] = 0 and the rest to INF, which would prevent the DP from propagating correct costs.
Using Python lists or comprehensions to build item masks in an inner loop, rather than once per item during input; constructing masks repeatedly can inflate constant factors.

Iterating dp states in the wrong order (e.g., reversed when not needed) could matter if the problem allowed multiple uses of the same item; in this problem it does not, but maintaining the forward iteration pattern as in Code A is safe.

Choosing INF too small (e.g., sum of costs might exceed 10^7). Code A uses 10^7 assuming the total cost bound is below that; changing constraints may require increasing INF to avoid overflow-like behavior.
If n is increased significantly (e.g., n ≥ 20), even O(m * 2^n) becomes too slow and memory-heavy; the chosen algorithm depends critically on the small-n constraint.

constraints_guess.notes: Single array, one-shot computation. Original brute-force over range(min(a)..max(a)) would TLE if values span is large (e.g., up to 1e9). Real contest versions of this task often have much smaller ranges (e.g., Xi <= 1000), where even the slow version passes.

dominant_ops: Outer loop over all integer candidate points P in [min(var_7), max(var_7)]
Inner list comprehension computing (var_7[i] - P)**2 for every element at each P
Summation over that list for each P

complexity.why: Let n = number of elements, R = max(var_7) - min(var_7) + 1. min() and max() are O(n) once. The outer for-loop iterates R times. In each iteration, the list comprehension builds a length-n list of squared differences (O(n)), then sum(var_4) traverses that list again (another O(n)). Thus each iteration is O(n) and total is O(n * R). The temporary list var_4 holds n integers, so extra space is O(n).

bottlenecks.detail: Brute-force search over every integer between min(var_7) and max(var_7) when the minimizer of sum (xi - P)^2 can be characterized analytically (near the mean). This introduces a factor R = max - min into the runtime.
Nested structure: for each candidate P (outer loop of size R), it recomputes squared differences for all n elements and sums them, leading to O(n * R) operations.
On each outer-loop iteration, a new list var_4 of length n is allocated just to sum its contents, incurring repeated allocations and GC overhead.
Using eval(input()) for reading an integer is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()). This is minor compared to the O(n * R) cost but still unnecessary.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the fact that the sum of squared deviations Σ(xi − P)^2 is minimized (over real P) at P = mean(xi). For integer P, the minimizer must be one of floor(mean) or ceil(mean). The fast solution computes the average once, chooses the closer integer (between floor and floor+1), and then computes the sum of squared deviations for that single P in one pass.

complexity.why: One pass to compute sum(var_7) (O(n)), constant-time arithmetic to derive candidate P (floor/ceil), and one pass to accumulate Σ(xi − P)^2 (O(n)). No per-iteration temporary lists are built; only a few scalar accumulators are used, so extra space is constant.

complexity_delta.from: O(n * R) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: Removed dependence on the value range R = max(var_7) - min(var_7) by replacing brute-force search with a closed-form characterization of the optimal P based on the mean.

transformation_steps: Recognize the mathematical structure: the objective is to minimize Σ (xi - P)^2 over integer P.
Use calculus / algebra: Σ (xi − P)^2 is a convex quadratic in P with its real-valued minimum at P = mean(xi).
Restrict to integer P: the optimum integer lies in {floor(mean), ceil(mean)}; it suffices to check these two candidates.
Replace the outer loop over P in [min, max] with a constant number of candidates derived from the mean.
Eliminate the inner list allocation by accumulating the sum of squared differences in a single scalar variable within one loop.
Compute sum(var_7) once to obtain the mean instead of recomputing any aggregate for each candidate P.
trigger_signals: A loop over all integers between min(array) and max(array) calling a full O(n) computation in each iteration.
Objective function is a sum of (xi − P)^2, a classic pattern where the mean (or median for absolute values) gives the optimum.
Creation and summation of a full-length list on every outer-loop iteration, which scales poorly when either n or the value range grows.
Independent candidate evaluations: the cost for each P is recomputed from scratch, indicating a potential for using a formula or precomputed aggregates.
pitfalls: Floating-point precision: var_8 = sum(var_7) / var_3 is a float. For extremely large values or large n, float rounding could make the chosen integer P differ from the true argmin. For typical contest constraints (small to moderate integers), this is safe, but an exact rational or integer-based approach (e.g., using integer division and testing both floor and floor+1 from integer mean) is more robust.

Assuming only one candidate integer: the real minimum is at mean, but when constrained to integers, both floor(mean) and ceil(mean) must be considered. The modified code correctly effectively chooses between them based on proximity, but this reasoning must be preserved if refactored.
Type handling: using eval(input()) is unnecessary and unsafe; switching to int(input()) avoids unexpected behavior if the input is malformed.

Overflow in other languages: while Python integers are unbounded, in fixed-width integer languages the computation of (xi - P)^2 and the sum may overflow; one would need 64-bit integers or explicit checks.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic unbounded knapsack / minimum cost to reach weight >= W. W (first input) is up to about 1e4–1e5, number of item types N (second input) up to ~100. Original 2D DP with size (N+1) x (W+1) is near Python's memory/time limit.

dominant_ops: Allocation and initialization of 2D DP table var_4 with size (var_9 + 1) x (var_5 + 1)
Nested loops over item types (var_9) and weight states (var_5) performing DP transitions and min comparisons

complexity.why: The DP table var_4 has (N+1)*(W+1) entries. Each entry var_4[i+1][w] is filled exactly once via constant-time work (a few integer additions and min operations). Memory holds the entire 2D table simultaneously.

bottlenecks.detail: The 2D list var_4 of size (var_9 + 1) x (var_5 + 1) stores O(NW) integers. For W ~ 1e5 and N ~ 100 this is ~1e7 entries, which can exceed memory limits and harm cache locality in Python.
Building var_4 via nested list comprehensions already costs O(NW) time and allocates large contiguous Python list structures before any DP step runs.
Two Python-level nested loops (over var_6 in range(var_9) and var_7 in range(var_5)) incur significant interpreter overhead when NW is large.
The item index dimension is not strictly needed for unbounded knapsack; each state only depends on weights, so carrying the item dimension multiplies both time and space by N unnecessarily.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the unbounded nature of items and rewrite the DP by weight only: dp[w] = min(dp[w - wi] + ci) over all items, for all w up to W + max(wi). This 1D DP removes the item-index dimension, drastically reducing memory and improving cache behavior while keeping the same asymptotic time.

complexity.why: dp has length L = W + max(wi). For each w in [1, L) we take the minimum over all N items, so time is O(NL). Since L ≤ W + max_w and max_w ≤ W in typical constraints, this is O(NW). Only a 1D array of size O(W + max_w) is stored, instead of an (N+1) x (W+1) table.

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time remains O(NW), but the constant factors and especially memory usage improve significantly by dropping the item-index dimension.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the original recurrence is an unbounded knapsack / coin change style DP where the optimal cost for a weight w depends only on smaller weights and not on the exact sequence of item indices.
Replace the 2D DP table var_4[item_index][weight] with a 1D DP array var_5[weight] that directly stores the minimal cost to achieve each weight.
Extend the DP array size to W + max(weight_i) so that states able to exceed the required weight W are available, allowing the final answer to be min(dp[w]) for w >= W.

Rewrite the transition so that for each weight w, dp[w] is computed as the minimum over all items of dp[w - weight_i] + cost_i (when the index is valid), collapsing the item dimension into a single min operation.
Return the minimal value in dp[W:] as the answer, instead of using dp[N][W] from a 2D table.
trigger_signals: 2D DP table size is N x W with N and W both potentially large (e.g., N ~ 100, W ~ 1e5), causing heavy memory usage and slow initialization in Python.

The transition for state (i, w) depends on (i, w - wi) and (i-1, w) in a way that suggests the item index is not required to characterize the optimal cost for weight w (typical unbounded knapsack pattern).
Python implementation experiences Memory Limit Exceeded or is close to time limits despite having acceptable asymptotic O(NW) complexity (common when porting C++ DP to Python).
Observation that DP decisions for each weight w across items are symmetric and can be aggregated into a single dimension over w.
pitfalls: When converting to a 1D DP, careful ordering of loops is crucial; for unbounded knapsack, iterating weight in increasing order is appropriate, but negative indexing (w - weight_i < 0) must be guarded against to avoid reading from the end of the list.

Using a generator inside min (min(dp[w - wi] + ci for ...)) is convenient but still loops in Python; if N is large, further micro-optimizations (e.g., pre-unrolling for small N, avoiding repeated attribute lookups) may be necessary.
The choice of INF (here pow(2, 31) - 1) must be greater than any achievable cost to avoid overflow or incorrect minima; too small an INF can silently corrupt results.
Extending dp up to W + max(weight_i) assumes that exceeding W by at most max(weight_i) is sufficient; if the problem definition or constraints are changed, this range must be reconsidered.

Removing the item dimension eliminates per-item results; if the problem later requires reconstruction of which items were used, additional backtracking information or a different DP structure would be required.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical for this AtCoder-style problem: N up to around 1e5 (so that factorial arrays of size N+O(log M) fit in memory), M up to around 1e9–1e12 so that prime factorization by trial division up to sqrt(M) is fine. Number of distinct prime factors and total exponent sum are O(log M). Only a single test case per run.

dominant_ops: Global precomputation of factorials and inverse factorials up to a fixed bound var_7 = 10**6 using numpy (func_3 and func_2)
2D reshape and prefix-product sweep over a var_3 x var_3 array inside func_2 (effectively computing a 1D prefix product using a cache-unfriendly 2D scheme)
Prime factorization of M by trial division in func_4 (standard sqrt(M) loop; not the main bottleneck compared to the numpy precomputation)

complexity.time: O(F + sqrt(M)), where F = var_7 = 10^6 is the unconditional factorial bound; more precisely O(F) for factorial/inv-factorial precompute plus O(sqrt(M)) for prime factorization.
complexity.space: O(F) additional memory for factorial and inverse factorial arrays, plus temporary O(F) numpy buffers due to 2D reshape in func_2.
complexity.why: func_3 allocates arrays of length var_7 and calls func_2 twice. func_2 computes prefix products by resizing the length-F array into a var_3 x var_3 matrix (var_3 ≈ sqrt(F)), then performing two nested sweeps: one over columns, one over rows. This remains Θ(F) operations but with a large constant factor and extra memory traffic. This precomputation is executed globally irrespective of the actual required maximum n in combinations, so time is dominated by the fixed F = 10^6 setup even if the test case only needs much smaller n.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorials and inverse factorials are precomputed up to fixed var_7 = 10**6 regardless of the actual maximum needed n (which is only N + max_exponent(M) ≈ N + O(log M)). For many inputs this is orders of magnitude larger than necessary.

func_2 reshapes a 1D array of length F into a var_3 x var_3 matrix and performs 2D prefix products to emulate a 1D prefix. This incurs extra memory, cache misses, and Python–numpy overhead compared to a simple 1D loop.

Using numpy in a competitive programming context introduces large constant factors: array allocation, dtype management, and Python–C boundary crossings. The work being done (modular prefix products) is simple integer arithmetic and is often faster in plain Python with tight loops for these constraint sizes.
var_13 and var_14 (factorial and inverse factorial arrays) are computed at import time (top level), so the O(10^6) precomputation cost is paid even if the program exits early or if N is small.

numpy arrays are created with dtype=int64; repeated modular multiplications rely on staying within 64-bit range. While mod 1e9+7 is safe mathematically, careless operations or intermediate overflows could cause correctness issues in other settings. Pure Python ints avoid this class of bugs.

FastAudit.core_idea: Factorize M into primes M = Π p_i^{e_i}. For each exponent e_i, compute the number of ways to distribute e_i identical items into N bins: C(N + e_i - 1, e_i) (stars and bars). The final answer is the product over all prime factors of these combinations modulo 1e9+7. Precompute factorials and inverse factorials only up to N + max(e_i) + small_margin using a single linear pass, then evaluate each binomial coefficient in O(1).

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + N), where sqrt(M) comes from prime factorization by trial division up to sqrt(M) and N from linear precomputation of factorial and inverse factorial arrays of size ≈ N + O(log M).
complexity.space: O(N) for factorial and inverse factorial arrays, with N replaced by (N + max_exponent + margin), which is still Θ(N) given max_exponent = O(log M).
complexity.why: Prime factorization of M by testing divisibility by integers up to sqrt(M) is O(sqrt(M)) in the worst case (when M is prime or has a large prime factor). After collecting exponents, the maximum n needed in combinations is N + max(e_i) - 1, which is at most N + O(log M). The code allocates arrays of length var_2 + 50, enough for typical constraints. Factorials are computed iteratively in one forward loop, inverse factorials in one backward loop using a single modular inverse via Fermat's little theorem, giving Θ(N) arithmetic operations with very low constants.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(F + sqrt(M)) with F fixed at 10^6 for factorial precomputation, space O(F), plus heavy numpy constants from 2D operations; factorization cost O(sqrt(M)).
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(N + sqrt(M)) and space O(N), with N being the actual input parameter and factorial bound ≈ N + O(log M); no numpy overhead and only 1D loops.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time remains linear in the precomputation bound plus sqrt(M), but the bound is reduced from a fixed worst-case F=1e6 to the problem-driven N+small_margin, and numpy-based 2D prefix products are replaced by lightweight Python loops. This yields substantial real-world speedups and lower memory use.

transformation_steps: Remove global numpy-based factorial precomputation (func_2 and func_3) and the fixed bound var_7 = 10**6.
Switch from numpy arrays to plain Python lists for factorial (var_7 in fast_code) and inverse factorial (var_6) storage.
Compute factorials iteratively in a single forward loop: fact[i+1] = fact[i] * (i+1) % MOD up to size ≈ N + 50.
Compute inverse factorials using one modular inverse of fact[-1] via pow(fact[-1], MOD-2, MOD), then a single backward loop inv_fact[i-1] = inv_fact[i] * i % MOD.
Retain the existing prime factorization logic (trial division up to sqrt(M)) to produce the exponent list var_5.
For each exponent e in var_5, compute C(N + e - 1, e) in O(1) via fact and inv_fact and multiply into the answer under modulo.
Avoid any unnecessary dimensions or reshaping: all operations remain 1D and contiguous, improving cache locality and reducing overhead.
trigger_signals: Use of numpy and 2D reshaping for a simple prefix-product computation, which is usually a red flag in competitive-programming environments.
Fixed precomputation bound var_7 = 10**6 that does not depend on the actual input N or exponent sizes, indicating possible over-allocation.
Global initialization of heavy data structures (factorials/inv-factorials) at module import time.
The presence of an alternative simple implementation (fast_code) that uses straightforward loops and scales directly with N and log M.
Environment constraints typical of online judges where numpy is slower or even disallowed, making pure-Python solutions preferable.
pitfalls: When resizing the factorial array bound from a fixed F to N + margin, it is essential to ensure the bound always covers the maximum n used in combinations (here max is N + max_exponent - 1). Under-allocating will cause index errors or incorrect binomial computations.
The margin (+50 in fast_code) is tuned to expected max_exponent ≈ O(log M) under given constraints; if M's upper bound increases significantly, the margin (or bound computation) must be revisited.

Switching away from numpy means all multiplications are on arbitrary-precision Python ints; although correct and generally fast for these sizes, accidentally dropping the modulo in loops could cause large integer blow-up and performance regression.
The modular inverse via pow(fact[-1], MOD-2, MOD) relies on MOD being prime; changing MOD to a non-prime value would break the inverse factorial logic.
Trial division for factorization is O(sqrt(M)); if constraints on M become much larger (e.g., up to 10^18), a more advanced factorization method or an adjusted complexity analysis may be needed.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical Lunlun number problem: input is k (1-indexed), need the k-th positive integer whose adjacent digits differ by at most 1. Upper limit 3234566667 in slow_code is just chosen to cover the maximum needed k (likely around 10^5).

dominant_ops: Recursive DFS expansion of all Lunlun numbers up to numeric limit 3,234,566,667 regardless of requested k
Appending every generated number into a global list var_2
Sorting the full list of generated numbers with sorted(var_2)

complexity.why: Let M be the number of Lunlun numbers <= 3,234,566,667. The DFS explores every such number (each node visited once) giving O(M) generation cost, then sorted(var_2) incurs O(M log M). Memory usage is O(M) because every generated number is stored in var_2 at once.
