The range-query func_1 is truncated (incomplete conditional on var_10) and the build loop range(var_9 - 2) appears off by one for standard 0-based segment trees. These bugs can cause extra work or incorrect recomputations; even when fixed, the pattern remains less efficient than the fast version.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a generic, 1-based, array-backed segment tree with a supplied associative operation (dot) and identity element, performing iterative bottom-up build and range queries with minimal branching and no extra list allocations.

complexity.why: The tree size is ~2 * n_ceil where n_ceil is the next power of two. Building runs one pass over all internal nodes (O(n)). Each update walks from a leaf index up to the root (height O(log n)). Each range query uses the standard half-open [l, r) pattern, moving l and r upwards with at most a constant number of operations per level (bit tests & increments/decrements), thus O(log n) per query. No extra lists are allocated in the inner loops, keeping memory overhead at Θ(n).

complexity_delta.from: O((n + q) log n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O((n + q) log n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity remains the same, but constants are reduced significantly via cleaner indexing, elimination of temporary lists, fewer branches, and a more cache-friendly layout.

transformation_steps: Change the tree layout from a 0-based scheme with leaves at index n-1 and hand-rolled parent/child math to a 1-based layout with leaves at indices [n, 2n), simplifying parent/child relationships (parent i, children 2i and 2i+1).
Replace reversed(list(range(...))) with a simple descending range loop (for i in range(n-1, 0, -1)), removing the extra list allocation and traversal.

Make the segment tree generic by injecting the combination function (__dot) and identity value (__e), so the logic is unified instead of hardcoding max/0. This enables reuse and keeps core operations tightly implemented once.
Streamline update logic into a single method func_2 that uses integer division by 2 while climbing to the root, eliminating duplicated/overridden func_3 definitions.
Use the standard half-open interval [l, r) for queries in func_1 with bitwise checks (l & 1, r & 1) to decide when to include nodes, minimizing branching and handling at most two nodes per level.
Store references to frequently used fields locally inside hot methods (e.g., var_17 = self.__node) to avoid attribute lookups within tight loops.
trigger_signals: Observed or anticipated TLE (time limit exceeded) on large inputs where both N and Q are around 1e5–2e5 despite using a segment tree.

Profiling shows a large fraction of runtime in the range-query function and tree-building function, with surprising time spent in list construction (reversed(list(range(...)))) and attribute/function calls.
Memory profiling indicates unnecessary temporary list allocations during build despite a conceptually O(n) structure.
Difficulty maintaining correctness due to multiple func_3 definitions and complex parity-based range traversal, signaling the need for a cleaner, canonical segment-tree implementation.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when switching between 0-based and 1-based indexing, especially in how leaves and ranges are mapped to indices.
Mixing inclusive [l, r] and half-open [l, r) semantics between the old and new query code, which can produce subtle wrong answers while still appearing to work on small samples.
Choosing an incorrect identity element (__e) for the operation (e.g., using 0 for min instead of +∞), which breaks associativity and leads to incorrect results.
Forgetting that the operation (__dot) must be associative; arbitrary functions will not work correctly in a segment tree.

In the provided fast code, using eval for input conversion (int(eval(input()))) is unnecessarily slow and potentially unsafe; standard int(input()) should be used to avoid significant per-line overhead.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical for AtCoder ABC083B / 'Some Sums': 1 <= N <= 10^4, 1 <= A <= B <= 36. Single-pass loop over all integers 1..N, each with small digit count.

dominant_ops: Outer for-loop over all integers from 1 to N
Inner while-loop performing repeated division and modulo per digit
math.floor calls and float arithmetic due to '/=' operator

complexity.why: For each integer in [1..N], the code iteratively strips digits using modulo and division. This is proportional to the number of digits D = O(log10 N). Overall cost is O(N * D), i.e., O(N log N). No extra data structures beyond a few scalars.

bottlenecks.detail: Per-number digit sum is implemented in pure Python with an inner while-loop, doing one iteration per digit. That adds extra Python-level loop overhead on top of the outer loop over N.
Uses math.floor on every digit. math.floor is a Python function call invoking C-level code but still adds function call overhead per digit, which is unnecessary when working with integers.

Uses '/=' (true division) instead of integer division. This converts var_4 to float, making '%' and comparisons operate on floats, which are slower and can be numerically problematic. Correct integer digit extraction should use '//=' instead.

With '/=' and a float, var_4 approaches 0 asymptotically and may never hit exactly 0, risking a very long or non-terminating loop. Even if it terminates, many extra iterations near 0 greatly increase runtime.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace the explicit digit-stripping loop and math.floor operations with Python’s built-in string conversion and sum(map(int, str(x))) for each number. This leverages highly optimized C code for most work and avoids float arithmetic.

complexity.space: O(1) extra (O(log N) transient per iteration)
complexity.why: Each integer in [1..N] is converted to a string of length D = O(log10 N). map(int, ...) and sum iterate over these D characters. Thus per number cost is O(D), giving O(N * D) = O(N log N) overall. Temporary strings and small ints are created per number but are discarded immediately, so peak extra memory usage is bounded by the size of one number’s digit representation.

complexity_delta.from: O(N * log N) time, O(1) space (but with float arithmetic and possible non-termination if '/=' is kept)
complexity_delta.to: O(N * log N) time, O(1) extra space (using C-optimized digit handling)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged, but the constant factors and reliability improve significantly by avoiding float loops and replacing Python-level per-digit logic with built-in operations.

transformation_steps: Remove the manual while-loop that extracts digits via modulo and division.
Replace digit accumulation (var_7 += ...) with sum(map(int, str(current_number))) to compute the digit sum in one expression.
Eliminate math.floor and any float arithmetic by operating directly on string digits and ints.
Simplify variable roles: loop directly over 1..N (var_5 in the fast code) and accumulate into a single sum variable.
Preserve the same filter condition var_1 <= digit_sum <= var_2 and summation of qualifying numbers.
trigger_signals: Inner loops that manually peel digits using '% 10' and '/ 10' or '// 10' inside another loop over many numbers.
Use of math.floor or other heavy math.* calls inside tight loops over each digit.
Accidental use of '/=' with integers causing implicit float conversion and slower operations.
Observed slowness or risk of timeouts when N is large, especially if per-digit operations are all in Python.
Profiling showing a large fraction of time spent in math.floor or in integer division/modulo operations inside nested loops.
pitfalls: String-based digit sums (str(x), map(int, ...)) allocate temporary objects; for extremely large N these allocations can be a bottleneck, even though they are faster than Python-level digit loops in many practical cases.

Relying on sum(map(int, str(x))) is concise but may be slightly slower than a carefully written integer-only loop using '// 10' and '% 10' if that loop avoids function calls and stays in pure arithmetic; actual performance can depend on Python version and cache behavior.
If the original intent was integer division, failing to change '/=' to '//=' is both a correctness and performance issue; always double-check division semantics in Python 3.

For very tight performance budgets, further micro-optimizations (e.g., avoiding map, using a local reference to int, or precomputing digit sums) might be needed; the current change greatly improves clarity but is not the only high-performance approach.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder ABC 110 D style: N up to 1e5, M up to about 1e9. Need to factor M and compute a product of binomial coefficients C(N+e-1, e) modulo 1e9+7. Number of distinct primes of M is small; each exponent e <= ~30.

dominant_ops: Trial-division prime factorization of M up to sqrt(M).
One large math.factorial(N-1) computation on a growing big integer.
For each prime exponent e: O(e) multiplications of large integers to build numerator of C(N+e-1, e), followed by integer division by factorial(e).

complexity.time: O(√M + F(N) + P * e_max * M_mul(N)) in bit-operations, where F(N) is the complexity of math.factorial(N), P is number of distinct primes of M, e_max is the maximum exponent, and M_mul(N) is the cost of multiplying ~Θ(N log N)-bit integers. In simple algorithmic terms: trial division O(√M) plus one very heavy super-linear-in-N factorial and several large-integer multiplications.
complexity.space: O(1) integers beyond input, but with a single big integer of size Θ(N log N) bits for (N-1)! and similar intermediates.
complexity.why: M is only up to about 1e9, so trial division is fine. The heavy part is that all combinatorial calculations are done on exact Python big integers: factorial(N-1) constructs a huge integer (~500k bits for N=1e5) and repeated multiplications in the loop keep working on such large values. Those big-int operations dominate runtime compared to the modest combinatorial dimensions.

bottlenecks.detail: Uses exact integer factorials and integer division to compute binomial coefficients instead of working modulo 1e9+7 with precomputed factorials/inverses. This introduces super-linear big-integer cost where O(1)-per-combination modular arithmetic would suffice.

For each exponent e, the code builds the numerator of C(N+e-1, e) via an explicit loop with e multiplications of large integers. Even though e is small, those multiplications act on very large integers (size linked to N), making each step expensive.
math.factorial(N-1) constructs the full exact factorial once, which is significantly more expensive than building factorials modulo a prime up to N+e_max using fixed-width integers.
Uses Python input() instead of buffered sys.stdin, which is minor but still slower in tight contest environments.

FastAudit.core_idea: Switch from exact integer combinatorics to modular combinatorics: precompute factorials and inverse factorials modulo 1e9+7 up to a global limit (~1e5+100) using a vectorized NumPy-based prefix-product trick, then evaluate each binomial C(n, k) in O(1) as fact[n] * invfact[k] * invfact[n-k] mod MOD. Keep prime factorization of M, but compute the product of binomials using these precomputed tables.

complexity.time: O(√M + L) where L is the precomputation limit (≈1e5). Factorization remains O(√M). The factorial and inverse factorial arrays are built in O(L) modular multiplications via NumPy vectorized prefix products. Each binomial coefficient is then O(1). Overall dominated by O(L) with small constant factors once M is modest.
complexity.space: O(L) integers for factorial and inverse factorial arrays (each stored as NumPy int64), plus O(P) for prime exponents. No huge big integers are kept.
complexity.why: All heavy combinatorial work is reduced to linear-time precomputation in fixed-width modular arithmetic. The NumPy-based prefix-product technique minimizes Python-loop overhead by doing multiplications in C over blocks laid out as a near-square matrix. Selecting L ≈ 1e5+100 safely covers all n = N+e-1 needed for the binomials.

The prime factorization remains trial division, and the final count is built by multiplying these efficient combinatorial contributions.

dominant_ops: Trial division up to sqrt(M) in func_1 (many Python-level division/mod operations)
Small-number binomial coefficient construction via integer multiplications/divisions in func_2 for each prime exponent

complexity.why: func_1 loops var_7 from 2 to floor(sqrt(original_M)) and for each candidate performs at least one divmod; repeated divisions when var_7 is a factor. Total factorization cost is Θ(sqrt(M)) in the worst case (M prime). The combination part iterates over the exponents of prime factors: each exponent e_i is at most O(log M), and the sum of all exponents is O(log M). func_2 runs in O(e_i) per prime, so overall O(log M). Thus time is dominated by O(sqrt(M)). The dictionary of prime factors has at most O(log M) entries, giving O(log M) space.

bottlenecks.detail: Prime factorization uses a for-loop up to int(sqrt(original_M)) computed once, even though M shrinks as factors are removed. This keeps the upper bound fixed at sqrt(initial_M), preventing early termination based on the reduced value.

Inside the factorization loop, divmod(var_9, var_7) is called on every iteration of the inner while True loop, creating a tuple and doing both division and modulo even when only the remainder check is needed. This is heavier than separate % and // and happens Θ(sqrt(M)) times.
The structure `for var_7 in range(2, var_6): var_4 = 0; while True: ... break` forces at least one divmod for every var_7, even when var_7 is not a divisor of M, increasing constant factors.

The use of list(var_3.values()) in the final loop materializes a list of exponents; iterating directly over var_3.values() would avoid an extra small allocation. It is minor but still unnecessary overhead.

In func_2, all multiplications and divisions are done on potentially large Python integers and only at the end is the result reduced modulo var_7. Although exponents are small so this is acceptable, inserting intermediate modular reductions can reduce integer magnitude and improve constant factors.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the same mathematical approach (factorize M, then for each prime exponent e compute a combinatorial term C(N+e-1, e) and multiply them modulo 1e9+7) but streamline the factorization loop and combination computation to reduce per-iteration overhead: use a while var_7*var_7 <= current_M pattern, avoid divmod, and construct binomial coefficients with simple integer products before taking modulo.

complexity.why: The optimized func_1 uses a classic trial division loop: var_7 increases while var_7*var_7 <= current_M and divides out each prime factor completely when found. This is Θ(sqrt(M)) in the worst case but benefits from an early reduction of the bound as M shrinks. The combination computation for each exponent e still requires O(e) multiplications/divisions with sum_e O(log M). As before, the prime factor map requires O(log M) space and no additional large structures are allocated.

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(M) + log M) time, O(log M) space
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + log M) time, O(log M) space
complexity_delta.note: Both versions perform trial division factorization and binomial coefficient computations with similar big-O complexity, but the modified version significantly reduces Python-level overhead inside the hot loops (factorization and combination), yielding practical speedups while keeping the same asymptotic bounds.

transformation_steps: Replace the for-loop factorization pattern `for var_7 in range(2, int(sqrt(M)) + 1)` with a while-loop `while var_7 * var_7 <= var_8` that automatically tightens the stopping condition as M is reduced.
Avoid divmod in the inner loop: use `if var_8 % var_7 == 0` followed by repeated `var_8 //= var_7` when divisible to separate modulo and division and avoid tuple creation.
Switch from a plain dict to collections.defaultdict(int) for factor counts, simplifying increment logic (no explicit existence checks) and slightly reducing branching overhead.

Inline or simplify the binomial coefficient logic so that for each exponent e you build numerator and denominator linearly with small loops, then do a single integer division followed by modulo, keeping the loops simple and predictable.
Remove minor inefficiencies such as unnecessary list(...) materialization around dict values and avoid recomputing or storing values that can be derived on the fly.
Standardize the modulus as a constant (10**9 + 7) and perform modulo operations at appropriate points to keep intermediate values from growing too large.
trigger_signals: Trial division up to sqrt(M) implemented with nested loops and divmod, indicating heavy per-iteration overhead for a large number of iterations.
Usage of `while True` with a break condition inside an already large loop, typical of patterns that can be expressed more simply and efficiently.
Factorization using a bound derived from sqrt(initial_M) rather than the current reduced M, suggesting non-tight loop bounds.
Repeated creation of temporary objects in hot loops (divmod tuple results, unnecessary list(...) calls) in performance-sensitive number-theoretic code.
Binomial coefficient computations done via large integer products/divisions without structure optimizations, signaling room for micro-optimizations in numeric handling.
pitfalls: When changing the factorization loop to `while var_7 * var_7 <= n`, it is crucial to update the loop condition using the *current* n after divisions to avoid missing a remaining prime factor or looping infinitely.

Replacing divmod with separate % and // requires care to ensure that operations are ordered correctly and that integer division is only performed when divisibility is guaranteed, to avoid subtle off-by-one or rounding issues.
The inner loop that counts prime exponents must divide out the factor completely; forgetting the inner while or not updating n correctly can lead to incorrect exponent counts.
In binomial coefficient construction, integer division `//` must be exact; changing the loop order or applying modulo at the wrong time could break exact divisibility and lead to incorrect results.

Delaying modulo too long in the presence of many multiplications could theoretically lead to very large intermediate integers and performance degradation; conversely, applying modulo too early (especially before division) would break exact binomial computation.

Assuming that the sum of exponents is small (O(log M)) is safe for this problem but may not hold in variants where M can be large and highly composite; reusing this pattern blindly in such contexts could lead to slower-than-expected performance.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic AtCoder-style 'pairwise/setwise/not coprime' problem. Number of elements n up to around 2e5, each a[i] up to about 1e6. Single test case. Needs sieve over max(a[i]) and GCD over the array.

dominant_ops: 1) Building an SPF-like sieve up to ~1e6 using nested loops and a separate boolean array. 2) Factoring each input number using the sieve and incrementing a prime-frequency array. 3) A full scan of the frequency array via max(var_2). 4) GCD fold over the array.

complexity.time: O(M log log M + N log A_max + M)
complexity.why: M ≈ 1e6 is the sieve limit; the inner while for each prime behaves like a standard Eratosthenes sieve, giving O(M log log M). Each of the N numbers is factorized by repeatedly dividing by its smallest prime factor; this costs O(log A_max) per number on average. After factoring, max(var_2) scans the whole O(M) frequency array. Space is dominated by the sieve/SPF array and helper arrays (size O(M)) plus the input array (O(N)).

bottlenecks.detail: The sieve loop uses a Python while var_6 * var_7 <= var_11 per prime, doing explicit multiplications and bound checks in Python. This has higher constant overhead than a range-based loop stepping by the prime value.

The boolean array var_10 is allocated and touched for every composite marking, in addition to var_3. A more compact SPF sieve can avoid a separate primality array in inner loops, improving cache behavior and constants.
The list of booleans var_10 is constructed as [True for ...] instead of [True] * (var_11 + 1), incurring unnecessary Python-level loop overhead.
Use of int(eval(input())) is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()), though this is a minor constant-factor issue relative to sieve and factorization costs.

After factoring, max(var_2) scans the entire length ~1e6 frequency array even if a conflict appears much earlier. With large N this extra O(M) pass can be avoided by early detection during factorization.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a more streamlined SPF sieve that writes smallest prime factors using stride-based for-range loops, then during factorization track seen primes via sets to detect any prime shared by two different numbers on the fly. Also separate the overall GCD check to distinguish pairwise vs setwise coprimality without scanning a large frequency array.

complexity.time: O(M log log M + N log A_max)
complexity.why: The SPF sieve uses for var_6 in range(var_5, M+1, var_5) for each prime, which corresponds to the standard Eratosthenes complexity O(M log log M) with better constants due to tight C-level loops. Each number is factorized by repeatedly dividing by its smallest prime factor; this is O(log A_max) per number. While factoring, set membership checks detect conflicts; there is no additional full O(M) scan like max(var_2). Space is O(M) for the SPF array plus O(N) for inputs and transient factorization state.

complexity_delta.from: Asymptotically O(M log log M + N log A_max + M) time and O(M + N) space.
complexity_delta.to: Asymptotically O(M log log M + N log A_max) time and O(M + N) space.
complexity_delta.note: Big-O is essentially the same in practice for the sieve+factorization core, but the modified (fast) version removes an extra linear scan over M and uses more efficient range-based loops, reducing constant factors and improving real runtime.

transformation_steps: Replace the while-based composite marking (var_7 loop with var_6 * var_7) with range-based loops stepping by the prime value, e.g., for m in range(p, M+1, p). This leverages CPython's optimized range iteration and reduces per-iteration Python overhead.
Use a single SPF array as in func_2(var_7) from the fast_code, avoiding an extra boolean primality array in the inner marking path and simplifying memory access patterns.
Change factorization to operate directly on the SPF array and use sets to track which primes have appeared for which numbers, enabling early exit when a prime is detected in more than one number.
Remove the final max(var_2) scan over the entire 1e6-sized frequency array and instead detect conflicts online while factorizing, so the algorithm can short-circuit as soon as it knows the result.
Avoid eval(input()) and prefer int(input()) for reading n, slightly reducing overhead and removing unnecessary dynamic evaluation.
trigger_signals: Runtime close to or exceeding limits when M ≈ 1e6 and N is large (e.g., 2e5), especially if implemented in Python.
Profiling or timing shows a large fraction of time spent in the sieve's inner loops or in a final pass over a large auxiliary array (like max(var_2)).
Memory pressure or cache misses observed due to maintaining multiple large arrays (e.g., SPF plus a separate primality bitmap) when one can suffice.
Code reviewers or performance tools indicating heavy use of Python-level while loops in hotspots instead of tight range-based loops.
pitfalls: Ensuring the SPF/sieve array is sized to at least max(a[i]); under-allocating causes index errors or incorrect factorization, while over-allocating excessively beyond ~1e6 wastes memory.

When using sets for detecting shared primes, it is important to distinguish primes reused within a single number (prime powers) from primes reused across different numbers; the inner per-number set var_8 in the fast_code handles this correctly.
Recomputing the sieve multiple times (e.g., per query) would drastically increase cost; the SPF should be built once and reused for all factorizations.
Mixing global mutable arrays (SPF, counters) with nested functions can lead to subtle bugs if reused across multiple runs; ensure arrays are initialized exactly once in a controlled scope.

For very tight time limits, even set operations may be relatively heavy; an array-based counter (like in the slow_code) can be faster if used with online conflict detection instead of a trailing max(var_2) pass.

constraints_guess.notes: First input (var_6 / var_3, call it n) is the DP length and iteration bound. Second input (var_5 / var_1, call it m) appears only in arithmetic in the fast code, so it can safely be as large as about 1e9. The slow version incorrectly precomputes factorials up to m, which is infeasible when m is large. Likely constraints: n up to around 2e5, m up to around 1e9.

dominant_ops: Precomputing factorial and inverse-factorial arrays up to var_1 (m) in func_3 (O(m) multiplications and memory writes), then an O(var_3) loop performing constant-time combinatorial queries and modular arithmetic each iteration.

complexity.why: func_3(var_13) builds two arrays var_12 and var_11 of length var_13 + 1 (where var_13 = var_1 = m), filling them in two linear passes: O(m) time, O(m) space. The main loop runs for var_3 + 1 (≈ n) iterations. Each iteration executes a constant number of O(1) operations: array lookups, multiplications, additions, one modular exponentiation with exponent 2 (O(1)), and a few modulo operations. Hence total time O(m + n), memory dominated by arrays of size m. With m potentially up to 1e9, this is both too slow and impossible in memory.

bottlenecks.detail: func_3(var_1) allocates two lists of size var_1 + 1. If var_1 = m is as large as 1e9, this would require multiple gigabytes of RAM and cannot run.
The factorial and inverse-factorial precomputation in func_3 performs O(m) modular multiplications. For large m (even around 1e7), this alone approaches or exceeds typical time limits.

The algorithm’s work scales linearly with m in addition to n. The fast solution only scales with n, so as m grows large while n remains moderate, the slow solution becomes disproportionately expensive.
The combinatorial formulation (using general C and P via factorial tables) is more general than needed for this problem; it forces precomputation up to m where a direct recurrence in n suffices.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid explicit combinatorial sums and factorial tables by deriving a direct DP recurrence in n for the required combinatorial quantity, combined with a single running product that represents the falling factorial (m)_n. This keeps all precomputation and iteration linear in n only, independent of the potentially large m.

complexity.why: The fast code initializes dp array var_3 with one element and iterates var_4 from 0 to var_6 - 1 (n - 1). In each iteration it performs O(1) arithmetic: one recurrence update for var_3[var_4 + 1] and one multiplicative update for var_2. This yields O(n) time. The array var_3 grows to length n + 1, so space is O(n). There is no dependence on m beyond constant-time arithmetic per step.

complexity_delta.from: O(m + n) time and O(m) space, which is infeasible when m is large (e.g., up to 1e9).
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time and O(n) space, with no linear dependence on m.
complexity_delta.note: The key improvement is removing factorial precomputation up to m by switching from a closed-form combinatorial sum to a direct DP recurrence in n.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the combinatorial expression being computed in the slow code (using combinations C(n, t) and permutations P(m, t)) corresponds to a value that satisfies a simple linear recurrence in t (or n), with coefficients depending on m and n.

Derive or use the known recurrence relation for the target combinatorial quantity, resulting in the DP transition used in the fast code: dp[i+1] expressed as a linear combination of dp[i] and dp[i-1] with coefficients involving m and n.
Replace general-purpose factorial-based C and P computations with direct DP updates on a length-(n+1) array var_3, eliminating the need for O(m) precomputation and large auxiliary arrays.
Maintain the falling factorial (m)_n as a single running product var_2 updated in each iteration instead of using factorial and inverse-factorial tables, further keeping work to O(n).
trigger_signals: Problem constraints or editorial indicating that the second parameter m can be as large as around 1e9, making factorial precomputation up to m impossible.
Empirical timeouts or memory errors when attempting to precompute factorials/inverses up to var_1.
Code review observation that the slow solution’s complexity depends linearly on m while the DP solution depends only on n.
Awareness that inclusion–exclusion or combinatorial-sum solutions often admit simpler recurrences that avoid factorial tables and large parameters.
pitfalls: When converting to the DP recurrence, off-by-one errors in indices (e.g., using dp[i] vs dp[i-1] at the boundaries) can silently produce incorrect results.
The recurrence uses terms like (m - n + i) and i; failing to keep all intermediate results reduced modulo MOD can lead to overflow or negative values in languages without automatic big integers.
Maintaining the falling factorial (m)_n as var_2 requires correct loop bounds; updating it too many or too few times (using range(n) vs range(n+1)) changes the final answer.

If one tries to keep the combinatorial-table approach but only precompute up to n instead of m, the formulas for C and P used in the slow code no longer hold; a correct optimization must change the formula itself, not just the precomputation range.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical zero-sum subarray counting using prefix sums; likely n up to 2e5 based on style and need for O(n) or O(n log n) solution.

dominant_ops: Building prefix sum array in a Python loop: O(n)
Counting prefix sums with Counter: O(n)
Sorting Counter entries via most_common(): O(k log k) where k is number of distinct prefix sums

complexity.why: Prefix sum construction and Counter population are O(n). Counter.most_common() sorts entries by frequency, which is O(k log k) with k ≤ n+1 distinct prefix sums, making overall time O(n log n). Space is O(n) for storing prefix sums and the Counter.

bottlenecks.detail: Using Counter.most_common() sorts all distinct prefix sums by frequency, which is unnecessary when the task only requires summing combinations over counts. This introduces an O(k log k) factor.
func_1 computes nCk via range + reduce + mul for a general k, but in this problem it is always invoked with k = 2, adding Python-level function call and small but avoidable overhead.
Using eval(input()) instead of int(input()) is slower and unsafe, though in competitive programming judges this is more a style/safety issue than a dominant performance cost.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid sorting Counter entries and avoid generic combinatorics helper: directly compute prefix sums, count occurrences, and for each frequency f add f * (f - 1) // 2 in a single pass over the counts.

complexity.why: Prefix sums and Counter population remain O(n). Iterating over Counter.values() is O(k) without sorting, so overall time is O(n + k) = O(n). Space usage stays O(n) for the prefix sums and frequency map.

complexity_delta.from: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: The key asymptotic improvement comes from removing the Counter.most_common() sort; other changes (closed-form combination, itertools.accumulate) reduce constant factors.

transformation_steps: Replace manual prefix-sum loop with itertools.accumulate to keep prefix-sum construction concise and efficient.
Build the prefix-sum list as [0] + list(accumulate(var_1)) instead of manually appending to an initially [0] list.
Count frequencies of prefix sums using Counter directly on the prefix-sum list, as in the original.
Remove Counter.most_common() and instead iterate over Counter.values(), avoiding a full sort of the frequency table.
Inline the combination formula for k = 2, replacing the generic func_1(n, 2) logic with f * (f - 1) // 2 for each frequency f.
Simplify the outer logic by iterating over frequencies only, eliminating the need to break when counts drop below 2; the closed-form formula naturally yields 0 when f < 2.
Drop eval() in favor of a direct integer read (int(input())) if further safety and micro-optimizations are desired.
trigger_signals: Use of Counter.most_common() in a context where only aggregate computations over frequencies are needed (no need for sorted order).
Presence of a generic nCk helper function invoked exclusively with k = 2, suggesting replaceable constant-time arithmetic.
Overall pattern of counting subarrays via prefix sums and frequency counts, where the known optimal solution is O(n) without sorting.
Performance concerns or timeouts on large inputs (e.g., n ≈ 2e5) indicating that an O(n log n) solution may be borderline in Python.
pitfalls: When replacing combination logic with f * (f - 1) // 2, ensure integer (floor) division is used to avoid floating-point inaccuracies.
Do not accidentally iterate over Counter.items() or sort keys again; the benefit relies on a plain O(k) pass over counts.
Be mindful that removing the break condition from the most_common() loop is correct only because the new formula handles small counts (f < 2) by yielding 0; logic must match the original semantics.
If further refactoring I/O, avoid eval(input()) for safety and consistency, but ensure you preserve the exact input format handling (e.g., int(input()) vs split-based reading).

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case. N is up to around 1e5; M up to around 1e9–1e12 (trial division sqrt(M) is used). Need many nCk modulo 1e9+7 with n up to N + max_prime_exponent(M).

dominant_ops: Global precomputation of factorials and inverse factorials up to a fixed size 1e6 using NumPy 2D prefix products (func_3 -> func_2).
Resizing and reshaping large NumPy arrays to sqrt(N)^2, then iterating over rows/columns to build prefix products.
Trial-division prime factorization of M up to sqrt(M) (func_4).

complexity.time: O(N0 + sqrt(M)) where N0 = 10^6 (fixed upper bound for factorials), independent of the actual input N.
complexity.space: O(N0) ≈ O(10^6) for factorial / inverse factorial arrays plus temporary O(N0) 2D NumPy buffers.
complexity.why: func_3 always runs with var_7 = 10**6, so it precomputes factorials up to 1e6 regardless of the required maximum n. func_2 does two passes over a sqrt(N0) x sqrt(N0) array, i.e. Θ(N0) ops but with large constant factors and heavy NumPy memory traffic. Prime factorization is an additional O(sqrt(M)) but cheaper than the global precomputation.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorials / inverse factorials are precomputed up to a fixed 1e6 (var_7) on import, even if the actual maximum n in nCk is much smaller. This is wasted work for typical constraints (~1e5).

Using NumPy (np.resize, reshape, 2D arrays) introduces heavy allocation and Python–C boundary overhead. For N0=1e6 the constant factors overshadow the simple integer loop approach, especially in competitive programming environments where NumPy may not be optimized or even allowed.

The code repeatedly reshapes to a sqrt(N0) x sqrt(N0) array. This inflates peak memory usage (multiple ~8 MB int64 arrays) and adds cache-unfriendly access patterns, compared to simple contiguous Python lists.

The precomputation (var_13, var_14 = func_3(var_7, var_5)) runs at module import time, not after reading input. That means cost is paid even for trivial inputs or when the module is imported but not used.

func_4 returns 'va' (truncated) and global var_1 is left hanging, suggesting this modified version is not only slower but also broken. While not a performance issue per se, it indicates fragile refactoring around critical logic.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use classic factorial and modular inverse precomputation with plain Python lists, sized just to the needed maximum (N + a small margin), and compute combinations in O(1) per query. Factor M by trial division and for each prime exponent e, multiply C(N-1+e, e) modulo 1e9+7.

complexity.time: O(N + sqrt(M)) where N is the input var_3 (plus a small constant offset for safety in factorial range).
complexity.space: O(N) for factorial (var_8), inverse factorial (var_7), and inverse (var_10) arrays.
complexity.why: func_3 builds factorials and modular inverses up to var_12 = N+100 using a single forward loop. Each binomial coefficient func_1 then uses O(1) arithmetic. Prime factorization remains O(sqrt(M)) via trial division in func_4. Unlike the slow version, N is data-dependent, so precomputation is proportional to the actual input size, and operations are simple scalar integer multiplications without NumPy overhead.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(N0 + sqrt(M)) with N0 fixed at 10^6, plus large constant factors from NumPy 2D prefix products; Space: O(N0) int64 arrays plus extra temporary 2D buffers.
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(N + sqrt(M)) where N is the actual input size (var_3), with small constants using simple Python lists; Space: O(N) for factorial / inverse arrays with no large temporary buffers.
complexity_delta.note: As soon as the actual required maximum n is much smaller than 10^6 (typical for AtCoder constraints), the fast solution does strictly less work and with lower constant factors. Even when N is near 10^6, the plain-loop implementation typically outperforms the NumPy-based 2D approach in this setting.

transformation_steps: Remove NumPy and Counter imports and all uses of NumPy arrays; operate directly on Python lists of integers.

Replace the 2D prefix-product trick (func_2 + func_3 with reshape to sqrt(N)^2) by a straightforward 1D linear precomputation of factorials and modular inverses up to max_n = N + margin using a single loop (func_3 in the fast code).
Use a standard linear-time inverse construction: maintain an array of modular inverses var_10 where var_10[i] is the inverse of i modulo 1e9+7, and build inverse factorials var_7 from these.
Compute only as many factorial entries as needed: invoke func_3(var_3 + 100, var_2) after reading N, not at import time and not up to a fixed upper bound like 10^6.
Keep the prime factorization step (func_4) essentially the same, as its O(sqrt(M)) cost is appropriate and not the main bottleneck.
Use func_1 to get combinations in O(1) for each prime exponent e: multiply the running answer by C(N-1+e, e) modulo 1e9+7.
trigger_signals: Presence of heavy scientific libraries (NumPy) in a competitive programming solution, especially for simple tasks like factorial precomputation.
Fixed large precomputation size (var_7 = 10**6) independent of the real input N.
Module-level precomputation executed before reading any input.
Use of reshaping to 2D sqrt(N) x sqrt(N) arrays for what is fundamentally a 1D prefix-product problem.
Memory footprint and time both dominated by array operations that do not scale with input size.
pitfalls: When replacing NumPy with plain Python arrays, ensure the factorial / inverse arrays are large enough for the maximum n used in nCk (here up to N - 1 + max_exponent(M)), including any safety margin.
The linear modular-inverse recurrence used in the fast code assumes the modulus is prime (1e9+7); using it with a non-prime modulus would break correctness.
Precomputation should happen after reading input so you can size arrays correctly; doing it at import time risks wasted work or sizing mistakes for multiple testcases.
Watch for off-by-one errors in factorial indexing: var_8[0] and var_8[1] are both initialized as 1, and loops must start at 2 up to the inclusive maximum.
If constraints were ever raised so that N approaches 1e7+, even the fast O(N) precomputation might need further optimization or a different combinatorial method.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case. Effective N is roughly (x + y) / 3 coming from the combinatorial term C(N, k). Coordinates up to about 2e6 so that an O(N) factorial precomputation is acceptable in Python.

dominant_ops: Python for-loops up to ~1e6+ iterations for factorial computation
Python for-loops up to ~1e6+ iterations for modular inverse precomputation (done twice)
Modular multiplication and indexing in tight Python loops

complexity.time: O(L + N + k + m) ≈ O(N) but with multiple passes; concretely about 3 full linear scans where N ~ (x + y) / 3 and L is the fixed 1e6 inverse precompute
complexity.space: O(max(L, N)) for storing inverse arrays; a single list of size up to ~1e6 at a time
complexity.why: The slow_code precomputes modular inverses up to 1e6 (L) regardless of the actual needed range, then runs additional O(N) loops to build factorial and to multiply by inverse values. It then rebuilds the inverse array a second time up to var_12. All heavy work is from these large Python loops and list growth.

bottlenecks.detail: var_7 (array of modular inverses) is built once up to a fixed 1_000_000 and then rebuilt again up to var_12+1, even though the needed range is only up to max(var_10, var_12).

First inverse precomputation uses var_1 = 1000000 irrespective of the actual problem size. If coordinates were larger, this would be both insufficient and wasteful; for moderate size it is just extra work.

Factorial of (var_10 + var_12) is built by a loop from 1 to var_10 + var_12; then two more loops multiply in inverses for var_10 and var_12 separately. A single precomputation of factorials and inverse factorials can compute C(n, k) in O(1) after one O(N) setup.
Using `var_7 += [expression]` in the inverse precomputation loop is slower than simple append and repeatedly allocates small temporary lists.
Uses default input() rather than buffered sys.stdin.readline; minor but still slower under tight limits.

FastAudit.core_idea: Derive the number of paths as a single binomial coefficient C(N, k) modulo a prime and compute it efficiently using one pass of factorial and modular inverse precomputation up to N, then evaluate C(N, k) using factorial * inv_factorial products.

complexity.time: O(N) where N = (x + y) / 3 (var_14) for a single setup loop over n from 2 to N building factorials and modular inverses, then O(1) to compute the final combination.
complexity.space: O(N) for three arrays: factorial, inverse factorial, and modular inverses up to N.
complexity.why: The fast_code’s func_1 constructs factorials and inverse factorials in one linear loop and directly uses the closed-form C(n, k) = fact[n] * ifact[k] * ifact[n-k] mod MOD. It also reduces k via k = min(k, n-k) to minimize work and accesses. No repeated or wasted precomputation is performed.

complexity_delta.from: Single-test O(N) overall but with multiple O(N) and O(1e6) passes and redundant precomputations; high constant factors.
complexity_delta.to: Single-test O(N) with a single linear precomputation and O(1) combination evaluation; significantly smaller constant factors.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity remains linear in N, but the fast version eliminates redundant loops and fixed-range work, making it viable for larger N and stricter time limits.

transformation_steps: Mathematically re-express the path-counting problem as a binomial coefficient C(N, k) under the condition (x + y) % 3 == 0; derive N and k directly from x and y.
Replace the manual factorial and per-parameter inverse multiplications with a standard factorial + inverse-factorial precomputation up to N in one loop.

Use a single modular inverse construction leveraging the linear-time recurrence (inv[i] = -inv[MOD % i] * (MOD // i) mod MOD) inside func_1, instead of building a large global inverse array multiple times.
Optimize the combination evaluation by using the symmetry k = min(k, n - k) to limit access to the inverse factorial array and minimize arithmetic.
Remove hardcoded bounds like var_1 = 1000000 and size all arrays based solely on the actual N derived from input.
Switch from input() to buffered sys.stdin.readline to reduce I/O overhead in tight environments.
trigger_signals: Presence of magic constant loop bounds (var_1 = 1000000) that ignore actual input size.
Multiple passes building similar data structures (var_7 inverses built twice).
Sequential loops doing factorial and inverse multiplications separately rather than using canonical C(n, k) formula with precomputed factorials and inverse factorials.
Use of `+= [value]` in loops, indicating suboptimal list extension patterns.
Single test case with potentially large coordinates, meaning any extra linear pass can significantly impact runtime.
pitfalls: Incorrectly sizing precomputation arrays: N must be at least as large as the maximum factorial index used; underestimating N causes index errors, overestimating too much hurts performance.
Forgetting to use modular inverses properly (e.g., using integer division instead of modular inverse) would break correctness under modulus.
Not handling impossible cases early ((x + y) % 3 != 0 or coordinate ratio constraints) can lead to unnecessary heavy computation or incorrect combinatorial parameters.
Miscomputing k in C(N, k) when translating from the geometry of moves to combinatorial counts can yield wrong answers even if the precomputation is efficient.
Using Python recursion or per-query recomputation of factorials/inverses (if generalized to multiple queries) would dramatically increase time; precomputation must be shared.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case, integers likely up to about 1e9. A linear loop in terms of the answer can time out if the quotient (var_3 / (var_4 + var_5)) is large; intended solution is O(1) arithmetic.

dominant_ops: A while-loop repeatedly increments var_2 by (var_4 + var_5) and counts iterations in var_1 until var_2 exceeds var_3.

complexity.time: O(K), where K ≈ max number of iterations s.t. var_4 + 2*var_5 + K*(var_4 + var_5) <= var_3
complexity.why: The only unbounded work is the while-loop; each iteration performs a constant amount of arithmetic and comparison, so runtime is proportional to the number of loop iterations. Only a fixed number of scalar variables are used.

bottlenecks.detail: The loop iterates once per unit increase in the count var_1, effectively one iteration per step of an arithmetic progression var_2 = var_4 + 2*var_5 + t*(var_4 + var_5). If (var_3 - (var_4 + 2*var_5)) / (var_4 + var_5) is large (up to around 1e9 in worst cases), the loop becomes too slow.
The sequence of var_2 values forms a simple arithmetic progression. The required count can be obtained by solving an inequality and using integer division instead of simulating each step.

FastAudit.core_idea: Recognize that the loop counts how many times a fixed step (var_4 + var_5) fits into a linear range and replace the iterative simulation with a closed-form integer division on a transformed variable: compute a shifted upper bound then divide by the step size.

complexity.why: The modified code performs a constant number of arithmetic operations and a single integer division, independent of the magnitude of the inputs or the would-be number of loop iterations.

complexity_delta.from: O(K) where K is the number of loop iterations (~ (var_3 - (var_4 + 2*var_5)) / (var_4 + var_5) when positive)
complexity_delta.to: O(1) time with the same O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: The transformation replaces counting via a while-loop over an arithmetic progression with a direct integer-division formula that yields the same count.

transformation_steps: Identify the progression in the slow code: var_2 starts at var_4 + 2*var_5 and increases by (var_4 + var_5) each iteration while var_2 <= var_3, incrementing var_1 on each step.
Express this as an inequality: count t such that var_4 + 2*var_5 + t*(var_4 + var_5) <= var_3; algebraically solve for t to get the count in terms of a quotient.
Reparameterize to a simpler form (e.g., using k = t + 1 or an equivalent shift) so the result can be expressed as a single floor division.

Rewrite the code so that initial adjustments to the upper bound and step size are done via a couple of additions/subtractions (e.g., var_3 = var_2 + var_4; var_1 -= var_4), and the loop is replaced by var_1 // var_3.
Verify integer edge cases (bounds, non-negativity conditions) so that the arithmetic formula matches the original loop semantics for all valid inputs.
trigger_signals: A loop whose body only performs additions and comparisons over a variable that evolves as an arithmetic progression.
Loop termination condition depends on crossing a numeric threshold (var_2 <= var_3) with constant increments.
The number of iterations is proportional to a large input-derived value, suggesting that constraints with large upper bounds will cause timeouts.
Presence of a single test case with potentially very large integers, a typical pattern where an O(1) math solution is expected instead of simulation.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when translating the inequality for the progression into a division-based formula (e.g., whether to use floor((upper - shift) / step) or need an additional +/-1).

Differences between mathematical floor and language-specific integer division behavior for negative values; although the original problem likely constrains inputs to avoid negative intermediate results, relying on this without checking can cause subtle bugs.

Assuming the count is always non-negative; in the original loop, if the initial var_2 > var_3, the loop never runs and the answer is 0, whereas a naive arithmetic formula might produce a negative quotient if not guarded.
Potential division-by-zero if the step size were allowed to be zero; this is typically prevented by problem constraints (var_2 + var_4 > 0), but must be ensured.

Renaming and reordering variables, as in Code B, can obscure the connection to the original loop; one must carefully match the transformed formula to the original semantics, not just rely on positional arguments.

constraints_guess.notes: N is the index of a special integer sequence (Lunlun-like: adjacent digits differ by at most 1). Typical constraints around 1e5; only a single query.

dominant_ops: Recursive DFS generation of all valid numbers up to 11 digits, repeated string conversions per node, then global sort of the entire generated list.

complexity.why: Let M be the total count of generated Lunlun numbers up to 11 digits. Each recursive call appends one value to var_4 and does O(1) work plus string conversions. After generating all M numbers, var_4.sort() costs O(M log M). Space is dominated by storing all M numbers in the list.

bottlenecks.detail: func_1 recurses until length > 10 regardless of the requested index var_1, generating the full search tree up to depth 11 even if var_1 is small.
After generating all numbers, the code sorts the entire list var_4 with var_4.sort(), adding an O(M log M) phase that is unnecessary if numbers were generated in order.
Deep recursion (up to 11 levels) with many calls increases Python call overhead compared to an iterative loop.
Each node computes len(str(var_2)) and int(str(var_2)[-1]), incurring repeated str() calls for every generated number.
All generated numbers are stored in var_4 simultaneously, even though only the first var_1 elements are ultimately used.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use an iterative BFS-like expansion starting from digits 1–9, always generating the next valid numbers in ascending order, and stop as soon as the sequence reaches length N. This avoids global sorting and avoids generating unused tail elements.

complexity.why: Each loop iteration processes exactly one existing number and appends at most 3 new numbers; the loop runs until len(var_2) >= N, so the number of generated numbers is O(N). No sorting is required because BFS preserves order. Space is linear in N for storing the prefix in var_2.

delta_type: algorithmic_restructuring (DFS+sort over full space -> incremental BFS generation up to N)

complexity_delta.from: O(M log M) time, O(M) space (M = total count of valid numbers up to max digit length, independent of N)
complexity_delta.to: O(N) time, O(N) space (N = requested index in the sequence)
complexity_delta.note: The optimized version scales with the requested prefix length N instead of the full search-space size M and removes the O(M log M) sorting cost.

transformation_steps: Replace recursive DFS (func_1) that explores all numbers up to a fixed maximum length with an iterative process that grows numbers in a queue-like list.
Initialize the sequence with base digits [1..9] and maintain an index (var_3) to the current element, effectively simulating BFS.
For each current number, compute the next candidates by appending digits differing by at most 1 from the last digit, and append them to the list in the order they are discovered.
Terminate the generation loop once len(var_2) reaches var_1, instead of exploring deeper levels unconditionally.
Remove the global sort; the BFS ordering ensures var_2 is already in ascending order, so var_2[var_1 - 1] is directly the answer.
trigger_signals: Full enumeration of a combinatorial search space (all Lunlun numbers up to length 11) even when the problem only requires the N-th element.
Presence of a large global sort on a generated list before indexing (var_4.sort() followed by var_4[var_1 - 1]).
Deep recursion with simple state transitions that can be naturally modeled via an iterative BFS or queue.
Performance insensitive to N (runtime stays roughly constant as N decreases), indicating overgeneration.
High memory footprint from storing all generated candidates when only a prefix is needed.
pitfalls: Ensuring BFS preserves the correct numeric order: the generation rules must match the intended sequence definition so that the list stays sorted without an explicit sort.
Avoiding off-by-one errors in stopping criteria: the loop must run until len(var_2) >= var_1, and the final index is var_1 - 1.
Handling edge digits correctly (0 and 9) to prevent generating invalid candidates (e.g., last digit 0 cannot append -1; last digit 9 cannot append 10).

String conversions are still used in the BFS implementation; while acceptable for given constraints, they could be a secondary optimization target (using arithmetic last-digit extraction) if N were much larger.

For very large N, even O(N) memory for storing the entire list might be high; a more advanced approach could stream or use a true queue with discarding of earlier elements, but this is unnecessary under typical constraints for this problem.

constraints_guess.notes: Single array input of size N; typical AtCoder-style constraints where O(N) with small constants is required. Memory is not extremely tight but extra O(N) temporaries may hurt in Python for large N.

dominant_ops: Reading N integers into a Python list
Creating a NumPy array from the Python list (np.array(var_2, dtype='int32'))
Computing np.sum(var_2)
Computing (var_2 - var_4) ** 2 which allocates a full temporary array
Computing np.sum on the squared-difference array

complexity.why: Input reading is O(N). Creating the NumPy array is O(N). Both np.sum calls and the elementwise operations on var_2 are linear in N. The vectorized expression (var_2 - var_4) ** 2 constructs a temporary array of size N, so total work still scales linearly. Memory usage is dominated by storing the array plus the temporary squared-difference array, both O(N).

bottlenecks.detail: Converting a Python list to a NumPy array (np.array(var_2, dtype='int32')) for a single short computation introduces overhead that may not be repaid when N is only up to ~1e5–2e5.
The expression (var_2 - var_4) ** 2 allocates a new array of size N for the differences and another for the squares (depending on NumPy's fusion); this adds memory traffic and allocation cost.

The mean is computed as np.sum(var_2) / var_1 (float) then rounded. This incurs floating-point operations and an extra rounding step, while the objective is integer-valued and can be minimized using purely integer arithmetic with floor/ceil of the mean.
Using NumPy just for sum and squared differences increases startup/import overhead and may be slower than pure-Python arithmetic for a single pass over a moderately sized array.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid building difference/squared temporary arrays by using the algebraic expansion of the squared-error objective in terms of sum(a_i) and sum(a_i^2), and evaluate the objective only at the two relevant integer points (floor and ceil of the mean). This reduces per-element work to a couple of scalar accumulations and eliminates vectorized intermediate arrays.

complexity.why: The algorithm still needs to read and store N integers. It computes sum(a_i) and sum(a_i^2) in O(N). The objective for the two candidate centers uses only O(1) scalar arithmetic. var_7 = np.power(var_6, 2) still creates one O(N) array, but there are no additional O(N) temporaries beyond that. Asymptotically it remains linear in N with one pass for sums; constants are reduced relative to multiple NumPy passes and temporaries.

from.time: O(N) with multiple NumPy passes and temporaries
from.space: O(N) for data plus O(N) for temporary difference/squared arrays

to.time: O(N) with a single pass for sums and O(1) post-processing (but with some redundant sums in the given code)
to.space: O(N) for the input list and one O(N) squared array

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity remains O(N) time and O(N) space, but the operation count and temporary allocations are reduced by using a closed-form expression for sum (a_i - x)^2. The provided fast_code still has minor inefficiencies (eval for input, repeated sum(var_6), keeping NumPy) that can be further optimized away.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the objective sum (a_i - x)^2 can be expanded as sum(a_i^2) - 2x * sum(a_i) + N * x^2, so only sum(a_i) and sum(a_i^2) are needed rather than all individual (a_i - x)^2 values.
Replace the direct vectorized computation np.sum((var_2 - var_4) ** 2) with scalar computations using precomputed S = sum(a_i) and SQ = sum(a_i^2) in the formula N * x^2 - 2 * S * x + SQ.

Avoid floating-point rounding of the mean; instead compute the integer candidates x = floor(S / N) and x = ceil(S / N) using integer division and check both, since the quadratic is minimized near the real-valued mean.
Eliminate the NumPy difference operation that created a temporary O(N) array; instead, perform a single pass to accumulate sums, then O(1) arithmetic with the formula.

Optionally (not done in the given fast_code but recommended), remove redundant sum(var_6) calls by storing S once, and drop NumPy entirely by computing SQ = sum(a * a for a in var_6), further reducing overhead.
trigger_signals: The original code computes np.sum((array - c) ** 2) where c is a scalar, which suggests a sum of squared deviations from a center—a classic case where an algebraic simplification to sums of a_i and a_i^2 is possible.
Presence of multiple NumPy passes (conversion to np.array, separate np.sum, and another np.sum on a transformed array) for a single final scalar result.

Objective depends only on aggregated statistics (sum, sum of squares) rather than on the individual positions of elements, indicating that a more compact representation can replace full elementwise operations.
Floating-point computation of the mean followed by round(), hinting that integer-only reasoning (floor/ceil around the mean) could simplify both correctness and performance.
Use of NumPy in a competitive-programming style problem where import overhead and temporary arrays can be a liability under tight time limits.
pitfalls: The fast_code uses eval(input()) instead of int(input()), which is slower and unsafe; from a performance standpoint this is a regression relative to the original code and should be replaced by int(input()).
The fast_code recomputes sum(var_6) several times (for var_2, var_3, var_4, var_5), adding unnecessary O(N) work; sum should be stored in a variable and reused.

The current fast_code still depends on NumPy (np.power) and builds an O(N) array of squares; pure-Python computation of SQ = sum(a * a for a in var_6) would remove the NumPy dependency and avoid the NumPy import and array-allocation overhead.

Switching from round(mean) to floor/ceil changes the exact integer center used; for this particular quadratic objective, checking both floor and ceil is correct, but blindly replacing round with floor could be wrong if only one side is tested.

When porting this pattern to other problems, ensure that the objective truly decomposes into simple sums (like sum(a_i), sum(a_i^2)); using the formula where cross terms or position-dependent weights exist can lead to incorrect results even if performance improves.

constraints_guess.n_max: a few thousand intervals per test case (likely <= 3000–5000)
constraints_guess.notes: Multiple test cases until a 0 line. Times are in fixed zero-padded HH:MM:SS format within a 24-hour day (86400 seconds). Task: compute maximum number of overlapping intervals.

dominant_ops: Per test case: allocation and full traversal of a 86400-length integer list regardless of actual interval count
For each interval: multiple string slices and int() conversions to translate HH:MM:SS into seconds
Use of eval(input()) instead of int(input()), adding overhead and potential safety issues

complexity.why: For each test case, the code does O(n) work to apply a +1/-1 difference on a fixed 86400-length array and then always runs a full O(86400) prefix-sum loop, even when n is small. Space is dominated by the fixed 86400-element array.

bottlenecks.detail: The loop over 86400 seconds runs in every test case, independent of how many intervals exist. When n is small (e.g., hundreds or a few thousand), this fixed cost dominates runtime.
Time parsing is done with repeated slicing and int() calls for both start and end times (six int conversions per interval), which adds non-trivial constant overhead.
Using eval(input()) to read the interval count is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()).
Each test case allocates a full 86400-length list (~3–400 KB) even if only a few intervals are provided, increasing memory traffic and cache pressure.

FastAudit.core_idea: Convert each interval into two events (start and end), sort all events by time, and sweep once while maintaining the current number of active intervals and tracking the maximum.

complexity.why: For each test case, 2n events are stored, then sorted (O(n log n)); a single linear sweep over the events computes the maximum overlap. No dependence on the 86400-second domain, so there is no fixed-cost loop per day.

complexity_delta.from: O(T * (n + 86400)) time, O(86400) space
complexity_delta.to: O(T * (n log n)) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: When n is modest (e.g., n <= a few thousand), n log n is significantly smaller than the fixed 86400 cost, making the sorting-based sweep-line faster overall despite the asymptotic log factor.

transformation_steps: Replace the fixed-size 86400-second difference array with a dynamic list of 2n events representing interval starts and ends.
Avoid converting times into seconds; instead, keep them as HH:MM:SS strings and rely on lexicographic sorting (valid because of zero-padded fixed-width format).
For each interval, append (start_time, True) and (end_time, False) into the events list.
Sort the events list once per test case; events are primarily ordered by time string and secondarily by the boolean flag.
Sweep through the sorted events, incrementing a counter on start events and decrementing on end events, tracking the maximum counter value.
Use int(input()) instead of eval(input()) to read the interval count, reducing overhead and avoiding security risks.
trigger_signals: Presence of a full-day loop: a for-loop over range(86400 - 1) independent of n, indicating heavy fixed per-test work.
Fixed-size large array var_7 = [0] * 86400, suggesting domain-based discretization rather than data-dependent computation.
Multiple repeated string slicing/int() patterns for each time conversion, hinting at avoidable parsing overhead.
Use of eval(input()) instead of int(input()), a classic red flag for both performance and safety in competitive-programming-style tasks.
pitfalls: Relying on lexicographic comparison of time strings works only if the input is strictly zero-padded HH:MM:SS; if formats vary, explicit numeric time conversion is required.

Tie-breaking at equal times is crucial: in the sweep-line approach, sorting ensures end events (False) come before start events (True) at the same timestamp so that intervals are treated as [start, end) and simultaneous leave+enter does not overcount.
If n becomes very large (e.g., >> 10^4), the n log n sort may surpass the cost of a fixed 86400 loop, making the array-based method comparatively better; the optimal approach is constraint-dependent.
Allocating and sorting 2n tuples adds memory and GC pressure; in extreme cases one may need to optimize event representation (e.g., using smaller structures or custom keys).
Changing the representation from numeric seconds to strings means any later arithmetic on times must be adjusted or reintroduced explicitly if required for extended features.

constraints_guess.notes: Undirected graph with N vertices and M edges (third value per edge unused). Need number of connected components. Must be ~O(N+M) with low constant factors to pass in Python.

dominant_ops: Building adjacency list: pushing 2*M endpoints into N lists
Graph traversal via BFS over all components using queue.Queue
Frequent queue put/get operations with thread-safe queue implementation

complexity.time: O(N^2 + M) in worst-case due to repeated enqueues + BFS over adjacency list
complexity.space: O(N + M) for adjacency + visited, with worst-case transient queue size up to O(N^2) due to duplicates
complexity.why: Each edge is stored once per endpoint (O(N+M)), but BFS marks vertices visited only when dequeued, not when enqueued. On dense graphs, a vertex can be enqueued from many neighbors before it is first dequeued, causing up to O(N^2) queue operations. Using queue.Queue adds large constant overhead for each operation (locking, etc.).

bottlenecks.detail: Visited array is updated only when a node is popped from the queue, not when it is enqueued. This allows the same vertex to be enqueued many times by different neighbors in dense graphs, inflating queue operations from O(N+M) to O(N^2) in the worst case.

Using queue.Queue (thread-safe, intended for multi-threading) for BFS instead of collections.deque introduces heavy per-operation overhead for put/get, significantly slowing down an otherwise linear-time traversal.
Maintaining an explicit adjacency list of size O(N+M) is not strictly bad, but combined with potentially enormous numbers of queued entries (duplicates) can increase memory pressure and cache misses.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace BFS-based connected-component counting with a Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) structure that unions endpoints of each edge and tracks the current number of groups. This avoids building or traversing an adjacency list explicitly and keeps per-operation cost extremely low.

complexity.why: Initialization creates parent and rank arrays of size N. Each of the M edges results in one union operation, which is amortized inverse-Ackermann time with path compression and union by rank. No explicit adjacency list is stored, so memory is linear in the number of vertices.

complexity_delta.from: Empirical: O(N^2 + M) worst-case BFS with heavy queue.Queue overhead and an O(N+M) adjacency list.
complexity_delta.to: O((N + M) * α(N)) ≈ O(N + M) using Union-Find with path compression and union by rank, with O(N) space.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both can be O(N+M) if BFS is implemented carefully with correct visited marking and a deque; however, the given slow code is effectively worse (up to O(N^2)) and has much larger constants than the DSU approach.

transformation_steps: Remove the explicit adjacency list construction; instead of storing all edges in per-vertex lists, process each edge once as it is read.
Introduce a Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) class maintaining parent and rank arrays for N nodes, initialized so each node is its own parent and grp = N.
For each edge (u, v, _), convert to 0-based indices and call the union operation (e.g., unite/func_4) on u-1 and v-1.
Within union, find the roots of the two nodes (with path compression) and, if distinct, merge by rank and decrement the group counter grp.
After all edges are processed, output the DSU’s grp value as the number of connected components.
Avoid queue.Queue and any BFS/DFS traversal entirely, eliminating the repeated-enqueue bug and the heavy synchronization overhead.
trigger_signals: Constraints that allow M to be large (e.g., up to 2e5 or more), where O(N^2) behavior or heavy constant factors in BFS become problematic.
Use of queue.Queue for BFS in single-threaded competitive programming code, which is a known performance anti-pattern due to locking and Python overhead.
Visited nodes marked only after dequeue instead of at enqueue time, a common bug leading to multiple enqueues of the same node in dense graphs.
Task structure is purely about counting connected components of an undirected graph with no need for traversal order, a classic fit for Union-Find.
pitfalls: When implementing Union-Find, ensure method names in the class and calls in main are consistent (e.g., find vs func_1, unite vs func_4); mismatches will cause runtime errors even if the performance is good.
Remember to convert input node indices from 1-based to 0-based exactly once; double-adjusting or forgetting the adjustment changes the connectivity structure.

If find is implemented recursively, very deep trees could, in principle, hit recursion limits. Path compression and union by rank mitigate this, but an iterative find is safer for extreme constraints.
If one chooses to keep a BFS/DFS solution instead, they must: (1) use collections.deque instead of queue.Queue, and (2) mark visited when enqueuing, not when dequeuing, to maintain O(N+M) behavior.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AOJ-style problem: multiple testcases until '0 0'. n is small enough that O(n^2) passes but O(n^3) risks TLE when summed over many cases.

dominant_ops: Triple nested loops over i<j<k in [1..n], computing and comparing sums for all combinations.

complexity.why: There are three nested loops: i from 0..n-3, j from i+1..n-2, k from j+1..n-1. This enumerates all C(n,3) = Θ(n^3) triples. An auxiliary list var_2 of size n is created, and var_1 stores all matches (at most O(n^3), but typically much smaller); asymptotically dominated by the input range list O(n).

bottlenecks.detail: Brute-force enumeration of all triplets (i, j, k) with i<j<k, leading to Θ(n^3) combinations even though only their count is needed.
The code stores each successful sum in var_1 and only prints len(var_1). Maintaining the list is unnecessary; a simple counter would suffice and slightly reduce overhead.
Repeated indexed accesses var_2[var_6], var_2[var_7], var_2[var_8] in the innermost loop; although cheap, they are executed Θ(n^3) times.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the structure a + b + c = S with 1 ≤ c < b < a ≤ n: fix a (the largest number), derive starting b and c from algebra, then slide along the (b, c) solution line by decrementing b and incrementing c while maintaining a + b + c = S and the ordering constraints. This removes one summation loop, reducing enumeration from all triples to all feasible (a, b) pairs.

complexity.why: The outer loop decreases a (var_1) roughly from n down to a minimum where any valid triple is still possible: O(n) iterations. For each a, the inner while enumerates all feasible (b, c) pairs along the solution line b + c = S - a, with b>c>0; in the worst case this is O(n) per a. Thus total time Θ(n^2). Only a few scalar variables are used, so space is constant.

complexity_delta.from: O(n^3) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n^2) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: One summation loop is eliminated by solving for c and iterating only over feasible (a, b) pairs under ordering constraints.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the numbers are exactly from 1 to n and we only need the count of triples (a, b, c) with 1 ≤ c < b < a ≤ n such that a + b + c = S.
Fix a (the largest value) and note that for each a we only need to consider (b, c) pairs satisfying b + c = S - a and 1 ≤ c < b < a.
For each chosen a, initialize b = a - 1 and c = S - a - b. This ensures a + b + c = S at the start and b is as large as possible.
Check the feasibility condition a > b > c; if it fails at initialization for a, further smaller a will not yield valid triples, so break early.
Within the inner loop, maintain the invariant a + b + c = S by decrementing b and incrementing c together (b -= 1; c += 1), moving along the line of solutions b + c = S - a while preserving sum S.
For each position in the inner loop, count the triple whenever a > b > c > 0 holds, thus avoiding recomputation and extra storage.
Remove the auxiliary array of [1..n] and the result list; retain only counters and scalar variables to keep memory usage constant.
trigger_signals: Presence of three nested loops over the same O(n) range (i, j, k) indicating O(n^3) behavior.
Constraints (in the original problem context) where n can be up to a few thousand, making n^3 too slow over multiple testcases.
The operation inside the innermost loop is very simple (integer addition and comparison), a classic sign that algorithmic complexity dominates runtime.
The task requires only the count of valid triples, not the triples themselves, suggesting that full enumeration is unnecessary and can be replaced by a combinatorial or algebraic approach.
pitfalls: Ordering constraints must be strict: ensure the inequalities c < b < a and positivity c > 0 are correctly encoded; a small off-by-one mistake can overcount or undercount solutions.

The early-break condition `if not var_1 > var_2 > var_3` assumes that once a given a fails the ordering at initialization, no smaller a will work; this relies on problem-specific reasoning and must be justified carefully for other variants.
Because the inner loop mutates b and c, their initialization for each new a must be correct (b = a - 1, c = S - a - b). Reusing stale values across iterations would break the invariant a + b + c = S.
When porting or refactoring, it is easy to inadvertently allow non-distinct values (e.g., b = c or a = b). Always double-check the strictness of comparisons, especially when changing loop boundaries.
The fast code's reliance on integer arithmetic is safe in Python due to arbitrary-precision integers, but in other languages overflow or type limits might need attention.

constraints_guess.notes: Two strings, likely of equal or similar length; classic string-rotation or substring check. Single test case, input size dominated by total string length.

dominant_ops: Building a doubled string and running a substring membership test `var_3 in var_4` on it.

complexity.why: Let n be the length of the first string. `var_4 = var_4 + var_4[:-1]` allocates a new string of length ~2n, which is O(n). The subsequent membership test `var_3 in var_4` is implemented in C and runs in linear time average-case in the length of the haystack (and pattern), so also O(n). Total is O(n) time and O(n) extra memory for the doubled string.

bottlenecks.detail: Creating `var_4 + var_4[:-1]` copies the original string and almost all of it again, allocating ~2n characters. This dominates runtime for large n due to memory bandwidth and allocation cost.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical unbounded knapsack-style DP: H (target sum) up to around 1e4, number of item types N up to ~1e2, item values up to ~1e4. DP array sized to H + max(a_i) (+ small margin) in original; modified code hardcodes +1e4, implying max(a_i) ≤ 1e4.

Repeated use of max(0, i - a_j) inside the innermost loop, adding a conditional operation to every transition.

The outer loop runs for each state index var_5 from 1 to L-1, and the inner loop iterates over all N items. Each iteration does O(1) work (a few array accesses, an addition, a min). Thus time is O(L * N) = O((H + maxA) * N). The dp array itself stores one integer per index, so space is O(L) = O(H + maxA); input arrays var_1 and var_2 add O(N).

bottlenecks.detail: The DP iterates over all indices up to H + maxA, and for each index it uses that index as a base state in transitions. However, to compute the minimal cost to reach at least H, it is sufficient to use only base states < H and allow transitions to jump beyond H. Using states >= H as base states is redundant and costs O(maxA * N) extra operations.

The code does not skip dp positions that remain at the INF sentinel (sys.maxsize). It still performs N transitions for those indices, even though they cannot improve any future states, wasting work especially when many states are unreachable.

Each transition uses max(0, var_5 - var_1[var_7]) to guard against negative indices. This adds a conditional operation inside the innermost loop for every DP update. For large (H + maxA) * N it becomes a noticeable constant-factor overhead.

The dp length scales with maxA. When maxA is large relative to H, the number of DP states and thus total work increases, even though many of those high indices are only needed as final overshoot targets and not as transition bases.

FastAudit.core_idea: Reformulate the DP as a forward, reachable-state propagation: iterate over heights i from 0 up to H-1, skip unreachable dp[i], and for each reachable state update dp[i + a_j] using dp[i] + b_j. This avoids using overshoot states (>= H) as base states and prunes unreachable states, reducing the number of transitions. Additionally, use faster input (stdin.readline) and a fixed upper bound (H + 1e4) for dp size instead of computing max(a_i) at runtime.

complexity.time: O(H * N) in practice, with pruning reducing the constant factor
complexity.why: The outer loop iterates var_7 from 0 to H-1 (H iterations). For each reachable dp[var_7] (dp[var_7] != INF), it loops over all N items and performs O(1) transitions, updating dp[var_7 + a_j]. Because only indices < H are used as bases, the number of base states is H; overshoot states ≥ H serve only as targets and do not generate further work. Thus the base complexity is O(H * N). The dp array var_6 is sized to H + 1e4 + 1, matching the constraint-based upper bound on max a_j, so space remains O(H + maxA_max), where maxA_max (~1e4) is the maximum allowed a_j. Pruning unreachable states further cuts the effective time cost when many states are never reached.

complexity_delta.to: O(H * N) time in terms of base states, O(H + maxA_max) space
complexity_delta.note: By restricting base states to indices < H and allowing transitions to overshoot H, the algorithm no longer uses indices ≥ H as sources in the DP recurrence. This effectively removes an O(maxA * N) component from the time complexity. In worst-case asymptotics where maxA ≈ H the big-O notation remains similar, but the constant factor is significantly reduced and for maxA >> H the improvement is substantial. Unreachable-state pruning further reduces practical runtime.
