complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + P * F(N)) where P is number of distinct prime factors of M and F(N) is the cost of computing factorial(N) with big integers; the big-int factorial and divisions dominate for N≈1e5
complexity.space: O(P + K * size_of_factorial_values) big-int space, where K is number of cached factorial arguments; factorial values grow to Θ(N log N) bits
complexity.why: Prime factorization uses a standard while var_5**2 <= var_9 loop (O(sqrt(M))). For each exponent e_i, the code calls func_1, which uses math.factorial to compute factorial(var_8), factorial(var_8 - var_12), factorial(var_12) as arbitrary-precision integers. These factorials for N≈1e5 have hundreds of thousands of bits; each multiplication/division on such numbers is expensive. Caching avoids recomputation for identical arguments but still stores huge integers and performs big-int division var_2 // (var_3 * var_4) without modular reduction until the very end.

bottlenecks.detail: math.factorial returns full-precision integers of enormous size (factorial(1e5) has ~456k digits). All subsequent multiplications and divisions in computing combinations operate on these huge numbers before a single modulo operation is applied.

Modulo 1e9+7 is applied only once at the end: print((var_12 % var_7)). This forces all intermediate combinatorial calculations to use full big integers instead of cheap modular integers, drastically increasing runtime and memory pressure.

Each combination C(n, k) is recomputed from factorials and big-int divisions instead of using precomputed factorials and modular inverses. Even with a cache dictionary, factorials are built via math.factorial rather than incremental modular multiplication.

In func_2 (factorization), the membership test uses 'if var_5 in list(var_11.keys()):', which allocates a list of keys for every check. A direct dict membership 'if var_5 in var_11:' would avoid repeated list creation. This is a minor overhead compared to big-int costs but still wasteful.

The cache var_1 stores multiple huge factorial integers. Storing several factorial values of order ~1e5 results in tens of megabytes of memory usage, which can trigger GC overhead and slow down CP environments.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep all combinatorial computations under modulo 1e9+7 and precompute factorials and inverse factorials once up to the required maximum (N + small margin). Replace big-int factorial and division with O(1) modular nCr using precomputed factorials and multiplicative inverses; perform essentially the same prime factorization, but represent factors as a list of (prime, exponent) pairs and use the combinatorial formula nCr(e_i + N - 1, N - 1) directly.

complexity.why: Factorization via trial division remains O(sqrt(M)). The key improvement is in computing combinations: factorial array var_6 and inverse factorial array var_7 are built in a single O(N) pass (N ≈ var_2 + 100). Modular inverses var_9 are also computed in O(N) using the standard linear recurrence inv[i] = -(MOD//i) * inv[MOD % i] mod MOD. Each binomial coefficient C(n, k) is then computed in O(1) as fact[n] * inv_fact[k] * inv_fact[n-k] % MOD. All operations are performed modulo 1e9+7, so integers remain bounded and operations are cheap. Overall, the dominant cost is the linear precomputation plus the trial division, both easily within limits for N≈1e5 and M≈1e9.

complexity_delta.from: Effectively dominated by big-integer factorial computations and divisions: O(sqrt(M) + P * F(N)) with F(N) superlinear in N due to growing bit-length of factorial(N); large constant factors and memory usage cause TLE/MLE for N≈1e5.
complexity_delta.to: O(N + sqrt(M)) time and O(N) space with all operations in modular arithmetic; practical and fast for N≈1e5, M≈1e9.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically in terms of arithmetic operations, both approaches perform a similar number of loop iterations in N, but the slow code uses huge big integers, making bit-complexity enormous. The fast code constrains all values modulo 1e9+7 and thus has small, fixed-size integers, reducing both runtime and memory usage by orders of magnitude.

transformation_steps: Replace the math.factorial-based combination calculation with a precomputed factorial and inverse factorial scheme under modulo 1e9+7. Introduce arrays var_6 (fact), var_7 (inv_fact), and var_9 (inv) computed up to var_2 + 100 to cover all required n in C(n, k).

Compute modular inverses iteratively using inv[i] = -inv[MOD % i] * (MOD // i) mod MOD, then build inverse factorials via inv_fact[i] = inv_fact[i-1] * inv[i] mod MOD, achieving O(N) precomputation instead of repeated big-int divisions.

Redefine the combination function func_1(var_11, var_14, var_10) to return 0 for invalid k, symmetrize k via k = min(k, n-k), and compute C(n, k) using precomputed fact and inv_fact arrays entirely under modulo arithmetic.

Keep the prime factorization logic conceptually similar but change the representation from a dict of prime→exponent to a list of [prime, exponent] pairs (var_4). Slightly refactor the factorization loop to be a clean for-loop up to int(sqrt(M)) + 1 and ensure the remaining factor is appended if >1.
Apply modulo 1e9+7 during accumulation of the final answer (var_3) after each multiplication, preventing integer growth and keeping all intermediate values bounded.
Eliminate the factorial cache dictionary of big integers and all big-int divisions. All heavy numerical work is replaced with light modular multiplications and a single upfront precomputation.
trigger_signals: Use of math.factorial on arguments derived from N where N can be as large as 1e5, combined with integer division to compute C(n, k), and modulo applied only at the end.

Recognition of the pattern product over primes of C(e_i + N - 1, e_i), which is a standard combinatorics-with-modulo pattern where factorial/inverse factorial precomputation is the canonical optimization.
Presence of a dictionary cache storing large factorial values, hinting at both repeated expensive computations and potential memory overuse.
-like constraints (single query, N up to around 1e5) where O(N) precomputation is typical and big-integer math is known to be too slow.
Inner loop in factorization creating list(var_11.keys()) repeatedly, a sign of micro-inefficiency that, while minor here, indicates the code has not been tuned for performance.
pitfalls: Ensuring the precomputation range for factorials (var_2 + 100) is sufficiently large to handle all n in C(n, k). In this problem exponents are small (for M<=1e9, max exponent ~30), so N + 100 is safe; in other problems this margin must be adjusted carefully.

Correctness of the modular inverse recurrence: var_9.append((-var_9[var_10 % var_8] * (var_10 // var_8)) % var_10) assumes var_10 is prime and uses a standard formula; any typo or incorrect modulus would silently produce wrong combinations.

Need to use 64-bit safe operations (Python ints are unbounded, so this is fine) and apply modulo after each multiplication to avoid overflow in other languages; in Python it's more about performance than correctness.
When generalizing, mixing big-int factorials with modular arithmetic can lead to incorrect results if modulo is applied inconsistently or divisions are attempted in modular space without inverses.

The trial-division factorization still has O(sqrt(M)) complexity; if M were larger (e.g., up to 10^12 or more), further optimization (e.g., precomputed primes or Pollard Rho) might be required. The current change improves combination computation but not factorization asymptotics.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style graph problem: up to ~2e5 nodes and edges, must run in ~1s in Python. Third value per edge is unused (probably a weight or type).

dominant_ops: Building adjacency list O(N+M) and running BFS over all components using queue.Queue with many put()/get() calls in Python.

complexity.why: Each vertex is enqueued and dequeued at most once, and each undirected edge is examined twice (once from each endpoint). The adjacency list stores all edges; the visited array and queue take O(N) extra.

bottlenecks.detail: Using queue.Queue (thread-safe, locking, designed for multithreading) for BFS in a tight loop. Its put()/get()/empty() involve locks and function-call overhead, making each queue operation significantly slower than deque operations.
Frequent calls to var_9.empty() instead of a cheap truthiness test (while var_9). queue.Queue.empty() is slower and not needed in this single-threaded setting.
queue.Queue is created once and reused, which is fine, but the main cost remains its heavy implementation compared to a simple deque. For large N,M, the number of queue operations dominates runtime.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the algorithm (BFS over all components) but replace queue.Queue with collections.deque, using popleft()/append() and a simple truthiness check for the queue. This removes locking and reduces per-operation overhead while preserving O(N+M) complexity.

complexity.why: The traversal work is unchanged: each node and edge is processed a constant number of times. deque operations (append, popleft) are amortized O(1) with very low constant factors, so overall complexity stays O(N+M) but is much faster in practice.

complexity_delta.from: O(N + M) with high constant factors due to queue.Queue locking and method overhead.
complexity_delta.to: O(N + M) with low constant factors using collections.deque for BFS.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is identical, but the constant factor improvement is substantial for large graphs, often turning TLE into AC in Python.

transformation_steps: Replace 'import queue' and 'var_9 = queue.Queue()' with 'from collections import deque' and per-component 'var_9 = deque([var_4])'.
Change the BFS loop condition from 'while not var_9.empty():' to 'while var_9:'.
Replace 'var_5 = var_9.get()' with 'var_5 = var_9.popleft()'.
Replace 'var_9.put(var_6)' with 'var_9.append(var_6)'.
Keep the graph construction and visited-array logic identical to preserve correctness and O(N+M) behavior.
trigger_signals: Using queue.Queue in competitive programming / single-threaded BFS (import queue with many put/get calls).
TLE or borderline time on large graphs despite an O(N+M) algorithm.
Hotspot profiling showing high time spent in queue.Queue methods (put, get, empty).
Code review recognizing that thread-safe queues are unnecessary in a single-threaded algorithm.
pitfalls: Accidentally using a plain list as a queue with pop(0), which leads to O(N^2) behavior due to O(N) per pop from the front.
Forgetting to mark nodes visited before or as they are enqueued, which can cause multiple enqueues and effectively increase the constant factor (or even worse behavior in dense graphs).
Misusing deque (e.g., using appendleft/popleft inconsistently) and inadvertently changing traversal order, though correctness for connected-component counting is usually unaffected.
Confusing queue.Queue semantics (blocking, threads) with deque and assuming methods like put()/get()/empty() exist on deque.
Allocating an excessively large per-component queue structure in other contexts; here, per-component deque reallocation is negligible since total enqueues remain O(N+M).

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AOJ-style problem: count triples (i,j,k) with 1 <= i < j < k <= n and i+j+k = x, repeated for multiple (n,x) pairs until sentinel (0,0). Limits likely up to low thousands, making O(n^3) too slow and O(n^2) acceptable.

dominant_ops: Triple nested loops over (var_2, var_3, var_4) with a simple sum and equality check in the innermost loop.

complexity.why: var_2 ranges from 1..n-2, var_3 from var_2+1..n-1, var_4 from var_3+1..n, leading to Θ(n^3) combinations. Only a few integer variables are kept, so space is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: Enumerating all ordered triples (var_2, var_3, var_4) with 1 <= var_2 < var_3 < var_4 <= n is Θ(n^3). For n in the low thousands this leads to ~O(10^9) iterations, which is infeasible in Python.
Each of the Θ(n^3) iterations incurs Python loop overhead and integer additions/comparisons; even if the arithmetic is cheap, the sheer loop count dominates runtime.
The sum var_2 + var_3 + var_4 is recomputed for every candidate triple, even though for fixed (var_2,var_3) the needed var_4 could be solved directly from the target sum.

FastAudit.core_idea: Eliminate the innermost loop by solving directly for the third variable: for fixed (var_3, var_4), compute var_2 = target_sum - var_3 - var_4 and then just check whether var_2 is within range and respects the ordering constraints (var_2 > var_4 would be incorrect; the code correctly uses var_2 > var_4 as a condition for the chosen index order). This reduces the search from all triples to all pairs.

complexity.why: The optimized code loops over var_3 in [1, n-2] and var_4 in (var_3, n-1], yielding Θ(n^2) pairs. For each pair, var_2 is computed in O(1) and validated with O(1) checks; no inner loop remains. No additional data structures are used, so space is constant.

complexity_delta.from: O(n^3) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n^2) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time improved by removing one loop through algebraic substitution; memory usage stays constant.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the triple (var_2, var_3, var_4) is constrained by var_2 + var_3 + var_4 = var_5[1] (or var_6 in the modified code) and by 1 <= var_2 < var_3 < var_4 <= n.
Observe that for any chosen pair (var_3, var_4), the corresponding var_2 is uniquely determined as var_2 = target_sum - var_3 - var_4.
Replace the innermost loop over var_4 (or over one of the three indices) and the sum check with a direct computation of var_2 from the equation instead of enumeration.

Change the nested loops to iterate only over two variables (var_3 and var_4), compute var_2 in O(1), and then apply range and ordering constraints: var_2 > var_4 / var_3 / 0 as required by the chosen variable order, and var_2 <= n.
Preserve the input sentinel logic (n == 0 with x == 0 implied) while simplifying the parsing: unpack into var_5, var_6 and break on var_5 == 0.
Retain constant extra memory by not introducing any arrays or caching structures; keep only scalar integer variables.
trigger_signals: Presence of three nested for-loops each depending on n, indicating O(n^3) behavior.
Constraints where n can be in the high hundreds or thousands, making n^3 operations infeasible for Python under typical time limits.
The inner loop body performing only a simple arithmetic check, suggesting that algebraic manipulation could remove one dimension of iteration.
A pattern of counting combinations (i < j < k) subject to a linear sum constraint, a classic case where one variable can be solved directly from the others.
pitfalls: Off-by-one and ordering errors: when removing the innermost loop and computing var_2 directly, the ordering constraint (1 <= var_2 < var_3 < var_4 <= n) must still be enforced correctly. The specific inequalities (e.g., var_2 > var_4 vs var_2 < var_3) depend on which variable is being solved for and how the loops are structured.

Range validation: after computing var_2 = target_sum - var_3 - var_4, it is essential to check that var_2 is at least 1 and at most n; missing one of these checks can count invalid triples or index out of the allowed range (even if Python itself won’t index with it here, the combinatorial interpretation would be wrong).

Sentinel handling: the original problem uses (0,0) as the terminator. The optimized code breaks when var_5 == 0, which is correct only if the input guarantees that x is 0 whenever n is 0. If the judge specification differed, this change could mis-handle termination.

Integer arithmetic assumptions: this transformation relies on exact integer arithmetic. In Python that is safe, but in other languages with potential overflow, computing var_2 via subtraction might overflow if not within bounds, altering correctness.

Symmetry and double-counting: when switching from explicit triple enumeration to a derived third variable, it is easy to count the same combination multiple times if the loop bounds and inequalities are not carefully matched to the original 1 <= i < j < k <= n constraint.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case. Second input (n) is factorized in O(sqrt(n)), so n is likely up to about 1e12. First input (k) is used inside binomial coefficients C(k + e - 1, e); original code precomputes up to 2e5, suggesting k + max_exponent <= 2e5 in the intended constraints, but the fast version adapts this bound dynamically.

dominant_ops: Trial division prime factorization of n up to sqrt(n).
Precomputation of factorials var_10[0..2*10^5-1] modulo MOD.
Precomputation of inverse factorials var_12[1..2*10^5-1] via one modular inverse using pow and a backward DP.
O(1) binomial coefficient evaluations per distinct prime factor.

complexity.why: Factorization by trial division iterates divisors up to sqrt(n), giving O(sqrt(n)) divisions. Factorial and inverse factorial arrays are built with L = 2*10^5 elements, with simple O(1) work per element, giving O(L) time and space. The number of distinct primes in n is at most O(log n), so the loop over prime exponents is negligible compared with these two major costs.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorials and inverse factorials are precomputed up to a fixed global limit L = 2*10^5 regardless of the actual required maximum n in C(n, k). For small k and small exponents, this does more work and allocates more memory than necessary.

The global constant L = 2*10^5 is assumed to be >= max over primes of (k + e_i - 1). If the judge’s constraints allow larger k or exponents such that k + max_e - 1 > 2*10^5, the code will either index out of bounds or compute incorrect results. This is a robustness and potential performance issue if L must be increased significantly.

Using defaultdict(int) and iterating func_1(var_1).items() is slightly heavier than necessary when only the exponents are needed to form the product; the fast version simplifies this via a list and Counter. This is minor compared with the precomputation cost.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the same mathematical approach—factor n into primes, use stars-and-bars to get C(k + e_i - 1, e_i) for each exponent, and multiply modulo MOD—but size the factorial and inverse factorial tables exactly up to the maximum needed n = k + max_exponent instead of a fixed global constant. Factorization is expressed as a flat list of prime factors combined with Counter to get exponents, and a standard combinatorics helper uses dynamically sized precomputed factorials.

complexity.why: Factorization remains O(sqrt(n)) using trial division, unchanged asymptotically. Let max_e be the maximum exponent among n’s prime factors and k be the first input. The largest n used in C(n, r) is k + max_e - 1, so the fast code sets K = k + max_e and builds factorial and inverse factorial arrays of size O(K). Each element is filled in O(1), and only one modular inverse via fast exponentiation is used. The number of binomial evaluations is still O(number of distinct primes), which is O(log n) and negligible compared with O(sqrt(n) + K).

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(n) + L) time, O(L) space, with L fixed at 2*10^5 regardless of actual k and prime exponents.
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(n) + K) time, O(K) space, where K = k + max_exponent is computed from the specific input instance.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both are linear in the chosen precomputation bound, but the fast version replaces a fixed global bound with a tight input-dependent bound. This improves constants, memory footprint, and scales correctly when k or exponents grow beyond 2*10^5.

transformation_steps: Change prime factorization representation from a defaultdict(prime -> exponent) to a list of prime factors returned by func_2 and aggregated by collections.Counter to obtain exponents.
Compute the maximum exponent over all prime factors via Counter(values), and derive the true maximum binomial n parameter as var_4 = k + max_exponent.
Allocate factorial array var_9 of size var_4 + 1 and fill it iteratively, instead of using a preallocated global array of size 2*10^5.
Compute a single modular inverse of var_9[var_4] using a fast binary exponentiation helper func_3, then build the inverse factorial array var_10 bottom-up from var_4 to 0.

Replace the original combination helper func_2(n, r) that relied on globally precomputed arrays with func_1(n, r) that uses the newly computed factorial and inverse-factorial arrays sized to the exact required maximum.
Preserve the core formula (for each prime exponent e, multiply by C(k + e - 1, e) mod MOD) while restructuring the implementation to eliminate fixed-size assumptions.
trigger_signals: Presence of a magic constant L = 2*10^5 used to bound factorial precomputation, with no derivation from input constraints.
Potential or observed out-of-range access when k + exponent exceeds the fixed bound for factorial tables.
Memory or time issues when L must be increased to meet tighter problem constraints, suggesting the need for input-sensitive precomputation sizes.
Code review noticing that many test cases use small k and exponents, making precomputation up to a large fixed L wasteful.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when computing the required maximum n = k + max_exponent - 1 for C(n, r) and sizing the factorial/inverse factorial arrays; the implementation must ensure arrays are at least length max_n + 1.

For n = 1 (no prime factors) the Counter is empty; the code must handle this case correctly (the product over an empty set should remain 1) and avoid deriving an invalid var_4 from max on an empty sequence.

Manual modular exponentiation (func_3) is correct but slower than Python’s built-in pow with three arguments; it should not be called in inner loops, and its use must be limited to a small, fixed number of invocations.

When switching from dict-based exponent storage to a list + Counter approach, it is important to ensure that all residual factor > 1 at the end of trial division is appended correctly to avoid losing prime factors.
The factorial and inverse factorial tables depend on the modulus being prime for Fermat-based inversion; changing MOD to a non-prime would require a different inverse computation strategy.

constraints_guess.notes: AtCoder-style problem: given N and a single special edge (X,Y), count for each distance k how many vertex pairs have shortest path length k in a path graph 1..N plus one extra edge. Typical constraints: N ≤ 2000, no separate queries.

dominant_ops: Running Dijkstra's algorithm (via a heap) from each vertex over a sparse graph, with heavy Python class and list-walk overhead inside the main loop.

complexity.why: The underlying graph is a path of N nodes plus one extra edge, so edges E ≈ N. The code structure (Class_1 with func_9 using a heap) indicates Dijkstra's algorithm. To get all-pairs distances for counting, Dijkstra must be run from each vertex: O(N) sources × O(E log N) per run ≈ O(N · N log N) = O(N^2 log N). The adjacency list and distance arrays are O(N + E) = O(N) in size.

bottlenecks.detail: Using full Dijkstra from every vertex for an almost-linear graph (a line plus one extra edge) is overkill. Distances between i and j can be expressed in closed form as min(j−i, |X−i| + 1 + |Y−j|), avoiding repeated shortest-path computations.

All-pairs distances are obtained by recomputing shortest paths from each node independently, even though the graph structure is fixed and extremely simple. This repeats heap relaxations and list scans N times.

Graph edges are wrapped in Python classes (Class_1, inner Class_2/Edge) with method calls (func_5, func_6, func_7, func_9) inside the tight Dijkstra loop. Combined with heap operations, this creates substantial interpreter overhead at O(N^2 log N) scale.
Input is read via eval in func_2 (int(eval(var_10()))), which is both slow and unsafe. While not the dominant factor vs Dijkstra, it is unnecessary overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the specific structure of the graph (a line 1..N plus one extra edge between vertices X and Y) to derive a direct formula for the shortest path between any pair (i, j). For i < j, the distance is min(j−i, |X−i| + 1 + |Y−j|). Iterate over all ordered pairs with i < j once in a double loop, compute this formula in O(1), and increment a frequency array for the resulting distance.

complexity.why: The fast code does two nested loops: for var_5 in range(1, N), for var_6 in range(var_5+1, N+1), which enumerates all O(N^2) unordered pairs (i, j) with i < j. Each iteration performs O(1) arithmetic and an array increment using min(j−i, |X−i| + |Y−j| + 1), so total time is O(N^2). Only an array of length N (var_1) is stored to count how many pairs achieve each distance k, giving O(N) additional space.

complexity_delta.from: O(N^2 log N) time, O(N) space with heavy constant factors from heap operations and Python classes.
complexity_delta.to: O(N^2) time, O(N) space with simple arithmetic in tight loops.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically, the log N factor is removed and constant factors are drastically reduced by replacing generic all-pairs Dijkstra with a direct arithmetic formula tailored to the line-plus-one-edge graph.

transformation_steps: Recognize the graph structure: vertices 1..N connected in a path, with one extra edge between X and Y. This yields at most two fundamentally different shortest path patterns between any pair (i, j): either the direct path along the line or the path that uses the special edge once.

Derive the closed-form shortest path distance between i and j. For i < j, without the special edge, distance is j−i. A path using the extra edge is min(|X−i| + 1 + |Y−j|, |Y−i| + 1 + |X−j|). The fast code embodies one of these symmetric expressions as abs(var_3−var_5) + abs(var_4−var_6) + 1.
Replace the generic graph representation and Dijkstra routine (Class_1 with adjacency lists and heaps) with a simple counting array var_1 where index k stores the number of pairs whose distance is k.

Instead of running Dijkstra from each vertex, iterate over all pairs (i, j) with i < j via two nested loops and compute the distance via the formula: d = min(j−i, |X−i| + |Y−j| + 1). Increment var_1[d].
Finalize by printing the counts for k = 1..N−1 (after deleting the unused index 0), matching the problem's required output format.
trigger_signals: The graph is nearly a path with only one extra edge, suggesting strong structure that likely admits a direct combinatorial or formula-based solution instead of generic shortest-path algorithms.

The original approach (implied by the slow code) needs all-pairs shortest paths in a sparse graph with N up to around 2000, which in Python is borderline when implemented as N Dijkstra runs with heavy object overhead.
The problem asks only for counts of distances, not the actual paths or full distance matrix, indicating that aggregating via analytic formulas could be sufficient and more efficient.
Use of classes, methods, and a priority queue in a deeply nested context is a red flag for performance in Python, especially when the same work pattern is repeated many times (once per source node).
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors: vertices in the fast code are treated as 1-based (loops from 1 to N, and X, Y are used directly). Mixing 0-based and 1-based indices from the original graph code can easily misalign distances.
Double counting pairs: the fast solution loops over i < j only once. A naive translation from all-pairs shortest paths might mistakenly consider both (i, j) and (j, i), doubling counts.

Incorrect distance formula: the shortest path via the extra edge must consider both directions (i → X → Y → j and i → Y → X → j). The compact expression abs(X−i) + abs(Y−j) + 1 works because X and Y are symmetric; mis-deriving this can lead to off-by-one or asymmetry issues.

Index handling in the count array: distances range from 1 to N−1. The fast code allocates size N, uses indices directly as distances, and then deletes var_1[0]. Forgetting this alignment or printing an extra element can break the output format.

Performance regressions if generalized: extending the fast pattern to more special edges without rethinking the formula can silently reintroduce O(N^3) or worse behavior; the optimization relies critically on having exactly one extra edge.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic lattice-move / knight-move style combinatorics problem: given two non-negative integers (x, y), count number of paths under specific step constraints using combinations modulo 1e9+7. Original code precomputes up to 1e6 unconditionally, suggesting n (max coordinate or effective steps) is up to about 1e6.

dominant_ops: Precomputing modular inverses up to a fixed bound (1e6) using repeated list concatenation in a loop.
Factorial product loops up to O((x + y) / 3) to compute n! modulo 1e9+7.
A second, smaller but similar precomputation of modular inverses for var_12.

complexity.why: Let M be the fixed precomputation bound (var_1 = 1_000_000) and N ≈ (x + y) / 3. In the slow code, var_7 is constructed via `var_7 += [value]` inside a loop from 2 to M (and again up to var_12+1). Each `+= [value]` creates a new list and copies all existing elements, so building a list of length M this way is Θ(1 + 2 + ... + M) = Θ(M^2) operations, not Θ(M). The factorial products and the second inverse-precomputation loops are linear in their ranges (O(N)), but are dominated by the quadratic cost of repeated list concatenation. Memory holds arrays up to size M, hence O(M) space.

bottlenecks.detail: Using `var_7 += [expr]` in a loop from 2 to var_1 (1e6) causes list reallocation and copying on every iteration, leading to quadratic time and heavy allocator pressure.
Precomputation is done up to a fixed upper bound of 1e6 regardless of the actual input sizes; when x and y are much smaller, this wastes time and memory.
The code recomputes modular inverses in a second array-building loop for var_12, instead of reusing a single global precomputation.
Multiple passes over ranges with Python big integers and modular arithmetic (factorial loops and inverse loops) add significant constant factor overhead on top of the already high asymptotic cost.

FastAudit.core_idea: Precompute factorials and modular inverse factorials up to the maximum needed index using a single linear-time pass over preallocated arrays, then answer the combinatorial query with an O(1) binomial coefficient function. Avoid repeated list reallocation by indexing into fixed-size lists and limit precomputation size to max(x, y), which is enough because the combination parameter n = (x + y) / 3 is always strictly less than max(x, y) for positive coordinates under the problem constraints.

complexity.why: Let N = max(x, y). The optimized code allocates lists var_4, var_5, var_7 of length N and fills them once in func_2 using simple recurrences: var_4[i] = var_4[i-1] * i mod MOD (factorial), var_7[i] = MOD - var_7[MOD % i] * (MOD // i) mod MOD (modular inverse), and var_5[i] = var_5[i-1] * var_7[i] mod MOD (inverse factorial). Each index i in [0, N-1] is visited a constant number of times, so precomputation is Θ(N). The final answer is computed by a single call to func_1, which performs O(1) modular multiplications to evaluate C(n, k). Memory usage is linear in N for the three arrays.

complexity_delta.from: Approximately O(M^2 + N) time and O(M) space, where M is the fixed precomputation bound (1e6) and N ≈ (x + y) / 3. Dominated by quadratic behavior from repeated list concatenation.
complexity_delta.to: O(N) time and O(N) space, where N = max(x, y). Linear precomputation with O(1) query using preallocated arrays.
complexity_delta.note: The key improvement is replacing quadratic list-building with linear-time preallocation and indexed updates, and reducing the precomputation size from a fixed 1e6 to the minimum necessary derived from the actual inputs.

transformation_steps: Replace `var_7 += [expr]` (which reallocates and copies the list every iteration) with preallocated lists `var_4`, `var_5`, `var_7` and simple indexed assignment inside the loop (e.g., `var_4[i] = ...`).
Limit the precomputation size to `max(var_2, var_3)` instead of an unconditional constant 1e6, leveraging the problem structure that n = (x + y) / 3 is always < max(x, y) when a solution exists.

Compute factorials and modular inverse factorials in a single pass using the standard linear-time recurrence for modular inverses: `inv[i] = MOD - inv[MOD % i] * (MOD // i) % MOD`, and accumulate inverse factorials with `inv_fact[i] = inv_fact[i-1] * inv[i] % MOD`.

Abstract the binomial coefficient into a helper function `func_1(n, k)` that uses precomputed factorial and inverse factorial tables to compute C(n, k) in O(1), instead of recomputing factorials or inverses for each use.
Remove the second redundant inverse-precomputation loop by relying entirely on the single global precomputation (func_2) for all needed factorial and inverse values.

Preserve and centralize the early-invalid checks on (x + y) % 3 and the linear constraints between coordinates, so the expensive precomputation is only used when the combinatorial parameters are valid.
trigger_signals: Use of `list += [value]` or `list = list + [value]` inside a large loop with bounds on the order of 1e6, indicating hidden quadratic behavior.
A fixed precomputation upper bound (e.g., var_1 = 1000000) that does not depend on the actual input size, suggesting avoidable work on small inputs.
Multiple similar precomputation loops for modular inverses or factorial-like arrays, hinting at redundant computation and missed opportunities for reuse.
Heavy loops performing Python big-integer modular arithmetic in pure Python, where any unnecessary repetition strongly impacts runtime.
Recomputing structures that can be expressed as simple recurrences (like factorials and modular inverses) without leveraging their incremental nature.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors in precomputation ranges: when switching from building lists via append/concatenation to indexed assignment on preallocated arrays, it is essential to ensure that the loop bounds and array sizes cover every index that will be used in binomial calculations (here, ensuring factorials and inverse factorials are computed at least up to n = (x + y) / 3 and k).

Index coupling between problem parameters and precomputation size: the optimization relies on the fact that n = (x + y) / 3 is strictly less than max(x, y) under valid problem constraints; if the formula or constraints change in a variant problem, those inequalities must be re-verified or the precomputation bound adjusted.

Correctness of the modular inverse recurrence: the formula `inv[i] = MOD - inv[MOD % i] * (MOD // i) % MOD` is only valid when MOD is prime and i is not divisible by MOD; changing the modulus or allowing gcd(i, MOD) > 1 would break this approach.

Sign and boundary checks in the combination function: func_1 guards against negative or inconsistent (n, k) values; omitting such checks or changing the derivation of n and k without updating the guards can lead to index errors or wrong answers.

Memory usage scaling: although the optimized version is linear, allocating three arrays of length N can still be heavy if constraints are increased substantially (e.g., N ≫ 10^6); in such cases, further techniques (like on-demand precomputation or more compact structures) may be needed.

constraints_guess.notes: Two integers (n,k). Typical AtCoder-style bounds: n up to about 1e5, k up to about 1e9. Single computation, no multiple queries.

dominant_ops: For each starting value i in [1..n], repeatedly double i until it reaches at least k (counting doublings), then add (1/n) * (1/2)^{doublings} using np.power.

complexity.why: Outer loop over n starting values; inner while loop doubles the current value until it reaches k. Each doubling multiplies by 2, so the number of iterations per i is O(log(k/i)) ⊆ O(log K). No extra data structures of size proportional to input are used.

bottlenecks.detail: np.power is called on scalar arguments inside the innermost loop. Importing NumPy and doing Python-to-NumPy boundary crossings for simple scalar exponentiation significantly increases constant factors.
Nested while loops perform repeated multiplications and comparisons for each i rather than using a direct formula like ceil(log2(k/i)), keeping the cost per element at O(log K).
Importing NumPy for a small, tight computation is unnecessary and slow in typical competitive-programming environments.

FastAudit.core_idea: Eliminate NumPy and perform the same expected-value computation using only Python built-ins. The code still simulates, for each starting value, how many times it must be doubled to reach at least k, but uses (0.5) ** steps instead of np.power and avoids the heavy NumPy import.

complexity.why: It retains the same algorithmic structure: for each of the n starting values, it runs a while loop that doubles up to O(log K) times. Only constant-factor changes were made (no extra data structures).

complexity_delta.from: O(n log K)
complexity_delta.to: O(n log K)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time and space complexities are unchanged, but removing NumPy and using plain Python exponentiation reduces overhead in the tight loop.

transformation_steps: Removed the NumPy import and replaced np.power(1 / 2, var_5) with the built-in exponentiation operator (0.5) ** var_1.

Reordered the iteration over starting values: first handled the case i = n explicitly, then iterated over the remaining starting values by computing n - offset. This preserves behavior but does not change asymptotics.
Maintained the same probability formula (1/n) * (1/2)^{steps} while restructuring variable names and loop ordering.
Kept all state local and scalar, avoiding any external library calls in the hot path.
trigger_signals: Use of np.power for scalar exponentiation inside a deeply nested or frequently executed loop.
Importing a heavy numerical library (NumPy) in a competitive-programming style problem where I/O and simple arithmetic dominate.
Observed pattern of repeated exponentiation by 1/2 with small integer exponents, which is efficiently handled by Python's built-in exponentiation.
No need for vectorized operations or large arrays, making NumPy unjustified overhead.
pitfalls: Both versions remain O(n log K); for very large n and k this may still be slow, and a more mathematical/log-based approach could be required for further optimization.

Floating-point accumulation over many terms can introduce small rounding errors; changes in evaluation order or exponentiation method might slightly alter the final printed value at the least significant digits.
The modified code uses more indirection in indices (e.g., n - offset). When refactoring like this, off-by-one mistakes or misordered ranges are easy to introduce.
Variable names are opaque (var_1, var_2, etc.); when reworking loops, this can make reasoning about correctness harder and increase risk of subtle bugs.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic beginner problem: N people, M item types, each person lists liked items; count items liked by everyone. Typical constraints N,M <= 30–100, total input size small.

dominant_ops: Building a flat list of all liked items across all people (append per item).
Counting frequencies of all items with collections.Counter over the flat list.
Calling Counter.most_common(), which sorts all distinct items by frequency.

complexity.why: Let K be total number of item occurrences (sum of all k_i per person) and U the number of distinct items. Building var_7 costs O(K). Counter(var_7) is O(K). most_common() sorts all U keys by frequency, which is O(U log U). The list var_7 stores K entries and Counter stores up to U keys.

bottlenecks.detail: Counter.most_common() sorts all distinct items, but the task only needs to count those whose frequency == N. A single pass over the counts would suffice without sorting.
All item occurrences are stored in a single flat list var_7 before counting. This duplicates information that could be aggregated incrementally or via per-person sets.
The code first flattens data then re-groups by counting. Using set intersection or direct counting keyed by item while reading would avoid some intermediate structure.

FastAudit.core_idea: Model each person’s liked items as a set and compute the intersection of all these sets. The size of the intersection is exactly the number of items liked by everyone, avoiding both a global flat list and sorting by frequency.

complexity.time: O(K) on average, O(N * M) in the worst case
complexity.space: O(K) total for all sets, typically O(N * M) in worst case, O(M) live working set for intersections
complexity.why: Building each person’s set from their k_i items costs O(K) overall. Intersecting N sets of size at most M is O(N * M) in the worst case, but intersections quickly shrink when there are few common items, making it close to linear in practice. No O(U log U) sort is performed.

complexity_delta.from: O(K + U log U) time, O(K + U) space using a flat list and Counter.most_common().
complexity_delta.to: O(K)–O(N * M) time without an O(U log U) sorting step, O(K) space using set intersections.
complexity_delta.note: The primary improvement is the removal of the O(U log U) sort from Counter.most_common(), replacing it with direct set intersections that better match the problem semantics. As U grows, this avoids an unnecessary log U factor.

transformation_steps: Stop accumulating all items into a single flat list; instead, read each person’s list into a set immediately.
Replace global frequency counting via Counter with logical intersection of all per-person sets to directly obtain items present in every person’s list.
Remove the use of Counter.most_common(), avoiding the full sort of all distinct items by frequency.
Return the size of the final intersection set as the answer, matching the count of universally liked items.
trigger_signals: Use of Counter.most_common() when only a simple frequency criterion (count == N) is needed.
Pattern of building a large temporary flat list of all items before any aggregation.
Problem semantics that naturally map to set intersection (elements common to all groups).
Small per-person lists but potentially many distinct items, making a global sort wasteful.
pitfalls: In the modified code, input().split()[0] is called inside the list comprehension header, consuming the first line separately from the main loop; this is easy to misread and can be brittle if input format changes.
The sets are built from strings (input tokens) rather than ints; this is correct for equality/intersection but might surprise readers expecting numeric types.
Using functools.reduce with '&' requires N >= 1; if N could be 0, reduce would raise a TypeError without an initializer.

Set intersection order can affect constant factors; intersecting large sets with much smaller ones first is typically faster, though here all sets are built and intersected in a simple left-to-right order.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical Lunlun-number BFS problem (e.g., AtCoder-style). Input is a single integer N; performance-sensitive around N up to 1e5–1e6 due to large BFS frontier.

dominant_ops: queue.Queue.get() and queue.Queue.put() for each generated number
Integer arithmetic per state: modulo, multiplication, addition
Python loop overhead across ~N iterations

complexity.why: The BFS pops one number per iteration for N-1 iterations, generating up to 3 children each time. Each queue get/put is amortized O(1), so overall O(N) operations with a queue that can hold O(N) numbers in the worst case.

bottlenecks.detail: queue.Queue is a thread-safe, locking queue designed for multi-threading. In single-threaded competitive programming code, its locking and synchronization overhead makes each get/put significantly slower than a deque-based queue.

Four queue operations (1 get + up to 3 puts) per iteration with a heavy object (queue.Queue) dominate runtime. With N up to about 1e5–1e6, this overhead is enough to cause TLE or borderline performance.
Thread-safety and internal condition variables in queue.Queue are never used here but are paid for on every operation.
Use of eval(input()) instead of int(input()) is slightly slower and unsafe, though not the main performance issue.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace the heavy, thread-safe queue.Queue with collections.deque to get lightweight O(1) append/popleft operations, and avoid unbounded queue growth by only enqueuing children while the queue length is below N.

complexity.why: The algorithm still processes one element per loop for N-1 iterations. Each step performs one popleft() and up to three append() calls on a deque, all O(1). The len(var_5) < var_2 check caps growth of the queue to O(N), preserving linear time and space while reducing constants.

complexity_delta.from: O(N) time, O(N) space with high constant factors due to queue.Queue locking and heavier operations.
complexity_delta.to: O(N) time, O(N) space with much smaller constants using collections.deque and bounded queue growth.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged but the runtime becomes practical for large N; the queue-length guard may also slightly reduce the total number of generated states.

transformation_steps: Replace queue.Queue() with collections.deque() to avoid thread-safety overhead.
Initialize the BFS queue directly with deque([1..9]) instead of multiple put() calls in a loop.
Use popleft() instead of get() and append() instead of put() for queue operations.
Introduce a guard condition if len(var_5) < var_2: before enqueuing children to limit queue growth.
Maintain the same BFS pattern of generating neighbors by looking at the last digit and appending numbers with last_digit-1, last_digit, last_digit+1 when valid.
trigger_signals: Single-threaded contest environment using queue.Queue, which is known to be slow.
Profiling or intuition shows the majority of time spent in queue.put/get rather than arithmetic.
TLE or near-timeout behavior despite nominal O(N) complexity.
Large N (e.g., >= 1e5) where Python’s per-operation overhead becomes critical.
pitfalls: Behavioral change risk: The condition if len(var_5) < var_2: alters which nodes are enqueued compared to the original, which enqueues all possible children. For some problem settings, this pruning may change the logical result if not carefully justified.
Correctness must be re-verified: For Lunlun-like problems, limiting the queue size to N is typically safe, but this depends on the fact that we only need the first N numbers in BFS order.
Still uses eval(input()): This is unsafe for untrusted input and slightly slower than int(input()); for production or contest code, int(input()) is preferred.
Assuming deque length checks are O(1): They are for collections.deque, but this assumption is important when reasoning about complexity.
Memory behavior: Even though space is O(N), large N may still hit memory limits; pruning helps but does not change the asymptotic bound.

constraints_guess.notes: Input is the index (1-based) of a number in a special sequence of integers where adjacent decimal digits differ by at most 1 (often called Lunlun numbers). Code bounds maximum length to 10 digits, so the total pre-generated sequence size is about 9 * (3^10 - 1) / 2 ≈ 2.6e5.

dominant_ops: Recursive DFS over all valid digit-strings for each target length var_5 in [1,10]
For each recursive step, loop over all 10 candidate digits and filter using abs difference
Appending all generated numbers into a list and sorting it at the end

complexity.time: O(10 * 9 * 3^9) ≈ O(3^10) with a large constant from 10-way digit loops and repeated DFS per target length
complexity.space: O(M) where M is the total count of generated numbers (≈ 2.6e5)
complexity.why: The DFS enumerates all digit strings of length up to 10 that satisfy |adjacent digits difference| <= 1. For each final length L (var_5), it performs a fresh DFS from depth 1 to L, exploring a ternary-like branching (at most 3 valid next digits) at each level. There are about 9 * 3^{L-1} numbers of length L, and summing L from 1 to 10 yields Θ(3^10) nodes. At each node, the inner loop still iterates over all 10 digits and filters, and the outer var_4 loop repeats DFS work for each length.

bottlenecks.detail: Inside func_2, the code iterates var_7 in range(10) and rejects most digits with an abs((var_8 % 10) - var_7) >= 2 check. Only up to 3 digits are ever valid, so this wastes roughly a factor of ~3–4 in the inner loop.

The outer loop for var_4 in range(1, 11) runs a separate DFS for each target length var_5. Prefix paths of length k are recomputed for every larger length, rather than reusing them in a single DFS that naturally visits all depths.
setrecursionlimit(10**6) and nested function definition add small but non-zero overhead; recursion depth never exceeds 10, so the high recursion limit and repeated import sys are unnecessary.

FastAudit.core_idea: Perform a single DFS that grows numbers from 1 to 10 digits, but at each step only consider the at most 3 valid next digits (last_digit-1, last_digit, last_digit+1). Append the current number at every recursion depth, so all lengths are covered in one traversal. This reuses prefixes across all lengths and removes the inefficient 10-digit scan.

complexity.time: O(9 * 3^9) ≈ O(3^10) but with a much smaller constant factor due to 3-way branching instead of scanning 10 digits and no repeated DFS per length
complexity.space: O(M) where M is the number of generated numbers (≈ 2.6e5), plus recursion stack O(10)
complexity.why: Starting from each initial digit 1..9, the DFS branches only to neighbors (last_digit-1, last_digit, last_digit+1) that remain in [0,9], giving at most 3 children per node. It continues to depth 10 exactly once, collecting all prefixes along the way. The total size of the visited search tree is sum_{k=1}^{10} 9 * 3^{k-1} = Θ(3^10), with minimal constant factors.

complexity_delta.from: O(3^10) DFS over valid numbers, but implemented with 10-digit scans per node and repeated DFS per target length
complexity_delta.to: O(3^10) DFS with direct 3-way branching and a single traversal covering all lengths
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity class (in terms of maximum digit length) remains exponential, but the constant factor improves substantially by removing wasteful candidate scans and redundant recomputation.

transformation_steps: Replace 10-way digit scanning with bounded neighbor-based generation: instead of looping var_7 in range(10) and filtering by abs difference, loop var_3 in (-1, 0, 1) and compute var_7 = last_digit + var_3 with bounds check 0 <= var_7 <= 9.

Unify per-length DFS runs into a single DFS: rather than looping var_4 (target length) and running a fresh recursion for each, use one recursive function that continues until depth 10 and records numbers at every depth.
Simplify recursion interface: pass the current depth and current value only, with a shared list for results; remove the inner closure and per-call definition overhead.
Drop unnecessary configuration: remove sys.setrecursionlimit(10**6) and inline input reading once at the top-level since the maximum recursion depth is fixed and small.
Maintain global result list and sort once: generate all valid numbers into var_1, sort it once at the end, and index the (var_4 - 1)-th element.
trigger_signals: Inner loop scanning all 10 digits on every recursive step while the condition effectively restricts choices to at most 3.
Outer loop over target lengths that repeatedly recomputes similar recursion paths.
Low maximum depth (<=10) indicating that recursion itself is not the main cost; instead, per-node work and recomputation dominate.
Performance symptoms when N is moderately large (e.g., 1e5), where naive enumeration with excessive constant factors becomes slow in Python.
pitfalls: Changing the branching logic incorrectly (e.g., using last_digit ± 1 only and missing the 'same digit' case) would generate a different sequence than intended.
Removing the depth limit (var_2 == 10 condition) would cause the DFS to grow numbers indefinitely and never terminate for large N.
Relying on sorted order of generation: the DFS does not inherently guarantee numeric order; explicit sort is still required before indexing.
If constraints changed to allow much longer lengths, even the optimized DFS would become infeasible due to exponential growth, requiring a more incremental or queue-based generation approach.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case, exactly three integers read from stdin. Likely competitive programming (AtCoder-style) with values up to about 10^9–10^18, but input size is constant (3 numbers).

dominant_ops: Importing NumPy at runtime
Creating a NumPy array for just three integers
Repeated NumPy vector operations (mod 2, integer division) inside a Python while-loop
Python-NumPy boundary crossings for any()/all() each iteration

complexity.why: k is the number of iterations until at least one element becomes odd; in the worst case k ≈ floor(log2(max(a,b,c))). Each loop iteration performs constant-size NumPy vector ops and any()/all() checks, so time grows linearly with k. Input size is constant (three ints), so asymptotically it is O(1) in terms of input length, but practically dominated by O(k) loop cost and heavy NumPy overhead.

bottlenecks.detail: Importing NumPy for a problem that handles only three integers adds substantial startup and runtime overhead compared to pure Python.
Using a NumPy array and vectorized operations for just three scalars incurs more cost (array allocation, dtype handling, ufunc dispatch) than simple scalar arithmetic.
The while True loop performs var_2 % 2, any(), all(), and division on every iteration through Python↔NumPy calls; this dominates runtime when the numbers are divisible by many powers of two.
Each any(var_2 % 2) and all(var_2 % 2) triggers Python-level function calls and NumPy ufuncs on a tiny array, which is inefficient for such a small, fixed-size operation.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace iterative halving and parity checks with a closed-form bitwise computation on the three integers. Detect the special case (all equal and even) via (a-b)|(b-c) and combined parity, and otherwise compute the needed exponent using bit tricks and bit_length(), all in constant time without loops or external libraries.

complexity.why: Only a fixed number of integer arithmetic and bitwise operations plus one bit_length() call on scalar integers. No loops and no external library overhead; cost is constant regardless of the magnitude of the input values.

complexity_delta.from: O(k) time with high constant factors due to NumPy and Python↔NumPy crossings (k ≈ number of halvings until an odd appears); O(1) space.
complexity_delta.to: O(1) time with very small constant factors using pure integer bit operations; O(1) space.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically in terms of input count both versions are O(1), but the modified version incurs loop and NumPy overhead proportional to the number of halving steps, whereas the fast version is truly constant-time with only primitive operations.

transformation_steps: Remove NumPy entirely and operate directly on three scalar integers read via map(int, input().split()).
Recognize that (a-b)|(b-c) equals 0 iff a == b == c; this allows detecting the 'all equal' special case without loops.
Use (a|b|c) % 2 to detect whether any number is odd in constant time (LSB parity), instead of looping or vectorized modulo checks.
Combine the checks into bool(var_4 | (a|b|c) % 2) to distinguish the special infinite/equal-even case from all others in a single Boolean factor.

Use the bit trick (x ^ (x-1)).bit_length() - 1 (implemented as (var_4 ^ ~-var_4).bit_length() - 1) to compute the required exponent directly from the bit pattern of (a-b)|(b-c), eliminating the halving loop.
Return -1 via the Boolean multiplier being 0 when var_4 == 0 and all numbers are even, matching the original special-case behavior.
trigger_signals: Use of NumPy for extremely small (constant-size) inputs in a competitive programming context.
Presence of a Python while-loop whose body only applies simple arithmetic and parity tests that could be expressed via bit operations.
Pattern of repeated division by 2 / modulo 2 checks, which often indicates that a power-of-two or bit-position computation is possible.
Special casing of the 'all equal' scenario (returning -1), which suggests there may be a structural, closed-form characterization.
The problem domain being purely integer arithmetic with no need for high-level linear algebra, making NumPy suspicious from a performance standpoint.
pitfalls: The bitwise formulation is far less readable and maintainable; future modifications or debugging may be difficult without documenting the derivation of the bit trick.
Relying on subtle identities like ~-x == x-1 and properties of x ^ (x-1) requires careful reasoning; an incorrect manipulation can silently produce wrong answers.
Assuming two's complement behavior is safe in CPython for ints, but porting the trick to other languages or non-standard integer models may need reconsideration.

Edge cases such as negative inputs need to be clearly defined; bit_length() and bitwise ops on negative integers behave differently, so the formula assumes non-negative or suitably constrained inputs.
Micro-optimizations with bit magic can obscure the original mathematical intent, increasing the chance of logical errors if the problem statement or constraints change.

constraints_guess.notes: Single array optimization problem; brute-force over target integer t is used. Typical AtCoder-style constraints suggest n <= 100, element values up to ~100–200, making O(n * value_range) acceptable.

dominant_ops: Triple-nested looping over (value_range)^2 * n when searching for the minimizing integer t; repeated recomputation of the same sums within an unnecessary outer loop.

complexity.why: Let n = len(var_7), L = min(var_7), U = max(var_7), R = U - L + 1. Sorting costs O(n log n). The outer loop over var_4 runs R times but its index is never used. Inside each iteration, a first loop computes a sum over n elements, then an inner loop over t in [L+1, U-1] (~R) recomputes a sum over n elements. So per outer iteration: O(n + R * n) = O(R * n). Multiplied by R outer iterations gives O(R^2 * n). Space is just the array plus a few scalars → O(n).

bottlenecks.detail: Loop `for var_4 in range(var_7[0], var_7[len(var_7) - 1] + 1):` does not use var_4 at all, causing every computation inside to be repeated R times unnecessarily.
For each candidate t (var_2), the code recomputes `sum((t - a_i)^2)` from scratch over all n elements, and this entire scan is itself repeated in the redundant outer loop, leading to O(R^2 * n) work.

The first inner loop in each outer-iteration computes `sum((var_7[0] - var_7[i])**2)` into var_6 and assigns it to var_5, but this same value is identical on every outer pass and could have been computed once—or avoided entirely by merging logic.
Sorting the array O(n log n) is not needed for a brute-force scan over t if you only care about min and max or max; contributes small overhead relative to the inflated O(R^2 * n) term.

FastAudit.core_idea: Enumerate every candidate integer t in a single pass over [0, max(a)], and for each t compute the total squared distance to all elements. Track the minimum sum encountered. This removes the redundant outer loop and quadratic factor in the value range.

complexity.why: Let n = len(var_2), M = max(var_2). The outer loop runs over t indices `var_4` from 0 to M (M+1 iterations). For each t, the inner loop scans all n elements once to accumulate `sum((a_i - (t+1))^2)`, costing O(n). Total time is O((M+1) * n) = O(R * n) where R ≈ M. Space usage is O(n) for storing the array and O(1) extra for accumulators.

complexity_delta.from: O(R^2 * n + n log n)
complexity_delta.to: O(R * n)
complexity_delta.note: By eliminating a redundant outer loop that did not affect the calculations and by scanning the value range only once, the algorithm improves from quadratic to linear in the value range R (min-to-max).

transformation_steps: Recognize that the outer loop over var_4 in the slow code does not use var_4 and thus simply repeats the exact same inner computations R times.
Remove the redundant outer loop, keeping a single loop over candidate t values; conceptually, keep only what the fast code does: one loop over t, one loop over the array for each t.
Avoid repeated recalculation of the same initial sum `sum((var_7[0] - var_7[i])**2)` on every outer iteration by either computing it once or directly folding it into the main candidate enumeration.
Drop unnecessary sorting because the brute-force method in the fast code needs only max(a) (and optionally min(a)); retrieving max is O(n) without sorting.
Resulting structure: single outer loop over t (value range) and single inner loop over n elements, tracking a running minimum of the sum of squared differences.
trigger_signals: Presence of three nested loops where the innermost work depends only on the loop indices and array values, suggesting O(R^2 * n) behavior.
A loop variable (var_4) that is never used in its body, indicating redundant repetition of the same computation.
Recomputing `sum((constant - a_i)^2)` multiple times with the same constant instead of computing once.
Sorting the array even though the subsequent algorithm does not actually rely on order beyond min/max.
Comparing to the original/fast version reveals that the search over t only needs one pass over the value range, not two nested passes.
pitfalls: If the range of values (R = max(a) - min(a)) were very large (e.g., up to 1e9), even the fast O(R * n) brute force would be too slow; in that scenario, a mathematical solution using the mean and precomputed sums would be needed.
Using `eval(input())` for reading integers is unsafe and slower than `int(input())`; while not the main performance issue here, it is a bad practice.

The slow code’s arithmetic uses `(var_7[0] - var_7[var_1])**2`, which is logically wrong for exploring candidates t; fixing the logic while keeping the same nested-loop structure would still leave you with the O(R^2 * n) performance problem.
Relying on sort just to get min and max is unnecessary overhead; for larger n, always prefer single-pass min/max unless sorted order is required for another reason.

constraints_guess.notes: Single pair of integers (var_2, var_3), each likely up to around 1e6–1e7 based on linear loops; must be small enough that O(min(x,y)) is acceptable.

dominant_ops: Two linear loops building numerator and denominator of a binomial coefficient, plus a custom recursive modular exponentiation for modular inverse.

complexity.why: Let k = var_13 = one of the move counts (roughly O((var_2+var_3)/3)). The code performs two for-loops each running k iterations: one for the numerator product and one for the denominator product, giving O(k). Modular inverse is computed with a custom recursive binary exponentiation func_2(var_4, var_1-2), which takes O(log MOD) time and O(log MOD) call stack space.

bottlenecks.detail: Computes C(var_11+var_13, var_13) via two separate loops over the same range, instead of a single loop that accumulates numerator and denominator simultaneously.
Uses a Python-level recursive fast exponentiation (func_2) instead of the built-in pow(base, exp, mod). Built-in pow is implemented in C and significantly faster with less overhead.
Recursive exponentiation introduces Python function call overhead and non-zero recursion depth, which is unnecessary given pow(var_4, var_1-2, var_1) is available and iterative under the hood.
Uses exponentiation operator (**2) inside recursion instead of simple multiplication; this has slightly higher overhead than a direct a*b multiply in tight loops.

FastAudit.core_idea: Reduce the number of Python-level operations by (1) computing numerator and denominator for the binomial coefficient in a single linear loop and (2) using the built-in pow(base, exp, mod) for modular inverse instead of a custom recursive exponentiation.

complexity.why: Let k = min(var_10, var_5 - var_10) = min(number of each move type). The function func_1(var_10, var_12) performs a single loop from 1 to var_12 inclusive, doing constant work per iteration to accumulate numerator and denominator, so O(k). The modular inverse is computed with pow(var_13, var_9 - 2, var_9), whose complexity is O(log MOD) in C, but with very small constant factors and no Python recursion; space is O(1) from Python’s perspective.

complexity_delta.from: O(k + log MOD) time, O(log MOD) space (due to recursion)
complexity_delta.to: O(k + log MOD) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time complexity in terms of k (move count) is the same, but the optimized code reduces constants (fewer loops, C-implemented pow) and removes recursion, which materially improves performance in Python for large k.

transformation_steps: Reformulated the combinatorial computation to iterate only once over the relevant range, accumulating both the numerator and denominator products in the same loop instead of two loops over the same size.
Replaced the custom recursive fast exponentiation (func_2) with Python’s built-in pow(base, exp, mod) to compute modular inverses using Fermat’s little theorem.
Adjusted variables so that the loop length is effectively min(n1, n2) where n1 and n2 are the counts of each move type, minimizing the linear factor in the binomial computation.
Kept all arithmetic under modulo during accumulation, avoiding large intermediate integers and keeping operations fast.
trigger_signals: Presence of a custom recursive binary exponentiation while using a fixed prime modulus (1e9+7), which suggests replacing with pow(base, exp, mod).

Two separate loops computing numerator and denominator for what is effectively a binomial coefficient C(n, k), indicating an opportunity to streamline into a single loop or use a well-known combinatorial identity.
Recursion depth proportional to log exponent for a primitive integer operation (modular exponentiation) in performance-sensitive code.
Integer loops directly dependent on input magnitude (var_13) without clear minimization to min(k, n-k).
pitfalls: Incorrectly changing pow(var_13, var_9 - 2, var_9) to pow(var_13, var_9 - 2) (omitting the modulus) would produce enormous intermediate integers and drastically degrade performance or memory usage.
Attempting to precompute factorials and inverses up to max(var_2, var_3) without checking constraints may result in excessive memory use if the inputs are large.
Rewriting the modular inverse logic without Fermat’s little theorem (e.g., using extended Euclidean algorithm incorrectly under a prime modulus) could lead to wrong answers or slower performance.

If recursion is retained and exponent accidentally becomes dependent on input size (e.g., O(k) instead of O(log MOD)), recursion depth could exceed Python’s recursion limit and crash, or dramatically slow down.

Changing the binomial coefficient logic without preserving the constraints checks ((var_2 + var_3) % 3 != 0 or negative move counts) can lead to off-by-one errors or negative loop bounds, causing incorrect counts or runtime errors.

constraints_guess.n_max: 1e5 (order of 10^5; N is the index of the lunlun number)
constraints_guess.notes: Classic 'lunlun numbers' task (adjacent digits differ by at most 1), equivalent to AtCoder-style problem where N up to about 10^5 and answers fit in < 10^10, so depth 10 is enough.

dominant_ops: Recursive DFS (func_1) generating all valid numbers up to fixed depth for each starting digit
Repeated list append into global list var_1
Final full sort of var_1 (var_1.sort())
Single random-access indexing var_1[var_4 - 1]

complexity.time: O(M log M), where M is the total count of generated lunlun numbers up to depth 10 (independent of N but potentially much larger than N).
complexity.why: func_1 performs a DFS over all digit-strings of length ≤ 10 that satisfy the lunlun condition, appending each to var_1. This is O(M) work (with small constant depth). After that, var_1.sort() costs O(M log M). N only affects which index we read in the already-built array; it does not limit enumeration.

bottlenecks.detail: The DFS generates all lunlun numbers up to length 10 regardless of the requested index N (var_4). For small N this does far more work than necessary.
The algorithm sorts the entire list var_1 even though it only needs the N-th smallest value, adding an O(M log M) term that can dominate for larger M.

Python recursion for each generated number (func_1 calls itself at each level) adds function-call overhead compared to an iterative approach; while depth is capped at 10, the call count equals the number of nodes in the search tree.
All lunlun numbers up to depth 10 are stored at once in var_1, instead of generating only the first N and discarding the rest.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a BFS-like incremental construction where var_4 acts as a queue: start from 1..9, repeatedly expand the next number by appending allowed neighbor digits (last_digit-1, last_digit, last_digit+1), and stop as soon as we have generated N numbers. The BFS order coincides with increasing numeric order, so no sorting is needed.

complexity.time: O(N * D), where D is the number of digits of the N-th lunlun number (D is small, ≤ 10 in typical constraints). Effectively O(N).
complexity.why: Each loop iteration consumes one existing number (at index var_3) and appends up to 3 new ones. We run the loop until len(var_4) == N, so the number of processed/generated nodes is O(N). Extracting the last digit via string conversion is O(D) per iteration, with D bounded. The list keeps at most O(N) numbers.

complexity_delta.from: O(M log M) time, O(M) space (M = total lunlun numbers up to max depth, independent of N).
complexity_delta.to: O(N * D) ≈ O(N) time, O(N) space, where N is the requested index and D is small (≤ 10).
complexity_delta.note: The optimized version scales linearly with the requested index N and avoids full-space enumeration and sorting. For cases where N << M, this is a significant improvement.

transformation_steps: Switch enumeration order from DFS + global collection to iterative BFS using a growing list (var_4) as an implicit queue.
Exploit the BFS property that generated numbers naturally appear in increasing numeric order (by length, then lexicographically), removing the need for var_1.sort().
Introduce an early-stopping condition: terminate generation once len(var_4) reaches N, instead of exploring all numbers up to a fixed maximal depth independent of N.
Replace recursive function calls with an iterative while-loop over indices (var_3), eliminating recursion overhead and stack management.
Access only the needed result directly from the BFS-generated list (var_4[var_1 - 1]) without any additional processing.
trigger_signals: Presence of a full sort (list.sort()) on a large generated search space when only the k-th element is needed.
Generation of all solutions up to a fixed size limit before considering the input N, rather than generating on-demand.
Deep or wide recursion (DFS) where an iterative queue/level-order traversal (BFS) could naturally produce results in the desired order.
Large global list accumulating all candidates without early pruning or stopping criteria tied to N.
pitfalls: While the BFS version is faster asymptotically, it still uses string conversion to get the last digit (str(var_4[var_3])[-1:]); for larger N or tighter time limits, switching to arithmetic (x % 10) would reduce constant factors.

Both approaches rely on the fact that the first N lunlun numbers fit within the chosen digit limit (10 digits in the slow DFS code, implicit via growth in the BFS code); if constraints changed and N required more digits, the DFS depth limit or assumptions might need adjustment.
If one attempted to generalize the slow DFS approach by increasing maximum depth to support larger N, the M in O(M log M) could grow explosively, leading to time and memory issues.
Using eval(input()) is unsafe in general and should be replaced by int(input()) in production or contested environments, though this does not affect algorithmic complexity.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic 'pairwise/setwise/not coprime' problem (e.g., AtCoder-style). Typical constraints: N up to ~1e5, each A_i up to 1e6; frequency array sized to 1e6+1 supports this.

dominant_ops: Building frequency array var_7 up to U = 10^6+2
Double loop over var_5 in [2..U) and slice var_7[var_5::var_5] to sum counts of multiples (sieve-like pass)
Final linear pass computing gcd across all input numbers

complexity.time: O(U log U + N log A_max)
complexity.why: The inner pattern 'for var_5 in range(2, U): for var_4 in var_7[var_5::var_5]' effectively visits indices ~U/2 + U/3 + ... ≈ U log U times (harmonic series). Each visit is O(1). The gcd accumulation is O(N log A_max), but N is at most 1e5 while U is 1e6, so the sieve-like traversal dominates. Space is dominated by the frequency array var_7 of size ~U.

bottlenecks.detail: The loop over var_5 from 2 to var_1 never breaks early. Even when a shared divisor is found (var_3 > 1), the code only flips var_8 = False and continues scanning all remaining divisors, doing all O(U log U) work regardless of input.
var_1 is set to 10**6 + 2 while max A_i is effectively up to 10**6; the extra entries are unused overhead (minor but unnecessary).
Using var_7[var_5::var_5] creates an implicit stride-based view that still causes Python-level iteration over many elements; combined with the full-scan behavior this amplifies constant factors.

FastAudit.core_idea: Introduce early termination in the sieve-like loop: as soon as any divisor var_5 divides at least two numbers (var_3 > 1), break out and proceed directly to the setwise-coprime gcd check. Use a for-else construct so that if no such divisor is found (no break), the numbers are classified immediately as 'pairwise coprime'. Also tighten the upper bound of the frequency array to 10**6 + 1.

complexity.time: Worst case: O(U log U + N log A_max). Best/average case: often much less due to early exit when a small prime divides multiple numbers.
complexity.why: The structure of the loops is unchanged at a worst-case level: we may still inspect ∑_{k=1..U} U/k = O(U log U) multiples if the array is pairwise coprime (no early break). However, on typical inputs where many numbers share small prime factors, the loop breaks after examining only a small prefix of divisors (e.g., var_5 = 2 or 3), substantially reducing the practical running time. Space remains dominated by the frequency array.

delta_type: early-termination optimization with minor array bound adjustment

complexity_delta.from: Always performs a full sieve-style scan over all divisors up to U (≈10^6), regardless of when a shared divisor is detected: Θ(U log U + N log A_max) for every input.
complexity_delta.to: Retains Θ(U log U + N log A_max) in the worst case (pairwise coprime inputs) but in many cases stops after the first shared divisor is found, typically at a small var_5, reducing actual runtime substantially while keeping asymptotic bounds unchanged.
complexity_delta.note: This is an improvement in best-case and average-case behavior rather than asymptotic worst-case; for competitive programming constraints this difference is often enough to avoid TLE on adversarial or dense-input distributions.

transformation_steps: Replace the boolean flag pattern (var_8 initialized to True, possibly set to False inside the divisor loop) with a for-else + break pattern to support immediate exit from the heavy loop upon detecting var_3 > 1.
Move the 'pairwise coprime' return into the for-else clause: if the divisor loop completes without a break, return 'pairwise coprime' directly, eliminating the need for a separate flag check.
Ensure that when a break occurs (i.e., not pairwise coprime), control naturally falls through to the gcd accumulation loop used to decide between 'setwise coprime' and 'not coprime'.
Tighten var_1 from 10**6 + 2 to 10**6 + 1 to better match the maximum possible value of input elements and avoid one extra unused frequency slot.
trigger_signals: Profiling or timing reveals that the vast majority of runtime is spent inside the nested divisor-multiples loops, even on inputs where pairwise coprimality clearly fails early (e.g., many even numbers).
Code inspection shows a loop that detects a terminating condition (var_3 > 1) but merely sets a flag and continues scanning through all remaining candidates.
Observed TLE or borderline performance on large inputs with many shared small factors, indicating that the algorithm is not exploiting early knowledge that pairwise coprimality has already failed.
Static reasoning that the decision 'pairwise vs not pairwise coprime' does not require complete information about all divisors once a single violating divisor is found.
pitfalls: Misusing the for-else construct: the 'else' clause executes only if the loop terminates without a 'break'. Placing the 'pairwise coprime' return incorrectly (e.g., inside the loop body rather than in 'else') would change semantics.

Forgetting to keep the gcd phase reachable after a 'break': if gcd computation were incorrectly placed inside the 'else' or inside the loop, the classification between 'setwise coprime' and 'not coprime' would be wrong.

Off-by-one errors when adjusting var_1: the frequency array must be at least max(A) + 1 in length; setting var_1 too small would raise index errors or silently miss some values, while excessively large values waste memory and time.

Assuming asymptotic improvement where there is only average-case improvement: the worst-case time complexity remains O(U log U), so for inputs specifically constructed to be pairwise coprime, performance will still hit the upper bound.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic AtCoder pattern: count shortest-path lengths between all pairs on a line graph of size N with one extra edge between nodes X and Y. N≈2e3 inferred from known task (ABC160 D / Line++). No separate queries; all-pairs over indices 0..N-1.

dominant_ops: For each start node, a full BFS over the line-plus-one-edge graph (deque popleft/append operations).
Re-initializing distance array of size N with float('inf') for every BFS.
Inner while-loop performing many repeated comparisons and min assignments for already-visited nodes.

complexity.why: There are N starting nodes (outer for var_4 in range(var_7)). For each start, BFS explores all N nodes in a constant-degree graph (line plus one extra edge), so O(N) per BFS. Total time O(N * N) = O(N^2). Space: distances var_3 is O(N); queue size is O(N); result array var_2 is O(N).

bottlenecks.detail: Per-node BFS (N times) on a graph with very special structure (a path plus one extra edge). This discards exploitable structure and incurs large constant factors from Python-level BFS.
var_3 = [float('inf')] * var_7 is executed N times, performing O(N^2) float writes and repeated allocations; significant overhead for Python.
In BFS loop, each pop checks if var_3[var_5] != float('inf') and performs min assignments even when already finalized, causing extra branches and work on every node visit.
Deque operations (popleft/append of tuples) are heavier than simple arithmetic; repeated for O(N^2) total operations.
