FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the graph’s structure (a line 0..N-1 with one extra edge between X and Y) to derive a closed-form expression for the shortest distance between any two nodes i<j. The distance is the minimum of: (1) the direct line distance |i-j|, and (2) the path using the special edge via X→Y or Y→X. Thus all pairwise distances can be computed by pure arithmetic in a double loop, eliminating BFS and heavy data structures.

complexity.why: There is a double loop over all unordered pairs (var_4, var_6) with var_4 < var_6. Number of iterations is N*(N-1)/2 = O(N^2). Each iteration performs O(1) arithmetic and a small constant number of abs/min operations. The result array var_3 has size N to count frequencies of each distance, so O(N) space. No per-start BFS or auxiliary per-start arrays are needed.

complexity_delta.from: O(n^2) time via N BFS runs over a size-N graph; heavy constant factors from deque operations, per-iteration branching, and repeated distance-array initialization.
complexity_delta.to: O(n^2) time via pure arithmetic over all pairs; very small constants and no BFS or re-allocation per start node.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time and space complexities remain O(n^2) and O(n), but runtime improves substantially in practice by replacing graph traversal with a closed-form distance computation.

transformation_steps: Model the graph explicitly as a path of nodes 0..N-1 plus a single extra edge between nodes X and Y (1-based in input, converted to 0-based).
For any pair of nodes (i, j), derive formulas for three candidate path lengths: direct line distance |i-j|; path using the special edge via i→X→Y→j; and path via i→Y→X→j.
Express the shortest distance as: min(|i-j|, |i-X|+1+|Y-j|, |i-Y|+1+|X-j|). Implement this as func_1.
Replace the BFS from each node with a double loop over all unordered pairs (i<j), computing func_1(i, j) in O(1) time per pair.
Accumulate counts of distances directly into a single result array indexed by distance; then output counts for distances 1..N-1.
trigger_signals: Presence of an outer loop over all start nodes combined with a full BFS for each start, suggesting an all-pairs shortest path approach on a highly structured graph.
The graph definition is extremely simple (line plus one extra edge), which is often amenable to a direct formula for distances rather than generic BFS.
N is modest (~2000) but the per-BFS overhead (deque, list initialization, Python branching) is still high, indicating room for constant-factor optimization.
Distance queries are only needed between all pairs of nodes on a one-dimensional index set, hinting at using absolute differences and simple arithmetic instead of graph traversal.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when converting from 1-based input indices (var_8, var_9 in fast code) to 0-based internal indices used in arithmetic.
Ensuring that only unordered pairs (i<j) are counted once; double-counting symmetric pairs or including i==j would distort the distance frequency counts.
Correctly including both possible uses of the special edge: i→X→Y→j and i→Y→X→j; omitting one path can overestimate some distances.
Maintaining consistency in distance indexing: distance 0 should not be counted in the output, so the result array needs size N and output should skip index 0.
Preserving integer operations: the formula uses abs and additions only; introducing floats or incorrect min logic could subtly change results for larger N.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical of AtCoder-style problems: N up to around 1e5 points, choose exactly M of them. Time limit ~1–2s in Python, so anything worse than ~O(N log N) or O(N * polylog N) is risky.

dominant_ops: Nested loops over selected count (M) and all points (N)
Repeated abs and arithmetic in Python inside tight loops
Greedy selection with O(N) scan per chosen element

complexity.why: For each of the M selections, the algorithm scans all N points (skipping already taken ones): inner loop over N inside outer loop over M, giving O(N*M). Storage is dominated by the list of N triples plus a few O(N) boolean/index arrays.

bottlenecks.detail: Core selection is a greedy incremental heuristic: for each of M iterations, it scans all N remaining points to find the best improvement, giving O(N*M) time. With N,M up to ~1e5, this is on the order of 1e10 operations and completely infeasible in Python.
The inner loop is Python-level with many abs() calls and list accesses per iteration; this exacerbates the already bad O(N*M) complexity.
The slow code attempts multiple heuristic passes (starting from points with largest |x|, |y|, |z|, etc.), which add more O(N*M) and O(N^2)-like work without changing the fundamental complexity class.

FastAudit.core_idea: Transform each 3D point (x,y,z) into scalar scores for all 4 essential sign combinations: (+x +y +z), (+x +y -z), (+x -y +z), (+x -y -z). For each sign pattern, sort these scores once, take the best M points (either largest or smallest depending on maximizing absolute value), and compute the objective. The maximum over these 4 patterns is the answer. This replaces per-element greedy selection with a one-shot sort per sign pattern.

complexity.why: Building 4 arrays of length N is O(N). Sorting each array is O(N log N), done 4 times: O(4 * N log N) = O(N log N). For each sign pattern, summing the top/bottom M elements is O(M), and M ≤ N, so total additional cost is O(4M) ⊆ O(N). Overall dominated by sorting: O(N log N). Space-wise, we store the N original triples and 4 arrays of length N, so O(N).

complexity_delta.from: O(N * M) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N log N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: Replaced incremental greedy selection (scanning all N points M times) with a sort-based strategy over fixed linear functionals (sign patterns) and a single pass per pattern.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the objective |sum x| + |sum y| + |sum z| can be represented as maximizing a linear functional for some choice of signs (sx, sy, sz) in {+1, -1}, up to a global sign flip.
Observe that it suffices to evaluate 4 distinct sign combinations ((+,+,+), (+,+,-), (+,-,+), (+,-,-)), since the remaining 4 are just global negations and give the same absolute-value objective.
For each point (x,y,z) and each of the 4 sign patterns, precompute a scalar score s = sx*x + sy*y + sz*z and store it in an array corresponding to that pattern.
For each of the 4 arrays, sort the scores once in O(N log N).
For each sorted array, compute the sum of the best M scores by taking either the largest M or the smallest M (since abs(sum) is used) and track the maximum absolute sum over all patterns.
Eliminate the O(N)-per-selection greedy inner loop and all repeated rescans; the new approach uses only one sort per pattern and linear passes, turning the quadratic-ish behavior into O(N log N).
trigger_signals: Nested loop where the outer loop runs up to M (~N) times and the inner loop runs over all N points: clear O(N*M) structure.
Constraints inferred to be around N up to 1e5, where O(N^2) is too slow.
Per-iteration recomputation of improvement scores using abs() and multiple array accesses in pure Python.
Greedy heuristic structure (pick best next point each time) for a combinatorial optimization problem, often a red flag when constraints are large.
Known competitive-programming pattern: maximize sum of absolute values of coordinate sums by enumerating sign patterns and sorting once.
pitfalls: Using the greedy O(N*M) selection and expecting it to pass when N and M are large; it may appear to work on small samples but will time out on full constraints.
Forgetting that only 4 distinct sign patterns are needed due to global sign symmetry; using all 8 is correct but doubles the constant factor (still acceptable in C++ but less ideal in Python).
Recomputing sums in an inefficient way (e.g., sorting every time a point is added, or repeatedly calling sum() on large slices inside performance-critical loops).
Incorrect handling of the M = 0 corner case; the fast code explicitly checks this and returns 0 immediately, while some naive refactors might overlook it.
Mixing heuristic local improvements with the sign-enumeration method; this can reintroduce O(N*M) behavior without improving optimality.
In languages without big integers, one must watch for overflow when summing up to 1e5 values, but Python’s unbounded ints avoid this issue.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case, input is two integers on one line; operations are purely arithmetic so constraints can be large (up to around 1e9) but count of operations remains constant.

dominant_ops: Heavy use of decimal.Decimal construction and arithmetic (var_1(...) calls) for simple integer operations: repeated Decimal() wrapping, modulo, multiplication, addition, and floor division.

complexity.why: The algorithm inspects only two input integers and performs a fixed number of arithmetic operations and condition checks. No loops or data structures that scale with input size; however, each operation is implemented via high-overhead Decimal objects, inflating constant factors.

bottlenecks.detail: Using decimal.Decimal (via from decimal import * and treating var_1 as Decimal) for all arithmetic on small integers. Decimal has much higher overhead than native int due to context management and arbitrary-precision semantics.
Deeply nested calls like var_1(var_1(var_7[0]) % 2) and var_1(var_1(var_1(var_7[0]) - 1) // 2) cause multiple redundant Decimal constructions and conversions for the same value.
Intermediates are recomputed instead of reused (e.g., multiple var_1(var_7[0]) calls instead of storing once), further increasing the number of Decimal operations.
from decimal import * pulls many names into the global namespace; var_1 is implicitly bound to Decimal, making the code obscure and harder for both humans and tools to reason about performance.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace all Decimal-based arithmetic and nested conversions with straightforward integer arithmetic on native ints, computing essentially ceil(var_1 * var_2 / 2) with a special-case for when either dimension is 1.

complexity.why: The improved solution still uses a constant number of operations on two input integers, but all operations are direct int additions, multiplications, modulo, and floor division. Python ints are highly optimized, so the constant factor is much smaller than when using Decimal.

complexity_delta.from: O(1) time, O(1) space with very high constant factors due to Decimal usage and redundant computations.
complexity_delta.to: O(1) time, O(1) space with low constant factors using native integer arithmetic and minimal operations.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged, but runtime is significantly reduced in practice because heavy Decimal overhead and duplicate work are removed.

transformation_steps: Eliminate dependency on decimal by removing from decimal import * and all uses of Decimal via var_1(...).
Read the two integers directly into simple variables (var_1, var_2) using map(int, input().split()) instead of building a list and then wrapping values in Decimal.

Replace nested Decimal operations and branching logic with a clear integer formula: handle the special case when either input equals 1, otherwise compute var_1 * var_2, then apply parity check to implement ceil(product / 2).
Remove redundant recomputation of intermediate values by computing the product once and reusing it for modulo and division.
Simplify the final output to directly print the computed integer (var_3) instead of converting from Decimal and performing unnecessary wrapping.
trigger_signals: Use of decimal.Decimal for what appears to be basic integer arithmetic with no high-precision requirements.
Nested and repeated calls to the Decimal constructor (var_1(...)) around every arithmetic operation, indicating avoidable conversion overhead.
Very small input size (constant, two integers) but potentially observed slow performance or unnecessary complexity in code review.
Obfuscated control flow and arithmetic expressions suggesting the original code may have been auto-generated or intentionally convoluted, making performance characteristics worse than necessary.
pitfalls: Ensuring semantic equivalence: the simplified formula uses integer operations; care must be taken to match the behavior for corner cases such as when either input is 1 (the fast code preserves this with an explicit if).
Avoiding integer overflow is generally not a concern in Python due to arbitrary-precision ints, but in other languages similar transformations must account for product overflow.

Misinterpreting the role of parity: the condition var_1 * var_2 % 2 != 0 encodes an odd product to decide between floor(product/2) and floor(product/2)+1; changing this logic incorrectly would break correctness.

Overlooking that removing Decimal changes numeric types: if the surrounding system depended on Decimal-specific behavior (e.g., quantization, context precision), direct int arithmetic would not be a drop-in replacement. In this competitive-programming-style problem, that dependency does not exist, so the change is safe.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: choose integer P to minimize sum_i (ai - P)^2. Inputs are N and N integers, each usually in [1,100]. Even if N is larger, both solutions are linear in N up to a constant factor.

dominant_ops: Double loop over candidate P in [1,100] and all N elements, computing abs() and square for each pair, plus a min() reduction over candidates.

complexity.why: The outer loop runs over 100 candidate target values (1..100), and the inner loop scans all N elements to accumulate squared differences. This leads to 100 * N cost evaluations. Storing the N input values costs O(N) space; only O(1) extra space is used for accumulators.

bottlenecks.detail: The algorithm explicitly checks every integer P from 1 to 100 instead of using the closed-form property that the minimizing P is the (rounded) mean of the data. This multiplies the cost by ~100.
For each of the 100 candidate P values, the code scans the entire array, performing N abs() and squaring operations, leading to repeated work on the same data.

Each of the 100*N iterations performs multiple Python-level operations (abs, subtraction, exponentiation, addition) in pure Python, which is costly in an interpreted language even if asymptotic complexity is still linear in N.
Using eval(input()) to read an integer is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()). While not the primary performance bottleneck, it adds overhead and risk.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical fact that the sum of squared deviations Σ(ai − P)^2 is minimized when P equals the mean of ai. For integer P, the optimal value is the nearest integer to the mean, so one can compute the mean once, round it, and then compute the total squared deviation in a single pass.

complexity.why: The code reads N numbers into a list (O(N)), computes their sum once (O(N)), then computes the squared deviations from the chosen P in a single list comprehension (another O(N)). Total work is proportional to N with a small constant factor. The list of inputs requires O(N) space; other variables are O(1).

complexity_delta.from: O(100 * N) ≈ O(N) with large constant factor due to brute-force over all candidate P in [1,100].
complexity_delta.to: O(N) with a small constant factor by computing the optimal P directly from the mean.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity in big-O terms is the same, but the constant factor is reduced by roughly 100x by eliminating the outer candidate loop and using a formula-based solution.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the objective function is f(P) = Σ(ai − P)^2, a convex quadratic in P whose minimizer over the reals is the arithmetic mean of ai.

Note that restricting P to integers means the optimum is achieved at the integer nearest to the mean (either floor(mean) or ceil(mean)); using round() is sufficient because when the mean is exactly x.5, both neighbors yield the same cost.
Replace the outer loop over P=1..100 with a single computation of P as the rounded mean: P = round(sum(ai)/N).
Retain a single pass over the data to compute the total squared deviation Σ(ai − P)^2.
Avoid per-candidate recomputation by computing sum(ai) only once instead of using it implicitly 100 times.
Optionally (for safety and minor speed), replace eval(input()) with int(input()) for reading N.
trigger_signals: Objective function is a sum of squared distances to a single scalar parameter P, a classic pattern where the mean is optimal.
Presence of a fixed-range outer loop (for var_5 in range(1, 101)) coupled with an inner loop over all data, suggesting brute-force over candidate parameters.
Inner loop performing repeated abs() and square operations on the same dataset for each candidate, indicating redundant computation.
The candidate range [1,100] suggests constraints on values but not on N, making the constant factor (100x passes) an obvious optimization target.
pitfalls: Using round() in Python applies banker's rounding (ties to even). For this quadratic objective, when the mean is exactly halfway between integers, both neighboring integers give the same cost, so this does not break correctness, but this nuance should be understood.

If the domain of allowed P were not all integers (e.g., restricted subset), directly using the rounded mean might violate constraints; here, the brute-force version implicitly assumes P ∈ [1,100]. The formula-based approach assumes any integer P is allowed, so constraints must be consistent.

Relying on floating-point mean computation (sum / N) can introduce rounding error for very large sums, though within typical competitive programming constraints with small integers this is negligible.
Continuing to use eval(input()) remains unsafe and slower than int(input()); correcting algorithmic inefficiency should not obscure the need for safe, simple parsing.

constraints_guess.n_max: ≈ 10^4 (upper bound on var_6 / var_7, inferred from needing faster than O(n^3))
constraints_guess.notes: Cubic solution over min(var_6, var_8) would be too slow for n around 10^3–10^4, implying the intended solution is closer to linear or low polynomial in n.

dominant_ops: Three nested loops over candidate triplets (var_2, var_3, var_4) with a simple integer-sum check (var_2 + var_3 + var_4 == var_8). The overwhelming cost is the iteration count, not the arithmetic.

complexity.why: For each test case, var_2 ranges from var_7 down to var_5 (≈O(K)); for each var_2, var_3 ranges down from var_2-1 (≈O(K)); for each var_3, var_4 ranges down from var_3-1 (≈O(K)). This yields O(K^3) iterations, where K ≈ min(var_6, var_8). Only a few integer operations per iteration, so asymptotic time is dominated by the cubic loop; no significant extra memory is used.

bottlenecks.detail: Triple nested loops: for var_2 in [...], for var_3 in [...], for var_4 in [...]. This performs on the order of K^3 iterations even though all that’s needed is counting valid (var_2, var_3, var_4) with var_2 > var_3 > var_4 >= 1 and var_2 + var_3 + var_4 == var_8.
The condition (var_2 + var_3 + var_4) == var_8 is checked by brute force enumeration, instead of exploiting the fixed-sum constraint to derive closed-form counts for each var_2.

Although var_2 is restricted between min(var_8 − 3, var_6) and max(var_8 / 3, 3), var_3 and var_4 still scan full ranges below var_2, leading to many iterations that cannot satisfy the sum constraint.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the fixed sum var_8 and ordering constraints to eliminate two inner loops. For each possible largest value var_2 (bounded appropriately), compute directly how many (var_3, var_4) pairs exist such that var_2 > var_3 > var_4 >= 1 and var_2 + var_3 + var_4 = var_8, using arithmetic to find the valid range of var_3 and count solutions in O(1) per var_2.

complexity.why: The optimized code loops var_2 from var_5 to var_3 (both O(K) in magnitude), and for each var_2 computes var_4 (upper bound for var_3) and var_6 (lower bound for var_3) via constant-time arithmetic, then increments var_1 by (var_4 − var_6 + 1). This yields O(K) work per test case with constant extra memory.

complexity_delta.from: O(T * K^3) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(T * K) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: K ≈ min(var_6, var_7, var_8). Transition is from explicit enumeration of all triplets to a closed-form counting approach over a single loop variable.

transformation_steps: Recognize the combinatorial structure: the slow code counts strictly decreasing positive integer triplets (var_2, var_3, var_4) such that var_2 + var_3 + var_4 == var_8 and var_2 ≤ var_6, with derived bounds giving var_2 in [var_5, var_7].

Fix var_2 and rewrite the constraint on (var_3, var_4): var_3 + var_4 = var_8 − var_2, with 1 ≤ var_4 < var_3 < var_2. This reduces the problem to counting integer pairs with a fixed sum and inequality constraints.

Derive the feasible interval for var_3 for each var_2: lower bound is derived from var_3 > var_4 and var_3 > (var_8 − var_2)/2, while upper bound comes from var_3 < var_2 and var_4 ≥ 1, giving an upper bound of min(var_2 − 1, var_8 − var_2 − 1).
Compute the count of valid var_3 for each var_2 in O(1): number_of_solutions = max(0, upper_bound − lower_bound + 1). This replaces the inner two loops over var_3 and var_4.

Optimize bounds on var_2 itself: use var_3 = min(var_8 − 3, var_7) as an upper bound (since we need at least 1+2 for the other two terms) and var_5 = max(var_8 // 3 + 1, 3) as a lower bound (largest term must exceed a third of the sum and be at least 3).
Implement a single loop over var_2 from var_5 to var_3 (ascending), updating var_1 with the closed-form count for each var_2, thus eliminating the combinatorial explosion of triple nested loops.
trigger_signals: Presence of three nested for-loops iterating over integer ranges whose bounds are linearly tied to the input size (classic O(n^3) pattern).
The inner-most body only performs a simple arithmetic condition check (var_2 + var_3 + var_4 == var_8), suggesting that the sum constraint might be exploitable mathematically.
Constraints on variables (strict ordering var_2 > var_3 > var_4 >= 1 and fixed sum var_8) are typical of problems solvable via closed-form counting rather than brute-force enumeration.
Use of min/max expressions in the loop bounds indicates the author already uses problem-specific structure, implying further algebraic simplification may be possible.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors in bounds: The fast code carefully uses var_4 = min(var_2 − 1, var_8 − var_2 − 1) and var_6 = (var_8 − var_2) // 2 + 1. Misplacing +1 or −1 will undercount or overcount solutions.

Integer division semantics: Using integer division (//) is crucial. Replacing it with float division or incorrect rounding (e.g., using int(...) inconsistently) can shift the lower bound on var_3 and change the count.

Loop direction and inclusivity: The slow code iterates var_2 downward and inner loops in descending order; the fast code iterates var_2 upward. Care must be taken that the ranges [var_5, var_3] in the fast code exactly cover the same valid var_2 values as [var_7, var_5] in reverse without missing or duplicating cases.

Boundary constraints from problem limits: var_2 must satisfy both the upper bound from var_6 (or var_7) and the feasibility bound from the sum constraint var_8. Incorrectly setting var_3 = min(var_8 − 3, var_7) or var_5 = max(var_8 // 3 + 1, 3) can allow impossible states or exclude valid triplets.

Assuming symmetry where it does not exist: The ordering constraint var_2 > var_3 > var_4 breaks symmetry among the three variables. Any closed-form derivation must respect this ordering; otherwise, one might count permutations instead of strictly ordered triplets.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style problem: given N (up to around 10^4–10^5) and bounds A,B on digit sums, sum all i in [1,N] whose digit sum is within [A,B]. Straightforward brute force over all integers is expected.

dominant_ops: For each integer up to N, repeatedly compute var_7 % 10 and var_7 /= 10 in a while loop until var_7 == 0, using float division and a cast int(var_7 % 10).

complexity.time: intended O(N * log10(N)), but actually may be non-terminating due to float division and equality check with 0
complexity.why: The outer loop runs over all integers from 0 to var_6. Inside, a while-loop processes each digit of var_4. Intended digit peeling is O(d) per number, where d is digits count. However, using '/=' on an int converts it to float in Python 3, and checking 'while var_7 != 0:' with floats may never hit exactly 0 due to precision, so the loop might not terminate or run for far more iterations than necessary.

bottlenecks.detail: Using 'var_7 /= 10' on an integer promotes var_7 to float. All subsequent '% 10' operations become float modulo, which is significantly slower than integer arithmetic.
Loop condition 'while var_7 != 0:' compares floats to 0.0. Because var_7 is repeatedly divided by 10 as a float, it may never be exactly 0.0, leading to a non-terminating or extremely long loop.
The expression 'int(var_7 % 10)' is unnecessary if var_7 is kept as an integer; the modulo is already an int. With var_7 as float, this adds a cast on top of a slower float modulo.
The range 'for var_4 in range(var_6 + 1):' starts at 0. The problem is usually defined for 1..N; iterating 0 is harmless but wasted work (constant-factor overhead).

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep all arithmetic in integer domain and peel off digits using integer division // 10. Iterate i from 1 to N, compute digit sum with repeated 'var_7 % 10' and 'var_7 //= 10', and accumulate i when its digit sum lies in [A,B].

complexity.why: For each integer from 1 to var_5, the while-loop runs once per digit (base-10). An integer of size up to N has O(log10(N)) digits, so the overall number of iterations is proportional to N * log10(N). Only a constant amount of extra memory is used for counters and accumulators.

complexity_delta.from: Intended O(N * log10(N)) but with float division inside the digit loop it can become non-terminating or disproportionately slow; practical time complexity is unbounded.
complexity_delta.to: O(N * log10(N)) with predictable, tight constant factors using pure integer arithmetic.
complexity_delta.note: The asymptotic intent of both versions is the same, but the slow version’s incorrect use of '/' instead of '//' turns the digit loop into a floating-point computation that may never terminate and is much slower per iteration.

transformation_steps: Change the loop range from 'range(var_6 + 1)' to 'range(1, var_5 + 1)' to skip the unnecessary 0 case and to match the problem’s 1..N domain.
Replace 'var_7 /= 10' with 'var_7 = var_7 // 10' to keep var_7 as an integer and ensure exact digit peeling and guaranteed termination.
Remove the redundant 'int(...)' cast around the modulo by accumulating directly into an integer (as in 'var_6 += var_7 % 10').
Use consistent integer comparisons and boundaries in the if-condition ('var_6 >= var_1 and var_6 <= var_3'), equivalent to 'var_1 <= var_6 <= var_3' but explicit.
trigger_signals: Use of '/=' on an integer inside a digit extraction loop, which in Python 3 promotes to float.
Loop condition 'while var_7 != 0:' combined with repeated float division by 10, which is a classic red flag for non-terminating or unstable loops.
Presence of 'int(var_7 % 10)' indicating that modulo is being applied to a non-integer or that unnecessary casting is happening.
Performance symptoms: program hangs or times out even for small N where an integer-based digit loop is known to be fast.
pitfalls: In Python 3, '/' always produces a float. Using it for digit extraction (base-10 peeling) is incorrect and can break loop termination.
Using 'while x != 0' with floating-point x is unsafe: due to rounding, x may never become exactly 0. Prefer integer counters or explicit step counts.
Relying on implicit type promotions (int -> float) can silently change algorithmic behavior and complexity, not just performance.
Assuming that adding 'int(...)' around a modulo fixes type issues; it hides the root cause (wrong numeric type) rather than correcting it.
Even though both versions look nearly identical, small operator differences ('/' vs '//') can change the algorithm from linear-time digit peeling to one that effectively never finishes.

constraints_guess.notes: Two integers with combinatorial / polynomial-style computation. Original uses factorials up to max(n, m), typical for n <= 2e5~1e6 in AtCoder-style tasks.

dominant_ops: Linear-time factorial and inverse-factorial precomputation (two arrays up to max(n, m))
Main summation loop over k with multiple modular multiplications per iteration
Repeated modular exponentiation pow(x, 2, MOD) inside the main loop

complexity.why: func_1 builds factorial and inverse factorial arrays up to max(n, m), which is O(N) time and memory. The main summation loop runs for k = 0..n (O(n)). Each iteration does O(1) arithmetic, including pow(x, 2, MOD) with a constant exponent, so asymptotically still O(N). Overall dominated by N = max(n, m).

bottlenecks.detail: Precomputes full factorial and inverse-factorial tables even though the final formula can be evaluated via a single linear recurrence without them.
Stores two arrays (factorials and inverse factorials) of size max(n, m) + 1. For large constraints this increases memory usage and cache pressure.
Main loop performs several modular multiplications and a modular exponentiation pow(x, 2, MOD) per iteration, which adds a noticeable constant factor for large n.
Uses an inclusion–exclusion style sum of binomial coefficients, which is algebraically overkill compared to the simplified DP recurrence in the fast version.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial / inverse factorial tables and the explicit inclusion–exclusion sum by deriving and using a one-dimensional linear recurrence that computes the required combinatorial quantity in a single pass, while maintaining a separate running product term.

complexity.why: The loop runs n times (for var_4 in range(var_6)), each iteration doing O(1) modular arithmetic and one list append. Only a single DP array var_3 of size n+1 is stored, and the product var_2 is updated in-place.

from.time: O(max(n, m)) with a large constant factor due to factorial tables and repeated pow operations
from.space: O(max(n, m)) for two arrays (factorials and inverse factorials)

to.time: O(n) with a smaller constant factor via a simple recurrence and no general modular exponentiation
to.space: O(n) with a single DP array plus scalars

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time remains linear but the constant factors and memory footprint are significantly reduced by eliminating factorial tables and heavy inner-loop operations.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the original inclusion–exclusion sum of binomial terms can be rewritten as the value of a polynomial / combinatorial function satisfying a linear recurrence in k.
Replace explicit binomial coefficient computations (via factorial and inverse factorial arrays) with a one-dimensional DP recurrence: var_3[k+1] depends only on var_3[k] and var_3[k-1].
Introduce a running product variable var_2 to accumulate the multiplicative term \prod (m - i) incrementally instead of building it from factorials and inverses.
Eliminate factorial and inverse factorial precomputation (func_1) and the large arrays var_8, var_7, thereby avoiding extra memory and setup time.
Remove repeated modular exponentiation inside the main loop; all operations are now basic additions and multiplications modulo 1e9+7.
Streamline the final result computation to a single expression: print((var_2 * var_3[-1]) % MOD).
trigger_signals: Presence of factorial and inverse factorial arrays sized up to the maximum input value, even though only a one-dimensional progression in k is needed.
Use of combinatorial sums with alternating signs (pow(-1, k)) and multiple binomial factors, suggesting an inclusion–exclusion formula that may have a simpler DP or polynomial recurrence.
Repeated pow(base, 2, MOD) calls inside a loop over n, indicating unnecessary modular exponentiation overhead.
Memory usage dominated by auxiliary tables rather than the minimal state actually needed for the final result.
pitfalls: The recurrence in the fast code must be derived correctly; a small algebraic mistake will silently produce wrong answers while still passing small tests.
Indices in the recurrence (var_3[var_4] and var_3[var_4 - 1]) rely on the list being correctly initialized with var_3 = [1]; off-by-one errors can be subtle.

Because the factorial-based implementation inherently encodes combinatorial symmetry, switching to a custom recurrence requires extra care to ensure the same boundary conditions and sign patterns (e.g., those from inclusion–exclusion) are respected.
All intermediate operations must remain under modulo arithmetic; forgetting a % MOD on an update can lead to overflow or incorrect wrap-around behavior.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AOJ-style 'count triples i<j<k with i+j+k=X' problem. N is likely up to a few thousand; brute-force O(N^3) in Python is too slow for worst cases with many test pairs.

dominant_ops: Triple nested for-loops over (var_6, var_4, var_2) with ranges up to O(n)
Per-iteration creation of a temporary list [var_6, var_4, var_2] and sum(...) computation
Repeated equality check of var_7 == sum([var_6, var_4, var_2]) for every triple

complexity.why: For each test case (n=var_5, target=var_7), the code iterates var_6 from 1 to n-2, var_4 from var_6+1 to n-1, and var_2 from var_4+1 to n, visiting every strictly increasing triple (var_6, var_4, var_2). The number of iterations is C(n,3) = O(n^3). All work inside the innermost loop is O(1), so overall time per test is Θ(n^3). Only a constant number of scalar variables are used, so space is O(1) aside from negligible input parsing overhead.

bottlenecks.detail: Brute-force enumeration of all combinations (i,j,k) with 1 ≤ i < j < k ≤ n leads to Θ(n^3) checks per test case.
Using sum([var_6, var_4, var_2]) allocates a new list and sums it on every innermost iteration instead of using var_6 + var_4 + var_2.
Pure Python nested loops with up to O(n^3) iterations incur significant interpreter overhead and cannot handle upper-end constraints efficiently.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid enumerating all triples explicitly. For each possible choice of the largest element k, count in O(1) time how many pairs (i,j) with 1 ≤ i < j < k satisfy i + j = X − k, using arithmetic bounds on j derived from the inequalities. Sum these counts over feasible k, yielding an O(n) algorithm per test case.

complexity.why: For each test case (n=var_6, X=var_9), the optimized solution loops var_1 (interpretable as k, the largest value in the triple) from approximately X/3 up to n: O(n) iterations. Each iteration calls func_1, which performs only a few integer operations and min/max calls, so its cost is O(1). Therefore, each test case runs in Θ(n) time. Inputs are accumulated in list var_8, giving O(T) additional memory usage (storing all (n,X) pairs), but per-test computation itself is O(1) extra space.

complexity_delta.from: O(T * n^3) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(T * n) time, O(T) space
complexity_delta.note: The main improvement comes from replacing triple nested loops with a single loop over k and a closed-form count of valid (i,j) pairs. Extra O(T) space is used only to store all inputs before processing; this is not fundamental and could be reduced back to O(1) if desired.

transformation_steps: Reformulate the problem: count the number of triples (i,j,k) such that 1 ≤ i < j < k ≤ n and i + j + k = X.
Fix k (the largest element) and set S = X − k. Then count pairs (i,j) with 1 ≤ i < j < k and i + j = S instead of iterating over all three indices.
Express the pair constraints in terms of j: with i = S − j, inequalities become 1 ≤ S − j < j < k.
Derive bounds on j from the inequalities: 1 ≤ S − j gives j ≤ S − 1; S − j < j gives j > S/2; and j < k gives j ≤ k − 1.
Combine bounds to get j_min = floor(S/2) + 1 = S // 2 + 1 and j_max = min(k − 1, S − 1). The number of valid pairs for fixed k is max(j_max − j_min + 1, 0). This logic is encapsulated in func_1.
Restrict the k loop: k must be large enough for any triple to exist (k is around X/3 at minimum), so iterate k from X // 3 up to n, adding func_1(k, X − k) to the answer.
Optionally batch input: read all (n,X) pairs into a list and then process them, as done in the optimized code (this affects memory but not asymptotic time).
trigger_signals: Presence of three nested loops over ranges up to n with only a simple arithmetic condition inside.
Problem semantics are purely counting-based with linear constraints on variables (sums and inequalities), which often admit combinatorial or arithmetic closed forms.
Use of sum([...]) in the innermost loop, signalling extra overhead on top of already heavy iteration.
Typical competitive-programming context (p02412) where N can be large enough that O(n^3) is untenable in Python.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when translating inequalities into index ranges: the correct j bounds are j > S/2 and j ≤ min(k − 1, S − 1), implemented as j from S // 2 + 1 to min(k − 1, S − 1).
Handling cases where the computed lower bound exceeds the upper bound; func_1 uses max(var_4 − var_5 + 1, 0) to safely yield zero in those cases.
Ensuring that integer division (//) is used so that floor(S/2) is correctly computed for odd S.
Choosing the k loop range: starting at X // 3 is safe but includes some k that yield zero pairs; starting too high or too low could miss valid triples or waste work.
Storing all inputs (var_8) increases memory usage to O(T); in memory-constrained settings it may be preferable to process each test case as it is read instead of buffering.

constraints_guess.notes: Single sequence of N jobs (read as N lines). Typical AtCoder-style scheduling / deadline feasibility check: O(N log N) via sort is intended and acceptable.

dominant_ops: Reading N lines of integer pairs from stdin
Storing N pairs in a Python list
Sorting the list of N pairs by deadline: list.sort()
Single linear pass accumulating times and checking deadlines

complexity.why: The main cost is sorting the N tasks (func_2.sort()), which is O(N log N). Input storage requires holding all N pairs, giving O(N) additional memory. The subsequent feasibility check loop is O(N).

bottlenecks.detail: Sorting the list of N tasks (func_2.sort()) dominates runtime at O(N log N), which is expected and necessary for this greedy scheduling approach.
Use of eval(input()) inside func_4 and multiple tiny wrapper functions around input(). This adds Python call overhead and eval parsing overhead on top of raw input reading.
eval(input()) is substantially slower and less safe than int(input()) for reading integers, due to expression parsing and security concerns.

Modules such as itertools, bisect, decimal, Counter, copy and helper functions func_2, func_3, func_5, func_6 are imported/defined but unused, slightly increasing load/parse time and code complexity (though not asymptotic cost).

Multiple small wrappers (func_1, func_4, etc.) add function-call overhead during input, and variable names are re-used (func_2 as both function and list), which can make maintenance and micro-optimizations harder.

FastAudit.core_idea: Preserve the same greedy scheduling algorithm (sort tasks by deadline and check cumulative time) while simplifying I/O and data handling: avoid unused helpers and imports, read directly in the main loop, store pairs, sort, then perform a single linear feasibility check.

complexity.why: The algorithm is unchanged: reading N tasks is O(N), sorting them by deadline is O(N log N), and the verification loop is O(N). All tasks are stored, requiring O(N) memory. Minor structural changes (using deque then list, removing helpers) do not change asymptotic complexity.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(N log N), Space: O(N)
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(N log N), Space: O(N)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is identical; improvements are primarily in constant factors and code clarity (fewer function calls, fewer imports, less indirection).

transformation_steps: Removed unused imports (sys, math, itertools, bisect, copy, Counter, Decimal) and helper functions (func_2, func_3, func_5, func_6) that were not required by the core scheduling algorithm.
Eliminated wrapper functions around input (func_1, func_4) in favor of direct reading in the main loop; this removes extra Python function-call overhead.
Replaced the indirect construction of the task list (func_2.append followed by indexed access in a for-range loop) with a more direct for-each iteration over the sorted list.

Simplified variable naming and removed shadowing between function names and variables (e.g., func_2 as both function and list, func_4 as both function and loop index), reducing cognitive load and potential for subtle bugs.

Used deque for intermediate storage and then converted to list before sorting; functionally equivalent to appending to a list directly, but emphasizes queue-like construction (impact on performance is negligible for append-only usage).
trigger_signals: Use of eval(input()) for simple integer input, which is slower and unnecessary compared to int(input()).
Multiple tiny I/O wrapper functions that simply forwarded to input().split() or list(map(int, ...)), adding overhead with no algorithmic benefit.
Presence of many unused utilities and imports, which is a common sign of template code not trimmed for the specific problem and can marginally increase start-up and parsing time.
Shadowing names (func_4 as function and then as loop index), indicating potential confusion and making profiling/optimization more difficult.
pitfalls: The modified version still uses eval(input()) for reading the first integer (var_2); replacing this with int(input()) would be safer and faster without changing logic.

Using deque here provides no performance benefit over a list, since only append operations are used before a full conversion to list; developers might wrongly assume a speedup where there is effectively none.

Relying on exit() inside the loop for control flow is fine in contest code but can complicate integration or unit testing in larger systems; raising an exception or returning from a function is often preferable.
While unused imports and helpers are removed, one should ensure this cleanup does not accidentally remove needed utilities if the script later grows or is reused in other contexts.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: N up to ~1e5, M up to ~1e9. Need to factor M and compute products of binomial coefficients C(N+e-1, e) modulo 1e9+7.

dominant_ops: Prime factorization loop up to sqrt(M)
Repeated calls to math.factorial with large arguments (~N + e)
Big-integer multiplications and divisions when forming combinations without modulus

complexity.why: sqrt(M) from trial division factorization. For each distinct prime factor (P of them), math.factorial is called on arguments up to N+e_max, N-1, and e. A factorial of k uses O(k) multiplications on increasingly large big integers, so the effective cost is superlinear in k due to big-integer arithmetic. Caching avoids recomputing the same factorial values, but the largest factorials (around N+e_max) still dominate both time and memory. The dictionary of factorials grows up to O(N+e_max) distinct entries, hence O(N) space.

bottlenecks.detail: Using math.factorial on arguments up to N+e_max builds enormous integers (thousands of bits) and performs O(k) big-int multiplications per call. This dominates runtime when N is large (e.g., 1e5).

The combination C(n, k) is formed as var_2 // (var_3 * var_4) using full-precision integers with no intermediate modulo reduction. This causes huge intermediates and very expensive big-int division and multiplication.
Computing combinations via full factorials is overkill for small k=e (exponent of a prime). A direct multiplicative formula in O(e) avoids factorials up to N+e.

The factorization function checks `if var_5 in list(var_11.keys())`, creating a new list of keys each time. This is O(#primes) per check. Although #primes is small here, it is an unnecessary overhead compared with direct dictionary access.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the prime factorization step, but replace factorial-based combination computation with a direct multiplicative formula for C(N+e-1, e) that iterates only e times, and apply the modulus at each multiplication to keep integers small.

complexity.why: Factorization via trial division remains O(sqrt(M)). For each prime with exponent e, the code computes C(N+e-1, e) using two running products over a loop of length e. The sum of exponents sum_e (over all primes) is at most O(log M). All intermediate multiplications are reduced modulo 1e9+7, so numbers stay bounded and big-integer growth is avoided. Space holds only the prime exponent map plus a few scalars, so O(#primes) = O(log M).

complexity_delta.from: Factorization O(sqrt(M)) + factorial-based combinations with large big-integer cost roughly O(P * F(N+e_max)), where F(k) is the cost of computing k! and handling huge intermediates.
complexity_delta.to: Factorization O(sqrt(M)) + binomial via multiplicative formula O(sum_e), with all arithmetic in O(1) per op under modulo; effectively O(sqrt(M) + log M).
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic factorization cost is unchanged, but the combination part drops from large factorial computations on huge integers to short loops over small exponents with modular reduction, removing the practical bottleneck.

transformation_steps: Replace the factorial-based combination function with an in-place multiplicative computation of C(N+e-1, e): multiply successive terms of the numerator and denominator in a loop of length e.
Apply the 1e9+7 modulus after each multiplication to keep intermediate results bounded and avoid large big-integer growth.
Factor the second input (M) into primes once, storing exponents in a dictionary (defaultdict(int) for simpler updates).
Iterate over the exponents, computing C(N+e-1, e) via the new multiplicative method, multiply these into the running answer, and reduce modulo 1e9+7 after each step.
Simplify dictionary usage in factorization by using direct `dict[key]` updates (or defaultdict) instead of repeated `in list(dict.keys())` checks.
trigger_signals: Use of math.factorial with arguments proportional to N (up to ~1e5) in a tight combinatorial loop.
Absence of modular reduction during combination construction, leading to extremely large intermediate integers.
Runtime dominated by big-integer multiplication and division rather than the O(sqrt(M)) factorization step.
Dictionary of cached factorials growing up to O(N) distinct keys when only a narrow band of factorials is actually needed.
pitfalls: When switching to modular arithmetic, performing division directly under the modulus is generally invalid; you must either divide before taking modulus (as done here with exact integer arithmetic) or use modular inverses. The fast code carefully divides numerator and denominator before the final modulo, preserving correctness.
If N or exponents e were large (e.g., up to 1e5), the inner O(e) loops might also become heavy; in such cases, a factorial+inverse-factorial table with modular inverses is preferable.
Trial division up to sqrt(M) can still be too slow if M is much larger than assumed (e.g., >>1e12); in that case, more advanced factorization methods or tighter constraints are required.
Care must be taken to avoid integer overflow in languages without arbitrary-precision integers; always apply modulo after multiplications when porting this approach outside Python.

constraints_guess.notes: Classical 'count triples (i<j<k) in [1..n] with i+j+k=x' style problem (e.g., AOJ Sum of Three Integers). Typical constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 50, 1 ≤ x ≤ 100, multiple test cases until '0 0'. Even if n were a few hundreds, O(n^3) vs O(n^2) matters.

dominant_ops: Triple nested for-loops over (var_6, var_4, var_2) in the range [1..n] with strictly increasing indices, and inside them construction of a 3-element list and sum() each time to compare against target var_7.

complexity.why: The loops iterate over all ordered triples 1 ≤ var_6 < var_4 < var_2 ≤ n. The number of such triples is C(n,3) = Θ(n^3). The body does O(1) work but includes a list allocation and sum() call per triple. No extra structures beyond a few scalar variables, so space is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: Enumerates all O(n^3) triples (i,j,k) satisfying 1 ≤ i < j < k ≤ n even though the relation i+j+k = x restricts the feasible triples heavily. This cubic enumeration is the main cost driver and becomes expensive as n grows.

For each triple, constructs a 3-element list [var_6, var_4, var_2] and calls sum() on it. This causes repeated small list allocations and function overhead inside the tightest loop; while asymptotically still O(1), it is a nontrivial constant factor in the innermost O(n^3) loop.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid explicit enumeration of all triples by leveraging the equation and ordering constraints. Fix the largest element (var_1) in an outer loop, then for each fixed var_1, treat the remaining two elements as a constrained 2-sum: start with var_2 = var_1 - 1 and compute var_3 = target - var_1 - var_2, then slide var_2 down and var_3 up while maintaining var_1 > var_2 > var_3 and var_3 > 0. This effectively converts the triple loop into a double loop (two-pointer-like scan) and solves for the third value algebraically instead of looping over it.

complexity.why: The outer while over var_1 effectively iterates over possible values of the largest element in roughly O(n) steps (from n down to about 3). For each fixed var_1, the inner while loop moves var_2 monotonically downward (and var_3 upward) until var_2 <= var_3, which takes at most O(var_1) steps. Summed over all var_1, this gives O(1 + 2 + ... + n) = O(n^2). Only a fixed number of integer variables are used, so space remains constant.

complexity_delta.note: One dimension of the triple enumeration is eliminated by solving for the third element and using a monotone (two-pointer style) scan instead of a full nested loop over all three indices.

transformation_steps: Recognize the mathematical structure: we need to count triples (i,j,k) with 1 ≤ i < j < k ≤ n and i + j + k = x.
Observe that if we fix one variable, say the largest element k, then j and i must satisfy i + j = x - k with 1 ≤ i < j < k, significantly restricting possibilities.
Replace the innermost loop over the third index with an algebraic computation: for fixed k and j, compute i = x - k - j instead of iterating i. This already removes one loop conceptually.

Exploit ordering constraints (i < j < k) and positivity to define monotone movement: initialize j near k (j = k - 1) and i derived from the sum constraint; then move j downward and i upward (or vice versa) while the inequalities remain valid. This is akin to a two-pointer approach on the (i,j) pair.

Implement the above as an outer loop over k (var_1 in the fast code) and an inner loop that adjusts j (var_2) and i (var_3) while maintaining var_1 > var_2 > var_3 > 0, counting valid configurations and stopping when no further ordered triple is possible.
Remove per-iteration allocations and sum() calls by using direct integer arithmetic and comparisons, improving constant factors within the now-quadratic algorithm.
trigger_signals: Presence of three nested loops over ranges tied to the same parameter (n), indicating O(n^3) behavior.
The core condition inside the innermost loop depends only on a simple linear relation among the loop indices (var_6 + var_4 + var_2 == var_7), suggesting algebraic elimination of one loop variable.
Redundant operations in the innermost loop, such as creating a new list and calling sum() for each triple, which can be replaced with direct additions.
Typical constraints of this class of problem (n on the order of tens to hundreds) where cubic-time solutions may be borderline or clearly suboptimal compared to available quadratic strategies.
pitfalls: Correctness of inequality constraints: ensuring the fast version faithfully preserves 1 ≤ var_3 < var_2 < var_1 ≤ n and does not count invalid permutations or out-of-range values.

Edge cases where no valid triple exists; the outer termination condition (`if not var_1 > var_2 > var_3`) must be carefully designed so the loop stops correctly and does not miss any remaining valid triples.

Potential off-by-one errors in initialization of var_1 and var_2 (e.g., starting var_1 at n vs n+1, or var_2 at var_1-1) that could either skip valid triples or access indices effectively outside the intended domain.

The algorithm assumes monotone movement of var_2 and var_3 is sufficient to cover all feasible pairs for each var_1; an incorrect update rule or condition could result in skipping some combinations that satisfy the sum and ordering constraints.

Even though the new algorithm is asymptotically faster, the control flow (nested while True with breaks) is less transparent than the straightforward triple for-loop, which can make reasoning about termination and correctness more error-prone if modified further.

constraints_guess.notes: Single array processed in one pass; typical competitive constraints n≈1e5–2e5. Values irrelevant to complexity.

dominant_ops: Reading n integers into a list
Single linear scan over the array with adjacent comparisons
Constant-time max and assignments inside the loop

complexity.why: The algorithm performs one pass over the n-element array, doing O(1) work per element, so O(n) time. It stores the input array of size n and only O(1) extra scalars, leading to O(n) space overall.

bottlenecks.detail: No true algorithmic bottleneck: the core is already optimal O(n) for scanning the entire array once.

Multiple unused imports and helper functions (factorial-based combination, divisor listing, duplicate check) are defined but never called. They incur minor definition-time overhead and obscure the core logic but do not change asymptotic complexity.

Use of opaque variable names (var_1, var_2, etc.) and indirection via func_4 for input harms readability and maintainability, potentially leading to mistakes when modifying code, though not affecting raw performance materially.

FastAudit.core_idea: Streamline the implementation to a direct single-pass DP-like approach that tracks, for each position i, the length of the current non-increasing suffix ending at i and then takes the maximum over these lengths. Remove unused helper functions and imports, and read input inline.

complexity.why: Still a single pass over the array with O(1) work per element, so O(n) time. It stores both the input array and an auxiliary array of length n (var_4), hence O(n) total space.

from.note: Input array of size n plus O(1) extra working variables.

to.note: Input array of size n plus an auxiliary DP array of size n.

complexity_delta.note: Both versions are linear-time. The modified version trades slightly higher memory usage (one extra length-n array) for clearer, more explicit state tracking. Asymptotic complexity is unchanged.

transformation_steps: Inline input reading instead of using a helper function: directly read n and then the list of integers with map(int, input().split()).
Remove unused imports and helper functions (combinatorics, divisor enumeration, duplicate detection) that were never invoked in the solution path.
Replace the manual tracking of the current run length and running maximum with an auxiliary array var_4 that stores, for each index i, the length of the current non-increasing suffix ending at i.
Compute the answer as max(var_4) instead of manually maintaining a running maximum during the loop.
Simplify loop indices and conditions: iterate i from 1 to n-1 and compare var_2[i] <= var_2[i-1], aligning semantics with the original condition a[i] <= a[i-1] (equivalent to a[i-1] >= a[i]).
trigger_signals: Desire to remove dead code and unused imports for clarity and minor startup overhead reduction.
Interest in making the state evolution (current non-increasing run length) explicit at each index via an array, which can be easier to reason about or extend.
Code review feedback pointing out overly obfuscated variable names and auxiliary functions that obscure the core O(n) scan.
Maintenance concerns where the presence of unused helper functions could mislead future contributors about the intended algorithm.
pitfalls: The auxiliary array var_4 requires O(n) extra space; while asymptotically acceptable, it is a regression in memory usage relative to the original, which used only O(1) extra space beyond the input.
When rewriting the condition, it is easy to flip the inequality or indexing direction, inadvertently switching between non-increasing and non-decreasing segments.
Using max(var_4) at the end requires correct initialization: var_4[0] must be 0 so that runs start counting correctly from index 1.

Both versions continue to use eval on input for reading n, which is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; replacing eval(input()) with int(input()) is recommended for robustness even though performance impact is negligible here.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical scheduling-with-deadlines greedy problem (sum durations vs deadlines after sort by deadline). Sorting O(n log n) is intended; n likely up to ~1e5–2e5, times/deadlines up to ~1e9.

dominant_ops: Reading n lines of two integers each via helper wrappers around sys.stdin.readline
Creating an extra list copy per row (list(func_3()) where func_3 already returns a list)
Sorting list of length n by second element using a Python lambda key
Single linear pass over sorted list to accumulate durations and compare with deadlines

complexity.why: Input reading and the final linear scan are O(n). The sort on n 2-element lists dominates at O(n log n). All task pairs are stored at once, requiring O(n) additional space.

bottlenecks.detail: Multiple small wrapper functions (func_3, func_8, func_7, etc.) around sys.stdin.readline add Python-level call overhead for every line read. var_7.readline() is not locally bound to a shorter name for faster attribute access.
Each row is built as list(func_3()) while func_3 already returns a list; this creates an unnecessary second list object per input line.
Sorting uses key=lambda var_8: var_8[1], which invokes a Python lambda for each element; using operator.itemgetter(1) is slightly faster and more memory-friendly.
The loop continues even after detecting a violation (var_5 > var_4). This wastes time on remaining iterations when the answer is already known to be 'No'.
Several unused helpers (func_2, func_4, func_5, func_6, func_1) and sys.setrecursionlimit(10**7) are defined or called despite recursion not being used, adding minor startup overhead and noise.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the same greedy algorithm (sort jobs by deadline, accumulate durations, and ensure the cumulative time never exceeds each job's deadline) but reduce constant factors via faster I/O, avoiding redundant list construction, using itemgetter for the sort key, storing rows as tuples, and exiting early on the first detected violation.

complexity.why: Algorithmic structure is unchanged: reading n lines is O(n), sorting the n pairs by deadline is O(n log n), and the feasibility check is an O(n) scan. All tasks are still stored in memory, requiring O(n) space. Improvements are purely in constant factors (less function-call overhead, fewer allocations, early exit).

complexity_delta.from: O(n log n) time, O(n) space (baseline greedy scheduling with overhead from lambdas, extra list copies, and no early exit).
complexity_delta.to: O(n log n) time, O(n) space (same asymptotics, but with lower constant factors due to faster I/O, more efficient data structures, and early termination).
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged, but per-element and per-line overhead is reduced significantly, which matters for large n near contest limits.

transformation_steps: I/O optimization: Bind sys.stdin.readline to a local name (var_5) and use it directly instead of multiple wrapper functions and attribute lookups.
Remove unused helpers: Delete func_2, func_4, func_5, func_6, func_1, and the unnecessary recursion limit adjustment, reducing startup and call overhead and clarifying the data flow.

Avoid redundant copies: Read each pair with tuple(map(int, var_5().rstrip().split())) instead of list(func_3()) where func_3 already builds a list, eliminating an extra list construction per line and favoring tuples for immutable records.
Faster sort key: Replace key=lambda var_8: var_8[1] with key=itemgetter(1) to cut per-element key-function overhead during sorting.
Early termination: Inside the loop, print 'No' and return immediately when var_6 > var_4, avoiding unnecessary work on the remaining tasks once infeasibility is detected.
Control structure cleanup: Wrap the main logic in func_1 and guard it with if __name__ == '__main__': for clearer execution entry and slightly reduced module-level side effects.
trigger_signals: Presence of many tiny wrapper functions around sys.stdin.readline with no algorithmic benefit.
Redundant list(list(...)) construction indicating unnecessary copying of input rows.
Use of a Python lambda as sort key in a critical O(n log n) section where itemgetter is preferable.
Loop continues after the result is known, doing extra comparisons when a violation has already been found.
Contest context suggests large n; any avoidable per-element or per-line overhead can risk TLE even with correct asymptotics.
pitfalls: Behavioral equivalence: When adding early returns, ensure that all paths still print exactly one of 'Yes' or 'No' and that no additional output or missing newline is introduced.

Input format assumptions: The optimized code strips trailing whitespace via rstrip() before split(); this is usually safe but must not rely on any unusual whitespace semantics beyond standard contests.
Data mutability: Switching from lists of lists to lists of tuples is safe here because the records are not mutated; in other problems, later in-place updates to rows would break after this change.

Global vs local I/O bindings: Binding readline locally improves speed but can be confusing if later code relies on reassigning sys.stdin; modifications to the global stream after binding will not affect the bound function.
Error handling: Early exit on infeasibility removes the chance to perform any additional checks or cleanup afterward; ensure no important post-processing is needed after the loop in other problems.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical of AtCoder ABC110 D-style problem: N up to 1e5, M up to about 1e9. Need to factor M and compute products of combinations C(N+e-1, e) modulo 1e9+7.

dominant_ops: Computing factorial(var_2 - 1) as a huge Python integer (math.factorial) with no modular reduction
Handling very large intermediate integers in multiplications before final modulo
Trial division prime factorization up to sqrt(M) (moderate but not the bottleneck)

complexity.time: O(√M + N^2 · polylog(N)) in bit operations (dominated by building (N-1)! as a big integer)
complexity.space: O(N · log N) bits for representing (N-1)! as a big integer
complexity.why: Factorization is O(√M) which is fine for M≈1e9. The killer is math.factorial(N-1) on N≈1e5: the result has Θ(N log N) bits, and factorial is implemented via many big-integer multiplications whose cost grows with operand size. All combinatorial computations are done on these huge integers before the final modulo, so both time and memory blow up.

bottlenecks.detail: Using math.factorial on N-1 directly (N up to ~1e5) creates an enormous integer (~4.5e5 decimal digits), incurring very expensive big-integer arithmetic.
A large factorial var_5 = factorial(var_2 - 1) is computed but never actually used, wasting substantial time and memory.

Combinatorial terms are computed via exact integer arithmetic (multiplying and dividing large integers) and only reduced modulo 1e9+7 at the very end, causing unnecessary growth of intermediate values.
Integer division (// factorial(var_12)) on very large numerators is significantly slower than using modular inverses with precomputed factorial tables.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid gigantic intermediate integers by performing all combinatorial computations modulo 1e9+7 using precomputed factorials and inverse factorials. For each prime exponent e in the factorization of M, compute C(N + e - 1, e) in O(1) with nCr = fact[n] * invfact[r] * invfact[n-r] % MOD after an O(N) precomputation. Factorization of M remains trial division but is not the bottleneck.

complexity.why: Prime factorization via trial division is O(√M). Precomputing factorials and inverse factorials up to about N+max_e uses two linear passes over arrays of size ≈N (one forward, one backward) plus one modular exponentiation pow(fact[-1], MOD-2, MOD) in O(log MOD). Each combination C(N+e-1, e) is then O(1). No huge integers are created; all arithmetic is modulo 1e9+7.

complexity_delta.from: O(√M + cost_of_bigint_factorial(N)) with massive intermediate integers; practically too slow and memory-heavy for N≈1e5.
complexity_delta.to: O(√M + N) arithmetic modulo 1e9+7 with modest memory usage.
complexity_delta.note: The key shift is from exact big-integer factorial arithmetic to modular combinatorics with precomputed factorials and inverse factorials, turning an effectively superlinear big-int workload into a linear-time modular one.

transformation_steps: Remove math.factorial-based computation of combinations on full Python integers; avoid computing unused factorial(var_2 - 1).
Factor M (var_1) into prime exponents e exactly as before but store only the exponents in a list (var_5).
Determine an upper bound for n in combinations C(N+e-1, e) and allocate arrays for factorial (var_7) and inverse factorial (var_6) up to N + margin (here N+50) to cover all N+e-1.
Precompute factorials modulo MOD iteratively: fact[i] = fact[i-1] * i % MOD.
Compute invfact[max] via Fermat's little theorem: invfact[max] = pow(fact[max], MOD-2, MOD) (since MOD is prime).
Fill the rest of the inverse factorial array backwards: invfact[i-1] = invfact[i] * i % MOD.
For each exponent e in var_5, compute C(N+e-1, e) as fact[N+e-1] * invfact[N-1] * invfact[e] % MOD and multiply into the answer modulo MOD.
Print the final product directly (already reduced modulo 1e9+7).
trigger_signals: Use of math.factorial on an argument linear in N (~1e5) in a competitive programming context.
Performing large integer products and divisions with no intermediate modulo, followed by a single final modulo.
Presence of a huge factorial result that is computed but not used (clear red flag for wasted work).
Time limit exceeded (TLE) or memory limit issues observed for larger N despite relatively simple number-theoretic logic.
pitfalls: The precomputation size for factorials must be large enough: need max_n >= max(N + e - 1) for all exponents e. Using N+50 relies on the fact that max exponent e is small (for M up to ~1e9). If M were larger, N+50 could be insufficient and cause index errors or incorrect results.
The modulus must be prime for Fermat-based modular inverse (pow(x, MOD-2, MOD)) to be valid; here MOD=1e9+7 is prime, but this assumption must be checked for other problems.
Off-by-one mistakes in factorial/inverse factorial indexing (e.g., using N+e instead of N+e-1) will silently produce wrong combinatorial values.
Integer division should never be used with modular arithmetic; always replace a/b with a * inv(b) % MOD, where inv(b) is computed modulo MOD.
Sorting var_5 is not algorithmically necessary for correctness; while it does not hurt asymptotically here, one must ensure such steps do not inadvertently change logic in more complex variants.

constraints_guess.notes: Single array input, length n; magic constant 400005 suggests original constraints like n, |a[i]| <= 2e5. Overall intended solution is O(n).

dominant_ops: One O(400000) initialization loop for var_4, then a single pass over n elements performing constant-time list indexing and integer arithmetic.

complexity.why: var_4 is populated using a for-loop of fixed length C=400005, giving O(C). The main logic iterates once over the n-element array with O(1) work per element, giving O(n). Memory holds the input array (O(n)) plus the fixed-size var_4 array (O(C)). Since C is a small fixed upper bound relative to constraints, overall is effectively linear in n.

bottlenecks.detail: var_4 is filled with zeros by appending inside a Python loop over range(400005). This is slower than using a vectorized construct like [0] * 400005 and costs ~400k Python-level iterations regardless of n.
The use of a hard-coded size 400005 for var_4 reserves that many integers even if n is much smaller, increasing memory footprint and unnecessary initialization work when n << 400000.
Using eval(input()) to read an integer is slower and unnecessarily flexible compared to int(input()). For large test counts this can measurably hurt performance.

Although the algorithm is O(n), every iteration performs two bounds checks, two index computations, and up to two list accesses. With large n, the constant factors of a pure Python loop can become the limiting factor.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace the fixed-size index array with sparse hash maps (defaultdict) keyed by transformed indices (i + a[i] and i - a[i]); first count occurrences of each transformed index for both forms, then aggregate by multiplying matching counts, instead of maintaining a streaming count in a single array.

complexity.why: The first loop processes each of the n elements once, performing a constant number of dictionary updates; average-case hash operations are O(1). The second loop iterates over all keys in var_1 (at most n) and performs an O(1) membership test and lookup in var_3, so total time is O(n). Memory holds the input array plus up to O(n) keys/values in the two defaultdicts.

complexity_delta.from: Time O(n + C), Space O(n + C) with a fixed-size array of length C=400005 used as a frequency table for indices derived from i + a[i].
complexity_delta.to: Time O(n), Space O(n) using two hash maps (defaultdict) keyed by transformed indices i ± a[i], aggregating counts then combining them.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both approaches are linear; the change primarily trades a fixed-size dense array and streaming update for sparse hash maps and a second aggregation pass. Depending on n relative to C and Python’s overhead, this may or may not be faster in practice.

transformation_steps: Replace the preallocated list var_4 of length 400005 with two defaultdict(int) structures to separately accumulate counts of indices where i + a[i] and i - a[i] fall into a valid range.

Change from an online counting strategy (updating and querying var_4 as the loop advances) to a two-phase strategy: first build histograms (var_1 and var_3) over transformed indices, then in a second pass over var_1’s keys, combine counts via multiplication when a key exists in both maps.

Restrict storage and lookups to indices within the range [0, n) (and i - a[i] > 0) instead of the broader [0, 400005) window, making the structure size dependent on actual data rather than a global constant.
