constraints_guess.notes: Typical of AtCoder-style problem: N up to ~2e5, M up to ~1e9. Need prime factorization of M and combinatorics (stars and bars) modulo 1e9+7. Precomputation size chosen around 2e5 to cover worst-case N and sum of prime exponents.

dominant_ops: Precomputing factorials, modular inverses, and inverse factorials up to a fixed limit var_2 = 2*10^5+10
Trial-division prime factorization of var_1 up to sqrt(var_1)
A few modular multiplications over the list of prime exponents

complexity.time: O(F + sqrt(M)) where F ≈ 2e5 is the fixed factorial precomputation bound and M = var_1
complexity.why: Three arrays var_6, var_7, var_9 of size F are built with a single linear pass. Factorization loop runs up to sqrt(M) in the worst case (breaks when var_8*var_8 > var_11). The final loop over exponents is bounded by the number of distinct primes of M (≤ log M), negligible compared to precomputation and factorization.

bottlenecks.detail: The factorial & inverse arrays are always built up to a fixed upper bound F = 2e5+10 irrespective of the actual input N (var_4). For small N, this is wasted work and memory.
Prime factorization uses a Python for-loop up to sqrt(M) with integer divisions/modulo in the inner while-loop. This is fine for M up to ~1e9, but it is still one of the heaviest per-test operations.
All precomputation is executed at import time (before reading input), which can be noticeable in environments running many small test cases or when this file is imported as a module.

FastAudit.core_idea: Scale the combinatorial precomputation to the actual input N instead of a fixed global bound, and streamline factorization and data structures. Factorials, modular inverses, and inverse factorials are computed only up to var_2 + 100, where var_2 is the input N. Factorization returns a compact list of [prime, exponent] pairs. The combination function is an inlined nCk using these precomputed arrays.

complexity.time: O((N + c) + sqrt(M)) where N = var_2 (input) and c ≈ 100 is a small safety margin
complexity.why: Factorials and inverses are computed only up to N + 100, replacing the fixed bound 2e5+10 with a bound proportional to the actual input size. Factorization remains trial division up to sqrt(M). The remaining work is a small loop over prime factors of M, each performing O(1) binomial computations.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(F + sqrt(M)), Space: O(F) with fixed F ≈ 2e5 (independent of input N).
complexity_delta.to: Time: O((N + c) + sqrt(M)), Space: O(N) where N is the input and c is a small constant (≈ 100).
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic order in terms of worst-case input bounds is the same if N can reach 2e5. The main gain is reducing unnecessary work and memory when N is significantly smaller than the global upper bound. Micro-optimizations in factorization and data layout also reduce constant factors.

transformation_steps: Move from global, fixed-size factorial/inverse precomputation (up to 2e5+10) to local precomputation sized by the actual input N (var_2 + 100).
Inline and slightly refactor the binomial coefficient logic into func_1(var_11, var_14, mod), eliminating the separate global combinatorics helpers and using min(k, n-k) symmetry.

Change the factorization result representation from a defaultdict(int) of prime -> exponent to a list of [prime, exponent] pairs, avoiding defaultdict overhead and dict lookups in the main multiplication loop.
Adjust the factorization loop bounds using a precomputed ceil(sqrt(n)) expression, instead of iterating up to n with a break condition; both are O(sqrt n), but the upper bound is made explicit.
Localize all core computation inside a single func_3() entry point, reducing global side effects and allowing faster startup in repeated-run environments.
trigger_signals: Observed that factorial precomputation dominated runtime for inputs where N is much smaller than the fixed limit 2e5.
Memory profiling or constraints hinted that a 2e5-sized precomputation might be overkill for many test cases.
Noticed that combinations only require n up to roughly N + max_exponent, permitting a tighter bound around N plus a small safety margin.
Desire to encapsulate logic into a single callable function for cleaner structure and reduced global initialization.
pitfalls: The factorial/inverse precomputation now depends on N (var_2). If constraints allow N larger than the chosen upper bound (var_2 + 100), the code must ensure that all needed n for nCk (here, var_2 + exponent - 1) are within the precomputed range; otherwise, results will be incorrect or IndexError will occur.

Using floating-point sqrt (var_11**0.5) to determine the loop upper bound in factorization relies on the fact that M is not too large; for much larger integers, floating precision could cause off-by-one issues. Within typical constraints (M ≤ 1e9 or even 1e12) this is safe.
The new code removes defaultdict and uses plain lists; any later modification expecting missing-prime keys to default to 0 must handle that explicitly.
All logic is now inside func_3(); reusing combinatorial helpers elsewhere would require refactoring them back out or duplicating code.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case. Elements likely up to |a_i| <= 1e9. Original solution brute-forces over [min(a), max(a)], which would TLE if the value range is large; intended solution uses mean-based formula for minimizing sum of squared distances.

dominant_ops: Sorting the array of n integers
Nested loop over all candidate centers x in [min(a), max(a)] and all n elements to compute sum of squared differences

complexity.why: The list is sorted once: O(n log n). Then for each integer var_4 in the inclusive range from min(a) to max(a) (range size R = max(a) - min(a) + 1), the code loops over all n elements and accumulates (a_i - var_4)^2, giving O(R * n) additional time. The array itself requires O(n) memory; only O(1) extra scalars are used.

bottlenecks.detail: Brute-force search over every integer x between min(a) and max(a) to find the minimum of sum_i (a_i - x)^2, leading to O(R * n) time where R can be very large if the values are spread out.
The array is fully sorted even though only min and max are needed for the brute-force range; this adds an O(n log n) cost that does not contribute to the final value computation.
Use of eval(input()) to read an integer is unsafe and slower than int(input()); it is not a performance bottleneck at scale compared to the O(R * n) loop but is a bad practice.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical fact that for f(x) = sum_i (a_i - x)^2 over real x, the minimizer is the mean of a_i. For integer x, the optimum is attained at floor(mean) or ceil(mean). Compute the mean via sum(a_i)/n, test these two integer candidates, and choose the smaller sum of squared differences.

complexity.why: Reading n integers and computing their sum is O(n). The candidate centers var_4 are computed as floor and ceil of the mean in O(1). For each of the at most two candidate centers, a single pass over the n elements computes sum (a_i - x)^2, giving O(2n) = O(n) time. No sorting or range scanning is needed. Memory usage is dominated by storing the n-element list.

complexity_delta.from: O(n log n + R * n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: The critical improvement removes the linear scan over the value range [min(a), max(a)] by replacing brute-force search with an analytic solution based on the mean, reducing dependency on the potentially large value range R.

transformation_steps: Recognize the objective function as f(x) = sum_i (a_i - x)^2, which is a convex quadratic in x.
Use calculus/variance properties to note that the real-valued minimizer of f(x) is the mean mu = (sum_i a_i) / n.
Observe that when restricting x to integers, the minimum must occur at one of the nearest integers to mu, i.e., floor(mu) or ceil(mu).
Replace the outer loop over all integers in [min(a), max(a)] with a constant-size set of candidate centers: (sum(a)//n) and (sum(a)+n-1)//n.
Compute the objective f(x) for each candidate center in a single pass over the array and take the minimum.
Eliminate the unnecessary sort, since min and max or the full ordering are no longer needed for the optimized method.
trigger_signals: A loop over every integer between min(a) and max(a) used for optimization, which is suspicious when the range can be much larger than n.
Objective function is a sum of squared differences, a classic pattern where mean/variance formulas often apply.
Time complexity tied to numeric magnitude (R = max - min) instead of just the number of elements n.
Presence of nested loops where the inner loop scans all elements for each candidate parameter value.
pitfalls: When using the mean-based approach, it is important to test both floor(mean) and ceil(mean) as candidates; using only integer division (floor) can be incorrect when the mean is not an integer.
If the language had overflow-prone integer types (unlike Python), sum of squared differences could overflow for large |a_i|; careful use of 64-bit or big integers would be necessary.

Removing the sort is safe for this optimization because only sum(a_i) and the individual a_i values are needed; if other parts of the solution relied on the sorted order, that dependency must be checked before removing sorting.
Using eval(input()) is unsafe and unnecessary; although not the main performance issue, it can introduce security risks and subtle bugs if the input is not trusted.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case with two integers; typical AtCoder-style A problem. Integer magnitude likely up to about 1e9–1e18, but runtime is O(1) regardless.

dominant_ops: Importing many heavy standard-library modules (math, itertools, heapq, collections, random, etc.) that are never used
Creating global direction arrays var_3 and var_4 that are never used
Single line input parse via sys.stdin.readline and list comprehension
A few arithmetic operations: max, min, subtraction, modulo, integer division
One function call indirection to func_6()

complexity.why: The algorithm performs a constant amount of work: reading two integers and doing a fixed number of arithmetic operations and comparisons. No data structures grow with input size. However, there is significant constant-factor overhead from importing many modules and creating unused globals.

bottlenecks.detail: Many large modules are imported (math, itertools, heapq, collections, random, etc.) despite never being used. In competitive-programming environments, this increases startup time and can be a noticeable overhead for a trivial O(1) task.
Global variables var_3, var_4, var_5, var_6 are defined but not used. They add unnecessary overhead in both initialization time and a tiny amount of memory.

The solution logic is wrapped in func_6() and depends on helper func_2(), adding a couple of Python function calls for a problem that can be solved with a single expression. This slightly increases call overhead, though still O(1).

The midpoint is computed via max/min and difference instead of directly using (a + b) // 2, which is slightly more verbose and adds a couple more primitive operations. The impact is negligible but still a constant-factor cost.

FastAudit.core_idea: Read two integers directly, compute their sum, and return the integer midpoint if the sum is even, otherwise print "IMPOSSIBLE". All done in a single expression without extra imports or helper functions.

complexity.why: Only a constant number of arithmetic operations and a single input read are performed. No additional data structures or unused modules are created, so both time and space usage remain constant with minimal overhead.

complexity_delta.from: O(1) time, O(1) space with high constant factors from imports and unused structures
complexity_delta.to: O(1) time, O(1) space with minimal constant factors
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged, but the modified fast_code significantly reduces startup time and runtime constants by removing unused imports, globals, and function call overhead.

transformation_steps: Remove all unused imports (math, itertools, heapq, collections, random, etc.) to avoid their import-time cost.
Remove unused global variables and constants (var_3, var_4, var_5, var_6) that are never referenced in the solution.
Eliminate helper functions (func_1 to func_5) that are unused, and inline the logic of func_6 into the main script.
Simplify the arithmetic by directly computing the midpoint as (var_1 + var_2) // 2 instead of using max/min and differences.
Use a single-line conditional expression for printing the result, avoiding an extra return path and function call overhead.
Use the built-in input() with map(int, ...) directly in the main code instead of routing through sys.stdin helper wrappers for such a small input.
trigger_signals: Very simple problem with O(1) logic but a bloated template containing many unused imports and helper functions.
Noticeable compilation/import phase relative to the actual computation, especially in environments with tight time limits or many test runs.
Use of a generic competitive-programming template for a trivial A-level task, suggesting many pieces of code are unnecessary.
Code length and complexity are disproportionately large compared to the problem description and required operations.
pitfalls: While replacing max/min-based midpoint computation with (a + b) // 2 is correct in Python (no overflow due to big integers), in some languages this pattern could cause integer overflow; the template logic may have been written to avoid such issues.
Switching from sys.stdin.readline to input() is fine here because input size is tiny; for large input problems, this change may have the opposite effect on performance.
Over-aggressive template stripping should ensure no needed utility functions are removed for more complex problems; here, only problem-specific logic is required so removal is safe.
Using the bitwise check (sum & 1 == 0) for evenness is correct but must be applied to integers only; mixing types or strings would cause errors. Both versions correctly ensure they operate on ints.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical of AtCoder-Style problem 'Factorization'-like: one query, M up to about 1e9–1e12, N up to around 1e4–1e7. Number of distinct prime factors of M is small (O(log M)), and each exponent is <= log2(M) (~30).

dominant_ops: Trial division prime factorization of var_6 up to sqrt(var_6) in func_2
Linear precomputation of factorials up to var_8 = var_9 + max(exp_i)
Linear precomputation of modular inverse factorials up to the same bound via backward scan
O(#prime_factors) modular combination evaluations using precomputed factorials

complexity.why: Factorization via trial division is O(sqrt(M)) where M = var_6. The arrays var_2 and var_5 are sized to var_8 = var_9 + max_exp, so both time and space for factorial precomputation are linear in N (var_9) plus the maximum exponent of prime factors of M. Only O(#primes) combinations are evaluated afterwards, so the O(N) precomputation dominates when N is large.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorial and inverse-factorial precomputation up to var_8 = var_9 + max(exp) costs O(var_9) time and memory even though only O(#distinct_primes) combination values are ever needed. For large N (var_9) and small max_exp, this linear work is unnecessary overhead.
Arrays var_2 and var_5 of size O(var_9 + max_exp) can be very large (e.g., N ~ 1e7 or higher), risking high memory usage or MLE for a single combinatorial query.

Every combination uses three modular multiplications with array lookups in func_1, but this cost is minor compared to the large one-time O(N) precomputation that may be wasted if N is big relative to the very small number of combinations.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial precomputation and instead compute each required combination C(N + e - 1, e) directly with a short multiplicative loop whose length depends only on the exponent e of each prime factor, not on N. This removes the linear dependency on N in both time and memory; only O(#primes * max_exp) simple multiplications/divisions and a final modulo are performed.

complexity.why: Factorization of M is still via trial division, O(sqrt(M)). After that, for each prime with exponent e, the code runs a loop of length e to form the numerator and denominator of C(N + e - 1, e). Since the total sum of exponents is bounded by log2(M), this part is O(sum_exp), independent of N. Space is just the prime->exponent map plus a few scalars, O(#primes).

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(M) + N + max_exp) time, O(N + max_exp) space
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + sum_exp) time, O(#distinct_primes) space
complexity_delta.note: The change removes the linear dependency on N by dropping factorial arrays and switching to per-exponent multiplicative computation of combinations. This is asymptotically better when N is large and exponents are small (which they are, since sum_exp = O(log M)), but relies on Python big integers for intermediate C(n,k) values.

transformation_steps: Replace the list-of-primes factor representation (via Counter(func_2(...))) with a direct exponent map (defaultdict(int)) produced during factorization, avoiding a separate Counter pass.
Remove global factorial and inverse-factorial arrays (var_2 and var_5) and the comb helper func_1 that used them.

For each prime exponent e, compute C(N + e - 1, e) via a short multiplicative loop over j = 1..e, multiplying numerator by (N + e - j) and denominator by j, then divide the two integers before taking modulo.
Apply the modulus only on the final combination value for each prime factor (and when multiplying into the running answer), instead of maintaining factorial tables modulo throughout.
Eliminate the O(N)-sized state (arrays) so that both time and memory scale with the number and size of prime exponents, not with N.
trigger_signals: Constraints or profiling indicate that N (var_9/var_3) can be as large as 1e6+ while the factorization of M yields only a handful of primes with very small exponents.
Only a single or very small number of combination values C(N + e - 1, e) are needed, making heavy O(N) combinatorics precomputation overkill.
Memory usage for factorial arrays approaches or exceeds limits (e.g., var_8 ~ 1e7+), or precomputation time dominates the total runtime.
The problem requires just one test case instead of many; amortizing a large precomputation over many queries is not possible.
pitfalls: The fast_code computes the exact integer combination C(n, k) using Python big integers, then reduces modulo 1e9+7. This is correct but can become slow if either n or k grows large enough that C(n, k) has hundreds or thousands of digits; constant factors may explode for higher constraints.

In languages without arbitrary-precision integers (e.g., C++ 64-bit), computing C(n, k) with plain integers and then taking modulo would overflow; a modular inverse-based approach (like slow_code) is required there.

If future constraints change and exponents (e) become large (e.g., e up to 1e5), the multiplicative combination loop O(e) per prime may again become a bottleneck; in that setting, reverting to factorial precomputation up to N + max_exp can be better.

The slow_code’s factorial-based approach is asymptotically sound for moderate N and many combinatorial queries (or larger exponents), but for this single-query, small-exponent setting it wastes time and memory; misjudging this tradeoff can lead to choosing the wrong implementation for the actual constraints.

Care must be taken that integer division (//) in the fast_code is always exact when forming combinations; this relies on the mathematical property that C(n, k) is an integer. Any mistake in the multiplicative loop or overflow behavior (in other languages) can break this assumption.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case; three integers a,b,c. Typical AtCoder-style constraints likely 0 <= a,b,c <= 1e9 or up to about 1e18. Only three numbers, so performance issues stem from number of loop iterations or infinite loops, not input size.

dominant_ops: Iterative loop repeatedly applying a linear transformation to (a,b,c) with modulus and integer division until at least one value becomes odd, or a 1-second wall-clock timeout triggers.

complexity.time: O(T), where T is the number of iterations before some of a,b,c becomes odd; T is typically O(log(max(a,b,c))) but can be infinite for some inputs (e.g., a=b=c even).
complexity.why: Each iteration performs a constant amount of arithmetic (3 mods, 3 divisions, 3 additions, some assignments). No extra data structures are used, so space is constant. The number of iterations depends on how long the values stay all-even under the transformation; in the worst pathological case a=b=c even, the values never change so the loop does not terminate logically, relying only on the time-based bailout.

bottlenecks.detail: When a == b == c and they are even, the transformation a'=(b+c)/2, b'=(a+c)/2, c'=(a+b)/2 leaves (a,b,c) unchanged. The parity condition remains satisfied forever, so the loop is logically infinite; the only termination is the time.time()-based bailout. This can hit TLE or rely on undefined timing behavior.

The loop simulates each step instead of using a closed-form or direct computation of how many times the triple can be halved while keeping all-even parity. This makes runtime proportional to the answer, rather than O(1).

The frequent calls to time.time() inside the loop add overhead, particularly for many iterations. While each call is cheap, putting it in the innermost loop magnifies the cost relative to pure arithmetic.
Using a wall-clock timeout to decide that the answer is -1 is brittle. Execution speed can vary, and the chosen 1-second threshold is tied to environment performance rather than problem logic.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace iterative simulation of the transformation with a direct arithmetic/bitwise formula. Detect the special non-terminating case (a == b == c even) via (a-b)|(b-c) == 0, and otherwise compute the number of iterations using bit operations on that difference pattern to derive how many times the system can be halved while staying all-even. All work is done in O(1) using integer arithmetic, bitwise operators, and bit_length.

complexity.why: The fast code performs a constant number of arithmetic operations: two subtractions, a few bitwise OR/XORs, a modulo by 2, one bit_length call, and a couple of boolean/arithmetical combinations. No loops and no recursion are involved, so runtime does not depend on the magnitude of the integers or the number of theoretical iterations.

complexity_delta.from: O(T) time, where T is the number of simulated steps until parity breaks (or effectively infinite for the equal-even triple), O(1) space.
complexity_delta.to: O(1) time, O(1) space.
complexity_delta.note: The main gain is eliminating potentially unbounded or large-step simulation and replacing it with a direct, constant-time computation based on differences and bit-level properties. It also removes reliance on wall-clock timing for correctness in the infinite-loop case.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the transformation a'=(b+c)/2, b'=(a+c)/2, c'=(a+b)/2 is linear and, except for the special case a=b=c, reduces the problem to tracking parities and factors of 2 rather than explicit values at each step.
Observe that the only non-terminating configuration is when a == b == c and they are even; the triple then remains constant and all-even forever. This can be detected via (a-b)|(b-c) == 0.

Express the number of halving steps until some value becomes odd in terms of the powers of 2 dividing certain combinations/differences of a, b, and c. This allows a direct formula instead of step-by-step simulation.

Encode this formula using bitwise operators, leveraging that the index of the least significant set bit of an integer encodes the exponent of 2 dividing it. The code uses a bit trick `(x ^ ~-x).bit_length() - 1` and boolean masking to compute the needed count.
Remove the loop and the time-based bailout. Replace them with a single evaluation of the arithmetic/bitwise expression, which directly yields either the number of steps or -1 in the equal-even case.
trigger_signals: A loop repeatedly applies a deterministic transformation to a fixed small number of integers (here 3) and stops when a simple predicate (parity condition) fails.
The state space is clearly structured (linear combinations, halving, parity), suggesting the possibility of a closed-form solution or an invariant-based analysis instead of simulation.

The original solution resorts to time-based escape (`time.time()` checks) to avoid infinite loops, which is a strong smell that a logical condition for non-termination exists and can be characterized mathematically.

The per-iteration work is constant but the potential number of iterations is proportional to the logarithm of input magnitude, or even unbounded, making the simulation susceptible to TLE or fragile timeouts.
Bitwise operations and factor-of-two reasoning (parity and powers of 2) are central, indicating that trailing-zero or least-significant-bit techniques may yield an O(1) solution.
pitfalls: The bit-hack expression `(var_4 ^ ~-var_4).bit_length() - 1` is opaque and easy to misuse; small changes (e.g., using a different intermediate or missing a negation) can silently yield incorrect answers.

Python’s handling of negative integers and two’s-complement-style bit operations can be non-intuitive. If constraints ever allow negative inputs or values outside the original problem’s range, the bit-level trick may break or require re-derivation.

Readability and maintainability suffer: future readers (or the author, later) may find it hard to understand or verify the formula-based solution without redoing the math. A more explicit trailing-zero count or clearer formula would be safer.
Relying entirely on clever bit tricks can hide edge cases, such as the all-equal-even case, if not explicitly considered. Missing that case could restore the risk of non-termination or wrong outputs.

Portability: if the solution is ported to another language or environment with different integer/bit semantics (fixed-width vs arbitrary-precision), subtle overflow or sign issues might arise if the derivation assumes Python’s unbounded integers.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical of problems like AtCoder ABC-156 D: n up to ~1e9, with parameters a,b (here var_1,var_5/var_3) up to ~2e5. Loops depend on a,b, not on n.

dominant_ops: math.factorial on moderately large a,b (huge intermediate big integers)
loops computing n*(n-1)*... with modular reduction
modular exponentiation for inverse via pow(x, MOD-2, MOD)

complexity.time: O(a + b + T_fact(a) + T_fact(b)), with T_fact(k) being the cost of computing k! as a full big integer (practically superlinear in k due to growing operand size). Overall dominated by factorial computations.
complexity.space: O(a log a + b log b) bits for storing a! and b! as full big integers before reduction modulo MOD.
complexity.why: The numerator products for C(n,a) and C(n,b) are kept small by taking modulo at every step, so their integer size stays bounded (~30 bits). However, math.factorial(a) and math.factorial(b) compute exact factorials with no modulus until after the fact. For a,b up to around 2e5, a! and b! have on the order of 1e6 decimal digits, so each factorial call builds and stores a huge integer, and pow(fact, MOD-2, MOD) must first reduce this huge integer modulo MOD, incurring large big-integer division cost.

bottlenecks.detail: Using math.factorial(var_1) and math.factorial(var_5) computes enormous integers (a! and b!) before any modular reduction. This causes heavy CPU and memory usage even though only the values modulo 1e9+7 are needed.

pow(var_4, var_12 - 2, var_12) and pow(var_8, var_12 - 2, var_12) are called with huge bases var_4 and var_8 (a! and b!). Python pow will reduce the base modulo MOD, but that initial reduction requires a big-integer modulo operation whose cost is proportional to the size (in digits/bits) of the factorial.

The algorithm conceptually needs factorials under modulo arithmetic, but the implementation computes them exactly over Z (full integers) first, then reduces. This mismatch between needed precision and performed precision is the primary source of slowness.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid ever constructing huge factorial integers by computing both numerator and denominator products directly under modulo arithmetic, and then use modular inverses of these small (mod-reduced) factorial values to form C(n,k). All multiplications are kept within the modulus, so integer sizes remain small and operations fast.

complexity.time: O(a + b + log MOD) ≈ O(a + b)
complexity.space: O(1) extra space beyond input/output (only a handful of integers modulo MOD are stored).
complexity.why: func_1 computes products over ranges (for numerator n*(n-1)*... and denominator 1*2*...*k) while taking modulo after each multiplication, keeping values bounded by MOD. Each combination computation func_2 does O(k) modular multiplications plus one modular exponentiation pow(var_6, MOD-2, MOD), which runs in O(log MOD) multiplications on constant-size integers. Since a,b are up to ~2e5, the linear loops dominate but remain feasible, and integer sizes no longer grow with k, eliminating the huge big-integer overhead seen in the slow version.

complexity_delta.from: O(a + b + T_fact(a) + T_fact(b)) time with large big-int operations; O(a log a + b log b) bits of peak memory due to full factorials.
complexity_delta.to: O(a + b + log MOD) time with only fixed-size modular multiplications; O(1) extra memory (no large intermediate integers).
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically in terms of the loop counts a,b the big-O looks similar, but the removal of full big-integer factorials dramatically reduces constant factors and memory usage, which is crucial for a,b up to ~2e5.

transformation_steps: Replace math.factorial(k) with an explicit loop that multiplies 1*2*...*k while taking modulo MOD at each step, so the intermediate value never exceeds MOD.
Abstract repeated product logic into func_1(start, end, MOD), which computes the product of a contiguous integer range modulo MOD.
Implement combination calculation C(n,k) in func_2 using: numerator = product(n-k+1..n) mod MOD, denominator = product(1..k) mod MOD, then C(n,k) = numerator * inverse(denominator) mod MOD.
Use pow(denominator, MOD-2, MOD) to compute modular inverses under the assumption that MOD is prime (Fermat's little theorem), now applied to small mod-reduced values instead of huge factorials.
Inline or hoist input reading and constant MOD initialization outside of heavy loops to avoid repeated work and minor overheads.
trigger_signals: Use of math.factorial or similar exact big-integer factorial routines in a modular arithmetic problem, especially when only results modulo a prime are needed.
Very large intermediate integers in a profile or memory snapshot that are later reduced modulo a small-ish prime like 1e9+7.

Combination or binomial coefficient calculations with parameters up to ~2e5 or more, where a naive factorial-based approach may still pass complexity checks on paper but performs poorly in practice due to big-int overhead.
Calls to pow(x, MOD-2, MOD) where x is computed as a full factorial instead of a value already reduced modulo MOD.
pitfalls: Modular inverse correctness: The formula pow(x, MOD-2, MOD) assumes MOD is prime and x is not divisible by MOD. Reusing this pattern in other problems where the modulus is not prime would be incorrect.
Range bounds: func_1(var_12, var_13, var_10) multiplies from var_12 up to and including var_13. Off-by-one mistakes here will silently produce wrong combination values.

Zero and edge cases: When k == 0, C(n,0) should be 1. The current fast pattern assumes k >= 1. Adapting this pattern to handle k=0 requires an explicit check to avoid empty ranges and undefined inverses.

Performance regressions for very large k: If k could approach n and n itself were up to 2e5 or more, computing full factorial tables once and reusing them could be faster than recomputing products per query. Here, with only two k values (a and b), the current approach is appropriate; but in multi-query settings, precomputation might be necessary.

Integer overflow assumptions: While Python integers are unbounded, in other languages one must ensure the intermediate multiplications are done in a type wide enough or with modular multiplication that avoids overflow before the modulus is applied.

dominant_ops: Triple nested loops over a,b,c in [1,100] (1e6 iterations)
Integer multiplications and additions computing a^2+b^2+c^2+ab+bc+ca
Array increments var_1[value] for qualifying sums
Use of eval() in input parsing (heavy and unsafe)

complexity.time: O(K^3) with K=100 (effectively ~1e6 iterations, independent of N)
complexity.space: O(M) with M=10001 (fixed-size array) + O(1) temporaries
complexity.why: The runtime is dominated by the three for-loops each running 100 iterations, giving 100^3 computations of the polynomial regardless of the actual input N. Memory is dominated by the fixed array of length 10001 used to accumulate counts.

The loops only explore (a,b,c) where the partial sums can still reach <= N, breaking out once further increments are guaranteed to exceed N.

complexity.space: O(N) for the result array + O(1) for loop temporaries

Nested loops over a,b,c up to sqrt(N) give O((sqrt(N))^3) iterations. Early break conditions prune the loops when even the minimal continuation would exceed N. Memory is now a dynamic array sized to N+1 instead of a fixed 10001.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(K^3) with fixed K=100 (~1e6 iterations regardless of N); Space: O(10001).
complexity_delta.to: Time: O((sqrt(N))^3) = O(N^(3/2)) with strong pruning; Space: O(N).
complexity_delta.note: Under the original AtCoder-style constraints (N<=10000), the worst-case asymptotic work remains similar in scale (since sqrt(10000)=100), but the optimized version greatly reduces work for smaller N and is structurally scalable if N were increased, while also reducing constant factors (no eval, fewer iterations via early breaks, and better memory locality).

constraints_guess.notes: Typical job scheduling with deadlines; N up to ~1e5–2e5, processing times/deadlines up to ~1e9. Needs O(n log n) or better with efficient I/O.

dominant_ops: Reading N job pairs and sorting them by deadline; linear scan to accumulate processing times and check feasibility.

complexity.why: We store all N jobs in a list, then sort that list once (O(n log n)) and perform a single O(n) pass over it. Extra helper functions and imports do not change asymptotic complexity, only constants.

bottlenecks.detail: Uses eval(input()) wrapped inside func_4 for reading N, and func_1 plus list(map(int, input().split())) in a loop, with function-call overhead on every line. eval is slower than int and unsafe.
Every line of job input goes through func_1, and N is read through func_4, adding Python call overhead inside the hot path.

Imports math, itertools, bisect, copy, deque, Counter, Decimal and sets recursionlimit, defines multiple unused helpers (func_2, func_3, func_5, func_6). These add slight startup cost and noise but not major runtime impact.

Reuses names like func_2 as both a function and later a list, and func_4 as both a function and a loop variable. This does not slow down asymptotically but harms clarity and can complicate maintenance or debugging.

FastAudit.core_idea: Read all jobs directly, sort by deadline (and then by processing time for tie-breaking), accumulate processing times in order, and verify that the cumulative time never exceeds each job's deadline. This is the standard greedy schedule feasibility check.

complexity.why: Same algorithm as the slow version: store N jobs, sort once by deadline with a key function, and perform a single linear pass. Using direct input calls and list comprehensions minimizes constant factors but not big-O.

complexity_delta.to: O(n log n)

constraints_guess.notes: Single query: given k (up to about 1e5), output the k-th 'Lunlun' number (non-negative integer whose adjacent digits differ by at most 1). Depth of generation in original code is fixed to at most 10 digits, giving O(3^10) total candidates (~1.7e5).

dominant_ops: Recursive DFS over digit strings up to length 10, branching factor up to 3 per level.
Appending every generated number to a Python list.
Sorting the entire list of generated numbers at the end (var_1.sort()).

complexity.time: O(B^D + N log N) where D is max digit length (~10), B≈3 (branching factor), and N is number of generated numbers (~B^D). With fixed D=10 this is effectively constant (~1e5 operations), but asymptotically exponential in D and includes a full sort.
complexity.space: O(N + D) where N is number of generated numbers (list storage) and D is recursion depth (call stack). For D=10, N≈O(3^10) ≈ 1.7e5.
complexity.why: func_1 does a full DFS, appending on every node before checking depth; this explores the complete search tree of all valid numbers up to length 10, regardless of k. After generation, it sorts the entire list to obtain the order, which costs O(N log N). Recursion retains a call stack of depth up to D.

bottlenecks.detail: Generates all valid numbers up to 10 digits even if k is small; work is proportional to total search space, not to requested index k.
Sorts the full list of generated numbers (var_1.sort()) just to select the k-th number, adding an O(N log N) step that is avoidable with ordered generation.
Recursive calls for every node in the search tree incur function-call overhead and use the Python call stack; this is less cache-friendly and more overhead-heavy than an iterative BFS.
If max digit length D were increased, DFS enumeration cost grows as O(3^D) and quickly becomes infeasible, while k may remain modest.
Using eval(input()) is unsafe and slower than int(input()); not the main hotspot but bad practice and unnecessary overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Generate Lunlun numbers in increasing order iteratively (BFS-style) by expanding existing numbers to their valid children and appending them to the same list, stopping as soon as the list length exceeds k. This avoids generating the entire search space and eliminates the final sort.

complexity.time: O(k * d) where k is the requested index and d is the digit length of the k-th Lunlun number (at most ~10 here). Each of the first k numbers is expanded at most once, and digit operations are linear in number length.
complexity.space: O(k) to store the generated Lunlun numbers up to index k. There is no recursion; no extra stack beyond loop variables.
complexity.why: The loop `for var_1 in var_4:` effectively performs a BFS over the state space: starting with [1..9], it expands each number exactly once, appending its children (next digits differing by at most 1) to the end of the same list. Because BFS visits numbers in non-decreasing numeric order, the k-th generated element is the desired answer, so we can break once `len(var_4) > k` and avoid sorting or exploring deeper nodes unnecessarily.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(3^D + N log N), Space: O(N + D), where D is max digit length and N≈O(3^D) generated numbers (full search space).
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(k * d), Space: O(k), where k is requested index and d is digit length of the k-th number.
complexity_delta.note: With D fixed at 10 and k up to 1e5, the original is borderline but still OK; the refactor makes the cost linear in k rather than in the theoretical maximum search space and avoids the O(N log N) sort.

transformation_steps: Replace depth-first recursive generation (func_1) with iterative BFS-like expansion by looping over the evolving list of numbers.
Exploit the invariant that children of a number are formed by appending digits that differ by at most 1 from its last digit (handling boundary digits 0 and 9 specially).
Generate children in numeric order for each parent (from last_digit-1 to last_digit+1), ensuring global non-decreasing order under BFS traversal.
Accumulate generated numbers directly into the same list that is being iterated (queue-like behavior), so each number is processed exactly once.
Introduce an early stopping condition (`if len(var_4) > var_3: break`) to stop generating as soon as the k-th number is obtainable, removing the need for full-space enumeration.
Drop the global sort step and instead rely on BFS generation order to guarantee that `var_4[k-1]` is the answer.
Avoid recursion and its stack overhead by using simple loops and list appends.
trigger_signals: Algorithm generates all combinatorial candidates (full DFS) even when only the k-th in order is needed.
Presence of a global sort on all generated candidates simply to pick the k-th element.
Recursive depth bounded but search space size grows exponentially with digit length or allowed depth.
Performance constraints where k is relatively small compared to the full search space.
Stack-depth concerns or function-call overhead from heavy recursion.

constraints_guess.n_max: ≈1e9 for each of the three integers (must assume large to justify O(1) math solution)
constraints_guess.notes: Three scalar integers; slow code does a double loop up to (var_1+1)*(var_4+1), which becomes infeasible once var_1 and var_4 are much above ~10^4. The fast solution suggests the intended constraints require constant-time arithmetic.

dominant_ops: Two nested for-loops over var_7 in [0, var_1] and var_8 in [0, var_4], performing simple arithmetic and comparisons each iteration.

complexity.why: The algorithm visits every pair (var_7, var_8) in the (var_1+1) by (var_4+1) grid exactly once, doing O(1) work per pair, and keeps only a few scalar variables.

bottlenecks.detail: The exhaustive search over all (var_7, var_8) combinations causes O(var_1 * var_4) iterations, which is prohibitive when var_1 and var_4 are large (e.g., 10^5 → 10^10 iterations).

Within the nested loops, the expression var_2 - (var_1 - var_7) * (var_4 - var_8) recomputes multiplications every iteration. Even if algebraically simplified, it cannot fix the asymptotic O(var_1 * var_4) behavior.
Using eval(input()) is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()), but its overhead is negligible compared to the double loop when inputs are large.

FastAudit.core_idea: Interpret var_2 - (var_1 - var_7) * (var_4 - var_8) as the number of affected cells when selecting var_7 rows and var_8 columns in a var_1 by var_4 grid. Each selected row covers var_4 cells, each selected column covers var_1 cells, and overlaps are subtracted as var_7 * var_8. To reach at least var_3 cells with the minimum number of selections (var_7 + var_8), it is always optimal to select only along the longer side of the grid, because each selection on the longer side covers at least as many new cells as any selection on the shorter side. Thus the minimal number of selections is ceil(var_3 / max(var_1, var_4)), which can be computed directly as (var_3 + max_side - 1) // max_side.

complexity.why: The optimized code performs a constant number of integer operations and a single print, independent of the magnitudes of var_1, var_4, and var_3.

complexity_delta.from: O(var_1 * var_4) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(1) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: The exhaustive search over all row/column selections is replaced with a derived closed-form solution using a ceiling division by the larger dimension.

transformation_steps: Recognize that var_2 = var_1 * var_4 is the total number of cells in a var_1 by var_4 grid, and (var_1 - var_7) * (var_4 - var_8) is the count of untouched cells after selecting var_7 rows and var_8 columns.
Rewrite var_6 = var_2 - (var_1 - var_7) * (var_4 - var_8) as the number of affected cells: var_6 = var_1 * var_4 - (var_1 - var_7)(var_4 - var_8) = var_1 * var_8 + var_4 * var_7 - var_7 * var_8.
Formulate the optimization problem explicitly: find nonnegative integers (var_7, var_8) minimizing var_7 + var_8 subject to var_1 * var_8 + var_4 * var_7 - var_7 * var_8 >= var_3.

Observe that each selection on the longer side of the rectangle (max(var_1, var_4)) initially covers that many distinct cells; combining selections along both sides yields overlaps that reduce marginal gain, so mixing sides is never better than taking all selections along the longer side for minimizing the count.

Deduce that the optimal strategy is to select only along the dimension max(var_1, var_4), giving at least max_side new cells per selection until the target var_3 is achieved; thus the minimum number of selections is ceil(var_3 / max_side).
Implement the closed-form answer as (var_3 + max_side - 1) // max_side, replacing the double loop with a constant-time calculation.

pitfalls: Incorrectly assuming the closed form without a proof: for some grid-based problems, combinations of rows and columns can be optimal; the derivation must justify that taking all selections along the longer side indeed minimizes var_7 + var_8.

Reliance on eval(input()) is unsafe and unnecessary; while not a performance bottleneck here, it should generally be replaced with int(input()) in production or contest code.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical for this AtCoder task: N up to 1e5, each A_i up to 1e6; need to classify as pairwise / setwise / not coprime.

dominant_ops: Building a full prime-factor table up to 1e6 with a sieve-like method, then factoring each input number by repeated division using precomputed prime factors; plus a pass to compute global GCD.

complexity.time: O(M log log M + N log A_max)
complexity.why: func_2(10**6) builds an array var_2 of size M=1e6+1 and runs a modified sieve: even loop O(M/2) and odd loop similar to Eratosthenes, totaling O(M log log M). Then func_3 factors each of the N numbers by repeatedly dividing by var_2[var_3]; each factorization takes O(log A_max) divisions in worst case. func_1 does an O(N) GCD accumulation. The sieve array var_2 dominates memory: O(M) integers.

bottlenecks.detail: func_2 always constructs a sieve up to 10**6 regardless of the actual maximum value present in var_1, doing up to ~1e6 operations and allocating an array of size ~1e6 even for small inputs.
The sieve stores one integer per value up to 10**6; this is acceptable for the given constraints but is the main memory cost and would not scale well if A_max were larger.

In func_3, for numbers with high prime powers (e.g., p^k), the while-loop repeatedly divides by the same prime factor; although the per-number complexity is still logarithmic, there is a nontrivial constant factor from repeated divisions.
Using eval(input()) to read var_7 is slower and potentially unsafe; however, its performance impact is negligible compared to sieve and factorization work.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid constructing a runtime sieve up to 1e6 by hard-coding the list/set of primes up to sqrt(1e6)=1000 and using that fixed small prime table for trial division when factorizing each input number. This trades one large O(M) precomputation and O(M) memory for a small, constant-sized prime set and per-number trial division.

complexity.why: With primes up to √A_max pre-listed (here primes up to about 1000), each number is factorized by testing divisibility against this fixed prime set. For A_i ≤ 1e6, at most 168 primes up to 997 are tested, which is a constant. Thus factorization is effectively O(1) per number and the total time is O(N). No O(M)-sized sieve array is built; the prime set is a constant-sized literal, so asymptotic extra memory is O(1).

from.time: O(M log log M + N log A_max)

to.time: O(N * π(√A_max)) (≈ O(N) for fixed A_max ≤ 1e6)

complexity_delta.note: The modified approach removes the O(M) sieve over all values up to 1e6 and replaces it with trial division using a constant-size prime table, yielding lower memory usage and lower or comparable time for the given constraints. For much larger A_max, the original sieve scales better, but under A_max=1e6 the constant-size table is competitive or faster.

transformation_steps: Remove the dynamic sieve construction func_2(10**6) and the associated O(M)-sized array of prime factors.
Introduce a hard-coded set/list of prime numbers up to sqrt(A_max) (here up to around 1000), so the prime table is created at import time as a constant literal with effectively O(1) cost.
Replace factorization via indexed lookup in sieve (var_2[var_3]) with trial division by primes from the constant prime set until the residual becomes 1 or a prime > sqrt(A_max).

Maintain the same global and per-number prime-factor tracking logic (var_8 for per-number uniqueness, var_9 for across-all-numbers uniqueness) to detect shared prime factors and conclude pairwise coprimality.
Rely on the problem’s numeric bounds (A_i ≤ 10^6) so that primes up to 1000 suffice for complete factorization, making π(√A_max) a small constant.
