dominant_ops: For each integer from 1 to N, repeatedly divide by 10 and take % 10 to accumulate digit sum (implemented using float division and math.floor).

complexity.time: O(N * log10(N)) (intended), but actual code risks non-termination due to float division / overflow in loop iterations.
complexity.why: Each number i in [1, N] is processed digit-by-digit; number of digits is O(log10(i)), so total work is proportional to sum over i of digits(i) ≈ O(N log N). Only a few scalar variables are used.

bottlenecks.detail: Digit extraction inside the outer loop produces O(N log N) work; this is expected for this direct approach.

Uses `var_4 /= 10` (true division) instead of integer division. `var_4` becomes a float and approaches 0 without ever reaching 0, so `while var_4 > 0:` may effectively never terminate (or at least does many more iterations than intended).
`var_7 += math.floor(var_4 % 10)` and `var_4 /= 10` make `%` and division operate on floats, which are slower and less precise than integer ops here.
Repeated `math.floor` calls inside the tight inner loop add overhead that is avoidable when working with integers.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use only integer arithmetic for digit extraction: integer division `// 10` to drop the last digit and `% 10` to get the last digit, eliminating floating-point operations and `math.floor`. Loop until the temporary value becomes exactly 0.

complexity.why: Same asymptotic algorithm (iterate 1..N and strip digits), but each digit operation is now a constant-time integer op without extra overhead. No additional memory structures are introduced.

complexity_delta.from: Intended O(N log N) but with potential non-termination / huge overhead due to float division in the digit loop.
complexity_delta.to: Reliable O(N log N) with low constant factors using only integer ops.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is the same in big-O terms, but the modified code both fixes a correctness/termination bug and significantly reduces per-iteration cost.

transformation_steps: Replaced `var_4 /= 10` with integer division `var_5 = var_5 // 10` in the digit-stripping loop to ensure the value eventually hits 0 and stays integral.
Changed loop condition from `while var_4 > 0:` to `while var_5 != 0:` to avoid issues caused by floating-point approximation; integer comparison is exact.
Removed `math.floor` and relied on integer `% 10` directly: `var_7 += var_5 % 10` instead of `var_7 += math.floor(var_4 % 10)`.
Eliminated the use of floats in digit processing, thereby removing the need for the `math` module and reducing function-call overhead in the inner loop.
Kept the same high-level algorithm (iterate from 1 to N and sum qualifying indices), preserving the O(N log N) structure but with lower constant factors and correct termination.
trigger_signals: Use of `/=` (true division) inside a loop intended to strip digits, combined with a `> 0` termination condition.
Presence of `math.floor` around a `% 10` operation, suggesting unnecessary float handling for what should be integer digit extraction.
Tight inner loop performing function calls (`math.floor`) and float arithmetic, a classic hotspot in performance traces.
Loop variable type changes from int to float mid-loop, which is suspicious for digit-processing code.
pitfalls: Even after optimization, the algorithm is O(N log N); for significantly larger N (e.g., 10^8), a different strategy would be required.
Using `/` instead of `//` anywhere in digit-stripping logic reintroduces float behavior and potential non-termination or precision bugs.
Changing the loop condition back to a float-based comparison (like `> 0` on a float) can again depend on subtle floating-point behavior.
If the input constraints were much larger than anticipated, additional optimizations or mathematical shortcuts (e.g., counting by digit DP) might be necessary.

constraints_guess.notes: State space uses bitmasks of size 2^n; Python solution with O(m * 2^n) is still used, so n is likely <= 20. Number of items m (var_7 / var_4) appears moderate (<=100) from typical set-cover DP problems.

dominant_ops: Nested enumeration over all bitmasks and many of their submasks, plus scanning all items for each mask. Heavy use of bin(x).count('1') and mask-relationship checks inside large loops.

complexity.why: Building var_22 and var_19 costs O(2^n * n) due to bin().count('1'). Computing var_13 uses an outer loop over all 2^n masks and an inner loop over all m items: O(2^n * m). The final DP for var_12, which tries all ways to split a mask into two submasks, effectively behaves like a subset-convolution style DP: for each of the 2^n masks it iterates over subsets of all sizes up to half its popcount. This leads to ~O(3^n) behavior overall, which is prohibitive for n around 20.

bottlenecks.detail: The DP over var_12 performs a near subset-convolution: for every mask, it considers combinations of two submasks by iterating over all masks in var_19[k] and filtering by subset tests. This induces roughly O(3^n) time, which blows up quickly for moderate n.
Computing var_13 by scanning all items for every mask is O(2^n * m); while acceptable alone, combined with the O(3^n) subset splitting becomes too slow.

Uses bin(mask).count('1') for every mask to compute popcount, which is relatively slow in Python when repeated 2^n times. A DP or builtin bit-counting (int.bit_count in newer Python) would be faster, though this is secondary to the algorithmic issue.
var_19 groups masks by popcount and is iterated many times; repeatedly scanning these lists for every outer mask adds substantial overhead in Python due to interpreter-level loop costs.

FastAudit.core_idea: Define dp[mask] as the minimum total cost to achieve exactly the set of skills represented by 'mask'. For each item with cost c and skill-mask s, update dp[new_mask] = min(dp[new_mask], dp[mask] + c) where new_mask = mask | s over all existing masks. This is a standard forward subset DP that grows reachable skill sets item by item.

complexity.why: There are 2^n possible skill sets. For each of m items, the algorithm iterates once over all masks (0 .. 2^n - 1) and performs O(1) work per mask (one OR, one addition, one comparison and assignment). The dp array holds one value per mask, so space is linear in 2^n.

complexity_delta.from: O(2^n * m + 3^n) time, O(2^n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(m * 2^n) time, O(2^n) space
complexity_delta.note: The improved solution eliminates the expensive subset-convolution-style DP and uses a direct item-by-item subset DP, reducing the exponential factor from ~3^n to ~2^n.

transformation_steps: Redefine the DP state to be directly over skill subsets achieved by some combination of items: dp[mask] = minimal total cost for exactly this mask (rather than trying to precompute single-item superset costs and then combine arbitrary submasks).
Replace the subset-splitting DP over var_12 with a simple forward DP over masks: for each item (cost, skill-mask), iterate all masks once and relax dp[mask | skill_mask].
Remove the grouping by popcount (var_19, var_22) and the costly triple nested loops that attempt to split each mask into two smaller masks; this is unnecessary when we accumulate items sequentially.

Avoid scanning all masks per popcount for each outer mask; instead, structure the loops as 'for item in items: for mask in range(1 << n): ...', which is cache-friendly and minimizes Python-level loop overhead.

Keep a single dp array updated in-place for each item, relying on the fact that reusing an item multiple times cannot improve the mask (bitwise OR is idempotent), so forward iteration over masks is safe.
trigger_signals: Presence of nested loops over all masks combined with another iteration over masks grouped by popcount (i.e., masks-in-masks loops), a hallmark of 3^n subset-convolution-like complexity.
Use of popcount-based bucketization (var_19) and repeated subset checks (mask_a & mask_b == mask_a) inside inner loops, indicating expensive subset enumeration.
Overall loop structure: 'for mask in 2^n: for size in O(n): for candidate_mask in many masks of that size', which scales very poorly in n.
DP logic attempting to combine two arbitrary submasks for each mask (var_18 and var_17 = mask ^ var_18), rather than a more direct incremental construction over items.
Use of bin(x).count('1') in a 2^n loop, which hints at per-mask overhead that becomes significant at n close to 20.
pitfalls: When switching to the item-by-item DP, one must ensure the update order does not accidentally allow beneficial reuse of the same item in a way that changes reachable masks. Here, since OR-ing the same skill set multiple times does not change the mask, in-place forward iteration is safe; in other problems (e.g., knapsack on sums) backward iteration would be required.

It is easy to mistakenly define dp[mask] as 'minimum cost of an item that covers mask' (as in var_13) and then try to combine masks; this invites complicated and slow subset-convolution logic. Defining dp over combinations of items from the outset simplifies both correctness and complexity.
Care must be taken to initialize dp correctly: dp[0] = 0 and all others = INF. Forgetting this or mishandling INF checks can cause incorrect -1 outputs or overflow-like behavior.

For large n, storing explicit lists like var_19 of all masks per popcount is extremely memory- and time-inefficient; such structures should be avoided unless a true subset-convolution with efficient implementation is intended.

Bitmask operations are fast, but Python-level loops are not. Seemingly modest algorithmic overhead like an extra factor of n or another exponential (3^n vs 2^n) quickly dominates; always compute rough operation counts for n near its limit.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer N, need to output the N-th specially-constructed integer (Lunlun-like). N up to about 1e5 in typical tasks.

dominant_ops: heap pushes/pops for each generated number
set membership and insert operations
repeated string<->int conversions on every popped value
final conversion of set to list and full sort

complexity.why: Each accepted number is inserted into a set and later into a list; a heap is used for priority processing with heappop/heappush costing O(log M) where M is heap size. Up to a constant multiple of new candidates (up to ~6) are pushed per pop. Finally, all collected numbers are sorted, costing O(M log M). Overall, for N outputs and M = Θ(N) unique numbers, this yields Θ(N log N) time and Θ(N) memory.

bottlenecks.detail: Uses a min-heap plus a deduplication set and then an additional full sort, even though only the N-th smallest value is needed and the generation can be done in sorted order directly.
Priority queue (heap) is unnecessary; a simple queue/linear list traversal suffices because the generative process naturally forms a BFS tree whose visitation order is already non-decreasing.
Generates many duplicate candidates (same integer from different parents) and filters them with a set, increasing heap and set traffic.
For each popped number, converts int->str, then extracts first/last digits, then reconverts to int multiple times when pushing neighbors, adding significant constant-factor overhead.
After collecting all values in the set, converting to list and sorting them performs an additional O(N log N) pass that could be avoided by streaming the sequence in order.

The loop condition `while var_3 + 100 >= 0` forces at least N+100 heap pops even though only N distinct numbers are required, and the termination is not tightly coupled to the number of unique outputs collected.

FastAudit.core_idea: Generate the sequence in BFS order directly using a growing list as a queue: start from digits 1–9, and for each current number append its valid neighbors formed by adding digits differing by at most 1 at the end. This visitation order is already non-decreasing, so once the list length exceeds N you can stop and take the N-th element without any heap or sorting.

complexity.why: Each number in the list is processed at most once. For each processed number, we append up to three children (based on last digit), and we stop when we have generated just over N numbers. All operations on the Python list are amortized O(1), and there is no final sort or priority queue maintenance, giving linear time and linear memory in N.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: By eliminating the heap, deduplication set, and final sort, and instead performing a single BFS-style pass that yields numbers in order, the asymptotic time improves from N log N to N while using comparable memory.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the required numbers form a tree where children are constructed by appending digits differing by at most 1 from the last digit.
Observe that a simple BFS traversal over this tree, starting from digits 1–9, naturally visits numbers in non-decreasing order; no heap or sorting is needed.
Replace the heap-based loop with a linear traversal over a list that is simultaneously used as a queue: iterate `for x in list`, appending each node’s children to the same list.
Stop the traversal as soon as the list length exceeds N instead of using an approximate bound like `var_3 + 100 >= 0`, tying termination directly to the amount of data actually needed.
Access the answer directly as the (N-1)-th element of the list, avoiding any postprocessing such as converting sets to lists or sorting.
trigger_signals: Use of a priority queue plus a final sort despite needing only the N-th value of a monotonically generatable sequence.
Presence of a deduplication set (`var_5`) that indicates many duplicates are being generated and then discarded.
Loop condition independent from the exact count of produced results (`while var_3 + 100 >= 0`), suggesting over-generation of candidates.
Heavy string<->integer conversions inside the inner loop for basic digit operations that can be structured more simply.
Asymmetry between a conceptually BFS-like generation pattern and the choice of a heap instead of a FIFO queue or list.
pitfalls: When switching to a BFS-on-list implementation, ensure the list iteration semantics allow appending while iterating (as in Python) and that the loop will eventually terminate once N elements are generated.
Be careful to handle edge digits 0 and 9 correctly so that you do not generate invalid successors (e.g., negative digits or digits > 9).
Do not introduce an explicit queue pop(0) operation on Python lists, which is O(N); rely on index-based iteration or collections.deque if you need explicit queue semantics.
Avoid unnecessary global over-generation: always tie the stopping condition directly to the required count N to keep memory and time linear.
Confirm that the BFS generation order indeed matches the required sorted order for the problem; if a different ordering is required, a heap or sorting step might still be necessary.

constraints_guess.notes: Single array of N integers; need to compute sum of squared deviations from an integer center close to the mean. Typical AtCoder-style constraints suggest N up to 1e5–2e5, values up to ~1e9.

dominant_ops: Import and initialization of NumPy
Conversion of Python list to NumPy array (O(N))
Vectorized subtraction, squaring, and summation over N elements

complexity.why: Reading N integers into a list is O(N). Converting to a NumPy array is O(N). The vectorized (var_2 - var_4) ** 2 and subsequent np.sum each touch all N elements, so overall linear in N. The array itself requires O(N) extra memory.

bottlenecks.detail: Importing NumPy and creating a NumPy array for a single linear pass is heavy; import time plus array allocation overhead dominate for competitive-programming-style input sizes.
Data is read as a Python list, then copied into a NumPy array (int32), then upcast to float64 when dividing by var_1 and subtracting var_4 (float). Multiple conversions increase constant factors.

var_4 is obtained via floating-point division and round(...), so the expression (var_2 - var_4) ** 2 is executed in floating point, which is slower and adds unnecessary precision concerns for a pure-integer objective.
Using NumPy for a straightforward O(N) scalar reduction is less efficient than pure-Python integer arithmetic in environments where NumPy is not optimized (e.g., many online judges).

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid NumPy and floats entirely. Use pure Python integers: compute the sum of the array, derive candidate integer centers as floor and ceil of the average, and evaluate the sum of squared deviations for each candidate with a simple loop, taking the minimum.

complexity.why: Reading N integers into a list is O(N). For each of at most two candidate centers, we compute sum((a_i - center)^2) over all elements, which is 2 * O(N) = O(N). The list of N elements is stored, so memory is O(N).

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(N), Space: O(N) using NumPy with float operations
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(N), Space: O(N) using pure Python integer operations
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity remains O(N), but constant factors are reduced by eliminating NumPy import/array allocations and float arithmetic; correctness is also clarified by checking both floor and ceil centers explicitly.

transformation_steps: Remove NumPy import and the conversion of the input list into a NumPy array.
Replace np.sum(var_2) / var_1 and round(...) with a purely integer-based approach: compute total sum and derive floor and ceil of the average via integer division.
Evaluate the objective sum((a_i - center)^2) using Python loops (list comprehension or generator) for each candidate center and take the minimum.
Avoid float intermediates by keeping all quantities as Python ints, leveraging arbitrary-precision integers to prevent overflow and precision issues.
trigger_signals: Use of a heavy numerical library (NumPy) just for a single linear scan and reduction.
Additional O(N) data copy from Python list to NumPy array with no subsequent reuse.
Float division and round in a problem that is naturally expressed with integer arithmetic.
Competitive-programming context where import and allocation overhead are often the dominant cost for such simple tasks.
pitfalls: The modified code uses int(eval(input())) instead of int(input()), which is slower and unsafe in general; eval is unnecessary and should be avoided.

The inner sum uses a list comprehension ([...]) instead of a generator expression, incurring a small extra O(N) transient list allocation; using sum((...) for ...) would be slightly more memory-friendly.
Care must be taken that the number of read integers matches N; neither version performs validation, so malformed input will behave unpredictably.

When porting the idea, ensure integer centers are handled correctly: for quadratic cost functions, checking floor and ceil of the mean is sufficient, but using only round(mean) can be ambiguous due to tie-breaking conventions of round.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case. N and the total sum of prime-factor exponents of M are bounded so that N + sum_exponents <= ~2 * 10^5. M is up to around 10^9–10^12 so that trial division up to sqrt(M) is acceptable.

dominant_ops: Precomputation of factorials and inverse factorials up to ~2 * 10^5 with modular multiplications.
Prime factorization of M using trial division over consecutive integers from 2 up to sqrt(M).
Dictionary updates for storing prime -> exponent during factorization.
A small number of binomial coefficient evaluations using precomputed tables.

complexity.time: O(L + sqrt(M)) where L = 2 * 10^5 (fixed upper bound for factorials).
complexity.space: O(L) for factorial, inverse, and inverse-factorial arrays.
complexity.why: Factorials/inverses are built once in a loop of length L. Prime factorization loops i from 2 upward and stops when i * i > M; in the worst case this is O(sqrt(M)). The number of combinations computed is bounded by the number of distinct prime factors of M, which is small, so that part is negligible.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorization loop increments by 1 over all integers (2, 3, 4, ...) instead of skipping even numbers after handling 2. This roughly doubles the iterations in the factorization phase for large M.
Use of a defaultdict(int) for prime exponents adds some overhead (hashing, dynamic growth) when only a small fixed number of factors is expected.
Factorial and inverse tables are always built up to 2 * 10^5 + 10 regardless of the actual N + sum_exponents needed, incurring a constant but non-trivial preprocessing cost.

FastAudit.core_idea: Maintain a combinatorics helper class that precomputes factorials and inverse-factorials using a single modular exponentiation and a backward pass, and perform a slightly more efficient prime factorization that treats factor 2 separately and then iterates only over odd candidates while updating the square bound incrementally. This preserves asymptotic complexity but reduces constant factors in both the factorization and combinatorics preprocessing.

complexity.time: O(L + sqrt(M)) where L is the maximum needed n in nCk (typically ~2 * 10^5), plus an extra O(log MOD) for one modular exponentiation.
complexity.space: O(L) for factorial and inverse-factorial arrays.
complexity.why: Factorials are built in a single forward pass. Inverse-factorials are generated from a single pow(fact[L], MOD-2, MOD) followed by a linear backward loop, so total precomputation remains O(L). Factorization still considers O(sqrt(M)) trial divisors but halves the search space by skipping even numbers and uses lighter-weight counters instead of a dictionary. The number of combination calls is small and each is O(1) with table lookups.

complexity_delta.from: O(L + sqrt(M)) time, O(L) space, with linear trial division over all integers and dictionary-based accumulation of exponents.
complexity_delta.to: O(L + sqrt(M)) time, O(L) space, but with ~1/2 the factorization iterations and cheaper combination/inverse-factorial computation (O(L) + one O(log MOD) pow).
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic bounds remain the same; improvements are mainly in constant factors and cleaner separation of concerns via a combinatorics class.

transformation_steps: Replace the dictionary-based prime factorization (trial division over every integer) with a factorization that handles 2 separately and then tests only odd divisors, updating the square limit incrementally.
Replace global factorial/inverse/inverse-factorial arrays with a combinatorics helper class that encapsulates these tables and exposes an O(1) nCk method.

Change inverse-factorial computation from accumulating the product of modular inverses to a backward pass starting from fact[n]^(MOD-2), reducing conceptual complexity and centralizing the use of Fermat's little theorem.
Add symmetry optimization in combination computation (use k = min(k, n-k)) to reduce lookup and multiplication work in edge cases with large k.
trigger_signals: Precomputation over a fixed large bound (2 * 10^5) dominates runtime when M has a small factorization and only a few combinations are needed.
Profiling would show a large fraction of time spent in the trial-division factorization loop, especially for M near its upper limit.
Desire to reuse combinatorial tables cleanly and avoid scattering global arrays and helper functions across the solution.
pitfalls: The optimized prime-factorization routine must be careful to keep track of the remaining unfactored part; failing to yield a final exponent of 1 for a leftover prime would give incorrect results.
The factorial/inverse-factorial tables must be sized to at least max_needed_n = max over all combination arguments; under-allocating by even 1 leads to index errors or incorrect nCk values.
The use of pow(x, MOD-2, MOD) assumes MOD is prime (so that Fermat's little theorem applies); changing MOD to a non-prime value would silently break the fast version.
When applying the symmetry optimization k -> min(k, n-k), the code must still handle edge cases like k < 0 or k > n correctly and return 0 in those cases.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic scheduling-with-deadlines feasibility check (sum of durations vs deadlines after sorting). Typical contest constraints suggest up to 1e5–2e5 jobs; time cost dominated by sort and I/O.

dominant_ops: Reading N lines of integer pairs via helper function func_3
Sorting list of N pairs by second element using lambda key
Single pass over N sorted pairs to accumulate and compare deadlines

complexity.why: All meaningful work is: (1) reading O(N) pairs, (2) sorting N elements by key (O(N log N)), (3) linear sweep O(N). Sort dominates asymptotically; loop and I/O add linear cost with sizable constants.

bottlenecks.detail: Input is read through sys.stdin with multiple small wrapper functions (func_3, func_7, etc.). Each call to func_3 incurs a Python function call + list() construction overhead on hot path, instead of an inlined parse around a locally bound readline.
sort(key=lambda var_8: var_8[1]) uses a Python lambda as key, which is slightly slower than using operator.itemgetter(1) due to per-call overhead and attribute lookup.

Even after detecting a missed deadline (var_5 > var_4), the code only flips var_3 = False and continues iterating over all remaining tasks. No break/return, so worst-case always processes all N elements.

Several input helpers (func_2, func_4, func_5, func_6, func_8, func_1) are defined but unused. While they do not affect runtime after import, they indicate an over-generic template and distract from optimizing the main hot path.

Accessing var_7.readline through the sys.stdin object each time is marginally slower than binding readline to a local variable (e.g., var_5 = sys.stdin.readline), which avoids repeated attribute lookups in tight loops.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the same greedy scheduling algorithm (sort by deadline, track cumulative time) but reduce constant factors on the hot path: bind readline locally, parse inputs in-line without extra helper calls, use operator.itemgetter for the sort key, and exit early from the loop as soon as a deadline violation is found.

complexity.why: The algorithm remains the same: read N pairs, sort by the second component (O(N log N)), then scan once (O(N)). Only constant factors improve via more efficient I/O, key functions, and early termination when possible.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N log N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity unchanged; performance gains come from reduced interpreter overhead (I/O, sorting key, loop exit behavior), which is crucial near tight contest time limits for large N.

transformation_steps: Bind sys.stdin.readline to a local variable (var_5) to avoid repeated attribute lookups and indirection via helper functions for each line read.
Inline integer parsing inside the list comprehension: use list(map(int, var_5().rstrip().split())) instead of calling func_3, eliminating an extra Python function call per line.
Replace sort(key=lambda var_8: var_8[1]) with sort(key=itemgetter(1)) to use a faster C-implemented key function and avoid lambda overhead.
Move all work into a dedicated function func_1 with a local scope to slightly speed up variable access (locals are faster than globals in CPython).
Introduce early termination: when cumulative time exceeds the current deadline (var_6 > var_4), print("No") and return immediately instead of scanning the remaining tasks.
Remove generic/unneeded parsing helpers from the hot path so that only the minimal logic needed for this problem executes.
trigger_signals: Runtime close to or exceeding time limits on large N despite an O(N log N) algorithm, hinting at Python interpreter overhead rather than algorithmic complexity.
Profile or contest feedback showing that the sort + loop region is hot but algorithmically optimal already.
Use of lambda as sort key and multiple thin wrapper functions on the critical input-reading path, both of which are common constant-factor offenders in Python.
Workload with many lines of input and no opportunity to amortize I/O overhead, making efficient use of readline and minimal parsing essential.
pitfalls: Early-return logic must ensure output is produced exactly once and covers all branches; forgetting the final print("Yes") path or misplacing return can change behavior.
Relying on itemgetter(1) assumes all items have at least two elements; if input format changes, this can cause IndexError instead of a clearer failure.
Aggressive micro-optimizations can harm readability; over-templated I/O wrappers as in the slow_code can obscure the actual data being read and make future maintenance harder.
Removing rstrip() must be done carefully: trailing newline characters can interfere with split() or int() parsing if assumptions change.

Assuming that skipping a break after a deadline is safe: in problems where later tasks might reset or otherwise influence the feasibility, early exit would be incorrect. For this classic greedy condition, it is safe, but the pattern is not universally applicable.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer input used as sequence index. Original code preallocates array of size 1e6, suggesting upper bound around 1e6; sequence is Fibonacci-like (F0=2, F1=1, Fn=Fn-1+Fn-2).

dominant_ops: Allocation of a fixed-size list of length 1,000,000 regardless of input n
O(n) loop computing each term via one addition and two indexed loads per iteration
Storing all intermediate sequence values up to index n

complexity.why: The loop executes from 2 to n inclusive, doing constant work per iteration (two index reads, one addition, one write), giving O(n) time. The list var_1 has fixed length 1e6, which is O(n) in the intended constraints, and all intermediate results up to n are stored, so space is linear in the maximum supported n.

bottlenecks.detail: Always allocates a list of size 1,000,000 even if the input n is much smaller, leading to unnecessary memory usage and potential MLE for tighter limits or multiple test cases.
Stores the entire sequence up to index n although only the final value var_1[var_2] is used; this increases memory footprint and cache pressure without algorithmic benefit.
If n can exceed 999,999, the fixed-size array leads to IndexError; if constraints grow, both the fixed-size allocation and full history storage become inefficient.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the fact that this Fibonacci-like recurrence only needs the last two values to compute the next term, so maintain two running variables updated in a loop instead of storing the entire sequence. The loop runs n steps starting from (2,1) and prints the current value corresponding to the n-th term.

complexity.why: The optimized logic does one constant-time update per iteration, still O(n) time in the sequence index. It no longer stores all sequence values, but it builds a list [0]*n solely to drive the loop, which itself is length n, so the worst-case asymptotic auxiliary space remains O(n). However, the stored objects are small (repeated references to 0) rather than large growing integers, significantly reducing practical memory usage compared to storing all sequence values.

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time complexity remains linear. Asymptotic space is also linear, but the optimized version avoids storing n distinct large integers for the sequence and instead uses two running integers plus an O(n) loop-control list of small repeated values, greatly reducing memory in practice. A further tweak using range(n) instead of [0]*n would reduce space to O(1) truly.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the recurrence Fn = Fn-1 + Fn-2 requires only the two previous terms, so the full DP array is unnecessary when only the nth term is required.
Replace the DP array var_1 with two scalar variables var_1, var_2 representing consecutive terms in the sequence.
Initialize these scalars to match the original base cases: var_1 = F0 = 2, var_2 = F1 = 1.

Iterate exactly n times, updating (var_1, var_2) = (var_2, var_1 + var_2) each step so that var_1 holds the next term; align the loop count so that the final printed value matches var_1[var_2] from the original implementation.
Remove all array indexing and assignment inside the loop, reducing per-iteration overhead and memory traffic.
Drive the loop with a size-n iterable ([0]*n in the given fast code), and optionally improve further by switching to range(n) to avoid the extra O(n) list allocation.
trigger_signals: The slow code allocates a fixed 1e6-element list regardless of the input, which is a red flag for memory-heavy DP when only one output value is needed.
The loop writes every DP state into the array but the program only reads a single element at the end, indicating redundant storage.
Performance or memory issues when n approaches the upper limit (e.g., around 1e6), especially in environments with strict memory limits.
Recognition that the underlying problem is a simple Fibonacci-like recurrence, which is known to have an O(1)-space iterative solution.
pitfalls: Using [0]*n as the loop iterable still allocates O(n) memory; for best performance and minimal memory, range(n) should be used instead.

Care must be taken to align the number of iterations and initial values so that the final printed term corresponds exactly to the original DP definition; off-by-one errors are easy when switching from index-based DP to step-based iteration.
The use of eval(input()) is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; int(input()) is sufficient and safer, although this does not directly affect performance in typical competitive programming settings.
If constraints increase far beyond 1e6, even O(n) time may become a bottleneck; more advanced methods (e.g., fast doubling or matrix exponentiation) would then be required for near-logarithmic time.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer N; both solutions rely on iterating up to roughly sqrt(N) and enumerating divisors, suggesting N up to about 1e12 is intended.

dominant_ops: Linear scan over candidate k (var_4) up to about sqrt(N) with repeated modulo operations
Repeated re-factorization of N for each candidate (inner while var_5 % var_4 == 0)
Second full scan up to sqrt(N) to check if N is a pure power of k (var_5 == 1)
Divisor enumeration of N-1 via func_1(var_6 - 1) in O(sqrt(N))
Building and deduplicating a potentially large list of candidates (var_7) then converting to a set

complexity.why: The first while loop over var_4 increments var_4 from 2 until the break condition var_4 - N/var_4 > 2 holds, which algebraically happens at var_4 > 1 + sqrt(N+1); thus it runs for Theta(sqrt(N)) iterations, each doing at least one modulo and maybe a few divisions. The second while loop also runs var_4 from 2 up to floor(sqrt(N)), performing similar factor-removal work. Finally, func_1(var_6 - 1) enumerates all divisors of N-1 in O(sqrt(N)) time. Overall this yields a constant number (~3) of full sqrt(N)-scale scans plus some extra divisibility work, so the asymptotic time is O(sqrt(N)). Space is dominated by storing divisors/candidates in lists and sets whose size is at most on the order of the number of divisors, i.e., O(sqrt(N)) in the worst case.

bottlenecks.detail: N is repeatedly re-factorized from scratch for each candidate var_4 in both main while loops (var_5 is reset to N on every iteration), leading to many repeated modulo/division operations on the same number.

There are effectively three separate O(sqrt(N)) passes: first while over var_4, second while over var_4, and divisor enumeration for N-1 in func_1. The fast version combines the N and N-1 divisor work into a single sqrt(N) loop.

The flag var_1 is never reset inside the first while loop; once set to 1 it remains 1, so the condition (var_5 % var_4 == 1 and var_1) effectively degrades to just checking var_5 % var_4 == 1 after the first divisible case. While primarily a correctness issue, it also means the code may perform unnecessary appends/tests for many var_4.

Candidates are generated by scanning all integers up to about sqrt(N) with ad-hoc conditions instead of restricting checks to true divisors of N and N-1. This increases the constant factor via many extra modulo operations on values that will never be valid k.

var_7 accumulates candidates with duplicates, and only at the end is converted to a set for deduplication; this imposes O(K) extra work for insertions and then an O(K) set construction, where K can be O(sqrt(N)) in the worst case.
Using eval(input()) instead of int(input()) is slower and unsafe, and provides no benefit here; while not the dominant cost, it is an unnecessary overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit number-theoretic structure: any valid k must be a divisor of N or N-1. Enumerate all divisors of N and N-1 in a single loop up to sqrt(N), then for each divisor d of N test whether repeatedly dividing N by d leaves a remainder 1 modulo d ((N' - 1) % d == 0). This focuses work only on promising candidates and merges the N and N-1 divisor scans.

complexity.why: A single for-loop over var_5 from 2 to floor(sqrt(N)) collects all divisors of N and N-1. Enumerating divisors up to sqrt(N) has O(sqrt(N)) iterations, and each divisor insertion is O(1) on average. The total number of divisors of an integer is at most O(sqrt(N)), so the size of var_2 and var_3 is O(sqrt(N)). For each divisor var_7 in var_2 (divisors of N), func_1(var_7) repeatedly divides N by var_7 until it is no longer divisible; the total number of such divisions over all divisors is bounded by a small multiple of the sum of exponents in the prime factorization of N, i.e., O(log N) overall. Thus the extra cost of func_1 over all candidates is negligible compared to the O(sqrt(N)) divisor enumeration. Space is O(sqrt(N)) to store the divisor sets.

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(N)) with roughly three separate sqrt(N)-scale scans, repeated refactorizations of N, and many checks on non-divisor candidates.
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(N)) with a single sqrt(N) scan to build divisors of N and N-1, plus O(log N) total extra work to test candidates via repeated division.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity remains O(sqrt(N)), but the fast code sharply reduces the constant factors and removes redundant work by restricting checks to actual divisors and merging passes.

transformation_steps: Restrict candidate k values to divisors of N and N-1 instead of scanning all integers up to around sqrt(N).
Merge the processing of N and N-1 into a single loop over i from 2 to floor(sqrt(N)), simultaneously collecting divisors into two sets.

Replace repeated ad-hoc refactorizations of N in multiple loops with a dedicated helper function (func_1) that, for each candidate divisor k of N, divides N by k until it no longer divides, then performs a single modular check ((N' - 1) % k == 0).
Use sets from the beginning for divisor storage to avoid duplicates and to make membership and combination operations O(1) average case, instead of building lists and deduplicating late.
Eliminate the second sqrt(N) pass that checks for pure powers (var_5 == 1) by leveraging the structure encoded in func_1.
Simplify control flow: a single for-loop over sqrt(N) replaces multiple nested whiles and a non-obvious break condition (var_4 - N/var_4 > 2), improving both performance and readability.
trigger_signals: Presence of multiple while-loops each iterating up to roughly sqrt(N) and repeating similar computations on the same N.
Manual scanning over all integers up to sqrt(N) with modulo conditions to select candidates rather than directly iterating over divisors.
Re-initialization of the same large value (var_5 = N) and refactorization inside nested loops.
Late deduplication via len(set(list_of_candidates)), indicating possible redundant work and memory usage.
Use of float-based break conditions (var_4 - var_5 / var_4 > 2) inside tight loops, hinting at nontrivial constant factors and potential numeric overhead.
pitfalls: Assuming both versions differ in asymptotic complexity: they are both O(sqrt(N)); the performance gain comes from fewer passes and less redundant work, not from changing big-O class.
Over-aggressive micro-optimizations (e.g., tricky break conditions) can obscure logic while providing little benefit compared to a clean divisor-based approach.
Keeping global state (like var_1 in the slow code) across iterations without resetting can silently introduce correctness bugs and affect the pattern of work performed.
Using eval(input()) is unnecessary and risky; replacing it with int(input()) avoids security issues and small overhead without changing the algorithm.

When reusing the fast pattern in other problems, one must ensure that the property truly only depends on divisors of N and/or N-1; blindly applying the divisor-enumeration trick can miss valid candidates in different settings.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical Lunlun-number style problem (e.g., AtCoder ABC161 D). n up to around 1e5; answer magnitude bounded by generating all valid numbers up to ~10 digits.

dominant_ops: Depth-first recursive generation of ALL valid numbers for lengths 1..10, storing them in a list, then a full sort, and finally indexing the n-th element.

complexity.why: Let M be the total count of generated numbers (all lengths from 1 to 10). func_2 recursively explores a branching factor up to 3 per digit (except at boundaries 0/9) for each starting digit 1..9 and for each target length 1..10, generating all possible values regardless of the requested index n. All generated numbers are stored in var_2 (size M) and then sorted, costing O(M log M). Space is O(M) for storing the entire collection, plus O(L_max) recursion stack (L_max=10). M is significantly larger than n for typical inputs.

bottlenecks.detail: The algorithm generates all candidate numbers up to the maximum considered length (1..10) for all starting digits, even if the user only needs the n-th smallest number for small n. Work is essentially independent of input size n, leading to unnecessary enumeration.
After generation, sorted(var_2) performs an O(M log M) sort over all candidates. This dominates for larger M and is unnecessary if generation order can be made to match the required output order.

func_2 uses recursive calls for every digit extension, incurring Python function-call overhead at each level. Although depth is small (~10), the sheer number of calls adds significant constant-factor cost compared to an iterative approach.

All generated numbers across all lengths and starting digits are retained in memory (var_2) simultaneously, instead of generating only the first n values needed. This raises memory usage to O(M) instead of O(n).

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a BFS-like iterative construction over the space of numbers where adjacent digits differ by at most 1 (Lunlun numbers). Maintain a queue/list var_4 of valid numbers in ascending order and extend numbers from the front by appending allowed next digits (last_digit-1, last_digit, last_digit+1 within [0,9]) until len(var_4) reaches n. Then directly output var_4[n-1] without any final sorting.

complexity.why: Each generated number is appended exactly once and processed exactly once: when it becomes var_4[var_3], it spawns its successors and var_3 is incremented. The loop terminates as soon as len(var_4) == n, so the total work is proportional to n. There is no global sort; the BFS nature of the construction maintains ascending order implicitly. Memory usage is O(n) to store the first n numbers plus O(1) temporary overhead.

complexity_delta.from: O(M log M) time, O(M) space where M is the total number of generated numbers up to max length (independent of n).
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space where n is the requested index of the number.
complexity_delta.note: The fast solution scales with the actual input parameter n and removes the expensive global sort and unnecessary enumeration of unused larger-index numbers.

transformation_steps: Replace global DFS generation for every length (1..10) and every starting digit with an incremental BFS-style generation that maintains numbers in ascending order as they are produced.
Introduce a queue-like list var_4 initialized with 1..9, representing all valid one-digit numbers in sorted order.

Iteratively process var_4 from the front (indexed by var_3), deriving successors by appending last_digit-1, last_digit, and last_digit+1 (within bounds 0..9), mimicking a BFS on the implicit digit graph.
Stop generation as soon as len(var_4) reaches the required n, instead of exploring the full search space up to a fixed maximum length.
Remove the global list accumulation and the final sorted(var_2) call; correctness is ensured by BFS producing numbers in non-decreasing order by value.
trigger_signals: Presence of nested loops over starting digits and lengths (for var_6 in range(1, 10), for var_4 in range(1, 11)) combined with a recursive DFS suggests a full-space enumeration irrespective of the input n.
Use of a global container (var_2) that stores all candidates followed by sorted(var_2)[n-1] indicates that ordering is being fixed post hoc by sorting instead of being preserved during generation.
Input n only influences the final index into the sorted list, not the amount of work done, signaling a potential mismatch between algorithmic complexity and the actual query size.
Recursive calls with small but fixed depth and no pruning based on n imply that the algorithm's work is bounded by a large constant M, which can still be too big for tight time limits in Python.
pitfalls: When converting to BFS, it is easy to get the generation order wrong, e.g., by pushing successors in an incorrect order or by using a stack instead of a queue-like pattern, which would break the ascending numeric order assumption.

Edge digits 0 and 9 require special care: only two successors are valid (0 -> {0,1}, 9 -> {8,9}), whereas middle digits have up to three. Incorrect handling can miss valid numbers or create invalid ones.

Off-by-one errors in stopping criteria (e.g., looping while len(var_4) <= n instead of < n, or indexing var_4[n] instead of var_4[n-1]) can easily slip in when changing from global enumeration to incremental generation.
Although not the main performance issue, both versions use eval(input()), which is unnecessary and potentially dangerous; replacing it with int(input()) is safer and slightly faster.

constraints_guess.n_max: ≈1e9 for N, ≈2e5 for A,B (bouquet sizes)
constraints_guess.notes: Classic AtCoder-style problem: compute (2^N − 1 − C(N,A) − C(N,B)) mod 1e9+7. N can be very large (cannot iterate up to N), while A,B are relatively small (≈2e5), allowing O(A+B) combinatorial computation.

dominant_ops: Exact factorial computation using math.factorial for A and B, which builds huge arbitrary-precision integers before reducing modulo 1e9+7. Additional O(A) and O(B) loops to form N P A and N P B.

complexity.time: O(A + B + log N) Python steps, but factorial(A) and factorial(B) dominate with O(A log A) and O(B log B) big-integer work (bit complexity).
complexity.space: O(A log A + B log B) bits for holding factorial(A) and factorial(B) as big integers.
complexity.why: The loops computing products over N down to N−A+1 and N−B+1 are only O(A+B). However, math.factorial(A) and math.factorial(B) construct exact factorials as enormous integers (~A log A bits), requiring many big-int multiplications and large temporary memory. Only after this is done are the results reduced modulo 1e9+7 via pow(fact, MOD−2, MOD). All intermediate big integers are unnecessary for a purely modular answer.

bottlenecks.detail: Using math.factorial(var_1) and math.factorial(var_5) computes exact factorials of size O(k log k) bits, which is expensive when k is up to ~2e5.
The problem only needs values modulo 1e9+7, but the code first builds full-precision factorials and only then applies modular exponentiation, inflating both time and memory costs.
C(N, k) is not simplified using k = min(k, N−k). For cases where k > N/2, this doubles the number of multiplicative steps in the partial product compared to a symmetric approach.

FastAudit.core_idea: Compute combinations C(N, k) directly in modular arithmetic using only O(k) multiplications on values already reduced modulo 1e9+7, and shorten the product length via k = min(k, N−k). Avoid building full exact factorials and avoid any O(N) dependence.

complexity.time: O((A + B) + log N) operations on machine-word-sized integers; each combinatorial term uses O(k) modular multiplications plus a single modular inverse via pow(_, MOD−2, MOD).
complexity.space: O(1) extra space beyond a few integers (all bounded by MOD).
complexity.why: func_3 computes the numerator N·(N−1)…(N−k+1) using k multiplications modulo MOD. func_1 computes k! also modulo MOD, so numbers never exceed MOD. The combination C(N,k) is then numerator * inv(denominator) mod MOD. Using k = min(k, N−k) limits both loops to at most min(k, N−k) steps. No huge big integers are created, so both time and memory are linear in k with small constants.

complexity_delta.from: Practical cost dominated by big-integer factorial computations: O(A log A + B log B) bit-operations and large intermediate integers, plus O(A + B + log N) modular work.
complexity_delta.to: All heavy arithmetic done modulo 1e9+7 on word-sized integers: O(A + B + log N) operations with much smaller constants and O(1) extra space.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically in terms of primitive Python operations, both versions are O(A+B+log N), but the original hides expensive big-int internals (factorial) whereas the revised version maintains all values modulo a prime, eliminating unnecessary big-int growth and halving loop lengths via k = min(k, N−k). This yields a significant real-world speedup under large constraints.

transformation_steps: Replace math.factorial(k) with a custom modular factorial function func_1 that multiplies 1..k under modulo, keeping all intermediates < MOD.
Introduce func_3 to compute the partial product N·(N−1)…(N−k+1) modulo MOD, directly forming the numerator of C(N,k).
Compute C(N,k) as func_3(N,k,MOD) * inv(func_1(k,MOD)) mod MOD using func_2, where pow(den, MOD−2, MOD) provides the modular inverse (Fermat's little theorem).
Apply the symmetry optimization k = min(k, N−k) before constructing products so that combination computation does not exceed min(k, N−k) multiplicative steps.
Compute the final answer in a single expression: (2^N − 1 − C(N,A) − C(N,B)) mod MOD, ensuring subtraction is done under modulo to avoid negative intermediate values.
trigger_signals: Use of math.factorial with arguments up to ~2e5 or higher in a problem where only answers modulo a prime are required.
Constraints featuring very large N (≈1e9) but relatively small k (A,B), suggesting that any solution depending linearly on N would be impossible, and that combinatorial terms must be handled in O(k).
Performance issues or timeouts in Python due to heavy big-integer arithmetic, despite apparently linear loop bounds in A and B.
Presence of modular exponentiation pow(_, MOD−2, MOD) combined with non-modular factorials, indicating a mismatch between exact arithmetic and modular needs.
pitfalls: Relying on pow(x, MOD−2, MOD) assumes MOD is prime and x is non-zero modulo MOD; this holds for 1e9+7 and factorial-based denominators here but may not in other problems.
When using k = min(k, N−k), it is essential that 0 ≤ k ≤ N; invalid inputs or lack of checks could produce negative ranges in the numerator product.
Subtractions like 2^N − 1 − C(N,A) − C(N,B) must be taken modulo MOD carefully; forgetting the final '% MOD' or intermediate adjustments can yield negative answers.

If constraints change and A,B can approach N/2 at scale (e.g., N up to 2e6, many test cases), further optimization via precomputed factorials and inverse factorials may be necessary; the current approach is O(A+B) per query and might be too slow for large multi-test scenarios.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic AtCoder-style problem: given N and M, factorize M and count ways to write M as a product of N positive integers. Precomputation size 2*10^5 in the original code suggests N + max_exponent <= ~2e5; M is up to around 10^9 so that trial division up to sqrt(M) is acceptable.

dominant_ops: Trial-division prime factorization of M up to sqrt(M) in func_3
Linear precomputation of factorials up to MAXN = 2*10^5+10
Linear precomputation of modular inverses and inverse factorials up to MAXN using recurrence

complexity.why: func_3 performs trial division until p^2 > current_n, which is O(sqrt(M_initial)). The arrays var_6 (fact), var_9 (inv), and var_7 (inv_fact) are always built up to the fixed MAXN, taking linear time and memory regardless of the actual N and exponents. Computing each combination via func_1/func_2 is O(1) using the precomputed tables.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorial, inverse, and inverse factorial arrays are precomputed up to a hard-coded upper bound (2*10^5+10) even if N + max_exponent is much smaller, wasting time and memory on small inputs.

The fixed size MAXN couples the implementation to a particular constraint. If N + max_exponent ever exceeds 2*10^5+10, the code would index out of bounds or require increasing MAXN, making it less reusable for different constraints.

The modular inverse array var_9 is filled using the common O(MAXN) recurrence; this is fine asymptotically but has a somewhat higher constant factor compared to the single pow + backward inverse-factorial method used in the fast code.
func_3 accumulates prime exponents in a defaultdict(int). While asymptotically fine, it has slightly more overhead than building a list of prime factors and then counting them, as in the fast code.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the same mathematical approach (factor M, then for each prime exponent e compute C(N+e-1, e) modulo a prime), but size the combinatorics precomputation exactly to N + max_exponent instead of a fixed constant, and use a factorial + inverse-factorial scheme based on a single modular inverse via pow and a backward pass. Factorization returns a list of prime factors and uses Counter to obtain exponents, reducing overhead compared to a defaultdict.

complexity.why: Prime factorization of M remains trial division up to sqrt(M). After factorization, the code computes var_8 = N + max_exponent and builds factorial and inverse factorial arrays of length var_8+1 in linear time. Each binomial coefficient C(n, k) is then evaluated in O(1) using fact and inv_fact. Compared to the original, the asymptotic form is parameterized by actual N + max_exponent instead of a fixed global MAXN, so on smaller instances the precomputation is lighter while still remaining linear in the necessary range.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(MAXN + sqrt(M)), Space: O(MAXN) with MAXN fixed at 2*10^5+10 regardless of input.
complexity_delta.to: Time: O((N + max_exponent) + sqrt(M)), Space: O(N + max_exponent), where the precomputation size is adapted to the actual input.
complexity_delta.note: Big-O under the official constraints (where N + max_exponent <= 2*10^5) is effectively the same, but the fast version avoids unnecessary work for smaller inputs and is less tightly bound to a hard-coded upper limit. It also uses a slightly more efficient inverse-factorial construction.

transformation_steps: Replace defaultdict-based factorization (mapping prime -> exponent) with a function that returns a flat list of prime factors, then wrap it with collections.Counter to obtain exponent counts.

Remove the hard-coded MAXN = 2*10**5 + 10 and compute the required combinatorial precomputation bound dynamically as var_8 = N + max_exponent, where max_exponent is the largest prime exponent in the factorization of M.

Switch from the linear modular-inverse recurrence to a standard factorial / inverse-factorial approach: precompute factorial array fact up to var_8, compute inv_fact[var_8] using pow(fact[var_8], MOD-2, MOD), then fill inv_fact backwards with inv_fact[i-1] = inv_fact[i] * i % MOD.

Redefine the combination function func_1 to use fact and inv_fact directly: C(n, k) = fact[n] * inv_fact[n-k] % MOD * inv_fact[k] % MOD, and assert argument ranges instead of relying on implicit bounds.
Streamline the main loop over prime exponents: for each exponent e in Counter.values(), compute and multiply C(N + e - 1, e) using the new combinatorics utilities.
trigger_signals: Presence of a hard-coded global limit (var_2 = 2 * 10**5 + 10) used for precomputations, which suggests potential overkill on small inputs and fragility if constraints change.
Linear precomputation of modular inverses and inverse factorials up to the global MAXN even though the actual required n in combinations is clearly bounded by N + max_exponent from the factorization.
Defaultdict and repeated dictionary increments in the factorization routine, which may indicate avoidable overhead in a hot path that runs for every prime factor.
Desire to reuse the logic for different problem sizes (e.g., different tasks) where a fixed MAXN is no longer appropriate, prompting a more flexible, parameterized precomputation.
pitfalls: If N + max_exponent becomes large (e.g., approaching 10^6 or more), the dynamic factorial precomputation will scale accordingly; while still linear, in other environments this may require reevaluating memory and time limits.

The factorial/inverse-factorial method assumes the modulus is prime so that pow(x, MOD-2, MOD) yields a valid modular inverse via Fermat's little theorem; changing MOD to a non-prime would break the fast approach.

Edge cases such as M = 1 must be handled explicitly: the fast code short-circuits when var_6 == 1; any refactoring must preserve that behavior to avoid miscomputing the answer for trivial factorizations.

The dynamic bound var_8 = N + max_exponent must be computed before allocating factorial arrays; off-by-one errors or miscomputations of max_exponent can lead to out-of-range accesses in fact or inv_fact.

Using Counter over a list of prime factors introduces overhead proportional to the number of total factors; although small for typical M (<= 10^9), for other constraints with heavier factorization this overhead must be considered.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer input N. Original solution is O(N) with a Python loop over ~N/2 iterations, which becomes slow around N ≳ 1e7. Modified version uses NumPy and allocates arrays of length N, so memory becomes a concern for very large N (e.g., N=1e8 would be too large).

dominant_ops: Python for-loop over i from 1 to N//2 (~N/2 iterations)
Integer floor division N // i in each iteration
Multiple integer multiplications and additions per iteration
Final arithmetic progression sum for i in (N//2, N]

complexity.why: The main cost is the loop: for var_2 in range(1, var_4 + 1) where var_4 = N//2, so ~N/2 iterations. Each iteration performs O(1) arithmetic (a constant number of integer divisions, multiplications, additions). No data structures grow with N, so extra space is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: The core loop in pure Python runs ~N/2 iterations, each with several operations. The per-iteration dispatch and Python integer object overhead dominates runtime for large N.
Each iteration performs integer floor division var_3 = var_1 // var_2, which is more expensive than basic arithmetic and is repeated O(N) times.
Using eval(input()) is slower than int(input()) or sys.stdin.readline(), and is also unsafe. It adds parsing overhead unrelated to the core computation.
All arithmetic is executed as scalar Python operations, missing opportunities for C-level vectorization or SIMD that libraries like NumPy provide.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace the Python loop with NumPy vectorized operations over the full range 1..N. Compute floor divisions, products, and the final sum in bulk using contiguous arrays and C-level loops, while also improving input handling.

complexity.why: Arrays var_5, var_4, and var_2 are all of length N (from 1 to N). NumPy still needs O(N) operations internally, but they are implemented in optimized C loops with low per-element overhead and potential vectorization. This preserves the asymptotic time complexity but drastically improves the constant factor. Space is O(N) because these arrays are materialized in memory.

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time complexity remains O(N) but the execution is moved from a Python-level loop to efficient C-level vectorized operations, greatly reducing wall-clock time. This comes at the cost of increasing space usage from constant to linear due to NumPy arrays.

transformation_steps: Input handling: Replaced eval(input()) with stdin.readline and int(...) to avoid the overhead and security risk of eval, and to use faster buffered I/O.
Loop elimination: Removed the explicit Python for-loop over var_2 in range(1, var_4 + 1) and instead constructed a vector var_5 = np.arange(1, var_3 + 1, dtype=np.int64) representing all i in [1, N].
Vectorized division: Computed var_2 = var_3 // var_5 in a single NumPy operation, producing an array of floor(N / i) for all i at once, instead of recomputing in Python for each iteration.

Vectorized product and sum: Computed var_4 = var_3 // var_5 * var_5 to form N//i * i for all i, then used var_1 = (var_2 * (var_5 + var_4) // 2).sum() to evaluate the arithmetic expressions in bulk and sum them via NumPy's optimized reduction.

Consolidation of cases: Instead of separating i <= N//2 and i > N//2 (with a second arithmetic progression term), the modified version handles the entire range 1..N uniformly within the vectorized formula.
Use of 64-bit integers: Explicitly chose dtype=np.int64 to reduce Python bigint overhead and allow efficient native integer arithmetic, as long as results fit within 64-bit range.
trigger_signals: The original solution contains a tight Python loop with about N/2 iterations where N can be large, and each iteration uses integer division.
Profiling or reasoning shows the majority of runtime would be spent in this loop for large N, with minimal memory use—indicating a CPU-bound hot loop.
The loop body consists solely of pure arithmetic on integers, with no data-dependent branching or complex Python objects, making it an ideal candidate for vectorization.
The structure of the computation (operations applied elementwise over i in [1, N]) maps naturally to array operations like arange, elementwise division, multiplication, and reduction via sum.
Use of eval(input()) is an anti-pattern and performance smell, suggesting that I/O and input parsing could also be tightened.
pitfalls: Memory usage: Creating arrays of size N with dtype=int64 consumes about 8 * N bytes per array. With multiple arrays, memory may become problematic for N much larger than about 1e7, depending on the environment.
NumPy availability: Some online judges or restricted environments do not allow third-party libraries like NumPy, making the fast_code non-portable in those contexts.
Small-N overhead: For small N, the overhead of importing NumPy and allocating arrays may outweigh the benefit of vectorization, making the vectorized version slower than the simple loop.

Integer overflow: Using np.int64 can overflow if the mathematical result exceeds 2^63 - 1, whereas Python's int is arbitrary-precision. For very large N, this may produce incorrect results or wraparound.

Semantic consistency: While floor division and arithmetic are preserved for positive integers, any change to include negative inputs or different types might alter the behavior when moved to fixed-width NumPy dtypes.

Cache and GC behavior: Large arrays may exert pressure on memory bandwidth and cache, and repeated use in a larger program could interact with Python's garbage collector differently than the scalar loop.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: compute number of divisors of n! modulo 1e9+7. Constraints likely up to n≈1e4; original O(n*sqrt(n)) solution is acceptable there, while O(n^2) is borderline/too slow.

dominant_ops: The slow code first performs a naive primality test for every number up to n (nested loops in func_2), then for each k from 1 to n it scans all indices up to k to factor k using those primes (func_1), and finally performs an O(n) vector addition for each k to accumulate exponents (rebuilding var_9 via list comprehension). This leads to roughly O(n^2) scalar operations plus an O(n^{3/2}) naive sieve.

complexity.why: func_2 runs a naive primality check: for each var_2 in [2..n], it tries divisors var_4 up to sqrt(var_2), giving about O(n^{3/2}) time. FastAudit.core_idea: Instead of building and updating a full exponent vector for each k, factor each integer from 2 to n directly and increment a global exponent counter per prime. constraints_guess.notes: Classic AtCoder-style combinatorics problem (likely ABC110 D 'Factorization'): input (n, m). n up to around 1e4, m up to about 1e9–1e12. Single query; need prime factorization of m and products of binomial coefficients modulo 1e9+7.

Precomputation of factorials and inverse factorials up to n + max_exponent.
Single modular exponentiation pow(fact[max], MOD-2, MOD) for inverse factorial seed.
O(#prime_factors) calls to nCr via precomputed factorial/inv_factorial.

complexity.why: Prime factorization by trial division is O(sqrt(m)). Factorial and inverse-factorial precomputation loops over range(1, n+E+1), doing a modular multiplication at each step. For larger n this dominates after factorization.
Stores two arrays of length n+E+1 for factorials and inverse factorials. Space is linear in n, which is fine for ~1e4 but can become heavy if n grows to ~1e6+.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial/inverse-factorial precomputation. Instead, compute each required binomial coefficient C(N, K) directly via multiplicative formula using reduce(operator.mul, ...) and integer division, then reduce modulo 1e9+7. This trades O(n) precomputation for O(K) work per combination and reduces auxiliary memory to O(1).

complexity.why: Factorization cost remains O(sqrt(m)). For each prime factor with exponent e, it computes C(n+e-1, e). The function func_1 forms products over ranges of length K = min(e, n+e-1-e), which in this problem is essentially O(e). The sum of all exponents in the factorization is O(log m). No arrays of size ~n are built, and each combination computation is linear in its (small) K but involves big-integer multiplications.

Second pass: for each i, add the count of (i - a[i]) from the dictionary. This keeps work proportional to n and uses memory proportional to the number of distinct transformed indices, not a guessed global bound.

complexity.why: Both loops run over the n elements once. Dict get/set operations are O(1) on average, so the total expected time is O(n). The dictionary stores up to n keys (one per index in the worst case), so its size is O(n). No extra dependence on a large fixed bound like 10**7.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: choose integer p minimizing sum_i (a_i - p)^2. Original editorial usually uses brute force over p in [1,100], implying a_i and p are small (1..100), but N itself can be moderately large (e.g., up to 2e5). The brute-force loop over p is constant-factor 100, so asymptotically O(N).

dominant_ops: Nested loop: for each candidate p in [1,100], iterate over all N elements to accumulate squared deviations
Per-element arithmetic: abs, subtraction, squaring, addition

complexity.time: O(R * N) with R = 100 (i.e., O(N) with a constant factor of ~100)
complexity.why: The outer loop runs over 100 candidate p values. For each p, the inner loop scans all N elements and performs O(1) arithmetic work. That is 100 * N iterations overall. The input array of size N dominates space; only O(1) extra variables are used.

bottlenecks.detail: The array is fully scanned 100 times to recompute sums of squared deviations for each candidate p, even though the objective function is a simple quadratic in p with a known minimizer around the mean.
Abs and exponentiation via `** 2` are done N * 100 times. While still O(N) asymptotically, the constant factor can be significantly larger than necessary.
Use of `eval(input())` for reading an integer is slower and unsafe compared to `int(input())`, though this is a minor performance issue relative to the nested loops.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the mathematical property that f(p) = sum_i (a_i - p)^2 is a convex quadratic in real p, minimized at the mean of a_i. For integer p, the optimum lies at floor(mean) or ceil(mean). Compute the mean once, evaluate the objective at these two integer candidates, and choose the better. This reduces the problem to a single pass over the data plus O(1) extra work.

complexity.why: The algorithm performs a single pass to read the N elements and compute their sum, then one more pass to accumulate squared deviations from the chosen p. All other operations are O(1). The array storage remains O(N), with only a constant number of auxiliary scalars.

complexity_delta.from: O(R * N) with R = 100 (brute-force enumeration of all candidate p)
complexity_delta.to: O(N) (single evaluation around the mean, with constant extra candidates)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both are O(N) because R is constant, but the optimized version removes a ~100x constant factor in the number of passes over the array. The key improvement is reducing repeated scans with a direct formula-based choice of p.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the objective function f(p) = sum_i (a_i - p)^2 is a convex quadratic in p. Its derivative vanishes at p* = (sum_i a_i) / N, the arithmetic mean.
Note that when p is constrained to integers, the minimizer must be one of the integers closest to the mean, namely floor(mean) or ceil(mean).
Replace the outer loop over all p in [1,100] with a computation of the mean: var_8 = sum(var_7) / var_3.
Compute the two integer candidates var_5 = floor(mean) and var_6 = var_5 + 1, then choose the one closer to the mean using a constant-time comparison.
Perform a single pass over the array to compute the sum of squared deviations from the chosen integer p. This replaces the 100 repeated passes in the original solution.

Simplify input reading by avoiding `eval` and using direct integer parsing (e.g., int(input())) for both correctness and minor speed gains (even though the provided fast_code still uses eval, the main speedup is from the algorithmic change).
trigger_signals: A simple scalar decision variable (p) with brute-force iteration over a fixed small range (1..100) combined with a sum of squared differences is a classic sign that a convex or quadratic structure might be exploited.
Objective function uses squared deviations ( (x - p)^2 ), suggesting a direct link to the arithmetic mean as the minimizer.
Repeated full scans over the same array for each candidate p, indicating redundant work that might be collapsible via a formula or partial sums.
No dependency of the optimal p on any discrete structure like ordering or combinatorial constraints, making a calculus-based or algebraic solution plausible.
pitfalls: Domain constraints on p: The optimized code does not enforce the original search bound p ∈ [1,100]. If the problem constraints truly require p to lie within [1,100], and the mean lies outside this interval, the correct minimizer under the constraint will be 1 or 100, not floor/ceil(mean). The transformed solution may produce a mathematically valid unconstrained minimizer but violate the problem’s specified domain.

Floating-point precision: Computing the mean with floating-point division can introduce rounding errors. While comparing distances to floor/ceil(mean) is usually safe when values are small, for larger numbers or extreme sums it is safer to work with rational comparisons or integer arithmetic to avoid subtle off-by-one issues.

Integer division semantics: In Python 3, `/` performs float division and `//` integer division. Accidentally using integer division for the mean would bias the candidate selection if one relied directly on the mean’s value instead of comparing floor/ceil explicitly.

Readability vs. obfuscation: Variable names like var_1, var_2, etc., obscure the underlying math (mean, candidate, sum_of_squares), making it harder to verify the correctness of the optimization and increasing the risk of off-by-one or domain errors when modifying the algorithm.
Safety of eval: Both versions use `eval(input())` for reading integers. Besides being unnecessary and slower, this is unsafe in general contexts and should be replaced by `int(input())`.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: N up to ~1e5, M up to ~1e9 or slightly larger; number of distinct prime factors of M is small (<= 9 for M <= 1e9).

dominant_ops: Trial division prime factorization of M up to a fixed bound sqrt(M_initial).
Naive multiplicative computation of binomial coefficients using integer multiplication/division under modulo.

complexity.why: func_1 does trial division for divisors 2..floor(sqrt(M_initial)); each inner while divides M by the current prime factor until it no longer divides, so factorization is O(sqrt(M)) in the worst case. The sum of prime exponents sum_e is small (<= O(log M)), and each combination uses O(min(e, N-1)) operations, which is O(e) since e << N; number of distinct primes p is also small, so total extra time from combinations is O(sum_e). Memory holds at most p prime-exponent pairs, so O(p) = O(log M) in the worst case but very small in practice.
