pitfalls: The fast_code collects all prime factors into a list, which can be memory-heavy when n is large (O(n log n) factors). For higher constraints this could cause memory issues or cache inefficiency.

Trial division by all odd integers (rather than just primes) increases the number of modulus operations. For large n this may actually be slower than using a well-implemented sieve-of-SPF-based factorization despite less Python-level control flow.
Using eval(input()) to read an integer is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; input() with int() is safer and clearer.

Both codes remain O(n * sqrt(n)) and will not scale to very large n (e.g., 1e6) under typical time limits. A fundamentally different approach (e.g., Legendre’s formula for exponents in n! or an SPF sieve with O(n log log n) complexity) would be required for such constraints.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic 'coprime / setwise coprime / not coprime' problem (AtCoder-style). Typically: 1 <= N <= 2e5, 1 <= a_i <= 1e6. Need to distinguish pairwise coprime, setwise coprime via gcd, or not coprime.

dominant_ops: Allocate frequency array var_7 of size ~1e6: O(A_max) space and initialization
Outer loop over all integers var_5 from 2 to 1e6+1: O(A_max)
For each var_5, create slice var_7[var_5::var_5] and iterate it: total O(A_max log A_max) element visits plus O(A_max log A_max) list construction overhead
Final gcd accumulation over all input numbers: O(N log A_max)

complexity.time: O(A_max log A_max + N log A_max)
complexity.why: The critical section is the double loop: for each d in [2, A_max], it iterates over var_7[d::d]. The total length of all such slices is sum_{d<=A_max} A_max/d = A_max * H_{A_max} = O(A_max log A_max). Python list slicing creates a new list each time, so both constructing slices and looping over them dominate. N only affects the initial frequency fill (O(N)) and the gcd fold (O(N log A_max)). Space is dominated by the fixed-size frequency array of length about 1e6.

bottlenecks.detail: Performs a sieve-like scan over all integers up to a fixed bound 1e6 regardless of the actual maximum input value, leading to O(A_max log A_max) work even if input is small.
Checks for pairwise coprimality by scanning all multiples of each d instead of working directly with the prime factors of the input numbers.
Uses slicing var_7[var_5::var_5] in the inner loop, which allocates a fresh list for each divisor var_5; this adds substantial overhead on top of the pure algorithmic cost.
Even after detecting that the numbers are not pairwise coprime (var_8 set to False), the code continues scanning all divisors up to 1e6 instead of breaking early.
Uses input() and eval(input()) instead of fast buffered I/O; this is minor compared to the algorithmic bottleneck but still slower under large input.

FastAudit.core_idea: Instead of scanning all possible divisors up to a global bound, factor each input number individually into its distinct prime factors. Maintain a boolean array indexed by prime to record which primes have appeared. If any prime appears in more than one number, the set is not pairwise coprime. In parallel, compute the gcd of all numbers to distinguish setwise coprime vs not coprime. This turns a global sieve-like scan into per-element prime factorization plus a single gcd fold.

complexity.time: O(N * sqrt(A_max)) in the worst case, often closer to O(N log A_max) on typical data
complexity.why: func_1 does trial division up to sqrt(x) per number, extracting each distinct prime factor once. For each a_i, the work is O(sqrt(a_i)) in the worst case (when a_i is prime or has a large prime factor), but smaller for composite numbers because n shrinks during factorization. Across N numbers with a_i <= A_max, this is bounded by O(N * sqrt(A_max)) and is typically faster in practice. The prime-usage array var_4 has size max(a_i) + 1, so space is O(A_max). The gcd computation via recursive func_2 is O(N log A_max) but with very small constants.

complexity_delta.from: O(A_max log A_max + N log A_max) time, O(A_max) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N * sqrt(A_max) + N log A_max) time, O(A_max) space
complexity_delta.note: Original cost is dominated by scanning all multiples for every divisor up to 1e6, independent of N. The modified version scales with N and the actual values via per-number factorization. For typical constraints (N up to 2e5, A_max up to 1e6) and non-adversarial data, the factorization-based approach is faster in Python despite the theoretical sqrt(A_max) factor, especially due to removal of massive list-slicing overhead.

transformation_steps: Replaced global sieve-like divisor scanning over [2..1e6] with per-number prime factorization using trial division (func_1).
Introduced a boolean presence array var_4 of size max(a_i)+1 to track which prime factors have been seen across the entire array and detect repeated primes quickly.
Embedded an early conflict check: as soon as a prime factor is found that has already appeared in a previous number, mark the set as not pairwise coprime and avoid further pairwise work.
Switched from math.gcd to a custom gcd (func_2) that is called once per number as part of a running fold; complexity remains similar, but this is integrated tightly into the main loop.
Retained the setwise coprime check via gcd over all numbers (var_12); the gcd result is used only after pairwise coprime has been ruled out.
Replaced input() with sys.stdin.readline to reduce I/O overhead for large N.
Eliminated creation of large slices var_7[d::d] in inner loops, thus removing repeated allocations and iterations over mostly zero frequencies.
trigger_signals: Presence of a fixed upper-bound loop up to 1e6 regardless of actual input size or values.
Nested loops where the inner loop uses list slicing (var_7[var_5::var_5]) inside a large outer range, indicating repeated large allocations and iterations.
Global divisor scanning pattern where each possible divisor d is considered even if no number in the input is a multiple of d.
No early termination after detection of non-pairwise coprimality, meaning unnecessary continued heavy computation.
Target environment (Python) where high-constant-factor O(A_max log A_max) sieve-like operations over 1e6-scale arrays are often too slow compared to more input-sensitive strategies.
pitfalls: The trial-division factorization in func_1 is worst-case O(sqrt(a_i)); if many a_i are large primes near A_max and N is large, total operations can approach the Python performance limit.
The prime presence array var_4 uses size max(a_i)+1; if constraints on a_i were much larger than 1e6, memory and performance could degrade.
The gcd implementation func_2 is recursive; although recursion depth is bounded by O(log a_i) and safe for typical values, iterative gcd would be safer if a_i could be extremely large.
The algorithm assumes integers are positive; zeros or ones in the input are not specially handled in the prime-factorization logic (though ones simply produce no factors).

Using eval on the first line of input (var_10 = int(eval(var_7()))) is unconventional; if the input format were ever to change or contain leading/trailing spaces or comments, this could misbehave. A simple int(var_7()) would be safer.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer N, likely 1 <= N <= 10000. Task: for each 1 <= n <= N, count the number of triples (a,b,c) with small bounds (<= ~sqrt(N) or <=100) such that n = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + ab + bc + ca.

dominant_ops: Triple nested loops over fixed range 1..100 computing expression v = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + ab + bc + ca and conditionally incrementing counts; plus use of eval() for input parsing.

complexity.time: O(100^3 + N) ≈ O(1e6 + N) ~ effectively O(1) w.r.t N but with a large constant (~1,000,000 iterations).
complexity.why: The loops over var_5,var_6,var_7 each go from 1 to 100 regardless of N, making at most 100^3 = 1,000,000 iterations. The array var_1 has fixed length 10001, independent of N. N only affects the final output loop.

bottlenecks.detail: Always performs 100^3 iterations even when N is small; no pruning based on partial sums. For small N this does far more work than needed.
For many (a,b,c), the computed value var_4 will exceed N; these combinations are fully evaluated then discarded by the `if var_4 <= var_3` condition instead of being pruned earlier.
Using eval() inside int(eval(func_2())) is significantly slower and unsafe compared to directly using int() on the input string.
var_1 is always length 10001, even if N is much smaller. This is minor but still unnecessary space and cache overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Adapt loop bounds to sqrt(N) and use early-break pruning based on partial sums so that the triple loop explores only combinations that can produce values ≤ N. Also eliminate eval() and size the result array exactly to N+1.

complexity.time: O((sqrt(N))^3) = O(N^{3/2}) in the worst case, but with strong pruning; for N ≤ 10000 this is at most about 1e6 iterations and often much less for smaller N.
complexity.why: The loops on var_4,var_7,var_8 each go up to var_9 ≈ sqrt(N), not a fixed 100. The innermost loop breaks when the partial expression exceeds N, so many combinations are skipped early. The result array scales with N (size N+1) to store counts for each value.

complexity_delta.from: Fixed triple loop of 100^3 iterations plus O(N) output; worst-case work ~1e6 operations regardless of N.
complexity_delta.to: Triple loop bounded by (sqrt(N))^3 with early breaks when partial sums exceed N, plus O(N) output; worst-case ~1e6 operations at N=10000 but significantly less for smaller N.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both are acceptable under given constraints, but the fast version scales with N, prunes unnecessary work, and avoids eval(), improving constant factors and typical runtime.

transformation_steps: Replace eval-based input parsing (`int(eval(func_2()))`) with direct integer parsing via `int()`.
Resize the count array based on the actual input N (`[0] * (N + 1)`) instead of a fixed upper bound like 10001.
Change triple loop bounds from fixed 1..100 to 1..sqrt(N) so the search space adapts to the actual constraint.
Introduce precomputation of partial sums (e.g., var_5 = var_4**2, var_6 = var_5 + var_7**2 + var_4*var_7) to avoid redundant arithmetic.
Add early-break conditions in the middle and inner loops to stop iterating once the partial expression can no longer yield values ≤ N.
Print results using a single `print(*arr[1:N+1], sep='\n')` call for simpler and efficient output.
trigger_signals: Static inspection shows a 100x100x100 nested loop, a classic red flag for performance in Python.
Recognition that the mathematical form allows bounding variables by sqrt(N) and pruning via partial sums.
Use of eval() on input, which is both slow and unsafe, suggesting an easy optimization opportunity.
Problem constraints (N up to about 10000) indicate that solutions must be close to 1e6 operations at most; any unnecessary constant-factor work risks TLE.
pitfalls: When tightening loop bounds to sqrt(N), off-by-one errors (e.g., not including the upper bound or adding +1 incorrectly) can cause missing or extra solutions.
Over-aggressive pruning (breaking too early on partial sums) can skip valid triples if the pruning condition does not correctly upper-bound the remaining terms.
Changing array size from fixed to N+1 requires careful index management to avoid out-of-bounds errors when N is at its maximum.
Relying on floating-point sqrt and int casts must be done carefully to avoid truncation issues; better ensure the loop upper bound safely covers all needed integer values.

constraints_guess.notes: Each test case: first integer n (var_3), then n integers in [0,9]. Loop ends when n==0. Likely online judge style; upper bounds inferred from typical constraints, not from statement.

dominant_ops: For each test case, builds a full list of n values, then for each digit d in 0..9 calls var_2.count(d) twice (once for the stars, once for the zero-check), where list.count scans the entire list.

complexity.time: O(n) per test case (10 * 2 calls to count over n elements => 20n operations; linear with a large constant factor)
complexity.why: The list var_2 of size n is stored. list.count(d) is O(n), but it is invoked 20 times (2 per digit, 10 digits). The digit range is constant [0,9], so asymptotically it is still O(n), but with a high constant. Memory is proportional to n because all inputs are kept.

bottlenecks.detail: var_2.count(var_1) scans the entire list for each digit; it is called twice per digit, causing 20 full list scans per test case.
All n inputs are stored in var_2 even though only their frequency per digit (0-9) is needed.
Use of eval(input()) for integers is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()), though this is secondary to the counting overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Accumulate counts for digits 0-9 in a fixed-size array as inputs are read, avoiding repeated full-list scans and avoiding storing all values.

complexity.why: Each of the n inputs is processed exactly once with a constant-time increment into an array of size 10. Output then iterates over 10 entries. The array size does not depend on n, so extra memory is constant.

from.time: O(n) with ~20n list scans per test case

to.time: O(n) with ~n updates + 10 outputs per test case

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time remains linear, but the constant factor is drastically reduced by eliminating repeated list.count calls. Space improves from storing all inputs to storing only 10 counters.

transformation_steps: Replace building the full list var_2 with an in-place counting structure var_1 of size 10 initialized to zeros.
On reading each input value x, immediately increment var_1[x] instead of appending x to a list.
After all inputs are processed, iterate directly over the counts in var_1 to produce output, instead of calling list.count for each digit.
Avoid calling list.count(var_1) twice per digit (once for stars, once for zero-check); instead use the stored count value to decide between '*' * count and '-'.
Partially reduce eval usage by reading counts with eval(input()) once and inner values with int(input()); ideally, eval could be removed entirely for further robustness and speed.
trigger_signals: Use of list.count or similar scanning operations inside a loop over possible keys/categories.
Recomputing the same aggregate (frequency) multiple times instead of caching it.
Storing all inputs when only simple aggregated statistics (like counts per small fixed domain) are required.
Fixed small domain (digits 0-9) but algorithm still iterates over the entire data set per domain element.
pitfalls: Using eval(input()) for numeric parsing, which is both slower and unsafe; int(input()) is preferred.
Assuming list.count is O(1); it is O(n) and quickly dominates runtime when used repeatedly on the same list.
Forgetting that the alphabet size (0-9) is constant; failing to exploit this can lead to unnecessary list traversals.
Off-by-one or index errors when mapping input values to indices in the count array; must ensure inputs are within [0,9].

constraints_guess.notes: Classic task: given N integers, choose integer x minimizing sum (ai - x)^2. Typical competitive-programming constraints push for O(N) or O(N log N) solutions; N can be up to ~1e5-2e5, values up to around 1e9.

dominant_ops: Triple-nested looping over the entire integer range [min(a), max(a)] and over all elements for each candidate center, recomputing the same squared-distance sums many times.

complexity.why: Let N = len(var_7), and V = var_7[-1] - var_7[0] + 1 (value range). The outer loop over var_4 iterates V times but does not affect the computation, effectively repeating the entire inner work. Inside it, there is a first loop over N elements, then another loop over var_2 from min+1 to max-1 (~V iterations), and for each var_2 a loop over all N elements. So work per outer iteration is O(N + V*N) = O(V*N). Multiplied by outer V iterations yields O(V^2 * N). The array itself is stored once, so space is O(N).

bottlenecks.detail: The algorithm scans every integer from min(a) to max(a) (via var_2) and recomputes sum (a[i] - x)^2 for each candidate x, which is already O(V * N). On top of that, an outer loop over var_4 repeats the entire scan, blowing this up to O(V^2 * N) with no change in result.
var_4 is unused in the cost computation; for every var_4 the code recomputes the same sequence of sums for var_2. This multiplies runtime by approximately V for no reason.
Runtime depends on the numerical spread V = max(a) - min(a). If inputs are up to, say, 1e9 with a wide spread, the loops over that range are infeasible regardless of N.

All squared differences are recomputed in pure Python loops, missing the simple analytical fact that the minimizer of sum (ai - x)^2 is the mean of ai, so only a single pass over the data is actually needed.
Using eval(input()) for an integer N is unnecessary and slightly slower/unsafe compared to int(input()), though this is negligible compared to the algorithmic bottlenecks.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical property that the function f(x) = sum_i (ai - x)^2 is minimized at x equal to the mean of ai; for integer x, only floor(mean) or ceil(mean) need to be considered. The code effectively picks the appropriate integer around the mean and computes the sum once.

complexity.why: Computing the mean is a single pass over N elements. Then the code adjusts the mean via simple constant-time checks and builds a list of squared differences in one more pass (O(N)), followed by sum over that list (O(N)). No loops over the value range; total time is linear in N. The input list and the list of squared differences both store N values, giving O(N) space.

complexity_delta.from: O(V^2 * N) with redundant scanning over the entire value range [min, max] and repeated recomputation of sums.
complexity_delta.to: O(N) using a direct formula based on the mean, with only two linear passes over the data.
complexity_delta.note: The optimization removes dependence on the numeric spread V and eliminates two extra nested loops, turning an effectively cubic-style behavior (in terms of mixed parameters) into a single-pass linear solution.

transformation_steps: Recognize the underlying mathematical structure: minimizing sum (ai - x)^2 is a least-squares problem whose minimizer over real x is the arithmetic mean of ai.
Reduce the search space: for integer x, the minimum is attained at floor(mean) or ceil(mean); you do not need to loop through all integers between min(a) and max(a).
Eliminate the outer redundant loop (over var_4) and the inner exhaustive search (over var_2), replacing them with a single computation of mean and a constant-time rounding decision.
Compute the target integer x once (based on mean and tie-breaking rules), then perform a single pass over the data to compute sum (ai - x)^2.
Avoid recalculating the squared distance sums for every candidate x; instead, compute them once for the analytically determined optimal x.
trigger_signals: Presence of nested loops where one or more loop bounds depend on the numeric range (max(a) - min(a)) rather than solely on N.
An outer loop whose index variable (var_4) is not used in the computation, indicating redundant re-execution of inner logic.
An inner loop that recomputes sum (ai - x)^2 from scratch for each candidate x, despite the function being a simple quadratic in x.
Problem statement suggesting minimization of a sum of squared distances, a classic indicator that a mean-based or variance-based closed form likely exists.
Potential constraints from the original problem (large N or large value ranges) making any O(V * N) or worse approach non-viable.
pitfalls: Floating-point rounding: computing the mean as a float and comparing var_7 == 0.5 or using var_7 % 1 can be sensitive to floating-point representation; in practice this usually works for small integers but can be risky for large or extreme values.

Overcomplicated tie-breaking: the special case for mean exactly equal to 0.5 and counting elements greater than the mean is more complex than necessary. Usually checking floor(mean) and ceil(mean) explicitly and picking the better one is clearer and avoids floating subtleties.
Using eval(input()) for reading integers is unnecessary and potentially dangerous; int(input()) is safer and slightly faster.
Assuming that brute-force over the integer range [min, max] is acceptable without checking constraints; large spreads in values immediately make such approaches infeasible.

When refactoring, care must be taken to ensure the integer rounding convention matches the original problem’s definition (e.g., if multiple minimizers exist, any is allowed, or there is a specific tie-breaking rule).

constraints_guess.notes: N is the number of pieces; effective search space is 4^N (assign each piece to {unused, A, B, C}). Original AtCoder problem ABC119C uses N<=8, but the approach scales up to about N≈10 with pruning/constant-factor care.

dominant_ops: Iterating over all 4^N assignments using itertools.product([0,1,2,3], repeat=N).
For each assignment, looping over all N positions to accumulate three group sums.
Constructing a Counter and a set for each assignment to count usage per group and to check that exactly three groups are used.
Computing penalties and updating the best answer for every assignment.

complexity.why: There are 4^N tuples from product([0,1,2,3], repeat=N). For each tuple, the code: (1) scans all N entries to accumulate the three sums, (2) builds a set and a Counter over N entries to check usage and compute penalties. This yields Θ(N) work per assignment, giving O(4^N * N) time. Memory usage is dominated by temporary containers and per-iteration local variables, which are O(N) in size.

bottlenecks.detail: Recomputes group sums and per-group counts from scratch for each of the 4^N assignments instead of reusing partial aggregates along a search tree.
Allocates a new Counter and a new set for every assignment inside the main loop, incurring heavy interpreter and allocation overhead at each of the 4^N states.
Inner per-assignment loop performs an if/elif chain for each of the N positions, which adds Python-level branching overhead on top of the exponential state space.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a depth-first recursive search over the 4 choices per piece (unused, A, B, C) while carrying partial sums for A, B, C and the count of used pieces. At the leaf (after N pieces), compute the total cost in O(1) and update the best answer. This avoids building full assignment tuples, avoids Counter/set construction, and avoids rescanning all N pieces for each state.

complexity.why: The recursion explores a tree with branching factor 4 and depth N, giving 4^N leaves and O(4^N) total nodes. At each node, updates to partial sums and used-count are O(1). At each leaf, cost computation is O(1) because all necessary aggregates have been maintained incrementally. The recursion depth is at most N, so additional stack space is O(N).

complexity_delta.note: Both implementations are exponential in N, but the recursive version removes an extra multiplicative N factor and eliminates heavy per-state allocations (Counter, set), which substantially reduces runtime when 4^N is near the practical limit.

transformation_steps: Replace flat enumeration over product([0,1,2,3], repeat=N) with a recursive DFS that branches 4 ways at each index, passing index and current aggregates as arguments.
Maintain the three group sums (for targets A, B, C) incrementally in the recursion parameters (var_4, var_6, var_7) instead of recomputing them from the full assignment tuple for every state.

Track the total number of used pieces (var_12) along the recursion and compute the penalty term (var_12 - 3) * 10 only at leaf nodes, removing the need for a Counter and per-group counting in O(N) time.
Eliminate construction of temporary set and Counter objects by enforcing the non-empty constraint via a simple check on the final sums (var_4, var_6, var_7) at the recursion base case.
Keep the current best answer (var_5) in outer scope and update it only at leaf nodes, avoiding repeated min computations inside inner loops over N positions.
trigger_signals: Use of itertools.product over 4^N combinations combined with non-trivial O(N) work inside the main loop.
Creation of Python collections such as Counter and set within the innermost combinatorial loop.
Constraints indicating small N (≈8–10) where 4^N is large but still borderline feasible so constant factors and per-state overhead dominate performance.
Recomputation of simple aggregate values (group sums, counts) from scratch for every assignment instead of maintaining them incrementally along a search path.
pitfalls: When refactoring to recursion, shared state such as the best answer (var_5) must be handled carefully (global/nonlocal or passed by reference) to avoid scoping bugs that silently break correctness.
Recursion depth must remain within Python's recursion limit; this is safe for N up to about 10 but would require adjustment if N were significantly increased.
All four options per piece (unused, A, B, C) must be preserved to maintain the same search space as the original product-based enumeration; omitting a branch changes the problem.

The penalty must be based on the total count of used pieces (var_12) rather than incorrectly recomputing or miscounting per-group usage; otherwise the objective function will differ from the specification.

Base-case checks must correctly enforce that each of the three target groups is non-empty (e.g., by verifying var_4, var_6, var_7 are non-zero) to match the original constraints captured via the Counter in the slow version.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical for AtCoder ABC110 D: N, M up to 1e9; need to factor M and compute product of combinations C(e_i + N - 1, e_i) mod 1e9+7. Number of distinct prime factors and exponents is small (sum exponents = O(log M)).

dominant_ops: Global precomputation of factorial and inverse factorial arrays using NumPy vectorized prefix products
NumPy array reshaping and resizing for prefix product computation
Trial division factorization up to sqrt(M) (moderate but not dominant compared to NumPy overhead)

complexity.why: Factorization by trial division takes O(sqrt(M)). Combinatorics are implemented via precomputed factorials/inverse factorials up to some limit F (var_7 = 1e5+100 in the snippet), generated using NumPy prefix products. This adds O(F) work and memory even though the number of actual nCr evaluations and k-values is tiny (sum of prime exponents is O(log M)). The use of NumPy also introduces significant constant-factor overhead (import, array creation, reshaping, modulo operations in vectorized loops).

bottlenecks.detail: Use of NumPy (np.arange, np.resize, reshape, vectorized multiplication and modulo) for factorial precomputation is heavy in a competitive programming environment. Startup and per-operation costs are large compared to pure Python integer arithmetic for the small number of operations actually needed.

Precomputes factorials and inverse factorials up to a fixed bound (1e5+100) regardless of input sizes. For this problem, combinations are only needed for small k (prime exponents) but potentially enormous n (N up to 1e9), so factorial precomputation at a fixed array size is both mismatched and overkill for the real bottlenecks.

The factorial-based nCr formula assumes the ability to precompute factorials up to n_max, which can be as large as N+max_exponent. With N up to 1e9, this approach does not scale conceptually; the fixed bound var_7=1e5+100 risks incorrect results or implicit constraint violations.

The NumPy prefix product routine func_2 repeatedly multiplies and mod-reduces entire columns/rows of an array of size O(F). This is memory-bandwidth-heavy and wastes time relative to the few scalar multiplications actually needed to evaluate each combination multiplicatively.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial precomputation and NumPy entirely. Factorize M by trial division and for each prime exponent e, compute the combination C(e + N - 1, e) directly via a multiplicative formula using only O(min(e, N-1)) scalar multiplications/divisions. Because e is very small (sum exponents = O(log M)), the total work remains small and independent of N’s magnitude.

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + sum_e min(e, N-1)) ≈ O(sqrt(M) + log M)
complexity.why: Factorization remains O(sqrt(M)) via trial division. For each prime exponent e, we compute C(e+N-1, e) via: multiply numerator terms in a loop of length min(e, N-1), then divide by factorial(min(e, N-1)) in another loop of the same size. Since e is bounded by O(log M), these loops are tiny. No large arrays or precomputation are required; memory usage is constant aside from a small dict of primes to exponents.

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(M) + F) time, O(F) space, with large constants due to NumPy vectorization and array management (F ≈ 1e5 in the provided code). Conceptually cannot scale factorial precomputation to N up to 1e9.
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + log M) time, O(1) space (beyond small prime-exponent map). All operations are scalar integer arithmetic with very small constant factors and no dependence on a precomputation bound F.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically, both versions share the sqrt(M) factorization cost, but the slow version adds unnecessary O(F) work and memory and cannot be extended to support large N. The fast version’s combination calculation cost depends only on the small prime exponents, not on N or a large factorial table.

transformation_steps: Remove NumPy-based factorial/inverse-factorial precomputation (func_2 and func_3) and the associated global arrays var_13, var_14.

Replace the factorial-table-based nCr implementation with a multiplicative combinatorics routine: compute C(n, k) by multiplying n * (n-1) * ... * (n-k+1) and dividing by 2 * 3 * ... * k, with k = min(k, n-k).

Ensure modular reduction is applied only at the end (after integer division), or structure the computation such that intermediate values remain exact integers before taking modulo. In the fast_code, integer arithmetic is exact and the final result is reduced mod 1e9+7.
Keep the trial-division factorization but implement it in pure Python using integer operations and math.sqrt; store exponents in a dictionary keyed by prime factors.
Compute the final answer as the product over all prime exponents of C(exponent + N - 1, exponent) modulo 1e9+7, using the new multiplicative combination routine.
Avoid any large auxiliary arrays or fixed-size bounds tied to factorial tables, so the method remains valid even when N is as large as 1e9.
trigger_signals: Presence of NumPy for a primarily integer-arithmetic, combinatorial number theory problem (highly unusual in competitive programming and a red flag for performance).
Global factorial precomputation (var_7 = 10**5 + 100) when the problem involves a parameter N that can be as large as 1e9, indicating an approach that cannot scale to theoretical constraints.
Use of factorial-table-based nCr for single or very few combination evaluations where k is known to be small (prime exponents), suggesting that a multiplicative formula would be far cheaper.
Heavy reshaping/resizing of NumPy arrays (np.resize, reshape, 2D prefix products) for a one-dimensional factorial sequence, implying unnecessary memory traffic and overhead.
Competitive programming environment where Python + NumPy is typically too slow and large imports are discouraged unless absolutely necessary.
pitfalls: When replacing factorial-table-based nCr with a multiplicative implementation, ensure integer division (//) is used and that the numerator is always divisible by the denominator at each step; otherwise, the result can be incorrect or non-integer. The provided fast_code computes the full product then divides by all integers 2..k, which is safe for exact binomial coefficients.

Beware of attempting to apply the modulo during the division phase of the multiplicative nCr algorithm; modulo arithmetic does not commute with division unless modular inverses are used carefully. The fast_code avoids this by performing all divisions in exact integer arithmetic before taking modulo.

If constraints on N and M change and k becomes large (e.g., k up to 1e5 or more), the naive multiplicative combination method may become too slow, and a factorial/inverse-factorial approach with O(maxN) precomputation and O(1) per nCr might be preferable.

Factorization via trial division assumes M is not extremely large (here up to about 1e9). For significantly larger M, trial division O(sqrt(M)) would be too slow and a more advanced factorization method or different problem structure would be necessary.

Care must be taken to keep all intermediate values within Python’s integer capabilities when using multiplicative combinations without modular reduction; Python’s big integers handle this well, but in other languages overflow would be a concern and modular inverses would be required instead.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer N; need count of 1..N whose decimal length is odd. Code B only handles up to 6 digits, suggesting N ≤ 10^6.

dominant_ops: Loop from 1 to N
Per-iteration conversion of integer to string via str(var_2)
Per-iteration len() on the created string
Conditional check and possible increment

complexity.why: The loop runs N times. Each str(var_2) is O(log_10 var_2) characters, so total cost sums to Θ(∑ log i) = Θ(N log N). Only a few scalar variables are kept, so auxiliary memory is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: Linear scan over all integers up to N with per-element work proportional to the number of digits, instead of using a direct digit-count formula.
Creating a new Python string and computing its length on every iteration causes heavy allocation and GC overhead for large N.
Using eval(input()) is slower and unsafe; plain int(input()) is sufficient and safer.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the structure of decimal lengths: all 1-digit numbers (1–9) and 3-digit numbers (100–999), 5-digit numbers (10000–99999), etc., form contiguous ranges. Count full ranges with odd digit length and add the partial range for the highest digit length of N, avoiding per-number iteration.

complexity.why: The solution performs a constant number of comparisons and arithmetic operations based on thresholds (10, 100, 1000, ...). No loops or data structures grow with N.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log N) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(1) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: Replaced a digit-counting loop using string conversion with a closed-form, range-based counting formula over digit lengths.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the property checked (odd number of digits) depends only on the magnitude range of the integer, not on the specific value.
Derive counts for ranges with odd digit lengths: all numbers in those ranges contribute fully, while ranges with even digit lengths contribute zero.
For the highest relevant odd digit length <= digits(N), compute the partial contribution as N - lower_bound + 1 (e.g., N - 90, N - 9090).
Implement a sequence of if/elif branches on N’s magnitude to select the correct closed-form expression.
Replace eval(input()) with int(input()) for correctness and safety (even though this does not affect asymptotic complexity).
trigger_signals: Presence of a large loop over the entire range 1..N with per-element string operations.
Use of str() and len() inside the hot loop, which are relatively expensive in Python.
Potential or stated constraints where N can approach 10^6 or higher, making O(N log N) with heavy per-iteration work borderline in Python.
The mathematical pattern of digit lengths over integer ranges, suggesting a formulaic approach.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors at digit-boundary thresholds (e.g., handling N = 9, 10, 99, 100, etc.).
Forgetting to include all odd-digit full ranges below N (e.g., always including 1–9 and 100–999 when N is large enough).
Writing branch conditions in the wrong order, which may cause incorrect ranges to be applied.
Hard-coding thresholds up to a certain maximum (here 10^6) and silently failing or producing wrong results if the actual constraints allow larger N.
Assuming base-10 representation; the logic does not generalize without adjustment to other bases.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer N. Modified solution hard-codes ranges up to 10^5 (1..9, 100..999, 10000..99999), strongly suggesting N ≤ 10^5. If N could be larger, Code B would be incorrect/incomplete.

dominant_ops: Outer loop over all integers from 1 to N
Per-number digit-count loop using division by 10
Function-call overhead for each i in 1..N
Use of floating-point division in digit loop (var_4 / 10) instead of integer division

complexity.why: For each i in [1, N], func_1 repeatedly divides by 10 until the value drops below 1. The number of iterations is proportional to the number of digits, i.e., O(log_10 i). Summed over i = 1..N this is Θ(N log N) in the worst case. Only a few scalar variables are used, so auxiliary space is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: Digit length is recomputed by repeated division for every number in 1..N, leading to Θ(N log N) operations instead of using a direct counting-by-ranges or arithmetic formula.
Each iteration of the outer loop calls func_1, adding Python function-call overhead N times.
The digit loop uses floating-point division (var_4 / 10 >= 1) rather than integer operations, which is slower and unnecessary; int-only logic would be cheaper and clearer.
If N were as large as 10^7–10^8 or more, the Θ(N log N) work in pure Python risks TLE; the pattern (nested work in a 1..N loop) is a typical performance red flag.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the structure of numbers with an odd number of digits: they come in contiguous ranges (1–9, 100–999, 10000–99999, ...). Instead of counting digits for each number, explicitly iterate over fixed odd-digit ranges and stop once the current number exceeds N. This bounds the work to a small constant number of iterations for the given constraints.

complexity.time: O(min(N, 10^5)) (effectively O(1) under the intended constraint N ≤ 10^5)
complexity.why: The code iterates over at most three ranges: 1..9 (9 iterations), 100..999 (900 iterations), 10000..99999 (90000 iterations). That is ≤ 90,909 iterations regardless of N, provided N ≤ 10^5. No auxiliary data structures are used beyond a few scalars, so space remains constant.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log N) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(min(N, 10^5)) time, O(1) space (effectively constant-time for the intended N range)
complexity_delta.note: The new approach caps the number of iterations by hard-coding the few relevant odd-digit ranges within the constraint N ≤ 10^5, eliminating the per-number digit-count loop and function-calls.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the property 'number of digits is odd' defines contiguous numeric intervals: [1, 9], [100, 999], [10000, 99999], etc.
Replace the generic digit-count function with logic that directly processes these intervals.
For each odd-digit interval, loop from its lower bound upward, incrementing the count while the current value ≤ N, and break when it exceeds N.
Specialize to the problem's constraint bound by only implementing intervals up to 5 digits (≤ 10^5), thereby keeping the total loop iterations bounded by a small constant.
Remove the inner digit-count loop and associated floating-point division, as well as the cost of function calls inside the main loop.
trigger_signals: A loop from 1 to N where each iteration performs non-trivial work (another loop with divisions).
Use of a helper function doing repeated division per number, called N times.
Checking a numerical property (digit length) that is known to form simple contiguous ranges in base 10.
Presence of logarithmic inner loops whose bounds are derived from value magnitude (here, digit count) rather than fixed constants.
pitfalls: Correctness bounds: The modified code only covers up to 5-digit ranges. If N can exceed 99,999, additional odd-digit ranges (7 digits, 9 digits, ...) must be included; otherwise the answer becomes wrong for large N.
Maintainability: Hard-coded numeric ranges (1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000, 100000) are less self-explanatory than a formula-based approach and are easy to mis-extend or mis-copy for different constraints.
Off-by-one risks: Intervals like 1–9, 100–999, 10000–99999 need careful inclusive/exclusive handling; mistakes at boundaries can silently skew the count.
Input handling: Both versions use eval(input()), which is unsafe and unnecessary; using int(input()) is safer and typically faster.
Base dependence: The logic assumes base-10 representation. If the problem or environment changed to another base, the range constants would need full re-derivation.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style problem: choose integer p minimizing sum (ai - p)^2, with N up to ~100 and ai in [1,100]. Bounded value range allows brute-force over p in [1,100].

dominant_ops: Triple-nested loops over value range and array indices
Integer subtraction, squaring, and addition in tight loops
Redundant recomputation of the same sums across outer iterations

complexity.why: Let n = len(var_7), R = var_7[-1] - var_7[0] + 1. Outer loop: for var_4 in range(min, max+1) runs R times. Inside each outer iteration: one loop over n for p = var_7[0] (O(n)) plus an inner loop over all candidate p (var_2 in [min+1, max-1]) of size ~R, and for each candidate another loop over n, giving O(R * n). Total per outer iteration: O(n + R*n) = O(R*n). Multiplied by R outer iterations gives O(R^2 * n). Array storage is O(n); only a few scalar variables beyond that.

bottlenecks.detail: The loop `for var_4 in range(var_7[0], var_7[len(var_7) - 1] + 1)` does not use var_4 at all, yet repeats the entire computation of sums for all candidate p on every iteration. This multiplies the work by a factor of R unnecessarily.

Within the outer loop, `var_6` for p = var_7[0] is recomputed from scratch in every outer iteration. Likewise, for each candidate p (var_2) the sum over all elements is recomputed, even though this same set of computations is repeated for every outer-iteration of var_4.

`var_7.sort()` is only used to derive min and max, but the algorithm then loops over the full min..max range redundantly. Sorting adds O(n log n) setup cost without enabling a more efficient search strategy.

There is a nested loop: outer over `var_4` in [min, max], and inner over `var_2` in [min+1, max-1]. Both ranges are essentially the same size R, causing the R^2 factor. Only a single loop over candidate p values is needed.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the known bound on ai to brute-force over a fixed small range of candidate p values [1, 100], computing the sum of squared differences for each p in a single pass over the array, and track the minimum.

complexity.why: The loop `for var_5 in range(1, 101)` iterates over at most C = 100 candidate p values (a constant from problem constraints). For each p it performs a single O(n) pass over var_1 to accumulate `sum((ai - p)^2)`. Total time is O(C * n) = O(n). Space is O(n) for storing the array plus O(1) for scalars.

delta_type: remove_redundant_value-range nesting and fix candidate-range strategy

complexity_delta.from: O(n * R^2) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n * C) ≈ O(n) time (with C=100), O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: By eliminating an unnecessary outer loop over the value range and iterating directly over a single fixed candidate range [1,100], the algorithm moves from quadratic in the value range (R^2) to linear in n with a small constant factor.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the optimization target is `min_p sum_i (ai - p)^2`, and that p only needs to be considered over a bounded domain [1,100] given by the problem constraints, rather than dynamically scanning [min(ai), max(ai)] in nested loops.
Remove the redundant outer loop that iterated over `var_4` without using it, which caused a full recomputation of all candidate sums for every outer iteration.
Flatten the candidate search to a single loop over p: for p in allowed_range: compute `sum((ai - p)^2)` exactly once per p.
Replace index-based inner loops over `range(len(var_7))` with direct iteration over list values (`for var_3 in var_1:`), simplifying the code while preserving O(n) cost per candidate.
Use a running minimum (`var_4 = min(var_4, var_6)`) to track the best objective value instead of nested comparisons across repeated full scans.
trigger_signals: Presence of a loop variable (`var_4`) that is never used in the loop body, indicating likely redundant repetition.
Nested loops where both ranges depend on roughly the same span of values (min..max), inflating complexity to R^2 unnecessarily.
Recomputation of the same sum for the same candidate p in multiple loop iterations instead of caching or computing once.
Knowledge from the problem statement that ai ∈ [1,100], which allows a simple fixed-range brute force instead of an expansive dynamic search.
Complexity smell: three nested loops over n and value ranges, where the conceptual problem only requires trying each candidate p once.
pitfalls: Hard-coding the candidate range [1,100] is correct only if guaranteed by the problem constraints; applying this pattern generically without checking bounds could miss optimal p outside the chosen interval.
Both versions use `eval(input())`, which is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; `int(input())` is sufficient and safer.

If the value range of ai were large (e.g., up to 1e9) and not tightly bounded, even the fast solution’s `for p in range(1, 101)` style enumeration would need to be replaced by an analytic solution (using properties of quadratic functions) rather than brute force.
Relying on sorting for this problem is unnecessary; in other contexts keeping the sort when it’s not needed introduces extra O(n log n) cost without benefit.
When refactoring nested loops, it is easy to change control flow or variable scoping in ways that alter correctness; verifying that each candidate p is evaluated exactly once is essential.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder setting: N up to ~1e5, M up to ~1e9. One-shot computation, no multiple queries.

dominant_ops: Trial division prime factorization up to sqrt(M)
Naive multiplicative binomial coefficient per prime exponent with integer multiply/divide and per-call modulo

complexity.why: func_1 runs a for-loop up to floor(sqrt(original_M)) regardless of how much var_9 shrinks; trial division is therefore O(sqrt(M)). Each exponent e contributes a binomial C(e+N-1, e) computed in O(min(e, N-1)) basic arithmetic steps; with typical constraints, max e is tiny (<= ~30 for M<=1e9), so sum_e is small and factorization dominates.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorization loop uses a fixed upper bound int(sqrt(var_9_initial)) + 1 and keeps iterating up to that even after var_9 is reduced by extracted factors, performing unnecessary divisor checks.
Use of math.sqrt and int conversion for the loop bound introduces small but avoidable overhead compared to the simple arithmetic condition i * i <= n that naturally tightens as n shrinks.

Binomial func_2 performs integer multiplication and division with a modulo operation only at the end but still uses floor-division per step; repeated divisions can become non-trivial cost if exponents were larger.

Although the modulo is not applied inside the loop (good), func_2 is recomputed for each exponent instead of reusing global factorial/precomputed combinatorics, which would be more scalable for larger N or many queries.

FastAudit.core_idea: Tighten the factorization loop to stop at i * i <= current_n so the bound shrinks as factors are stripped, and implement the binomial coefficient as separate numerator and denominator products using plain integer arithmetic with a single modulo at the outer level, avoiding extra structure and math calls.

complexity.why: Factorization func_2 uses while d*d <= n with n decreasing as factors are removed, eliminating redundant checks beyond sqrt(remaining_n); asymptotically still O(sqrt(M)) but with a smaller constant. Binomial func_1 performs O(e) multiplications for numerator and denominator (e = exponent), exactly matching the previous asymptotics but with a simpler inner loop and no per-step modulo, thus reducing constant factors.

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(M) + sum_e) time, O(#prime_factors) space
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + sum_e) time, O(#prime_factors) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged; improvements come from tighter loop bounds, simpler arithmetic, and better placement of expensive operations like sqrt and modulo.

transformation_steps: Replaced for-loop with fixed upper bound int(sqrt(M_initial)) + 1 by a while-loop condition d*d <= current_M, allowing the effective upper bound on divisors to shrink as factors are removed.
Removed dependency on math.sqrt for the factorization loop bound, reducing function-call overhead and avoiding recomputation of a bound based on the initial value.
Changed factorization result representation from a dict {prime: exponent} to a list of (prime, exponent) tuples; iteration cost is similar but avoids dict overhead in this context.

Reimplemented the binomial coefficient as a direct multiplicative ratio: multiplying the descending numerator and denominator sequences and then performing a single integer division, rather than two loops with dynamic min(k, n-k) and repeated divisions.
Applied the modulus only once per prime factor contribution in the outer loop, keeping inner arithmetic purely integer, which generally performs better in Python.
Removed unnecessary casts and list-materialization (e.g., list(var_3.values())) in favor of direct iteration over the factorization result.
trigger_signals: Factorization loop iterating up to a precomputed sqrt bound even after the candidate number had been significantly reduced by division.
Use of math.sqrt inside performance-critical code where a simple arithmetic condition (i * i <= n) is sufficient.
Binomial coefficient computed via repeated integer division without leveraging the small, fixed exponent size and without reducing structural overhead.
No precomputation of factorials or reuse of combinatorial structures, acceptable here but a potential concern for larger or repeated inputs.
pitfalls: The new binomial implementation assumes that intermediate integer products remain manageable; in Python they do (arbitrary precision) but extremely large parameters would increase big-integer overhead. Here exponents are small, so this is safe.

Moving modulo operations out of inner loops is beneficial, but it requires careful use of integer division (//) to avoid floating-point behavior; using / instead would silently introduce precision bugs.
The factorization loop now depends on the invariant d*d <= n with n mutated; incorrect updates to n or d could prematurely terminate the loop and miss a remaining composite factor.
The new representation of prime factors as a list of tuples changes the access pattern; code relying on dictionary-style lookups would need adaptation if extended.

constraints_guess.notes: Array size and number of operations are on the order of 3e5. Operations are range updates and range max queries; naive per-element handling will TLE.

dominant_ops: Building a segment tree over the initial array
Point updates on the segment tree (func_3) called repeatedly for each element in an update range
Range max queries (func_1) on the segment tree
Extra list allocation in build: reversed(list(range(...)))

complexity.time: O(n log n + sum_over_updates(len_range) * log n + q_query * log n)
complexity.why: The class implements a standard max segment tree with point updates (func_3) and range max queries (func_1). A single point update or query is O(log n). If the problem’s logical operation is a range update [l, r) and it is implemented as a loop of point updates, each such operation costs O((r-l) log n), leading to O(n * q * log n) in the worst case. Tree build is O(n log n) in this implementation due to the inefficient reversed(list(range())) pattern, and the segment tree itself stores O(n) elements.

bottlenecks.detail: Range updates are likely realized as many point updates via func_3 inside a loop over all indices in the interval, giving per-update time O(range_length * log n) instead of O(log n). With up to ~3e5 operations and large ranges, this becomes prohibitive.

Tree build uses reversed(list(range(var_9 - 2))) which constructs an intermediate list of size O(n) and then iterates it in reverse, instead of a direct reversed range (e.g., range(var_9 - 2, -1, -1)). This adds unnecessary allocation and time.

Heavy use of method calls (Class_1.func_3 / func_1), attribute lookups (self.node), and a separate func_2 wrapper around max() adds call overhead on every internal node visit, amplifying the cost of each O(log n) operation when executed hundreds of thousands of times.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace repeated point updates with a segment tree supporting true range assignment updates via lazy propagation, implemented iteratively with flat arrays and bit operations. This reduces per-update complexity from O(range_length * log n) to O(log n) and aggressively minimizes Python-level overhead by avoiding classes, recursion, and intermediate allocations.

complexity.why: The fast code preallocates segment tree arrays sized to the next power of two >= 300001 (var_5). It supports range assignment updates and range maximum maintenance with lazy propagation: func_4 performs a range update [l, r) in O(log n) by updating O(log n) segment tree nodes and lazily marking them in var_15. func_1 computes the nodes on the paths that need their lazy values pushed down, and func_2 pushes those values to children before updates. Each operation touches only O(log n) nodes, giving overall O((n + q) log n) time. The tree arrays var_9 (values) and var_15 (lazy tags) are O(n) in size.

complexity_delta.from: Per range update implemented as O(range_length * log n) via repeated point updates; total worst case O(n * q * log n) when ranges are large. Build phase also has extra O(n) allocation overhead.
complexity_delta.to: Per range update and per range query in O(log n) using an iterative lazy segment tree; overall O((n + q) log n).
complexity_delta.note: The key asymptotic change is in how range updates are handled (true lazy propagation vs. many point updates). Additional gains come from removing per-operation Python overhead (classes, extra lists, redundant function wrappers).

transformation_steps: Identify that problem operations are range-based (assign or update over [l, r)) combined with range maximum queries, making repeated point updates asymptotically suboptimal.
Redesign the data structure from a point-update segment tree to a lazy segment tree that directly supports range assignment updates in O(log n) per operation.
Switch from an object-oriented, method-based segment tree to a flat-array, function-based implementation to reduce Python attribute lookup and call overhead.
Avoid intermediate list allocations in tree processing by using bit-level index arithmetic and compact loops instead of reversed(list(range(...))).

Introduce lazy tag array (var_15) to defer propagation of range assignments, and a targeted push-down mechanism (func_1 + func_2) that only touches necessary nodes on paths relevant to each operation.
Use fast I/O (sys.stdin.readline) and precomputed tree size (next power of two) to reduce input parsing and allocation overhead.
trigger_signals: Constraints suggest n and q up to ~3e5 with many range operations; a solution with per-element loops inside each operation is likely to exceed time limits.
Original design provides only point updates (func_3) but the problem semantics require range updates, implying a loop over the range in user code.
Profiling or reasoning shows that the majority of time is spent in repeated calls to update over contiguous ranges, each performing log n work.
Presence of reversed(list(range(...))) and small wrapper functions around built-ins (func_2 wrapping max) indicates avoidable Python overhead in inner loops.
pitfalls: Implementing lazy propagation incorrectly (e.g., failing to push tags before reading children, or mishandling overlapping ranges) can lead to subtle wrong answers that only appear on specific corner cases.

Off-by-one errors in translating between array indices and segment tree positions (0-based vs 1-based, [l, r) vs [l, r]) are easy to introduce when converting from a simple point-update tree to an iterative lazy one.

Mixing assignment semantics (overwrite) with max semantics in the tree requires clear invariants: lazy values must represent the operation correctly, and internal node values must always be recomputable from children.

Using Python recursion for segment tree operations with large n risks hitting recursion limits or incurring extra overhead; an iterative design like in the fast code avoids this but is more index-arithmetic heavy and error-prone.
Relying on bit operations for path decomposition (e.g., (x & -x).bit_length()) is efficient but can be fragile if indices or inclusivity rules change without carefully updating the logic.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: given N and M (up to about 1e9), factorize M and count distributions of prime exponents among N slots using combinations C(N+e-1, e) modulo 1e9+7.

dominant_ops: Trial division prime factorization up to floor(sqrt(M)) on the original M
Recursive computation of binomial coefficients using multiplicative identity with Python big integers

complexity.why: Factorization loop iterates var_6 from 2 to floor(sqrt(original M)), regardless of how much var_1 has shrunk, giving O(sqrt(M)) trial divisions. For each prime exponent e, func_1 makes e recursive calls, so total O(sum_e e) = O(log M) given exponents are small; this is dominated by factorization.

bottlenecks.detail: for var_6 in range(2, floor(sqrt(var_1)) + 1) uses sqrt of the *initial* var_1; the loop does not shorten when var_1 is divided down, so it keeps trying unnecessary divisors after full factorization.

func_1 uses recursion for C(n, k): func_1(var_8 - 1, var_7 - 1) * var_8 // var_7. Even though depth is small (exponent size), each recursive call has Python frame setup/teardown overhead and function-call overhead.
Combination is built step-by-step as big integers with multiply-then-divide on each recursive step; while mathematically efficient, it is still done at Python level, not in tight C loops.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the algorithm the same (factorize M then multiply C(N+e-1, e)), but (1) factorize using a while loop whose upper bound shrinks with the current remaining value, and (2) compute each binomial coefficient iteratively using Python's C-level reduce and operator.mul for faster loops instead of Python recursion.

complexity.why: Factorization uses while var_3 * var_3 <= var_6 with var_6 updated as factors are removed; this can stop earlier than sqrt(original M) when M has small factors, improving constants while keeping O(sqrt(M)) worst-case. For each exponent e, computing C(n, e) via reduce(mul, range(...)) and range(...) for the denominator is O(e) with tight C-level loops, again dominated overall by factorization.

delta_type: implementation-level optimization with constant-factor and robustness improvements

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(M) + sum_e e) with larger constant factors due to over-long factorization loop and Python recursion overhead.
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + sum_e e) with smaller constants by early-stopping factorization and using C-level iteration for products.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged, but runtime is reduced by (a) not iterating up to sqrt(initial M) once the remaining value has shrunk, and (b) eliminating Python recursion and replacing it with faster C-driven loops.

transformation_steps: Change factorization from a for-loop up to floor(sqrt(initial_M)) to a while-loop with condition var_3 * var_3 <= current_remaining_value, so the upper bound shrinks as factors are removed.
Replace recursive combination func_1(n, k) with an iterative formulation using ranges and reduce(operator.mul, ...) to compute numerator and denominator products.
Normalize k by k = min(k, n-k) to reduce the number of multiplicative steps when applicable.
Apply modulo 1e9+7 only at the aggregation stage (same as before) while relying on more efficient intermediate arithmetic.
trigger_signals: Use of recursion in a tight numeric loop (combination computation) where iteration would suffice.
Factorization loop whose upper bound is based on the original M rather than the shrinking remaining value.
Observed TLE or high runtime despite correct high-level algorithm (factorize-then-combine).
High function-call counts in profiling concentrated in func_1 (recursive combinatorics).
pitfalls: Both versions still do full big-integer arithmetic for combinations and only apply the modulus at the end; if constraints were larger (e.g., N and exponents much bigger), a factorial + modular inverse approach would be necessary to avoid huge integers.
Using recursion for combinatorics risks hitting Python's recursion limit if exponents or usage patterns were increased in future changes.
Care must be taken that the modified factorization loop correctly handles the remaining prime > sqrt(remaining) (both codes address this by appending the last var_1 if != 1).

The iterative combination code must guard against invalid parameters (n < k) and handle k = 0 properly, as the fast version does; omitting these checks could cause incorrect integer division or empty ranges.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic AtCoder-style task: choose integer p that minimizes sum_i (a_i - p)^2. Typical constraints: n <= ~100, a_i in [1,100]. The fast solution brute-forces p in [1,100], consistent with small bounded value range.

dominant_ops: Python-level loop over candidate p values spanning [min(a), max(a)]
Inside loop: np.sum over full array each iteration
Inside loop: repeated min(var_2) on numpy array

complexity.why: Let N = len(var_2), D = max(var_2) - min(var_2) + 1. max(var_2) and min(var_2) outside loop are O(N) once. The loop executes D times. In each iteration: (1) min(var_2) is called again: O(N) because numpy's min over the array; (2) (var_2 - var_5) ** 2 allocates a size-N temporary array; (3) np.sum over that array is O(N). So each iteration is O(N), giving O(D * N) overall. Memory is dominated by the N-sized numpy array and temporary arrays: O(N).

bottlenecks.detail: The loop iterates over all integers from min(var_2) to max(var_2), which can be large if the input values are not tightly bounded. This makes the factor D potentially big, leading to slow runtime when value spread is large.
min(var_2) is recomputed in every iteration of the loop even though the array does not change. This adds an extra O(N) per iteration overhead.
Each iteration performs numpy vectorized operations and a sum over the entire array. While vectorized, these are still O(N) and incur Python-to-C boundary overhead every iteration.
Using eval(input()) to read an integer is slower and risky; eval is unnecessary and adds parsing overhead. input() is also slower than buffered sys.stdin.readline used in the fast code.
Importing numpy is heavy for competitive programming style tasks and can noticeably impact execution time for small N and small constant loops where pure Python is sufficient.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the small, fixed search domain for p (1..100) and use simple nested Python loops over N and at most 100 candidate values, avoiding numpy and repeated expensive operations. This turns the outer loop count into a small constant and keeps the implementation cache-friendly with minimal overhead.

complexity.why: The algorithm tries every candidate p from 1 to 100, and for each p scans all N elements, accumulating the squared distances. The outer loop is over a fixed constant size (100), so the cost is 100 * O(N) = O(N). Memory use is O(N) for storing the list of integers; only scalar temporaries are used otherwise.

complexity_delta.from: O(D * N) with D = max(a) - min(a) + 1, plus unnecessary O(N) work per iteration from repeated min() calls
complexity_delta.to: O(N) by constraining the candidate search space to a fixed small range (1..100) independent of input spread
complexity_delta.note: The theoretical worst-case of both approaches may look similar if D is small, but in practice the slow code allows D to scale with the value range, and adds redundant O(N) work per iteration. The fast code exploits the known bounded domain for p, making the outer loop a small constant and removing library overhead in the hot path.

transformation_steps: Replace dynamic search range based on [min(a), max(a)] with a fixed small range [1, 100] consistent with problem constraints, reducing D to a small constant.
Remove repeated computation of min(var_2) inside the loop; in the fast solution, no min/max on the array are needed at all.
Drop numpy entirely and switch to plain Python lists and scalar arithmetic, avoiding Python-to-C overhead in each iteration and temporary array allocations.
Optimize IO by switching from input()/eval to sys.stdin.readline and explicit int conversion, eliminating eval and reducing per-line parsing overhead.
Accumulate the squared differences in a simple inner loop using integers, maintaining the running minimum cost in a Python variable.
trigger_signals: Use of numpy operations inside a Python for-loop over many iterations, each performing a full-array computation.
Recomputation of min(var_2) inside the p-iteration loop despite the array being immutable.
A search range for p that depends on max(a) - min(a) rather than on known small constraints from the problem statement.
Use of eval(input()) for reading integers in a performance-sensitive context.
Competitive programming environment where importing heavy libraries and using slow IO are known to cause timeouts.
pitfalls: If the actual constraints for p are not strictly limited to [1, 100], hard-coding the range could miss the true optimal p. The optimization assumes the contest/problem guaranteed a small bounded range.

Removing numpy is beneficial here because N and the outer loop bound are small. For very large N and a fixed small D, a well-structured numpy solution without Python-level loops might be competitive or faster, but that is not the pattern used in the slow code.

Assuming that using numpy is always faster is incorrect: numpy shines when you can move the entire computation into vectorized operations and minimize Python loops. Here, a Python loop over p calling numpy every iteration is suboptimal.

Over-aggressive micro-optimization of IO (like switching to sys.stdin) is only helpful if algorithmic complexity is already appropriate; in the slow code, IO is not the primary bottleneck compared to O(D * N) computation.

If one tried to further optimize by using the mean of a_i analytically as the best p (rounding to nearest integer), care must be taken with integer rounding and checking both floor/ceil candidates to avoid off-by-one errors.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case; typical competitive constraints where n up to ~1e5-2e5 and each value up to ~1e4–1e5. Original O(n * max(a_i)) loop would be too slow if max(a_i) is large (e.g., up to 1e9), suggesting intended O(n) or O(n log n) solution.

dominant_ops: Double loop over candidate centers (0..max(var_2)) and all array elements; for each candidate, recomputes sum of squared differences.

complexity.why: Outer loop runs over V = max(var_2)+1 candidates; inner loop scans all n elements and does O(1) work per element. So total operations proportional to n * V. Only a few scalar variables and the input array are stored, giving O(1) extra space beyond input.

bottlenecks.detail: Brute-force search over all integer x in [1, max(var_2)] to minimize sum (a_i - x)^2. This is unnecessary because the sum of squared deviations has a known minimizer related to the mean, allowing O(n) instead of O(n * max(a_i)).
For each candidate x, a full pass over the array is performed. When max(var_2) is large, this leads to potentially billions of iterations.
The expression (var_7 - (var_4 + 1)) ** 2 is recomputed from scratch for every (element, candidate) pair instead of using precomputed aggregates like sum(a_i) and sum(a_i^2).
Use of eval(input()) is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()); while not the primary performance bottleneck, it adds unnecessary overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical property that the sum of squared deviations ∑(a_i - x)^2 is minimized near the mean of the data. Compute the (rounded) average once, then compute the sum of squared differences to that single candidate value in one pass over the array.

complexity.why: Two linear passes over the array: one to compute the sum (for the mean), one to compute the sum of squared deviations. Each pass is O(n) with constant work per element. No additional data structures beyond a few scalars are needed, so extra space is O(1).

complexity_delta.from: O(n * V) time, O(1) extra space
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(1) extra space
complexity_delta.note: V = max(a_i). The transformation removes dependency on the numeric range of values and relies only on the array length.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the objective function is sum of squared deviations: f(x) = ∑(a_i - x)^2, which can be expanded as ∑a_i^2 - 2x∑a_i + n x^2, a convex quadratic in x with a unique minimum.
Use calculus / algebra to note that the continuous minimizer is x* = (∑a_i) / n, the mean of the data.
Since x must be an integer, restrict attention to integer points near the mean (e.g., round, floor, or ceil of the mean) instead of scanning the entire range [1, max(a_i)].
Implement an O(n) solution: compute mean = sum(var_2) / var_1, choose an integer candidate (here, round(mean)), and compute the sum of squared deviations to that value in one pass.
Remove the outer loop over candidate x (0..max(var_2)) and keep only a single linear-time aggregation over the array.
trigger_signals: Appearance of a loop over all possible values from 0 to max(array) combined with an inner loop over all elements, suggesting O(n * max_value) complexity.
Potential input sizes that allow array elements to be large (e.g., up to 1e5 or 1e9), making a value-range loop suspicious.
Mathematical structure of the objective function is a sum of squared differences, a standard case with a known minimizer (mean), signaling that brute-force enumeration is unnecessary.
Time-limit exceeded or noticeably slow runtime when max(var_2) is large, even if n is moderate.
pitfalls: Integer vs. real minimizer: The true minimizer of ∑(a_i - x)^2 over reals is the exact mean; over integers, the optimal x is one of floor(mean) or ceil(mean). Using round(mean) alone may fail in edge cases where ties or asymmetries occur; a robust solution should typically check both candidates and take the better.

Floating-point rounding: Using floating-point division and round() can introduce subtle off-by-one issues, especially if sums are large; using exact integer arithmetic (e.g., checking floor(sum/n) and floor(sum/n)+1) avoids such problems.
Still using eval for input: eval(input()) is unnecessary and unsafe; while not a performance bottleneck here, it is a bad practice and can cause security issues in other contexts.

List vs generator in sum: sum([(var_4 - var_3) ** 2 for var_4 in var_2]) builds an intermediate list; for very large n, sum((var_4 - var_3) ** 2 for var_4 in var_2) would be slightly more memory-efficient, though both are O(n) and the asymptotic space remains O(1) beyond input.

constraints_guess.notes: Multiple test cases until '0 0'. Count triples (i,j,k) with 1 <= i < j < k <= n and i+j+k == x. Typical AOJ ITP1_7_B style constraints: n <= 100, x <= 300.

dominant_ops: Triple nested loops over candidates 1..var_6 for (var_1, var_2, var_3) with an O(1) check per triplet (including a sum over a 3-element list).

complexity.why: For each test case, the code computes var_6 = min(n, x) and iterates var_1 from 1..var_6, var_2 from var_1+1..var_6, var_3 from var_2+1..var_6. This is Θ(var_6^3) triplets in the worst case; with var_6 = O(n), time is Θ(n^3) per test case. The sum([var_1,var_2,var_3]) is constant-time but adds interpreter overhead inside the innermost loop. Only O(1) extra variables are stored.

bottlenecks.detail: Explores all O(n^3) ordered triples (var_1,var_2,var_3) with 1 <= var_1 < var_2 < var_3 <= var_6, even though only a small fraction satisfy var_1 + var_2 + var_3 == var_8.
The innermost loop depth is 3, so the interpreter overhead for Python-level loops becomes significant as n grows (e.g., up to 100).
Uses sum([var_1, var_2, var_3]) inside the innermost loop, which allocates a list and calls a generic sum function on every iteration instead of using a simple var_1 + var_2 + var_3 expression.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid the explicit O(n^3) enumeration by fixing var_1, deriving the initial var_2 and var_3 from the sum constraint var_1 + var_2 + var_3 == var_7, and then walking all valid (var_2,var_3) pairs for that fixed var_1 in a single inner loop. This reduces the search space to O(n^2) states while maintaining the ordering constraints var_1 > var_2 > var_3 > 0.

complexity.why: For each test case, var_1 starts from var_6+1 and is decremented until the inequality var_1 > var_2 > var_3 fails, where var_2 and var_3 are functions of var_1 and the fixed sum var_7. Thus the outer loop runs O(n) times in the worst case. For each fixed var_1, the inner while-loop adjusts var_2 downward and var_3 upward, preserving var_2 + var_3 = const; the difference var_2 - var_3 shrinks by 2 each iteration until var_2 <= var_3 or either bound fails. The maximum initial gap is O(n), so the inner loop is O(n) for each var_1. Combined, this yields O(n^2) iterations per test case. Only a constant number of scalar variables are used, so space remains O(1).

complexity_delta.note: Reduced the search dimension from three nested loops over candidates to effectively two degrees of freedom by using the sum constraint to derive the third value and iterating along the valid (var_2,var_3) line for each var_1.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the constraint var_1 + var_2 + var_3 == target allows computing one variable from the other two, so only two variables need to be looped over explicitly.
Replace the triple nested loops over (var_1,var_2,var_3) with an outer loop over a single variable (var_1) and algebraic initialization of var_2 and var_3 using the sum equation.

Within each outer iteration, iterate over possible (var_2,var_3) pairs by updating them in opposite directions (var_2--, var_3++) while preserving their sum, and stopping when the ordering constraints var_1 > var_2 > var_3 > 0 break.
Exploit the fact that once var_1 is too small to satisfy var_1 > var_2 > var_3 under the sum constraint, no further smaller var_1 can work, allowing an early break from the outer loop.
Keep memory usage constant by only storing a few scalar counters instead of maintaining explicit collections of candidates.
trigger_signals: Presence of three nested loops over the same bounded range (1..n) with a simple arithmetic constraint tying the loop variables together.
The innermost body is just a constant-time condition check (sum equality), with no dependence on complex data structures.
The problem is combinatorial counting of triples under a linear constraint, which is a classic pattern for reducing one dimension via algebra.
Performance issues or timeouts when n or the number of test cases grows, indicating cubic complexity is too slow.
Use of sum([...]) and list construction inside the innermost loop, which is a sign of inefficiency in Python for tight loops.
pitfalls: Incorrectly handling the order constraint (i < j < k). When reducing dimensions, it is easy to allow permutations or double-counting unless inequalities are carefully maintained.
Forgetting to enforce bounds 1 <= var_3 and var_3 <= n when deriving var_3 from var_1 and var_2, which can introduce invalid triples.
Stopping conditions in the optimized while-based loops are subtle; incorrect inequalities can either miss valid triples or lead to infinite loops.
Over-optimizing with opaque loop logic (as in the fast_code) can reduce readability and make verification harder, increasing the risk of logical off-by-one errors.

Assuming that shrinking one dimension always makes it faster without considering Python interpreter overhead; if the new control flow is too complex, constant factors can erode some of the theoretical gains.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical greedy scheduling with deadlines: sort N jobs then linear scan. Python solution with O(N log N) is standard for N up to ~2e5 when using fast I/O.

dominant_ops: Reading N lines of two integers each from stdin
Allocating list of N pairs
Sorting the list of N jobs by the second element (deadline) using a key function
Single linear pass computing prefix sums and comparing to deadlines

complexity.why: The bottleneck is sorting the list of N jobs by deadline, which costs O(N log N). Input reading and the linear validation loop are both O(N). The extra helper functions do not change asymptotic complexity.

bottlenecks.detail: Although using sys.stdin.readline is already fast, the numerous unused helper wrappers add tiny overhead in readability but negligible runtime cost. Core I/O is appropriate for large N.
Sorting with key=lambda x: x[1] introduces a key-function call per comparison; this is still efficient and idiomatic in Python and not a real bottleneck at this scale.
No algorithmic bottleneck beyond the necessary O(N log N) sort; the algorithm is already optimal for this greedy scheduling check.

FastAudit.core_idea: Same greedy scheduling algorithm: read N jobs, sort by deadline, accumulate required times in ascending deadline order, and fail immediately if any prefix sum exceeds its deadline. Implementation changes revolve around I/O style and how the sort key is encoded (reordering fields instead of using a key function), not the algorithm.

complexity.why: Still sorts N jobs (now by constructing pairs as [deadline, duration] and using default sort), followed by a single O(N) pass. Using deque and then converting to list does not change the asymptotic behavior.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N log N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged, but constants are likely worse in the modified code due to using eval(input()) and plain input() instead of buffered sys.stdin, plus an unnecessary deque-to-list conversion.

transformation_steps: Replaced sys.stdin.readline-based input helpers with direct input() calls and eval(input()) for the first integer.
Switched representation of each job from [duration, deadline] to [deadline, duration] to rely on default sort order instead of a key function.
Introduced a deque to collect jobs, then converted it back to a list before sorting.
Changed the validation loop from using a boolean flag and printing at the end to early exit on failure via print('No'); exit().
trigger_signals: Desire to avoid an explicit key=lambda var_8: var_8[1] in sort, possibly under the misconception that this is slower than sorting by default order of transformed pairs.
Attempt to simplify the control flow by using early exit instead of carrying a boolean flag.
