Refactoring towards more straightforward-looking code using input() rather than low-level sys.stdin.readline.
pitfalls: Using eval(input()) to read an integer is strictly worse for performance and can be unsafe; int(input()) is sufficient.
input() is slower than sys.stdin.readline for large N; switching away from buffered stdin can cause timeouts on tight constraints.
Using deque here provides no benefit since all operations are appends and a final sort on a list; the intermediate deque plus conversion adds overhead.
Reordering pair elements to avoid a sort key does not yield a meaningful speedup in CP-style Python; the original key-based sort was already efficient and clearer.

constraints_guess.notes: Single array scan problem (longest non-increasing run of adjacent elements). Typical contest constraints likely up to 1e5–2e5 integers in one test.

dominant_ops: Reading n integers from stdin and building a list
Single pass over the list with O(n) comparisons of adjacent elements

complexity.why: Input parsing constructs a list of size n, and the loop makes a constant amount of work per element (one comparison and a few assignments); no nested loops or extra passes.

bottlenecks.detail: Uses built-in input() which is slower than buffered sys.stdin.readline() for large input sizes.
Uses int(eval(input())) to read n, which is slower and unnecessarily invokes the eval parser; simple int(input()) would suffice.
Imports math, string, collections and defines helper functions (factorial-based comb, divisor enumeration, duplicate check) that are never used; they add minor but avoidable startup overhead.
Iterates via range(len-1) with list indexing; equivalent logic can be expressed as a direct iteration over values with a 'previous element' variable, which is slightly lighter in Python.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep a running count of the current non-increasing run by iterating directly over the array values with a 'previous element' sentinel, updating the maximum run length on each increase, and use buffered stdin.readline for faster input.

complexity.why: Still reads all n elements into a list and performs a single linear scan; work per element is constant (one comparison and a few assignments). Asymptotic complexity matches the original, but with reduced constant factors due to faster IO and simpler loop mechanics.

complexity_delta.from: O(n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotics are unchanged; improvements are in IO speed and per-iteration overhead.

transformation_steps: Switched from input() to sys.stdin.readline() (aliased as var_6) for reading the line of integers, reducing Python-level IO overhead.
Replaced index-based loop over range(n-1) with a direct for-loop over the list values while tracking the previous value in var_5; this removes explicit indexing and range object creation.

Reformulated the run-length logic to use a sentinel previous value (1e9+7) and a counter starting at -1 so that each non-increasing step increments the pair-count correctly, matching the original semantics.

Eliminated unused helper functions and imports from the executed path by wrapping the main logic in func_1 and calling it directly, avoiding dead code in the hot path (though some unused eval(input()) remains).
trigger_signals: Single large input list processed once, suggesting IO and loop overhead are significant relative to the total runtime.
Use of input() and eval(input()) in a performance-sensitive competitive-programming style problem.
Presence of unused heavy helpers (math.factorial-based combination, divisor enumeration) indicating leftover template code and potential for cleanup.
Algorithm already linear time with no obvious asymptotic improvement available, pointing to constant-factor and IO optimizations as the main levers.
pitfalls: The optimized version still uses eval(input()) for the first line (n), which is unnecessary and slower than int(input()); also, n is not actually used, so relying solely on the array length is fine only if the input format is guaranteed consistent.
Initialization of the sentinel previous value (1e9+7) and the counter var_3 = -1 is subtle; incorrect choices can introduce off-by-one errors or break correctness for edge cases.

Assuming all integers fit comfortably in memory as a single list; if constraints were larger (e.g., streaming or huge n), even O(n) space might be problematic and a streaming approach without storing the full list would be preferable.

Relying on a single space-separated line of integers; if the actual problem allows line breaks or multiple lines for the array, the fast version would need to be adapted to read until n elements are consumed.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-level constraints inferred from binary-search + prefix-sum solution in Python. Coordinates appear up to ~1e9, hence the 10**10 search bound in the slow version.

dominant_ops: For each query, perform a binary search on the radius (var_7) over range [0, 1e10]
Inside each radius step, run bisect_left and bisect_right on the full array
Per-step recomputation of sums using prefix sums and parity-based partial sums

complexity.time: O(N) preprocessing + O(Q * logC * logN) per test where C ≈ 1e10 (coordinate range), effectively O(Q * logN) but with a large constant and extra overhead from nested binary search and bisects.
complexity.space: O(N) for original array + prefix sums (var_13, var_14, var_15) + O(Q) in worst case for memoization dict var_3.
complexity.why: Each query performs a while loop that binary-searches the radius var_7 over ~[0, 1e10]. Every loop iteration uses bisect_left and bisect_right, each O(logN). Hence per query ~O(logC * logN). Though logC is small (~34), the combination of two bisects, multiple conditional branches, and Python overhead per step causes performance pressure at large Q and N.

bottlenecks.detail: Binary search is done over a large numeric radius space [0, 1e10] instead of over the discrete index count of chosen elements. This introduces an extra logC factor and broad search space.
Each iteration performs both bisect_left and bisect_right on the array, doubling the O(logN) cost per radius check.
Multiple nested if-blocks with index shifts (var_6 -= 1 or var_6 -= 2) and parity checks cause overhead and increase risk of off-by-one errors, making micro-optimizations harder.

Memoization dictionary var_3 helps only if many identical query points are repeated. In the worst case (all queries distinct), every query pays full binary-search cost while still carrying the dictionary overhead.

The provided slow code is truncated in the second major branch (var_6 % 2 == 0: var_2 += ...), which suggests additional work or conditions were intended. A more complex inner logic would further increase per-iteration cost.

FastAudit.core_idea: Change the binary-search domain from a continuous radius on the coordinate axis to the discrete count of elements taken from the right end. Precompute total prefix sums and a parity-aware prefix sum array over the original sequence (reversed in logic), then for each query binary-search the optimal number of elements to select from the right. This eliminates repeated bisects, shrinks the search space, and turns the problem into a single binary search over indices.

complexity.time: O(N) preprocessing + O(Q * logN) for queries.
complexity.space: O(N) for the input array, total prefix sums (var_9), and parity-based prefix array (var_10). No per-query auxiliary structures.
complexity.why: Preprocessing computes cumulative sums once in linear time. For each query, a single binary search on k (the number of elements from the right) is performed. All checks inside the search are O(1), relying only on index arithmetic and prefix sums. The final answer is composed with O(1) operations using var_9 and var_10.

complexity_delta.from: O(N) + O(Q * logC * logN) with C ≈ 1e10 (binary search on radius plus bisect on array)
complexity_delta.to: O(N) + O(Q * logN) (single binary search over index count with O(1) checks)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both may appear close for realistic C, but removing the extra logC factor and the two bisect calls per step significantly reduces constant factors and Python overhead, making the optimized version robust for N, Q up to about 2e5.

transformation_steps: Reinterpret the geometric/radius-based condition in terms of discrete indices: express the balanced / distance conditions with indices from the end of the array instead of explicit coordinate radius.
Precompute simple prefix sums (var_9) for the entire array to allow O(1) sum queries for any suffix.

Precompute a parity-aware prefix sum array (var_10), defined so that var_10[i] stores the cumulative contribution of positions whose parity matches the needed pattern when considering a suffix from the right.
Replace the outer binary search over radius [0, 1e10] with a binary search over k, the number of rightmost elements selected (domain [0, N]).

Within the binary search, use only O(1) computations: compare values at positions var_1[var_6 - k] and var_1[var_6 - 2*k + 1] using the problem’s balance condition, avoiding bisect operations entirely.
Compute the final answer as the sum of the last k elements (via prefix sums) plus the appropriate remainder from the left (via parity prefix sums), all in O(1).
Remove memoization on query values, as each query is cheap enough (O(logN)) and repeated queries do not significantly affect performance.
trigger_signals: Presence of a while loop over a huge numeric range (var_10 = 10**10) combined with bisect_left and bisect_right inside the loop.
Use of bisect in every iteration of an outer binary search, implying nested logarithmic factors.
Complex conditions relating distances between query value and array endpoints (e.g., comparisons of counts on left and right) that suggest an alternative representation via indices.
Performance pressure in Python for N, Q near 2e5, where logC * logN overhead becomes non-trivial.
Visible parity-based prefix arrays (var_14, var_15) indicating that the logic can be encoded in simpler prefix structures, but currently recomputed in a more complicated way.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when converting from radius-based logic to index-based logic, especially with expressions like var_6 - var_5 and var_6 - 2 * var_5 + 1.
Incorrect handling of boundary cases when 2 * k - 1 > N; the optimized code includes explicit checks for this, which must be preserved.

Parity handling: in the slow version, separate arrays var_14 and var_15 track even/odd indices; in the fast version, this is folded into var_10. Miscomputing parity or prefix indices will silently corrupt answers.

Misuse of prefix sums when translating from 0-based to 1-based reasoning. For example, var_9[-1] - var_9[var_6 - var_4 - 1] must match the intended suffix; changing indices requires careful re-derivation.

The fast code uses eval(input()) for reading query integers, which is unsafe and unnecessary. While not a performance bottleneck, it is a security and robustness concern and should be replaced with int(input()).

constraints_guess.notes: One-dimensional array scan; typical competitive constraints suggest n up to 1e5–2e5 or possibly 1e6. Requires O(n) or better solution in Python.

dominant_ops: Single pass over the array computing comparisons a[i] >= a[i+1] and maintaining current and maximum run lengths

complexity.why: After reading n and the list of n integers, the code performs a single for-loop over indices 0..n-2; each iteration does O(1) work (one comparison, a few assignments, one max), and only O(1) extra variables are maintained.

bottlenecks.detail: Multiple imports (math, string, collections) and helper functions (func_1, func_2, func_3) are defined but never used in the main logic. This adds constant-time startup overhead (module loading and function definitions) but does not affect asymptotic complexity.
Uses eval(input()) to read n. This is slower and less safe than int(input()) but still O(1) per test; impact is constant factor only.

The main loop is already optimal for this problem structure: a single pass computing the length of the longest contiguous non-increasing run via adjacent comparisons. There is no avoidable superlinear work.

FastAudit.core_idea: Refactor the logic into two phases: (1) build a boolean array representing whether each adjacent pair is non-increasing (a[i] >= a[i+1]); (2) scan this boolean array to compute the longest streak of True values. Also drop unused imports and helper functions to reduce constant startup overhead.

complexity.why: The modified code makes two passes over data of size n: first over the original array to fill an (n-1)-length boolean list, then over this boolean list to compute the maximum consecutive run length. Each pass is O(n), so total time remains O(n). However, it now allocates an O(n) auxiliary list (var_6), increasing space usage from O(1) to O(n).

complexity_delta.note: Algorithmic complexity in time remains linear, but the modified version introduces an O(n) auxiliary boolean array and an extra full pass over it. Any speed differences are due only to constant factors (some reduced by removing unused imports, some increased by the extra pass and memory traffic).

transformation_steps: Remove unused imports and helper functions (math, string, collections, Counter, func_1, func_2, func_3) from the main script.
Replace the helper-based input reading (func_4) with an inline list(map(int, input().split())).
Introduce a preallocated list var_6 of length n-1 to store boolean results of adjacent comparisons a[i] >= a[i+1].
Perform a first loop over indices 0..n-2, filling var_6[i] with True if a[i] >= a[i+1] and False otherwise.
Perform a second loop over var_6, computing the length of the longest contiguous subsequence of True values via a running counter (var_1) and a maximum tracker (var_4).
Print the maximum run length (var_4) directly, instead of tracking it in the same loop that reads comparisons.
trigger_signals: Presence of many unused imports and helper functions around a very small core logic, suggesting opportunity to remove constant overhead.
Simple linear scan pattern that is already optimal in asymptotic terms, leaving only micro-optimizations or structural refactors possible.
Desire to separate concerns: first record pairwise relationships, then process them, leading to an intermediate boolean array design.
pitfalls: The modified approach uses extra O(n) memory for var_6; on very large inputs, this can increase memory pressure and may reduce cache locality compared with the in-place single-pass version.

Any belief that the modified code is asymptotically faster would be incorrect; both are O(n), and the second pass plus extra allocations can easily outweigh the benefit of removed imports in practice.
Use of eval(input()) remains in the modified code for reading n (var_5). This is slower than int(input()) and can be unsafe if input is not trusted, even though it does not change complexity.

Off-by-one interpretation: the computed value is the maximum number of consecutive indices i such that a[i] >= a[i+1] (i.e., run length in terms of edges, not elements). Both versions share this semantics; any change to count elements instead would require adjusting how runs are tracked.

constraints_guess.notes: Problem is the classic: count triples (i < j < k), 1..n, with i + j + k = s. Typical AOJ-style input until '0 0'. Naive O(n^3) Python approach is often too slow if n is in the low thousands, but fine for n <= ~100. Here we assume the 'slow' label implies n can be large enough that cubic time may TLE.

dominant_ops: Triple nested for-loops over indices (O(n^3) triplets)
Integer additions and equality checks in innermost loop
Appending to a list for every matching triplet

complexity.why: The three nested loops iterate over all combinations 0 <= i < j < k < n, which is Θ(n^3) triplets. Each triplet performs a few O(1) operations. The list `var_2` stores numbers 1..n (Θ(n)), and `var_1` stores all matching sums, which is O(answer) ≤ O(n) in worst reasonable cases.

bottlenecks.detail: Enumerating all triples (i, j, k) with three nested loops leads to Θ(n^3) operations, which becomes prohibitively slow when n is a few hundred to a few thousand.
The heavy use of Python-level loops and list indexing in the innermost loop magnifies the cost of the cubic iteration compared to a lower-level language.
List `var_1` stores each successful sum even though only the count is needed. This incurs extra append operations and memory traffic. A simple scalar counter would be cheaper.
`var_2 = list(range(1, var_4 + 1))` is unnecessary because the values are just index+1; direct arithmetic on indices would avoid the list creation and array lookups.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid explicit enumeration of all triples by converting the problem into counting valid pairs arithmetically for each choice of one variable. For each candidate value (e.g., one element of the triple), compute in O(1) how many pairs of the remaining two elements can satisfy the sum and ordering constraints (distinct and ordered). This reduces the complexity from cubic to essentially linear in n per test.

complexity.space: O(T) total or O(1) per test case
complexity.why: The main loop for each test case runs `for var_1 in range(var_9 // 3, var_6 + 1)`, which is O(n) iterations in the worst case. Each iteration calls `func_1` which performs constant-time arithmetic to count valid pairs; there are no nested loops inside. Input pairs are stored in `var_8`, so space is O(T) for T test cases (or O(1) if processed on-the-fly).

complexity_delta.from: O(n^3) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time per test, O(1)–O(T) space
complexity_delta.note: The key speedup comes from replacing triple enumeration with a single loop plus closed-form counting of the remaining two elements. This reduces the number of iterations by roughly a factor of n^2.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the problem is to count distinct triples (i < j < k) with i + j + k = s over 1..n, and that brute-forcing all triples is unnecessary.
Fix one element of the triple (e.g., one of i, j, or k) and derive algebraic constraints on the other two elements to maintain ordering and distinctness.
Derive a closed-form formula (or simple O(1) computation) for the number of integer pairs (b, c) satisfying the sum and inequality constraints for each fixed first element.
Replace the triple nested loop with a single loop over the chosen element, calling an O(1) helper (`func_1`) that counts valid pairs.
Eliminate unnecessary data structures: avoid constructing the list of all numbers (1..n) and avoid storing each successful triple or sum; maintain only an integer counter.
Optionally, batch input reading and result output for small additional I/O efficiency, as seen in collecting test cases into `var_8`.
trigger_signals: Presence of three nested loops where all loop bounds are on the order of the main input parameter n.
Each loop index ranges roughly over up to n with simple arithmetic in the innermost loop, indicating Θ(n^3) operations.
The problem structure is pure counting of combinations, which is often amenable to combinatorial formulas instead of explicit enumeration.
Use of a list (`var_1`) merely to count matching configurations, rather than maintaining a single integer counter, signalling extra overhead.
Constraints or performance expectations (e.g., online judge time limits) that make O(n^3) borderline or clearly infeasible for the anticipated upper bounds of n.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when translating index-based loops (0..n-1) to value-based loops (1..n) and when enforcing i < j < k.
Incorrect handling of the distinctness and ordering constraints in the arithmetic formula; it is easy to accidentally count cases where indices are not strictly increasing or values are not distinct.
Integer division edge cases when computing midpoints or bounds (e.g., using `// 2` vs. floating division) can cause missed or extra solutions.

Boundary conditions when the target sum s is too small or too large relative to n (no valid triples) must be handled carefully to avoid negative counts in formulas; `max(..., 0)` as in `func_1` mitigates this.

Storing all test cases in a list before processing (`var_8`) can be unnecessary and slightly increases memory usage; in environments with very many test cases, streaming the processing might be preferable.

constraints_guess.notes: Two integers N (var_3) and M (var_1/var_2) are given. M is factorized; for each prime exponent e, we compute C(N-1+e, e) mod 1e9+7 and multiply. Typical AtCoder-style constraints: N up to around 2e5, M up to around 1e9–1e12. Only a single test query per run.

dominant_ops: Linear precomputation of factorials, modular inverses, and inverse factorials up to O(N) in func_3
Trial-division prime factorization of M up to sqrt(M) in func_4

complexity.why: func_3(var_3 + 100, MOD) iterates from 2 to N+100, appending to three global arrays (factorials, inverses, inverse factorials), which costs O(N) time and space. func_4 uses trial division up to sqrt(M). Each binomial query in func_1 is O(1) after precomputation, but there are only O(log M) such queries, so the O(N) precompute dominates when N is large.

bottlenecks.detail: func_3 precomputes factorials and inverses up to N+100 even though the code only performs O(number_of_prime_factors(M)) binomial evaluations, each with small k (exponents of prime factors). This O(N) work is not amortized and is excessive for a single query.
Three global lists var_8, var_7, var_10 grow to size O(N). For large N this increases memory usage and can degrade cache/locality performance.

The loop in func_3 is pure Python with several list appends and modular multiplications per iteration. For N up to ~2e5 or higher, this can be noticeably slower than a solution that only performs O(log M) arithmetic operations.
func_4 uses trial division up to sqrt(M). This is acceptable under typical constraints, but combined with the O(N) precomputation it further contributes to the total runtime.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial and inverse precomputation entirely and compute each required binomial coefficient C(n, k) directly using the multiplicative formula in O(k) time, where k is the prime exponent (small), after factorizing M by trial division.

complexity.why: func_2 factorizes M (var_2) in O(sqrt(M)) via trial division. For each prime factor with exponent e, func_1 computes C(N-1+e, e) with a loop of length e (O(e)). The sum of exponents over all primes is O(log M). Thus total time is O(sqrt(M) + log M). No arrays growing with N are allocated; space usage is constant apart from a small list of prime factors.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(N + sqrt(M)); Space: O(N)
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(sqrt(M) + log M); Space: O(1)
complexity_delta.note: N is the first input (var_3). M is the second input (var_1/var_2). The slow version pays an O(N) precomputation cost even though only O(log M) binomial coefficients with small k are needed.

transformation_steps: Eliminate the factorial/inverse precomputation (func_3) and the associated global arrays var_8, var_7, var_10. These were designed for many or large binomial queries but are unnecessary when the count of queries is small and each k is small.

Replace the O(1)-after-precompute binomial evaluation func_1(n, k, MOD) with a direct multiplicative binomial computation func_1(n, k) that uses a loop of length k to build numerator and denominator and then performs exact integer division before applying the modulus.
Keep the same trial-division factorization strategy (func_2/func_4) to decompose M into prime powers; the factorization cost is comparable in both versions and typically dominated by sqrt(M).

Apply the modulus only after each binomial coefficient is computed, instead of incorporating modular inverses into every multiplication, thereby reducing the constant-factor overhead and simplifying the arithmetic.
Use simple local variables rather than large globally-grown lists, reducing memory footprint and improving locality.
trigger_signals: Presence of a large O(N) loop that precomputes factorials and inverse factorials even though the code ultimately evaluates only a handful of binomial coefficients.
Global arrays whose size scales with the maximum n in C(n, k) and not with the actual number of queries or actual k values.
Single test case (or very few queries) combined with a heavy one-time precomputation that is not amortized across multiple uses.
k values in C(n, k) bound by prime exponents of a single integer M, which are typically tiny (sum of exponents is O(log M)), suggesting that a direct O(k) method is cheaper than O(N) preprocessing.
Use of intricate modular inverse precomputation patterns (like the linear-time modular inverse sieve) in a context with very few combinatorial queries.
pitfalls: When replacing factorial-based binomial computations with a multiplicative formula, one must ensure that the intermediate numerator/denominator computation stays within reasonable size. This works here because each exponent e is small, but for large k an O(k) multiplicative approach could be slow and cause large intermediate integers.

Direct computation of C(n, k) with integer division then modulo relies on exact division; reordering or applying the modulus too early would break correctness because modular division is not the same as integer division.

If problem constraints were different (e.g., many test cases or large k values), the removed factorial precomputation could become beneficial; the choice between precomputation and on-the-fly computation must be guided by actual constraints.

Trial-division factorization remains O(sqrt(M)); if M were much larger than assumed, this step would dominate regardless of how binomials are computed, so further optimization (e.g., precomputed primes) might become necessary.

Changing the combination implementation without re-checking index ranges (e.g., ensuring that n in C(n, k) never exceeds the precomputed factorial bound in the old approach) can introduce subtle bugs; in the fast approach, this risk is removed but correctness still depends on k remaining small as assumed.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case. Input is n followed by n integers. Value range of elements potentially large (e.g., up to 1e9), which makes iterating over [min, max] dangerous in the slow solution if max-min is large.

dominant_ops: Sorting the array: sorted(list(map(int, input().split())))
Outer loop over candidate centers var_2 in range(var_8 + 1), where var_8 = max(a) - min(a)
Inner loop computing sum of squared distances for each candidate: sum((var_2 - var_3[j]) ** 2 for j in range(n))

complexity.why: Reading and storing n elements costs O(n). Sorting costs O(n log n). Let R = max(a) - min(a). The outer loop iterates R+1 times, and for each candidate value, the inner loop scans all n elements to compute the sum of squared differences. This is O(R * n). When R is large, R * n dominates the complexity. Extra space is for storing the list of n integers.

bottlenecks.detail: Brute-force search over all integer centers from min(a) to max(a) (range size R = max(a) - min(a)). If R is large (e.g., up to 1e9), this is completely infeasible.
For each candidate center, an O(n) traversal computes the sum of squared distances, producing O(R * n) work.

Sorting the array only to get min and max is overkill; min and max can be obtained in O(n) without sorting. Sorting adds an O(n log n) overhead even though the objective function does not require order.
Using eval on input for reading an integer is slower and unsafe compared to direct int(input()). Not a dominant complexity issue, but a poor practice that adds overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical property that the sum of squared deviations S(x) = sum_i (x - a_i)^2 is minimized (over real x) at the mean of the data. For integer x, the minimizer is one of the integers nearest to the mean, so taking x = round(average) yields an optimal or near-optimal integer center. Compute the mean once and evaluate the sum of squared differences in a single pass, eliminating the O(R) search over the value range.

complexity.why: The modified code reads n numbers into a NumPy array (O(n)), computes their average using np.average (O(n)), and then computes the sum of squared differences via vectorized operations (conceptually O(n)). No search over the value range is done, so total time is linear in n. Space is O(n) for storing the array; additional overhead from NumPy’s internal structures is still linear in n.

complexity_delta.from: O(n log n + (max(a) - min(a) + 1) * n)
complexity_delta.to: O(n)
complexity_delta.note: The outer search over all possible integer centers in [min(a), max(a)] was replaced by a direct computation using the mean, eliminating the factor proportional to the value range. Sorting is also avoided conceptually (NumPy does not require sorted input for this computation).

transformation_steps: Recognize the problem: minimize S(x) = sum_i (x - a_i)^2 over integer x. Observe this is a convex quadratic function in x.
Use calculus/algebra: expand S(x) = n*x^2 - 2x*sum(a_i) + sum(a_i^2). The derivative dS/dx = 2n*x - 2*sum(a_i) = 0 gives x* = mean(a_i) as the minimizer over reals.
Handle integer constraint: for integer x, the minimizer lies at one of the integers nearest to the real mean. Using round(average) gives a candidate that is optimal or tied for optimal.
Replace the O(R * n) search: instead of iterating var_2 across all values in [min(a), max(a)], directly set var_2 = round(mean(a)).

Vectorize computation: use NumPy to represent the data as an array, compute the mean via np.average, and compute the total squared deviation as np.sum((var_2 - var_3) ** 2) in one vectorized expression, dropping explicit Python-level loops.
trigger_signals: Presence of an outer loop iterating over all values between min(a) and max(a) suggests dependence on value range R rather than on n.
Inner loop recomputes a full O(n) sum for each candidate, leading to nested loops and high runtime when R is large.
Objective function is a sum of squared differences, a standard form where mean minimization is a known result.
Sorting is used only to access min and max, indicating potential inefficiency since the order is irrelevant to the optimization.
Use of float('inf') and manual min-tracking around a simple quadratic objective suggests a generic search instead of applying closed-form optimization.
pitfalls: {'kind': 'numerical', 'detail': 'Using floating-point mean and round can introduce subtle issues if sums are large (e.g., overflow in intermediate double representation or precision loss). For huge values, a purely integer arithmetic formulation (e.g., using sum and sum of squares) is safer.'}

{'kind': 'integer_rounding', 'detail': "When the mean is exactly halfway between two integers (e.g., 0.5, 1.5, ...), round’s tie-breaking behavior matters. NumPy’s average returns a float; Python’s round uses banker's rounding (ties to even). In this specific sum-of-squares context, both neighboring integers often give the same minimal value, but if constraints require a specific tie-breaking rule (e.g., smallest integer), explicit handling is needed."}

{'kind': 'library_overhead', 'detail': 'Importing NumPy and creating arrays has nontrivial overhead. In competitive programming environments with small n or strict import limits, a pure-Python O(n) solution using basic arithmetic might be faster or required, even though the asymptotic complexity is the same.'}

{'kind': 'environment_compatibility', 'detail': 'Some online judges disallow external libraries like NumPy. The algorithmic improvement (using the mean) is valid, but the specific implementation might not be accepted in such environments.'}

{'kind': 'input_safety', 'detail': 'Both versions still use eval to parse the first line as an integer, which is unsafe and slower than int(input()). While not a complexity issue, it is a robustness and security concern.'}

constraints_guess.notes: Classic digit-sum enumeration (e.g., AtCoder-style). N small enough that O(N * digits) is fine; A,B are small bounds on digit sum.

dominant_ops: Outer loop over all integers from 1 to N (var_5)
Inner while-loop extracting digits via modulo and division for each integer
math.floor calls on every digit
Floating-point division ("/=") in tight inner loop

complexity.why: For each integer up to N we repeatedly divide by 10 until it becomes 0; this takes O(number_of_digits) = O(log_10 N) iterations, with constant extra state.

bottlenecks.detail: math.floor(var_4 % 10) is redundant since var_4 % 10 is already an integer; calling into the math module on every digit adds overhead.

var_4 /= 10 uses floating-point division, converting var_4 to float and incurring extra cost and potential precision issues; integer floor division (var_4 //= 10) is cheaper and semantically correct for digit stripping.
Digit extraction is done in Python with a while-loop and multiple operations per digit (mod, floor, division) rather than leveraging a tighter C-level implementation.
While asymptotically OK for N≈1e4, if N were increased (e.g., 1e7), the per-digit overhead (math.floor + float division) in pure Python would become a practical performance problem.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace manual digit extraction in Python with string conversion and built-in aggregation (sum(map(int, str(x)))), shifting most work into optimized C-level routines and removing unnecessary math.floor and float operations.

complexity.why: Each number is converted to a string and its characters are iterated once; the number of characters is the number of digits (O(log_10 N)), repeated for all N values.

complexity_delta.from: O(N * log_10(N)) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N * log_10(N)) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged, but constant factors are improved by avoiding math.floor and float division, and by using C-level operations via str+map+sum.

transformation_steps: Removed the inner while-loop-based digit extraction and replaced it with var_6 = sum(map(int, list(str(var_4)))), eliminating explicit modulo and division operations.
Eliminated math.floor calls entirely by relying on integer digits from string conversion instead of numeric floor operations.
Avoided float division in the digit loop (var_4 /= 10) by not using arithmetic stripping at all; in a purely arithmetic alternative, this would be replaced by integer division (var_4 //= 10).
Kept the outer enumeration loop structure but simplified the condition to more idiomatic comparisons (var_1 <= var_6 <= var_2).
trigger_signals: Tight inner loop performing multiple Python-level operations (%, /=, math.floor) per digit.
Use of math.floor on values that are already integers.
Use of floating-point division where integer operations are sufficient, indicating unnecessary type conversions.
Digit-sum pattern recognizable as a candidate for str-based or precomputed-digit optimization.
pitfalls: String conversion for every number adds overhead; for extremely tight constraints or lower-level languages, arithmetic digit extraction with integer division might be preferable.
Using list(str(var_4)) is slightly more allocation-heavy than iterating directly on str(var_4); a further micro-optimization would be sum(map(int, str(var_4))).

If constraints became very large (e.g., N ~ 1e9), both solutions would be asymptotically too slow; a fundamentally different approach (mathematical or digit DP) would be needed rather than micro-optimizing this pattern.

constraints_guess.notes: Matches AtCoder-style problem where first line is `N M` (people × items) and each of N lines lists liked items. Typical official constraints for this task are small, e.g. N,M ≤ 30, sum of listed items ≤ N*M.

dominant_ops: Allocating a (N+1) × M 2D Python list (var_1)
Iterating over N people and over each listed item, performing indexed assignments into the 2D list
Summing the final row of length M

complexity.why: The code allocates an (N+1)×M DP table upfront (O(N*M) time just for list construction). For each of the N people it reads a line, slices off the first element (k), then iterates over the remaining k items and performs constant-time assignments to var_1[var_7][var_8-1]. The sum over k across all rows is at most N*M in the worst case, so total time is O(N*M + Σk) = O(N*M). Space holds the entire DP table of size (N+1)×M, giving O(N*M) memory.

bottlenecks.detail: The DP table var_1 has (N+1) rows and M columns, storing integers. For large N,M this O(N*M) memory becomes prohibitive, especially in Python where list-of-lists and per-element overhead are high.
Constructing var_1 with nested list comprehensions creates N+1 Python lists of length M each, which is O(N*M) object work before even processing input.

The algorithm potentially touches each of the N*M cells via Python-level operations (allocation plus assignments), which is slower than leveraging more compact representations such as sets of present indices.

The pattern `var_1[current_row][j] = var_1[previous_row][j]` for a sparse set of columns leaves most columns untouched per person, yet all columns exist in memory, wasting cache and allocation effort.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid an explicit N×M DP table and instead represent each person's liked items as a set, then compute their intersection directly. This keeps only actual liked items in memory and uses the set-intersection operation, which efficiently finds items common to all people.

complexity.why: The code reads N from the first line via `int(input().split()[0])`. It then builds N sets, each from one input line: `set(input().split()[1:])`. Creating these sets costs O(k_i) for the i-th person, so total set construction is O(Σk). `set.intersection(*sets)` processes elements across these sets; with the typical implementation it runs in time proportional to the total number of elements involved (again O(Σk) in this problem). The final `len(...)` is O(1). Space-wise, it stores all sets at once, with total number of elements equal to the total number of listed items, so O(Σk) memory.

complexity_delta.note: The slow DP approach pre-allocates and maintains a dense N×M table even though each row is sparse (most items are unmentioned for each person). The fast approach stores only actually mentioned items in per-person sets and uses a set intersection, so runtime and memory scale with the number of provided likes Σk instead of the dense product N*M.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the DP table var_1 is logically tracking, for each item, whether it has remained liked by all people up to that row; this is equivalent to intersecting the sets of liked items across all people.
Eliminate the explicit (N+1)×M DP matrix and any row-by-row propagation of values.
Represent each person's liked items directly as a set constructed from the line `input().split()[1:]`.
Apply `set.intersection` across the N sets to compute the set of items liked by everyone in a single conceptual operation.
Return the size of the intersection via `len(...)` instead of summing a DP table row.
trigger_signals: Presence of a full 2D table whose rows are derived from the previous row with only selective updates suggests a bitmask/intersection semantics rather than needing all intermediate rows.
First line provides both N and M but the actual logic only needs the item identifiers; this hints that using M to size a full matrix is unnecessary.
In problems where each row only lists a few indices (sparse data), dense O(N*M) storage and processing are a red flag; treating each row as a set is more natural.
The final result is simply the count of positions where all rows have a 1, which is exactly the size of the intersection of per-row item sets.
pitfalls: {'kind': 'edge_case', 'detail': 'The fast code calls `set.intersection(*list_of_sets)`. If N could be 0, `list_of_sets` would be empty and `set.intersection(*[])` raises a TypeError. The original problem typically guarantees N ≥ 1, but this assumption should be explicit if reused elsewhere.'}

{'kind': 'data_type', 'detail': 'The fast solution keeps item identifiers as strings because it uses `input().split()[1:]` directly. This is fine when identifiers are only compared for equality, but if later numeric operations are required, they should be converted to integers (`map(int, ...)`).'}

{'kind': 'memory_pattern', 'detail': 'Although asymptotically better than the DP table, the fast solution constructs all sets in memory before intersecting them. For extremely large inputs, a streaming approach (start with the first set, then intersect with each subsequent set one by one and discard intermediate sets) can further reduce peak memory.'}

{'kind': 'readability/maintainability', 'detail': 'The fast one-liner is concise but dense: nested comprehensions, unpacking, and `set.intersection` in one expression can be harder to read and debug than a stepwise version. For production code, splitting into named variables (`N`, `M`, `food_sets`, etc.) improves clarity without affecting performance.'}

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style problem: minimizing sum of squared distances over integer x. Values may be up to ~1e9, so value range (max-min) can be very large, making brute-force over x infeasible for large n.

dominant_ops: Double loop: for each candidate center x in [min(a), max(a)] compute sum over all elements of (ai - x)^2.

complexity.why: Let n be the number of elements and R = max(a) - min(a). The outer loop iterates over every integer x in this range (R+1 candidates). For each x, the inner loop scans all n elements to compute the sum of squared differences. Thus time is proportional to n * R. The array of n integers dominates space, giving O(n) space; other variables are O(1).

bottlenecks.detail: The outer loop `for var_4 in range(var_2[0], var_2[var_1 - 1] + 1)` iterates over every integer between the minimum and maximum array values. If the values are large and far apart (e.g., min=0, max=1e9), this becomes on the order of 1e9 iterations regardless of n, which is far too slow.
For each candidate x, the inner loop recomputes `sum((ai - x)**2)` from scratch over all n elements, yielding O(n * R) operations. This pattern is a classic TLE trigger when R can be large.

The list is fully sorted via `sorted(var_2)` just to access min and max. While sorting is O(n log n) and may be dominated by the O(n * R) scanning, it is still unnecessary; min and max could be computed in O(n) without sorting.
Each inner iteration performs a subtraction and a squaring (`(var_6 - var_4) ** 2`), which are not extremely heavy individually but are repeated potentially billions of times when R is large.

Using `eval(input())` to read an integer is slower and unsafe compared to plain `int(input())`. This is minor compared to the algorithmic bottleneck but still a small performance and security concern.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the convexity of the quadratic function: the sum of squared deviations S(x) = Σ(ai - x)^2 is a convex parabola in x, whose real-valued minimizer is the mean μ = (Σai)/n. For integer x, the minimum must be attained at floor(μ) or ceil(μ). Thus compute S at these two candidates only and take the minimum.

complexity.why: The optimized code reads n integers into an array (O(n)), computes the sum once to get μ (O(n)), and then performs a single loop over all n elements to accumulate squared differences for at most two candidate centers (floor(μ) and ceil(μ)), which is O(n). No iteration over the value range is needed, so time is linear in n. Space is O(n) for storing the input array; other variables are O(1).

complexity_delta.from: O(n * R) with R = max(a) - min(a)
complexity_delta.to: O(n)
complexity_delta.note: The solution replaces an exhaustive scan over all possible integer centers in [min(a), max(a)] with a constant-number-of-candidates approach (floor and ceil of the mean) derived from the properties of quadratic functions.

transformation_steps: Reformulate the objective: Recognize that the function to minimize is S(x) = Σ(ai - x)^2, a quadratic polynomial in x, which is convex. Derive that its derivative w.r.t. x is -2 Σ(ai - x) = -2(n x - Σai), and setting this to zero gives the real-valued minimizer μ = (Σai)/n.

Restrict to integer candidates: Since x must be an integer, observe that for a convex quadratic, the minimal integer point must lie at either floor(μ) or ceil(μ). Therefore, only two candidate centers need to be checked instead of all possible values between min(a) and max(a).

Implement constant-candidate evaluation: Compute total = Σai once, derive var_6 = total // n (integer floor of μ) and var_7 = var_6 + 1 (which acts as ceil(μ) when μ is not already an integer). Then perform a single pass over the array, accumulating the sum of squared deviations for these two candidates and taking their minimum as the final answer.

Eliminate range-based outer loop and sorting dependency: Remove the outer loop over x in [min(a), max(a)] and the need to access sorted boundaries for min and max, thereby avoiding the O(R) factor and reducing preprocessing to a simple read plus sum operation.
trigger_signals: The brute-force pattern of scanning x from min(a) to max(a) and recomputing a full sum for each x indicates a value-range-based approach that is vulnerable to large coordinate ranges.

The potential value range (max(a) - min(a)) is unbounded by the input specification in the code and can be much larger than n (e.g., inputs like 0 and 1e9). When R can be >> n, O(n * R) is infeasible.
The objective function is a sum of squared differences with respect to a single scalar x, a strong hint that statistical properties (mean, variance) or calculus on quadratics can be exploited.
Performance issues such as timeouts or extremely long runtimes on tests with large element values but modest n would point directly to the outer range loop as the bottleneck.
pitfalls: Forgetting the integer constraint: The theoretical minimizer of Σ(ai - x)^2 is μ = (Σai)/n, which may not be an integer. Taking only floor(μ) or only ceil(μ) can be wrong in edge cases; both candidates must be evaluated and the smaller sum chosen.

Precision and overflow: Using floating point to represent μ could introduce rounding issues and, in some languages, lead to precision errors for very large sums. The provided code uses integer division and integer arithmetic for squared differences, which is safer. However, in languages with fixed-width integers, ensure that squaring differences (possibly up to ~1e9) and summing them fits into 64-bit integers.

Recomputing the sum unnecessarily: The fast code calls `sum(var_1)` twice. While this does not change asymptotic complexity and is acceptable in many constraints, it performs an extra O(n) pass. For very large n or stricter limits, it is better to compute the sum once and reuse it.

Assuming sorted order is needed: The original code sorts the array to get min and max. In the optimized approach, there is no need to sort because the optimal x depends only on the sum (and indirectly on n), not on the ordering or even the individual min/max. Sorting would add unnecessary O(n log n) time.

Using eval for input: `eval(input())` is unnecessary and potentially unsafe. It should be replaced with `int(input())`. While this has minor impact on performance compared to the algorithmic change, it is still a best-practice correction.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical 'Lunlun/stepping numbers' style problem: given N (up to about 1e5), output the N-th number whose adjacent digits differ by at most 1. Only a single query.

dominant_ops: Recursive DFS over all valid numbers up to fixed length (depth 10)
Appending every generated number to a global list
Full sort of the entire generated list of numbers

complexity.time: O(S log S), where S is the total count of generated numbers up to 10 digits (about 2e5, constant w.r.t. input N)
complexity.why: The DFS explores all valid sequences up to depth 10 regardless of the requested index var_4. Each generated number is appended to var_1, then var_1.sort() is applied, costing O(S log S). Space is proportional to storing all S numbers at once.

bottlenecks.detail: Generates the full set of Lunlun numbers up to 10 digits even if the input var_4 is small and only a few smallest numbers are needed.
Sorts the entire list var_1 after generation, even though the numbers could be produced directly in sorted order using a BFS-like construction.
Uses recursive calls func_1 for a tree of height 10, adding Python call overhead at every node. While bounded, it contributes unnecessary constant-factor cost.

FastAudit.core_idea: Generate Lunlun numbers in increasing order using an iterative BFS-style process starting from 1..9, appending successors of each number on-the-fly until reaching the N-th element, thereby avoiding full enumeration and sorting.

complexity.time: O(N * L) ~ O(N), where N is the requested index and L is the digit length (small constant for given constraints)
complexity.why: At each loop iteration, the algorithm takes one existing number, examines its last digit, and appends 2 or 3 successors. The loop runs until the list length reaches N, so the number of iterations and appended elements is proportional to N. Each step does constant work (with small-cost string conversions), so total time is linear in N; space is linear in N due to storing only the first N numbers.

complexity_delta.from: O(S log S) time and O(S) space for S precomputed numbers independent of N
complexity_delta.to: O(N) time and O(N) space, generating only as many numbers as needed for the N-th answer
complexity_delta.note: S (all Lunlun numbers up to 10 digits) is a large fixed constant (~2e5). The new approach scales directly with N and avoids the sort, offering better constants and memory usage, especially when N is much smaller than S.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the DFS + sort is effectively constructing the sequence of Lunlun numbers in sorted order but via overkill: full enumeration followed by sorting.
Reformulate the generation as a BFS over numbers: start from digits 1..9 and, for each number, create successors by appending digits in {last-1, last, last+1} within [0,9].
Observe that BFS over this graph, when processing nodes in queue order, naturally yields numbers in increasing order of magnitude and value, matching the sorted order required.
Replace the recursive DFS and global list aggregation with an iterative loop using indexing (var_3) into var_2, appending successors to the same list.
Remove the final sort and early-stop the generation once len(var_2) reaches the requested index, avoiding generation of unneeded numbers.
Eliminate recursion, reducing function-call overhead and risk of stack issues, and rely on plain Python loops and list operations.
trigger_signals: The original code fully explores a fixed-depth recursion tree regardless of the input N, indicating work that does not scale with the query size.
A large global list var_1 is built and then sorted, which is typically a smell when the sequence has a known constructive ordering.
The sort cost is unnecessary because Lunlun numbers can be generated in ascending order directly via a BFS-like approach.
Presence of recursion with fixed depth and repeated branching where an iterative queue-based solution is natural.
pitfalls: Ensuring that the BFS generation order exactly matches the sorted order; mistakes in the neighbor-generation logic or starting seeds (1..9) can yield incorrect indexing for the N-th element.
Handling boundary digits 0 and 9 correctly when creating successors (need to avoid digits outside [0,9]; the optimized code uses separate cases for last digit 0 and 9).
Relying on string conversion to construct successors may be slower than pure arithmetic; for very large N or longer numbers, avoiding str()/int() conversions can further improve performance.
Off-by-one errors in stopping condition (len(var_2) < var_1) and in indexing the result (var_2[var_1 - 1]) can easily lead to incorrect answers if changed.

Assuming recursion depth is always safe; while depth 10 is fine, extending the approach to larger digit lengths with recursion would risk hitting Python's recursion limit, which the iterative BFS approach avoids.

constraints_guess.notes: Single input N (var_5/var_6) and bounds A,B (var_1,var_2). Typical AtCoder-style digit-sum problem, likely N up to around 10^4–10^5.

dominant_ops: Outer loop over all integers 1..N
For each integer, while-loop extracting digits using % and /
Repeated float modulo and float division operations
math.floor calls on every digit

complexity.time: Unbounded / non-terminating in practice (intended: O(N * log10(N)))
complexity.why: Intended logic: for each i in [1..N], peel off digits with modulo/division -> ~O(log10(i)) per i -> O(N log N) overall. However, using `/` makes var_4 a float that never reaches 0, so the inner while-loop does not terminate, effectively making runtime unbounded.

bottlenecks.detail: Digit stripping uses `var_4 /= 10` (true division) instead of integer division `var_4 //= 10`. After the first iteration, var_4 becomes a float and asymptotically approaches 0 without ever hitting 0 exactly (e.g., 123 -> 12.3 -> 1.23 -> ...), so `while var_4 > 0` can loop indefinitely or for a huge number of iterations due to floating-point behavior.

Using `math.floor(var_4 % 10)` inside the inner loop is unnecessary: `var_4 % 10` is already integral for integer arithmetic, and even with floats it’s more expensive than strictly needed. Each digit requires an extra function call into the math module.
Modulo and comparison are performed on floats after the first division. This is slower than pure integer arithmetic and can introduce subtle precision issues (e.g., `var_4 % 10` for large floats).

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace manual digit peeling with string conversion and per-character integer summation. This avoids float arithmetic and math.floor, leveraging optimized C-level string and integer operations to compute digit sums reliably and efficiently.

complexity.space: O(1) extra (aside from transient string for each number)
complexity.why: For each integer i in [1..N], `str(i)` produces a string of length ≈ number of digits (O(log10(i))). Summing digits via a simple for-loop over the string is O(digits). Summed over i from 1 to N, this yields O(N log N) time with a small constant factor. Memory usage is O(1) extra because each string is created and discarded per iteration.

complexity_delta.from: Practically non-terminating / unbounded due to buggy float-based digit extraction (intended O(N log N))
complexity_delta.to: O(N log N) with low constant factors using string-based digit summation
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity matches the intended algorithm, but the key improvement is fixing the infinite/very-long loop and reducing per-digit overhead by avoiding float operations and math.floor.

transformation_steps: Eliminate float-based digit extraction: stop using `/` on the loop variable to peel off digits.
Replace math.floor and modulo-based digit accumulation with string conversion of each number (`str(var_3)`) and sum of digit characters via `int()`.
Use simple integer arithmetic and string operations instead of mixed int/float arithmetic to ensure termination and better constant factors.
Preserve the same filtering logic on digit sums (`var_1 <= digit_sum <= var_2`) and same accumulation of qualifying integers.
trigger_signals: Program appears to hang or run extremely slowly even for small inputs.
Inner digit-extraction loop uses `/` instead of `//`, causing suspicion of non-terminating or very long loops.
Use of `math.floor` around `% 10` which is unnecessary for integer digit extraction and suggests confusion between float and int arithmetic.
High CPU usage with no progress, typical for a tight non-terminating while-loop.
pitfalls: If attempting to fix the original approach without changing to strings, one must use integer division (`var_4 //= 10`) and keep everything as ints; mixing floats and ints here is error-prone.
String-based digit summation is efficient in Python, but for extremely large N (well beyond typical contest limits) the O(N log N) pattern can still be too slow; no asymptotic improvement is gained.
When refactoring, keep track of variable roles carefully (e.g., `var_5` vs `var_6`) to avoid off-by-one or misread-input bugs; the modified code renames the main upper bound variable.
Ensure the range condition `var_1 <= digit_sum <= var_2` is preserved inclusively; changing operators (e.g., `<` vs `<=`) would change the set of counted numbers.
Avoid unnecessary imports like `math` in the optimized version to keep the code minimal and avoid implying the need for floating-point operations.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case. N numbers, each likely constrained to a small integer range (e.g., 0–100). Intended solution is linear O(N) with simple arithmetic; no need for heavy libraries or multi-pass brute-force over candidate centers.

dominant_ops: Conversion of input list to NumPy array
Loop over 100 candidate integer centers with full-array NumPy arithmetic each iteration: (var_6 - var_2) ** 2 and np.sum(...)

complexity.time: O(K * N) with K = 100 (effectively linear but with a large constant and repeated full-array passes)
complexity.space: O(N) for the array plus O(N) transient temporaries each iteration created by NumPy expressions
complexity.why: For each of ~100 candidate centers, NumPy performs vectorized subtraction and squaring over all N elements, materializing temporary arrays before reduction. This multiplies both work and memory traffic by ~100 versus a single-pass analytic solution.

bottlenecks.detail: Brute-force scan over all integer centers in range(100) instead of using the analytic fact that the optimal integer center is around the mean (floor/ceil).
Each expression (var_6 - var_2) ** 2 allocates temporary NumPy arrays; repeated 100 times, causing extra memory traffic and cache pressure.
Importing and using NumPy for a simple O(N) scalar computation adds startup and runtime overhead, especially in contest or short-running scripts.
The same var_5 array is reused; var_6 = var_5 does not copy, but the arithmetic still recomputes N-element expressions for each candidate center.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the analytic minimizer of sum_i (a_i - x)^2: the real-valued optimum is the mean of the data; for integer x, only floor(mean) and ceil(mean) need consideration. The code effectively rounds the mean with a custom tie-breaking rule, then computes the squared deviations in a single pass.

complexity.space: O(N) for the input list plus O(1) extra working memory
complexity.why: The list of N numbers is read once, the mean is computed in O(N), and the sum of squared differences is computed in a single additional O(N) pass using scalar arithmetic. No extra factor from scanning many candidate centers or building large temporaries.

complexity_delta.from: O(K * N) with K = 100 and repeated vectorized passes over the data
complexity_delta.to: O(N) with a single analytic computation around the mean
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic big-O is linear in both, but removing the explicit factor K and the heavy NumPy temporaries significantly reduces constant factors and memory traffic, which matters for large N and tight time limits.

transformation_steps: Recognize the objective: minimize sum_i (a_i - x)^2 over integer x, which is a standard least-squares problem.
Use the fact that the real-valued minimizer is the mean of the data; only its floor and ceil (or a well-defined rounding rule) need to be checked for integer x.
Replace the brute-force loop over all candidate centers in range(100) with a direct computation of the (possibly tie-broken) rounded mean.
Compute the sum of squared differences once using simple Python arithmetic instead of repeated NumPy expressions.
Avoid importing NumPy and allocating temporary arrays for each candidate center; rely on built-in functions (statistics.mean, math.floor/ceil, list comprehension).
trigger_signals: Presence of a small outer loop over candidate integer parameters (here range(100)) where the inner computation scans the entire dataset each time.
Use of heavy vectorized operations (NumPy) in a loop when a closed-form or near-constant-time decision exists.
Objective function of the form sum of squared distances to a scalar x, which is a classic case where the mean is optimal.
Contest-style I/O (single N, single list of numbers) where typical constraints suggest preference for simple O(N) solutions without expensive libraries.
pitfalls: Floating-point rounding of the mean can cause tie-breaking issues at exactly .5; the original fast code includes a special case when mean == 0.5 and uses counts to decide floor vs ceil.
Using equality checks on floats (e.g., var_7 == 0.5) can be fragile if the mean is not exactly representable; however, with small integer inputs and controlled ranges this may still work in practice.
Over-reliance on NumPy in tight loops may degrade performance rather than improve it when the problem is naturally scalar and requires only a few passes over the data.
Brute-forcing over a fixed range (0..99) assumes all values lie in that range; this can silently give wrong results if constraints change or were misread.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder setting for this problem (ABC160 D). n up to ~2e3 so O(n^2) is acceptable, O(n^3) is not.

dominant_ops: Breadth-first search (BFS) from every vertex (n BFS runs)
Per-BFS O(n) scanning of neighbors in a path + 2 teleport edges
Reallocation and initialization of distance array inside outer loop
Deque popleft/append operations in inner while loop

complexity.why: Outer loop over start node runs n times. Each BFS on a path graph with O(n) vertices and O(n) edges costs O(n). So total ~O(n * n) = O(n^2). Distance array var_3 is size n per BFS; var_2 is size n globally, giving O(n) auxiliary space.

bottlenecks.detail: Running a full BFS from every node duplicates a lot of work; distances on a path with a single teleport pair can be computed directly from indices.
Outer loop over starting node (n) + inner BFS loop (O(n) pushes/pops) + another inner loop over targets (up to n) leads to heavy constant factors even though asymptotic complexity is O(n^2).
var_3 = [float('inf')] * var_7 reallocates and initializes an O(n) list for each of the n start nodes, adding O(n^2) element inits.
Deque popleft/append in pure Python within a tight loop is relatively expensive compared to simple arithmetic in nested for-loops.
Distances on an unweighted line graph with one extra edge have a simple closed form; BFS recomputes them from scratch instead of using the formula.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the 1D structure of the graph (a line with one extra edge between nodes x and y) to derive a direct formula for the shortest distance between any pair (i, j). Instead of BFS, iterate over all i < j once and compute the minimal of three candidate path lengths: direct line distance, path using teleport (i -> x -> y -> j), and the symmetric teleport path (i -> y -> x -> j). Count how many pairs have each distance.

complexity.why: Two nested loops over var_5 (1..n-1) and var_6 (var_5+1..n) enumerate all O(n^2) pairs exactly once. For each pair, only O(1) arithmetic and array access are performed. The counts array var_1 is size n, so O(n) space.

complexity_delta.from: O(n^2) time, O(n) space via n BFS runs on an n-node graph
complexity_delta.to: O(n^2) time, O(n) space via direct O(1) distance formula per pair
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time remains O(n^2), but the constant factor drops significantly by replacing BFS + deque operations and repeated allocations with simple arithmetic in nested loops.

transformation_steps: Recognize the graph structure: nodes 1..n in a line with edges (i, i+1), plus a single extra edge between nodes x and y.

Derive the closed-form shortest path distance between any two nodes i and j: min(|i-j|, |x-i| + 1 + |y-j|, |y-i| + 1 + |x-j|). These correspond to: direct line, using teleport via x->y, and using teleport via y->x.
Replace the outer loop over starting nodes and inner BFS with a double loop over all pairs (i, j) with i < j.
Within the pair loop, compute the three candidate distances using abs and additions, then take their minimum and increment the corresponding counter.
Remove BFS-related state: drop the deque, distance array per start node, and float('inf') initializations, leaving only the global counts array.
Optimize output: print all results in one print call using unpacking and sep='\n'.
trigger_signals: BFS (or any graph traversal) being invoked once per vertex in a dense or structured graph where distances might have a formula.
Distance queries over all pairs (i, j) in a very regular graph (like a path or cycle) with few extra edges.
Re-initialization of an O(n) array inside an O(n) loop (suggests potential for formula or reuse).
Use of a general-purpose algorithm (BFS) where all edge weights and topology are very simple and symmetric.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors: original code uses 0-based indices internally, while the formula-based solution in fast_code uses 1-based indexing for nodes. Careful alignment is required when porting logic.
Forgetting both teleport directions: the extra edge is undirected, so both i->x->y->j and i->y->x->j paths must be considered; omitting one can give incorrect distances.
Misinterpreting distance counting: the answer array index corresponds to the distance value; ensure that array size and indexing (0..n-1 vs 1..n) match the distance range.

Assuming improved asymptotic complexity: while the optimized solution is much faster in practice, its big-O time remains O(n^2); it will not scale to substantially larger n (e.g., 1e5) without a different approach.
Integer vs float sentinel: the slow version uses float('inf') as a sentinel in var_3, which is unnecessary and slower; if reusing BFS elsewhere, prefer an integer sentinel or visited boolean array.

constraints_guess.notes: Grid is (N+1) x (N+1). Original solution is O(N^3), which suggests N is at most a few thousand; otherwise it would be infeasible. Problem is counting segments [l, r] fully contained in query intervals [L, R].

dominant_ops: Precomputing var_1 with three nested loops over indices (start i, end j, and intermediate k) leading to O(N^3) additions over an N x N grid.

complexity.why: var_7, var_2, and var_1 are each (N+1) x (N+1) => O(N^2) space. Building var_2 is O(N^2). Computing var_1 uses loops: for i in [1..N], j in [i..N], inner k in [0..(j-i)], so total ~sum_{i=1}^N sum_{j=i}^N (j-i+1) = O(N^3). Query answers are O(Q).

bottlenecks.detail: The computation of var_1[i][j] uses an extra inner loop over all rows between i and j for each (i, j) pair, resulting in O(N^3) operations.
Each prefix segment sum is recomputed repeatedly for overlapping sub-intervals instead of using a global 2D prefix-sum structure.
All three dimensions of the O(N^3) work are implemented as Python-level for-loops, which are slower than vectorized or library-based implementations for large N.

FastAudit.core_idea: Model the counts of segments as points in an (N+1) x (N+1) grid and build a 2D prefix-sum array using numpy.cumsum. Each query [L, R] becomes a constant-time rectangle-sum query over the square submatrix [L..R] x [L..R], which equals the number of segments fully contained in [L, R] because counts exist only for indices with left <= right.

complexity.why: Filling the count grid var_5 is O(M). Computing the 2D prefix sums via two cumsum operations is O(N^2) (library-optimized). Each of the Q queries is answered in O(1) using four prefix-sum lookups and a few arithmetic operations. Arrays remain (N+1) x (N+1), so space is O(N^2).

complexity_delta.from: O(N^3 + Q) time, O(N^2) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N^2 + M + Q) time, O(N^2) space
complexity_delta.note: Time complexity improves by a factor of roughly O(N) by replacing per-interval nested accumulation with a global 2D prefix-sum and O(1) rectangle queries. Space usage stays the same order.

transformation_steps: Interpret the original problem geometrically: each segment [l, r] is a point at (l, r) in a 2D grid with l and r in [1..N]. The query [L, R] asks for points inside the square [L..R] x [L..R].
Instead of precomputing var_1[i][j] via a triple loop, build a single global count grid var_5 where var_5[l][r] is incremented for every segment [l, r].
Compute the 2D prefix sums var_3 using np.cumsum along rows and columns, so var_3[i][j] stores the sum of var_5[y][x] for 0 <= y <= i, 0 <= x <= j.

Replace the O(N) inner accumulation for each (i, j) pair with a constant-time 2D range-sum formula using the prefix-sum array: sum over [L..R] x [L..R] = S(R, R) - S(R, L-1) - S(L-1, R) + S(L-1, L-1).

Rely on the fact that there are no segments with left > right, so the lower-triangular part of the [L..R] x [L..R] square contains only zeros; thus the square-sum equals the number of valid segments with L <= l <= r <= R.
Use numpy to perform the O(N^2) prefix-sum computation in optimized native code, greatly reducing Python-level loop overhead.
trigger_signals: Triple nested loops over N-sized ranges (i, j, k) in pure Python, with one dimension spanning triangle indices and an inner loop whose length depends on interval widths.
Explicit summation var_13 += var_2[...] inside the innermost loop, indicating O(1) work repeated O(N^3) times.
The structure of var_1 as all-pairs interval aggregates over an N x N grid, which is a typical sign that a prefix-sum or cumulative approach can reduce complexity.
Use of multiple large 2D arrays (var_7, var_2, var_1) that represent cumulative information in subtly different ways, suggesting they can be unified into a single 2D prefix-sum representation.
pitfalls: Indexing off-by-one: arrays are built with size (N+1) and indices starting from 1 in the problem domain, while numpy arrays are 0-based. Careful handling of 0th row/column as the zero-padding layer is required for correct prefix-sum formulas.

Rectangle formula correctness: for 2D prefix sums S, the sum of submatrix [L..R] x [L..R] must use S(R, R) - S(R, L-1) - S(L-1, R) + S(L-1, L-1); mixing up row/column ordering or L/R positions will silently give incorrect counts.

Assuming segments always satisfy l <= r: the square [L..R] x [L..R] includes pairs with l > r, but these cells must be guaranteed to be zero; otherwise they would corrupt counts. The input format must ensure l <= r.

Memory constraints: an (N+1) x (N+1) integer grid can be large if N is big (e.g., N=5000 => ~25e6 cells). Using numpy changes the internal representation; one must ensure it fits within memory limits and uses an appropriate dtype.

Numpy environment: on some competitive programming platforms, numpy may not be available or may be slower to import than pure Python methods for very small N. The algorithmic idea (2D prefix sums) is independent of numpy and can be implemented with pure Python lists if needed.

Conversion cost: calling np.cumsum on a Python list-of-lists incurs an O(N^2) conversion to an ndarray before cumsum. This is acceptable here because O(N^2) is already the target complexity, but it should be kept in mind if the grid were sparse and could be represented differently.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic AtCoder 'Coprime' task: N up to ~2e5, each A[i] up to ~1e6. Need to classify pairwise/setwise/not coprime using sieve + prime factorization + gcd.

dominant_ops: Building smallest-prime-factor sieve up to 10**6 in func_2 (two nested loops over range up to 1e6).
Prime factorization of each A[i] by repeated division using the SPF array.
Set membership and insertion operations while tracking used prime factors across all numbers.
GCD chaining over all A[i] using math.gcd for the setwise coprime check.

complexity.time: O(M log log M + N * log A_max), with M fixed at 10^6 and A_max <= 10^6
complexity.space: O(M + N), with M = 10^6 for the SPF array and N for input storage and auxiliary sets
complexity.why: func_2 runs a sieve-like process: initializing an array of size M and iterating over all numbers and their multiples is O(M log log M). Each A[i] is factorized via successive division by its smallest prime factor, costing O(log A[i]) per element. Pairwise coprime detection uses sets for prime factors but each prime factor is inserted at most once globally, so its overhead remains linear in the number of distinct prime factors.

bottlenecks.detail: func_2 always builds the SPF array up to 10**6 regardless of the actual maximum value in var_1. If max(var_1) << 10**6, this wastes work and memory; even when max(var_1) is 10**6, the constant overhead is large for Python.
The sieve in func_2 implies a full O(10^6 log log 10^6) preprocessing even if N is small, which can be significant near time limits in Python.

During factorization in func_3, for each division step there is a set membership test and insert into var_8 and var_9. This per-factor overhead adds up for many elements with multiple prime factors, increasing constant factors.
func_1 repeatedly calls math.gcd in a Python loop. While asymptotically fine, it adds small overhead compared with a tight custom gcd loop fused into the main code path.

FastAudit.core_idea: Reduce the sieve range to max(A[i]) instead of a fixed 10**6 and streamline factorization and coprime checks using a single global SPF array and simpler loops, minimizing constant factors while keeping the overall algorithm the same.

complexity.time: O(M' log log M' + N * log A_max), where M' = max(A[i]) <= 10^6
complexity.why: The modified sieve builds an SPF array only up to the actual maximum value in the input, reducing precomputation when max(A) < 10**6. Factorization is still done via repeated SPF divisions, and each prime factor is inserted at most once into the global set var_11. The gcd-based setwise check uses a straightforward iterative gcd implementation, maintaining O(N log A_max) behavior with low overhead.

complexity_delta.from: O(10^6 log log 10^6 + N log A_max) time, O(10^6 + N) space, with M hard-coded to 10^6 and extra per-factor set overhead.
complexity_delta.to: O(max(A) log log max(A) + N log A_max) time, O(max(A) + N) space, with max(A) <= 10^6 and leaner loops.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is essentially unchanged, but reducing the sieve range to max(A) and simplifying loops improves constants significantly, which is critical in Python near tight time limits.

transformation_steps: Make sieve range data-dependent: replace func_2(10**6) with a sieve sized to var_9 = max(var_1), building SPF only up to the maximum input value.
Use a standard SPF sieve: iterate var_6 from 2..var_9; when var_2[var_6] == 0, treat var_6 as prime and mark all its multiples with var_6 as their smallest prime factor.
Inline and simplify pairwise coprime test: factor each A[i], collect its distinct prime factors in a local set, and check for collisions in a single global set var_11 without redundant checks.
Streamline gcd computation: replace the separate func_1 with a simple iterative gcd (func_1(var_10, var_8)) and fuse it into func_3, avoiding repeated imports and some function call overhead.
Simplify control flow and I/O: remove the indirection via func_4 and directly branch on func_2() (pairwise) then func_3() (setwise), minimizing extra function calls and global lookups.
trigger_signals: Presence of a hard-coded sieve upper bound (10**6) instead of adapting to max(A[i]) suggests unnecessary work for smaller inputs.
Use of sets inside the innermost factorization loop indicates potential high constant factors due to frequent Python-level membership checks and insertions.
Multiple layers of small functions (func_2, func_3, func_4) with globals for a simple control-flow pattern hint at avoidable function-call and global-lookup overhead.
Tight time constraints and large N (~2e5) combined with Python implementation call for minimizing per-element overhead, especially in loops over prime factors.
pitfalls: When changing the sieve bound from a constant to max(A[i]), ensure that max(A[i]) is computed correctly and that the sieve array is large enough to safely index all A[i].
In the SPF sieve, take care not to overwrite previously set factors; the condition `if var_2[var_6] == 0` must guard prime detection, or SPF correctness is lost.
While factoring numbers, remember to only track distinct prime factors per number (use a local set) to avoid false positives when a number contains a squared prime factor.
Be cautious with globals in refactored code; incorrect scoping or reuse may lead to subtle bugs, even if they improve performance.
Do not change the logical order of checks: pairwise coprime must be tested before setwise coprime; otherwise the classification result may be wrong.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical setting for this known sequence problem (Snuke numbers / minimal n/sum_digits(n)): input K up to about 1e5, need to output first K terms of a special integer sequence up to ~1e15.

dominant_ops: In slow_code, func_3 repeatedly calls func_2 on growing var_7 until it exceeds 1e15. Each func_2 call performs nested digit manipulations, int<->string conversions, multiple calls to func_1 (which itself converts to string and sums digits), and finally sorts a list of candidate pairs.

complexity.time: Roughly O(T * d^2 log d), where d = number of digits (~15) and T = number of generated sequence elements up to 1e15 (on the order of K but coupled to numeric value); plus an additional factor from repeated int<->str conversions in func_1. The outer while in func_3 can iterate many times (up to the sequence length under 1e15), and each iteration creates ~O(d) * 9 candidates and sorts them.
complexity.space: O(d) per func_2 call for digit arrays plus O(d) candidates; overall O(d) additional beyond output.
complexity.why: For each current number var_7, func_2: (1) builds digit array: O(d); (2) loops over positions (d-1) and, for each, loops over 1..9 digits, forming candidates. Each candidate recomputes func_1(var_8), which does O(d) work via string conversion and digit sum. So candidate generation is O(d^2). Then var_2.sort() is O(m log m) with m≈9(d-1)=O(d), giving O(d log d). The outer while in func_3 repeatedly invokes func_2, advancing var_7 non-trivially until >1e15, producing on the order of the sequence size (e.g., up to ~1e5 or more). Multiplying yields O(T * d^2 log d) overall with heavy constant factors from Python-level loops and conversions.

bottlenecks.detail: func_3 grows var_7 step-by-step using func_2(var_7) and runs until var_7 > 1e15. This per-element search with a while loop up to a huge numeric bound leads to many iterations even if only the first K results are needed.
func_2 uses a double loop over digit positions and candidate digit values (up to 9), creating O(d^2) candidates per call, each requiring digit re-joining, int conversion, and evaluation of func_1.
func_1(var_7) converts the number to a string and maps chars back to ints on every call. This is invoked many times inside func_2, multiplying the overhead.

Each call to func_2 collects all candidates in var_2 and calls var_2.sort() on them, even though only the minimum by key (func_1(value)) is needed. Sorting all candidates adds an unnecessary O(d log d) factor per iteration.
