dominant_ops: math.factorial(var_1) and math.factorial(var_5) producing huge exact integers (~(min(a,b))! without modulo reduction)
Python big-integer multiplications inside factorial and later modular exponentiation pow(huge_factorial, MOD-2, MOD)
Loops over ranges [n, n-a] and [n, n-b] with Python-level multiplication and modulo per step

complexity.time: Superlinear in a and b due to big-integer growth in factorial; roughly O((a + b) * M(digits)) where digits ~ Θ(min(a,b) log min(a,b)) and M is big-int multiplication cost. Practically, factorial(2e5) is enormous and dominates runtime.
complexity.space: Θ(size of factorial(a)) + Θ(size of factorial(b)) digits, i.e., Θ((a + b) log(a + b)) digits of big integers, far beyond what is needed modulo 1e9+7.
complexity.why: The code computes exact factorials of size up to a! and b! with math.factorial before applying modulo. For a,b ~ 2e5, factorial values have on the order of 10^6 decimal digits, making big-int operations extremely expensive in both time and memory. Modular reduction happens only after these huge integers are fully constructed.

bottlenecks.detail: Using math.factorial(var_1) and math.factorial(var_5) to get full factorials instead of factorials modulo MOD leads to huge intermediate integers and very slow big-int arithmetic.
pow(factorial(k), MOD-2, MOD) must first reduce a massive factorial(k) modulo MOD, incurring heavy big-int cost before the actual O(log MOD) modular exponentiation.
Combinations C(n, a) and C(n, b) are computed directly for a and b, without using C(n, k) = C(n, n-k), so when k > n/2 the numerator loops and factorial magnitude are larger than necessary.
The logic for computing C(n, a) and C(n, b) is duplicated, each with its own loop and factorial call, instead of sharing precomputed factorial/falling-factorial values.

FastAudit.core_idea: Work entirely modulo 1e9+7 using precomputed falling factorials and factorials up to max(a, b), exploiting symmetry k -> n-k to keep k small. Represent C(n, k) as (n * (n-1) * ... * (n-k+1)) * inv(k!) mod MOD. Precompute arrays of these values in O(max(a, b)) time, then use a single modular inverse via fast exponentiation per k.

complexity.time: O(max(a, b) + log MOD). The loop up to var_7 = max(var_3, var_5) builds numerator and denominator arrays in linear time; two pow calls for modular inverses contribute O(log MOD) each but are negligible compared to max(a, b) for typical constraints (~2e5).
complexity.space: O(max(a, b)) for the arrays var_1 and var_2 storing falling factorials and factorials modulo MOD.
complexity.why: By always reducing intermediate results modulo 1e9+7, all integers stay within machine-friendly big-int sizes (~30 bits), eliminating factorial-sized blowup. Precomputing up to max(a, b) reuses state for both C(n, a) and C(n, b), and using min(k, n-k) cuts work when k is large.

complexity_delta.from: Time dominated by big-int factorial and modular exponentiation on huge integers; effectively superlinear and impractical for a,b up to ~2e5. Space dominated by enormously large factorial values.
complexity_delta.to: Time O(max(a, b)) with modest constants plus a few O(log MOD) exponentiations; space O(max(a, b)) with only modulo-sized integers.
complexity_delta.note: The key improvement is avoiding construction of enormous exact factorials and instead maintaining values modulo MOD throughout all multiplications.

transformation_steps: Replace math.factorial(k) (exact factorials) with iterative multiplication modulo MOD to build factorial-like sequences (var_2) and falling factorials (var_1).
Introduce symmetry reduction var_3 = min(var_3, var_9 - var_3) and var_5 = min(var_5, var_9 - var_5) so that combinations C(n, a) and C(n, b) are computed using the smaller of k and n-k.
Precompute var_1[i] = n * (n-1) * ... * (n-i+1) mod MOD and var_2[i] = i! mod MOD in a single linear loop up to var_7 = max(var_3, var_5).
Compute each binomial coefficient as var_1[k] * pow(var_2[k], MOD-2, MOD) % MOD using Fermat's little theorem for modular inverse, operating only on modulo-sized integers.
Reuse the same precomputed arrays for both C(n, var_3) and C(n, var_5), removing duplicated work and big-int allocations.
Perform final expression assembly ((2^n - 1) - C(n, a) - C(n, b)) modulo MOD with careful modular normalization to avoid negative results.
trigger_signals: Use of math.factorial on inputs that can be as large as 2e5 or similar, combined with modular arithmetic, indicating unnecessary exact big-int factorial computation.
pow(factorial(k), MOD-2, MOD) where factorial(k) is not reduced modulo MOD before exponentiation.
Observed or potential TLE/MLE when a and b are large (e.g., near upper constraint) even though the conceptual combinatorial formula is simple.
Duplicated combination-computation logic for C(n, a) and C(n, b) without shared precomputation.
pitfalls: Assuming math.factorial(k) is cheap when k is large; in pure modular problems, computing full factorials is almost always unnecessary and harmful.
Forgetting to apply modulo at each multiplication step, causing integer sizes to grow uncontrollably before the first mod reduction.
Overlooking the symmetry C(n, k) = C(n, n-k), which can approximately halve work and reduce intermediate value sizes.
Mismanaging negative values after subtraction of combinations; must normalize with modulo (as done in the fast code by wrapping in % var_8).
Assuming that a direct descending product for the numerator alone solves performance: while that part is O(k), pairing it with exact factorial for the denominator reintroduces big-int costs.

constraints_guess.notes: Single permutation of size N, integer K up to about 1e18 (fits in 63 bits). Need to compute applying permutation K times starting from position 1 using binary lifting / repeated squaring.

dominant_ops: For each of 63 bits, two full Python for-loops over N elements to square the permutation: var_2[i] = var_1[var_1[i]] then copy back var_1[i] = var_2[i].

complexity.why: The algorithm performs up to 63 iterations (log2 of max K), and each iteration does O(N) work to compose the permutation twice (compute into var_2, then copy into var_1). The position update var_7 = var_1[var_7] is O(1) per bit. Space is dominated by the permutation arrays var_1 and var_2 of size N.

bottlenecks.detail: Two explicit for-loops over range(var_4) per bit for permutation squaring cause heavy Python overhead: 2 * 63 * N index assignments.
Squaring uses a temporary array var_2 then copies back element-by-element, doubling the per-iteration work instead of building the next permutation in one pass.
Uses input().split() twice, which is slower than reading all stdin at once for large N.
The inner loops perform Python-level indexing and assignment for each element, which is significantly slower than a list comprehension implemented in C.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the same binary-lifting / permutation exponentiation algorithm but implement the permutation squaring as a single list comprehension over the current mapping (including index 0) and use read-all-at-once I/O. This reduces Python-level loop overhead while preserving O(N log K) behavior.

complexity.why: The while var_3 loop runs proportional to the number of bits in K (~log K). Each iteration performs a single list comprehension var_1 = [var_1[var_2] for var_2 in var_1], which is O(N) but executed in optimized C; the position update var_5 = ... is O(1) per bit. Only one permutation array of size N+1 is maintained, so space is O(N).

complexity_delta.from: O(N log K) time, O(N) space (with high Python-interpretation overhead per element via nested loops).
complexity_delta.to: O(N log K) time, O(N) space (same asymptotics, but drastically reduced constant factors via list comprehensions and faster I/O).
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time/space do not change, but the implementation shifts heavy work into C-level loops and avoids redundant passes and copies, making the solution fast enough for large N.

transformation_steps: Replace manual 0-based permutation handling and two-step squaring (compute into var_2, then copy to var_1) with a single list comprehension: var_1 = [var_1[var_2] for var_2 in var_1], using a 1-based permutation array prefixed with a dummy 0 entry.
Inline the binary decomposition of K by using var_3 % 2 and var_3 //= 2 directly in a while var_3 loop instead of precomputing bits into an auxiliary array var_8.
Use a compact boolean-expression update for the current position: var_5 = var_3 % 2 and var_1[var_5] or var_5 to avoid branches and extra indexing when the bit is zero.
Switch from repeated input().split() calls to open(0).read().split() to reduce input overhead for large N.
Eliminate the auxiliary array var_2 and its associated copy-back loop, reducing memory traffic and per-iteration passes over the permutation.
trigger_signals: Presence of two explicit for-loops over range(N) for each of 63 iterations, indicating 100+ million Python-level operations for large N.
Use of a temporary buffer var_2 solely to copy back into var_1, suggesting redundant work.
Precomputation of K's bits into an array and then always looping 63 times regardless of the actual highest set bit.
Use of Python input() for large data volumes instead of bulk reading stdin.
TLE or near-timeout behavior when N is large (e.g., N around 1e5–2e5) combined with K up to 1e18.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when changing from 0-based with -1 adjustments to 1-based indexing with a dummy element at index 0. The position variable and the permutation array must be consistently indexed.
Ensuring the composition var_1 = [var_1[var_2] for var_2 in var_1] includes the dummy index 0 at the start so that the mapping remains valid and closed over its index set.
The compact boolean expression var_5 = var_3 % 2 and var_1[var_5] or var_5 relies on var_1[var_5] being non-zero when used; misuse in other contexts could cause subtle bugs if valid targets can be 0.
When switching to open(0).read().split(), all input must be consumed in the correct order and count; miscounting how many integers belong to the permutation can corrupt the mapping.

Relying on K fitting within the assumed bit range (here up to 63 bits). If constraints changed to allow larger K, the fixed 63-loop version would break, whereas the while var_3 approach naturally scales.

constraints_guess.q_max: unknown; likely up to 1e4–1e5 queries (input until EOF)
constraints_guess.notes: Both versions precompute primes up to 999999 (~1e6). Each query gives an n and asks for the count of primes ≤ n.

dominant_ops: Sieve precomputation up to 1e6 using nested for-loops
For each query: Python-level while loop that decrements n and accumulates var_5[n]

complexity.time: O(N log log N + Q * N) with N = 1e6 (sieve is O(N log log N); each query is O(n_query))
complexity.space: O(N) for the sieve array; O(1) extra per query
complexity.why: The sieve uses the standard i*i start optimization and loops i up to sqrt(N), so precomputation is near-optimal. However, each query scans from n down to 1 in pure Python, which is linear in n with high constant factors due to Python while-loop overhead.

bottlenecks.detail: For each input n (var_4), the code does a Python while loop: var_1 += var_5[var_4]; var_4 -= 1. This performs O(n) Python-level iterations per query; if many queries are large, total work becomes Q * N.
The counting loop uses explicit Python bytecode for each step (load, add, store, compare, branch), which is slow compared to C-level tight loops used in comprehensions or built-ins.
No prefix sums or pre-aggregated counts are used; the code recomputes the count of primes from scratch for each query.

FastAudit.core_idea: Still precompute primality with a sieve once, but for each query count primes via a list comprehension over a slice of the sieve list. The heavy per-query iteration is executed in optimized C-level loops (list building and iteration), which significantly reduces Python interpreter overhead compared to a manual while loop.

complexity.time: O(N log log N + Q * N); asymptotically the same as the slow version, but with a much smaller constant factor in the per-query part.
complexity.space: O(N) for the sieve array plus O(n_query) temporary space per query due to slicing and list creation inside len([...]).
complexity.why: The sieve is a variant of the Eratosthenes algorithm, slightly less optimized (starts marking from 2*i instead of i*i), but only run once so it’s not the bottleneck. The main speedup comes from using a list slice and comprehension, which loops in C over contiguous memory, reducing per-iteration overhead even though it allocates temporary lists.

delta_type: lower constant factors in critical per-query loop)

complexity_delta.from: O(N log log N + Q * N) with high constant factors due to Python while-loop for each query
complexity_delta.to: O(N log log N + Q * N) with reduced constant factors by using list slicing and comprehensions (C-level loops) for counting
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity remains linear per query, but the fast version is substantially quicker in practice. A fully optimal solution would introduce a prefix sum array to achieve O(1) per query, but that is not what was changed here.

transformation_steps: Retain one-time sieve precomputation of primality up to 999999 (structure preserved, though exact bounds/inner-start differ).
Replace the explicit Python while loop that decremented n and summed var_5[n] with a list comprehension plus len(...) over a slice of the sieve list.
Leverage CPython’s optimized C-level loops for iteration and counting, even at the cost of temporary list allocation.
Stop doing per-iteration Python arithmetic and branching in the query loop; push as much work as possible into built-in operations.
trigger_signals: You see a Python while/for loop running up to O(1e6) iterations per query, with very simple operations inside (e.g., array access + integer addition).
Profiling shows that most time is spent in a tight Python loop that conceptually is a reduction (sum/count) over a list or range.
The problem pattern is repeated counting/aggregation over the same precomputed boolean/int array for many different query endpoints.
The algorithmic structure cannot easily be changed (e.g., contest constraints fixed), but you still need a significant speedup.
pitfalls: Using slicing and comprehensions per query increases temporary memory usage to O(n_query); with very large n and many queries this can lead to higher memory pressure or cache misses.

Both versions remain O(N * Q) in the worst case; for very large Q the overall approach can still time out. The real algorithmic fix is to precompute a prefix-count array and answer each query in O(1).
Reliance on eval(input()) is unsafe and also slower than int(input()); while not the main performance issue here, it is a bad practice and can cause security or robustness problems.

The sieve implementation in the fast code starts marking from 2*i instead of i*i, which increases constant factors in precomputation. This is acceptable here but would matter for significantly larger N.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder setting: N up to around 1e5, M up to around 1e9. Single test case; need fast factorization of M and many combinatorial computations C(e+N-1, e) under mod 1e9+7.

dominant_ops: Trial-division factorization up to sqrt(M) in func_2
Repeated computation and manipulation of very large factorial integers via math.factorial in func_1
Integer division of huge factorial values to form combinations before taking modulo
Repeated creation of list(var_11.keys()) inside the tight inner loop of factorization

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + K * cost_factorial) where cost_factorial is the time to compute factorials of size up to about N+max_exponent using Python big integers; effectively near-linear in N with high constant factors and big-integer overhead
complexity.space: O(K * size_of_factorial_values) where K is the number of distinct factorial arguments cached; factorial values grow as Θ(N log N) bits each, so memory is dominated by large big integers
complexity.why: func_2 performs naive trial division var_5 = 2..sqrt(M), which is O(sqrt(M)) operations. func_1 calls math.factorial on large arguments like N+e-1 and N-1, returning big Python integers with Θ(N log N) bits. Combinations are computed via exact integer division var_2 // (var_3 * var_4), which requires expensive big-integer multiplication and division. Furthermore, list(var_11.keys()) is allocated anew on each inner loop iteration, adding avoidable overhead, although the number of primes is small.

bottlenecks.detail: Combinatorial values C(n, k) are computed using raw factorials and integer division on huge integers instead of using modular factorials and inverse factorials. This keeps numbers enormous until the very end, making arithmetic slow.
math.factorial is called on large arguments multiple times (even if somewhat cached in a dict), and each call builds a fresh big integer instead of reusing a linear factorial table under modulo.
list(var_11.keys()) in func_2 is rebuilt on every inner-loop iteration, adding an O(#primes) overhead to each factor division step for no benefit.

All arithmetic in the original version is done on unbounded Python ints with thousands of bits; even when asymptotic complexity is acceptable, the constant factors from big-int multiplication/division are high compared with modular arithmetic on 64-bit-sized ints.

FastAudit.core_idea: Precompute factorials and inverse factorials modulo a prime (1e9+7) up to a global limit and use them to evaluate combinations C(n, k) in O(1) per query. Keep all arithmetic under the modulus to avoid huge integers, and slightly optimize prime factorization by handling 2 separately and iterating over odd factors with a tighter loop.

complexity.time: O(L + sqrt(M) + P) where L is the precomputation limit for factorials (≈ N + max_exponent), sqrt(M) is for factorization, and P is the number of prime factors; each combination query is O(1) after precomputation.
complexity.space: O(L) for factorial and inverse factorial arrays, storing O(L) modular integers (machine-sized).
complexity.why: The Class_1 constructor precomputes fact[i] and invs[i] for i up to var_11 in a single forward and backward pass, each O(L). C(n, k) is then computed as fact[n] * invs[k] * invs[n-k] mod MOD in constant time. func_2 performs trial division but in an optimized pattern (2 first, then odd numbers with updated square), which remains O(sqrt(M)) but with low overhead. Since all values are reduced modulo 1e9+7 at each multiplication, big-int growth is eliminated and operations are effectively on fixed-width integers.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(sqrt(M) + K * cost_bigint_factorial_and_division); Space: O(K * size_of_big_factorials). All combinatorial arithmetic uses large Python integers with heavy multiplication/division.
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(L + sqrt(M) + P) with O(1) per combination after precomputation; Space: O(L) with only modular-sized integers.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically, both approaches are polynomial and involve a sqrt(M) factorization term plus something linear in the maximum n used in combinations. The key improvement is moving from heavy big-integer factorial/division per query to a single linear precomputation of modular factorials and inverse factorials with O(1) combination queries, alongside tighter low-level factorization. This drastically reduces constant factors and makes the solution safe under typical constraints (N up to ~1e5, M up to ~1e9).

transformation_steps: Replace the on-demand math.factorial-based combination function func_1 with a combinatorics helper class (Class_1) that precomputes factorials modulo MOD up to a chosen limit.
Compute inverse factorials using Fermat's little theorem: inv_fact[maxN] = fact[maxN]^(MOD-2) mod MOD, then fill lower entries via inv_fact[i] = inv_fact[i+1] * (i+1) mod MOD.
Implement nCr(n, k) as fact[n] * inv_fact[k] * inv_fact[n-k] % MOD, and expose it through Class_1.func_1 so each combination is computed in O(1).
Update the factorization function: count factors of 2 separately, then loop over odd candidates and update the loop bound using the square (var_10), avoiding list(dict.keys()) and redundant work.
Apply the modulus at every multiplication step (var_12 *= nCr(...) % MOD) instead of only once at the end to keep intermediate values bounded and efficient.
Remove dynamic dictionary-based factorial caching and large intermediate integers; rely solely on the precomputed arrays of modular factorials.
trigger_signals: Presence of math.factorial on arguments that can be as large as N+max_exponent (~1e5), combined with exact integer division to form combinations.
Lack of intermediate modulo operations: results are reduced modulo 1e9+7 only at the very end, implying huge interim integers.
Repeated use of list(dict.keys()) inside a tight loop in func_2, indicating unnecessary allocations and linear scans.
Competitive programming context (single test case, constraints around 1e5) where the standard pattern is to precompute factorials and inverse factorials once.
Use of combinatorial formula C(e+N-1, e) multiple times, a classic signal for needing precomputed nCr mod prime.
pitfalls: The modulus 1e9+7 must be prime for Fermat-based inverse factorials; changing MOD to a non-prime requires a different inversion strategy.
The factorial/inverse factorial arrays must be sized to at least max_n used in combinations (here roughly max(e_i + N - 1)); underestimating this limit will cause index errors or incorrect results.
Care is needed to handle edge cases in nCr: when k < 0 or k > n, the function should return 0; some fast implementations rely on callers to avoid invalid ranges.

In the optimized factorization, yielding exponents for each candidate factor must align with how the caller interprets them; mixing zero-exponent yields with omitted primes can lead to off-by-one issues if the consumption logic changes.

When refactoring to class-based combinatorics helpers, ensure that all referenced methods (e.g., a combination helper) are actually implemented and that func_1 correctly delegates to them; otherwise, runtime errors (like missing self.combination) can occur.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style coprimality problem: n up to ~1e5, each a_i up to ~1e6. Single test, no separate queries.

dominant_ops: Full smallest-prime-factor (SPF) sieve up to 10**6 irrespective of actual max(a_i).
Per-element gcd accumulation over all n values.
Prime factorization of each a_i using repeated division by SPF with Python-level while loop and array accesses.

complexity.time: O(M log log M + N log A)
complexity.why: Let M = 10**6 (fixed upper bound), A = max(a_i). The SPF sieve writes to var_7 for every multiple of each prime: harmonic sum over primes gives O(M log log M). For each of N numbers, gcd(var_5, a_i) is O(log A); prime factorization via repeated division by SPF uses at most O(log A) iterations per number. Arrays var_7 and var_9 both have size M+1, so space is O(M).

bottlenecks.detail: Sieve always runs up to var_2 = 10**6 even if max(a_i) is much smaller. On small inputs this dominates runtime unnecessarily.
The SPF sieve is implemented with nested Python for/while loops assigning into var_7 for every multiple; this is many millions of Python-level operations.
Each a_i is factorized with a Python while loop, repeatedly indexing var_7 and var_9 and dividing var_4. Even though asymptotically O(log A), the constant factors are high in Python.

The SPF sieve and exact factorization compute more information (full prime factors) than needed; the problem only requires whether any gcd>1 shared across elements exists and whether primes repeat across different elements.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid prime factorization entirely. Count frequency of each integer value up to max(a_i), then for each d from 2 to max(a_i) aggregate counts of all multiples of d via var_2[d::d]. The maximum such aggregate indicates the maximum number of elements sharing a common divisor. Combine this with n and simple comparisons to classify pairwise/setwise/not coprime.

complexity.why: M = max(a_i). Building the frequency array var_2 costs O(M + N). For each d in [2..M], sum(var_2[d::d]) touches roughly M/d entries; summing over d yields M * (1/1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/M) = O(M log M) operations. Arrays scale only up to M (the actual maximum in input), so space is O(M). Despite the O(M log M) bound, the operations are simple integer additions and lookups, and M is at most around 1e6, making this practical.

complexity_delta.from: O(M log log M + N log A) time, O(M) space (full SPF sieve and factorization up to fixed M = 10**6).
complexity_delta.to: O(M log M + N) time, O(M) space (frequency counting and divisor-based aggregation up to actual max(a_i)).
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically the sieve-based approach has a slightly better dependency on M, but in this problem the modified version wastes work on a fixed upper bound 10**6 and incurs heavy Python overhead in sieve and factorization loops. The frequency+multiples method operates only up to max(a_i) and uses simpler operations, yielding better real-world performance under the given constraints.

transformation_steps: Remove the global SPF sieve and replace it with a direct frequency array var_2 sized to max(a_i) instead of a fixed 10**6.
Eliminate per-element prime factorization and instead rely on counting how many input values are multiples of each candidate divisor.
Loop over d from 2 to max(a_i), and for each d compute the total count of elements divisible by d using sum(var_2[d::d]); track the maximum such count as var_6.

Replace gcd-based setwise coprime detection with logic based on var_6 and n: if no divisor >1 divides at least two numbers (var_6 < 2) then pairwise coprime; else if not all share a divisor (var_6 < n) then setwise coprime; otherwise not coprime.
Allocate data structures only up to the observed maximum value in the input to avoid unnecessary O(10**6) work when the actual range is smaller.
trigger_signals: Presence of a full SPF sieve up to a constant 10**6 regardless of actual input values.
Nested loops over all multiples of each prime in Python (sieve) combined with additional per-element factorization loops.
Use of gcd and prime factor tracking for each element when the final decision only depends on aggregate divisibility properties.
Memory allocation of multiple arrays of size 10**6 per run in a language with non-trivial per-element overhead.
pitfalls: The fast approach uses sum(var_2[d::d]), which creates a new sliced list for each d. For significantly larger max(a_i) this could become a bottleneck; an even faster version would accumulate counts in-place without creating slices.

Both approaches assume an upper bound around 10**6. If the true constraints allow much larger values, both memory and time complexities may become unacceptable and a more sophisticated number-theoretic optimization would be needed.

Care must be taken that the divisor-based aggregation correctly reflects the coprimality logic: while any composite divisor hitting multiple numbers implies a shared prime, summing over all multiples can create large constants if implemented naively.
Using eval(input()) for reading integers is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; although not a performance bottleneck here, it should be avoided in general.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer seconds value, likely within typical 32-bit range (e.g., 0 <= t <= 10^9). Time-conversion / implementation problem; performance constraints trivial.

dominant_ops: Module-level doctest discovery and execution (doctest.testmod)
Full stdin read via sys.stdin.read for a single integer
Float division (/) instead of integer division (//) for hour and minute components
Modulo operations for seconds and residual minutes

complexity.time: O(L) where L is length of stdin; O(1) with respect to numeric value range
complexity.space: O(L) for buffer of sys.stdin.read plus minor O(1) locals
complexity.why: doctest.testmod scans the module and may run embedded tests; sys.stdin.read reads entire input stream into memory even though only a single integer is needed. Arithmetic itself is O(1); overheads are from I/O and doctest.

bottlenecks.detail: doctest.testmod() runs at program start, incurring module scanning and potential test execution overhead that is completely unnecessary in a competitive-programming / online judge setting.
sys.stdin.read() reads the entire stdin into a single string, which is wasteful when only one integer should be parsed. This increases memory use and time proportionally to total input size.

Using / for division produces floats in Python 3 (var_2, var_3 become floats). Even though they are printed with %d (which truncates), float operations are marginally slower and can introduce subtle correctness issues if the problem expects strict integer arithmetic.
Using old-style printf formatting with %d requires implicit type coercions from float to int; while minor, it adds unnecessary work compared to staying in integer domain.

FastAudit.core_idea: Remove doctest and full-stream read; use standard input() for a single integer and integer-only arithmetic (// and explicit remainder construction) to compute hours, minutes, and seconds, then print with simple sep=":" formatting.

complexity.time: O(1) with respect to both input size (single integer) and value magnitude
complexity.why: input() reads only one line, and all computations are simple integer divisions and subtractions (constant number of operations). No module-level testing or full-stream buffering is performed.

from.time: O(L) due to sys.stdin.read and doctest.testmod scanning module; plus constant arithmetic

to.time: O(1) for single-line read and constant arithmetic

complexity_delta.note: As typically used on an online judge with a single integer input, both versions behave effectively O(1) in practice, but the original incurs unnecessary overhead from doctest and full-stream reading. The modified version removes these overheads and uses integer arithmetic, improving both performance constants and correctness robustness.

transformation_steps: Remove doctest.testmod() call so that no tests are run at runtime in the submission environment.
Replace sys.stdin.read() with input() to read only a single line (single integer) instead of the entire input stream.
Switch from float division (/) to integer division (//) and explicit remainder construction using subtractions to keep all intermediate results as integers.
Change formatted output from old-style "%d:%d:%d" % (h, m, s) to print(h, m, s, sep=":") for simpler, direct integer printing.
Rename and reorder variables (var_1, var_2, var_3) to reflect hour, minute, second roles more clearly and avoid reuse of a float-typed variable.
trigger_signals: Presence of doctest.testmod() inside __main__ in a competitive-programming-like solution, which is unusual and costly.
Use of sys.stdin.read() with a problem statement that clearly implies a single integer input.
Use of / for divisions where the problem is integer-based time decomposition (hours, minutes, seconds), suggesting a potential correctness and type-efficiency issue.
Float values being formatted with %d, implying implicit truncation or coercion rather than intended integer computation.
pitfalls: Behavioral change if the judge or environment feeds multiple numbers or trailing content into stdin: sys.stdin.read() would see all of it, while input() only reads one line. For typical problems with exactly one integer, this is safe; otherwise, behavior differs.

Using / in Python 3 yields floats; relying on %d formatting to coerce to int can mask subtle bugs (e.g., non-integer results due to miscalculated expressions). The optimized version correctly uses // to avoid this.
Recomputing remainders via subtraction, as in var_3 - var_1 * 3600 - var_2 * 60, must be carefully ordered to avoid algebraic mistakes; misplacing a factor (e.g., 60 vs 3600) leads to wrong results.

If later extended to handle very large integers or non-standard input formats, input() assumptions (single line, clean integer) might require validation; currently no error handling is present in either version.

constraints_guess.n_max: ≈1e9 for the number being factorized; combinatorial parameter up to ≈1e5–2e5
constraints_guess.notes: Typical of AtCoder-style problem: given K and N, factorize N and compute ∏ C(e_i + K - 1, e_i) mod 1e9+7, where e_i are prime exponents of N.

dominant_ops: Precomputation of factorials and modular inverse factorials up to some max_n (var_11) in Class_1.__init__
Trial-division style factorization in func_2 up to roughly sqrt(N) using incrementing odd candidates
Per-prime binomial computations via precomputed factorials (O(1) each)

complexity.why: Class_1.__init__ builds two length-(max_n+1) arrays (factorials and inverse factorials) in O(max_n) time and memory. func_2 performs trial division using candidates up to about sqrt(N). The number of distinct prime factors P of N is small (≤ log N), so per-prime combination queries are O(1) each compared to the precomputation and factorization costs.

bottlenecks.detail: Class_1.__init__ always computes factorials/inverse factorials up to var_11 regardless of how few C(n, k) queries are actually needed; in this problem only O(P) combinations (P very small) are used.
Two integer arrays of size O(max_n) (fact and invs) are stored even though only a handful of binomial coefficients are needed, which is wasteful when max_n is large.

func_2 loops odd candidates while candidate^2 <= original N (var_13), not the shrinking remainder, so it may continue checking larger candidates even after the residual var_15 is small; this misses an easy constant-factor improvement compared to using candidate^2 <= var_15.
func_2 yields an exponent for every candidate (including zeros); if the caller consumes all yields, it may do unnecessary combination computations for primes that are not actually factors.

Class_1.func_1 calls self.combination, which is not defined in the provided snippet; even if intended as a symmetry optimization, miswiring this function can introduce recursion or attribute lookups that hurt performance and correctness.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial precomputation and modular inverse arrays. Instead, factorize N by simple trial division while updating the remainder, count prime exponents in a dictionary, and compute each binomial coefficient C(n, k) directly via multiplicative formula with integer arithmetic; finally reduce the product modulo 1e9+7.

complexity.why: func_2 performs trial division while var_1 * var_1 <= current var_5, so the divisor bound effectively shrinks as factors are removed, keeping factorization O(sqrt(N)) in the worst case. For each exponent e_i, func_1 computes C(e_i + K - 1, e_i) using O(e_i) multiplications/divisions (after applying symmetry k = min(k, n-k)); since exponents come from factorization, Σ e_i = O(log N) and P is small, giving near-linear-in-sqrt(N) time with very small overhead beyond factorization. No large O(max_n) arrays are allocated; only a dictionary of size O(P) is used.

delta_type: constant-factor reduction and removal of unnecessary precomputation

complexity_delta.from: O(max_n + sqrt(N) + P) time, O(max_n) space (max_n depends on combinatorial parameters, typically K + max_exponent)
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(N) + Σ e_i) time, O(P) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both approaches share the O(sqrt(N)) factorization cost, but the original code adds an O(max_n) factorial precomputation that dominates when K (or max_n) is large compared to the number of actual binomial queries. The optimized code removes this overhead, making runtime depend mainly on sqrt(N) and small exponents e_i.

transformation_steps: Removed the Class_1 factorial and inverse factorial precomputation and the associated O(max_n) memory footprint.

Replaced O(1)-per-query modular binomial using precomputed tables with an on-demand multiplicative binomial (func_1) that runs in O(k) where k is the smaller of r and n-r; in this problem k equals the prime exponent and is very small.

Reimplemented prime factorization (func_2) using trial division that updates the working value var_5 and checks while var_1**2 <= var_5, reducing unnecessary iterations when the composite collapses quickly.
Eliminated generator-based factorization that produced zero exponents for non-dividing candidates; instead, only actual prime factors and their positive exponents are stored in a dictionary.
Removed class indirection and potential miswired method calls (self.combination) in favor of straightforward top-level functions, reducing object overhead and possible recursion/lookup costs.

Deferred modulo reduction until the final product, relying on Python’s big integers to handle intermediate values; this reduces per-operation overhead of modular multiplications in exchange for slightly larger integer sizes, which is acceptable given the tiny Σ e_i.
trigger_signals: Only O(P) binomial coefficients are needed where P (number of distinct prime factors of N) is very small, making a global O(max_n) factorial precomputation suspiciously heavy.
Memory footprint dominated by two arrays of size proportional to the combinatorial parameter, despite a single test case and very few combination queries.
Presence of a combination helper class with big precomputation in a problem whose constraints suggest that K is moderate and exponents e_i are tiny (≤ log N).
Generator-style factorization that can yield many zeros hints at unnecessary work for non-factors.
Method call to an apparently missing self.combination method inside func_1 suggests possible design/logic issues that can both harm performance and cause runtime errors.
pitfalls: The fast version’s direct combinatorial calculation uses integer division and only applies the modulo at the end; while fine for small Σ e_i, for larger k or many queries this can cause very large intermediate integers and slowdown.

In other languages without arbitrary-precision integers, the same strategy (compute full C(n, k) then mod) would overflow; the factorial+mod-inverse approach from the original is safer and more general in such environments.

If future changes increase the number of combination queries (e.g., multiple test cases or additional combinatorial subproblems), the lack of a reusable precomputed factorial table could become a new bottleneck; in that scenario, the original pattern (with a correctly implemented combination class) might be preferable.
The optimized factorization still has worst-case O(sqrt(N)) behavior; for much larger N or many test cases, more advanced factorization (e.g., precomputed primes or Pollard’s Rho) would be needed.

Deferring modulo until after all multiplications assumes that intermediate integers fit comfortably in memory and that Python big-int operations remain fast; this assumption may fail if the structure of the problem changes (e.g., significantly larger K or exponents).

constraints_guess.notes: Typical 'sum of numbers whose digit sum is within [A,B]' problem (e.g., AtCoder ABC083B uses N <= 10^4). Single input N, A, B; loop from 1..N.

dominant_ops: For each integer from 1 to N, a while-loop repeatedly divides a value by 10 using float division (`/=`) and calls `math.floor` on `var_4 % 10` to accumulate digit sum. This inner loop runs many times due to floating-point underflow behavior.

complexity.why: The outer loop is over N numbers. Intended digit extraction via division by 10 should take O(D) where D is the digit count (≈ log10 N). However, because `var_4` is divided using float division (`/=`), it becomes a float and never reaches exactly 0; it only stops when it underflows to 0.0. This leads to a large, effectively constant K (~1000) iterations per number, independent of the actual number of digits. Thus total time ≈ N * K with a huge constant factor. Memory usage is constant aside from a few scalar variables.

bottlenecks.detail: Using `var_4 /= 10` (float division) instead of integer division (`var_4 //= 10`) causes `var_4` to be a float that approaches 0 but does not reach it until floating-point underflow, massively increasing loop iterations and distorting complexity.
Calling `math.floor` inside the tight while-loop for every digit-like step adds significant overhead, especially combined with float modulo operations.
Each iteration computes `var_4 % 10` where `var_4` is a float and 10 is an int, leading to mixed-type arithmetic and more expensive operations than simple integer arithmetic.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace the manual float-based digit extraction loop with Python's high-level operations: convert the number to a string, map each character to int, and sum them. This computes the digit sum in a bounded number of steps proportional to the number of digits and avoids the float underflow issue.

complexity.why: For each of the N numbers, `str(var_5)` creates a string of length D (number of digits), `map(int, ...)` iterates over D characters, and `sum(...)` sums D integers. Thus digit-sum computation per number is O(D), yielding O(N * D) overall. D ≈ log10 N and is small in typical constraints (<= 5 or 6). Space per number is O(D) for the temporary string and list; overall auxiliary space remains O(D).

complexity_delta.from: O(N * K) with large hidden constant due to float-division-driven while-loop until underflow
complexity_delta.to: O(N * D) where D is number of digits (~log10 N) with small constant factors via string-based digit sum
complexity_delta.note: The asymptotic form remains linear in N, but the actual runtime improves drastically: the inner loop no longer depends on floating-point underflow and uses far fewer, simpler operations per number.

transformation_steps: Remove the manual while-loop that repeatedly divides by 10 using float division (`/=`) to extract digits.
Eliminate `math.floor` and float modulo; rely on integer digit values instead.
For each number `var_5`, convert it to a string (`str(var_5)`), map each character to an integer (`map(int, ...)`), and sum them with `sum(...)` to get the digit sum.
Use a simple range check `var_1 <= digit_sum <= var_2` and accumulate the qualifying numbers into the running total.
Optionally (further micro-optimization, not present but possible): remove the unnecessary `list()` around `map` to avoid an extra list allocation.
trigger_signals: Inner loop pattern `while var_4 > 0: var_4 /= 10` (or similar) indicating float division where integer division is intended.
Use of `math.floor` or other math library calls inside a tight per-element loop for simple digit extraction.
Mixed float-int arithmetic (`float % int`) in numeric loops that are expected to be purely integer-based.
Unexpectedly high runtime or timeouts for small upper bounds N in problems that conceptually should be O(N * log N) or better.
pitfalls: In the original approach, using `/=` instead of `//=` subtly changes ints to floats and leads to many extra iterations; such bugs are easy to miss because the code may still terminate and produce correct results for small inputs.

In the modified approach, repeatedly creating strings and lists has overhead; for extremely large N, a more optimized integer-only digit-sum (`while x: s += x % 10; x //= 10`) can be faster, though for typical contest constraints the string approach is fine.
Including `list()` around `map(int, ...)` is unnecessary; it materializes a list when `sum` can consume the iterator directly, adding extra allocations.
Relying on float behavior (underflow, precision) for control flow is fragile; always ensure digit extraction and similar operations use integer arithmetic when working with integers.

constraints_guess.notes: First solution reads all integers in one shot and uses a DP array of fixed size 6**8 (~1.7e6). The optimized solution allocates a segment tree over a value domain var_17=300001, suggesting value coordinates and/or N are on the order of 3e5. Time limits typical of competitive programming (1–2s) make O(N) with heavy Python-level loops or O(N * window_size) borderline at this scale.

dominant_ops: Outer DP loop over var_5 (O(N) iterations)
For each i, a Python-level max(...) over up to 99 candidates with a generator comprehension and conditional filter
Repeated abs()/comparison and list indexing inside the inner generator
Allocation and zero-initialization of a large list var_2 of length 6**8 (~1.7e6) and concatenation var_1 = var_2 + var_1

complexity.time: O(N * W) where W = 99 (effectively O(N) but with ~100 Python-level operations per state)
complexity.space: O(N + M) where M = 6**8 (~1.7e6) due to the oversized DP array and padded value array
complexity.why: The while loop decrements var_5 from its initial value (N) down to 1. In each iteration it scans the range [var_5, var_5+99) and checks a condition per candidate before computing max(var_2[var_3]) + 1. That is Θ(W) work per DP state with W fixed at 99, so asymptotically linear but with a large constant factor in pure Python. Additionally, var_2 and the padded prefix of var_1 both scale with 6**8, giving large but input-independent memory usage.

bottlenecks.detail: The core DP transition is implemented as a Python generator in max(...) inside an outer Python while loop. For N≈3e5 and window size 99, this is ~3e7 iterations of Python bytecode, which is close to or beyond typical contest time limits in CP environments.

var_2 is allocated with length 6**8 regardless of N, and var_1 is rebuilt as var_2 + var_1. This introduces ~1.7M extra integers and a large concatenation, impacting both memory and startup time without being tied to actual input size.

Using a huge prefix (var_2) to enable negative indexing into var_1 (var_1[-var_5], var_1[-var_3]) obscures locality and forces the large allocation; while asymptotically harmless, it contributes to cache-unfriendly access patterns and makes it harder to shrink the data structures to the true N.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace the per-position linear scan over candidate transitions with a segment tree that supports range updates and range-maximum queries over the value domain. Instead of checking up to ~100 future DP states in a Python loop for each index, maintain DP information in a tree indexed by value (or a compressed coordinate). For each new element, query the segment tree over the range of values allowed by the |a[i] - a[j]| <= D constraint to get the best reachable DP value, then update the appropriate range/node. Lazy propagation (var_15) amortizes range assignments so each operation is O(log M), where M is the value-domain size (~3e5).

complexity.time: O(N log M) where M ≈ 300001 is the segment tree size
complexity.space: O(M) for the segment-tree arrays plus O(N) for the sequence, with M rounded up to a power of two (~2 * 2**19 nodes)
complexity.why: The main work is in segment-tree operations. func_1 computes the set of segment-tree nodes covering a range [l, r); func_2 pushes pending lazy tags down; func_4 performs a range update (and the missing remainder likely performs range-max queries). Each DP step performs O(log M) tree operations rather than scanning all candidate positions in Python loops. Although asymptotically this is slightly worse than a truly constant-width O(N) DP, it dramatically reduces Python-level loop overhead by offloading iteration to tight numeric loops over indexes and leveraging tree structure, which is more efficient in Python for large N.

complexity_delta.from: Naive DP with an explicit per-state scan over a fixed-size window: O(N * W) with W=99, implemented using Python generators and list indexing.
complexity_delta.to: DP powered by a segment tree over the value domain, with range updates and range-max queries in O(log M) per state, yielding O(N log M) total.
complexity_delta.note: The theoretical asymptotics go from linear in N with a small constant window (O(N)) to O(N log M), but the practical performance improves because the hot inner loop is replaced by structured tree operations with fewer Python-level iterations and better use of contiguous arrays. Additionally, the huge fixed array of size 6**8 is replaced by a tree sized to the value domain (~3e5).

transformation_steps: Remove the giant fixed-size padding array and negative-indexing trick; instead treat the sequence positions and/or value range explicitly.

Identify that the DP transition is a max over states constrained by both index distance and value difference. Reformulate it as queries over ranges in the value domain (e.g., all values within [a[i]-D, a[i]+D]) combined with a sliding index window.
Introduce a segment tree (var_9 for values, var_15 for lazy tags) whose leaves correspond to value coordinates (or compressed ranks).
Implement lazy propagation helpers: func_1 to compute the relevant tree nodes for a range, func_2 to push pending updates down to children before operating on them.

Implement range-update and range-query operations (func_4 and likely a missing symmetric query function) so each DP step does: (1) a range-max query over the allowed value interval; (2) a point or range update to store the new DP value.
Iterate through the sequence using these tree operations instead of nested Python loops, then take the maximum value recorded in the tree as the final answer.
trigger_signals: Empirical or judged TLE when N is large (e.g., N≈1e5–3e5) with the original DP that runs ~3e7 Python-level operations.
Profiling or simple reasoning indicating the max(...) generator inside the DP loop dominates runtime.
High and input-independent memory footprint due to var_2 = [0] * 6**8 and the concatenation var_1 = var_2 + var_1.
Awareness that the transition constraints form ranges over a coordinate (values) and a bounded index window, which is a classic fit for segment trees or similar range-query data structures.
pitfalls: Segment-tree indexing is subtle: off-by-one errors when mapping value ranges to [l, r) indices or when computing internal node indices (shifts, +var_5/-1) can silently give wrong answers.
Lazy propagation (var_15) must be pushed correctly before reading or updating children; forgetting to propagate tags or double-applying them leads to inconsistent tree states.
The transformation assumes that the value range can be bounded or compressed to about 3e5; if actual values exceed this domain and are not compressed, index errors or wasted memory can occur.
Using eval() for input parsing in the fast code adds overhead and potential security issues; in a pure performance context, eval is slower than int() and can negate some gains on very tight limits.

The sliding-window aspect (index distance constraint) needs explicit handling in the segment-tree version (e.g., expiring contributions from positions that are more than 98 away). Failing to remove or neutralize out-of-window states yields overcounting and incorrect DP results.
Refactoring from a simple DP loop to a segmented tree structure significantly increases code complexity, raising the risk of bugs and making it harder to maintain or adapt the solution.

constraints_guess.notes: var_2 = 2*10^5+10 used as precomputation bound for factorials and inverse factorials, so N (first input) is likely up to ~2e5. Second input (number to factor) likely up to around 10^9–10^12, since trial division up to sqrt(M) is used once.

dominant_ops: Precomputation of factorials and modular inverse factorials up to var_2 ≈ 2e5 using linear DP-style loops.
Single trial-division prime factorization of var_1 up to sqrt(var_1).
O(1) modular nCk computations per prime-exponent using precomputed arrays.

complexity.time: O(var_2 + sqrt(var_1)) ≈ O(2e5 + sqrt(M)), with very small extra cost per distinct prime factor.
complexity.space: O(var_2) for three integer arrays (factorials, inverses, inverse factorials).
complexity.why: The factorial/inverse precomputation loops each touch every index up to var_2 once with constant-time modular arithmetic on small integers (< MOD). Prime factorization runs a while/for loop up to sqrt(M) in the worst case. Each combination call is O(1) due to precomputed factorials and inverse factorials.

bottlenecks.detail: The three size-O(var_2) arrays (var_6, var_7, var_9) are filled in a loop up to 2*10^5, which dominates for small M but is well within typical contest limits.
Trial division factorization func_3(var_11) is O(sqrt(M)); for M near its upper bound this is noticeable but still acceptable once per test.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace explicit modular combinatorics precomputation with Python's math.factorial and direct integer arithmetic for combinations, then take the result modulo 1e9+7 at the end; keep a similar trial-division factorization.

complexity.time: Dominated by math.factorial(var_2 - 1) on large var_2 plus big-integer multiplications in the combination loops; roughly superlinear in var_2, around O(var_2^2 log var_2) bit-operations, plus O(sqrt(var_1)) for factorization.
complexity.space: Θ(number_of_bits(factorial(var_2))) ≈ Θ(var_2 log var_2) bits for big integers, far larger than O(var_2) machine-word arrays.
complexity.why: math.factorial(var_2 - 1) constructs a single enormous integer with ~Θ(var_2 log var_2) bits; arithmetic on such integers is significantly more expensive than modular arithmetic on bounded 64-bit integers. Additionally, this factorial is computed once per run and not even used in the final formula, so its cost is pure overhead. The per-prime combination loop also multiplies large integers without reducing modulo until the very end.

complexity_delta.from: O(var_2 + sqrt(var_1)) time and O(var_2) space with fixed-width modular integers (arrays of size ~2e5).
complexity_delta.to: O(var_2^2 log var_2 + sqrt(var_1)) bit-operations time and Θ(var_2 log var_2) bits space due to huge big-integer factorials and intermediate products.
complexity_delta.note: The supposed 'fast' version abandons modular precomputation and instead builds enormous Python integers via math.factorial; this is significantly slower and more memory-intensive for var_2 up to ~2e5.

transformation_steps: Replaced precomputed factorials and inverse factorials modulo 1e9+7 with calls to math.factorial producing full big-integer factorials.
Removed the O(1) combinatorics via precomputed arrays and implemented combinations by explicit big-integer multiplication and division (var_3 loop and division by factorial(var_12)).
Deferred modulus application to the very end (var_11 % (10**9 + 7)), allowing intermediate values to grow to huge sizes.
Introduced an unused computation var_5 = factorial(var_2 - 1), which is very expensive and provides no benefit.
Kept trial-division factorization essentially the same complexity-wise, so the main change is entirely in the combinatorics implementation.
trigger_signals: Use of math.factorial on inputs as large as var_2 - 1 ≈ 2e5, which yields integers with hundreds of thousands to over a million decimal digits.
Intermediate products in combination loops are not reduced modulo 1e9+7, which causes big-int sizes to grow unnecessarily.
Presence of an expensive factorial computation whose result (var_5) is never used in subsequent calculations.
Loss of precomputed modular inverses and O(1) nCk in favor of repeated big-int multiplications and divisions.
pitfalls: Severe performance degradation (TLE risk) due to computing factorial(var_2 - 1) as a full big integer for large var_2 instead of working modulo 1e9+7.
High memory consumption (MLE risk) caused by storing and operating on large factorial integers instead of compact modular values.

Integer division var_3 // factorial(var_12) relies on exact arithmetic; while mathematically correct, it is costly and fragile if any arithmetic is modified, and offers no advantage over modular inverse-based combinatorics.
Deferring the modulo until the end prevents Python from keeping intermediate integers small; always applying % MOD or using precomputed modular factorials keeps numbers bounded and operations cheap.
Renaming and reusing function names (func_1) with different semantics can confuse maintenance and audits, making it easier to introduce subtle bugs beyond performance issues.

constraints_guess.notes: Input is a single integer N; this is the classic Lunlun-number style problem (e.g., AtCoder ABC 161 D) where N is typically up to about 1e5.

dominant_ops: Recursive DFS expansion of all valid numbers up to length 10
Frequent string conversions: len(str(var_2)) and str(var_2)[-1]
Appending every generated number to a Python list
Final full sort of all generated numbers

complexity.why: Let L be the max number of digits (here 10), and K the count of all generated numbers (all Lunlun-like numbers of length 1..L). DFS visits each such number once: O(K). Each step does string conversions costing O(L). After generation, var_4.sort() costs O(K log K). Memory stores all K numbers. For this particular code, L is capped at 10 so K is on the order of 3^L (~6e4 per starting digit, overall up to ~5e5–1e6), which is large but bounded.

bottlenecks.detail: Generates the entire search space of all valid numbers up to length 10 regardless of the requested index N, then sorts and only uses the N-th element. Work is independent of N and can be far larger than necessary when N is small or moderate.
Sorting the complete list var_4 (size K) is O(K log K). The BFS approach inherently produces numbers in ascending order and avoids this cost.
At each recursion, the code calls str(var_2) twice (for len and last digit access). This is done for every generated node and adds significant constant-factor overhead.
Deep recursive calls (depth up to 10 per starting digit) introduce function call overhead and potential risk if depth or branching were increased. Iterative methods are cheaper for this pattern.
Stores all generated numbers (var_4) before using only a single index. Peak memory is proportional to the total number of generated numbers K, not to N.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a BFS (queue-based) generation of numbers, starting from digits 1..9 and repeatedly appending allowed neighbor digits (last_digit-1, last_digit, last_digit+1). Because BFS in this construction visits numbers in strictly increasing order, the N-th generated element is exactly the answer, so there is no need to generate the full space or sort.

complexity.why: Each loop iteration dequeues one number and enqueues up to 3 new ones. After N-1 expansions, the next dequeued number is the answer. The number of operations is linear in N, and the queue size is on the order of the frontier, which is O(N) in the worst case. Arithmetic-based digit handling avoids expensive string operations, lowering constants.

complexity_delta.from: O(K log K + K * L) time, O(K) space, where K is the total count of all valid numbers up to max length 10 (roughly up to ~1e6) regardless of N.
complexity_delta.to: O(N) time, O(N) space, proportional directly to the requested index N.
complexity_delta.note: The modified fast solution scales with N instead of with the full search-space size up to length 10, and removes the global sort and most per-node overheads.

transformation_steps: Switch from global DFS enumeration (generate-all-then-sort) to incremental BFS generation that naturally yields numbers in ascending order.
Replace recursive function calls with an explicit queue-based loop to reduce call overhead and better control iteration count.
Eliminate string conversions by using arithmetic to obtain the last digit (var_3 % 10) and construct new numbers.
Stop generation as soon as the N-th number is reached instead of generating all possible numbers up to a digit-length cap.
Remove the final sort of the full list of generated numbers, since BFS already preserves the correct order.
trigger_signals: Presence of a global list that accumulates all generated candidates even though only one indexed value is ultimately needed.
Use of recursion over a combinatorial search tree with a fixed but high branching factor and depth cap.
Use of var_4.sort() after full enumeration, signaling O(K log K) work that may be avoidable if generation order can be controlled.
Repeated str(...) conversions and length checks inside tight recursive loops.
Knowledge that the problem asks for the N-th smallest number in a monotone-constructible sequence, a pattern that is well-suited to BFS or priority-queue generation.
pitfalls: Although queue.Queue works, it is thread-safe and slower; in single-threaded competitive settings, collections.deque is typically faster for BFS.
Using eval(input()) is unnecessary and potentially unsafe in general; int(input()) is sufficient and safer.
In the DFS version, if the digit-length bound were increased or removed, recursion depth and branching could explode and hit recursion limits or timeouts.
For extremely large N, even the BFS approach would need consideration of integer size and queue memory, though within typical constraints (~1e5) it is safe.

Any reimplementation must preserve the exact generation rules (neighbors differ by at most 1 in the last digit) to maintain sorted order; otherwise, the assumption that BFS output is sorted may break.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case. var_3 is the main size parameter (used in combinations). var_1 (to be factorized) is likely up to around 1e9–1e12 (square-root factorization is used). Number of distinct prime factors of var_1 is small (O(log var_1)), so the core bottleneck is iterating up to var_3 for each prime factor.

dominant_ops: Trial division prime factorization of var_1 up to sqrt(var_1)
For each distinct prime factor exponent e: computing C(var_3 + e - 1, var_3 - 1) via a loop of length var_3 - 1
Inside that loop, repeated modular exponentiation pow(var_5, var_2 - 2, var_2) for each var_5 in 1..(var_3 - 1)

complexity.why: Factorization loop runs var_5 from 2 while var_5^2 <= var_1, giving O(sqrt(var_1)) trial division. Let P be the number of distinct prime factors of var_1. For each exponent we call func_1(var_3 + e - 1, var_3 - 1). Inside func_1 we loop var_5 from 1 to var_6 = var_3 - 1, and in each iteration we perform a modular inverse via pow(var_5, MOD-2, MOD) which is O(log MOD). Hence O(P * var_3 * log MOD) for all combination computations. Memory only stores a defaultdict of exponents (size P) plus a few scalars.

bottlenecks.detail: func_1(var_7, var_6) iterates var_5 from 1 to var_6 = var_3 - 1 for every prime factor, making each binomial coefficient O(var_3). When var_3 is large, this is prohibitive even if the number of primes P is small.

Inside func_1, the code calls pow(var_5, var_2 - 2, var_2) for every var_5 in 1..var_3-1. Each pow is O(log MOD) and repeated O(var_3) times per prime factor, causing a significant constant-factor and asymptotic overhead.
The same sequence of inverses 1^{-1}, 2^{-1}, ..., (var_3-1)^{-1} is effectively recomputed for each prime factor, instead of being precomputed once and reused.
Use of input() is not the main bottleneck here, but combined with Python-level heavy loops it can contribute slightly for large inputs. It is minor compared to the combinational loop cost.

FastAudit.core_idea: Precompute factorials up to a sufficient limit once, then compute binomial coefficients using the closed form C(n, k) = fact[n] * inv(fact[k]) * inv(fact[n-k]) mod MOD. This converts each combination from O(var_3 * log MOD) to O(log MOD) with a small constant. Factorization remains via trial division; the primary speed-up is eliminating the inner O(var_3) loops and repeated inverses.

complexity.why: func_4 factorizes var_1 similarly via trial division to sqrt(var_1), which is unchanged. func_3 precomputes factorials up to var_12 = var_3 + 100, requiring O(var_3 + E) simple mul/mod operations (E is a small safety margin related to the sum of exponents, bounded by O(log var_1)). Each func_1 call then computes C(n, k) via three factorial array lookups and two pow calls for inverses, giving O(log MOD) per prime factor, so total O(P * log MOD). Memory now stores factorials up to var_3 + 100, so O(var_3 + E) space, which is acceptable for var_3 up to around 1e5–1e6.

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(var_1) + P * var_3 * log MOD) time, O(P) space
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(var_1) + (var_3 + E) + P * log MOD) time, O(var_3 + E) space
complexity_delta.note: The key improvement is replacing O(var_3 * log MOD) work per prime factor (multiplicative binomial computation with repeated modular inverses) by O(log MOD) per prime factor (factorial-based binomial with precomputed factorials). This trades extra O(var_3) precomputation time and memory for removing a multiplicative factor of var_3 from the hot loop.

transformation_steps: Recognize that func_1 is computing a binomial coefficient C(var_7, var_6) in O(var_6 * log MOD) using the multiplicative formula and repeated modular inverses.
Replace the on-the-fly multiplicative approach with the standard factorial-based formula: C(n, k) = fact[n] * inv(fact[k]) * inv(fact[n-k]) mod MOD.
Introduce a global factorial array var_8 initialized with [1, 1] and a precomputation function func_3 that fills var_8 up to the maximum n needed (here var_3 + 100 to cover var_3 - 1 + max_exponent).
Modify func_1 to use the precomputed factorials: it now just does constant-time array accesses and two pow calls for modular inverses of factorial values.

Retain the same prime factorization logic in func_4 (trial division up to sqrt(var_1)), but make it return a list of (prime, exponent) instead of using a defaultdict, which is slightly simpler and more cache-friendly.
Aggregate the final answer in func_2 by iterating over the factor list and multiplying the corresponding binomial coefficients computed via the factorial-based func_1.
Switch I/O from input() to sys.stdin.readline() for marginal speed improvement and to match typical competitive programming patterns.
trigger_signals: Presence of a loop inside func_1 running up to var_6 = var_3 - 1, and func_1 being called multiple times in the outer computation (once per prime factor).
Use of pow(..., MOD-2, MOD) inside a loop, indicating repeated modular inverse computation for varying bases where many of those inverses could be shared or precomputed.
Combination-like multiplicative pattern var_9 = var_9 * (var_7 - var_5 + 1) * inv(var_5), a textbook sign that a binomial coefficient is being computed iteratively.
Problem structure suggesting that var_3 can be large while the number of prime factors (and exponents) is small, making any O(var_3 * P) approach suspicious for tight constraints.
Use of Python and large theoretical bounds (like up to 1e5 or more) where nested or repeated O(N) loops are often too slow in practice.
pitfalls: The factorial precomputation size must be large enough to cover the maximum n in C(n, k). Here n = (var_3 - 1) + exponent, and the code uses var_3 + 100 as a simple upper bound assuming exponents are small (bounded by log2(var_1)). If var_1 could be extremely large, or if more general use is desired, the bound must be carefully computed as var_3 - 1 + max_exponent.

While factorial-based C(n, k) reduces asymptotic complexity, calling pow for each inverse still costs O(log MOD) time. If the number of binomial evaluations P were large, it might be beneficial to precompute factorial inverses as well (inv_fact) in O(N), allowing O(1) C(n, k) evaluations.

Using global mutable arrays (var_8 for factorials) requires care to avoid double-precomputation or inconsistent sizes if func_3 is called multiple times in extended code. Here it is safe because func_3 is called once before any queries.

The trial division factorization is unchanged and still O(sqrt(var_1)). For very large var_1 (e.g., up to 1e12) this is usually fine, but for much larger limits (1e15–1e18) a faster factorization approach might be required, otherwise factorization itself becomes a bottleneck.
Modular inverses via pow(x, MOD-2, MOD) rely on MOD being prime (which holds for 1e9+7). Reusing this pattern with a non-prime modulus would break correctness.
I/O optimizations (sys.stdin.readline) do not fix algorithmic issues; they only provide marginal gains. The core improvement here is algorithmic (factorial precomputation), not I/O.

constraints_guess.notes: Pattern matches classic 'number of divisors of n!' mod 1e9+7' tasks (e.g., AtCoder ABC style) where n is usually <= 1000–10^4. Original code with O(n^{2.5}) behavior suggests intended n is not huge (else it would trivially TLE).

dominant_ops: For each k in [1..n], recomputing primality for all numbers up to k via nested trial division up to sqrt(i)
Triple-nested looping structure: outer over k=1..n, inner over i=2..k, innermost over trial divisor d up to sqrt(i)
Per-k prime factorization of k using only primes detected by the naive primality routine

complexity.time: Theta(n^{5/2}) in terms of the input n (var_1), dominated by sum_{k=1}^n sum_{i=2}^k O(sqrt(i)) ≈ O(n^{5/2})
complexity.space: Theta(n) for arrays that track prime exponents across 1..n plus per-call working arrays up to size k<=n
complexity.why: func_2(k) constructs a boolean array of length k and tests each i in [2..k] for primality by trial division up to sqrt(i). That costs sum_{i<=k} O(sqrt(i)) ≈ O(k^{3/2}). func_2 is called for every k in [1..n], so total ≈ sum_{k<=n} k^{3/2} = O(n^{5/2}). Other work (per-k factorization and final product) is at most O(n^2) and does not dominate.

bottlenecks.detail: func_2 recomputes primality information from scratch for every k in [1..n], instead of building a single sieve up to n once and reusing it.
Primality of each i is checked via trial division starting from 2 up to sqrt(i), giving O(sqrt(i)) per number and O(k^{3/2}) per call to func_2(k).

Global structure is: loop over k in [1..n] → inside call func_2(k) (O(k^{3/2})) → then loop again up to k for factorization. This yields effectively three levels of iteration and super-quadratic time.
The algorithm never reuses the prime information or factorization results from previous k. Each step k recomputes what was already known for k-1.

FastAudit.core_idea: Compute n! once using math.factorial, factor that single large integer by trial division (collecting prime exponents via a Counter), then use the multiplicative formula for the number of divisors: if n! = ∏ p_i^{e_i}, answer = ∏ (e_i + 1) mod 1e9+7.

complexity.time: Roughly O(T_fact(n) + T_factor(n)), where T_fact(n) is the cost of computing math.factorial(n) on big integers (sub-quadratic in n in CPython but with large constant factors) and T_factor(n) ≈ O((sum of exponents in n!) * cost(big-int division)). In high-level n-steps terms, ignoring bit-costs, the factoring loop performs about Θ(∑_{p<=n} v_p(n!)) ≈ Θ(n log log n) divisions/mods, but each on integers with Θ(n log n) bits.
complexity.space: Theta(size(n!)) = Theta(n log n) digits for storing factorial plus O(#primes <= n) for exponent counts.
complexity.why: Instead of re-factoring each k (1..n) separately, it aggregates all prime factors into n! directly: factorial builds a single huge integer; the while-loop factors this integer by incrementally dividing out small integers starting from 2. The number of divisions corresponds to total prime exponent count in n!, but arithmetic is on big integers whose bit-length grows roughly linearly with n log n.

complexity_delta.from: Super-quadratic in n: about Theta(n^{2.5}) operations on small integers with Theta(n) memory.
complexity_delta.to: Fewer high-level iterations: about O(n log log n) factorization steps, but each operating on huge integers of size Theta(n log n) bits, plus the cost of computing n! itself.
complexity_delta.note: At the level of loop counts, the modified code drastically lowers the combinatorial complexity by avoiding a triple-nested structure and repeated primality computation. However, it shifts cost into big-integer arithmetic and trial division on n!, which can explode for larger n and may exceed time/memory limits if n is bigger than the classic ~1000 range.

transformation_steps: Removed the outer loop over k=1..n that repeatedly factors each k and recomputes primality.
Replaced incremental factor accumulation across 1..n with a single computation of n! using math.factorial(var_1).
Introduced a trial-division loop over candidate divisors starting from 2 that repeatedly divides the factorial value, collecting all prime factors into a list.
Used collections.Counter to count exponents of each prime factor in n! (i.e., multiplicity of each prime in the factor list).
Computed the final answer as the product over (exponent+1) for each prime factor count, applying modulo 1e9+7 incrementally.
trigger_signals: Presence of a loop over k in [1..n] where each iteration recomputes primes and factors up to k, indicating O(n^3/2) or worse behavior.
Use of a naive primality checker (trial division up to sqrt(i)) embedded inside loops that go up to n.
Overall three-level nesting pattern: over k, over i<=k, over divisors of i, which is a classic red flag in combinatorial number-theory tasks.
Recognition that the quantity being computed only depends on the combined factorization of n! (or the union of factorizations for 1..n), making per-k recomputation unnecessary.
pitfalls: Computing n! explicitly as a big integer causes extremely rapid growth in both time and memory; for n much larger than ~1000, this approach will likely become infeasible even if loop counts look small.

Factoring n! by naive trial division (incrementing var_5 by 1) remains inefficient; the algorithm does not skip composite divisors or leverage prime sieves, which can still be a bottleneck for larger n.

The modified approach is tightly coupled to Python's big-int performance (math.factorial and arbitrary-precision division); the theoretical loop-count improvement does not directly translate to a proportional speedup.
Using eval(input()) is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; while not the performance bottleneck, it is a bad practice and could be problematic in other contexts.
For very small n, overhead of big-int factorial and Counter may outweigh benefits compared to a well-designed O(n log n) or O(n sqrt n) prime-sieve-based factor accumulation.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case. Values appear bounded in [1,100] from the loop range and typical AtCoder patterns. Even if n is up to 1e5, an O(100*n) solution is borderline but acceptable; optimizing to O(n) is still desirable.

dominant_ops: Double loop: outer loop over candidate centers (100 iterations) and inner loop over all n elements computing squared differences and accumulating the sum.

complexity.why: The input list var_6 of size n dominates memory. For each of 100 candidate values (var_1 from 0 to 99, used as var_1+1), the code scans all n elements and performs arithmetic; there are no additional asymptotic-space structures beyond storing the input.

bottlenecks.detail: The squared differences (var_6[var_2] - (var_1 + 1)) ** 2 are recomputed for every candidate center across 100 passes over the entire array, even though an analytic minimizer is available for sum of squared deviations.
The outer loop over range(100) brute-forces possible centers from 1 to 100. This is a fixed 100x slowdown versus computing the optimal center directly via the mean.
Using eval on input for an integer (int(eval(input()))) is slower and unsafe compared to a direct int(input()) call, though this is a minor performance impact compared to the double loop.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical fact that the sum of squared deviations \sum_i (a_i - x)^2 is minimized (over real x) at the mean of the data. Since x must be an integer (and in the original problem likely within [1,100]), the optimal integer center is at or near the rounded mean. The fast code computes the mean once, rounds it, and then makes a single pass to sum squared deviations around that center.

complexity.why: The algorithm reads n numbers into a list and performs two linear passes over them: one to compute the sum (for the mean) and one to accumulate squared deviations. No extra asymptotic-space structures are introduced beyond the input list itself.

complexity_delta.from: O(100 * n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time complexity in terms of big-O remains linear, but the constant factor is reduced by approximately 100x by removing the brute-force search over candidate centers. This can be significant for large n.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the objective function is a sum of squared deviations: f(x) = sum_i (a_i - x)^2.
Use calculus / algebra to note that the derivative of f(x) with respect to real x is zero at x = mean(a_i); hence the mean minimizes the sum of squared deviations over the reals.
Since x must be an integer, choose an integer close to the mean. The provided fast solution uses round(sum / n) to pick the nearest integer to the mean.
Replace the outer brute-force loop over x in [1,100] with a single computation of this near-optimal center.
Keep a single linear pass over the data to compute the sum (for the mean) and another to compute the sum of squared deviations to that chosen center.
trigger_signals: Presence of a fixed-range brute-force search (for var_1 in range(100)) on top of a full scan over the data, suggesting potential mathematical optimization.
The cost function is smooth and convex in x (a quadratic polynomial), which often admits a closed-form minimizer.
Repeated evaluations of essentially the same expression (var_6[var_2] - (var_1 + 1)) ** 2 with only the center changing.
Typical competitive programming pattern: minimize sum of squared distances from a set of points to a single point is solved via the mean.
pitfalls: Rounding behavior: Using round(sum / n) in Python 3 applies bankers’ rounding (ties to even). Depending on the exact problem statement, this may or may not match the expected tie-breaking rule; sometimes floor or checking both floor and ceil of the mean is safer.
Domain constraints on x: If the optimal mean-based center falls outside a required range (e.g., [1,100]), it may be necessary to clamp x to the allowed interval or test boundary values explicitly.

Numerical issues are minimal with small integers, but if values or n become large, using floats for the mean could introduce rounding errors; using integer arithmetic (e.g., examining floor(sum // n) and sum // n + 1) can be more robust.
Retaining eval in input processing is unnecessary and unsafe; it should be replaced with int(input()) for both clarity and security, though this is secondary to the algorithmic change.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic task: count ways to choose var_2 numbers from {1..var_3} whose sum is var_4. Common online judge versions typically have var_3 <= 12 and multiple queries until var_3 == 0.

dominant_ops: Recursive backtracking exploring subsets of {var_1..var_3} with include/exclude branching, plus integer arithmetic and comparisons for pruning.

complexity.time: O(2^n) in the worst case, with pruning reducing the effective search space for many (var_2, var_4).
complexity.space: O(n) recursion depth and call stack; O(1) extra data aside from stack.
complexity.why: func_1 makes two recursive calls per level (include or skip the current number), yielding a binary recursion tree over up to n = var_3 - var_1 + 1 elements. The pruning condition var_4 < var_1 * var_2 + var_2 - 1 cuts subtrees that cannot reach the required sum, but worst-case when pruning is ineffective still approaches 2^n nodes. Each node uses constant extra memory aside from recursion stack.
