bottlenecks.detail: Exponential-time backtracking (include/exclude pattern) without memoization or dynamic programming. For larger var_3 this does not scale.
Deep Python recursion with two calls per node introduces significant function call overhead in Python’s interpreter, even when n is modest.

Only a lower-bound sum check is used (var_4 < var_1 * var_2 + var_2 - 1). There is no upper-bound or other stronger pruning, so many partial states that can never reach sum var_4 may still be explored when var_4 is large relative to remaining numbers.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace explicit recursive backtracking with itertools.combinations to generate all k-combinations (size var_2) of {1..var_3} in C, then count how many have sum == var_4 in Python.

complexity.time: O(C(n, k) * k), where n = var_3 and k = var_2.
complexity.space: O(n) for the list(range(1, var_3 + 1)) plus O(k) for each generated combination tuple at a time.
complexity.why: itertools.combinations generates each k-subset once, so there are C(n, k) tuples. For each tuple, sum(var_1) performs O(k) additions in Python. The generator is streaming, so memory use is proportional to the input list plus one tuple at a time.

complexity_delta.from: Exponential backtracking with some pruning over subsets of {1..var_3} (worst case O(2^n), but can be much smaller in practice due to early pruning by sum bounds).
complexity_delta.to: Direct enumeration of all size-k combinations via itertools.combinations with per-combination sum check: O(C(n, k) * k) operations and no pruning by sum.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically, both approaches are exponential in n. The new version eliminates Python-level recursion and leverages C-level combination generation, but also removes sum-based pruning and always enumerates all C(n, k) combinations. For typical constraints (n <= 12) performance may be similar; there is no clear big-O improvement and for some (n, k, target) patterns the modified code can be slower.

transformation_steps: Replaced recursive function func_1 with a single loop using itertools.combinations over range(1, var_3 + 1).
Changed the stateful recursion (var_1, var_2, var_4) and pruning logic into a flat generator expression that tests sum(var_1) == var_4 for each size-var_2 combination.
Removed sum feasibility pruning (the var_4 < var_1 * var_2 + var_2 - 1 check) and any early stopping; every combination is evaluated.
Introduced a list(range(1, var_3 + 1)) as the base iterable for combinations, adding an O(n) list allocation per query.
trigger_signals: Desire to avoid recursion depth and potential recursion-limit issues in Python.
Desire to use concise, standard-library-based combinatorics (itertools.combinations) which is implemented in C and often faster than Python recursion for small search spaces.
Perception that the original code is complex or hard to reason about due to multiple recursive parameters and pruning conditions.
pitfalls: For larger var_3 or for k close to n/2, C(n, k) grows very quickly; enumerating all combinations with Python-level sum is expensive and has no pruning, potentially slower than the original pruned backtracking.
The modified solution always evaluates all combinations even when the target sum var_4 is impossible, whereas the original can cut off many branches early via the lower-bound check.
Repeatedly constructing list(range(1, var_3 + 1)) per query has an O(n) overhead that could be avoided by reusing a list or using range() directly (itertools.combinations works with any iterable).

If constraints on var_3 were to increase beyond small values (e.g., n > 20), both approaches would become impractical, but the lack of pruning in the combinations-based solution would be particularly problematic. A proper dynamic programming or memoized solution would then be preferable.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AOJ-style problem: count triples 1<=a<b<c<=n with a+b+c=x, repeated until input 0 0. Exact constraints unknown; many references use n<=50.

dominant_ops: Three nested for-loops over var_2, var_3, var_4 in [1..n], checking sums and incrementing a counter.

complexity.why: For each test case, the code iterates var_2 from 1..n-2, var_3 from var_2+1..n-1, and var_4 from var_3+1..n, generating Θ(n^3) triplets and doing O(1) work per triplet. Only a few scalar integers are stored.

bottlenecks.detail: Naive enumeration of all combinations (var_2, var_3, var_4) without using the sum constraint to remove a loop.
The innermost loop over var_4 simply checks var_2 + var_3 + var_4 == target; var_4 is fully determined by var_2 and var_3, so iterating over it is unnecessary.
Python-level triple nested loops are relatively slow; Θ(n^3) iterations can become a bottleneck if n grows beyond small values, even if asymptotically acceptable on paper.

FastAudit.core_idea: Eliminate the third loop by solving for the third value algebraically (k = x - i - j) and only checking if that implied k satisfies ordering and range constraints, reducing from O(n^3) to O(n^2).

complexity.why: var_1 (i) ranges 1..n-2 and var_2 (j) ranges i+1..n-1, yielding Θ(n^2) pairs. For each pair, the code computes the implied third value and checks inequalities in O(1). The list comprehension materializes a list with one element per valid triple, giving O(ans) ≤ O(n^2) extra space; scalar overhead is constant.

complexity_delta.from: Time O(n^3), Space O(1)
complexity_delta.to: Time O(n^2), Space O(n^2) due to list materialization
complexity_delta.note: The third loop over the candidate k was removed by deducing k = x - i - j and verifying bounds and ordering, cutting one factor of n from the runtime at the cost of storing matches in a list.

transformation_steps: Recognize that for a fixed pair (i, j), the third value k in i + j + k = x is uniquely determined as k = x - i - j.
Remove the explicit innermost loop over k and instead compute k directly from i and j.
Encode the validity of k (1 <= i < j < k <= n) as inequality checks: j < k <= n, with k computed as x - i - j.
Implement the O(n^2) enumeration over i and j using a nested loop and count valid k using a comprehension, then take its length.
trigger_signals: Presence of three nested loops each depending linearly on n is a standard red flag for O(n^3) time.
The loop body only checks a simple linear equation (sum equals target), which suggests the possibility of solving for one variable instead of iterating it.
The third loop index appears only in the sum check and ordering, indicating it is not needed as a free iterator.
In Python, cubic-time nested loops are often problematic even for moderate n, so any avoidable loop should be targeted.
pitfalls: When removing the innermost loop, it is easy to break the strict ordering condition i < j < k; the inequality checks must mirror the original loop bounds exactly (j < k <= n).
Using a list comprehension and len(...) allocates a list that can use unnecessary memory; a generator with sum(1 for ...) could reduce peak space to O(1) if memory is a concern.
Off-by-one errors in the loop ranges for i and j (e.g., ending at n instead of n-1 or starting j at i instead of i+1) will subtly change the count.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: input (N, M). N up to about 1e5, M up to about 1e9. Need to factorize M (trial division up to sqrt(M)) and compute products of combinations C(N + e_i - 1, e_i) modulo 1e9+7. Number of distinct prime factors of M is small (<= ~9 for M<=1e9), and exponents sum is O(log M).

dominant_ops: Precomputation of factorials, modular inverses, and inverse factorials up to 2*10^5 (three lists: var_6, var_7, var_9), each step involving modular multiplications.
Trial division factorization of M up to sqrt(M) in func_2.
O(1) binomial coefficient queries via table lookups and modular multiplications in func_1.

complexity.why: L is the fixed precomputation limit (2*10^5). The factorial/inverse precomputation loop dominates and runs in O(L). Factorization by trial division runs in O(sqrt(M)) in the worst case because the loop goes up to ceil(sqrt(M)), independent of the progressive reduction of var_15. P is the number of prime factors, which is small and only incurs O(1) work per factor due to precomputed factorials. Space is dominated by three arrays var_6, var_7, var_9 of size L.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorials and inverse factorials are precomputed up to 2*10^5 for every run regardless of the actual N and the exponents e_i. For small N and tiny exponents, this O(2e5) precomputation dominates total runtime.
The precomputation cannot be reused across test cases in this implementation (single-run script); if embedded or repeated, this linear setup cost would be paid for each input.

func_2 uses a for-loop with an upper bound computed via floating-point sqrt and ceiling: range(2, int(-(-(var_11**0.5) // 1)) + 1). This introduces extra overhead versus a simple integer loop condition (while p*p <= n) and does not exploit the shrinking of var_15 to reduce the effective bound.

Storing three lists of length 2*10^5 (factorials, modular inverses, inverse factorials) uses more memory than necessary for the tiny number of binomial evaluations actually required (one per prime factor).

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial/inverse precomputation and instead compute each required binomial coefficient directly using a short multiplicative loop, exploiting that the exponent e in C(N+e-1, e) is small (sum of prime exponents of M). Also use a simple trial division factorization loop with a dynamic bound (while p*p <= n) that naturally shrinks as n is divided.

complexity.why: Factorization in func_2 uses a while loop with condition var_7*var_7 <= var_9; as var_9 is reduced by dividing out found factors, the effective bound decreases, but worst-case still O(sqrt(M)). For each prime factor with exponent e_i, func_1 computes C(e_i + N - 1, e_i) via an O(e_i) loop: sum e_i = S = O(log M). No factorial tables are stored; only a small list of prime factors is kept, so auxiliary memory is constant relative to input size.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(L + sqrt(M)) with L = 2*10^5 precomputation; Space: O(L) for factorial and inverse tables.
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(sqrt(M) + S) where S = sum of prime exponents of M (O(log M)); Space: O(1) auxiliary.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both versions are dominated by the sqrt(M) factorization term, but the slow_code adds a large fixed O(L) cost and O(L) memory, whereas the fast_code replaces this with a tiny O(S) per-binomial cost and constant memory.

transformation_steps: Remove global precomputation of factorials, modular inverses, and inverse factorials (var_6, var_7, var_9), which incurred O(L) time and O(L) space.

Replace the O(1)-per-query combinatorial primitive based on precomputed factorials with a direct multiplicative implementation (func_1) that computes C(n, k) as a product ratio over k steps, O(k), where k is the small exponent e.
Simplify the factorization function: use a while-based trial division loop with condition p*p <= n, allowing the upper bound to adapt as n shrinks, and avoid float-based sqrt/ceil computations.

Apply the modulus only at the aggregation step when multiplying binomial results, rather than inside the combinatorial computation; this reduces the number of modular operations at the cost of working with larger Python integers, which is acceptable given very small k and S.
Eliminate large auxiliary arrays and keep only the list of prime factors and minimal scalar state, reducing memory footprint and object allocation overhead.
trigger_signals: Observation that only a handful of binomial coefficients are needed (one per prime factor), and each involves a small exponent e, while the slow_code builds factorial tables up to 2e5 regardless of actual e.
Profiling or mental estimation revealing that the linear O(2e5) precomputation dominates runtime when M is small or moderate and the number of factors is tiny.

Recognizing that factorial-based combinatorics is beneficial when n and k are large or when many binomial queries are needed, but is overkill and memory-heavy when both the number and size of binomial evaluations are small.
Detection of per-run memory usage and setup-time patterns that are disproportionate to the simple nature of the end computation.
pitfalls: The fast_code computes binomial coefficients using plain integer arithmetic without reducing modulo 1e9+7 at each step. For larger n or k this can cause extremely large intermediate integers, leading to significant slowdown or memory pressure; it is only safe because k (the exponent) is tiny under the assumed constraints.

constraints_guess.notes: n is a single integer; original code allocates sieve of fixed size 10000, so n is likely <= 9999. Task: compute number of divisors of n! modulo 1e9+7.

dominant_ops: Sieve of Eratosthenes over [2..n] using array var_8
For each prime p <= n, repeated division/multiplication to accumulate exponent of p in n!

complexity.why: The sieve up to n using i*i stepping is O(n log log n). For each prime p, summing floor(n/p^k) takes O(log_p n); summing over all primes up to n gives about O(n) additional work. Overall dominated by the sieve.

bottlenecks.detail: Sieve array var_8 has fixed size 10000, so for n >= 10000 the code will index out of bounds. This limits scalability even though the algorithmic complexity is otherwise near-optimal.
Use of eval(input()) is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()) and unnecessary for a single integer.
For n up to ~1e4, the algorithm (sieve + prime exponent accumulation) is already asymptotically optimal for this task; no major algorithmic bottleneck relative to typical constraints.

FastAudit.core_idea: Iterate all integers from 2 to n; for each, factor it by trial division over all potential divisors from 2 up to its current value, incrementing a global count array for each factor found. Then take the product (mod 1e9+7) of all entries in this count array.

complexity.why: For each k in [2..n], the inner loop tries all divisors from 2 up to k (range is fixed at loop start), performing a small number of divisions per divisor. The total work is roughly sum_{k=2}^n O(k) = O(n^2). The array var_2 has length n+1, so space is linear.

complexity_delta.from: O(n log log n)
complexity_delta.note: The change replaced a sieve-based prime enumeration plus efficient n! exponent counting with per-number trial-division factorization, which is asymptotically worse.

transformation_steps: Removed the global sieve of size 10000 and prime-only outer loop; replaced it with an outer loop over all integers from 2 to n.
Replaced the explicit computation of exponent of each prime in n! via repeated multiplication by p with factoring each k in [2..n] independently using trial division.
Changed the representation of exponents from a prime-indexed array (implicitly via sieve) to an array var_2 indexed by all integers up to n, incremented on every division in trial factorization.
Replaced incremental modular multiplication of (exponent+1) per prime with a final reduce-based modular product over all entries of var_2.
trigger_signals: Presence of nested loops where both bounds scale with n (for var_4 in 2..n, then for var_3 in 2..var_4) indicating O(n^2) behavior.
Inner while loop performing repeated divisions inside the already quadratic double loop.
Loss of sieve structure and direct prime iteration, replaced by generic trial division.
Use of factorization per integer in [2..n] rather than aggregating prime contributions directly to n!.
pitfalls: Algorithmic: The modified approach is asymptotically slower than the original sieve-based method and will perform poorly as n grows (beyond a few thousand).
Correctness: Counts are accumulated for all divisors, including composites, not just primes; this does not correspond cleanly to prime exponents in n!, so the mathematical result is suspect.

Implementation: Reusing var_4 as both the outer-loop index and as a mutable value being divided inside the inner loop is confusing and error-prone, even though Python’s range prevents it from breaking the outer iteration sequence.
Scalability: Although the original code had a fixed 10000 limit, simply extending n in the modified code without changing the algorithm leads to severe performance degradation due to O(n^2) time.

constraints_guess.notes: This matches the typical AtCoder ABC161 D 'Lunlun numbers' task: given N (≈ up to 1e5), output the N-th Lunlun number. Upper bound 3234566667 in code matches known solution bounds; only a single query.

dominant_ops: In func_2, a digit DP over all digit positions with nested loops over digits and adjacency transitions; in func_1, a binary search repeatedly invoking func_2 ~O(log U) times.

complexity.time: O(log U * D * 10 * 2 * 10 * 3) ≈ O(D * log U)
complexity.why: Let U be the search upper bound (≈3.2e9) and D the max number of digits (≤10). Each func_2 call builds a DP table var_5 of size (D+1)×2×11 and runs loops: for each digit position (≈D), it iterates over var_9 in 0..9 and var_11 in [var_9−1,var_9,var_9+1] for both tight states (2), all inside the digit-position loop. So each DP call is O(D * 10 * 2 * 3 * constant). func_1 performs a standard binary search on [0,3234566667], which requires O(log U) ≈ 32 calls. Total is O(D * log U) operations, with very small constants and strictly bounded D and U, so effectively O(1) per input in practice. Space is dominated by var_5 with (D+1)*2*11 entries, i.e., O(D).

bottlenecks.detail: func_2 performs multiple nested Python loops (over positions, digits, tight states, and neighbor digits). Even though the state space is small, this introduces a relatively high constant factor from many interpreted operations.

The DP is recomputed from scratch for each mid in the binary search. For this problem with fixed constraints and monotonic counting, a single constructive generation of Lunlun numbers suffices; recomputing the DP log U times is asymptotically fine but unnecessary for the given small N.

For N up to about 1e5, the total number of Lunlun numbers required is far below the DP’s theoretical capacity (all Lunlun numbers up to 3234566667). The DP is sized for the worst-case digit length, not tailored to the small N, which may make it slower than a direct constructive approach despite better asymptotic scaling.

FastAudit.core_idea: Generate Lunlun numbers in increasing length using a BFS-like layer expansion from 1–9, where each number spawns successors by appending a digit whose difference from the last digit is at most 1. Accumulate numbers level by level until the total count reaches N, then flatten and sort to select the N-th smallest.

complexity.time: O(K * b + K log K) ≈ O(K log K)
complexity.why: Let K be the total count of generated Lunlun numbers needed to cover the N-th one, and b the average branching factor (≤3). The while-loop expands each number at most once and creates up to b children, so the generation cost is O(K * b). At the end, all generated numbers are collected into var_11, then sorted, which costs O(K log K). For Lunlun numbers with digits ≤10, K is bounded (on the order of 10^5–10^6 at most, and in practice much less for N≤1e5), so this is effectively linearithmic with a small K. Space holds all generated numbers at once, so O(K).

delta_type: replaced a general digit-DP + binary search with a direct BFS enumeration tailored to the problem’s small constraints.

complexity_delta.from: O(D * log U) time, O(D) space (digit DP with binary search on answer).
complexity_delta.to: O(K log K) time, O(K) space (BFS-style enumeration plus final sort), where K is the number of Lunlun numbers generated up to the N-th.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically in U, the DP+binary-search solution is better (independent of K), but given problem constraints (N small, number of digits bounded), K is small and the BFS construction tends to be faster in practice due to simpler logic and fewer nested loops. So the transformation sacrifices theoretical scaling in U in exchange for lower constant factors and straightforward implementation.

transformation_steps: Abandon binary search on the numeric range [0, 3234566667] and the digit DP counting function func_2; instead, work directly in the space of Lunlun numbers.
Initialize the first layer of Lunlun numbers as the set {1,2,...,9}. These are the 1-digit Lunlun numbers.
Iteratively expand each layer: for every number, look at its last digit and append allowed neighbor digits (same, +1, -1 within [0,9]) to form new numbers, collecting them into the next layer’s set.
Maintain a running count var_3 of how many Lunlun numbers have been generated so far; once var_3 >= N, stop expanding further layers.
Flatten all per-layer sets into a single list var_11, sort it, and output var_11[N-1] as the N-th Lunlun number.
trigger_signals: Input consists of a single N with known upper bound on the order of 1e5, and the domain of valid Lunlun numbers is relatively small and structurally constrained.
The original DP solution includes multiple nested loops and recomputation for each binary search step, which can be overkill when the answer domain is small and can be enumerated directly.
The problem requires only the N-th smallest value, not answering many queries or dynamic ranges, suggesting that one-off generation up to N may suffice.
The BFS structure on digit transitions is natural and simple for Lunlun numbers (adjacent digit difference ≤1), making direct constructive generation both easy and efficient under given constraints.
pitfalls: Memory growth: The BFS solution stores all generated Lunlun numbers (var_1 as list of sets and then var_11 as a flat list). If constraints were increased substantially (N much larger or digit length unbounded), this O(K) storage could become prohibitive, while the DP solution stays O(D).

Sorting overhead: The final var_11.sort() is O(K log K). For very large K, this dominates the runtime. A more scalable enumeration would maintain numbers in order (e.g., using a queue or min-heap) to avoid a full sort, or would avoid storing all layers at once.
Use of eval(input()): Both versions use eval(input()), which is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; using int(input()) is safer and marginally faster.

String conversions on every expansion: In the BFS code, each extension converts integers to strings and back for digit manipulation. For larger K this adds overhead; using arithmetic operations (mod 10, integer division, and multiplication/addition) is more efficient.

Assuming fixed small constraints: The BFS solution is fast here because the problem naturally caps the required digit length and N. If reused in a context with larger N or more digits without adjustment, this approach may degrade, while the digit DP method would scale more predictably.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: given N integers (likely each in [0, 99] since slow/modified code scans range(100)), find integer x minimizing sum (a_i - x)^2. N probably up to about 1e5.

dominant_ops: For each candidate integer var_2 in range(100), compute np.sum((var_5 - var_2) ** 2) over all N elements using NumPy broadcasting, and take the minimum.

complexity.time: O(V * N) where V = 100 (candidate x values) => effectively O(N) but with a large constant factor 100.
complexity.why: The input list of size N is stored as a NumPy array. Each iteration over var_2 performs a vectorized subtraction and square over N elements, producing a temporary array of size N, followed by a reduction (np.sum). This repeats V=100 times.

bottlenecks.detail: Brute-force over all 100 candidate centers (0..99) instead of using the fact that the minimizing integer lies at floor/ceil of the mean of the data. This multiplies the cost by ~50x compared to checking only two candidates.
Each iteration in range(100) creates a temporary array for (var_6 - var_2) ** 2 of size N, causing repeated allocations and memory traffic.
Using NumPy inside a Python loop for small, fixed-size candidate set adds per-call overhead (100 separate vectorized operations) instead of a single linear pass in pure Python.
Variable var_6 is reassigned to var_5 every loop iteration but never changes; this extra binding does nothing but slightly increases per-iteration overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical property that the sum of squared deviations is minimized at the mean; for integer x, it suffices to check floor(mean) and ceil(mean). Compute the average once, then evaluate the objective for at most two candidates in a single pass over the data.

complexity.why: The list of N integers is stored once. Computing the average is O(N). Then for each of at most 2 candidate integers (floor and ceil of the mean), a single pass over the N elements computes the squared differences and their sum. Total passes are constant (≈3), so time is linear in N; additional memory is only the input list and a few scalars.

complexity_delta.from: O(V * N) with V = 100 (brute-force over all possible integer centers in [0, 99])
complexity_delta.to: O(N) by checking only floor(mean) and ceil(mean)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both are linear in N because V is constant, but the constant factor drops from 100 passes using NumPy (with temporary arrays) to 2 passes in pure Python, yielding a substantial speedup in practice.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the objective sum (a_i - x)^2 is a convex quadratic in x and is minimized at the mean of {a_i}. For integer x, the optimum is attained at floor(mean) or ceil(mean).
Replace the brute-force loop over all candidate x in range(100) with a loop over just two candidates: math.floor(average) and math.ceil(average).
Avoid NumPy inside the main loop; use Python lists and built-in sum with a comprehension to compute the squared differences in a single pass, eliminating per-iteration temporary arrays.
Remove redundant variable reassignments (e.g., var_6 = var_5 inside the loop) and unused variables (var_3 in the slow version), slightly reducing overhead and clarifying the logic.
trigger_signals: The code scans all integer candidates in a small fixed range (range(100)) to minimize a smooth, quadratic-like cost function, which suggests there may be a closed-form or near-closed-form solution.
The cost function has the structure sum((a_i - x) ** 2), a classic case where the minimizing x is the mean of the a_i's, signaling that brute-force search is unnecessary.

Repeated vectorized operations in a Python loop (NumPy broadcasting plus np.sum called many times) indicate a pattern where algorithmic improvements or aggregation of operations could drastically cut overhead.

The candidate space size (100) is independent of N, but the cost is still dominated by N; any reduction in the number of passes over the data (from 100 to a constant like 2) is a strong optimization opportunity.
pitfalls: When switching to the mean-based solution, it is crucial to handle the integer constraint correctly: using only round(mean) may fail on tie cases; checking both floor(mean) and ceil(mean) is safer.

For very large magnitude inputs, computing squared differences can overflow typical 32-bit integer types; in Python integers are arbitrary precision, but care would be needed in languages with fixed-width types (e.g., use 64-bit or wider).

If one keeps NumPy for other reasons, mixing Python loops and NumPy in tight performance-critical sections can backfire; better to vectorize fully or to stay in pure Python where vectorization cannot be leveraged effectively.

Using eval(input()) for reading numbers is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; while not the main performance issue here, it is a bad practice and could cause problems if inputs are not strictly trusted.

constraints_guess.notes: Input is a single integer K, asking for the K-th 'Lunlun' number (adjacent digit differences <= 1). This matches AtCoder ABC161 D; K <= 1e5 in the original problem.

dominant_ops: Repeated conversion of integers to strings and per-digit checks in func_2
Nested while-loop in func_11 that manipulates powers of 10 (10**var_8) and uses modulo / rounding to search for the next valid number
Potentially scanning through many non-Lunlun integers to reach the next Lunlun number

complexity.time: O(V * D) in the worst interpretation, where V is the magnitude of the K-th Lunlun number and D is its digit length; practically this can approach iterating over up to ~1e9+ integers, each with O(D) digit work
complexity.space: O(1) or O(D); only a handful of integers and temporary strings are kept at once
complexity.why: func_2 checks each candidate by stringifying and comparing adjacent digits in O(D). func_11 uses a while True loop with power-of-ten arithmetic to move to the next candidate but still appears to require scanning a large contiguous region of integers (or near-contiguous), leading to work essentially proportional to the numeric gap between successive Lunlun numbers rather than just their count. With K up to 1e5, the K-th Lunlun number is very large, so blindly scanning by value is prohibitive in Python.

bottlenecks.detail: Search progresses in the integer line (by value) rather than in the smaller graph of Lunlun numbers, so it touches enormous numbers of invalid states.
Each validity check converts the entire candidate integer to a string and loops over all digits; this is done for many more numbers than necessary.
The nested while True in func_11 repeatedly computes powers of 10 and uses modulo-based rounding, which is costly when executed for a large number of candidate values.
A large number of heavy modules (bisect, heapq, decimal, itertools, etc.) and timing decorators are imported/defined but not needed; while not the main TLE cause, they add noise and overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Generate Lunlun numbers directly as a graph/BFS over digits: start from all 1-digit Lunlun numbers (1–9), then for each number extend by one digit using only neighbors (last_digit-1, last_digit, last_digit+1). Collect generated numbers in a set until at least K are obtained, then sort once and pick the (K-1)-th element.

complexity.why: The BFS-like generation ensures that essentially each Lunlun number is generated a constant number of times (at most once with each valid last digit transition), so the number of produced elements is O(K). All heavy work is the final sort of these O(K) numbers, which costs O(K log K). Intermediate per-number work is O(1). Space is dominated by storing the set of generated numbers.

complexity_delta.from: Effectively O(V * D), where V is the numeric value of the K-th Lunlun number (potentially ~1e9 or more), due to scanning many invalid integers with O(D) digit checks.
complexity_delta.to: O(K log K) time and O(K) space by generating only valid Lunlun numbers and sorting them once.
complexity_delta.note: The fast solution changes the search domain from 'all integers up to the answer, filtered by a digit predicate' to 'only Lunlun numbers, generated via a digit-transition graph'. This is the main reason for the speedup.

transformation_steps: Stop scanning the entire integer line and instead conceptualize Lunlun numbers as nodes in a graph where edges connect numbers whose digits can be extended by a neighbor digit (diff <= 1).
Initialize the frontier with 1-digit Lunlun numbers {1..9} instead of starting from 1 and incrementing.
For each current number, look only at its last digit and generate the next-level numbers by appending last_digit-1, last_digit, or last_digit+1 (with boundary checks at 0 and 9).
Accumulate all generated numbers in a set to avoid duplicates while growing levels until the set size reaches at least K.
After generation, convert the set to a list, sort it once, and output the (K-1)-th element as the K-th Lunlun number.
Remove unused imports, timing wrappers, and other general-purpose utilities, keeping only the minimal input-processing logic and the core BFS generation.
trigger_signals: The original code uses a while True inner loop over arithmetic with powers of 10 and modulo operations, suggesting per-number search for the next candidate rather than structured generation.

Presence of a general digit-check helper (func_2) coupled with no explicit queue/graph structure indicates a filter-over-integers pattern, which is a red flag when the answer index K is large but individual numbers are big.

Knowledge of the domain (Lunlun digits only depend on adjacent digits) indicates that a state is fully characterized by its last digit and length, making a BFS over digit states natural and much smaller than scanning all integers.
Constraints (K up to around 1e5) coupled with the likely magnitude of the K-th Lunlun number make any linear scan up to the answer infeasible in Python.
pitfalls: Using a set for var_2 and var_5 is fine at this scale, but for much larger K this could become memory-heavy; one should then consider a true BFS with a queue ordered by value rather than storing all numbers in a set and sorting.

Sorting all generated numbers at the end is O(K log K); if K or constraints grow, a priority-queue-based generation (always popping the smallest next Lunlun number) could yield O(K log K) without a final sort, or even better with careful deduplication.
Care must be taken with the transitions at digit 0 and 9 to avoid generating invalid digits or missing valid ones; off-by-one errors here silently produce wrong answers.

The BFS-like generation in the fast code relies on the fact that Lunlun numbers grow roughly in layers of increasing digit length; if applied blindly to other digit-constraint problems, the branching factor or total count might explode.

If the input constraints were significantly larger (e.g., K >> 1e5), the current use of Python integers and sets might still become a bottleneck; further optimizations (e.g., using a min-heap and generating in sorted order without storing all elements) would then be necessary.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case; typical AtCoder-style combinatorics with n,k up to around 2e5–1e6 where O(n log MOD) is acceptable but heavy constants or extra precomputation can TLE.

dominant_ops: O(N) precomputation of factorials and inverse factorials in func_3
O(K log MOD) modular exponentiations in func_1 inside the main loop
Large import set including numpy and other unused libraries increasing startup and memory footprint
Repeated Python-level multiplications and indexing into large arrays for each term in the sum

complexity.why: func_3 builds factorial and inverse factorial arrays of size N=var_14 => O(N) time and memory. The main loop over var_11 in range(var_9+1) calls func_1 (binary exponentiation) with exponent about O(N), each in O(log N) ~ O(log MOD), giving O(K log MOD). Arrays var_5 and var_8, and other intermediates, hold O(N) elements.

bottlenecks.detail: Building full factorial and inverse factorial tables (func_3) when only a sequential run of binomial coefficients is needed. This adds O(N) time and memory overhead.
Imports of numpy, decimal, heapq, queue, copy, fractions, itertools, collections, bisect, math, etc., are unused for the core logic but increase startup time and memory usage, especially numpy.
Custom modular exponentiation func_1 runs entirely in Python, whereas Python's built-in pow(base, exp, mod) is implemented in C and significantly faster.
Creating large helper arrays (factorials, inverse factorials) and keeping them for the whole run increases memory footprint and cache misses compared to an O(1)-space iterative recurrence.
Multiple lambda-based input wrappers on top of sys.stdin.readline add minor but unnecessary overhead in tight time limits.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial precomputation and explicit binomial formula; instead maintain the combination coefficient iteratively in O(1) per step using C(n-1, i+1) = C(n-1, i) * (n-1-i)/(i+1) (mod MOD), and use Python's built-in pow(base, exp, mod) and pow(x, -1, mod) for exponentiation and modular inverses in a single simple loop.

complexity.why: The loop runs for var_5+1 iterations. Each iteration performs a constant number of modular multiplications plus two pow calls: pow(var_6-1, exponent, MOD) and pow(var_4+1, -1, MOD). Each pow is O(log MOD), so the loop is O(K log MOD). No arrays proportional to input size are kept; only a few scalar variables are maintained, yielding constant additional space.

from.time: O(N + K log MOD) with high constant factors

to.time: O(K log MOD) with low constant factors

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically, the logarithmic factor from pow is unchanged for the summation, but the removal of the O(N) factorial precomputation and all large arrays significantly reduces both memory and practical runtime. Using built-in pow further lowers constants.

transformation_steps: Remove all unused heavy imports such as numpy and other standard-library modules not required for the combinatorial sum.
Eliminate factorial and inverse-factorial table construction (func_3) and any combinatorial expressions that index into those tables.
Replace explicit nCk computations via factorials with an iterative recurrence that updates the binomial coefficient C(n-1, i) to C(n-1, i+1) using modular multiplication and a modular inverse.
Replace the custom modular exponentiation func_1 with Python's built-in pow(base, exp, mod) for both exponentiation of (var_6-1) and modular inverses via pow(x, -1, MOD).
Collapse the logic into a single tight loop that accumulates the answer var_2 and updates the current coefficient var_3, avoiding intermediate arrays and function-call overhead.
Use a single fixed modulus var_1 = 998244353 consistently and remove unrelated constants (e.g., 10**16) and extraneous global settings like excessively high recursion limits.
trigger_signals: Time-limit exceeded or borderline runtimes when N,var_14 or K,var_9 are near their upper bounds.
High memory usage observed due to factorial arrays of size O(N).
Profiler or simple timing pointing to func_3 and func_1 as hot spots, along with non-trivial overhead in imports.
Observation that binomial coefficients are needed sequentially for successive k, suggesting an iterative recurrence instead of random-access nCk queries.
pitfalls: Using pow(x, -1, MOD) assumes MOD is prime and x is not divisible by MOD; this holds for 998244353 but must be reconsidered for non-prime moduli.
Integer division inside the recurrence must be performed as multiplication by a modular inverse; using Python's // instead of modular inverse would break correctness under modulo arithmetic.
Rewriting to an iterative recurrence requires careful handling of off-by-one indices (e.g., using n-1-i versus n-i) to ensure the combinatorial identity matches the original formula.

Removing factorial precomputation is only safe if the algorithm never again needs random-access combinations for arbitrary (n, k); if such queries were required, a different optimization strategy (e.g., precompute once or use prefix products) might be needed.
Assuming that removing imports alone solves performance issues; the primary gains come from algorithmic simplification and use of built-in pow, not just from cleaning imports.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder 'Coprime' settings: 1 <= n <= 2e5, each a_i in [1, 10^6]. Need to decide if numbers are pairwise coprime, setwise coprime, or not coprime.

dominant_ops: Building smallest-prime-factor (SPF) table up to 10^6 via a sieve skipping composites
Factorization of each input number using the SPF table
Tracking last index for each prime factor to detect reuse (pairwise coprime check)
Running a cumulative gcd over all elements (setwise coprime check)

complexity.time: O(M log log M + N log V)
complexity.why: Let M = 10^6 (fixed upper bound), V = max(a_i), N = number of elements. The SPF sieve only iterates inner loops for primes because composites are skipped by `if var_7[var_6] > 0: continue`, giving ~M (1/2 + 1/3 + 1/5 + ...) = O(M log log M). Each a_i is factorized by repeatedly dividing by its smallest prime factor, costing O(log a_i) steps, so total factorization is O(N log V). The index tracking array `var_9` is size M, giving O(M) space.

bottlenecks.detail: SPF table is built up to a fixed 10^6 regardless of the actual maximum value in the input. If max(a_i) << 10^6, significant unnecessary work is done and extra memory is allocated.
Two arrays of size 10^6+1 (`var_7` for SPF and `var_9` for last-index tracking) consume noticeable memory even when input values are small.
The sieve loop over 2..10^6 with an inner loop over multiples is the dominant hotspot; all other parts (gcd and factorization loops) are relatively minor.

FastAudit.core_idea: Adapt the sieve upper bound to the maximum input value and replace positional last-seen tracking with set-based tracking of prime factors to determine pairwise/setwise coprimality. All input is read at once for reduced I/O overhead.

complexity.time: O(V log V + N log V)
complexity.why: Let V = max(a_i), N = number of elements. The modified SPF construction loops `var_7` from 2..V and for each runs `for var_8 in range(var_7, V+1, var_7)`, regardless of whether var_7 is prime. This gives total work sum_{k=2..V} V/k = V * (H_V - 1) = O(V log V), which is asymptotically worse than the prime-only variant. Factorization of each number still costs O(log a_i) using the SPF table, totaling O(N log V). Each number’s prime factors are stored in a small set (number of distinct primes of a_i is small for a_i <= 10^6), so set unions and intersections add only small constant factors. Memory is O(V) for the SPF table plus transient small sets.

from.time: O(M log log M + N log V) with fixed M = 10^6
from.note: Original code uses an efficient SPF sieve that skips composite bases, but always up to 10^6 even if max(a_i) is much smaller.

to.time: O(V log V + N log V)
to.note: Modified code scales the sieve up to the actual maximum input value V, which may save work when V << 10^6, but the sieve itself is implemented in an O(V log V) style instead of O(V log log V).

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically, the new sieve is worse (log V vs log log V), but for typical constraints (V <= 10^6) both versions are usually fast enough in Python. The main practical improvement is avoiding unnecessary work when the max input is well below 10^6; the main regression is the more expensive nested loop pattern over all k = 2..V.

transformation_steps: Input handling changed from iterative `input()` calls to `open(0).read().split()` with argument-unpacking to get n and the array in one pass, reducing Python I/O overhead.
Upper bound for sieve changed from a fixed 10**6 to `max(var_1)`, so preprocessing and memory scale with actual input magnitude.

SPF construction changed from a prime-only outer loop (skipping composites via `if var_7[var_6] > 0: continue`) to a double loop over all k in [2..V] and their multiples, setting the factor when first visited.
Prime factorization logic moved into a helper `func_2` returning a `set` of distinct prime factors for each number.
Pairwise coprimality detection reworked from an array of last-used indices (`var_9`) to directly checking intersections of prime-factor sets across numbers (`var_3 & var_12`).
Setwise coprimality detection reworked from cumulative gcd to intersection of prime-factor sets across all numbers (`var_4 &= var_12`).
Final decision is encoded as an index into a list of result strings, improving clarity of the output mapping.
trigger_signals: Use of a fixed-size sieve and auxiliary arrays up to 10^6 regardless of actual max(a_i), suggesting wasted work and memory.
Reliance on repeated `input()` calls instead of bulk input reading, which is often a bottleneck in Python under tight time limits.
Desire for a more declarative, set-based structure to reason about coprimality (pairwise vs setwise) rather than index bookkeeping.
pitfalls: The new SPF construction is asymptotically slower (O(V log V)) because it loops over all bases 2..V and their multiples, including composites. The original sieve, which skips composite bases, is closer to O(V log log V). This can matter if V is large and near the upper limit.

Set-based operations (`var_3 & var_12`, `var_3 |= var_12`, `var_4 &= var_12`) add overhead compared to simple integer index checks. For a_i <= 10^6 the number of distinct primes per number is small, but using sets still introduces Python object and hashing overhead.
If future constraints increase V substantially (e.g., V >> 10^6), the O(V log V) sieve and Python-level loops may become a performance bottleneck, risking TLE.

Both versions rely on correct SPF entries for all values encountered. Any change that allows a number > max(a_i) to be passed into `func_2` would cause incorrect behavior or errors, so the invariant that all inputs are <= V must be maintained.
Direct I/O via `open(0).read()` requires enough memory to hold all input at once; this is benign for typical competitive-programming constraints but could be problematic under extreme input sizes.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical 'number of divisors of N! mod 1e9+7' task (e.g., AtCoder ABC052 C). N appears to be <= 1000 from the sieve bound func_4(10**3).

dominant_ops: Sieve of Eratosthenes up to ~N to precompute primes (func_4)
For each k in [2..N], trial division of k by all precomputed primes up to sqrt(k) (func_2)
Creation of a new defaultdict for every k and iterating list(func_2(k).items()) (func_3)
Python-level dict increments for prime exponents across all k

complexity.time: O(N * sqrt N / log N) ≈ O(N^{3/2}) for N up to 1000
complexity.why: func_4 runs a sieve in O(M log log M) with M≈N (negligible for N=1e3). The heavy part is func_3: for each integer k from 2 to N, func_2 factors k by trying all primes ≤ sqrt(k), which takes O(π(√k)) ~ O(√k / log k) operations. Summed over k=2..N this gives ≈∑√k/logk ≈ O(N^{3/2}/log N). All prime-exponent totals are stored in a defaultdict keyed by primes, giving O(number_of_distinct_primes≤N)=O(N/log N) space, which is dominated by O(N) overheads.

bottlenecks.detail: func_3 creates a fresh defaultdict via func_2 for every k in [2..N], leading to O(N) small dict allocations and deallocations. Dict construction overhead dominates for small N.
list(func_2(var_4).items()) materializes a temporary list of (prime, exponent) pairs for every k, adding extra allocations and iteration overhead.
Prime sieve func_4 is run even though N is only 1e3; its asymptotic benefit is minor while it still introduces another nested loop in Python.

Entire pipeline is Python-loop-heavy: triple layering of loops (sieve, per-k factorization, per-prime accumulation) with dict-based bookkeeping, which is slower than using vectorized C-level operations where possible.

FastAudit.core_idea: Directly prime-factor each integer from 2 to N using simple trial division, append all prime factors into one global list, then use collections.Counter (implemented in C) to aggregate multiplicities and compute the product over (exponent + 1). This pushes aggregation work into efficient C-level code and avoids per-number dict allocations.

complexity.space: O(T) where T is the total number of prime factors in 2..N (≈O(N log log N) for general N, but very small for N<=1000)
complexity.why: func_1 factors a single k by trial division up to sqrt(k), skipping even composites. Worst-case per k is O(√k) trial divisions, and summing over k=2..N gives O(N√N). The global list var_8 stores each prime factor once per multiplicity; its length is the sum of prime factor counts Ω(k) over k≤N, which is ≈O(N log log N) in general but tiny for N=1e3. Counter aggregates in C, so aggregation overhead is effectively linear in |var_8| with low constant.

delta_type: implementation/constant-factor optimization with simpler data flow (no asymptotic change but large practical speedup for given constraints)

complexity_delta.from: O(N * sqrt N / log N) factoring using primes + O(M log log M) sieve, dominated by many Python dict creations and updates
complexity_delta.to: O(N * sqrt N) trial division using integers, but with aggregation pushed into C via Counter and far fewer Python objects
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both are around O(N^{3/2}); the key improvement is reducing Python-level overhead (dicts, temporary lists, multiple passes) and using a single flat list + Counter.

transformation_steps: Removed per-number defaultdict accumulation and replaced it with a single global list of prime factors across all k in [2..N].
Eliminated explicit prime sieve and prime list; instead, used direct trial division by integers up to sqrt(k) with a simple even-number skip.
Replaced manual defaultdict-based exponent aggregation with collections.Counter, leveraging highly optimized C loops.
Simplified data flow so factorization returns a list of primes rather than a dict, allowing tight inner loops and fewer allocations per k.
trigger_signals: Multiple nested Python loops with dictionaries inside the innermost loops (profilers would show heavy time in dict operations and function calls).
Creation of a new mapping object (defaultdict) per integer k in [2..N].
Use of list(dict.items()) in hot paths, indicating unnecessary intermediate containers.
Relatively small input bound (N≈1000), meaning algorithmic improvements from sieving do not offset Python overhead.
pitfalls: The fast_code’s trial division strategy would become too slow if N were much larger (e.g., N ≥ 1e5); a true SPF-based sieve factorization would then be needed.
Building a global list of all prime factors (var_8) is fine for N<=1000 but could become memory-heavy for much larger N; a streaming aggregation method would be preferable in that case.
Using eval(input()) in fast_code is unsafe and unnecessary; while not a performance issue here, it is a security and robustness pitfall.

If one reintroduces a sieve approach, care must be taken to avoid off-by-one errors and to ensure that the sieve and factorization loops still keep most work in C (e.g., by using arrays or precomputed SPF rather than Python dicts in inner loops).

constraints_guess.notes: Counts number of subarrays with sum 0 via prefix sums and frequency map. Typical AtCoder-style constraints: n up to ~2e5, |a_i| up to ~1e9.

dominant_ops: Building prefix sum array of length n (single pass over input).
Counting frequencies of all prefix sums with collections.Counter.
Sorting frequency items via Counter.most_common() (O(m log m) for m distinct prefix sums).
Computing nC2 via reduce/mul and small temporary lists for each distinct prefix sum value.

complexity.time: O(n + m log m)  (with m <= n+1, effectively O(n log n))
complexity.why: Prefix sums and Counter construction are O(n). The call to Counter.most_common() sorts the m distinct prefix sums by frequency, which is O(m log m). Combination computation is O(1) per key but has non-trivial constant overhead from reduce/mul and list creation.

bottlenecks.detail: Counter.most_common() sorts all distinct prefix sums by frequency, even though only the frequencies themselves are needed and order is irrelevant. This adds an O(m log m) step.
Computing nC2 via reduce(mul, ...) over tiny ranges and constructing intermediate lists incurs extra Python overhead compared to a direct arithmetic formula c*(c-1)//2.
Storing all prefix sums explicitly in a list, then wrapping with Counter, instead of streaming directly into Counter or using accumulate, adds minor but avoidable overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use prefix sums and a frequency map as before, but avoid sorting and heavy helpers by iterating directly over Counter.values() and computing combinations in O(1) with the closed form c*(c-1)//2. Handle the initial zero-prefix separately by adding the count of prefix sums equal to 0.

complexity.why: Computing prefix sums via itertools.accumulate and counting them with Counter are both linear in n. Iterating once over the frequency values to sum c*(c-1)//2 is O(m) with m <= n+1. No sorting step remains, so total time is linear.

complexity_delta.from: O(n + m log m) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: Removed the O(m log m) sorting from Counter.most_common() and replaced the combination helper with a direct O(1) arithmetic formula, significantly improving performance for large n.

transformation_steps: Replace the explicit prefix sum loop with itertools.accumulate to compute prefix sums in a single, iterator-based pass.
Feed the accumulate iterator directly into collections.Counter to build the frequency map without an intermediate full list of prefix sums (other than what Counter itself stores).
Remove Counter.most_common() and instead iterate directly over Counter.values(), since the ordering of prefix sums is irrelevant when summing over cC2.
Inline the combination logic specialized to k=2: replace the generic nCk helper using reduce(mul, ...) with the closed-form formula c*(c-1)//2 for each frequency c.

Account for the initial prefix sum 0 (which was part of the list in the original code) by adding var_2[0] to the final answer so that pairs among zero prefix sums are correctly computed as C(count_0+1, 2).
trigger_signals: Use of Counter.most_common() where only aggregate frequency information is required, indicating unnecessary sorting.
Generic combination function based on reduce and list(range(...)) used repeatedly for the fixed case k=2.
TLE or slow runtime on large inputs (e.g., n up to 2e5) due to extra log factor and Python-level overhead.
Profiling or code inspection showing a large fraction of time spent inside Counter.most_common and reduce/mul.
pitfalls: Correctness around the initial prefix sum 0: when switching from an explicit [0] + prefix list to using accumulate, you must remember to treat the implicit starting sum 0 as one extra occurrence, which is handled here by adding var_2[0] to the total.
Integer overflow is not an issue in Python due to arbitrary-precision ints, but in other languages the c*(c-1)//2 formula could overflow if c is large; care would be needed there.
Using eval(input()) is unnecessary and can be unsafe in general; while unchanged between versions, it should be avoided in broader contexts.

Although Counter(values) and accumulate are both O(n), they still store O(n) data; this approach is not suitable if memory constraints are extremely tight and a more streaming-based or compressed approach is required.

constraints_guess.notes: Single array-processing pass; pattern closely matches AtCoder-style constraints where n is up to 2e5 or similar.

dominant_ops: Single O(n) loop over the array, performing integer comparisons and assignments
Input parsing of n integers via map(int, input().split())

complexity.why: The core logic scans the array once, updating two scalar counters. No auxiliary data structure grows with n.

bottlenecks.detail: Many unused imports (copy, math, string, collections, etc.) and helper functions (func_1, func_2, func_3) add minor startup and code noise but do not impact asymptotic complexity.
Use of int(eval(input())) is slower and less safe than int(input()), but time impact is negligible compared to the O(n) scan for typical competitive-programming constraints.
The algorithm is already optimal O(n) for this problem; there is no fundamental algorithmic bottleneck, only stylistic/micro-performance concerns.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a DP-like prefix array where var_4[i] stores the length (in edges) of the current non-increasing run ending at index i, then take the maximum of this array.

complexity.why: The code still performs a single pass over the n elements, but it now maintains an auxiliary array var_4 of size n to store run lengths.

complexity_delta.note: The new version trades constant extra space for an O(n) DP array without changing the overall time complexity; asymptotically it is not faster and may use more memory.

transformation_steps: Removed unused helper functions and extraneous variables from the core logic.
Changed the run-length computation from two scalar counters (current streak and best streak) to a DP-like array var_4 that accumulates streak lengths.
Re-expressed the condition as var_2[i] <= var_2[i-1] while preserving the non-increasing run semantics from the original a[i] >= a[i+1] check.
Kept the same input pattern (int(eval(input())), map(int, input().split())) but simplified the subsequent processing structure.
trigger_signals: Single-pass contiguous-condition counting over an array, a pattern amenable to either scalar counters or prefix/DP arrays.
Presence of unused imports and functions signaled that the original snippet likely came from a more complex template and could be streamlined.
No need for sub-quadratic optimization since the original algorithm was already O(n). Changes were driven by style/structure rather than big-O improvement.
pitfalls: The DP-array version increases memory usage from O(1) to O(n); for very large n and tight memory limits this can be worse than the original scalar-counter implementation.
Both versions still use int(eval(input())), which is unnecessary and unsafe for untrusted input; int(input()) should be preferred.
If n can be 0 or 1, care must always be taken that the loop bounds and max(var_4) / max(var_1, var_2) are well-defined; the given patterns assume at least one element but behave benignly for n=1.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: single test, n relatively small (<=100 or a few hundred), values likely in a small integer range (e.g., 0–100).

dominant_ops: Triple-nested loops recomputing sum of squared differences for many candidate centers, with a completely redundant outer loop over the same range.

complexity.why: Let n = len(var_7), R = var_7[max] - var_7[min] + 1. The code sorts the array in O(n log n), then: outer loop over var_4 runs R times; inside, the first inner loop over var_1 runs O(n) once; then a second loop over var_2 runs ~R times, and inside that an inner loop over var_1 runs O(n). Overall per outer iteration is O(n + R*n) = O(R*n), multiplied by R outer iterations gives O(R^2 * n). The array itself is size n, and only O(1) extra scalars are used beyond it, so space is O(n).

bottlenecks.detail: The outermost loop `for var_4 in range(var_7[0], var_7[len(var_7) - 1] + 1):` does not use var_4 and simply repeats the entire inner computation R times for no effect, multiplying runtime by O(R).

The sum of squared differences `(candidate - var_7[var_1]) ** 2` is computed in pure Python inside nested loops (over candidates and indices). This results in O(R * n) arithmetic operations even without the redundant outer loop, and O(R^2 * n) with it.

For each candidate center (var_2), the sum of squared distances to all points is recomputed from scratch instead of leveraging algebraic formulas or incremental updates; no partial sums or precomputations are used.

The array is sorted but the subsequent cost computation only uses values and min/max; sorting is not strictly needed to evaluate the sum of squared distances, contributing an extra O(n log n) though it is dominated by the R^2 * n term.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace nested Python loops with a small fixed-range loop and vectorized NumPy operations, computing squared differences for all elements at once for each candidate center, reducing complexity to linear in n with low constant factors.

complexity.why: The code parses input into a NumPy array of length n, then loops `for var_2 in range(100):` a fixed constant T = 100 times. Inside each iteration, `(var_6 - var_2) ** 2` and `np.sum(...)` are vectorized operations over n elements, each O(n) in C-level code. Overall runtime is O(T * n) = O(n). Space is O(n) for the NumPy array plus O(1) scalars.

complexity_delta.to: O(n)
complexity_delta.note: The slow version redundantly repeats an O(R * n) candidate-evaluation process R times, yielding O(R^2 * n). The fast version uses a fixed small number of candidate centers (100) and NumPy vectorization, giving O(n) with respect to input size. As long as the candidate range is indeed bounded by a small constant, the asymptotic complexity improves drastically.

transformation_steps: Remove the unused outer loop over var_4 that was recomputing the same logic R times.
Collapse the explicit nested loops over indices into a single loop over candidate centers, with the per-candidate cost computed in a vectorized way using NumPy arrays.
Replace manual accumulation `var_6 = var_6 + (...) ** 2` with `(array - candidate) ** 2` followed by `np.sum(...)`, offloading the heavy work to optimized C code.
Keep only O(1) scalar state for the running minimum (var_1) instead of reassigning and recomputing across unnecessary scopes.
Use a fixed, small candidate range (0..99) instead of scanning every integer between the minimum and maximum values when problem constraints permit that simplification.
trigger_signals: Presence of three nested Python loops where the innermost loop performs simple arithmetic over all elements of an array for each candidate parameter.
Loop variable (var_4) that is never used in its body, indicating accidental redundant repetition.
Pattern of recomputing the same type of reduction (sum of squared differences) from scratch for many similar candidate values.
Arithmetic on every element of an array inside Python loops instead of leveraging vectorized libraries like NumPy.
pitfalls: Correctness risk: The fast code assumes candidate centers in the fixed range 0..99; if the optimal center can lie outside this range (e.g., data values >99 or <0), the result may be incorrect even though performance is good.
Using `eval(input())` is unsafe and unnecessary; `int(input())` should be used instead to avoid security risks and overhead.
For very small n, the overhead of importing NumPy and creating arrays may outweigh performance gains over pure Python, though asymptotics still improve for larger n.

If the true constraints require scanning between the actual minimum and maximum of the input values (R possibly large), then replacing that with a constant 100-range is only valid if guaranteed by the problem; otherwise, an O(R * n) but correct solution with no redundant outer loop may be preferable.

Portability consideration: NumPy may not be available or allowed in some competitive-programming environments; in such cases, one should still remove the redundant outer loop and, if needed, derive an O(n) or O(n log n) formula using precomputed sums (e.g., using sum(x_i) and sum(x_i^2) to compute sum (x_i - p)^2 efficiently).

constraints_guess.n_max: ≈100–200 (typical for triple-sum counting problems)
constraints_guess.q_max: multiple test cases until '0 0' sentinel (≈10^2–10^3 lines)
constraints_guess.notes: Compute number of distinct triplets (1 ≤ i < j < k ≤ n) such that i + j + k = X.

dominant_ops: Triple-nested loops over (var_6, var_4, var_2) with an O(1) sum and comparison inside; executed for each input pair (n = var_5, x = var_7).

complexity.why: Outer loop var_6 runs ~n times, middle loop var_4 runs up to ~n times, inner loop var_2 runs up to ~n times → ~n^3 iterations; only a few scalars are stored, so memory is constant aside from input.

bottlenecks.detail: Unnecessary enumeration of all (i, j, k) triples with 1 ≤ i < j < k ≤ n and explicit checking of i + j + k = X via three nested loops leads to cubic time.
The condition uses sum([var_6, var_4, var_2]), which allocates a temporary list and then sums it; direct arithmetic var_6 + var_4 + var_2 would be cheaper.
Python’s per-iteration loop overhead in three nested for-loops (inner loop up to O(n)) is substantial when n is non-trivial and there are many test cases.

FastAudit.core_idea: Eliminate the innermost loop by solving for the third value algebraically: for each pair (i, j) with 1 ≤ i < j ≤ n, deduce k = X − i − j, and only count it if it satisfies j < k ≤ n. This reduces one dimension of iteration.

complexity.space: O(n^2) in the given code, O(1) if counting directly
complexity.why: Two nested loops over (var_1, var_2) yield O(n^2) pairs; for each pair, k is computed in O(1) and checked with constant-time inequalities. The current implementation builds a list with one element per valid triplet, giving O(#solutions) additional space; in the worst case #solutions = O(n^2), but could be reduced to O(1) by using a simple counter.

complexity_delta.from: O(n^3) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n^2) time, O(1)–O(n^2) space (depending on whether a list or counter is used)
complexity_delta.note: Main improvement comes from algebraically determining the third element of the triplet instead of iterating over all possibilities in a third nested loop.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the condition var_6 + var_4 + var_2 = var_7 defines the third variable uniquely as var_2 = var_7 − var_6 − var_4 for each (var_6, var_4) pair.
Remove the innermost loop over var_2 and instead compute k = var_4_target − var_1 − var_2 directly for each pair (var_1, var_2).
Replace the triple nested loops (over i, j, k) with double nested loops (over i, j) and constrain k using inequalities ensuring 1 ≤ i < j < k ≤ n.
Use an existence/counting strategy (increment a counter or append a dummy value to a list) whenever the computed k satisfies j < k ≤ n.
Optionally, replace list construction and len() with a direct integer counter to avoid O(#solutions) extra space and allocation overhead.
trigger_signals: Presence of three nested loops over ranges derived from n, indicating potential O(n^3) behavior.
A simple linear constraint i + j + k = X, which suggests that one variable can be expressed in terms of the others.
Performance or time-limit issues when n or the number of test cases increases.
Use of sum() over a small fixed-size list inside a hot loop, signaling avoidable per-iteration allocation overhead.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when translating loop bounds into inequality constraints (ensuring 1 ≤ i < j < k ≤ n is correctly mirrored by ranges and comparisons).
Forgetting to enforce the j < k constraint when eliminating the third loop, which could lead to counting non-distinct or unordered triplets.
Relying on building a list purely to count elements, which increases memory usage unnecessarily; a simple counter is enough.

Assuming algebraic optimization is always necessary: given small constraints (e.g., n ≤ 50) the cubic solution might still pass in faster languages but may be borderline in Python with many test cases.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case, three integers. The slow version hard-caps the answer search at 1e5, implying the true answer is guaranteed <= 1e5. Input values likely up to around 1e9.

dominant_ops: A descending for-loop from 10**5 down to 1 performing a multiplication and comparison each iteration until a break condition on an inequality is satisfied.

complexity.time: O(K) where K = 10^5 (linear scan over bounded range)
complexity.why: The body of the loop has O(1) work and can execute up to 10^5 times in the worst case; no additional data structures are used.

bottlenecks.detail: The loop linearly searches for the maximum integer var_4 satisfying var_1 >= var_4 * (var_2 + var_3) + var_3, even though this is directly expressible as floor((var_1 - var_3) / (var_2 + var_3)).
The range(10**5, 0, -1) bound forces up to 100k iterations per run regardless of actual answer size, wasting time when a constant-time arithmetic solution exists.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use algebra to transform the inequality into a direct integer-division formula instead of scanning over all possible answers. Compute the result with one subtraction and one floor division.

complexity.why: The optimized code performs a constant number of arithmetic operations and no loops or extra data structures.

complexity_delta.from: O(K) time, O(1) space with K up to 10^5
complexity_delta.to: O(1) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: Replaces a bounded linear search over candidate answers with a closed-form computation via integer division.

transformation_steps: Start from the slow code condition: var_1 >= var_4 * (var_2 + var_3) + var_3.
Isolate the term involving var_4: var_1 - var_3 >= var_4 * (var_2 + var_3).
Solve for var_4 as a real number: var_4 <= (var_1 - var_3) / (var_2 + var_3).
Because var_4 must be an integer and we want the maximum such value, use floor: var_4 = floor((var_1 - var_3) / (var_2 + var_3)).
Implement this with integer arithmetic using // for floor division, eliminating the loop.
Re-map variable names to match the fast_code convention and compute the result directly after a simple subtraction.
trigger_signals: A for-loop over a large fixed bound (10**5) searching for an integer satisfying a simple inequality.
Loop variable appears only in linear arithmetic inside a comparison, suggestive of an underlying formula.
Break-on-condition pattern typical of a search for extremal integer satisfying an inequality.
No dependence on previous loop iterations beyond the candidate value itself, indicating the loop is not inherently sequential.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when translating the inequality to floor division; the boundary must match the original condition exactly.
Ensuring subtraction order matches the algebraic rearrangement ((var_1 - var_3) vs (var_3 - var_1)); a sign mistake changes the result.
Division by zero if (var_2 + var_3) could be zero; constraints likely forbid this, but an implementation must respect problem assumptions.
Differences between mathematical floor and language-specific division for negative numbers; here inputs are presumably non-negative, making // safe.
Maintaining the intended variable roles when renaming (var_1, var_2, var_3, var_4) between the slow and fast versions to avoid mixing up parameters.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test with an array that is a permutation of 1..n. Original O(n^3) solution suggests intended n is large (e.g., 1e5–2e5), making triple nested loops infeasible.

dominant_ops: Enumerating all index pairs (i, j) with i < j: O(n^2) pairs
For each pair, copying the entire array: O(n) per pair
For each swapped version, scanning linearly to check sortedness: O(n) per pair
Total dominant operations: O(n^3) element copies and comparisons

complexity.why: There is a preliminary O(n) sortedness check. Then a nested loop over all pairs (var_3, var_4) is O(n^2). Inside, the code creates a new list var_7 of size n and checks sortedness in another O(n) loop. Thus per pair cost is O(n), giving O(n^2) * O(n) = O(n^3). The extra temporary array uses O(n) space.

bottlenecks.detail: Brute-force over all O(n^2) index pairs and checking if swapping them yields a sorted array, instead of reasoning about the small structural change that a single swap can cause.
For every candidate swap, the algorithm copies the whole array (var_7 = [var_6[var_3] for var_3 in range(var_1)]) even though only two positions differ. This incurs heavy O(n^3) element copying.
Triply nested structure (two index loops plus an inner check loop) scales very poorly as n grows, making it unsuitable for typical constraints like n up to 10^5.
Use of Python list comprehensions and repeated allocations inside tight loops amplifies overhead on top of the already poor asymptotic complexity.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit that the array is a permutation of 1..n. A permutation can be sorted with at most one swap if and only if the number of positions where a[i] != i+1 is at most 2. Count mismatches once in O(n) and answer YES if mismatches <= 2, otherwise NO.

complexity.why: The algorithm reads the array once and then performs a single linear pass counting indices where var_3[i] != i+1. This is O(n) time. Besides storing the input list of size n, it uses only O(1) extra variables, so the additional space is O(1) and total space dominated by the input array is O(n).

complexity_delta.from: O(n^3) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: By replacing exhaustive simulation of all swaps and full-array copies with a single pass mismatch counter leveraging the permutation property.

transformation_steps: Recognize the structural property of the target sorted array: since the input is a permutation of 1..n, the sorted array is exactly [1, 2, ..., n].

Replace the brute-force enumeration of all index pairs and swap simulations with an analytical condition: a permutation is sortable by at most one swap if the number of indices i with a[i] != i+1 is 0 or 2.
Implement a single linear pass to count mismatches between a[i] and i+1 instead of creating a new list and checking sortedness for each candidate swap.
Remove the inner sortedness checks and array copies, thus eliminating the nested O(n^2) * O(n) structure and collapsing the process into O(n).
trigger_signals: Code iterates over all O(n^2) index pairs to test swaps.
Creation of a full copy of the array inside nested loops.
Repeated full-array sortedness checks for slightly modified arrays.
Problem statement mentioning 'at most one swap' or 'almost sorted' for permutations, which typically admits O(n) or O(n log n) solutions using mismatch counting.
pitfalls: The O(n) solution assumes the array is a permutation of 1..n. If the input can contain duplicates or arbitrary values, the condition var_3[i] != i+1 is not equivalent to 'not sorted'; a different check (e.g., comparing to sorted(var_3)) would be needed.
Off-by-one errors when relating positions (0-based indices in Python) to expected values (1-based in the sorted permutation). The correct comparison is a[i] != i+1, not a[i] != i.
Relying on eval(input()) is unnecessary and unsafe; int(input()) suffices and avoids evaluating arbitrary expressions.
If multiple test cases were present (not in this snippet), reusing global variables or not reinitializing counters would cause logical errors even though the complexity is optimal.

constraints_guess.notes: Heuristic: var_3 initialized as 10**6 suggests worst-case sum of squares around 10^6, consistent with n ≤ 100 and |a_i|, |a_i - p| ≤ 100. Typical of AtCoder beginner problems where elements are small integers.

dominant_ops: Nested loops: for each candidate integer center p in [min(a), max(a)] re-scan entire array and compute (a_i - p)**2 and accumulate.

complexity.why: Let n be number of elements, R = max(a) - min(a). Sorting costs O(n log n). Outer loop over p runs R+1 times. Inner loop scans n elements per p, so O(nR). This dominates for large R. The algorithm stores the list of n integers, so O(n) space.

bottlenecks.detail: The brute-force search over all integer centers p between min(a) and max(a) leads to O(nR) evaluations of the quadratic objective. For large R this is much slower than necessary.
For every candidate p the code recomputes sum((a_i - p)**2) from scratch, discarding previous work, even though the cost function is a simple quadratic in p with a closed-form minimizer at the mean.
The list is sorted just to obtain min and max. min(var_2) and max(var_2) could be computed in O(n) without the O(n log n) sort. This is minor compared to O(nR) but still avoidable.
The exponentiation operator '**2' is executed nR times. Although each operation is O(1), the sheer count makes it a noticeable constant-factor cost in Python.
Using eval(input()) to read an integer is slow and potentially unsafe. It should be replaced by int(input()) or int(sys.stdin.readline()).

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical fact that the sum of squared deviations Σ(a_i − p)^2 is minimized at p = mean(a). For integer p, any integer nearest to the mean (floor or ceil) is optimal. Compute the (rounded) mean once and evaluate the objective in a single pass.

complexity.why: Compute the sum of elements in O(n) to obtain the mean, then a single pass to compute Σ(a_i − mean)^2 in O(n). Input storage for the list is O(n); no dependence on the value range R remains.

complexity_delta.from: O(n * R + n log n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: Eliminates the dependence on the value range R = max(a) − min(a) by replacing brute-force search with a closed-form solution based on the mean.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the objective function f(p) = Σ(a_i − p)^2 is a quadratic in p with its minimum at p = (Σ a_i) / n.
Observe that when p is restricted to integers, any integer closest to the real mean (floor or ceil) yields the minimal sum of squares; the function is symmetric around the mean.
Replace the outer loop over p in [min(a), max(a)] with a direct computation of the mean: mean = round(sum(a) / n).
Compute the sum of squared deviations once: ans = Σ(a_i − mean)^2 via a single loop or list comprehension.
Remove the sort, since min and max are no longer needed for candidate enumeration.
Optionally replace eval(input()) with int(input()) to avoid overhead and safety issues.
trigger_signals: Runtime grows significantly when the numeric range of a_i expands even if n remains modest, indicating a hidden dependency on value magnitude (R) rather than just count (n).
Code structure contains a loop over all possible candidate values between min and max, a classic sign of brute-force over an ordered domain when the cost function looks smooth or polynomial.
Objective function involves a sum of squared differences, a standard case where the minimizing point is known analytically (mean for L2, median for L1).
Profiling or mental counting shows nR evaluations of a simple expression, disproportionate when R can be as large as input values (e.g., up to 10^4 or 10^5).
pitfalls: Using round in Python 3 performs banker's rounding (ties to even). For this problem this is safe, because both floor and ceil of the mean yield the same minimal Σ(a_i − p)^2, but in other contexts this choice may matter.
If porting to languages without arbitrary-precision integers, computing Σ(a_i − mean)^2 may overflow; one may need 64-bit types or modular arithmetic as required by the problem.
Replacing brute-force with a mean-based formula is valid specifically for squared error (L2). For absolute deviation (L1) the median is the minimizer; reusing this trick blindly would be incorrect.
Over-optimizing micro-aspects (like changing '**2' to 'x*x') without fixing the O(nR) algorithm would not resolve the fundamental performance issue.
Relying on eval(input()) is unnecessary and harmful: aside from overhead, it can execute arbitrary code if the input is not trusted.

constraints_guess.notes: Input is a single integer k (1-indexed) asking for the k-th 'Lunlun/stepping' number where adjacent digits differ by at most 1. Typical contest versions use k up to around 1e5.

dominant_ops: Recursive DFS generating all valid numbers up to fixed digit length (depth 10)
List append for every generated number
Full sort of the generated list of numbers
Indexing into sorted list to get k-th element

complexity.why: Let M be the total count of generated Lunlun numbers up to 10 digits. The recursive DFS explores a 3-ary branching tree of depth up to 10 starting from digits 1..9, so M is on the order of 9 * 3^9 (plus all shorter prefixes). After generation, the code sorts all M numbers, costing O(M log M). Space is O(M) to store all numbers plus recursion stack O(depth)=O(1) relative to M.

bottlenecks.detail: Generates the complete set of Lunlun numbers up to 10 digits regardless of the requested index k; work does not scale down when k is small.
Performs a full sort of all generated numbers even though only the k-th smallest is needed, adding an O(M log M) factor.
Uses deep recursive calls (max depth 10) with a branching factor up to 3, incurring Python function call overhead for each generated number.
