The DFS stops at depth 10, so if the true k-th Lunlun number requires more digits, this approach cannot scale by simply increasing a limit without causing exponential blowup in time and memory.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use BFS over the implicit graph of Lunlun numbers, starting from 1..9 and iteratively expanding numbers by appending a digit that differs by at most 1 from the last digit. BFS naturally generates Lunlun numbers in ascending order without needing to precompute all up to a fixed digit length or to sort.

complexity.why: The BFS loop runs exactly k-1 iterations, each iteration dequeuing one number and enqueuing up to 3 successors. Every generated number participates in O(1) queue operations and constant arithmetic, so total time is O(k). The queue size is proportional to the frontier of generation, which is O(k) in the worst case, giving O(k) additional space. No global sort is required.

complexity_delta.from: O(M log M) time, O(M) space, where M is the total number of Lunlun numbers up to a fixed digit limit (here roughly constant but grows exponentially if extended).
complexity_delta.to: O(k) time, O(k) space, scaling directly with the requested index k.
complexity_delta.note: Conceptually changes from full precomputation + sort of all candidate numbers to on-demand ordered generation via BFS. This both removes the sorting step and ties the work directly to k rather than an arbitrary depth cap.

transformation_steps: Model Lunlun numbers as nodes in an implicit graph where edges connect a number to numbers formed by appending a digit that differs by at most 1 from the last digit.
Replace the recursive DFS that explores all paths up to fixed depth 10 with an iterative BFS starting from seeds 1..9.
Use a FIFO queue to maintain the BFS frontier: repeatedly pop the smallest not-yet-expanded Lunlun number in generation order.
For each dequeued number, compute its last digit and enqueue up to three valid successors: last_digit-1 (if >=0), last_digit, last_digit+1 (if <=9).
Run this BFS expansion exactly k-1 times so that the next number dequeued is the k-th Lunlun number; output it directly without sorting.
Eliminate the global list of all numbers and the final sort, reducing both memory usage and time complexity.
trigger_signals: Presence of a global list accumulating all generated candidates before using only a single indexed element.
Use of sort() on a large list when the problem only asks for the k-th value in order, not the full ordering.
Recursive generation with fixed maximum depth that is unrelated to the actual input size k, suggesting potential exponential growth if extended.
Access pattern where numbers could be generated inherently in order (graph/sequence structure) but are instead post-processed by sorting.
pitfalls: Ensuring BFS generation order matches numeric ascending order: the starting seeds and enqueue order must be chosen carefully. Using initial queue [1..9] and always expanding the front of the queue with successors in increasing digit order preserves ascending numeric order.

Using Python's recursion for deeper limits would be unsafe due to recursion limits and exponential blowup; the iterative BFS avoids this but must be coded correctly to prevent infinite loops or incorrect termination.

Queue implementation choice: Python's queue.Queue is thread-safe and slightly heavier; for single-threaded competitive programming, collections.deque is often faster. However, both preserve O(1) amortized enqueue/dequeue.
Edge handling for last digits 0 and 9 must be correct to avoid generating invalid digits or missing valid successors.
If k becomes extremely large, even O(k) generation can be too slow or memory-heavy; in such cases a more analytical counting/DP approach might be needed instead of explicit generation.

constraints_guess.notes: This is AtCoder ABC122 D ("We Like AGC"). N (string length) is up to about 100, alphabet size is fixed at 4 (A,C,G,T), DP state tracks the last 3 characters.

dominant_ops: Creation and use of a large generic competitive programming template (many imports, helper functions, classes) even though the actual task is very small (N ≤ ~100)
Method-call-based modular arithmetic via Class_1.add/sub/mul/etc. for each arithmetic operation in the core DP, instead of direct integer operations
Extra layers of indirection for I/O and possibly for the main logic via helper functions and decorators
Potential use of debugging/time-measurement decorator func_4 wrapping the main solving function, adding overhead on every call
Dictionary or array updates for DP transitions over all possible 4-length suffixes per position (same asymptotic DP work as the fast code, but with heavier per-operation overhead)

complexity.time: O(N * A^(L+1)) with large constant factors (here A=4, L=3, so O(256N))
complexity.space: O(A^L) (here O(4^3) = O(1) for fixed alphabet and pattern length)
complexity.why: The algorithm needs to consider all possible length-(L+1) windows when extending the DP (all 4^4=256 patterns) for each of the N positions. The slow code uses the same basic DP idea but implements arithmetic and control flow through a heavy abstraction layer (ModInt-style class, decorators, many helper functions), increasing constant factors without changing asymptotics.

bottlenecks.detail: Modular arithmetic is performed via a Class_1 instance (methods add, sub, mul, etc.). Each DP update requires one or more Python method calls plus argument passing and attribute access, instead of a single primitive `+` or `*` on ints. For a DP that performs thousands of updates, this overhead is significant.

The file imports many standard-library modules (bisect, heapq, random, decimal, etc.), defines multiple generic helpers (I/O wrappers, decorators, ModInt-like class, etc.) that are either unused or only lightly used. Importing and defining all of this increases startup time and memory footprint for a problem that only needs a tiny core DP.

Input reading and possibly the main solution are routed through wrapper functions (func_8, func_9, func_10, etc.) and potentially decorated with func_4 for timing. This adds extra function calls in the hot path as opposed to reading input directly and running a flat main loop.
The timing decorator func_4 uses time.time() and stderr printing. If accidentally left enabled around the main solver, it adds system calls and I/O in addition to Python function-call overhead.

Although the DP’s logical complexity is small (N ≤ ~100, 256 transitions per step), placing costly abstractions (class methods, decorators, possibly lambdas) inside this inner loop can dominate runtime when run many times (e.g., multiple test cases or tight time limits).

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a compact, specialized DP over the last 3 characters of the string, directly on integers and tuples, with precomputed forbidden 4-character patterns that would create "AGC" (or its near variants) when appending a new character. For each length from 3 up to N, iterate over all 4^4 possible 4-length windows, skip those in the forbidden set, and update a DP dictionary keyed by the last 3 characters. Use plain integer arithmetic with a final modulo pass per layer, and avoid any extra abstraction or unused tooling.

complexity.time: O(N * A^(L+1)) where A is alphabet size (4) and L is the DP memory length (3), concretely O(256N) with a very small constant factor
complexity.space: O(A^L) for the DP state (here at most 4^3 = 64 states per layer, i.e., O(1) for fixed A and L)
complexity.why: For each of the N−L extension steps, the code enumerates all length-(L+1) sequences over the alphabet (`product(var_2, repeat=var_4+1)`) to test validity and perform transitions. This yields A^(L+1) candidate windows per step. The DP dictionary contains only A^L states (all 3-length suffixes). Both A and L are constants fixed by the problem, so asymptotically the runtime is linear in N, and memory usage is constant in N.

complexity_delta.from: O(N * A^(L+1)) with high constant factors from method-based modular arithmetic, generic helpers, decorators, and extensive unused imports
complexity_delta.to: O(N * A^(L+1)) with low constant factors using direct integer arithmetic, minimal data structures, and no extraneous framework
complexity_delta.note: The asymptotic complexity is unchanged; the improvement is entirely in constants by removing layers of abstraction and unused machinery from the core DP loop.

transformation_steps: Remove the large generic competitive programming template: drop unused imports (bisect, heapq, random, decimal, etc.), unused helper functions, and the ModInt-like Class_1 when the problem only requires addition and modulo on Python ints.

Replace method-based modular arithmetic (e.g., obj.add(a, b), obj.mul(a, b)) with direct integer expressions and a single modulo operation per DP layer (as seen in the loop that mod-reduces all DP states).
Eliminate debugging and timing decorators (func_4) from the hot path; if timing is needed, run it externally rather than wrapping the main solve function.
Inline I/O: read N with a direct `int(input())` (or equivalent) instead of routing through multiple input helper functions that add function-call overhead.
Express the DP directly in a flat, tight loop that uses builtin types (dict, tuple, range, itertools.product) without extra wrappers or class abstractions.
Precompute the set of forbidden 4-character patterns once (var_17) and then reuse it directly, relying on tuple membership checks, which are efficient and simple.

Rely on Python’s built-in big integers only where necessary and keep values reduced modulo 1e9+7 regularly (once per layer) to avoid growth of integer sizes without incurring method-call overhead on every update.
trigger_signals: Profiling or timing shows that, for a very small theoretical workload (N ≤ ~100, about 256 transitions per step), the runtime is still significant, suggesting heavy constant-factor overhead.
Call-graph or profiler output indicates a large fraction of time spent in helper methods (ModInt operations, decorators, input wrappers) rather than in bare arithmetic or simple loops.
Import-time overhead is noticeable (or memory footprint is higher than expected) due to many unused library imports and class/function definitions.
Inspection of the code reveals multiple layers of abstraction around simple operations (addition, modulo, input reading) inside inner loops.
Unit tests or local runs show that removing or bypassing the template and using a simpler script drastically reduces runtime without changing the algorithm.
pitfalls: When removing a ModInt-like class and switching to raw integers, it is easy to forget to apply the modulo in all necessary places (especially after subtractions) or to rely on Python’s negative modulo behavior without adjusting the logic.

Over-optimizing the modulo placement (e.g., never applying modulo until the very end) can cause intermediate integers to grow very large in other problems with bigger N, harming performance; the current approach of modding once per DP layer is a safe compromise here.

Using `eval(input())` (as in the fast code) instead of `int(input())` is not necessary and is unsafe in general contexts, even though it is benign on controlled online judge inputs; replacing it should be considered if reusing the code elsewhere.

Aggressively stripping the template may accidentally remove genuinely needed utility functions or constants if they are intertwined with the solution logic; refactoring should be done carefully with tests.

If one later generalizes the solution (e.g., variable alphabet size or pattern length), hard-coded assumptions used to simplify and specialize the fast code (like fixed ranges and pattern construction) must be revisited to maintain correctness and performance.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic bitmask DP for minimum-cost set cover where N is number of skills/attributes (<= ~12–15) and M is number of items/books (<= ~1000). Overall DP size is 2^N; constraints must be small enough for O(M * 2^N) in Python.

dominant_ops: Double-buffer DP over items and all bitmasks: outer loop over M items, inner loop over all 2^N states
Two min() calls per state transition (one for keeping state, one for adding item) plus an if-branch for subset check
Bitwise operations (mask & subset, mask | subset) in the inner loop
Inefficient construction of masks from input using a list comprehension per line
Use of a 2D DP array var_8 with size 2 x 2^N instead of a single 1D DP

complexity.why: For each of the M items (outer loop over enumerate(var_3)), the code iterates over all 2^N bitmasks (var_6 in range(2**var_5)). Each iteration performs several constant-time operations: a subset check (var_7 & var_6 == var_6), one or two min() calls, and one or two bitwise ORs. The DP table var_8 has 2 rows and 2^N columns, so memory is proportional to 2^N.

bottlenecks.detail: Inside the inner loop, each state update does multiple min() calls and a conditional subset check, significantly increasing constant factors compared with a straightforward single-transition DP.
Using var_8 as a 2x(2^N) DP adds cache and copying overhead (swapping and repeatedly touching two rows) instead of in-place updates on one 1D array.

var_8[1][var_6] is always updated (with or without the subset branch) and var_8[1][var_7 | var_6] is also updated immediately afterward; many of these updates are redundant compared with a single dp[new_mask] = min(...) form.

The loop `for var_7 in [int(var_9) for var_9 in var_10().split()]:` builds an intermediate list for every item line. Combined with Python-level loop for OR-ing bits, this adds overhead over a more direct map-based construction.

The 2D list var_8 = [[float('inf')] * 2**var_5 for _ in range(2)] allocates a large contiguous structure twice; although still O(2^N), it doubles the memory footprint relative to a single 1D dp array.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a simple 1D bitmask DP where dp[mask] = minimum total cost to achieve exactly the skill set 'mask'. For each item, precompute its bitmask and relax dp[new_mask] for all masks via new_mask = mask | item_mask with a single transition dp[new_mask] = min(dp[new_mask], dp[mask] + cost).

complexity.why: There are M items, and for each item the algorithm iterates over all 2^N masks (var_9 in range(1 << var_8)). Each iteration performs constant-time work: one bitwise OR and a single min() on dp. The DP array var_4 has size 2^N and is updated in place for each item, so memory is linear in the number of states.

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged, but the DP formulation in the fast_code has significantly smaller constant factors: one DP array instead of two, one core min() update per state, no subset-check branch, and simpler memory access patterns. This tends to be the difference between passing and TLE at the upper bounds in Python.

transformation_steps: Collapse the 2D DP var_8[2][2^N] into a single 1D DP array var_4[2^N] representing minimal cost for each mask.

Remove the subset-check-based transition (if var_7 & var_6 == var_6) and instead use the standard cover DP transition new_mask = mask | item_mask with dp[new_mask] = min(dp[new_mask], dp[mask] + cost).
Avoid repeated min() chains per state; perform only one straightforward relaxation per (item, mask) pair.
Precompute each item's bitmask directly as a sum of bit contributions (or an OR over bits) and then reuse that mask for all transitions.
Initialize dp[0] = 0 and all others to a large sentinel (10**9) instead of float('inf') in a 2D table; this is slightly faster and simpler.
Use in-place updates on dp for each item, relying on the bitmask OR to encode the union of skills, eliminating the need for double buffering.
trigger_signals: Nested loops of the form: for item in items: for mask in range(1 << N): with complex inner logic involving multiple min() calls.
DP tables dimensioned as [2][2^N] or similar when the state is naturally representable as a single 2^N-length array.
Branch-heavy inner loops (subset checks, multiple paths) where mathematically only one canonical transition is necessary.
Use of float('inf') and 2D lists for a scalar DP problem that only needs one dimension over bitmasks.
Attempted micro-optimizations on I/O (sys.stdin.readline) while the core DP transitions remain over-complicated.
pitfalls: Changing the DP formulation must preserve the problem semantics; an over-complicated transition (like the subset-check approach) can both slow the program and risk incorrect results compared with the standard mask-OR DP.

Converting from double-buffer to in-place updates requires ensuring that each state transition uses only the previous item’s values, not partially updated ones; the chosen order of iteration (over masks) must not introduce unwanted dependencies.
Using 1 << var_8 to size the DP requires that var_8 (N) is small (e.g., <= 20); larger N would be infeasible regardless of implementation details.
Relying on Python’s large constant factors in triple-nested logic can still cause TLE even when asymptotic complexity looks acceptable; keeping the inner loop as lean as possible is crucial.

Switching away from sys.stdin.readline to input() in Python can be fine for moderate constraints, but for very heavy input scenarios, using the slower input method could become a bottleneck; here the DP dominates so it is acceptable.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer N; task is to count integers i in [1, N] whose decimal representation has an odd number of digits. Piecewise conditions (N < 100, N < 10000, N <= 100000) strongly suggest N <= 100000.

dominant_ops: Loop from 1 to N
Per-iteration int-to-string conversion
Per-iteration string-to-list conversion and length/modulo check

complexity.why: The code iterates over every integer from 1 to N. For each integer, it converts the number to a string and then to a list of characters to compute its length. If D is the maximum number of digits (≈ log10 N), each iteration costs O(D), yielding total time O(N * D). The only extra memory is the temporary list of digits of size O(D) per iteration (reused each time), so asymptotic space is O(D).

bottlenecks.detail: The algorithm performs a full linear scan over all integers up to N to count how many have an odd number of digits. Since the property depends only on digit-length ranges, a direct formula exists and the O(N) loop is unnecessary.

For every integer, the code allocates a new string (via str(var_3)) and a new list of characters (via list(str(...))). These repeated small allocations create overhead and generate garbage that the interpreter must clean up.

Calling str() on every integer inside a tight loop is relatively expensive, especially compared to simple arithmetic or direct digit-counting logic; this conversion work dominates runtime when N is large.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit that the count of numbers with an odd number of digits up to N can be expressed in closed form by summing contributions over digit-length ranges (1-digit, 3-digit, 5-digit, ...), avoiding any per-number iteration.

complexity.why: The optimized code uses a fixed, small number of comparisons and arithmetic operations regardless of N, branching on whether N is below 100, 10000, or 100000 and using prederived formulas like min(N, 9), min(N - 90, 909), and min(N - 9090, 90909). There is no loop over values up to N and no per-value allocations, so both time and space are constant in N.

complexity_delta.from: O(N * D) time, O(D) space
complexity_delta.to: O(1) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: The transformation removes the O(N) loop and all per-integer string/list conversions by replacing them with a constant-time arithmetic formula based on digit-length ranges. As a result, runtime no longer grows with N, and extra space for digit lists is eliminated.

transformation_steps: Observe that the condition "has an odd number of digits" depends only on the length of the decimal representation of each number, not on its specific digits.

Partition the domain [1, N] into intervals where all numbers share the same digit length: [1, 9] (1 digit), [10, 99] (2 digits), [100, 999] (3 digits), [1000, 9999] (4 digits), [10000, 99999] (5 digits).
Note that only intervals with odd digit lengths (1, 3, 5, ...) contribute to the result; intervals with even digit lengths (2, 4, ...) can be ignored.

For each odd-length interval, derive how many numbers up to N lie in that interval: for 1-digit numbers this is min(N, 9); for 3-digit numbers it is max(0, min(N, 999) - 99); for 5-digit numbers it is max(0, min(N, 99999) - 9999).

Algebraically simplify and encode these contributions into compact piecewise formulas using constants such as 90, 909, and 9090, resulting in branches like: if N < 100 use min(N, 9); elif N < 10000 use min(N - 90, 909); elif N <= 100000 use min(N - 9090, 90909).
Eliminate the explicit for-loop and all string/list conversions, retaining only a single input read, the constant-time arithmetic, and a single print statement.
trigger_signals: A for-loop that scales linearly with N (`for var_3 in range(1, var_1 + 1):`) where N can be as large as 100000, coupled with non-trivial work in the loop body.

Per-iteration use of `str()` and `list()` on numeric values, which are relatively heavy operations; this is a common sign that a numeric property is being computed via string manipulation instead of arithmetic.
The underlying task—counting integers by the number of digits—naturally suggests reasoning in terms of ranges [1, 9], [10, 99], [100, 999], etc., hinting that an O(1) formula should exist.

The presence of small powers-of-10 thresholds (100, 10000, 100000) in the faster solution indicates that breakpoints are determined by digit count, not by individual values, making iteration avoidable.
pitfalls: The closed-form solution assumes N is at most 100000; if the problem constraints change (e.g., larger N), additional branches for higher digit ranges (7 digits, 9 digits, etc.) must be added or a more general formula used.
It is easy to introduce off-by-one errors at digit-boundary values (9/10, 99/100, 999/1000, ...); inequalities (`<` vs `<=`) and constants (e.g., 90 vs 89) must be double-checked.
The use of magic constants like 90, 909, and 9090 makes the intent less obvious; without clear derivation or comments, future modifications risk breaking correctness.
Both versions read input via `eval(input())`, which is unsafe and unnecessary; while it does not significantly impact performance here, replacing it with `int(input())` is important for robustness.

constraints_guess.notes: Two integers n,k (or similar) are read. Fast solution is O(n) and typical AtCoder combinatorics tasks keep n ≤ 2e5 so that linear DP or factorial precomputation is feasible. Second parameter is used only in arithmetic, not as a loop bound in the fast solution.

dominant_ops: Linear precomputation of factorials and inverse factorials up to L = max(n, m)
O(1) binomial evaluations per term via factorials/inverses
pow(-1, k) without modulus in the main summation loop (O(log k) exponentiation)
Modular multiplications and additions inside the O(n) summation

complexity.time: O(L + n log n) where L = max(n, m)
complexity.why: func_1 builds factorials and inverse factorials up to L in two linear passes → O(L). The main loop runs for k = 0..n and in each iteration performs a constant number of modular multiplies/adds plus pow(-1, k) which is implemented as exponentiation by squaring → O(log k). Summed over k this gives O(n log n). Arrays var_8 and var_7 each have size L+1, so space is O(L).

bottlenecks.detail: Factorials and inverse factorials are precomputed up to L = max(n, m), even though the core combinatorial quantity can be computed using a DP depending only on n. If m is comparable to n or larger, this doubles memory and work versus an n-only DP.

Using inclusion–exclusion with pow(-1, k) inside the main loop introduces an extra log factor (O(n log n) instead of O(n)), and repeated calls to pow for signs are more expensive than a simple alternating sign variable.

Each loop iteration performs multiple modular multiplications, a modular exponentiation with exponent 2, and several factorial/inverse lookups. Although asymptotically linear in n, the constant factor is significantly larger than for a simple recurrence-based DP.
Two arrays of length L+1 (factorials and inverse factorials) are kept, which is overkill when only a single DP array of size O(n) is actually required by the problem.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid general inclusion–exclusion and explicit binomial coefficients by deriving a direct linear recurrence in n for the needed combinatorial quantity. Maintain a DP array over n that encodes the recurrence and a single scalar product representing a falling factorial in the second parameter, then combine them at the end.

complexity.why: The loop runs from 1 to n and for each iteration performs O(1) arithmetic operations: updating dp[k] using the two previous dp values and updating a single scalar var_2 with a multiplication. No pow inside the loop and no precomputation depending on m are needed. The dp list stores n+1 entries, so space is O(n).

complexity_delta.from: O(L + n log n) time, O(L) space, with L = max(n, m)
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: By replacing a factorial-based inclusion–exclusion sum with a tailored DP recurrence in n and a simple falling-factorial product in m, the solution removes the dependence on max(n, m) precomputation and avoids pow(-1, k) inside the main loop.

transformation_steps: Mathematically analyze the inclusion–exclusion expression implemented in the slow version and recognize that it can be represented via a recurrence relation in n (often involving Stirling numbers or surjection counts).

Derive a linear recurrence for the key combinatorial sequence dp[k] that uses only dp[k-1] and dp[k-2], with coefficients expressed in terms of the second parameter (m) and n, eliminating the need for factorials and binomial coefficients in the main computation.

Replace the summation and factorial-based binomial computations with a single forward DP pass over k = 1..n, and track any required m-dependent multiplicative factor as a simple falling factorial updated in O(1) per step.
Eliminate pow(-1, k) by removing the explicit inclusion–exclusion sum, thereby avoiding O(log k) exponentiation per iteration and significantly cutting constant factors.
Keep only the O(n)-size dp array and one scalar accumulator instead of O(L)-size factorial and inverse-factorial tables.
trigger_signals: Presence of factorial and inverse-factorial precomputation up to max(n, m) for a problem whose natural parameter of iteration is only n.
Use of inclusion–exclusion (alternating signs, pow(-1, k), large combinatorial coefficients) when the answer depends on a single small-ish dimension.
A linear DP recurrence in editorial/solution hints that avoids explicit binomial sums.
Repeated pow calls inside the main loop, especially pow(-1, k) without a modulus, suggesting unnecessary exponentiation overhead.
Memory footprint dominated by factorial tables even though the conceptual object is a 1D sequence in n.
pitfalls: Deriving an incorrect recurrence relation when moving from inclusion–exclusion to DP; any off-by-one in indices (e.g., using m-n+k vs m-n+k-1) will silently produce wrong answers.
Mishandling the falling factorial term (var_2 in the fast code): the bounds and order of multiplication must exactly match the combinatorial interpretation or the final multiplier will be wrong.
Forgetting modulo at intermediate steps in the recurrence, which can cause overflow or incorrect results before the final mod.

If one tries to optimize the slow version instead (rather than switching to the recurrence), it is easy to miss that pow(-1, k) each iteration is more expensive than maintaining an alternating sign variable.

Assuming that factorial precomputation up to max(n, m) is always safe; if constraints change or m is larger than expected, the slow approach can become infeasible in memory or time, whereas the recurrence-based solution scales with n only.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic task: choose integer p minimizing sum_i (a_i - p)^2. Typical constraints allow up to ~1e5-2e5 numbers with values up to around 1e9, so an O(n) or O(n log n) solution is intended; naive triple-nested loops over value ranges will time out.

dominant_ops: Integer additions and squaring inside triple-nested loops: outer loop over candidate p values (var_4), inner loop over candidate p values (var_2), and innermost loop over all array elements (var_1).

complexity.why: Let n = len(var_7), R = max(var_7) - min(var_7) + 1. The outer loop over var_4 runs R times. For each iteration it recomputes a full O(n) sum for p = var_7[0], then runs an inner loop over var_2 that spans about (R - 2) values, each doing an O(n) pass over the array. So per outer iteration: O(n + n * (R - 2)) = O(nR). Multiplied by R outer iterations gives O(nR^2). The array itself is stored once: O(n) space.

bottlenecks.detail: Unnecessary outer loop over var_4: the loop variable is never used, so the full candidate-scan work is repeated R times for no effect, inflating complexity from O(nR) to O(nR^2).
For p = var_7[0] the sum (var_7[0] - var_7[var_1])**2 is recomputed in every outer iteration, even though it is identical each time.

The code iterates over every integer p between min(var_7) and max(var_7) and recomputes the full sum of squared distances for each p, instead of using the known property that the minimizing p is near the mean.
Sorting the list just to obtain min and max costs O(n log n) and is not required; min() and max() would give these in O(n). This is minor compared to the O(nR^2) bottleneck but still suboptimal.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical fact that the sum of squared deviations Σ(a_i - p)^2 is minimized at p equal to the mean of a_i. For integer p, the optimum is attained at one of the integers nearest to the mean (floor/ceil or rounding). Compute the (rounded) mean once and a single pass to accumulate squared deviations.

complexity.why: Reading the n integers: O(n). Computing sum(var_2) is O(n). One pass to accumulate (var_2[i] - mean_rounded)**2 is O(n). No loops over the value range R of the numbers. The list itself is stored: O(n) space; only O(1) extra scalars are used.

complexity_delta.from: O(n * R^2) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: R is the numeric range max(a) - min(a) + 1. Eliminating the redundant outer loop and then replacing a full scan over all candidate p with the closed-form mean-based choice removes dependence on R entirely.

transformation_steps: Recognize the mathematical objective: minimize Σ(a_i - p)^2 over integer p.
Observe that for real p, the derivative-based minimizer is p = mean(a_i). For integer p, the minimum is achieved at floor(mean) or ceil(mean), i.e., at one of the integers nearest to the mean.
Replace the brute-force enumeration of all p between min(a) and max(a) with computing the (rounded) mean once.
Remove the unused outer var_4 loop that redundantly repeats the entire inner search.
Implement a single O(n) pass to compute the sum of squared deviations from the chosen mean.
Avoid the sort used only to obtain min and max (not needed anymore once p is determined from the mean).
trigger_signals: Triple-nested loops where two loops iterate over ranges of values and the innermost loop scans the entire array.
Loop variable (var_4) that is never used inside its body, suggesting redundant repetition of the same work.
Recomputing the same sum of squared deviations for the same candidate p multiple times.
Awareness of a standard mathematical result: sums of squared deviations are minimized at the mean.
pitfalls: Rounding behavior: For integer optimization, the minimum can be at floor(mean) or ceil(mean). Using round() is acceptable here because when the mean is exactly x.5, both x and x+1 yield the same sum of squares, and for any other fractional part the nearest integer is optimal. However, one must be aware that Python uses bankers rounding (0.5 to even); in other problems this might matter.

Potential overflow in other languages: Σ(a_i^2) can exceed 32-bit ranges when a_i is large; in Python this is safe due to arbitrary-precision integers but in fixed-width integer environments a 64-bit type or modular arithmetic might be needed.
Using eval(input()) for reading integers is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; int(input()) should be preferred, though this is not a performance issue.

Assuming the mean-based shortcut always applies: this transformation is specific to squared-loss optimization. For absolute deviations (|a_i - p|) or other cost functions, the minimizer would be different (e.g., median for absolute deviations).

constraints_guess.n_max: ≈1e9 for coordinates (x, y)
constraints_guess.notes: Single query with large coordinates; modulus is fixed at 1e9+7. Solution must avoid any O(x) or O(y) scans and minimize modular exponentiation calls.

dominant_ops: Linear search over all candidate move counts var_4 in range(0, var_6 + 1) to solve the linear system relating (x, y) to move counts.
Inside the binomial coefficient loop, repeated modular inverses via pow(var_4, var_5 - 2, var_5) for every var_4 from 1 to var_2.

complexity.why: The for-loop `for var_4 in range(var_6 + 1)` does O(var_6) work to find a valid pair (var_2, var_3). If a valid pair is found, the second loop `for var_4 in range(1, var_2 + 1)` computes C(var_2+var_3, var_2) multiplicatively. Each iteration uses pow(var_4, var_5-2, var_5), which is O(log MOD) modular exponentiation. Thus the combination part is O(var_2 * log MOD). Only O(1) extra variables are stored, so space is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: Solving the linear constraints between (x, y) and the move counts is done via a brute-force scan over var_4 in [0, var_6]. This is a linear-time search where a constant-time algebraic solution exists.
The loop computing the binomial coefficient calls pow(var_4, var_5 - 2, var_5) on every iteration, performing O(var_2) modular exponentiations instead of a single exponentiation.
For large coordinates (e.g., up to ~1e9), O(var_6) scanning and O(var_2 * log MOD) repeated exponentiations are too slow for typical contest time limits.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace the brute-force search for move counts with a direct algebraic solution of the linear system and compute the binomial coefficient using a single modular inverse. Specifically, derive closed-form counts (a, b) from (x, y) via linear equations and then compute C(a + b, a) by building numerator and denominator products once, followed by one modular exponentiation to invert the denominator using Fermat's little theorem.

complexity.time: O(k + log MOD), where k = min(a, b)
complexity.space: O(log MOD) due to recursion depth in binary exponentiation (effectively O(1) for constraints here)
complexity.why: Deriving (a, b) from (x, y) with arithmetic and divisibility checks is O(1). The numerator and denominator products for C(a + b, a) are each computed in a single O(k) loop. Only one modular inverse is computed via func_1(var_5), which is a binary exponentiation taking O(log MOD) time. The recursion depth for exponentiation is O(log MOD) and does not grow with the input coordinates.

complexity_delta.from: O(var_6 + var_2 * log MOD) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(k + log MOD) time, O(log MOD) space (effectively O(1))
complexity_delta.note: Improvements come from (1) eliminating the O(var_6) linear search for feasible move counts and (2) reducing the number of modular exponentiations from O(var_2) to 1.

transformation_steps: Model the movement as a system of linear equations: x = a + 2b, y = 2a + b for counts of the two move types. Solve this system algebraically instead of scanning.
Derive closed-form formulas for the move counts: a = (2*y - x)/3 and b = (2*x - y)/3 (up to variable renaming), with constraints that a, b are integers and non-negative.
Replace the brute-force loop over var_4 in range(var_6 + 1) with O(1) arithmetic checks: (x + y) % 3 == 0, then compute candidate counts and validate non-negativity.
Reformulate the combinatorial count as a single binomial coefficient C(a + b, a) or C(a + b, b).

Change the combination computation from per-step modular inverses in the loop to accumulating full numerator and denominator products in O(k), then computing exactly one modular inverse of the denominator using fast binary exponentiation (func_1).
Implement binary exponentiation (func_2) recursively to compute pow(base, MOD-2, MOD) in O(log MOD), and wrap it in func_1 for clarity.
trigger_signals: A loop scanning over all values from 0 to x (var_6) attempting to satisfy a simple linear equality between derived expressions of the loop variable and inputs.
Presence of a linear system with small integer coefficients, which suggests that a direct algebraic solution is possible instead of search.
Modular combinations computed via a loop that repeatedly calls pow(..., MOD-2, MOD) inside the loop body.
Very large possible coordinate inputs (suggesting ~1e9 scale), which are incompatible with naive O(n) scans or O(n * log MOD) operations.
pitfalls: When moving to the algebraic solution, it is essential to ensure that (x + y) is divisible by 3 and that the resulting move counts are integers and non-negative; neglecting these checks yields incorrect positive counts where the answer should be 0.
Integer division must be used carefully: using // instead of / is critical to avoid float inaccuracies and to preserve exact arithmetic for divisibility checks.

The recursive binary exponentiation (func_2) must correctly apply modulus at each multiplication to prevent overflow in languages without big integers; in Python this is safe but still a good practice.

Recursion depth for func_2 is O(log MOD) and safe for MOD ≈ 1e9+7, but in other environments or with different implementations, converting to an iterative binary exponentiation can avoid potential recursion limit issues.

The multiplicative formula for the binomial coefficient relies on the denominator being invertible modulo MOD; this is only valid because MOD is prime (1e9+7). Using the same approach with a non-prime modulus would fail.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case. var_4 (N in combinations) is likely up to ~2e5 (factorial precomputation size), var_1 (number to factor) up to around 1e9–1e12 (trial division up to sqrt(N) is used).

dominant_ops: Trial division factorization of var_1 up to sqrt(var_1) in func_3
Global precomputation of factorials and inverse factorials up to var_2 = 2*10^5+10
O(1) binomial coefficient queries via precomputed factorials in func_1/func_2 for each prime exponent

complexity.time: O(MAXN + sqrt(M)) where MAXN ≈ 2e5 (factorial precompute) and M = var_1 (number to factor)
complexity.space: O(MAXN) for three arrays of length ~2e5 (factorials, modular inverses, inverse factorials)
complexity.why: Factorization uses trial division up to sqrt(M) in func_3, which is O(sqrt(M)) for a single M. The three arrays var_6, var_7, var_9 are each size O(MAXN), and they are all filled in a single O(MAXN) loop. Each combination query is then O(1) using precomputed factorials and inverse factorials.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorials and inverse factorials are precomputed up to a fixed upper bound var_2 = 2*10^5+10 regardless of the actual input sizes. For a single query, this O(2e5) setup can dominate runtime when the factorization itself is cheap.
Three int arrays of size ~2e5 are always allocated. This is acceptable but unnecessary if N (var_4) is small and only a few binomial coefficients are needed.

The code relies on a hard-coded var_2. If constraints changed so that var_4+max_exponent exceeded 2e5, this implementation would break or require increasing var_2 further, increasing memory and precomputation cost.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial/inverse factorial precomputation by computing the required binomial coefficients on the fly using the multiplicative formula and modular inverses via fast exponentiation, while still using trial division to factor var_1 and iterating only over the exponents of its prime factors.

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + sum_e (e * log MOD)) where M = var_1 and e ranges over prime exponents of M
complexity.space: O(1) auxiliary space besides a few integers; no large precomputed arrays
complexity.why: Factorization in func_1 still uses trial division up to sqrt(var_7), so it is O(sqrt(M)). For each prime exponent e, combinations C(var_3-1+e, e) are built multiplicatively: a loop of length e, each step doing a modular inverse via pow(., MOD-2, MOD), which is O(log MOD). Since sum_e e = O(log M) (total exponent of prime factorization is small for typical constraints), the binomial-related work is negligible compared to factorization, and there is no O(MAXN) precomputation.

complexity_delta.from: O(MAXN + sqrt(M)) time, O(MAXN) space with MAXN ≈ 2e5 due to factorial and inverse factorial tables
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + sum_e (e * log MOD)) time, O(1) extra space; practically dominated by O(sqrt(M)) with small extra overhead from modular inverses
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time remains dominated by the trial division factorization in both versions; the main practical win is removing the O(MAXN) precomputation and memory, trading it for small per-binomial costs.

transformation_steps: Replace global factorial and inverse factorial precomputation with on-the-fly computation of binomial coefficients using the multiplicative formula C(n, k) = product_{i=0..k-1} (n - i) * inv(i + 1) mod MOD.
Compute modular inverses as needed via pow(x, MOD-2, MOD) (Fermat’s little theorem) instead of maintaining a full inverse table.
Refactor prime factorization to a generator (func_1) that yields exponents of prime factors, then iterate over those exponents directly in func_2.
Eliminate large global arrays (var_6, var_7, var_9) and the associated initialization loop, reducing space to O(1) and cutting fixed startup cost.
Preserve the overall mathematical structure: the final answer is still the product over prime exponents of combinations C(N + e - 1, e), just computed differently.
trigger_signals: The original code precomputes factorials and inverse factorials up to a fixed large bound (≈2e5) for only one or very few combination queries.
Memory footprint includes multiple arrays of length ≈2e5 even though the number of necessary combinations is only proportional to the number of prime factors (O(log M)).
Performance profiling would show a significant portion of time spent in the factorial/inverse precomputation loop rather than in the problem-specific logic.
Need to adapt to potentially larger constraints without linearly scaling the precomputation size.
pitfalls: In the fast version’s factorization, the loop condition uses var_6 * var_6 <= var_7 instead of the reduced var_8, so the outer factorization loop continues up to sqrt(original N) even when var_8 has become 1. This does not break correctness but wastes time and forfeits a possible early stop optimization present in the original code.

The generator yields exponents for every odd candidate var_6 (including composites), outputting many zeros. While zeros are later ignored (inner range(var_5) is empty), this still adds generator and loop overhead.

On-the-fly modular inverses via pow(x, MOD-2, MOD) add a log MOD factor; if exponents e or the number of binomial evaluations became large, the cost could surpass the original O(1) per-query factorial-based method.
Care is needed to maintain correct modular multiplication order and avoid overflow; although Python ints are unbounded, in other languages one would need explicit 64-bit modular arithmetic handling.

The removal of precomputed factorials means losing the ability to answer many different binomial queries efficiently; this trade-off is only beneficial when the number of queries is small (as in this problem).

constraints_guess.notes: Typical 'number of divisors of N!' problem (e.g., AtCoder ABC 052 C) with N up to around 10^4. Original code precomputes primes only up to 10^3, consistent with sqrt(N_max) for N_max≈10^6, but an O(N*sqrtN) factorization loop suggests intended N is closer to 10^4 for runtime feasibility.

dominant_ops: Repeated prime factorization of every integer k in [2, N] using trial division by precomputed primes up to sqrt(k)
Heavy use of defaultdict and per-k temporary dictionaries for factorization results
Iteration over dictionary items via list(func_2(k).items()), creating many short-lived lists

complexity.time: O(N * sqrt(N)) (more precisely O(N * pi(sqrt(N))) where pi is prime-counting function)
complexity.space: O(N / log N) for prime list + O(number_of_distinct_primes_in_[2,N]) for the cumulative exponent map
complexity.why: func_3 iterates k from 2 to N. For each k, func_2 runs trial division by all primes <= sqrt(k). That yields Θ(sqrt(k)/log(sqrt(k))) trial divisions in the worst case, so total work is ≈ Σ_{k=2..N} sqrt(k)/log k = Θ(N*sqrt(N)/log N). Memory is dominated by the list of primes up to 10^3 and the global map of prime exponents.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorization is performed independently for every k in [2, N], each via trial division up to sqrt(k). No reuse of partial results across k.
func_2 allocates a new defaultdict for each k and func_3 materializes list(func_2(k).items()), causing many small heap allocations and dictionary operations.
Nested loops: outer over k in [2, N], inner over primes up to sqrt(k), and potentially inner-most while loops extracting repeated prime factors. This triple-nesting multiplies overhead.
Modulo is applied inside the multiplication loop (var_10 *= var_3 + 1; var_10 %= var_1), incurring extra Python integer operations each step.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep a single global array var_2 indexed by factor value to accumulate exponents across all k in [2, N], and factor each k in-place using simple trial division (2 then odd numbers). This removes dictionary allocations and per-k maps, instead using a flat integer array and direct indexing. Also apply the modulus only once at the end.

complexity.why: Each number k is still factorized by trial division up to sqrt(k), so the asymptotic factorization cost is unchanged: Σ_{k=2..N} O(sqrt(k)) = O(N*sqrt(N)). However, replacing dictionaries with a single integer array eliminates per-k allocation and hashing overhead, dramatically reducing constant factors. Space is O(N) for var_2 of length N+1, which directly stores exponents for all possible factors.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(N * sqrt(N)) with high constant factors due to dictionaries and prime list traversal. Space: O(N / log N + P) where P is number of distinct primes needed.
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(N * sqrt(N)) with substantially smaller constant factors via contiguous array and fewer allocations. Space: O(N) for a single exponent array.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time complexity remains O(N * sqrt(N)), but practical runtime improves significantly due to elimination of hash maps, list constructions, and repeated item-views, and by aggregating exponents directly into a flat array.

transformation_steps: Removed the global sieve and precomputed prime list; factorization now uses plain trial division by 2 and subsequent odd integers.
Replaced per-call defaultdict factor maps with a single global integer array var_2 sized N+1, where index i holds the total exponent of factor i across all k in [2, N].
Inlined factorization into func_1(var_7) and called it for each k in the range, avoiding constructing and merging many small dictionaries.
Eliminated list(func_2(k).items()) overhead; exponents are accumulated directly into var_2 as integers without temporary containers.

Moved modulo operation: instead of applying % 1e9+7 on every multiplication, the fast code multiplies into var_3 and applies the modulus once at the end (trading slightly larger intermediates for fewer modular reductions).
Simplified I/O and control flow, reducing function-call overhead and nested iteration over prime lists.
trigger_signals: Use of defaultdict for every k in [2, N], indicating heavy dynamic allocation and hashing in the innermost computation.
Nested factorization: an outer loop over k with an inner loop over primes for each k, which is borderline for N around 10^4–10^5 in Python when combined with dictionaries.
Creation of list(func_2(k).items()) for each k, a clear signal of repeated short-lived list allocations in hot paths.
Modulo operations inside a tight loop, which are relatively expensive on Python big integers.
pitfalls: The fast code still uses naive trial division and thus retains O(N * sqrt(N)) time; for substantially larger N (e.g., N>=10^5..10^6), both versions would likely TLE, and a sieve-based exponent accumulation for N! (e.g., using prime sieving plus exponent summation via floor divisions N/p + N/p^2 + ...) would be preferable.

The exponent array var_2 has length N+1 and indexes by factor value. For very large N, this direct-index array becomes memory-heavy; a sparse mapping (e.g., dictionary keyed by primes only) may be more space-efficient.

The fast code computes var_3 without intermediate modulo; for larger N, this product can become extremely large, causing performance issues due to Python big-int arithmetic, even if it fits in memory. Applying modulo periodically would cap integer sizes.

The fast code uses eval(input()) for reading N, which is slower and unsafe in general contexts; in competitive programming it may pass, but for production or online judges, int(input()) is safer and clearer.

Care must be taken that exponents are only accumulated for actual primes. While naive trial division over 2 and odd numbers works correctly (composites will not divide the residual once their prime factors are removed), any modification that skips smaller factors or changes the traversal order could introduce composite-factor entries and break the divisor-count formula.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic 'pairwise/setwise/not coprime' classification. Values ai up to about 1e6 (matching sieve limit). Single test case, time limit ~1–2s typical of AtCoder/AOJ.

dominant_ops: Building smallest-prime-factor (SPF) array up to 1e6 via sieve
Factoring each input number using SPF and checking prime reuse
Running cumulative gcd over all numbers

complexity.time: O(M log log M + n log A_max)
complexity.why: Sieve-like SPF construction over M = 1e6 costs about sum_{p prime<=M} M/p = O(M log log M). For each of n numbers, factorization via SPF is O(#prime_factors(ai)) ⊆ O(log ai), and cumulative gcd is O(n log A_max). Auxiliary arrays (SPF and last-seen index) are size M.

bottlenecks.detail: SPF is always built up to var_2 = 1e6 even if max(input) is much smaller; this costs fixed O(1e6 log log 1e6) operations regardless of actual data.

The sieve is a straightforward SPF variant but loops from 2..M and then through all multiples. Asymptotically fine, but it dominates runtime for typical n (≤1e5) because factorization and gcd are cheaper.
Using eval(input()) instead of int(input()) adds overhead and is unsafe, though it is minor compared to the sieve cost.

FastAudit.core_idea: Refactor the logic into separate functions: build an SPF array with a slightly optimized sieve (pre-filling even multiples), use sets to track seen prime factors for pairwise coprimality, and compute gcd in a dedicated function for setwise coprimality detection.

complexity.time: O(M log log M + n log A_max)
complexity.why: func_2 builds SPF up to 1e6 with a typical Eratosthenes-style process: evens filled in O(M), then primes fill their multiples in total O(M log log M). func_3 factorizes each number using SPF (O(#prime_factors(ai))) and uses sets to track primes, adding a logarithmic factor in practice for hash operations but not changing big-O. func_1 runs cumulative gcd in O(n log A_max). Sets var_8 and var_9 store distinct primes seen, bounded by number of distinct primes dividing all inputs.

complexity_delta.from: O(M log log M + n log A_max) time, O(M) space
complexity_delta.to: O(M log log M + n log A_max) time, O(M + P) space (P = #distinct primes used in sets)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged. The modified version reorganizes the code and may alter constant factors (SPF construction slightly optimized; set-based tracking adds overhead vs array).

transformation_steps: Extracted SPF construction into func_2, pre-filling even indices with factor 2 to reduce work in the main sieve loop.
Replaced array-based last-seen index tracking (var_9 indexed by prime) with set-based tracking (var_8 for current number, var_9 for global primes) in func_3.
Separated gcd aggregation into func_1, computing overall gcd in a clean loop over the list.
Wrapped decision logic into func_4 returning 0/1/2, then mapped to output strings via an index into ["pairwise", "setwise", "not"].
Adjusted printing to build a structured result (though currently printing a tuple rather than a single concatenated string).
trigger_signals: Desire to modularize code into reusable functions (SPF builder, coprimality checker, gcd aggregator).
Recognition that SPF building is a reusable operation and should be factored out of the main input-processing logic.
Interest in more declarative data handling via sets for prime usage tracking instead of manual index bookkeeping.
pitfalls: Using sets for prime tracking introduces extra per-operation overhead compared to integer-indexed arrays; for large n and many factors per number, the original array-based approach may actually be faster in practice despite similar big-O.
func_2 still builds SPF up to a hard-coded 1e6; if input values are much smaller, both versions do unnecessary sieve work. A better optimization is to limit SPF size to max(var_1).

The final print in fast_code outputs a Python tuple (e.g., ('pairwise', 'coprime')) instead of the exact original string 'pairwise coprime'; this is a functional/formatting difference, not a performance one.

Calling func_2 inside func_3 rebuilds the SPF every time func_3 is called; this is fine here because func_3 is called once, but in a multi-testcase setting SPF should be built once and reused to avoid repeated O(M log log M) cost.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical of AtCoder ABC-level math problem: N up to 1e5, M up to about 1e9. Need factorization of M and binomial coefficients C(e_i + N - 1, e_i) modulo 1e9+7. Only one query per run.

dominant_ops: Precomputing factorials var_10[0..var_2-1] with modular multiplication (O(var_2) ~ 2e5 steps).
Precomputing inverse factorials var_12[0..var_2-1] using one modular exponentiation pow(fact[var_2-1], MOD-2) + backward loop (O(var_2) + O(log MOD)).
Trial-division factorization of M up to sqrt(M) with repeated division for each prime factor.
A few O(1) modular multiplications per prime factor to evaluate binomial coefficients via precomputed factorials.

complexity.time: O(var_2 + sqrt(M)) ≈ O(N_max + sqrt(M)) per run, with var_2 fixed at 2*10^5, plus very small overhead per distinct prime factor of M.
complexity.space: O(var_2) for factorial and inverse-factorial arrays, i.e., Θ(2*10^5) integers.
complexity.why: The factorial and inverse-factorial precomputation loops run over the full fixed range var_2, independent of the actual N and of the small exponents in M’s factorization. Factorization itself is O(sqrt(M)), but for the intended constraints the O(var_2) precomputation is the main cost and memory consumer.

bottlenecks.detail: var_2 is hard-coded to 2*10^5, so factorials and inverse factorials are computed for the entire range even if the actual maximum n in C(n, k) = e_i + N - 1 is significantly smaller. For a single query this dominates runtime.

Two arrays of size 2*10^5 (factorials and inverse factorials) are allocated and filled. This is not huge but is overkill given the tiny k (exponents of prime factors) and one-shot nature of the computation.
Even when M is small or N is small, the code still pays the full O(var_2) cost every run. The factorization part is relatively cheap compared to the unconditional precomputation.
The pow(fact[var_2-1], MOD-2, MOD) call is O(log MOD). It is not the main bottleneck, but it is an extra fixed cost that disappears in the fast version.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial/inverse-factorial precomputation and compute each needed binomial coefficient C(n, k) directly via a multiplicative formula using big integers. Since all k (prime exponents) are tiny, this reduces the dependence on N and removes the O(N)-sized precomputation altogether.

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + Σ e_i) ≈ O(sqrt(M)), where e_i are the exponents in M’s prime factorization and each C(n, e_i) is computed in O(e_i) time. For M up to around 1e9, e_i ≤ ~30, so the binomial part is effectively O(1).
complexity.space: O(1) extra space beyond a small list of prime factors; no large factorial tables.
complexity.why: The factorization is similar to the slow code (trial division up to sqrt(M)). The key improvement is replacing O(var_2) factorial precomputation with an on-the-fly multiplicative computation of C(n, k) that only loops up to k, and k (exponent) is bounded by log M, not by N.

complexity_delta.from: O(var_2 + sqrt(M)) time and O(var_2) space, with var_2 fixed at 2*10^5 (effectively O(N_max + sqrt(M))).
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + Σ e_i) time and O(1) extra space, with Σ e_i ≤ O(log M) and no dependence on N in loops.
complexity_delta.note: The optimized (fast) version removes the O(N_max) precomputation cost and large auxiliary arrays by exploiting that the binomial parameters have very small k (prime exponents) and only a single query is processed.

transformation_steps: Removed global factorial and inverse-factorial precomputation arrays (var_10 and var_12) of size 2*10^5.

Replaced the combinatorial helper func_2(n, k) that used precomputed factorials with a new func_1(n, k) that directly computes C(n, k) via a multiplicative formula: numerator = n * (n-1) * ... * (n-k+1), denominator = k * (k-1) * ... * 1, and returns numerator // denominator.

Dropped the modular inverse logic and per-index inverse factorial recursion; instead, rely on integer arithmetic to compute exact C(n, k) and only then take modulo 1e9+7 at the final aggregation step.

Kept a simple trial-division factorization (func_2 in fast code) that returns a list of primes with multiplicity; used Counter to turn it into exponents e_i, matching the mathematical structure product_i C(e_i + N - 1, e_i).
Simplified state: no global precomputed tables, the only per-run heavy work is factorizing M, then a few small loops for binomials.
trigger_signals: Profiling or timing shows that the majority of runtime in the slow version is spent in the O(var_2) loops that build factorial and inverse-factorial tables, despite only a handful of binomial coefficients being needed.
Inspection of constraints reveals that exponents of primes in M are tiny (e_i ≤ ~30), meaning C(e_i + N - 1, e_i) has small k and can be computed in O(k) without precomputation.
Observation that the problem only has a single query, so the standard competitive-programming pattern of building reusable factorial tables is unnecessary overhead here.
Recognition that the binomial n values depend on N (up to 1e5) but k values do not, making an O(k) multiplicative method attractive compared to an O(N)-sized precomputation.
pitfalls: The fast version relies on computing C(n, k) using big integers without modular reduction inside the loop. This works well because k is very small; for larger k (e.g., k up to 1e5), intermediate integers would become enormous, causing severe slowdown and memory pressure.

Integer division (//) in func_1 assumes that the numerator is exactly divisible by the denominator. For standard binomial coefficients this is mathematically correct, but any accidental mismatch or integer overflow in other contexts would cause bugs.

The optimized approach is less general: it is tailored to small k and a single query. For many queries or large k, the original factorial/inverse-factorial precomputation can become superior in practice.

Because the binomial computation no longer reduces modulo 1e9+7 at each multiplication, the intermediate big integers are larger than in the slow version that keeps all arithmetic modulo MOD. This is acceptable here but would be problematic for much larger parameters.

Both versions use naive trial-division factorization up to sqrt(M); if M’s upper bound were significantly larger (e.g., 10^12 or higher), more advanced factorization techniques or precomputed primes would be required to keep performance acceptable.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style problem: minimize sum_i (xi - p)^2 over integer p. N likely up to 1e2–2e5, |xi| up to about 1e9. No separate queries; single batch computation.

dominant_ops: Sorting the array: O(n log n).
Outer loop over var_4 from min_x to max_x (range length R = max_x - min_x + 1): O(R) iterations.
Inside each outer iteration, a full recomputation of the minimum over all candidate centers var_2 in [min_x+1, max_x-1], each requiring a loop over all n elements: O(R * n) per outer iteration.
Overall, the triple-nested loops perform on the order of n * R^2 evaluations of (candidate - xi) ** 2.

complexity.why: Let R = max(var_7) - min(var_7) + 1. The array is sorted once: O(n log n). The outer loop over var_4 runs R times. For each iteration, it first computes one O(n) sum (using var_7[0], which does not depend on var_4), then runs an inner loop over var_2 across ~R candidates, and for each var_2 it loops over all n elements. This yields O(R * (n + R * n)) = O(n * R^2) time. All computations are done in-place using a fixed number of scalar variables, so space usage is O(1) beyond the input array.

bottlenecks.detail: The outer loop `for var_4 in range(var_7[0], var_7[len(var_7) - 1] + 1)` does not affect any computation inside (var_4 is never used). It redundantly repeats the entire search for the best center R times.

For each candidate center var_2, the code recomputes `sum((var_2 - xi)**2 for xi in var_7)` from scratch, instead of using any incremental update or mathematical shortcut. Coupled with the unused outer loop, this leads to O(n * R^2) work.

The objective is a convex quadratic function in p: f(p) = sum_i (xi - p)^2, which has a known analytic minimizer at the mean of xi (with the integer optimum at floor/ceil of the mean). Brute-forcing all integer p in [min_x, max_x] ignores this structure.

Both inner cost computations use `var_7[0]` and `var_2` but never `var_4`. The outer loop is therefore logically redundant and misleading, suggesting a design error that also massively inflates runtime.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical property that the sum of squared deviations f(p) = sum_i (xi - p)^2 is minimized at the mean of xi. Since p must be an integer, the minimum occurs at either floor(mean) or ceil(mean). Compute the mean once, choose the closer integer (or check both), and then compute the sum of squared differences in a single pass over the array.

complexity.why: The optimized code performs: (1) one pass to read the numbers and compute their sum: O(n); (2) O(1) work to compute the mean and select between floor/ceil; (3) one pass to compute the final sum of squared differences: O(n). No loops over the value range [min_x, max_x] are needed, and no sorting is required. Total time is thus O(n), with only a constant amount of extra scalar storage, giving O(1) additional space.

complexity_delta.to: O(n)
complexity_delta.note: R = max(x) - min(x) + 1. The original code brute-forced candidate centers across the entire value range in nested loops (and even redundantly repeated the search). The optimized code exploits the quadratic structure of the objective and uses the mean to directly find the optimal integer p, removing two levels of looping over R.

transformation_steps: Recognize the problem as minimizing f(p) = sum_i (xi - p)^2 with respect to an integer p, a one-dimensional least-squares problem.
Use calculus/known identity: for real p, the minimizer of sum_i (xi - p)^2 is p* = (1/n) * sum_i xi (the mean).
Since p must be integer, note that the optimal integer lies among floor(p*) and ceil(p*); either pick the closer one or explicitly check both.

Remove the brute-force loops over all candidate p in [min_x, max_x] and the redundant outer loop, keeping only two linear passes: one to compute the mean, one to compute the final sum of squared deviations.
Drop the unnecessary sort, because the objective and the mean depend only on the multiset of values, not on their order.
Implement the final solution as: read n and array, compute mean = sum / n, choose integer center nearest to mean, accumulate sum((xi - center)**2) in a single loop, and print the result.
trigger_signals: Nested loops where the innermost loop is over all n elements for each candidate center value, suggesting an O(n * R) or worse pattern.
A brute-force search over a contiguous integer range [min_x, max_x] for a minimum of a smooth-looking function based on squared differences.
Repeated evaluation of `(candidate - xi)**2` where the candidate shifts by 1 between iterations, indicating a structured quadratic objective with potential analytic solution.
The target expression being the sum of squared deviations, a classic scenario where the mean (and its neighbors for integer constraints) is known to be optimal.
pitfalls: Floating-point mean: `var_8 = sum(var_7) / var_3` uses float division. For typical constraints (e.g., n up to 1e5–1e6 and |xi| up to 1e9), Python’s double precision is exact for the integer sum, but rounding can slightly shift the mean. The code mitigates this by comparing distances to floor and floor+1, which is robust for this problem; however, for extremely large magnitudes or different languages this might require extra care.

Integer candidate set: The mathematical minimizer is the real mean, but the feasible set is integers. A common bug is to fix p = round(mean) without checking neighboring integers; here the code correctly compares floor and floor+1 via absolute differences.

Unnecessary use of eval: `int(eval(input()))` is slower and unsafe compared to `int(input())`. While not a performance bottleneck in typical contest settings, it is a bad practice and can pose security risks in other contexts.

Overflow/precision in other environments: Python’s big integers avoid overflow when summing xi and squaring differences, but in fixed-width integer languages, intermediate values (especially (xi - p)^2 and the total sum) may overflow and require 64-bit types or explicit checks.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task scheduling / feasibility check with N up to ~2e5 and 1s time limit; I/O overhead is critical.

dominant_ops: High-overhead input parsing via eval(input()) and tiny wrapper functions
Building and sorting an O(N) list of jobs

complexity.why: The main cost is sorting the list of N job entries. Input parsing is linear but with heavy constant factors due to eval and function wrapper calls.

bottlenecks.detail: Uses eval(input()) for the first integer and a chain of small Python functions (func_1, func_4, etc.) around input(), adding multiple Python-level calls and eval overhead per read.
eval(input()) is not only slow (parsing arbitrary Python expression) but also unsafe for untrusted input; a simple int(input()) would suffice.

Imports math, itertools, bisect, copy, deque, Counter, Decimal, and defines multiple helper functions that are unused in the core logic; they don’t change asymptotics but reflect unnecessary complexity and minor startup overhead.
Stores each job as a separate list element and sorts all N entries. If many jobs share the same deadline, this misses an opportunity to aggregate, leading to a larger sort than necessary.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use fast buffered input (sys.stdin.readline), avoid eval and wrapper functions, and aggregate jobs by deadline using a defaultdict so that sorting is performed on the set of unique deadlines instead of all raw entries.

complexity.time: O(K log K) with K ≤ N (number of unique deadlines)
complexity.why: Reading and aggregating is linear in N. Sorting occurs on K dictionary entries (unique deadlines) rather than N raw pairs. In worst case K = N, matching the original O(N log N), but in practice K can be much smaller and constant factors are significantly reduced via cheaper I/O and simpler logic.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log N) time, O(N) space on N raw jobs with heavy I/O and eval overhead.
complexity_delta.to: O(K log K) time, O(K) space where K is number of unique deadlines, with low-overhead I/O; asymptotically same worst case but often faster in practice.
complexity_delta.note: The theoretical big-O does not fundamentally change in the worst case, but constants drop substantially and the effective input size for sorting can shrink from N to K.

transformation_steps: Replace eval(input()) with faster and safer integer reading via sys.stdin.readline and int().
Remove or bypass small input wrapper functions (func_1, func_4, etc.) to avoid extra Python call overhead per line.
Eliminate unused imports and helper functions, keeping only what is needed for the core algorithm.
Introduce a defaultdict(int) keyed by deadline to aggregate required times for identical deadlines during the read loop.
Convert the aggregated dictionary to a list of (deadline, total_required) pairs and sort it by deadline.
Iterate the sorted aggregated list, maintaining cumulative work and checking feasibility (cumulative <= deadline), exiting early on failure.
trigger_signals: Use of eval(input()) to parse integers, which is a classic red flag for performance and safety.
Multiple thin wrapper functions around input() in a tight loop, indicating unnecessary function call overhead.
Large N (typical competitive programming upper bounds ~1e5–2e5) combined with pure Python and 1s limit, making I/O optimization important.
Presence of many unused imports, suggesting template code where performance tuning was not yet applied.
Sorting a potentially large list of raw entries when aggregation by key is possible.
pitfalls: Replacing input() with sys.stdin.readline requires manually stripping newlines and converting types; forgetting this can cause subtle bugs.
Using eval on arbitrary input is dangerous in any real system; switching to int() is both faster and safer.
When aggregating into a dictionary, one must ensure the key is correct (deadline vs duration) and that the accumulation (+=) is applied to the required amount, not the time bound.
If deadlines can be very large but sparse, switching to a list indexed by deadline instead of a dict would be wrong or memory-inefficient; dict/defaultdict is appropriate here.
Early exit (exit() or break) must preserve correct final output; ensure 'Yes' vs 'No' logic remains identical after refactoring.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style problem: given n and m (≈1e9), factorize m and compute a product of binomial coefficients C(e_i + n - 1, e_i) modulo 1e9+7. Prime exponents e_i are small (O(log m)).

dominant_ops: math.factorial on arguments as large as n (~1e9)
arbitrary-precision integer multiplications and divisions on extremely large factorial values
repeated creation of list(dict.keys()) inside tight factorization loop

complexity.why: Factorization func_2 runs in O(sqrt(m)) divisions which is fine. The main cost is func_1: factorial(k) for k up to N = n + e - 1 (≈ n) has time at least linear in k due to multiplying all integers up to k with large big-int sizes. Even with memoization, factorial(n) and factorial(n-1) are each computed once, making total work Θ(N) big-int multiplications. The size of factorial(N) is Θ(N log N) bits, so space grows linearly with N and intermediate arithmetic cost is enormous.

bottlenecks.detail: Computing binomial coefficients via full factorials: C(a, b) = factorial(a) // (factorial(a-b) * factorial(b)) with a ≈ n (~1e9). This creates factorial(1e9)-sized integers (billions of digits), which is infeasible in time and memory.

No modular reduction is applied during factorial computation or during binomial construction. All arithmetic is on huge exact integers, leading to massive big-int multiplications and divisions before finally taking % 1e9+7 at the end.

In func_2, membership check `if var_5 in list(var_11.keys())` recreates a list of keys on every iteration, turning an O(1) dict lookup into O(#keys). Although #keys is small here (few prime factors), this is still unnecessary overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid gigantic factorials by computing each binomial coefficient C(e + n - 1, e) using a multiplicative formula that runs only O(e) steps, where e is the prime exponent (≤ O(log m)). This keeps integers at the scale of the binomial value itself (≈ (n^e) / e!), which is only a few hundred bits, instead of building factorial(n) with billions of digits. The prime factorization is retained but represented as a list of (prime, exponent) pairs.

complexity.why: Factorization remains O(sqrt(m)). For each prime exponent e_i, func_1 runs a loop of length e_i, multiplying and dividing numbers of size O(e_i * log n) bits. Since m ≤ 1e9, e_i ≤ ~30, so sum e_i is small. The largest intermediate integer in constructing C(e_i + n - 1, e_i) has bit-length O(e_i log n) (about a few hundred bits), so both time and space are tiny compared to building factorial(n) with Θ(n log n) bits.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(sqrt(m) + N) with N ≈ n due to factorial(N). Space: O(N log N) bits from factorial(N) and related intermediates.
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(sqrt(m) + sum e_i) with sum e_i ≤ O(log m). Space: O(log n * max e_i) bits, i.e., a few hundred bits.
complexity_delta.note: The key reduction is in the argument size of factorial-like operations: from computing factorial(N) for N ≈ 1e9 (billions of digits) to computing a binomial via O(e) multiplicative steps where e ≤ ~30. This changes practical runtime from impossible/TLE to easily acceptable.

transformation_steps: Replace factorial-based binomial computation with a multiplicative nCr formula: for C(a, b), iteratively multiply numerator and denominator over b terms instead of calling factorial(a), factorial(b), factorial(a-b).
Ensure the multiplicative binomial operates only over the smaller parameter (here the exponent e) so that loop length is O(e) not O(a). In this problem, use C(e + n - 1, e) with a loop of length e.

Keep all arithmetic integer-based and only perform final modulo operations after the exact binomial value is obtained (or optionally reduce modulo after safe integer operations) to avoid precision issues.
Simplify prime factorization storage from a dict with repeated key-list generation to a list of (prime, exponent) tuples, avoiding unnecessary overhead in the factorization loop.

Accumulate the product of binomial coefficients under modulo 1e9+7 during the aggregation step so the final result is always kept small, even though exact binomial computations themselves are inexpensive in this setting.
trigger_signals: Use of math.factorial directly on values derived from input n, especially when n can be as large as 1e9.
Binomial coefficient computed via factorial(a) // (factorial(b) * factorial(a-b)) with a tied directly to a potentially huge input parameter.
No modulo applied until the very final print statement, despite working toward an answer modulo 1e9+7.
Observation that combinatorial parameters like r (here exponent e) are much smaller than n, suggesting a multiplicative O(r) binomial is preferable to factorial-based O(n) methods.
Frequent appearance of enormous intermediate integers (very long decimal strings or extremely slow arithmetic) in profiling or during test runs.
pitfalls: Attempting to combine modular arithmetic with binomial computation by taking modulo on both numerator and denominator and then using integer division; this breaks correctness because division in modular arithmetic requires multiplicative inverses, not integer division.
Implementing the multiplicative nCr incorrectly (e.g., off-by-one in the loop bounds or mixing up which parameter is smaller), which can change complexity back to O(a) or produce wrong results.
Assuming that factorial-based methods are safe because n is 'just' up to 1e9; factorial(1e9) is astronomically large and infeasible to compute exactly.
Overusing list(dict.keys()) or similar patterns inside tight loops during factorization, which may not dominate for very small m but can still contribute unnecessary overhead.

Porting the approach to languages without arbitrary-precision integers and trying to store the full binomial value before applying modulo; in such cases, one must use modular multiplication and modular inverses throughout.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer N, computing number of divisors of N! modulo 1e9+7. Typical constraints likely N in [1e3, 1e5]; original code would TLE for much larger N due to ~O(N^2) work.

dominant_ops: Naive primality detection up to N using trial division inside func_2 (for each x up to N, try all integers up to sqrt(x)).
For each k in [1..N], func_1 scans all indices up to k and, for prime indices, repeatedly divides k by that prime to count exponents.
For each k in [1..N], allocates a length-N list of exponents (var_6) and performs a full element-wise addition var_9 = var_9 + var_3, costing O(N) per k.

complexity.why: func_2 performs O(N * sqrt(N)) trial divisions, but the main cost is the outer loop k=1..N calling func_1. Each func_1 runs a loop up to k (O(k)) and allocates/initializes a length-N list. Additionally, for each k, an O(N) list-comprehension sums var_9 and var_3. Summing over k gives Θ(N^2) element operations and allocations. Auxiliary data (prime flags, exponent arrays) is linear in N.

bottlenecks.detail: Primality is computed via trial division for every number up to N (func_2) instead of using a sieve, leading to O(N * sqrt(N)) rather than O(N log log N).
Prime exponents of each k are recomputed from scratch, scanning all candidates up to k and doing trial divisions, yielding a cumulative Θ(N^2) pattern.
For each k, a new length-N list of exponents is allocated and then combined with var_9 via an O(N) list comprehension, resulting in Θ(N^2) element-wise additions and repeated allocations.

Uses true division (/) when updating var_5 in func_1 instead of integer division (//). Python 3 keeps it as float and then implicitly converts, which is slower and potentially unsafe for large integers.

FastAudit.core_idea: Precompute all primes up to N via a Sieve of Eratosthenes, then factor every integer from 2 to N using only these primes while aggregating prime exponents in a single global map. Finally, compute the number of divisors of N! using the formula ∏(e_p + 1) modulo 1e9+7, without building per-k exponent vectors or performing repeated vector additions.

complexity.time: O(N^2 / log^2 N) in the worst case; empirically much faster than the original O(N^2) for typical contest bounds.
complexity.why: The sieve runs in O(N log log N). The factorization loop iterates k from 2..N and, for each prime p, divides k by p until not divisible, updating the exponent map. Every successful division corresponds to one factor in the factorization of N!, giving a total of O(N log log N) successful divisions. However, for prime k near N, the code still tests all smaller primes before finding k itself, leading to ~π(k) checks for that k.
