Summed over all primes this yields ~Θ(N^2 / log^2 N) trial checks in the worst case. Memory is dominated by the sieve array (size N) and a dictionary entry per prime up to N.

complexity_delta.from: O(N^2) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N^2 / log^2 N) worst-case time (and roughly O(N log log N) successful factorizations), O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: The new code removes repeated length-N vector work and naive primality checks, instead using a sieve plus aggregated factor counts. Asymptotically still superlinear, but substantially faster for typical constraints due to eliminating Θ(N^2) list operations and expensive primality tests.

transformation_steps: Replace naive primality detection (func_2) with a Sieve of Eratosthenes over [2..N], producing a reusable list of primes.
Stop building a full exponent vector per k; instead, factor each k directly into a global defaultdict(int) that accumulates exponents for primes across all k in [2..N].
Eliminate per-k vector additions var_9 = var_9 + var_3; the aggregated exponent map var_5 already holds the total exponents for N!.
Compute the final answer as a single pass over var_5.values(), multiplying (e_p + 1) modulo 1e9+7, instead of iterating over N-length arrays.
Use integer division (//) during factorization to keep numbers as ints and avoid floating point overhead.
trigger_signals: Presence of nested loops over k in [1..N] with inner loops up to k and list sizes of N (typical O(N^2) pattern).
Repeated construction and summation of full-length exponent arrays per iteration, indicating avoidable redundancy.
Naive prime-checking via trial division up to sqrt(x) for every x, instead of a sieve.
Use of per-number recomputation of factorizations rather than aggregating factors globally for N!.
pitfalls: The optimized factorization still iterates over the prime list for each k without an early stop based on p * p > remaining_k; for very large N, consider using a smallest-prime-factor sieve or Legendre’s formula for exponents to achieve O(π(N) log N) time.
Be careful to use integer division (//) consistently; using / can introduce floats and subtle bugs for larger N.
The outer factorization loop mutates the loop variable var_6, which is safe in Python but can be confusing; future modifications should avoid relying on mutated loop indices.
Using eval(input()) is unsafe and slower; int(input()) is sufficient for numeric input and avoids security risks.
If constraints grow (e.g., N ≥ 10^6), this method might still be too slow; a more advanced approach (SPF sieve or direct exponent summation for each prime) would scale better.

constraints_guess.notes: Task: count the number of distinct triples (a < b < c) with 1 ≤ a, b, c ≤ n whose sum is x. Inputs are small but allow naive O(n^3) to be borderline in Python when combined with heavy inner-loop work.

dominant_ops: Triple nested loops over candidates 1 ≤ var_6 < var_4 < var_2 ≤ n, with a list allocation and sum() call inside the innermost loop for every triple.

complexity.why: The loops enumerate all combinations (var_6, var_4, var_2) with 1 ≤ var_6 < var_4 < var_2 ≤ var_5. The count of such triples is Θ(n^3). For each triple, the code allocates a new list [var_6, var_4, var_2] and calls sum() on it. There is no additional data structure growing with n, so space usage is constant apart from tiny, short-lived lists.

bottlenecks.detail: Enumerates every possible ordered triple (var_6, var_4, var_2) with 1 ≤ var_6 < var_4 < var_2 ≤ n, giving Θ(n^3) iterations. For n≈100, that is on the order of 10^6 iterations per test case.

In the innermost loop, sum([var_6, var_4, var_2]) allocates a new list of length 3 and then sums it, for every triple. That is ~Θ(n^3) tiny list allocations and function calls, which are very expensive in Python relative to simple integer arithmetic.
Calling sum() in the innermost loop adds Python-level function call overhead for every triple, instead of using a simple arithmetic expression var_6 + var_4 + var_2.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid explicit enumeration of the third element of the triple by algebra: for each choice of two elements, the third is determined by the target sum. Re-parameterize the search space so the third value is implied, then just validate inequalities (ordering and bounds), reducing from O(n^3) to roughly O(n * X) ≈ O(n^2) work and eliminating per-iteration allocations.

complexity.time: O(n * X) ≈ O(n^2) under typical constraints (X = O(n))
complexity.space: O(1) aside from a small list used only to count matches
complexity.why: Outer loop: var_1 ranges over candidate largest elements, 3..n → O(n). Inner loop: var_2 (middle element) ranges from 2 up to var_4 - var_1 - 1 (var_4 is target sum X), so each inner loop is O(X - var_1). Over all var_1 this is O(n * X) operations. In typical constraints with X ≤ 3n, this is effectively O(n^2). The third value is computed implicitly as var_4 - var_1 - var_2 and checked via inequalities; no third loop and no sum() calls or list allocations are needed.

complexity_delta.from: O(n^3) time, O(1) space with heavy inner-loop allocation and function-call overhead
complexity_delta.to: O(n * X) ≈ O(n^2) time, O(1) space with only simple arithmetic in the inner loop
complexity_delta.note: The main gain is eliminating one loop dimension and removing per-iteration list allocation and sum() calls. For typical n≤100, this cuts operations by ~30–100× and removes costly Python overhead.

transformation_steps: Recognize that for triples (a, b, c) with a < b < c and a + b + c = X, fixing two variables determines the third: a = X - b - c (or analogous).
Re-parameterize the search in terms of two loop variables (largest and middle elements) and compute the third implicitly via subtraction from the target sum, instead of looping over it explicitly.
Replace the innermost sum([a, b, c]) call with direct arithmetic and inequality checks: X - var_1 - var_2 < var_2 < var_1 encodes a < b < c.
Drop the innermost loop entirely by relying on algebraic derivation, reducing triple nested loops to effectively double nested loops.
Avoid per-iteration list allocation inside the deepest loop. The fast version performs only arithmetic and comparisons during enumeration.
Compact the counting logic into a comprehension, so the only list built is proportional to the number of valid triples (often very small), rather than all explored candidates.

Use of sum([var_6, var_4, var_2]) inside the innermost loop, indicating repeated small list allocations and function calls.
Knowledge that constraints are modest (n≈100) but that Python’s per-iteration overhead makes 10^6+ heavy operations per test case expensive.
A clear algebraic relationship between loop variables (a + b + c = X), suggesting one variable can be eliminated.
Performance-sensitive environment (online judge) where Python needs lean inner loops to pass time limits.

Forgetting to enforce the ordering a < b < c when re-encoding the constraints as inequalities (e.g., var_4 - var_1 - var_2 < var_2 < var_1).
Neglecting bounds on the implied third value (must be ≥1 and ≤n); these must be ensured via either loop ranges or explicit checks.

constraints_guess.notes: Single-input problem, dominated by a loop over n with integer division. The presence of an optimization that halves the loop range suggests n is large enough that a 2x speedup matters but not so large that O(n) is impossible.

Each iteration performs an integer division var_3 = var_1 // var_2, which is relatively expensive compared to simple arithmetic. With n iterations, this is the main per-iteration cost.
For all var_2 > n/2, var_1 // var_2 == 1, so the loop computes the same simple expression repeatedly where a closed-form summation (arithmetic series) could be used.
Using eval(input()) is slower and riskier than int(input()). It’s a minor performance issue relative to the O(n) loop, but still unnecessary overhead.

The summand then reduces to var_2, whose total contribution over that range is just the sum of an arithmetic progression. By looping only up to floor(n/2) and adding a closed-form sum for the tail, the number of iterations is roughly halved while preserving correctness.

Asymptotically, this is still linear in n (O(n)), but with a constant factor of about 0.5 in the dominating loop cost. Split the original summation over var_2 = 1..n into two parts: 1..floor(n/2) (where floor(n / var_2) >= 2 and varies) and floor(n/2)+1..n (where floor(n / var_2) = 1).
Keep the explicit loop for the first part only: for var_2 in range(1, var_4 + 1) where var_4 = n // 2.

Accumulate both contributions into var_5 and print the result, preserving the original semantics.
Optionally (not in provided fast_code but advisable), replace eval(input()) with int(input()) to avoid unnecessary parsing overhead and security risks.

Observation that beyond a certain threshold (here n/2), the quotient var_1 // var_2 takes on a constant value (1), which often allows replacement of that loop segment with a closed-form sum.
Performance issues (e.g., time limit exceeded) specifically when the input is near the maximum allowed size, indicating that the O(n) loop is the bottleneck.
Mathematical structure: the summand can be expressed as a simple formula in ranges where the integer division result is constant, hinting at summation simplifications.

Incorrect handling of the arithmetic series formula: the term ((var_4 + 1) + var_1) * (var_1 - var_4) // 2 must match sum_{k=var_4+1}^var_1 k exactly. Any miscalculation of the count (var_1 - var_4) or endpoints changes the result.

Assuming this is more than a constant-factor optimization: both versions remain O(n). For much larger constraints (e.g., n up to 1e9), an O(n) solution would still be too slow; more aggressive math (e.g., grouping by equal floor(n / i) values) would be needed.

Integer overflow concerns in languages with fixed-width integers: the product ((var_4 + 1) + var_1) * (var_1 - var_4) may overflow if not using 64-bit or arbitrary-precision integers, though Python itself is safe.
Using eval(input()) can be dangerous if inputs are not trusted and also slightly slower than int(input()). While not the main bottleneck here, it is a reliability and minor performance pitfall.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer N, likely up to 1e5 (from explicit branch N<=100000). Task: count how many integers in [1, N] have an odd number of decimal digits.

dominant_ops: For-loop from 1 to N
Per-iteration digit-length computation via math.log10 and floor
Conditional check and possible increment

complexity.why: The code iterates over every integer from 1 to N and performs a constant amount of work (log10, floor, mod, branch, optional increment) per iteration. No extra data structures allocated proportional to N.

bottlenecks.detail: Linear scan over all numbers from 1 to N, which is unnecessary because the property (odd digit length) can be counted with a constant-time arithmetic formula based on ranges of digit lengths.
Using math.log10 and math.floor for each number adds function call overhead and floating-point operations; although asymptotically constant, this is slower than integer arithmetic or direct formulae.
Using eval(input()) is unsafe and slower than int(input()); this is not the main performance bottleneck but is a poor practice.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the structure of digit lengths: numbers with 1 digit (1–9), 3 digits (100–999), and 5 digits (10000–99999) all have odd digit counts. For a given N up to 100000, we can directly compute counts for each complete range and the partial last range using simple min / subtraction expressions, avoiding iteration.

complexity.why: The code performs a constant number of comparisons and min operations regardless of N. No loops or recursion; memory usage consists only of a few scalar variables.

complexity_delta.from: O(N) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(1) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: Replaced a linear scan with a closed-form arithmetic count over digit-length ranges. This primarily benefits large N (near the upper constraint), turning per-element work into constant work.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the property being tested (odd number of digits) depends solely on the length of the decimal representation, not on the specific value of each number.
Observe that digit-length ranges are contiguous powers of 10: 1–9 (1 digit), 10–99 (2 digits), 100–999 (3 digits), 1000–9999 (4 digits), 10000–99999 (5 digits), etc.
For N <= 100000, identify the relevant odd-length ranges: [1, 9], [100, 999], [10000, 99999].
Derive a piecewise formula for the count of numbers with odd digit length up to N: for each odd-length range, add max(0, min(N, range_max) - range_min + 1).

Simplify these expressions for the given constraint into the implemented branches: if N < 100, answer = min(N, 9); elif N < 10000, answer = min(N - 90, 909); elif N <= 100000, answer = min(N - 9090, 90909).
Remove the O(N) loop and math.log10 calls, replacing them with the constant-time branch logic.

The condition depends on digit count, a classic pattern where counting by ranges (powers of 10) yields a direct formula.
N being as large as 1e5 (or possibly greater in general versions) suggests seeking a solution that does not touch every integer if avoidable.
Use of floating-point math for integer digit counts hints at an opportunity to switch to pure integer arithmetic or closed-form expressions.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: given N and M (e.g., 1 <= N <= 1e5, 1 <= M <= 1e9), count ways to write M as product of N positive integers. Solution uses prime factorization of M and combinations with repetition: ∏ C(N + e_p - 1, e_p) mod 1e9+7, where e_p are prime exponents of M.

dominant_ops: Trial division factorization of M up to sqrt(M).
Precomputation of factorials up to N+O(1) under modulo.
Precomputation of inverse factorials using one modular exponentiation and a reverse loop.
For each prime exponent e, a constant-time combination lookup using factorial and inverse factorial arrays.

complexity.why: Factorization loop iterates up to O(sqrt(M)). Then factorial and inverse factorial arrays of size O(N) are filled with linear-time loops. The number of distinct primes in M and their exponents is very small (<= ~30 total exponent, <= ~9 primes for M<=1e9), so the final product over prime exponents is O(1). Space is dominated by the factorial and inverse factorial arrays of length N+50.

bottlenecks.detail: Precomputes factorial and inverse factorial arrays up to N+50 even though combinations are only needed for small k (prime exponents <= ~30). This forces O(N) time and memory regardless of how small the exponents are.
Each factorial step and inverse factorial step performs a modular multiplication; for large N this is a noticeable constant-factor overhead compared to doing only O(sum of exponents) work.
Two arrays of size O(N) (factorial and inverse factorial) are allocated; this is acceptable for N≈1e5 but unnecessary for the small combination sizes actually required.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial/inverse factorial precomputation and instead compute each required binomial coefficient C(n, k) directly with a multiplicative formula using small k (the prime exponents). Keep the same trial-division factorization but shrink the combinatorial work from O(N) to O(sum of exponents).

complexity.why: Factorization still uses trial division up to sqrt(M), with an extra O(#primes) factor from dictionary operations that is negligible (few primes). For each exponent e, func_1 computes C(n, e) in O(e) multiplications and O(e) divisions. Since for M<=1e9 we have e<=30 and the number of primes is small, the total combinatorial cost is O(sum_e e) = O(log M) with modest big-integer sizes. No arrays of size N are allocated; only a few scalar variables and a small dict are used.

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(M) + N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + log M) time (sum of small exponents), O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: The factorization cost remains essentially unchanged; the main win is eliminating the O(N) factorial infrastructure when only combinations with small k are needed.

transformation_steps: Replaced the array-based modular nCr implementation (factorial + inverse factorial tables) with a direct multiplicative nCr function func_1 that runs in O(k) for C(n, k).
Removed global factorial and inverse factorial precomputation, thus eliminating O(N) time and memory usage.
Kept trial-division factorization but refactored it into func_2 that returns a dictionary mapping primes to their exponents instead of a list of exponents only.
Changed the final aggregation to iterate over prime exponents from the dictionary and multiply the corresponding C(N + e - 1, e).

Deferred modulo reduction to the very end of the computation instead of applying modulo at every multiplication, relying on the fact that exponents are small so intermediate values stay within manageable big-integer sizes.
trigger_signals: The original solution builds factorial and inverse factorial tables up to N even though each combination uses only small k (exponents of M's prime factors).
The number of combinations evaluated is bounded by the number of distinct prime factors of M (very small), so O(N) preprocessing is disproportionate.
Use of two O(N) arrays and one modular exponentiation suggests potential to avoid heavy precomputation by leveraging problem-specific constraints (small k).
pitfalls: The new combinatorial routine func_1 performs integer multiplications/divisions without modulo; this is safe when prime exponents are small (e<=~30), but would become slow or memory-heavy if exponents or N became much larger, as big integers would grow significantly.
Modulo is applied only at the very end; if future changes increase the size or number of combinations, inserting intermediate modulo operations would be necessary to keep big integers small.

The factorization helper func_2 uses `if var_1 in list(var_7.keys())`, which constructs a new list of keys each time. For this problem the number of keys is tiny, but in a more general context this pattern would be unnecessarily slow; direct `if var_1 in var_7` should be preferred.

The refactored code relies on integer division in func_1 to exactly compute binomial coefficients; any inadvertent changes that break the exact division property (e.g., adding modulo inside the loops) would corrupt the result.

Input variable roles were swapped (var_4, var_2 vs. var_2, var_1 in the original), which is logically equivalent here but could be a source of confusion or bugs if further modifications are made without careful tracking of variable semantics.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer input, constant-time processing; typical online judge I/O limits irrelevant.

Calling func_1 for a single modulo-like computation using np.floor

np.floor and floating-point division are used instead of Python's built-in integer modulo operator (%), incurring conversion and dispatch overhead.
func_1 is defined and called once for a trivial calculation that can be inlined directly in the conditional.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace the custom numpy-based remainder computation with Python's built-in integer modulo operator (%) and remove all unnecessary abstraction and imports, keeping the logic in a single expression.

complexity_delta.to: O(1) time, O(1) space with minimal constant factors using native integer operations only.

trigger_signals: Use of numpy for simple scalar arithmetic that can be handled by Python built-ins.
Manual reimplementation of the modulo operation via division and floor instead of using the % operator.
Presence of a helper function that is called only once for trivial logic.
Heavy dependency (numpy) in a problem that requires only basic integer math.
pitfalls: When replacing custom remainder logic with %, ensure behavior matches for negative numbers; here, with divisor 2 and Python semantics, the results coincide.
Avoid using eval on raw input in general; although both versions do this, it is usually unnecessary and less safe than int(input()).
Be careful not to introduce integer vs float behavior changes when removing numpy; keep all operations in integer space for consistency.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic AtCoder-style problem: count integers in [1, N] whose decimal representation has an odd number of digits (similar to ABC 136 B). N is likely up to about 1e5, so a simple O(N * digits) loop is acceptable.

dominant_ops: Iterating from 1 to 100000 and converting each integer to string (len(str(var_4)))
Storing all odd-digit numbers up to 99999 into a list, then building a dictionary from that list
Iterating from 1 to N and repeatedly converting to string to check digit parity
Dictionary membership checks var_4 in var_2 in the second loop

complexity.why: The first loop always runs from 1 to 99999, independent of N, doing a string conversion and list append each iteration: O(100000 * d_fixed), where d_fixed ≤ 5. It then builds a dictionary over that list: O(100000). The second loop runs from 1 to N; in each iteration, it converts var_4 to a string to check digit parity (O(d)) and may do an O(1)-average dictionary membership test. Overall this is O(100000 + N * d) time, and the list + dictionary for numbers up to 99999 require O(100000) memory.

bottlenecks.detail: Precomputes all odd-digit numbers from 1 to 99999 regardless of the actual input N, even if N is much smaller. This adds a fixed but significant overhead.

Builds a list var_3 and then a dictionary var_2 mapping each number to itself, only to check membership later. Since the second loop already iterates over the same numeric range and rechecks digit parity with len(str(var_4)), the dictionary is redundant.

Within the main counting loop, it both checks len(str(var_4)) % 2 == 0 to continue and then checks if var_4 in var_2, where var_2 is defined precisely by the same condition. This repeats the same logical test twice.
Uses explicit Python lists, a dictionary, and two full scans with string conversions instead of a single pass with a simple predicate, increasing constant factors significantly.
Uses eval(input()) instead of int(input()), which is slower and unsafe, though this does not dominate runtime for typical constraints.

FastAudit.core_idea: Perform a single pass from 1 to N, selecting numbers with an odd digit count using a generator expression, and count them directly. Avoids any precomputation or auxiliary dictionaries.

complexity.why: The generator expression iterates from 1 to N, converting each number to a string once and checking len(str(var_3)) % 2 == 1, which is O(d) per number where d is the number of digits (bounded by about 5 when N ≤ 1e5). Converting the generator to a list to take len(list(var_1)) materializes all qualifying elements, so space is O(K) where K ≤ N; asymptotically O(N). The time is O(N * d).

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both solutions are linear in N (up to digit factor), but the slow version includes an unconditional O(100000) preprocessing step plus extra data-structure overhead, whereas the fast version performs a single streamlined pass. For typical N up to 1e5, this yields a noticeable constant-factor speedup. Space in the fast version is dominated by building the list solely to call len; this could be improved to O(1) by using sum(1 for ...) instead of len(list(...)).

transformation_steps: Remove the separate preprocessing loop that scans 1..99999, the intermediate list var_3, and the dictionary var_2 used for membership checks.
Collapse the logic into a single loop from 1 to N, applying the odd-digit predicate directly instead of checking membership in a precomputed set.
Replace explicit accumulation in a counter with a generator expression that filters numbers with odd-length decimal representations.
Count the qualifying numbers in a single operation by taking len(list(generator)) (or preferably sum(1 for ...) to avoid materializing the list).
Simplify input handling from eval(input()) + int() to int(input()) for safety and minor performance improvement.
trigger_signals: A loop whose upper bound is a fixed large constant (100000) independent of the input N, followed by another loop over 1..N doing similar work.
Construction of a dictionary whose keys and values are identical and are only used for membership tests, especially when the membership condition is recomputable with a cheap predicate.
Redundant conditional logic where a property (odd digit count) is both precomputed into a container and recomputed inline in the main loop.
Presence of unused or pointless variables (e.g., var_6 never used), indicating possible overcomplication or leftover scaffolding.
Use of eval(input()) for numeric input when int(input()) suffices, hinting at non-idiomatic and potentially inefficient I/O.
pitfalls: While len(list(generator)) is concise, it materializes all matching elements; for larger N this can cause unnecessary memory usage. Prefer sum(1 for ...) to count matches in O(1) additional space.
Relying on fixed upper bounds (like 100000) instead of the actual input N can silently become the bottleneck if constraints change (e.g., N grows beyond 1e5).
Using eval(input()) is unsafe (can execute arbitrary code) and slightly slower; always parse numeric input with int(input()).
Overusing dictionaries or sets for membership when a simple arithmetic or string-based predicate suffices increases both time and space constants without improving asymptotic complexity.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic combinatorics/number-theory problem: count ways to express N as a product of M positive integers modulo 1e9+7 via prime factorization and combinations. Factorials precomputed up to about 2*10^5 suggests M <= 10^5 and max n in nCk <= 2*10^5. N is likely <= 1e9 so that trial division up to sqrt(N) is acceptable.

dominant_ops: Trial-division prime factorization of N up to sqrt(N)
Linear precomputation of factorial and inverse-factorial arrays up to ~2*10^5 in pure Python
O(#distinct_primes) binomial coefficient evaluations using precomputed tables

complexity.time: O(F + sqrt(N)) where F ≈ 2*10^5 is the factorial table size
complexity.space: O(F) for factorial and inverse-factorial tables
complexity.why: func_1 does trial division up to floor(sqrt(N)) with a small number of divisions per prime factor, giving O(sqrt(N)). Two arrays var_10 and var_12 of size F are filled in simple for-loops, i.e., O(F). The final loop over prime factors is tiny because the number of distinct prime factors of N <= log2(N).

bottlenecks.detail: Factorial and inverse factorial arrays are filled using Python for-loops with modular multiplications for each index up to ~2*10^5. For larger F (e.g., >= 10^6) this becomes a dominant cost and could threaten time limits.

Trial-division prime factorization runs in O(sqrt(N)). With N up to about 1e9 this is fine, but if N were significantly larger (e.g., up to 10^12–10^13) the factorization would become a real bottleneck.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the same mathematical formulation (prime-factorize N; for each prime exponent e compute C(e+M-1, e) mod 1e9+7) but accelerate the factorial and inverse-factorial precomputation via NumPy vectorized prefix products. This reduces Python-level loop overhead while preserving O(F) arithmetic work. The combination queries then use the same O(1) formula nCk = fact[n] * invfact[k] * invfact[n-k] mod MOD.

complexity.time: O(F + sqrt(N)) with a smaller constant factor for the O(F) part due to vectorized NumPy operations
complexity.space: O(F) for factorial/inverse-factorial arrays plus transient O(F) NumPy arrays during prefix-product computation
complexity.why: func_3 builds factorial and inverse factorial arrays by applying func_2 (a 2D prefix-product trick) over a size-F array, which is still linear in F but runs largely in optimized C code. Factorization func_4 is still essentially trial division up to sqrt(N). Asymptotically this matches the original solution, but Python interpreter overhead is reduced on the heavy precomputation segment.

complexity_delta.from: O(F + sqrt(N)) time, O(F) space using pure-Python loops for factorial/inverse factorial precomputation and trial division for factorization.
complexity_delta.to: O(F + sqrt(N)) time, O(F) space where the O(F) factorial-related work is pushed into NumPy vectorized operations, reducing Python-level overhead but not changing big-O complexity.
complexity_delta.note: The algorithmic design (prime factorization + combinatorics with precomputed factorial tables) is unchanged; only the implementation of factorial-related precomputation is optimized using NumPy prefix products.

transformation_steps: Replace the manual factorial precomputation loops over var_10 and var_12 with a NumPy-based routine (func_2/func_3) that computes prefix products over an array using 2D reshaping and column/row cumulative products, then flattens back.
Introduce a general nCk helper func_1 that uses globally precomputed fact (var_13) and invfact (var_14) arrays and handles out-of-range k by returning 0 immediately.
Refactor the prime factorization routine into func_4 that collects prime factors (likely to be used with Counter) instead of building a defaultdict of exponents directly.
Switch all input handling to sys.stdin.readline-based lambdas to reduce input overhead and prepare for potential multiple uses of the combinatorial utilities.
Centralize MOD as var_5 and ensure all NumPy computations are done with integer types (e.g., np.int64) and modular reductions to avoid overflow.
trigger_signals: Observation that factorial precomputation up to size around or above 10^5–10^6 using pure Python loops can dominate runtime in tight time limits.
Need to handle potentially larger factorial bounds or to reuse the combinatorial precomputation across multiple combinations, making the precomputation cost more critical.
Profiling or intuition indicating that the pure-Python for-loops over large arrays are the main consumer of CPU time, while the combinatorial logic and factorization are relatively cheap.
Availability of NumPy in the runtime environment, making vectorized arithmetic a viable option for reducing Python overhead.
pitfalls: NumPy may not be available or allowed in some competitive programming environments; relying on it can make the solution non-portable.
For modest F (around 10^5), the overhead of importing and using NumPy can offset or even outweigh the benefit of vectorization, leading to no speedup or a slowdown.
Mixing Python ints with NumPy scalars (e.g., np.int64) in pow or modular arithmetic can cause type issues or unexpected performance penalties if conversions are frequent.
The 2D reshape and prefix-product trick in func_2 relies on careful handling of array sizes; off-by-one errors in resizing or slicing can silently corrupt factorial arrays.

Vectorized operations still need explicit modulo reductions to prevent overflow and ensure results remain within the finite field; forgetting a modulo step can break correctness for large intermediate products.
NumPy uses additional memory; for very large F or constrained memory environments this can lead to higher peak memory usage than a simple Python list implementation.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AOJ-style problem: repeatedly given n and x (here var_7 and var_8) until 0 0. Need count of triples 1 <= i < j < k <= n with i + j + k = x. Values are small/medium; n likely up to a few thousand so O(n^3) Python is at risk, O(n^2) is safe.

dominant_ops: Three nested for-loops over i, j, k up to O(n) each
sum([var_1, var_2, var_3]) allocation and summation in the innermost loop

complexity.why: Outer loop: var_1 from 1..var_6, middle: var_2 from var_1+1..var_6, inner: var_3 from var_2+1..var_6. This is Θ(n^3) combinations in the worst case. Aside from input, only a few scalars and tiny lists are used, so asymptotic extra space is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: Triple nested loops over (var_1, var_2, var_3) with all three dimensions proportional to n leads to ~n^3 iterations; this dominates runtime for larger n.
Using sum([var_1, var_2, var_3]) in the innermost loop creates a new list and calls sum for every triple, adding significant overhead on top of the O(n^3) iteration count.
The third variable var_3 is explicitly iterated even though it is fully determined by var_1, var_2, and the target sum var_8; this wastes an extra factor of O(n).

FastAudit.core_idea: Eliminate the third loop by computing the third value algebraically as var_4 = target - (var_2 + var_3), then check if it respects ordering and bounds. This reduces the enumeration from triples to ordered pairs (var_2, var_3), turning O(n^3) into O(n^2) while preserving correctness.

complexity.why: Two nested loops over var_2 and var_3, each up to n, give Θ(n^2) iterations. For each pair, only O(1) arithmetic and comparisons are performed, with no extra data structures that scale with n.

complexity_delta.from: O(n^3) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n^2) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: The main win comes from removing the third loop (k) by deducing it from i and j. Also removes per-iteration list construction and sum() call in the innermost loop.

transformation_steps: Reformulate the counting: for each pair (a, b) with 1 <= a < b <= n, the third value c is uniquely determined by c = x - (a + b). We only need to check if c is an integer in (b, n] (i.e., b < c <= n).
Remove the innermost loop over c (var_3 in Code A) and instead compute var_4 = var_5[1] - (var_2 + var_3) directly in Code B.
Replace sum([var_1, var_2, var_3]) with simple arithmetic to avoid list creation and function-call overhead inside the deepest loop.

Simplify upper bounds: iterating up to n instead of min(n, x) is safe because for positive integers, any i, j, k > x cannot sum to x; the inequality checks on var_4 ensure only valid triples are counted.
Maintain ordered triple constraint i < j < k by: choosing loop ranges var_2 in [1..n], var_3 in [var_2+1..n], then enforcing var_4 > var_3 and var_4 <= n.
trigger_signals: Presence of three nested loops with bounds proportional to the same parameter n.
An extra loop dimension (third loop) where one variable can be algebraically derived from the others and the target sum.
Use of sum(list_of_small_fixed_length) inside a hot path, indicating avoidable allocation and function overhead.
Typical competitive-programming pattern: counting triples with a fixed-sum constraint almost always has an O(n^2) solution.
pitfalls: Incorrect ordering constraints: forgetting to enforce i < j < k (or using <= by mistake) will miscount solutions; the fast code encodes this by loop ranges and var_4 > var_3.

Bounds on the third value: var_4 must be at least 1 and at most n; in the optimized code it is checked via var_4 > var_3 and var_4 <= var_5[0], implicitly ensuring var_4 >= 3 and within range, but if n or domain assumptions change, explicit lower-bound checks may be needed.
Changing the upper loop bound from min(n, x) to n is correct only because all variables are positive; if zeros or negatives were allowed, this adjustment could introduce invalid candidates.

Using continue with redundant conditions: the check if var_3 <= var_2: continue is unnecessary given the loop range var_3 in range(var_2 + 1, ...); altering ranges later without adjusting this check could introduce logical errors or dead code.
Integer vs. floating arithmetic: the approach relies on exact integer arithmetic for equality and range tests; introducing floating-point intermediates would risk precision issues and miscounts.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: choose integer P in [0,100] to minimize sum_i (a_i - P)^2. Elements appear bounded in [0,100]. n likely <= 100 or a small few hundred, but the solution pattern is general.

dominant_ops: Outer loop over candidate centers P in range(0, 101) (101 iterations)
For each P: vectorized subtraction (var_6 - P) over n elements
For each P: elementwise squaring over n elements
For each P: Python built‑in sum() over a NumPy array, incurring Python‑level iteration over n elements
Repeated min() updates across 101 candidates

complexity.time: O(R * n), where R is the number of candidate P values (here R ≈ 101)
complexity.why: var_6 (size n) is allocated once. The loop over P runs 101 times; each iteration performs O(n) work: building a temporary NumPy array (var_6 - P) ** 2 and then summing it via Python sum(), which iterates over n elements in Python space. Thus overall time ≈ 101 * O(n).

bottlenecks.detail: Brute-force search over all integer P in [0,100] instead of using the analytical minimizer (the mean) of the quadratic objective sum_i (a_i - P)^2.
Using Python built-in sum() on a NumPy array each iteration: sum((var_6 - var_3) ** 2). This defeats NumPy’s vectorized reduction and forces Python-level iteration, adding significant overhead.
Recomputes the full squared differences array and its sum for 101 different P values, despite the known closed-form solution for the optimal P.
Creating temporary arrays (var_6 - var_3) and (var_6 - var_3) ** 2 in every loop iteration increases allocations and memory traffic.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical fact that the sum of squared deviations sum_i (a_i - P)^2 is minimized at the (possibly rounded) mean of the data. Compute P as the rounded average once, then compute the sum of squared deviations in a single vectorized NumPy operation.

complexity.why: Reading input and forming the NumPy array var_3 is O(n). np.average(var_3) and np.sum((var_2 - var_3) ** 2) each perform a single vectorized pass over n elements, so both are O(n). There is no extra multiplicative factor from an outer loop over candidate P values.

complexity_delta.from: O(R * n) time, R ≈ 101; O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time; O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: Removed the outer loop over 101 candidate P values and avoided Python-level sum() over NumPy arrays by using the analytical optimum (mean) and fully vectorized NumPy reductions.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the objective function sum_i (a_i - P)^2 is a convex quadratic in P, minimized at the arithmetic mean of the a_i values.
Replace the brute-force loop over P in range(0, 101) with a single computation of P using np.average(var_3), then round to the nearest integer to respect the integral P requirement.
Compute the sum of squared deviations once using NumPy vectorized operations: np.sum((var_2 - var_3) ** 2), eliminating repeated temporary arrays.
Avoid Python built-in sum() on NumPy arrays; rely on NumPy’s own reduction (np.sum), which runs in compiled code and is significantly faster.
Simplify input handling to read n explicitly and then the list of values once, instead of unpacking with var_2, *var_5 from open(0).read().split().
trigger_signals: Presence of an outer loop over a small fixed range of candidate parameters (0..100) with an inner pass over the entire dataset for each candidate.
Objective is a sum of squared deviations with respect to a single scalar parameter P, a classic pattern where the minimizer is known to be the mean.
Use of Python built-in sum() on a NumPy array, indicating vectorization benefits are being negated by Python-level iteration.
Repeated allocation of intermediate NumPy arrays inside a loop performing essentially the same computation for different scalars.
pitfalls: When using the mean as the minimizer, P must be an integer and possibly constrained (e.g., in [0,100]); you must decide between floor, ceil, or round. The provided fast code uses round(), which matches the behavior of brute-force search over integer P when the quadratic is symmetric around the mean.
np.average returns a floating-point value; ensure correct casting or rounding before using it as an integer P to avoid off-by-one differences from the brute-force solution.

If the original problem restricts P to a bounded interval (e.g., 0..100), a pure mean-based solution might need clamping to this interval; otherwise, the result might differ from the brute-force constrained optimum.

In competitive programming, importing NumPy can have nontrivial startup overhead. If constraints are tiny, pure Python loops may suffice; but when using NumPy, always leverage its reductions (np.sum, np.mean) rather than Python sum() over arrays.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer N. The original code precomputes primes up to 10^3, which is sufficient to factor all integers up to about 10^6 via trial division since every composite ≤ 10^6 has a prime factor ≤ 10^3.

dominant_ops: For each integer k in [2, N], func_3 calls func_2(k) to perform trial-division factorization using the precomputed prime list, and accumulates exponents in a global dictionary. This per-number factorization dominates runtime.

complexity.time: ≈O(N^{3/2} / log N), often written as O(N^{3/2}) integer operations for rough analysis
complexity.space: O(N / log N) for the map of prime exponents plus O(1_000) for the sieve
complexity.why: The sieve in func_4 runs once up to 10^3, which is effectively constant relative to N. In func_3, for each k from 2 to N, func_2 does trial division by primes up to min(10^3, sqrt(k)); the number of trial primes is approximately π(√k) ≈ √k / log k. Summing over k gives ∑_{k=1..N} √k / log k ≈ (2/3) N^{3/2} / log N. The dictionary in func_3 holds all primes that divide some k ≤ N, which is up to π(N) ≈ N / log N.

bottlenecks.detail: Repeatedly factors each integer k from 2 to N individually, instead of using a direct formula (e.g., Legendre’s formula) or a sieve of smallest prime factors to accumulate exponents more efficiently.
func_2 constructs a new defaultdict for every k and returns it; func_3 then iterates list(func_2(k).items()), creating many short-lived dictionaries and lists.
Heavy use of Python-level loops and modulo operations inside nested loops (outer over k, inner over prime factors), which are relatively slow in CP-style workloads.

FastAudit.core_idea: Compute N! once using math.factorial, then factor this single large integer by incremental trial division starting from 2. For each distinct factor, count its multiplicity (var_3), multiply the running answer by that multiplicity, and proceed to the next divisor. This avoids per-k factorization loops and accumulates the answer directly from the factorization of N!.

complexity.time: Dominated by big-integer operations: O(N * M(bitlen(N!)) + T_division(N!)), where M is big-int multiplication cost and T_division is the cost of repeated trial-division of a huge integer up to about N. In terms of N, this is super-quadratic in N with naive big-int arithmetic and, asymptotically, *worse* than the small-integer O(N^{3/2}) approach, though it may be acceptable for very small N (e.g., N ≲ 100).
complexity.space: O(N log N) bits to store N! plus a few scalar accumulators
complexity.why: math.factorial builds the full value of N!, whose bit-length is Θ(N log N). Each trial division var_1 % var_4 and var_1 //= var_4 operates on this big integer and is much more expensive than small-int division. While the number of distinct trial divisors is only O(N), each division has cost proportional to the size of N!, so overall asymptotic cost grows quickly with N.

delta_type: algorithmic reformulation with a different cost profile (fewer factorizations but on a vastly larger integer

complexity_delta.from: O(N^{3/2} / log N) small-integer trial divisions and dictionary merges; space O(N / log N)
complexity_delta.to: Big-int factorial computation plus O(N) big-int trial divisions on N!, effectively super-quadratic in N with much higher constant factors; space O(N log N) bits for N!
complexity_delta.note: The modified approach reduces the number of factorization calls from O(N) on small numbers to a single factorization of N!, but each operation becomes much more expensive due to the size of the integer. For large N, this is asymptotically and practically slower, though for very small N it can appear competitive because it avoids Python-level nested loops.

transformation_steps: Replace iterative accumulation of prime exponents across all k in [2, N] with a single computation of N! via math.factorial.
Remove the sieve-based precomputation of primes and the per-number factorization func_2 / func_3 pipeline.
Introduce a single while loop that performs trial division of N! by an incrementing divisor var_4 starting at 2, counting multiplicities in var_3.
Accumulate the product of multiplicities (var_2 *= var_3) as a proxy for multiplying (exponent + 1) for each prime and apply the modulo only once at the end.
trigger_signals: Original code has a nested pattern: outer loop over k from 2 to N, inner loop over primes to factor each k, with lots of small dictionary allocations and merges.
func_2 is called N−1 times and always creates a new defaultdict; the repeated overhead is a natural optimization target.
Observation that the mathematical goal depends only on the factorization of N!, suggesting a direct factorization of N! as a single number as an alternative approach.
Desire to eliminate Python-level nested loops in favor of a single loop, even at the cost of heavier arithmetic.
pitfalls: Computing factorial(N) for large N leads to enormous integers: memory and time blow up quickly. For N in the thousands or higher, this approach is typically infeasible in Python.
Trial-dividing N! as a big integer is asymptotically worse than factoring each k individually; for realistic contest constraints (e.g., N up to 10^5 or 10^6) this will time out or run out of memory.
Using eval(input()) is unsafe and slower than int(input()); it can execute arbitrary code if input is not trusted.
Modulo is applied only at the end; while Python’s big ints avoid overflow, intermediate integers become extremely large, increasing both time and memory costs.

The algorithm implicitly relies on the fact that divisors are tried in increasing order, but it does not explicitly skip non-prime divisors; although this still yields correct multiplicity counting, it wastes time dividing by many composite numbers.

notes: Primes are precomputed up to 110000, so input n (first query parameter) is likely <= 100000.
Each query: two ints (n, k); termination when n == -1.
Original code always takes the next 100 primes strictly greater than n and forms all pair sums with replacement, so k is probably in [1, 5050].
Multiple queries: while-loop reading until sentinel, so Q can be large (several thousands).

dominant_ops: Sieve of Eratosthenes up to 110000 using nested Python for-loops.
For each query: generate all O(m^2) pair sums from the next 100 primes using itertools.combinations_with_replacement (m = 100).
Sorting a list of ~5050 sums for every query.
Python-level loop appending each sum to a list var_7.

time.overall: O(N log log N + Q * m^2 log(m^2)) with N = 110000 and m = 100
time.precomputation: O(N log log N) for the sieve over N = 110000.
time.per_query: O(m^2 + m^2 log m^2) ~ O(m^2 log m) with m fixed at 100 → about 5k pair sums and a sort.
time.why: The sieve is near-linear and done once; the per-query cost is dominated by generating all O(m^2) combinations_with_replacement and sorting the resulting list. Although m is fixed (100), with many queries this constant factor becomes the bottleneck in Python.

space.details: O(N) for the sieve boolean array and prime list (≈110k elements), plus O(m^2) temporary storage per query for the list of pair sums (≈5050 integers).
space.why: The sieve array dominates globally; per query, the full list of pair sums is materialized before accessing the k-th element.

bottlenecks.detail: for var_4, var_6 in cwr(var_3, 2): var_7.append(var_4 + var_6) performs ~5050 iterations in Python per query; across many queries this dominates runtime.
var_7.sort() sorts ~5050 elements per query; sorting cost is non-trivial when Q is large.
Always using the next 100 primes, even if the requested index k is small, increases the constant factor (m^2 with m = 100).
Inner sieve loop uses Python for var_6 in range(var_4 * var_4, var_1, var_4): var_11[var_6] = False, which is less cache-friendly and slower than a slice-based or more vectorized marking approach.

core_idea: Replace the inner sieve loop with slice assignment to mark multiples in bulk, moving more work into optimized C-level list operations.

Reduce the number of primes used per query from 100 to a smaller fixed number (30) and generate pair sums via a more direct construction (combinations + doubled primes) instead of combinations_with_replacement plus a Python append loop.
Use itertools.combinations and list comprehensions to generate sums in C-heavy paths rather than manual loops.

time.overall: O(N log log N + Q * m'^2 log(m')) with N = 110000 and m' = 30
time.precomputation: O(N log log N) in theory; practically improved by list slicing: var_6[2 * i + 1 :: i + 1] = 0 for marking composites.
time.per_query: O(m' + m'^2 log m') with m' = 30 (≈465 sums), much smaller constant factor than m = 100.
time.why: The sieve still has near-linear complexity but faster constants due to slice-based marking. Per query, the number of prime pairs is reduced from ~5000 to ~465, reducing both the generation and sorting costs.

space.details: O(N) for var_6 sieve array (≈110k ints/bools) and O(m'^2) for the per-query list of sums, with m' = 30 (≈465 integers).
space.why: Same asymptotic behavior as the original but with smaller per-query temporaries due to fewer primes used.

from.time: O(N log log N + Q * m^2 log m) with m = 100 primes per query (~5050 sums)
from.space: O(N + m^2) with m = 100 (≈5050 per-query sums)

to.time: O(N log log N + Q * m'^2 log m') with m' = 30 primes per query (~465 sums)
to.space: O(N + m'^2) with m' = 30 (≈465 per-query sums)

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic forms are the same in terms of N and Q, but the per-query constant factors are significantly reduced (≈10x fewer pair sums). Sieve constants are also improved via slice operations.

transformation_steps: Sieve optimization: Replace the nested inner loop for marking composites with list slice assignment: var_6[2 * i + 1 :: i + 1] = [0, 0, ...], pushing the heavy work into C-level operations.

Prime representation tweak: Switch from a boolean list var_11 and explicit prime list var_10 to a single list var_6 that stores primality flags directly indexed by value-1, and infer primes on the fly.

Per-query prime collection: Instead of taking the next 100 primes from a precomputed list via bisect_right, collect a smaller fixed number (30) of primes greater than the query value by scanning forward and checking var_6.

Combinatorics refactor: Replace combinations_with_replacement over 100 primes and a Python append-loop with itertools.combinations over 30 primes plus a separate list of doubled primes, built using list comprehensions.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder ABC177 E-style: 1 <= n <= 1e5, 1 <= A_i <= 1e6. Need to distinguish pairwise coprime / setwise coprime / not coprime.

dominant_ops: Building a smallest-prime-factor (SPF) table up to 1e6 with a nested sieve loop, then factoring each A_i using repeated division by SPF while also computing a global gcd and counting prime occurrences.

complexity.time: O(V log log V + n * log V) where V ~ 1e6
complexity.space: O(V) for SPF table and auxiliary arrays
complexity.why: func_1 runs a sieve-like process up to var_11 ~= 1e6: outer loop over all integers, and for each prime p an inner loop over multiples of p, yielding O(V log log V) operations. func_3 then repeatedly divides each A_i by its smallest prime factor, costing O(log A_i) per number. Together with a linear pass for gcd, this is O(V log log V + n log V) time and O(V) memory.

bottlenecks.detail: The sieve always runs up to 10^6+5 regardless of the actual maximum value in the input, doing more work than necessary when max(A_i) is smaller.

The SPF sieve uses an inner while-loop with var_7 starting from 2 for each prime, performing repeated multiplications var_6 * var_7; this is heavier in Python than a standard for-loop over range(var_6*2, var_11+1, var_6).
Allocates multiple arrays of size O(10^6): var_3 (SPF table), var_10 (sieve boolean), and var_2 (prime occurrence counts). This is acceptable but larger than necessary compared to sizing by max(A_i).
The nested sieve loops and SPF-based factorization introduce more Python-level loop iterations and array accesses than the simpler per-number trial division approach for these particular constraints.

FastAudit.core_idea: Factor each number individually using trial division up to sqrt(A_i), keeping only distinct prime factors per A_i, and track whether any prime factor is reused across different elements via a boolean array; in parallel, compute the gcd of all elements to determine if the set is at least setwise coprime.

complexity.time: O(n * sqrt(maxA)) in the worst case, typically much less due to early division by found factors
complexity.space: O(maxA) for the prime-used boolean array
complexity.why: func_1 performs trial division per value up to sqrt(A_i), but divides out all multiples of a found prime before continuing, so each prime divisor is handled once per A_i. With maxA <= 1e6, sqrt(maxA) <= 1e3, yielding roughly up to 10^8 simple operations in the worst configuration but usually significantly fewer in practice. The gcd computation is O(n log maxA) and negligible compared to factorization. The boolean array var_4 has length max(var_2) + 1, i.e., O(maxA).

complexity_delta.from: O(V log log V + n log V) time, O(V) space with V fixed at ~10^6 regardless of input size.
complexity_delta.to: O(n * sqrt(maxA) + n log maxA) time, O(maxA) space with maxA determined from the actual input.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically the SPF sieve is more scalable for very large V, but for this problem where maxA <= 1e6 and n <= 1e5, the simpler per-number sqrt factorization with tight bounds and smaller constant factors can be faster in Python, especially since it avoids the global 10^6 sieve and associated overhead.

Replaced SPF-based factorization with a localized trial-division factorization (func_1) that operates only up to sqrt(current_value), dividing out prime factors fully to minimize work.

Changed the pairwise-coprime detection mechanism from counting prime occurrences in var_2 to a boolean prime-used array (var_4) sized only by max(A_i), short-circuiting as soon as a repeated prime is detected.
Kept and simplified the gcd-based setwise coprimality check by using a straightforward recursive gcd (func_2) over the array, instead of intertwining gcd logic with the sieve.
Used fast I/O via sys.stdin.readline instead of input(), slightly reducing overhead for large n.

Nested Python loops in the sieve (outer for over 1e6, inner while per prime) are relatively expensive for an interpreted language.

The problem pattern (pairwise vs setwise coprime with A_i <= 10^6) is well-known to be solvable efficiently either with a sieve or with direct factorization; empirical slowness of the sieve-based attempt indicates that constant factors and implementation details dominate.
The alternative solution avoids global preprocessing and works on-demand per input value, making its runtime scale more tightly with n and the actual distribution of A_i.

Using recursion for gcd (func_2) is safe here because recursion depth is bounded by log(A_i), but copying this pattern blindly in other contexts with deeper recursion could cause RecursionError.

The boolean tracking array var_4 is sized by max(var_2); if values could be much larger (e.g., > 10^7 or > 10^8), memory usage would grow and could become a bottleneck.

The SPF-based approach in the slow code is algorithmically sound, but implementing sieves in Python demands attention to micro-optimizations (range step usage, avoiding redundant multiplications, and minimizing Python-level loops) to realize their theoretical benefits.

constraints_guess.notes: Matches AtCoder 'Coprime' (ABC 177 E) style: 1 <= N <= 1e5, 1 <= A_i <= 1e6. slow_code hardcodes var_4 = 10**6, consistent with A_max = 1e6.

dominant_ops: Per-element trial division to factor numbers combined with repeated marking of multiples up to 1e6 for each newly seen prime factor.

complexity.time: O(n * sqrt(A_max) + A_max log log A_max)
complexity.why: Each of the n numbers is factored via trial division from 2 upward, costing up to O(sqrt(A_max)) modulo operations per element. For each new prime factor p, a loop marks all multiples up to A_max in steps of p, and the total marking over all primes is ~A_max * sum(1/p) over primes p <= A_max = O(A_max log log A_max). Both phases are implemented with Python loops, so constant factors are high.

bottlenecks.detail: func_1 starts var_8 at 2 and repeatedly tests var_11 % var_8, incrementing var_8 until var_8 * var_8 >= var_11. In worst cases this performs O(sqrt(A_max)) modulo operations per number, leading to ~1e8 operations when n ~ 1e5 and A_max ~ 1e6.

When a prime factor var_8 of a number is found, func_1 runs a loop var_10 from var_8 to var_4 in steps of var_8, setting var_3[var_10] = 1. Across all distinct primes up to 1e6, this resembles a sieve and touches ≈ A_max log log A_max positions, but done via many Python-level loops.

Both factoring (while var_11 > 1) and marking (while var_10 <= var_4) use tight Python while-loops with divisions, modulo, and assignments, creating a large interpreter overhead that dominates runtime at upper constraints.
Sorting the array var_1 (var_1 = sorted(var_1)) adds O(n log n) work that is not required for the gcd-based or pairwise-coprime logic, mildly increasing runtime.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid per-number factorisation. Instead, build a frequency array over all values up to max(A_i) and, for each possible factor i, accumulate how many input values are multiples of i by summing freq[i], freq[2i], freq[3i], …. The maximum such count reveals whether any prime divides at least two numbers, which suffices to classify pairwise/setwise/not coprime.

complexity.why: Building the frequency array var_2 takes O(A_max) initialization plus O(n) increments. For each i in [2..A_max], the sum over var_2[i::i] touches indices i, 2i, 3i, …; each position j participates once for each divisor of j. The total work is proportional to sum_{j<=A_max} d(j) = O(A_max log A_max). The loops are simple and linear-style, minimizing overhead.

complexity_delta.from: ≈O(n * sqrt(A_max) + A_max log log A_max) with heavy Python while-loops for trial division and marking
complexity_delta.to: ≈O(A_max log A_max + n) using a single global frequency array and divisor-based accumulation
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both use sieve-like ideas, but the slow version combines trial division and repeated marking per number, yielding far more Python-level operations. The fast version centralizes work into a single pass over all possible factors with predictable, cache-friendly loops.

Drop the global marker array var_3 and the sorting step, simplifying the state and removing unnecessary work.

Presence of nested-effect loops: for each number, trial division up to sqrt(A_max), and for each new prime factor, a full multiples-marking pass up to 1e6.
Rough back-of-the-envelope estimate indicating ~1e8+ Python loop iterations, which is typically too slow.
Detection that the problem only needs to know multiplicities of shared prime factors, not full factorisation of each number.

Marking multiples for each newly encountered prime factor duplicatively simulates a sieve; doing this per number adds substantial redundant work.
Using eval(input()) is unnecessary and unsafe for plain integer input; int(input()) should be used instead.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style problem: given two integers (coordinates) up to about 1e6, compute number of paths with allowed moves and answer modulo 1e9+7. Only one test case; uses combinatorics and modular arithmetic.

dominant_ops: Precomputing modular inverses up to 1e6 using a linear recurrence with division and modulus in each iteration
Factorial loop up to (var_10 + var_12) ~ O(n) multiplications with modulus
Second precomputation of modular inverses up to var_12 + 1 (another O(n) loop)
Multiple passes over ranges involving heavy int arithmetic (division, modulus) and list growth

complexity.why: Let n be the maximum relevant coordinate (~1e6). The code builds an inverse-like table var_7 up to size var_1 = 1e6 in O(var_1) with division and modulus per step, then performs factorial and inverse-multiplication loops whose bounds are O(n). It later rebuilds another inverse table up to var_12 + 1 = O(n). Overall the algorithm runs a few linear passes with heavy operations and stores arrays of size O(n).

bottlenecks.detail: Linear precomputation of var_7 (modular inverses) up to 1e6 using var_7 += [ ... ] in a Python loop; each iteration performs integer division, modulus, multiplication, and list append.
Recomputes a second inverse table var_7 for range up to var_12 + 1 even though only a small number of inverses are ultimately needed.
Uses var_7 += [value] per iteration instead of preallocating or simple append; repeated list concatenations add overhead on top of Python loop cost.
The modular inverse recurrence has per-iteration operations: var_2 % var_6 and int(var_2 / var_6), which are relatively expensive compared to multiplications and additions.
Stores arrays of size up to 1e6 twice in the same run (first for global inverse table, then for a second range up to var_12), increasing memory footprint to O(n).

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global O(n) inverse precomputation and large arrays; instead compute the needed binomial coefficient directly via a single O(k) multiplicative loop and one modular inverse using fast exponentiation (Fermat's little theorem), where k is the smaller of the two derived parameters from the coordinates.

complexity.why: The function func_1 computes C(var_7, var_11) by iterating var_11 times, maintaining the numerator product (var_7 - i) and denominator product (var_11 - i) modulo MOD. This is O(k) where k = var_11. It then computes the modular inverse of the denominator with a single exponentiation via func_3 using exponentiation by squaring in O(log MOD), with MOD ≈ 1e9+7. No arrays of size O(n) are built, so memory usage is constant.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(n) with multiple full linear passes (2 inverse-table builds + factorial loops), heavy per-iteration work; Space: O(n) due to storing large inverse tables.
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(k + log MOD) where k ≤ n is the combination parameter (single linear pass plus one fast exponentiation); Space: O(1) using only scalar variables.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both approaches are linear in the size of the relevant coordinate (n), but the modified fast version eliminates large O(n) precomputations and uses faster operations, significantly reducing constant factors and space from O(n) to O(1). This yields a practical runtime improvement and lower memory use, especially near the upper bound (≈1e6).

transformation_steps: Identify that the mathematical core is computing a single binomial coefficient C(N, K) modulo a prime (1e9+7), after validating reachability conditions ((x+y) % 3 == 0 and bounds on coordinates).

Replace the global O(n) inverse precomputation (the var_7 table built via a recurrence) with a direct modular inverse of a single denominator using fast exponentiation (func_3 implementing exponentiation by squaring).

Remove all large arrays (var_7) and associated loops; switch to a multiplicative formula for C(N, K): compute the numerator product N*(N-1)*...*(N-K+1) and denominator product K*(K-1)*...*1 in a single O(K) loop, maintaining values modulo 1e9+7.
Apply Fermat's little theorem to compute the denominator inverse: denom^(MOD-2) mod MOD, and multiply numerator * denom_inverse mod MOD to obtain the binomial value.
Simplify the control flow to compute only once and avoid rebuilding inverse structures for different ranges; leverage the fact that only one combination is needed per input.
Ensure that all intermediate computations are reduced modulo MOD to keep integers bounded and operations fast.
trigger_signals: Presence of a fixed upper bound var_1 = 1000000 and a full linear loop up to this bound regardless of the actual input values.
Use of list-based inverse precomputation var_7 += [var_7[var_2 % var_6] * (var_2 - int(var_2 / var_6)) % var_2] with heavy per-iteration operations (division and modulus).
Reconstruction of a similar inverse table (var_7) a second time for a different upper limit within the same program.
Large memory allocation for arrays proportional to the maximum coordinate instead of the actual minimal parameter required for the combination.
Problem structure indicating that only a single binomial coefficient is required, making global precomputation unnecessary and wasteful.
pitfalls: If constraints were significantly larger (e.g., coordinates up to 1e9), even the O(k) multiplicative combination method would become too slow; in that case, a factorial + inverse factorial precomputation (O(n)) with multiple queries or a different combinatorial approach would be needed.

The fast exponentiation function func_3 is implemented recursively; though depth is only O(log MOD) (~30) and safe in Python, rewriting it iteratively would avoid any dependence on recursion limits in case of adaptation.
The correctness of func_2 (modular inverse) relies on MOD being prime; changing MOD to a non-prime would invalidate this approach and require an extended Euclidean algorithm instead.
Care must be taken to keep all products reduced modulo MOD during the multiplicative combination loop to avoid extremely large intermediate integers and potential performance degradation.

When refactoring such code, it is easy to mix up the derived parameters (var_12, var_13 vs N, K); incorrect mapping will give wrong answers while still passing trivial tests, so the algebra relating coordinates to combination parameters must be rechecked.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style problem generating the N-th 'Lunlun-like' number; N is likely up to around 1e5. Single query.

dominant_ops: Repeated string<->int conversions for every generated number
Set construction and membership for each BFS layer
Flattening many sets into a list
Full sort of all generated numbers at the end

complexity.why: The algorithm generates O(N) numbers across BFS layers, but then flattens them and performs a global sort of size O(N), costing O(N log N). Each generation step also uses multiple str/int conversions whose cost is proportional to the number of digits, but this is dominated asymptotically by the final sort. All generated numbers are stored in memory, giving O(N) space.

bottlenecks.detail: Final sort of var_11 (all generated numbers) introduces O(N log N) time even though BFS can generate numbers in sorted order inherently.
For each number var_5, the code converts it to str multiple times and back to int (str(var_5), int(var_9), int(str(...))). This adds significant constant-factor overhead.
Using sets for each layer and accumulating all layers in var_1 keeps every number ever generated, increasing memory usage and requiring an explicit flattening pass.
Flattening: for var_10 in var_1: var_11 += list(var_10) repeatedly creates and extends lists, adding overhead before the final sort.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a queue (deque) to perform BFS directly over valid numbers, generating them in non-decreasing order. Maintain the queue up to size N and simply pop the N-th number without global sorting or heavy string conversions.

complexity.why: Each iteration processes exactly one number from the deque, performing O(1) arithmetic operations to generate up to 3 successors. The loop runs N-1 times, so processing is O(N). No final sort is needed because BFS with the given transition rules naturally yields numbers in increasing order. The deque is capped (len(var_5) < var_2), so at most O(N) numbers are stored at any time.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: Removing the global sort and using arithmetic-based BFS generation reduces time complexity and constant factors significantly.

transformation_steps: Replace layered set-based BFS (var_1 holding all levels) with a single deque that holds the current frontier of numbers.
Avoid storing all layers and flattening; instead, process numbers in queue order and stop after generating the N-th element.
Eliminate string-based digit extraction (str(var_5)[-1]) and concatenation; use arithmetic: last_digit = var_3 % 10 and build new numbers with var_3 * 10 + delta.
Remove the final sort of all generated numbers; rely on the BFS order to be non-decreasing so the N-th popped element is the answer.
Limit queue growth by checking len(var_5) < var_2 before appending new candidates to keep memory bounded.
trigger_signals: Presence of a global sort over all generated candidates before selecting the N-th number.
Use of string concatenation and repeated str/int conversions inside the tight generation loop.
Storing all intermediate BFS layers and then flattening them, rather than streaming the sequence.
Observation that BFS according to these transitions already respects numeric order, making sorting redundant.
pitfalls: Ensuring generated sequence remains correctly ordered when switching from layered sets to a single deque; the transition rules must preserve non-decreasing order.
Careful handling of edge digits 0 and 9 when using arithmetic operations (avoiding invalid neighbors like -1 or 10).
Queue size control: dropping the len(var_5) < var_2 check could increase memory usage, especially if constraints are larger than expected.
Retaining eval(input()) mirrors the original but is unnecessary and unsafe in general; int(input()) should be preferred in real-world code.

constraints_guess.notes: AtCoder-style candy distribution / attendance counting problem: N people, K events, each event lists some subset of people. Typical ABC-B constraints: N,K <= ~100, total listed indices sum d_i <= ~10^4.

dominant_ops: Building a temporary list of indices for each event (var_5)
Copying all these indices into a large preallocated array (var_4)
Constructing a set over a large fixed-size list (set(var_4))
Repeated use of eval() for simple integer parsing

complexity.why: Let N be number of kids, K number of events, M = sum d_i total listed indices, L = 10001 (fixed array size), d_max = max d_i. The slow code: (1) allocates var_4 of size L: O(L); (2) for each event, parses size with eval (costly constant factor), builds list var_5: O(d_i), then copies var_5 into var_4: another O(d_i), giving O(M) overall for all events; (3) builds a set from the entire var_4: O(L) time and O(L) memory. So total time is O(L + M + K) with relatively high constant factors (extra list build + copy + set construction), and peak memory is dominated by var_4 (size L) plus the largest per-event list var_5.

bottlenecks.detail: Each event's indices are first stored in var_5 and then copied element-by-element into var_4. This doubles the number of writes per index compared to directly updating a per-kid counter.
var_4 is always length 10001 regardless of N or total M. set(var_4) must process all 10001 entries, including many unused zeros, adding unnecessary work and memory usage.

To get the number of kids with no candy, the code first collects all indices, computes the number of distinct indices via a set, then derives N - distinct_count. This uses global deduplication where a simple per-kid frequency array and zero-counting would suffice, avoiding the set construction.
Using eval() to read an integer (var_1 = int(eval(input()))) incurs heavy parsing overhead and is unsafe, compared to int(input()) or reading via split(). This cost is paid K times.
The indices for an event are read into a list (var_5) even though they are only needed once to populate var_4. This contrasts with streaming them directly into the final data structure.

The fixed length 10001 for var_4 assumes the total number of listed indices never exceeds 10001; if constraints are larger, this risks index errors or silent truncation. This also decouples memory use from actual N and M.

FastAudit.core_idea: Maintain a frequency array of length N that directly tracks whether each kid appears in any event. For each event, stream indices from input and increment the corresponding positions in this array. At the end, count how many entries remain zero. This avoids global deduplication via set and any intermediate storage of all indices.

complexity.why: Allocate var_1 of length N once: O(N). For each of the K events, parse and discard the size (eval(input())), then stream each of the d_i indices and do a constant-time increment in var_1: total O(M). Finally, var_1.count(0) scans the N-length array once: O(N). No global set construction or extra copies are performed, and memory usage is linear in N only.

complexity_delta.from: Asymptotically O(L + M + K) time and O(L + d_max) space with high constants due to extra list copies and set construction over a large fixed-size buffer.
complexity_delta.to: O(N + M + K) time and O(N) space with minimal constants by using a direct per-kid frequency array and streaming updates.
complexity_delta.note: Both approaches are linear in total indices M, but the slow code ties itself to an arbitrary constant L=10001 and adds extra passes and allocations. The fast code’s cost scales directly with the problem’s natural parameters N and M and removes redundant work.

transformation_steps: Replace the global collection of all indices (var_4 plus set(var_4)) with a direct frequency array of length N, where each index represents a kid and is incremented whenever that kid appears in an event.
Eliminate the intermediate per-event list var_5 and the subsequent copy into var_4; instead, iterate directly over map(int, input().split()) and update the frequency array in-place.
Drop the oversized fixed buffer of length 10001. Size the main array exactly to N (number of kids), aligning memory use and processing cost with the actual problem size.

Replace the distinct-count-via-set pattern with a zero-frequency count: after processing all events, count how many positions in the frequency array remain zero to obtain the number of kids who never appeared.

Avoid global deduplication (set construction) and associated hashing overhead by relying on per-kid state; each kid is represented once in the frequency array, regardless of how many times they appear.
Optionally (not done in the given fast_code but recommended), replace eval(input()) for reading event sizes with a safe integer parse like int(input()) to reduce parsing overhead and improve safety.
trigger_signals: Use of a large fixed-size array (size 10001) unrelated to N and M, followed by a set() call on the entire array.
Presence of an intermediate full copy of event indices (var_5 into var_4) indicating redundant data movement.
Counting distinct elements via set() and then deriving the answer indirectly, instead of maintaining direct per-entity state.
Use of eval() in tight input loops, which is a strong indicator of avoidable overhead and potential safety issues.
Multiple passes over essentially the same data (list creation, then copying, then set construction) where a single streaming pass would suffice.
