constraints_guess.notes: Structure matches AtCoder ABC160 D (Line++): single integer N up to ~2000, plus two special positions X,Y. Output counts for distances 1..N-1.

dominant_ops: Running a full BFS from every starting node (N BFS runs on a graph with O(N) edges)
Per-source allocation and initialization of distance array var_11 of size O(N)
Final nested loop over all node pairs via for var_5 in 1..N and inner for var_7 in var_5..N

complexity.why: The graph is a path of N nodes plus one extra edge, so edges M = O(N). For each start node var_5 (N choices), a BFS visits all N nodes/edges in O(N) time, giving O(N^2) total. The final accumulation loop also touches ~N(N+1)/2 entries but does not change the asymptotic bound. Space is dominated by adjacency list O(N), distance array var_11 O(N), and counts var_3 O(N); no structure is O(N^2).

bottlenecks.detail: N separate BFS traversals over essentially the same sparse graph; each BFS recomputes distances that are highly structured and derivable by formula.
Distance array var_11 of length N+1 is reallocated and reinitialized for each of the N BFS runs, adding significant constant-factor overhead.
Heavy use of deque.popleft(), list appends, and Python-level loops inside BFS in a nested fashion leads to large interpreter overhead for N^2-scale operations.

Distances for all node pairs are derived indirectly via BFS-from-each-node and a second nested loop (var_5,var_7), rather than directly iterating over unordered pairs with a simple arithmetic formula.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the special graph structure (a path 1..N with one extra edge between positions X and Y) to compute the shortest path between any pair (i,j) by a closed-form formula, and then count distances by iterating over all unordered pairs with that formula instead of running BFS from every node.

complexity.why: The code uses itertools.combinations over range(1, N+1) to enumerate all unordered pairs (i,j), i<j, which are O(N^2) in number. For each pair, it performs O(1) arithmetic: distance = min(|i-j|, |X-i|+1+|Y-j|, |Y-i|+1+|X-j|). Counting into a Counter is also O(1) amortized per pair. Thus time is O(N^2). Space usage is O(N) for the Counter (at most N-1 keys) plus the initial list(range(1,N+1)) of size O(N).

complexity_delta.from: O(N^2) time, O(N) space (multiple BFS traversals with high constant factors)
complexity_delta.to: O(N^2) time, O(N) space (direct arithmetic over all pairs with small constant factors)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity in terms of N remains quadratic, but the constant factor drops substantially by removing BFS and repeated allocations in favor of direct distance formulas using simple arithmetic.

transformation_steps: Recognize the graph as a path 1..N with a single additional undirected edge between nodes X and Y, which yields a highly regular shortest-path structure.

Derive a closed-form expression for the distance between any pair of nodes (i,j): the direct path distance is |i-j|, and alternative paths using the special edge are |X-i| + 1 + |Y-j| and |Y-i| + 1 + |X-j|; the true distance is the minimum of these three.
Replace the per-source BFS loop with a direct iteration over all unordered pairs (i,j) using itertools.combinations(range(1, N+1), 2).
For each pair (i,j), compute the distance with the O(1) formula and accumulate the frequency of that distance using a Counter keyed by distance.
Finally, output the counts for distances from 1 to N-1 by reading from the Counter, defaulting to 0 for distances with no pairs.
trigger_signals: The slow code builds a nearly linear chain graph plus one extra edge, which is much simpler than a general graph; this often admits closed-form distance formulas.
BFS is executed N times on a graph with O(N) edges, a classic pattern for shortest-path distribution tasks on structured graphs that can often be replaced by O(1)-per-pair arithmetic.
The goal is not to retrieve explicit paths but only to count how many pairs have each distance k, suggesting that direct combinatorial or formula-based counting may be possible.
The distances in the BFS solution depend only on indices along the line and the positions of the special edge, hinting that distances can be expressed via absolute differences of indices.
pitfalls: The optimized solution still has O(N^2) time complexity; if N were significantly larger (e.g., 10^5), this approach would still time out. It is an optimization of constants, not of the asymptotic order.

Using combinations(list(range(1, N+1)), 2) creates an intermediate list of size N; for very large N, one might want to avoid the intermediate list and use range directly, though here N is small enough.

Off-by-one errors are easy when translating between 1-based node labels and Python indices; the distance formula must correctly reflect that nodes are labeled from 1 to N and that indices in the output run from 1 to N-1.
It is important to account for both possible paths using the special edge (i->X->Y->j and i->Y->X->j); omitting one can give incorrect distances for pairs on opposite sides of the special edge.

When using Counter for counts, missing keys default to 0; the print loop must iterate from distance 1 to N-1 explicitly, not over Counter keys, to ensure all distances are reported (including those with zero count).

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer input n; typical AtCoder constraints suggest n up to around 1e7 for Python with O(n) acceptable, but O(n log n) with heavy Python-level loops is risky.

dominant_ops: Build a sieve-like smallest-prime-factor table up to n, then for every i in [1, n-1] factorize i using repeated division and compute its number of divisors, summing these.

complexity.time: O(n log log n + n log n) ≈ O(n log n)
complexity.why: The sieve over odds up to n requires roughly n log log n operations. For each i < n, factorization via repeated division by its prime factors costs O(omega(i)) steps where omega(i) ≤ O(log n), and additional loop/control overhead in Python. Summed over all i this yields O(n log n) Python-level work. The SPF array var_1 has size Θ(n).

bottlenecks.detail: Using full prime factorization of every integer 1..n-1 to compute the divisor count is asymptotically heavier than directly summing floor((n-1)/i).
Nested Python loops in sieve (over primes and their multiples) plus loops inside the factorization for every i create a large number of interpreted operations.
Each i triggers allocation of a list of factor pairs, multiple integer divisions, and while-loops, all in Python, amplifying constant factors.
The SPF array of size Θ(n) stresses memory and cache behavior for large n compared to the O(1) memory approach.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the identity sum_{k=1}^{n-1} d(k) = sum_{i=1}^{n-1} floor((n-1)/i), and compute the right-hand side directly with a single loop and integer division, avoiding any explicit factorization or sieve.

complexity.why: A single for-loop iterates i from 1 to n-1, performing one integer division and one addition per iteration, yielding Θ(n) operations. Only a few integers are stored, so memory usage is constant.

complexity_delta.from: O(n log n) time, O(n) space (sieve + factorize each i)
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(1) space (direct floor-sum loop)
complexity_delta.note: Better asymptotics and drastically reduced Python-level overhead; removes sieve construction and per-number factorization.

transformation_steps: Recognize the mathematical equivalence sum_{k=1}^{n-1} d(k) = sum_{i=1}^{n-1} floor((n-1)/i).
Observe that the original slow implementation explicitly computed d(k) via prime factorization, whereas the same result is obtainable by summing floor((n-1)/i).
Remove the SPF sieve (func_2) and the factorization routine, along with the inner loops that build factor lists and compute divisor counts.
Replace the entire factorization-based accumulation with a single loop: for i in range(1, n): ans += (n-1) // i.
Keep I/O minimal and avoid unnecessary allocations (no large arrays, no per-iteration list creations).
trigger_signals: Presence of a sieve (O(n log log n)) followed by additional O(log n) factorization work per number, suggesting compounded overhead.
Nested loops and while-loops inside the main counting routine, especially ones involving integer division in Python.
Large auxiliary arrays (size proportional to n) when the target quantity is a simple arithmetic sum.
Mathematical nature of the task (sum of divisor counts / floor-sums), which often admits simpler direct formulas.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors: the identity uses n-1; the code must consistently use var_2 = n-1 and loop i from 1 to n-1, not to n.
Assuming O(n) is always sufficient: for much larger n (e.g., 1e9), even the fast O(n) solution would be too slow and a sqrt-decomposition of the floor-sum would be required.
Accidentally using floating-point division instead of integer division (//) would both slow down and change results.
Overcomplicating with prime-factorization-based divisor computations when a direct arithmetic formulation exists; this adds heavy overhead in Python for no benefit.

constraints_guess.notes: Likely AtCoder ABC126 C (Dice and Coin). Typical constraints: 1 <= N <= 1e5, 1 <= K <= 1e9. Single test, no queries.

dominant_ops: For each starting value i (effectively from 1 to N), repeatedly double i until it reaches at least K, counting steps, then add (1/N) * (0.5 ** steps) to the answer.

complexity.why: For each of the N starting values, the inner while loop doubles the value until it is >= K. The number of doublings for a given starting value x is ceil(log2(K/x)) <= O(log K). Summed over x in [1, N], this yields O(N log K). Only a constant amount of extra memory is used.

bottlenecks.detail: The first while-loop handles the case starting from N separately, then the for-loop handles N-1 down to 1. This splits the logic and repeats setup work without reducing asymptotic complexity.

For each i, the code computes (0.5) ** var_1 using Python’s pow on floats. Although var_1 is small (<= ~60), calling pow repeatedly introduces overhead compared to updating a running multiplier inside the inner loop.

Variables var_1 and var_4 are reset multiple times inside the for-loop body (`var_1 = 0` twice, reassigning var_4 then subtracting var_2). This does not change complexity but adds interpreter overhead.
Uses `input()` instead of `sys.stdin.readline()`. This is minor here (only one line of input) but still slightly slower.
Per-iteration floating point exponentiation and multiplication are done in the tight loop, which dominates runtime at N up to ~1e5.

FastAudit.core_idea: Iterate i from 1 to N. For each i, start with probability weight var_7 = 1. While i < K, repeatedly double i and halve var_7 (multiply by 0.5). After the loop, add var_7 / N to the result. This fuses the step-counting and probability update into a single inner loop using only multiplications, avoiding repeated pow calls.

complexity.why: Same logical process: for each i, the inner loop doubles i until i >= K, which takes O(log2(K/i)) steps, upper-bounded by O(log K). Total cost across all i is O(N log K). Only a few scalar variables are kept.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log K)
complexity_delta.to: O(N log K)
complexity_delta.note: Both versions have the same asymptotic complexity, but the fast version significantly lowers constant factors by using cheaper operations in the inner loop and slightly more efficient I/O.

transformation_steps: Unify the handling of all starting values i into a single for-loop from 1 to N, instead of treating N separately and then looping over N-1..1.
Replace repeated computation of (0.5 ** steps) with an incremental update of a probability multiplier: start at 1.0 and multiply by 0.5 each time i is doubled.
Avoid redundant reinitializations and assignments in the inner loop; keep the logic minimal: update i and the multiplier only.
Use sys.stdin.readline() instead of input() to slightly reduce input overhead (though input size is tiny here).
trigger_signals: Presence of pow or exponentiation in a hot inner loop (`(0.5) ** var_1` executed O(N) times).
Redundant variable assignments and resets inside loops (multiple `var_1 = 0` statements).
Duplicated control flow handling a single starting value (N) separately with almost identical logic to the main loop.
Overall runtime being borderline for N up to ~1e5 when implemented in pure Python with heavy float operations.
pitfalls: Both versions rely on floating point arithmetic; reordering operations can change rounding behavior slightly, though here differences should be well within acceptable error for contest problems.
Over-optimizing around pow vs incremental multiplication only helps if the inner loop remains small; if constraints changed to much larger exponents, a different approach might be required.
Switching to sys.stdin.readline() has no effect if the real bottleneck is CPU in the inner loop, so relying on I/O tweaks alone would not fix performance issues.
Refactoring loops must preserve the exact range of starting values i (1..N) and the conditions for doubling; off-by-one or misordered ranges can silently change the probability calculation.

constraints_guess.notes: Problem is equivalent to counting pairs (i, j) with 1 <= i <= j <= N and pre‑given M points (i, j). Then answer Q queries [L, R] asking for how many points lie in the square L <= i <= j <= R. Fast solution uses an (N+1) x (N+1) 2D prefix sum, so N is moderate (a few thousand) but Q and M can be large.

dominant_ops: Building and updating a segment tree in pure Python using loops and function calls
Range-sum queries via a bottom-up segment tree traversal for each query
Multiple levels of Python control flow and function indirection (func_3, func_7, func_8, func_9) on every operation

complexity.time: Likely O(K log K) where K is the number of segment-tree leaves being managed per build/update, and potentially O((N^2 + Q) log N) or worse if the tree is used over a 2D-flattened structure or rebuilt repeatedly.
complexity.space: O(K) for the segment tree array plus any associated arrays; if K ~ N^2 this becomes O(N^2).
complexity.why:
The slow code is organized around a segment tree:
- func_3 builds the tree: one pass to set leaves (O(K)), another to compute internal nodes (O(K)) => O(K).
- func_9 performs point updates: O(log K) per update.
- func_7 performs range-sum queries: O(log K) per query (standard iterative segment-tree pattern with left/right pointers).
However, these are all implemented in pure Python with small integer operations, while the underlying problem structure is inherently 2D and can be preprocessed once into a 2D prefix-sum table with O(N^2) work and O(1) per query. If the segment tree is being used over a 2D encoding (e.g., handling many ranges or rebuilding for each i), the effective complexity easily inflates to something like O(N^2 log N) or O(N Q log N), which is too slow for large N, M, Q.

bottlenecks.detail: Using a segment tree for a problem that admits a simple 2D prefix-sum solution. Segment trees are well-suited for online dynamic updates, but this problem is static with all points known in advance and queries that are pure range sums, making segment trees unnecessary overhead.

Segment-tree operations are implemented entirely in Python: many small integer operations, while loops, and function calls per query/update (func_3, func_7, func_8, func_9), resulting in high constant factors compared to a vectorized or C-backed implementation.

func_7’s iterative range-query loop has multiple branches inside a tight loop (bit tests on indices, conditional accumulation, integer divisions), which are all interpreted by CPython for each query. With large Q this becomes a dominant cost.

Heavy reliance on globals (var_16, var_17, var_22, var_9) and small wrapper functions (func_8 for simple addition) adds layers of indirection, slightly increasing overhead per operation and obscuring simple arithmetic that could be done more directly or vectorized.

The problem’s natural 2D grid structure (indices (i, j) with i <= j) is not exploited; instead, the logic is implemented through 1D structures and trees, losing the cache-friendly, contiguous memory access patterns that 2D prefix sums offer.

FastAudit.core_idea: Represent the counts of pairs (i, j) directly as a 2D grid and precompute a 2D prefix-sum (integral image) once using NumPy’s highly optimized cumsum. Each query [L, R] then becomes a single O(1) 2D prefix-sum rectangle lookup over this grid, fully exploiting the problem’s static nature and spatial structure.

complexity.why:
Let N be the maximum station index (var_7), M the number of given pairs (var_6), and Q the number of queries (var_8).
- Building var_5: For each of the M pairs (var_1, var_2), we increment var_5[var_1][var_2] in O(1), for total O(M).
- Computing 2D prefix sums: var_3 = np.cumsum(var_5, axis=0).cumsum(axis=1) performs two passes over the (N+1) x (N+1) array in C, for O(N^2) time with a very small constant.
- Answering each query: Each [var_1, var_2] query uses four array accesses and three integer operations:
    ans = var_3[r][r] - var_3[r][l-1] - var_3[l-1][r] + var_3[l-1][l-1]
  which is O(1); total O(Q).
Overall complexity: O(N^2 + M + Q) time, O(N^2) space. There are no Python-level nested loops over N^2; the heavy lifting is delegated to NumPy’s vectorized C loops, leading to much better performance in practice.

complexity_delta.from: Approximately O(K log K) per build and O(log K) per query/update in the segment-tree approach, with effective total cost likely around O(N^2 log N) or O(N Q log N) in the intended use, all in pure Python.
complexity_delta.to: O(N^2 + M + Q) total using a single 2D prefix-sum computation with O(1) per query, with the N^2 work done in optimized C via NumPy.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically, the segment tree is overkill for a static 2D counting problem and introduces extra log factors and Python overhead. The NumPy 2D prefix-sum solution both removes log factors and drastically reduces constant factors by vectorizing in C.

transformation_steps: Reformulate the problem in terms of a 2D grid var_5 of size (N+1) x (N+1), where var_5[i][j] counts how many given pairs (i, j) exist.
Accumulate all input pairs (var_1, var_2) by simply incrementing var_5[var_1][var_2] += 1; do not update any tree or data structure per query.
Replace all segment-tree-based range-sum logic with a 2D prefix-sum approach: compute var_3 as the cumulative sum along rows and columns using NumPy’s cumsum (axis=0 then axis=1).
Derive the constant-time query formula: for a query [L, R], answer is the sum over the square L <= i <= j <= R, which equals var_3[R][R] - var_3[R][L-1] - var_3[L-1][R] + var_3[L-1][L-1].
Implement the computation of var_3 using NumPy to offload the O(N^2) work to optimized C loops, avoiding Python-level nested loops.
Keep all query answering in pure Python but only as O(1) index arithmetic and array reads, which is cheap even for large Q.
trigger_signals: The slow code uses a segment tree (func_3, func_7, func_9) to answer many range-sum queries in Python for a problem that has no dynamic updates, indicating a likely algorithmic mismatch.
Presence of complex tree-building and query traversal logic with multiple while loops and conditionals, suggesting high constant factors and potential TLE under larger constraints.
The core data is inherently 2D (indices (i, j) with constraints like i <= j), but the original logic is not directly leveraging a 2D prefix-sum or matrix representation.

The fast solution’s use of np.cumsum in two axes shows that a straightforward 2D prefix-sum approach is sufficient; this is a strong indication that any log-factor data structure is unnecessary overhead.
If profiling or estimation shows N up to the low thousands, then an O(N^2) precomputation is acceptable, while O(N^2 log N) in Python is not.

{'kind': 'indexing_off_by_one', 'detail': 'The 2D prefix-sum formula relies on 1-based indexing semantics using an extra row/column (index 0). Off-by-one errors in accessing var_3[r][l-1] or var_3[l-1][r] can silently produce wrong answers. Carefully maintain the (N+1) x (N+1) layout and boundary checks.'}

{'kind': 'numpy_import_overhead_and_environment', 'detail': 'Using NumPy in competitive programming or constrained environments may be disallowed or introduce import overhead. Ensure the judge environment supports NumPy and that startup cost is acceptable. In some contests, a pure-Python 2D prefix-sum (still O(N^2 + Q)) could be preferred if N is smaller (e.g., <= 2000).'}

{'kind': 'data_type_selection', 'detail': 'By default, NumPy may choose platform-dependent integer types. If M and Q are large, ensure that the chosen dtype (e.g., int64) is sufficient to avoid overflow; explicitly setting dtype=np.int64 when creating var_5 may be safer in general solutions.'}

constraints_guess.notes: Classic AtCoder-style task: given N and M (here var_3/var_2 or var_2/var_1), factor M and for each prime exponent e compute C(N + e - 1, e) modulo 1e9+7. Likely from ABC110 D 'Factorization': N ≤ 10, M ≤ 1e9, so max prime exponent is O(log M) ≈ 30, and N + max_e ≲ 50.

dominant_ops: Trial division factorization of M up to floor(sqrt(M))
Precomputation of factorials up to L = N + max_exponent
Precomputation of inverse factorials via one modular exponentiation (binary exponentiation) and a backward loop
O(1) binomial queries using precomputed factorial and inverse factorial

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + L + log MOD), where L = N + max_exponent and MOD ≈ 1e9+7
complexity.why: Factorization uses a loop up to sqrt(M). Factorials and inverse factorials are stored in arrays var_8 and var_9 of size L+1. Modular inverse of var_8[L] uses binary exponentiation with exponent MOD-2, which is O(log MOD). Each call to func_1 is then O(1).

bottlenecks.detail: Factorial (var_8) and inverse factorial (var_9) arrays of size L are built even though the number of binomial evaluations is only equal to the number of distinct prime factors (typically very small, O(log M)). When N is large, L becomes large and dominates runtime and memory.

The loops `for var_10 in range(1, var_4 + 1)` and the reverse loop to fill var_9 are pure Python loops whose cost is linear in L. For large N this becomes the main cost despite each iteration being simple arithmetic.

All factorial and combination computations are done under modulo at every step. Modular multiplications are relatively cheap but still add constant-factor overhead compared with working in plain integers and reducing modulo only at the end when constraints allow it.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial/inverse-factorial precomputation and compute each binomial coefficient C(n, k) directly using the multiplicative formula with recursion, where the number of steps depends on k (the exponent) rather than on n. This cuts out the O(L) precomputation when N (n) is large while prime exponents remain small.

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + sum_e e), where e runs over prime exponents of M
complexity.space: O(1) auxiliary (aside from recursion stack O(max_e))
complexity.why: Factorization is unchanged: O(sqrt(M)). For each exponent e, func_1(n, e) executes e recursive steps, each doing one multiplication and division on integers. The total work across all primes is proportional to the sum of exponents, which is O(log M). No arrays of size N + max_e are allocated, and no O(L) loops are required.

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(M) + L + log MOD) time, O(L) space with L = N + max_exponent
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + sum_e e) time, O(1) space (plus O(max_e) recursion stack)
complexity_delta.note: For typical constraints where N can be much larger than the sum of prime exponents of M, eliminating the O(L) factorial precomputation and the two O(L) loops significantly reduces runtime and memory. For the specific AtCoder-style constraints (N ≤ 10, M ≤ 1e9), both are fast, but the new approach scales better in N while keeping factorization cost identical.

transformation_steps: Remove global factorial (var_8) and inverse factorial (var_9) arrays and the associated O(L) forward/backward loops.
Replace modular combinatorial formula using factorials/inverse factorials with a direct multiplicative computation of C(n, k) via recursion: C(n, k) = C(n-1, k-1) * n // k.
Defer modulo reduction until the final product over all primes, operating in Python big integers throughout combination computation.
Reuse the same trial division factorization logic but store exponents directly in a defaultdict.
trigger_signals: Observed that N appears directly in the bound L = N + max_exponent for factorial precomputation, suggesting potential O(N) overhead even though only a few combinations are needed.
Prime exponents of M are bounded by O(log M), so k in C(N + e - 1, e) is small even if N is large, making a k-dependent algorithm attractive.
Memory profiling or reasoning shows O(L) arrays are unnecessary for a handful of binomial evaluations.
Performance concern about Python-level loops over large ranges (L) compared with a small constant number of combinations.
pitfalls: The recursive combination function func_1 has recursion depth equal to k (the exponent). While k is small (O(log M)) in this problem, this pattern would be unsafe for large k due to Python's recursion limit and overhead.

Deferring modulo until the end causes intermediate integers to potentially grow large when N and exponents are big. Python can handle big integers, but they are slower; for substantially larger inputs this could offset the gains from avoiding factorial precomputation.

Using integer division (`// var_7`) assumes the multiplicative recursion always yields exact integers (which it does for nCk). Any change to the formula must preserve exact divisibility or it will silently produce wrong results.

The slow/original code structure (with factorials and modular inverses) is more suitable when many binomial queries with varying n and k are required; replacing it with per-call combinatorial computation might be a regression in multi-query or larger-k scenarios.

constraints_guess.n_max: ≈1e4 (effective target sum N; worst-case double loop ~1e8 ops if small denominations)
constraints_guess.notes: Only four integers are read. Core work is a double loop over non‑negative coefficients of two denominations whose linear combination must not exceed N and must match N modulo the third denomination. To keep a pure Python double loop feasible, N is likely around 1e4 or less when the first two denominations can be as small as 1.

dominant_ops: Two nested for-loops over candidate counts of the first two denominations; in each iteration: a few integer multiplications/additions, a comparison, and a modulo operation.

complexity.time: Θ((N/a + 1) * (N/b + 1)) where N is target sum, a=var_7, b=var_4; in worst case a=b=1 this is Θ(N^2).
complexity.why: Outer loop: var_2 ranges over 0..N/a. Inner loop: var_1 ranges over 0..N/b independent of outer loop. Each pair (var_2, var_1) performs O(1) arithmetic/modulo checks and possibly increments the counter, so total time is proportional to the product of the loop lengths. No additional data structures are used; memory is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: The algorithm checks all (var_2, var_1) in [0, N/var_7] × [0, N/var_4] regardless of whether var_2*var_7 already uses most of N. This yields ~ (N/var_7) * (N/var_4) iterations even when many combinations are impossible because var_2*var_7 is large.

The inequality (var_2 * var_7 + var_1 * var_4 - var_6) <= 0 is partially redundant given the modulo check: every pair is examined even when the sum heavily exceeds var_6; they are only filtered by the inequality after doing the multiplications.

Expression var_2 * var_7 + var_1 * var_4 is recomputed fully for each (var_2, var_1), and both the subtraction by var_6 and modulo by var_5 are applied each time. Although O(1), this adds noticeable constant factor inside a potentially large double loop.
Uses built-in input() which is slightly slower than sys.stdin.readline() in tight time limits. Here it is a minor factor compared to the loop cost but still a relative inefficiency.

FastAudit.core_idea: Maintain the same brute-force counting of non‑negative integer solutions but tighten the inner loop bound based on the remaining sum and hoist repeated arithmetic out of the inner loop. Also use sys.stdin.readline() for marginally faster input.

complexity.time: Θ((N/a + 1) * (N/b + 1)), but with a reduced average inner loop length due to dependency on the remaining sum; effectively up to about half the iterations compared to the independent bounds in the slow version when a and b are of similar magnitude.
complexity.why: Outer loop: var_7 from 0..N/var_4 (a). For each var_7, the maximum feasible var_6 (coefficient of the second denomination, b) is limited by the remaining sum: 0..(N - var_7*var_4)/var_2. This avoids scanning values of var_6 that would immediately overshoot N. Each iteration still performs only O(1) arithmetic and a modulo test, so the asymptotic complexity remains quadratic in the worst case, but with a better constant (fewer iterations and fewer arithmetic operations per iteration). Memory usage remains constant.

complexity_delta.from: Time: Θ((N/a + 1) * (N/b + 1)) with inner bound independent of outer index; Space: Θ(1).
complexity_delta.to: Time: Θ((N/a + 1) * (N/b + 1)) but with inner bound (N - a*i)/b depending on the outer loop, reducing average iterations (often ≈50% fewer when a and b are comparable); Space: Θ(1).
complexity_delta.note: Big‑O time and space complexities are unchanged, but hoisting arithmetic and tightening loop bounds reduce the constant factor significantly, which matters under tight limits for large N.

transformation_steps: Input remapping and naming: Reorder and rename the four input integers to more naturally align with the roles of the three denominations and the target sum (var_4, var_2, var_1, var_3).

Tighter inner loop bound: Instead of iterating the inner index up to N/second_denom for all outer indices, compute the remaining sum after fixing the outer coefficient (var_3 - var_7*var_4) and limit the inner loop to (remaining_sum)//second_denom. This avoids exploring combinations that necessarily exceed the target.

Hoist linear combination: Precompute var_12 = var_7 * var_4 once per outer iteration and reuse it in the inner loop to compute var_13 = var_12 + var_6 * var_2, reducing multiplications of the outer index inside the inner loop.

Simplify condition: Replace the inequality plus modulo on (var_2 * a + var_1 * b - N) with a single modulo check on the remaining sum (var_3 - var_13) % var_1 == 0, since the inner loop already ensures var_13 <= var_3.
Faster input: Switch from input() to sys.stdin.readline() (wrapped in lambdas) to reduce I/O overhead in competitive environments.
trigger_signals: The body of the inner loop performs non-trivial arithmetic and runs potentially up to ~1e8 times in worst cases, making any reduction in iterations or operations per iteration impactful.
Inner loop upper bound does not depend on the outer loop index, even though feasibility clearly depends on how much of the target sum is already consumed by the outer loop's choice.
The same partial sum (outer_index * denom) is recomputed repeatedly for each inner iteration.
A redundant inequality check is performed for every pair before (or along with) the modular check, which can be logically folded into the loop bounds and remaining-sum formulation.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when tightening bounds: The ranges must remain inclusive of combinations where the remaining sum is exactly zero; hence the +1 in the range upper bounds and careful use of floor division.

Logical equivalence: When removing the explicit inequality (sum <= N), one must ensure that the new bounds for the inner loop guarantee sum <= N for all iterated pairs; otherwise valid solutions might be lost or invalid ones counted.

Integer division vs modulo: The transformation relies on (N - current_sum) % denom3 == 0 being equivalent to the original condition involving (sum - N) % denom3 == 0 and sum <= N. Any sign or off-by-one mistake in this algebra breaks correctness.
Assuming asymptotic improvement: Despite fewer iterations, both versions remain Θ(N^2) in worst case; relying on this change to handle N an order of magnitude larger could still lead to timeouts.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical 1D array scan problem; N is likely up to 1e5–2e5. Single read of N integers, then one pass to find longest non-increasing run.

dominant_ops: Reading N integers from input into a list
Single O(N) loop comparing adjacent elements to count longest non-increasing streak

complexity.why: The algorithm stores all N elements in a list and performs a single pass over them. Extra imported modules and unused helper functions add constant overhead at import time but do not change the asymptotic complexity.

bottlenecks.detail: Many heavy modules (math, collections, decimal, fractions, itertools, etc.) and multiple copy imports are loaded but never used. This increases startup time and memory footprint slightly.
Helper functions func_1, func_2, func_3 and arrays var_3, var_4 are defined but never used, adding to code size and minor load-time overhead.
Use of eval(input()) to parse the integer size is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()), though it does not dominate for typical constraints.
The array-read is wrapped in func_4, adding an extra function call layer; this is a micro-overhead but still constant-factor only.

FastAudit.core_idea: Perform a single linear scan over the array, maintaining the length of the current non-increasing streak of adjacent pairs and the maximum streak length seen so far, with minimal code and no unused imports.

complexity.why: The optimized code still needs to store all N elements to compare neighbors and performs a single linear pass using a while loop, keeping only O(1) extra counters.

complexity_delta.from: O(N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged; improvements are in constant factors (startup time, memory footprint, and loop overhead) and code clarity.

transformation_steps: Removed all unused imports (math, collections, decimal, fractions, itertools, copy, etc.) to reduce startup overhead.
Removed unused helper functions (func_1, func_2, func_3) and unused arrays (var_3, var_4) to simplify the module and avoid dead code.
Inlined the input parsing for the array instead of using a separate func_4 wrapper, reducing function call overhead.
Rewrote the for-loop over indices into a clear while-loop that explicitly tracks the current index and streak length.
Simplified the maximum-tracking logic so that the maximum is updated each iteration, eliminating the need for a sentinel value (-1) and a final max over two variables.
Adjusted the comparison direction and index usage to maintain the same semantics (count of consecutive non-increasing steps) with clearer indexing: compare a[i] to a[i-1] instead of a[i] to a[i+1].
trigger_signals: Presence of many imported modules that are never referenced in the core logic.
Helper functions and variables that are defined but never used in the main computation.
Algorithm already O(N), but code size and indirection (extra functions, sentinels) suggest avoidable constant-factor overhead.
Simple scan pattern where performance concerns are more about overhead and clarity than algorithmic redesign.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when changing from a for-loop over range(N-1) with a[i] and a[i+1] to a while-loop with a[i] and a[i-1].
Changing the comparison direction (>= vs <=) must preserve the meaning of a non-increasing sequence; incorrectly flipping it could change problem semantics.
Incorrect initialization of counters (e.g., starting the streak length at 1 instead of 0) can shift outputs by 1.
Relying on eval(input()) can be both slower and unsafe; replacing it with int(input()) requires ensuring inputs are plain integers.
When removing dead code and imports, ensure that no subtle side-effect (none in this case) is actually required by the runtime environment.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AOJ/ICPC-style problem: for each pair (n,x), count triples 1<=a<b<c<=n with a+b+c=x until '0 0'. Published versions use n<=50, x<=100 and a modest number of test cases.

dominant_ops: Triple nested loops over var_1, var_2, var_3: ~n^3 iterations.
Creation of a 3-element list [var_1, var_2, var_3] and calling sum() on every innermost iteration.
Per-test-case input parsing via list comprehension (minor vs loops).

complexity.space: O(1) auxiliary (but with repeated small list allocations in the inner loop)
complexity.why: var_1 runs 1..n, var_2 runs var_1+1..n, var_3 runs var_2+1..n, giving Θ(n^3) triple combinations checked. The sum() call on a constant-size list is O(1), but its cost is multiplied by the Θ(n^3) iterations.

bottlenecks.detail: Unnecessary third loop over var_3; the sum constraint var_1 + var_2 + var_3 == var_7 can be solved algebraically for var_3, reducing the search to O(n^2).
Using sum([var_1, var_2, var_3]) allocates a new list and iterates over it in every inner-loop iteration; a simple arithmetic expression var_1 + var_2 + var_3 is faster and allocation-free.

FastAudit.core_idea: Eliminate the third loop by computing the third value directly: for each pair (i,j) with 1<=i<j<=n, set k = x - (i + j) and count it if k is in (j,n] (maintaining i<j<k and bounds). This reduces the complexity from cubic to quadratic.

complexity.why: Two nested loops over (var_2,var_3) generate Θ(n^2) pairs. For each pair, var_4 (the third number) is computed in O(1) and checked against range/order conditions. No third loop over var_4 is required.

complexity_delta.from: O(n^3) time, O(1) space with heavy constant factors from list+sum in inner loop
complexity_delta.to: O(n^2) time, O(1) space with lightweight arithmetic in inner loop
complexity_delta.note: For n up to about 50, both pass, but the O(n^2) solution is significantly faster and scales better; it also removes unnecessary allocations and sum() calls.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the problem is counting triples (i,j,k) with 1<=i<j<k<=n and i+j+k==x, i.e., structured combinations where one variable can be derived from the others.
Observe that for any fixed pair (i,j), the third value is uniquely determined as k = x - (i + j); there is no need to iterate over all possible k.
Replace the innermost loop over var_3 with an O(1) computation of var_4 = x - (var_2 + var_3) (naming differences aside) and a constant-time range/order check (var_4 > var_3 and var_4 <= n).
Remove the use of sum([var_1, var_2, var_3]) in favor of direct arithmetic to avoid per-iteration list allocation and function overhead.
Preserve the ordering constraint i<j<k by carefully choosing loop bounds (second index starts at first+1) and validating the third index via comparisons rather than an explicit third loop.
trigger_signals: Presence of three nested loops whose only purpose is to test a simple linear relation i + j + k == target under ordering and bound constraints.
Use of sum() over a small, fixed-size list in the innermost loop, indicating avoidable overhead.
Problem structure where one variable in a constraint can be algebraically solved from the others (linear equation in three variables with bounds).
Performance concerns or timeouts when scaling n, or noticing Θ(n^3) behavior in profiling or complexity inspection.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when ensuring 1<=i<j<k<=n; mis-specifying inequalities (>= vs >) can overcount or undercount triples.
Forgetting the ordering constraint when removing the third loop; if you only check bounds on k but not k>j, you will count permutations of the same combination multiple times.
Incorrect upper or lower bounds on the computed third value (e.g., allowing k==j or k>n) will violate the problem conditions.
Changing the algorithm but keeping sum() over a list in the inner loop would leave a noticeable constant-factor overhead even with fewer iterations.
Assuming input always well-formed without handling the terminating '0 0' condition correctly could lead to infinite loops or errors; the fast code preserves this termination pattern.

constraints_guess.notes: Single array of up to ~2e5 integers, each possibly up to around 1e9 in magnitude. No separate queries; just one minimization over all elements.

dominant_ops: Triple-nested looping over candidate integer p in [min(a), max(a)] and over all elements to recompute sum((a_i - p)^2) from scratch many times.

complexity.why: Let n = len(var_7) and R = max(var_7) - min(var_7). The code has an outer loop over var_4 spanning ~R values (though var_4 is unused), an inner loop over var_2 spanning ~R values of p, and an innermost loop over all n elements to compute the squared-difference sum. This yields O(R * (R * n)) = O(n * R^2). The list of inputs var_7 is stored once, so auxiliary space is O(n).

bottlenecks.detail: Brute-force scan over all integer p in [min(a), max(a)] and, for each, recompute sum((a_i - p)^2) with a full pass over the array.
The outermost loop over var_4 does not affect any computation; the entire inner work is repeated identically R times, wasting a factor of ~R in runtime.
The expression (var_7[0] - var_7[var_1]) ** 2 is recomputed inside a loop even though it does not depend on the loop index var_4 or the candidate p, and is repeated every outer iteration.
Runtime depends on the numeric spread R = max(a) - min(a); for wide ranges (e.g., values near 1e9) the R^2 factor makes the approach infeasible even for moderate n.
Use of eval(input()) for integers is unnecessary and potentially unsafe, though it does not materially affect performance compared to the algorithmic bottlenecks.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the algebraic expansion of the objective S(p) = sum_i (a_i - p)^2 = n*p^2 - 2*p*sum(a_i) + sum(a_i^2), a convex quadratic in p. Its real-valued minimum is at p = mean(a), and since p must be integer, it suffices to evaluate S(p) at floor(mean) and ceil(mean) and take the minimum.

complexity.why: The algorithm makes a single pass to read the n elements, compute sum(a_i), and (via numpy) sum(a_i^2). It then evaluates the quadratic S(p) for two candidate p values derived from the mean. All subsequent work is O(1). Space is O(n) due to the list of inputs and the numpy array; the core math uses only O(1) extra memory.

complexity_delta.from: O(n * R^2) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space (O(1) extra beyond input storage)
complexity_delta.note: R = max(a) - min(a). The change removes dependence on the value range and eliminates two nested loops by replacing brute-force enumeration of p with a closed-form quadratic evaluated at just two integer candidates around the mean.

transformation_steps: Recognize the objective as minimizing S(p) = sum_i (a_i - p)^2 over integer p.
Expand S(p) algebraically to S(p) = n*p^2 - 2*p*sum(a_i) + sum(a_i^2), separating terms that depend on p from those that do not.
Observe that S(p) is a convex quadratic in p with derivative 2*n*p - 2*sum(a_i), whose zero is at p* = sum(a_i)/n (the mean).
Since p must be an integer and S is convex, the optimum lies at floor(p*) or ceil(p*); evaluate S at both and take the smaller value.
Implement this using a single pass to compute sum(a_i) and sum(a_i^2), then compute S(p) for the two candidate p values instead of scanning the full range [min(a), max(a)].
Optionally, use numpy (or plain Python) to compute the sum of squares in O(n) time without any nested loops.
trigger_signals: Presence of triple-nested loops combining an outer range over possible p with inner loops over the entire array.
Outer loop variable var_4 not used in the body, indicating repeated identical work.
Runtime scaling with the numeric range of values (max(a) - min(a)) rather than just the number of elements.
Computation of sum((a_i - p)^2) from scratch for every p instead of reusing partial results or exploiting algebraic structure.
Known structure of the objective (sum of squared distances) suggests a connection to mean/variance, hinting that a closed-form solution should exist.
pitfalls: When switching to the mean-based solution, using only floor(mean) or only ceil(mean) can be incorrect; both integer neighbors must be checked because the real minimizer may be non-integer.
Integer division must be handled carefully: sum(a)//n and -(-sum(a)//n) correctly produce floor and ceil in Python; off-by-one errors here lead to wrong answers.
In languages with fixed-width integers, computing n*p^2 or sum(a_i^2) can overflow; while Python ints are arbitrary precision, this is a concern in other environments.
Importing numpy inside a tight loop or per test case can add overhead; for this single computation it is acceptable, but a pure-Python sum of squares is also sufficient and may be simpler.
Retaining the brute-force range loop in addition to the formula-based computation would negate the performance gain; all superfluous loops over p must be removed.
Using eval(input()) for reading integers is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; while not a performance issue, it should be replaced with int(input()) or equivalent.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical for AtCoder-style 'coprime' problems: N up to ~2e5, each A_i up to about 1e6. The hard limit appears to be max(A_i) ≈ 1e6 from the fixed sieve size and frequency-array size.

dominant_ops: Building smallest-prime-factor sieve up to 10^6
Prime factorization of each array element using the SPF table
GCD folding over the entire array

complexity.time: O(M log log M + N log M), where M = 10^6 and N is the array length
complexity.space: O(M + K), where M = 10^6 for the SPF table and K is number of distinct primes encountered
complexity.why: func_2 first builds an Eratosthenes-style table var_14[0..10^6] by visiting all multiples of each i: this is O(M log log M). Then each of the N values is factorized by repeatedly dividing by its largest prime factor, costing O(log A_i) per number in the worst case, so O(N log M) overall. The GCD reduction over N numbers is O(N log M). The SPF table consumes O(M) memory.

bottlenecks.detail: Sieve is always built up to var_1 = 10**6, regardless of the actual maximum value in the input; if max(A_i) << 10^6 this does unnecessary work.
The sieve loop `for var_6 in range(2, var_1 + 1)` with inner `for var_10 in range(var_6, var_1 + 1, var_6)` performs on the order of M log log M iterations (~2e7 when M=1e6) in pure Python.
Each number is factorized via repeated division using the SPF table. This per-element loop adds O(N log M) operations and Python-level loops / set operations for each input value.
The GCD function func_1 is written recursively, incurring Python call overhead for each modulus step. This is a minor cost but still slower than an iterative gcd or math.gcd.
Using eval on input (e.g., int(eval(var_7()))) is slower and unsafe compared to direct int() parsing, though this is a small fraction of total time.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid explicit prime factorization and global SPF construction by using a frequency array up to max(A_i) and, for each potential divisor d, summing counts over multiples d, 2d, 3d, ... to detect whether any prime divides at least two numbers (pairwise coprimeness). The logic then classifies as pairwise, setwise, or not coprime based on the maximum multiple-count and N.

complexity.time: O(M log M + N), where M = max(A_i)
complexity.why: A frequency array var_2[0..M] is built in O(M + N). Then for each d in [2..M], the operation `sum(var_2[d::d])` iterates over ~M/d entries. Summed over all d, this costs about sum_{d=1..M} M/d ≈ M log M. The main memory cost is the O(M) frequency array.

complexity_delta.from: O(M log log M + N log M) time, O(M) space (SPF sieve + per-element factorization + gcd)
complexity_delta.to: O(M log M + N) time, O(M) space (frequency array + divisibility sweep)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both are near-linear in M with a slowly growing factor. The modified code removes explicit factorization and the global SPF table, instead using a divisor-sweep over frequencies. In practice, the use of Python slicing in `sum(var_2[d::d])` may increase constant factors despite similar big-O.

transformation_steps: Removed the global smallest-prime-factor table construction (SPF sieve) that ran up to a fixed 10^6 irrespective of input values.
Replaced per-element prime factorization via the SPF table with a single frequency array var_2 sized to max(A_i), populated by counting occurrences of each input value.

Introduced a divisor-sweep loop over d in [2..max(A_i)] that aggregates counts of numbers divisible by d via `sum(var_2[d::d])`, tracking the maximum such count (var_6) to detect whether any prime divides at least two numbers.
Eliminated the explicit gcd-based setwise check from the original solution and instead inferred setwise vs not coprime using `var_6 < var_5` as the condition for 'setwise coprime'.
Simplified input handling by using input() directly instead of sys.stdin.readline and removed recursion for gcd entirely (no gcd computation).
trigger_signals: Detection that a full SPF sieve up to a fixed upper bound (10^6) might be unnecessary when the actual maximum input value is smaller.
Concern about the overhead of per-element factorization loops in Python, which can be significant when N is large.
Observing that coprimality properties can be deduced via counting multiples, without constructing explicit prime factorizations.
Desire to avoid recursive gcd computations and additional data structures (defaultdict, sets) in the hot path.
pitfalls: {'kind': 'performance', 'detail': 'Using `sum(var_2[d::d])` creates a new list slice for every d, copying O(M/d) integers each time. This adds significant allocation and memory bandwidth overhead, and can be slower than an explicit `for j in range(d, M+1, d): s += var_2[j]` loop that reuses the array without creating slices.'}

{'kind': 'performance', 'detail': 'The divisor-sweep remains O(M log M). For M around 10^6 this is typically acceptable but may become borderline in slower environments or with tight time limits, especially given Python-level loops and slicing.'}

{'kind': 'correctness', 'detail': "The modified code infers 'setwise coprime' via `elif var_6 < var_5:` without actually checking gcd of the entire set. This can misclassify some inputs where gcd(A_1,...,A_N) > 1 but no single prime divides all numbers; a gcd-based check is required for full correctness even if pairwise coprimeness is handled via the multiple-count method."}

{'kind': 'scalability', 'detail': 'Both versions scale linearly with M = max(A_i). If M were increased significantly beyond 10^6, both approaches would likely need optimization (e.g., lower-level language, optimized libraries) to meet strict time limits.'}

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style problem: N nodes on a line plus one extra edge (X,Y). Need counts of pairs (i,j) by shortest-path distance. O(N^2) is acceptable; O(N^2 log N) is borderline but usually passes; O(N^3) is too slow.

dominant_ops: Building an explicit graph with adjacency lists for N nodes
Running Dijkstra’s algorithm (heap push/pop, adjacency scans) repeatedly
Heavy object usage (nested classes, attribute lookups for edges)
Use of eval() on input lines

complexity.why: The intended structure of slow_code is: construct a graph with O(N) vertices and edges (line edges plus one (X,Y) edge), then run Dijkstra from each start node to get all-pairs distances. A single Dijkstra run costs O(E log V) = O(N log N). Doing that for all N start nodes gives O(N^2 log N). Space is O(N) for adjacency lists and distance arrays.

bottlenecks.detail: Uses general Dijkstra for all-pairs shortest paths on a very simple, almost-1D graph (line plus one extra edge) where distances can be derived by a closed-form formula.
Runs a full Dijkstra from every node instead of exploiting symmetry and structure; recomputes very similar paths many times.
Dijkstra’s priority queue introduces a log N factor (heap push/pop) for each edge relaxation, inflating runtime from O(N^2) to O(N^2 log N).
Nested Class_1 and Class_2 (Edge) with attribute access (self.Edge, self.G, self.V(), etc.) on every edge insertion and relaxation add heavy Python-level overhead.
func_2 uses eval() on input, which is much slower and less safe than int(). This is unnecessary for reading integers.
The class code is convoluted (e.g., self.Edge vs Class_2, self.V()/func_5 naming) and partially incomplete, which further increases maintenance cost and likelihood of subtle inefficiencies or bugs.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the special structure of the graph (a line 0..N-1 with edges between neighbors and one extra edge between X and Y) to derive a direct formula for the shortest distance between two nodes. For each pair (i, j), the distance is the minimum of the direct line distance |i-j| and the two paths that use the special edge: |i-X| + 1 + |Y-j| and |i-Y| + 1 + |X-j|. Count how many pairs realize each distance by a simple double loop and accumulate counts in an array.

complexity.why: There are O(N^2) unordered pairs of nodes. The fast code iterates i from 0..N-1 and j from 0..i-1, i.e., about N(N-1)/2 iterations. Each iteration performs O(1) arithmetic and comparisons via func_1, and increments a counter. The result array var_3 has size O(N). Thus total time is O(N^2), space is O(N). The log N factor from Dijkstra’s heap operations is completely removed.

complexity_delta.from: O(N^2 log N) time, O(N) space (all-pairs via Dijkstra on a line-plus-chord graph)
complexity_delta.to: O(N^2) time, O(N) space (direct combinational formula for distances)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically removes the log N factor and also dramatically cuts constant factors by avoiding heavy graph and heap machinery.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the graph is a simple path (line) 0..N-1 with an extra edge (X,Y), so shortest-path distances have a simple closed-form expression.
Derive the direct formula for distance(i,j): min(|i-j|, |i-X|+1+|Y-j|, |i-Y|+1+|X-j|).
Replace repeated Dijkstra calls with a double loop over all i>j and compute distances using this O(1) formula.
Accumulate counts of distances directly into an array indexed by distance, avoiding storage of all-pairs distances.
Simplify I/O by using built-in input().split() and int conversion instead of eval-based helpers and unnecessary indirection.
Remove custom graph classes, nested Edge objects, and heapq usage to avoid Python object and attribute-access overhead.
trigger_signals: The graph is almost a simple path with a single extra edge: strong hint that a math/closed-form solution might exist.
All-pairs shortest path is required, but N is only up to around 2000, suggesting an O(N^2) combinational approach is feasible.
The code runs Dijkstra from every node (or conceptually plans to), which is often redundant when the graph has strong structure (line, tree, or nearly so).
Heavy use of classes and per-edge objects in tight loops, plus heap operations inside nested loops, signals high constant-factor overhead.
Use of eval() in input parsing is a red flag for unnecessary overhead and complexity in competitive-programming context.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when converting problem’s 1-based positions X,Y to 0-based indexing; the fast solution adjusts by var_8 -= 1 and var_9 -= 1 correctly.
Forgetting to count only unordered pairs (i<j); using both (i,j) and (j,i) would double-count and distort frequency results.
Mis-indexing the result array var_3: distance 0 never occurs and should not be printed; the code correctly skips the first element with next(var_5).
Attempting to further optimize to sub-O(N^2) without care may introduce logical complexity and risk overshadowing the already acceptable O(N^2) solution given N≈2000.
Porting back to a graph-based solution (e.g., to other languages or variants) without reusing the closed-form insight can reintroduce unnecessary Dijkstra overhead.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic AtCoder ABC119 C-style brute force: N sticks (~<=8), target lengths A,B,C up to ~1e3. Exponential-in-N solutions are acceptable; factorial blowups are not.

dominant_ops: Generation of all assignments of N sticks into 3 labeled groups (3^N) via itertools.product
Exponential recursive search in func_1 over subsets of each group to approximate the target length
Repeated list slicing and reallocation in recursion (var_12[:i] + var_12[i+1:])
Materialization of the full Cartesian product into a list (list(itertools.product(...)))

complexity.why: Outer layer: all assignments of N sticks to 3 groups -> 3^N tuples (via itertools.product). For each assignment, each group of size k is processed by func_1. func_1 recursively tries subtracting each element and recurses on the remaining list, effectively exploring permutations/subsets of the group without memoization: T(k) ≈ k * T(k-1) => O(k!). Combined, worst case ~3^N * N!. Space: the full product is materialized as a list of size 3^N; recursion depth is O(N).

bottlenecks.detail: func_1 explores all permutations/subsets of a group without memoization. T(k) ~ k * T(k-1) + O(k^2) => O(k!), which is catastrophic even for moderate k.
Outer loop enumerates all group assignments with 3^N patterns. Combined with factorial per-pattern recursion, this yields ~3^N * N! operations.
Subproblems in func_1 are identified by (target, multiset of remaining lengths) but are recomputed from scratch; no caching of (var_18, subset) results.
var_8 = list(itertools.product([0, 1, 2], repeat=var_5)) holds all 3^N assignments in memory instead of streaming via an iterator.
Recursive calls constantly create new lists via slicing (var_12[:var_9] + var_12[var_9 + 1:]), adding per-call O(k) overhead on top of the factorial recursion.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace the inner exponential subset-sum recursion with a direct enumeration of disjoint index subsets for the three targets and compute the cost from sums in one pass. Enumerate partitions of indices into three non-empty labeled groups (and an implicit unused group) via combinations, avoiding recursive search inside each group.

complexity.space: O(4^N) in worst combinational enumeration (practically much smaller for N<=8)
complexity.why: The algorithm enumerates all triples of non-empty, pairwise-disjoint subsets (A,B,C) of the N indices, with remaining indices implicitly unused. The number of labeled 4-way partitions (A,B,C,unused) is 4^N; enforcing A,B,C non-empty only reduces this by a constant factor. For each partition, it computes sums over the chosen indices and a constant amount of arithmetic, costing O(N) per partition in the naive implementation. For N<=8, O(4^N * N) is easily feasible and avoids any factorial blowup.

complexity_delta.from: O(3^N * N!) time, O(3^N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(4^N * poly(N)) time, O(4^N) space (practically fine for N<=8)
complexity_delta.note: The key improvement is eliminating the factorial-in-group-size recursive search and replacing it with a single combinational enumeration whose growth is exponential only in N.

transformation_steps: Eliminate recursive subset-sum-like search (func_1) over group elements; instead, directly use the sum of a chosen subset as the constructed length for a target.
Reframe the problem as selecting disjoint subsets of indices for targets A, B, and C (remaining sticks unused); enumerate these subsets combinatorially.
Loop over possible group sizes (len(A), len(B), len(C)) to guide combinations generation and ensure groups are non-empty.
For each combination triple, compute sum of lengths for A, B, and C in O(size_of_group) and compute the cost directly via (k-1)*10 + |sum - target|.
Track the minimum total cost over all valid combination triples and output it as the answer.
trigger_signals: Presence of recursion over all subsets or permutations without memoization (func_1 recursing on smaller lists while exploring all removal positions).
Outer enumeration already exponential (3^N via itertools.product) combined with inner exponential recursion.
Repeated list slicing and concatenation (var_12[:i] + var_12[i+1:]) inside a deep recursion.
Small N (<=8) in a contest problem, which typically invites direct brute-force over partitions without additional factorial factors.
Materialization of huge Cartesian products via list(itertools.product(...)) indicating brute force with potential inefficiencies.
pitfalls: Even the improved algorithm is exponential (≈4^N); if N were larger (e.g., >12), further pruning or DP would be required.
Repeated creation of sets in the fast code (var_15 - set(var_6) - set(var_8)) can be a minor overhead; for higher N, caching or incremental updates would be preferable.
Care must be taken to enforce non-empty groups for A, B, and C; forgetting this leads to invalid solutions with zero sticks for a target.
Using eval() on numeric input is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; it should be replaced with int(input()) for robustness and speed.
If porting the approach, ensure sums and costs are not recomputed redundantly inside deeper loops where they could be accumulated incrementally.

constraints_guess.n_max: ≈ 2e5 .. 1e6 for var_3; var_2 (to be factorized) up to ≈ 1e12 or so
constraints_guess.notes: Pattern matches typical AtCoder-style problem: given N=var_3 and M=var_2, factorize M and compute ∏ C(e_i + N - 1, e_i) mod 1e9+7. Practical constraints must keep var_3 + max_exponent small enough for factorial precomputation in Python (<= ~2e6). var_2 is factorized by trial division, so sqrt(var_2) must also be manageable (<= ~1e6..1e7).

dominant_ops: Trial-division prime factorization of var_2 up to floor(sqrt(var_2))
Linear precomputation of factorials and inverse factorials up to var_4 = var_3 + max_exponent
Binary exponentiation for a single modular inverse of factorial[var_4]

complexity.time: O( sqrt(var_2) + var_4 + log MOD ) where var_4 = var_3 + max_exponent
complexity.why: func_2 performs trial division up to sqrt(var_2), giving O(sqrt(var_2)). Building factorial array var_8[0..var_4] and inverse factorial array var_9[0..var_4] is linear in var_4. One binary exponentiation in func_3 is O(log MOD). The final loop over prime factors is over at most O(log var_2) factors and uses O(1) time per factor due to precomputed factorials.

bottlenecks.detail: Trial-division factorization in func_2 is O(sqrt(var_2)). This is usually acceptable for var_2 up to ~1e12, but it is the dominant term if var_3 is modest.
Factorial / inverse-factorial precomputation up to var_4 = var_3 + max_exponent is O(var_4) time and space. For large var_3 this dominates and may hit time/memory limits.
Custom binary exponentiation func_3 in Python is slower than the built-in pow(base, exp, mod), especially for large exponents like MOD-2.

Use of defaultdict(int) for factor counts is marginally slower than using a normal dict with explicit handling, though this is a small constant-factor issue compared to sqrt(var_2) and factorial precomputation.

The call var_9[var_4] = func_3(var_8[var_4], mod=var_12) does not match the signature of func_3(var_17, var_12) (no 'mod' keyword parameter). In real code this would raise a TypeError; assuming it was intended as func_3(var_8[var_4], var_12). While not a performance issue, it is a fragility point.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the same mathematical formula but streamline implementation: (1) use fast I/O via sys.stdin; (2) precompute only factorials (no inverse factorial array), and compute modular inverses on the fly using Python's built-in pow with exponent MOD-2; (3) use a straightforward factorization loop and slightly relaxed upper bound for factorial precomputation (var_3 + 100) that is independent of the actual exponents but safely above their maximum under the intended constraints.

complexity.time: O( sqrt(var_1) + (var_3 + C) + P * log MOD ) where var_1 is the input M, P is the number of distinct prime factors, and C is a small constant margin (~100).
complexity.why: func_4 still uses trial division up to sqrt(var_1) ⇒ O(sqrt(var_1)). func_3 precomputes factorials in array var_8 up to var_3 + 100 ⇒ O(var_3). For each of P prime factors, func_1 computes one binomial C(n, k) using three factorial lookups and two modular inverses via pow(., MOD-2, MOD). Each inverse is O(log MOD), so combination cost is O(log MOD) and total P * O(log MOD). No inverse-factorial array is stored, reducing memory and the O(var_4) time for building it.

delta_type: micro-optimizations and data-structure simplification while preserving overall asymptotic complexity

complexity_delta.from: O( sqrt(M) + (N + E_max) + log MOD ) time, O(N + E_max) memory
complexity_delta.to: O( sqrt(M) + (N + C) + P * log MOD ) time, O(N + C) memory (C small, P = num_distinct_primes(M))
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically, both versions are dominated by sqrt(M) for factorization and O(N) for factorials. The fast version trades one global binary exponentiation plus inverse-factorial array construction for multiple built-in pow calls and a single factorial array. This usually improves constant factors and reduces memory, especially when N is large but the number of prime factors P is small (typical for bounded M).

transformation_steps: Replaced input() with sys.stdin.readline (and related aliases) to avoid overhead of the high-level input wrapper, even though there is only one line of input; this is a standard competitive-programming optimization pattern.

Removed the custom binary exponentiation func_3 for modular inverse factorial and instead used Python's built-in pow(base, exp, mod) with exponent MOD-2 to compute modular inverses when needed; this reduces Python-level loop overhead and leverages C-optimized power.

Eliminated the inverse-factorial array var_9 and its O(var_4) backward fill loop. In the fast code, each binomial coefficient uses on-the-fly modular inverses of factorial values (pow(var_8[k], MOD-2, MOD)), simplifying the code and reducing memory usage.

Changed factorial precomputation to a single forward loop func_3(max_n, MOD) that appends to a global var_8 array, rather than managing two arrays (factorial and inverse factorial) with linked indices.

Adjusted the bound on factorial precomputation from var_3 + max_exponent to var_3 + 100, relying on the fact that under intended constraints the maximum prime exponent of M is small (≤ ~30). This sacrifices tightness for simplicity while still being safe for the problem's inputs.

Simplified factor representation: the fast code stores prime factors and exponents as a list of (prime, exponent) tuples rather than a defaultdict, shaving some overhead and making loops over factors simple for the combination computation.
trigger_signals: Observation that the original code constructs both factorial and inverse-factorial arrays even though the number of binomial evaluations is only equal to the number of distinct prime factors, which is very small compared to N. This suggests on-the-fly inverses might be cheaper than a full inverse-factorial array.
Presence of a custom modular exponentiation routine in Python for a single inverse-factorial computation, which is likely slower than built-in pow for the same task.

Recognition that the combination parameters (N-1+e_i, e_i) only require factorials up to N + max_exponent, and that max_exponent is tightly bounded by the constraints on M, making it safe to precompute up to N + small_constant.

General performance heuristics in competitive programming: prefer sys.stdin over input(), avoid unnecessary data structures, and move heavy computations into built-in C-optimized functions when possible.
pitfalls: The fast code assumes that precomputing factorials up to var_3 + 100 always suffices. This relies on a bound for the maximum exponent of prime factors of var_1 (M). If constraints on M were increased such that some exponent exceeds 100, indexing var_8[n] in func_1 could go out of range and crash or produce incorrect results. The safe upper bound must be aligned with the actual constraints.

Computing modular inverses via pow for each binomial coefficient introduces O(P * log MOD) overhead. If the number of prime factors P were large (e.g., with artificially constructed inputs with many small primes), this could offset the gains from avoiding the inverse-factorial array. Under realistic constraints, P is small, but this tradeoff must be considered if the problem changes.

Both versions still rely on trial division up to sqrt(M). If future constraints allow M to be much larger (e.g., ≫ 1e12), this approach will become too slow, and a more advanced factorization method (e.g., Pollard's Rho) would be necessary.

The original code's mismatch between func_3 signature and its call (using mod=var_12) indicates fragility: small refactors can introduce runtime errors. In performance-sensitive code, ensuring function signatures and calls are consistent is crucial to avoid unexpected failures that overshadow performance improvements.

Using global mutable arrays (var_8) in the fast code is efficient but can be error-prone if the module is reused or extended: inadvertent reuse of precomputed factorials with incompatible sizes or MOD values would cause subtle bugs. Any extension must maintain the invariant that var_8 is built exactly once for the relevant MOD and maximum n.

constraints_guess.notes: Single query. Likely AtCoder-style: input N,M (here var_3/var_2 = N, var_1 = M). Typical bounds: N up to ~1e5, M up to ~1e9–1e12. Goal: factorize M, then compute product over prime exponents e of C(N+e-1, e) mod 1e9+7.

dominant_ops: Trial division factorization up to sqrt(M) in a for-loop
For each combination, O(N) loop with modular multiplications and modular exponentiation pow(i, MOD-2, MOD) per iteration

complexity.why: Factorization loop runs i from 2 upward until i*i > M -> O(sqrt(M)). For each distinct prime factor (P ≈ O(log M)), func_1 is called with var_6 = N-1 and runs a loop of length N-1. Each iteration does a modular multiplication plus a modular inverse via pow(base, MOD-2, MOD), costing O(log MOD). So combination part is O(P * N * log MOD). Space is dominated by storing the prime-exponent map.

bottlenecks.detail: Combination computation func_1(var_7, var_6) is O(var_6 * log MOD) using per-step modular inverse pow(var_5, var_2-2, var_2), where var_6 ≈ N. This dominates when N is large.
Repeated pow(var_5, MOD-2, MOD) inside the loop does a full modular exponentiation (~30 multiplications) per iteration instead of reusing precomputed inverses or using factorial tables.

Factorization loop is written as for var_5 in range(2, var_1+1) with an early break at var_5*var_5 > var_1. Asymptotically still O(sqrt(M)), just a slightly less explicit upper bound than using floor(sqrt(M)).

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the same O(sqrt(M)) factorization but replace the O(N * log MOD) per-prime modular nCr with an O(e) exact-integer nCr using the multiplicative recurrence C(n,k) = C(n-1,k-1) * n / k, where k is the (small) exponent of the prime. Perform all arithmetic in Python integers and only reduce modulo 1e9+7 once at the end.

complexity.why: Factorization still O(sqrt(M)). For each prime factor with exponent e, func_1 computes C(N+e-1, e) via a recursion of depth e, doing O(e) multiplications/divisions on Python integers. Since sum e over primes is O(log M), this is O(P * E) with small E. Big-int cost grows with number of digits, but here n ≈ N+e-1 (up to ~1e5) and e is small (≤ log2 M), so the total digit count stays moderate. Space usage remains dominated by the dictionary of prime -> exponent.

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(M) + P * N * log MOD) time, O(P) space
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + P * E * cost_bigint) time with E ≈ max exponent (≪ N), O(P) space
complexity_delta.note: The critical change is reducing the dependence on N in the combination computation to dependence on small exponents e, and eliminating per-iteration modular exponentiation.

transformation_steps: Keep the prime factorization phase; change the upper bound to floor(sqrt(M)) + 1 for clarity, but asymptotics remain O(sqrt(M)).

Replace the modular combinatorics loop (iterating k=1..N-1 and computing modular inverses via pow) with a recursive multiplicative formula func_1(n, k) that computes C(n, k) exactly using integers: C(n,k) = C(n-1,k-1) * n // k.
Change the parameters of func_1 to directly use k = exponent (e) instead of N-1, computing C(N+e-1, e) with O(e) recursion depth.
Accumulate the product of these binomials in a Python integer and apply modulo 1e9+7 only once at the end, avoiding repeated modular reduction inside the combination routine.
Maintain the same mathematical result by using the identity C(N+e-1, N-1) = C(N+e-1, e), just adjusting which argument is used as k.
trigger_signals: N is relatively large (e.g., up to 1e5), but each prime exponent e is small (O(log M)), so an O(N)-per-prime combinatorial routine is wasteful.
Presence of pow(base, MOD-2, MOD) inside an inner loop is a strong indicator of potential performance issues, especially when the loop is long.
Number of distinct primes P is small (≈ log M), meaning it is advantageous to make combination cost depend on e rather than N.
pitfalls: The recursive implementation of func_1 depends on recursion depth equal to k = e. With exponents bounded by log2(M), this is safe for typical constraints but would need conversion to an iterative loop if exponents could be large to avoid hitting recursion limits.
All arithmetic is done using Python big integers before taking modulo; while safe here, for significantly larger N or many primes, big-int multiplication cost could become non-negligible.

The integer division // in func_1 must be exact at every step; this relies on the combinatorial identity and correct recurrence. Any change to the formula that breaks exact divisibility would introduce subtle correctness bugs.

In the original (slow) code, the modular arithmetic kept intermediate values small; in the modified version, loss of modular reduction inside the combination routine means memory and time characteristics depend more heavily on the magnitude of the binomial coefficients.

constraints_guess.notes: Input is a single integer N (1 <= N <= 100000). Task: count integers i in [1, N] whose decimal representation has an odd number of digits.

dominant_ops: Two full loops over ranges up to 100000
Repeated conversion of integers to strings to measure digit length
Building an intermediate list and dictionary of all odd-digit numbers up to 99999
Dictionary membership checks inside a loop

complexity.why: The code builds a list and dict of all odd-digit numbers up to 99999 (O(1e5) memory) and then iterates from 1 to N (N <= 1e5), doing string conversions and dictionary lookups in each iteration. Overall cost scales linearly with the maximum range size.

bottlenecks.detail: Precomputes all integers from 1 to 99999 with odd digit length into a list var_3 and then into a dict var_2, even though the final loop only needs to count such numbers up to N and could be done directly or via formula.

Uses len(str(var_4)) inside loops up to 100000 twice (once for precomputation and once during counting). Converting every integer to a string just to read its digit length is relatively expensive compared with simple arithmetic.

Creates both a list (var_3) and a dictionary (var_2) to hold the same values. The dictionary is then used only to re-check membership for numbers from 1 to N, which is redundant because the odd-digit property is re-checked via len(str(var_4)) anyway.

The code first determines which numbers up to 99999 have odd digit length, then later re-applies the digit-length check in the second loop and also checks membership in var_2. The membership test is logically unnecessary given the length test.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the structure of decimal digit lengths to derive a closed-form piecewise count of numbers with an odd number of digits up to N, instead of iterating. The counts are: 1-digit numbers: 1..9 (9 numbers), 3-digit numbers: 100..999 (900 numbers), 5-digit numbers: 10000..99999 (90000 numbers). For a given N <= 100000, we sum the contribution from each fully covered odd-length block plus the partial contribution from the current block, implemented via simple min and subtraction operations.

complexity.why: The modified code performs a fixed sequence of comparisons and arithmetic operations based on N's magnitude. There are no loops or data structures whose size depends on N, so both time and memory usage are constant with respect to the input size.

complexity_delta.from: O(N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(1) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: Replaced iterative construction and scanning of ranges up to 100000 with direct arithmetic formulas counting the numbers with odd digit lengths in each relevant magnitude range.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the condition len(str(i)) % 2 == 1 depends only on the number of digits of i, which corresponds to fixed numeric intervals: 1..9 (1 digit), 10..99 (2 digits), 100..999 (3 digits), 1000..9999 (4 digits), 10000..99999 (5 digits).
Observe that the original code effectively counts how many i in [1, N] lie in the 1-digit, 3-digit, or 5-digit ranges. Thus, instead of iterating, we can derive counts from interval lengths.
Derive formulae: for N < 100, the answer is min(N, 9) (only 1-digit numbers contribute).

For 100 <= N < 10000, the count is all 1-digit numbers plus the 3-digit numbers up to N: 9 + max(0, min(N, 999) - 99). This is algebraically represented as min(N - 90, 909), which accounts both for partial and full coverage of 3-digit numbers.

For 10000 <= N <= 100000, we similarly account for 1-digit and 3-digit blocks fully, and then the 5-digit prefix up to N: 9 (1-digit) + 900 (3-digit) + max(0, N - 9999). This is compactly encoded as min(N - 9090, 90909), which caps at the total possible odd-digit numbers up to 99999.
Implement the final piecewise logic using if-elif branches and min expressions, eliminating all loops, string conversions, and auxiliary collections.
trigger_signals: Loop upper bounds are small but fixed (100000), suggesting that the problem structure may allow a non-iterative solution.
Digit-length checks (len(str(x))) are used as the primary condition, hinting that the number of digits and thus the numeric ranges could be reasoned about directly.

The presence of precomputed containers (list and dict) whose content is entirely determined by digit-length properties, not by input data, indicating that the work is independent of N and can be folded into arithmetic.
Counting problem over a simple range [1, N] with property depending only on order-of-magnitude, a common pattern where closed-form formulas exist.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when translating between digit lengths and numeric intervals (e.g., ensuring that 9, 99, 999, etc., are included or excluded correctly in each branch).
Incorrect capping of counts when N spans multiple digit-length blocks; for example, failing to limit the 3-digit contribution when N < 999, or the 5-digit contribution when N < 99999.
Using eval on input can be unsafe in general; although the task environment likely provides clean numeric input, in real-world code int(input()) is preferable.
The final branch handles N <= 100000; if problem constraints were extended beyond 100000, additional branches for 7-digit (and higher) ranges would be required to maintain correctness.
