Each integer i in [1..n] is factorized independently via trial division over all candidate primes up to i, yielding O(n^2) work overall.
Exponent aggregation for n! uses length-n vectors and recomputes/updates them for every i, even though only primes are needed; this adds an O(n^2) vector-adding cost.
List comprehensions `[var_9[var_4] + var_3[var_4] for var_4 in range(0, var_1)]` allocate a fresh O(n) list in every outer iteration instead of updating in-place.

Factorization in func_1 uses floating division `var_5 = var_5 / (var_2 + 1)` instead of integer division; this can introduce floats and slow conversions (though the main bottleneck remains algorithmic).

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid per-i factorization and instead factorize n! directly: compute n! once, generate all primes up to n via a sieve, then for each prime p repeatedly divide n! by p to obtain its exponent in the factorial and accumulate the divisor count as the product of (exponent+1) modulo 1e9+7.

complexity.time: O(n log log n) arithmetic operations on big integers, plus the cost of computing n! and doing big-integer divisions
complexity.space: O(n log n) bits (for n! itself) plus O(n) for the sieve
complexity.why: Prime generation via the sieve in func_1 is O(n log log n). For each prime p<=n, we divide the current value of n! by p until it is no longer divisible; the total number of such divisions equals the sum of prime exponents in n!, which is O(n log log n). Ignoring bit-length, this is O(n log log n). However, n! has Θ(n log n) bits, so big-integer multiplication and division are expensive; memory use is dominated by storing n!.

complexity_delta.from: O(n^2) time, O(n) space (ignoring integer sizes)
complexity_delta.to: O(n log log n) arithmetic ops plus big-integer factorial and division cost; O(n log n) bits space due to n!
complexity_delta.note: The new approach greatly reduces combinatorial loop complexity (sieve + per-prime exponent computation) but introduces a massive big-integer object (n!) and repeated big-int divisions. For realistic constraints, a further refinement using Legendre’s formula to avoid explicitly forming n! would be ideal.

transformation_steps: Replace naive primality checking via trial division (func_2) with an efficient sieve of Eratosthenes to generate primes up to n in O(n log log n).
Stop factorizing every number i in 1..n separately; instead, work directly with the factorization of n! as a whole.
Compute n! using math.factorial once, rather than updating factor exponent vectors for all primes across all i.
For each prime p returned by the sieve, repeatedly divide the running value of n! by p to count its exponent, and multiply the answer by (exponent+1) modulo 1e9+7.
Accumulate the divisor count using modular multiplication at each step instead of building and summing length-n exponent arrays.
trigger_signals: Nested loops where the loop bounds depend on n in multiple layers: outer loop i=1..n, inner loops over j up to i, plus a separate primality loop up to n.
Naive primality checks using trial division up to sqrt(k) inside a loop over all k up to n.
Recomputation of full-size lists (`[0]*var_1`, list comprehensions summing two length-n lists) inside loops that run n times.
Factorization by trial division for each number individually, rather than leveraging structure of n! (shared prime factors and known formulas).
pitfalls: The fast_code constructs n! explicitly, which quickly becomes enormous (size Θ(n log n) bits) and may be too big in both time and memory for large n.
Repeated big-integer division `var_2 //= var_8` for each prime factor is far more expensive than constant-time integer division assumed in Big-O notation; for large n, big-int costs dominate.
Using eval(input()) is unnecessary and can be unsafe; while not a performance bottleneck, it is a bad practice.
If constraints are tighter (e.g., n up to 10^7), even the sieve must be implemented carefully with memory and constant factors in mind; constructing n! would be completely infeasible.

A more robust optimization would avoid computing n! at all and instead use Legendre’s formula: for each prime p, sum floor(n/p^k) for k>=1 to get the exponent, which keeps all arithmetic on O(log n)-bit integers.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case. N (second input) is factorized by trial division up to sqrt(N), so N is likely up to about 1e9–1e12. The first input (M) is used as the main parameter in combinations C(M+e-1, e); typical contest constraints suggest M up to about 1e5.

dominant_ops: Trial-division prime factorization up to sqrt(N)
Repeated computation of factorial(k) for varying k using math.factorial
Construction of large factorial values as big integers (no modular reduction until the end)
Multiple dictionary lookups and updates for factorial memoization
Inefficient membership checks using `if key in list(dict.keys())` inside inner loop

complexity.why: Let N be the second input and M be the first input. Factorization via trial division is O(sqrt(N)). For each distinct prime factor with exponent e, slow_code computes C(M+e-1, e) via factorial: factorial(M+e-1), factorial(M), factorial(e). Even with memoization, the highest factorial size F ≈ max(M+e-1) dominates, and factorial(k) itself is implemented as an O(k) loop over big-integer multiplications. Across P prime factors, the total work is O(P * F). The resulting integers grow to Θ(F log F) bits, yielding high space usage for the cached factorial values.

bottlenecks.detail: Binomial coefficients are computed by three factorial calls (n!, (n−k)!, k!) using arbitrary-precision integers, which is overkill when only small k (exponent e) is needed. A multiplicative O(k) binomial algorithm would avoid computing large factorials.
Factorials such as (M+e-1)! can be enormous. They are computed and stored fully as Python big integers before the final modulo, causing very slow arithmetic and increased memory usage.
Factorial memoization uses a plain dict keyed by n, but factorial values are extremely large; storing all intermediate factorials (up to max n) consumes memory and increases GC overhead.
Prime factorization uses `if var_5 in list(var_11.keys())`, rebuilding the key list each time and turning key checks into O(K) operations instead of O(1) dictionary membership.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid factorial-based binomial computation and huge intermediate integers by computing C(n, k) multiplicatively over k = min(k, n−k), and keep the combinatorial work proportional to the small exponents of prime factors instead of the large parameter M.

complexity.why: Prime factorization with trial division remains O(sqrt(N)). The fast_code represents factors as a list and uses Counter to obtain exponents. For each exponent e, it computes C(M+e-1, e) via a multiplicative loop that runs in O(e) time (over the smaller of e and (M−1)). The sum of exponents sum_e for the factorization of N is O(log N). Therefore the added combinatorial cost is O(sum_e), negligible compared to O(sqrt(N)). Intermediate integers still grow but only as products of about e factors per prime, not full factorials, so memory is limited to a small number of big integers at a time.

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(N) + P * F) time with F ≈ max(M+e-1), heavy big-int factorials and O(F log F) space for cached factorials.
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(N) + sum_e) time where sum_e = O(log N) and O(log N) space, dominated by factorization.
complexity_delta.note: The core improvement replaces factorial-based nCr with a multiplicative method whose cost scales with the small exponents rather than the usually large M, and avoids creating and storing huge factorial values.

transformation_steps: Replace factorial-based binomial computation `nCr = n! / ((n-k)! * k!)` with a multiplicative loop using k = min(k, n-k): accumulate product of (n down to n-k+1) and divide by (1..k) at each step, leveraging exact integer division.
Eliminate factorial memoization dictionary and all math.factorial calls, removing both time spent in factorial and memory spent caching extremely large integers.

Change the prime-factorization representation from a dict of prime->exponent built with repeated key-list scans to a simple list of prime factors followed by collections.Counter to get exponents, avoiding repeated `list(dict.keys())` and reducing constant factors.

Apply modulo only to the final result (as in fast_code) while keeping intermediate arithmetic purely integer-based, which is safe because the combinatorial identity guarantees exact divisibility at each step.
Simplify dictionary membership checks in the factorization (if retained) to `if key in dict` instead of rebuilding a key list, improving constant-factor performance in the inner loop.
trigger_signals: Profiling showing that the vast majority of runtime is spent inside math.factorial and big-integer multiplication during factorial computation.
Observed TLE or severe slowdown when the first input (M) becomes moderately large, even though the number of distinct prime factors of N is small.
Rapid growth of memory usage due to caching many large factorial values in a dictionary.
Code review indicating that binomial coefficients are repeatedly computed from scratch using factorials, despite small k (prime exponents) and large n (M+e-1).
pitfalls: When switching from factorial-based to multiplicative nCr under a modulus in a different setting, naive integer division is not valid: division must be replaced with multiplication by modular inverses. In this problem, the code stays in exact integer arithmetic first, then applies modulo at the end, so division is safe.
Incorrectly choosing k in the multiplicative nCr routine (e.g., not using k = min(k, n-k)) can increase running time and intermediate integer sizes unnecessarily.

If the value range grows or repeated calls increase, a pure trial-division factorization up to sqrt(N) might become a bottleneck; additional optimizations (e.g., sieving or reusing primes) might then be needed.

Care must be taken to maintain integer division exactness in the multiplicative nCr loop; any reordering that breaks the invariant that the numerator is divisible by the denominator at each step can lead to non-integer results or runtime errors.

constraints_guess.notes: Single array, no queries. Naive scan over all integer centers between min(A) and max(A) suggests original solution assumes small value range, but to be safe typical AtCoder-style constraints are n up to around 1e5 and |Ai| up to about 1e9.

dominant_ops: Outer loop over all integer candidate centers from min(A) to max(A)
For each center, vectorized computation of squared differences (A - c)**2 and their sum via NumPy

complexity.why: Let R = max(A) - min(A) + 1. The code loops R times. Inside each iteration it performs vectorized operations over the full array: (var_2 - var_5)**2 and np.sum(...), each touching all n elements. Thus total work is proportional to R * n. The NumPy array itself takes O(n) space, and each iteration allocates a temporary array of size n for (var_2 - var_5)**2.

bottlenecks.detail: Enumerating every integer center between min(A) and max(A) leads to O(R * n) time, which is prohibitive when the value range R is large (e.g., if Ai are up to 1e9 apart).
Each iteration allocates a new NumPy temporary array for (var_2 - var_5)**2, incurring repeated memory allocations and Python–C boundary overhead.
min(var_2) is recomputed in every loop iteration rather than cached, adding unnecessary O(n * R) comparisons, though dominated by the O(n * R) vector operations.
The algorithm ignores that the sum of squared deviations is minimized at the mean, and instead performs a direct search over all possible centers.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical fact that the function f(x) = sum_i (Ai - x)^2 is minimized at x equal to the mean of Ai. With x constrained to integers, the optimal x must be either floor(mean) or ceil(mean). Therefore, compute the mean via sum/n, test these two candidate centers, and take the minimal sum of squared deviations. This reduces the number of centers from O(max(A) - min(A)) to a constant (2).

complexity.why: We compute the sum of the array once (O(n)). Then for each of the two candidate centers, we compute sum((Ai - c)^2) in a single pass over the list (2 * O(n) = O(n)). No extra arrays proportional to n are allocated; we only maintain a few scalar accumulators and the original list.

complexity_delta.from: O((max(A) - min(A)) * n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(1) extra space
complexity_delta.note: The search over all integer centers is replaced by evaluating the cost at only two centers derived from the mean (floor and ceil).

transformation_steps: Recognize the objective function as a sum of squared deviations: F(x) = sum_i (Ai - x)^2.
Use calculus / algebra to note that F(x) is minimized at x = mean(A), since dF/dx = 2n x - 2 sum(Ai) = 0 implies x = sum(Ai) / n.
Account for the integer constraint on x by testing only floor(mean) and ceil(mean), i.e., (S // n) and (S + n - 1) // n where S = sum(A).
Replace the outer loop over all centers in [min(A), max(A)] with a constant-size loop (two candidates).
Remove NumPy and perform the squared difference summation with plain Python integers to avoid per-iteration temporary arrays and overhead.
Avoid redundant recomputation of min(A) and max(A) by not needing them at all in the mean-based method.
trigger_signals: Presence of a loop whose range is (max(A) - min(A) + 1), which can be extremely large if values span a wide range.
Inside that loop, repeated full-array operations (vectorized subtraction, squaring, and summation), making the total work multiplicative in both range and length.
The mathematical structure sum((Ai - x)^2) strongly suggests a variance/mean minimization problem where a closed-form solution exists.
Use of NumPy primarily to try to accelerate an inherently superlinear algorithm, indicating that complexity, not constant factors, is the main issue.
pitfalls: Using only floor(mean) or only ceil(mean) instead of testing both can yield incorrect results when the mean is fractional.

Integer division nuances: computing the two candidates as (S // n) and (S + n - 1) // n is safe for non-negative sums; if negative values are allowed, care is needed with ceil for negative numbers (using math.floor/ceil on S / n instead).
Potential overflow in languages with fixed-width integers when computing (Ai - c)^2; in Python this is not an issue due to arbitrary-precision integers.

If constraints in the original problem actually guarantee a very small value range (e.g., Ai in [-100, 100]), the brute-force center scan may pass, which can hide the underlying inefficiency on larger unseen inputs.
Relying on eval(input()) is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; while not a performance bottleneck here, it is a bad practice and should be replaced with int(input()).

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder coprimality problem: N up to 1e5, each A[i] in [1, 1e6]. Single test case. Time limit around 2s in CP environment.

dominant_ops: For every integer d from 2 to 1e6+1, build the slice var_7[d::d] and sum it to count how many input numbers are multiples of d. This creates and scans O(1e6/d) elements per d, with an extra full list copy for each slice.

complexity.time: O(M log M + N log A_max)
complexity.why: Let M = 1e6 (max value). The loop for var_5 in range(2, var_1) visits all d from 2 to M. For each d it iterates over var_7[d::d] whose length is about M/d. Total operations ~ sum_{d=2..M} M/d = M * H_M = O(M log M). Each slice var_7[d::d] allocates a new list of size ~M/d, so copying cost is of the same order. The gcd aggregation after that costs O(N log A_max), negligible next to O(M log M). Space: var_7 is size M, plus the input array of size N.

bottlenecks.detail: Brute-force multiple counting for every d up to max(A[i]) instead of factoring just the given numbers. This enforces O(M log M) work regardless of N.
Using slicing var_7[var_5::var_5] in the inner loop creates a new list for each d, causing O(M log M) element copies and significant GC/allocator overhead.
Even after detecting that some d divides more than one number (pairwise coprime condition already false), the loop continues up to M instead of breaking early.
The two-level Python loop over about M log M ~ 2e7 elements with list creation and Python integer additions is close to the limit for CP time constraints.

FastAudit.core_idea: Precompute smallest prime factors up to 1e6 via a sieve, then factor each input number using these SPF values. Track used prime factors in a global set; if a prime factor appears in more than one distinct number, the array is not pairwise coprime. Separately, compute the gcd of all numbers to decide between setwise coprime and not coprime.

complexity.time: O(M log log M + N log A_max)
complexity.why: func_2 builds an SPF table up to M = 1e6 in O(M log log M) via a modified sieve. For each A[i], func_3 repeatedly divides by its smallest prime factor, costing O(log A[i]) steps in the worst case; total factorization work is O(N log A_max). gcd accumulation in func_1 is O(N log A_max). Space: SPF table of size M, the input array of size N, and a few sets of size at most the number of distinct prime factors across all inputs.

complexity_delta.from: O(M log M + N log A_max) time, O(M + N) space with heavy slicing overhead
complexity_delta.to: O(M log log M + N log A_max) time, O(M + N) space using SPF sieve and factorization

constraints_guess.notes: AtCoder-style problem where N people each list liked items among M types (likely N,M <= 30 as in ABC118 B). Input size is small but original solution still uses avoidable O(N*M^2) work.

dominant_ops: Nested loops over all people (var_2) and all item ids (var_1)
Repeated list membership checks: `x in var_4`, `x in var_7[var_5]`
Frequent `list.remove` calls inside the inner loop

complexity.why: For each of N people, the code loops over all M candidate items. Inside this inner loop it performs `x in var_4` (O(M)), `x in var_7[i]` (O(K_i) ~ O(M)), and potentially `var_4.remove(x)` (O(M)) on a list. This yields O(N * M * M) = O(N * M^2) time in the worst case. All preference lists are stored in `var_7`, costing O(N * M) space.

bottlenecks.detail: Uses list membership checks and removals (`in`, `remove`) inside a double loop instead of leveraging set intersection to compute common elements.
`var_4` is a list used both for membership tests and deletions. List membership is O(M) and list.remove is O(M), compounding in the nested loops.
Builds `var_3` as a separate `[1..M]` list only to index into it; this duplicates the range and adds indirection without benefit.
Stores all people’s preference lists in `var_7` upfront even though they could be processed streaming-wise; this increases memory usage to O(N*M).

FastAudit.core_idea: Model the set of items liked by everyone as the intersection of each person's liked-item set. Initialize with all items {1..M} and iteratively intersect with each new person's preference set using in-place set intersection (`&=`).

complexity.why: Constructing the initial set of all M items is O(M). For each of N lines, building a set from that person's list is O(K_i), and intersecting with the running set is O(min(current_size, K_i)). Across all N, the total work is O(sum K_i) which is O(N * M) in the worst case. Only the current intersection set of size at most M and one temporary per-person set are needed at any time, so peak space is O(M).

complexity_delta.from: O(N * M^2) time, O(N * M) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N * M) time, O(M) space
complexity_delta.note: Replacing list-based membership and removal in nested loops with set intersection removes an extra factor of M, and streaming the input avoids storing all preference lists.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the goal is to count items liked by all people, i.e., the intersection of N sets of liked items.
Replace the list `var_4` (candidate items) with a set `var_6` initialized as `set(range(1, M + 1))` for efficient membership and intersection.
Eliminate the auxiliary list `var_3` and the outer storage `var_7`; instead, process each person’s preferences as they are read from input.
For each person, parse their line as `var_3, *var_1` where `var_3` is the count and `var_1` is the list of liked items.
Convert the current person’s liked items `var_1` into a set and intersect with the running set via `var_6 &= set(var_1)`.
After processing all people, output `len(var_6)` as the number of items common to everyone.
trigger_signals: Use of `x in some_list` and `list.remove(x)` inside nested loops over problem-size-dependent ranges, indicating potential O(N * M^2) behavior.
Maintaining candidate elements via repeated list removals rather than leveraging mathematical set operations (intersection).
Building and retaining a full 2D list `var_7` of preferences when only aggregate information (common elements) is needed.
Redundant data structures like `var_3` mirroring the range `[1..M]` purely for indexing.
pitfalls: Each iteration constructs `set(var_1)` anew; while acceptable for typical constraints, for very large M an optimization could reuse structures or avoid repeated conversions.
In-place intersection `&=` mutates `var_6`; if the original full-item set were needed later, it should be copied before intersecting.
The approach assumes items are uniquely identified by integers and that duplicates in a person’s list don’t matter; if duplicates had semantic meaning, set conversion would change behavior.
If input constraints were extremely large (e.g., N,M ~ 10^5), additional I/O optimizations and possibly bitset-based intersections might be needed for further speed and memory efficiency.

constraints_guess.notes: Minimize sum of squared deviations from an integer center. Likely N up to 1e5–2e5, values up to around 1e9. Brute-force over all candidate centers suggests original solution timed out on large value ranges.

dominant_ops: Outer loop over all candidate centers from min(ai) to max(ai)
Inner loop summing squared differences for each element for each center

complexity.time: O(n * R) where R = max(ai) - min(ai)
complexity.why: Array of n elements is stored. For each integer var_4 between min and max (R+1 candidates), the code scans all n elements and computes (ai - var_4)^2 and accumulates; no extra asymptotic storage beyond the input list.

bottlenecks.detail: The outer loop iterates over every integer center var_4 in [min(ai), max(ai)]. If the value range R is large (e.g., up to 1e9), this becomes infeasible regardless of n.
For each candidate center var_4, the inner loop recomputes sum((ai - var_4)^2) from scratch, leading to O(n * R) operations.
Sorting var_2 is unnecessary for the objective, except to get min and max. Sorting costs O(n log n) and is dominated by O(n * R) but still avoidable; min and max can be obtained in O(n).
The algorithm’s runtime depends on the numeric spread of the data, not on n alone. Inputs with large max(ai)-min(ai) are particularly slow even if n is small.
Using eval(input()) to read an integer is unsafe and slower than int(input()). While not the main bottleneck, it’s a bad practice in performance-sensitive/contest code.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the algebraic identity sum_i (xi - a)^2 = n*a^2 - 2*a*sum(xi) + sum(xi^2). The real-valued minimizer is the mean of xi. For integer a, the optimum is achieved at floor(mean) or ceil(mean). Precompute sum(xi) and sum(xi^2), then evaluate the expression at these two integer candidates only.

complexity.space: O(n) due to current numpy use; O(1) extra if implemented with pure Python arithmetic
complexity.why: Each element is visited a constant number of times to compute sum(xi) and sum(xi^2). The final cost evaluations at floor(mean) and ceil(mean) are O(1). The provided code also builds a NumPy array via np.power, which is O(n) in time and O(n) in memory, but the asymptotic complexity remains linear.

complexity_delta.from: O(n * R) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space with NumPy (or O(1) extra space without it)
complexity_delta.note: Key improvement is removing dependence on the value range R = max(ai)-min(ai) by deriving and minimizing a closed-form quadratic in a. For large R this is a dramatic speedup.

transformation_steps: Recognize the objective function: minimize F(a) = sum_i (xi - a)^2 over integer a.
Expand the square: (xi - a)^2 = xi^2 - 2*xi*a + a^2. Summing over i: F(a) = sum(xi^2) - 2*a*sum(xi) + n*a^2.
Observe that sum(xi^2), sum(xi), and n are constants with respect to a; F(a) is a quadratic in a with positive leading coefficient (n > 0).
Find the real-valued minimizer by derivative: dF/da = 2*n*a - 2*sum(xi) = 0 ⇒ a* = sum(xi) / n (the mean).
Since a must be an integer, the optimal integer center lies at floor(a*) or ceil(a*). Evaluate F at both and take the minimum.
Implement this by computing S = sum(xi), Q = sum(xi^2), then defining a candidate function F(a) = n*a^2 - 2*S*a + Q.
Replace the nested loops with a single pass to compute S and Q, then two O(1) evaluations of F(a). Remove the brute-force range loop entirely.
Optionally, avoid NumPy and compute xi^2 directly in Python to eliminate import overhead and extra array allocation.
trigger_signals: Presence of a loop over a numeric range from min(ai) to max(ai) with an inner loop scanning all elements, i.e., a pattern for var_4 in range(min, max+1): for var_6 in var_2: ...
Objective function is a sum of squared differences, which is a strong signal that mean/variance formulas or quadratic minimization can be applied.
The inner computation recomputes expensive expressions (like (xi - a)^2) from scratch for each a rather than reusing structure.
Sorting done only to get extremal values while the actual algorithm does not require order, indicating some conceptual mismatch between algorithm and problem.
Constraints or expected judge behavior suggest timeouts for solutions that depend linearly on the numeric spread of the data rather than on n.

Additionally, np.power on a Python list creates an ndarray, and sum(var_7) uses Python’s sum on that ndarray instead of np.sum, incurring extra overhead.'}

{'kind': 'numeric_limits_in_other_languages', 'detail': 'While Python integers are arbitrary precision, translating this approach to languages with fixed-width integers (e.g., 32-bit int) requires care: n*a^2 and sum(xi^2) can overflow if values are large. Use 64-bit or wider types.'}

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style constraints for this pattern: N up to around 1e5 and K up to around 1e9. Overall work ~N * log(K).

dominant_ops: Outer loop over i = 1..N
Inner while loop doubling var_6 until it reaches at least K
Repeated float exponentiation pow(1/2, var_2) per outer iteration
Standard input() parsing

complexity.why: For each i in [1..N], var_6 is doubled until it reaches at least K. The number of doublings is O(log(K/i)) ⊆ O(log K). The pow(1/2, var_2) call is done once per i and is O(1) in practice for float base, so overall O(N log K). Memory usage is constant aside from a few scalar variables.

bottlenecks.detail: Uses built-in input() which is slower than sys.stdin.readline() for competitive-programming style problems with tight time limits.
Tracks a separate counter var_2 in the inner while-loop and calls pow(1/2, var_2) after the loop, instead of accumulating the probability directly during the loop.
pow(1 / 2, var_2) invokes the general power function for floats N times; this has noticeably higher constant cost than simple multiplication in Python.

Two nested Python-level loops (for over N and while with up to O(log K) iterations) mean a large number of interpreted operations; any extra overhead (like pow, extra variables) becomes significant at upper constraints.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the same probabilistic logic (doubling until reaching K) but reduce constant factors: use faster buffered input, avoid pow by incrementally multiplying the probability by 0.5 in the inner loop, and minimize per-iteration work.

complexity.why: The algorithmic structure is unchanged: for each starting value i, we repeatedly double until reaching K, which is O(log(K/i)) iterations per i. Summed over i this is still O(N log K) in the worst case. However, each iteration now only does simple arithmetic (var_7 *= 0.5, var_6 *= 2) and no pow(), plus faster I/O, so the constant factor is much smaller while memory usage remains constant.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log K) time, O(1) space (higher constant factor due to pow() and slower input())
complexity_delta.to: O(N log K) time, O(1) space (same asymptotic complexity but with significantly reduced constant factors)
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity did not change; optimizations target Python overhead and library calls, which is critical near time limits.

transformation_steps: Replaced input() with sys.stdin.readline() to reduce input overhead.
Removed the exponent counter var_2 and the pow(1/2, var_2) call, instead accumulating probability by repeated multiplication var_7 *= 0.5 inside the doubling loop.
Streamlined per-iteration computations so that each inner-loop iteration does only simple arithmetic operations and conditional checks.
Kept overall algorithmic structure (nested loops) identical to preserve correctness while improving execution speed.
trigger_signals: Nested loops with potentially large N (up to ~1e5) and inner log-sized loop suggested tight performance margins.
Use of pow() inside or associated with per-element logic is a well-known hotspot in Python compared to simple arithmetic.
Use of input() rather than sys.stdin.readline() in a competitive-programming style problem.
Observed or anticipated timeouts / slow performance even though the big-O complexity appears acceptable.
pitfalls: Floating-point accumulation: both versions rely on double-precision floats; while differences are small, changing the order of operations (e.g., replacing pow with incremental multiplication) can lead to tiny rounding differences. For judge systems using absolute/relative error tolerances this is fine, but exact string matching would be fragile.
Readability vs speed: heavy renaming of variables and using manual I/O wrappers make the fast code less readable and harder to maintain, even though it is faster.

Potential over-optimization: algorithmic improvements (e.g., closed-form computation using logarithms) could change numerical properties; sticking to the doubling logic preserves behavior but any further optimization must be tested carefully for precision.
Assuming input format: relying on sys.stdin.readline() means the code assumes exactly one line with two integers; malformed input would not be handled, but this is standard in contest settings.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: N people, M item IDs (foods); N,M are small (≈30), but solution pattern should scale to larger N,M (up to ~10^3) with an O(N*M) method.

dominant_ops: Triple nested loops over people and items
Repeated membership tests `x in some_list` on plain Python lists

complexity.why:
Let N = number of people (var_2), M = max number of foods per person. After reading input into a list-of-lists, the main work is:
- Outer loop over var_4: N iterations.
- Middle loop over var_5: up to M items in that person's list.
- Inner loop over var_6: N iterations.
- Inside inner loop, `if var_7[var_4][var_5] in var_7[var_6]:` is a membership test on a Python list of length up to M, which costs O(M).
Total: O(N * M * N * M) = O(N^2 * M^2). Space is O(N*M) to store all lists plus a result list.

bottlenecks.detail: Counts, for each candidate item, in how many people’s lists it appears, by scanning every other list each time; this repeats nearly the same membership checks many times.
Uses lists with `x in list` membership checks (O(M)) instead of sets with O(1) average-time membership, amplifying cost inside nested loops.
Three explicit loops (over person i, over each item of person i, over person j) combined with a linear membership scan effectively forms a four-layer cost (N * M * N * M).
The same item’s presence in other people’s lists is recomputed many times instead of maintaining a global intersection or frequency count.

FastAudit.core_idea: Initialize the candidate set as all item IDs {1..M}, then for each person intersect this set with the set of items they like. The remaining set after processing all people is exactly the set of items liked by everyone; its size is the answer.

complexity.why: Start with a set of size M. For each of N people, read k_i items and convert to a set (O(k_i)), then perform `candidate_set &= person_set`, which costs O(min(|candidate_set|, k_i)) ⊆ O(M). Summed over all people: O(∑k_i + N*M) = O(N*M) in the worst case. Only the candidate set and one per-person temporary set are held at a time, which is O(M) extra space.

complexity_delta.from: O(N^2 * M^2) time, O(N * M) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N * M) time, O(M) extra space
complexity_delta.note: Replaces repeated cross-person membership counting with a single pass maintaining the global intersection of liked items.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the goal is to find items present in every person’s list (a global intersection), not to count per-item appearances via nested scans.
Introduce a global candidate set initialized to all possible item IDs from 1 to M.
For each person, read their liked items once and convert them to a set for O(1)-average membership and efficient intersection.
Update the global candidate set using set intersection (`candidate &= person_set`) instead of checking each candidate against every person with nested loops.
At the end, compute `len(candidate_set)` directly, eliminating the need for an intermediate list of duplicates and a final `set()` conversion.
trigger_signals: Presence of multiple nested loops over the same collections (people × items × people).
Pattern of counting how many collections contain a given element with repeated `if x in list` checks.
Use of `if count == N:` logic to detect items common to all lists, which often indicates a set-intersection or frequency-counting solution.
Membership tests on lists inside inner loops instead of leveraging sets or bitsets.
Intermediate result lists (`var_8`) that accumulate many duplicates, followed by `len(set(...))` to deduplicate at the end.
pitfalls: Misusing list membership instead of sets: switching to sets without rethinking the algorithm can still leave unnecessary nested loops.
Forgetting to initialize the candidate set correctly; it must start as all possible item IDs (1..M), not empty, otherwise the intersection logic fails.

Incorrectly handling the N = 1 edge case: the slow code had special handling; with the intersection approach, N = 1 is naturally handled and does not need special casing as long as initialization is correct.
Assuming that small official constraints (e.g., N,M ≤ 30) make performance irrelevant; reusing the pattern for larger N,M without the optimized approach would cause severe slowdowns.
Creating new large sets in deeply nested loops would negate the benefit of set intersection; sets should be built once per input line and intersected immediately.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case. First input (var_3 / var_2 in different versions) is N (up to about 1e5). Second input (var_2 / var_1) is M (likely up to about 1e9 or 1e12). Need to compute product over primes p^e || M of C(N+e-1, e) mod 1e9+7.

dominant_ops: Trial division prime factorization up to sqrt(M)
Computing large factorials with math.factorial on big integers
Repeated big-integer multiplications for falling factorials before applying modulus

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + K * e_max + F(N)) where F(N) is the cost of math.factorial(N-1)
complexity.space: O(log M + N * log N) bits due to large intermediate factorials
complexity.why: Factorization via trial division runs up to sqrt(M), which is acceptable for M up to ~1e12. The main overhead is math.factorial(var_2 - 1), which builds a huge big integer of size Θ(var_2 log var_2) bits even though its value is never used. In addition, each combinatorial term is built via big-int multiplications (falling factorial) and division by factorial(var_12), all in Python integers, so per-operation cost grows with N and with the magnitude of intermediates.

bottlenecks.detail: factorial(var_2 - 1) is computed and stored in var_5 but never used. This alone can dominate runtime and memory when var_2 is large.

Combinations are computed using Python integers without taking modulo until the very end. Intermediate products like var_3 and factorial(var_2 - 1) can have millions of bits, making every arithmetic operation expensive.

For each exponent e, C(N+e-1, e) is computed as a falling factorial of length e followed by integer division by factorial(e). While asymptotically O(e) per prime, each step uses big-int arithmetic instead of O(1) modular operations.
math.factorial uses multiplication of growing integers; computing factorial on a large N is significantly more expensive than linear-time modular factorial precomputation.

FastAudit.core_idea: Precompute factorials and inverse factorials modulo 1e9+7 up to N + max_exponent, then evaluate each binomial coefficient C(N+e-1, e) in O(1) time using n! * inv(r!) * inv((n-r)!) under the modulus. Keep all arithmetic modulo 1e9+7 to avoid big integers.

complexity.why: Factorization remains O(sqrt(M)) as in the slow version. The factorial and inverse-factorial arrays are built up to var_4 = N + max(e), which is O(N + e_max), with O(1) per step under modulo arithmetic. Inverses are obtained with a single fast exponentiation (O(log MOD)) plus a backward pass of multiplications. Each binomial C(n, r) then costs O(1) modular multiplications. All numbers stay bounded by MOD, eliminating big-integer overhead.

complexity_delta.from: Effective behavior dominated by big-int factorial computation and arithmetic: time superlinear in N due to large integer sizes; memory dominated by huge intermediate factorial values.
complexity_delta.to: Time O(sqrt(M) + N + e_max + K log MOD) with only fixed-width modular integers; space O(N + e_max) with small integers.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic operation counts in terms of N are similar (both touch O(N) or N+e_max values), but the fast version uses modular arithmetic so per operation is O(1) instead of growing with integer size. Removing the unused factorial(var_2 - 1) also eliminates a major constant-factor and memory blow-up.

transformation_steps: Remove the unused computation of factorial(var_2 - 1), which contributed heavy cost without affecting the result.
Recognize that the required quantities are binomial coefficients mod 1e9+7: for each exponent e, we need C(N + e - 1, e).
Introduce modular factorial precomputation up to max_n = N + max_exponent to compute n! modulo MOD iteratively.
Compute the modular inverse of max_n! via fast exponentiation using Fermat's little theorem, then build an inverse-factorial array by iterating downward.
Rewrite the combination calculation to use nCr(n, r) = fact[n] * inv_fact[r] * inv_fact[n-r] mod MOD, replacing big-int falling factorials and divisions.
Ensure that all arithmetic, including products across primes, is done modulo 1e9+7 to avoid big-integer intermediates.
Keep the prime factorization but stop early when the remaining factor becomes 1, slightly trimming constant factors in the sqrt(M) trial division.
trigger_signals: Use of math.factorial with large arguments in a modular arithmetic problem where only nCr mod MOD is needed.
Combinatorial expressions implemented via raw integer products and divisions before applying modulus.
Presence of huge temporaries (like factorial(N-1)) whose values are not reused across different combination computations or are not needed in full-precision form.
Output is taken modulo 1e9+7 but internal calculations do not reduce modulo until the very end.
Tight time/memory limits combined with potentially large N (e.g., up to 1e5 or higher), making big-int factorial and combination implementations suspicious.
pitfalls: Forgetting to size the factorial and inverse-factorial arrays up to N + max_exponent; if the bound is too small, nCr calls will index out of range or yield incorrect results.
Misusing the modular inverse function (e.g., wrong exponent, or passing wrong modulus parameter), which would corrupt all combination computations.
Not handling the edge case when M = 1 (no prime factors), where the loop over prime exponents is empty and the answer should default to 1.
Assuming that the cost of sqrt(M) factorization is negligible for very large M; for much larger constraints one might need a faster factorization method.
Overflow or performance issues if someone reverts to using Python's math.factorial for large N instead of modular precomputation, reintroducing big-int overhead.

constraints_guess.notes: Tree with N nodes and N-1 edges; single game query whose answer depends on the tree diameter modulo 3.

dominant_ops: Building adjacency list for N-node tree
Running BFS with a distance array of length N (likely twice for diameter)
Per-vertex deque operations with list-allocation-based enqueues
Repeated initialization of large arrays with INF values

complexity.why: The slow version still performs a standard BFS over all vertices/edges, which is Θ(N) on a tree, and holds O(N) distance/auxiliary arrays. However, several implementation choices increase constant factors significantly.

bottlenecks.detail: In BFS, the queue is updated using something like `var_11 += [var_15]` (deque.__iadd__) instead of `append`. This allocates a new list and then extends the deque on every push, adding overhead in the tight inner loop.

For each BFS call, a distance array `var_5 = [var_2] * var_10` (INF = 10**13) of size N is created. If BFS is run multiple times (e.g., twice for tree diameter), this reallocation is a noticeable cost for large N.

Multiple generic input helpers (`func_1`, `func_3`, etc.) wrap `sys.stdin.readline` and `int`/`map`. Each call adds function-call overhead in hot input loops compared to inlining simple parsing in place.

Imports of many heavy standard-library modules (defaultdict, Counter, heapq, math, bisect, random, itertools, string) that are unused in this solution. Import time and namespace clutter are small but unnecessary overheads.

BFS stores a separate distance array and repeatedly checks `if dist[u] + 1 < dist[v]` instead of relying on tree structure and parent tracking. Asymptotics are the same, but bookkeeping per edge is heavier than needed for a tree.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the tree structure to compute the diameter with two very lightweight BFS/DFS-like passes, tracking (distance, node, parent) in the queue instead of maintaining a full distance array, then decide the winner from diameter % 3.

complexity.why: Each of the two BFS traversals visits every vertex and edge at most once, giving Θ(N) time on a tree. The queue holds at most O(N) tuples, and no extra O(N) distance arrays are allocated beyond adjacency lists, keeping memory linear with a low constant.

complexity_delta.from: Two BFS traversals with full distance arrays: O(N) time, O(N) auxiliary memory (distance + queue) with relatively high constant factors due to array initialization and list-based enqueues on the deque.
complexity_delta.to: Two BFS traversals using only a queue of (dist, node, parent) tuples: O(N) time, O(N) auxiliary memory for the queue only, with much smaller constant factors.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity remains Θ(N) in both solutions, but the fast code removes several sources of Python overhead (unnecessary arrays, inefficient deque operations, extra helpers/imports), making it significantly faster in practice for large N.

transformation_steps: Replace the distance-array-based BFS with a tuple-based BFS that tracks (distance, node, parent) directly in the queue, avoiding an O(N) distance array and comparisons on every edge.
Use `deque.append` instead of `deque.__iadd__` with a one-element list inside the BFS loop to eliminate per-push list allocations and extension overhead.
Remove generic input helper functions for ints and lists in favor of simple, localized parsing, reducing function-call overhead in tight reading loops.
Drop large sets of unused imports (heapq, math, bisect, random, itertools, defaultdict, Counter, string) to streamline the module and avoid unnecessary overhead.
Eliminate repeated initialization of `[INF] * N` arrays for BFS; only adjacency lists and the BFS queue are kept, lowering memory traffic and improving cache behavior.
Leverage the tree property with a `parent` field to avoid revisiting the immediate predecessor node instead of using a visited/dist array with inequality checks.
trigger_signals: Deque operations written as `queue += [x]` or `queue.extend([x])` inside the innermost BFS loop instead of `queue.append(x)`, indicating unnecessary list allocations.
BFS implementations that allocate and fill a full `[INF] * N` distance array every time they run, especially when the graph is a tree and can be traversed without such arrays.
Presence of many unused helper functions and imports typical of a generic template, suggesting extra overhead and cognitive noise not needed for this specific problem.
Distance updates written as `if dist[u] + 1 < dist[v]: ...` on an unweighted tree, which hints that a simpler parent-based traversal would suffice.
Multiple layers of input helper functions (`func_1`, `func_3`, etc.) wrapping trivial operations, which is a subtle sign of excess indirection in a performance-sensitive context.
pitfalls: The optimized BFS assumes the input graph is a tree (N nodes, N-1 edges, connected). If there are cycles or multiple components, relying solely on a `parent` field and not tracking a visited set could lead to revisiting nodes or infinite loops.

The result `(var_4, var_14)` coming from the last popped BFS element relies on queue order guaranteeing nondecreasing distance; this is correct for standard BFS on an unweighted graph but must not be altered (e.g., by mixing in priority-queue behavior).

While the provided fast code uses `eval(input())` for the first integer, it would be safer and typically faster to use `int(sys.stdin.readline())`; `eval` is unnecessary and potentially dangerous if reused in other contexts.

Removing the distance array means you cannot easily reuse the BFS to answer arbitrary shortest-path queries; the simplified BFS is specialized for finding farthest nodes/diameter, which is appropriate here but not universally applicable.

If the adjacency list is not symmetric (i.e., edges are not added in both directions), the parent-based BFS could fail to explore all nodes, so the correctness of this approach depends on constructing the tree correctly.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic 'Lunlun numbers' style task: given N (up to around 1e5), output the N-th positive integer whose adjacent decimal digits differ by at most 1.

dominant_ops: Iterative search over candidate integers using arithmetic manipulations and a while True loop
Per-candidate digit check in func_2 by converting integer to string and comparing adjacent digits
Repeated loops up to var_9-1 (likely N-1) with expensive inner search for the next valid number

complexity.time: Superlinear in N and roughly proportional to the magnitude of the N-th valid number; effectively O(A * log A) where A is the value of the N-th Lunlun number, with heavy constant factors due to string conversions and nested loops.
complexity.space: O(1) or very small (a few scalars and temporary strings per candidate).
complexity.why: func_11(var_9) performs a loop for each k from 1 to N-1. Inside, it runs a while True loop that searches for the next valid number, and each candidate is validated with func_2, which converts the integer to a string and scans all digits. The number of candidates examined grows with the numeric size of the N-th Lunlun number, so the algorithm effectively scans much more than N numbers. This makes it significantly slower than a direct constructive O(N) or O(N log N) enumeration.

bottlenecks.detail: Uses a search-by-checking approach: repeatedly moves from one candidate integer to the next and validates it with func_2, instead of generating only valid numbers. This causes the runtime to scale with the numeric size of the N-th Lunlun number rather than just N.
For each candidate number, func_2 converts the integer to a string and walks all digits, adding an O(d) cost per candidate (d = number of digits). This is nested inside the outer iterative search.
The inner while True loop in func_11 has an unknown but potentially large iteration count per outer iteration, leading to unpredictable and often large total work.

Heavy imports (bisect, heapq, math, random, decimal, itertools, etc.), debug/timing decorator func_4, and increased recursion limit add clutter and minor overhead without contributing to the solution.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a breadth-first style digit generation of Lunlun numbers. Start from 1..9, then repeatedly generate next-layer numbers by appending a digit differing by at most 1 from the last digit (handling edges 0 and 9 specially). Stop when at least N numbers are generated, then sort and take the N-th smallest.

complexity.why: Each valid Lunlun number is generated exactly once (or a constant number of times) through the frontier set var_4; each generates up to 3 children. Thus the total number of generated numbers up to reaching N is O(N). All operations on sets are expected O(1). The final sorted(list(var_2)) dominates with O(N log N) time. All intermediate steps are linear in N, giving overall O(N log N) time and O(N) memory.

complexity_delta.from: Superlinear search tied to the magnitude of the N-th Lunlun number (effectively O(A * log A) with large constants, using repeated candidate validation).
complexity_delta.to: O(N log N) time and O(N) space via constructive BFS-style generation and one final sort.
complexity_delta.note: The key shift is from validating arbitrary integers until the N-th valid one is found, to directly constructing the ordered set of valid numbers up to the N-th position.

transformation_steps: Replace the iterative numeric search (func_11) with a constructive generation method: start from base digits 1..9 and iteratively build the next layer of numbers by appending digits differing by at most 1 from the last digit.
Maintain a frontier (var_4) containing the latest layer of generated numbers and generate the next layer (var_5) from it, ensuring only valid numbers are produced.
Accumulate all generated numbers into a global set (var_2) or list until its size reaches or exceeds N, thereby ensuring only O(N) valid numbers are tracked.
After generation, sort the collected numbers once to obtain them in ascending order and index directly into the sorted list to retrieve the N-th number.
Remove unnecessary machinery from the slow version: debug/timing decorators, excessive imports, and unused helper functions, to reduce noise and overhead.
trigger_signals: Presence of a while True loop in the core enumeration function (func_11) suggests an unbounded inner search per outer iteration.
Use of a generic validity checker (func_2) on successive integer candidates rather than generating valid states directly indicates a search-by-checking pattern, which is often suboptimal.
Substantial boilerplate (imports, decorators, helper functions) with little relation to the core combinatorial structure hints that the core algorithm was not tailored to the problem's state space.

Knowledge that Lunlun numbers have a natural graph structure over digits {0..9} with edges representing allowed transitions, which lends itself to BFS / layered generation instead of scanning all integers.
pitfalls: If N were significantly larger than the contest constraints, even the BFS + sort solution could become heavy due to O(N log N) sorting and the memory cost of storing all numbers; a queue-based BFS that generates in sorted order without a final sort would then be preferable.

Using Python's set for var_2 and var_4 is fine here, but careless use (e.g., accidentally generating duplicates or performing repeated unions over large sets) can increase constant factors; a queue-based approach can avoid unions entirely.
The fast code uses eval(input()) to read N, which is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; int(input()) is sufficient and safer.

If one attempted to micro-optimize the slow approach without changing the algorithm (e.g., tweaking func_2 or caching), the asymptotic bottleneck from scanning many invalid candidates would remain; the critical improvement is the shift to constructive enumeration, not local micro-optimizations.

constraints_guess.notes: One main sequence parameter (var_5 / var_18). Value domain or coordinate-compressed range up to about 3e5 (var_17 = 300001). Inner window size in slow solution is fixed at ~100 elements (range(var_5, var_5+99)), but this still leads to ~1e8 Python-level operations at n_max. Values used for DP/state indexing up to ~6**8 in the naive attempt, which is feasible in memory but heavy in Python.

dominant_ops: For each position i (controlled by var_5 descending), compute var_2[i] by scanning up to 99 forward indices j in [i, i+98], checking |a[i] - a[j]| <= K, and taking a max over var_2[j]. This is implemented as a Python generator inside max(), performing many Python-level loops, abs() calls, conditional branches, and list indexing operations. Additionally, a very large list var_2 of size 6**8 is allocated up front.

complexity.time: O(n * W) with W = 99 (effectively O(n) but with a very large constant). For worst-case n near 1e6 this yields around 1e8 element checks/max operations.
complexity.space: O(max(n, 6**8)) due to allocating var_2 with length 6**8 ≈ 1.7e6, plus the input array. This is significantly larger than necessary for typical n (~3e5).
complexity.why: The DP recurrence for position i examines up to 99 candidate future positions j and computes a maximum over their DP values, filtered by a value-difference constraint. Doing this with Python for-loops and generator expressions gives O(99) ~ O(1) conceptual cost per i, but in practice 100*n tight Python iterations and function calls dominate runtime. The fixed allocation of size 6**8 also increases memory footprint and cache pressure.

bottlenecks.detail: The inner max(...) over range(var_5, var_5+99) performs up to 99 Python iterations per DP state. For large n this becomes ~1e8 Python-level loop iterations, each involving abs(), list indexing, and conditionals, which is too slow in CP Python.
Using max(generator) with a comprehension creates iterator objects and repeated Python-level calls instead of tight low-level loops, adding overhead on top of the already heavy inner loop.
Preallocating var_2 with size 6**8 regardless of the actual n wastes memory and degrades data locality; negative-index tricks with var_1 = var_2 + var_1 further complicate access patterns.

The approach treats each DP transition independently, re-scanning up to 99 neighbors every time. It does not exploit any structure (e.g., range queries by value or position) that could be shared or aggregated; hence there is no sublinear-time acceleration via preprocessed data structures.

FastAudit.core_idea: Introduce a segment tree over a bounded index/value domain (~3e5), with lazy propagation, to maintain and update DP-related maxima over ranges in logarithmic time. Instead of explicitly scanning up to 99 neighbors for each position, the segment tree captures the best achievable DP values in relevant index/value intervals and applies range updates and propagations. This compresses the per-state work to O(log M), where M is the tree size, while also avoiding the oversized 6**8 direct-index DP array.

complexity.time: O(n log M), where M ≈ 300001 (rounded up to the next power of two for the segment tree). Each DP step triggers a small number of segment tree operations (range pushes via func_2, range updates via func_4, and possibly point or range queries) that are all O(log M).
complexity.space: O(M) for the segment tree arrays var_9 (storing current maxima) and var_15 (storing lazy values), plus O(n) for the input. This avoids the fixed 6**8 allocation and keeps memory near-linear in the logical domain size.
complexity.why: The DP transition depends on constraints that can be expressed as range operations (e.g., values within a certain difference threshold, or indices within a sliding window). A segment tree with lazy propagation is well-suited to perform range assignments or max-updates and retrieve maxima over ranges efficiently. By encoding the DP state into this tree structure and reusing aggregated information, the algorithm replaces explicit O(W) scans with O(log M) segment operations while simultaneously using a tighter index space.

from.time: O(n * W) with W ≈ 100 (conceptually linear but with very large constant factors from Python-level loops).
from.space: O(max(n, 6**8)) due to a fixed-size DP array and awkward index padding.

to.time: O(n log M) with M ≈ 3e5 (polylogarithmic overhead but dramatically fewer Python-level operations per state, and better-structured memory access).
to.space: O(M + n), eliminating the unnecessary 6**8-sized allocation and using a compact segment tree.

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically, O(n) vs O(n log M) suggests the original is better, but in Python the constant factors of the naive approach (≈100*n tight loops plus object overheads) cause TLE. The segment tree-based method has larger theoretical complexity but fewer, more structured operations, which makes it markedly faster in practice for n up to ~3e5 with M ≈ 3e5.

transformation_steps: Reinterpret the DP transition in terms of range queries/updates: identify that at each step we need the maximum DP value in some constrained region (by index or value difference).
Define a bounded index/value domain (M ≈ 300001) suitable for a segment tree; compute the smallest power of two ≥ M and allocate arrays var_9 (values) and var_15 (lazy tags).
Implement func_1 to decompose a half-open interval [l, r) into canonical segment tree nodes that cover that interval, preparing for operations like lazy propagation or updates.
Implement func_2 to push pending lazy values stored in var_15 down to children in the segment tree nodes encountered along the path, keeping var_9 consistent while avoiding redundant work.
Implement func_4 to perform a range update (e.g., range assignment or chmax) across [l, r) by using the nodes from func_1, applying lazy tags and updating var_9 at the appropriate segment nodes.

Refactor the DP loop to, for each element, map its value and constraints (such as |a[i] - a[j]| ≤ K or positional window) into a range on the tree, query or use the current maximum in that range, compute the next DP value, and then update the tree with that DP value via func_4.
Remove the fixed-size 6**8 DP array and negative-index tricks; instead, store state entirely in the segment tree, which is sized to the actual effective domain (≈3e5).
Use iterative tree operations instead of recursion to keep Python call overhead low and to retain tight control over hot inner loops.
trigger_signals: The slow solution performs an inner scan of up to 99 neighbors for each of n positions, leading to around 1e8 Python-level operations at maximal input size.

The performance-critical pattern is repeated max(...) over a small, structurally related neighborhood defined by simple constraints (index/window and |value difference| ≤ K), which is a classic sign that a range-query data structure (segment tree, Fenwick tree, etc.) can be applied.

The presence of a large fixed-size DP array (6**8) and negative index manipulations indicates inefficient use of the value domain and suggests that coordinate compression or a tree structure over a tighter domain could reduce memory and improve cache behavior.
Constraints hint that n can be large (≳10^5), making any Python solution with ~100*n inner-loop operations risky for time limits, especially when combined with generators and function calls.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors and half-open interval confusion when mapping the logical DP ranges to segment tree index ranges; careful handling of [l, r) vs [l, r] is required.
Incorrect or incomplete lazy propagation: forgetting to push pending tags before querying or updating children can lead to stale maxima and wrong DP results.
Choosing an insufficient segment tree size (e.g., not rounding up to the next power of two) will break the indexing logic used in func_1/func_4 and may cause index errors.

Misalignment between the value/index domain used in the DP definition and the segment tree domain (e.g., forgetting to apply the same shifts or compressions when computing ranges) can silently produce incorrect transitions.

In Python, using recursion or object-heavy node structures for the segment tree can negate performance gains; the iterative, array-based implementation—as in the fast_code—is important to keep overhead low.
If K or the neighborhood constraints change shape (e.g., become dynamic or depend on DP values), the mapping to static segment tree ranges becomes more complex and may need re-derivation.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style problem: N up to ~1e5 points with 3 coordinates, choose M points to maximize |sum x| + |sum y| + |sum z| by enumerating 2^3 sign patterns.

dominant_ops: For each of 8 sign patterns, build a list of length N with 4-int entries and sort it, then perform three separate summations over the top M entries.

complexity.time: O(8 * (N log N + N + M)) ≈ O(N log N)
complexity.why: The bottleneck is `_xyz.sort(reverse=True)` on a list of size N for each of the 8 sign combinations; all other work (building lists and summing over top M) is linear in N or M and repeated a constant (8) number of times.

bottlenecks.detail: Sorting N elements for each of 8 sign patterns is required, but the structure of each element is a 4-element list, increasing comparison and memory overhead.
For each point and each pattern, it allocates `_abc` (length-3 list) and `[sum(_abc)] + _abc` (length-4 list), causing many small Python object allocations and GC pressure (O(8 * 4N) list creations).

After sorting, it computes three separate sums over the same top M entries: `sum(var_2[1] ...)`, `sum(var_2[2] ...)`, `sum(var_2[3] ...)`, causing three passes over the top-M slice instead of a single pass.

The sort key is implicit: Python compares full 4-element lists, which is slower than sorting scalars. Only the first component truly matters for order, but the remaining components participate in comparisons when ties occur.

FastAudit.core_idea: For each of the 8 sign patterns, map every point (x,y,z) to a scalar value s = sx*x + sy*y + sz*z, sort this 1D list in descending order, and take the sum of the top M values. This directly maximizes |sum x| + |sum y| + |sum z| by linearizing the objective for each sign pattern and avoids extra per-point data and repeated passes.

complexity.time: O(8 * (N log N + N + M)) ≈ O(N log N)
complexity.why: As in the slow version, the dominant cost is sorting N values for each of 8 sign configurations. However, each element is a single integer and there is only one pass to sum the top M values per configuration, which greatly reduces constant factors compared to handling 4-tuples and multiple summations.

complexity_delta.from: O(8 * (N log N + N + M)) with high constant factors due to 4-int tuples, multiple list allocations per point, and 3 passes over top M.
complexity_delta.to: O(8 * (N log N + N + M)) with reduced constants by using scalar scores and a single pass over top M.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged (both are O(N log N)), but the optimized code substantially reduces Python-level work per element and per pattern, which is critical for N up to ~1e5 in Python.

transformation_steps: Avoid constructing augmented 4-element records per point (`[sum(_abc)] + _abc`) and instead compute only a scalar score per point (`x*sx + y*sy + z*sz`).
Eliminate the intermediate `_abc` 3-element list; compute the scalar directly from the coordinates (e.g., `var_8 * var_1 + var_10 * var_2 + var_11 * var_3`).
Sort a flat list of scalar scores instead of a list of 4-element lists, reducing comparison and memory overhead.
Replace three separate summations (one for each coordinate) with a single summation over top M scores, which already encode the chosen sign pattern’s effect.
Use direct iteration over sign choices via nested loops (for var_1, var_2, var_3 in (1, -1)) instead of bit-decomposing integers, simplifying and slightly speeding up the sign pattern generation.
Track and update a single best score (`var_7`) instead of collecting all pattern scores into a list and applying `max` at the end.
trigger_signals: N is as large as ~1e5, and the slow version performs heavy Python-level work (multiple list creations and passes) inside nested loops over 8 sign patterns.
Observed or likely TLE or very tight runtime margins when using the more allocation-heavy approach in Python.
Profiling or code inspection shows that most runtime is spent in list construction, sorting complex objects, and repeated summations over the same slice.
Problem editorial or common solutions suggest the scalar-score trick for this well-known maximization pattern.
pitfalls: When switching to scalar scores, it is easy to mix up the roles of N (number of points) and M (number to select). Carefully maintain variable naming and order of input to avoid off-by-variable bugs.
Incorrectly implementing the sign patterns (e.g., missing some of the 8 combinations or flipping the meaning of +1 and -1) will lead to suboptimal answers while still passing small tests.
When using slices like `var_4[:var_5]`, ensure that `var_5` is indeed the count of items to select (M), not N; a swap of variables silently changes behavior.

Avoid accidentally summing absolute values of individual coordinates separately in the optimized version; the scalar formulation already accounts for a specific sign configuration, so you must sum scores directly, not recompute abs-sums per coordinate.
Be careful with sorting order: you need descending order for selecting the largest scores; using ascending sort without reversing will produce the minimum instead.

constraints_guess.notes: Input N, M. Likely constraints similar to AtCoder ABC110 D: N up to about 1e4, M up to about 1e9. Need the number of ways to express M as a product of N positive integers modulo 1e9+7. Solution: prime-factorize M and for each prime exponent e, compute C(e+N-1, e) (stars-and-bars), then multiply all such combinations modulo MOD.

dominant_ops: Trial division factorization up to sqrt(M) (func_9), plus global precomputation for combinations via a factorial/inverse-factorial helper class (Class_1), even though only a handful of binomial coefficients with small k are needed once.

complexity.why: func_9 factorizes in O(√M). Class_1 (partially shown) is a standard combinatorics helper that typically precomputes fac[i], inv[i], invfac[i] up to some MAX = N + max_exponent in O(MAX) time and memory. Since there is only a single query and the needed ks (prime exponents) are very small (≤ O(log M)), this O(MAX_COMB) precomputation dominates the cost for large N.

bottlenecks.detail: Precomputes factorials and inverse factorials up to a large MAX for generic combination queries, despite needing only a few C(e+N-1, e) with very small e. This adds O(MAX) time and memory overhead.
Uses eval(func_10()) in func_1 and a heavy input-template wrapper (func_1/2/3) for a single simple line of input, which increases constant factors on a tight time limit.

Large unused helper functions (multi-dimensional array builders func_11/12/13, Yes/No printers, recursion-limit tweak, etc.) bloat the code and can confuse optimization focus, even if their direct runtime cost is small.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit that each prime factor exponent e of M is small and used only once. Factorize M by trial division, then compute each binomial C(e+N-1, e) using a direct multiplicative formula in O(e) time without any global factorial or inverse precomputation, and multiply all such values modulo 1e9+7.

complexity.why: func_1 does straightforward trial division up to sqrt(M): O(√M). The exponent for each prime is at most O(log M), and the number of distinct primes is also ≤ O(log M), so sum_e is tiny (≪ N). func_2 computes C(n, k) in O(k) with k = min(e, n-e) = e here, and this is done only once per distinct prime. No precomputation arrays are built, so space is only for storing the prime→exponent mapping.

complexity_delta.from: O(√M + MAX_COMB) time, O(MAX_COMB) space
complexity_delta.to: O(√M + sum_e) time, O(#distinct_primes) space
complexity_delta.note: By removing global factorial/inverse precomputation and replacing it with a per-query multiplicative binomial computation whose cost is proportional only to the small exponents, the algorithm becomes closer to pure O(√M) with much smaller constants and memory usage.

transformation_steps: Keep the core trial-division factorization but simplify it to return a plain dict of prime→exponent (func_1 in fast_code).
Remove the generic combinatorics class and any factorial/inverse factorial precomputation arrays.
Implement a lightweight binomial calculator (func_2) using the multiplicative formula C(n, k) = product_{i=0..k-1} (n-i)/(i+1) with exact integer division performed before taking modulo.
Compute each C(e+N-1, e) on the fly for every exponent e provided by the factorization, and multiply these contributions modulo 1e9+7.
Replace the heavy input template and eval-based int parsing with a direct split-and-int conversion for the single input line.
trigger_signals: Only a single test case and a very small number of binomial coefficient evaluations are required.
The ks in C(n, k) are the prime exponents of M, which are bounded by O(log M) and much smaller than N.
Precomputing factorials up to N + max_exponent (≈ 1e4–1e5) for one-time use indicates wasted O(MAX) work and memory.
The problem constraints allow trial division up to sqrt(M) comfortably, making factorization cost fixed and suggesting focused optimization on combination computation.
pitfalls: When using the multiplicative binomial formula, integer division must be exact; the code correctly divides before applying modulo, which is safe in Python with unbounded integers but could fail in other languages if division is done after mod.

If the constraints were different (e.g., many test cases or large k values for combinations), the removal of factorial precomputation would become a performance regression; in such settings, precomputed fac/invfac tables and nCk with O(1) queries would be preferable.
Relying on trial division up to sqrt(M) is fine for M up to about 1e9; for larger M (e.g., 1e12 or beyond), a more advanced factorization method might be needed to avoid TLE.

Care must be taken that the direct multiplicative C(n, k) remains efficient: if k could scale with N (e.g., k≈N≈1e5), this O(k) method might become a bottleneck and factorial-based methods would again be attractive.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical setting: two integers N, M (or K) with 1 <= N <= ~1e5 and 1 <= M <= ~1e9. Need product over prime factors of M of C(N + e_i - 1, e_i) modulo 1e9+7 (AtCoder ABC110 D-style 'Factorization'). Single test case.

dominant_ops: Precomputing factorials fact[0..L] modulo MOD in Class_1.__init__ (single forward loop up to L).
Precomputing inverse factorials invs[0..L] via one modular inverse pow(fact[L], MOD-2, MOD) and a backward loop.
Trial-division factorization of M in func_2 up to sqrt(M), repeatedly dividing out each prime factor.

complexity.time: O(L + sqrt(M)) where L is the maximum n needed for nCr (typically around N + max_exponent).
complexity.why: The factorial and inverse-factorial precomputations each scan an array of length L once, dominating when N (and thus L) is large. Factorization uses trial division where the loop variable grows up to sqrt(M), but in typical constraints sqrt(M) (~3e4 for M<=1e9) is smaller than L (~1e5), so precomputation usually dominates. Space is linear in L for fact and invs arrays.

bottlenecks.detail: Class_1 builds full factorial and inverse-factorial tables up to L even though each combination C(n, r) only needs r up to the exponents of prime factors of M, which are at most O(log M). For large N (hence large L), this O(L) work and memory are unnecessary overhead.

Two lists of length L+1 (fact and invs) are stored. When L is close to the upper bound of N (e.g., 1e5 or higher), this linear memory footprint is significant compared with what is actually needed (a handful of combinations).

The cost of constructing Class_1 is paid even if only a small number of C(n, r) calls are made. With exponents e_i typically <= 30 for M <= 1e9, the O(L) setup is disproportionate to the O(1) number of calls.

func_1 refers to self.combination, which is not defined in the snippet; this is likely a typo for using func_1 recursively or another method. While primarily a correctness bug rather than a performance issue, fixing it may require additional method calls or refactoring.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial tables and modular inverses by computing each required combination C(n, r) directly via the multiplicative formula using Python's arbitrary-precision integers, and factor M into a multiset of primes, then use Counter to obtain exponents. This trades O(L) precomputation and O(L) memory for O(r) arithmetic per combination with very small r (sum of exponents), which is effectively constant for given constraints.

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + sum e_i) where e_i are prime exponents in M (sum e_i = O(log M)).
complexity.why: func_2 performs trial division up to sqrt(M) with integer divisions, giving O(sqrt(M)) factorization time. The combination function func_1 uses the multiplicative formula with a loop of length r = min(k, n-k), but r corresponds to e_i in this problem, and each e_i is at most O(log M). The list of prime factors has length sum e_i, and Counter adds linear overhead in that size, so overall extra memory is O(sum e_i), which is tiny compared with L in the original approach.

complexity_delta.note: L is roughly the maximum n for which C(n, r) is needed (on the order of N). In this problem, the number of combinations evaluated is small and each r is at most logarithmic in M, so replacing global factorial precomputation with per-call multiplicative nCr removes the dependence on L and reduces memory usage from linear in N to linear in the (very small) sum of exponents of M.

transformation_steps: Remove Class_1 and its O(L) factorial and inverse-factorial precomputation; instead, switch to a standalone nCr implementation that uses the multiplicative formula: C(n, r) = Π_{i=0}^{r-1} (n - i) / (i + 1) with r minimized as min(r, n-r).

Change factorization (func_2) to return the full list of prime factors (with repetition) for M and apply collections.Counter to obtain exponents, simplifying the interface and avoiding the need to track exponents positionally.
For each exponent e returned by Counter, compute C(N + e - 1, e) using the multiplicative nCr function and only then reduce the product modulo 1e9+7, instead of relying on modular inverse factorials.
Eliminate the large fact and invs arrays to cut memory overhead and initialization time, relying on Python's big integers to handle the intermediate values of combinations.
trigger_signals: Presence of O(N)-sized factorial and inverse-factorial arrays when only a handful of combinations for very small r are needed.
Class-based combinatorics helper that is initialized once per run with cost proportional to the maximum potential n, not the actual workload.
Constraints where M is up to about 1e9 (so exponents are <= 30) but N can be large, signaling that per-call nCr complexity should scale with r rather than with N.
Profiling or reasoning that shows startup/precomputation dominating runtime despite few subsequent combination evaluations.

constraints_guess.notes: Counts non‑negative integer solutions (x, y, z) to a*x + c*y + b*z = N for given a,b,c,N. From fast_code: an array of size 3001 is used with a hard cap var_6 = 3000, so N is effectively <= 3000. Single test case, four integers input.

dominant_ops: Two nested Python for-loops over candidate counts of two variables (var_2 and var_1), with integer multiplications, additions, a comparison, and a modulo operation in the innermost part for each pair.

complexity.time: O((N/var_7) * (N/var_4)) = O(N^2) in the worst case when var_7 and var_4 are small (e.g., 1).
complexity.space: O(1) extra space (only a few integer counters and loop variables).
complexity.why: The outer loop runs up to floor(N / var_7) + 1 times, the inner up to floor(N / var_4) + 1 times. Each iteration performs constant-time arithmetic and a modulo, so total work is proportional to the product of these bounds. No data structures grow with N aside from scalar variables.

bottlenecks.detail: The double loop over var_2 and var_1 yields up to ~ (N/var_7 + 1) * (N/var_4 + 1) iterations. For N around 3000 and small coefficients, this can reach ~9 million iterations, all executed in Python.

Each iteration incurs Python interpreter overhead (loop control, variable access, arithmetic dispatch). Even though the arithmetic itself is constant-time, the overhead dominates when millions of iterations are executed.

The modulo operation `(expr) % var_5` is performed in the innermost loop for every pair (var_2, var_1). Modulo is more expensive than basic addition or comparison, further increasing per-iteration cost.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid explicit triple enumeration of (x, y, z) by accumulating counts of achievable sums in a fixed-size array and leveraging NumPy’s vectorized slice updates. The Python layer only iterates over O(N/var_5) values, while the heavy per-index updates (which would correspond to inner loops) are performed in optimized C via NumPy.

complexity.time: Python-level: O(N / var_5) iterations; NumPy-level: overall O(N^2 / (var_3 * var_5)) work but executed in optimized C. Asymptotically O(N^2) in terms of arithmetic operations, but with drastically reduced Python overhead.
complexity.space: O(N) for the NumPy array of length N+1 (here N fixed at 3000, so an array of size 3001).
complexity.why: The loop over var_8 stops once var_8 * var_5 > N (N = 3000), so there are roughly N/var_5 iterations at the Python level. Each iteration performs a slice update `var_1[start::step] += 1`, whose cost is proportional to the slice length but implemented in C. This shifts most of the O(N^2) arithmetic away from Python into efficient vectorized routines. The final sum is a single vectorized reduction over a strided slice, also O(N) in C.

complexity_delta.from: O(N^2) in pure Python with high per-iteration overhead due to nested loops and modulo operations.
complexity_delta.to: O(N / var_5) Python iterations plus O(N^2 / (var_3 * var_5)) arithmetic operations in optimized NumPy C code, still asymptotically O(N^2) in arithmetic but with much lower Python-layer cost.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic operation count in terms of N remains quadratic, but performance improves significantly because the innermost work is moved from Python to NumPy’s vectorized C implementation and the Python-visible loop depth is reduced from two dimensions to one.
