Trial division prime factorization of m up to sqrt(m).
Constant number of binomial coefficient evaluations using precomputed factorials.

complexity.why: Factorization runs in O(sqrt(m)). The large cost is initializing three arrays of size N (factorial, inverse, inverse factorial) and filling them with O(1) operations each. Each nCk query is then O(1) using precomputed tables, and there are only as many queries as distinct prime factors of m (small).

bottlenecks.detail: Building factorial (var_6), inverse (var_9), and inverse-factorial (var_7) arrays up to 2e5 dominates runtime and memory when there is only a single test case and only a handful of binomial evaluations are required.
Three integer arrays of size ~2e5 each are allocated regardless of the actual exponents of prime factors; this is overkill when the number of combinations needed is tiny.

All intermediate factorial and combination computations are done modulo 1e9+7 at every step, which is efficient but still adds overhead compared to computing a few exact binomials with small parameters.

FastAudit.core_idea: Eliminate global factorial / inverse factorial precomputation and instead compute each binomial coefficient C(n+k-1, k) directly via the multiplicative formula with exact integer arithmetic, leveraging that k (prime exponent) is very small. Factorization remains O(sqrt(m)), but memory and fixed precompute cost are drastically reduced.

complexity.space: O(1) additional (beyond storing the factor list/counter)
complexity.why: Factorization is still trial division up to sqrt(m). After that, exponents of prime factors (e) are computed via Counter. For each exponent e, the binomial C(n+e-1, e) is calculated in O(min(e, n-1)) multiplications/divisions. In this problem e is small (total number of prime factors of m is O(log m)), so sum_e e is tiny compared to N = 2e5 and even compared to sqrt(m). No large precomputed tables are used, so memory is essentially constant.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(N + sqrt(m)), Space: O(N) for N ≈ 2*10^5 due to factorial/inverse tables.
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(sqrt(m) + sum_e e) ≈ O(sqrt(m)), Space: O(1) extra beyond small lists and counters.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically in terms of N (the precompute bound), time improves by removing the O(N) term and space drops from linear to constant. In absolute terms, for a single test with small exponents, this avoids building 2e5-sized tables to answer only a handful of combination queries.

transformation_steps: Replaced factorial + modular inverse precomputation with a direct multiplicative binomial function func_1 that computes C(n, k) by multiplying numerator terms and dividing by denominator terms in integer arithmetic.

Changed the representation of factorization results from defaultdict(int) of prime → exponent to a flat list of prime factors followed by Counter to obtain exponents; this keeps asymptotic cost but simplifies code and avoids managing a map during factorization.

Removed repeated modular inverses and modular multiplications inside combination logic; combinations are computed exactly as Python integers and reduced modulo 1e9+7 only once at the end of the global product.
Used an explicit sqrt upper bound for trial division (for var_7 in range(2, floor(sqrt(n)) + 1)) instead of iterating to n with a break, slightly clarifying and tightening the loop bound.
trigger_signals: Single test case with only a small number of required nCk evaluations makes heavy factorial precomputation suspiciously expensive.
Presence of large static arrays (size ~2e5) used only to evaluate a few binomials points to over-precomputation.
Constraints on exponents of prime factors of m are very small (sum of exponents is O(log m)), suggesting that on-the-fly binomial computation will be cheap.
Memory-sensitive or startup-time-sensitive environments benefit from removing large global tables.
pitfalls: The direct multiplicative binomial implementation relies on exact integer division (var_5 //= var_8) at each step; this is mathematically safe for C(n, k) but must not be altered (e.g., changing loop order arbitrarily or doing modulo in between) or it may break integrality.

Doing all binomial arithmetic without intermediate modulo can lead to big integers; while safe in Python for these constraints (e small), porting this approach to languages without big-int support or with much larger k could cause overflow or performance regressions.

If the problem constraints were changed so that exponents e (or the effective k in C(n+k-1, k)) can be large (e.g., up to 1e5) or if many queries are needed, the precomputation-based approach can become faster overall due to O(1) per query vs O(k) for the multiplicative method.

The refactored approach is tailored to a prime modulus 1e9+7; if the modulus or arithmetic requirements change (e.g., non-prime modulus, need for modular inverses), the exact-integer combination formula followed by one modulo may no longer be directly applicable.
Factorization logic still uses trial division O(sqrt(m)); if m could grow significantly beyond ~1e9, a more advanced factorization method or precomputed primes might be necessary to avoid TLE.

constraints_guess.n_max: ≈ 2000–5000 (number of digits in the upper bound string)
constraints_guess.notes: The original solution is O(L * K * 10) in Python with three nested loops, which becomes borderline or too slow once L and K are in the low-thousands range. The use of NumPy in the modified code suggests constraints large enough that pure-Python triple loops risk TLE but not so large that O(L*K*10) is asymptotically impossible.

dominant_ops: Triple nested Python loops over (position, modulo_state, digit_choice)
Frequent modulo operations on inner-loop updates
Random-access updates to a 3D Python list structure

complexity.why: L = len(var_2) is the number of digits of the upper bound; K = var_1 is the modulus of the digit-sum. For each position (L), the code iterates over all modulo states (K) and all 10 possible next digits, performing several additions and mod operations plus 3D list indexing. The DP table has dimensions (L+1) x K x 2.

bottlenecks.detail: The core DP loop is explicitly written as three nested Python for-loops: for each digit position, each modulo class, and each candidate digit 0–9. That yields L*K*10 iterations at the Python level, with heavy per-iteration overhead.

Each inner iteration performs multiple list lookups and updates: var_4[var_5 + 1][(var_6 + var_3) % var_1][...] += ... plus two modulo operations. These are all executed in Python, magnifying interpreter overhead.
The DP array var_4 is a nested Python list structure of size (L+1) x K x 2. Python list-of-lists incurs pointer chasing and poor cache locality compared to flat numeric arrays.
Modulo by var_7 is applied on every inner-loop iteration for both tight states. This is functionally correct but increases the constant factor; it could be batched or reduced.

FastAudit.core_idea: Reformulate the digit DP transitions as convolutions with short uniform kernels and implement the modulo-state transitions using NumPy arrays, thereby vectorizing the DP and moving the heavy loops from Python into optimized C code. Precompute DP distributions for suffix lengths, then accumulate contributions for each prefix digit using offset management instead of explicit tight/loose dimensions.

complexity.time: O(L * K * 10) in arithmetic operations, but with most work done in NumPy over contiguous arrays rather than Python loops
complexity.why: func_1(var_14, var_7) constructs the transition for adding a digit in [0, var_14-1] via array slicing and accumulation. Its cost is O(var_14 * K) ≈ O(10 * K). This is called O(L) times for precomputations and O(L) times in the main accumulation, so the total arithmetic remains Θ(L*K*10). However, these loops run inside NumPy’s C implementation over contiguous int64 arrays, which is dramatically faster than equivalent Python-level loops. The DP over tight/loose is replaced by prefix-sum style composition using precomputed suffix distributions.

complexity_delta.from: Theoretical: O(L * K * 10) time, O(L * K) space, with all iterations and updates at Python level (triple nested loops over position, modulo, digit).
complexity_delta.to: Theoretical: O(L * K * 10) time, O(L * K) space, but with the core DP transitions implemented as NumPy array operations, eliminating Python from the innermost loops and reducing constant factors significantly.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time/space complexity is unchanged. The optimization is primarily in moving work from Python to optimized numeric kernels and simplifying the DP structure (no explicit tight dimension in the main DP).

transformation_steps: Recognize that the original 3D DP over (position, sum_mod_K, tight_flag) can be expressed in terms of transitions that depend only on (sum_mod_K) when the digit choices are unrestricted or bounded by a small integer d.

Isolate the transition for adding a digit in [0, d-1] to a modulo distribution as a convolution-like operation: each state distributes its count to a band of consecutive modulo classes. Implement this via a helper function func_1(var_14, var_7) using NumPy arrays and slicing instead of a Python for-loop over digits.

Precompute DP arrays var_11[i] for suffix lengths i where all remaining digits are free in [0, 9], using repeated application of func_1(10, ·). This effectively captures, for each remaining length, the counts of modulo sums for all completions.

Redesign the handling of the tight constraint by iterating over the digits of the upper bound string from left to right: for each position, combine suffix DP for lengths still to come with the current digit upper bound var_14 using func_1(var_14, var_11[remaining_length]). This accumulates contributions from choices where the current digit is strictly less than the corresponding digit of the bound.

Track the cumulative offset of the digit sum modulo K (var_8) as the fixed prefix grows, and accumulate contributions into var_10 using shifted slices (var_10[var_8:var_8 + var_1] += var_7). This replaces explicit tight/loose DP with an offset-based aggregation.

At the end, add the exact-prefix-equal path (var_10[var_8] += 1) and then sum var_10[::var_1] to aggregate counts where the total digit sum is divisible by K, adjust by -1 to exclude zero, and take the result modulo 10**9+7.
Use contiguous NumPy int64 arrays for DP vectors to improve memory locality, leverage SIMD and BLAS-like optimizations, and reduce overhead from Python-level dynamic typing and list indirection.
trigger_signals: Presence of triple nested loops with bounds (len(var_2), var_1, 10), suggesting potentially millions to tens of millions of Python iterations.
Inner-loop structure consisting almost entirely of arithmetic and array indexing, which is a classic candidate for vectorization using NumPy or similar numeric libraries.
DP over a modulo dimension with uniform or near-uniform transitions (digit choices 0–9), which is naturally expressible as convolution or sliding-sum operations.
Explicit tight/loose DP flag (Boolean third dimension) and digit-iterating logic indicating a standard digit DP pattern that can often be algebraically simplified using precomputation over suffixes.

constraints_guess.n_max: ≈1e5 (N: number of factors / length parameter)
constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style: N moderately large (up to around 1e5), M up to about 1e9. Need O(sqrt(M)) prime factorization and combinatorics up to N + max prime exponent (max exponent ≲ 30 for M ≤ 1e9).

dominant_ops: Global precomputation of factorials and inverse factorials up to var_7 = 10**6 using NumPy (func_3 + func_2).
NumPy-based 2D sqrt-decomposition style prefix-product construction in func_2 (reshape to sqrt(n) x sqrt(n), then row/column cumulative products).
Trial-division prime factorization in func_4 up to sqrt(M) (this part is fine asymptotically).

complexity.time: O(F_max + sqrt(M)), where F_max is the fixed factorial limit (here F_max = 10^6) independent of the actual needed range (N + max_exponent).
complexity.space: O(F_max) for factorial and inverse-factorial tables stored as NumPy arrays, plus additional overhead from temporary 2D arrays in func_2.
complexity.why: The code always precomputes factorials and inverse factorials up to 10**6 via NumPy, regardless of the input N and the actual maximum n needed for combinations. The 2D prefix-product trick in func_2 has linear work in array size but with large constant factors (reshape, broadcasting, modulo in NumPy), and it materializes a 2D array of size about 10**6 elements. These dominate over the relatively cheap O(sqrt(M)) trial division for factorization.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorials/inverse-factorials are precomputed up to a fixed var_7 = 10**6, regardless of the input N and required maximum of (N + max_prime_exponent). For typical constraints this is significant over-allocation and wasted work.

Use of NumPy for modular prefix products (func_2) introduces high constant factors: array resizing/reshaping, vectorized multiplications, and modulo operations on large arrays. In contest environments like , this is often slower than a tight pure-Python loop for ~10^5–10^6 operations.
The sqrt-decomposition 2D layout (reshape to var_3 x var_3, cumulative products across columns then rows) increases memory traffic and hampers cache friendliness vs. a single flat 1D factorial loop.
The heavy factorial precomputation runs at module import / before reading input. Even for small N, the program pays the full cost of building size-10**6 tables.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace the fixed, NumPy-based factorial precomputation with on-demand factorial and inverse-factorial arrays sized just up to N + max_prime_exponent, using straightforward 1D Python loops; keep simple trial-division factorization; and compute combinations via standard nCr = fact[n] * invfact[r] * invfact[n-r] mod MOD.

complexity.why: Prime factorization of M by trial division runs in O(sqrt(M)). Let e_i be exponents of primes in M, and E_max = max(e_i). The algorithm builds factorial and inverse-factorial arrays up to N + E_max, then computes each combinatorial term C(N + e_i - 1, e_i) in O(1). For typical constraints, E_max is small (≲ 30) and N is the dominant term, so both time and space are linear in the actually required combinatorial range instead of a fixed 10**6.

complexity_delta.from: O(F_max + sqrt(M)) time and O(F_max) space with F_max = 10**6 fixed, using NumPy 2D prefix products for factorials.
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + (N + max_exponent)) time and O(N + max_exponent) space, with simple 1D Python arrays for factorials.
complexity_delta.note: As long as N + max_exponent ≪ 10**6 (typical for this problem), the optimized version asymptotically and practically reduces both work and memory, and more importantly avoids the heavy NumPy overhead and global over-initialization.

transformation_steps: Remove the global NumPy-based factorial precomputation (func_2/func_3, var_13/var_14, var_7 = 10**6).
Replace factorial construction with a simple 1D Python loop: fact[i] = fact[i-1] * i % MOD for i in 1..(N + max_exponent).
Build inverse-factorial array via a single modular inverse of fact[max_n] followed by a backward loop: invfact[i] = invfact[i+1] * (i+1) % MOD.
Implement nCr as fact[n] * invfact[r] * invfact[n-r] % MOD with assertions/assumptions that 0 ≤ r ≤ n.
Use a straightforward trial-division factorization function that returns the multiset of prime factors as a list, then compress with Counter to get exponents.
Loop over prime exponents e and accumulate the result as the product of C(N + e - 1, e) modulo MOD.
Avoid importing NumPy and any 2D reshaping/resizing; keep all combinatorial data as flat Python lists.
trigger_signals: Fixed-size precomputation of factorials up to 10**6 regardless of input, indicating possible overkill vs. required range.
Use of NumPy for heavy inner loops in a competitive-programming context, where interpreter overhead and array conversions often make NumPy slower for ≤10**6 scale workloads.
Nontrivial 2D sqrt-decomposition logic to compute prefix products where a trivial 1D loop is sufficient.
Global initialization running before reading input, suggesting that small inputs still pay the cost of maximum precomputation.
pitfalls: Ensuring that the factorial and inverse-factorial arrays are sized to at least N + max_exponent; off-by-one errors in sizing or indexing can cause incorrect nCr results or IndexError.
Handling edge cases such as M = 1 (no prime factors) correctly; in the fast_code this is treated separately (if var_6 == 1: print(1)).
Confirming that all nCr calls satisfy 0 ≤ r ≤ n; in the optimized solution this is guaranteed by construction but should not be violated if the formula is modified.
Using modular inverses correctly: invfact construction via pow(fact[max_n], MOD-2, MOD) assumes MOD is prime (true for 1e9+7); changing the modulus would require a different approach.

If problem constraints on N were ever raised (e.g., N up to 10**7+), even the optimized linear factorial precompute could become too slow or memory-heavy; then one would need combinatorial formulas that avoid O(N) precomputation.

constraints_guess.notes: Two main parameters: N groups and M item IDs (1..M). Typical constraints likely N,M up to ~10^3; slow version degrades badly when both are a few hundred or more.

dominant_ops: Nested loops over people (N) and items (M) with repeated list membership checks and removals: `x in var_4`, `x in var_7[i]`, and `var_4.remove(x)` inside the inner loop.

complexity.why: There are N*M iterations of the inner loop. Each iteration performs `x in var_4` (O(|var_4|) ≈ O(M)), `x in var_7[i]` (O(K_i) ≤ O(M)), and potentially `var_4.remove(x)` (O(|var_4|) ≈ O(M)). Thus worst-case per-iteration cost is Θ(M), giving Θ(N*M^2). Memory holds all N preference lists (total size ≈ N*K_avg) plus two M-sized lists.

bottlenecks.detail: Using Python lists (`var_4`, `var_7[i]`) for membership checks leads to O(M) `in` operations and O(M) `remove` operations inside nested loops.
Filters the candidate list by scanning all items for every person, instead of using a direct set intersection of liked items.
Calling `var_4.remove(...)` while iterating over indices of `var_3` causes repeated shifting of elements and magnifies cost to O(M) per removal.

FastAudit.core_idea: Represent the set of candidate items as a Python `set` and iteratively intersect it with each person's liked-item set, leveraging O(1)-average membership and linear-time set intersection.

complexity.why: Initial candidate set of size M costs O(M). For each of N people, we build a set from their list in O(K_i) and intersect it with the current candidate set in O(min(|candidate|, K_i)), which in the worst case (all sizes ≈ M) sums to O(N*M). Memory holds the candidate set (≤M) plus one temporary set per line (≈K_i).

complexity_delta.from: O(N * M^2) time, O(N * K_avg + M) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N * M) time, O(M + K_avg) space
complexity_delta.note: Switching from list-based membership and removals in nested loops to set intersection removes an extra factor of M from the inner work.

transformation_steps: Replace the list `var_4` (candidate items) with a `set` initialized as all items 1..M.
For each person, read their liked items and convert that list to a `set` instead of keeping it as a list for membership checks.
Replace the manual nested scan and conditional removal (`if x in var_4 and x not in person_list: var_4.remove(x)`) with a single set intersection operation `var_4 &= person_set`.
Avoid mutating the candidate collection via `remove` inside the inner loop; instead rely on the bulk `&=` operation which is internally optimized.
Drop redundant arrays (`var_3` copy of 1..M and full `var_7` storage, if not otherwise needed) to simplify logic and reduce overhead.
trigger_signals: Membership tests (`x in list`) and `list.remove(x)` calls appearing inside nested loops over both N and M.
Problem semantics naturally describing 'items common to all groups', which maps directly to set intersection.
Performance issues or TLE when N and M grow, particularly with O(N*M^2) patterns.
Shrinking a list while iterating over indices of a related list, which is a known anti-pattern for performance and correctness.
pitfalls: Rebuilding sets from lists more often than necessary can add overhead; in this pattern building one set per input line is appropriate, but avoid extra conversions.

Initializing the intersection set incorrectly (e.g., from the first person's preferences instead of the full 1..M universe) can change behavior if some items never appear; the original logic used the full range 1..M, so the rewrite must preserve that.
Assuming set operations are always O(1); while average-case is good, extremely large sets with adversarial data can still be slower, though far better than list-based O(M) membership in this context.
Mixing lists and sets inconsistently (e.g., `x in list` instead of `x in set`) can accidentally reintroduce O(M) factors even after a partial refactor.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style constraints; task is to multiply N integers (N up to about 2e5) and cap result at 1e18.

dominant_ops: Reading N integers from stdin
Linear scan to detect zero in the list
Linear scan to multiply all elements until product exceeds 1e18
Big-int multiplication and comparison against 10**18

complexity.why: The algorithm reads an array of size n, performs an `in` check (O(n)) and then a single pass loop (O(n)) to multiply elements and check against a fixed limit; extra imports and helpers do not change asymptotic complexity. The list itself requires O(n) space.

bottlenecks.detail: Large number of unused imports (`bisect`, `math`, `itertools`, `collections`, etc.) slightly increases startup time and memory footprint.
Custom lambda-based input helpers wrapping `sys.stdin.readline` add minor indirection overhead, though they are still relatively fast.
The flags and ternary-style final print (`var_13`, `print((var_14 if not var_13 else -1))`) are more complex than necessary, though the cost is negligible compared to the O(n) loop.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the same linear algorithm—early-out on zero, otherwise multiply elements and stop if product exceeds 1e18—but simplify control flow and avoid auxiliary helpers, printing immediately on detecting overflow.

complexity.why: The modified code still reads an array of size n and performs two linear passes (zero check and multiplication with early exit). No additional asymptotic work is introduced, and memory use remains dominated by storing the n integers.

complexity_delta.from: O(n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: Both versions are linear-time and linear-space; changes are primarily about code style and constant factors. In fact, using `eval(input())` may slightly hurt performance compared to the original `sys.stdin.readline`-based approach.

transformation_steps: Removed large sets of unused imports and global helper lambdas, leaving only the core logic.
Replaced custom `sys.stdin`-based input wrappers with direct `input()` calls and simple parsing.
Eliminated function wrapper and global utility structure; moved logic to top level with straightforward variables.
Simplified control flow: on encountering zero or overflow, print the result and `exit()` immediately instead of using a flag and conditional final print.
Replaced flag-based overflow handling (`var_13`) with direct early termination.
trigger_signals: Code cluttered with many unused imports and helpers for a very small computational task.
Desire to simplify solution template for contest submissions.
Potential perception that helper-heavy templates add overhead for simple problems.
pitfalls: Using `eval(input())` is unsafe in general and also slower than simply `int(input())`; it should be avoided in competitive programming and production code.
Switching from `sys.stdin.readline` to `input()` can be a performance regression for very large inputs; the original I/O method was already efficient.
Relying on `exit()` at top-level can be fine in scripts but is less clean if the code is ever reused as a module or within a larger application.
Both versions still perform two passes over the list (`0 in var_1` and then the multiplication loop); if needed, these could be merged into a single pass without changing asymptotic complexity.

constraints_guess.notes: Input: N followed by N integers. Values likely up to around 1e9. Task: compute the greatest common divisor (GCD) of all N integers.

dominant_ops: Sorting the entire array of N numbers
Enumerating all divisors of the minimum element up to its square root
For each candidate divisor, scanning the full array to test divisibility

complexity.time: O(N log N + sqrt(M) + N * τ(M)) where M = min(A), τ(M) is the number of divisors of M
complexity.why: The code sorts the N-element array (O(N log N)), then iterates all i from 1 to floor(sqrt(M)) to collect divisors of the minimum element M (O(sqrt(M))). The number of collected divisors is τ(M). For each divisor, it checks divisibility for all N elements (O(N * τ(M))). Arrays of size N are stored plus a list of divisors, so space usage is linear in N.

bottlenecks.detail: Uses divisor enumeration of the minimum element and checks each divisor against all elements instead of directly computing the GCD. This introduces an extra factor τ(M) in the time complexity.
Sorts the entire array just to obtain the minimum value, which could be obtained in O(N) with a single pass.
Uses eval(input()) for reading N, which is slower and unsafe compared to direct int(input()).

FastAudit.core_idea: Compute the GCD of the array by iteratively applying the Euclidean algorithm: start from the first number and fold GCD over the list. This avoids enumerating divisors and scanning the array multiple times.

complexity.why: Each GCD computation between two integers up to A_max takes O(log A_max) with the Euclidean algorithm. Folding over N numbers performs N-1 such GCD operations, so O(N log A_max). The algorithm keeps only a running GCD and the array, so asymptotic space is linear in N (dominated by input storage), with O(1) extra working memory.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log N + sqrt(M) + N * τ(M)) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N log A_max) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: Replaced divisor enumeration and repeated full-array checks with a single linear pass using the Euclidean GCD, and removed the need for sorting and storing all divisors.

transformation_steps: Eliminate sorting of the input list; read all numbers and directly use them for GCD computation.
Replace divisor enumeration (looping up to sqrt(min(A))) with a running GCD variable initialized to the first element.
Iterate once over the remaining N-1 elements and update the running GCD using the Euclidean algorithm (iterative gcd function).
Remove the outer loop over candidate divisors and the inner divisibility checks, since the final GCD from the fold is by definition the largest integer dividing all elements.
Switch to faster input handling via sys.stdin.readline and avoid eval on simple integer inputs.
trigger_signals: Presence of nested loops: candidate divisors × all array elements.
Sorting performed only to get the minimum element, which signals unnecessary O(N log N) work.
Mathematical structure: problem asks for a greatest common divisor over a set of integers, which has a well-known optimal solution via the Euclidean algorithm.
Potentially large N and large integer values, making repeated full scans per divisor costly in worst-case scenarios.
pitfalls: Handling edge cases like N = 1, where the answer should just be the single element; the fold-style GCD must handle this correctly.
Ensuring all numbers are non-negative or taking absolute values before GCD if negative inputs are possible.
Avoiding eval for input parsing to prevent security risks and overhead.
Remembering that Python’s built-in math.gcd or a hand-written Euclidean function should be used, not a naive O(min(a,b)) divisor search.
Maintaining integer types throughout (no floating-point operations like **(1/2) for square root when not needed).

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style job scheduling / deadlines problem: N jobs (duration, deadline). Need to check if jobs can be ordered (by deadline) so cumulative time never exceeds each job's deadline. Constraints likely around N ≤ 2e5, durations and deadlines up to ~1e9.

dominant_ops: Reading N lines of two integers each
Sorting N jobs by deadline using a Python lambda key
Single linear scan over sorted jobs accumulating processing time and checking deadlines

complexity.why: The input is stored as a list of N pairs. The sort on var_1 dominates with O(N log N). The input reading and final loop are O(N). No extra asymptotic memory beyond storing all jobs.

bottlenecks.detail: Sorting N jobs with a Python key function is inherently O(N log N); for large N (≈2e5), the sort dominates total runtime. This is necessary for the greedy approach, so it cannot be removed but defines the performance envelope.

Multiple tiny wrapper functions (func_1–func_8) create small overhead via extra Python function calls, though only func_3 and func_7 are actually used. This adds call overhead for every read and parse.

Using var_7 = sys.stdin and then var_7.readline() is fine, but not aliasing readline directly (e.g., var_4 = sys.stdin.readline) misses a micro-optimization where the function lookup is slightly cheaper.

The final decision logic keeps a flag (var_3) for the entire loop and prints once at the end instead of exiting early when a violation is found, which can waste some iterations in negative cases (though still O(N)).

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the same greedy scheduling algorithm (sort jobs by deadline and ensure cumulative processing time never exceeds each job’s deadline), but streamline I/O, remove unused helpers, add an explicit tie-break in sorting, and exit immediately when a violation is detected to reduce constant factors.

complexity.why: The algorithm is unchanged asymptotically: building the list is O(N), sorting by a tuple key (deadline, duration) is O(N log N), and the single scan is O(N). Memory is dominated by storing the N pairs.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(N log N), Space: O(N)
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(N log N), Space: O(N)
complexity_delta.note: The asymptotic bounds are identical; improvements come from reduced Python-level overhead (fewer function calls, direct readline alias, early exit) and a slightly more specific sort key, which may help with worst-case constant factors but does not change big-O.

transformation_steps: Replaced multiple small input helper functions with a direct alias to sys.stdin.readline (var_4 = sys.stdin.readline) to avoid repeated Python function call overhead for simple operations.

Simplified reading of N: var_6 = func_7() became var_5 = int(eval(var_4())). This removes a wrapper call but introduces eval; using int(var_4()) would be simpler and safer while preserving the benefit of the readline alias.
Constructed the job list in a single expression using the readline alias and map(int, ...): var_1 = [list(map(int, var_4().split())) for _ in range(var_5)]. This removes the func_3 indirection.

Adjusted the sort key from sorting by deadline only (key=lambda var_8: var_8[1]) to sorting by (deadline, duration) (key=lambda var_7: (var_7[1], var_7[0])). This adds a deterministic tie-breaker but keeps the same optimal greedy structure and asymptotic cost.

Changed the loop logic to perform the violation check before updating the cumulative time fully in the stored variable, and to exit immediately on the first violation: if var_6 + var_2 > var_3: print('No'); exit(). This avoids unnecessary iterations in failing instances and removes the need for a boolean flag.
Simplified the final output to unconditional print('Yes') at the end of the loop when no early exit has occurred, dropping the ternary print and boolean state.
trigger_signals: Problem constraints suggest N can be large (≈1e5–2e5), making Python implementations sensitive to constant factors around sorting and I/O.
The original solution already uses the correct O(N log N) algorithm but may be close to time limits on heavy test data, prompting micro-optimizations rather than algorithm changes.
Profiling or intuition for similar tasks reveals input reading and sort-key application as dominant costs, so reducing function call overhead and early termination in failing cases are natural steps.
pitfalls: Using eval on raw input is generally unsafe and slower than necessary; var_5 = int(var_4()) (or stripping whitespace) is preferred. Although for competitive programming with trusted inputs it often passes, it is a bad habit for production code.

Calling exit() (from the site module) is slightly non-idiomatic; sys.exit() is more explicit and avoids potential differences in some environments. In strict judges, abrupt termination may be discouraged; breaking the loop and printing carefully can be safer.

Adding a tie-breaker to the sort key (sorting by (deadline, duration)) does not change correctness for this decision problem, but one must ensure it does not conflict with any subtle problem-specific requirements when porting patterns between tasks.

Over-optimizing for constant factors can obscure code readability. In many contexts, the clearer original version with small helper functions is more maintainable, and only needs optimization when profiling or time-limit evidence justifies it.

constraints_guess.notes: Input is a fixed 3x3 integer grid. Values are likely small (e.g., in [0,100]). Task: determine if there exist arrays A[3], B[3] such that grid[i][j] = A[i] + B[j] for all i,j.

dominant_ops: Triple nested loops over candidate values (0..100) for three variables, with constant-time consistency checks for the 3x3 grid in the innermost loop.

complexity.time: O(K^3) where K is the range size of guessed values (here K=101, ~10^6 iterations, effectively constant but heavy).
complexity.why: The algorithm enumerates all triples (var_6, var_7, var_8) in [0,100]^3. For each triple, it performs a fixed number of arithmetic operations and comparisons on the small 3x3 grid, without additional data structures.

bottlenecks.detail: Exhaustively tries all combinations of three parameters (a0, b0, b1) via three nested loops, instead of solving the linear relations directly.
Once var_1 is set to True (a valid assignment found), the loops continue until all 101^3 combinations are processed; no early break out of the loops.
Values var_2, var_3, var_4 depend only on var_6 but are recomputed inside the innermost loop over var_7 and var_8, increasing constant factors.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the structure c[i][j] = A[i] + B[j]. Fix A[0] = 0 (or equivalently use row/column differences), derive B[j] from the first row, derive A[i] from the first column using B[0], then verify that A[i] + B[j] equals every grid cell. This removes the search over candidate values and uses direct algebraic consistency checks.

complexity.time: O(1) for the fixed 3x3 grid (more generally O(n^2) for an n×n grid).
complexity.why: The code constructs two small arrays of length 3 and runs two nested loops over the 3x3 grid (9 checks total). There is no dependence on any large value range or search space—only on the fixed grid size.

complexity_delta.from: O(K^3) over the value range (triple nested search over 0..100) with relatively high constant factors.
complexity_delta.to: O(1) for the fixed 3x3 grid (or O(n^2) over grid size) with very small constant factors.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both are constant for this particular problem instance, but the brute-force method performs about 10^6 iterations whereas the direct method performs only a handful of operations. This is a large constant-factor speedup and is more scalable if the grid size or value range were increased.

transformation_steps: Recognize that each cell satisfies c[i][j] = A[i] + B[j], so the grid is determined by row- and column-wise offsets.
Fix a baseline (e.g., set A[0] = 0 or more generally absorb any constant shift between A and B), and derive B[j] directly from the first row: B[j] = c[0][j] - A[0].
Use the first column to derive A[i]: A[i] = c[i][0] - B[0].
Verify consistency: check for all i,j that A[i] + B[j] == c[i][j]; if any mismatch occurs, answer "No", else answer "Yes".
Remove all enumeration over candidate values (no nested loops over the value range), keeping only loops over the fixed grid cells.
trigger_signals: Presence of triple nested loops over a small bounded range (0..100) to solve a simple additive relation on a tiny 3x3 grid.
The mathematical form of the condition (grid[i][j] = A[i] + B[j]) suggests a linear, directly solvable system instead of search.
Recomputing similar expressions for each candidate combination, indicating that the structure of the equations is not being exploited.
No early termination of the brute-force loops even after a satisfying assignment is found.
pitfalls: When moving from brute-force to algebraic derivation, one must correctly handle the invariance A[i] -> A[i] + k, B[j] -> B[j] - k; choosing a normalization such as A[0] = 0 (or using differences) must be done consistently.
All cells must be checked for consistency; skipping any check or only validating a subset of rows/columns can produce false positives.
If generalized to larger grids or different constraints, care is needed to keep indexing correct and avoid off-by-one errors in row/column derivations.
In other languages or larger ranges, attention to integer overflow may be necessary when computing differences A[i] and B[j].

constraints_guess.notes: Classic 'count items common to all groups' pattern (e.g., N people, M item types, each line: k a1 ... ak). Competitive programming versions often allow N,M,Σk up to around 1e5–2e5, where quadratic or worse in N,M becomes too slow.

dominant_ops: For each item id var_7 in [1..M], scan every person's list (var_5 in var_1) and perform membership test `var_7 in var_5` (linear in length of var_5)
Creation of all lists of liked items and storing them in memory (var_1)

complexity.why: Let N = var_4 (number of people), M = var_3 (number of item types), and K_i be the size of person i's list. The code computes `sum(all(var_7 in var_5 for var_5 in var_1) for var_7 in range(1, var_3 + 1))`. The outer comprehension iterates over all M item IDs. For each item ID var_7, `all(...)` scans all N lists. Each membership `var_7 in var_5` on a Python list is O(K_i) in the length of that list. Therefore a single var_7 costs Θ(Σ_i K_i), and repeated for all M items gives Θ(M * Σ_i K_i). All lists are stored, so space is Θ(ΣK_i).

bottlenecks.detail: Triple-nested behavior: loop over all M items, for each item loop over all N people, and for each person perform a linear search within that person's list. This effectively becomes O(M * ΣK_i) membership work, which can degenerate toward O(N * M^2) if K_i ≈ M.

Using Python lists for membership checks (`x in list`) results in O(K_i) time per check. For this problem, each person's liked items should be represented as a set for O(1) average membership to avoid the extra factor of K_i.

The slow code retains all users' lists (var_1) and then re-scans them M times. It does not exploit the fact that the operation needed is a global intersection of sets, which can be maintained incrementally in a single pass.

Use of `sum(all(...) for ...)` over a large range creates many generator frames and Python-level iterations. Even if the asymptotics were acceptable, this implementation style has significant constant overhead in CPython compared to a tighter loop or vectorized set operations.

FastAudit.core_idea: Maintain a running intersection of the sets of liked items: start from the set of all items {1..M} and intersect it with each person's liked-item set as the input is read. The final intersection size is exactly the count of items liked by everyone.

complexity.time: O(M + ΣK_i + N * M') (with M' shrinking as the intersection gets smaller; in typical cases close to O(M + ΣK_i))
complexity.why: Let initial set S have size M. For each person i, we build a set from their K_i items in O(K_i) time, then intersect it with S. Each intersection is O(min(|S|, K_i)). The size of S is non-increasing and bounded by M, and often shrinks quickly. Total time is O(M) to build the initial set plus O(ΣK_i) to parse and build per-person sets plus O(Σ min(|S_{i-1}|, K_i)) for intersections. This is typically near-linear in ΣK_i+M, and even in the pessimistic case bounded by O(N*M + ΣK_i). Space only needs to hold the current intersection S and the current person's set, i.e., O(M).

complexity_delta.from: O(M * ΣK_i) time, O(ΣK_i) space
complexity_delta.to: O(M + ΣK_i + Σ min(|S_{i-1}|, K_i)) time (≈ O(M + ΣK_i) in practice), O(M) space
complexity_delta.note: The slow version effectively does a repeated linear search of lists for every item-person pair; the fast version transforms the computation into a single global set intersection, replacing repeated scanning with efficient set operations and eliminating an extra factor proportional to list lengths.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the goal is to find items present in every person's list, which is exactly the intersection of all N sets of liked items.
Change the representation of each person's liked items from lists to sets to achieve O(1) average-time membership and efficient intersection operations.
Initialize a set S with all candidate items `{1, 2, ..., M}` instead of iterating over items as the outermost loop.
For each input line/person, parse their liked items and immediately intersect S with the set of these items (`S &= set(person_items)`), updating the global intersection incrementally.
At the end, replace the computationally heavy `sum(all(...) for ...)` over all item IDs with a simple `len(S)` to get the count of items common to all.
trigger_signals: Presence of nested comprehensions: `sum(all(var_7 in var_5 for var_5 in var_1) for var_7 in range(1, var_3 + 1))`, which encodes a loop over items and, inside it, a loop over people and lists.
Use of `x in list` membership checks inside an inner loop, which scales linearly with the list size and is repeated many times.
Algorithm structure that re-traverses all data M times instead of progressively reducing the candidate set of answers in a single pass.
Problem semantics matching a classic 'intersection of sets' or 'common elements in all groups' pattern, signaling that direct set operations are likely optimal.
pitfalls: If per-person sets are very large and the global intersection remains large, repeated set intersections still cost O(N*M); however, this is usually much better than O(M * ΣK_i) when K_i are also large.

Converting each list of items to a set has an upfront O(K_i) cost; for tiny lists and very small N,M, the constant factors might dominate and differences become negligible, though asymptotically the set-based approach remains preferable.

When translating from the slow pattern to the fast one, off-by-one or indexing mistakes can occur (e.g., misinterpreting N vs M or ignoring the first integer k on each line). Care is needed to ensure that the intersection uses the correct universe of items and that all inputs are consumed correctly.

If the universe of items is extremely large but each person’s list is tiny, initializing S as `set(range(1, M+1))` may be more costly than intersecting from a smaller starting set, e.g., beginning from the first person’s set instead of the full range.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style problem: minimize sum_i (a_i - t)^2 over integer t. Input usually n ≤ 100 and 1 ≤ a_i ≤ 100, consistent with np.arange(1, 101).

dominant_ops: Python for-loop over candidate t values; each iteration performs a NumPy vector operation (var_2 - t)**2 and sum over the full array.

complexity.why: Let n = len(var_2) and V = max(var_2) - min(var_2) + 1 (number of candidate t values). For each of V candidates the code computes (var_2 - t)**2 and np.sum(...), both O(n) on a length-n array. Thus total O(V*n). Space: var_2 plus a length-n temporary per iteration, but at any time only O(n) is live.

bottlenecks.detail: The main loop over var_4 is in pure Python, calling NumPy (vectorized) operations V times. Each iteration incurs overhead for Python-level loop control and function calls.
min(var_2) is recomputed in every loop iteration when constructing var_5, even though it is constant. This adds unnecessary overhead, especially if V grows.
Each iteration allocates a temporary array (var_2 - var_5)**2 of size n. Repeated allocation and deallocation of these temporaries increases memory traffic and cache pressure.
var_1 = int(eval(input())) is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()). While not a major performance bottleneck here, it is a bad practice and can impact startup latency.

FastAudit.core_idea: Eliminate the Python loop over candidate t values and instead evaluate the objective for all candidates at once using NumPy broadcasting over a fixed, small candidate range (1..100). This turns many small NumPy calls into one larger, fully vectorized computation.

complexity.why: The code builds a 2D array of shape (T, n) via (var_2 - np.arange(1, 101).reshape(100, 1))**2. Here T=100 is a small constant (candidate t values). Computing the squared differences and summing along axis 1 both require touching all T*n elements, so time is O(T*n) ≈ O(n). Space is O(T*n) for the temporary 2D array, which is acceptable given small T.

complexity_delta.from: O(V * n) time, O(n) space (Python loop over V candidate t; each iteration does O(n) work).
complexity_delta.to: O(T * n) time with T=100 treated as constant (≈ O(n)), O(T * n) space via a single broadcasted 2D array.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both are O(range * n), but in the fast version the range T is fixed and small (1..100), and the loop is moved entirely into NumPy’s C-level implementation, yielding a substantial constant-factor speedup and eliminating Python-loop overhead.

transformation_steps: Removed eval-based input and switched to fast I/O using sys.stdin.readline to avoid overhead and unsafe evaluation.
Replaced the explicit Python for-loop over candidate t values with a single broadcasted NumPy expression that evaluates the squared errors for all t simultaneously.
Hard-bounded the candidate t range to 1..100 via np.arange(1, 101), exploiting known constraints on a_i to keep the candidate set small and constant-sized.
Used np.sum(..., axis=1) followed by np.min to compute the objective for each candidate and then select the minimum in pure NumPy.
Avoided repeated recomputation of min(var_2) and max(var_2) by discarding the dynamic range in favor of the fixed known range.
trigger_signals: Presence of a Python for-loop whose body performs NumPy vector operations on the same array for many different scalar parameters.
Repeated calls to min(var_2) and max(var_2) suggesting invariant quantities inside the loop.
Problem structure: minimizing sum (a_i - t)^2 over integer t, which is convex and lends itself naturally to evaluating all candidates at once.
Known small bounds on data values (likely 1..100), making it feasible to enumerate all candidate t in a small fixed range and vectorize across them.
pitfalls: Hardcoding np.arange(1, 101) assumes all relevant t lie within [1, 100]. If the actual input domain for a_i extends beyond this range, the solution may miss the true optimum.

The vectorized version allocates a (100, n) temporary array; for much larger ranges or n this pattern could become memory-intensive. If T were not a small constant, we would need a different strategy (e.g., analytical solution or chunked computation).

Relying on NumPy’s default integer dtype assumes no overflow when squaring differences. On platforms where int is 32-bit and data can be large, explicit use of a larger dtype (e.g., int64) may be necessary.
The unused assignments var_5 = sys.stdin.read and var_7 = sys.stdin.readlines add minor clutter and could confuse maintainers, though they do not impact performance materially.

constraints_guess.notes: N people, M food types. Each person lists some foods they like; total (person, food) pairs on the order of 1e5–2e5 for the fast solution to be necessary.

dominant_ops: Triple-nested loops with an inner `x in list` membership test: for each person, for each food they like, scan every other person's list linearly to check membership.

complexity.time: O(N^2 * K^2) in the worst case (≈ O(N^2 * M^2) when each person lists most foods).
complexity.why: Let N = number of people, K = average number of foods per person. Outer loop over people (N), middle loop over foods person i likes (≈K), inner loop over all people again (N), and inside that an `in` check over a list of size ≈K (O(K)). This multiplies to O(N * K * N * K). All input lists are stored, giving O(N*K) space.

bottlenecks.detail: The core logic is: for each (person i, food f they like) pair, check every person j to see if f is in their list, using `f in list_j` which is linear. This effectively enumerates all quadruples (i, j, position-of-f-in-i, position-of-f-in-j) in the worst case.

Using plain Python lists for membership testing (`x in some_list`) is O(L) per test. With L ≈ K and tests nested inside O(N*K) loops, this becomes O(N*K^2 * N). Sets or a global frequency array would reduce membership/counting to O(1).
The code does not deduplicate foods per person before counting, so the same food can be re-checked multiple times for the same person, adding redundant work inside the nested loops.

`pop(0)` on lists is O(len(list)) because it shifts all remaining elements. It is done once per person, adding an extra O(N*K) overhead. This is smaller than the main O(N^2*K^2) term but still unnecessary.

FastAudit.core_idea: Count, for each food type, how many people like it using a frequency array indexed by food ID; then count how many food types have frequency equal to N (liked by everyone). Each (person, food) pair is processed exactly once.

complexity.why: Reading and processing input per person is O(K_i) for that person. Summed over all people this is O(sum K_i) = O(N*K). Each food ID increments a counter in O(1). Finally, scanning the count array of size M once gives O(M). No nested membership tests or re-scans of other persons' lists are performed. Space is a single array of size M+1 for counts.

complexity_delta.from: O(N^2 * K^2) time, O(N * K) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N * K + M) time, O(M) space
complexity_delta.note: The optimization removes the quadratic dependence on both N and K by aggregating counts globally instead of re-checking membership across all lists for every (person, food) pair.

transformation_steps: Replace per-food global membership checking across all people with a single global frequency array `var_5` of length M+1, where index is the food ID.
Process each input line (one person) once: read K_i and the list of foods, ignore K_i for logic, and increment `var_5[food]` for every food in that line.
After all input is processed, compute the answer by counting how many entries in `var_5` equal N (var_4), which directly gives the number of foods liked by all people.
Remove all nested loops that iterate over other peoples’ lists for every food; each (person, food) pair contributes to the count exactly once.
Avoid costly operations like `pop(0)` and linear `x in list` membership checks; use direct indexing into the frequency array instead.
trigger_signals: Presence of three nested `for` loops over people and foods, with an additional `in` membership test inside the innermost loop.
Running time growing very quickly with N and K (e.g., acceptable for N,M≈30 but timing out or slowing dramatically as they reach ~1e3+).
Use of `x in list` inside nested loops, a common pattern leading to O(N^2) or worse behavior.
Redundant recomputation: the same food's presence across all people being re-evaluated multiple times instead of being accumulated once.
pitfalls: Off-by-one indexing: food IDs in the problem are typically 1-based. The fast solution correctly allocates `var_5 = [0] * (var_3 + 1)` and uses indices directly; using 0-based indexing inadvertently without adjusting IDs would cause incorrect counts or IndexError.

Misinterpreting memory trade-offs: while storing all lists plus a frequency array is possible, the optimized approach never needs to keep all lists simultaneously if memory is tight—it can update counts on the fly and discard per-person lists immediately.

Using Python `list.count` in the hot path: in the fast code, `var_5.count(var_4)` is applied once at the end, which is fine (O(M)); repeatedly using `.count` inside loops would re-introduce quadratic behavior.

Changing to sets but keeping the same triple nesting: converting each person’s list to a set speeds up membership checks but keeps the O(N^2 * K) structure; the main gain comes from changing the algorithm to a single aggregation pass, not just swapping data structures.

Incorrect handling of the N=1 edge case: the slow code has a special branch `if var_2 == 1: var_8 = var_7[var_4]`. The fast solution naturally handles N=1 via the frequency counts, so extra special-casing is unnecessary and could introduce bugs if ported incorrectly.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style single-query generation of the N-th 'Lunlun' number (numbers whose adjacent digits differ by at most 1). N is usually up to about 1e5; BFS queue size grows proportionally to N.

dominant_ops: Repeated deque.popleft/append operations for BFS-like expansion of numbers
Per-number overhead from Python function calls/wrappers
Potential per-number digit/condition checks (e.g., via helper like func_2 using str() and iterating digits)
Large unused import set and debug/timing utilities increasing startup/interpretation overhead
While-loop control and conditional branching around each generated number

complexity.why: func_11 builds numbers in increasing 'Lunlun' order using a deque, starting from digits 1..9 and repeatedly popping from the front and appending up to three children per node (last digit ±1 or 0). To reach the N-th valid number, it generates and enqueues O(N) states. Each state involves constant-time integer arithmetic plus some overhead from Python-level control structures; if a digit-check function like func_2 is used, that adds an extra O(D) factor per state where D is the number of digits (bounded by log10 of the resulting number, so still O(N) overall). The queue length and number of stored numbers also grow linearly with N, giving O(N) space.

bottlenecks.detail: The slow_code is wrapped in a large competitive-programming template with many unused imports (bisect, heapq, math, random, decimal, itertools, Counter, defaultdict, etc.), generic I/O helpers, debugging print (func_1 to stderr), and a timing decorator (func_4). Even if some are unused at runtime, they add parsing/import overhead and clutter, and any active debug/timing calls add cost on the critical path.

Helper like func_2(var_13) converts numbers to strings and scans digit-by-digit to check the |diff|<=1 property. If func_11 relies on this for validation, then each generated candidate incurs an O(D) digit scan on top of the BFS structure. This increases constant factors significantly compared with generating only valid neighbors structurally without validation.

func_11 uses a while True loop with manual popping, nested for loops over (-1, 0, 1), and multiple conditionals around each candidate, plus potential external counters. In Python, such deep control-flow and function-call overhead on each of O(N) iterations increases runtime despite the same asymptotic complexity as the optimized solution.

I/O is funneled through var_8 = sys.stdin.readline and wrapper functions func_7/func_8/etc. While not asymptotically bad, each extra layer (parsing helpers, mapping via list(map(...))) adds overhead relative to the simple single read-and-parse needed for this problem.

FastAudit.core_idea: Model Lunlun numbers as nodes in an implicit graph where each node x transitions to up to three children by appending a digit whose difference from the last digit of x is -1, 0, or +1 (subject to staying in 0..9). Run a straightforward BFS starting from 1..9: pop from the front, generate its children, append them to the back, and repeat N times. The N-th popped number is the answer. This leverages structural generation so that all queue contents are valid Lunlun numbers; no explicit digit-checking or filtering is required.

complexity.why: The fast_code processes exactly N pop operations from the deque, and for each popped number generates at most 3 children with constant-time arithmetic and modulo operations. Thus, work is Θ(N) (with a small constant). The deque size grows in proportion to how many numbers are generated before the N-th; this is linear in N for this BFS, so memory is Θ(N) as well. There are no per-number string conversions or complex helper calls, so the constant factors are small.

complexity_delta.from: O(N) time, O(N) space, but with heavy Python-level overhead (possible O(N * D) if per-number digit checks via string are used)
complexity_delta.to: O(N) time, O(N) space with minimal constant factors and only integer arithmetic and deque operations on the critical path
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic big-O remains linear, but the new solution eliminates unnecessary layers (string digit checks, debug wrappers, complex control flow), leading to a substantial practical speedup.

transformation_steps: Replace generic BFS-plus-property-check pattern with a specialized constructive BFS that only generates valid Lunlun numbers as children. This removes the need for a separate validation function (like func_2) and its per-number digit scans.
Collapse the logic into a single, tight loop: read N, initialize deque with [1..9], and perform exactly N iterations of pop-and-expand, tracking the last popped value as the answer.

Remove timing decorators, debug print to stderr, and other profiling utilities from the hot path. These are useful during development but inappropriate inside the main algorithm for performance-critical submissions.
Eliminate unused imports and general-purpose helper functions that are not needed for this particular problem, reducing overhead and potential confusion.
Use direct integer operations on the last digit (var_3 = var_2 % 10) to determine which children to generate, avoiding all string conversions and digit-by-digit loops.

Simplify I/O to a single integer read (int(input()) via eval(input()) in the provided fast_code) with no extra abstraction layers. Although eval is not ideal stylistically, it is invoked only once and does not affect complexity.
trigger_signals: Presence of a property-check function (func_2) that converts numbers to strings and inspects digits, suspicious in a problem that can be solved by structural generation of numbers.
Use of a while True loop with an implicit termination condition based on counters or checks, rather than a clearly bounded for-range loop, suggesting potentially unnecessary iteration or overhead.
Large template with many unused imports and helpers in a problem whose core logic is quite simple, implying a mismatch between problem complexity and implementation overhead.
Debug printing and timing decorators around the main logic, which are red flags for performance in a competitive-programming environment.
Redundant modeling of the same concept (Lunlun property) in multiple ways (BFS generation plus possible post-hoc validation), instead of using one tight representation.
pitfalls: While simplifying, it is important to preserve the BFS order (which corresponds to increasing value for Lunlun numbers) so that the N-th popped number is indeed the N-th smallest; changing queue behavior (e.g., using a stack or incorrect append order) would break correctness.
The queue can grow to size Θ(N); for much larger N than expected, memory usage could become an issue. However, for typical constraints (N up to around 1e5), this is safe in Python.

The fast_code uses eval(input()) to read the integer; this is unnecessary and potentially unsafe in general. For production or contest code, prefer int(input()) to avoid evaluating arbitrary expressions.

Removing all validation checks is safe here only because children are constructed so that they always satisfy the Lunlun property; if this invariant is broken in modifications, the lack of validation would cause subtle bugs.

Extremely large N might lead to very large integers (many digits). Python can handle big integers, but arithmetic becomes slower; constraints should remain moderate (as is typical for this problem) to keep runtimes acceptable.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case. Loop upper bound is 1e5, suggesting the intended search space for var_4 is [1, 1e5]. Input values are chosen so that the answer does not exceed 1e5.

dominant_ops: A descending for-loop from 1e5 to 1 with an arithmetic expression and comparison in each iteration.

complexity.time: O(N) where N = 1e5 (the search bound for var_4)
complexity.why: The code performs at most 1e5 iterations, each doing constant-time arithmetic and a comparison, and uses only a few scalar variables.

bottlenecks.detail: The for-loop `for var_4 in range(10**5, 0, -1)` may execute up to 100000 iterations, which dominates the runtime even though each iteration is O(1).

The loop is effectively searching for the maximum integer var_4 satisfying `var_1 >= var_4 * (var_2 + var_3) + var_3`, but this inequality can be solved directly with integer arithmetic instead of iterative search.

FastAudit.core_idea: Solve the inequality `var_1 >= var_4 * (var_2 + var_3) + var_3` algebraically for var_4 to get `var_4 <= (var_1 - var_3) / (var_2 + var_3)` and use integer division to obtain the maximal integer var_4 directly.

complexity.why: The optimized code performs a constant number of arithmetic operations and a single print, independent of the 1e5 bound.

complexity_delta.from: O(N) with N up to 1e5 due to a linear search loop.
complexity_delta.to: O(1) using a closed-form integer arithmetic expression.
complexity_delta.note: The worst-case runtime is reduced from proportional to the search bound (1e5 iterations) to constant time by replacing the loop with direct computation.

transformation_steps: Start from the loop condition: find the largest integer var_4 in [1, 1e5] such that `var_1 >= var_4 * (var_2 + var_3) + var_3` holds.
Rearrange the inequality: `var_1 - var_3 >= var_4 * (var_2 + var_3)`.
Solve for var_4: `var_4 <= (var_1 - var_3) / (var_2 + var_3)`.
Recognize that we need the maximum integer var_4 satisfying the inequality, so use floor division: `var_4 = (var_1 - var_3) // (var_2 + var_3)`.
Replace the entire descending loop and break logic with a single print of this expression.
trigger_signals: Loop runs over a fixed numeric range (1e5) rather than input-dependent size.
Loop body only checks a monotone inequality and breaks on first success, indicative of searching for a threshold value.
Inequality structure is linear in the loop variable, enabling a direct algebraic solution.
No side effects inside the loop that depend on intermediate iterations, so the result depends solely on the inequality’s boundary.
pitfalls: Integer division correctness: must ensure that using floor division `//` matches the original "largest integer satisfying inequality" semantics; ceiling division would be incorrect.
Off-by-one and bounds: original code implicitly caps var_4 at 1e5; if constraints did not guarantee the solution is <= 1e5, a pure formula without min(1e5, ...) could change behavior.

Handling small var_1: when `var_1 < var_3`, `(var_1 - var_3)` becomes negative and floor division yields a non-positive result; the original loop would then never satisfy the condition and var_4 would exit as 0, so any direct formula must be consistent with this behavior or explicitly clamp to 0 if required.
Division by zero: relies on the guarantee that `(var_2 + var_3) > 0`. If that were not true, both the original and optimized codes would be problematic; the math optimization assumes this constraint.

Type and overflow: in Python this is safe due to arbitrary-precision integers, but in other languages an analogous optimization could require attention to integer overflow when computing `var_4 * (var_2 + var_3)` or `(var_1 - var_3)`.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer N; count numbers in [1, N] whose decimal digit-length is odd. Typical AtCoder-style constraint N ≤ 1e5.

dominant_ops: For each integer i from 1 to N, compute its digit count using repeated division in func_1
Floating-point division var_4 / 10 inside the digit-counting loop
Function-call overhead for func_1 on every iteration

complexity.why: The outer loop runs for every integer from 1 to N. For each i, func_1 repeatedly divides by 10 until the value becomes < 1, costing O(number_of_digits(i)) operations. Summed over i=1..N this is Θ(N log10 N), usually written O(N log N). Only a few scalar variables are used, so space is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: Counts digits for each number separately via a while-loop and division, rather than exploiting the structure of digit ranges to compute a closed-form answer.
Calls func_1 for every i in range(1, N+1), incurring Python function-call overhead N times.
Uses var_4 / 10 in the while condition, which creates floats and is more expensive than integer comparison; integer arithmetic (var_4 >= 10 and var_4 //= 10) would be cheaper.
Uses eval(input()) instead of int(input()); eval is slower and unsafe, though this is negligible compared to the O(N log N) loop.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid per-number digit counting by reasoning about contiguous ranges of numbers with fixed digit lengths and deriving a direct formula for how many have an odd number of digits up to N. Then implement this as a small set of conditional branches computing the count in O(1) time.

complexity.why: The solution performs a constant amount of arithmetic and at most a few branches regardless of N. No loops over N or per-number digit counting remain, so both time and space are constant with respect to the magnitude of N.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log N) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(1) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: Replaces a loop that individually inspects every integer up to N and counts its digits with a closed-form computation based on digit-length ranges.

transformation_steps: Identify the problem being solved by the slow code: counting how many integers in [1, N] have an odd number of decimal digits.
Observe the structure of decimal numbers: 1–9 (1 digit), 10–99 (2 digits), 100–999 (3 digits), 1000–9999 (4 digits), 10000–99999 (5 digits), etc.
Recognize that within each digit-length block, all numbers have the same digit count, so you can add entire blocks at once for those with odd digit length instead of checking each number.

Derive piecewise formulas for N up to 1e5: for N < 100, count is min(N, 9); for 100 ≤ N < 10000, add the full 1-digit block (9) plus the partial 3-digit block up to N → min(N - 90, 909); for 10000 ≤ N ≤ 100000, add 1-digit and 3-digit full blocks (9 + 900 = 909) plus the partial 5-digit block → min(N - 9090, 90909).
Encode these formulas as a small if/elif cascade performing only constant-time arithmetic and comparisons, eliminating the loop and func_1 entirely.
Simplify input handling by using int(input()) instead of eval(input()) to avoid unnecessary overhead and security risks.
trigger_signals: A for-loop iterating from 1 to N with a helper function called on every iteration.
The helper function performs repeated division to determine digit count, implying O(log i) work per number.
Constraints (or typical contest patterns) suggest N can be as large as 1e5 or more, making O(N log N) overkill when the pattern depends only on digit ranges.
The mathematical structure of the problem (properties depending only on number of digits) naturally lends itself to aggregation by ranges instead of per-element checks.
pitfalls: Hard-coded thresholds (100, 10000, 100000) assume the original constraint N ≤ 1e5; if N can be larger, the formula code must be generalized to handle more digit ranges instead of relying on fixed constants.
Off-by-one errors at boundaries like N = 9, 10, 99, 100, 999, 1000, etc.; the inequalities (< vs <=) must be chosen carefully so that each N falls into exactly one correct branch.
Using floating-point division in digit counting (var_4 / 10) can introduce both performance overhead and subtle bugs; integer comparisons (var_4 >= 10) with integer division (//) are preferable.
Relying on eval(input()) is risky and slower; for competitive programming and performance-critical code, int(input()) is both safer and faster.

When generalizing this optimization to different limits or bases, you must re-derive the constants and piecewise structure; copying the existing magic numbers without understanding them can miscount in new ranges.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic 'pairwise/setwise/not coprime' classification: first line N, second line N integers. Typical constraints: N up to 1e5, each a_i up to about 1e6.

dominant_ops: Per-number processing based on a hard-coded prime set up to 1000 (var_9). This strongly suggests trial division or repeated divisibility checks for each input value against all these primes, likely followed by aggregating which primes divide which numbers.

complexity.why: The code defines a literal set of all primes up to 997 (≈ √10^6). The usual way to use such a set in this problem is: for each of the n input numbers, test divisibility by every prime in the set until the square root bound is exceeded. That yields O(π(√A_max)) trial divisions per number. Any bookkeeping for prime usage across numbers adds at most linear factors.

bottlenecks.detail: Trial-dividing each input number by all prelisted primes up to 1000 scales as O(n * π(√A_max)). With n around 1e5 and π(1000)≈168 this implies ~1.7e7 Python-level modulo operations, which is heavy and fragile under strict time limits.
Using a Python set literal of ~170 primes and then iterating it repeatedly introduces hashing/iteration overhead compared to tight numeric loops over contiguous ranges or indices.

The hard-coded prime set is truncated with non-prime values at the end ('... 983, 991, 997, 100'). Any algorithm that relies on this as the complete prime basis up to √A_max risks both correctness and the need for extra guards, complicating the logic and overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace per-number factorization with a global sieve and divisor-multiplicity counting. First, compute primality for all integers up to max(a_i) using a sieve-like marking. Then build a frequency array of input values. For each prime p, walk through its multiples k = p, 2p, 3p, ... and sum how many input numbers equal each k. The maximum such count over all primes determines whether the set is pairwise coprime (max < 2), setwise coprime (max < n), or not coprime (max == n).

complexity.time: O(A_max log log A_max + A_max + n)
complexity.why: The sieve loop over var_6 and multiples var_7 is the standard Eratosthenes marking whose cost is Θ(A_max log log A_max). Building the frequency mapping var_2 over values up to A_max is linear in A_max plus n. For each prime, summing over its multiples uses the harmonic series over primes, Σ_p A_max/p = O(A_max log log A_max). Overall this gives near-linear time in the maximum value, independent of n beyond the initial counting.

delta_type: algorithmic re-design (from per-number trial division to global sieve + multiple-counting) and data representation change (from ad-hoc prime set to range-based sieve over [2

complexity_delta.from: O(n * π(√A_max)) ≈ O(n * √A_max / log A_max)
complexity_delta.to: O(A_max log log A_max + n)
complexity_delta.note: The slow approach scales primarily with n times the cost to factor a single number; the fast approach flips the perspective to scale with A_max and treats all numbers in aggregate. For typical constraints n≈1e5, A_max≈1e6, this reduces heavy per-number modulo work and makes runtime far more predictable.

transformation_steps: 1. Abandon the hard-coded small-prime set and instead compute primality for all integers up to max(a_i) using a sieve (dictionary var_3 in the provided code, though a list would also suffice).
2. Build a frequency structure var_2 that counts how many times each integer up to max(a_i) appears in the input. This lets us query 'how many numbers are equal to k' in O(1) time.

3. Enumerate only primes (keys in var_3 with True) and, for each prime p, iterate over its multiples k=p,2p,3p,... up to max(a_i), accumulating var_2[k] into var_4[p]. This replaces individual factorization of each a_i with a single pass over all multiples for each prime.

4. Compute the maximum value of var_4, i.e. the largest number of input elements sharing a common prime factor. Use this single statistic to classify the set as pairwise coprime, setwise coprime, or not coprime.

5. Remove any pairwise-gcd nested loops or per-number factorization logic that scales as O(n^2) or O(n * π(√A_max)), ensuring the main work is done once per prime/multiple rather than once per input element.
trigger_signals: Observed or anticipated TLE when n reaches around 1e5 with a trial-division-based solution (too many modulo operations).
Asymptotic mismatch: pairwise gcd checks or repeated factorizations give O(n^2) or O(n * √A_max) behavior, which is clearly incompatible with typical /competitive constraints.
Problem structure hint: requirements are about global coprimality properties, suggesting counting shared prime factors across the entire multiset rather than processing numbers independently.
Presence of a fixed, hard-coded prime list (up to 1000) which does not adapt to the actual max(a_i), leading to a combination of correctness and scalability concerns.
pitfalls: Using `eval(input())` instead of `int(input())` is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; while not a performance bottleneck here, it is a bad practice.

The fast solution uses dictionaries (var_3, var_2, var_4) keyed by integers up to A_max; for tight constraints a list-based representation is both faster and more memory efficient. Large A_max values (e.g., > 1e7) would require attention to memory usage.

When converting a trial-division or pairwise-gcd solution to the sieve-based method, it is easy to miscount multiplicities (e.g., double counting numbers that are powers of a prime) or to forget to handle the 'all gcd==1 but not pairwise coprime' distinction correctly. The use of max over counts per prime must be consistent with the classification logic.
If the input values can be 1, they should be handled correctly: 1 contributes nothing to any prime's count, so the algorithm must ensure it does not misclassify cases with many ones.

Attempting micro-optimizations (e.g., partial hard-coded primes) instead of changing the core algorithm often yields fragile solutions that may still TLE or fail on edge cases; the key improvement is the algorithmic switch to global sieve + multiple counting.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical Lunlun-number problems (e.g., AtCoder ABC161 D) have K up to 1e5. Only one query: find the K-th smallest Lunlun number (digits adjacent differ by at most 1).

dominant_ops: Recursive DFS generation of all Lunlun numbers up to 10 digits starting from each initial digit 1..9.
Repeated string conversion of the current number to get its last digit and length for every recursive call.
Appending every generated number to a global list var_4.
Final full sort of the entire generated list var_4 to get ascending order before indexing.

complexity.why: Let T be the total count of Lunlun numbers with up to 10 digits (a fixed but fairly large constant, roughly on the order of 10 * 3^9). The DFS explores all such numbers regardless of the input K, doing O(1) work per generated number plus overhead of recursion and string conversions, so generation is O(T). A full sort of all T numbers adds O(T log T). Memory stores all T numbers in var_4, so space is O(T). Complexity is effectively independent of K as long as K <= T.

bottlenecks.detail: Generates the full set of Lunlun numbers up to 10 digits even when the requested index var_1 (K) is small. Work does not scale with K.
After exhaustive generation, var_4 is fully sorted (O(T log T)) even though a construction in sorted order or a BFS-by-value approach could avoid sorting entirely.
Each new number is produced via recursive calls, which add Python call overhead and stack operations for every generated number.
Every recursive step calls str(var_2) at least once (for len and for the last digit). This repeated conversion is significantly more expensive than arithmetic operations on digits.
Using and mutating a global list var_4 from inside func_1 slightly complicates reasoning and makes optimizing or refactoring harder, though it is not the main performance cost.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use an iterative BFS-like generation of Lunlun numbers in increasing order and stop as soon as the list size exceeds K, avoiding exhaustive generation and the final sort. The BFS is implicitly performed by iterating over a list that is being extended (var_4), producing numbers in the required order.

complexity.why: The loop over var_4 effectively performs a breadth-first traversal of Lunlun numbers ordered by value. Each number up to the K-th is processed once; from each number only up to 3 children are generated. The loop breaks when len(var_4) > K, so the total number of generated numbers is Θ(K). No final sort is needed because the BFS generation order aligns with non-decreasing numeric order. Memory is proportional to the number of generated numbers, which is Θ(K).

complexity_delta.from: O(T log T) time, O(T) space (T = total count of Lunlun numbers up to max digits, independent of K).
complexity_delta.to: O(K) time, O(K) space, directly proportional to the requested index K.
complexity_delta.note: The optimized approach eliminates the dependence on the full search space (T) and the sorting step by generating numbers in ascending order and stopping as soon as enough numbers are produced.

transformation_steps: Change from recursive DFS that fully explores all Lunlun numbers up to a fixed depth (10 digits) to an iterative BFS-like expansion starting from 1..9.
Preserve natural non-decreasing order of generated numbers by leveraging BFS over the implicit graph of Lunlun numbers instead of generating then sorting.
Introduce an early stopping condition: break the generation loop as soon as len(var_4) > K (var_3), so that only O(K) numbers are generated instead of the entire search space.

Replace explicit depth control via length check (len(str(var_2)) > 10) with an implicit bound derived from K; for typical constraints (K up to around 1e5), Lunlun numbers do not exceed 10 digits anyway.
Remove the final sort operation and direct indexing into the already-ordered list var_4 to obtain the K-th number.
Refactor from recursive calls to iterative list growth (mutating var_4 while iterating over it), which reduces Python function call overhead and stack usage.
trigger_signals: The original solution generates all possible valid numbers up to a fixed maximum digit length, regardless of the requested index K.
