Presence of a full list sort at the end of the computation suggests that generation order is not exploited and that work might be avoidable.
The recursive function func_1 performs string conversions and branching logic on every node, indicating high constant factors for each of many calls.
The input K (var_1) is only used at the very end as an index into the sorted list, not to limit or prune the search.
pitfalls: The fast_code still uses eval(input()), which is unsafe and slower than int(input()); for competitive programming, int(input()) is sufficient and safer.

The fast_code performs multiple string conversions per iteration (str(var_1), slicing, and int()), which are unnecessary overhead—using modulo and integer arithmetic for the last digit would be faster.

Modifying var_4 while iterating over it relies on Python’s specific behavior of for-loops over dynamic lists; it works but can be error-prone if future changes alter the invariant or if additional filtering is added.

The fast_code relies on the fact that BFS over Lunlun transitions from seeds 1..9 yields numbers in non-decreasing order; if transition rules change, this property might break and would need revalidation.

The optimized approach implicitly assumes that, for the given constraints, K is small enough that the needed Lunlun numbers do not exceed practical digit lengths; if K were much larger, an explicit digit-length bound or a more formal DP might be necessary.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: given N (up to about 2e5) and a threshold K, read N numbers, transform ai -> ai-K, build prefix sums, and count pairs (i<j) with S[i] <= S[j]. This equals counting subarrays whose average >= K. Needs ~O(N log N) to pass.

dominant_ops: Fenwick/BIT operations (point updates + prefix-sum queries) inside a loop over all prefix sums, plus nontrivial template overhead (wrapper I/O functions, eval-based parsing, possible unused multi-dimensional array builders).

complexity.why: The visible core data structure is a Fenwick tree (Class_1) with O(log N) per update/query. Such operations are typically called once per prefix sum, giving O(N log N). However, the implementation is wrapped in a large generic template with extra function layers and potential inefficiencies, which substantially increase constant factors even though the asymptotic class is acceptable.

bottlenecks.detail: Using a Fenwick tree implemented as a class with method calls (func_15/func_8) inside tight loops adds Python attribute lookup overhead and extra indirections for every O(log N) step.

Each prefix sum requires multiple log N steps in the BIT (while loops with bitwise operations). Compared to a carefully implemented merge-based counting that does only linear work per level, the BIT-based solution tends to be slower for the same theoretical O(N log N) bound.

Numerous helper functions (func_11, func_1, func_2, func_3, etc.) wrap basic I/O and parsing. Some use eval() for simple integer parsing, which is significantly slower than int(). The extra function calls and generic utilities add overhead in a performance-critical environment.

Template utilities like func_12/func_13/func_14 can allocate large 2D/3D lists if used; even if not used for this problem, their presence can encourage inefficient patterns. A BIT tree sized to next power of two is fine, but combined with any unnecessary auxiliary arrays can raise memory usage.
Fenwick methods rely on while loops with repeated index arithmetic and conditions in Python. These per-step Python-level operations dominate runtime compared to a contiguous, linear merge over lists.

FastAudit.core_idea: Transform the problem to counting pairs of prefix sums (S[i], S[j]) with i<j and S[i] <= S[j] by first shifting each element ai -> ai-K. Build prefix sums S, then use a divide-and-conquer (merge-sort-like) procedure to sort S while counting such pairs during the merge phase. The merge processes two sorted halves in descending order and, whenever a right value is taken because it is >= left, it adds the number of remaining left elements to the global answer. This yields an O(N log N) algorithm with excellent constants and cache-friendly memory access.

complexity.why: Building the prefix sum array is O(N). The recursive func_1 performs a merge-sort-like division of the array: the depth of recursion is O(log N), and each level merges disjoint subarrays in total O(N) time, for an overall O(N log N) time. The counting is done in the merge step without extra asymptotic cost. Extra memory is linear for temporary merged arrays.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log N) using a Fenwick tree and heavy template wrappers
complexity_delta.to: O(N log N) using a specialized divide-and-conquer merge-based counter
complexity_delta.note: Both approaches are asymptotically optimal for this problem, but the merge-based method has much smaller constant factors and better cache locality, making it significantly faster in Python for N up to ~2e5.

transformation_steps: Remove generic competitive-programming template utilities (multi-dimensional list builders, assorted print helpers, and eval-based integer input) that are unnecessary for this problem.
Replace the Fenwick tree (Class_1) and its update/query calls with a direct divide-and-conquer counting approach that works directly on the prefix sum array.
Compute prefix sums once using itertools.accumulate and store them in a simple list, avoiding extra layers of abstraction.
Implement the pair-counting logic in the merge-phase of a custom merge function (func_2) that both merges and updates the global count via arithmetic on indices instead of multiple BIT operations.
Use a sentinel value (var_7 = 1<<60) at the end of each half to simplify boundary checks and keep the merge loop branch-light and linear.
trigger_signals: Runtime close to or exceeding time limits on large inputs (e.g., N ~ 2e5) despite an ostensibly O(N log N) algorithm, with profiling showing most time spent in BIT methods and template I/O wrappers.
High call counts to helper functions (func_1, func_2, func_3 for I/O and the Fenwick methods) in profiler output, indicating Python overhead dominates.
Observed that the algorithmic pattern is a classic prefix-sum pair counting problem, for which a merge-sort-based solution is known to be simpler and faster in Python than a BIT-based implementation.
Concern about Python recursion limits or per-operation overhead in while-based BIT loops, pushing toward a more contiguous, linear-access style implementation.
pitfalls: The merge-based solution relies on recursion; for extremely large N, recursion depth must stay within sys.getrecursionlimit, but here depth is O(log N) so it is safe. Still, careless changes (e.g., deeper recursion patterns) could break this.
In func_2, the code declares 'global ans' but actually uses 'var_2' as the accumulator; any refactoring must ensure that the intended global variable is correctly referenced and updated.

Sentinel values appended to the lists (var_1.append(-var_7), var_5.append(-var_7)) mutate the argument lists in-place; reusing these lists elsewhere or making assumptions about their lengths after func_2 would be incorrect.

The correctness of the pair count depends critically on sorting order (descending) and on the inequality direction in the merge condition (var_1[var_9] <= var_5[var_10]); altering these without re-deriving the counting logic will silently produce incorrect results.

If one attempts to reintroduce a BIT-based approach, forgetting coordinate compression or mis-sizing the Fenwick tree to the value range instead of the compressed rank space can lead to excessive memory usage and slower-than-expected performance.

constraints_guess.notes: Given an integer K (up to about 1e5), output the K-th smallest positive integer whose adjacent decimal digits differ by at most 1 ("Lunlun numbers").

dominant_ops: Iterating over many candidate integers and checking the Lunlun property via string conversion and per-digit difference tests (func_2), or equivalently, generating candidates in a less-structured way with high constant overhead.

complexity.time: O(A * d) in the naive scan interpretation, where A is the value of the K-th Lunlun number and d is the number of digits (~10); effectively on the order of scanning up to ~1e10 for K=1e5, which is infeasible. Even if func_11 does BFS, the surrounding code structure is cluttered and not tightly focused on enumerating exactly K numbers.
complexity.space: O(1) to O(K) depending on implementation details (if only counting, space is constant; if storing all found numbers in a list, it becomes O(K)).
complexity.why: The presence of func_2 suggests a naïve approach: increment an integer, convert to string, and check all adjacent digit differences. For large K, the K-th Lunlun number has up to ~11 digits, so the search space up to that value is astronomically large. The repeated string allocations and per-character integer conversions dominate runtime. The code also imports many unused modules and has timing/debug wrappers that add overhead without addressing the core cost.

bottlenecks.detail: Linear scan over the integer line combined with a per-number Lunlun check (func_2) leads to time proportional to the numeric value of the answer rather than to K, which is far too slow when the K-th Lunlun number is around 1e10.

Each candidate check does: int -> str conversion, looping over characters, converting digits back to int and taking absolute differences. These are relatively heavy Python operations inside a very large loop.

Many heavyweight imports, recursion limit changes, decorators, and helper functions add noise and overhead but do not improve the asymptotic behavior. They also make it harder to see that the core algorithm is just a linear scan + test.

FastAudit.core_idea: Generate Lunlun numbers directly by BFS over digit strings (or integers), instead of scanning all integers. Start from 1–9 as the first layer; for each number, append digits whose difference from the last digit is -1, 0, or +1 (within [0,9]). Repeat layer by layer until at least K numbers are generated, then sort and pick the K-th smallest.

complexity.time: O(K log K) for the provided fast_code: O(K) Lunlun numbers are generated using a BFS-like expansion from the frontier set, and then sorted once at the end, adding a log K factor.
complexity.space: O(K) to store all generated Lunlun numbers in the set var_2 until K elements are available.
complexity.why: The BFS-style generation only explores valid Lunlun numbers and stops once at least K such numbers exist. The branching factor is at most 3 per number (last digit can go to last-1, last, last+1), so the total count of generated numbers is proportional to K. Sorting the K-sized set to extract the K-th smallest dominates the runtime, but K is only around 1e5 so O(K log K) is easily fast enough.

delta_type: algorithmic (from property-testing scan to constructive BFS generation over digits)

complexity_delta.from: Roughly O(A * d) where A is the numeric value of the K-th Lunlun number (on the order of 1e10 for K≈1e5), dominated by enormous numbers of string conversions and digit differences.
complexity_delta.to: O(K log K) time and O(K) memory: generate ~K Lunlun numbers via BFS on digits and sort once; effectively proportional to the answer count instead of its numeric magnitude.
complexity_delta.note: The key change is to parameterize the work by the number of Lunlun numbers needed (K), rather than by the magnitude of the search range on the integer line.

transformation_steps: Stop scanning all integers and checking them with a per-number predicate (func_2). Instead, treat Lunlun numbers as nodes of a graph where edges represent appending a digit whose difference from the last digit is in {-1,0,1}.
Initialize the search with all 1-digit Lunlun numbers (1 through 9). This forms the first BFS layer (var_2 / var_5).

For each current frontier number, compute its last digit and generate all valid successors by appending last-1, last, and/or last+1 if they remain in [0,9]. Collect these in a new frontier set (var_6).

Accumulate all generated numbers in a global set (var_2) and repeat expansions until var_2 contains at least K elements. This ensures only valid Lunlun numbers are explored and that the search space grows only as needed.
After enough numbers are generated, sort the set var_2 and output the (K-1)-th index. This ensures the correct K-th smallest number is retrieved.
Keep all operations purely arithmetic on integers (no int->str conversions per candidate) and avoid per-number digit loops except in the controlled BFS digit extension.
trigger_signals: Time limit exceeded or extremely slow performance when K is moderately large (e.g., 1e4–1e5) because scanning up to the K-th Lunlun number requires exploring an enormous integer range.
Profiler or logging showing that the majority of time is spent inside the Lunlun checker (func_2) converting numbers to strings and iterating over digits.
Empirical observation that the K-th answer is large (many digits), implying that a naive scan will have to examine far more than K integers.
Code complexity dominated by repetitive loops over candidate integers, with little structural exploitation of the specific digit-difference constraint.
pitfalls: Using eval(input()) as in fast_code introduces unnecessary overhead and potential security issues; int(input()) is sufficient and safer.
When generating successors for each number, it is easy to forget edge conditions for digits 0 and 9; failing to handle these correctly can generate invalid digits or miss valid numbers.

Storing all generated numbers in a Python set and sorting them is acceptable for K≈1e5 but can become memory-heavy for larger K; an optimized BFS that emits numbers in sorted order and stops exactly at the K-th pop avoids the final sort and reduces memory traffic.

If one mixes the two approaches (still scanning regular integers while also generating via BFS), one can accidentally revert to O(A) behavior; the key is to rely solely on the constructive digit-based BFS.

Relying on string-based digit operations inside the BFS (e.g., converting every intermediate number to string to examine its last digit) would reintroduce large constant factors and should be avoided in favor of integer arithmetic (n % 10 and n * 10 + delta).

constraints_guess.notes: Input is two month indices in [1,12]; effective problem size is constant but original code scales with total number of months stored in collections.

dominant_ops: Iterating over dictionary keys and then over each list of months
Linear search for each of the two target months inside each list

complexity.why: Let K be the total number of stored months across all groups (7 + 4 + 1 = 12 here). The outer loop iterates over each key of var_2 and the inner loop scans each list fully, leading to a linear scan over all K elements. Only a few scalar booleans and small fixed-size structures are used, so auxiliary space is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: Performs a full scan over all month entries in the dictionary to determine group membership, even though each month could be mapped directly to its group.
Both target months are checked against each element of each list, resulting in repeated comparisons and branches.

The condition `if var_1 == True and var_8 == False or var_1 == False and var_8 == True` is evaluated on every dict key, adding branching overhead and complexity for a conceptually simple equality-of-groups test.

FastAudit.core_idea: Precompute a direct mapping from month to its group (number of days) in an array, then compare the group IDs of the two input months with a single O(1) lookup each.

complexity.why: The lookup table var_1 has fixed length 13 and is independent of input size. For each query, only two array accesses and one comparison are performed, so runtime does not grow with any problem parameter. The table itself is constant-sized, so auxiliary space remains constant.

complexity_delta.from: O(K) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(1) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: Both versions are effectively constant-time for this specific task, but the modified code removes linear scans and expresses the logic as two direct table lookups, improving clarity and constant factors.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the dictionary of lists encodes a partition of months into a small number of groups (31-day, 30-day, February).
Replace the dictionary-of-lists structure with a fixed array var_1 where the index is the month and the value is a compact group ID.
Eliminate the nested for-loops and boolean state tracking (var_1, var_8) in favor of two direct lookups var_1[month1], var_1[month2].
Reduce the final decision logic to a simple equality comparison between the two group IDs and a single if/else print.
trigger_signals: Nested loops over a small, fixed classification structure (dictionary of lists) to perform membership tests.
Boolean flags set inside loops with early-break conditions that effectively implement a simple classification comparison.
Hard-coded data (month groupings) that naturally lends itself to a direct indexing or lookup-table representation.
pitfalls: The lookup table assumes valid month indices; missing input validation can cause IndexError if months outside 1–12 are given.
The mapping in var_1 must accurately reflect the original grouping (e.g., all 31-day months share one ID, 30-day months share another); any mistake silently changes behavior.
Using 1-based month indices with a 0-based Python list requires a placeholder at index 0; omitting or misaligning this placeholder shifts all group mappings.

constraints_guess.notes: Single string input, typical AtCoder/contest scale where |S| can be up to 2e5 or similar. Needs linear-time solution with low constant factors and O(1) extra memory to be safe in Python.

dominant_ops: Materializing all groups as lists via itertools.groupby and list(var_5)
Building an array of all groups (var_7) before processing
Processing string twice (original and reversed) including recomputation of all groups
Creating a full reversed copy of the string (var_13[::-1])
Heavy debug I/O to sys.stderr inside per-group loop

complexity.why: For a string of length n: groupby runs in O(n), but every run is converted to list(var_5) and stored in var_7, generating O(n) element constructions and allocations. The algorithm is then executed twice (original, reversed), plus an O(n) string reversal, so the time is still linear but with ~3 passes and substantial overhead. Space is O(n) because all groups and the reversed string are stored explicitly.

bottlenecks.detail: var_7 collects all groups as lists: for _, var_5 in groupby(var_15): var_7 += [list(var_5)]. This duplicates the entire string data into grouped lists, increasing memory and allocation overhead to O(n).
Each group list(list(var_5)) is a separate Python list, causing many small allocations and pointer indirections, slowing iteration compared to simple index-based string traversal.
func_1(var_13) and func_1(var_13[::-1]) both perform full O(n) passes with grouping, effectively doubling the heavy work. var_13[::-1] itself is another O(n) pass and allocation.

Debug prints inside the main per-group loop: print(var_6, file=sys.stderr) and print(var_6, var_2, var_3, file=sys.stderr). Per-iteration I/O to stderr is extremely slow and dominates runtime for large n.
Building var_7 = [] then iterating again over var_7 instead of processing groups on-the-fly from groupby doubles traversal overhead and keeps all intermediate data alive longer than needed.
The wrapper func_2 performs max(func_1(var_13), func_1(var_13[::-1])), recomputing the same structure twice rather than deriving the needed answer in a single directional pass.

FastAudit.core_idea: Scan the string once from left to right, maintaining a small current pattern (var_5) and a segment count (var_2). At each position, compare the next character with the current pattern; extend or reset this pattern and increment the count when needed. This avoids any grouping structures, avoids reversing the string, and uses only O(1) extra state in a single pass.

complexity.why: The loop advances var_3 monotonically from 0 to len(var_1), performing O(1) work per iteration. No additional collections proportional to n are created; only a few scalar variables and a small pattern string var_5 are maintained. Thus runtime is linear in the string length and memory overhead remains constant.

from.time: O(n) with high constant factors (multiple full passes, group materialization, heavy stderr I/O)
from.space: O(n) due to storing all grouped runs and a reversed copy

to.time: O(n) with low constant factors (single simple pass over the string)
to.space: O(1) extra beyond the input string

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time complexity stays linear, but the fast version removes secondary passes, data duplication, and debug I/O, yielding a very large practical speedup and lower memory footprint.

transformation_steps: Eliminate itertools.groupby usage and per-group list materialization; instead, traverse the string directly via indices and maintain only a small pattern variable.
Remove construction of var_7 (the list of all groups) and process characters on the fly, reducing both allocations and memory usage.
Drop the second computation on the reversed string and avoid creating var_13[::-1]; design the one-pass logic to capture the required behavior in a single direction.
Remove all debug print calls inside tight loops (stderr logging) to prevent I/O from dominating runtime.
Simplify state: use a few scalar variables (current index, current pattern, answer count) rather than multiple flags and per-group metadata, minimizing Python overhead per character.
trigger_signals: Use of itertools.groupby followed by list() on each group and collecting into a master list for a large input string.
Presence of prints (especially to sys.stderr) inside loops that run O(n) times over the input data.
Creation of a full reversed copy of a large string and re-running an O(n) algorithm on both original and reversed variants.
Overall O(n) algorithm that performs several full passes and constructs many temporary lists when the problem only needs a simple linear scan with constant state.
pitfalls: Rewriting from grouped-runs logic to a single-pass index-based approach risks off-by-one errors in how segments are counted and when the pattern var_5 is updated.

Removing the reverse-pass logic changes behavior if the original algorithm relied on symmetry or special handling at the ends; the single-pass logic must be carefully reasoned to preserve the intended count.
Using string concatenation to extend var_5 (var_5 = var_5 + var_1[var_3]) is fine here because var_5 remains very small, but care must be taken not to let it grow to O(n) length in other problems.
Eliminating debug prints makes profiling more difficult; if diagnostics are needed, they should be guarded or removed in the final submission to avoid performance regressions.

constraints_guess.notes: Likely AtCoder ABC 126 C 'Dice and Coin': N up to about 1e5 and K up to about 1e9, single test case.

dominant_ops: For each of N iterations: float division var_1/(var_4+1), a math.log call, list allocation for max([...]), math.ceil, and float exponentiation 0.5**var_3.

complexity.why: There is a single for-loop over var_4 in range(var_2) (N iterations). Inside, the work per iteration does not depend on N or K asymptotically (math.log, ceil and pow are treated as O(1)), so total time is O(N). Only a few scalar variables are stored, so extra space is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: math.log and math.ceil are called once per iteration; these transcendental/rounding functions are significantly slower than basic integer arithmetic.
max([math.log(...), 0]) allocates a new list object on every iteration just to take its max; this adds allocation and GC overhead.
The expression var_1 / (var_4 + 1) and math.log(..., 2) operate on floats, and 0.5**var_3 uses generic float exponentiation, all more expensive than simple integer operations.
0.5**var_3 is evaluated N times; generic pow on floats is slower than repeated doubling/bit operations on integers.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid logarithms and other heavy floating-point operations inside the main loop by computing the needed exponent via a small integer while-loop that doubles until the threshold is reached, then accumulate the probability using that exponent.

complexity.why: Outer loop runs N times (var_1 from 1 to var_4). For each i, the inner while-loop increases var_3 until var_1 * 2**var_3 >= K. This takes O(log(K/i)) steps, bounded by O(log K). Thus total time is O(N log K). With typical constraints (K <= 1e9), log2 K <= ~30, so the log factor is a very small constant and the code behaves like a fast O(N) solution in practice. Only a fixed number of scalars are used, giving O(1) extra space.

complexity_delta.from: O(N) with heavy per-iteration floating-point and library-call costs
complexity_delta.to: O(N log K) with very small log K (<= ~30) using cheap integer operations
complexity_delta.note: The modified (faster) code introduces a theoretical log K factor due to the inner while, but replaces costly math.log/ceil/float pow with a few integer operations. Given problem constraints, this yields a substantial practical speedup despite the slightly worse asymptotic bound.

transformation_steps: Replace the direct logarithm-based exponent computation var_3 = ceil(max(log2(K / i), 0)) with an integer while-loop that increments var_3 until i * 2**var_3 >= K.
Remove per-iteration list creation for max([...]) by encoding the non-negative clamp in the while-loop logic (loop never runs when i >= K, so var_3 naturally stays 0).
Shift from floating-point heavy expressions (float division, math.log, math.ceil) to primarily integer arithmetic and comparisons, delaying or minimizing float use.
Keep the exponentiation base as 2 in the while condition (2**var_3) and 0.5 in the final accumulation, aligning with powers of two and avoiding repeated float logs.
Use simpler input parsing (map(int, input().split())) instead of a list comprehension, slightly reducing overhead at startup (minor but consistent).
trigger_signals: Presence of math.log (and possibly math.ceil) inside a loop that runs up to around 1e5 or more iterations.
Use of max([...]) with a list literal in the loop body, implying repeated allocations per iteration.
Use of generic float exponentiation (a ** b with non-integer or float base) inside a hot loop.
Overall tight loop dominated by Python-level function calls and allocations rather than plain arithmetic.
pitfalls: When translating from the log-based formula to the while-loop, it is easy to get an off-by-one error in the inequality (using > vs >= or starting var_3 at 1 instead of 0). The correct condition is to increment while i * 2**var_3 < K.

If K could be extremely large in another setting, the while-loop could iterate many more times and the O(N log K) behavior might become a real bottleneck; in such cases, a direct integer log2 approach would be preferable if implemented carefully and efficiently.

Using floating-point logs (as in the slow code) risks subtle precision issues for very large or very small ratios; rounding via math.ceil on an inexact log can produce off-by-one exponents for edge values.
If the inner while-loop condition were mistakenly reversed (e.g., while K > i * 2**var_3 without a correct stopping condition), it could lead to non-termination or incorrect probabilities.
Assuming exact symmetry when swapping input variable order (var_4, var_2) vs (var_2, var_1) can introduce logical bugs; the optimization must preserve the original mathematical meaning of N and K.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: choose integer x to minimize sum (a_i - x)^2. Original brute-force solutions often rely on small bounds like n ≤ 100 and |a_i| ≤ 100, giving manageable search range. However, algorithmic solution scales to much larger n and value ranges.

dominant_ops: Two nested loops: outer loop over all candidate centers x in [min(a), max(a)], inner loop over all elements to compute sum of squared differences for each candidate.

complexity.why: Sorting the n values costs O(n log n). Then we iterate over R = var_2[-1] - var_2[0] + 1 candidate integers; for each candidate we scan all n elements and compute (a_i - x)^2, giving O(R * n). No extra asymptotic memory beyond a few scalars.

bottlenecks.detail: Outer loop `for var_4 in range(var_2[0], var_2[-1] + 1)` scans every integer between min and max value. If the value range is large (e.g., up to 1e9), R becomes enormous and the loop is intractable.
Inner loop `for var_5 in var_2:` recomputes the full sum of squared distances from scratch for each candidate center. This leads to R full passes over the data, yielding O(R * n) operations.
The expression sum (a_i - x)^2 is recomputed naively for each x even though it has a closed form in terms of sum(a_i) and sum(a_i^2). This misses an O(n) or O(1) per-query formulation.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical fact that the sum of squared deviations is minimized at the mean. Since x must be an integer, the optimum lies at either floor(mean) or ceil(mean). Compute the mean once, test the two integer candidates, and choose the better. Then compute the sum of squared differences exactly once for the chosen x.

complexity.why: We scan the array once to compute the sum (O(n)), derive the mean, pick the nearest integer (constant time), and then make one pass to accumulate sum (a_i - x)^2 (O(n)). No sorting or multi-candidate scanning is done; memory usage is constant aside from storing the input list.

complexity_delta.from: O(R * n + n log n)
complexity_delta.to: O(n)
complexity_delta.note: Replaces brute-force search over all candidate centers in the value range with a direct computation using properties of the mean; removes the dependence on the numeric range R = max(a) - min(a).

transformation_steps: Recognize the objective as minimizing f(x) = sum_i (a_i - x)^2 over integer x.
Use algebra: f(x) = sum_i (a_i^2) - 2x * sum_i a_i + n * x^2, a convex quadratic in x, minimized at x* = (sum_i a_i) / n (the mean).

Account for the integer constraint: the optimal integer x is either floor(mean) or ceil(mean). For integer arithmetic, this can be implemented by testing both candidates and choosing the one with smaller cost.
Replace the outer loop over all candidates with a constant-time selection of x from the two candidates.
Keep a single O(n) pass to compute the final sum of squared distances for the chosen x.
trigger_signals: Presence of a loop over all integers between min and max data values (`range(var_2[0], var_2[-1] + 1)`), suggesting dependence on numeric range rather than input size.
Nested loops where the inner loop recomputes a global cost from scratch for each candidate value.
Objective function of the form sum of squared distances to a variable x, which is a classic pattern minimized by the mean.

Known small constraints in the reference problem make brute force acceptable, but recognizing that such structure often admits a direct formula that yields better asymptotic complexity and robustness to larger constraints.
pitfalls: Floating-point precision: Using `var_8 = sum(var_7) / var_3` introduces a float mean. For large values (big n or large a_i), floating-point rounding could misidentify whether floor or ceil is closer to the exact rational mean. With the original small constraints, this is safe, but for large-scale use it’s better to avoid floats or to test both floor and ceil of the exact rational mean using integer arithmetic.

Integer division differences: In Python 3, `/` yields float and `//` yields integer division. The current code relies on `/` to obtain a float and uses comparison of distances to floor and ceil. Rewriting without care could accidentally revert to pure integer division and change behavior.

Assuming bounds for INF: The slow code uses `var_3 = 10**6` as an initial large value, which only works if the true minimum sum of squares never exceeds 1e6. For larger constraints, this sentinel would be too small and break correctness.

Sorting cost vs. necessity: The slow version sorts the list even though the algorithm doesn't actually rely on internal order, only on min and max. For large n, this is an unnecessary O(n log n) overhead; any optimization should either avoid sorting or use a single pass to find min and max.

Overlooking the quadratic form: Another common misstep is attempting incremental updates between consecutive x values instead of directly leveraging the closed form in terms of sum(a_i) and sum(a_i^2), which is both simpler and more numerically stable when done in integers.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style constraints; list length up to about 1e5, each value up to around 1e9. Need to compute product and return 0 if any element is 0, -1 if product would exceed 1e18.

dominant_ops: Single pass multiplying all elements in the list
Additional scan to test membership `0 in var_3`

complexity.why: Reading n integers into a list requires O(n) space and time. The multiplication loop visits each element once in the worst case, and the membership test `0 in var_3` is another O(n) scan. Extra imports and globals add constant initialization overhead but do not change asymptotic complexity.

bottlenecks.detail: The list is scanned in the multiplication loop and then scanned again with `0 in var_3`, doubling the number of Python-level iterations in the worst case.

Many heavy modules are imported (`bisect`, `itertools`, `collections`, etc.) and lambdas/globals are defined but never used, introducing avoidable constant-time overhead before any problem logic runs.

The accumulator `var_4` is a Python integer that can grow, and multiplying large integers is more expensive than small ones. The guard `if var_4 > var_9` limits how far this can grow, but the per-iteration cost still increases until the threshold is crossed.

FastAudit.core_idea: Read all numbers, immediately short-circuit if any element is zero, then multiply sequentially and terminate early with -1 if the running product exceeds 1e18; otherwise print the final product. Avoid unnecessary imports and globals.

complexity.why: The algorithm still performs at most one membership scan for zero and one pass for multiplication, each O(n). It stores the input list, requiring O(n) space. Removing unused imports and helpers improves constant factors but not asymptotic complexity.

complexity_delta.from: O(n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged. Improvements are primarily in constant factors: eliminated heavy unused imports, reduced indirection, and simplified control flow and checks.

transformation_steps: Remove all unused imports (`bisect`, `math`, `itertools`, `collections`, `array`, etc.) and unused global lambdas/constants to reduce startup cost and code noise.
Inline input reading using `input()` instead of `sys.stdin.readline()` plus extra globals, keeping I/O simple and avoiding unnecessary global variables.
Perform the zero check (`0 in var_1`) up front and immediately return 0 if found, clarifying control flow; the original simple version does this cleanly with an early return.
Keep the overflow guard inside the multiplication loop and return -1 as soon as the running product exceeds 1e18, avoiding further big-int multiplications.
Avoid extra flags and nested conditionals (like `var_6`) by using early returns, reducing branching and making the hot loop and post-loop decision logic more direct.
trigger_signals: Presence of many imports and global utilities that are never used in the solution, indicating template or boilerplate bloat.
Use of additional state (`var_6` flag) and nested conditionals to express simple control flow where early returns would suffice.
Multiple passes over the same list (loop for multiplication plus separate `0 in var_3` scan) without a strong reason.
Reliance on big-int multiplications in a tight loop, where guarding and early termination can reduce the number of heavy operations.
pitfalls: Changing the order of checks (zero-check versus overflow-check) must not alter the required behavior: if a zero exists anywhere, the answer must be 0 regardless of intermediate overflow.
Using early returns requires care to ensure all paths print exactly one result; missing a return can lead to printing multiple outputs or none.
Removing `sys.stdin.readline()` in favor of `input()` can be slightly slower for extremely large input; for this problem size it is acceptable, but this trade-off may not generalize.
Any refactor involving the overflow threshold must keep the comparison strictly greater than 1e18, matching the problem’s definition and avoiding off-by-one errors around the boundary.

constraints_guess.n_max: 1e12 (N up to about 10^12; needs sqrt-based divisor scan)
constraints_guess.notes: Two integers M, N. Need to find the largest divisor d of N such that N / d >= M. Constraints implied by need for O(√N) solution; O(N) scan would TLE for N around 10^9–10^12.

dominant_ops: Single loop in func_1 scanning candidate divisors from roughly N/M down to 1 with a modulo operation per iteration.

complexity.time: O(N / M) in typical reasoning, but worst-case O(N) when M = 1
complexity.why: var_3 = int(var_2 / var_1) ≈ N / M. In the worst case var_1 = 1 so var_3 ≈ N. func_1 then iterates from var_3 + 1 down to 1, performing a modulo var_2 % var_4 each time. No extra containers used, so constant space.

bottlenecks.detail: Linear scan over up to ~N candidates in func_1: for var_4 in range(var_3 + 1, 0, -1). For N up to 10^9–10^12 this leads to 10^9+ modulo operations and will TLE.
Does not exploit the fact that divisors come in pairs (d, N/d). It checks potential divisors one by one instead of limiting search to O(√N).

FastAudit.core_idea: Iterate only up to sqrt(N), enumerating divisor pairs (d, N/d). For each divisor candidate d, check whether the quotient N / d is at least M; keep the maximum d satisfying this constraint. This reduces the number of checks from O(N) to O(√N).

complexity.why: The loop for var_6 in range(1, int(var_1**0.5) + 1) runs up to floor(√N). Each iteration does O(1) work: a couple of modulo/division operations and comparisons. No additional data structures are stored, so memory usage stays constant.

complexity_delta.from: O(N) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(√N) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: The main improvement is reducing the candidate divisor search space from all integers up to ≈N to only up to √N using divisor pair properties.

transformation_steps: Reinterpret the target property mathematically: search for the largest divisor d of N such that N / d >= M.
Observe that divisors of N appear in pairs (d, N/d); if d <= √N then N/d >= √N, and vice versa.
Replace the linear downward scan from ~N with an upward scan var_6 = 1..√N, testing if var_6 divides N.
For each divisor var_6, compute the paired divisor var_1 // var_6 and check whether the quotient condition (partner >= M) holds for each of the pair treated as candidate d.
Maintain the maximum valid divisor in a running variable (var_4), outputting it after the loop.
trigger_signals: Presence of a loop whose bound depends directly on the magnitude of input (range(var_3 + 1, 0, -1) where var_3 ≈ var_2 / var_1 and can be as large as N).
Use of expensive modulo operations in that large loop, which will dominate runtime for large N.
Typical competitive-programming constraints where N can be 10^9 or higher, making O(N) divisor scans infeasible.
Number-theoretic structure (divisors) that strongly suggests an O(√N) divisor enumeration approach.
pitfalls: Incorrect handling of divisor pairs: must ensure both d and N/d are considered as candidates d with correct quotient checks (N/d >= M).
Off-by-one in the sqrt loop: the upper bound must be int(var_1**0.5) + 1 to include floor(√N).

Integer division vs. float: var_1**0.5 returns float; casting to int must not cause precision issues for very large N (in Python it is safe up to problem constraints, but in other languages one must be careful).
Ensuring constant-time operations per iteration and avoiding redundant computations or repeated modulo checks for the same divisor.

constraints_guess.notes: var_2 is target length N; var_3/var_5 is number of (length, cost) pairs M. The original code allocates N + 10^4, suggesting max step length or safety margin around 10^4 and N up to about 10^5 for Python to be feasible.

dominant_ops: Python-level loop over N, and in each iteration multiple NumPy array indexings and temporary array creations (including np.arange and fancy indexing) of size M, followed by a reduction (min).

complexity.why: For each state var_6 in [1..N], the code builds index arrays of length M (np.arange) and performs vectorized indexing into var_7 and var_4, then a min reduction over M values. This yields O(M) work per N, so O(N*M) total. Arrays var_1, var_4, and var_7 are all O(M) or O(N + max(var_1)), giving O(N+M) space.

bottlenecks.detail: NumPy is called inside a Python for-loop over all N states. Each DP step allocates np.arange(var_5, dtype=np.int16) and performs fancy indexing, which is much more expensive per-iteration than simple integer arithmetic in pure Python.
np.arange(var_5, dtype=np.int16) is recomputed on every iteration, creating a new array of length M each time. This adds significant O(N*M) allocation and garbage-collection overhead.

Fancy indexing (var_7[var_6 - var_1[idx]] and var_4[idx]) creates temporary arrays and forces extra memory traffic and bounds checks, increasing constants despite the same asymptotic O(N*M) complexity.
The index array uses dtype=np.int16; for M >= 32768 this overflows and corrupts indices. It is also unnecessary and can reduce performance due to type conversions.

States are not initialized with an INF sentinel, so unreachable states are treated as cost 0. Also, indexing var_7[var_6 - var_1[...]] can go negative for var_6 < var_1[i], causing wrap-around indexing from the end of the array. These issues both impact result correctness and can hide performance problems during testing.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a straightforward 1D DP over total length with a large sentinel value for unreachable states, iterating all (length, cost) pairs for each reachable state and relaxing transitions. Only simple integer operations and list indexing inside tight Python loops; no heavy NumPy overhead.

complexity.why: For each length var_7 in [0..N-1], the inner loop scans all M (length, cost) pairs once and tries to relax state var_7 + length. This is O(M) per state, giving O(N*M) total. The DP array var_6 has size N + 10^4 + 1 (effectively N + A_max), and the list of pairs is size M, so space is O(N + A_max + M) ≈ O(N + A_max). In practice, this is efficient in CP constraints when N and M are up to around 10^5 and 10^2–10^3 respectively.

complexity_delta.from: O(N * M) with heavy per-iteration NumPy overhead, extra allocations, and misuse of vectorization inside a Python loop.
complexity_delta.to: O(N * M) using simple integer arithmetic and list indexing in tight Python loops, skipping unreachable states and correctly handling overshoot with a sentinel INF.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time complexity remains O(N*M), but the constant factors are dramatically reduced. In practice, the pure-Python DP is significantly faster and also correct wrt the original problem (min cost to reach at least N), while the NumPy version computes a different and often incorrect DP.

transformation_steps: Replace the Python for-loop + per-iteration NumPy vectorized expression with a doubly nested pure-Python loop: outer over current length (var_7), inner over (length, cost) pairs.
Introduce a DP array initialized with a large sentinel INF value and set dp[0] = 0; skip transitions from unreachable states to avoid propagating garbage values.
Extend the DP array by a fixed margin (10**4) to safely handle overshoot beyond the target length N, then take the minimum over dp[N:] as the final answer.
Use plain Python lists and integers instead of NumPy arrays and fancy indexing, removing repeated allocations like np.arange() and avoiding dtype issues.
Read input via sys.stdin.readline to reduce I/O overhead for many lines compared to plain input().
trigger_signals: Runtime significantly worse than expected for O(N*M) DP despite modest N and M, especially when using NumPy in a tight Python loop.
Profiling shows the majority of time spent in NumPy array creation (np.arange) and fancy indexing, not in the core arithmetic.
Memory churn and frequent allocations observed (many temporary arrays per DP step).
Incorrect outputs or suspicious results due to negative indices and missing INF initialization, particularly when some lengths cannot be formed exactly.
Use of small integer dtypes (e.g., int16) for indices or large counts M, indicating potential overflow and hidden bugs.
pitfalls: The sentinel value (100000000) must exceed any possible valid cost; if input costs can sum above this, the INF choice must be increased to avoid overflow-like behavior.
The DP array size N + 10**4 assumes step lengths are bounded (e.g., <= 10^4). If the maximum step length can be larger, the buffer must be adjusted to at least N + max_step.
Skipping unreachable states is essential; without the dp[var_7] == INF check, you may propagate invalid large costs and degrade performance.

Using Python lists is faster here, but for extremely large N*M (e.g., > 10^8 operations), even the optimized version may still TLE in Python; in such cases, an algorithmic improvement (e.g., different DP optimization) or a faster language might be required.

Care must be taken to maintain the original problem semantics: Code A computes min cost to reach at least N, while the NumPy version effectively targeted exact N without overshoot handling and with different state initialization, leading to incorrect behavior even if it were fast.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: given N and M (here var_8, var_5), factorize M (<= ~1e9) and compute product over primes of C(N + e_p - 1, e_p) mod 1e9+7, where e_p are exponents in prime factorization of M. Number of distinct primes and exponents is small (O(log M)).

dominant_ops: Global precomputation of factorials and inverse factorials up to var_7 = 10^6 using numpy-based prefix products (func_2, func_3).
Large numpy array creations and reshapes (np.resize to var_3**2, reshape(var_3, var_3)).
Vectorized modular multiplications over ~10^6 elements in multiple passes.
Trial-division prime factorization of M (func_4, partially shown) up to sqrt(M).

complexity.time: O(L + sqrt(M)) where L = var_7 (10^6) for factorial/inv-factorial precompute, plus O(sum e_p) for a few binomial evaluations.
complexity.space: O(L) = O(10^6) for factorial and inverse factorial tables, plus temporary numpy arrays of similar size.
complexity.why: The algorithm precomputes factorials and inverse factorials up to a fixed upper bound L = 10^6 using numpy. This is linear in L irrespective of actual input sizes (N, exponents e_p). Given that the number of binomial coefficients needed is tiny (exponents of prime factors of M, typically <= O(log M) and sum e_p small), the O(L) precomputation dominates runtime and memory. Additionally, numpy import and large array handling add substantial constant-factor overhead.

bottlenecks.detail: Factorials/inverse factorials are precomputed up to 10^6 even though only a handful of binomial coefficients with very small k (exponents of prime factors of M) are needed.
Importing numpy and operating on 10^6-sized arrays introduces large startup and memory overhead, which is disproportionate for a single test case and small combinatorial parameters.

func_2 builds a sqrt-decomposed 2D numpy array of size var_3^2 ≈ L and performs multiple full passes of modular multiplication over it, which is bandwidth-heavy compared to simple scalar integer multiplications.
The precomputation limit var_7 = 10^6 is hard-coded, so the work does not scale with the real needed bound (max over N + e_p - 1); it may be far larger than necessary for given inputs.

The numpy-based prefix-product trick (reshape to square, cumulative products by row/column) is algorithmically O(L) but complicated and brittle; debugging or modifying it risks mistakes and makes the solution less transparent.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the very small number and size of prime exponents of M. First, factorize M by trial division up to sqrt(M), recording exponents e_p. For each exponent e, compute C(N + e - 1, e) directly with a multiplicative formula in O(e) using plain integers, and multiply all these contributions modulo 1e9+7. No global factorial precomputation or heavy libraries are needed.

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + sum e_p) where sum e_p is small (at most O(log M), typically much less).
complexity.space: O(#distinct_primes) = O(log M) at most, effectively O(1) for this constraint range.
complexity.why: Trial division up to sqrt(M) suffices to factorize M ≤ ~1e9 (sqrt(M) ≤ ~3×10^4), which is fast in CP. The number and size of exponents e_p are tiny, so using a multiplicative binomial formula C(n, k) in O(k) is extremely cheap. All work is done with scalar Python integers, avoiding large precomputed tables and numpy overhead.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(sqrt(M) + sum e_p) with only small constant factors; Space: O(1).
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(L + sqrt(M) + sum e_p) with L = 10^6 and heavy per-element numpy overhead; Space: O(L).
complexity_delta.note: The modified (slow) version generalizes binomial computation via factorial tables and numpy, which adds an O(L) precompute cost and large constant factors, while the problem only requires a few small-k combinations that the original direct method handles in negligible time.

transformation_steps: Recognize that only combinations of the form C(N + e - 1, e) where e are prime exponents of M are needed, and that e is small (O(log M)).
Remove the global factorial/inverse-factorial precomputation up to a fixed large bound (var_7 = 10^6).
Replace the generic nCk implementation using factorial tables with a direct multiplicative formula for C(n, k) that runs in O(k) and uses plain integer arithmetic.
Eliminate all numpy usage (np.arange, np.resize, reshape, vectorized products) and rely on simple Python loops, which are sufficient at this scale.
Keep the straightforward trial-division factorization of M up to sqrt(M) from the original fast code, as its complexity is appropriate for M up to about 1e9.
Apply modulo 1e9+7 only as needed (e.g., after each combinatorial multiplication) to keep integers within reasonable size, while still letting Python big integers handle intermediate products safely.
trigger_signals: The input involves factoring a single integer M and then using only a small number of exponents to form combinations.
The code performs a large, fixed-size precomputation (10^6 elements) independent of any obvious upper bound derived from N and M.
The solution imports heavy numerical libraries (numpy) for what is fundamentally integer combinatorics on small parameters.
Runtime or memory usage is high despite simple-looking problem constraints (e.g., single test case, small M).
Profiling or logging would show most time/memory spent inside the factorial precomputation and numpy operations rather than factorization or core combinatorial logic.
pitfalls: When reverting to a direct multiplicative binomial formula, ensure the symmetry C(n, k) = C(n, n - k) is used (choose smaller k) to avoid unnecessary iterations.

Be careful with integer division: in the multiplicative formula, always divide exactly after each multiplication step to avoid non-integer intermediate results; Python integers handle large numerators safely.

Remember to apply modulo after multiplications (and possibly periodically) to control integer size, but not in a way that breaks the exact integer division when using multiplicative formulas over integers; a safe pattern is to build C(n, k) as an exact integer first, then take modulo.
Avoid hard-coding excessively large precomputation bounds (like 10^6) unless they are proven necessary by constraints; derive bounds from max(N + e_p - 1) when factorial tables are truly needed.
Do not rely on numpy in environments where it may be unavailable or slow (e.g., many online judges); even when available, the overhead may dominate for problems with small to moderate input sizes.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic scheduling-by-deadline greedy check. Needs O(n log n) solution; typical n up to ~2e5 in Python. Each job has (duration, deadline).

dominant_ops: Reading O(n) lines of two integers each from stdin
Sorting n pairs by deadline: O(n log n)
Single linear pass over sorted list to check feasibility

complexity.why: All variants perform the same algorithm: store n jobs, sort by deadline, then single pass accumulating processing time and checking against deadlines. Sorting dominates at O(n log n); storage of all jobs is O(n).

bottlenecks.detail: Input helpers func_3/func_7 wrap var_7.readline in Python function calls for every line, adding call overhead on top of already heavy IO. For large n, this overhead is noticeable though still O(n).
Use of multiple small wrapper functions (func_3, func_7, etc.) for simple one-liners adds extra global lookups and call frames compared to inlining readline/map directly.

sys.setrecursionlimit and several unused helpers (func_1, func_2, func_4, func_5, func_6, func_8) do not affect asymptotic complexity but indicate a generic template; this can bloat code and slightly increase module import and name-resolution overhead.

The loop sets a flag var_6 and breaks, then prints after the loop. This still processes until the first violation but cannot terminate the program immediately, so any framework/outer logic executes after; a direct exit at first violation is marginally cheaper.

FastAudit.core_idea: Same greedy algorithm (sort jobs by deadline, then accumulate durations and ensure each partial sum is within its job’s deadline) but with tighter IO and control-flow: a local alias to stdin.readline, no generic helper wrappers, and early process termination on first failure.

complexity.why: Algorithmic structure is unchanged: read n jobs -> sort by (deadline, duration) -> single pass check. Sorting still dominates with O(n log n) time, and all jobs are stored in memory simultaneously, giving O(n) space. Improvements are constant-factor only (less function-call overhead, localized IO, earlier termination).

complexity_delta.from: O(n log n) time, O(n) space (with heavier per-iteration overhead from wrappers and generic template code).
complexity_delta.to: O(n log n) time, O(n) space (same asymptotics but with reduced function-call and attribute-lookup overhead and earlier termination in failing cases).
complexity_delta.note: No change in big-O; improvements are in constant factors and average-case work when an early failure occurs.

transformation_steps: IO aliasing: Replaced generic var_7 + helper functions with a direct alias var_4 = sys.stdin.readline and used it inline, cutting one layer of Python function calls per input line.

Inline parsing: Inlined int/tuple parsing into the list comprehension [list(map(int, var_4().split())) for _ in range(var_5)] instead of via func_3, eliminating extra call overhead and global lookup of func_3.

Simplified control flow: Removed the boolean flag var_6 and post-loop conditional print in favor of printing "No" and exiting as soon as a deadline violation is detected, avoiding any trailing logic and making the main loop straightforward.

Sort key adjustment: Changed sort key from key=lambda var_8: var_8[1] to key=lambda var_7: (var_7[1], var_7[0]); this does not change asymptotics and only marginally affects constant factors. The secondary key (duration) is a tie-breaker and usually harmless.
Removed unused template code: Dropped recursion-limit adjustment and unused input helpers, slightly reducing module-level overhead and making the code lighter for the interpreter.
trigger_signals: Same algorithm in both versions but one version timing out or running noticeably slower suggests overhead in IO and Python-level function calls rather than algorithmic flaws.
Presence of multiple generic helper functions for simple reads (func_1..func_8) is a typical sign of template code that can be inlined for performance.
Problem type (greedy with single sort and pass) is already optimal algorithmically for this task; remaining optimizations naturally focus on constant factors.
High input size (large n) makes repeated Python call overhead (wrappers around readline/map) and non-local attribute lookups relatively expensive compared to the arithmetic being performed.
pitfalls: Use of eval: fast_code uses int(eval(var_4())). eval on raw input is generally unsafe and slower than int(var_4()) because it runs the Python parser. For competitive programming on trusted judges it may work but should be avoided; using int(var_4()) or int(var_4().strip()) is safer and faster.

Correctness dependence on ordering: Changing the sort key structure (e.g., forgetting to sort by deadline) would break correctness even though complexity remains O(n log n). Any further micro-optimizations must preserve the primary sort by deadline.

Early exit semantics: Using exit() terminates the whole process immediately. In some environments (unit tests, online judges with multiple testcases per run, or embedded interpreters) this may be undesirable; sys.exit or structured returns from main-like functions are usually safer.

Memory vs streaming: Both versions read all jobs into memory before processing. Attempting to stream jobs without sorting would change the algorithm and break the greedy correctness; do not trade away the sort for linear IO to save memory.

Over-focusing on micro-optimizations: The current improvements are reasonable, but further micro-optimizations (e.g., overusing eval or clever one-liners) can hurt readability and may not yield meaningful speed gains compared to algorithmic or IO-structure changes.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer input; original code is O(n) with a loop up to n//2, which would only be acceptable up to around 1e7 in Python. The optimized code is O(sqrt(n)), suggesting n may be as large as ~1e12.

dominant_ops: Single for-loop from 1 to n//2 performing integer division n//i
O(1) arithmetic per iteration (multiplications, additions, integer division)

complexity.why: The main loop iterates from i = 1 to i = n//2, which is Theta(n) iterations in the worst case. Each iteration performs a constant amount of arithmetic and one integer division, so total time is linear in n. Only a fixed number of scalar variables are used, so space is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: The for-loop runs for n//2 iterations, which is too large when n is up to around 1e10–1e12.
Each iteration performs n//i; integer division is relatively expensive, and it is executed O(n) times.
For intended constraints inferred from the optimized solution (n up to ~1e12), O(n) is not feasible in Python, leading to timeouts.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit divisor-pair symmetry and arithmetic series sums to rewrite the sum so that it can be computed by iterating only over d up to sqrt(n). For each d ≤ sqrt(n), contributions from both d and its paired divisors n//d are captured using prefix-sum-like closed forms via func_1 (sum of first k integers). This reduces the iteration range from O(n) to O(sqrt(n)).

complexity.why: The loop runs for var_3 = 1..floor(sqrt(n)); it stops as soon as var_3 * var_3 > n. Inside the loop, only O(1) arithmetic is done (a few multiplications, additions, and integer divisions), so total time is proportional to sqrt(n). No additional data structures are allocated beyond a constant number of scalar variables, so space usage remains constant.

complexity_delta.from: O(n)
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(n))
complexity_delta.note: Replaced a linear scan up to n//2 with a sqrt-based divisor-pair iteration using closed-form arithmetic series sums.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the original summation over i up to n//2 involves structured terms depending on floor(n / i) and can be reformulated using properties of divisors and arithmetic series.
Introduce a helper function func_1(k) = k * (k + 1) // 2 to compute sums of consecutive integers in O(1) time.
Change the iteration variable to var_3 and restrict it to 1..floor(sqrt(n)), breaking when var_3 * var_3 > n, so each var_3 corresponds to a divisor range through n // var_3.

For each var_3, accumulate the diagonal term var_3 * var_3 and then use 2 * var_3 * (func_1(var_4) - func_1(var_3)) to capture symmetric contributions from both var_3 and its paired divisors, avoiding explicit iteration over the larger range.

Preserve correctness by ensuring that all contributions that were previously covered by iterating to n//2 are now covered via divisor pairs and arithmetic series identities, avoiding double-counting by careful limits (using func_1(var_4) - func_1(var_3)).
trigger_signals: The original loop bound is proportional to n (specifically n//2), with a non-trivial integer division inside the loop.
Use of integer arithmetic and n//i pattern strongly suggests that divisor-based or floor-division-based optimization (grouping by equal n//i values or iterating up to sqrt(n)) is possible.
The presence of an optimized reference (Code B) that stops at var_3 * var_3 > n is a direct indication that a sqrt(n) approach is intended.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when translating between ranges 1..n//2 and 1..sqrt(n); incorrect bounds can lead to missing or double-counted contributions.
Misusing the arithmetic series helper func_1 (e.g., computing func_1(var_4) - func_1(var_3 - 1) instead of func_1(var_4) - func_1(var_3)) would shift the summation range and break equivalence.

For large n, intermediate products (e.g., var_3 * var_3 or 2 * var_3 * (func_1(var_4) - func_1(var_3))) can become very large; Python handles big integers, but in other languages overflow would be a critical concern.
Retaining eval(input()) is unsafe from a security perspective; while not a performance problem, replacing eval(input()) with input() and int() is important in real contest or production settings.

constraints_guess.notes: Structure matches AtCoder-style expected value problem (e.g., ABC126 C: N up to 1e5, K up to about 1e9). Single test, no extra queries; inner loop length bounded by O(log K).

dominant_ops: Outer loop over i from 1 to N (var_4)
Inner while loop that repeatedly evaluates exponentiation 2**var_3
Per-iteration floating-point power (0.5)**var_3

complexity.why: For each i in [1..N], var_3 is incremented until var_1 * 2**var_3 >= var_2 (≈ log2(var_2/var_1) steps). Worst case is O(log K) iterations of the while loop per i. Each while iteration recomputes 2**var_3, which is more expensive than a simple multiplication, so the effective cost is N * log K exponentiations. The accumulation uses O(1) extra space.

bottlenecks.detail: Inside the inner while loop, the condition uses var_1 * 2**var_3, recomputing 2**var_3 from scratch every iteration instead of reusing the previous value or using iterative doubling. This makes the innermost work more expensive than necessary.
Exponentiation (2**var_3) in the loop condition is significantly slower than integer multiplication; it dominates runtime when N is large and K is large (so var_3 goes up to around 30–60).

Although (0.5)**var_3 is only done once per outer iteration, it is still a power operation. Its cost is smaller than the inner 2**var_3 because it runs O(N) times instead of O(N log K), but it is non-trivial compared to simple arithmetic.
Using input() instead of sys.stdin.readline() adds minor overhead. This is not the primary bottleneck here but can matter under tight time limits.

FastAudit.core_idea: Preserve the same probabilistic computation but replace recomputed exponentiation inside the inner loop with iterative doubling of an integer, turning an expensive pow-style operation into cheap multiplications, and use faster I/O. The exponent of 0.5 is tracked as an integer counter (var_4) while a separate variable (var_7) is doubled until it reaches the threshold.

complexity.why: For each starting value var_5 in [1..var_2], the code doubles var_7 until it reaches var_1, which still takes O(log K) steps in the worst case. However, each step now performs constant-time integer multiplication and increment, eliminating repeated exponentiation. The expected-value accumulation is still O(N), and only O(1) extra variables are used.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log K * cost_pow) with exponentiation in the inner loop condition
complexity_delta.to: O(N log K) with only integer multiplications inside the inner loop and a single pow per outer iteration
complexity_delta.note: The asymptotic Big-O in terms of N and K is unchanged, but the dominant inner-loop operation changed from pow-style exponentiation to simple multiplication, significantly reducing the constant factor. Faster input reading further trims overhead.

transformation_steps: Change I/O from input() to sys.stdin.readline() to reduce Python function call overhead on read.
Reinterpret the inner loop condition K > i * 2**c as doubling a temporary variable: start var_7 = i and repeatedly do var_7 *= 2 until var_7 >= K, counting the doublings in var_4.
Remove the recomputation of 2**var_3 on every while-iteration and instead track only the number of doublings (var_4), which directly becomes the exponent used for 0.5.
Retain a single power computation per outer iteration as pow(0.5, var_4), which is acceptable because var_4 is at most O(log K).
Keep accumulation in a running float and division by N (var_2/var_4) outside the inner loop to avoid redundant work.
trigger_signals: Inner while loop whose bound depends logarithmically on another input (doubling pattern) combined with an expensive exponentiation in the loop condition.
Use of exponentiation operator (**) inside a nested loop in Python, which is known to have higher constant cost.
Known competitive-programming constraints where Python solutions with pow in an inner loop are prone to TLE even if asymptotic complexity seems acceptable.
Pattern matching to standard problem (expected value via doubling), where canonical solutions use iterative doubling rather than exponentiation inside loops.
pitfalls: Changing the inequality direction or loop condition incorrectly when switching from K > i * 2**c to var_7 < K can alter off-by-one behavior and produce wrong probabilities.

Floating point precision: repeated use of pow(0.5, exponent) is generally safe for exponents up to about 60, but reformulations that accumulate many tiny increments could accumulate rounding error if not careful.

Mis-ordering of input variables: the modified code swaps the naming (var_2, var_1) vs (var_4, var_2). Any further refactor must preserve the logical roles (N vs K) rather than rely on original variable names.

Assuming that removing exponentiation changes asymptotic complexity: it does not; the benefit is from lowering the constant factor. Further scaling beyond typical contest constraints might still require a more analytical formula to avoid the N log K loop entirely.
Using pow with three arguments (modular exponentiation) by mistake instead of floating-point pow would change semantics; here pow(0.5, var_4) must remain a float call.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style array/prefix-sum problem: Python O(n^2) tends to TLE while O(n) passes. Input is just n and an array of length n.

dominant_ops: Building full prefix-sum array var_2 of length n+1
For each prefix sum, converting dict keys to a list and doing membership test: str(s) in list(var_5.keys())
Final pass computing combinations over frequency map

complexity.why: Computing prefix sums is O(n). The second loop iterates over n+1 prefix sums; for each it calls list(var_5.keys()) (O(k)) and then checks membership in that list (another O(k)), where k is current number of distinct prefix sums (up to O(n)). This yields ~sum_{k=1..n} O(k) = O(n^2). The final combination pass over frequencies is O(n). Arrays and dict store O(n) elements, so space is O(n).

bottlenecks.detail: Membership check written as `str(var_3) in list(var_5.keys())` turns an intended O(1) dict lookup into O(k) linear search over keys for every element, making the counting step O(n^2).
Calling list(var_5.keys()) on every iteration repeatedly allocates new lists of growing size, adding large constant overhead and memory churn.
Converting numeric prefix sums to strings for keys (str(var_3)) prevents direct O(1) numeric dict lookup and adds conversion cost.
Storing all prefix sums in an array var_2 instead of updating a running sum increases memory usage and adds an extra pass, though this is secondary compared to the O(n^2) lookup pattern.
Using eval(input()) instead of int(input()) is slower and unsafe, though it does not dominate asymptotic complexity.

FastAudit.core_idea: Maintain a running prefix sum and a hash map (dict) that counts how many times each prefix sum has occurred so far. For each new element, update the running sum, add the current frequency of that sum to the answer (counting subarrays ending here with sum 0), then increment the stored frequency. This streams the array in one pass using O(1) expected time per element.

complexity.why: Each of the n elements is processed once with a constant number of average O(1) dictionary operations (get and set). No nested loops or repeated scans of growing structures are used. The dict may store up to O(n) distinct prefix sums, so space is O(n).

complexity_delta.from: O(n^2) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: The main improvement is replacing repeated list-based key scans with direct O(1) dict lookups and streaming the prefix sum instead of scanning prefix arrays with quadratic behavior.

transformation_steps: Replace eval(input()) with int(input()) for safe and slightly faster integer parsing.
Avoid building a full prefix-sum array; instead, maintain a single running prefix sum variable updated in the main loop.
Use a dictionary directly keyed by integer prefix sums (no str() conversion).
Replace `if str(s) in list(var_5.keys())` pattern with `count = var_4.get(s, 0)` and then `var_4[s] = count + 1`, eliminating O(k) key-list creation and linear search.
Accumulate the answer on the fly: for each new prefix sum s, add its previous frequency to the result (counting all subarrays ending at this index with sum 0).
Initialize the frequency map with {0: 1} so that subarrays starting from index 0 are counted correctly without special cases.
Avoid building intermediate lists (like var_6 of combinations) just to sum them; update the total incrementally to reduce allocations and passes.
trigger_signals: Use of `list(dict.keys())` inside a loop where the dict grows with input size, combined with membership checks, indicates a hidden O(n^2) pattern.
Observed TLE or very slow performance when n reaches typical contest upper bounds (e.g., 10^5–2*10^5).
Conversion of numeric values to strings solely to be used as keys in a dict, then repeatedly reconverted or compared, suggests unnecessary overhead and possibly missed O(1) operations.
Two-pass structure over the data (build prefix array, then iterate again to count) where a one-pass streaming solution exists.
Use of eval for numeric input in competitive programming code, which often hints at non-optimized/boilerplate or unsafe patterns.
pitfalls: Forgetting to pre-seed the frequency dictionary with {0: 1} will undercount subarrays that start at index 0 and sum to 0.
Using the dict incorrectly (e.g., incrementing frequency before adding to the answer) changes the combinatorial counting logic and yields off-by-one errors.
If ported to languages with fixed-size integer types, large prefix sums could overflow; Python avoids this but other environments may require 64-bit integers.
Retaining the string conversion for dict keys (using str(sum)) while adopting the fast pattern would still incur unnecessary conversion costs and complicate reasoning; keys should remain integers.
Accidentally reverting to patterns like `if key in dict.keys()` or creating lists from dict views in the main loop can reintroduce hidden linear factors and degrade performance.

constraints_guess.notes: Fixed structure: 3 groups, each with 8 lines of input (3 * 8 = 24 contestants/items). Time constraints negligible; main concern is code complexity and constant factors.

dominant_ops: Per-item Python-level branching and assignments inside nested loops
Repeated float parsing via map(float, input().split())
Manual tracking of top-2 values per group and overall via comparisons
String formatting with printf-style (%d %4.2f) for each output line

complexity.why: There are G=3 groups and K=8 entries per group. For each of the 24 entries, the code does a constant amount of work: one input read, conversion to two floats, and a fixed chain of comparisons/assignments. No per-item auxiliary data structures grow with input size; only a constant number of scalar variables is maintained.

bottlenecks.detail: All comparisons and state updates are implemented as Python bytecode in nested loops. Even though the total number of items is small (24), each item incurs multiple interpreted branches and assignments, which increases constant-factor overhead.

The logic for updating per-group and global top-2 values has multiple nested if/elif blocks. This not only makes the code harder to reason about, but also causes extra branching and repeated checks for each item.

For each new score, it potentially compares against up to four tracked minima (group first/second, global first/second). Some comparisons are repeated in multiple branches, increasing the per-item cost.
Manually implementing top-2 tracking per group and globally duplicates logic that could be handled more efficiently and more clearly by leveraging built-in sorting on a small list.

FastAudit.core_idea: Accumulate each group’s 8 items into a small list, then use Python’s built-in sorted (implemented in C) to obtain ordering and slice out the top candidates. Then, collect the second-tier candidates and again sort this small list to get the overall next-best two. This replaces intricate per-item branching with a couple of small, highly optimized sorts.

complexity.why: For each of G=3 groups, the code builds a list of K=8 entries and calls sorted once, costing O(K log K) per group. This dominates the per-group time, while list construction is O(K). Afterward, it performs one more sort on up to 6 items (the collected second-tier candidates), which is O(1) in practice. Space is O(G*K) to store all contestants of all groups (24 small records) plus intermediate slices.

complexity_delta.from: O(G * K) manual selection with constant auxiliary space
complexity_delta.to: O(G * K log K) via sorting small lists plus O(G * K) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically, the modified (slow) code is O(n) while the original (fast) code is O(n log n) in the number of contestants per group. However, with K fixed at 8, log K is a tiny constant and built-in sort is highly optimized C code, so the sort-based approach is effectively faster and far simpler in practice.

transformation_steps: Replace manual per-item top-2 tracking logic with collection of items into temporary lists per group.
Use input().split()[::-1] to store items in an order that makes lexicographic sorting yield the desired ranking, then rely on sorted(...) to order the 8 items within each group.
Select the top 2 items in each group via slicing (var_1[0:2]) and the next 2 via var_1[2:4], instead of repeated conditional updates.
Aggregate all group-level 3rd/4th-place candidates into a single list (var_4) and run a final sorted(...) on this tiny list to extract the global next-best two.
Simplify output formatting by iterating over the final ordered list and joining string components, avoiding the explicit float formatting logic.
trigger_signals: Very small, fixed-size collections (K=8) where sort-based solutions have negligible log K overhead.
Complex nested if/elif chains that attempt to maintain top-k elements manually.
Multiple variables representing different ranking positions (group and global first/second) with overlapping update paths.
Desire to offload comparison-heavy work from Python-level loops to C-level built-ins like sorted for better constant factors and clearer code.
pitfalls: Relying on lexicographic sort of string tokens (as in the original fast_code) can be incorrect if numeric values are not zero-padded or consistently formatted; converting to numeric types may be needed for correctness in general.
The sort-based approach assumes that the number of items per group remains small; if K became large, the O(K log K) cost might outweigh a carefully implemented O(K) selection algorithm.
Using list slicing and concatenation (var_3 += var_1[0:2], etc.) creates intermediate lists; while negligible here, such patterns can matter with larger inputs.
Switching from explicit numeric types (floats) to string-based comparisons changes semantics; any refactor must confirm that ordering rules remain correct for the problem’s intended input format.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: single query, N up to around 1e5, M up to around 1e9; must factor M and compute combinations with repetition under mod 1e9+7.

dominant_ops: Trial division prime factorization up to sqrt(M) in func_1
Computation of factorial(var_2 - 1) with a large argument (unused result)
Creation and manipulation of very large Python integers due to factorial calls and delayed modulo
Per-prime-exponent loop doing multiplicative construction of combinations and another factorial(var_12)

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + N * log N) in theory; factorization is O(sqrt(M)), but the heavy constant factor comes from factorial(N-1) on large N with big integers.
complexity.space: O(log M) for factorization map plus O(N log N) bits transiently for the huge factorial value and intermediate products.
complexity.why: The algorithmic structure is fine (factor M, then for each exponent e compute C(e+N-1, e)), but using math.factorial on potentially large N-1 and postponing modular reduction leads to massive big integers. These dominate both time and memory despite not affecting asymptotic big-O of the numeric loops.

bottlenecks.detail: var_5 = factorial(var_2 - 1) is computed but never used. For large var_2 this single call creates a huge integer (hundreds of thousands of digits), wasting substantial CPU and memory.
var_11 accumulates the product of all combination values with no modulo until the very end. Intermediate values can grow very large, slowing down multiplication and increasing memory usage.
The modulo 1e9+7 is applied only once at the final print; all intermediate combinatorial products are handled as exact big integers instead of being reduced early.

math.factorial is used repeatedly (once on N-1, once per exponent). Although implemented in C and optimized, factorial(N-1) in particular is overkill for this task and dominates runtime when N is large.
Imported sqrt and ceil are unused; they do not affect performance meaningfully but indicate some leftover / unused math heavy setup.
