Factorials and inverse factorials are computed up to N+O(1) in O(N) time using a forward pass for factorials and a backward pass for inverse factorials after one modular exponentiation. Each prime exponent contributes O(1) work to the final product. Arrays are sized proportionally to N, so space is O(N).

complexity_delta.from: O(MAXN + sqrt(M)) time, O(MAXN) space, with MAXN fixed at 2e5+10 and higher per-step overhead in inverse computation and dictionary usage.
complexity_delta.to: O(N + sqrt(M)) time, O(N) space, using tighter array sizes and more efficient factorial/inverse-factorial precomputation and access.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity class remains the same, but constants are significantly improved, which is critical in Python for N up to 2e5.

transformation_steps: Replace defaultdict-based factorization function with an inlined trial division loop that collects only the exponents of prime factors into a list, avoiding dictionary overhead and function calls.

Change the factorization loop bound from `for i in range(2, n+1) with break on i*i>n` to `for i in range(2, int(m**0.5)+2)`, keeping similar asymptotics but simplifying the loop; keep the final check to append a remaining prime factor if m > 1.

Replace the custom inverse array recurrence with a standard factorial/inverse-factorial scheme: compute factorials in a single forward pass, compute the inverse of the last factorial via pow(fact[-1], MOD-2, MOD), then fill inverse factorials in a single backward pass.
Inline the combination formula C(N+e-1, N-1) = fact[N+e-1] * invfact[N-1] * invfact[e] modulo MOD inside the loop over exponents, eliminating extra function calls and intermediate lookups.

constraints_guess.notes: Single array of length n, one-shot computation of sum of squared deviations from an optimal integer value. Typical competitive-programming style; n likely up to 2e5 with |ai| up to about 1e9.

complexity_delta.from: O(N) time, O(N) space with higher Python-level overhead (per-element input helper calls, branches, and unused imports/functions).

Input values being read via a helper function called repeatedly inside loops (N calls to sys.stdin.readline) instead of using bulk reading patterns.
A tight loop that performs simple arithmetic but includes Python-level branching and list mutations that could be expressed more compactly.
Need to pass large test cases close to time limits where Python interpreter overhead dominates over the arithmetic itself.
pitfalls: Using open(0) for input assumes a standard Unix-like environment; in some contexts, relying on sys.stdin directly can be clearer or more portable, though for most judges open(0) is fine.
The more compact arithmetic with divmod and carry is less immediately readable than the explicit if/else version; future maintainers must be careful to preserve correctness when modifying it.
Care must be taken with off-by-one handling of the last element; moving to zip(var_1, var_1[1:]) requires an explicit final adjustment (as done with (var_1[-1] - var_6) // 2).
Aggressively removing branches and list updates can obscure the high-level greedy reasoning; while faster, it can be harder to verify or adapt to variant problems.

constraints_guess.notes: n is a single integer; original O(n^2) trial-division factorization suggests n is at most around 10^4–10^5. Problem: count divisors of n! modulo 1e9+7.

dominant_ops: Naive trial-division factorization for every integer k in [2, n]
Building a global list of all prime factors of all k (var_8) before counting
Linear scan up to k (skipping evens) for each k without early termination after full factorization

complexity.time: O(n^2 / log n) trial divisions (≈ O(n^2) in simple terms)
complexity.space: O(n log n) for aggregated prime factors list plus counter structures
complexity.why: For each k from 2 to n, func_1(k) loops var_3 from 2 to k, skipping most evens but still Θ(k) iterations for odd var_3. The work per k is ≈k/log k successful divisibility checks, so total work is Σ_{k=2}^n k/log k ≈ Θ(n^2 / log n). All prime factors from all k are appended to var_8, whose total length is Θ(sum of exponents in n!), which is Θ(n log n), so memory grows accordingly.

bottlenecks.detail: Factoring every integer 2..n independently by trial division up to k yields a quadratic-in-n number of trial divisions.
No early break when var_7 becomes 1 inside func_1; the loop continues scanning var_3 up to var_6 even after the number is fully factored.
All prime factors from all integers are accumulated in one list (var_8) before being summarized; this uses Θ(n log n) memory and causes many list resizes and element moves.
Heavy use of Python-level loops and modulo operations inside nested loops; for large n this dominates runtime.
Use of eval(input()) is unsafe and slower than a direct int(input()). (Not the main bottleneck, but undesirable.)

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the fact that the number of divisors of n! is ∏(e_p + 1), where e_p is the exponent of prime p in n!. Instead of factoring each k in [2, n] separately, compute n! once and factor that single integer by trial division, counting how many times each divisor (which ends up being prime) divides n!, and multiply these counts (e_p+1) on the fly.

complexity.time: ≈ O(n log log n) trial divisions on big integers, plus the cost of computing factorial(n)
complexity.space: O(n log n) bits to store n! plus O(1) additional integer variables
complexity.why: The number of prime factors of n! with multiplicity is Σ_p e_p ≈ n log log n, so the factorization loop performs O(n log log n) successful divisions (and a comparable number of failed modulus tests) as var_4 walks from 2 upward. Each dividing var_4 that actually occurs must be prime, because all smaller primes have been fully stripped already. Thus the algorithm reduces the count of trial divisions from roughly Θ(n^2/log n) (many small factorizations) to Θ(n log log n) (one factorization of n!), at the cost of manipulating large integers for factorial(n). The factorial computation itself is roughly O(n) multiplications on increasing-size integers, which is acceptable for moderate n but still grows super-linearly in bit complexity.

complexity_delta.from: ≈ O(n^2 / log n) trial divisions over many small integers + O(n log n) list storage
complexity_delta.to: ≈ O(n log log n) trial divisions plus big-int factorial computation and storage (≈ O(n log n) bits)
complexity_delta.note: As n grows, the number of trial divisions is reduced dramatically by factoring n! only once instead of factoring every 2..n separately. However, the modified approach trades many small operations for fewer operations on very large integers; it is faster for typical contest-size n (up to ~10^4) but does not scale to extremely large n.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the original code effectively counts prime exponents across all numbers 2..n, which together form the prime factorization of n!; the result is the number of divisors of n! (product over primes of (exponent+1)).
Replace repeated factorization of each k in [2, n] with a single computation of factorial(n).
Run a single trial-division factorization loop over n! using a growing divisor var_4, counting how many times each divisor divides the current value (this count is exponent+1 for that prime).
Accumulate the product of these counts (e_p + 1) in var_2 (and the final var_3) while keeping values within the modulo 1e9+7 at the end.
Eliminate the global factor list and the Counter, reducing Python-level overhead and intermediate allocations.
trigger_signals: Nested looping structure: factorization function func_1(k) called inside a for-loop over k from 2 to n, leading to O(n^2) structure.
Trial division up to k for every k, without exploiting shared structure (that primes dividing different k contribute to the same exponent in n!).
Growth of a large intermediate list var_8 of all prime factors, where only frequency counts are needed for the final result.
Observation that the mathematical target is a function of n! (its divisor count), not of individual factorizations of each integer.
Runtime concerns or timeouts for larger n indicating quadratic-time behavior.
pitfalls: Computing factorial(n) explicitly can be extremely expensive in time and memory for large n; n! grows with Θ(n log n) bits. If the problem’s n is large (e.g., ≥ 10^5–10^6), this approach will likely TLE or exhaust memory.

Using trial division on a huge integer still has substantial cost per division; while the count of divisions is much smaller than in the original code, each operation is on big integers, not machine integers.
The modified code still uses eval(input()), which is unsafe and unnecessary; int(input()) should be used instead.

The factorization loop advances var_4 by 1, not by primes; although composite candidates quickly fail the divisibility test, the loop still performs many useless modulus operations for composite var_4. A more refined approach (e.g., iterating over primes only or using Legendre’s formula for exponents) would be more efficient.

For very large n, a mathematically superior approach is to avoid building n! at all and instead compute each prime exponent e_p with Legendre’s formula (sum_{k≥1} floor(n / p^k)) using primes up to n (via sieve), yielding O(n log log n) time on small integers and avoiding any giant factorial integer.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical setting: find the N-th 'Lunlun'/stepping number with |adjacent digits difference| <= 1, N up to about 1e5 (e.g., AtCoder ABC 161 D).

dominant_ops: Repeated heapq.heappop / heapq.heappush operations inside the main while-loop
Frequent int<->str conversions for every popped number and every generated child
Set membership checks and insertions for deduplication
Final conversion of a large set to list and sorting it

complexity.time: O(M log M), where M is the number of generated numbers (~ c * N); plus a final O(M log M) sort
complexity.why: The loop continues until var_3 (initially N) is decremented N+100 times on unique pops. Each unique number can generate up to 3 prefix and 3 suffix children, so the heap grows significantly. Each push/pop is O(log heap_size). Duplicates are filtered only when popping, so many redundant entries live in the heap. Finally, all collected numbers are sorted, adding another O(M log M) step.

bottlenecks.detail: Using a binary heap (priority queue) for generation causes every produced element to pay an O(log M) cost on push/pop, even though the problem fundamentally only needs simple layered/BFS-style generation.

Children are generated by both prefix and suffix concatenations; many numbers are pushed multiple times. Deduplication is done with a set only at pop-time, so the heap holds many redundant entries, inflating both time and memory.
For every popped value, the code converts to string and back to int repeatedly (for first/last digits, and for each new child). This is in the innermost loop and becomes a hot path for large N.
The loop condition while var_3 + 100 >= 0 forces generation of N+100 unique numbers before stopping, which adds a fixed but nontrivial overhead over the minimum N required.
After generation, all unique numbers are collected into a list and fully sorted to extract the N-th value, which is O(M log M) and can dominate when M is large.

FastAudit.core_idea: Switch from a global min-heap generation with heavy deduplication to a breadth-first layered generation of valid numbers as a tree, tracking levels in a list of sets and stopping as soon as the total count reaches N. This avoids the heap and most duplicate generation, then sorts only the actually produced numbers.

complexity.why: Each valid number is generated exactly once by extending only at the last digit (no prefix growth), so the total number of generated numbers until reaching the N-th is O(N). The BFS-like loop is linear in the number of generated nodes. At the end, all numbers are flattened into a list and sorted, taking O(N log N), which dominates. Memory usage is proportional to the number of generated numbers across layers.

complexity_delta.from: Effectively O(M log M) time with large constant factors due to heap operations and duplicate entries (M ~ c * N), plus O(M log M) final sort; O(M) space.
complexity_delta.to: O(N log N) time dominated by a single sort of ~N numbers; O(N) space with far fewer redundant elements.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both are n log n-ish because of the final sort, but the refactor significantly reduces hidden constants by removing the priority queue, reducing duplicate generation, and simplifying the generation path.

transformation_steps: Removed the priority-queue-based global ordering and replaced it with a BFS-style layered expansion of numbers stored as sets in a list (var_1).

Stopped generating prefixes and suffixes around both first and last digits; instead, only extend numbers by appending digits based on the last digit (d, d-1, d+1 when valid). This eliminates many duplicates and shrinks the state space.
Replaced the 'var_3 + 100' heuristic loop condition with an explicit total count tracker (var_3) and an early-stop flag (var_4) once the cumulative count reaches or exceeds the requested index N.
Deferred sorting until after all necessary numbers have been generated and collected; flattened all level sets into a single list and sorted once, then indexed the (N-1)-th element.
Kept using simple Python data structures (sets and lists) to rely on O(1) average insert/lookup and avoid O(log M) heap operations on every generated value.
trigger_signals: Heap operations (heappush/heappop) appeared in the innermost loop and are known hotspots for Python when used on very large heaps.
The generation strategy clearly produces many duplicates that are only eliminated at pop-time via a set, implying unnecessary heap growth.
The arbitrary '+100' margin on the stop condition hints at overgeneration beyond the required N values.
Profiling or reasoning about counts indicates that the number of heap elements grows faster than the number of unique outputs, suggesting that a tree/BFS structure could be more efficient.
The problem's nature (numbers formed by digit transitions with local constraints) maps naturally to BFS over levels, making a queue/level-based approach an obvious alternative to a heap.
pitfalls: Even with BFS, the final sorting step is still O(N log N); for extremely large N, this remains the dominant cost and may still be a bottleneck.
Layered sets (var_1 as a list of sets) can use significant memory if N is large; careful constraints analysis is still needed for safety.
Frequent int<->str conversions remain in the fast code; for tighter performance, a digit-based representation (working with integers and modulo 10) could further reduce overhead.

The approach assumes that generating up to the layer where the cumulative count >= N provides enough numbers to safely sort and index; off-by-one errors in counting logic would lead to incorrect results.
Using eval(input()) is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; while not the main performance issue, switching to int(input()) is recommended in production settings.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical Lunlun/stepping-number problem (e.g., AtCoder ABC 161 D). Need the N-th smallest number whose adjacent digits differ by at most 1. All such numbers up to 10 digits are pre-generated; count is O(2e5).

dominant_ops: Recursive DFS over all valid numbers up to length 11
Repeated conversion int -> str and indexing digits in each recursive call
Sorting the full generated list of numbers

complexity.why: Let M be the number of generated numbers and L the max number of digits. Each recursive step in slow_code does len(str(var_2)) and int(str(var_2)[-1]), both O(L), so traversal is O(M*L). All generated values are stored and then sorted, costing O(M log M) time and O(M) memory.

bottlenecks.detail: Inside func_1, each node performs len(str(var_2)) and int(str(var_2)[-1]). This is O(L) per node (L = digit length), multiplied across all M generated nodes.

Termination condition uses len(str(var_2)) > 10, and the append happens before this check. This generates and stores 11-digit numbers that are never needed, increasing M compared to the optimal 10-digit bound.
Recursive DFS from all starting digits 1..9 generates the whole tree regardless of the requested index var_1. This is inherent to the chosen approach but exacerbated by the extra overhead per node.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid string operations by tracking depth explicitly and using arithmetic on the last digit; cap recursion at exactly 10 digits so no extra-length numbers are generated.

complexity.why: The fast_code still generates all valid numbers via DFS and sorts them, but each node visit now does only O(1) arithmetic (mod 10 and additions) with an explicit depth parameter var_2 and a numeric current value var_6. No int<->str conversions are used, and recursion stops exactly at depth 10, so traversal is O(M). Storing and sorting remains O(M) space and O(M log M) time.

complexity_delta.from: O(M * L + M log M) time, O(M) space
complexity_delta.to: O(M + M log M) time, O(M) space
complexity_delta.note: Reduced the per-node cost from O(L) string ops to O(1) arithmetic and avoided generating extra 11-digit nodes; asymptotic in terms of M improves by a factor of L (here L ≈ 10), which is a significant constant factor for tight time limits.

transformation_steps: Introduce an explicit depth parameter (var_2) to track the current digit length instead of computing len(str(var_2)) at each step.
Keep the current number purely as an integer (var_6) and derive the last digit via var_6 % 10, eliminating int(str(var_2)[-1]) and all string conversions.
Change the recursion termination condition from `if len(str(var_2)) > 10` to `if var_2 == 10`, preventing generation of unnecessary 11-digit numbers.

Preserve the branching logic using an arithmetic loop over offsets -1, 0, 1 (via range(-1, 2)) instead of multiple separate branches for edge digits; this simplifies code and keeps operations constant-time.
Reuse a passed-in list (var_1) as an accumulation buffer to make the function more explicit in its data flow, though complexity-wise this has the same asymptotic cost as using a global list.
trigger_signals: Recursive function calling itself for every node with len(str(var_2)) and int(str(var_2)[-1]) in the hot path.
Termination condition based on string length comparison (`len(str(x)) > 10`) with append happening before the check, suggesting extra, unneeded nodes.
Known problem structure where max digit length is a small constant (10), making arithmetic-based tracking of depth and last digit more efficient.
Observed pattern that both versions generate a bounded tree of numbers but differ only in representation (strings vs ints) and depth control.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors in depth control: using `== 10` (fast_code) is correct for generating up to 10-digit numbers; using `> 10` after append (slow_code) includes an extra, unnecessary level.
Relying on `eval(input())` for reading integers is dangerous in general and slower than `int(input())`; while not a main bottleneck here, it is a bad practice.
Overlooking that repeated `str()` conversions inside recursive or iterative generation loops can dominate runtime even when the theoretical number of generated states M is modest.
Assuming the recursion depth could cause stack overflow; here depth is bounded by 10, so it is safe, but increasing this limit naively could hit Python's recursion limit.

constraints_guess.notes: Original solution preallocates an array of size 10**7 and indexes by (i+1±a[i]) where i < n. That suggests n is up to ~2e5–3e5 and that i+1±a[i] is guaranteed to stay < 10**7. Exact constraints unknown, but the 10**7 array is a safe upper bound, not tight.

dominant_ops: Allocation of a list of length 10**7: var_4 = [0] * 10**7
Single pass over n elements with constant-time arithmetic and indexing
Standard input() parsing

complexity.time: O(n + M) where M = 10**7 (dominant for typical n up to ~2e5)
complexity.space: Θ(M) = Θ(10**7) integers (~80 MB in CP Python)
complexity.why: The main loop is O(n), but the upfront allocation and implicit initialization of var_4 of size 10**7 dominates both time and especially memory usage. The array size is independent of n and chosen as a large constant upper bound.

bottlenecks.detail: var_4 = [0] * 10**7 allocates a huge dense array, even if only O(n) positions are actually touched. This can cause high memory usage and cache inefficiency.
Initializing 10**7 zeros requires touching all 10**7 entries, which is expensive compared to the linear work in n (where n is likely much smaller).
Using a hardcoded bound 10**7 instead of an n-based structure can be fragile if problem constraints change, and hides the true problem scale.
Use of eval(input()) is unnecessary, slower, and unsafe compared to int(input()). Not a big performance issue, but a code-smell and slight overhead.
Using input() repeatedly is slower than buffered sys.stdin.readline for large inputs, though this is minor compared to the 10**7-allocated array.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace the large fixed-size counting array with a frequency map over only the actually used keys. Compute arrays L[i] = i - a[i] and R[i] = i + a[i], count frequencies of R[i] in a defaultdict, then for each L[i] add the count of matching R values. This avoids the 10**7-sized dense array and keeps both time and memory proportional to n.

complexity.why: Building L and R is O(n). Populating var_11 (a defaultdict frequency map) iterates over R once, O(n). Summing var_11[v] for v in L is another O(n) pass. All operations are O(1) average for hash map access, so overall O(n) time. Space is O(n) for L, R, and the frequency map, which only stores keys that actually occur.

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both are linear in n plus a constant, but the original has a large fixed factor 10**7 which dominates for realistic n. The new version removes this hard bound, making both time and memory scale with actual input size.

transformation_steps: Eliminate the global dense counting array var_4 of fixed size 10**7.

Reformulate index expressions: original code uses positions (i+1 - a[i]) and (i+1 + a[i]); new code captures equivalent values as L[i] = i - a[i] and R[i] = i + a[i], which are consistent up to a constant offset and thus preserve matching relationships.
Build a frequency map (defaultdict(int)) over R[i] values instead of incrementing counts in a huge preallocated array.
Compute the result by summing frequencies for each L[i]: result = sum(var_11[x] for x in L), which conceptually mirrors the original accumulation var_3 += var_4[index].
Switch to faster, buffered input via sys.stdin.readline and remove eval usage for parsing integers.
Structure the code into small functions for input (func_1) and computation (func_2), improving clarity and testability (neutral to performance).
trigger_signals: Presence of a very large fixed-size list ([0] * 10**7) unrelated to exact n.
Memory usage dominated by a sparse counting structure where only O(n) indices are touched.
Hard-coded bounds (10**7) suggesting over-approximation rather than tight constraints.
Use of eval(input()) for reading an integer.
Performance issues (or risk thereof) on platforms with tight memory limits where 10**7 integers is excessive.
pitfalls: {'issue': 'Changing index formulas incorrectly', 'detail': 'The original code uses i+1±a[i] while the new code uses i±a[i]. Off-by-one mistakes can silently change which pairs are counted. The shift must be consistent so equivalence classes (i+1 - a[i] == j+1 + a[j]) map correctly to (i - a[i] == j + a[j]) or similar; here, both sides were shifted by 1 so equality is preserved.'}

{'issue': 'Hash map vs dense array performance tradeoff', 'detail': 'For extremely tight ranges and very large n, a dense list can be faster than a dict due to lower constant factors and better cache locality. The dict-based solution trades dense-array speed for much lower memory when the used index range is sparse or not well-bounded.'}

{'issue': 'Unnecessary list materialization in sum', 'detail': 'sum([var_11[var_9] for var_9 in var_3]) creates an intermediate list. Using a generator expression sum(var_11[x] for x in var_3) avoids this extra allocation and is slightly more memory-efficient.'}

{'issue': 'Unused imports and settings', 'detail': 'Imports of product, math, bisect and setting sys.setrecursionlimit are unused; they do not hurt performance significantly but add clutter and may confuse readers about recursion or algorithmic needs.'}

constraints_guess.notes: Single test case. Three integers (N, M, K) read once. Modulus is 998244353 (NTT-friendly prime). Typical AtCoder-style constraints where N,K are up to about 2e5–2e6 and an O(N log MOD) or O(N) solution is intended.

dominant_ops: Precomputing factorials and factorial-inverses up to N via a Class_1 helper: O(N) modular multiplications and one modular exponentiation.
In the main loop over k in [0..K]: per-iteration modular exponentiation pow(M-1, N-1-k, MOD): O(log MOD) multiplications.
Per-iteration combination lookup via nCr(n, k) using precomputed factorials: O(1) but with Python attribute and list index overhead.
General Python loop and function/class call overhead (func_* wrappers, method calls).

complexity.why: Class_1.__init__ builds factorial and inverse tables up to N => O(N) time and memory. The summation loop runs K+1 iterations, each with at least one modular exponentiation pow(M-1, N-1-k, MOD) => O(log MOD) time per iteration. nCr itself is O(1) thanks to precomputation. Overall time is O(N + K log MOD), space is O(N) for the factorial/inverse arrays.

bottlenecks.detail: Class_1 precomputes factorials and inverse factorials up to N even though only binomial coefficients C(N-1, k) for k in [0..K] are required. For large N this O(N) setup can dominate both runtime and memory, especially when K << N.

Inside the main loop, pow(M-1, N-1-k, MOD) is recomputed from scratch for every k. Each call is O(log MOD), so the loop is O(K log MOD). If K is large, this becomes a significant cost; it’s not amortized across iterations.

Using a Class_1 instance and calling var_11.nCr(...) introduces Python method lookup, attribute access, and list indexing inside the tight loop. This doesn’t change asymptotic complexity but adds constant-factor overhead compared with an in-place recurrence on a scalar variable.

Numerous unused imports and tiny wrapper functions (func_3/func_4/func_5) slightly increase startup and call overhead and obscure the core numerical loop, making it harder to optimize or reason about performance.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial precomputation and class/method overhead by maintaining the needed binomial coefficient C(N-1, k) incrementally in O(1) per step using the multiplicative recurrence C(n, k+1) = C(n, k) * (n-k)/(k+1) (implemented with a modular inverse), while directly accumulating the sum in a flat loop.

complexity.why: The loop runs for k in [0..K]. Each iteration performs: (1) one modular exponentiation pow(M-1, N-1-k, MOD) with O(log MOD) cost; (2) O(1) modular multiplications/additions; and (3) one modular inverse via pow(k+1, -1, MOD), which is also O(log MOD). Constants are low and there is no O(N) preprocessing. Memory usage is O(1) aside from a few scalar variables and the input.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(N + K log MOD), Space: O(N) due to factorial/inverse tables.
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(K log MOD), Space: O(1) using only scalar state for the current binomial coefficient.
complexity_delta.note: When K is on the order of N, both are effectively O(N log MOD) time, but the fast version removes the O(N) factorial precomputation and heavy memory footprint, and reduces constant factors. When K << N, the savings can be very large. Space usage improves from linear in N to constant.

transformation_steps: Eliminate the Class_1 combinatorics helper and its factorial/inverse table construction, thereby removing O(N) preprocessing time and O(N) memory.

Replace the generic nCr(N-1, k) calls with an in-loop recurrence for the binomial coefficient: maintain a running coefficient var_3 initialized to 1, and update via var_3 = var_3 * (N-1-k) * inv(k+1) mod MOD each iteration.
Use Python’s built-in pow(x, -1, MOD) to compute modular inverses on the fly, which leverages Fermat’s little theorem for prime MOD and avoids storing per-index inverses.
Flatten the logic into a single tight loop with only scalar variables (var_2 accumulator, var_3 current C(N-1, k)), reducing Python-level overhead from object/method dispatch and attribute lookups.
Keep the core summation structure identical mathematically: accumulate var_2 += C(N-1, k) * M * (M-1)^(N-1-k) over k in [0..K], ensuring correctness while simplifying implementation.
trigger_signals: Profiler or timing shows a large fraction of runtime in combinatorics precomputation (factorial/inverse table construction) even though only a small subset of binomial coefficients is used.
Memory usage scales linearly with the maximum N due to large factorial and inverse arrays, risking MLE or cache inefficiency.
The hot path includes frequent Python method calls for nCr and repeated attribute accesses inside tight loops, visible in profiling stacks.
Problem constraints indicate that a single-pass O(K) or O(K log MOD) solution should suffice, making an O(N) preprocessing step suspicious or unnecessarily heavy.
pitfalls: Using pow(x, -1, MOD) for modular inverses assumes MOD is prime and x is not divisible by MOD. In this problem (MOD=998244353, x in [1..K+1] with K << MOD), that is safe, but the pattern should not be blindly generalized to non-prime moduli or x multiples of MOD.
The recurrence var_3 = var_3 * (N-1-k) * inv(k+1) must apply the modulus at each step to avoid integer blow-up; omitting '% MOD' can quickly lead to large Python integers and severe slowdown.

The expression N + ~k in the fast code is a compact way to express N-1-k (since ~k == -k-1). This bitwise-not trick is concise but can be confusing and error-prone; incorrect manipulation or reuse elsewhere may introduce off-by-one or sign errors.

Although factorial precomputation is removed, the algorithm still performs O(K log MOD) modular exponentiations. For extremely large K, a further optimization (e.g., maintaining (M-1)^(N-1-k) incrementally) might be required; otherwise pow in the loop can remain a bottleneck.

constraints_guess.notes: Single array, choose integer x minimizing sum (a_i - x)^2. Original brute-force over 0..max(a_i) suggests intended constraints small (e.g., n <= 100, a_i <= 100), but scalable solution must handle much larger n and value range.

dominant_ops: Nested loops: for each candidate center x in [0..max(a_i)] recompute sum of squared distances over all elements.

complexity.why: Outer loop over V = max(a_i)+1 candidate values (range(var_5+1)), inner loop scans all n elements to accumulate (a_i - x)^2. Only a few scalars are stored, so extra space is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: Searches all possible centers from 0 to max(a_i)+1 regardless of n, even though the objective is a convex quadratic with a known closed-form minimizer.
For each candidate x, recomputes sum (a_i - x)^2 from scratch instead of reusing aggregated information (sum(a_i), sum(a_i^2)).
If max(a_i) is large (e.g., 1e5 or 1e9), the outer loop makes the algorithm infeasible despite linear dependence on n.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the fact that f(x) = sum(a_i - x)^2 is a convex quadratic in x with its minimum at the mean of a_i. For integer x, the optimum lies at floor(mean) or ceil(mean); evaluate the cost at these at most two candidates only.

complexity.why: Compute sum(a_i) in O(n) to get the mean candidate(s), then evaluate sum(a_i - x)^2 for up to two x values in another O(n). No extra data structures beyond a few scalars.

complexity_delta.from: O(n * V) where V = max(a_i)
complexity_delta.to: O(n)
complexity_delta.note: Replaced exhaustive search over all integer centers in the value range with a constant-number candidate check derived from quadratic minimization properties.

transformation_steps: Recognize the cost function f(x) = sum(a_i - x)^2 as a convex quadratic in x.
Express f(x) as n*x^2 - 2*x*sum(a_i) + sum(a_i^2), whose continuous minimizer is x = mean(a_i).
Note that with integer x, the optimal solution must be among floor(mean) and ceil(mean).
Compute sum(a_i) once to derive these two candidates instead of scanning all x in [0..max(a_i)].
For each candidate x, compute the total squared error in a single pass over the array and take the minimum.
trigger_signals: Nested loops where the outer loop iterates over a value range [0..max(a_i)] rather than indices or input size.
Objective function is a sum of squared differences (typical least-squares structure) which is known to have a closed-form minimizer.
Recalculation of a global cost from scratch for each candidate value.
Dependence on the magnitude of array values instead of the number of elements suggests poor scalability.
pitfalls: When using the mean-based optimization, x may not be an integer; must check both floor and ceil of the mean to guarantee correctness for integer x.
Care must be taken with integer division semantics; using // and (sum + n - 1) // n correctly obtains floor and ceil for non-negative sums.
In other languages (unlike Python), sum(a_i^2) or intermediate quadratic terms may overflow; using 64-bit integers or wider types is necessary.
The original fast code still uses eval(input()) to read n, which is unsafe in general; prefer int(input()) although it does not affect asymptotic performance.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: given N (<=100) and N integers in [1,100], choose integer P in [1,100] minimizing sum_i (a_i - P)^2.

dominant_ops: Double loop over candidate centers P (1..100) and all elements to compute squared deviations
Integer arithmetic for (var_7 - var_1) ** 2 and accumulation

complexity.why: Input is read into a list of length N (var_6). For each candidate P in the fixed range 1..100, the code performs a full pass over that list, leading to 100 * N iterations of the inner body. The 100 factor is constant, so asymptotically O(N), but with a relatively high constant factor. Memory is dominated by storing the N integers.

bottlenecks.detail: The sum of squared deviations is recomputed from scratch for each P in 1..100, causing 100 passes over the same array.
Although 100 is constant, the double loop multiplies runtime by ~100 compared to a single-pass or two-pass O(N) method based on the mean.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical fact that the sum of squared deviations sum_i (a_i - P)^2 is minimized when P is the (nearest integer to the) mean of the values, so we only need to compute that single P instead of scanning all candidates.

complexity.why: The code computes the sum of all elements once to obtain the mean (O(N)), then makes a single pass to accumulate squared deviations from that mean (another O(N)). No outer loop over candidate P is needed, so the 100x factor is removed, while still storing all N elements.

complexity_delta.from: O(100 * N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically both are O(N) since 100 is constant, but the optimized version removes the 100x constant factor by avoiding repeated full scans for each candidate P.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the objective function is sum_i (a_i - P)^2, a convex quadratic in P whose minimizer over reals is the mean of the a_i.
Replace the brute-force enumeration over P in [1,100] with a direct computation of P as the rounded average of the input values.
Compute sum(var_2) and len(var_2) to get the mean, then compute a single sum of squared deviations from this chosen P, eliminating the outer loop over candidate P.
Keep the data structure as a simple list of integers; only the algorithm for choosing P changes.
trigger_signals: Presence of a fixed-range outer loop (for var_1 in range(1, 101)) wrapping a full pass over the array, indicating repeated recomputation.
Objective has a simple analytical form sum (x_i - P)^2, which is a standard pattern where the minimizer is related to the mean.
Number of candidate P values is small but still large enough to introduce noticeable constant-factor slowdown compared to a single-pass formula.
pitfalls: Mathematical correctness: The exact integer P minimizing sum (a_i - P)^2 is the integer closest to the mean; for ties, either neighboring integer yields the same cost. Using round() is usually fine but can be affected by language-specific rounding rules (banker’s rounding in some environments).
Domain constraints: If the original problem restricts P to [1,100], the mean-based P may need clamping into this range; failing to do so might violate problem constraints in edge cases.

Floating-point precision: Computing the mean as sum / len uses floating-point and round(); for large sums or different constraints, integer-based reasoning (e.g., trying floor(mean) and ceil(mean)) would avoid precision issues.
Security / style: The fast_code uses eval(input()) to read an integer, which is unnecessary and unsafe in general, although not a performance issue.

constraints_guess.notes: Input size suggests up to about 3e5 values; coordinates are clamped to [0, 300005]. Time limit typical of contest problems (~1-2 seconds) requires around O(n log n) or better in Python.

dominant_ops: A backward loop over var_5; for each i it computes max(...) over a generator that scans up to 99 indices, performing abs and conditional checks in Python and feeding them into max(). Also allocates and copies large arrays of size 6**8.

complexity.time: O(n * W) where W = 99 (effectively O(n) but with a large constant; about 100 scalar operations plus generator overhead per element, totaling ~3e7 iterations for n≈3e5).
complexity.space: O(M + n) where M = 6**8 ≈ 1.68e6 (two big lists var_2 and var_1, each on the order of millions of integers).
complexity.why: For each position var_5 it iterates var_3 from var_5 to var_5 + 98 (99 elements) inside a generator used by max(). This is done for every var_5 down to 1, giving ~99 * n iterations. Python-level generator, abs, and max calls dominate runtime. Additionally, var_2 = [0] * 6**8 and var_1 = var_2 + var_1 both allocate and copy large arrays, which adds significant overhead at startup.

bottlenecks.detail: For each index i, the code rescans a fixed-size window [i, i+99) with a Python max over a generator instead of using a data structure to maintain range maxima. This makes the constant factor per step large.

Use of max(...) over a generator comprehension combined with abs and conditional logic per candidate incurs heavy interpreter overhead (function calls, iterator protocol, Python conditionals) for every of the ~100 * n inner iterations.

var_2 = [0] * 6**8 creates a list of about 1.68 million integers; then var_1 = var_2 + var_1 copies that entire list again. This large preallocation and copy costs time and memory, and is unrelated to actual n (wasted space).

Accesses like var_2[var_3] and var_1[-var_3] bounce around a large array that includes a huge zero-padding prefix, which is not cache-friendly and adds more overhead versus a compact structure sized to the problem.

The window size is hard-coded to 99 instead of being derived from the value-radius constraint; while this is more of a correctness issue, it also prevents leveraging problem structure to choose an optimal complexity bound like O(log N) via a segment tree.

FastAudit.core_idea: Model the recurrence as a DP over value coordinates and implement range-maximum queries with a segment tree. For each value x, query the maximum DP value over [x - d, x + d] and then update the segment tree at position x with that maximum + 1. Track the global maximum as the answer.

complexity.time: O(n log M) where M is the coordinate range (≈300005). Each of the n values performs one segment-tree range-maximum query and one point update, both O(log M).
complexity.space: O(M) for the segment tree array, plus O(n) for storing the input values.
complexity.why: The tree is sized as power-of-two >= 300005 and stored in a flat array var_11 of size 2 * var_4. func_1 performs an iterative segment-tree range maximum over [L, R) in O(log M) by climbing from the leaves, and func_3 does a point update with upward recomputation also in O(log M). No per-step rescanning of windows is needed; all historical data is summarized in the segment tree.

complexity_delta.from: O(n * W) with W = 99 using heavy Python generator and max overhead; effectively linear but with large constant factors and large extra memory allocations (6**8).
complexity_delta.to: O(n log M) with small constant factors (tight iterative segment-tree loops) and memory scaled to the coordinate domain M ≈ 3e5 instead of a fixed 6**8.
complexity_delta.note: Although both are theoretically near-linear for the intended constraints, the segment-tree solution concentrates work into low-level integer operations (≈log M ≈ 19 per query/update) and avoids large fixed-size preallocations and Python generator overhead, yielding a substantial constant-factor speedup and more predictable memory usage.

transformation_steps: Identify the DP structure: for each value x, the best DP state depends on the maximum DP value among prior states whose values lie within [x - d, x + d]. This is a range-maximum query over a coordinate axis, plus a point update at x.
Replace the explicit per-step window scan (range over var_3 and max over a generator) with an abstract range-maximum data structure. Choose a segment tree for O(log M) queries and updates.

Fix the state space explicitly over the value domain rather than over index windows: clamp coordinates to [0, 300005], choose var_4 as the smallest power of two ≥ 300005, and allocate a segment tree array var_11 of size 2 * var_4.

Implement an iterative segment tree point-update function (func_3) that sets the leaf corresponding to a coordinate and recomputes parent nodes on the path to the root using max. This avoids recursion and keeps operations simple and fast.

Implement an iterative segment tree range-maximum function (func_1) with the classic [L, R) traversal pattern: convert to leaf indices, then while L < R, consider contributions when endpoints are odd, move inward, and shift both endpoints upwards. This provides O(log M) query time.

Eliminate the oversized fixed arrays (like [0] * 6**8 and concatenation var_1 = var_2 + var_1). Instead, allocate only what is needed: an array for the segment tree and an array var_7 for the input values.
Maintain the global answer incrementally by tracking the maximum DP value over all updates (var_8), instead of recomputing max(var_2) over a large array at the end.
Use direct integer indexing and simple loops in place of high-level constructs (generator expressions, repeated abs and max inside comprehensions), reducing interpreter overhead per DP step.
trigger_signals: Presence of a while var_5 loop combined with an inner max(...) over a comprehension that itself iterates over a range per element, indicating a per-element scan rather than a data-structure-based query.
Hard-coded constant window size (range(var_5, var_5 + 99)) that scales the runtime by a large constant and suggests a naive sliding-window approach.
Very large, fixed-size arrays (var_2 = [0] * 6**8 and var_1 = var_2 + var_1) that are unrelated to the actual input size, signaling wasteful memory use and extra copying.
Use of Python generator expressions and function calls (abs, max) in tight nested loops, typically much slower than flat loops or iterative segment-tree operations in performance-critical code.
End-of-program global max(var_2) across a huge array, which is another linear pass over an oversized data structure and unnecessary if the maximum is maintained incrementally.
Lack of any logarithmic-time data structure (segment tree, Fenwick tree, etc.) despite a pattern that clearly requires repeated range-maximum queries and point updates.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors in segment-tree range queries: func_1 uses a half-open [L, R) convention, clamping and shifting indices carefully. Incorrect bounds (e.g., including R as inclusive) would change the set of elements considered.

Incorrect tree sizing: the code uses var_4 = 2 ** (300005).bit_length() to ensure the base size is a power of two ≥ 300005. Using a smaller base or forgetting to use a power-of-two size would break the traversal logic or waste more space.

Misalignment between value coordinates and tree indices: updates use var_9 as the position in the tree; queries use transformed ranges based on var_9 - var_2 and var_9 + var_2. Any mismatch in how coordinates are mapped to indices will yield wrong results.

Inefficient or recursive segment-tree implementations: using recursion or object-heavy node structures in Python would reintroduce heavy overhead; an iterative, array-based implementation is critical for speed.

Unsafe or slow input parsing patterns: in the fast_code, eval(input()) is used to read integers; this is unnecessary and potentially dangerous. It should be replaced by int(input()) to avoid overhead and security issues.

Maintaining large global arrays unnecessarily: copying or concatenating big arrays (as in the slow_code var_1 = var_2 + var_1) is a major performance trap. The optimized solution avoids such copies and only stores strictly needed structures.

Assuming that a small constant window (99) is always safe: while O(n * 99) is asymptotically linear, in Python an extra factor of 100 with heavy high-level operations can be enough to TLE under tight contest limits when n is large (around 3e5).

constraints_guess.notes: Task is to compute the number of divisors of n! modulo 1e9+7. Typical contest constraints for this pattern are n <= 100 (or a few thousand), small enough that O(n^2) is acceptable but anything like O(n^{2.5}+ ) in Python becomes slow.

dominant_ops: Repeated primality testing in func_2 using nested trial division for every k <= n
Rebuilding prime table func_2(var_5) for each call to func_1
O(n) scans and list updates of length n inside the outer loop when aggregating exponents into var_9

complexity.time: Theta(n^{5/2}) for repeated naive primality checks + Theta(n^2) for repeated length-n list additions
complexity.why: For each k from 1..n, func_1(k, n) calls func_2(k). func_2 runs a naive primality test for each i in [2..k] by trial dividing up to sqrt(i), costing sum_{k=1..n} sum_{i=2..k} O(sqrt(i)) = O(n^{5/2}). Additionally, the aggregation step var_9 = [var_9[j] + var_3[j] for j in range(n)] is O(n) and executed n times, adding an O(n^2) term.

bottlenecks.detail: func_2 recomputes a primality table up to var_5 for every call to func_1, even though primality of numbers <= n does not change. This leads to an extra nested loop structure inside another loop over 1..n.

In func_2, for each candidate var_2 up to var_5, the code trial divides by all var_4 from 2 up to sqrt(var_2). This naive primality test is O(sqrt(var_2)) and is repeated for all k and all i <= k, producing O(n^{5/2}) behavior.

The aggregation step var_9 = [var_9[j] + var_3[j] for j in range(0, var_1)] rebuilds the entire length-n list on every iteration of the outer loop (n times), resulting in O(n^2) Python-level list work.

func_1 uses var_5 = var_5 / (var_2 + 1) instead of integer division. This creates floats, adds conversion overhead, and is slower and risky for correctness, although its asymptotic impact is still dominated by the algorithmic redundancy.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid factoring every integer 1..n separately. Instead, treat n! as a single number, build a list of primes up to n on the fly, and for each discovered prime p, count its exponent in n! by repeatedly dividing a copy of n! by p. This collapses many redundant primality computations and per-number factorizations into a single pass up to n.

complexity.time: Roughly Theta(n^2 / log n) candidate checks plus O(total_prime_exponent) big-integer divisions; for small contest n this behaves close to Theta(n^2) at the Python operation level.
complexity.why: The outer loop considers all integers 2..n. Primality is decided by trial division with already-found primes, costing O(pi(i)) per i, which sums to ~O(n^2 / log n). For each actual prime p, the code repeatedly divides n! by p, performing as many divisions as the exponent of p in n!; the total exponent sum over all primes is O(n log log n), so the loop count for divisions is modest compared to the outer n^2 / log n candidate checks. The primes and exponents lists grow only to size pi(n).

complexity_delta.from: Theta(n^{5/2}) + Theta(n^2) Python list ops in the slow version
complexity_delta.to: Approximately Theta(n^2 / log n) candidate checks + O(n log log n) big-int divisions in the fast version
complexity_delta.note: The optimized code removes the repeated O(k^{3/2}) primality table recomputation for each k and avoids refactoring each 1..k separately, trading it for a single pass over 2..n with incremental primality checks and exponent counting for n!.

transformation_steps: Replace per-k primality table recomputation (func_2 called inside func_1 for every k) with a single incremental prime list built as we scan 2..n.
Stop factoring each integer i in 1..n individually; instead treat n! as a whole and compute exponents of each prime p in n! directly by repeated division.
Eliminate the repeated length-n vector aggregation var_9 = [var_9[j] + var_3[j] for j in range(n)]; instead, maintain a compact list of primes and their exponents.
Use a more direct mathematical structure (prime factors of n!) instead of an implicit frequency vector over all 1..n.
trigger_signals: func_2 (primality computation) being invoked inside func_1, which itself is called in a loop over all k from 1..n (clear sign of duplicated heavy work).
Nested loops: an outer loop over k, an inner loop in func_2 over all i <= k, and a trial-division loop up to sqrt(i), indicating roughly cubic-like behavior in practice for moderate n.
Rebuilding entire lists (var_9) of size n in each iteration, suggesting O(n^2) Python-level overhead.
Use of naive trial division for primality instead of reusing results or using a sieve, indicating that the prime computation cost may dominate.
pitfalls: The fast version recomputes math.factorial(n) inside the loop for every candidate var_3, which is unnecessary and expensive for larger n; computing n! once and using integer arithmetic (e.g., Legendre’s formula) would be asymptotically better.
Big-integer arithmetic on n! (mod, division) becomes expensive as n grows; if constraints were larger than the typical contest setting, even the fast version would likely time out.
Both versions rely on eval(input()), which is slow and unsafe; while not the main complexity issue, this is a potential security and performance pitfall in real environments.

The slow version’s use of floating-point division (`/`) when factoring numbers can lead to precision and performance issues; any refactoring should replace it with integer division (`//`) to avoid subtle bugs and overhead.

constraints_guess.notes: Inputs are two integers (x,y). Effective combinatorial parameter is n = (x+y)/3. Typical AtCoder-style constraints suggest x,y up to ~1e6, so n up to ~2e6. Single query.

dominant_ops: Linear scan over all possible counts to solve a small system of equations
Per-iteration modular exponentiation inside a loop to build nCr multiplicatively

complexity.time: O(X + K log MOD) where X is first input (var_6) and K is the chosen step count (var_2); asymptotically O(n log MOD) with n ~ (x+y)/3
complexity.why: The code linearly searches var_4 from 0 to var_6 to find (var_2,var_3), which is O(X). After that, it computes a binomial coefficient via a loop from 1 to var_2, and in each iteration calls pow(var_4, MOD-2, MOD), which is O(log MOD). This yields O(var_2 log MOD) additional time. Only a few scalar variables are used, so space is constant.

bottlenecks.detail: The loop `for var_4 in range(var_6 + 1)` linearly searches for a solution to a simple linear system; the solution can be obtained in O(1) with algebra.

The binomial coefficient computation runs a Python loop up to var_2 iterations, calling `pow(var_4, var_5 - 2, var_5)` each time. Repeated modular exponentiation (O(log MOD) per iteration) dominates runtime for large inputs.
All arithmetic is done in Python-space loops (both the search loop and the nCr loop), which adds overhead when var_6 and var_2 are large (up to ~1e6).

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical characterization of the steps so that the number of moves of each type is derived in O(1) from (x,y), then compute the result as a binomial coefficient C(n,k) with precomputed factorials and inverse factorials using a linear-time modular inverse sieve. This replaces per-iteration modular exponentiation with a single O(n) precomputation and an O(1) query.

complexity.time: O(n) where n = (x+y)/3 (for factorial and inverse factorial precomputation), plus O(1) for the final nCr evaluation
complexity.why: Arrays var_4 (fact), var_5 (inv_fact), and var_7 (inv) of size about n = (x+y)/3 are filled in one linear pass. Computing C(n,k) from these precomputed tables is a constant-time product of three table lookups modulo MOD. Memory is linear in n due to the arrays.

complexity_delta.from: O(X + K log MOD) time, O(1) space (effectively O(n log MOD) with linear search and per-iteration pow in the nCr loop)
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space (linear precomputation of factorials/inverses and O(1) nCr)
complexity_delta.note: Replaces linear search and repeated modular exponentiation with direct algebra for parameters and a single linear precomputation for factorial-based combinatorics.

transformation_steps: Eliminate the linear search over var_4 by solving the underlying linear equations for the move counts directly, leading to n = (x+y)/3 and k = x - n.
Introduce an early feasibility check: if (x + y) % 3 != 0, immediately return 0, since the state is unreachable.
Precompute factorials modulo MOD up to n_max = (x+y)//3 + small_margin using a single forward loop.
Precompute modular inverses 1..n_max using the linear-time recurrence inv[i] = MOD - inv[MOD % i] * (MOD // i) % MOD and build inverse factorials from them.
Replace the iterative multiplicative nCr computation (loop with repeated pow) by a single table-based formula C(n,k) = fact[n] * inv_fact[k] % MOD * inv_fact[n-k] % MOD.
Guard the combination function to return 0 when k or n-k is negative or larger than n, to avoid invalid indexing and to cover unreachable states cleanly.
trigger_signals: Constraints or observed inputs where x,y are as large as 10^6 or more, making O(n log MOD) loops with modular exponentiation borderline for time limits.
Presence of `pow(..., MOD-2, MOD)` inside a loop that iterates up to n ~ 10^6, indicating repeated modular inverses being computed instead of reused.
A linear search loop that solves for variables which appear only linearly and can be obtained by simple algebra.
Need to compute combinatorial values exactly once but at near upper-bound sizes, where precomputing factorials is standard and significantly faster.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when sizing the factorial and inverse arrays; arrays must be at least length n+1 to index up to fact[n]. The fast code uses `var_9 = (var_2 + var_3) // 3 + 3` to be safely above the required maximum.
Incorrect handling of impossible cases (e.g., negative k or (x+y) not divisible by 3); failing to early-return 0 can lead to wrong combinatorial parameters or index errors.
Miscomputing modular inverses: the recurrence for inv[i] relies on inv[1] being initialized correctly and the modulus being prime.
Higher memory usage: O(n) arrays can be large; if constraints were much bigger, this would require reconsideration or more memory-efficient techniques.
Integer division subtleties: using `//` is required; using `/` (float division) would break the computation for large inputs and lead to precision issues.

constraints_guess.notes: Input is the index N of a specially constrained integer sequence (digits differ by at most 1). Typical tasks of this form (e.g., 'Lunlun numbers') use N up to about 1e5 and the answer has at most ~10 digits.

dominant_ops: Recursive DFS over all valid numbers up to fixed depth (10 digits)
Appending every intermediate number to a Python list
Sorting the entire list of generated numbers
Indexing into sorted list to get the N-th element

complexity.why: Let K be the total count of numbers generated up to the maximum depth (here depth 10). The DFS systematically explores all valid digit extensions from starting digits 1..9, appending every prefix to var_1. This visits every such number once, taking O(K) to generate. After generation, it sorts the full array var_1, which costs O(K log K). Space is dominated by storing all K numbers in the list simultaneously.

bottlenecks.detail: The algorithm generates *all* valid numbers up to 10 digits and sorts them even if the input N is small and only the first N numbers are needed.
Sorting the entire list var_1 of size K to then take a single element (K-th) adds an O(K log K) factor that is not needed if numbers were produced directly in the desired order.
All generated numbers are kept in memory in var_1, which can be relatively large (all valid numbers up to depth 10) instead of only maintaining a frontier or prefix of size O(N).
Deep recursion (depth up to 10) with Python function calls in tight loops adds overhead compared to iterative traversal; while depth is bounded, the number of calls is proportional to K.
Using eval(input()) is slower and potentially unsafe compared to int(input()). This is minor for performance but a clear code smell.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use BFS (queue) from initial digits 1..9 to generate numbers in lexicographic / sequence order, popping the smallest-indexed current number and pushing its valid digit-extensions. Stop as soon as the N-th number has been popped instead of generating and sorting the entire set.

complexity.why: Each iteration of the while loop processes exactly one sequence element (the current N-th candidate) and enqueues at most three successors (last_digit-1, last_digit, last_digit+1). To obtain the N-th number, the loop runs N-1 iterations, giving O(N) operations overall. The deque may hold up to O(N) elements in the worst case (when many successors are added before being popped), leading to O(N) space.

complexity_delta.from: O(K log K) time, O(K) space (full enumeration + sort, independent of N beyond being bounded by fixed depth)
complexity_delta.to: O(N) time, O(N) space (BFS generating only the first N sequence elements)
complexity_delta.note: K is the total number of valid numbers up to the maximum digit length; N is the requested index. Since K is fixed by depth but potentially larger than typical N, avoiding full enumeration and sorting gives clear speedups and scales better if depth grows.

transformation_steps: Replace recursive DFS with an iterative BFS using collections.deque to avoid deep recursion and to control generation order explicitly.
Initialize the queue with the base digits '1' through '9', mirroring the original starting points but in a structure that naturally supports FIFO processing.
Change representation of numbers from integers to strings so that the last digit can be accessed as var_3[-1] without repeated modulo/division operations.

In each BFS step, pop the front element (current smallest-indexed sequence element), decrement remaining N, and when N reaches 1, output this element directly instead of building all numbers ahead of time.
Generate successors by inspecting the last digit and appending valid neighbors (d-1, d, d+1) as new strings to the queue, preserving the sequence generation rule.
Remove the global list var_1 and the final sort; the BFS generation order already matches the desired sequence order, eliminating the O(K log K) sorting cost.

Replace eval(input()) with int(eval(input())) in spirit with int(input()) for safer and slightly faster parsing (though in the provided fast_code eval is still used, the intended optimization would be to drop eval).
trigger_signals: Code generates all combinatorial candidates (via DFS) into a large list and then sorts before taking only one element.
Result requires the k-th element of a breadth-like, adjacency-based sequence, suggesting natural BFS ordering rather than full enumeration and sorting.
Use of recursion with many calls and a fixed depth where an iterative queue-based approach would yield natural incremental results.
Presence of a clear local transition rule (extend number by appending digits differing by at most 1 from last digit), which is ideal for graph-like BFS traversal.
Memory footprint dominated by storing all generated states when the task only needs the first N in a specific order.
pitfalls: BFS must ensure that generation order exactly matches the intended sorted/sequence order; mismanaging the queue or extension order can produce incorrect k-th results.
Using strings instead of integers simplifies last-digit access but may introduce overhead for very large N; care is needed if constraints grow much larger.
For extremely large N, the queue size can grow linearly and exhaust memory; additional pruning or streaming techniques might then be required.
Off-by-one errors when counting down N in the BFS loop are common; the current pattern (loop while N>1, then output front element) should be carefully preserved.
Continuing to use eval(input()) in the fast version retains a security and minor performance issue; this should ideally be replaced with int(input()).

constraints_guess.notes: Bitmask DP over 2^n states; n (var_5/var_7) must be small (≈10–12, at most ~20) for Python to handle full 2^n scans per item. Number of items var_4/var_6 likely up to O(10^2).

dominant_ops: For each item (var_4), scanning all 2^var_5 bitmasks and doing two DP updates per mask: skip and take transitions via min.
Building bitmasks var_3[var_9] via per-token loop and bit shifting.

complexity.why: DP table var_8 has 2 * 2^var_5 entries (two layers). Outer loop over items (size var_4), inner loop over all bitmasks (2^var_5). Each inner step performs constant-time list indexing and min comparisons. Bitmask construction per item is linear in the number of bits listed.

bottlenecks.detail: Full DP transition over all 2^var_5 states for every item (var_4). This O(var_4 * 2^var_5) pattern dominates runtime for larger var_5.
Using a 2×2^var_5 table and writing both layers every iteration causes extra memory traffic: var_8[1][var_6] is always written for the 'skip' case even when unchanged.
Computes 2**var_5 inside the outer DP loop header (range(2**var_5)) on every item; also performs two min calls per mask even if values cannot improve.
Inner loop does multiple Python-level operations (two list indexings, two min calls) per state transition, which is costly when repeated O(var_4 * 2^var_5) times.
Uses sys.stdin.readline, which is already near-optimal for large input; I/O is not the limiting factor relative to the DP cost.

FastAudit.core_idea: Collapse the 2D DP (previous/current layers) into a 1D DP array over bitmasks, compute the number of masks 2^n once, and perform in-place relaxation with a conditional update instead of always calling min. This reduces memory and some constant factors while keeping the same subset-DP structure.

complexity.why: For each of var_6 items, the code iterates over all var_8 = 2^var_7 masks and performs a constant amount of work per mask (one or two array accesses and one comparison/assignment). The DP table is a single array of size 2^var_7, so memory is linear in the number of bitmasks.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(var_4 * 2^var_5), Space: O(2^var_5) with a 2×2^n table and two transitions per state.
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(var_6 * 2^var_7), Space: O(2^var_7) with a 1D table and one conditional relaxation per state.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity remains O(m * 2^n) time and O(2^n) space. Improvements are mainly lower constants from less memory and fewer unconditional writes. However, the in-place forward DP changes the semantics (can reuse the same item multiple times) and switching from sys.stdin.readline to input() may hurt performance on large inputs.

transformation_steps: Replaced the 2-layer DP table var_8[2][2^n] with a 1D DP array var_4[2^n], eliminating the extra dimension and the need to swap layers each iteration.
Removed the explicit 'skip' transition layer by reusing the same DP array and only relaxing states when a strictly better cost is found (if var_4[var_10] > var_4[var_9] + var_1).
Precomputed the number of bitmasks var_8 = 2**var_7 once before the item loop, avoiding repeated exponentiation inside the DP outer loop.

Changed bitmask construction from an in-loop OR of shifted bits to var_3 = sum([2 ** (int(var_5) - 1) for var_5 in input().split()]), trading a small constant-factor change in bitset building for a more compact expression.
Switched from sys.stdin.readline-based input processing to the higher-level input() function inside func_1(), encapsulating the solution in a function and guarding it with if __name__ == '__main__':.
trigger_signals: Presence of DP over 2**n states (2**var_5, 2**var_7) combined with a loop over items, a classic subset DP/set cover pattern.
Use of a 2D DP array where one dimension is of size 2 (previous/current), indicating potential for 1D DP optimization.
Full scan over all bitmasks for each item, suggesting that any reduction in writes or memory layers can significantly improve constants.
Use of bitmask operations (1 << (k-1), mask | subset) to model covering/combining sets.
pitfalls: The fast_code performs in-place DP updates over masks in increasing order for each item. For a 0/1 choice per item (each item can be taken at most once), this is logically incorrect because it allows the current item to be effectively used multiple times within the same iteration via already-updated states. Correct 1D 0/1 DP would require iterating masks in a direction that avoids reusing updated states (typically descending) or keeping separate prev/next arrays.
Switching from sys.stdin.readline to input() slows down I/O and can become a bottleneck if the number of items or bit entries per line is large.

Building the bitmask via sum of powers (2 ** (int(var_5) - 1)) inside a list comprehension introduces extra exponentiation overhead compared with using bit shifts (1 << (k-1)); for many bits per item this may offset some of the DP-side constant-factor gains.

In-place DP updates without careful ordering are easy to get wrong; subtle bugs may only appear on cases where the optimal solution would require combining multiple items and the erroneous reuse of the same item leads to a smaller (but invalid) cost.

Using float('inf') is convenient but repeated comparisons against floating infinity add slight overhead; this is minor relative to the DP but worth noting if further micro-optimizations are considered.

constraints_guess.notes: Likely AtCoder-style: n up to ~1e5–2e5, values up to around 1e9. Any solution with loops depending on (max(a) - min(a)) is too slow if values are large.

dominant_ops: Outer loop over all candidate target values in [min(a), max(a)]
Inner loop over all array elements for each candidate
Repeated integer exponentiation and additions in the double loop
Initial sort of the array

complexity.time: O(n log n + n * R), where n = number of elements and R = max(a) - min(a)
complexity.why: Sorting the list costs O(n log n). Then for each integer shift var_6 in 0..R, the code scans all n elements and computes (candidate - a[i])**2. This nested loop is O(n * R). The array itself is stored explicitly, giving O(n) space.

bottlenecks.detail: Brute-force enumeration of every integer target between min and max of the array leads to O(n * (max-min)) operations, which is prohibitive when the range of values is large (e.g., up to 1e9).
The inner loop recomputes (var_2 - var_3[var_7]) ** 2 for all elements for every candidate var_2, resulting in a large constant factor and wasted recomputation.
Sorting is only used to obtain min and max; both could be obtained in O(n) using min() and max() without sorting, so the O(n log n) sort is avoidable overhead.
Using Python’s ** for exponentiation with large integers inside tight nested loops further slows down execution.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use the mathematical fact that the sum of squared deviations S(x) = sum_i (a[i] - x)^2 is minimized at the mean of the values. Since the target x must be an integer, it suffices to check the two integers nearest to the mean: floor(mean) and ceil(mean), and pick the one with smaller S(x). This reduces the search to O(n) without dependence on the numeric range.

complexity.why: Compute the sum of all elements in O(n), derive the (possibly non-integer) mean, then evaluate S(x) for at most two candidates (floor and floor+1) with a single O(n) pass. The array storage itself is O(n); no extra structures or nested loops over the value range are used.

complexity_delta.from: O(n log n + n * R) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: Removed dependence on the numeric range R = max(a) - min(a) by replacing brute-force enumeration of candidate centers with a constant-number-of-candidates solution based on the mean.

transformation_steps: Recognize the objective function as S(x) = sum_i (a[i] - x)^2, which is a convex quadratic in x whose minimum over real numbers occurs at the arithmetic mean of the data.
Observe that the required x must be an integer, so the minimizing integer must be one of the integers nearest to the mean, specifically floor(mean) or ceil(mean).
Eliminate the outer loop over all candidates in [min(a), max(a)] and instead compute the mean in O(n) using sum(a) and the count n.
Evaluate the sum of squared deviations S(x) for the two candidates floor(mean) and floor(mean)+1 (which covers ceil(mean)) in a single linear pass over the array, picking the smaller result.
Remove the sort, since min and max are no longer needed for candidate enumeration; this also eliminates the O(n log n) term.
Retain only one main loop over the data for computing S(x), yielding an overall O(n) algorithm.
trigger_signals: Nested loops where the outer loop iterates over every integer in a potentially huge value range (max-min).
Time complexity depends on the magnitude of the numbers, not just on the number of elements n.
The cost per candidate evaluation is O(n), and candidates are simple shifts of a base value (var_3[0] + k), suggesting a closed-form or analytic approach.
The objective function is a sum of squares of linear terms, hinting at well-known results from statistics/optimization (mean minimizes squared error).
Presence of an initial sort that seems unrelated to the core sum-of-squares computation aside from obtaining min/max.
pitfalls: Using floating-point mean: sum(a) / n can be a non-integer float. Relying on rounding rules implicitly can cause off-by-one errors; explicitly checking both floor(mean) and ceil(mean) avoids this.

Precision issues: while Python’s float can exactly represent many integers, very large sums can lose precision. For competitive-programming constraints (e.g., up to ~1e5 * 1e9), double precision is usually safe, but in stricter settings you might want to avoid float altogether and reason directly with integer arithmetic.
Assuming the mean is always an integer and only checking that single value can be wrong; the true minimizing integer may be either floor or ceil of the real-valued mean.

For n = 1, the brute-force code has a special case returning 0. The optimized mean-based code should be verified to also return 0 (it does: the only candidate equals the single element, so the squared deviation is 0).
If porting to a language with fixed-width integer types, computing sum(a[i]^2) or (a[i] - x)^2 can overflow; wide integer types or modular arithmetic care may be required.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style constraints: n up to 2e5, |a[i]| up to about 2e5. Need O(n) or O(n log n) with low constant factors.

dominant_ops: Python for-loops over a fixed large range (0..400004) for array initialization
Random indexed access and updates to a large list (var_4[idx])
Per-element arithmetic for indices (i - a[i], i + a[i])

complexity.why: The first loop initializes var_4 with 400005 zeros: O(M) where M=400005. The second loop processes n elements with O(1) work each: O(n). var_4 has size M, so auxiliary space is O(M).

bottlenecks.detail: The loop `for var_3 in range(400005): var_4.append(0)` performs ~4e5 Python-level append calls regardless of n. When n is much smaller than 4e5, this dominates runtime.
Using a fixed-size array of length 400005 forces work proportional to M even if the effective index range used is much smaller, preventing scaling strictly with n.
Allocating an array of size 400005 costs O(M) memory, whereas the number of distinct i+a[i] indices might be closer to O(n), making this wasteful for smaller n.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid scanning and storing a large fixed index range; instead, use hash maps (defaultdict) to count only actually occurring transformed indices i+a[i] and i-a[i], then sum over matching keys with a frequency product.

complexity.why: Each element contributes O(1) work to update var_1 and var_2: O(n) for building counts. The number of distinct keys k is at most n, so iterating over var_1.items() is O(k) ⊆ O(n). Memory is proportional to the number of distinct transformed indices, O(k).

complexity_delta.from: O(n + M) time, O(M) space (M = 400005 fixed upper bound)
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(k) space (k ≤ n distinct transformed indices)
complexity_delta.note: For large M and moderate n, removing the O(M) initialization yields a noticeable speedup and better memory behavior; asymptotically, the dependence on the artificial constant M is removed.

transformation_steps: Replace the fixed-size list var_4 of length 400005 with two defaultdict(int) maps var_1 and var_2 keyed by the transformed indices i+a[i] and i-a[i].
In the single pass over the array, for each index i and value a[i], increment var_1[i + a[i]] and var_2[i - a[i]] instead of updating a preallocated array.
After building the frequency maps, iterate over the keys in var_1 and, for each key present in both var_1 and var_2, add var_1[key] * var_2[key] to the answer.
Remove the separate O(M) initialization loop; all storage is now allocated lazily as keys are encountered.
Let Python manage the effective key range via hashing rather than enforcing explicit index bounds and sentinel checks like `if idx < 400005`.
trigger_signals: Presence of a large magic constant (400005) used as an upper bound for an index space and for initializing an array.
A for-loop whose runtime depends only on the constant bound (range(400005)) instead of the input size n.
Manual zero-initialization via appends instead of using built-ins (e.g., [0]*M) or sparse structures.
Index range checks (`if var_1[var_3] + var_3 < 400005`) indicating a forced, possibly oversized index domain.
pitfalls: Switching to dict-based counting adds hashing overhead; for very small index ranges and very large n, a tightly bounded list-based solution might be faster, but here M is decoupled from n and dominates.
The array-based approach relies on a correctly chosen bound (400005). If the true range of i+a[i] or i-a[i] exceeds this, it silently drops valid pairs; dict-based counting avoids this class of bugs.

When using dicts, be cautious with iterating and mutating simultaneously; the chosen pattern `for k, v in list(var_1.items())` avoids mutation during iteration, but copying to a list has its own cost if var_1 is large.

Both versions use `eval(input())` for reading n, which is unnecessary and potentially unsafe; replacing with `int(input())` is advisable for robustness even though it does not materially affect performance here.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style problem: first integer N, then N integers. Needs O(N) or O(N log N) solution; O(N^2) will TLE for N≈2e5.

dominant_ops: A for-loop over N elements where each iteration calls sum(var_1), an O(N) operation

complexity.why: The loop runs N times; inside each iteration sum(var_1) scans the entire array (O(N)), yielding O(N) * O(N) = O(N^2). The array itself requires O(N) space.

bottlenecks.detail: sum(var_1) is recomputed in every loop iteration instead of using the already computed total (var_5). This turns a conceptually linear algorithm into quadratic time.
The formula for sum of pairwise products can be computed in one pass using prefix sums or the identity: (total^2 - sum(a_i^2)) / 2. Current code does not exploit this.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a single prefix-sum pass: for each element a[i] (i>=1), multiply it by the sum of all previous elements (prefix[i-1]); summing these products yields the sum over all pairs i>j of a[i]*a[j] in O(N).

complexity.why: Computing the prefix sums via itertools.accumulate is O(N). Zipping var_1[1:] with the prefix sequence and summing the products is another O(N) pass. The input array and the prefix sums each require O(N) space.

complexity_delta.from: O(N^2) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: The key improvement is eliminating the repeated O(N) sum inside the loop by restructuring the computation into a single-pass prefix-sum-based accumulation.

transformation_steps: Recognize the target quantity as the sum over all distinct pairs i<j of a[i]*a[j].
Observe that this can be computed incrementally: when processing a[i], all earlier elements contribute prefix_sum * a[i], where prefix_sum = sum of a[0..i-1].
Replace the loop with an accumulate-based prefix sum to maintain the running total of previous elements.
Compute the final answer as the sum over i>=1 of a[i] * prefix_sum[i-1] in one linear pass, removing the inner O(N) summation.
Optionally, avoid constructing intermediate lists (e.g., do not wrap the generator in list()) to reduce overhead, though this does not change asymptotic complexity.
trigger_signals: Presence of sum(var_1) or any O(N) aggregate function inside a loop that itself runs O(N) times.
Constraints suggesting N up to ~10^5 or 10^6, where O(N^2) is infeasible.
Pattern of computing pairwise interactions (i<j) using a double loop structure or equivalent repeated full-array operations.
Observing that a precomputed global value (like total sum) is recomputed in each iteration.
pitfalls: Recomputing total sums or other reductions inside loops, rather than caching them.
Using sum(var_1) instead of a maintained running total when only incremental updates are needed.
Neglecting mathematical identities such as (sum(a))^2 = sum(a_i^2) + 2*sum_{i<j} a_i*a_j, which can reduce quadratic pairwise computations to linear time.
Minor: constructing unnecessary lists around generators (e.g., list(...) inside sum) adds overhead, though it is not the main performance issue here.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer N, likely up to 1e5–1e6 (typical 'count numbers with odd digit length' problem, matching piecewise thresholds 10, 100, 1000, 10000, 100000, 1000000).

dominant_ops: Iterating over all integers from 1 to N
Converting each integer to string via str()
Computing len(str(x)) for each x
Building a list from a generator solely to take its length
