complexity.time: O(N * log10(N)) (effectively O(N) for these N, but with nontrivial per-element overhead from string conversion and length computation)
complexity.why: The code generates all integers from 1 to N, converts each to a string, checks its length, and then materializes all passing elements into a list just to call len() on it. The loop over N dominates time; list() storing all qualifying numbers dominates space.

bottlenecks.detail: Counting is done by explicit enumeration of all numbers instead of using a direct arithmetic formula for the count of numbers with odd digit length in [1, N].
Each integer in 1..N is converted to string str(var_3), and len() is called; repeated string allocation and length computation are expensive in Python.
len(list(var_1)) materializes all matching numbers into a list, requiring O(N) additional memory instead of counting on the fly.
Pure-Python loop and generator over a large numeric range leads to significant interpreter overhead when N is large (e.g., up to 1e6).

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the structure of digit lengths: all 1-digit numbers (1–9) and 3-digit numbers (100–999) and 5-digit numbers (10000–99999), etc., contribute fixed-size or simple-range blocks. Use piecewise arithmetic based on N’s magnitude to directly compute the count of numbers with odd digit length without iterating through all numbers.

complexity.why: The solution only performs a constant number of comparisons and simple arithmetic operations, with no loops over N and no extra data structures. Each branch handles an entire digit-length block in constant time.

complexity_delta.note: Eliminated per-number iteration, string conversions, and list materialization by replacing them with a closed-form, piecewise arithmetic count based on digit ranges.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the property "number has an odd number of digits" depends only on the digit length, which follows predictable ranges (1–9, 10–99, 100–999, etc.).
Derive formulas for counts of numbers with odd digit lengths up to N: e.g., for N < 10, answer is N; for 10 <= N < 100, answer is 9; for 100 <= N < 1000, answer is 9 + (N - 99), etc.
Replace the generator and list-based counting over range(1, N+1) with a series of if/elif branches that compute the count directly per digit-length segment.
Avoid building any intermediate collections; compute the result in local scalar variables and print it directly.
(Optional refinement, not shown in code): Replace eval(input()) with int(input()) for safety and minor performance benefits.
trigger_signals: Use of range(1, N+1) where N can be large, combined with non-trivial per-element work (str(), len()).
len(list(generator)) pattern, which forces full materialization of potentially large iterables.
Timeouts or slow execution in Python when N is near the upper constraint (e.g., 1e5–1e6).
Recognition that the condition depends only on the number of digits, which has a known, structured distribution over the integers.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors at digit boundaries (e.g., mishandling 9 vs 10, 99 vs 100, 999 vs 1000). Each if/elif range must be carefully checked to be inclusive/exclusive correctly.
Forgetting to extend the piecewise logic if the problem’s N_max exceeds the largest covered range (e.g., if N can be >= 1e6 or 1e7, additional branches are needed).
Decreased readability or maintainability if many explicit thresholds are used without comments explaining the pattern.
Relying on eval(input()) can be unsafe and is unnecessary; while not the primary performance issue here, it is a security and robustness pitfall.

constraints_guess.notes: Directed graph with N nodes and M edges; compute the length of the longest path in a DAG. Typical competitive constraints N,M up to ~2e5. Graph is guaranteed acyclic or answer defined on DAG.

dominant_ops: Building NumPy array from edge list: np.asarray(var_7) -> O(M)
Constructing SciPy csr_matrix for adjacency: csr_matrix(...) -> O(N + M) but with high constant and Python↔C overhead
Running scipy.sparse.csgraph.connected_components on directed graph (strongly connected): O(N + M) in theory
Python-level loops over edges to fill var_7 and adjacency list var_4: O(M)
Sorting list of N component labels: var_11.sort(reverse=True) -> O(N log N)

complexity.why: Graph representation (lists + CSR) uses linear space in N+M. SciPy's connected_components on a sparse CSR graph is linear in N+M. Additional O(N log N) from sorting component-label pairs. Asymptotically fine, but dominated in practice by heavy SciPy/NumPy import and sparse-matrix machinery.

bottlenecks.detail: Importing NumPy and SciPy and initializing SciPy’s sparse graph routines is extremely heavy for a competitive-programming environment, likely exceeding time and memory limits even before computation.
Most online judges do not provide SciPy; the solution is functionally invalid despite good asymptotics.
Building a SciPy CSR matrix and running connected_components is significantly more expensive than a simple Python adjacency list plus DFS/BFS/topological sort for this DAG longest-path problem.
Computing strongly connected components on a graph that is effectively used as a DAG adds conceptual and runtime overhead; a direct topological sort would avoid SCC computation and sorting.
The list of (label, node) pairs is sorted with O(N log N) cost. For large N, this is noticeable compared to an O(N+M) pure BFS/DFS topological ordering.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use Kahn’s algorithm (BFS-based topological sort) on the directed acyclic graph, and perform DP along the topological order to compute the longest distance to each node. Track in-degree, push all in-degree-0 nodes into a queue, relax edges while decrementing in-degree, and update dp[next] = max(dp[next], dp[cur] + 1).

complexity.why: Each edge and node is processed a constant number of times. Building adjacency lists and in-degree counts is O(N+M). The queue-based topological traversal is linear. DP updates occur once per edge, keeping overall time O(N+M). Memory holds adjacency lists, in-degrees, and dp arrays, all linear in N+M.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log N + M) time, O(N + M) space, but with large constant factors and heavy external SciPy/NumPy dependencies.
complexity_delta.to: O(N + M) time, O(N + M) space using only Python built-ins and collections.deque.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic improvement in time (removing the sort and SCC computation) and massive reduction in constant factors and startup overhead by eliminating SciPy/NumPy and sparse-matrix operations.

transformation_steps: Replace NumPy/SciPy-based graph modeling (np.asarray + csr_matrix + connected_components) with a simple Python adjacency list representation.
Remove SCC computation and instead compute a true topological ordering using Kahn’s algorithm (in-degree array + queue).
Maintain an in-degree array var_4 to identify initial sources (in-degree 0 nodes) and drive the BFS topological process.
Introduce a DP array var_1 storing the longest path length ending at each node; during BFS, propagate and relax dp values along outgoing edges.
Use sys.stdin.readline for fast input and avoid function-call overhead around main logic, aligning with CP performance idioms.
Eliminate sorting of component labels by relying on the inherent topological order produced by Kahn’s algorithm.
trigger_signals: Use of SciPy (scipy.sparse, scipy.sparse.csgraph) in a competitive-programming style problem, which is typically unsupported or too heavy.
Heavy numerical and sparse-matrix infrastructure for a simple graph DP problem that only requires adjacency lists.
Presence of connected_components(strong) on what is logically treated as a DAG, suggesting unnecessary SCC work.
Sorting of component labels before DP, indicating avoidable O(N log N) work and hinting at a simpler topological-order-based DP.
Need for improved runtime and memory in Python under tight judge constraints (large N,M and strict limits).
pitfalls: Algorithm assumes the graph is acyclic; if there were cycles, Kahn’s algorithm would not visit all nodes and the longest path would be ill-defined. The problem statement must guarantee a DAG.
Correct handling of 1-based to 0-based indexing is crucial when reading edges (var_11 - 1, var_12 - 1).
Using recursion-based DFS for topological sort in Python could hit recursion limits on deep graphs; the chosen deque-based BFS avoids this.
Ensuring dp updates happen at the correct time: updates must be done when edges are relaxed (upon in-degree reaching zero and node enqueued) to reflect longest paths respecting topological order.
Care must be taken not to forget to update dp for nodes that start with in-degree 0; they should have initial dp = 0, and only successors get incremented.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical pattern looks like AtCoder-style DP: N items (var_10/var_6) up to ~2e3 and capacity/target H (var_5/var_3) up to ~1e4. A full (N+1)*(H+1) 2D DP in Python risks MLE or cache-inefficient access when N*H ≳ 1e7.

problem_type_tags: min-cost to achieve at least/exact value

dominant_ops: Nested DP over items and capacity: for each of N items (var_10) iterate over all capacities 0..H-1 (var_5) and compute a few min() expressions involving table lookups.

complexity.why: The DP table var_4 has size (N+1) x (H+1). The main loops do N iterations (var_6) and for each, H iterations (var_8), performing O(1) work (a couple of min operations and array accesses) per cell.

bottlenecks.detail: The 2D list var_4 of size (var_10+1) x (var_5+1) stores an integer in every cell. For N*H on the order of 1e7, memory usage and allocation time become significant in Python.
Access pattern jumps between rows (var_4[var_6+1][*] and var_4[var_6][*]) which is fine but the large 2D structure still leads to poor cache behavior compared to a compact 1D/2-row DP.

Each DP transition uses min() over up to three expressions, each involving an indexed access and an addition with a large sentinel (10**15). Combined over N*H cells, this constant factor is non-trivial.
Uses input() repeatedly, which is slower than buffered sys.stdin.readline() for large inputs.

FastAudit.core_idea: Compress the 2D DP table to a rolling 1D/2-row DP (only current and previous row are kept) and speed up input by using sys.stdin.readline via helper functions. The DP transition logic stays essentially the same, but memory usage is reduced from O(N*H) to O(H) and allocation/GC overhead is lowered.

complexity.why: The optimized code still runs a double loop over N items and H capacities, so the time complexity is unchanged. However, it keeps only a single row (or two rows: previous and current, via var_8 and var_9) of size H+1 instead of an entire (N+1) x (H+1) table, reducing space to linear in H.

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time remains the same, but memory is reduced by a factor of ~N. In practice, constant-factor speedups also arise from smaller allocations, better cache locality, and faster I/O.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the DP recurrence for cell (i+1, w) depends only on row i and (optionally) the partially computed row i+1, so full (N+1) rows are not required simultaneously.
Replace the 2D DP table var_4 with 1D arrays: one representing the previous row (e.g., var_8) and one representing the next/current row (e.g., var_9).

For each item, initialize a new current-row array with 'inf' sentinel values, then fill it using min transitions that read from the previous-row array and already-updated cells of the current-row array.
After processing an item, assign the current-row array to be the previous-row array for the next iteration (rolling array technique).
Swap Python's built-in input() with sys.stdin.readline() wrapped in small helper functions to lower overhead for large input sizes.
Optionally standardize the sentinel for 'infinity' (using a large constant or float('inf')) and ensure all DP transitions are consistent with this sentinel.
trigger_signals: Memory Limit Exceeded (MLE) or very high memory usage when N*H is large (e.g., 1e7 or more DP cells).
Observed slow startup time due to allocation of a huge (N+1) x (H+1) list of lists.
Profiling shows that memory allocation and list creation dominate runtime, even though the algorithm is only O(N*H).
Problem constraints where N and H are both moderately large (hundreds to thousands), making N*H borderline for Python in a 2D DP.
I/O accounts for noticeable overhead: input() in a tight read loop for large instances.

constraints_guess.notes: Reads an unknown number of integer pairs until a (0, 0) sentinel. Typical online judge IO-bound beginner problem; performance driven mainly by per-line IO overhead rather than asymptotics.

dominant_ops: Repeated input().split(" ") calls, separate int() conversions, and a function call per pair for swapping.

complexity.why: For T input pairs, each iteration does a constant amount of work: one read, two string-to-int conversions, a constant number of comparisons and assignments, and a print. No data structure grows with T; only a fixed set of scalar variables is used.

bottlenecks.detail: func_1 is called on every iteration just to perform a simple conditional swap, adding call/return overhead in the tight IO loop.
The code calls input().split(" ") and then int() twice separately instead of using map(int, ...), causing more Python-level operations and attribute lookups.
The sentinel check is expressed as while (0 != var_1) or (0 != var_2), which is more verbose and slightly more expensive than a direct sentinel break on (0, 0).
Swapping via a temporary variable (var_4) inside func_1 is more verbose than using Python’s tuple-unpacking swap; while asymptotically the same, it adds extra bytecode operations.
The input-reading and int-conversion logic is duplicated before the loop and inside the loop, increasing code size and maintenance cost and slightly harming locality.

FastAudit.core_idea: Tighten the IO loop by combining input parsing and conversion (map(int, input().split())), inlining the conditional swap using tuple assignment, and using a simple infinite loop with a clear sentinel break condition.

complexity.why: The optimized version still processes each of the T input pairs once with a constant amount of work per pair. It reduces constant factors by removing a function call, minimizing Python-level operations in the loop, and simplifying the sentinel logic, but does not change the overall linear time nor the constant-space nature of the solution.

delta_type: constant-factor optimization and structural refactor of the IO loop

complexity_delta.from: O(T) time, O(1) space with higher constant factors due to function calls and redundant conversions
complexity_delta.to: O(T) time, O(1) space with lower constant factors via inlined logic and compact input parsing
complexity_delta.note: Both versions are linear in the number of input pairs, but the modified version executes fewer Python bytecodes per pair, making it faster for large T under tight time limits.

transformation_steps: Inline the swap logic from func_1 directly into the main loop using tuple-unpacking: if var_1 > var_2: var_1, var_2 = var_2, var_1.
Replace separate input().split(" ") and two int() calls with list(map(int, input().split())), reducing attribute lookups and Python-level operations.
Convert the while condition from while (0 != var_1) or (0 != var_2) to an infinite loop while 1 with an explicit sentinel break when not (var_1 + var_2).
Remove the now-unnecessary wrapper function func_2 and the __main__ guard boilerplate, turning the script into a straightforward top-level loop.
Avoid temporary variables for swapping (var_4) by using Python’s native multiple assignment, which is clearer and usually compiles to fewer bytecodes.
trigger_signals: A helper function (func_1) is invoked on every iteration of a simple, IO-heavy loop to perform trivial work (conditional swap).
Repeated patterns of parsing and converting input (input().split(" "); int() for each) appear both before and inside the loop.
The problem is clearly IO-bound: the core logic is only comparisons and assignments on small integers, so micro-optimizing logic and IO can meaningfully improve runtime.
Use of verbose conditions for sentinel loops (while (0 != var_1) or (0 != var_2)) instead of a direct and cheap break mechanism hints at unnecessary overhead.
The language (Python) is relatively slow per operation, so high-frequency, per-line overheads such as function calls and extra bytecodes can dominate runtime on large input sizes.
pitfalls: Behavioral equivalence: ensure the new sentinel condition (if not var_1 + var_2: break) exactly matches the old termination condition (both values zero). With this logic, (0, 0) terminates; other sums like (5, -5) do not terminate, matching the original semantics.

Input splitting: using split() instead of split(" ") can change behavior when there are multiple spaces or other whitespace; typically safe (and better) for online judge inputs that use arbitrary whitespace, but worth verifying against the judge’s specification.

Output format: both versions currently print a Python tuple (e.g., '(1, 2)') rather than space-separated values ('1 2'); if the judge expects the latter, this is a specification bug, not a performance issue, and should be corrected alongside optimization.

Readability vs. brevity: collapsing everything into a top-level while 1 loop is fast but can reduce clarity in more complex problems; in production code, balancing clarity with performance is important.
Error handling: the tight loop assumes all lines are well-formed with exactly two integers; in more robust contexts, additional checks may be needed, which would add some overhead back.

constraints_guess.notes: Single integer N; task is to compute the number of divisors of N! modulo 1e9+7. The hard-coded sieve limit 10^3 suggests sqrt(max N) ≈ 10^3 → max N ≈ 10^6. Practical setters often use N in the 10^4–10^6 range.

dominant_ops: Sieve of Eratosthenes up to 10^3 to generate small primes
For each integer k in [2..N], trial division by all primes ≤ sqrt(k) (subset of precomputed primes)
Dictionary updates accumulating total prime exponents over all k ≤ N
Extra overhead from repeatedly constructing dicts and converting .items() to list() in the inner loop

complexity.time: O(N * π(√N)) ≈ O(N^(3/2) / log N) for factorization over k = 2..N; sieve cost O(P log log P) with P = 10^3 is negligible.
complexity.space: O(P + π(N)) ≈ O(N / log N) for storing sieve up to 10^3 and a map of all primes ≤ N with their exponents in N!.
complexity.why: func_3 iterates k from 2 to N and calls func_2(k) each time. func_2(k) divides k by each prime p up to min(√k, 10^3) until fully factored, so cost per k is O(π(√k)). Summing over k ≤ N yields Σ_k π(√k) ≈ N * π(√N), giving ≈ O(N^(3/2)/log N). The final divisor-count computation is linear in the number of distinct primes, which is lower order.

bottlenecks.detail: Redundant trial division: each number from 2 to N is factorized independently. This repeats similar work and yields N separate factorizations instead of leveraging properties of factorial or precomputing smallest prime factors.

func_3 calls func_2(k) for each k, and inside func_3 uses list(func_2(k).items()), creating a temporary dict and list for every k. This adds significant Python overhead beyond the arithmetic operations.

Using a sieve only up to 10^3 forces trial division for all k with primes up to min(10^3, √k). While correct up to about 10^6, using a sieve/SPF up to N would allow much faster factorization or direct exponent accumulation.
Frequent dictionary lookups and updates in Python inside nested loops (over k and primes) contribute noticeably to runtime for large N.

FastAudit.core_idea: Compute N! as a single Python big integer via math.factorial, then factorize N! itself by trial division (repeatedly dividing by the current divisor and counting multiplicities) and finally compute the product over (exponent + 1) using the exponent multiplicities obtained from factoring N!.

complexity.time: At least O(N^2 log N) in terms of bit operations: O(cost_factorial(N) + N * M(B)), where B ≈ size in bits of N! and M(B) is big-integer division cost. The trial-division factorization of N! dominates, giving super-linear and practically very large cost.
complexity.space: Θ(B) = Θ(N log N) bits to store N! as a single huge integer, plus smaller overhead for storing factor multiplicities.
complexity.why: math.factorial(N) constructs N! as a big integer with roughly B ≈ Θ(N log N) bits. The subsequent loop tries divisors var_5 = 2, 3, ..., up to roughly N, performing at least one big-int division per step. Each division on a B-bit integer is at least linear in B (and often worse), so the factorization alone costs ≈ O(N * B) = O(N^2 log N) bit operations. This is asymptotically and practically far worse than factoring each k ≤ N when N is large.

complexity_delta.from: O(N * π(√N)) ≈ O(N^(3/2) / log N) time and O(N / log N) space in the original code, with only small integers handled during factorization.
complexity_delta.to: At least O(N^2 log N) time and Θ(N log N) bits of space in the modified code due to constructing N! as a huge integer and then trial-dividing it.
complexity_delta.note: The modified (so-called 'fast') code is asymptotically and practically slower and more memory-intensive than the original approach for realistic N; it changes the performance bottleneck from many small factorizations to a single extremely expensive big-integer factorial and factorization.

transformation_steps: Replaced incremental factorization of each integer k in [2..N] with computing N! once using math.factorial(N), creating a huge intermediate integer.
Switched from factoring many small numbers (≤ N) to factoring the single large number N! by trial division from 2 upward.
Removed the sieve and prime-list-based factorization, instead relying on naive incrementing of the trial divisor until N! is reduced to 1.
Changed I/O from sys.stdin.readline to eval(input()), which is slightly slower and introduces unnecessary overhead and security risk, though negligible compared to the factorial/factorization cost.
trigger_signals: Runtime grows extremely fast as N increases; even moderate N (e.g., a few thousands) cause significant slowdown or timeouts due to big-int arithmetic.
Memory usage spikes because factorial(N) is stored explicitly as a giant integer with Θ(N log N) bits.
CPU profiling would show most time spent inside math.factorial and big-integer modulo/division operations within the factorization loop.
Observation that the loop while var_2 != 1 with var_5 increasing one by one implies scanning all integers up to roughly N on a massive big integer.
pitfalls: Assuming that computing N! and then factoring it is faster than aggregating prime exponents over 2..N. In reality, big-int operations dominate and are much slower than many small-integer operations for this problem.
Using naive trial division on N! instead of using number-theoretic formulas: the exponent of a prime p in N! can be computed efficiently via sum_{k>=1} floor(N / p^k) without ever forming N!.
Creating a huge intermediate object (N!) that is not needed for the final answer; the problem only requires the exponents of primes in N!, not the factorial value itself.
Using eval(input()) for reading a single integer: it is slower and unsafe, and provides no benefit for this task.
Ignoring better data structures such as smallest prime factor (SPF) arrays or direct prime exponent summation, both of which yield O(N log log N) or better behavior without big integers.

constraints_guess.notes: Single sequence length N, typical AtCoder-style constraints where N can be up to ~2e5 or similar. Need linear-time solution with efficient I/O in Python.

dominant_ops: One linear scan over the array of length n, performing adjacent comparisons and max updates; plus linear-time input parsing.

complexity.why: Reads n integers into a list and then iterates once over indices 0..n-2, doing O(1) work per element. Extra helper functions are defined but never invoked in the hot path, so they do not change asymptotic complexity.

bottlenecks.detail: Uses input() for reading the line of integers and eval(input()) for reading n, which is slower and potentially unsafe compared with direct integer parsing or bulk reading from stdin.
Index-based loop over var_5 with repeated list indexing var_5[var_6], var_5[var_6+1] creates slightly higher overhead than iterating directly over the values.

Multiple heavy imports (math, decimal, fractions, collections, etc.) and unused helper functions (factorial-based combinatorics, divisor enumeration, duplicate check) inflate startup time and may hurt performance in tight contest time limits.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep a running count of the current non-increasing contiguous segment while streaming through the values once, tracking only the previous value and the current/best segment lengths. Optimize I/O by reading all integers at once with open(0).read() and skipping the first token (n).

complexity.why: Still reads all n values into a list and performs a single pass over them, doing O(1) work per element. The core algorithmic structure remains linear; improvements are purely in constant factors (faster I/O, simpler loop, no unused imports).

complexity_delta.from: Time O(n), Space O(n) with slower per-element and I/O constants due to input(), eval(), and superfluous code.
complexity_delta.to: Time O(n), Space O(n) but with reduced constant factors via bulk I/O, direct iteration, and removal of unused overhead.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged; the optimization primarily targets Python runtime overhead and I/O speed for large n.

transformation_steps: Replaced eval(input()) and input().split() with open(0).read().split(), parsing all integers in one bulk read and avoiding eval.
Skipped the first token (n) by slicing [1:], eliminating the need to store or use the size explicitly in the loop.
Switched from index-based adjacency checks over var_5[i] and var_5[i+1] to a direct iteration over values while remembering the previous value in a scalar variable.
Initialized the previous-value sentinel var_5 to a large number (1e9+7) so the first actual element always starts a non-increasing run correctly.
Tracked current non-increasing-run length in var_3 and best length in var_2, updating best both inside the loop on breaks and once more after the loop terminates.
Removed unused imports and helper functions (deepcopy, factorial combinatorics, divisor enumeration, duplicate detection, etc.), reducing startup and module loading overhead.
trigger_signals: Presence of eval(input()) on hot-path input, which is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()).
Use of input() for potentially large inputs where open(0).read() or sys.stdin.buffer.read() is preferred for speed.
Multiple heavy imports and helper functions that are never used in the actual solution logic.
Single-pass linear algorithm already in place, indicating the main remaining gains are from micro-optimizations and I/O improvements rather than algorithmic changes.
pitfalls: Bulk-reading stdin with open(0).read() loads the entire input into memory; while fine for typical contest constraints, it can be problematic if input size is extremely large.

The algorithm computes the length in terms of the number of comparisons in the non-increasing segment (effectively run_length - 1). Any change to problem interpretation (e.g., wanting full segment length) would require adjusting the counting logic.
The sentinel initialization (var_5 = 1e9+7) assumes all input values are <= 1e9+7; if the domain changes and values can exceed this, the first comparison semantics may be affected.
The code assumes at least one element after the first token; edge cases with n = 0 or malformed input are not handled and could cause incorrect behavior or errors.
Directly slicing tokens with [1:] relies on the first token being exactly the count n; if the input format changes, this will silently misinterpret the data.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical for AtCoder ABC110 D-like tasks: N up to ~1e5, M up to ~1e9. Need to factor M and compute products of combinations C(N-1+e_i, e_i) modulo 1e9+7.

dominant_ops: Trial-division factorization of M up to sqrt(M)
Precomputation of factorials up to N + max_exponent
Precomputation of inverse factorials via one modular inverse and a reverse loop
O(1) nCr queries using precomputed factorials/inverse factorials

complexity.why: Factorization of M by trial division runs in O(sqrt(M)). Building factorial and inverse-factorial arrays up to var_8 = N + max_exponent (max_exponent ≲ log M) is O(N). Each combination evaluation is O(1) and used only for a handful of distinct primes.

bottlenecks.detail: Allocating and filling two arrays of size ~N (factorials and inverse factorials) dominates runtime and memory, even though only a small number of combinations are evaluated.
Storing both factorial and inverse-factorial arrays requires O(N) integers; if N were much larger, this would be a limiting factor.
Using Counter over the full multiset of prime factors and an assertion in func_1 introduces small overhead, though negligible for typical constraints.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep a single factorial array and compute nCr using modular inverses via pow() on demand, avoiding the inverse-factorial array and simplifying factorization to return (prime, exponent) pairs directly. Use faster I/O primitives.

complexity.why: Factorization remains O(sqrt(M)). Factorials are precomputed once up to N+O(1), giving O(N) time and space. Each nCr call uses two modular exponentiations (for 1/fact(k) and 1/fact(n−k)), each O(log MOD). The number of distinct primes P in M is small (P ≲ 9 for M ≤ 1e9), so the extra P log MOD term is minor.

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(M) + N) time, O(N) space with two arrays (factorials + inverse factorials).
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + N + P log MOD) time, O(N) space with a single factorial array.
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic behavior in N and M is effectively unchanged. Memory is slightly reduced by dropping the inverse-factorial array. Time includes a small extra factor from a constant number of pow() calls, which is negligible for small P.

transformation_steps: Replaced factorization that returns a flat list of prime factors with one that returns (prime, exponent) pairs directly, eliminating the Counter construction.
Removed the global inverse-factorial array; nCr is now computed as fact[n] * inv(fact[k]) * inv(fact[n-k]) using modular exponentiation pow(..., MOD-2, MOD).
Kept factorial precomputation but encapsulated it in func_3 and drove it with N+constant (N+100) as an upper bound.
Switched input handling from built-in input() to sys.stdin.readline for marginally faster I/O.
Simplified combination boundary checks by returning 0 for invalid (n, k) instead of using assertions.
trigger_signals: Need to reduce memory footprint from dual factorial/inverse-factorial arrays when only a small number of combinations is required.
Desire to simplify combinatorics code by removing explicit inverse-factorial precomputation and using modular exponentiation for inverses.
Recognition that the number of nCr evaluations is very small (one per distinct prime factor), making on-the-fly pow() inverses acceptable.
Interest in slightly faster or more robust I/O handling via sys.stdin for competitive programming environments.
pitfalls: Using pow() to compute modular inverses for each combination becomes expensive if the number of combination queries grows large; in that case the original inverse-factorial precomputation may be faster.
The factorial array must be precomputed up to at least max_n used in nCr (here N-1+max_exponent); choosing too small a bound (e.g., N+100) without verifying max_exponent can cause index errors.
The modular inverse via pow(x, MOD-2, MOD) assumes MOD is prime; changing the modulus to a non-prime requires a different inverse strategy.
Removing the assertion in nCr shifts error handling from immediate failure to silent 0 return; logic bugs in the ranges of n and k may become harder to spot.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style task: given N and M (e.g., 1 ≤ N ≤ 1e5, 1 ≤ M ≤ 1e9), factor M and for each prime exponent e compute C(N+e-1, e) mod 1e9+7. Precomputation in the original up to 2*10^5 suggests N+max_e <= 2*10^5.

dominant_ops: Trial division prime factorization up to sqrt(M)
Global precomputation of factorials and modular inverses up to 2*10^5 for binomial coefficients

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + L) where L = 2*10^5 (factorial + inverse precomputation dominates for small M)
complexity.space: O(L) for factorial, inverse, and inverse-of-index arrays (L = 2*10^5)
complexity.why: Factorization iterates divisors up to sqrt(M), which is cheap for M ≤ 1e9. The loop that fills var_6, var_7, var_9 from 2 to 2*10^5 is always executed, regardless of N, M, or the actual exponents, and allocates three arrays of length ≈2*10^5.

bottlenecks.detail: Always precomputes factorials and modular inverses up to 2*10^5 (var_6, var_7, var_9) even though the number of needed binomial coefficients is only equal to the number of distinct prime factors of M (typically small).
Keeps three arrays of length 2*10^5 in memory for a single computation of a handful of binomial coefficients.
Each factorial index requires multiple modular multiplications and divisions during the linear inverse sieve, increasing constant factors though still linear in 2*10^5.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid global factorial/inverse precomputation and compute each required binomial coefficient C(N+e-1, e) on the fly via a multiplicative formula using plain integer arithmetic, then reduce modulo 1e9+7. Keep the factorization as trial division but expressed as a while loop with var_7*var_7 <= var_8.

complexity.time: O(sqrt(M) + sum_e) ≈ O(sqrt(M) + log M), since sum of exponents e over distinct prime factors of M is O(log M), and each binomial C(N+e-1, e) is computed in O(e). There is no O(L) precomputation term.
complexity.space: O(P) where P is the number of distinct prime factors of M (size of the defaultdict for exponents), plus a few scalar big integers during combination computation.
complexity.why: Factorization remains trial division up to sqrt(M). After factorization, only one binomial coefficient per prime factor is needed. Computing each via a simple product/quotient loop in e avoids storing and computing factorials up to a global max L = 2*10^5, removing the largest linear-time and linear-space component.

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotically, the sqrt(M) factorization term is unchanged; the main improvement is eliminating the unconditional O(2*10^5) factorial/inverse precomputation and their storage. For typical constraints (N up to 1e5, M up to 1e9) this significantly reduces constant factors in both time and memory.

transformation_steps: Replaced the factorial + inverse precomputation (var_6, var_7, var_9) with no global combinatorial precomputation at all.

Changed binomial coefficient computation from table lookup C(n, k) via factorials and modular inverses to an on-the-fly multiplicative formula: C(N+e-1, e) = ∏_{j=1..e} (N+e-j)/j as exact integer arithmetic, then applied modulo 1e9+7 to the result.
Refactored prime factorization: retained trial division but used a while var_7*var_7 <= var_8 loop and a defaultdict(int) to accumulate exponents, simplifying control flow and memory usage.
Reduced memory footprint by storing only prime-exponent pairs in a small dictionary instead of large factorial/inverse arrays.

Applied modulo reduction only on the accumulated answer var_9, not on every intermediate factorial and inverse value, trading frequent modular ops for a small number of big-int multiplications/divisions.
trigger_signals: Observation that only a handful of binomial coefficients (one per prime factor of M) are needed, while the original code precomputes up to 2*10^5 factorial values and their inverses.
The presence of a large, fixed precomputation bound (2*10**5) that does not depend on the actual factorization of M or the number of test cases.
Single-shot computation (no multiple queries) means amortization of heavy precomputation is poor and motivates per-query/on-the-fly computation.
N can be large but exponents e from factorization of M are typically small (sum_e ≈ O(log M)), so a multiplicative binomial formula is efficient.
pitfalls: The fast version relies on exact integer division var_4 // var_10 in the multiplicative formula. This is mathematically safe because each step maintains that the numerator is divisible by the denominator, but any change that introduces intermediate modulo operations before division would break correctness.

Intermediate binomial values can grow large as Python big integers when N is large, increasing the bit-complexity of multiplications. For substantially larger constraints, the original modular factorial method might scale better than big-int arithmetic.
Care must be taken not to move `% var_2` (mod 1e9+7) inside the loop that forms var_4 and var_10 before performing exact division, since modular division without modular inverses is not valid.

If constraints required many different binomial coefficients (e.g., many queries or variable N, M), the lack of reusable precomputed factorials could become a performance disadvantage compared to the original precomputation approach.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic AOJ/ITP-style problem: given N and X, count triples 1 <= i < j < k <= N with i + j + k = X, terminated by '0 0'. Typical constraints N <= 100, X <= 300; multiple test cases until sentinel.

dominant_ops: Triple nested for-loops over i, j, k in [1..N] with i < j < k
sum([var_1, var_2, var_3]) list construction and summation inside innermost loop
Equality check against target sum in innermost loop

complexity.why: Three nested loops: var_1 ranges ~N, var_2 ~N, var_3 ~N/2 on average (due to ordering constraint), so the number of iterations is Theta(N^3). Each iteration does constant work plus an avoidable list allocation for sum; asymptotically still O(N^3). No extra data structures are kept, so auxiliary space is O(1).

bottlenecks.detail: Triple nested loops scale as N^3; if N is up to ~1000, this leads to ~1e9 iterations which is far too slow in Python for an online judge.
Using sum([var_1, var_2, var_3]) creates a temporary list on every innermost iteration, adding overhead (~3-element list allocation and deallocation) on top of the already heavy cubic loop.
Python's per-iteration overhead for nested loops is high; a cubic algorithm that might pass in C/C++ is likely to TLE in Python under similar constraints.

FastAudit.core_idea: Eliminate the explicit third loop by deriving the third value from the sum constraint and count valid triples via a double loop plus inequality checks, effectively reducing the search space from all (i, j, k) triples to all (i, j) pairs and inferring k = S - i - j.

complexity.time: O(N * X)  (often effectively O(N^2) for typical constraints)
complexity.space: O(K) for the list in the comprehension, where K is the number of valid triples (conceptually O(N * X), but usually small); O(1) auxiliary space if implemented with a streaming counter instead of building a list.
complexity.why: var_1 loops from 3..N, var_2 loops up to roughly (X - var_1). For typical bounds X = O(N), the total iterations are on the order of sum_{i=1..N} O(X - i) = O(N * X). Within each iteration, only constant-time arithmetic and comparisons are performed. The current implementation uses a list comprehension and len(), which temporarily stores one item per valid triple, hence O(K) transient space, but no asymptotically large persistent structure.

complexity_delta.from: O(N^3) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N * X) time (often ~O(N^2)), O(K) transient space (or O(1) with streaming counting)
complexity_delta.note: By deriving the third value from the sum constraint and enforcing ordering via inequalities, the algorithm moves from exploring all O(N^3) triplets to only O(N * X) (i, j) pairs. Given typical constraints (N <= 100, X <= 300), the operation count drops from up to ~1e6–1e9 checks to on the order of 10^4–10^5, easily within Python limits.

transformation_steps: Recognize that the triple (i, j, k) must satisfy i + j + k = X and 1 <= i < j < k <= N; thus k is uniquely determined once i and j are fixed: k = X - i - j.
Remove the innermost loop over k and instead compute k directly from X - i - j inside a double loop over i and j.

Replace explicit i < j < k constraints (encoded via loop bounds in slow_code) with inequality checks relating j and inferred k (fast_code uses var_4 - var_1 - var_2 < var_2 < var_1 to enforce ordering).
Constrain the range of the inner loop using the sum constraint (var_2 in range(2, X - var_1)), which implicitly ensures k remains positive and reduces unnecessary iterations.
Aggregate counts using a comprehension and len(); for further micro-optimization, this could be converted to a streaming counter (e.g., sum(1 for ...)) to avoid allocating a list.
trigger_signals: Presence of a triple nested loop over a variable with maximum size on the order of up to 100–1000 (N), implying potential N^3 = 1e6–1e9 iterations.
Innermost loop body containing only a simple numeric condition (sum equality), suggesting that part of the search can be derived algebraically instead of fully iterated.
Use of sum() with a list in the innermost loop, which is a clear micro-optimization target and a hint that arithmetic can be simplified.
Problem type is combinatorial counting with a fixed-sum constraint, which commonly admits reduction from k nested loops to (k-1) loops by solving for the final variable.
pitfalls: Off-by-one errors when translating the i < j < k <= N constraints into loop ranges and inequalities can lead to missing or double-counting triples.

Ensuring k = X - i - j is within [1, N] is essential; the fast_code partially encodes positivity and ordering through the inequality var_4 - var_1 - var_2 < var_2 < var_1 and inner-loop range, but mis-setting these bounds will include invalid triples.

Using a list comprehension with len() (as in fast_code) allocates a list of size equal to the number of valid triples; for worst-case inputs or similar problems with larger counts, this may be wasteful compared to using an incremental counter.
Relying on short-circuit termination via sentinel (0 0) means input parsing must be robust; incorrect handling may cause unnecessary loops or missed termination.

If constraints differ from the assumed AOJ-style bounds (e.g., N much larger than X or vice versa), the perceived complexity O(N * X) might behave closer to O(N^2) or worse; it is important to reason in terms of actual problem constraints when generalizing this optimization pattern.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical of AtCoder-style problem: N points (≈1e5), coordinates up to about 1e9, need GCD of |Ai - X| over all i.

dominant_ops: O(N) integer conversions and absolute-value computations to build the difference array
O(N) calls to a Python-implemented Euclidean GCD (while loop with modulo)
Per-iteration modulo operations inside func_1, implemented in Python space

complexity.why: Building var_5 as a list of |Ai - X| costs O(N). Each GCD computation via the Euclidean algorithm costs O(log M) where M is the magnitude of the numbers. The code computes GCD across all N elements, leading to O(N log M) total time. All differences are stored in var_5, giving O(N) extra space.

bottlenecks.detail: Custom GCD func_1 is written in Python and executed at the Python level, incurring function call overhead and a Python while-loop with modulo operations for each pairwise GCD. This is slower than using the C-optimized math.gcd.

var_5 is created as a list of strings via input().split(), then each element is converted individually with int() inside a list comprehension. This doubles the work for parsing and conversion compared to mapping input directly to int.

The logic splits into special cases var_6 == 1, var_6 == 2, and var_6 >= 3 with separate GCD handling. While asymptotically fine, it prevents a simple uniform streaming reduction that would be more concise and easier for the interpreter to optimize.

The loop for var_6 >= 3 uses range(2, len(var_5) - 1), which stops at the second-to-last index and omits the last element from the GCD computation. This is a logic/edge-case bug rather than a performance issue, but it affects output correctness for N >= 3.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a single-pass streaming GCD over |Ai - X| using the C-optimized math.gcd, initializing the accumulator to 0 so gcd(0, x) = x, and parse input directly as integers.

complexity.why: The loop computes gcd(var_3, |X - Ai|) once per element, and each gcd call is O(log M). This yields O(N log M) time. The code still stores all Ai in var_5, so auxiliary space is O(N). The main improvement is a significantly smaller constant factor from using math.gcd and direct int parsing.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log M) time, O(N) space (Python-level GCD, extra int conversions, off-by-one loop on GCD aggregation).
complexity_delta.to: O(N log M) time, O(N) space (C-optimized math.gcd with simple streaming reduction and direct integer parsing).
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged, but runtime constant factors are significantly reduced and the off-by-one correctness bug is eliminated.

transformation_steps: Replace the custom Euclidean GCD implementation func_1 with the standard library math.gcd, leveraging a C-optimized implementation.
Change input parsing for the list from list(input().split()) followed by per-element int() conversion to list(map(int, input().split())), doing conversion in one pass.
Eliminate special-case branching for N == 1, N == 2, and N >= 3 by using a single streaming GCD accumulator initialized to 0 and iterating uniformly over all elements.
Embed the absolute difference computation abs(var_2 - var_5[var_4]) inside the GCD loop instead of precomputing and storing a separate difference array.
Fix the off-by-one error in the aggregation loop by iterating over the full range range(var_1) instead of range(2, len(var_5) - 1), ensuring all elements are included in the GCD.
trigger_signals: Presence of a manual Euclidean GCD implementation in Python where math.gcd is available.
Multiple passes and conversions over input data (strings then ints) indicating redundant work.
Conditional control flow branching only on N (1, 2, >=3) for what is fundamentally a uniform reduction operation.
Tight typical constraints (N up to about 1e5) where Python-level loops and function calls can risk timeouts.
Suspicious loop bounds range(2, len(var_5) - 1) that both miss the last element and obscure the intended aggregation pattern.
pitfalls: Assuming that using math.gcd changes the asymptotic complexity; it does not, but it drastically improves constant factors, which is crucial in Python.
Forgetting that gcd(0, x) = x is what allows initializing the accumulator to 0; any other initialization would require special-casing the first element.
Retaining the original off-by-one loop bounds when refactoring; the safer pattern is always to iterate over the exact number of elements (range(N)) or directly over the list.
Assuming that precomputing the difference array is necessary; it is not, since |Ai - X| can be computed on the fly in the streaming GCD loop.
Not considering that storing the full list var_5 still uses O(N) memory; if memory were tighter, one could stream input and immediately fold into the GCD without keeping all Ai in a list.

constraints_guess.notes: Classic AtCoder-ABC-style brute-force search (ABC119 C: Synthetic Kadomatsu). N is small (≈8); 4^N search is intended and acceptable.

dominant_ops: Enumerating all assignments of N sticks into 4 groups via itertools.product([0,1,2,3], repeat=N) -> 4^N combinations
For each assignment, O(N) loop to update 4 running sums and accumulation of cost
Minor overhead: per-assignment check for zero-length groups, abs computations, and min update

complexity.why: The outer product enumerates 4^N group assignments. For each, there is a single pass through N positions doing O(1) work per position (few integer ops and array accesses). Additional work per state (final cost, comparisons) is O(1). The auxiliary storage is a 4-element array plus O(N) for the input lengths.

bottlenecks.detail: Core search is a brute-force 4^N enumeration of all ways to assign each stick to one of three targets or to waste. This dominates runtime but is required by the straightforward solution for small N.
Each of the 4^N states performs an O(N) loop. For N≈8 this is fine, but any larger N would explode.
The check `any([var_6 == 0 for var_6 in var_11[:3]])` allocates a temporary list every time; it could be `any(x == 0 for x in var_11[:3])` to avoid the list.
Using `eval` on each input line is unnecessary and slower (and unsafe in general); `int(input())` suffices.

FastAudit.core_idea: Instead of assigning each stick to a group in one pass, explicitly enumerate all non-empty disjoint subsets for the three target groups via combinations, with the remaining sticks implicitly treated as unused. For each triple of subsets, compute the cost directly from their sizes and sums and keep the minimum.

complexity.why: A configuration is defined by three disjoint non-empty subsets S_A, S_B, S_C ⊆ {0..N-1} (rest = waste). The number of such triples is still Θ(4^N) (it’s the 4^N assignments restricted to the cases where each of the 3 target groups is non-empty). The code iterates over all size triples (O(N^3)) and for each uses nested combinations: C(N, a) * C(N-a, b) * C(N-a-b, c). Summed over all (a,b,c) this equals the number of valid assignments, asymptotically Θ(4^N). Within each combination triple, it recomputes sums with generator expressions, adding another polynomial factor in N. Space: O(N) for lengths plus O(N^3) to store all (a,b,c) in `var_12`.

complexity_delta.from: Θ(4^N * N) time, Θ(N) space
complexity_delta.to: Θ(4^N * poly(N)) time, Θ(N + N^3) space
complexity_delta.note: Both versions remain exponential in N with a ~4^N factor. The modified version changes the enumeration strategy but does not improve big-O; it likely increases constant factors and space usage.

transformation_steps: Replaced direct 4-ary assignment enumeration via `product([0,1,2,3], repeat=N)` with a three-level nested choice of subset sizes (a,b,c) and then nested combinations to choose explicit disjoint subsets for each target.
Enforced non-empty groups structurally by limiting sizes (a,b,c >= 1) instead of post-filtering assignments where some group sum is zero.
Rewrote cost computation to use closed-form `(len(group)-1)*10 + abs(sum(group_lengths) - target)` based directly on chosen subset indices.
Introduced additional data structures (a precomputed list of size triples `var_12` and repeated use of sets to enforce disjointness) instead of a simple running-sum array.
trigger_signals: Explicit exponential loop over `product([0,1,2,3], repeat=N)` suggesting potential concern about 4^N growth.
Per-state O(N) inner loop inside the exponential outer loop.
Desire to avoid generating assignments with empty groups, leading to restructuring into combinations of non-empty subsets.
Use of `eval` for numeric input, hinting at interest in refactoring rather than pure performance.
pitfalls: The combination-based approach does not reduce asymptotic complexity; the number of valid (non-empty) groupings is still Θ(4^N). For the typical N≤8 this is fine, but for larger N it will still blow up.

The new code adds overhead: repeated construction of sets (`set(var_6)`, `set(var_8)`), more complex iterator nesting, recomputing sums from scratch per subset, and storing O(N^3) size tuples, all of which can be slower than the original straightforward product-based enumeration.
Using combinations with set differences can increase constant factors and memory allocations compared to the original tight inner loop using fixed-size arrays and simple integer indices.
The perceived optimization (avoiding empty-group cases) only removes a fraction of the 4^N states; the overall order of magnitude remains exponential and dominated by 4^N configurations.

Both versions rely on exponential search; if N were to be increased beyond ~8, a fundamentally different approach (still exponential but with better pruning, or a different DP/branching structure) would be required, not just a rearrangement of the enumeration.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder 'Lunlun number' problem (e.g., ABC 161 D) where N ≤ 10^5 and generated values fit within 64-bit integers.

dominant_ops: Repeated string conversions for each generated number (int -> str, indexing last digit, str concatenations, str -> int).
Building many intermediate sets of numbers level-by-level.
Flattening all generated sets into a single list.
Sorting the entire list of generated numbers before indexing the k-th element.

complexity.why: Approximately N numbers are generated in a tree where each node yields up to 3 children. Each expansion performs digit work via string conversion (factor d: number of digits). After generation, all numbers (~N) are flattened and sorted, costing O(N log N). The BFS-style level generation itself is O(N), but the final global sort dominates.

bottlenecks.detail: Performs a global sort of all generated numbers just to access the k-th smallest, even though generation order could be structured to be already sorted.
Stores levels as sets and then accumulates them in a list of sets, forcing a full flatten + sort instead of streaming results.
Heavy use of string conversions and concatenations in the inner loop (int->str, indexing, str->int), which is slow compared to pure integer arithmetic.
Keeps all generated numbers in memory until the end, rather than discarding earlier ones once they are no longer needed.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use a BFS over valid numbers directly in increasing order using a queue (deque). Start from digits 1–9, repeatedly pop the smallest current Lunlun number, generate its next valid neighbors using integer arithmetic on the last digit, push them to the back of the queue, and stop after popping the N-th number. This makes the generation order already sorted, eliminating the need for a final sort and avoiding string operations.

complexity.why: Each popped number produces at most 3 children. The BFS processes exactly N pops (each O(1) amortized with deque) and O(1) arithmetic operations per node, yielding O(N) time. The queue size is proportional to the frontier and bounded by O(N). No global sort or string manipulation is required.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log N * d) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: Eliminated the global sort and expensive string-based digit handling by using a queue-based BFS that inherently maintains increasing order.

transformation_steps: Replaced the list-of-sets level structure with a single queue (collections.deque) that holds candidate numbers in BFS order.
Switched from generating all levels until reaching or exceeding N and then sorting, to popping exactly N elements from the queue and using the N-th popped value as the answer.
Removed string conversions and concatenations; replaced them with integer arithmetic to compute the last digit and generate neighbors (using % 10 and * 10 ± 1).
Changed termination logic from 'count all generated numbers, then sort and index' to 'increment a counter for each pop and stop when the N-th is reached'.
Simplified control flow and data storage, discarding numbers as soon as they are popped from the deque instead of storing all of them for a final pass.
trigger_signals: Presence of a final sort over all generated candidates when only the k-th smallest is needed.
Use of sets and a list of all levels plus a flattening step, indicating unnecessary retention of all intermediate results.
Inner loop dominated by str() calls, string concatenation, and int() conversion for digit operations.
Overall pattern resembling BFS tree generation where a queue could maintain sorted order naturally.
pitfalls: In other languages with fixed-width integers, care is needed to avoid overflow when multiplying by 10 and adding digits; in Python this is safe due to arbitrary-precision ints.
Using a normal list as a queue (pop(0)) instead of deque would reintroduce O(N^2) behavior; deque is important for O(1) pops from the front.
Off-by-one errors when deciding whether to loop until var_1 < N or var_1 <= N; the solution must ensure the printed value is the N-th popped element.
If constraints were much larger (e.g., N ≫ 10^6), even O(N) generation might require attention to constant factors, but for typical N ≤ 10^5 this BFS is sufficient.

constraints_guess.notes: First line is n, followed by n integers (likely one per line). Typical competitive programming limits; linear O(n) solutions with small constant factors are required.

dominant_ops: O(n) integer division and addition operations over the array
O(n) input reads via a small wrapper function around sys.stdin.readline
Creation and storage of an O(n)-sized list of integers

complexity.why: Reads n integers into a list, then a single for-loop over indices 0..n-2 plus a final operation on the last element. Each element is processed a constant number of times with O(1) work (division, modulo, comparisons). The list of length n dominates memory usage.

bottlenecks.detail: Uses a function wrapper (func_1) around sys.stdin.readline() and int conversion for each integer read. This adds a Python function call per input, slightly increasing constant factors.

Imports many heavy modules (bisect, itertools, heapq, math, random, copy, collections) and defines multiple unused helper functions (func_2, func_3, func_4, func_5, etc.). This increases startup time and code size, though not asymptotic complexity.

Algorithm in func_7 processes pairs via neighbor interactions (checking current and next element, mutating the next). While still O(n), this introduces extra branches and list writes compared to a pure accumulator-based sweep.
Large generic template with many unused parts obscures the actual solution logic, making performance tuning and correctness validation harder.

FastAudit.core_idea: Perform a single linear sweep over the input sequence, aggregating sums of consecutive positive values and converting each contiguous segment sum into pairs via integer division by 2 when a zero (or sentinel) is encountered. Append a trailing zero sentinel to flush the last segment, and keep state in a small set of scalar variables instead of mutating neighbors in the array.

complexity.why: Reads n integers into a list of size n, then performs a single pass over that list plus one sentinel element. Each element is inspected once with O(1) work (additions, comparisons, and an occasional division). The list of inputs plus the sentinel accounts for O(n) memory.

complexity_delta.from: O(n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged; the main gains are reduced constant factors and a simpler, more cache-friendly traversal with fewer branches and mutations. Note that using eval() for input parsing may actually be slower and is less safe, even though the rest of the logic is streamlined.

transformation_steps: Replace the large generic competitive-programming template and unused helper functions with a minimal, problem-specific script.
Flatten the pairing logic into a single sweep using an accumulator for the current contiguous segment (var_4) and a result counter (var_3), instead of neighbor-based mutation over the array.
Introduce a sentinel value (0) at the end of the array to naturally flush the last segment without special-case index handling.
Eliminate explicit index-based final handling of the last element (var_1[var_2 - 1] // 2) by using the sentinel-driven flush logic.

Streamline IO by using a cached reference to sys.stdin.readline (var_6) and mapping to integers in one expression; however, this implementation uses eval() where int() or split-based parsing would be preferable for both performance and safety.
trigger_signals: Presence of a large, generic CP template with many unused imports and helper functions, suggesting unnecessary overhead and obscured core logic.
Core operation is clearly linear over n integers, indicating that a single-pass greedy/accumulator approach is appropriate and likely optimal.
Neighbor-based mutation logic (checking var_1[k] and var_1[k+1], then decrementing var_1[k+1]) hints that the solution can be expressed as operations on segments rather than local pair mutations.
Need to avoid edge-case handling for the last element; introducing a sentinel is a standard pattern for simplifying boundary conditions in linear sweeps.
pitfalls: Using eval() for numeric input parsing in the fast code is dangerous and slower than int(); it can execute arbitrary code and may degrade performance for large n. For robust performance, replace eval(var_6()) with int(var_6()).
Both implementations still allocate an O(n)-sized list of all inputs; if constraints were significantly higher, a streaming approach without storing all values might be required.

Relying on a trailing sentinel value requires care: any change in input format (e.g., multiple test cases back-to-back without clear separation) must preserve the invariant that an extra 0 is safe and not from the actual input.

The simplified accumulator logic changes the way values are grouped (by contiguous positive segments). If the original problem's intent depended on more localized pair formation (e.g., between explicit neighbors only), one must ensure that the segment-based interpretation is mathematically equivalent before refactoring.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder-style problem: N people, M item types (foods). Each of N lines lists a subset of items liked by that person. Need count of items liked by everyone. Even if actual N,M are small, the original numpy approach is asymptotically and practically heavy in Python.

dominant_ops: Repeated np.append on a growing numpy array inside a Python loop
For each item ID from 1..M, full-array equality comparison (var_6 == id) and summation over all K entries

complexity.why: Let N be number of people, M be number of distinct item IDs, and K = sum of all k_i (total listed likes). Building var_6 with np.append in a loop copies the whole array each time, giving ~O(K^2) behavior. Then for each item ID (M iterations), it computes var_6 == id (O(K)) and np.sum over that boolean array (O(K)), for O(M*K) additional work. var_6 itself stores K integers, so space is O(K), plus a temporary boolean array of size K inside each loop iteration (not all at once but large peak usage).

bottlenecks.detail: Using numpy arrays for incremental growth with np.append in a loop; numpy is optimized for bulk operations on fixed-size arrays, not repeated appends. Each np.append allocates and copies, leading to quadratic behavior in total appended size.

To determine which items are liked by everyone, the code scans the entire flattened likes array K times, once for each candidate item ID in 1..M, via np.sum(var_6 == id). This is a repeated global scan instead of leveraging per-person sets or counters.
Each comparison var_6 == id materializes a full boolean array of length K. Repeating this M times causes large allocation and deallocation overhead and stresses cache locality.

Mixing Python control flow with numpy operations (especially small vectors and many calls) incurs heavy function-call and boxing/unboxing overhead, providing little to no benefit over pure Python structures for these sizes.

FastAudit.core_idea: Represent each person's liked items as a Python set and compute the intersection of all these sets once; the size of the intersection is exactly the number of items liked by everyone.

complexity.why: Building N sets from the input takes O(K) total work (each listed item inserted once). The set.intersection(*sets) call intersects all sets. Each set has at most M elements, so the intersection cost is roughly O(M*N) in the worst case, typically implemented by intersecting from the smallest set outward. Overall this is O(K + M*N), which for common constraints (K ≤ N*M) is effectively O(N*M) and eliminates the quadratic np.append cost and the M repeated full scans over K elements.

from.note: Quadratic-like behavior from np.append in a loop and repeated O(K) scans for each of M item IDs.

to.note: Linear-time construction of per-person sets plus one multi-way set intersection; no repeated full-array scans and no quadratic-growth append.

complexity_delta.note: The key improvement is avoiding both the quadratic-growth pattern of np.append and the repeated global scanning of all likes for each candidate item.

transformation_steps: Recognize the logical property being computed: an item is counted if it appears in every person's list, i.e., it lies in the intersection of per-person item sets.
Replace the single global flattened numpy array with one Python set per person, created from each input line's item IDs (input().split()[1:]).
Use set.intersection over all per-person sets to compute items liked by everyone in a single operation rather than scanning all likes for every item ID.
Return the result as len(intersection_set) instead of counting via explicit loops and equality checks.
Eliminate numpy entirely to avoid overhead from np.append and repeated broadcasting operations; rely on Python's optimized hash-set implementation.
trigger_signals: Use of np.append in a Python loop to grow an array from size 0, which is a known anti-pattern and usually a performance red flag.
Pattern of recomputing a global predicate (var_6 == id) across the entire data for each candidate key, indicating redundant work and suggesting set or map-based aggregation.
Small to moderate data sizes where numpy’s vectorization advantages are outweighed by Python-level looping and repeated allocations.
Algorithm conceptually about set membership and common elements across groups, which maps directly to set intersection or counting via dictionaries.

This works for this problem but is brittle: if later logic needs M, it must be explicitly stored from the same input line instead of calling input() again.'}

{'kind': 'data_type', 'detail': 'The fast code treats item IDs as strings (from split()) instead of converting to ints. This is acceptable here because only equality and set membership are used; however, mixing string vs int representations can cause subtle bugs if further numeric operations are needed.'}

{'kind': 'readability_vs_golf', 'detail': 'The list comprehension [set(input().split()[1:]) for _ in [0] * n] and the nested set.intersection call are concise but obscure for many readers. For maintainable code, prefer an explicit loop to build the list of sets and then call intersection on them.'}

{'kind': 'memory_profile', 'detail': 'Both versions require O(K) memory to store all liked items. While the fast version removes large temporary boolean arrays, it still holds N sets in memory. For extremely large K, consider streaming strategies or counting with a single frequency dictionary if intersection sets per person cannot be held at once.'}

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder setting for this task (Factorization / ABC110D): N up to around 1e4, M up to around 1e9, single test case, modulo is 1e9+7.

dominant_ops: Repeated computation of binomial coefficients via a multiplicative formula inside a Python loop, calling pow(var_5, MOD-2, MOD) for each step, leading to many modular exponentiations.

complexity.why: Factorization loop runs up to O(sqrt(M)) trial divisions. For each distinct prime factor (P of them, P is small but >1 in worst cases), the code computes C(N+e-1, N-1) with func_1 using a loop of length N-1. Each iteration performs a pow(…, MOD-2, MOD), which is O(log MOD). Hence the binomial part is O(P * N * log MOD). No large arrays are stored; only a small dict of prime exponents and a few scalars, so asymptotic extra space is O(1).

bottlenecks.detail: Binomial coefficients are computed from scratch for each exponent using a loop of length k = N-1 with modular inverses via pow at every step. This multiplies the cost by an extra log MOD factor and a large constant due to Python-level looping.

The inner combinatorial loop performs many Python function calls to pow and modular multiplications in pure Python, which is significantly slower than using precomputed factorials and inverse factorials with O(1) binomial queries.
Prime factorization is done by trial division up to sqrt(current_M). This is O(sqrt(M)), which is acceptable for M up to ~1e9 and not the primary bottleneck compared to the combinatorial loop.

FastAudit.core_idea: Precompute factorials and modular inverses (via an inverse array) up to N + max_possible_exponent in O(N) time and use the identity C(n, k) = fact[n] * inv_fact[k] * inv_fact[n-k] mod MOD to evaluate each binomial coefficient in O(1). Combine this with a standard O(sqrt(M)) prime factorization. This removes the inner pow-based loop in the combinatorial part.

complexity.why: Prime factorization still costs O(sqrt(M)). Factorials, modular inverses and inverse factorials are precomputed once up to about N + 100 in a single O(N) loop (using the linear recurrence for modular inverses). Each binomial coefficient C(N+e-1, N-1) is then obtained in O(1). The product over primes is over at most a few terms, so its cost is negligible. Arrays of size O(N) (fact, inv, inv_fact) dominate memory usage.

complexity_delta.from: O(sqrt(M) + P * N * log MOD) time, O(1) extra space
complexity_delta.to: O(sqrt(M) + N) time, O(N) extra space
complexity_delta.note: The key improvement is replacing repeated O(N * log MOD) binomial computations with O(1) binomial queries after an O(N) precomputation of factorials and inverse factorials, trading a small linear memory usage for a large reduction in time complexity and constant factors.

transformation_steps: Recognize the combinatorial structure: the answer is the product over prime factors of M of C(N + e - 1, N - 1) modulo 1e9+7.

Replace the multiplicative binomial computation in func_1 (looping k from 1 to N-1 and using pow(k, MOD-2, MOD) each iteration) with a combinatorics toolkit based on factorials and inverse factorials.

Introduce arrays var_6 (factorials), var_9 (modular inverses of integers), and var_7 (inverse factorials) and precompute them up to var_2 + 100 using linear-time modular inverse recurrence and prefix products.
Redefine func_1 to compute C(n, k) as var_6[n] * var_7[k] * var_7[n-k] % MOD, giving O(1) per combination query.
Keep (or slightly refine) the prime factorization via trial division up to sqrt(M) to obtain exponents of prime factors efficiently.
Iterate over the list of prime factors and exponents, calling the O(1) binomial function for each and multiplying the results modulo MOD to form the final answer.
trigger_signals: The presence of a loop from 1 to N (or N-1) inside a function computing combinations, combined with a call to pow(x, MOD-2, MOD) at each iteration, is a red flag: binomial coefficients are being recomputed expensively and repeatedly.
Constraints where N is up to ~1e4 and combinations C(N+e-1, N-1) are evaluated multiple times suggest that precomputing factorials and inverse factorials is the intended solution.
The modulus is the standard prime 1e9+7, which allows using modular inverses and factorial-based combinatorics efficiently.
Observed pattern C(a, b) used repeatedly with varying a but similar scale reinforces that a combinatorics precomputation can amortize the cost.
pitfalls: The factorial and inverse factorial arrays must be sized to at least the maximum n used in C(n, k), here max n ≈ N + max_exponent(M). The fast code uses var_2 + 100 as a safe upper bound; using a smaller bound would cause index errors or incorrect results.
The modular inverse precomputation (using var_9 and the recurrence inv[i] = -inv[MOD % i] * (MOD // i) mod MOD) assumes MOD is prime; changing MOD to a non-prime would break the math.

Off-by-one errors in binomial arguments can be subtle: the problem needs C(N + e - 1, N - 1). Any shift mistake (e.g., using N + e instead of N + e - 1) silently yields wrong answers while still running quickly.
Allocating arrays of size significantly larger than needed (e.g., up to 1e7 instead of 1e4) could lead to memory issues or slower startup due to unnecessary precomputation.

While prime factorization via trial division is fine for M up to ~1e9, extending M much further without changing the factorization method would create a new bottleneck (O(sqrt(M)) would then be too slow).

constraints_guess.notes: Typical scheduling/deadline feasibility task: N up to ~1e5–2e5, times and deadlines up to ~1e9; Python needs fast I/O and low constant factors.

dominant_ops: Reading N lines using input() and eval() via small wrapper functions inside the main loop
Sorting N pairs of integers
Single pass over the sorted list to accumulate times and check deadlines

complexity.why: All variants build a list of N job pairs and sort it, which is O(N log N). The input reading and feasibility check each scan the N items once, which is O(N) and does not change the asymptotic bound. Memory is linear in N to store the pair list.

bottlenecks.detail: Uses built-in input() repeatedly in a loop, which is significantly slower than sys.stdin.readline for large N.
Uses eval(input()) to parse integers, which is much slower than int(...) and unsafe; also wrapped in extra functions (func_4, func_1) called per line.
Each line read goes through multiple Python function calls (func_4, func_1, etc.), adding overhead inside the tight O(N) loop.
Imports many unused modules (math, itertools, bisect, etc.) and sets a large recursion limit; these do not affect asymptotic complexity but add minor startup overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Keep the same greedy scheduling logic (sort by deadline, accumulate required times) but minimize constant factors by using sys.stdin.readline for I/O, avoiding eval, and eliminating unnecessary helper functions and imports.

complexity.why: Still builds and sorts a list of N job pairs by deadline, giving O(N log N) time and O(N) space; input parsing and the feasibility check remain linear passes over the data, only with smaller constant factors.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.to: O(N log N) time, O(N) space
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic complexity is unchanged, but I/O and parsing overhead are reduced substantially, which is critical under tight time limits.

transformation_steps: Replace eval(input()) and input() with sys.stdin.readline-based reading to accelerate I/O.
Remove small wrapper functions for reading input (func_4, func_1, etc.) and parse directly in the main code to avoid per-line function call overhead.
Eliminate use of eval for numeric parsing; use int(...) and map(int, ...) directly.
Construct the list of (deadline, time) pairs using a list comprehension and sort it once, instead of appending via a loop with extra function calls.
Remove unused imports and global constants that are not required for the actual algorithm to reduce startup and cognitive overhead.
trigger_signals: Use of input() in a large loop where N can be up to around 1e5–2e5.
Use of eval(input()) for integer input, which is both slow and unnecessary.
Multiple small I/O wrapper functions called per iteration in the hot path.
Problem pattern (greedy scheduling with sort) typically appearing in contests with tight Python time limits, where I/O dominates.
pitfalls: Mixing input() and sys.stdin.readline in the same solution can cause subtle bugs if not handled carefully; the fast version consistently uses sys.stdin.readline.
Using eval on input is unsafe and may be disallowed; replacing it with int(...) is both faster and safer.
When refactoring to comprehensions, ensure the pair order (time vs deadline) remains correct; the fast code intentionally reverses the parsed list before sorting.

Relying on sys.exit() or exit() inside loops can be fine in scripts, but care must be taken if integrating into larger systems; the fast version instead uses loop control (break/else) to determine output.

constraints_guess.notes: Computes sum of a[i]*a[j] over all pairs i<j. Quadratic solution suggests original constraints small, but presence of prefix-sum optimization implies intended support for up to ~1e5–2e5 elements.

dominant_ops: Nested loops over all index pairs (i, j) with i < j performing integer multiplications and additions.

complexity.why: The slow_code has two nested for-loops: outer loop over var_3 in range(var_5) and inner loop over var_4 in range(var_3+1, var_5). This results in n*(n-1)/2 iterations, each doing constant work (a multiplication and an addition). No extra data structures are allocated beyond the input array and a few scalars.

bottlenecks.detail: Enumerates all O(n^2) index pairs (var_3, var_4) with var_3 < var_4 explicitly, which is prohibitive for large n (e.g., n >= 10^5).
Inner loop range(var_3 + 1, var_5) combined with the outer loop produces approximately n^2/2 iterations; this is the primary runtime driver.
Uses eval(input()) in func_1 to parse an integer, which is slower and unsafe compared to int(input()); however, this is negligible relative to the quadratic loop cost.

FastAudit.core_idea: Use prefix sums to compute the sum over all i<j of a[i]*a[j] in linear time: rewrite the sum as sum_{j=1..n-1} a[j] * (sum_{i=0..j-1} a[i]) and maintain prefix sums (with itertools.accumulate) instead of iterating over all pairs.

complexity.why: The fast_code computes a single prefix-sum array via accumulate(var_1), then zips it with var_1[1:]. The generator expression runs once per element (excluding the first), so the operations scale linearly with n. The space is O(n) to store the input list var_1 and the accumulated prefixes produced by accumulate.

complexity_delta.from: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space (beyond input)
complexity_delta.to: O(n) time, O(n) extra space (prefix sums and iterators)
complexity_delta.note: Replaces explicit enumeration of all index pairs with a mathematical transformation using prefix sums, drastically reducing the time complexity while slightly increasing auxiliary memory usage.

transformation_steps: Recognize the mathematical form of the target sum in slow_code: S = sum_{0<=i<j<n} a[i] * a[j].
Algebraically transform the double sum: for each j, group terms by the second index: S = sum_{j=1..n-1} a[j] * (sum_{i=0..j-1} a[i]).
Introduce a prefix sum P[j] = sum_{i=0..j} a[i]. Then sum_{i=0..j-1} a[i] = P[j-1].
Compute prefix sums iteratively in O(n) (or via itertools.accumulate in Python) instead of nested loops.
Iterate once over j from 1 to n-1 (implemented as zip(var_1[1:], accumulate(var_1))) and accumulate the result of a[j] * P[j-1] into a single scalar.
Eliminate the nested loops from slow_code and replace them with this single linear pass, yielding the fast_code implementation.
trigger_signals: Presence of two nested loops over the same range (range(var_5)) with inner loop starting from var_3+1, indicating O(n^2) pairwise operations.
Problem requirement to compute a sum over all pairs (i, j) with i<j, which is a known pattern that can often be simplified with algebra or prefix sums.
Potential or observed timeouts/slow performance when n grows beyond a few thousand elements.
