constraints_guess.notes: Classic AtCoder-style 'deal at least H damage with N spells, minimize cost'. H (~var_3/var_5) up to about 1e4, number of spells up to ~1e2. Each spell has (damage, cost); unlimited uses.

dominant_ops: Building a (N+1) x (H+1) 2D DP table (nested list comprehensions)
Double nested loops over spells (var_6 up to var_10) and HP values (var_8 up to var_5)
Multiple min() calls and list index operations per DP cell update
Accessing DP states across two dimensions: var_4[var_6+1][*] and var_4[var_6][*]

complexity.why: The outer loop runs over all spells N (var_10) and the inner loop runs over all HP values H (var_5). For each (spell, HP) pair, it performs constant-time work (a few min operations and list accesses). This yields O(NH) time. The DP table var_4 is of size (N+1) x (H+1), so memory usage is O(NH).

bottlenecks.detail: The 2D DP table var_4 of size (var_10+1) x (var_5+1) stores a full row per spell, although only the previous row is needed at any time. This multiplies memory by roughly a factor of N compared to a 1D DP.

Every DP state update involves several Python-level operations: three list index lookups, up to three additions, and a min() over three values. This in a tight double loop (N * H iterations) results in heavy interpreter overhead.

All DP cells are updated regardless of whether they are reachable or not. There is no reachability pruning; even clearly suboptimal or unreachable states are processed, which increases constant factors.
2D indexing var_4[row][col] with frequent jumps between rows (var_6 and var_6+1) decreases locality compared to a single 1D DP array, causing more cache misses and slower Python list access patterns.

FastAudit.core_idea: Reduce the DP to a single 1D array over total damage, representing the minimum cost to reach each damage value, and iterate damage from 0 upward while relaxing transitions with all spells (unbounded knapsack). Use an overshoot margin and take the minimum cost over all states achieving at least the target damage. This removes the spell dimension from the DP, shrinks memory, and improves locality and pruning.

complexity.why: The outer loop runs from 0 to target damage H-1 (var_3), and the inner loop runs over all N spells (var_5). Each iteration performs constant-time comparisons and assignments, so time is O(NH_eff), where H_eff is roughly H (plus a small extra margin var_2 = 1e4 used to allow overshoot). The DP array var_8 has length H + var_2 + 1, so the space complexity is O(H_eff). Only one dimension over damage is kept, eliminating the multiplicative factor of N in memory.

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time remains O(NH) in the worst case, but the constant factor is significantly reduced by using 1D DP and pruning unreachable states. Space improves from O(NH) to O(H_eff), which is a substantial reduction when N is non-trivial.

transformation_steps: Reinterpret the state definition from dp[item_index][damage] to a simpler dp[damage] that stores the minimum cost to reach exactly that damage, independent of spell order.

Observe that the problem is an unbounded knapsack: each spell can be used any number of times, so transitions are from damage d to d + spell_damage with added spell_cost, without needing the spell index as part of the DP state.
Replace the 2D DP table var_4 with a 1D array var_8 sized to cover the target damage plus an overshoot margin (H + 1e4), initialized to +inf with dp[0] = 0.
Iterate damage (var_9) from 0 up to H-1 and, for each reachable damage (dp[var_9] != inf), relax transitions by trying all spells and updating dp[var_9 + damage] with the minimum cost.
At the end, instead of reading from a single exact cell, take the minimum over dp[H:] to allow damage values greater than or equal to the target.
Eliminate the spell dimension from the DP (no var_4[row][*]), cutting memory usage by a factor of ~N and reducing Python indexing overhead and cache-unfriendly access patterns.
Use a guard to skip updates from unreachable states (if var_8[var_9] == inf: continue), which avoids needless work and speeds up instances where many states remain unreachable.
trigger_signals: DP solution uses a 2D table where one dimension is the number of items/spells and the other is the total value/HP; only previous row is needed at any time.
Memory usage is O(NH) and close to or exceeding typical problem limits (e.g., N and H both ~10^4), risking MLE or slow performance in Python.
Inner loops over both dimensions perform multiple min and indexing operations per cell, indicating heavy constant factors in an interpreter.
The state space includes a dimension that is not logically necessary for the optimal substructure (e.g., the order of spells is irrelevant and item index does not need to be part of the state).

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder Factorization problem: N up to ~1e9, M up to ~1e9. Prime factorization cost is bounded by sqrt(M). Sum of exponents in factorization of M is small (<= ~30) because 2^30 > 1e9.

Prime factorization of M via trial division up to sqrt(M) in func_4
For each prime exponent e, computing C(N-1+e, e) using precomputed factorials and modular inverses

constraints_guess.notes: Static undirected graph with N nodes and M edges; task is to count connected components. Vertices appear to be 1-indexed in input and converted to 0-indexed in the original code.

Running BFS from each unvisited node using a deque: each vertex is enqueued at most once and each edge is inspected at most twice (once from each endpoint).

complexity.why: The adjacency list stores each undirected edge twice, giving O(N + M) space. The BFS loop iterates over all vertices and traverses every adjacency list once; across all components each vertex and each edge is processed O(1) times, leading to O(N + M) total time.

The BFS structure is more than needed if the only required output is the number of connected components; DSU can count components without storing full adjacency lists or exploring neighbors per node.

FastAudit.core_idea: Replace explicit graph traversal (BFS over an adjacency list) with a Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find) structure. For each edge, union its endpoints; the number of connected components is then the number of distinct roots after all unions. This removes the need to store or traverse adjacency lists and compresses connectivity computation into near-constant-time union/find operations.

complexity.why: Union-Find with path compression and union by rank performs m union/find operations in O((N + M) * α(N)) time, where α is the inverse Ackermann function (practically constant). The structure keeps only two arrays of size O(N): roots and ranks, so space is O(N).

complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time complexity remains effectively linear in N + M, but Union-Find avoids adjacency storage and repeated neighbor traversal, reducing memory usage and constant factors for very large graphs.

constraints_guess.notes: Typical AtCoder 'Coprime' task: N up to ~1e5, each a_i up to 1e6. Need to classify: not coprime, setwise coprime, pairwise coprime.

dominant_ops: Building smallest-prime-factor array var_3 with a sieve up to 10^6+5 on every run
Prime-factorizing each input value using var_3
Computing GCD over all input values

complexity.time: O(A_max log log A_max + N log A_max)
complexity.why: func_1 runs a prime sieve over [2..10^6+5], marking multiples only for primes (∑_{p≤A_max} A_max/p ≈ A_max log log A_max operations). Each value is then factorized via repeated division by its smallest prime factors (O(log a_i) per value). GCD fold over N numbers costs O(N log A_max). Arrays var_3, var_2, and sieve flags var_10 are all sized Θ(A_max).

bottlenecks.detail: Always builds SPF sieve up to 10^6+5 even if max(a_i) is much smaller, and pays this Ω(A_max) cost per test case.
Keeps multiple length-1e6 arrays of Python ints/bools (var_3, var_2, var_10), which is heavy in Python (tens of MB) and can approach memory limits.
Inner sieve loop uses explicit while var_6 * var_7 <= var_11 instead of a range step (for j in range(2*var_6, var_11+1, var_6)), increasing Python-level loop overhead.

FastAudit.core_idea: Avoid building a full 1e6-sized SPF sieve by using a precomputed set of primes up to 1000 (≈sqrt(1e6)) and factorizing each input number by trial division over this small fixed prime set. Track which primes appear to determine pairwise/setwise/not coprime, and rely on one global GCD for the setwise/not decision.

complexity.why: For each of N inputs, trial divide by each prime ≤ sqrt(a_i). There are π(√A_max) ≈ 168 primes ≤ 1000, so worst-case about 168 trial divisions per number, i.e., ~O(N * π(√A_max)) operations. Any remaining factor > 1 after trial division is prime and processed once. GCD over all numbers stays O(N log A_max). Memory is dominated by the constant prime table and small auxiliary structures (seen prime flags/sets), independent of A_max’s full range.

complexity_delta.from: Time: O(A_max log log A_max + N log A_max), Space: O(A_max)
complexity_delta.to: Time: O(N * π(√A_max) + N log A_max), Space: O(π(√A_max)) ≈ O(1) for fixed A_max=1e6
complexity_delta.note: Asymptotic time is similar for the given constraints, but the fast version removes the Θ(A_max) sieve cost and large arrays, trading it for per-number trial division with a small fixed prime set. Space improves from linear in A_max to effectively constant.

transformation_steps: Remove the global SPF sieve var_3 and its construction func_1 over [2..10^6+5].
Introduce a fixed precomputed list/set of primes up to 1000 (√1e6), as seen in var_9, at module scope.
For each input number, factor it by trial dividing over var_9 until the current prime squared exceeds the remaining value; treat any leftover > 1 as a prime factor.
Maintain a structure (e.g., boolean array or set) to record which prime factors have been seen before across all numbers; if a prime factor repeats, the sequence is not pairwise coprime.
Keep the overall GCD fold over all numbers to distinguish between 'not coprime' and 'setwise coprime' when pairwise coprime fails.
Drop the large auxiliary arrays var_3 and var_2 sized by 1e6; keep only small per-prime or per-number bookkeeping.
trigger_signals: Memory usage is high due to arrays of size 1e6+ for each run, approaching the language’s memory limits.
Profiling shows a large fraction of runtime inside the sieve construction even when many test cases use small maximum a_i.
Time limit issues appear specifically when using Python, while C++ passes comfortably with the sieve-based approach.
Need to simplify code and reduce global state while maintaining near-linear behavior in N.
pitfalls: When switching to trial division, it is easy to double-count the same prime factor for one number; ensure each distinct prime factor per number is only considered once when checking pairwise coprimeness.
Must handle the residual factor > 1 after trial division as a prime; forgetting this misses large prime factors.
Need to handle the value 1 specially: it has no prime factors and should not affect pairwise checks.
Precomputed prime list var_9 must cover at least all primes up to √A_max; if it is truncated, factorization can fail for some inputs.
Order of checks matters: check overall gcd == 1 before concluding 'setwise coprime'; if gcd > 1, the array is 'not coprime' regardless of pairwise prime-factor behavior.

constraints_guess.notes: Single test with N integers. Values likely up to around 10^4–10^5. Brute-force over full value range is not feasible if value spread is large.

dominant_ops: Sorting the array of N integers
Double loop: iterating over all candidate target values in [min(a), max(a)] and, for each, scanning all N elements to compute squared distances

complexity.why: Sorting costs O(N log N). Let R = max(a) - min(a). The outer loop runs R+1 times (one per candidate target value), and the inner loop iterates over all N elements each time, giving O(N * R). The list of N integers dominates memory usage.

bottlenecks.detail: The cost function is recomputed from scratch for every candidate center var_2 by looping over all N elements, leading to O(N * R) operations.
The outer loop scales with the numeric range max(a) - min(a), not with N. If values are large or spread out, R can be orders of magnitude larger than N, causing severe slowdown.
The sort (O(N log N)) is not needed for the final objective; only min, max, and aggregate statistics are required. This adds extra superlinear cost.

FastAudit.core_idea: Exploit the fact that the sum of squared deviations \sum_i (x - a_i)^2 is minimized when x is the (possibly rounded) mean of the values. Instead of brute-forcing all integer centers in a range, compute the mean once and evaluate the objective at that point in a single pass.

complexity.why: Reading and storing the N integers costs O(N). A single traversal computes the sum, then another traversal computes the sum of squared deviations from the chosen center (rounded mean). No sorting or outer search over candidate centers is needed, eliminating dependence on the value range.

complexity_delta.from: O(N log N + N * (max(a) - min(a)))
complexity_delta.to: O(N)
complexity_delta.note: Removed brute-force search over all integer centers in the value range and the unnecessary sort; replaced with a direct formula-based computation using the mean.

transformation_steps: Recognize the mathematical structure: the objective is to minimize the sum of squared distances to a common value.
Use the known property from least squares: the minimizer of sum_i (x - a_i)^2 over real x is the arithmetic mean of a_i.
Adapt to integer x by rounding the mean instead of scanning all integers in [min(a), max(a)].
Eliminate the outer loop over candidate centers and the inner recomputation of the full sum for each candidate.
Remove sorting; only the list of values and their aggregate (sum) are needed.
Compute the rounded mean once, then perform a single pass to sum squared deviations.
trigger_signals: Presence of nested loops where the outer loop iterates over a numeric range derived from data values (max - min).
Time complexity depends on the numeric spread of input rather than purely on N.
Recomputing a global cost function from scratch for each candidate parameter.
Mathematical form resembling a least-squares objective (sum of squared differences).
Use of sorting where only simple aggregates (sum/mean) are required.
pitfalls: Rounding choice: for integer-constrained x, the true optimum is attained at floor(mean) or ceil(mean). Using Python's round (banker’s rounding) can be subtly different when the mean is exactly halfway between two integers; in some edge cases, checking both floor and ceil is safer.
Assuming small value range: the slow version is only viable when max(a) - min(a) is very small. If constraints are not clearly small, this assumption leads to TLE.
Numerical concerns: although Python’s integers are unbounded, in other languages using 32-bit or 64-bit ints, the squared terms and sums may overflow without careful typing.
Unnecessary sorting: relying on sorted values in further optimizations when the sorted order is not mathematically required can cause additional, avoidable overhead.
Use of eval for reading integers: not a performance issue here, but generally unsafe and marginally slower than direct int(input()) parsing.

var_1 collects every matching sum even though only the count (len(var_1)) is printed. This allocates and stores O(#solutions) integers unnecessarily.
The inner loop breaks when var_5 < var_3 by iterating indices in descending order, but in worst or average cases this pruning is insufficient to avoid cubic behavior.
Deeply nested pure-Python loops magnify interpreter overhead, making Θ(n^3) especially slow for n near the upper constraint.

complexity.why: Two nested loops over a and b: ~n(n-1)/2 pairs => Θ(n^2) iterations. For each pair, compute c and do constant-time comparisons. Only a few scalar variables are kept (no solution list), so extra memory is Θ(1) beyond input.

complexity_delta.from: O(n^3) time, O(n^2) space
complexity_delta.to: O(n^2) time, O(1) space
complexity_delta.note: Reframed the problem from enumerating all triples explicitly to deriving the third value from each pair, eliminating one loop level and the result list.

transformation_steps: Recognize that values equal indices (1..n), so sums can be computed directly from loop variables without an auxiliary array.
Reformulate triple enumeration: for each pair (a,b) with 1<=a<b<=n, compute c = x - a - b instead of looping over all c.
Add constraints on c to encode distinct ordered triples: require c>b (to maintain a<b<c) and c<=n and c>=1 (implicitly ensured by inequality checks).
Replace the innermost loop and equality test with a constant-time computation and conditional, reducing from three loops to two.
Eliminate the solution list var_1 and simply maintain an integer counter of valid triples, matching the required output (count only).
Simplify termination and input parsing: switch from '[n,x]==[0,0]' to 'n==0' since x is irrelevant once n=0, and parse input directly into named scalars.

Inner body performs only simple integer arithmetic and comparisons, meaning total cost scales almost entirely with loop counts.
The problem is conceptual 3-sum over consecutive integers 1..n, a known pattern where one dimension can be eliminated analytically.
Unnecessary data structures observed: building list [1..n] even though indices suffice; accumulating all matching sums just to count them.
Potential TLE or performance issues when n approaches typical competitive-programming bounds (e.g., n≈50–100 with multiple test cases).

Incorrect inequality on c: condition must be 'c > b and c <= n'; using '>=', '<', or forgetting the '>' would count invalid or duplicate triples.

constraints_guess.notes: Reads one integer N then N integers. Candidate value in slow code is scanned over fixed range [0, 99]. Typical AtCoder-style task: choose integer p in a small bounded range that minimizes sum (a_i - p)^2. N can be large, but candidate range is tiny (100).

dominant_ops: For each candidate integer var_2 in range(100), compute a full vector difference (var_6 - var_2) over all N elements
For each candidate, compute squared array and sum via np.sum, which is O(N) per candidate
Overall: 100 passes over the length-N array

complexity.time: O(K * N) with K = 100 (effectively O(N) but with a 100x constant factor)
complexity.why: The loop runs for 100 candidate values; each iteration performs elementwise subtraction, squaring, and summation over the N-element array. No extra asymptotic memory beyond storing the input array.

bottlenecks.detail: Brute-force scan over all 100 candidate integers, even though the optimum of sum (a_i - p)^2 over integer p can be derived analytically from the mean.
Each of the 100 iterations performs a complete O(N) vector computation (subtraction, square, sum) over the same array.
var_6 = var_5 in the loop creates an extra reference each iteration without any benefit.
Using NumPy per-iteration operations incurs Python→NumPy call overhead 100 times; the operations are vectorized but redundantly repeated.

complexity.why: Computes the mean of the N elements in one pass, rounds it to get the best integer candidate, then performs a single elementwise (a_i - p)^2 and sum. Only one full pass for the sum of squares, no outer loop over candidates.

complexity_delta.from: O(K * N) with K=100 (conceptually O(N) but with heavy constant factor from 100 repeated passes)
complexity_delta.to: O(N)

Use calculus/known fact: for real p, S(p) is minimized at p = mean(a).
For integer p, choose p as the nearest integer to the mean (round), which minimizes S(p) over all integer p.
Replace the loop over all candidate p in range(100) with a single computation of the mean and a single evaluation of S(p) at p = round(mean).
Compute the squared deviations and their sum only once instead of 100 times.

Objective function is convex quadratic in the candidate variable p (sum of squares form), suggesting a closed-form optimum.
The repeated pattern np.sum((var_6 - var_2) ** 2) for many var_2 values indicates potential to use statistics (mean/variance).
Use of a brute-force search over a simple 1D parameter that often has a known analytical solution.
